title: Classification of high-dimensional data with spiked covariance matrix structure
claim_source: Table 1, page 13 (feature counts from Table 2, page 14)

official.background: Fisher's linear discriminant rule is Bayes-optimal for two Gaussian classes with a shared covariance, but its plug-in version can do no better than random guessing when the number of features p is comparable to or larger than the sample size n. Most high-dimensional fixes assume the discriminant direction β = Σ⁻¹(µ2 − µ1) is sparse and that Σ has bounded eigenvalues. Real high-dimensional data such as gene expression often have a few large (spiked) eigenvalues instead. The paper studies the common practice of reducing dimension with PCA before running LDA, and gives conditions under which this is asymptotically Bayes-optimal.
official.method:
lda∘pca (Algorithm 1) estimates the whitening matrix W = Σ^{-1/2} under a spiked model Σ = UΛUᵀ + σ²I. The top d eigenpairs (Û, Λ̂) of the pooled sample covariance are kept, σ̂² is set to (tr Σ̂ − tr Λ̂)/(p − d), and Ŵ = Û(Λ̂ + σ̂²I)^{-1/2}Ûᵀ + σ̂⁻¹(I − ÛÛᵀ). The method whitens the class means, keeps the s largest coordinates in absolute value of ζ̂ = Ŵ(X̄2 − X̄1), and applies the Fisher rule with threshold ln(n1/n2) on those whitened coordinates. d is the smallest k for which the top-k eigenvalues explain at least 90% of tr(Σ̂). s is chosen from {1,…,30} by five-fold CV, taking the smallest s on ties.

In simulation Model 1 (equal correlation), p = 800, Σ = ρ11ᵀ + (1 − ρ)I, µ1 = 0 and µ2 = (1₁₀, 0₇₉₀). Each class has 100 training and 100 test points. Every result is averaged over 200 Monte Carlo replicates. Baselines are CAT-LDA (R sda), DSDA (R TULIP), AdaLDA (ADAM Matlab code), DSDA and AdaLDA after the rotation preprocessing of Hao et al. (γ = 0.25), SLDA and NSC. All baseline tuning parameters are chosen by five-fold CV. The oracle is the Fisher rule with the true parameters, i.e. the Bayes error.
official.claim: In the equal-correlation simulation (p = 800, 100 training points per class, ρ = 0.5), lda∘pca has a test mis-classification rate of 1.74% (sd 1.00) against 3.27% (sd 1.47) for DSDA, the best non-oracle baseline. The Bayes error is 1.37%. lda∘pca uses about 12 whitened features, while DSDA uses about 96 raw features.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Mis-classification rate (%) with standard deviations (%) in parentheses for equal correlation setting (model 1), based on 200 independent Monte Carlo replicates.
official.metric: Test mis-classification rate (%), lower is better. Mean over 200 Monte Carlo replicates; the value in parentheses is the standard deviation across replicates, not a standard error.
official.comparison: lda∘pca vs. DSDA (strongest baseline at ρ = 0.5), AdaLDA, CAT-LDA, DSDA(rot), AdaLDA(rot), SLDA, NSC, and the oracle Bayes rule
official.falsification_criterion: Over 200 replicates of Model 1 with ρ = 0.5, the mean error of lda∘pca is not below DSDA's (or AdaLDA's), or the gap is smaller than one per-replicate standard deviation (about 1.0–1.5 points).

title: Generative Conformal Prediction with Optimized Coverage Allocation
claim_source: Table 3 (Appendix F.2), page 22; summarized in Figure 4, page 9

official.background: Split conformal prediction wraps any predictive model to give prediction sets with guaranteed marginal coverage (e.g. 90%), but the sets are often much larger than necessary when the conditional distribution p(Y | X) is multimodal or heavy-tailed. One line of work uses generative models: Probabilistic Conformal Prediction (PCP) draws K samples from a fitted conditional model and returns a union of balls of one common radius around them. Because every ball gets the same radius, sets can be wasteful in low-density regions. Smaller sets at the same coverage are more informative for downstream decisions.
official.method:
ORCA (Optimized Ranking and Coverage Allocation) draws K conditional samples per input from a fitted generative model (here a quantile regression forest for 1-D responses; K = 20, m = ceil(sqrt(K))) and ranks them by their average m-nearest-neighbor distance among the samples (a local density proxy). On an exploration split (500 points), each point gets a ranked distance vector E_i,r = |Y_i - Yhat_i,j(r)|. Stage 2 picks a per-rank radius Q_r (an empirical quantile of the rank-r distances) to minimize the sum of Q_r^d subject to at least ceil(n1(1-alpha)) exploration points being covered by some rank's ball, solved exactly as a MILP (LP-relaxation and greedy variants also given).

Stage 3 calibrates on a separate 500-point split: the score S_i = min_r E_i,r / Q_r, its conformal (1-alpha) quantile t gives final radii R_r = t * Q_r, and the test set is the union over ranks of balls of radius R_r around the r-th ranked sample. Baselines (CQR, CHR, DCP-CQR, DistSplit, CDSplit, CRD, R2CCP, PCP) use the same QRF base model except CDSplit (mixture density network) and R2CCP (its own network). For each dataset: 500 exploration, 500 calibration, 1,000 test, rest for training; alpha = 0.1; 30 runs.
official.claim: At alpha = 0.1 with all methods at ~0.90 marginal coverage, ORCA's mean prediction-set size is 3.61 ± 1.27 on Blog, 3.70 ± 1.75 on Fb1 and 5.68 ± 1.62 on Fb2, versus 8.27 ± 0.21, 7.79 ± 0.28 and 9.35 ± 0.21 for the best baseline (PCP), roughly a 39-56% reduction.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Summary of real data results. Metrics include marginal coverage (Cover), worst-slab conditional coverage (Cond_Cover), and prediction set efficiency (Eff). Values report mean ± standard error over 30 runs. The lowest efficiency per dataset is bolded and highlighted along with corresponding coverage metrics.
official.metric: Eff = average Lebesgue measure (interval length) of the prediction set on 1,000 test points (lower is better), subject to marginal coverage near 0.90; ± is standard error over 30 runs
official.comparison: ORCA vs. CQR, CHR, DCP-CQR, DistSplit, CDSplit, CRD, R2CCP and PCP under the same data splits, alpha and (mostly) the same QRF base model; PCP is the strongest baseline on these three datasets
official.falsification_criterion: On Blog, Fb1 or Fb2, ORCA's mean set size at ~0.90 test coverage is not clearly smaller than PCP's (difference within the reported standard errors), or ORCA reaches the smaller size only with marginal coverage below ~0.89.

title: Disentanglement as Identifiable Pushforward Factorisation

official.background: VAEs and β-VAEs often learn disentangled representations, where changing a single latent coordinate changes a single generative factor of the data, even though nothing in the objective explicitly asks for it. A common hypothesis is that the diagonal Gaussian posterior covariance, chosen for computational convenience, pushes the decoder's Jacobian toward orthogonal columns and so causes disentanglement. This paper defines disentanglement as factorisation of the pushforward density into 1-D factors along the SVD of the decoder Jacobian, proves this holds iff two derivative conditions (C1-C2) hold, and argues through an exact identity (Eq. 8) that diagonal posteriors promote C1-C2 in expectation, more strongly as β grows.
official.method:
Gaussian VAEs with latent dimension d = 10 are trained on dSprites (5 known generative factors) with either diagonal or full posterior covariances, for β ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1}; results are averaged over 5 runs. Disentanglement is measured from the mutual-information matrix between each latent coordinate and each ground-truth factor, using the mutual information gap (MIG, Chen et al. 2018) and a new axis alignment score, AAS = 0.5 (Σ row maxima + Σ column maxima) / Σ entries of the MI matrix (Appendix F), which equals 1 for a permuted diagonal MI matrix.

The paper also reports how diagonal the two derivative terms of Eq. 8 are (J_zᵀJ_z and (x − d(z))H_z), via the mean normalised off-diagonal magnitude, on train and test data. The prediction is that with diagonal posteriors disentanglement and derivative diagonality both increase with β, while with full posteriors there is no such trend.
official.claim: On dSprites with d = 10 Gaussian VAEs, diagonal-posterior models become more disentangled as β rises from 0.001 to 1 (MIG about 0.05 → 0.40, AAS about 0.41 → 0.87), whereas full-posterior models do not (MIG stays about 0.06-0.11; AAS falls from about 0.50 to about 0.02), so at β = 1 diagonal posteriors give MIG about 0.40 vs. about 0.10 for full posteriors.
official.claim_caption: Figure 6. Diagonal vs Full Posteriors: (left) (bottom) disentanglement metrics and estimated diagonality of Eq. 8 terms (see Appendix F). With diagonal posteriors, disentanglement and diagonality are correlated (supporting P1), relative to full posteriors; (top) heatmaps of mutual information between model latents and ground truth factors. (right) derivatives in Eq. 8. terms are less diagonal for lower beta or full posteriors. (All results averaged over multiple runs)
official.metric: MIG and AAS (higher = more disentangled), computed from latent-factor mutual information; lines are means over 5 runs with shaded bands whose definition is not stated; values are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Diagonal-posterior vs. full-posterior Gaussian VAEs on dSprites, same d = 10, at β ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1}
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both VAE variants on dSprites (d = 10, several seeds), diagonal-posterior MIG at β = 1 is not clearly higher than full-posterior MIG (e.g. gap under ~0.15 or overlapping seed spread), or diagonal-posterior MIG/AAS do not increase from β = 0.001 to β = 1.

title: Gradient descent inference in empirical risk minimization

official.background: Gradient descent is the standard way to fit empirical risk minimization models, but when the sample size m and the dimension n are proportional (the mean-field regime), the gradient descent iterates are biased and depend on one another in ways classical theory does not describe. Valid confidence intervals for individual coordinates of the unknown signal are usually built from the converged estimator, and only for convex losses. A way to do valid inference at any iteration of gradient descent, with convex or non-convex losses and without waiting for convergence, would make early-stopped or non-convex fits usable for statistical inference.
official.method:
The authors derive a non-asymptotic state evolution for the gradient descent iterates mu^(t) in models Y_i = F(<A_i, mu*>, xi_i). The theory says that the debiased iterate mu_db^(t) = mu^(t-1) + eta * sum_{s in [1:t]} omega_{t,s} A^T d1L(A mu^(s-1), Y), with omega^[t] = (tau^[t])^{-1} the inverse of an 'Onsager correction' matrix (Eq. 1.9), is approximately b_db^(t) mu* + sigma_db^(t) Z coordinatewise, with Z standard Gaussian; in linear regression b_db^(t) = 1, so mu_db^(t) is approximately mu* + sigma_db^(t) Z. Algorithm 1 (the 'gradient descent inference algorithm') estimates the Onsager matrices tau^[t] and rho^[t] from the data alone, which gives mu_db^(t), a variance estimate sigma_db^(t) (Eq. 3.2), and the coordinatewise 95% confidence intervals mu_db;l^(t) +/- sigma_db^(t) z_{0.025} (Eq. 4.4 for linear regression).

Simulation setting (Section 6.1-6.2): m = 1200, n = 1000; mu* has i.i.d. |N(0,5)| entries; sqrt(n)A has i.i.d. N(0,1), standardized t(10), or standardized Bernoulli(1/2) entries; mu^(0) ~ N(0, I_n); 50 gradient descent iterations with step size eta = 0.3; B = 1000 Monte Carlo repetitions. Two linear regression settings: squared loss with N(0,1) noise, and pseudo-Huber loss (delta = 1) with t(2) noise. No regularization. Coverage is the fraction of the n coordinates whose CI contains mu*_l, shown as a box plot over repetitions at iterations 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
official.claim: In linear regression with m = 1200, n = 1000 and no regularization, the 95% CIs built from the debiased gradient descent iterate via Algorithm 1 have median coordinatewise coverage of about 0.95 (repetition boxes roughly 0.94-0.96) at every iteration t = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, for both squared loss and pseudo-Huber loss with t(2) noise, under Gaussian, Bernoulli and t(10) designs.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1. Linear regression. Top row: Squared loss. Bottom row: Pseudo-Huber loss.
official.metric: Empirical coverage of nominal 95% CIs averaged over the n = 1000 coordinates (target 0.95); box plots show the spread over B = 1000 Monte Carlo repetitions. No other error bars.
official.comparison: Empirical coverage of the debiased-GD CIs vs. the nominal 95% level, across iterations, two losses and three design distributions. There is no competing inference method in the figure.
official.falsification_criterion: Following the paper's setup, the median coverage at some iteration in {10, ..., 50} falls clearly outside about [0.93, 0.97] (e.g. below 0.92) for either loss or any of the three designs, or the standardized debiased coordinate (mu_db;1 - mu*_1)/sigma_db departs clearly from N(0,1) in a QQ plot.

title: RaZeR: Pushing the Limits of NVFP4 Quantization with Redundant Zero Remapping

official.background: NVFP4 is the 4-bit format that NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs support natively for LLM inference: each block of 16 values is stored as FP4-E2M1 elements (±{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6}) sharing one FP8-E4M3 scale, plus a per-tensor FP32 scale. The format wastes some of its bits. FP4 has both +0 and -0, so one of its 16 codes is redundant, and the FP8 block scale is always positive, so its sign bit is unused. Removing more of the 4-bit quantization error without increasing memory would make 4-bit LLM deployment more accurate on hardware that already exists.
official.method:
RaZeR remaps the redundant FP4 negative-zero code to a per-block 'special value'. For weights, the block scale is stored as E3M3 instead of E4M3 (Table 1 shows no perplexity loss from this), which frees 2 bits per block when combined with the unused sign bit. Those 2 bits select one of 4 allowed special values for that block. For each 16-element block, after the usual NVFP4 tensor and block scaling, the special value v is chosen from the allowed set to minimise the block's squared quantization error when the FP4 grid is extended to Q_FP4 ∪ {v} (Eq. 6-7), and the block is then rounded to that extended grid. The memory footprint stays at 4.5 bits per element, the same as NVFP4.

The allowed special values are ±5 plus one extra model-specific pair, which is ±8 for Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B (Appendix B.2, Table 12). For the weight-only (W4A16) rows of Table 3, all block-wise methods use block size 16 with an 8-bit block scale. Activations and KV-cache stay in FP16. Perplexity is measured on WikiText-2 and C4 with 2K context, starting from the HuggingFace checkpoints.
official.claim: With weight-only 4-bit quantization (W4A16, block size 16), RaZeR gives lower perplexity than native NVFP4 on Llama-3.1-8B (WikiText-2 6.50 vs 6.63; C4 9.29 vs 9.48; FP16 6.24 / 8.96) and Llama-3.2-3B (WikiText-2 8.10 vs 8.24; C4 10.86 vs 11.10). In all four cases it also beats FourOverSix (6.60 / 9.42 / 8.21 / 11.05).
official.claim_caption: Table 3. Perplexity (↓) under different 4-bit weight-only and weight-activation quantization methods. KV-cache remains in FP16.
official.metric: Perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4 (2K context), lower is better; single deterministic runs, no ± reported
official.comparison: RaZeR (FP4 + per-block special value from {±5, ±8}, E3M3 block scale) vs. native NVFP4 (FP4, E4M3 block scale) and FourOverSix (4over6), all at block size 16 and 4.5 effective bits, weight-only quantization of Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B
official.falsification_criterion: Using the same block size, special values and evaluation protocol, RaZeR's perplexity on Llama-3.1-8B or Llama-3.2-3B (WikiText-2 or C4) is not lower than NVFP4's, or it closes less than about half of the reported NVFP4-to-RaZeR gap (for example, Llama-3.1-8B WikiText-2 RaZeR ≥ 6.57 when NVFP4 reproduces at about 6.63).

title: A Steerable Deep Network for Model-Free Diffusion MRI Registration

official.background: Nonrigid registration aligns one brain scan to another and is needed for cross-subject comparison and atlas building. Diffusion MRI (dMRI) is harder to register than structural MRI because each voxel stores direction-dependent diffusion measurements, which have to be reoriented when the image is warped. Existing deep-learning dMRI registration methods (DDMReg, MVCReg) work on derived representations such as fractional anisotropy, tract orientation maps or fiber orientation distribution functions (fODFs). Computing these takes extra offline work and commits the user to a modelling assumption. This paper asks whether a network can register the raw diffusion-weighted signal directly, without fitting a derived model first.
official.method:
The raw dMRI signal on each q-space shell is treated as a function on position-and-orientation space (R^3 x S^2), and registration is posed as finding an SE(3)-equivariant diffeomorphism of that space (the 'diff-pq' problem), so no explicit Jacobian reorientation is needed. A VoxelMorph-style UNet (encoder depth 3) built from SE(3)-equivariant steerable convolutions, with filters parameterised by SO(5)-equivariant MLPs, takes the concatenated moving and fixed signal attenuations (DWIs divided by the mean b=0 volume, affinely pre-aligned, q-space resampled to the fixed image's directions, and low-pass filtered with an l_max=5 spherical-harmonic fit plus spatial Gaussian smoothing). It outputs a 6D velocity field (3 spatial + 3 spherical tangent components), which is integrated by scaling-and-squaring (N=4). A spatial transformer warps the moving image using trilinear interpolation in p-space and spherical-RBF angular interpolation (sigma=0.1) in q-space. The loss is an MMD between ensemble average propagators, implemented as a Gaussian-weighted L2 on signal attenuations in q-space plus an L2 velocity regulariser.

Data: the same 400 HCP Young Adult subjects and the same fixed subject as MVCReg, downsampled from 145x174x145 to 72x88x72. There are 399 moving-to-fixed pairs: 349 train, 25 validation, 25 test. Training runs for 500 epochs with SGD + Nesterov momentum, batch size 1, lr 0.001 halved every 100 epochs. Evaluation: the warped test subjects are run through MRtrix3 fODF estimation and peak extraction, then TractSeg segments 72 white-matter bundles. The reported number is the Dice overlap with the fixed subject's bundles, averaged over the 25 test subjects and 72 tracts.
official.claim: On HCP test registrations to a single fixed subject, the raw-dMRI SE(3)-equivariant network reaches a mean tract Dice of 0.7468, above VoxelMorph on FA (0.7126), MVCReg on fODF (0.7317) and DDMReg on FA+TOM (0.7417), but below MVVSReg (0.7493) and the classical mrregister (0.7601).
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Test time performance of various registration methods, average over all 25 test subjects and all 72 available white matter tracts.
official.metric: TractSeg bundle Dice (higher is better), averaged over 25 test subjects and 72 tracts; single numbers with no error bars, seeds or per-subject spread reported
official.comparison: Proposed raw-dMRI network vs. mrregister (classical SyN on fODF), VoxelMorph (FA), DDMReg (FA + TOM), MVCReg (fODF), MVVSReg (fODF)
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained under the paper's protocol, the raw-dMRI network's mean tract Dice fails to exceed VoxelMorph-on-FA and MVCReg on the same 25 test subjects, or falls clearly below about 0.74.

title: Rational Tuning of LLM Cascades via Probabilistic Modeling

official.background: An LLM cascade sends each query to a small model first and passes it on to a larger, more expensive model only when the current model's confidence is below a threshold. The k-1 thresholds set the trade-off between error rate and inference cost. Tuning them is usually done by grid search or black-box Bayesian optimization, which gets expensive as cascades get longer and needs enough labeled data to estimate how the models' errors interact.
official.method:
Each model's raw confidence (max answer-choice probability for multiple choice, or P('Y') from a self-verification prompt for generation) is calibrated by logistic regression on a hyperparameter-free log transform. The method then fits a joint model of the calibrated confidences of k models. Each marginal is a mixture of two scaled beta distributions plus point masses at the min and max confidence. Each adjacent pair is linked by a Gumbel copula with θ = 1/(1-τ), where τ is Kendall's tau, and the joint is built with a Markov factorization (model i depends only on model i-1). This gives closed-form P(Correct) and E[Cost] for any threshold vector. The thresholds are tuned by minimizing (1 - P(Correct)) + λ E[Cost] with L-BFGS-B over a geometric sweep of λ.

Setup: all 26 cascades of length k ≥ 2 built from Llama 3.2 1B/3B and Llama 3.1 8B/70B/405B, run zero-shot on MMLU, MedMCQA, TriviaQA, XSum, GSM8K and TruthfulQA. Open-ended answers are judged by Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Baselines: Bayesian optimization (HEBO, GP surrogate, same objective and λ sweep) and grid search over 2.5%-quantile grids followed by a Pareto filter. In the low-sample setting, calibrators and models are fitted on a balanced subsample of 20-30 training examples (pairs of one correct and one incorrect example per model) and evaluated on the ~1000-example test sets. The metric is the area under the test error vs. normalized-cost curve (AUC, lower is better).
official.claim: With n ≤ 30 training examples, Rational Tuning's average test error-cost AUC over the 26 Llama cascades is 0.325, vs. 0.338 for Bayesian optimization (-4.29% on average). It beats BO on all 6 benchmarks, with paired Wilcoxon p < 0.01 on 5 of them (e.g. MMLU -7.74%, p = 1e-6); TruthfulQA (-0.73%, p = 0.12) is not significant.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Area under the error-cost curve (AUC) in the low-sample limit (n ≤ 30 training examples), showing that our Rational Tuning ("RT") framework for selecting confidence thresholds consistently outperforms both a Bayesian optimization baseline ("BO") and high-resolution grid search ("GS"). The mean percentage changes (%Δ) are statistically significant at the p < 0.05 on almost all benchmarks, as measured by Wilcoxon rank-sum tests paired by cascade (highlighted in bold).
official.metric: Area under the test-set error-rate vs. normalized-cost curve (lower is better); %Δ is the mean per-cascade percentage change in AUC; p is from a Wilcoxon test paired by cascade (26 cascades); no seed std reported
official.comparison: Rational Tuning (Markov-copula model + continuous optimization) vs. Bayesian optimization (HEBO) and high-resolution grid search, all tuning the same cascades on the same low-sample training subsets
official.falsification_criterion: With the same Llama cascades and a balanced 20-30-example training subsample, Rational Tuning's mean per-cascade AUC reduction vs. Bayesian optimization is near zero or positive on most of MMLU, MedMCQA, XSum and GSM8K, or is not significant under a paired Wilcoxon test.

title: Adaptive Prior Selection in Gaussian Process Bandits with Thompson Sampling
claim_source: Table 2 (Appendix F), page 28; cumulative-regret curves in Figure 2, page 7

official.background: In Gaussian process (GP) bandits an agent repeatedly picks one of a set of correlated arms to maximise an unknown function drawn from a GP, and its exploration depends on the assumed GP prior (kernel, lengthscale, relevant input dimensions). In practice the prior is unknown and is usually set by maximum likelihood, which has no guarantees in sequential decision making. Prior-Elimination GP-UCB (PE-GP-UCB) handles a finite set of candidate priors by choosing the arm and prior with the highest joint upper confidence bound and eliminating priors that predict badly. That joint maximisation adds two layers of optimism and can over-explore. This paper asks whether Thompson-sampling (TS) variants that remove some or all of that optimism get lower regret.
official.method:
Given a finite set of candidate priors P, PE-GP-TS draws one posterior sample f~_{t,p} from each still-active prior and plays the arm and prior that jointly maximise the samples. It then adds the prediction error y_t - mu_{t,p_t}(x_t) to that prior's running total and eliminates the prior if the total exceeds a threshold V_t, as in PE-GP-UCB (delta = 0.05). HP-GP-TS (equivalent to EGP-TS of Lu et al. 2023) samples a prior p_t from the exact hyperposterior, which starts uniform and is updated by the Gaussian predictive likelihood of each observation. It then draws one GP posterior sample under p_t and plays its argmax. MAP GP-TS is the same as HP-GP-TS except that it greedily takes the most probable prior (equivalent to maximum likelihood under a uniform hyperprior).

Synthetic setups (noise variance 0.25^2, horizon T = 500, the true prior drawn uniformly from P, the reward function drawn from that GP, 500 seeds). Kernel: 6 zero-mean priors (RBF, RQ alpha = 0.5, Matern-5/2, Matern-3/2, periodic rho = 5, linear v = 0.05^2), all with lengthscale 1, and 500 arms equally spaced on [0, 20]. Lengthscale: 8 RBF priors with lengthscales equally spaced in [0.5, 4] on the same 500 arms. Subspace: d = 16 with 500 arms uniform in [0, 20]^16, and 5 RBF priors (lengthscale 8), each assuming f depends only on 4 cyclically shifted dimensions [i, i+1, i+2, i+3] (indices wrapped modulo 5). The metric is total cumulative regret at T = 500.
official.claim: On all three synthetic GP-bandit setups (T = 500, 500 seeds), both Thompson-sampling prior-selection methods have far lower total regret than PE-GP-UCB. Kernel: HP-GP-TS 39.2 ± 1.4 and PE-GP-TS 62.0 ± 0.6 vs. 121.6 ± 1.2. Lengthscale: 31.4 ± 1.0 and 61.8 ± 0.5 vs. 114.2 ± 0.6. Subspace: 88.3 ± 0.9 and 177.1 ± 1.4 vs. 389.0 ± 1.5.

title: Why Transformers Struggle with Distribution-Independent In-Context Learning
claim_source: Table 1, page 4 (transformer row with ± std in Table 3, page 15)

official.background: In-context learning (ICL) lets a transformer solve a new task from input-output examples in its prompt without weight updates. A common interpretation is that the transformer implements a learning algorithm such as gradient descent or least squares in its forward pass. If it did, its predictions should stay accurate whenever the context uniquely determines the target function, even when the test distribution differs from training. The paper tests this in noiseless polynomial regression, where classical regression extrapolates exactly, and asks whether strong in-distribution ICL implies distribution-independent ICL.
official.method:
A GPT-style decoder-only transformer (12 layers, 8 heads, hidden size 256, scalar tokens embedded by a learned linear map and decoded by a learned linear readout, final LayerNorm) is trained from scratch with the Garg et al. (2022) objective: squared error on next-label prediction across prompts (x1, g(x1), ..., xk, g(xk), x). For the chosen claim, g is a degree-1 polynomial with coefficients from U(-1,1) and inputs from U(-1,1). Training uses Adam (lr 1e-4, batch 64) for 500k steps with fresh prompts each step and a curriculum on prompt length from 11 to 41 pairs.

At test time inputs stay in U(-1,1) but coefficients are drawn from U(-sigma, sigma) for sigma from 1 to 10. Evaluation uses 5 seeds x 100 functions x 64 prompts of 41 points; MSE is averaged over predictions after the first n+1 positions. Baselines get the same in-context examples: Nadaraya-Watson with an RBF kernel, kernel ridge regression (KRR) with an RBF kernel and with a polynomial kernel (lambda = 1e-3, RBF lengthscale = std of the training input grid, no tuning on shifted data). Ordinary least squares, which is exact here, is shown separately as the dotted baseline in Figure 1, not in Table 1.
official.claim: On degree-1 polynomial regression with inputs from U(-1,1), a transformer trained on coefficients from U(-1,1) has MSE 9e-6 at sigma=1, but 4.29 at sigma=5 and 27.06 at sigma=10 when test coefficients come from U(-sigma, sigma). On the same in-context examples, KRR with a polynomial kernel stays at or below 2.3e-3 and KRR with an RBF kernel at or below 0.23.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: The evolution of MSE for degree-1 polynomial functions distribution shift, comparing the Transformer with Nadaraya–Watson regression (NW) and kernel ridge regression (KRR). Test inputs are sampled from U(−1, 1) and coefficients from U(−σ, σ). All methods receive the same in-context examples. Kernel hyperparameters are specified in Appendix C.
official.metric: Test MSE (lower is better). Table 1 gives means with no error bars. Table 3 reports the transformer as mean ± std over 5 evaluation seeds (one trained model, 100 test functions per seed): 4.3 ± 0.2 at sigma=5 and 27.1 ± 2.3 at sigma=10. No error bars are given for the kernel baselines.
official.comparison: Transformer (trained on U(-1,1) coefficients) vs. Nadaraya-Watson (RBF), KRR (RBF) and KRR (polynomial kernel) on identical in-context examples, across coefficient scales sigma in {1,2,3,5,7,10}

title: MITO: A Millimeter-Wave Dataset and Simulator for Non-Line-of-Sight Perception

official.background: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar signals pass through everyday occluders such as cardboard, fabric and plastic, so they can image objects that cameras cannot see, for example inside a closed box. mmWave images look very different from optical images: they are mostly specular, have edge-diffraction artifacts, no color, and are complex-valued. Learning-based perception on them is held back by a lack of data. MITO provides a real dataset (550 3D SAR images of 76 YCB objects at 24 and 77 GHz, in line-of-sight and under cardboard) and an open-source simulator that turns any 3D triangle mesh into a synthetic mmWave image, so models can be trained on synthetic data.
official.method:
The simulator takes a mesh and a set of radar positions. For each position it finds the visible mesh vertices, models each vertex reflection as exp(-j 4π|l−v|/λ_j), sums them into a raw signal, and passes the signals through the same SAR imaging pipeline (Eq. 1) used for real data. There are two variants: a specular simulation keeps only vertices whose surface normal points back toward the radar (angle below a threshold τ), and an edge simulation keeps only vertices on sharp edges (dihedral angle above τ_e). A combined image is the normalized weighted sum (α1·I_s + α2·I_e)/(α1+α2).

To measure accuracy, real and synthetic images are each turned into point clouds (one point per voxel whose magnitude exceeds τ_P), aligned with ICP (Open3D), and compared with the 3D F-score at distance threshold τ_F. For the combined simulation, the F-score is the maximum over a set W of weight pairs (α1, α2). Specular-only is α=(1,0) and edge-only is α=(0,1). The 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of F-score over all objects in the dataset are reported.
official.claim: Across all objects in MITO, the combined (specular + edge, best weight) simulation matches real 77 GHz mmWave images with a 3D F-score of 85% / 94% / 98% at the 25th / 50th / 75th percentiles, versus 68% / 90% / 97% for specular-only and 49% / 71% / 88% for edge-only simulation.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Simulation 3D F-Score for combined (Comb), specular (Spec), & edge simulations.
official.metric: 3D F-score (higher is better) between thresholded, ICP-aligned real and simulated point clouds; percentiles over objects. No error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Combined simulation (best F-score over the weight grid W) vs. specular-only (α1=1, α2=0) vs. edge-only (α1=0, α2=1), all run by the authors on the same objects with the same pipeline
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the released simulator and evaluation on the MITO real images, the combined simulation's 25th-percentile F-score is not clearly above specular-only (e.g. the 85% vs 68% gap shrinks to a few points), or the median of edge-only is not well below both others.

title: RSQ: Learning from Important Tokens Leads to Better Quantized LLMs

official.background: Post-training layer-wise quantization (e.g., GPTQ) compresses an LLM's weights one layer at a time by minimizing the reconstruction error ||WX - W̃X||² on a small calibration set, weighting every token equally. Rotation-based methods like QuaRot first apply orthogonal (Hadamard) transforms to remove weight outliers and then run GPTQ, which makes 3-bit and lower quantization workable. However, LLMs do not treat tokens equally (attention sinks, heavy-hitter tokens), so a uniform reconstruction loss may spend the quantized model's limited capacity on tokens that matter little.
official.method:
RSQ (Rotate, Scale, then Quantize) has three steps: (1) rotate the model with a randomized Hadamard matrix as in QuaRot; (2) scale each token's input features by an importance score r_i, giving the weighted objective sum_i ||r_i (W x_i - W̃ x_i)||², which is equivalent to running GPTQ with the modified Hessian H = 2 X R² Xᵀ; (3) quantize with GPTQ using that Hessian. Importance is computed per layer by attention concentration (AttnCon): the total attention probability each token receives, summed over all query positions and heads, min-max normalized into [r_min, 1] with r_min = 0.01 (the best value in Fig. 3). The same importance is shared by all weights within a layer.

RSQ also uses dataset expansion with factor M = 8: each calibration sequence is cyclically shifted by T/M, 2T/M, ..., (M-1)T/M so that every token occupies an important position at some point. For Table 2, each model is quantized to 3-bit with 256 WikiText-2 calibration samples of 4096 tokens. Baselines are GPTQ and QuaRot (rotation + GPTQ, uniform token weights). WikiText-2 perplexity is evaluated with a context length of 2048 (Appendix C.4); downstream accuracy is reported on LAMBADA (openai and std), WinoGrande, ARC-C/E, HellaSwag, PIQA, MMLU, GSM8k and TruthfulQA.
official.claim: Quantizing LLaMA3-8B-Instruct to 3-bit with 256×4096-token WikiText-2 calibration, RSQ reaches WikiText-2 perplexity 9.046 ± 0.01 and 10-task average accuracy 65.4 ± 0.1%, versus 9.517 ± 0.11 and 63.8 ± 0.5% for QuaRot under the same setup.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Comparison of recent layer-wise quantization approaches with RSQ on multiple downstream tasks. We report perplexity for WikiText and accuracy for all other tasks. The model is quantized to 3-bit. The best-performing method across all quantization approaches is highlighted in bold. We denote the standard deviation across three runs as a subscript.
official.metric: WikiText-2 perplexity (lower is better, context length 2048) and average accuracy over 10 downstream tasks (higher is better); ± is the std across three runs (seeds)
official.comparison: RSQ (rotation + AttnCon token scaling + dataset expansion + GPTQ) vs. QuaRot (rotation + GPTQ with uniform token weights) and GPTQ, same model, bit-width and calibration data
official.falsification_criterion: On LLaMA3-8B-Instruct at 3-bit with matched calibration data and seeds, RSQ's WikiText-2 perplexity is not lower than QuaRot's by more than the seed std (i.e., the ~0.47 perplexity gap shrinks to within ~0.1), or RSQ's average accuracy is not above QuaRot's by more than about one std (~0.5 points).

title: Aligned Delta-Triplane Transformers as Occupancy World Models

official.background: Occupancy world models predict future 3D semantic voxel grids around an autonomous vehicle from past occupancy frames and the ego vehicle's past and planned motion. Most existing models compress each frame into a bird's-eye-view latent, use a large Transformer or diffusion model to align past frames implicitly, and predict the full future scene. That is costly and redundant, because once ego motion is removed most of the scene does not change over a few seconds.
official.method:
ADTT first pretrains a triplane autoencoder (xy, xz, yz feature planes, 16x100x100, 8 channels) to reconstruct 16x200x200 Occ3D-nuScenes occupancy grids. Historical triplanes are then explicitly warped into the target ego frame using the recorded ego poses (nearest-neighbour sampling, zeros where there is no historical correspondence). A lightweight conv tokenizer maps each aligned triplane to an 8x8x4 grid of 256 tokens (dim 96). A Transformer encoder builds a memory from the last 4 aligned frames. A Transformer decoder with 64 ego-motion queries (from an MLP on the future ego motion) and 192 learnable external queries predicts delta tokens. These are upsampled to a delta triplane, added to the latest aligned triplane and decoded to occupancy. Prediction is autoregressive. Training uses L1+L2 triplane losses plus cross-entropy/Lovasz occupancy losses, with the triplane encoder frozen and the decoder fine-tuned.

Evaluation follows the standard Occ3D-nus protocol: 4 past frames (2 s) are used to predict 6 future frames (3 s), reporting mIoU over 18 semantic classes and occupancy IoU averaged over 1 s, 2 s and 3 s. In the Table 4 ablation each variant removes one component from the full model M0. M4 removes motion compensation, so the historical triplanes are not warped into the target frame. M5 removes delta prediction, so the model predicts the full future triplane instead of a residual added to the aligned prior.
official.claim: On Occ3D-nus 3-second forecasting, full ADTT reaches 46.87 average mIoU and 52.63 IoU. Removing triplane motion compensation drops this to 31.87 mIoU and 37.48 IoU, and predicting the full future state instead of deltas drops it to 36.65 mIoU and 45.50 IoU.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Ablation on key designs in ADTT.
official.metric: Average mIoU (%) over 18 semantic classes and average occupancy IoU (%) across 1 s, 2 s and 3 s horizons, higher is better. Single runs with no seeds, std or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: Full ADTT (M0) vs. the same model without motion compensation (M4) and without delta prediction (M5), under the same training settings
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained variants without motion compensation, or with full-state instead of delta prediction, come within a few mIoU points of the full model (e.g. a gap under about 3 mIoU instead of 15 and 10), or match or beat it.

title: Reasoning Under 1 Billion: Memory-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
claim_source: Figure 2 (GSM8K panel), page 7; Memory-R+ K = 20 exact values in Table 2, page 8

official.background: RL fine-tuning with outcome rewards (as in DeepSeek-R1) improves chain-of-thought reasoning in large LLMs, but tiny models (1B parameters or fewer) rarely produce correctly formatted, correct answers early in training, so outcome rewards are sparse. Adding format-based rewards helps, but small models tend to overfit to those easy rewards or collapse in response length, and they have no explicit exploration mechanism. The paper proposes an intrinsic reward from episodic memory to give tiny models a denser, performance-driven training signal.
official.method:
Memory-R+ keeps two kNN episodic memories of past (query, responses) pairs, one for successful responses (correct answer) and one for failed ones, with queries and responses embedded by the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 Sentence Transformer. For a new query, the K most similar stored queries (cosine similarity) are retrieved. The exploit reward is minus the Euclidean distance between the response embedding and the centroid of retrieved successful responses; the explore reward is 1 minus the maximum cosine similarity to retrieved failed responses (after a warm-up of about 50 steps). Each is min-max normalized over a sliding window of w = 100, and they are summed (beta_s = beta_e = 1) and added to the outcome and format rewards in GRPO.

For the chosen claim, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct is trained with GRPO (Open-R1 codebase, one H100) on 2,000 random samples of AI-MO NuminaMath-TIR for 4 epochs, with lr 5e-6, batch 4, grad accumulation 16, 16 generations, max completion length 300, memory K = 20, L = 100. Baselines share the correctness, XML and reasoning-step format rewards: R1 (standard GRPO with those rewards) and Cosine (adds a length-based cosine reward). Checkpoints are evaluated zero-shot with Lighteval extractive match on GSM8K test, MATH-500 and AIME24, 3 seeds each.
official.claim: Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on 2,000 AI-MO samples, Memory-R+ (K = 20) reaches about 37.5-38% GSM8K test accuracy from step 100 onward, versus about 33-34.5% for both R1 and Cosine, a gap of roughly 4 points with non-overlapping std bands over 3 seeds.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Performance of fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AI-MO data. The test accuracy is evaluated at multiple checkpoints during training (mean±std. over 3 runs).
official.metric: GSM8K test extractive-match accuracy (Lighteval, zero-shot), higher is better; mean ± std over 3 training seeds (shaded bands)
official.comparison: Memory-R+ (K = 20) vs. R1 (GRPO with correctness + format rewards) vs. Cosine (adds length-based reward), same model, data and hyperparameters
official.falsification_criterion: With 3 seeds per method, Memory-R+'s GSM8K accuracy at the final checkpoint is not above both R1 and Cosine by more than the seed std, or the gap is under about 2 points.

title: Beyond Semantics: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Reasonless Intermediate Tokens
claim_source: Table 6, page 19 (Appendix A.2); seed-1 values also in Table 3, page 10

official.background: Reasoning models are trained to emit intermediate tokens ('chains of thought') before an answer, and these traces are often read as faithful records of the model's reasoning. It is unclear whether the semantic correctness of the traces is what makes them useful. In large pretrained models this cannot be checked, because traces are natural language with no ground truth. A small, fully controlled setting where traces are formally verifiable (A* search on grid mazes) lets one test directly whether training on semantically correct traces matters for final-answer accuracy.
official.method:
The authors train a Qwen2.5-0.5B architecture from scratch with a custom 944-token vocabulary (~380M parameters, 32k context) on 30x30 maze shortest-path problems. Each training example is a maze description, start and goal, a linearized A* execution trace (create/close x y cG cH operations, Manhattan heuristic), and the correct plan. Training sets have 500k problems; 250k steps, batch size 8, AdamW, peak LR 2.2758e-4, weight decay 0.1528, 100 warm-up steps, bf16. Mazes are generated either with Wilson's algorithm (acyclic) or with Searchformer-style random wall placement (SF-style, 30-50% walls, can contain loops).

The 'Swapped' dataset contains the same problems and correct plans, but each problem's A* trace is randomly permuted to a different problem, so traces have the right format but no relation to the maze they accompany. 'Normal' models train on the correct traces. Both are evaluated on 1000-problem test sets from five generators (Wilson, Kruskal, DFS, Drunkard's Walk, SF-style) by plan accuracy (a plan is valid if every move goes between adjacent free cells and ends at the goal; optimality is not required) and by trace validity among valid plans, checked by a formal A* trace verifier.
official.claim: For models trained from scratch on 500k SF-style maze problems, training on traces swapped between problems gives higher plan accuracy than training on correct A* traces, on both initialization seeds: 89.1% and 86.8% vs. 56.2% and 64.9% on in-distribution SF-style mazes, and 95.4% and 87.8% vs. 62.1% and 66.3% on out-of-distribution Drunkard's Walk mazes, while the swapped models have 0% trace validity.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: SF-style model performance across seeds. Original denotes the models whose performance were reported at Table 3. Seed 2 are the models trained on a different seed. Each cell shows Plan Accuracy (%) / Trace Validity within valid plans (%).
official.metric: Plan accuracy (%) on 1000 test problems per maze generator, higher is better; trace validity within valid plans (%) is also shown. No ± reported; two training seeds (original and Seed 2) are reported as separate rows.
official.comparison: Swapped (SF-style) vs. Normal (SF-style), same architecture, same problems and plans, same training budget, matched per initialization seed
official.falsification_criterion: A Normal (correct-trace) SF-style model trained under the same setup reaches plan accuracy within a few points of, or above, the Swapped model on the SF-style or Drunkard test sets, or the Swapped model's advantage disappears on a fresh seed.

title: HOPSE: Scalable Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder for Combinatorial Representations

official.background: Topological deep learning models data on higher-order domains such as simplicial and cell complexes, where nodes, edges and faces (triangles, cycles) all carry features. Most topological neural networks use higher-order message passing (HOMP) between cells of different ranks, which is expressive but slow, because the number of message routes grows quickly with the number of ranks and neighborhood types. This limits how well these models scale. HOPSE asks whether the message passing can be dropped altogether, with the higher-order structure computed once as positional and structural encodings, while keeping the predictive performance.
official.method:
HOPSE splits a complex into a set of strictly augmented Hasse graphs, one for each chosen neighborhood function (adjacencies A_{r,s} and incidences I_{s->t} between cells of different ranks). On each Hasse graph it computes standard graph positional and structural encodings once, as preprocessing. The encodings for cells of the same target rank are concatenated. During training, per-rank MLPs embed the encodings and the original cell features, another MLP mixes them into a representation for each rank, and a readout combines all ranks. No message passing happens during training or inference. HOPSE-M-C (the variant in the claim) uses four connectivity-only encodings: Laplacian eigenvectors (LapPE), electrostatic PE, random-walk SE and heat-kernel diagonal SE. HOPSE-M-F uses feature-aware encodings and HOPSE-GPSE uses a pretrained GPSE encoder.

All models run in TopoBench with shared encoders and readout, five stratified 50/25/25 train/val/test splits, and a hyperparameter grid search chosen by mean validation score over 5 seeds; test mean ± std is reported. On MANTRA (43,000+ triangulations of 2- and 3-manifolds, simplicial domain), the beta_2 task is predicting the second Betti number. Baselines are GCN, GAT and GIN (each run with and without the HOPSE encodings, best kept) and the simplicial HOMP models TopoTune, SCCNN and SANN.
official.claim: On MANTRA second-Betti-number prediction (simplicial domain), HOPSE-M-C reaches 83.70 ± 0.99, above the best higher-order message-passing baselines TopoTune (80.37 ± 1.62) and SCCNN (79.62 ± 1.23), and far above GIN (56.11 ± 0.53).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Overall Results Table. Evaluation of predictive performance on molecular and topological benchmarks. We report the test mean ± standard deviation over 5 seeds for best validation configurations. Bold highlights the top-performing model per column, while blue denotes models with no statistically significant difference from the best score (at a 95 % confidence level).
official.metric: Test score on the beta_2 task, higher is better (the paper says accuracy/F1 for up-arrow tasks without naming the exact one for beta_2); mean ± std over 5 seeds at the best validation configuration. title: Practical Adversarial Attacks on Stochastic Bandits via Fake Data Injection
claim_source: Figure 1b (and 1a), page 10; numbers stated in Section 5, page 9

official.background: Adversarial attacks on stochastic multi-armed bandits usually assume the attacker can change the reward of the chosen arm in every round, by any amount. Real systems such as recommenders and ad platforms do not allow this: an adversary cannot overwrite genuine user feedback but can create fake accounts that add a limited number of valid, bounded ratings or clicks. This paper proposes a 'fake data injection' threat model. The attacker adds fabricated (arm, reward) records with rewards in [r_min, r_max] to the learner's history, and the question is whether a small, sublinear number of such records can make UCB or Thompson Sampling pull a chosen low-reward target arm in almost every round.
official.method:
The attacks use a suppression principle. Once a non-target arm i has been pulled ⌈log T / δ0²⌉ times, the attacker injects enough fake samples with reward r_min to push its empirical mean below a high-probability lower bound on the target arm's mean, ℓ̂_K(t) = µ̂_K(t) − 2β(N_K(t)) − 3σδ0. After that, UCB essentially never explores arm i again (Lemma 4.1). SBI (bounded Simultaneous Injection, Algorithm 1) injects the required n_i samples at once. PBI (Periodic Bounded Injection, Algorithm 2) injects at most f samples per batch with a computed cooldown R_i between batches. LI injects one fake sample per triggered arm, with its reward chosen to meet the threshold. The control is a random-timing heuristic that uses SBI's fake rewards and per-arm sample counts (so the same cost) but injects them at random times.

UCB experiment (Section 5): K = 10 arms are 10 movies sampled from a MovieLens-derived binary rating matrix, with Bernoulli rewards at their mean ratings. The target is the least popular movie. Settings: σ = 0.5, δ = 0.05, δ0 = 0.2, r_max = 1, f = 10, 20 runs per horizon, T from K to 10^6 (T counts genuine plus fake records). All methods share the same genuine reward streams and pull each arm once at initialization. The metrics are the attack cost C^F(T) (cumulative |r^F − µ_arm| over fake samples) and the fraction of rounds in which the target arm is selected.
official.claim: Against UCB on a 10-arm MovieLens Bernoulli bandit with the least popular movie as target, SBI and PBI make the learner select the target arm in 99.68% of rounds at T = 10^6, with attack cost C^F(T) of about 3,800, while a random-timing heuristic with exactly the same fake samples (same cost) reaches only 0.02%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: UCB experiments with 20 repetitions. Shading shows one sample standard deviation. Panels: (a) Attack cost vs. T, (b) Target-arm ratio vs. T. Methods: SBI, PBI, LI, Heuristic.
official.metric: Target-arm selection ratio (higher is better for the attacker) and attack cost C^F(T) (cumulative reward deviation of fake samples, lower is better); means over 20 runs, shading = one sample standard deviation; values other than 99.68% / 0.02% are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: SBI and PBI (suppression-timed injection) vs. a random-timing heuristic with matched fake rewards and per-arm counts; LI (one optimized fake sample per arm) also shown
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the UCB setup (K = 10 MovieLens arms, σ = 0.5, δ0 = 0.2, δ = 0.05, f = 10, T = 10^6, 20 runs), SBI/PBI's target-arm ratio falls well below ~95%, or the matched-cost random-timing heuristic reaches a comparable ratio, or SBI/PBI's attack cost grows roughly linearly in T instead of flattening near a few thousand.

title: B-XAIC Dataset: Benchmarking Explainable AI for Graph Neural Networks Using Chemical Data

official.background: Graph neural networks are the standard model for predicting molecular properties, and many explainability (XAI) methods claim to show which atoms and bonds drive a prediction. Evaluating these explainers is hard because real molecular datasets rarely have known ground-truth rationales, and existing benchmarks are either synthetic or small single-task sets such as MUTAG. Common metrics also threshold importance maps or take top-k elements, which breaks down when no substructure is relevant at all. Without a benchmark with known rationales, it is unclear whether popular explainers recover the rules a model actually uses.
official.method:
B-XAIC samples 50K molecules from ChEMBL 35 (8/1/1 random split) and labels them for 7 rule-based binary tasks: presence of boron (B), phosphorus (P), halogens (X), indole, PAINS alerts, more than four rings (rings-count), and a ring with more than six atoms (rings-max). Each positive molecule has node- and edge-level ground-truth explanations (the atoms/bonds of the matched pattern). GCN, GAT, GIN and ProtGNN are trained on the tasks; GIN reaches weighted-F1 of 92.9-99.98% on all tasks (Table 3) and is the model the explainers are evaluated on in the main text.

Explanations are scored in two regimes. Null explanation (NE): for a molecule without the pattern, the explanation should contain no outliers; the score is 1 if Tukey's 1.5x IQR rule finds no outlier attributions and 0 otherwise, averaged over instances. Subgraph explanation (SE): for a molecule with the pattern, the AUROC of the attribution scores against the ground-truth nodes/edges. Explainers include gradient-based methods (Saliency, Deconvolution, InputXGradient, GuidedBackprop, IntegratedGradients), graph-specific methods (GNNExplainer, GraphMask, PGExplainer, PGMExplainer, FlowX, SubgraphX, GraphSHAP-IQ), perturbation-based (ShapleyValueSampling, EdgeSHAPer) and surrogate methods (DnX, FastDnX). Table 4 reports NE and SE averaged over the 7 tasks (nodes) or 4 ring/indole/PAINS tasks (edges).
official.claim: On B-XAIC with a trained GIN, node-level gradient-based explainers other than Deconvolution score low on null explanations (Saliency 0.51 ± 0.12, InputXGradient 0.54 ± 0.14, GuidedBackprop 0.41 ± 0.12, IntegratedGradients 0.39 ± 0.26, averaged over 7 tasks) while PGMExplainer scores 0.98 ± 0.02 and SubgraphX 0.94 ± 0.05, even though these gradient methods rank the true pattern well (SE 0.83-0.87); Deconvolution is the gradient-based exception (NE 0.79 ± 0.10).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Evaluation of the node and edge explanations for the GIN model. Explainers are grouped as gradient-based (GB), graph-specific (GS), perturbation-based (PB), and surrogate (SU). Bold marks the best score and those not significantly worse (one-sided Wilcoxon test). Avg is the mean of NE and SE; uncertainty is reported for NE and SE.
official.metric: NE: fraction of pattern-free molecules whose node attributions contain no 1.5x IQR outliers (higher is better). SE: node-level AUROC against ground-truth pattern atoms (higher is better). Values are means over the 7 tasks; the ± is the standard deviation across the 7 tasks (the Table 4 caption says only 'uncertainty', but Table 10 reports the same node NE values as 'mean ± standard deviation across seven tasks'). Bold marks scores not significantly worse than the best under the paper's one-sided Wilcoxon test.
official.comparison: Gradient-based explainers (Saliency, GuidedBackprop, IntegratedGradients, InputXGradient) vs. PGMExplainer and SubgraphX, all applied to the same trained GIN on the same B-XAIC test set.
official.falsification_criterion: Using a GIN trained to similar accuracy on B-XAIC, Saliency (or IntegratedGradients/GuidedBackprop) reaches a task-averaged node NE within about 0.2 of PGMExplainer, or PGMExplainer's node NE falls below about 0.8.

title: ER-Reason: A Benchmark Dataset for LLM Clinical Reasoning in the Emergency Room

official.background: LLMs score well on medical-licensing-style multiple-choice benchmarks, but prospective studies show much weaker clinical usefulness. A common critique is construct validity: most benchmarks measure knowledge recall or final diagnostic accuracy on stylized vignettes rather than clinical reasoning. The paper defines clinical reasoning as revising beliefs over a differential diagnosis as evidence accumulates (Ledley and Lusted's sequential testing loop). ER-Reason supplies 25,174 de-identified real emergency-room notes from 3,437 patients, with tasks across the ER workflow and Script Concordance Test (SCT)-style items, to measure whether models update diagnostic beliefs the way emergency physicians do.
official.method:
Emergency medicine attendings wrote 194 SCT-style cases from real ER provider notes. Each case gives a clinical scenario, 3-5 candidate diagnoses and a sequence of evidence steps (a lab, imaging, or exam finding), for 787 SCT items in total. At each step the respondent rates how the new evidence changes the likelihood of the diagnosis under consideration on a -2..+2 scale and re-ranks the differential. Two attending physicians annotated every item independently, a third adjudicated disagreements, and the consensus is the ground truth. The annotators also wrote a rationale for every step.

Eight LLMs (DeepSeek-R1, o4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5.2 Thinking, Claude Sonnet 4.5 Thinking, Phi-4, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5; temperature 0.1 where supported, via Azure OpenAI or OpenRouter) are prompted in three conditions. Zero-shot (ZS) gives the case, the differential and the new evidence. Single oracle (SO) also gives the physician rationale for the current step. Full oracle (FO) gives all physician rationales from steps 1..t. DxUpdate is the linearly weighted Cohen's kappa between model and physician ordinal scores, averaged over timesteps. DxTrajectory is the mean Spearman rho between model and physician differential rankings over all encounter-timestep pairs.
official.claim: On the 194-case ER-Reason SCT set, giving the model the physician's rationale for the current step (single oracle) raises DxUpdate for every one of 8 LLMs above the upper end of its zero-shot 95% CI, e.g. GPT-5.2 0.677 (0.646-0.701) -> 0.795 and o4-mini 0.691 (0.664-0.713) -> 0.809; DxTrajectory rises likewise (GPT-5.2 0.646 (0.618-0.680) -> 0.780 SO, 0.813 FO).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance in SCT reasoning tasks. (95% confidence intervals reported from 1,000 bootstraps.)
official.metric: DxUpdate = linearly weighted Cohen's kappa vs. physician consensus (higher is better); DxTrajectory = mean Spearman rho of differential rankings (higher is better). Parentheses are 95% CIs from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, reported for zero-shot only; SO/FO are point estimates with no CI. One run per condition.
official.comparison: Same model, same cases: zero-shot vs. single-oracle vs. full-oracle prompting, for each of 8 LLMs
official.falsification_criterion: For the same (or comparable current) models, single-oracle DxUpdate or DxTrajectory falls inside the zero-shot bootstrap 95% CI (a gain of less than roughly 0.03-0.04) for most models.

title: Equivariant Spherical Transformer for Efficient Molecular Modeling

official.background: SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks for molecules and materials usually build interactions from Clebsch-Gordan tensor products of steerable (spherical-harmonic) features. These products get expensive as the maximum degree L grows, and a fixed L limits what the network can express. For example, Joshi et al. showed that tensor-product models of degree L cannot tell apart n-fold rotationally symmetric structures with n > L. SCN/eSCN-style models instead project features onto sampled points on the sphere, but they process each orientation independently.
official.method:
The Equivariant Spherical Transformer (EST) maps each node's steerable features (degrees 0..L, C channels) onto S near-uniform sample points on the sphere (a Fibonacci lattice, optionally refined by repulsion). This gives a length-S sequence of C-dimensional vectors. EST applies pre-LayerNorm self-attention across all S orientations, plus an FFN, with query and key vectors augmented by the 3D sample coordinates (relative orientation embedding). It then maps back to steerable features with the inverse transform. The continuous operator is exactly equivariant. With finite sampling it is only approximately equivariant.

For the expressiveness test, following the geometric-WL benchmark of Joshi et al. [16], the authors build a single message-passing layer whose only interaction operation is EST (no steerable FFN). They test whether it can distinguish an n-fold rotationally symmetric structure from its rotated copy, reporting classification accuracy (50% = chance) for EST at L = 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 on 3-, 10- and 100-fold structures, and for a TFN/MACE tensor-product layer at the same L on 2-, 3-, 5- and 10-fold structures.
official.claim: A single EST layer with maximum degree L = 1 distinguishes 3-fold, 10-fold and 100-fold rotationally symmetric structures with 100.0 ± 0.0% accuracy, while a TFN/MACE tensor-product layer with L = 1 stays at chance (50.0 ± 0.0%) on 2-, 3-, 5- and 10-fold structures, and in general fails whenever n > L.

official.metric: Classification accuracy (%) for distinguishing the symmetric structure pair (higher is better; 50% = chance). The paper reports ± values but does not define them or state the number of runs or seeds.

official.falsification_criterion: An L = 1 EST layer (trained with the paper's setup and Fibonacci-lattice sampling) scores near 50% on 3-fold or 10-fold structures, or a TFN/MACE L = 1 layer, run under the same protocol, distinguishes those structures well above chance.

title: Diffusion Guidance Is a Controllable Policy Improvement Operator

official.background: Offline RL tries to learn a policy that is better than the behavior in a fixed dataset, but most methods that do so are harder to tune and less stable than plain behavioral cloning. Goal-conditioned behavioral cloning (GCBC) is simple and scalable, yet it only imitates the data and does not converge to the optimal goal-reaching policy. This paper argues that classifier-free guidance in diffusion/flow models is itself a policy improvement operator: raising the guidance weight sharpens the policy toward higher advantage, so a GCBC policy can be improved at test time without training any value function.
official.method:
A single flow-matching policy network is trained with the standard conditional flow-matching loss, conditioned on state and on a goal g that is dropped (set to null) 10% of the time, so the same network represents both the unconditional BC policy and the goal-conditioned GCBC policy. Goals are sampled uniformly from future states in the same trajectory (OGBench default). At sampling time, the velocity is v = (1 - w) v(a, t, s, null) + w v(a, t, s, g) with 16 flow steps. w = 0 recovers flow BC, w = 1 recovers flow GCBC, and CFGRL uses w = 3 for all tasks. The paper shows that w > 1 corresponds to a product policy pi_hat(a|s) p(g|s,a)^w, which provably improves on the w = 1 policy.

Experiments use the 'oraclerep' variants of OGBench goal-conditioned tasks (ground-truth goal representations), MLP [512]x4 with GELU, 1M gradient steps, batch 1024 for state-based tasks, success rate averaged over 8 seeds. Baselines are Gaussian BC, flow BC, Gaussian GCBC and flow GCBC.
official.claim: On OGBench pointmaze-giant-navigate (state-based, oraclerep), a flat flow policy sampled with CFG weight w = 3 (CFGRL) reaches 30 ± 10% success versus 4 ± 2% for flow GCBC (w = 1) and 2 ± 2% for Gaussian GCBC; on humanoidmaze-medium-navigate it reaches 19 ± 6% versus 8 ± 3% for flow GCBC.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Improving on GCBC. CFGRL consistently improves performance over GCBC across the board. Numbers at or above the 95% of the best performance in each category are boldfaced, as in OGBench [57].
official.metric: Goal-reaching success rate (%) on OGBench evaluation goals, higher is better; ± is standard deviation over 8 seeds (state-based tasks) or 4 seeds (pixel tasks)
official.comparison: CFGRL (flow policy, guidance w = 3) vs. flow GCBC (w = 1), flow BC (w = 0), Gaussian GCBC and Gaussian BC, all trained without a value function
official.falsification_criterion: On pointmaze-giant-navigate with 8 seeds, CFGRL at w = 3 does not exceed flow GCBC by more than the seed std (e.g. CFGRL mean below ~15% while flow GCBC stays near 4%), or on humanoidmaze-medium-navigate CFGRL is not above flow GCBC.

title: Accelerating Inference of Discrete Autoregressive Normalizing Flows by Selective Jacobi Decoding

official.background: Autoregressive normalizing flows such as TarFlow reach state-of-the-art likelihoods and image quality by splitting an image into a sequence of patches and transforming each one conditioned on all previous ones with a causal transformer. Training is parallel, but sampling requires inverting every flow block, and the inverse is strictly sequential: each patch must wait for all earlier patches. For a 256x256 model with 1024 patches and 8 blocks, this makes generation slow. Jacobi decoding, which updates all positions in parallel from the previous iterate until a fixed point is reached, has been tried for language models and autoregressive image models with modest gains. This paper asks whether it works better for the deterministic, continuous inverse of a normalizing flow.
official.method:
Inverting one autoregressive flow block is treated as solving a triangular system of L nonlinear equations. Jacobi decoding (Algorithm 1) starts from z^0 = 0 and, in each iteration, recomputes every patch z_{k,l} in parallel from the previous iterate's prefix z^{t-1}_{k,<l} and the block input z_{k+1}, stopping when the max-norm change between iterates is below tau = 0.5. It converges exactly in at most L iterations, and in practice in about 4-7 iterations for most blocks (Table A3). No retraining or architecture change is needed.

Selective Jacobi Decoding (SJD, 'Ours') keeps standard sequential decoding with a KV cache for the first inverted block (the one that starts from Gaussian noise, where dependencies are strongest) and uses Jacobi iteration for all remaining blocks. Baselines are standard sequential (KV-cached) inference and uniform Jacobi decoding (UJD, Jacobi on all blocks). Time is the average seconds per batch of 256 over 10 runs on two L40S GPUs. FID is computed against the real dataset using as many generated samples as the dataset has images. CLIP-IQA and BRISQUE are also reported. AFHQ uses the released TarFlow 256x256 checkpoint (patch size 8, L = 1024, 8 blocks).
official.claim: On AFHQ 256x256 with the released TarFlow checkpoint, selective Jacobi decoding generates a batch of 256 in 41.21 s vs. 186.28 s for sequential inference (4.5x faster) and 219.24 s for uniform Jacobi decoding, with FID 15.44 vs. 15.42 (sequential) and 15.44 (UJD).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of sequential inference, uniform Jacobi decoding, and our approach. The subscript indicates the maximum deviation in three runs.
official.metric: Wall-clock time per batch in seconds (lower is better; mean over 10 batches, two L40S GPUs) and FID (lower is better). For AFHQ no error bars are reported (single run); for CIFAR-10/100 the ± is the maximum deviation over three runs.
official.comparison: Selective Jacobi Decoding vs. standard sequential inference with KV cache and uniform Jacobi decoding (all blocks), same checkpoint, tau = 0.5, zero initialization
official.falsification_criterion: On the released AFHQ checkpoint, SJD gives less than about a 2x wall-clock speedup over a properly KV-cached sequential sampler at the same batch size and hardware, or its FID rises by more than about 0.5 over sequential sampling, or UJD turns out to be as fast as SJD.

title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures

official.background: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language-model activations into a dictionary of sparse, ideally interpretable features. Larger dictionaries reconstruct activations better, but they tend to split one concept into many narrow features and to absorb features into one another, which hurts interpretability. Standard SAEs treat the dictionary as a flat set, even though human concepts are often hierarchical (dog -> corgi, greyhound). Building that hierarchy into the architecture might improve reconstruction without giving up interpretability, at little extra compute.
official.method:
The Hierarchical SAE (H-SAE) is a top-level TopK SAE (encoder E, decoder D, LeakyReLU then TopK with k = 32, no bias, unit-normalized inputs) in which every top-level atom j has its own expert: a trainable down-projection to an s-dimensional subspace, a small low-level SAE with m_low sublatents that keeps only its top-1 sublatent, and a trainable up-projection back to the input space. An expert runs only when its top-level atom is among the active top k. The reconstruction is the sum of the top-level decoder output and the outputs of the active experts. The loss is ||x - x_hat||^2 + 0.1 ||x - Dz||^2 (top-level-only reconstruction), plus a 0.1-weighted bi-orthogonality penalty on the top-level encoder/decoder (||ED - diag(ED)||_F / (m_top^2 - m_top)) and a 0.001 L1 penalty on the pre-TopK top- and low-level latent values (the paper describes it as acting on latents outside the top k); the regularizers warm up from 0 over the first 1,000 steps. With 16 sublatents per expert the subspace dimension is 4; with 64 it is 8.

Training data is 1B residual-stream vectors from layer 20 of Gemma 2-2B, taken from the first 256 tokens of multilingual Wikipedia articles and normalized to unit norm. The baseline is a TopK SAE (Gao et al.) with the same k = 32, trained on the same data for the same 4 epochs, using a dead-latent auxiliary loss (coefficient 1/30). Both are trained with Adam, learning rate 5e-4, 1,000-step warmup, cosine decay, and batch size 32,512. Widths of 8k, 16k and 32k top-level latents are compared using 1 - explained variance (normalized L2 reconstruction error) and 1 - SAEBench CE loss score (downstream Gemma loss when the reconstruction is spliced in).
official.claim: On layer-20 Gemma 2-2B residual activations with k = 32, the H-SAE has lower 1 - explained variance than a standard TopK SAE of the same top-level width at 8k, 16k and 32k latents (e.g. 32k: about 0.29 with 16 sublatents and 0.26 with 64, vs. 0.33 for the SAE), and the 8k x 64 H-SAE (about 0.327) matches the 32k standard SAE (about 0.33).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance as measured by explained variance and the downstream CE loss of a Gemma 2-2B using SAE-reconstructed activation vectors. (a) 1 - CE Loss score across model sizes with 16 and 64 sublatents per expert (SAEBench CE loss score; lower is better). (b) 1 - Explained Variance across model sizes with 16 and 64 sublatents per expert (lower is better).
official.metric: 1 - explained variance and 1 - SAEBench CE loss score (both lower is better); single runs, no error bars or seeds reported

title: To trust or not to trust: Attention-based Trust Management for LLM Multi-Agent Systems

official.background: LLM multi-agent systems pass messages between agents, and each agent treats incoming messages as trusted context. Compromised agents, intercepted channels, or injected misinformation can therefore corrupt the whole system. Existing defenses usually target a single kind of harm, such as factual errors, and rely on prompting an LLM judge or on external verifiers. Both are slow, and prompted judges can be inconsistent. The paper asks whether the model's own attention patterns over an incoming message can be used to decide cheaply whether the message is trustworthy.
official.method:
The authors define six trust dimensions (factual accuracy, logical consistency, relevance, bias, clarity, language quality) and build a Trust Violation dataset (>20k samples). In each sample, a message M, paired with a context C (benign agent profile plus a math, code, or QA task), violates exactly one dimension or none. Factual and bias violations come from FEVER and StereoSet; the other four are generated with GPT-4o. For each message, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct computes the attention from the last token to each message token. Per layer and head, these weights are aggregated with a geometric mean over message tokens and then averaged over layers, giving a 32-dim per-head vector. For each dimension, a one-vs-rest logistic regression is trained on this vector (1,500 positives and an equal number of negatives). The six probabilities form the A-Trust score.

In the trust management system, every inter-agent message is scored and filtered if any dimension exceeds its threshold. Thresholds are chosen on the Trust Violation dataset to maximize TVR + TBR - FVR - FBR. For the factual dimension, messages in an uncertain band go to Gemini-2.0-flash with Google Search. The testbed is Camel with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct agents in Chain (4 agents), Tree (2 parents with 2 children each) and Complete (4 agents) structures, with one compromised agent or channel. The attacks are AiTM (DoS variant), AutoTransform, AutoInject and NetSafe (misinformation injection). The tasks are MMLU-physics, MBPP, StrategyQA and MATH-500. Inside the same system, the baselines are a perplexity score of M given C (Llama3.1-8B) and a prompted six-dimension trust rating (GPT-4o).
official.claim: Across all 4 datasets x 3 agent structures x 4 attacks (48 settings), A-Trust's message detection rate ranges from 77.1% to 90.4%, while the best baseline (perplexity or prompt-based) ranges from 50.5% to 67.7%. A-Trust leads the best baseline in every setting, by margins of 10.9 to 32.2 points (e.g. MMLU-Phy Chain AutoInject: 90.1 vs 57.9). Its false-detection rate on clean, correctly solved queries stays between 6.7% and 9.6%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Message Detection Rate (MDR) of different attacking methods on various datasets and agent structures, and higher rates denote better performance. Note that the clean detection rate is the proportion of messages detected as malicious on the queries correctly solved by the system, and a smaller value indicates better utility.
official.metric: Message Detection Rate (%), higher is better: the fraction of malicious messages flagged by the trust system. The 'Clean' column (lower is better) is the fraction of messages flagged on correctly solved clean queries. No error bars, seeds or sample counts are reported.
official.comparison: A-Trust (attention-based logistic-regression probes on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct) vs. perplexity-based score (Llama3.1-8B) and prompt-based six-dimension trust score (GPT-4o), all plugged into the same trust management system and multi-agent setup
official.falsification_criterion: In a reproduction, A-Trust's MDR does not exceed the better of the two baselines by at least ~10 points in most of the (dataset, structure, attack) settings, or A-Trust's clean false-detection rate rises well above ~10%.

title: Tactile MNIST: Benchmarking Active Tactile Perception
claim_source: Figure 42, page 44 (numbers in the Appendix H text, pages 44-45)

official.background: Tactile sensors such as the GelSight Mini give rich but very local information, so an agent has to choose where to touch and combine many touches over time to recognise an object (active tactile perception). The field has no standard benchmark. The paper introduces ap_gym (a Gymnasium-compatible active perception framework) and the Tactile MNIST Benchmark Suite (TMBS), which contains simulated tactile tasks, 13,580 3D-printable MNIST digit meshes, and a real dataset of 153,600 GelSight touches on 600 3D-printed digits. A CycleGAN trained on the real data renders realistic tactile images in simulation. Whether policies trained in simulation work on real tactile images is a key question for this kind of benchmark.
official.method:
The task is TactileMNIST classification with 16 touches per episode. Training uses TactileMNISTSnap, where each step the commanded sensor position snaps to the closest of 16 uniformly sampled positions. Real evaluation uses TactileMNISTRealSnap, which replays recorded real touches from the test split: the commanded position snaps to the closest of the next 16 prerecorded touches of the current digit. The agent is APPLE-SAC (a transformer actor-critic with a vision encoder), trained for 2.5M environment steps on 5 seeds per configuration.

The full sim-to-real recipe has four parts: (1) during training, simulated depth maps are rendered with the CycleGAN depth-to-RGB generator; (2) at test time, each real tactile image is passed through a CycleGAN round trip (RGB-to-depth, then depth-to-RGB); (3) during training, a background depth overlay adds the round-trip depth estimate of a random no-contact real touch to each simulated depth map; (4) contact geometry variation erodes or dilates and blurs the simulated indentation. Each ablation removes one part. 'No CycleGAN' renders with Taxim during training and evaluates on raw real images. The metric is accuracy after the last touch, averaged over evaluations between 2.0M and 2.5M steps, reported as mean ± std over the 5 seeds.
official.claim: With the full sim-to-real recipe, APPLE-SAC trained only in simulation reaches 65.7 ± 4.3% final classification accuracy on real TactileMNIST test digits. Removing the CycleGAN gives 12.4 ± 1.7%, removing the real-image round trip gives 19.0 ± 2.1%, and removing the background depth overlay gives 31.9 ± 7.7%. Simulated accuracy stays near or above 68% in every configuration, so simulated accuracy does not predict transfer.
official.claim_caption: Figure 42: Final classification accuracy of APPLE-SAC on real (TactileMNISTRealSnap, test split; solid) and simulated tactile data (TactileMNISTSnap; light) for the full sim-to-real recipe and its ablations. Each ablation removes one component from the full recipe; without the CycleGAN, we render with Taxim during training and, since the real-image round trip requires the CycleGAN, evaluate without it on the raw real images. Bars show the mean over 5 seeds of the accuracy averaged between 2.0M and 2.5M environment steps; lines show one standard deviation. The dashed line marks chance level (10%).
official.metric: Final-step classification accuracy (%) on TactileMNISTRealSnap test split (higher is better), averaged over evaluations between 2.0M and 2.5M env steps; ± is std over 5 seeds. Chance is 10%.
official.comparison: Full recipe vs. four single-component ablations (no CycleGAN / no real-image round trip / no background depth overlay / no contact geometry variation), all APPLE-SAC, same training budget; real vs. simulated accuracy for each.
official.falsification_criterion: The full recipe's real-data accuracy falls to or below the 'no real-image round trip' or 'no background depth overlay' ablation (or stays within about one std of either), or the full recipe does not clearly beat chance (10%) on the real test split.
