title: QUTCC: Quantile Uncertainty Training and Conformal Calibration for Imaging Inverse Problems
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (mean lengths and risks: Table 6, page 18)

official.background: Deep networks used for image reconstruction (denoising, accelerated MRI, phase microscopy) can produce plausible-looking but wrong outputs, so users want pixel-wise error bars with a statistical guarantee. Conformal methods for image-to-image regression, such as Im2Im-UQ (RCPS calibration) and K-RCPS, take heuristic quantile-regression bounds and widen them on a held-out calibration set until a target fraction of ground-truth pixels falls inside. They do this with one global scale factor λ, or K factors over a fixed pixel partition, so they cannot adapt the widening to the content of each image, and the resulting intervals are wider than they need to be.
official.method:
QUTCC trains a single attention U-Net f_θ(y, q) with a sinusoidal quantile embedding (as in diffusion time embeddings), fed to every residual block. At each training step q ~ U(0,1) is sampled per image and used both as the conditioning input and as the level of the pinball loss, so the network learns the full conditional quantile function. The point estimate is f_θ(y, 0.5).

Calibration does not scale the bounds. It binary-searches the two conditioning inputs (q_lo, q_hi) on the calibration set so that the lower-bound and upper-bound pixel miscoverage rates are each ≤ α/2 (with a finite-sample correction), giving the interval [f_θ(y, q̂_lo), f_θ(y, q̂_hi)]. This gives a nonlinear, spatially varying effective scaling. Baselines: Im2Im (upgraded to the same deep backbone, one λ), Im2Im-Asymm (two λs, one per bound), K-RCPS (k = 2, Otsu partition), all calibrated to α = 0.1. For Poisson denoising, FMD ground-truth images (180 train / 40 calibration / 20 held out, which the paper calls validation) are scaled by λ ~ U(50, 100), Poisson-sampled and clamped to [0, 1]. The metric is calibrated interval length, stratified by ground-truth pixel intensity.
official.claim: On synthetic Poisson denoising of FMD images calibrated to α = 0.1, QUTCC's interval length for bright pixels (intensity 0.80–1.00) is 0.187 ± 0.034, versus 0.225 ± 0.028 for K-RCPS and 0.294 ± 0.042 for Im2Im-Asymm (0.60–0.80 bin: 0.158 vs. 0.207 and 0.238), with mean interval length 0.040 vs. 0.046–0.047 (Table 6).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Uncertainty interval length stratified by pixel intensity. Blue entries denote the smallest uncertainty intervals within each bin, while bold black entries indicate the second smallest.
official.metric: Calibrated uncertainty-interval length (upper minus lower bound, in normalized intensity units), lower is better, at target total pixel miscoverage α = 0.1. The paper does not define ± for Tables 1 and 6; it appears to be the spread over test pixels/images within the bin, not over seeds. No seed repeats are reported.
official.comparison: QUTCC vs. the other conformal methods on the same deep attention U-Net backbone: Im2Im (single λ), Im2Im-Asymm (two λ), K-RCPS (k = 2). MC-Dropout and Deep Ensembles are also listed but are not the central comparison.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same backbone, data split and α = 0.1, QUTCC's calibrated interval length in the 0.60–1.00 intensity bins on Poisson denoising is not smaller than K-RCPS's by more than the reported per-bin spread, or QUTCC only achieves the shorter intervals while its test risk exceeds 0.1, or the gap disappears when the baselines are calibrated so their realized risk is close to 0.1.

title: Understanding the Interplay between Memorization and Learning in Large Language Models
claim_source: Figure 61, page 64 (appendix J.1); summary version for L2 in Figure 9, page 10

official.background: Memorization in LLMs is usually measured by how well a model recalls a training string, which mixes up rote memorization with recall that comes from having learned the language (for example, counting to 1000). The paper proposes 'contextual memorization': a training string counts as memorized only once its training loss falls below the lowest loss it would reach if it were left out of training. It studies this measure in a controlled setting where models are fine-tuned on strings sampled from probabilistic context-free grammars, so string frequencies and the language entropy are known exactly. It uses the measure to motivate a training scheme that reduces memorization without hurting learning.
official.method:
Mistral-7B is fine-tuned for 50 epochs (batch size 8, learning rate 5e-6, linear schedule with 0.05 warm-up) on strings sampled from a formal language (L2, L4 or L9, defined in Appendix F) and evaluated on 1024 held-out test strings from the same language. The 'optimal learning epoch' is the epoch with the lowest mean test cross-entropy loss, and all metrics are read at that epoch. Contextual memorization of a training string s is (min-over-epochs loss of s when s is not trained on − training loss of s) / that minimum, clipped at 0. The leave-one-out loss is approximated by the lowest test loss of test strings in the same frequency group. 'Weighted memorization' is the mean of this score over training strings.

Memorization-aware training (MAT): at each epoch, compute x = the fraction of test strings whose loss went up since the previous epoch, then drop the x fraction of training strings with the lowest training loss for the next epoch. Dropped strings come back if their loss rises again. Baselines are base training (a fixed training set every epoch) and deduplication (each distinct string kept once). MAT* is a more expensive variant that drops strings based on contextual loss. Results are averaged over multiple runs (three runs according to Section 3).
official.claim: When Mistral-7B is fine-tuned on formal language L2, MAT gives lower weighted contextual memorization at the optimal-learning epoch than base training (about 0.02 vs. 0.21) and lower test-loss std (about 0.090 vs. 0.094), with mean test loss no worse (about 0.177 vs. 0.188). MAT's memorization is also below base training on L4 with Mistral-7B (about 0.043 vs. 0.081) and on L9, where the per-seed figures show Pythia-1B was used (about 0.055 vs. 0.14). On every language MAT's memorization is also below deduplication's (L2: about 0.02 vs. 0.085).
official.claim_caption: Figure 61: Summary results on learning, memorization, and training cost efficiency on different formal languages, averaged across multiple runs. Lower values are better in all dimensions.
official.metric: Weighted contextual memorization at the optimal-learning epoch (lower is better). Also reported: std and mean of test cross-entropy loss over 1024 test strings at that epoch (lower is better), and cumulative number of training strings. Points are averages over runs; no error bars or ± values are reported.
official.comparison: MAT vs. base training and deduplication (and MAT*), same model, data and hyperparameters, on languages L2, L4 and L9
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running base training and MAT on L2 with the released code and several seeds, MAT's weighted contextual memorization at the optimal epoch is not clearly lower than base training's (for example, within seed variability, or not at least halved), or MAT's mean test loss is clearly higher than base training's.

title: MaPPO: Maximum a Posteriori Preference Optimization with Prior Knowledge

official.background: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aligns an LLM with preference pairs by maximizing the likelihood that the chosen response beats the rejected one under a Bradley-Terry model. The loss depends only on the gap between the two responses. So DPO pushes them apart even when both are good (near-ties), and it is known to lower the absolute likelihood of both the chosen and the rejected response (the 'squeezing effect'). When a reward model is used to build the pairs, DPO also throws away the reward scores and keeps only which response won.
official.method:
MaPPO turns the DPO maximum-likelihood objective into a maximum a posteriori objective by using the reward model's scores as a prior. In practice, the implicit reward of the rejected response is scaled by the reward gap: L = -log σ(β log[πθ(yw|x)/πref(yw|x)] - Δr · β log[πθ(yl|x)/πref(yl|x)]), with Δr = rw - rl ∈ [0, 1]. Rewards come from the BT reward model sfairXC/FsfairX-LLaMA3-RM-v0.1, mapped into [0, 1] with a logistic function. When Δr = 1 the loss is exactly DPO. MaPPO adds no hyperparameters.

Pairs are built from the UltraFeedback prompt set (RLHFlow/UltraFeedback-preference-standard). In the offline setting, the initial instruct model generates n = 8 responses per prompt at temperature 1.0, and the best and worst of the 8 under the reward model become yw and yl. DPO and DPO+MaPPO are trained on the same data with the same hyperparameters: global batch 128, learning rate 5e-7, 100 warmup steps, weight decay 0.01, AdamW, β = 0.1, bf16. Evaluation uses AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled win rate and Arena-Hard v0.1 win rate, both judged by GPT-4 Turbo (1106-preview), plus MT-Bench.
official.claim: With offline training on UltraFeedback prompts and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, DPO+MaPPO reaches 26.68 AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate and 35.1 Arena-Hard win rate, against 20.16 and 29.2 for DPO trained the same way. That is gains of +6.52 and +5.9, well above the reported evaluation error (AlpacaEval SE ≈1.0-1.7, Arena-Hard CI ≈±1.5).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Main evaluation results on three standard benchmarks. ↑ indicates the higher the better.
official.metric: AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled win rate (%) and Arena-Hard v0.1 win rate (%), both judged by GPT-4 Turbo, higher is better. The table has no per-cell error bars. The text reports AlpacaEval standard errors of 1.02-1.67 across model sizes and Arena-Hard 95% CIs of about ±1.5; these are judge-sampling errors, not variance across training seeds. MT-Bench is the average of 3 judge scores.
official.comparison: Offline DPO+MaPPO vs. offline DPO on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, with the same preference data, reward model and hyperparameters.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same pipeline on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, DPO+MaPPO beats DPO by less than about 2 points (≈ the reported SE) on AlpacaEval 2.0 LC, or by less than about 1.5 points (≈ the reported CI) on Arena-Hard, or DPO comes out ahead.

title: DINOv3
claim_source: Table 14, page 30 (Section 7, DINOv3 family); the 7B-scale counterpart is Table 3, page 19

official.background: Self-supervised vision foundation models such as DINOv2 are used as frozen, general-purpose image encoders, and the quality of their per-patch (dense) features determines how well they serve segmentation, depth estimation and correspondence without fine-tuning. Long, large-scale self-supervised training is known to improve global (image-level) features while dense feature maps degrade. DINOv3 scales data and model size (a 7B ViT teacher) and adds Gram anchoring to stop that degradation, then distills the 7B teacher into a family of smaller ViTs (S, S+, B, L, H+) and ConvNeXts that are released for public use.
official.method:
DINOv3 7B is trained with the DINO/iBOT self-distillation objectives on a curated 1.7B-image web dataset, followed by a Gram anchoring phase that regularizes the Gram matrix of patch features toward that of an earlier teacher checkpoint, and a high-resolution adaptation phase. Smaller ViTs (patch size 16) are distilled from the frozen 7B teacher. The claim concerns the released distilled ViT-L/16 (300M parameters) compared with DINOv2 ViT-L/14 with registers (Table 14 compares families at matched size).

Dense evaluation (Sec. 6.1.2, App. D.1-D.2): the backbone is frozen; a linear layer is trained on the last-layer patch features (after the backbone's layer norm), preceded by a trained batch-norm layer. Segmentation reports mIoU on ADE20k; depth reports RMSE on NYUv2. For every backbone the authors sweep AdamW learning rate in {1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3} and weight decay in {1e-4, 1e-3}. Input resolution is matched in number of patch tokens across patch sizes (for segmentation in Table 3: 1024 tokens, i.e. 448x448 for patch 14 and 512x512 for patch 16).
official.claim: With frozen backbones and a linear probe on patch features, the distilled DINOv3 ViT-L/16 reaches 54.9 mIoU on ADE20k and 0.352 RMSE on NYUv2 depth, versus 48.8 mIoU and 0.394 RMSE for DINOv2 ViT-L/14 (with registers) at a matched number of patch tokens; the same ordering holds at ViT-B (51.8 vs. 48.4 mIoU, 0.373 vs. 0.416 RMSE).
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Comparison of our family of models against open-source alternatives of comparable size. We showcase our ViT-{S, S+, B, L, H+} models on a representative set of global and dense benchmarks: classification (IN-ReAL, IN-R, ObjectNet), retrieval (Oxford-H), segmentation (ADE20k), depth (NYU), tracking (DAVIS at 960px), and keypoint matching (NAVI, SPair). We match the number of patch tokens for a fair comparison across models of different patch size.

title: When Language Overrules: Revealing Text Dominance in Multimodal Large Language Models

official.background: Multimodal LLMs take text together with images, video, audio, time series or graphs, but are often observed to lean on the text prompt and underuse the other input. The paper measures this 'text dominance' directly from attention: during generation, how much attention per input token goes to text tokens versus non-text tokens. It argues the imbalance is largely caused by attention dilution, because non-text inputs are encoded as many redundant tokens, and that removing redundant non-text tokens should rebalance attention.
official.method:
Two metrics are computed from the attention of generated output tokens to input tokens, aggregated over the generation of N output tokens and normalised so that text attention A_T plus non-text attention A_O equals 1. The Modality Dominance Index is MDI = (A_T/|T|) / (A_O/|O|), the ratio of average per-token attention to text versus non-text tokens (MDI > 1 means text dominance, 1 means balance). The Attention Efficiency Index is AEI_T = (A_T/(A_T+A_O)) / (|T|/(|T|+|O|)), the text attention share divided by the text token share. Both are reported for 'Early', 'Middle' and 'Late' layers, i.e. aggregated over the first two, middle two and last two LLM layers.

For the mitigation experiment, LLaVA-1.5-7B is run on MMMU-Pro with and without FasterVLM-style [CLS]-guided visual token pruning: each visual token's importance is the attention from the frozen vision encoder's [CLS] token, and only the top N(1 - r) visual tokens are kept before they enter the LLM, for reduction rates r = 75%, 90% and 95%. No training is involved; MDI and AEI are recomputed on the pruned inputs.
official.claim: On MMMU-Pro, pruning 90% of LLaVA-1.5-7B's visual tokens with [CLS]-guided FasterVLM reduces late-layer MDI from 17.37 to 1.84 and middle-layer MDI from 10.23 to 1.10 (0.86 at 95% pruning), bringing text/image per-token attention close to balance (MDI = 1).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Effect of token-reduction ratio on Modality Dominance Index (MDI) and Attention Efficiency Index (AEI). Statistics are reported for the first two layers (Early), the middle two layers (Middle), and the final two layers (Late).
official.metric: Modality Dominance Index (closer to 1 = more balanced; > 1 = text dominance) and text Attention Efficiency Index, averaged over the first/middle/last two layers. No ± reported: no seeds, error bars or number of evaluated samples given.
official.comparison: LLaVA-1.5-7B with all visual tokens (0% reduction) vs. the same model with FasterVLM [CLS]-guided pruning at 75%, 90% and 95% reduction, same benchmark
official.falsification_criterion: Recomputing MDI as defined in Eq. 1 on MMMU-Pro, LLaVA-1.5-7B's late-layer MDI at 90% visual-token pruning stays far from 1 (e.g. above ~5) or is not substantially below the unpruned value, or the unpruned late-layer MDI is not strongly text-dominant (e.g. near 1).

title: CrafterDojo: A Suite of Foundation Models for Building Open-Ended Embodied Agents in Crafter

official.background: Minecraft is the main testbed for open-ended embodied agents because foundation models trained on internet-scale data exist for it: VPT (behavior prior), MineCLIP (video-language grounding) and Steve-1 (instruction following). Minecraft is slow, crash-prone and hard to modify. Crafter is a lightweight 2D, pure-Python game with similar mechanics (procedural maps, resource collection, crafting, survival), but it has no comparable foundation models, so Crafter research has mostly used reinforcement learning from scratch on its 22 fixed achievements. CrafterDojo builds Crafter versions of the three Minecraft models from synthetic data so that hierarchical, instruction-following agents can be prototyped cheaply.
official.method:
A PPO-RNN expert trained for 10B steps in Craftax-Classic (symbolic) generates CrafterPlay, 20,000 pixel-observation episodes. C-VPT (ResNet + TransformerXL + policy head, VPT architecture) is behavior-cloned on CrafterPlay. A rule-based captioner (15 rules, 61 templates, each expanded with 40 LLM paraphrases) labels 6-frame clips to form CrafterCaption, on which C-CLIP (MineCLIP-style video/text encoders initialized from CLIP) is trained contrastively. C-Steve-1 fine-tunes C-VPT with LoRA as a goal-conditioned policy (goal embedding added after the TransformerXL) using event-based packed hindsight relabeling with C-CLIP video embeddings as goals, plus a CVAE prior mapping C-CLIP text embeddings to goal embeddings. At inference it uses classifier-free guidance (lambda = 1.5).

For long-horizon tasks, PPO-Steve is a hierarchical agent: a PPO high-level planner chooses one of the 61 template captions every 10 steps and passes it to frozen C-Steve-1 as the low-level controller. Baselines are PPO-RNN trained from scratch on pixels, C-VPT-RL (C-VPT base fine-tuned with PPO + LoRA r = 16, alpha = 16, with a 0.1-weighted KL to the pretrained policy), and C-Steve-1 prompted with a single instruction for the whole task (no training, shown as a dashed line). Tasks have sparse rewards given only for completing sub-tasks in the right order, with a 1,000-step episode limit: T1 eat plant (simplified env without health decay or mobs), T2 place plant then place table, T3 make wood pickaxe then obtain sapling, and T4 obtain coal, craft wood pickaxe, then obtain stone. Each agent is trained for 1M environment steps with 3 seeds.
official.claim: On the long-horizon Crafter task T4 (obtain coal -> make wood pickaxe -> obtain stone), after 1M environment steps the hierarchical PPO-Steve agent (PPO planner over C-Steve-1) reaches a success rate of about 0.6, compared with about 0.17 for PPO fine-tuning of C-VPT (C-VPT-RL), about 0 for PPO-RNN from scratch, and 0.33 for single-instruction C-Steve-1. On T3, PPO-Steve reaches about 0.96 vs. about 0.77 for C-VPT-RL.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Training performance of four models on four long-horizon tasks. The first task requires the agents to obtain sapling, place plant, and then eat plant. The second task requires the agents to place plant and then place table. The third task requires the agents to make wood pickaxe and then obtain sapling. The last task requires the agents to obtain coal, craft wood pickaxe, and then obtain stone. For all tasks, the agents receive a reward for completing the given tasks in the right order. We report training performance with success rates and standard deviations among three seeds for each agent.
official.metric: Episode success rate during training (higher is better) vs. environment steps; lines are means over 3 seeds and shaded bands are standard deviations across seeds. C-Steve-1 single-instruction is a fixed evaluation shown as a dashed line. Values are read off the plot and approximate.

official.falsification_criterion: Retraining PPO-Steve and C-VPT-RL on T4 for 1M environment steps with 3 seeds, PPO-Steve's final success rate is not clearly above C-VPT-RL's (e.g. the gap is under ~0.2 or the seed bands overlap), or PPO-Steve does not beat single-instruction C-Steve-1 on T4.

title: Data Auctions for Retrieval Augmented Generation

official.background: Data owners such as news publishers increasingly license content to generative-AI platforms for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The paper models a seller who auctions a database of points (documents or images) to several AI platforms, each data point going to at most one buyer. A buyer's value for a dataset is its private scalar type θ_i times a weighted coverage function: a database point j counts as covered if some allocated point lies within radius r_ij of it in embedding space. Maximizing total welfare under exclusive allocation is NP-hard even with two bidders, and standard combinatorial-auction allocators (greedy, continuous greedy) are not monotone, so they are not incentive compatible.
official.method:
LPR solves an LP relaxation with fractional allocation X̄_ij (each point's allocations sum to at most 1) and coverage C̄_ij ≤ Σ_{j' within r_ij of j} X̄_ij', then assigns each point independently to bidder i with probability X̄_ij, giving a (1 − 1/e) approximation. LPRMono adds 'data burning': bidder i receives its rounded dataset only with probability ρ_i = (1 − 1/e)·C̄_i / E[C_i] (otherwise nothing), so its expected coverage is exactly (1 − 1/e)·C̄_i, which is monotone in its bid and allows Myerson-style truthful payments. The baseline GREEDY loops over data points and gives each point to the bidder with the largest marginal value gain.

For the runtime experiment the database is ResNet embeddings of CIFAR-10 training images (d = 2048, public embeddings from MatthewWilletts), subsampled to n ∈ {1000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000}, with m = 3 buyers. Types θ_i are drawn uniformly from {0, 0.1, ..., 0.9}; radii r_ij = α_i·R_c with α_i ~ U[0, 1] and R_c the mean pairwise Euclidean distance among 100 random points of point j's class; weights w_ij are constant within a class, drawn U[0, 1] and normalized to sum to 1 per buyer. Each setting is repeated on 50 random instances and wall-clock runtime is recorded.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 embedding instances with m = 3 buyers, LPRMono runs much faster than GREEDY at every database size tested: log(runtime in seconds) is about −0.7 vs. 1.3 at n = 1000, 1.9 vs. 4.9 at n = 5000, and 4.65 vs. 8.2 at n = 20000, with non-overlapping 95% confidence bands (roughly a 20–35x speedup if the log is natural).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Runtime in seconds of each algorithm.
official.metric: log(runtime in seconds), lower is better; curves are means over 50 random instances with 95% confidence bands; values are read off the plot and approximate; the log base is not stated
official.comparison: LPRMono (LP solve + randomized rounding + data burning) vs. GREEDY allocation, same CIFAR-10 instances, varying n
official.falsification_criterion: With reasonable implementations of both algorithms on the same CIFAR-10 instances (m = 3, n = 5000–20000), GREEDY is not clearly slower than LPRMono (e.g. less than ~5x slower, or the gap shrinks or reverses as n grows).

title: Statistical Complexity of Soft Bellman Residual Minimization
claim_source: Table 6, page 28 (Appendix E); also Figure 1, page 10

official.background: Offline RL and inverse RL fit value functions or rewards from a fixed batch of logged transitions. Bellman residual minimization (BRM) fits a Q-function by minimizing the mean-squared Bellman error (MSBE). With entropy regularization ('soft' BRM) and a bi-conjugate reformulation, BRM becomes a min-max problem. Prior work showed that stochastic gradient descent-ascent (SGDA) converges globally on this problem under Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) geometry. How many offline samples SGDA needs was still open: earlier BRM sample-complexity results either assume an exact (oracle) solver or give O(n^-1/2) rates.
official.method:
Soft BRM is written as min over Q_w, max over an auxiliary function zeta_v, of the empirical average of a per-sample saddle loss f(w, v; s, a, s') = (TD loss of Q_w) - beta^2 (V_Q(s') - zeta_v(s, a))^2 (Eq. 3-5). It is solved by minibatch SGDA (Algorithm 1): a descent step on w and an ascent step on v with dual stepsize ratio kappa_v. Under PL, quadratic-growth and smoothness conditions, the paper proves O(1/n) on-average primal argument stability (Theorem 2) and an O(1/n + 1/T) excess population risk / excess MSBE for the SGDA output (Theorem 5).

Numerical check (Section 4, Appendix E): a soft MDP with |S| = 5, |A| = 3, beta = 0.9, eta = 1, rewards ~ Unif[0,1], P(.|s,a) = 1/2 delta_s + 1/2 Dirichlet(1), and a uniform behavior policy. Q_w (one-hot state -> |A| outputs) and zeta_v (one-hot state-action -> scalar) are two-layer softplus networks of width H in {8, 16, 32} with NTK parameterization. SGDA uses B = 32, eta_t = 400/(2000 + t), kappa_v = 2 and T = 40,000. The data are n in {100, ..., 6400} transitions, either i.i.d. from the stationary distribution mu or from a single stationary trajectory. The excess population MSBE of the output is computed exactly from P; since Q* is representable, it equals the excess risk. Each (n, H) setting uses 50 repetitions, and the slope is a least-squares fit of log(mean) on log n over n >= 200, with a 95% bootstrap interval over repetitions.
official.claim: On the 5-state, 3-action soft MDP with i.i.d. data and width-16 networks, the excess population MSBE of the SGDA output decays as n^-1: the fitted log-log slope over n = 200..6400 is -1.00 (95% bootstrap interval [-1.05, -0.95]), n x excess MSBE stays between 0.385 and 0.443, and every width and data regime has a slope interval that excludes -1/2.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: n times the excess population MSBE of the SGDA output (mean ± standard error), and of the exact empirical minimizer on the datasets of the i.i.d. H = 16 runs.
official.metric: n x excess population MSBE (mean +/- standard error over 50 repetitions) and the fitted slope of log(excess MSBE) vs log n over n >= 200, with a 95% bootstrap interval over repetitions
official.comparison: Observed decay rate of the SGDA output's excess MSBE vs the theorem's predicted n^-1 rate and the n^-1/2 rate of prior bounds, across widths H = 8/16/32, i.i.d. vs single-trajectory data, and against the exact empirical minimizer
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the stated setup gives a fitted slope (n >= 200) whose 95% bootstrap interval excludes -1 or includes -1/2 for H = 16 i.i.d. data, or n x excess MSBE grows steadily with n (for example, a clear upward trend from 0.44 at n = 200 to well above 1 at n = 6400).

title: The Algorithm Is Not the Behavior: Learned Priors Override Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network
claim_source: Figure 6 (right), page 8; exact values in Section 3.3 and Appendix O, page 84

official.background: Mechanistic interpretability work has found learned algorithms inside networks, including look-ahead in Leela Chess Zero's policy network (Jenner et al., 2024). Those studies show the algorithms exist and matter when the model succeeds. This paper asks whether a learned algorithm actually determines the output. It reports 'forgotten puzzles': tactical chess puzzles where intermediate layers of Leela's policy network pick the correct move but the final layer overrides it with a safer quiet move. The authors argue that learned safety priors cause the override, not a failure of look-ahead.
official.method:
The network is Leela Chess Zero T82-768x15x24h (15-layer Post-LN encoder transformer, one token per square), used as a policy network without search. Puzzles are the 10,000-puzzle Lichess set from Ruoss et al. (2024); a puzzle counts as solved if argmax move selection reproduces all of the player's principal-variation moves or delivers checkmate. The unsteered full model solves 88.6%.

Concepts are Stockfish 8 handcrafted evaluation terms. For a concept c, the concept preference of the full model is Delta c_L = sum over legal moves of pi(m) * (c(s') - c(s)). The steering vector for layer l is the gradient of Delta c_L with respect to the residual stream after layer l, averaged over 10,000 CCRL positions and all 64 squares and normalized to unit length. It is added to every square as h' = h + alpha * E[||h||] * v_hat, with alpha in {+-0.25, ..., +-1.5}. Strength is chosen per concept and layer on a random half of the puzzles and the solve rate is measured on the other half, repeated over 200 random splits. The control is 50 isotropic Gaussian unit vectors evaluated with the same protocol.
official.claim: Steering Leela's residual stream after layer 13 against the 'opponent threats' safety concept raises the held-out puzzle solve rate to 92.43 ± 0.25%, vs. 88.6% unsteered and about 89% for random directions under the same protocol; the fixed setting (alpha = -0.5) recovers 71.7% of the 8,595 held-out forgotten puzzles.
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Safety-related concept analysis across layers. Left: Mean concept preference Delta c_l for four safety-related concepts, measured in centipawns with 95% CI. Late layers shift from aggressive toward conservative concept preferences. Right: Held-out solve rate when steering with each concept's gradient, with the strength alpha in {±0.25, ±0.5, ..., ±1.5} selected per layer on half of the puzzles and evaluated on the other half. Lines show the mean and shaded areas one standard deviation across 200 random splits. Steering against the late-layer safety preferences substantially improves solve rates, peaking at layer 13. The gray line shows the mean of 50 random unit vectors under the same protocol, with 95% CI across vectors, while the dashed line indicates the unsteered baseline.
official.metric: Held-out puzzle solve rate (%) on the 10,000 Lichess puzzles (full principal variation correct), higher is better; ± is std over 200 random half/half cross-validation splits, not over seeds. Random baseline: mean of 50 random unit vectors, 95% CI across vectors.

title: Prompts to Proxies: Emulating Human Preferences via a Compact LLM Ensemble
claim_source: Table 3 (Appendix D.1), page 34; means also in Table 1, page 8

official.background: LLMs are increasingly used as stand-ins for human survey respondents, but off-the-shelf models collapse toward central tendencies, and demographic-conditioning approaches need individual profiles and still do not reliably match population response distributions. The paper asks whether aggregate survey response distributions of a target population can be reconstructed from public survey data alone, with no individual demographic data and no fine-tuning, by treating a set of prompted LLM 'proxy agents' as a basis and learning weights over them.
official.method:
Each survey's questions are split 7:1.5:1.5 into train/validation/test. Stage 1 (active endowment generation) builds a pool of up to 300 proxy agents with Gemini-2.0-flash: profiles ('endowments') are generated from an attribute bank organized into modes, plus survey- and question-specific attributes extracted by an LLM; over 5 update steps, modes are sampled via softmax over a variability score based on normalized response entropy on training questions, with question patching for the 3 lowest-entropy questions (75% of budget) and mixed modes triggered at t=2. Stage 1 never sees human ground truth.

Stage 2 fits constrained lasso weights over agents' one-hot answers to match ground-truth option proportions on train+validation questions (per-question mass constraint relaxed to a quadratic penalty, lambda=100; alpha by CV). Baselines use the same 300-agent budget and the identical Stage 2: Vanilla (LLM asked to generate diverse profiles conditioned on the survey topic) and PERSONA (300 profiles randomly sampled from the PERSONA census-derived dataset). Metric is option-level MSE on held-out test questions, over 14 Pew American Trends Panel waves from OpinionsQA.
official.claim: On 14 ATP waves with a 300-agent budget and identical lasso aggregation, P2P's held-out test MSE averages 0.014 versus 0.025 for Vanilla and 0.029 for PERSONA, and is lower than both baselines on every wave (e.g. W42: 0.011 ± 0.000 vs. 0.029 ± 0.005 and 0.036 ± 0.001; W82: 0.008 ± 0.002 vs. 0.021 ± 0.004 and 0.021 ± 0.002).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Full distribution metrics comparison across 14 ATP waves. MSE measures mean squared error of predicted response probabilities. 1-JSD (1 minus Jensen-Shannon Divergence) measures distributional similarity (higher is better). EMD (Earth Mover's Distance) measures distributional distance (lower is better). Each cell reports the mean over three runs, with the sample SD in parentheses below.
official.metric: Test MSE of option-level response proportions on held-out questions (lower is better); mean over 3 runs with sample SD in parentheses. 1-JSD (higher better) and EMD (lower better) also reported.

title: Nonconvex Decentralized Stochastic Bilevel Optimization under Heavy-Tailed Noise

official.background: Bilevel optimization (an outer problem whose objective depends on the solution of an inner problem) underlies hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning and model pruning. Decentralized versions let workers holding local data solve it by peer-to-peer communication. Existing decentralized bilevel methods assume a strongly convex inner problem and stochastic gradients with finite variance, but gradients in deep learning, for example on language data, are often heavy-tailed. The usual fix is gradient clipping, whose threshold is hard to tune.
official.method:
The bilevel problem with a nonconvex (PL) inner objective is rewritten via a penalty as a minimax problem min_{x,y} max_z f(x,y) + (1/delta)(g(x,y) - g(x,z)). D-NSVRGDA (Algorithm 1) has each worker keep STORM-style variance-reduced estimates of the gradients with respect to x, y and z, combine them with gradient tracking over the communication graph, and update each variable with a normalized step (step size times estimate / its norm), followed by neighbor averaging. No clipping is used.

Test problem (Synthetic Dataset I): hyperparameter optimization for a 2-layer MLP (100 -> 20 -> 1) for binary classification, where the inner problem fits the weights with per-unit exponentiated L2 penalties and the outer problem tunes the penalty hyperparameters x on validation loss. Data: X in R^{10000x100} and w standard Gaussian, labels y = sgn(Xw + alpha*xi) with Cauchy noise xi, alpha in {0.2, 0.1, 0.05}; equal-size validation and test sets. Eight workers on a line graph, batch 32 per worker, learning rate 0.001, momentum coefficient 0.9 and penalty parameter 0.3 for all methods. The key baseline D-SVRGDA is the same algorithm with the normalization step removed; D-SVRGDA-Clip adds clipping with thresholds 0.2-0.8; D-F2BSA variants are decentralized versions of a single-machine first-order bilevel method.
official.claim: On Synthetic Dataset I with Cauchy label noise, after 15,000 iterations D-NSVRGDA reaches an upper-level loss of about 0.02-0.04 for all three noise levels (alpha = 0.2, 0.1, 0.05), roughly a third of the un-normalized ablation D-SVRGDA (about 0.09-0.12) and below every clipped variant and D-F2BSA baseline (best about 0.10-0.14); final test accuracies are nearly identical (about 0.90-0.92).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: The upper-level loss function value and test accuracy on different datasets that are generated with different levels of heavy-tailed noise.
official.metric: upper-level (validation) loss vs. iteration, lower is better; test accuracy vs. iteration; single run per curve, no error bars
official.comparison: D-NSVRGDA vs. D-SVRGDA (same algorithm without normalization), D-SVRGDA-Clip (tau = 0.8, 0.6, 0.5, 0.2), D-F2BSA-VR and D-F2BSA-1/5/10, all with the same data, graph, batch size and learning rate
official.falsification_criterion: Over several seeds, D-NSVRGDA's upper-level loss at 15,000 iterations is not clearly below D-SVRGDA's (e.g. the gap is within seed-to-seed spread) at any of the three noise levels.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Just Classification and a Few Regressions

official.background: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) tries to recover a reward function from observed behaviour. In the maximum-entropy (Gumbel-shock dynamic discrete choice) model, the behaviour policy identifies the reward only up to potential-based shaping, so recovering a specific reward requires a normalization. DeepPQR (Geng et al., 2020) does this with an anchor action whose reward is known (e.g. r(s, a†) = 0). It estimates an anchor value function using only the transitions where the anchor action was taken, which becomes unreliable when that action is rare or there are many actions.
official.method:
GenPQR handles any statewise affine normalization Σ_a µ(a|s) r(s,a) = g(s). Step 1 estimates the behaviour policy and sets û = log π̂(a|s) (any classifier, behaviour cloning, or AIRL). Step 2 solves the linear Bellman equation Q(s,a) = û(s,a) − g(s) + γ E_{s'~P, a'~µ}[Q(s',a')] by fitted Q-evaluation over all observed transitions (s, a, s'). The reward is then r̂(s,a) = Q̂(s,a) − Σ_a' µ(a'|s) Q̂(s,a') + g(s). With an anchor action, µ(a|s) = 1{a = a†}, this targets the same reward as DeepPQR. The difference is that DeepPQR fits the anchor value W(s) only on anchor-action transitions, then reconstructs Q from log-policy ratios and fits a reward network.

Experiment (Section 6, Appendix C): an adaptation of DeepPQR's synthetic environment with 5-dim continuous states, |A| = 5, γ = 0.9, deterministic action-specific state shifts with uniform reset at the boundary, and trajectories of length 10. The behaviour policy comes from a soft-Q planner (α = 1). The normalization is r(s, a† = 0) = 0, and anchor frequency is controlled by an anchor-logit shift. Both methods share the same AIRL policy estimate (two-layer (64, 64) ReLU MLPs, 60 BC warm-start epochs, 80 adversarial updates) and neural FQE (dueling MLP (128, 128), Adam 5e-3, 8 Bellman iterations, 4 epochs each). Estimated probabilities are clipped to [0.01, 0.99]. Settings are (training trajectories, anchor shift) = (200, −1.0), (1000, −1.0) and (2500, 0.0), with 300 test trajectories and 100 seeds each. Metrics are reward MSE and correlation against the true normalized reward.
official.claim: With the same AIRL policy estimate and neural FQE, GenPQR recovers the anchor-normalized reward with much lower MSE than DeepPQR when the anchor action is rare (16% of transitions): 0.91 ± 0.11 vs. 2.60 ± 0.15 with 200 training trajectories, and 0.76 ± 0.08 vs. 1.48 ± 0.10 with 1000. With a common anchor (2500 trajectories, 25%) the gap shrinks to 0.60 ± 0.06 vs. 0.70 ± 0.07.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Matched DeepPQR vs. GenPQR comparison. Both use the same AIRL policy estimate and neural FQE. Entries are mean ± 95% CI over 100 seeds. Anchor count is the number of anchor-action transitions used by DeepPQR's anchor-Q step.
official.metric: Reward mean squared error against the ground-truth normalized reward (lower is better); also reward correlation (higher is better). ± is the half-width of a normal-approximation 95% confidence interval over 100 seeds.
official.comparison: GenPQR vs. DeepPQR, both using the same AIRL behaviour-policy estimate and neural FQE, in three (trajectory count, anchor frequency) regimes
official.falsification_criterion: In the rare-anchor regimes (200 or 1000 trajectories, anchor logit shift −1.0), GenPQR's mean reward MSE is not clearly below DeepPQR's: the 95% CIs overlap, or the ratio DeepPQR/GenPQR is below about 1.5 at 200 trajectories.

title: Enabling approximate joint sampling in diffusion LMs
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (all K from 1 to 8 in Table 4, Appendix C.1, page 12)

official.background: Masked diffusion language models such as Dream-7B and LLaDA-7B generate text by repeatedly unmasking tokens. Each forward pass gives only per-position marginal distributions, so unmasking several tokens in one pass samples them independently from the product of their marginals rather than from the joint distribution the model implies. Sampling exactly from that joint requires one token per forward pass, which is slow, and quality drops sharply as more tokens are unmasked per step. The paper asks whether a cheap add-on can approximate joint sampling of several tokens per full-model forward pass.
official.method:
ADJUST is a single transformer decoder layer (about 200M parameters, same layer architecture as the base model) placed on top of a frozen base diffusion LM. In each denoising step the base model runs once to give hidden states h0 = f(x); the first token is sampled from the base model's marginals at the position chosen by the base model's unmasking rule (lowest entropy for Dream). Then, for each further token, ADJUST takes the previous hidden states h and the updated token string (embedded with the frozen base token embeddings, concatenated with h, down-projected, passed through the decoder layer) and outputs new hidden states; the frozen LM head turns them into logits used to choose and sample the next position. So K tokens per step cost one base forward pass plus K-1 ADJUST passes. Naive parallel sampling instead samples all K tokens from the base marginals of h0.

Training: the base model generates trajectories with one token per step (K = 1, exact joint sampling); for Dream-7B-Base, 100K unconditional samples from a beginning-of-sentence prompt, length 128, temperature 1.0. From partially masked strings x along these trajectories and the next K positions the base model unmasked, ADJUST is unrolled with teacher-forced tokens and trained to minimise the summed per-position KL divergence between the base model's marginals on x with the extra tokens filled in and ADJUST's outputs (rollout K = 4, 2 epochs, constant LR 5e-5, batch 32). Evaluation: generate 128-token strings from the BOS prompt with K tokens per step; MAUVE (GPT2-Large features) is computed against samples from the same base model with K = 1, and NLL is scored by Qwen-2.5-7B.
official.claim: For unconditional 128-token generation from Dream-7B-Base at temperature 1.0 with K = 4 tokens unmasked per step, ADJUST samples reach MAUVE 0.87 against the model's K = 1 (true joint) samples, vs. 0.31 for naive parallel sampling and 0.39 for EDLM, and lower Qwen-2.5-7B NLL (5.58 vs. 6.52 and 6.18); the gap persists at K = 8 (MAUVE 0.84 vs. 0.19 and 0.16).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Unconditional Generation. In this table we compare the NLL and the MAUVE scores for three different methods : Marginal, Joint and Energy-based (EDLM). The base diffusion model is Dream-Base-7B. Across different number of tokens K sampled per step, and different sampling temperature, joint sampling consistently outperforms both of the baselines, parallel sampling and EDLM.
official.metric: MAUVE (GPT2-Large features) between generated strings and the base model's K = 1 samples, higher is better; generative NLL under Qwen-2.5-7B, lower is better. Single numbers, no error bars, seeds or sample counts reported (the checklist says standard errors are small but omitted).
official.comparison: ADJUST vs. naive parallel sampling and EDLM (two candidate completions, pick the lower Qwen-2.5-0.5B perplexity) on the same frozen Dream-7B-Base, same number of tokens per step K, same temperature and the base model's unmasking rule
official.falsification_criterion: With Dream-7B-Base, T = 1.0, K = 4, an ADJUST layer trained as described does not reach MAUVE (vs. K = 1 samples) at least ~0.3 higher than naive parallel sampling under the same evaluation, e.g. ADJUST MAUVE below ~0.6 while parallel is ~0.3.

title: Can Large Language Models Develop Gambling Addiction?
claim_source: Table 17, page 25 (same numbers as Figure 2a, page 3, and Table 7, page 16; differences with CIs in Table 8, page 16)

official.background: LLMs are increasingly deployed as agents that make sequential financial decisions, but it is unclear under what conditions they drift into self-defeating risk-taking. The paper borrows constructs from clinical research on pathological gambling (loss of bet-size control, loss chasing, goals that turn into moving targets) and asks whether giving an LLM more decision freedom in a negative-expected-value betting game makes it go broke more often, then probes whether those behaviours are readable from, and steerable through, the internal states of open-weight models.
official.method:
Six LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT) play a text slot machine with a 30% win rate and a 3x payout (each round loses 10% of the bet in expectation), starting from $100. Each round the model is shown its balance and the game history and chooses to bet or stop; the game ends at bankruptcy or voluntary stop. The design is 2 betting styles x 32 prompt conditions (all on/off combinations of five modules: G self-set goal, M maximise reward, H hidden pattern may exist, W win pays 3x, P win rate 30%), with 50 games per cell per model, i.e. 1,600 games per betting style per model.

Fixed betting locks every wager at $10; variable betting lets the model choose any integer bet from $5 up to its current balance (stated as $5-$100 in the body). The reported outcome is the bankruptcy rate (share of games ending at $0) per model and betting style, pooled over the 32 prompt conditions.
official.claim: In the slot-machine task, every one of six LLMs goes bankrupt more often under variable betting than under fixed $10 betting (1,600 games per arm), e.g. LLaMA-3.1-8B 0.4% -> 72.3%, Gemini-2.5-Flash 3.1% -> 48.1%, GPT-4o-mini 0.0% -> 21.3%, with the smallest gap on Gemma-2-9B (0.0% -> 5.4%).
official.claim_caption: Table 17: Participation, realised bet size and re-betting after a first loss beside the bankruptcy rate of every primary slot-machine cell (Figure 2a), n = 1,600 games per cell. Bankruptcy, participation and re-betting carry 95% Wilson intervals. The mean wager carries a 95% bootstrap interval over whole games. Definitions are as in Table 15, and the at-risk count behind re-betting is in parentheses. The fixed arm's wager is locked at $10 by construction.
official.metric: Bankruptcy rate (% of games ending at $0; higher = riskier), pooled over 32 prompt conditions x 50 games; brackets are 95% Wilson intervals over games. Table 8 gives variable-minus-fixed differences with Newcombe intervals (e.g. LLaMA +71.9 [+69.6, +74.0] pp, Gemma +5.4 [+4.4, +6.7] pp).
official.comparison: Variable betting ($5 up to balance, model chooses) vs. fixed $10 betting, same model, same prompts, same game, per model.
official.falsification_criterion: For a rerun model (e.g. LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct or GPT-4o-mini) over the 32 prompt conditions, the variable-arm bankruptcy rate is not clearly above the fixed-arm rate (95% intervals overlap), or for LLaMA-3.1-8B the variable-arm rate falls far outside the reported ~70-74% range.

title: Uncertainty Estimation for Pretrained Medical Image Registration Models via Transformation Equivariance

official.background: Deep learning registration networks predict a dense deformation field between two medical images but give no indication of where that prediction is unreliable, so misregistrations can silently corrupt downstream measurements. Existing uncertainty methods for registration (variational inference, MC-dropout, ensembles) require retraining or architectural changes, which rules them out for pretrained foundation registration models deployed as fixed components. An inference-time, model-agnostic uncertainty estimate that tracks actual registration error would make such models safer to use.
official.method:
Given a frozen registration network f, source image I_A and target I_B, the method samples N = 50 random spatial perturbations tau of the source (translation up to 1% of image size, scale U(0.9,1.1), shear U(-0.02,0.02), or B-spline deformation with 10-px grid and displacement U(-12.5,12.5) px), runs g_n = tau_n o f(I_A o tau_n, I_B), and computes the per-voxel sample covariance S(y) of the composed fields g_n. The uncertainty map is u(y) = sqrt(tr S(y)). If the network were perfectly transformation-equivariant, all g_n would coincide and u = 0.

To get ground-truth error, target images are created by warping each source with a known transformation: random translation (up to 10% of image size), random affine (plus shear U(-0.1,0.1), scale U(0.8,1.2)), a composition of two B-spline deformations, or a 'real' transformation estimated by ANTs between two real images. The error map is ||phi_AB(y) - phi_hat_AB(y)||_2. Pearson and Spearman correlation between u(y) and the error are computed over voxels inside an ROI, averaged across the dataset; AURC (area under risk-coverage curve, ranking voxels by uncertainty) is compared to the mean error (the AURC of a random ranking). Figure 5 uses the pretrained uniGradICON model on a curated brain MRI set (110 images for the simulated GTs, all 220 for the real/ANTs GT) and the 30-image Learn2Reg Abdomen CT training set (real GT: each of the 30 images paired with a randomly sampled target, ANTs affine followed by non-rigid registration).
official.claim: With pretrained uniGradICON on Learn2Reg Abdomen CT, the translation-perturbation uncertainty map has dataset-mean Pearson correlation with true voxel-wise registration error of about 0.70 (translation GT), 0.71 (affine GT), 0.64 (ANTs-derived real GT) and 0.39 (B-spline deformation GT); correlation is positive in all 32 GT x perturbation x dataset settings, and AURC is below mean error in every setting.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5. Correlation between the estimated uncertainty and the true registration error for a combination of varying ground truth transformation types (GT), perturbation transformation types, and datasets with uniGradICON.
official.metric: Pearson r and Spearman rho between uncertainty map and voxel-wise L2 registration error within ROI, averaged over the dataset (higher is better); mean AURC vs. mean mError (lower AURC than mError means better-than-random ranking). No error bars, seeds or CIs are reported.
official.comparison: Correlation of the proposed uncertainty map with true error across 4 ground-truth transformation types x 4 perturbation types x 2 datasets; AURC compared to the random-ranking baseline (mean mError). No competing uncertainty method is compared on this task.
official.falsification_criterion: On Learn2Reg Abdomen CT with uniGradICON, the translation-perturbation uncertainty map gives dataset-mean Pearson r clearly below ~0.5 under translation or affine ground truth (e.g. r < 0.4), or non-positive correlation in any setting, or AURC not below the mean error.

title: PATCH: Learnable Tile-Level Hybrid Sparsity for LLMs

official.background: Pruning cuts the memory and compute cost of LLMs, but the two common options pull in different directions. Unstructured sparsity keeps accuracy but cannot be accelerated on GPUs. NVIDIA/AMD 2:4 semi-structured sparsity is hardware-accelerated but forces exactly 50% sparsity in every layer, which hurts quality even when masks are learned end-to-end (MaskLLM). A format that gives an intermediate, non-uniform sparsity level while keeping GPU acceleration would let users trade off accuracy and speed.
official.method:
PATCH splits every weight matrix into 128x128 tiles and marks each tile as either dense or 2:4 sparse. Each tile has one learnable logit, sampled with Gumbel-Softmax to give a soft tile mask M_tile. This is merged with a MaskLLM-style differentiable 2:4 mask M_2:4 (a learnable categorical over the six 2:4 patterns per group of four) as M = M_tile + (1 - M_tile) * M_2:4. Model weights stay frozen; only the mask logits are trained. The loss is the language-modeling loss plus a penalty on the deviation of global model density from the target, plus MaskLLM's weight-magnitude regularizer. The temperature is annealed and the logit scale increased so masks become hard. At the end, tiles with a positive logit become dense. Because the sparsity target is global, layers end up with different sparsity levels.

In the PATCH-Joint variant used for small models, the tile logits and the 2:4 pattern logits are trained jointly. Masks are trained for 2000 steps, batch 256, sequence length 4096 (about 2B tokens of SlimPajama), with tile logits initialized from a SparseGPT prior. Baselines include one-shot 2:4 methods (magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT, Thanos, ProxSparse) and MaskLLM, which the authors reimplemented in PyTorch and trained under the same data budget. Evaluation is the average accuracy over eight zero-shot lm-eval-harness tasks (MMLU, PIQA, ARC-E, ARC-C, WinoGrande, OBQA, RACE, HellaSwag) and WikiText2 perplexity at sequence length 4096.
official.claim: On Qwen-2.5 0.5B, LLaMA-3.2 1B and Gemma-3 1B, PATCH-Joint at 45% global sparsity gets lower WikiText2 perplexity and higher eight-task average accuracy than 50% 2:4 MaskLLM: PPL 14.57 vs 15.22, 12.23 vs 12.93 and 11.96 vs 12.82; accuracy 40.29 vs 39.33, 42.08 vs 41.04 and 42.80 vs 41.84.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Model quality (average accuracy across eight zero-shot tasks and perplexity on WikiText2 dataset) for different pruning methods. By jointly optimizing the location of dense tiles and the sparsity pattern within the sparse tiles, PATCHJoint allows for a continuous sparsity ratio for the models, providing a flexible tradeoff between sparsity and model quality.
official.metric: WikiText2 perplexity (lower is better, seq len 4096) and average zero-shot accuracy over 8 tasks (higher is better). Table 1 is a single run with no error bars. Appendix J (Table 20) reports PATCH perplexity over 4 seeds: Qwen-2.5 0.5B at 45% gives 14.49-14.61 and LLaMA-3.2 1B at 45% gives 12.23-12.55. No seed variation is reported for accuracy or for MaskLLM.
official.comparison: PATCH-Joint (Dense/2:4 tiles, 45% global sparsity) vs. MaskLLM (learned 2:4, 50% sparsity), the strongest baseline. Both learn masks end-to-end on SlimPajama with frozen weights.
official.falsification_criterion: With masks trained under the paper's setup, PATCH-Joint at 45% fails to beat MaskLLM 2:4 on WikiText2 perplexity by more than the seed spread (about 0.1-0.3 PPL) on these models, or its eight-task average accuracy is not higher than MaskLLM's.

title: Knowledge-Level Consistency Reinforcement Learning: Dual-Fact Alignment for Long-Form Factuality

official.background: LLMs hallucinate in long-form answers, and RLHF preference rewards do not account for what the model actually knows. Earlier factuality-alignment methods score responses with retrieval-based checkers such as FActScore. These checkers are too slow for online RL, and because they reward precision alone, models learn to say less (over-conservatism). The paper treats long-form factuality as matching the facts the policy expresses to the base model's own verified parametric knowledge. The goal is to raise recall of facts the base model knows while keeping claims inside that boundary, using rewards that need no retrieval at training time.
official.method:
Offline, the base model (Qwen2.5-14B) is sampled 8 times per training query (ELI5, LongFact-Gen and LongWiki-Gen; about 13K queries). Atomic claims are extracted, and each is verified against a local Wikipedia index (Wiki20250716, top-10 retrieval) by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct. SUPPORT claims, after deduplication and importance filtering, form a per-query factual checklist. SUPPORT and REFUTE claims are used to train a lightweight truthfulness reward model that outputs P(true) for each claim. During online RL, a checklist verifier labels each checklist item as consistent, contradictory or missing for a response. This gives a Fact Recall reward (consistent / all items) and a Fact Precision reward (consistent / (consistent + contradictory)). The Truthfulness reward is the mean P(true) over the response's claims. The final reward is kappa*R_recall + gamma*R_precision + mu*R_truth + 0.1*R_general + length penalty + format reward, with (kappa, gamma, mu) = (1/4, 1/4, 1/2).

KLCF-zero applies GRPO (VeRL, 8 rollouts, lr 1e-6, 2 epochs, max response length 4096, think/answer format) directly to the Qwen2.5-14B base model. The matched baseline GRPO&FActScore is trained from the same base model with a retrieval-based FActScore reward in place of the KLC rewards. Evaluation covers FActScore (500 bios, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct extraction and verification against the local Wiki index), HalluLens-LongWiki (250), LongFact-Objects (250, VeriScore pipeline) and Factory-Hard (250, VeriScore). Metrics are FActScore, Recall@K, Precision, F1@K and win rate.
official.claim: Starting from the Qwen2.5-14B base model, GRPO with the KLC rewards (KLCF-zero) beats GRPO with a FActScore reward on FActScore (61.2% vs. 54.8%) and on LongFact-Objects F1@64 (0.733 vs. 0.663, recall@64 0.776 vs. 0.634), without losing precision (0.704 vs. 0.690).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results on Qwen2.5-14B. SFT denotes the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B. R@32 and Prec are Recall@32 and Precision. Best scores are bolded.
official.metric: FActScore (% supported atomic facts, higher is better) and VeriScore-style Recall@64 / Precision / F1@64 on LongFact-Objects (higher is better). These are single-run point estimates, averaged over test prompts. No seeds, std or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Qwen2.5-14B + GRPO with KLC rewards (KLCF-zero) vs. Qwen2.5-14B + GRPO with FActScore reward, both trained from the same base model. Base (10-shot), CoVe and Self-Eval-P(True) are also listed.
official.falsification_criterion: Using the paper's evaluation pipeline, KLCF-zero's FActScore lead over GRPO&FActScore shrinks below about 2 points, its LongFact F1@64 lead shrinks below about 0.02, or KLCF-zero's LongFact precision falls clearly below the FActScore-reward model. Any of these would refute the claim. So would retraining with a different seed showing that gaps of this size fall within run-to-run variation.

title: Sharpness of Minima in Deep Matrix Factorization

official.background: For gradient descent with step size η, a minimum is linearly (dynamically) stable only if the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian there, λmax, is at most 2/η. So λmax ('sharpness') decides which minima GD can settle in, and it is central to work on implicit bias, flat minima and edge-of-stability. For deep matrix factorization (and deep linear networks), closed forms for λmax were known only for special minimizers (flat or balanced ones), not for an arbitrary global minimizer.
official.method:
The loss is L(w) = ||M − W_L ··· W_1||_F^2 with all layer widths at least min(d_0, d_L). Theorem 3.1 states that at any global minimizer w* (M = W_L* ··· W_1*), λmax(∇²L(w*)) = 2 σmax( Σ_{i=1}^{L} (B_i^T B_i) ⊗ (A_i A_i^T) ), where A_k = W_L* ··· W_{k+1}* and B_k = W_{k-1}* ··· W_1* (empty products are the identity). Special cases: depth-2 M = L R^T gives λmax = 2(σmax(L)^2 + σmax(R)^2) (Corollary 3.3), and for scalar factorization λmax = 2 Σ_i σmax(A_i)^2 σmax(B_i)^2 (Corollary 3.2).

Experiment (Section 6, Figure 1): sample Gaussian factors W_1, W_2 ∈ R^{20×20} and W_3 ∈ R^{10×20} (entries N(0,1), no rescaling; seed numpy.random.default_rng(12)) and set M = W_3 W_2 W_1, so w* is an exact global minimizer. Compute λmax from Theorem 3.1, start full-batch GD at w* + r·v_1 with r = 1e-12, where v_1 is the top Hessian eigenvector, and run 2000 iterations in float64 with η = (2/λmax)×{1.0, 1.01, 1.02}. Track the normalized loss L(w_t)/||M||_F^2 and the normalized distance ||w_t − w*||^2/||w*||^2. Appendix E.2 repeats this for depth 2 (Fig. 2), 20-layer and 4-layer scalar factorization (Figs. 3–4, which include η = 0.97–0.99 × 2/λmax), and a 25×20 depth-2 case (Fig. 5).
official.claim: For a depth-3 Gaussian factorization of a 10×20 matrix, with GD started 1e-12 from the minimizer along the top Hessian eigenvector, GD with η = 2/λmax (λmax from Theorem 3.1) stays at the minimizer for 2000 iterations. With η = 1.01×2/λmax and 1.02×2/λmax, GD escapes after about 1250 and 650 iterations: the loss spikes to about 3e-4 and 1.3e-3 of ||M||_F^2, and the iterates settle at normalized squared distances of about 0.5e-5 and 2.05e-5 from w*.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: The setting is a depth-3 matrix factorization of a random 10 × 20 matrix with Gaussian factors W3 ∈ R^{10×20} and W1, W2 ∈ R^{20×20}. v1 and vN are the eigenvectors of ∇²L(w*) that correspond to its maximum and minimum eigenvalues respectively. λmax is computed via the closed-form expression in Theorem 3.1. GD runs with different step sizes are initialized within 10^−12 of the minimizer w* along v1. The contour plot in (c) projects the parameter space onto span{v1, vN} (Appendix E.1); darker (brighter) regions indicate higher (lower) loss. See Appendix E.2 for details.
official.metric: Normalized squared distance ||w_t − w*||_2^2/||w*||_2^2 after T = 2000 iterations, plus the normalized training loss L(w_t)/||M||_F^2. Escape means the final distance is far above the initial ~1e-24 scale. One random instance; no ± is reported.
official.comparison: GD at step sizes just below/at 2/λmax vs. just above 2/λmax, where λmax is the paper's closed form (Theorem 3.1). The implicit check is that the closed form equals the true top Hessian eigenvalue, so the stability threshold lands exactly at η = 2/λmax.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if the closed-form λmax differs from the top eigenvalue of the numerically computed Hessian at w* (beyond floating-point error) for random minimizers, or if GD at η = 2/λmax × 1.01 (started along v_1 at r = 1e-12) does not leave w* while η ≤ 2/λmax does, i.e., the observed stability threshold is not at 2/λmax.

title: TGPO: Temporal Grounded Policy Optimization for Signal Temporal Logic Tasks

official.background: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifies robot tasks with timed reach, stay and avoid requirements (e.g. 'reach A within [0,50], stay in C during [60,80], always avoid obstacles'). Solving STL with model-free RL is hard because satisfaction depends on the whole trajectory (non-Markovian) and the natural reward, the STL robustness score at the end of the episode, is very sparse. Prior RL methods either augment the state with history or flags and only handle shallow STL fragments, or use the terminal robustness score directly.
official.method:
TGPO flattens an STL formula into subgoals (Reach(mu, tau) or Inv(mu, W)) and invariant avoid constraints whose times depend on a few integer time variables (e.g. the instant tau in F[a,b]). Given a concrete assignment of the time variables, the subgoals become an ordered sequence. The state is augmented with the time index, the progress index (which subgoal is next), a reach-and-stay certificate flag and per-constraint satisfaction flags, and PPO is trained with reward R = 0.5*R_dist + 20*R_progress + 20*R_success - 3*R_inv (distance to current subgoal, subgoal completion, full-task success, invariant violation), plus the robustness score at the final step. Policy and critic are conditioned on the time-variable assignment.

TGPO* samples time-variable assignments each epoch from a mix of uniform sampling (40%), Metropolis-Hastings over exp(critic value) (50%) and an elite buffer of the best-robustness assignments (10%); at test time it picks one assignment by critic value and rolls out once. The ablation in Table 1b keeps everything else fixed and removes reward terms (keeping only the STL robustness, then adding invariance, progress, distance terms) or removes state augmentation (no flags; no flags and no time index). Evaluation: the Linear environment (2D single integrator, dt = 0.2, T = 100), 10 STL tasks (5 two-layer, 5 multi-layer, listed in Appendix A.7.1), 512 parallel envs, 1000 epochs, 512 test initial states, success rate averaged over states and the 10 STLs.
official.claim: In the Linear environment (10 STL tasks, T = 100), full TGPO* reaches 88.99 ± 9.60% test success, while the same method trained only on the STL robustness reward reaches 11.73 ± 2.67% and the method without state augmentation (no time index, no flags) reaches 11.43 ± 3.48%; adding the distance reward term alone lifts success from 49.80 ± 7.72% (STL+Inv+Prog) to 84.59 ± 7.88% (STL+Inv+Dist).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Ablation studies for TGPO on the linear dynamics environment. (a) Different time variables sampling strategies. (b) Different state augmentation and rewards.
official.metric: Test STL task success rate (%) over 512 initial states and 10 STL tasks, higher is better; ± is std over 7 random seeds
official.comparison: TGPO* with full augmented state and full dense reward vs. the same pipeline with (i) robustness-only reward, (ii) partial reward terms, (iii) no flags, (iv) no flags and no time index
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Linear-environment ablation with several seeds, full TGPO* success is not clearly above the robustness-only-reward variant and the no-augmentation variant (e.g. the gap is under ~30 points or within one seed std), or adding the distance term to STL+Inv does not raise success by well over one std.

title: Re-examining Low Rank adaptation for private LLM fine-tuning

official.background: DP-SGD makes fine-tuning differentially private by clipping per-example gradients and adding isotropic Gaussian noise, and this noise slows convergence. Fewer training steps at a fixed noise level also means less privacy budget spent. Gradients of transformer linear layers are close to low-rank, so their singular values decay quickly. DP noise inflates these singular values and destroys the fast decay. Random matrix theory gives estimators that partially recover a low-rank matrix from a noisy observation. Because these estimators only post-process the already-privatized gradient, they leave the privacy guarantee unchanged.
official.method:
At each DP-SGD step, after the noisy averaged gradient is formed, the gradient of every linear layer (here the LoRA factors) is treated as a noisy low-rank matrix with known noise std sigma = sigma_DP * C / |B|. The layer gradient is denoised with the Shabalin-Nobel optimal singular-value shrinkage estimator (Eqs. 8-9), which keeps the singular directions above the noise edge sigma(sqrt(m)+sqrt(n)) and shrinks their singular values. A layer is denoised only if its largest singular value exceeds kappa * sigma(sqrt(n)+sqrt(m)) with kappa = 1.02. Otherwise its noisy gradient is kept. Each denoised layer is rescaled to the norm of its noisy gradient. Non-linear-layer gradients are left unchanged. The result is passed to the optimizer.

GLUE setup (Appendix H): RoBERTa-base/large with LoRA r=16, alpha=16 on query, key, value, intermediate.dense and output.dense. Logical batch size 2000, lr 5e-4, clipping C=10, weight decay 0.01, 400 steps, target epsilon 6.7 with delta 1e-5 (1e-6 for MNLI/QQP), PRV accountant (Gopi et al.). The baseline is the same DP-LoRA run without denoising. Validation accuracy is evaluated every 50 steps, and each configuration is run 5 times.
official.claim: On QNLI with RoBERTa-base under DP-LoRA (epsilon = 6.7 over 400 steps), adding the spectral denoiser raises validation accuracy from 50.3 ± 2.3 to 78.2 ± 1.3 at step 200 and from 80.7 ± 0.9 to 84.4 ± 0.3 at step 400.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of our SVD denoising method with standard DP-LoRA on GLUE classification tasks. We report mean accuracy across runs ± the half-width of the 95% confidence interval, computed from the standard error over runs (Appendix H). Step speedup and ∆ϵ (privacy budget saved) represent the percentage of iterations and the absolute privacy budget saved by reaching the baseline's accuracy at a given step milestone. Speedup is calculated via linear interpolation.
official.metric: Validation accuracy (%), higher is better; mean over 5 runs ± half-width of the 95% t-confidence interval of the mean
official.comparison: DP-LoRA + per-layer RMT singular-value denoising vs. standard DP-LoRA, same hyperparameters, noise multiplier and privacy budget
official.falsification_criterion: Over 5 matched runs on QNLI with RoBERTa-base, the denoised run's mean accuracy at step 400 is not above the DP-LoRA mean, or the 95% CIs overlap. At step 200, the denoised run fails to beat DP-LoRA by a margin outside the CIs.

title: Words That Make Language Models Perceive

official.background: Text-only LLMs have never seen images or heard sounds, yet earlier work (the Platonic Representation Hypothesis) found that their embeddings of captions have a neighbourhood structure partly similar to that of vision encoders run on the paired images. That work measured alignment from single forward passes, so alignment was treated as a fixed property of the model. This paper asks whether alignment with a sensory encoder can be raised at inference time by prompting the LLM to 'see' or 'hear' the caption and letting it generate, which bears on whether LLMs encode perceptually grounded structure that context can bring out.
official.method:
Each caption c is wrapped in a prompt template: no cue 'Imagine: {caption}.', SEE cue 'Imagine what it would look like to see {caption}.', or HEAR cue 'Imagine what it would sound like to hear {caption}.'. A frozen Qwen3-32B generates a 128-token continuation. The generative representation z_g is the hidden state averaged over all layers and over all tokens of the generated continuation. The single-pass embedding z_e averages hidden states over all layers and the prompt+caption tokens without generating.

For a dataset of n paired items, a cosine-similarity kernel is built from the LLM's caption representations and from a frozen sensory encoder's representation of the paired image (DINOv2-Base ViT-B/14) or audio (BEATs-Iter3). Alignment is mutual-kNN: the average fraction of shared top-k neighbours between the two kernels. The vision comparison uses WiT (1024 Wikipedia image-caption pairs, as in Huh et al. 2024); the audio comparison uses AudioCaps 2.0 (975 pairs). Error bars are ±1 bootstrap standard error (B = 1000, resampling paired rows).
official.claim: With Qwen3-32B generative representations (128 tokens) on WiT, the SEE-cue prompt raises mutual-kNN alignment with DINOv2 from about 0.137 (no cue) to about 0.155, while the HEAR cue leaves it at about 0.136; with single-pass embeddings, the SEE cue does not help (about 0.113 vs 0.122 for no cue).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Sensory cues induce a generative text-only LLM representation that has higher alignment with the corresponding encoder. The star denotes matching cue-modality in generative representation. (a) Sensory cued alignment using single-pass embedding (z_e) and generative (z_g) representations. (b) Prompt templates used in generative representations.
official.metric: Mutual-kNN alignment between LLM caption kernel and DINOv2 image kernel (higher is better); error bars and shaded band are ±1 bootstrap standard error over resampled paired rows (B = 1000), about ±0.005. Values are read off the plot and approximate. No seed variation over generations is reported.
official.comparison: SEE cue vs. no-cue (and HEAR cue) prompt for Qwen3-32B generative representations z_g, same captions, same encoder; secondary contrast with single-pass embeddings z_e
official.falsification_criterion: On WiT with Qwen3-32B 128-token generations, SEE-cue z_g alignment with DINOv2 is not higher than no-cue z_g alignment by more than about 2 bootstrap SEs (e.g. gain < 0.01), or the HEAR cue matches or beats the SEE cue on DINOv2.

title: DELTA: Robustly Training Label-Conditional Diffusion Models with Weak Annotations

official.background: Label-conditional diffusion models are trained on (image, class label) pairs and assume the labels are clean. In practice labels are often noisy (wrong), ambiguous (a candidate set that contains the true class), or missing for most of the data. Training a conditional diffusion model directly on such weak annotations produces samples that do not match their class, collapse to a few modes per class, or degrade in quality. Earlier robust methods each handle only one kind of weak label and need extra information such as a known noise transition matrix or confidence scores.
official.method:
DELTA treats the true label as a latent variable and trains with an EM-style objective. In the generative term, the network's conditional score outputs for all classes are mixed with weights equal to the estimated posterior p(y | x_t, z) given the weak annotation z, and this mixture is regressed onto the standard denoising score-matching target (posterior-weighted score matching). The posterior is computed by the diffusion model itself (an EMA copy) as a diffusion classifier: Bayes' rule over class-conditional ELBOs, evaluated only on a short window of noise levels centred at the median of the EDM log-normal weight (log sigma = -1.2, window length 6.4) to make it cheap enough to run during training. For ambiguous labels the posterior is renormalized over the candidate set. A classification term (posterior-weighted cross-entropy) refines the model's posterior.

Vanilla is the internal ablation: the same joint objective and training setup, but the generative term trains directly on the weak pairs (x, z) without posterior reweighting. Both use EDM with a DDPM++ U-Net (about 55.7M parameters), trained from scratch for 200k iterations with Adam (lr 1e-3) and batch size 64 on CIFAR-10. In the 'Random' ambiguous setting each non-target label is added to the candidate set with probability 0.5. Samples are generated per class and scored with the DLSM evaluation code: FID, IS, Density and Coverage on the pooled samples, plus class-wise CW-FID, CW-Density and CW-Coverage averaged over classes.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with random ambiguous labels (each wrong class added to the candidate set with probability 0.5), DELTA reaches CW-FID 10.65 and FID 2.26, versus 27.18 and 7.76 for the Vanilla ablation trained identically without posterior-weighted score matching (clean-label upper bound: 9.83 and 2.05).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Generative results under various weak annotations. The gray-shaded 'Clean' column represents the best performance trained on the fully clean dataset. 'uncond'/'cond' denote unconditional/conditional metrics. Bold numbers indicate better performance.
official.metric: Class-wise FID (CW-FID, intra-class FID averaged over the 10 classes) and unconditional FID, lower is better; single runs, no error bars reported
official.comparison: DELTA vs. Vanilla (same architecture, data, weak labels and 200k-iteration budget; only the generative term differs), with a model trained on clean labels as reference
official.falsification_criterion: Training both models on CIFAR-10 with random ambiguous labels (q = 0.5) under the same budget, DELTA's CW-FID is not clearly below Vanilla's (e.g. less than about 1.5x lower, or the gap is within the spread of a few seeds), or DELTA's FID is not clearly below Vanilla's.

title: Test-Time Defense Against Adversarial Attacks via Stochastic Resonance of Latent Ensembles

official.background: Neural network classifiers and dense predictors can be pushed to wrong outputs by small, imperceptible adversarial input perturbations. Most defenses either retrain the model (adversarial training) or filter/smooth inputs or features with a fixed scheme, which loses information and can be bypassed by adaptive attackers. A defense that works purely at test time, needs no retraining, and plugs into existing architectures would be broadly useful, but test-time defenses for classification often look strong only because the attack does not account for the defense.
official.method:
Stochastic resonance (SR) applies a set of small integer-pixel translations g_{u,v} with |u| <= d, |v| <= d (N = (2d+1)^2 shifted copies) to the input image, runs each copy through the network up to a chosen layer, shifts each resulting feature map back by the inverse translation (A_g), and averages the aligned feature maps; the rest of the network then runs on the averaged features. Nothing is trained. For CIFAR-10 classification the ensembling is done at the bottleneck, right before the final linear layer, using translations implemented with torchvision's transforms.functional.affine.

The defense is added at test time to publicly released adversarially trained checkpoints (AT/Madry ResNet-18, TRADES WideResNet-34, MART ResNet-18) inside the FSR codebase and its evaluation protocol. Attacks are FGSM, PGD-20, PGD-100, C&W (all l_inf, eps = 8/255), a per-example worst-case 'Ensemble' over these attacks, and AutoAttack. The default 'Ours' row is described only as non-adaptive (the paper does not spell out how those attacks are generated); in the 'Worst-Case' adaptive setting the attacker has the weights and backpropagates through every SR forward pass. Baselines are other feature-level defenses (FD, CAS, CIFS, FSR) and the test-time output-ensembling method TTE, all on the AT ResNet-18.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with the AT ResNet-18 checkpoint, adding test-time stochastic resonance raises PGD-20 (eps=8/255) robust accuracy from 48.22% to 56.08% against a non-adaptive attacker and to 53.58% against a fully adaptive attacker that differentiates through all SR passes, while clean accuracy stays at 84.93% vs 85.02%; non-adaptively it also beats the best baseline, TTE (53.00%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Defense against adversarial attacks on CIFAR-10. Unlike baselines, we perform defense purely at test-time, and achieve state-of-the-art robustness under different attacks. Even in an adaptive setting (worst-case) where the attacker is fully aware of how defense is applied, the effectiveness of adversarial attacks is still notably reduced, while the computational cost for executing such attacks is significantly increased.
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%) on the CIFAR-10 test set under l_inf attacks with eps = 8/255, higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: AT ResNet-18 + SR (non-adaptive and worst-case adaptive attack) vs. the same AT ResNet-18 without defense, and vs. AT + FD / CAS / CIFS / FSR / TTE
official.falsification_criterion: Under an adaptive PGD-20 attack (eps=8/255) that backpropagates through the full SR ensemble (e.g. full white-box gradients, or EOT/BPDA if gradients are obfuscated), the SR-defended AT ResNet-18 scores no more than about 2 points above the undefended AT model's 48.22%, or its clean accuracy drops by more than about 1 point.
