title: Inference-Time Search Using Side Information for Diffusion-Based Image Reconstruction

official.background: Diffusion models are widely used as priors for inverse problems such as inpainting, super-resolution and deblurring. When the measurement is badly degraded, many reconstructions fit it equally well, and posterior sampling rarely recovers the true image. Side information, such as another photo of the same person, a text description or a second MRI contrast, could narrow the solution space. Existing diffusion solvers ignore it, and training a conditional model for each kind of side information needs paired data and retraining.
official.method:
The paper treats the posterior given side information s as the unconditional diffusion prior tilted by exp(r(x0; s)/τ), where r is an off-the-shelf reward that scores how consistent a reconstruction is with s. The reward is never differentiated. Instead, N particles of a standard solver (DPS, DAPS or MPGD) are run in parallel, and the reward is evaluated on each particle's Tweedie estimate x̂0|t. Particles are resampled greedily within groups: the best particle in each group is kept and copied. Greedy Search (GS) resamples all N particles every B steps. Recursive Fork-Join Search (RFJS) resamples groups of size N/2^j on a hierarchical schedule (all N every B steps, halves every B/2 steps, and so on), which keeps diversity between groups.

For the chosen claim, the target is a CelebA-HQ face and the side information is a different random image of the same identity. The prior is the FFHQ-pretrained diffusion model used by DPS, the base solver is DAPS (200 steps), and the task is box inpainting with a 96×96 box. The reward is the negative AdaFace identity distance (faces detected by MTCNN) between the reconstruction and the side image. RFJS uses N = 8 and B = 4. Baselines are plain DAPS, Best-of-N (N = 8, final selection by the same side-information reward), GS, and reward-gradient guidance (RGG, scale 13). The evaluation metric is FaceSimilarity: the AdaFace embedding distance between the reconstruction and the ground-truth image, which the method never sees.
official.claim: On CelebA-HQ 96×96 box inpainting with DAPS as the base solver and a reference image of the same identity as side information, RFJS (N=8, B=4) reaches a FaceSimilarity distance to ground truth of 0.423 ± 0.10, against 0.739 ± 0.18 for plain DAPS and 0.611 ± 0.14 for Best-of-8 with the same reward. PSNR, LPIPS and SSIM do not get worse (28.72 vs 28.29 dB PSNR).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Comparison of metrics for various inverse problems using DAPS as the base sampler. For each metric, the best result is shown in bold, and the second best is underlined. We observe that our RFJ Search-based algorithm has the best or the second-best performance in all the tasks.
official.metric: FaceSimilarity (AdaFace identity-embedding distance between reconstruction and ground truth, lower is better); PSNR, LPIPS and SSIM are secondary. ± is the per-image standard deviation across the test images (not seeds); the number of test images is not stated.
official.comparison: DAPS + RFJS vs. plain DAPS (primary), and vs. DAPS + Best-of-N, Greedy Search and reward-gradient guidance with the same AdaFace reward
official.falsification_criterion: With the stated setup (DAPS, 96×96 box inpainting, N=8, B=4, AdaFace reward on a different image of the same identity), mean FaceSimilarity for RFJS is not lower than plain DAPS by clearly more than the per-image std (e.g. the gap is under about 0.15, versus the reported 0.316), or RFJS does not beat Best-of-8 with the same reward.

title: Neural Bayesian Filtering
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (full budgets in Table 12, page 24)

official.background: Bayesian filtering tracks the posterior over a hidden state as noisy observations arrive. Gaussian filters such as the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) scale to high dimensions but cannot represent non-Gaussian or multimodal beliefs. Particle filters can represent any distribution, but in high dimensions their weights collapse onto a few particles, and repeated resampling makes the particle set lose diversity (impoverishment). A filter that represents complex beliefs and still works at moderately high state dimension would be useful for data assimilation and tracking.
official.method:
Neural Bayesian Filtering (NBF) represents the belief as an embedding θ from a Generative Distribution Embedding: a Set Transformer encoder (three rounds of Induced Set Attention Blocks with pooling) maps a weighted particle set to θ, and a conditional flow-matching generator samples states given θ. Each filter step draws n fresh particles from the generator, propagates each one through the known transition (bootstrap proposal), weights it by the known observation likelihood, and encodes the weighted set into the next embedding. Particles are never resampled. On Lorenz-96 the per-particle 'weight' given to the encoder is the vector of standardized residuals (y_j − x'_j)/σ_obs at the observed sites, clipped to [−20, 20], with zeros at unobserved sites. Encoder and generator are trained jointly on the particle sets that NBF produces during its own rollouts, with the flow-matching loss on the single realized true state as the target (100k AdamW steps, batch 256; 4096 rollout particles at K = 40).

Lorenz-96 setup: a ring of K ∈ {20, 40} sites, RK4 with dt = 0.01, observation window 0.4 time units, process noise std 0.25 per window, every second site observed with Gaussian noise. Training draws the forcing F from [5,7] ∪ [9,11] and σ_obs from [0.5, 1.1]. Evaluation uses the held-out F = 8 with σ_obs = 1, 20-step episodes, scores averaged after a 5-step spin-up over 500 episodes. Baselines: a stochastic EnKF (100 members, inflation 1.05, Gaspari–Cohn localization radius 4), a bootstrap PF, and a regularized PF (PF-Reg, Liu–West shrinkage jitter), each with up to 262,144 particles. Metrics: RMSE of the posterior mean, NLL of the true state (NBF via flow-matching density, EnKF via Gaussian density), and CRPS.
official.claim: On Lorenz-96 with K = 40 at the held-out forcing F = 8 (σ_obs = 1), NBF with 1024 particles reaches RMSE 1.060 and NLL 53.6. title: Efficient Prediction of Pass@k Scaling in Large Language Models

official.background: Repeated sampling raises both what LLMs can do (solving hard math and code problems) and the harm they can cause (jailbreaks succeed eventually). Forecasting pass@k, the chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds, at large k is useful for capability and safety evaluation, but measuring it directly takes at least k samples per problem. Common approaches fit a power law to low-k estimates with log-log linear regression, or fit a discretized scaled-beta distribution to per-problem success rates (Schaeffer et al., 2025). The paper argues that both are statistically flawed when data is limited.
official.method:
The proposed estimator models each problem's single-attempt success probability pass_i@1 as drawn from a Beta(α, β) distribution, so that the observed success count s_i out of b_i attempts follows a beta-binomial. α and β are fit by maximum likelihood on the (s_i, b_i) counts (Eq. 15-16), and pass@k is predicted as E_{p~Beta(α,β)}[1 - (1-p)^k] (Eq. 17). Sampling is dynamic (Algorithm 1-2): each new sample goes to the problem with the fewest successes so far, with ties broken by fewest attempts, and then uniformly at random. This concentrates the budget on hard problems, and it works because the beta-binomial likelihood allows a different b_i for each problem.

Baselines: (1) log-log linear regression of -log(pass@k) on log k, using unbiased pass@k estimates for k up to b and clipping predictions at 1; (2) the discretized-beta fit of Schaeffer et al. (log-spaced bins, multinomial likelihood), extended to predict pass@k via Eq. 14. Both baselines use uniform sampling: shuffle each problem's samples and take the first B/m. The data is the existing 10,000 samples per problem from Brown et al. (2024) (MATH, Pythia models) and Hughes et al. (2024), roughly 100-200 problems per dataset (Appendix F says 128). Ground truth is pass@k computed from all 10,000 samples. Predictions are made for log-spaced k from 100 to 10,000 and scored by squared error against ground truth; Figure 9 plots MSE against the total budget B from 10^2 to 10^4 (Appendix E says these plots are 'for fixed k', without naming the k).
official.claim: On MATH with Pythia models (160M-12B) and a total budget of 10^4 samples, the Dynamic + Beta-Binomial estimator reaches pass@k prediction MSE of about 2e-3 to 2e-2. Both log-log regression and the discretized-beta estimator stay at about 8e-2 or higher (roughly 0.08-0.3) on all six models, a gap of about 4x to 40x.
official.claim_caption: Figure 9: MSE scaling with increasing budget. As expected, more samples generally leads to a reduction in MSE across all approaches. For some models our approach reaches MSE more than 10x lower than its counterparts.
official.metric: Mean squared error between predicted and ground-truth pass@k (computed from all 10,000 samples); lower is better; log-scale y-axis. Appendix E describes these MSE-vs-budget plots as 'for fixed k', but the k used in Figure 9 is not stated (Section 5.1 predicts log-spaced k from 100 to 10,000). The shaded bands are not defined in the caption; Figure 1 states that its error bars are bootstrapped 95% CIs, and the bands here are presumably the same. No exact numbers are reported.
official.comparison: Dynamic sampling + beta-binomial MLE vs. log-log linear regression (uniform sampling, clipped at 1) vs. discretized scaled-beta fit of Schaeffer et al. (uniform sampling), all given the same total sample budget B drawn from the same 10,000-sample pool
official.falsification_criterion: At B = 10^4 on MATH/Pythia, the beta-binomial estimator's MSE is not clearly lower (e.g. less than about 3x lower) than the better of the two baselines on most of the six models, or the MSE does not drop steeply with budget as shown.

title: Correlating Cross-Iteration Noise for DP-SGD using Model Curvature

official.background: DP-SGD trains models with differential privacy by clipping per-example gradients and adding Gaussian noise, but this costs a lot of accuracy. DP-MF methods such as DP-BandMF instead add noise that is correlated across iterations through a mixing matrix C, so that later noise partly cancels earlier noise at the same privacy cost. C is chosen by minimizing a data-independent proxy for the error, which only counts the noise added to each gradient. It ignores the fact that earlier noise also moves the point where later gradients are taken, an effect governed by the loss curvature (Hessian).
official.method:
NoiseCurve keeps the DP-BandMF framework unchanged (banded X = C^T C with unit diagonal, the same batch sampling and privacy accounting, and C recovered by Cholesky) and replaces only the objective used to choose X. The new objective is Tr((V^T M V) X^{-1}), where M = Diag(mu_0..mu_{p-1}) holds the eigenvalues of a Hessian upper bound H_hat, and V[i,j] = (1 - eta*mu_i)^{T-j-1} depends on the learning rate eta and the number of steps T. It comes from an exact analysis of the expected final loss under quadratic loss.

H_hat is estimated from unlabeled public data (6,000 TinyImageNet samples for CIFAR-10, per Appendix A.1): the model is pre-trained on the public data with random labels, the Hessian is computed at the resulting weights, and negative eigenvalues are set to 0. For the Table 1(a) setting (only the last linear layer of an ImageNet-pretrained torchvision ResNet152 is finetuned on CIFAR-10, so the loss is convex), the full H_hat is computed. Training runs for 20 epochs with batch size 450, a constant learning rate, no momentum and delta=1e-5. Learning rate, clip norm and band size b (in [1,20]) are tuned with Optuna on a 10% validation split held out from the training set.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 last-layer finetuning of an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet152 (delta=1e-5), NoiseCurve reaches 78.3 ± 0.05% test accuracy at eps=2 and 80.14 ± 0.28% at eps=5, compared with DP-BandMF's 77.33 ± 0.09% and 78.35 ± 0.07% (DP-SGD: 77.14 ± 0.17% and 78.31 ± 0.23%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Test mean accuracy and standard deviation (over 6 runs). (a) Last layer finetuning of ResNet152 (convex loss). (b) Full finetuning of a small CNN (nonconvex loss).
official.metric: Test accuracy (%) on CIFAR-10, higher is better; mean ± std over runs (caption says 6 runs, text and Appendix A.3 say 3 seeds per cell)
official.comparison: NoiseCurve vs. DP-BandMF and DP-SGD, same model, data, epochs, batch size and validation-based hyperparameter tuning, at eps = 1, 2, 5
official.falsification_criterion: At eps=2 or eps=5, NoiseCurve's mean accuracy is within about one std of DP-BandMF's (e.g. less than ~0.3 points ahead), or DP-BandMF with tuned band size matches or beats it.

title: ESS-Flow: training-free guidance as Bayesian inference in source space

official.background: Training-free guidance steers a pretrained diffusion or flow model toward samples with a target property without retraining it. Most such methods (DPS, D-Flow, PnP-Flow, DAPS) need gradients of the reward or likelihood, and sometimes of the generative map too. In scientific design problems those gradients are often unavailable, for example when the generator rounds discrete atom types or the reward comes from an external simulator. Gradient-based guidance can also get stuck in disconnected modes of the data distribution, such as different atomic compositions.
official.method:
ESS-Flow treats a flow model with a Gaussian source as a deterministic transport map x = T(z), z ~ N(0, I), and samples the target pi(z) proportional to g(T(z)) N(z; 0, I) directly in source space using elliptical slice sampling (ESS). Each MCMC step draws nu ~ N(0, I), proposes z' = z cos(theta) + nu sin(theta) along the ellipse, and accepts if log g(T(z')) exceeds log g(T(z)) + log u. On rejection it shrinks the angle bracket and tries again. The method only needs forward evaluations of T and g, with no gradients and no tuning.

For materials, the prior is FlowMM (Riemannian flow matching on MP-20). The atom types are rounded to discrete values, so the generator is not differentiable. The potential is g = exp(-(P - y)^2 / 2 sigma^2), where P is predicted by ALIGNN models trained on JARVIS-DFT. Targets are bulk modulus 300 GPa (4 atoms, sigma = 10 GPa) and shear modulus 200 GPa (4 atoms, sigma = 10 GPa), both above the prior's 99th percentile. ESS-Flow uses 50 ODE steps and 1000 parallel chains run for 201 MCMC steps, keeping the final state of each chain (200 burn-in). The baselines are D-Flow, PnP-Flow, and DAPS. They use soft atom embeddings (D-Flow, PnP-Flow) or Metropolis-Hastings bit flips for atom types (DAPS), with hyperparameters given in Appendix Table 7. The metric is the absolute error between the predicted property and the target over the generated samples.
official.claim: When guiding FlowMM toward bulk modulus 300 GPa and shear modulus 200 GPa with ALIGNN-predicted properties, ESS-Flow reaches a mean absolute error of 8.99 ± 6.69 GPa and 10.53 ± 9.21 GPa. The best gradient-based baselines reach 39.14 ± 26.47 (DAPS) and 75.48 ± 33.45 (PnP-Flow).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Mean and standard deviation of absolute errors between the sample properties and targets, and of energy above hull values.
official.metric: Mean absolute error between the ALIGNN-predicted property of generated materials and the target, in GPa (lower is better). ± is the standard deviation across generated samples (1000 samples, one run), not across seeds.
official.comparison: ESS-Flow vs. D-Flow, PnP-Flow, and DAPS. All use the same FlowMM prior, the same ALIGNN predictor, and the same target and atom count.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same FlowMM prior, ALIGNN predictor and settings, ESS-Flow's mean absolute error on bulk or shear modulus is not clearly lower than the best of DAPS or PnP-Flow. For example, the best baseline comes within ~2x of ESS-Flow, or ESS-Flow's bulk-modulus MAE exceeds ~20 GPa.

title: Truthful Calibration Errors for Multi-Class Prediction
claim_source: Table 1 (Appendix F), page 22; illustrated in Figure 3, page 12 and Figure 1, page 3

official.background: Binned calibration errors such as the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) are widely used to evaluate and compare probabilistic classifiers, but prior empirical work (Nixon et al. 2019; Minderer et al. 2021) found that model rankings by calibration error can reverse when only the number of bins changes. The paper argues that this happens because standard binned errors are not truthful: a predictor can lower its measured error by reporting coarser, distorted probabilities instead of the true conditional distribution. It proposes truthful squared binned errors for multiclass prediction and argues that among nearly calibrated predictors they should rank models consistently with downstream loss, whatever the binning.
official.method:
The truthful classwise error LinCE^cw_B averages, over the k classes, a squared binned residual for each one-vs-all coordinate: for class r, bin the scalar reports p_i^(r) with an outcome-independent rule B, then compute (1/n^2) * sum over bins of (sum_{i in bin} (p_i^(r) - 1[y_i = r]))^2. The paper also defines a corrected confidence error ConfCE^corr (squared binned confidence residual plus a (1/n)(1 - accuracy) correction). The baselines are the standard l1 confidence ECE with fixed equal-width bins (ConfECE) and the squared confidence error without the correction (ConfCE), both of which the paper shows are non-truthful. Cal_(qua,m) means m quantile bins and Cal_(fix,m) means m fixed bins, with m in {2000, 20, 5}.

CIFAR-100 keeps the 50k training images, and the official 10k test set is split into 5k validation and 5k test (seed 42). The within-model pool uses 40 fine-tuning traces of ImageNet-pretrained timm mobilenetv3_small_100 trained on random subsets of 2.5% to 100% of the training data (steps of 2.5%), with 224x224 inputs, SGD (momentum 0.9), lr 1e-3, weight decay 5e-4, cosine schedule, batch size 256 and 100 epochs. Every epoch checkpoint (excluding warm-up epochs) is temperature-scaled on validation cross-entropy with L-BFGS and evaluated on the test split. Table 1 reports Spearman correlations across all checkpoints between classification error and each calibration error, and between the same error computed with different bin counts.
official.claim: On the within-model MobileNetV3-Small-1.0 CIFAR-100 checkpoint pool, the truthful classwise error with 5 quantile bins keeps a Spearman correlation of 0.884 ± 0.007 with classification error, whereas the standard confidence ECE with 5 fixed bins gives -0.277 ± 0.030 and the uncorrected squared confidence error with 5 quantile bins gives -0.121 ± 0.032. Across bin counts, LinCE^cw(2k) vs. LinCE^cw(5) correlate at 0.895 ± 0.007, against -0.285 ± 0.030 for ConfECE(2k) vs. ConfECE(5).
official.claim_caption: Spearman rank correlations on the test split for the calibration-error comparisons in our binning-robustness analysis. For each calibration-error family, the table reports the correlation between classification error and each calibration error, as well as the pairwise correlations among calibration errors computed with different bin choices. The last two columns compare the within-model MobileNetV3-Small-1.0 setting and the cross-model setting. The reported ± values denote 1.96 standard deviations for confidence estimation. Truthful calibration errors remain stable across binning choices, whereas non-truthful calibration errors are substantially more sensitive to the choice of bin size. In particular, truthful errors display better rank correlation among errors computed with different binning sizes.
official.metric: Spearman rank correlation over temperature-scaled checkpoints (higher = more consistent ranking); ± is 1.96 standard deviations (the paper does not say how the std is estimated); no seed replication
official.comparison: Truthful LinCE^cw (quantile bins) vs. non-truthful ConfECE (fixed bins) and ConfCE (quantile bins), with each error computed at 2000, 20 and 5 bins on the same checkpoints
official.falsification_criterion: On a re-run within-model pool, the Spearman correlation between classification error and LinCE^cw_(qua,5) is not clearly positive and not clearly higher than that of ConfECE_(fix,5) (e.g. LinCE^cw below about 0.6, or ConfECE_(fix,5) also above 0.6), or LinCE^cw_(qua,2k) and LinCE^cw_(qua,5) disagree in ranking about as much as ConfECE_(fix,2k) and ConfECE_(fix,5).

title: POME: Post Optimization Model Edit via Muon-Style Projection

official.background: Fine-tuning a pretrained LLM with Adam yields a weight update Delta W = W_ft - W_pre whose singular-value spectrum is dominated by a few directions. Matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon orthogonalize each step's update so that all directions contribute equally, but doing this every step is awkward in sharded (ZeRO/FSDP) training. The paper asks whether a fine-tuned model can be improved using only W_pre and W_ft, with no extra data or training, by applying a Muon-style projection once to the final accumulated update.
official.method:
For each selected layer, POME computes the SVD of Delta W = U Sigma V^T, keeps the top-k singular vectors (k = 0.5 * rank(Delta W) by default), sets all retained singular values to one, and rescales: Delta W_hat = alpha * U_k V_k^T, with alpha = beta * ||Delta W|| / ||U_k V_k^T|| (Eq. 12) and beta chosen on a small held-out validation set (Appendix A.3 suggests training accuracy can be used). The edited model is W_E = W_pre + Delta W_hat; all other layers are left unchanged. Based on a per-layer-type study (Table 1), the main experiments edit only the FFN up_proj matrices.

For the chosen claim, POME is applied to the publicly released MetaMath-Mistral-7B (huggingface.co/meta-math/MetaMath-Mistral-7B), with Delta W computed against its pretrained base checkpoint (the paper does not name it; presumably Mistral-7B-v0.1) and, per the paper's stated default for main experiments, only up_proj edited, and both the original and edited models are evaluated on GSM8K and MATH test sets (vLLM inference).
official.claim: Applying POME (up_proj layers, k = 0.5 * rank) to the public MetaMath-Mistral-7B checkpoint raises GSM8K accuracy from 77.9% to 79.5% (+1.6) and MATH accuracy from 28.1% to 28.5% (+0.4), with no extra data or training.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Effect of POME on the publicly available MetaMath-Mistral-7B model, demonstrating generalization to externally trained checkpoints.
official.metric: Test accuracy (%) on GSM8K and MATH, higher is better; single evaluation, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: MetaMath-Mistral-7B as released vs. the same checkpoint after the POME edit
official.falsification_criterion: With POME applied as described (up_proj, k = 0.5 * rank, beta tuned on held-out or training data, not the test set), the edited model does not improve GSM8K accuracy over the unedited checkpoint evaluated with the same prompt and decoding, or the gain is within the variation obtained across reasonable beta values / evaluation settings.

title: SCOPE-RL: Stable and Quantitative Control of Policy Entropy in RL Post-Training

official.background: GRPO is a common RL algorithm for post-training reasoning LLMs with verifiable rewards. During training its policy entropy tends to fall steadily (entropy collapse), so sampled outputs become homogeneous and exploration stops early. The usual fixes, entropy bonuses and clip-higher variants such as DAPO, can raise entropy, but the paper reports that they often make it oscillate and lower the reward. The paper wants a way to hold entropy at a chosen level so that exploration stays stable and the link between entropy and performance can be measured.
official.method:
SCOPE-RL adds an auxiliary policy-gradient term to the GRPO objective. At each update it samples extra rollouts at temperature T = clip(1 + H0 - H(pi_old), 0.8, 1.2), where H(pi_old) is the mean token entropy of the previous update and H0 = 0.5 is the target. Only correct (reward = 1) auxiliary trajectories are kept, with a target of 64 per update against 512 x 8 = 4096 standard rollouts. Their clipped likelihood ratio, taken against the untempered pi_old with no importance correction for the temperature, is added with weight alpha = 1/64. When entropy is below the target, high-temperature positive samples push it up; when it is above, low-temperature positive samples pull it down.

For the Llama extension (Appendix A.1), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is trained on Math12K for four epochs (91 updates) with seeds 1, 2 and 3. Rollout budgets are matched: the number of standard rollouts is reduced by the number of auxiliary rollouts, so every method uses the same total. Baselines are GRPO, DAPO, KL-Cov and CISPO (CISPO's training failed). Evaluation reports Pass@1 at sampling temperature 0.1, top-p 0.95 and 8192 max tokens on 12 math and knowledge benchmarks.
official.claim: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct trained on Math12K with matched rollout budgets (3 seeds), SCOPE-RL beats GRPO, DAPO and KL-Cov by more than the seed std on AIME24 (11.25 ± 1.00 vs. best baseline KL-Cov 8.58 ± 0.79, GRPO 7.74 ± 0.34) and on Minerva (29.17 ± 0.56 vs. best baseline GRPO 25.73 ± 1.33).
official.claim_caption: Additional results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over three independent random seeds. All methods use identical rollout budgets. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation.
official.metric: Pass@1 accuracy (%), higher is better; mean +/- std over 3 training seeds
official.comparison: SCOPE-RL vs. GRPO, DAPO, KL-Cov (CISPO failed to train) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, same data, same number of updates and same total rollout count
official.falsification_criterion: With 3 seeds under matched rollout budgets, SCOPE-RL's mean Pass@1 on AIME24 or on Minerva does not exceed the best of GRPO, DAPO and KL-Cov by more than the larger of the two seed stds.

title: SkipSR: Faster Super-Resolution with Token Skipping

official.background: Diffusion-based video super-resolution (SR) is the slow, expensive final stage of cascaded video generation and of video restoration, and its cost grows steeply with resolution because diffusion transformers use self-attention over all patches. Existing speed-ups reduce the number of diffusion steps or sparsify attention, but still spend the same compute on every patch. Many video regions (sky, plain walls, blurry backgrounds) have little high-frequency detail, so they could be upsampled cheaply instead of being refined by the transformer.
official.method:
The paper splits a high-resolution video I (T x H x W x 3) into non-overlapping 4 x 16 x 16 x 3 patches and calls a patch skippable if MSE(P, U(D(P))) <= tau, where D is 4x spatial area downsampling, U is bilinear upsampling and tau = 0.0002 (Eq. 1). To check that skipping does not degrade quality in the latent-diffusion setting, they encode I with the video VAE (8x spatial, 4x temporal compression; one skippable pixel patch corresponds to a 1 x 2 x 2 latent patch), replace the latents at skippable positions with the latents of U(D(I)), decode, and compute PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS against I. Expected speed-up is estimated by removing the skippable tokens from the SeedVR2 3B diffusion transformer and profiling it.

SkipSR itself trains a small 4-layer 3D-conv predictor on VAE latents of the low-resolution input to predict this mask, routes only unskipped tokens through the transformer (keeping their original RoPE positions and shifted-window assignments), and fine-tunes SeedVR/SeedVR2 3B with this masking. That training stage is not needed for the chosen claim.
official.claim: With the oracle mask (tau = 0.0002, 4x downsampling), 44.8% of patches are skippable on VBench 720p videos and 31.2% on VideoLQ 720p, and swapping them for bilinear-upsampled latents still gives PSNR 42.24 / 46.61 and LPIPS 0.0400 / 0.0239 against the original, with an estimated diffusion speed-up of 1.8x / 1.5x on SeedVR2.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Oracle Mask Analysis. Using the oracle mask, we measure the reconstruction error of upsampling and swapping simple patches, as well as the resulting expected speedup. We spatially downsample by 4x in all cases.
official.metric: Skippable % of 4x16x16 patches; PSNR (higher better), SSIM (higher better), LPIPS (lower better) of the VAE-decoded swapped video vs. the original high-resolution video; speed-up of the SeedVR2 diffusion transformer from dropping skippable tokens. Point estimates only; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Original high-resolution video vs. the same video with oracle-skippable latent patches replaced by latents of its 4x down-then-up-sampled version; dense SeedVR2 vs. SeedVR2 with skippable tokens removed (speed only).

title: HiLoRA: Adaptive Hierarchical LoRA Routing for Training-Free Domain Generalization

official.background: Community hubs host thousands of task-specific LoRA adapters, which suggests serving new inputs by reusing existing adapters instead of training new ones. In practice inputs come without task labels, may belong to tasks with no matching adapter, and activating a fixed number of whole adapters either brings in interfering parameters or leaves out useful ones. Existing routing methods often need task labels or trained gates, or use a fixed top-k, so a training-free router that adapts how much adapter capacity it activates per input would make LoRA reuse more practical.
official.method:
HiLoRA treats each rank of a LoRA (a row of the down-projection A paired with a column of the up-projection B) as a rank-one component (ROC). At the sequence level, each LoRA is represented by a Gaussian fitted to instructor-base embeddings of m = 20 examples from its training task; the input's length-normalised log-likelihood under each Gaussian is its score. If some score is positive, all LoRAs with positive score are kept; otherwise the top max(|max score|, k=3) are kept. A total ROC budget of gamma = 40% of the selected LoRAs' summed rank is split across them by multinomial sampling with softmax-of-score probabilities. At the token level, within each selected LoRA the o_i ROCs with the largest projection a^T x are activated, and the summed output is rescaled by sqrt(mean rank / budget). No parameters are trained.

In the within-cluster setting, ten FLAN-v2 NLI tasks are used: five are seen (their LoRAs are in the pool: ANLI-r1, ANLI-r3, MNLI, QNLI, SNLI) and five are unseen (ANLI-r2, CB, MNLI-mismatched, RTE, WNLI). LoRAs are downloaded from HuggingFace. Baselines, all training-free over the same pool except Phatgoose (trained gates), are Retriever (top-3 LoRAs by cosine similarity), LEGO (ROC clustering and merging), Arrow, Phatgoose, Ensemble (average all LoRAs), Merged (merge all LoRAs), plus two single-level ablations. Metric is per-task accuracy, averaged over the ten tasks.
official.claim: On the ten-task NLI within-cluster setting with LLaMA2-7B (five seen, five unseen tasks), HiLoRA reaches 63.41% average accuracy, versus 56.99% for the best non-HiLoRA baseline (Retriever) and 41.61% for Merged, close to the 65.13% of the oracle task-specific LoRA.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance on the NLI cluster using LLaMA2-7B and FLAN-T5-large. Tasks with a white background are set as seen tasks, while those with a gray background are set as unseen tasks. For each task, the best accuracy among all methods is in bold, and the second best is underlined.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) per task, higher is better, averaged over 10 NLI tasks; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: HiLoRA vs. Retriever, LEGO, Arrow, Phatgoose, Ensemble, Merged and the HiLoRA-GS / HiLoRA-ROC ablations; oracle per-task LoRA as upper reference
official.falsification_criterion: With the same LLaMA2-7B LoRA pool and seen/unseen split, HiLoRA's 10-task average accuracy is not at least about 3 points above Retriever (and the other external baselines), or the gap falls within the spread across several random seeds of HiLoRA's multinomial ROC allocation.

title: ViCO: A Training Strategy towards Semantic Aware Dynamic High-Resolution

official.background: Multimodal LLMs such as InternVL3.5 use dynamic high-resolution tiling: an image is split into up to 12 patches plus a thumbnail, each encoded as 256 visual tokens, so a single image can cost over 3,000 tokens and visual tokens dominate inference cost for documents, multi-image inputs and video. Existing token-reduction methods (e.g., FastV, SparseVLM) prune tokens with fixed hyperparameters, which tends to hurt vision-sensitive tasks such as OCR. The paper asks whether the number of tokens can be chosen per patch according to its semantic content instead.
official.method:
ViCO adds a second MLP connector with 16x downsampling (64 tokens per patch) beside the standard 4x connector (256 tokens per patch). In Consistency Training, a policy model sees images in which a random fraction (uniform in [0,1]) of patches use the 64-token connector, and is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its token-level response distribution and that of a frozen reference model that sees all patches uncompressed. In Router Training, the MLLM is frozen and a lightweight Visual Resolution Router (attention pooling over ViT features of a patch, then an MLP and softmax, ~50M parameters for 8B) is trained with cross-entropy to predict whether compressing that patch increases the consistency loss beyond a threshold (60th percentile of a sliding window of loss ratios).

At inference the router sends each patch to either 64 or 256 tokens. In Table 3, all variants are built on InternVL3.5-8B and evaluated on DocVQA (val), ChartQA, InfoVQA (val), TextVQA, OCRBench, AI2D, MMStar and BLINK. The comparison methods FastV and SparseVLM are applied to the original InternVL3.5-8B at a 'comparable average compression ratio'; the average column is performance relative to the uncompressed Vanilla model.
official.claim: On InternVL3.5-8B, ViCO (trained router, 55.0% of patches compressed on average) retains 99.6% of the uncompressed model's average score across 8 benchmarks, versus 95.9% for FastV and 91.2% for SparseVLM at comparable compression; the gap is largest on InfoVQA (78.6 vs 71.6 vs 55.2) and DocVQA (90.8 vs 87.5 vs 75.9).
official.claim_caption: Table 3. Ablation and comparative study of ViCO across general and strongly OCR-dependent benchmarks. Experiments are conducted on InternVL3.5-8B. For DocVQA and InfoVQA, the validation sets are used for performance evaluation.
official.metric: Benchmark accuracy/score (higher is better) and average relative to Vanilla InternVL3.5-8B (=100%); single runs, no error bars reported.
official.comparison: ViCO (InternVL3.5-8B with consistency training + patch-level router) vs. FastV and SparseVLM applied to vanilla InternVL3.5-8B at comparable average compression; Vanilla uncompressed model as the 100% reference.
official.falsification_criterion: With the released ViCO-8B (InternVL3.5-8B-Flash) checkpoint and FastV run on vanilla InternVL3.5-8B at a matched fraction of removed visual tokens, ViCO's InfoVQA/DocVQA scores are not clearly above FastV's (e.g., InfoVQA gap below ~2 points), or ViCO's average relative score falls below FastV's.

title: Assessing the robustness of heterogeneous treatment effects in survival analysis under informative censoring

official.background: Clinical studies often lose patients to dropout, and when dropout depends on survival time (informative censoring), standard estimators of the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) on survival time, which assume censoring is independent of survival, are biased and the CATE is not point-identified. The paper instead bounds the CATE: lower and upper bounds that remain valid under informative censoring, so clinicians can check whether a subgroup's treatment benefit stays positive regardless of how dropouts would have fared.
official.method:
For each treatment a, the conditional mean survival time is bounded below by mu-(x,a) = E[T~ | X=x, A=a] (the observed time min(T,C)) and above by mu+(x,a) = nu(0,x,a)[1 - xi(x,a)] + nu(1,x,a) xi(x,a) + gamma(x,a) xi(x,a), where nu(delta,x,a) = E[T~ | Delta=delta, X=x, A=a], xi(x,a) = P(censored | x,a), and gamma is a user-specified bound on expected post-dropout survival (Case 1, domain knowledge; gamma = 50 for the exponential scenario and 30 for sin and logistic-sin). Case 2 (conservative) uses t_max instead. CATE bounds are differences of these CAPO bounds.

The plug-in learner fits nu and xi with random forests and substitutes them into the bound formulas. The SurvB-learner is a two-stage, doubly robust meta-learner: nuisance functions (nu, xi, propensity pi) are fit with random forests under 3-fold cross-fitting, AIPW-style pseudo-outcomes (Eqs. 11-13) are built, and the pseudo-outcomes are regressed on X with a default random forest. Synthetic data (Appendix F): X ~ U[10,100], latent frailty U ~ N(0,1) that shortens both survival T and censoring time C (informative censoring), three treatment-effect functions (exponential, sin, logistic-sin), c0 tuned to censoring rates 0.2/0.4/0.6, 2000 samples per setting and seed. The metric is RMSE of the estimated bounds against oracle bounds computed from the true nuisance functions.
official.claim: With domain-knowledge bounds (Case 1) on synthetic informatively-censored data, SurvB-learner has lower bound-RMSE than the plug-in learner in all 9 scenarios, by margins several times the std over 5 runs, e.g. exponential xi=0.2: 2.541 ± 0.138 vs. 3.244 ± 0.152; sin xi=0.2: 0.799 ± 0.020 vs. 1.400 ± 0.067; logistic-sin xi=0.6: 1.739 ± 0.025 vs. 2.362 ± 0.051.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results for experiments with synthetic data. The experiments serve two purposes: (i) to show that our SurvB-learner obtains values close to the oracle bounds, and (ii) to demonstrate that the plug-in learner is not robust and therefore inferior. Experimental details are in Appendix H. We report the mean ± standard deviation of the RMSE compared to the oracle bound over 5 random runs for different synthetic datasets. Overall, we generate over 60 different datasets under varying scenarios. Our SurvB-learner outperforms the plug-in learner by a clear margin.
official.metric: RMSE of estimated CATE/CAPO bounds (upper and lower) vs. oracle bounds, lower is better; ± is std over 5 random runs
official.comparison: SurvB-learner (doubly robust two-stage meta-learner) vs. plug-in learner, both using default random forests for nuisance estimation, Case 1 domain-knowledge bounds
official.falsification_criterion: In the Case 1 domain-knowledge setting, SurvB-learner's mean RMSE is not lower than the plug-in learner's by more than one std over 5 seeds in a majority of the 9 (function, censoring strength) scenarios.

title: CanvasMAR: Improving Masked Autoregressive Video Prediction With Canvas

official.background: Masked autoregressive (MAR) models generate an image as continuous tokens, a few at a time in random order, with a small diffusion head per token. Applied to video prediction frame by frame, each frame starts from a fully masked grid. With only a few spatial sampling steps the early token sets have no global structure to build on, so frames become distorted, and the errors compound as frames are rolled out. That forces a trade-off between sampling speed and fidelity, which matters for low-latency or interactive video generation.
official.method:
CanvasMAR factorises generation into temporal and spatial autoregression. A Temporal ViT (causal across frames, bidirectional within a frame) encodes past latent frames into a temporal embedding. A Canvas ViT takes this embedding and the most recent frame and, in one deterministic forward pass, predicts a 'canvas': a blurred estimate of the next frame, trained with an L2 reconstruction loss through a linear head (weight 0.1). A Spatial MAR then generates the next frame's tokens set by set. Where vanilla MAR fills masked positions with a single learnable mask embedding, CanvasMAR uses the canvas embedding at those positions, and also conditions on the temporal embedding. The paper also adds a staticness head that orders sampling from low-motion to high-motion regions (MAS), and compositional classifier-free guidance.

For the claim, the authors train a model identical to CanvasMAR but without the canvas component, from scratch, and compare it with CanvasMAR (with and without MAS) under otherwise identical settings, without CFG, while varying the number of spatial autoregressive steps per frame. The BAIR setup is a 211M-parameter model on 64x64 frames (16x16 latents from a causal 3D CNN VAE), batch 192, 600 epochs, with 1 conditioning frame and 16 predicted frames. The metric is debiased FVD with K = 20 samples per test video over the 256 test videos.
official.claim: On BAIR video prediction without CFG, adding the canvas to an otherwise identical video MAR lowers debiased FVD at every step count from 1 to 8. At 4 autoregressive steps per frame (the default), FVD drops from about 50 without the canvas to about 32 with the canvas, and at 8 steps from about 35 to about 30.5.
official.claim_caption: Fig. 3: Component-level analysis. In the first two figures, classifier-free guidance is not used, and MAS represents the motion-aware sampling order. (a) Effectiveness of canvas and motion-aware sampling on BAIR. (b) Effectiveness of canvas and motion-aware sampling on UCF-101. (c) Effectiveness of compositional classifier-free guidance, where sCFG represents spatial (canvas) CFG, and tCFG represents the temporal CFG. The metric is FVD; the lower, the better.
official.metric: Debiased FVD on BAIR (lower is better), K = 20 generated clips per test video, 256 test videos. No error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported. Values are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: CanvasMAR (with canvas, with or without motion-aware sampling) vs. the same architecture trained from scratch without the canvas component, both without classifier-free guidance, across 1-8 spatial AR steps per frame
official.falsification_criterion: A matched re-implementation in which the no-canvas model reaches FVD within a few points of the canvas model at 2-4 AR steps on BAIR (e.g. no-canvas FVD below about 40 at 4 steps when the canvas model is about 32), or in which the gap shrinks to within seed-to-seed variation.

title: Catch Your Breath: Adaptive Computation for Self-Paced Sequence Production
claim_source: Table F.2 (Appendix F.1), page 22; seed replications in Section 4 text, page 6; same comparison shown in Figure 3 (right)

official.background: One way to give a transformer more computation per token without making it deeper is to insert <pause> tokens into the input stream, so each real token gets extra parallel forward steps before the next prediction. The standard recipe (Think Before You Speak, TBYS; Goyal et al. 2024) trains with ordinary cross-entropy read out only at the last pause, so the model cannot decide for itself when it is ready and, under causal masking, has to be ready to answer at every step. The paper asks whether letting the model choose when to read out within a fixed pause budget makes better use of the same compute.
official.method:
Catch Your Breath (CYB) inserts M-1 pause tokens after every real token (all pauses get the RoPE position of the preceding real token and distinct identities <pause1>, <pause2>, ...). At each step i the model outputs a <don't know> probability d_i (a repurposed unused vocabulary token, renormalised out of the next-token distribution and initialised with a high prior of 0.9 by adding a logit offset) and a next-token distribution whose target probability is t_i. With no forced stops (omega = 0:...:0:1) and no discounting (gamma_i = 1), the step at which the model answers has probability Pr(S=i) = (1 - d_i) * prod_{j<i} d_j (d_M = 0), and the loss per token is -log sum_i Pr(S=i) t_i. All pause steps are computed in parallel in one causal pass, so compute and memory equal TBYS.

TBYS uses the same pause insertion and position scheme but the loss -log t_M (cross-entropy at the final pause only). Pretrained Gemma3-4B is fine-tuned on 6.4M C4 sequences of 2048 real tokens (expanded to 4096/6144/8192 with 1/2/3 pauses), batch 64, 100k iterations, cosine LR with peak 1e-4/sqrt(d_model). Evaluation is perplexity of the real tokens on 160k C4 validation sequences (59.8M tokens); for CYB the prediction is the expected-accuracy mixture over readout steps implied by the loss. Baselines without pauses are fine-tuned on 2048 real tokens (data-matched) and on 8192 real tokens (compute-matched, 'Baseline 4xseq').
official.claim: Fine-tuning Gemma3-4B on C4 with 3 pause tokens after every real token, the CYB loss reaches C4 eval perplexity 10.131 vs. 10.359 for TBYS cross-entropy under identical pauses, data and compute (3-seed values 10.131/10.134/10.129 vs. 10.359/10.360/10.358); CYB with 1 pause (10.351) also matches TBYS with 3 pauses.
official.claim_caption: Table F.2: Results for fine-tuned (on C4) Gemma3-4B. Perplexity on eval set of C4. For relative improvement, we use the formula (5). In bold we highlight the best result – the lowest perplexity and the highest relative improvement.
official.metric: C4 validation-set perplexity (lower is better). The table reports single values; the text reports three replications (different data order) for baseline, CYB-3-pause and TBYS-3-pause only, with spread ~0.005. No error bars for 1- and 2-pause variants.
official.comparison: CYB vs. TBYS at 1, 2 and 3 pauses per token, matched in pause insertion, position encoding, data and compute; plus no-pause baselines (data-matched and 4x-sequence compute-matched)
official.falsification_criterion: With matched fine-tuning (same model, data, pauses and budget), CYB with 3 pauses does not achieve lower C4 eval perplexity than TBYS with 3 pauses by clearly more than the seed-to-seed spread (e.g., the gap is below ~1% relative or reverses).

title: STAR: Boosting Time Series Foundation Models for Anomaly Detection Through State-Aware Adapter

official.background: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used for multivariate time series anomaly detection. Industrial data often mixes numerical sensor channels (flow, speed) with discrete state variables (valve open/closed, machine position, day of week) that act as conditions on how the numerical channels should behave. TSFMs usually embed state variables with the same linear layers as numerical ones, and the authors show (Figure 1c) that adding state variables this way gives little benefit or even hurts detection. The paper asks whether a dedicated fine-tuning adapter that treats state variables as categorical conditions can recover that lost information.
official.method:
STAR is an adapter trained during fine-tuning while the TSFM backbone is frozen; only the numerical variables pass through the backbone. A State Extractor embeds each state variable from sinusoidal encodings of its variable index and current state value, routed (soft top-K) into a small learnable State Memory of N vectors with a load-balancing loss, followed by MLP intra/inter-patch temporal encoders and a weighted aggregation over state variables to give one state embedding per patch. A Conditional Bottleneck Adapter modifies backbone weights as ΔW = A R B ⊙ D, where A and B come from a frozen truncated SVD of the pretrained weight and the r×r matrix R (with a learned dynamic row mask) and vector D are generated per patch from the state embedding. A Numeral-State Matching module trains patch-level numeral and state embeddings with an InfoNCE contrastive loss (matched patch = positive).

Training loss is numerical reconstruction + λ1·load-balance + λ2·matching. At test time the anomaly score is the reconstruction MSE (averaged over numerical variables) multiplied by a softmax of the interpolated patch-level matching score. Table 1 fine-tunes each backbone (DADA, UniTS, Moment, Timer) on 10% of the downstream data under three regimes: standard fine-tuning, LoRA fine-tuning, and STAR, on MSL, SMAP, SWaT, Genesis and NYC, reporting threshold-free AUC-ROC, VUS-ROC and VUS-PR.
official.claim: On the Genesis dataset, adding STAR to a frozen TSFM gives higher VUS-ROC than the stronger of LoRA and standard fine-tuning of the same backbone for all four backbones: DADA 0.911 vs 0.832 (standard; LoRA 0.818), UniTS 0.850 vs 0.777 (LoRA), Moment 0.950 vs 0.908 (LoRA), Timer 0.944 vs 0.887 (LoRA).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results of adapters for different TFSMs. The better results are highlighted in bold.
official.metric: VUS-ROC (V-R), higher is better; AUC-ROC and VUS-PR also reported. Single numbers per cell; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Backbone + STAR vs. the stronger of Backbone + LoRA and standard fine-tuning (LoRA for UniTS, Moment and Timer; standard fine-tuning for DADA) for DADA, UniTS, Moment and Timer, each fine-tuned on 10% of the Genesis data
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the three fine-tuning regimes on Genesis, STAR's V-R fails to exceed the better of LoRA and standard fine-tuning for at least two of the four backbones, or the average margin over that baseline falls below ~0.02 or within the seed-to-seed spread of the reproduction.

title: Zeroth-Order Sharpness-Aware Learning with Exponential Tilting

official.background: Zeroth-order (gradient-free) optimizers such as MeZO fine-tune language models using only loss evaluations at randomly perturbed parameters, so they need about as much memory as inference. The standard two-point estimator implicitly minimizes the average loss in a neighborhood of the parameters, which acts as a weak sharpness penalty (the Hessian trace). First-order sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) instead penalizes the worst-case loss in the neighborhood, which tends to find flatter minima that generalize better and are more robust to label noise, but it needs backpropagation and extra memory. The paper asks whether a zeroth-order method can target a SAM-like objective at no extra cost.
official.method:
ZEST minimizes the tilted SAM objective F_t(x) = (1/t) log E_eps[exp(t f(x+eps))], which interpolates between the average loss (t -> 0, i.e. MeZO) and the max loss (t -> infinity, i.e. SAM). Per step it samples k random Gaussian directions v_i (regenerated from seeds rather than stored), evaluates the minibatch loss at x + rho v_i and x - rho v_i, forms a_i^± = exp(t f(x ± rho v_i)) normalized by their sum Z, and updates x <- x - eta (w_i / (t rho)) v_i for each i. ZEST_N uses w_i = ā_i^+ - ā_i^- (naive ratio-of-expectations plug-in). ZEST_BC multiplies this by a bias-correction factor.

Experiments use the MeZO code base, data processing and prompts (Malladi et al., 2023). RoBERTa-base is fine-tuned with prompts on 8 GLUE-style tasks, sampling 512 training examples per class. In the noisy variant, 30% of training labels are switched uniformly at random to another label. Zeroth-order settings: Gaussian perturbations, rho = 0.002, k = 5, batch size 128, learning rate tuned over {2e-5, 1e-5, 5e-6}, up to 700 epochs with early stopping, t tuned over {1, 5, 20} on validation data (MeZO is ZEST with t = 0). Test accuracy is reported.
official.claim: When RoBERTa-base is fine-tuned on 512 examples per class with 30% of labels flipped, ZEST_N beats MeZO in test accuracy by 5.9 points on QQP (68.3 vs. 62.4), 5.7 on SNLI (64.9 vs. 59.2) and 3.1 on MNLI (63.4 vs. 60.3), with identical zeroth-order budget and memory.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Experiments on RoBERTa-Base (512 training examples per class with 30% noisy labels). The objectives of each method are in Table 1.
official.metric: Test accuracy (%), higher is better; single number per cell, no error bars or seed count reported
official.comparison: ZEST_N (tilted zeroth-order estimator, t tuned in {1,5,20}) vs. MeZO (vanilla two-point zeroth-order estimator, equivalent to t = 0) on RoBERTa-base with 30% noisy labels; first-order SGD/ESAM/SAM/TSAM shown for reference
official.falsification_criterion: Over several seeds with the same tuning grids, ZEST_N's mean test accuracy on noisy QQP, SNLI and MNLI does not beat MeZO's by clearly more than the seed-to-seed spread (e.g. the gap falls below ~1 point or flips sign on at least two of the three tasks).

title: Prediction-Augmented Trees for Reliable Statistical Inference

official.background: Prediction-powered inference (PPI) and its tuned variant PPI++ build confidence intervals for a quantity such as a population mean from a small set of n labeled samples, a large set of N unlabeled samples, and a black-box ML predictor f. They add the mean prediction on the unlabeled data to a single global estimate of the mean residual Y - f(X) from the labeled data. When the residuals vary systematically across the feature space, one global correction leaves variance unexplained, so the intervals are wider than they need to be. Narrower intervals that still have valid coverage mean fewer expensive labels are needed for the same precision.
official.method:
PART (Prediction-Augmented Residual Tree) builds a CART-style binary tree over the feature space. Candidate split thresholds are midpoints between consecutive empirical quantiles (levels 1/n, ..., (n-1)/n) of each feature in the unlabeled data. Each split greedily minimizes the Variance of Mixture of Splits criterion VMS = p_left^2 * s_left^2 / n_left + p_right^2 * s_right^2 / n_right, where p is the unlabeled-data mass of the child region and s^2 is the sample variance of the labeled residuals in it. Splitting stops at maximum depth D or when a region has fewer than m labeled points. The estimate is mean_N f(X~) + sum_l p_l * rbar_l, where rbar_l is the mean residual in leaf l. The variance estimate is sum_l p_l^2 * s_l^2 / n_l, which gives a Wald interval. With depth 0, PART reduces to PPI.

For the wine experiment, the dataset is Vinho Verde wine quality (Cortez et al.) with 11 physicochemical features and a 0-10 quality score. The paper describes the dataset as 1,280 wine samples. A Random Forest classifier is trained on 20% of the data and predicts scores for the remaining 80%, which form the M evaluation samples (the paper does not state M; see caveats). For each n in {300, 375, 450, 525, 600}, n of the M samples are randomly kept as labeled and the other N = M - n are treated as unlabeled. PART with depth 2 and PPI++ are run on the same split, recording the interval width and whether the interval covers the true mean of all M labels. This is repeated 100 times per n.
official.claim: When estimating mean Vinho Verde wine quality with random-forest predictions, depth-2 PART gives narrower confidence intervals than PPI++ at every labeled size n from 300 to 600: about 0.128 vs 0.150 at n=300 and 0.093 vs 0.107 at n=600 (roughly 10-15% narrower). Both methods' coverage stays at or above the 0.90 target.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Estimating the mean quality of Portugese Vinho Verde wine [20] (see Section 5 for testing methodology).

title: Strengthening LLMs for Tabular Prediction with Structural Priors
claim_source: Figure 4, page 9 (exact gaps stated in Section 3.3, page 8)

official.background: Tabular prediction is dominated by gradient-boosted trees and specialised models such as TabPFN, while LLMs, despite cross-task transfer and readable reasoning, remain weak on tables. RL post-training with GRPO has improved LLM reasoning in maths, but on tabular prediction the outcome reward is sparse (a base model often gets few rollouts right), so group-relative advantages carry little signal. This paper uses a structural prior of tables, that the label does not change when columns are reordered, to obtain denser training signal from each labelled row.
official.method:
Each table row is serialised as 'The [feature] is [value].' sentences plus a task question. PRPO samples m label-preserving column permutations of a row, generates G rollouts per permutation, and gives each rollout a rule-based reward (classification: 1.0 correct, 0.1 wrong but well-formatted, 0 otherwise; regression: 1.0 if NMAE < 0.1, 0.1 if valid but NMAE >= 0.1, 0 otherwise). Advantages are computed both within each permutation group (intra) and over all m*G rollouts pooled (inter) and combined as alpha*intra + (1-alpha)*inter (alpha = 0.1 in Table 4), then used in the usual GRPO clipped objective with KL penalty. Base model Qwen3-8B-Base, verl, lr 1e-6, KL 0.001, batch 128, m = 4, G = 5, max response 1024 tokens.

The ablation (Figure 4) holds the rollout budget at 20 rollouts per original row and compares A0 standard GRPO (m=1, G=5), A1 GRPO with G=20, A2 GRPO with random column order per sample (m=1, G=20), A3 intra-only advantages (m=4, G=5), A4 inter-only advantages (m=4, G=5) and A5 full PRPO (m=4, G=5). Curves show mean test accuracy over the classification datasets and mean NMAE over the regression datasets as training proceeds to step 700. The final A5 values (0.843 / 0.150) match the fully supervised setting of Table 1 (50 classification and 15 regression OpenML datasets, trained and tested on each dataset's own split).
official.claim: Under a matched budget of 20 rollouts per row, full PRPO post-training of Qwen3-8B-Base reaches about 0.843 mean classification accuracy at step 700, versus about 0.745 for GRPO with 20 rollouts (A1), 0.739 for standard GRPO (A0) and 0.765 for GRPO with random column order (A2, a stated gap of +0.078); on regression PRPO reaches about 0.150 mean NMAE versus about 0.163-0.166 for the GRPO variants.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Attribution ablation on classification and regression datasets. A0 is standard GRPO; A1–A5 isolate rollout count, random column order, intra-only, inter-only, and full PRPO under matched rollout budgets.
official.metric: Mean test accuracy over classification datasets (higher is better) and mean NMAE over regression datasets (lower is better) against training step; single run, no error bars or seeds reported; values read off the plot are approximate except the gaps stated in the text
official.comparison: Full PRPO (A5, m=4, G=5) vs. standard GRPO (A0, G=5), GRPO with more rollouts (A1, G=20), GRPO with random column-order training (A2, G=20), intra-only (A3) and inter-only (A4) permutation advantages, all at 20 rollouts per original sample
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the compute-matched comparison on the same datasets, full PRPO's final mean classification accuracy is less than about 0.03 above GRPO with 20 rollouts (A1) or random column-order GRPO (A2), or the gap is within the spread across seeds; or PRPO's regression NMAE is not lower than the GRPO variants.

title: LIME: Link-based User-item Interaction Modeling with Decoupled XOR Attention for Efficient Test Time Scaling

official.background: Ranking models for recommendation trade accuracy against serving cost. Two-tower models are cheap because the user and item representations are computed independently, but they interact only through a final dot product. Target-attention transformers such as DIN or HSTU let each candidate attend over the user's interaction history and are more accurate, but their cost grows with history length (quadratically for self-attention) and linearly with the number of candidates, which makes them too expensive for large candidate sets. The paper aims for transformer-like accuracy at close to two-tower cost.
official.method:
LIME introduces ℓ learned global 'link embeddings' L. On the user side, L is contextualized with user features (MLP) and then personalized by attending over the user history E, producing L^P. In LIME-XOR this user module is a 3-layer HSTU-style block with an 'XOR' mask: history tokens attend only to link tokens and link tokens attend only to history tokens (no history-to-history attention), so the cost is O(ℓ·N) rather than O(N²). The personalized links are the sum of the layer outputs (Eq. 8).

On the candidate side, decoupled attention uses the raw, user-independent links as keys and the personalized links as values: O = φ(T Lᵀ) L^P (Eq. 4). The attention weights φ(T Lᵀ) depend only on the item and can be precomputed and cached, so per-candidate scoring is a weighted sum over ℓ vectors followed by a shallow MLP. Taobao-Ad experiments use the FuxiCTR preprocessing (max sequence length 50); Table 1 uses 32 links (VISTA with 32 seed embeddings as the matched budget), five seeds, and identical other components across models. TTSN is the sum-pooling two-tower baseline.
official.claim: On Taobao-Ad with five seeds, LIME-XOR (32 links) reaches AUC 0.646799 ± 0.000239, above the efficient baselines TTSN (0.645368 ± 0.000216) and VISTA with 32 seed embeddings (0.646075 ± 0.000224), and has the lowest log loss of all five models (0.192545 ± 0.000111).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Five-seed Taobao-Ad results (mean ± standard deviation). Lower log loss is better.
official.metric: AUC (higher is better), also gAUC and log loss (lower is better); mean ± standard deviation over 5 seeds (VISTA label says 32 seeds, which refers to its 32 seed embeddings)
official.comparison: LIME-XOR (32 links) vs. TTSN (sum-pooling two-tower) and VISTA (authors' implementation, 32 seed embeddings), with DIN and HSTU as more expensive target-attention references, all on the same Taobao-Ad split and training protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Over 5 seeds on Taobao-Ad (32 links, matched protocol), LIME-XOR's mean AUC does not exceed both TTSN's and VISTA's by more than one seed std. (The log-loss lead over VISTA, DIN and HSTU is smaller than one reported std, so log loss alone should not be used to confirm or refute the claim.)

title: Estimating Model-Level Membership Inference Vulnerability Without Reference Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (scatter in Figure 3, page 8; extended baselines in Table 4, page 23)

official.background: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) are the standard way to measure how much a trained model leaks about its training data, usually reported as the attack's true positive rate at a very low false positive rate. The strongest attack, LiRA, needs tens to hundreds of reference models trained like the target model, which makes privacy auditing too expensive for routine use such as hyperparameter search or repeated retraining. Cheaper attacks like RMIA still need at least one or two reference models. The paper asks whether a model's vulnerability to LiRA can be estimated from the target model's own train and test loss distributions, with no reference models.
official.method:
The target is an image classifier trained on a random 50% of a dataset's training split (members), with the other 50% held out (non-members), following Carlini et al. (2022). Ten architectures (ResNet-20, ResNet-18, WRN28-2, WRN40-4, WRN28-10, MobileNetV2, DenseNet121, VGG11, VGG16, plus ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B-16 fine-tuned on CIFAR-10 only) are trained on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CINIC-10 and CIFAR-100 (37 configurations) with SGD, momentum 0.9, cosine LR schedule, batch size 256, 50-200 epochs, weight decay and augmentation, to training accuracy above 90%. Ground truth is online LiRA with K = 64 reference models (32 IN, 32 OUT) and 2 mirror augmentations, reported as TPR at FPR = 1e-3.

The proposed reference-free estimator is the LOSS attack TNR: using only the target model's per-sample losses at the final epoch, choose the loss threshold so that the false negative rate on members equals 1e-3, then report the fraction of non-members whose loss is above the threshold. Each candidate statistic (LOSS TNR, LOSS AUC, LT-IQR AUC, KS distance, train-test accuracy gap, and the TPR of online RMIA with 2 reference models) is mapped to LiRA TPR with a one-parameter least-squares line anchored at that statistic's no-signal point (the origin, or 0.5 for AUC-type statistics), and the fit is scored by R^2, RMSE and MAE across the 37 configurations.
official.claim: Across 37 image-classifier configurations (10 architectures x 4 datasets), a one-parameter linear fit of reference-free LOSS TNR@FNR=1e-3 predicts online LiRA TPR@FPR=1e-3 (K=64) with RMSE 0.036 (R^2 0.944), better than RMIA with 2 reference models (RMSE 0.046) and the best reference-free baselines LT-IQR AUC and LOSS AUC (RMSE 0.068 each).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance of reference-free statistics and RMIA as predictors of LiRA TPR@FPR=10^-3, across the 10 image-classification architectures and 4 datasets of Section 4. Each statistic is mapped to LiRA TPR by a one-parameter least-squares fit anchored at that statistic's no-signal point: the origin for tail statistics, gaps and distances, and chance (0.5) for AUC-type statistics. Baselines are ordered by RMSE; our estimator is set off below them. LOSS TNR is the strongest predictor, ahead even of RMIA, which requires training two reference models.
official.metric: R^2, RMSE and MAE of a one-parameter anchored linear fit to LiRA TPR@FPR=1e-3 across configurations; lower RMSE is better. No error bars on these values (the paper reports only bootstrap confidence bands around the fitted line in Figure 3).
official.comparison: LOSS TNR (reference-free) vs. RMIA with 2 reference models, LT-IQR AUC, LOSS AUC, KS distance and train-test accuracy gap, all fit against the same LiRA TPR values
official.falsification_criterion: On a reproduced set of image configurations, the anchored linear fit of LOSS TNR to LiRA TPR@FPR=1e-3 has RMSE no lower than that of LOSS AUC (or of RMIA with 2 reference models), or its RMSE is far above 0.036 (e.g. above 0.068).

title: ARC-Encoder: learning compressed text representations for large language models

official.background: Long contexts from retrieval-augmented generation or chain-of-thought make LLM inference expensive, because prefill cost grows with the number of input tokens. Hard compression such as LLMLingua2 deletes tokens and works with any model, but it only achieves about 2x compression. Soft compression maps text to a few dense vectors (memory tokens, gist tokens, xRAG, PISCO), but most such methods fine-tune the target decoder, which can hurt its general abilities and ties each encoder to a single decoder. The paper asks whether an external trainable encoder can produce compressed representations that an unmodified decoder reads in place of token embeddings, at a fixed compression ratio, without losing much accuracy compared with reading the full text.
official.method:
ARC-Encoder is Llama3.2 3B with its last two layers removed and no causal mask. In the self-attention of its final layer, consecutive queries are averaged in groups of x (the pooling factor, 4 or 8) and attend to the unpooled keys and values, so the encoder outputs n/x vectors for n input tokens. A 2-layer MLP without activation (3072 -> 2048 -> 4096) maps these vectors into the decoder's embedding space. The decoder (Mistral 7B base) stays frozen; the compressed vectors replace the context's token embeddings, followed by a learned <Cont> token. The encoder, MLP and special tokens are pretrained on about 2.6B Common Crawl tokens (80k steps), alternating between reconstruction (20%) and continuation tasks. They are then fine-tuned (4k steps) on a mix of QA with retrieved passages, reading comprehension, summarization and synthetic translation data, in an interleaved 5-shot format. The training sets of the evaluation benchmarks are excluded. ARC4 uses the encoder pretrained at PF 8 and fine-tuned at PF 4.

Evaluation is 5-shot with every context document compressed: NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA (top-5 passages retrieved with NV-Embed v2 from Atlas Wikipedia) and SQuAD use exact match; FLORES (En->Da/Fr/De/Es) uses BLEU; CNN-DailyMail uses ROUGE-L. Baselines on the same decoder are closed-book, open-book (full text), LLMLingua2 (off-the-shelf), and ICAE-like, xRAG-like and PISCO-like re-implementations. The authors fine-tuned these re-implementations on their own data and few-shot format; PISCO-like also fine-tunes the decoder with LoRA, and one variant uses 128-token chunks to get a fixed 4x ratio.
official.claim: With a frozen Mistral 7B base decoder and 5-shot evaluation, ARC4-Encoder (4x pooling) averages 46.5 over NQ/TQA/HQA/SQuAD/FLORES/CNN, versus 41.4 for LLMLingua2 (1.9x), 39.5 for PISCO-like at 4x and 38.4 for ICAE-like; the open-book full-text score is 49.2. On SQuAD it scores 71.1 EM vs. 59.2 for the best baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main comparison of ARC-Encoder and other models. 'PF' (pooling factor): the token reduction factor (e.g., 4x) for fixed-ratio methods or the number of compressed tokens used, e.g. ~16, when this number is fixed as this yields benchmark-dependent ratios; 'Param.': number of parameters of the encoder; 'Avg. length': mean number of tokens per context document. The superscript on ARC-Encoder indicates if the model is specifically trained for one decoder (M for Mistral or L for Llama) or both simultaneously (⊗). † marks modified re-implementations, see details in Appendix D.1. Best context compression results are in bold, second best are underlined.
official.metric: Exact match (NQ, TQA, HQA, SQuAD), BLEU (FLORES), ROUGE-L (CNN), and their unweighted average; higher is better. Table 1 reports single runs (fine-tuning seed fixed to 0) with no error bars. For reference, Tables 5-7 report std over 3 fine-tuning seeds for a closely related ARC8 model: about 0.1-0.4 on the average and up to 2.0 on SQuAD.
official.comparison: ARC4-Encoder^M (Mistral-specific) vs. LLMLingua2, PISCO-like (~32 memory tokens and 4x chunked), ICAE-like and xRAG-like, all with the same frozen Mistral 7B decoder (PISCO-like also LoRA-tunes the decoder); closed-book and open-book as reference points.
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduced ARC4-Encoder on Mistral 7B averages within about 1 point of the best re-run compression baseline (LLMLingua2 or PISCO-like 4x) under the same 5-shot protocol, or fails to beat LLMLingua2 on average.

title: Optimal In-context Adaptivity and Distributional Robustness of Transformers
claim_source: Figure 4, page 10 (also Figure 2, page 2; more shifts in Figure 5, page 45)

official.background: In-context learning (ICL) theory usually assumes that a Transformer is tested on the same task distribution it was pretrained on. In practice, models are pretrained on a mixture of tasks of different difficulty and tested on a shifted distribution. The paper asks whether a Transformer pretrained on a mixture of nonparametric regression tasks with random smoothness can, in-context, reach the optimal convergence rate for the smoothness of each new test task (adaptivity), and whether this still holds when the test distribution is shifted from the pretraining prior (robustness). It proves that it can, by viewing the pretrained Transformer as an approximation of the posterior regression function and applying posterior contraction theory.
official.method:
Simulation (Section 5, Appendix I): single-index regression tasks with n = 30 in-context examples, ambient dimension d = 5, index dimension p = 1, noise sigma = 0.01 and covariates uniform on the unit ball. The regression link function is a random Besov function with smoothness alpha in {2, 2.5, 3, 4}, generated by a random wavelet-type expansion (eq. 41) with C0 = 2 and coefficients (a_k), (b_{l,gamma}) i.i.d. Unif[-1, 1]. One GPT-2-medium-style Transformer (L = 24, H = 16, d_model = 1024, d_ffn = 4096, GELU, pre-LN) is pretrained to predict the query output. It is trained with AdamW (lr 3e-4, cosine schedule, weight decay 1e-3, gradient clipping) for 200,000 steps of 576 sequences each (36 functions x 16 prompts). The curriculum is: d raised from 1 to 5 over the first 10k steps (alpha = 4), then a smoothness curriculum for 50k steps, then a uniform mixture over alpha for the last 140k steps.

Test: 100,000 fresh random functions for each fixed alpha, under (i) no shift (same generator as pretraining) and (ii) within-support shift, where the coefficients (a_k) are drawn from Unif[0, 1] instead of Unif[-1, 1]. The metric is query MSE with 90% CIs. Theorem 4.3 predicts a rate n^{-2alpha/(2alpha+1)}, so log MSE should be roughly linear in 2alpha/(2alpha+1).
official.claim: A single Transformer pretrained on a uniform mixture of single-index regression tasks with smoothness alpha in {2, 2.5, 3, 4} reaches test MSE that decreases strictly with alpha, from about 4.5e-3 at alpha = 2 to about 0.3e-3 at alpha = 4 (no shift), with log MSE approximately linear in 2alpha/(2alpha+1). Under the within-support coefficient shift, MSE stays close to the unshifted value (about 5.3e-3 vs. 4.5e-3 at alpha = 2, and nearly equal at alpha = 4).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: MSE and log MSE at test time based on 100,000 random test functions. Error bars represent 90% confidence intervals. (a) MSE against alpha. (b) Log MSE against 2alpha/(2alpha+1).
official.metric: Test-time query MSE (lower is better) over 100,000 random test functions per alpha; error bars are 90% confidence intervals over test functions (single training run, no seeds)
official.comparison: MSE across smoothness levels alpha for the same pretrained model, and shifted vs. unshifted test distributions. No competing estimator is evaluated.
official.falsification_criterion: MSE is not monotonically decreasing in alpha (CIs overlap or the order reverses between adjacent alpha levels), or log MSE departs clearly from a linear trend in 2alpha/(2alpha+1), or the shifted MSE is many times larger than the unshifted MSE at some alpha.

title: DEBATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Evaluating Opinion Dynamics in Role-Playing LLM Agents
claim_source: Figure 4 (left panels), page 8; numbers in Section 5.3 text and Appendix Q (page 28)

official.background: Researchers increasingly simulate how opinions change in groups by having role-playing LLM agents (RPLAs) talk to each other, but such simulations are known to drift toward unnatural consensus, and there has been little real human group data to check them against. DEBATE collects 4-person online deliberations on 107 controversial topics from U.S. Prolific participants (2,788 participants in 697 groups after cleaning), with private Likert opinions before and after three rounds of tweet-like posts and dyadic chats. This makes it possible to compare how much simulated groups converge with how much the matched real groups did.
official.method:
Each human participant is paired with a 'digital twin' agent whose prompt (memory) holds the participant's demographics, initial 6-point Likert opinion with free-text justification, their first tweet, and the interaction history. In Full Dynamics Simulation (the paper's primary setting), the four agents of a group roll out rounds 2 and 3 recursively: later tweets and chat utterances are generated by the agents and fed back into memory, starting from the human round-1 tweet and the human initial opinion. At the end, each agent produces a final private opinion (Likert rating plus justification). Public tweet stances are scored 1-6 by a gpt-5-mini stance judge; seven LLMs are evaluated zero-shot (gpt-5-mini, gpt-4o-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-32B, Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.1-8B), plus an SFT-tuned Llama-3.1-8B and a fitted DeGroot baseline.

Convergence for a group g is ΔSD_g = SD(final stances of the 4 members) − SD(initial stances); in the private channel these are the final and initial reported opinions. Figure 4 reports the mean ΔSD over groups of the group-generalization test split (136 groups) for humans and for each system, with bootstrap standard errors over groups. More negative means stronger convergence.
official.claim: On the DEBATE group-generalization test split under Full Dynamics Simulation, zero-shot Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct agent groups over-converge in private opinions relative to the matched human groups: mean within-group private-opinion ΔSD is −0.41 for the agents vs. −0.13 for humans (p ≈ 0.020), and every one of the seven zero-shot LLMs is more convergent than humans in the private channel.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Post-training convergence summaries and stance-SD trajectories on the group-generalization test split. The left two panels report public and private C^c(m); the right two show the matching stance-SD trajectories. More negative bars indicate stronger convergence. Error bars denote bootstrap standard errors, and the reference baselines are defined in Sec. 5.1. Appendix I gives DeGroot-fitting details, and Appendix S shows the same convergence summary on the topic-generalization split.
official.metric: Mean over groups of ΔSD = SD(final) − SD(initial) of the 4 members' 6-point private opinions (more negative = more convergence). Error bars are bootstrap standard errors over groups; the p-value is the paper's normal approximation on the aggregate bars. Single simulation run per model, no seed variance reported.
official.comparison: Simulated agent groups (zero-shot Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, plus the six other zero-shot LLMs) vs. the real human groups they are twins of, on the same 136 test groups and topics
official.falsification_criterion: Re-simulating the group-generalization test split with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in Full Dynamics Simulation gives a private-opinion mean ΔSD within about one bootstrap SE of the human value (≈ −0.13), or less negative than it.
