title: PORTool: Importance-Aware Policy Optimization with Rewarded Tree for Multi-Tool-Integrated Reasoning

official.background: LLM tool-use agents trained with reinforcement learning from outcome-only rewards face a credit-assignment problem: a single reward for the whole trajectory says nothing about which intermediate tool calls caused success or failure. GRPO-style methods broadcast the same advantage to every step, which can reinforce bad tool calls that happen to appear in successful rollouts and suppress necessary steps that co-occur with failures. Step-supervised alternatives need ground-truth intermediate tool calls, which fix a single canonical routine and handle dynamic, real-time tool outputs poorly.
official.method:
PORTool samples the n = 8 rollouts per query as a bounded-branching tree in which trajectories share prefixes and then diverge at selected tool-call steps. A GPT-4o judge labels each finished trajectory true / false / unable_to_answer (+1 / -1 / 0). Each step gets an importance score R(s) = G over descendant trajectories k of [γ^(T_k - t) R_out(τ_k)] + R_fm(s), where R_fm ∈ [-0.25, 0.25] is a tool-call format/execution reward, γ = 0.95, and G is max when sibling steps at the fork have different rewards and average otherwise.

The token advantage for a step is the average trajectory-relative (GRPO-style z-scored outcome) advantage over trajectories passing through it plus ω2 times a fork-relative advantage (the step's R(s) z-scored among its siblings), with ω2 set by Theorem 3.2. Training is a GRPO-style clipped objective without KL, after 5 epochs of SFT, for 15 RL epochs with LoRA (rank 16), batch 512, lr 1e-6, at most 6 tool-call steps. Baselines (GRPO, GRPO+format reward, DAPO, ARPO, ARPO+format reward, AgentFlow, SimpleTIR, ToRL) use the same SFT start, data and tools. Evaluation is on 535 held-out queries from a dataset of 3,607 real assistant queries across 8 domains; accuracy is judged by GPT-4o with five-vote majority plus human adjudication of unable_to_answer cases.
official.claim: On the 535-query held-out set, PORTool reaches 51.98 ± 1.09% final-answer accuracy with Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct versus 48.23 ± 1.06% for the best baseline (AgentFlow), and 46.60 ± 1.22% with Qwen-3-1.7B versus 42.76 ± 1.78% for the best baseline (GRPO with format reward), while also using the fewest tool-call steps (3.07 and 2.64).

Reported numbers are the average of the best three checkpoints during training (Appendix C.6). Also average tool-call steps (lower is better), unanswerable rate (lower is better), and formatting reward, all without error bars.

title: Outlier-Robust Multi-Output Gaussian Processes

official.background: Multi-output Gaussian processes (MOGPs) model several correlated response variables jointly and have a closed-form posterior when the noise is Gaussian. That assumption makes them fragile: a single outlier in one output distorts predictions for that output and, through the cross-output correlation, for the other outputs too. Existing robust alternatives swap in Student-t or Laplace likelihoods, which break conjugacy and need variational approximations that are much slower, on top of the already cubic O(N^3 T^3) cost of MOGPs.
official.method:
R-MOGP replaces the likelihood with a generalised-Bayes posterior built on a weighted Fisher divergence, extending robust conjugate GPs (RCGPs) to multiple outputs. Each observation y_{i,t} gets an inverse-multiquadric weight w_t = beta_t (1 + ((y_t - gamma_t)/c_t)^2)^(-1/2), where the centre gamma_t is the conditional mean of output t given the other outputs at the same input (borrowing strength across outputs), c_t is the (1 - eps_t) quantile of |y_{i,t} - gamma_t|, and beta_t = sigma_t/sqrt(2). The posterior stays Gaussian and closed form (same cost as an MOGP). Hyperparameters (kernel, noise) are fit with a weighted leave-one-out CV objective in which each LOO term is weighted by (w_{i,t}/beta_t)^2.

On the UCI Energy Efficiency dataset (d = 8 inputs, T = 2 outputs: heating and cooling load, standardised; 75/25 split, N = 576 train) an ICM kernel with a squared-exponential base kernel is used. 10% of heating-load training values are contaminated: Uniform (add or subtract U(6,9), half each), Asymmetric (add U(6,9)), or Student-t (add t_3(0,5)) noise. The baseline MOGP uses the same kernel, shared noise sigma_t = sigma, prior mean set to the output's mean, and an unweighted LOO-CV objective. Metrics are test RMSE and NLPD over 10 random train/test splits per scenario.
official.claim: On UCI Energy Efficiency with 10% of heating-load observations contaminated, R-MOGP reaches test RMSE 0.17 ± 0.02 (uniform outliers) and 0.16 ± 0.02 (asymmetric outliers) versus 2.27 ± 0.29 and 2.18 ± 0.18 for a standard MOGP with the same kernel, while matching the MOGP without outliers (0.12 ± 0.01 for both).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Average and standard deviation of RMSE and NLPD on the Energy Efficiency dataset under different outlier scenarios (10 seeds per scenario). Best results are highlighted in bold. Figure 4: Average runtime per function evaluation on the Energy Efficiency dataset across 40 runs.
official.metric: Test RMSE (lower is better) and NLPD (lower is better) on standardised outputs; ± is the standard deviation over 10 random train/test splits
official.comparison: R-MOGP (IMQ weights, w-LOO-CV) vs. standard MOGP (Gaussian likelihood, LOO-CV), same ICM kernel and data splits; t-MOGP and L-MOGP (variational GPflow) also reported
official.falsification_criterion: Under uniform or asymmetric 10% outliers, R-MOGP's RMSE is not clearly below the MOGP's (e.g. not at least 2x lower, or within a few std of each other), or R-MOGP's RMSE in the no-outlier setting is clearly worse than the MOGP's (outside ~1 std of 0.12).

title: Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Unordered Tasks: From Boolean to Coupled Reward Machines

official.background: Reward machines (RMs) are finite automata that expose a task's reward structure to an RL agent, so it can handle non-Markovian goals and learn more efficiently. When a task has N subtasks that may be done in any order (for example, collecting N boxes), a Boolean RM needs one state per subset of completed subtasks, which gives 2^N states. The agent then has to learn Q-values over the environment states times all of these RM states and explore many completion orders, so learning becomes slow or runs out of memory as N grows. The paper asks how to keep RM-based learning tractable for long-horizon tasks with many unordered subtasks.
official.method:
The paper introduces numeric RMs (unordered subtasks are folded into a counter), agenda RMs (each state is labelled <depth, remaining subtasks, current objective>, so symmetric states merge), and coupled RMs (an agenda state whose objective is a set of subtasks is split into one coupled state per subtask, and the agent occupies all of them at once). QCoRM learns one low-level Q-function per subtask over S x U', where U' is the set of subtasks plus Boolean objectives, so the low-level state space grows linearly in the number of subtasks. In coupled states, all subtask Q-functions are updated in parallel. A high-level policy treats the coupled states as bandit arms and picks the subtask with the lowest estimated steps-to-goal eta(u). The estimates are updated after each episode with step size alpha_eta = 0.005 and RM exploration xi. On subtask completion, the low-level reward R(K, tau) from Eq. (5) depends on the episode length and the subtask duration, which keeps tabular global optimality. Transitions between distinct RM states are buffered and replayed at the end of the episode.

The claim uses the tabular Delivery domain: a 10x10 four-connected grid with 8 randomly placed boxes that disappear when collected. The agent carries one box at a time and must deliver all boxes to a station. The reward is 1 on task completion and 0 otherwise. Tabular Q-learning uses alpha = 1e-5, gamma = 0.9, epsilon = 0.1. The baselines use the authors' agenda RMs with QRM, CRM (counterfactual experiences) and HRM (options-based hierarchical RL), plus DiRL. Boolean-RM baselines exceed memory beyond 5 boxes. Each run is limited to 1M environment steps and 40 hours on a single CPU core with 16 GiB, and the plots show the median over 10 seeds.
official.claim: On tabular Delivery with 8 unordered boxes, QCoRM reaches the optimal average reward per step within about 100k environment steps (median of 10 seeds). The strongest baseline, CRM with agenda RMs (T-CRM), is still well below that level after 1M steps (roughly 75% of QCoRM's plateau, read off the plot). Agenda-RM QRM stays near zero, and HRM and DiRL fail to converge.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Results of QCoRM (ours) and baselines, Q-learning (QRM), QRM with counterfactual reasoning (CRM), hierarchical HRM, and DiRL. Boolean RMs (B-QRM, B-CRM, B-HRM) and our agenda RMs (T-QRM, T-CRM, and T-HRM) were tested for Delivery (a,b), Office (e,f), Water (i,j), and HalfCheetah (m,n). As DiRL does not allow setting the number of environment interactions in advance and provides a complete evaluation only after training finishes, we cannot plot DiRL's learning curve. Instead, we run DiRL with an increasing number of iterations and mark its final performance as a single point per run against the total environment interactions consumed. QCoRM-0 stands for QCoRM without the joint optimisation from (5). (c,g,k,o) Time (in seconds) to run 10^6 steps in relation to the number of unordered objectives.
official.metric: Average reward per step during training (higher is better; the y-axis has no numeric ticks). The curve is the median over 10 seeds, and the shaded band is the 25th-75th percentile. No other error statistics are reported.
official.comparison: QCoRM vs. T-QRM, T-CRM, T-HRM and DiRL with the same tabular Q-learning hyperparameters and a 1M-step budget. Boolean-RM variants (B-QRM, B-CRM, B-HRM) could not be run at 8 boxes because they exceed memory.
official.falsification_criterion: With 8 boxes, T-CRM (or another baseline) reaches QCoRM's final average reward per step within 1M steps, with overlapping interquartile ranges, or QCoRM does not reach a stable optimal plateau within the first ~250k steps.

title: Rep2Text: Decoding Full Text from a Single LLM Token Representation

official.background: LLM hidden states are often treated as opaque, yet if the input text can be reconstructed from them, intermediate activations leak private input data and also reveal what information a model retains. Prior inversion work mostly targets sentence embeddings (e.g. Vec2Text) or uses the hidden states of all tokens. This paper asks how much of the input sequence can be recovered from a single last-token residual-stream representation of a decoder-only LLM, which is optimized for next-token prediction and so acts as an information bottleneck.
official.method:
Rep2Text takes the last-token residual-stream vector h from a fixed layer of a frozen target model (here Mistral-7B-v0.1 or Llama-3.1-8B, layer 10 by default) and maps it with a trainable adapter into k soft token embeddings in the input embedding space of a frozen decoding LLM (here Qwen-2.5-14B). The adapter is a two-layer MLP (LayerNorm, GELU, hidden size 0.5*d) whose output is reshaped into k vectors (k = number of tokens to invert, 32 here), each combined with a learned-gated skip projection of h and layer-normed. These k vectors are prepended to a fixed system prompt and user prompt and fed to the decoder, which generates the input text. Only the adapter is trained (teacher forcing, cross-entropy with label smoothing 0.075) on last-token representations of Wikipedia passages from The Pile (640K sequences by default); the decoder stays frozen.

For the Table 2 comparison, the baseline is Vec2Text (T5-base hypothesizer, plus optional corrector run for 50 steps) adapted to take the same last-token target-model representation as its 'embedding', trained 10 epochs on the same Wikipedia data with default Vec2Text settings (num repeat tokens 16, max length 64). Both are evaluated with an inversion length of 32 tokens on held-out Wikipedia and on an out-of-distribution clinical set: 2,500 patient notes from the Hugging Face dataset Sadaftb/clinical-nlp-patient-notes, each summarized by Qwen-2.5-32B into one sentence of at most 25 tokens including patient name, date of birth, gender and key symptoms. Metrics are ROUGE-1/2/L, Token F1, BLEU, BERTScore, and GPT-4.1-mini 0-5 ratings (normalized to 0-1) of structure, entity and topic preservation.
official.claim: Inverting Mistral-7B-v0.1 last-token representations of out-of-distribution clinical summaries, Rep2Text (adapter-only, frozen Qwen-2.5-14B decoder, trained only on Wikipedia) reaches ROUGE-1 0.37, Token F1 0.26 and topic score 0.64, versus 0.14, 0.13 and 0.21 for a Vec2Text hypothesizer trained on the same data; the same pattern holds for Llama-3.1-8B representations (ROUGE-1 0.34 vs 0.13).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Inversion comparison between Vec2Text and our method with input sequences of no more than 32 tokens. (* denotes Vec2Text; R1/R2/RL = ROUGE, BS = BERTScore, SS/ES/TS = structure/entity/topic scores from GPT-4.1-mini.)
official.metric: ROUGE-1, Token F1 (token level), BERTScore, and GPT-4.1-mini topic score (0-1, all higher is better), averaged over the test set. No standard deviations, seeds or confidence intervals are reported (single run).
official.comparison: Rep2Text vs. Vec2Text Base (T5-base hypothesizer) and Vec2Text + 50-step corrector, all inverting the same last-token representations and trained on the same Wikipedia data, evaluated on OOD clinical summaries (and on in-distribution Wikipedia for reference).
official.falsification_criterion: On the OOD clinical summaries, a Vec2Text hypothesizer trained on the same Wikipedia last-token representations reaches ROUGE-1 or Token F1 close to Rep2Text's (e.g. a gap under about 0.05 ROUGE-1 instead of about 0.23), or Rep2Text's clinical ROUGE-1 falls to the Vec2Text level of about 0.14.

title: Training Language Models to Explain Their Own Computations
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (input ablation columns); repeated in Table 6, page 20

official.background: When language models are asked to explain their decisions, the explanations often sound plausible but do not reflect the computation that actually produced the output. For example, models use a hint injected into a multiple-choice question without saying so. This paper asks whether a model can be fine-tuned to describe its own internal computations faithfully, using the outputs of interpretability procedures as ground truth. It also tests the 'privileged access hypothesis': whether a model explains itself better than a different model trained on the same explanations does.
official.method:
Input ablation task (Section 2.4, 5.2; Appendix G.3, H.3): MMLU multiple-choice questions c are given to the target model (Qwen3-8B, used with its chat template) with an injected hint x̃ = 'Hint: The answer is B' (the letter is chosen at random among the four options). The ground-truth explanation is obtained by also running the target on the question without the hint and comparing its most likely answer token: 'The most likely output would change to <<<Answer: M(c)>>>.' if M(c, x̃) ≠ M(c), and otherwise 'The output would remain unchanged from <<<Answer: M(c)>>>.' The data has 12,642 training examples (8,517 changed / 4,125 unchanged) and 1,395 test examples (929 / 466) (Table 8).

An explainer LM is fine-tuned with cross-entropy on the explanation given the prompt [system: answer-only MMLU instruction] [user: question c, hint x̃, 'If the hint were removed how would the assistant answer change?']. Two explainers are trained on the identical Qwen3-8B-derived data: Qwen3-8B itself (self-explanation) and Llama-3.1-8B (other-model explanation); an untrained, prompted Qwen3-8B is a reference. Metrics on the held-out split are Exact Match (the full explanation string is correct), Has-Changed macro-F1 over changed/unchanged, and Content Match (the predicted answer letter is correct).
official.claim: On the MMLU hint-ablation task with Qwen3-8B as the target, a Qwen3-8B explainer fine-tuned on Qwen3-8B's own ablation outcomes reaches 83.4 ± 1.0 Exact Match (87.0 Has-Changed F1, 90.6 Content Match), compared with 58.1 ± 1.3 Exact Match (70.5 F1, 71.6 Content Match) for Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned on the same data.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. A target model's intervention outcomes are best predicted by itself, shown through activation patching and input ablation. We train Qwen3-8B to verbalize its own intervention outcomes, and compare against training a different model (Llama-3.1-8B), and also against an untrained version of Qwen3-8B. Scores (mean ± standard error) are reported for three metrics—exact match, has-changed F1, and content prediction. For each task and metric, bold indicates no significant difference from the best entry (paired t-test, p ≥ 0.05). Results with Llama-3.1-8B as the target model can be found in Tables 5 and 6.
official.metric: Exact Match accuracy, Has-Changed macro-F1 and Content Match accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is the standard error reported by the paper ('mean ± standard error'; it does not say over what, presumably test examples, and reports no seed variance); the paper marks entries not significantly different from the best by a paired t-test (p ≥ 0.05)

title: Branching Flows: Discrete, Continuous, and Manifold Flow Matching with Splits and Deletions

official.background: Diffusion and flow matching models generate a state with a fixed number of elements, so they need the sequence length, the atom count, or the number of residues to be fixed in advance. That is awkward whenever the length is genuinely unknown, for example when designing the complementarity-determining region of an antibody between fixed flanking regions. Autoregressive models handle discrete length variation with stop tokens, but do not extend naturally to continuous or manifold-valued elements. Branching Flows is a generative framework in which the elements of the state evolve over a forest of binary trees, splitting and dying at rates the model learns, so the model itself controls how many elements exist at generation time.
official.method:
Branching Flows is formulated in Generator Matching. A latent Z = (X1+ø, X0, T, A) couples an initial sample x0 to a data sample x1: the data sequence is first augmented with 'to-be-deleted' states, then a forest of labelled binary plane trees T is sampled whose roots are the elements of x0 and whose leaves are the elements of the augmented x1, and 'anchors' A are attached to each node to steer the process along internal branches. Along each branch an element evolves under an arbitrary base generator (here, Discrete Flow Matching with unmasking and uniform noise for the antibody task) conditioned to end at the anchor ahead of it. Split events occur at rate (w_i - 1) * h_split(t) and deletion events at h_del(t) on to-be-deleted branches, which guarantees the conditional path ends exactly at x1. Training minimises a three-term Bregman loss over the base generator, the split intensity, and the deletion intensity; at inference the trees are marginalised out and elements duplicate in place or vanish according to the model's predicted rates.

For the antibody claim, models are trained on 15M filtered human heavy chains from the Observed Antibody Space (clustered at 95% identity). All three models share a diffusion-transformer architecture (dim 768, 12 heads, 8 layers, adaLN-Zero time conditioning), batch size 64, 234,375 steps, Muon with 2000-step warm-up and cosine decay 1e-3 -> 1e-7. The only architectural difference for Edit Flows (the authors' own re-implementation, since no reference implementation existed) is that its insertion head is as large as the alphabet, whereas Branching Flows needs one split rate per element. 10,000 sequences are generated per model with 1,000 uniform steps and compared to held-out natural sequences by 1 - KS statistic on five properties. The 'Oracle length' discrete flow matching model is given a true length drawn from the data distribution and serves as an upper reference, not as the comparison baseline.
official.claim: On unconditional antibody heavy-chain generation with architecture and training matched, Branching Flows matches the data distribution better than Edit Flows on diversity (1 - KS_D 0.894 vs 0.713), novelty (0.888 vs 0.770) and AbNatiV humanness (0.931 vs 0.769), while being roughly tied on sequence length (0.986 vs 0.989) and CDR3 length (0.989 vs 0.983).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Distribution agreement (1 - KS_D, higher is better) between properties of samples from each model vs. validation sequences. From left to right: Sequence Length, Diversity (within-samples min Cosine distance), Novelty (minimum edit distance to true sequence), CDR3 length, and AbNatiV 'humanness' score. Histograms of these properties are shown in Figure 6. Shown are results for an unconditional task where the entire sequence is generated, and a conditional task that generates multiple missing segments of the sequence. For the conditional task the 'Oracle length' model knows the length of each missing segment.
official.metric: 1 - KS_D, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the property distribution of 10,000 generated sequences and that of held-out validation sequences; higher is better, 1.0 is a perfect match. No error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Branching Flows vs. the authors' re-implementation of Edit Flows, same transformer backbone, same 15M-sequence training set, same batch size, optimiser and step count, same 1,000-step sampling and same 10,000 generated sequences. The 'Oracle length' DFM model, which is told the true length, is the reference ceiling rather than the baseline.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-training both models under the stated matched setup and regenerating 10,000 sequences each, Edit Flows reaches 1 - KS_D within run-to-run variation of Branching Flows on diversity, novelty and AbNatiV (i.e. the ~0.18 and ~0.16 gaps on diversity and AbNatiV largely vanish), or Branching Flows falls clearly behind on any of those three.

title: A Systematic Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Detection Under Representation and Training Paradigm Shifts
claim_source: Table 15, page 34 (Appendix F); summarized in Section 4.3, page 8

official.background: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors, or confidence scoring functions (CSFs), assign a score to each prediction so that unreliable inputs can be flagged. Rankings of these scores are unstable across datasets, architectures and training pipelines. The paper argues that which detector works depends mainly on the geometry of the learned penultimate-layer representation, and proposes a simple intervention on that geometry: reconstructing features from a low-rank PCA subspace before scoring.
official.method:
Projection filtering: fit PCA on the training-set penultimate-layer activations H of a trained classifier, keep the top-k eigenvectors P (k chosen by an explained-variance threshold tuned on an ID-only validation split), and replace each feature h by ĥ = P Pᵀ(h − µ) + µ before computing the CSF. 'Global' fits one P on all training features; 'class pred' (CPP) uses a per-class projector fit on that class's features, selected by the model's predicted class. Mahalanobis (Maha) is the class-conditional Mahalanobis-distance score to the class centroids on penultimate features, using the empirical covariance matrix Σ (Appendix C.3.5).

Models follow the FD-Shifts protocol: VGG-13 trained from scratch on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SuperCIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet under three training paradigms (ConfidNet / vanilla CE, DeVries, Deep Gamblers), 5 seeds per cell, with OOD sets iSUN, LSUN-crop, LSUN-resize, SVHN, Places365 and Textures. OOD detection compares OOD samples against correctly classified ID samples and is scored with AUGRC (lower is better). For each base CSF and projection variant, the paper computes paired AUGRC differences (base − variant) across source × OOD dataset × paradigm × run combinations and tests them with a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
official.claim: On VGG-13 (FD-Shifts setup), applying global PCA projection filtering to penultimate features before Mahalanobis scoring lowers AUGRC by a mean of 24.1 (median 16.6), winning 50 of 64 paired comparisons (Wilcoxon p < 0.001).
official.claim_caption: Table 15: Full paired AUGRC comparison: base CSF vs. projection variants on VGG-13 (Conv). ∆AUGRC = mean(base − variant); positive = variant better. Significant improvements (p < 0.05, variant better) are marked with ✓.
official.metric: AUGRC (lower is better; the paper does not state the scale, likely ×10³). ΔAUGRC = mean(base − variant) over paired source × OOD dataset × paradigm × run combinations; positive means the projected variant is better. title: ManipShield: A Unified Framework for Image Manipulation Detection, Localization and Explanation

official.background: Modern instruction-driven image editors (FLUX-Kontext, NanoBanana, GPT-Image, SeedDream, Qwen-Image-Edit) produce realistic local and global edits that go well beyond face swaps. Existing image manipulation detection and localization (IMDL) datasets cover few editing models and categories and mostly give only real/fake labels, so detectors trained on them learn model-specific artifacts and do not generalize to new editors. The paper builds a large benchmark of AI-edited images and an MLLM-based detector intended to detect, localize and explain such edits, and to generalize to editing models not seen in training.
official.method:
ManipBench: 22K real photos are edited by 25 editing models across 12 manipulation categories (add, remove, replace, color, background, size, action, material, expression, three kinds of text), giving about 455K manipulated images; 100K of them get human bounding boxes, judgment cues and textual explanations. Images are grouped by editor backbone (SD1.4, SD1.5, SD3, SDXL, FLUX, DiT) as in-distribution subsets, while four proprietary editors (FLUX-Kontext, NanoBanana, GPT-Image, SeedDream4) are held out as out-of-distribution test subsets. All fine-tuned models use the same 4:1:1 train/val/test split.

ManipShield is built on InternVL3.5 (8B). Stage 1 trains the vision encoder with LoRA using a contrastive loss on paired real/manipulated images. Stage 2 freezes the encoder, applies LoRA to the LLM, and attaches three MLP decoders (detection, unrealistic-attribute, bounding-box localization) to the hidden state of the first generated token at one LLM layer (layer 24), chosen by a 'layer discrimination selection' score (z-scored sum of KL divergence, local discriminant ratio and feature entropy between real and fake hidden states on 1% of the data). For detection, the classifier output is evaluated with accuracy and F1 at threshold 0.5. Baselines include CNN/Transformer classifiers, IMDL methods, AI-generated-image detectors, and other MLLMs (DeepSeekVL2-small, InternVL3-8B, Qwen3-VL-8B), each fine-tuned on ManipBench with the same strategy as ManipShield.
official.claim: On the ManipBench test split, ManipShield reaches 94.66% overall real/manipulated detection accuracy versus 92.58% for the best fine-tuned baseline (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 92.46% for fine-tuned AIDE, and on every held-out proprietary editor it beats all fine-tuned baselines (e.g. 81.45% vs 76.61% best baseline on FLUX-Kontext, 82.57% vs 79.37% on GPT-Image).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison results on different manipulation methods. ♠ standard CNN/Transformer baselines, ♡ image manipulation detection methods, ♣ AI-generated image detection methods, ♢ multimodal large language models. The fine-tuned results are marked with ✻. The best results are highlighted in red, and the second-best results are highlighted in blue.
official.metric: Detection accuracy and F1 (%, higher is better) at threshold 0.5. Single run; no standard deviations, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: ManipShield (fine-tuned InternVL3.5-8B with contrastive vision LoRA, LDS layer selection and task decoders) vs. fine-tuned baselines trained on the same split: ResNet50, Swin-T, MVSSNet, PSCCNet, HifiNet, FakeShield, CNNSpot, Lagrad, Univ, AIDE, DeepSeekVL2-small, InternVL3-8B, Qwen3-VL-8B. Zero-shot rows are reported but are not the comparison.
official.falsification_criterion: With matched training on ManipBench, a fine-tuned baseline (in particular Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3-8B or AIDE) matches or exceeds ManipShield's overall accuracy, or ManipShield does not beat the best fine-tuned baseline on the out-of-distribution editors (FLUX-Kontext, NanoBanana, GPT-Image, SeedDream4).

title: GLOBE: Accurate Surrogates for Boundary-Driven PDEs via Domain-Inspired Architectures and Equivariance

official.background: Steady RANS simulations of aerodynamic flows are expensive, so ML surrogates that predict flow fields from geometry are widely studied. Many such surrogates do not enforce basic physical structure: they break under rotation or reflection, depend on mesh discretization or units, or use local receptive fields even though elliptic PDEs need global information flow. Classical boundary-element and panel methods get large speedups by discretizing only the boundary and representing the solution as a superposition of Green's-function influences. This paper asks whether building that structure into a neural surrogate improves accuracy, particularly with little training data.
official.method:
GLOBE represents output fields at arbitrary query points as an area-weighted sum over boundary faces of a learned kernel K(source face -> target point). The kernel uses only relative positions nondimensionalized by reference lengths. It builds rotation-invariant features (smoothlog magnitudes, Legendre polynomials of pairwise angles), processes them with a Padé-approximant MLP of the form sgn(phi_n)|phi_n|^N/(1+|phi_d|^D), multiplies by a far-field decay envelope (~1/r^(d-1)), and reprojects vector outputs onto local basis vectors. This makes it translation-, rotation- and parity-equivariant, discretization-invariant and units-invariant. Several kernel branches with learned multiples of the reference lengths (chord and a viscous length) are summed, and H=2 communication hyperlayers pass latent scalars/vectors and source strengths between boundary faces before the final evaluation at query points. The AirFRANS model has 117,282 parameters (hidden sizes [64,64,64], 12 latent scalars and 6 latent vectors per hyperlayer, Padé N=D=2).

On AirFRANS (steady incompressible RANS over NACA airfoils), the Scarce split trains on 200 cases and tests on the official 200 test cases. Inputs are the airfoil boundary mesh, freestream direction and reference lengths; there is no signed-distance field. Training uses a Huber loss on nondimensional fields at 2,048 query points per iteration with Muon + RAdamW. Evaluation follows the released AirFRANS evaluator: pointwise MSE at all volume-mesh nodes (surface pressure on surface nodes), averaged equally over cases, divided by one point-pooled training-set variance per field.
official.claim: On the AirFRANS Scarce split (200 training cases), GLOBE's normalized test MSE (×10^-2) is 0.0238 (u_x), 0.0148 (u_y), 0.0496 (p) and 0.1889 (surface p), versus 0.1520, 0.1130, 0.2400 and 2.7000 reported for MARIO, the best published surrogate, i.e. 4.8-14.3x lower on every field.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: AirFRANS Scarce (low-data) task: mean squared error on the official test cases, normalized by the training-set field variance as in Table 1; lower is better. External values are as reported in the cited works (not rerun). GLOBE values are single-run point estimates.
official.metric: Mean squared error on official AirFRANS Scarce test cases, normalized by training-set field variance (released AirFRANS evaluator); lower is better. Single-run point estimates, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: GLOBE (trained by the authors) vs. published values for MARIO, Transolver, MLP, GraphSAGE, PointNet and GUNet (copied from Catalani et al. 2025b and Bonnet et al. 2023, not rerun)
official.falsification_criterion: A GLOBE model trained on the 200 Scarce training cases and scored with the official AirFRANS evaluator does not beat MARIO's reported MSE on all four fields, or the margin shrinks to under ~2x on volume pressure (p).

title: InTAct: Interval-based Task Activation Consolidation for Continual Learning

official.background: Continual learning asks a model to learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting earlier ones. In domain-incremental learning (DIL), every task has the same label set but a different input distribution, such as art styles or image corruptions. Prompt-based methods (L2P, DualPrompt, CODA-Prompt, KA-Prompt) keep a pre-trained ViT frozen and learn only prompts and a shared classifier head. Because the prompts and the head are shared across tasks, they still drift as new domains arrive, which causes forgetting. Most regularizers against forgetting constrain parameters directly, which does not by itself keep the network's function on old data unchanged.
official.method:
After each task, InTAct records a per-dimension activation interval (the 5% and 95% quantiles, alpha = 0.95) of the representations of that task, both for the [CLS] feature and for the inputs to the affine layers of the classifier head. It merges these intervals into a cumulative axis-aligned hypercube by element-wise min/max, and stores no data. When it trains on a later task, four losses are added to cross-entropy. L_IntDrift uses interval arithmetic to compute the exact lower and upper bounds of the output change (delta W z + delta b) of each protected affine layer over the stored hypercube, and penalizes their squares. L_Feat is an MSE between the current model's and the frozen previous model's features, applied only to the coordinates that fall inside the hypercube. L_Var penalizes the within-batch variance of features. L_Align pulls the batch mid-range toward the hypercube's center on non-overlapping dimensions. The backbone stays frozen, and only the prompts and the head are trained.

For the chosen claim, InTAct is added to L2P, DualPrompt and CODA-Prompt inside the official CODA-Prompt codebase, without changing prompt selection or training. The backbone is ViT-B/16 (ImageNet-21k pre-trained, fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k). ImageNet-R (200 classes) is split into 15 DIL tasks, and DomainNet has 6 domain tasks. The baselines and the InTAct variants use the same CODA-Prompt hyperparameters. The InTAct coefficients were chosen by grid search, giving lambda_Feat = 0.1, lambda_IntDrift = 1e-3, lambda_Var = 0.1 and lambda_Align = 1 for CODA-Prompt on ImageNet-R (Table 3). The metric is average accuracy (AA) over all tasks after the final task.
official.claim: On 15-task domain-incremental ImageNet-R with a frozen ViT-B/16, adding InTAct raises final average accuracy for every prompt method tested: CODA-Prompt from 61.21 ± 0.49 to 74.23 ± 0.16 (+13.0 p.p.), DualPrompt from 53.31 ± 0.36 to 61.85 ± 0.45 (+8.5 p.p.), and L2P from 50.34 ± 0.26 to 58.34 ± 0.24 (+8.0 p.p.).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Performance results of integrating InTAct with L2P, DualPrompt, and CODA-Prompt. We report AA for ImageNet-R and DomainNet in the DIL setting. Incorporating InTAct consistently yields performance gains over prompt-based baselines. Results are averaged over 5 independent runs.
official.metric: Average Accuracy (AA, %) over all tasks after training on the final task; higher is better. ± is the std over 5 independent runs (stated as an average over 5 runs; the paper does not say whether ± is std or SE).
official.comparison: Each prompt-based method (L2P, DualPrompt, CODA-Prompt) vs. the same method + InTAct, all run in the same CODA-Prompt codebase with the same backbone, task splits and baseline hyperparameters.
official.falsification_criterion: On ImageNet-R, CODA-Prompt + InTAct does not beat plain CODA-Prompt by clearly more than the run-to-run std (e.g., the gain is under about 3 p.p.), or InTAct gives no consistent gain for L2P and DualPrompt under matched settings.

title: Selective Disk Bispectrum: A Complete and Rotation Invariant Image Descriptor
claim_source: Figure 2 (panel a, MNIST, Image Size 28x28), page 8

official.background: Many vision tasks (microscopy, aerial imagery, cryo-EM) need features that do not change when the image is rotated. Hand-crafted rotation invariants (Hu/Zernike moments, SIFT-like descriptors) are cheap but throw away phase information, so different images can share a descriptor; learned equivariant networks are discriminative but need training, and pooling them to invariance also discards structure. The disk bispectrum, built from products of disk-harmonic coefficients, is a rotation invariant that keeps relative phase, but in full form it has O(m^3/N_m) coefficients and had no known inversion. The paper derives an inversion and shows that a small subset of coefficients, the selective disk bispectrum (SDB), is a complete rotation invariant.
official.method:
An L x L image is masked to a disk and expanded in disk harmonics a_{n,k} (Bessel-function radial part times e^{in theta}), keeping coefficients with lambda_{nk} below the bandlimit pi*L/2. The SDB (Definition 1) keeps only b_{0,0,k} = a_{0,1}^2 a*_{0,k} and b_{2,n,k} = a_{1,1} a_{n,1} a*_{n+1,k} for n = 0..N_m-1, which is O(m) complex values (feature size 194 / 194 / 406 for 28 / 56 / 112 pixel images per Fig. 2c). These are rotation invariant because a_{n,k} picks up the phase e^{in phi} under rotation and the phases cancel in each product. The SDB has no learned parameters.

Classification (Sec. 5, App. H): MNIST and FashionMNIST, train images rotated uniformly in [0, 90] degrees and test images in [90, 180] degrees, Gaussian noise of variance sigma^2 in {0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4} added to both splits. Each feature extractor feeds an MLP with a 10k/50k/500k parameter budget (0-2 hidden layers), trained 15 epochs, lr 0.005, dropout 0.1, batch 512, 20% of train held out for validation, 5 seeds. Baselines: max- and average-pooled G-CNNs, the Selective G-Bispectrum and the G-Triple Correlation layer (24 filters each, trained end-to-end with the MLP), and frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16, EVA-02 ViT-B and OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 features (images upsampled to 224 x 224).
official.claim: On rotated noisy MNIST (28x28, 50k-parameter MLP, test rotations disjoint from train rotations), an MLP on SDB features stays at roughly 0.85-0.70 test accuracy as noise variance rises from 0.1 to 0.4, while every convolution-based rotation-invariant baseline (pooled G-CNNs, Selective G-Bispectrum, G-Triple Correlation) falls to about 0.4 or below once any noise is added and to about 0.2-0.3 for sigma^2 >= 0.1; at sigma^2 = 0.4 the SDB (~0.70) also beats frozen DINOv3, EVA-02 and OpenCLIP features (~0.50-0.55).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Classification results on rotated noisy MNIST (left) and FashionMNIST (right). The SDB and transformers outperform convolution-based methods on noisy rotated images, across (a) image size (shown for 50,000 parameter MLP) and (b) MLP parameter budgets (shown for image size 28x28). Mean is reported across seeds, with standard deviation shaded. (c) The SDB encodes images into a lower-dimensional representation than the G-Triple Correlation, Selective G-Bispectrum, and transformers, as represented by marker sizes. However, unlike G-CNN max and average pooling, it does not discard structural information. Training time includes MLP training and feature computation; transformer training time would increase substantially without pre-trained models.

title: Aligning LLMs with Biomedical Knowledge using Balanced Fine-Tuning

official.background: Post-training LLMs on biomedical text with standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) gives every token equal weight, and Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT) down-weights each token by its own predicted probability to stabilize training. The authors argue that in biomedical text, low-confidence tokens often come in dense runs (rare entities, pathway steps, causal chains) that carry the actual knowledge, so DFT's absolute-confidence rule suppresses exactly the content that matters. They also want models that act as backbones for biomedical agent pipelines and that serve as good starting points for sparse-reward RL.
official.method:
Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT) changes only the per-token loss weights of SFT. For each response token t with confidence c_t = p(y_t | y_<t, x), it computes a local mean confidence C_loc over a centered window of g = 256 response tokens. The token weight is w_t = stopgrad(clip(c_t / (C_loc + eps), 0, 1)), so a low-confidence token inside a confident window is suppressed (much as in DFT), but one inside a uniformly low-confidence window keeps most of its signal. A sample weight s_b = stopgrad(1 - min_t C_loc) upweights sequences whose weakest local window is hard. The loss is the batch mean of s_b times the masked, weighted token cross-entropy average. BFT-token sets s_b = 1; BFT-sample sets w_t = 1.

DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B is full-parameter fine-tuned with SFT, DFT, or BFT under one recipe (LlamaFactory, AdamW, lr 1e-5, cosine, 2 epochs, global batch 64, cutoff 4096) on 51,056 synthetic samples: 2,820 HealthBench-Consensus medical responses written by GPT-5.1, and 48,236 instruction-response pairs generated by GPT-OSS-120B from NCBI gene/protein summaries (the GenePT corpus). Each fine-tuned model then replaces Gemini-2.5-Flash as the backbone of the unchanged VCWorld pipeline, which predicts Up / Down / No differential expression for chemical perturbations on five held-out cancer cell lines. The metric is 3-class accuracy.
official.claim: As the VCWorld backbone on chemical-perturbation reasoning (5 cell lines), DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B fine-tuned with BFT reaches 0.70 average accuracy, vs. 0.56 for SFT and 0.49 for DFT under the same recipe. Over three fine-tuning seeds the averages are BFT 0.696/0.679/0.708 (SD 0.015) vs. SFT 0.562/0.541/0.578 (SD 0.019).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Chemical perturbation reasoning accuracy for joint Up/Down/No classification. Upper block: original VCWorld; middle: aligned 70B replacements; lower: after GRPO. Cells are mean ± SD over eight stochastic inference passes of one checkpoint (decoding, not training, variability). Displayed averages are rounded to two decimals; tests use unrounded cell-line means. Best in each column is shown in bold.
official.metric: 3-class (Up/Down/No) accuracy averaged over 5 held-out cell lines, higher is better. In Table 1, ± is SD over 8 stochastic inference passes of a single checkpoint (decoding variability only). Table 6 gives SD across 3 independent fine-tuning seeds.

title: Test-time Scaling of Diffusions with Flow Maps
claim_source: Table 3 (Appendix D.1), page 30; summarized in Figure 5 and Section 3.4 of the main text

official.background: A common way to make a pretrained diffusion or flow model produce samples that score highly under a user-specified reward is to add the reward's gradient to the generative dynamics. The reward is usually defined only on clean data at the end of generation, so during sampling it has to be evaluated on a guess of where the current noisy state will end up. The usual guess is the one-step denoiser E[x1 | x_t], which is blurry and off the data manifold at high noise, so the reward signal early in the trajectory is weak or misleading. Flow maps, which learn the solution operator X_{s,t} of the probability-flow ODE, can jump from any x_t to its endpoint in one or a few steps.
official.method:
FMTT (Flow Map Trajectory Tilting) samples the reward-tilted distribution rho_1(x) exp(r(x)) / Z with the SDE dx_t = v_{t,t}(x_t) dt + eps_t [s_t(x_t) + grad r_t(x_t)] dt + sqrt(2 eps_t) dW_t, where v_{t,t} is the velocity implied by the flow map, s_t is the score derived from it, and the time-dependent reward is r_t(x) = t * r(X_{t,1}(x)), i.e. the reward evaluated at the flow-map look-ahead. The paper shows that with this choice the Jarzynski importance weights reduce to A_t = integral_0^t r(X_{s,1}(x_s)) ds, and uses them for SMC resampling (Sampling mode, used here) or top-n selection (Searching mode, used for images). The baselines replace the look-ahead with nothing (r_t(x) = t * r(x)) or with the one-step denoiser (r_t(x) = t * r(D_t(x))), with the weights from Eq. (17) in each case.

In the 2D toy (Appendix D.1), a flow-matching model is trained on a ring-shaped distribution and then distilled into a flow map (both 100,000 steps, batch size 8092). The reward is high on a zigzag-shaped subset of the ring and flat away from the data. SMC (Eqs. 13 and 17, default chi_t = 0) is run with 10,000 particles for 50, 100, 200 and 500 steps, resampling when the effective sample size drops below 0.9, with eps_t = 0.1 * (1 - t). Outputs are compared against ground-truth tilted samples obtained by rejection sampling using MMD and sliced Wasserstein-2 (SW2).
official.claim: In 2D SMC sampling of a ring distribution tilted toward a zigzag, flow-map look-ahead matches the tilted target far better than no look-ahead or denoiser look-ahead at every step count: MMD 0.043/0.065/0.065/0.031 vs. best baseline 0.996/0.460/3.016/3.459 and SW2 0.060/0.083/0.126/0.089 vs. 0.578/0.443/0.902/0.857 at 50/100/200/500 steps, with only 5-10 resampling events vs. 46-198.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Quantitative results for the 2D toy experiment. We compare no-lookahead, denoiser-lookahead, and flow map-lookahead across different numbers of SMC steps. Lower Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and Sliced Wasserstein-2 (SW2) indicate better agreement with the tilted target distribution.
official.metric: MMD and SW2 between SMC output and rejection-sampled tilted target (lower is better); number of resampling steps (lower = more stable weights). Single run per setting; no error bars reported.
official.comparison: Flow-map look-ahead vs. no look-ahead vs. 1-step denoiser look-ahead, same trained model, same SMC sampler, particles, schedule and stochasticity, at 50/100/200/500 steps
official.falsification_criterion: At any of the four step counts, the flow-map look-ahead's MMD or SW2 is not clearly lower (for example, within a factor of 2) than the better of the no-look-ahead and denoiser look-ahead baselines, or the flow-map variant needs a comparable number of resampling steps.

title: Guiding Visual Autoregressive Models through Spectrum Weakening

official.background: Visual autoregressive (AR) image generators usually rely on classifier-free guidance (CFG), which needs a trained unconditional branch and is undefined for unconditional generation. Diffusion models have alternatives that guide with a deliberately weakened copy of the model (e.g. perturbed attention, timestep or token perturbations), but these rely on diffusion timesteps or a full-image layout, which AR decoding with a KV-cache does not have. The paper asks whether a training-free, condition-free weak model can be built for AR generators so that they can be guided even without a prompt.
official.method:
Spectrum Weakening Guidance (SWG) builds the weak branch from the same pretrained model at inference time. In selected modules (e.g. the attention Q/K/V representations), each token's feature vector is mapped with a DFT along the channel dimension, a binary diagonal mask keeps only a subset of the spectral components (e.g. the first 10% in DFT order), and the inverse DFT's real part is taken. The magnitude is then restored either in the spectral domain (SWG-f, rescale the masked spectrum to the original spectral norm) or in the spatial domain (SWG-s, rescale the reconstructed vector to the original norm). No retraining or architectural change is involved.

At each decoding step the guided logits are z = z_c + w_s (z_c - z_p), where z_c is the normal prediction and z_p is the prediction of the spectrally weakened pass; CFG can optionally be added on top. For the claim, NOVA (0.3B continuous-token text-to-image AR model) generates unconditionally (null prompt) and is evaluated against COCO; SWG is compared with two other training-free weak branches: averaging feature elements (Avg) and pruning specific layers (Pruning).
official.claim: For unconditional NOVA generation evaluated on COCO, guiding with the spectrally weakened model gives FID 104.51 (SWG-f) / 105.98 (SWG-s), better than the alternative weak branches built by layer pruning (110.87) or feature averaging (112.79), and far better than no guidance (139.75).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison of unconditional generation on the COCO dataset. NOVA is used for evaluation. AS denotes aesthetic score. Bold indicates the best entries. SWG-s and SWG-f indicate spatial and spectral renormalization, respectively.
official.metric: FID (lower is better) against COCO; also IS and LAION aesthetic score (higher is better). Single numbers, no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: SWG-f and SWG-s vs. Avg-feature and layer-pruning weak-model guidance vs. no guidance, same NOVA model, unconditional generation
official.falsification_criterion: With a reasonable tuning of each method's guidance scale, SWG's unconditional FID on COCO is not lower than the layer-pruning weak branch's, or the gap is within the FID variation across sampling seeds.

title: FairMT: Fairness for Heterogeneous Multi-Task Learning

official.background: Most work on algorithmic fairness considers one classification task at a time. Multi-task models that jointly predict detection, classification and regression outputs, often from datasets where each sample is labeled for only some tasks, have no common fairness objective. Standard MTL optimizers such as MGDA constrain only the shared encoder, so the task heads can pick up group bias. Fairness methods usually equalize groups symmetrically, which can lower accuracy for the better-served group instead of raising it for the worse-served one.
official.method:
FairMT defines one-sided (asymmetric) per-task fairness violations: for binary detection, Asymmetric Equalized Odds penalizes only groups whose soft TPR falls below the best group's TPR or whose FPR rises above the lowest group's FPR (Eq. 1). Multi-class tasks use a class-wise version (Eq. 2) and regression uses Asymmetric Error Parity, the gap to the lowest group error (Eq. 3). Partial labels are handled by masks. The per-task violations are combined by AHFDA, max over simplex weights w of w^T Psi - (mu/2)||w||^2, solved with Frank-Wolfe, which puts the weight on the most-violated tasks (Eq. 4, Alg. 1).

Training is primal-dual: a dual multiplier eta on the constraint Phi <= epsilon is updated by projected ascent (Eq. 18). Task weights alpha come from an MGDA-style min-norm problem that includes the fairness gradient (Eq. 15). That problem is approximated by a head-aware quadratic program built from the final linear head weights W and average logit sensitivities u, with K = Diag(u) W W^T Diag(u) (Eqs. 19-22). Shared and head parameters then take gradient steps on the Lagrangian. On CelebA all 29 binary facial attributes are detection tasks, with age (Young/Old) and gender as sensitive attributes.
official.claim: On CelebA 29-attribute multi-task detection, FairMT reaches 88.4% (age) / 88.1% (gender) mean accuracy with EOD 3.4 / 6.4, versus MGDA's 87.7% with EOD 11.4 / 22.5, while the fairest baselines (UFaTE, MGDA-UFaTE) reach EOD 6.8 (age) and 12.2 (gender) only at 75-79% accuracy.
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Comparison of FairMT with multi-task (†), fairness-only (*), and hybrid fair-MTL (†*) baselines. Utility metrics (Acc, F1, CCC) are denoted with ↑ (higher is better), while fairness metrics (EOD, EO, KS, CSP) are denoted with ↓ (lower is fairer). (a) Attribute Detection (in %).
official.metric: Mean accuracy over the 29 attribute tasks (%, higher is better) and Equalized Odds / Equal Opportunity disparity across sensitive groups (%, lower is better); single numbers, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: FairMT vs. MTL optimizers (MGDA, GradNorm), fairness-only methods (LNL, UFaTE) and hybrids (MGDA-Mean, MGDA-UFaTE), separately for age and gender as the sensitive attribute
official.falsification_criterion: Re-run on CelebA, FairMT's age EOD is not clearly below the best baseline's (6.8) or its gender EOD is not clearly below 12.2, or its mean accuracy falls more than about 1 point below MGDA's.

title: StreamGaze: Gaze-Guided Temporal Reasoning and Proactive Understanding in Streaming Videos

official.background: Streaming video assistants (for example on AR glasses) must answer questions using only frames seen so far, and sometimes must decide on their own when to speak. Human eye gaze is a strong signal of what a user is attending to and what they will do next, but existing streaming video benchmarks ignore gaze, and existing gaze QA benchmarks use short clips and are not streaming. StreamGaze is a benchmark that tests whether multimodal LLMs can use gaze for past, present and proactive reasoning over egocentric video.
official.method:
The authors take egocentric videos with eye tracking from EGTEA+, EgoExoLearn and HoloAssist, extract fixations from the raw gaze (spatial-dispersion and minimum-duration thresholds plus a scene-consistency check), and use InternVL3.5-38B to list objects inside and outside a circular field-of-view around each fixation. Human annotators verify these object lists, and the resulting scanpaths are turned by an LLM into 8,521 QA pairs over 285 videos across 10 tasks: four past tasks (NFI, OTP, SR, GSM), four present tasks (OI easy/hard, OAR, FAP), all 4-way multiple choice, and two proactive alert tasks (GTA, OAA) scored as yes/no decisions at checkpoints around the target event.

Models are evaluated zero-shot and strictly causally: past tasks see video from 0 to the query time, present tasks a 60 s window, proactive tasks the cumulative prefix at each checkpoint. Gaze is given as a visual prompt (green dot at the gaze point, red circle for the FOV drawn on each frame) plus an instruction explaining the overlay. Metric is accuracy per task; Overall is the mean over the 10 task columns. A human score is reported for each task.
official.claim: On StreamGaze with visual gaze prompting, every evaluated MLLM scores far below humans: the best open-source model, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, reaches 0.478 overall accuracy and the best model overall (Claude Opus 4.8) 0.598, versus 0.827 for humans; humans lead on every one of the 10 tasks.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison of various MLLMs across StreamGaze tasks. We evaluate four categories of models, reporting accuracy for past, present and proactive tasks. Each section is sorted by overall performance, and the best per task across all models (excluding Human) is bolded.
official.metric: Accuracy (higher is better), per task and averaged over the 10 tasks (Overall); multiple-choice exact match for past/present tasks, per-checkpoint yes/no accuracy for proactive tasks. No ± reported (single run).
official.comparison: Human performance vs. 8 closed-source MLLMs, AssistGaze, 7 open-source MLLMs and 5 streaming MLLMs, all zero-shot under the same causal protocol and gaze overlay.
official.falsification_criterion: Running Qwen2.5-VL-7B (or another open 7-8B model in Table 2) with the paper's protocol and gaze overlay gives Overall accuracy far from the reported value (e.g. above ~0.6, closing more than half the gap to 0.827), or a re-measured human score on a sample of questions is close to the model scores.

title: Model-Free Assessment of Simulator Fidelity via Quantile Curves

official.background: Generative models, especially LLMs, are increasingly used as simulators of real systems, for example to stand in for human survey respondents. How far a simulator is from reality changes from one scenario (such as a survey question) to the next. Both the real and the simulated output distributions for each scenario are seen only through finite samples, often of different sizes. Average-error summaries hide rare large failures, and standard conformal methods cover observable outcomes, not latent per-scenario parameters. The paper aims to estimate the full quantile function of the per-scenario sim-to-real discrepancy, with finite-sample guarantees and no assumptions about the simulator.
official.method:
For each scenario j, the method builds a gamma_j confidence set C_j around the real-world plug-in estimate p̂_j from n_j human samples. It then takes the pseudo-discrepancy Δ̂_j = sup_{u in C_j} L(u, q̂_j), where q̂_j is the simulator estimate from k samples. V̂_m(τ) is the empirical τ-quantile of {Δ̂_j}. The calibrated curve evaluates V̂_m at the inflated index γ̄_m τ + (1 - γ̄_m), where γ̄_m is the average coverage (Eq. 3.5). Theorem 3.1 says this upper-bounds the τ-quantile of the true discrepancy Δ_ψ = L(p_ψ, q̂_ψ) up to finite-m terms. Coverage is set adaptively as γ_j = 1 - n_j^(-1/3).

Experiment (Section 5): WorldValueBench, 235 World Values Survey questions with answers mapped to [-1, 1], so p_j is the mean response. The confidence set is Hoeffding (Example 3.2), L(p, q) = (p - q)^2, and the simulator is GPT-4o prompted with demographic profiles, k = 200 samples per question. The mean over all available respondents for each question (up to 96,220) stands in for the true p_j and gives an oracle curve of Δ*_j = L(p_j, q̂_j). For n_j in {50, 500, 1000, 5000} subsampled respondents, the calibrated curve is compared with the oracle curve, under adaptive γ_j (Figure 5) and fixed γ_j = 1/2 (Figure 6).
official.claim: On 235 WorldValueBench questions with GPT-4o (k=200), adaptive-coverage calibrated quantile curves stay above the oracle curve at all τ. For n_j >= 500 they are close to it (at τ=0.5, about 0.07-0.11 vs. oracle about 0.04; n_j=50 gives about 0.34). With fixed γ_j=1/2, a clear gap remains even at n_j=5000: the curve is about 0.05 at τ=0 and about 0.17 at τ=0.5, vs. oracle about 0.00 and 0.04 (adaptive n_j=5000: about 0.01 and 0.07).
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Tightness analysis for varying n_j under GPT-4o. The dotted black curve is the oracle quantile curve Δ*; the colored curves are calibrated curves computed from subsamples with n_j = 50 (blue), n_j = 500 (orange), n_j = 1000 (green), and n_j = 5000 (red). The corresponding adaptive average coverage levels shown in the legend are γ̄ ≈ 0.73, 0.87, 0.90, and 0.94, respectively. Figure 6: Tightness analysis for varying n_j under GPT-4o with fixed γ_j = 1/2. Colors match Figure 5.
official.metric: Calibrated quantile value V̂ (squared error of the mean response on the [-1, 1] scale) as a function of quantile level τ; lower and closer to the oracle curve is tighter. It must not fall below the oracle curve. Single run, no error bars or repeated subsamples reported.
official.comparison: Calibrated curves at n_j in {50, 500, 1000, 5000} vs. oracle quantile curve (full-population p_j); adaptive γ_j = 1 - n_j^(-1/3) (Fig. 5) vs. fixed γ_j = 1/2 (Fig. 6)
official.falsification_criterion: Any of these refutes the claim: the calibrated curve falls clearly below the oracle curve over a non-trivial range of τ for some n_j; with adaptive γ_j at n_j >= 500 the curve stays as far from the oracle as the n_j = 50 curve; or fixed γ_j = 1/2 at n_j = 5000 is as tight as adaptive γ_j (no persistent gap at low τ).

title: LYNX: Learning Dynamic Exits for Confidence-Controlled Reasoning

official.background: Reasoning LLMs such as DeepSeek-R1 often keep generating chain-of-thought after they already have the answer. This wastes inference compute and sometimes talks the model out of a correct answer. Early-exit methods try to stop the reasoning once it is sufficient. Existing methods use token-entropy heuristics (DEER), extra speculative sampling (Think-or-Not), or external verifiers. They also need thresholds hand-tuned per model and temperature, and they give no statistical control over how often an early exit is wrong.
official.method:
LYNX considers exiting only at naturally occurring cue tokens ('hmm', 'wait', 'alternatively') inside the <think> block. To get training labels, the authors run one CoT rollout per Hendrycks MATH problem at T = 0.6. At each cue they force an exit: they cut the CoT before the cue, append '</think> Final Answer: \boxed{', let the same model produce a short answer, and label the cue 1 if that answer matches the gold answer and 0 otherwise. The probe input is the cue token's hidden states from two middle layers and the final layer, concatenated. The probe is a small MLP (Appendix B: hidden sizes [256, 64], GELU, Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4) trained with class-weighted BCE. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B the data is 400 training and 200 calibration problems per MATH category (2,800 / 1,400).

Split conformal calibration: on the calibration set, nonconformity scores s = 1 - p are computed for positive cues only. The threshold q is the (1 - δ) quantile of these scores, with confidence c = 1 - δ. At test time the model decodes normally and exits at the first cue where 1 - p ≤ q. The probe and thresholds are trained once on MATH and reused unchanged on GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC23, AIME24 and CommonsenseQA. Baselines are vanilla CoT, DEER and Think-or-Not, all run from the authors' public code with matched prompts, T = 0.0 and a maximum of 13,000 CoT tokens. Tokens are counted as all generated tokens, including the answer rollout after an exit and ToN's hidden sampling.
official.claim: On GSM8K (1,319 test problems, T = 0.0) with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, LYNX at c = 0.90 reaches 78.70% accuracy with 792 average generated tokens (-54.8% vs. baseline). DEER reaches 69.14% with 716 tokens (-59.1%), and the vanilla CoT baseline reaches 75.97% with 1,751 tokens. LYNX is about 9.6 points more accurate than DEER at a similar token budget and also beats the full-length baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs at temperature T = 0.0 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and QwQ-32B. For each dataset we report vanilla chain-of-thought (Baseline), DEER, Think-or-Not (ToN), and LYNX for multiple confidence levels c. ∆Acc vs base and ∆Tokens vs base are relative changes (%) with respect to each model's own Baseline. For ToN, the Tokens column reports total generated tokens.
official.metric: Pass@1 accuracy (higher is better) and mean generated tokens per question (lower is better); a single greedy (T = 0.0) run, no error bars or seeds reported. The '∆ vs base' accuracy column is a relative change in %, not percentage points.
official.comparison: LYNX (c = 0.90, probe trained and calibrated on Hendrycks MATH) vs. DEER and vanilla CoT on the same model, prompts, decoding settings and 13k-token cap; ToN (67.93%, 893 tokens) is a weaker secondary baseline.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running GSM8K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at T = 0.0, LYNX at a confidence level with token savings similar to DEER (about 50-60%) is not clearly more accurate than DEER (e.g. the gap is under ~3 points), or LYNX's accuracy falls clearly below the full-CoT baseline at that operating point.

title: From Next-Token to Next-Block: A Principled Adaptation Path for Diffusion LLMs

official.background: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can decode several tokens in parallel, but training them from scratch is expensive. A shortcut is to start from an off-the-shelf autoregressive (AR) LLM and adapt its weights into a DLM. Earlier adaptations either moved to full-sequence diffusion by randomly annealing the attention mask from causal to bidirectional, or dropped AR weights directly into a block-diffusion training recipe. Block diffusion decodes left-to-right one block at a time with bidirectional attention inside the block, so AR is the special case of block size 1. The paper asks what attention pattern and training path make this AR-to-block-diffusion adaptation work best.
official.method:
The model is trained as a block-diffusion LM with a parallel recipe: a noised copy of the sequence is concatenated with the clean sequence, and a structured 2L x 2L mask lets each noised block attend bidirectionally within itself and to all earlier clean blocks, while the clean copy never reads the noised copy. The masked-diffusion loss is computed on masked tokens in all blocks in one forward pass. Target block size is 32.

The claim compares two choices for how the clean context attends to itself. Block-Causal (as in Block Diffusion / SDAR / D2F): tokens in committed blocks attend bidirectionally within their block and causally across blocks. Context-Causal (proposed): the clean context stays strictly token-level causal, exactly as in the AR model, and only the active (noised) block is bidirectional. Each variant is adapted from the same (unnamed) AR model for 2000 iterations and evaluated on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP; the paper does not say whether the Table 1 runs also used the parallel recipe, AR loss or block growth. The full method additionally adds an auxiliary AR loss (lambda = 0.5) on the clean branch and grows block size 1 -> 2 -> ... -> 32 during training; Section 5 runs use sequence length 8K, global batch 1024, lr 1e-5, Adam.
official.claim: When adapting an AR LLM into a block-diffusion model (block size 32) for 2000 iterations, keeping the context strictly causal (Context-Causal) yields an average of 48.6 over GSM8K/MATH/HumanEval/MBPP vs. 31.4 for Block-Causal, winning every benchmark (GSM8K 68.8 vs. 60.1, MATH 36.8 vs. 1.6, HumanEval 41.5 vs. 24.4, MBPP 47.4 vs. 39.4).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of Block-Causal and Context-Causal attention schemes. Context-Causal gains a clear advantage in adaptation from AR.
official.metric: Benchmark accuracy / pass@1 (%), higher is better; single runs, no error bars reported
official.comparison: Context-Causal vs. Block-Causal context attention, same AR initialization and 2000-iteration adaptation budget
official.falsification_criterion: Under matched adaptation from the same AR checkpoint, Context-Causal does not beat Block-Causal on average across the four benchmarks by a clear margin (e.g., under ~5 points), or Block-Causal does not collapse on MATH relative to Context-Causal.

title: Exact Flow Linear Attention: Exact Solution from Continuous-Time Dynamics

official.background: Delta-rule linear attention (DeltaNet and its gated variants) keeps a matrix-valued memory that is updated at each token by erasing the component along the current key and writing a new key-value pair, giving linear-time sequence models with chunkwise-parallel training. The update is usually motivated as one gradient step of an online regression objective. The paper observes that, if key and value are held fixed within a token interval (zero-order hold), this update is exactly an explicit Euler step of a linear ODE. Euler steps are only first-order accurate and can become inaccurate or unstable when the effective step (learning rate times squared key norm) is large, for example with high-magnitude inputs.
official.method:
EFLA replaces the Euler step with the exact solution of the ODE dS/dt = -k k^T S + k v^T over one interval of length beta. Because k k^T is rank 1, the matrix exponential and the input integral collapse to closed form: S_t = (I - alpha_t k_t k_t^T) S_{t-1} + alpha_t k_t v_t^T, with alpha_t = (1 - exp(-beta_t lambda_t)) / lambda_t and lambda_t = ||k_t||^2. This is DeltaNet's update with beta_t replaced by alpha_t, so the parameter count, the WY/UT chunkwise kernels and the cost are unchanged. The numerator is computed with expm1, lambda is clipped below at 1e-12, and the authors report that scaling keys by sqrt(d), not L2-normalising them, is needed for EFLA to differ from DeltaNet.

Robustness test: each 28x28 MNIST image is flattened to a pixel sequence of length 784 and fed to a linear-attention classifier with hidden dimension 64, trained with AdamW at batch size 128, using either the DeltaNet or the EFLA update. The trained models are evaluated on test inputs perturbed by (i) Bernoulli pixel dropout with probability p, (ii) multiplying the input intensity by a scale factor (1 to 10), and (iii) additive Gaussian noise with std 0 to 1. The top row of Figure 1 uses learning rate 1e-3 for both models; the bottom row uses 3e-3 for EFLA and 1e-3 for DeltaNet.
official.claim: On pixel-level sequential MNIST with a d=64 linear-attention classifier and matched learning rate 1e-3, EFLA and DeltaNet both reach about 92% clean accuracy. Under input intensity scaling, EFLA keeps about 58% at scale 3 and 45% at scale 10, while DeltaNet drops to about 23% and 20%. Under additive Gaussian noise with std 0.2, EFLA keeps about 59% and DeltaNet about 19%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: EFLA outperforms DeltaNet in both convergence speed and robustness on sMNIST. The plots illustrate training dynamics and robustness against dropout, intensity scaling, and additive Gaussian noise. EFLA maintains higher accuracy as perturbation intensity increases, especially under the larger learning-rate setting 3 x 10^-3.
official.metric: Test classification accuracy (%) under perturbation, higher is better; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: EFLA update vs. DeltaNet (Euler) update in the same sMNIST linear-attention classifier at the same learning rate (1e-3), across perturbation strength for pixel dropout, intensity scaling and Gaussian noise
official.falsification_criterion: With matched architecture, training and learning rate, EFLA's accuracy under intensity scaling (scale >= 3) or Gaussian noise (std 0.2) is not at least ~15 points higher than DeltaNet's when averaged over several seeds, or the gap is within seed-to-seed spread.

title: Nemotron-Cascade: Scaling Cascaded Reinforcement Learning for General-Purpose Reasoning Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (SFT baseline from Table 2, page 14; final per-stage numbers in Table 8, page 28)

official.background: Post-training general-purpose reasoning LLMs with reinforcement learning usually mixes prompts from many domains (chat alignment, instruction following, math, competitive coding, software engineering) in one RL run. These domains differ a lot in response length and in how slow it is to check an answer (a rule-based math checker vs. running code tests vs. a reward model), which makes joint RL infrastructure, curricula and hyperparameters hard to manage. The paper instead runs RL one domain at a time and claims this gives strong reasoning models at 8B/14B scale without later stages undoing earlier gains.
official.method:
Starting from Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-14B-Base, the authors run two-stage SFT (16K then 32K tokens) on responses mostly generated by DeepSeek-R1-0528 / DeepSeek-V3-0324, giving an 8B unified model (switches between thinking and non-thinking with /think and /no_think flags per user turn) and 8B/14B thinking-only models. They then apply Cascade RL: GRPO with strict on-policy training and no KL term, run in sequence as RLHF (72B reward model) -> instruction-following RL -> math RL (AceReason-Math, length curriculum 24K->32K->40K) -> code RL (9.8K competitive programming problems, binary pass-all-tests reward) -> SWE RL (Agentless code repair, execution-free patch-similarity reward). Each stage starts from the checkpoint of the previous one.

Evaluation uses a 64K-token generation budget, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, and reports pass@1 averaged over k samples (avg@8 for LiveCodeBench v5/v6, avg@64 for AIME). LiveCodeBench v6 here is the 08/24-05/25 split (454 problems), after the training-data cutoff. The SFT-checkpoint numbers (Table 2) and per-stage numbers (Tables 4-8) come from the authors' own runs; the numbers for Qwen3, Nemotron-Nano, DeepSeek-R1 and Gemini in Table 1 are officially reported results.
official.claim: After the full Cascade RL pipeline, the unified Nemotron-Cascade-8B scores 71.1 pass@1 (avg@8, thinking mode, 64K budget) on LiveCodeBench v6 (08/24-05/25), up 14.4 points from its own SFT checkpoint (56.7) and above Qwen3-8B (58.3, official); on AIME 2025 it scores 80.1 vs. 72.8 for its SFT checkpoint and 67.3 for Qwen3-8B.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results. For unified reasoning models, we report reasoning-related benchmark results in thinking mode. For IFEval and IFBench, we report the higher score obtained from either thinking or non-thinking mode. LCB stands for LiveCodeBench. When comparing with our inital SFT models in Table 2, ↑number indicates the improvement achieved by applying the Cascade RL to initial SFT models. † Genini-2.5 uses its own scaffolds for SWE evaluation rather than Agentless setup.
official.metric: pass@1 accuracy (%), higher is better, averaged over k samples per problem (avg@8 for LiveCodeBench, avg@64 for AIME); no standard deviations, seeds or confidence intervals are reported
official.comparison: Nemotron-Cascade-8B after Cascade RL vs. the same model's SFT checkpoint (authors' run, same evaluation) and vs. Qwen3-8B in thinking mode (officially reported numbers, not re-run by the authors)

title: Soft geometric inductive bias for object centric dynamics

official.background: Learned world models of moving objects benefit from geometric priors, and strictly equivariant architectures (e.g. the Geometric Algebra Transformer) build exact rotation/translation symmetry into the network. Real environments often break those symmetries (walls, gravity, confining potentials, road layouts), and a hard equivariance constraint can then underfit. This paper proposes a soft alternative: keep the geometric-algebra representation and primitives, but use non-equivariant Clifford linear layers so the model is biased toward geometric transformations without being forced to respect a symmetry the data do not have.
official.method:
Each object's state is embedded as multivectors of a projective geometric algebra (Cl(3,0,1) in 3D: position as x e1 + y e2 + z e3 + e0, velocity as vx e1 + vy e2 + vz e3, charge as a scalar). An autoregressive transformer predicts the next state of all objects; every token is one object at one timestep, attention uses the geometric-algebra inner product with a block-causal mask (all objects at a timestep predicted in parallel), and the L2 loss is computed directly in multivector space. Three variants differ only in the MLP/linear layers: S-CliffordTransformer uses non-equivariant Clifford linear layers W_ij * x_j with multivector weights (soft bias); E-CliffordTransformer uses the exactly equivariant linear maps of Brehmer et al. (2023); the baseline Transformer is the same block-causal architecture with standard attention and an embedding size chosen to match the parameter count (~1.5M; 10 blocks, 8 heads, 24 multivector channels). A parameter-matched 2-layer ReLU MLP is also run.

Data: charged N-body simulation following Satorras et al. (2021), 5 particles with Coulomb interactions, leapfrog integration, 3000 training trajectories of 50 frames. Symmetry is broken by (a) constant gravity along z and (b) a harmonic confining potential F_z = -k_z z of increasing strength k_z, which breaks E(3) to E(2) in the xy-plane. Training: AdamW, lr 5e-4, batch 128. The metric is rollout RMSE against the ground-truth simulation.
official.claim: On 3D charged particles under harmonic confinement, the equivariant E-CliffordTransformer's rollout RMSE rises from ~0.19 (k_z = 0) to ~0.39 (k_z = 3) while the soft S-CliffordTransformer stays at ~0.19-0.25, so at k_z = 3 the soft model's RMSE is about half the equivariant model's; under constant gravity the soft model (~0.25) also beats the parameter-matched Transformer (~0.35).
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Symmetry-breaking ablations. Left: constant gravity along z. Right: harmonic confinement F_z = -k_z z with increasing strength. The soft S-CliffordTransformer maintains robust performance as symmetry breaking increases, while the equivariant E-CliffordTransformer degrades under strong harmonic confinement.
official.metric: Rollout RMSE against the ground-truth simulator (lower is better). Right panel: lines with shaded bands, left panel: box plots, presumably over seeds; the paper does not define the bands or state the number of seeds. Values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: S-CliffordTransformer vs. E-CliffordTransformer (strictly equivariant), parameter-matched Transformer, and MLP, trained on the same simulated data for each confinement strength / gravity setting
official.falsification_criterion: Re-training at k_z = 3, the E-CliffordTransformer's rollout RMSE is not clearly higher than the S-CliffordTransformer's (e.g. the gap is under ~0.1 or within seed spread), or E-CliffordTransformer degrades no more from k_z = 0 to k_z = 3 than S-CliffordTransformer does; or under gravity along z the Transformer matches the S-CliffordTransformer.
