title: Lifting Biomolecular Data Acquisition

official.background: Learning a map from protein sequence to activity normally means synthesizing and testing one sequence at a time, so the information gained is bottlenecked by how many (sequence, activity) pairs the lab can afford. The paper proposes increasing information density instead: deliver several different sequences into each cell and measure one composite activity per cell, then deconvolute the sequence-activity map algorithmically during model training. Whether this actually helps depends on both the experimental design (how many sequences per cell) and the training algorithm, and the paper's central claim is that only the combination of the two produces gains.
official.method:
LIFT assumes the measured activity of a cell is the sum of the activities of the sequences it received: y_i ~ Noise(sum_j f_theta(x_ij), sigma), with the number of sequences per cell m_i drawn from a Poisson with mean equal to the multiplicity of infection (MOI) and each x_ij drawn from a generative library model p(x). The unknown molecule-activity map f_theta is a neural network (a CNN here) fitted by MAP estimation under a functional prior exp(-lambda ||f_theta||_{1,p}), i.e. an L1 norm in function space approximated by Monte Carlo samples from p(x). This is a functional, neural version of the LASSO. Since only hits are sequenced, a LeaVS correction term n_0 log p(y = 0) is added to the log likelihood; the paper shows this correction implicitly supplies the L1 functional regularization.

The synthetic benchmark (Section 6.1, Appendix C) sets p(x) to a variational-synthesis model of human antibody CDRH3 sequences and defines f(x) deterministically: f(x) = 1 by default, multiplied by 10 for each of three rare amino-acid motifs present. Observed counts y are negative binomial with mean f(x) and dispersion phi = 2.28; only cells with total observable strength >= 10 are kept. For each MOI in {0.10, 0.18, 0.31, 0.55, 0.98, 1.73, 3.06, 5.42, 9.59, 16.96, 30.0}, N = 2000 cells are simulated and the experiment is repeated 10 times. The conventional baseline uses the identical CNN architecture and negative binomial noise model but splits each multi-sequence cell ({x_i1, x_i2, ...}, y_i) into separate pairs (x_i1, y_i), (x_i2, y_i), ... and trains in the standard supervised way. Both are evaluated on held-out (x, f(x)) pairs by PR AUC for predicting f(x) > 10.
official.claim: On the synthetic CDRH3 benchmark with 2000 simulated cells per run, LIFT training's PR AUC rises with MOI from about 0.31 at MOI 0.10 to about 0.81 at MOI 30.0, while conventional training on the same simulated data falls from about 0.24 to a minimum of about 0.05 at MOI 9.59 and recovers only to about 0.31 at MOI 30.0; the LIFT-vs-conventional gap at MOI >= 5.42 is many times the plotted standard error across the 10 independent simulations.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2. The predictive performance of LIFT training versus conventional training across different experimental designs, on synthetic data. Error bars are s.e. across independent simulations.
official.metric: PR AUC (higher is better) for predicting the binarized label f(x) > 10 on held-out sequences; shaded bands are standard error across 10 independent simulation repeats
official.comparison: LIFT (functional neural LASSO / LeaVS-corrected training on mixture datapoints) vs. conventional supervised training (same CNN, same negative binomial noise model, multi-sequence cells split into individual (x, y) pairs), both on identically generated synthetic datasets at each MOI
official.falsification_criterion: Conventional training matches or exceeds LIFT at high MOI (e.g. 9.59 or 30.0), or LIFT's PR AUC fails to increase with MOI, or the LIFT-conventional gap at high MOI falls within the standard error across simulation repeats.

title: ProEdit: Inversion-based Editing From Prompts Done Right

official.background: Training-free, inversion-based editing maps a source image (or video) back to noise with a flow model such as FLUX, then samples again with a target prompt. To keep the background and structure unchanged, these methods start from the inverted latent and inject source attention features (usually V, sometimes K) while sampling. The authors argue that this injects too much source information, so edits that change an attribute such as color, pose or count often fail: the result stays close to the source attribute (an orange cat stays orange when the prompt asks for black).
official.method:
ProEdit is a plug-in for flow-based inversion editors (RF-Solver, FireFlow, UniEdit) on FLUX.1-[dev] with 15 sampling steps. A mask M of the edited region is taken from the text-to-image attention map of the last Double block at the first inversion step, then dilated by one step. KV-mix: in all Double and Single blocks, on visual tokens only, the target K and V inside M are replaced by delta*target + (1-delta)*source (delta = 0.9), while outside M the source K and V are injected in full. Text attention always uses the target-prompt features (Eq. 7).

Latents-Shift: before sampling, the inverted noise z_T inside M is AdaIN-renormalized to the mean and std of fresh Gaussian noise and blended with the original latent, z_hat = M*(beta*z_tilde + (1-beta)*z_T) + (1-M)*z_T with beta = 0.25 (Eq. 8). The color-editing evaluation uses the color-change category of PIE-Bench and reports background SSIM on unedited regions plus CLIP similarity of the whole image and of the edited region.
official.claim: On the PIE-Bench color-editing category, adding ProEdit to RF-Solver (FLUX.1-dev) raises background SSIM (x100) from 80.21 to 86.63 and edited-region CLIP similarity from 20.86 to 22.88, and gives similar gains for FireFlow (80.14 -> 86.53 SSIM; 21.02 -> 22.55 edited CLIP).
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Quantitative comparison on Color Editing. The best and second-best results are shown in bold and underline.
official.metric: Background-preservation SSIM (x10^2, higher is better) on unedited regions; CLIP similarity for the whole image and the edited region (higher is better). Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: RF-Solver vs. RF-Solver+ProEdit, FireFlow vs. FireFlow+ProEdit, UniEdit vs. UniEdit+ProEdit, all on FLUX.1-dev and the PIE-Bench color-editing subset
official.falsification_criterion: When RF-Solver and RF-Solver+ProEdit are run on the PIE-Bench color-change subset with the stated settings (delta=0.9, beta=0.25, 15 steps), ProEdit fails to improve both background SSIM and edited-region CLIP similarity by a margin larger than the variation across random seeds (e.g. edited CLIP gain well below ~2 points or SSIM gain well below ~6 points).

title: Self-Rewarded Multimodal Coherent Reasoning Across Diverse Visual Domains
claim_source: Table 4, page 12 (appendix); SR-MCR-7B MMMU figure also in Table 1, page 5

official.background: Multimodal LLMs often give the right final answer with reasoning that is incoherent or not grounded in the image, partly because RL alignment usually rewards only the final answer. This paper asks whether cheap, label-free signals computed from the model's own outputs (semantic and lexical agreement between reasoning and answer, low repetition, CLIP-based visual grounding, NLI-based step consistency) can serve as a process-level reward to fine-tune a VLM without human preference labels or a learned reward model.
official.method:
SR-MCR scores each sampled response with five normalized signals: Sentence-BERT (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) cosine similarity between each reasoning sentence and the answer, ROUGE-L between reasoning and answer, 1 minus the fraction of repeated bigrams, CLIP similarity between spaCy-extracted text mentions and DETR-detected image regions, and DeBERTa-v3 NLI min(entailment, 1 - contradiction) between adjacent steps. Each score is winsorized and min-max normalized, then the scores are combined with softmax reliability weights (from validation correlation, inverse variance, EMA stability, or uniform). A cooling factor multiplies the reward by sigmoid(kappa (mean token NLL - c)), with gamma = 1, kappa = 5, c = 0.1, to down-weight trivial and overconfident samples. A LoRA adapter on Qwen2.5-VL-7B is trained with GRPO on this reward (4 generations per prompt, KL coefficient 0.01, lr 1e-6, rollout and global batch size 4 per Table 9, though Sec. 7.2 says 8xH800 with global batch 128). Training data is ScienceQA-IMG (hints removed) plus the full Visual7W.

The matched baseline (Appendix 7.1, Table 4) is Rejection-Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT): for each training prompt, draw N = 4 responses from the base model, score them with the same 5-term reward, keep the best one, and run standard SFT on it. Both models are evaluated on MMMU-val, MMBench v1.1, MME and V*Bench with think/answer prompt templates.
official.claim: Starting from Qwen2.5-VL-7B and using the same 5-term self-reward, online GRPO training (SR-MCR-7B) reaches 67.6% on MMMU-val versus 56.4% for offline best-of-4 rejection-sampling fine-tuning (base: 50.3%), and it is also ahead on MMBench (91.2 vs. 88.1), MME (94.5 vs. 91.2) and V*Bench (80.6 vs. 79.1).
official.claim_caption: Table 4. Necessity of Online Optimization. Comparison between the Base Model, Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT), and our SR-MCR on the 7B scale. RFT uses the same 5-term reward to select the best-of-N (N = 4) samples for supervised training. SR-MCR significantly outperforms RFT, demonstrating the critical value of online exploration.
official.metric: Benchmark accuracy (%), higher is better; single run per model, no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: SR-MCR-7B (online GRPO with the self-reward) vs. RFT-7B (best-of-4 under the same self-reward, then SFT) vs. untuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction of SR-MCR on Qwen2.5-VL-7B with the described reward and data does not beat a matched best-of-4 RFT baseline on MMMU-val by a clear margin (e.g. under 3 points), or SR-MCR-7B lands far below the claimed 67.6% on MMMU-val (e.g. within a few points of the 50.3% base).

title: Fusion or Confusion? Multimodal Complexity Is Not All You Need
claim_source: Figure 5, page 8 (numbers for the corrected protocol from Table 5, page 21)

official.background: Multimodal learning papers keep proposing more complex fusion, encoder, head, missing-modality and gradient-balancing mechanisms and report gains over earlier methods. Those gains are hard to interpret because papers differ in data splits, hyperparameter tuning, initialization and optimizer, and often skip cross-validation and significance testing. This paper reimplements 19 late-fusion methods under one protocol on nine datasets and asks whether any of them reliably beats a well-tuned simple baseline. It also includes a case study showing how evaluation choices in a recent NeurIPS 2025 oral method (AUG) change its reported ranking.
official.method:
SimBaMM is a simple late-fusion model. Each modality goes through its own encoder and a linear projection to a shared width d. The resulting tokens (one [CLS]-style token per modality in SimBaMM-CLS) form a sequence that a Transformer head processes, with an attention mask that hides missing modalities, followed by a linear output layer trained with cross-entropy. All methods share the same dataset-specific encoders, Kaiming initialization and ScheduleFree AdamW (SGD only where a method requires it). SimBaMM's hyperparameters come from a Bayesian search, and each competing method is then tuned on its method-specific and optimizer parameters under a controlled budget. Results are the mean ± SD over subject-wise 5-fold cross-validation.

In the CREMA-D case study (6-class emotion recognition, 7,442 clips, audio spectrogram + video frames, a ResNet encoder for each), AUG is generalized to M modalities, given the same Transformer head and tuned. Both methods are compared under (a) the original protocol inherited from OGM (train/test split only, model selection on the test set, speaker overlap between splits) and (b) the corrected protocol (speaker-independent splits, separate validation set for model selection, consistent tuning). The figure reports video-only, audio-only and multimodal accuracy for each method.
official.claim: On CREMA-D under the corrected protocol (speaker-independent 5-fold CV, validation-based model selection, both methods tuned), the simple late-fusion baseline SimBaMM-CLS reaches multimodal 6-class accuracy 0.6723 ± 0.031, versus 0.6105 ± 0.029 for AUG. Under the original leaky protocol, AUG ranks above SimBaMM (about 0.79 vs. 0.74).
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Case study on the CREMA-D dataset. Under a corrected data protocol with subject-independent splits and consistent hyperparameter tuning, the relative performance of methods changes.
official.metric: 6-class accuracy (Acc6) on CREMA-D, higher is better; ± is the standard deviation over the 5 subject-wise cross-validation folds. The original-protocol bars have no error bars.
official.comparison: SimBaMM(-CLS) vs. AUG, each under the original OGM/AUG data protocol and under the corrected speaker-independent protocol; the video-only and audio-only accuracies of each method are also shown
official.falsification_criterion: Under speaker-independent 5-fold CV with validation-based model selection and comparable tuning for both methods, AUG's multimodal accuracy matches or exceeds SimBaMM-CLS (e.g. the gap is under 1 fold SD, or reversed). Alternatively, the ranking does not depend on the protocol, i.e. AUG is not ahead of SimBaMM under the original leaky splits.

title: Imitation from Observations with Trajectory-Level Generative Embeddings

official.background: In offline imitation learning from observations (LfO), the agent gets a single expert demonstration that contains only states, no actions, plus a large unlabeled offline dataset that is mostly suboptimal. It must learn an expert-like policy without interacting with the environment. The leading methods (SMODICE, PW-DICE, DILO) estimate density ratios between expert and offline state distributions. These ratios become ill-conditioned when the offline data covers the expert's states poorly, for example when only a few expert trajectories are mixed into a medium-quality dataset. A reward signal that stays informative far from the expert's support could make standard offline RL usable in this regime.
official.method:
TGE trains a Diffuser-style temporal U-Net diffusion model (horizon H=32, 20 diffusion steps) on state-action segments from the offline dataset. The U-Net's downsampling half is treated as an encoder phi, and the clean-input embedding z = phi(tau, 0) is computed with the action dimensions masked, so states alone determine the embedding. Expert embeddings come from sliding windows (stride 1) over the single state-only expert episode. For each offline state s_t, the segment s_{t:t+H} is encoded, all embeddings are L2-normalised to the unit sphere, and the reward is the mean over the m=10 nearest expert embeddings of -log(1 + ||z_t - z_E|| / sigma) with sigma=1. The rewards are then normalised.

The relabelled dataset is used to train a standard offline RL algorithm. In TGE+ReBRAC, the actor's behaviour-cloning penalty is additionally weighted per transition by the normalised TGE reward (actor BC coefficient 0.4 on MuJoCo). Baselines are trajectory-level BC with Diffuser, SMODICE, PW-DICE and DILO, all run with their original implementations and hyperparameters. Each method gets the same offline dataset (1M D4RL medium transitions plus 30 unlabeled expert trajectories for medium+few-expert) and the same single state-only expert episode. The metric is the normalised D4RL score, mean ± std over 5 seeds.
official.claim: In the D4RL medium+few-expert offline LfO setting, TGE+ReBRAC reaches normalised scores of 97.24 ± 2.22 (hopper), 91.83 ± 0.80 (halfcheetah), 108.02 ± 0.76 (walker2d) and 130.23 ± 1.36 (ant). The best baseline in each task scores 61.97 ± 1.65 (TGE+IQL; best external baseline PW-DICE 56.79 ± 11.55), 66.07 ± 8.52 (DILO), 80.77 ± 3.14 (PW-DICE) and 101.26 ± 8.73 (PW-DICE).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main Results. TGE (combined with IQL or ReBRAC, highlighted in cyan) is compared against state-of-the-art offline LfO baselines. The results demonstrate that TGE achieves superior performance. We report the mean and standard deviation for each result with five random seeds. The top-performing results and those with overlapping standard deviations are highlighted in bold.
official.metric: Normalised D4RL return (higher is better; 100 = D4RL expert reference), mean ± standard deviation over 5 random seeds
official.comparison: TGE+ReBRAC vs. Diffuser (BC), SMODICE, PW-DICE, DILO (and TGE+IQL), same offline dataset and same single state-only expert episode
official.falsification_criterion: On medium+few-expert halfcheetah (or another of the four MuJoCo tasks), a 5-seed TGE+ReBRAC run does not beat the best of SMODICE/PW-DICE/DILO by more than the combined seed std, e.g. halfcheetah TGE+ReBRAC under about 75 or DILO above about 85.

title: AlignDrive: Aligned Lateral-Longitudinal Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

official.background: End-to-end autonomous driving models map camera images directly to planned motion. Recent state-of-the-art planners (e.g. HiP-AD) split planning into a lateral task (a drive path of spatially spaced waypoints for steering) and a longitudinal task (time-spaced trajectory waypoints for speed) and decode them with independent, parallel heads. Because the speed plan is not explicitly tied to the path the car will actually follow, it can ignore agents that cut into that path, which causes collisions in interactive scenarios such as merges and cut-ins. Closed-loop benchmarks like Bench2Drive in the CARLA simulator measure whether such planners actually complete routes safely.
official.method:
AlignDrive is a sparse, query-based camera-only driving model. A Drive Path Predictor first refines anchor-based drive-path, map and agent queries (deformable attention on multi-view image features, temporal and inter-task cross-attention) and outputs candidate drive paths (15 waypoints at 2 m spacing). A cascaded Longitudinal Planning module then predicts, for each candidate path, anchor-based 1D displacement sequences along that path (5 Hz, 3 s horizon); its queries attend to points sampled on the predicted path, to decoded-and-re-encoded agent boxes and future motions at each time step, and to map queries. Planning-oriented data augmentation inserts, with probability 0.1, a virtual agent heading toward a point on the ego ground-truth path; if it would collide, the ground-truth displacement sequence is uniformly scaled down to the maximal safe distance. Path and speed are tracked by two PID controllers.

Table 5 ablates three components on Bench2Drive (220 closed-loop CARLA routes, trained on the 950-clip Bench2Drive base set): LP (longitudinal planning conditioned on the predicted path), DP (1D displacement instead of 2D waypoint targets) and DA (data augmentation). Variant A has none of them and predicts the drive path and longitudinal trajectory in parallel, following HiP-AD; Variant E is the full AlignDrive. All variants use the same candidate-selection and control strategy. Training: 36 epochs (path predictor alone for the first 12; augmentation enabled after epoch 24), 64 RTX L20 GPUs, batch 512, AdamW, lr 1e-4.
official.claim: On Bench2Drive closed-loop evaluation, full AlignDrive (path-conditioned 1D displacement planning + planning-oriented augmentation) reaches Driving Score 89.07, Success Rate 73.18% and Collision Rate 11.4%, versus 83.21, 63.18% and 22.7% for the same model with parallel path/trajectory decoding (Variant A).
official.claim_caption: Ablation study on AlignDrive components. LP: uses lateral path prediction to condition longitudinal planning; DP: formulates longitudinal planning as displacement regression along the drive path; DA: applies planning-oriented data augmentation
official.metric: Bench2Drive Driving Score (higher better), Success Rate % (higher better), Collision Rate % = share of routes with a collision with a dynamic vehicle (lower better). Single run per variant, no error bars; Table 9 (p. 17) gives 3 simulator runs of the full model: DS 89.07 / 87.80 / 88.05 (mean 88.30), SR 73.18 / 71.36 / 70.00 (mean 71.50).
official.comparison: Variant E (LP + DP + DA, full AlignDrive) vs. Variant A (parallel lateral and longitudinal heads, HiP-AD style), with intermediate variants B (LP), C (LP+DP), D (LP+DA)
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained full model and a retrained parallel Variant A, each evaluated over several CARLA runs, differ by less than about 2 Driving Score points or 4 Success Rate points (roughly the run-to-run spread in Table 9), or Variant A has a collision rate no higher than the full model.

title: MCGI: Manifold-Consistent Graph Indexing for Billion-Scale Disk-Resident Vector Search

official.background: Disk-resident graph indexes such as DiskANN (Vamana) serve approximate nearest neighbor search over billions of vectors by keeping compressed (PQ) codes in RAM and reading full-precision vectors and adjacency lists from SSD during a beam search. Search cost is dominated by the number of disk reads per query, which is set by a single fixed candidate-list size L for all queries. Queries differ in difficulty: those in regions of high local intrinsic dimensionality (LID) need longer lists to reach high recall, while those in low-LID regions converge early, so a fixed L that is long enough for hard queries wastes disk reads on easy ones.
official.method:
MCGI keeps the standard DiskANN index and search engine and changes only the candidate-list size per query. After n0 = 24 expansions of the beam search, it computes five features from distances already computed: the log of an MLE (Hill) LID estimate over the exact distances of the k = 10 nearest expanded nodes, the same LID estimate over the PQ distances of the m = 64 best candidates, ln r1 and ln rk, and log(1 + number of candidates whose squared distance is within (1 + 0.2) rk^2). A ridge-regressed linear score w^T f(q) + b, fitted on 10,000 calibration queries disjoint from the test queries (target: log of the smallest list size at which the calibration query reaches its best recall), resizes the list once: L(q) = min{8 L̄, max{10, L̄ exp(γ (w^T f(q) + b − s̄))}}, where s̄ is the mean calibration score and γ is picked from {0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3} on calibration queries (0.7 for GIST1M). The search then continues without restart.

On GIST1M (1M vectors, 960-dim, 1,000 queries), one Vamana index is built with α = 1.2, Lbuild = 100, 322-byte PQ codes, at R = 32 and at R = 48. DiskANN (fixed list) and MCGI search the same index with the same PQ codes, beam width 2, 32 threads and requested list sizes L̄ in {10, ..., 400}. Each method gives one (Recall@10, QPS, reads) point per L̄; values at 95% Recall@10 are linearly interpolated along the recall axis. PipeANN (pipelined I/O) searches the same index files as a second baseline.
official.claim: On GIST1M at 95% Recall@10, MCGI's query-adaptive list issues 223.7 disk reads per query versus 272.7 for DiskANN's fixed list on the same R = 32 index (18% fewer), and 125.5 versus 146.7 on the R = 48 index (14% fewer), also fewer than PipeANN (268.3 and 143.8).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: QPS and disk reads per query at 95% recall.
official.metric: Mean disk reads (graph node reads) per query at 95% Recall@10, lower is better, interpolated along each method's recall curve; QPS also reported. Single run per setting, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: MCGI vs. DiskANN fixed-list beam search on the identical Vamana index (same PQ codes, beam width, list grid); PipeANN on the same index files as a secondary baseline.
official.falsification_criterion: On a GIST1M Vamana index with R = 32 (or 48), the query-adaptive list, calibrated on disjoint queries as described, does not reduce mean disk reads per query at 95% Recall@10 by clearly more than a few percent relative to the fixed-list DiskANN search on the same index (e.g., under 5% reduction), or the reduction vanishes when the calibration set is disjoint from the test queries.

title: Diffusion-DRF: Free, Rich, and Differentiable Reward for Video Diffusion Fine-Tuning
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (seed variance in Section D.4, page 20)

official.background: Post-training of text-to-video diffusion models usually relies on scalar rewards from reward models trained on human preference data (e.g. VideoAlign, PickScore) or on DPO/GRPO-style preference optimization. These rewards are costly to build, give only one global score per video, and are prone to reward hacking: quality improves early in training and then degrades, often toward unrequested stylization. The paper asks whether a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model can serve as a differentiable critic that gives richer, harder-to-exploit feedback without any reward-model training or preference data.
official.method:
Diffusion-DRF fine-tunes the DiT of Wan2.1-1.3B-T2V (VAE, text encoder and VLM frozen) on 5,077 caption-video pairs from OpenVid-1M. Offline, a text LLM (Qwen2.5-7B) decomposes each caption into scene elements and writes one Yes/No question per dimension: text-video alignment (TA), physical fidelity (Phy) and visual quality (VQ). Qwen2.5-VL-7B then produces reference answers (a Yes/No token plus a free-form explanation under 50 words) with near-greedy decoding, answering Phy/VQ on the paired real video; only samples whose reference answers are all Yes are kept (24,252 queries).

During training, each caption prompts an on-policy video (512x288, 49 frames, 25 denoising steps). The loss is the teacher-forced next-token NLL of the cached reference answers under the frozen VLM, conditioned on 10 subsampled frames of the generated video and, for Phy/VQ, 10 frames of the caption-matched real video. Gradients flow through the VLM, a lightweight H3AE decoder and only the last K denoising steps (K=4 in the reported run), with activation checkpointing. Training uses AdamW, lr 1e-5, 16 A100-80GB, batch 1 per GPU; the best checkpoint (step 1500) is reported. Baselines (Flow-DPO, Flow-GRPO, PickScore, VideoAlign, and Vanilla-DRF, which uses a single 'Does this video match the prompt?' yes/no log-prob) fine-tune the same base model on the same data, and each is reported at its best checkpoint.
official.claim: Fine-tuning Wan2.1-1.3B-T2V with Diffusion-DRF (Qwen2.5-VL-7B critic) reaches VBench-2.0 Overall 55.38 (3 seeds: 55.44 ± 0.26), versus 53.55 for VideoAlign (the strongest prior-method baseline), 53.70 for the authors' own single-question Vanilla-DRF (7B) variant, and 52.99 for the base model.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative results on VBench-2.0. In addition to the overall score, we report representative sub-dimension metrics closely related to text-video alignment and physical fidelity. The best results are highlighted in bold, and the second best are underlined. For completeness, we evaluate Diffusion-DRF with three different VLM backbones: InternVL3-1B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, denoted as Diffusion-DRF (1B), (3B), and (7B), respectively. All methods are trained with Wan2.1-1.3B-T2V as base model on the same datasets for fair comparisons.
official.metric: VBench-2.0 Overall score (higher is better), best checkpoint per method. Table 1 values are single runs; ± is std over 3 seeds and is reported only for Diffusion-DRF (7B). Baselines have no error bars.
official.comparison: Diffusion-DRF (7B) vs. VideoAlign differentiable reward tuning (strongest prior-method baseline), plus Flow-DPO, Flow-GRPO, PickScore, Vanilla-DRF and the untuned base model, all fine-tuning Wan2.1-1.3B-T2V on the same 5K prompts.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining under the paper's protocol (same base model, data and best-checkpoint selection) gives Diffusion-DRF a VBench-2.0 Overall no more than about 0.5 points above a VideoAlign-reward run, or below it.

title: Paradoxical noise preference in RNNs

official.background: Recurrent neural networks used as models of biological neural populations are usually trained with injected noise, both to mimic neural variability and as a regularizer. The usual assumption is that removing the noise at test time should keep or improve performance. This paper reports the opposite for continuous-time RNNs (CTRNNs) when the noise is injected inside the activation function, as is common in computational neuroscience: the trained networks perform best at a nonzero test noise close to the training noise, because the noise shifts the stationary states of the dynamics and the network learns to rely on that shift.
official.method:
The CTRNN is Euler-discretized as h_{t+1} = (1 - γ) h_t + γ f(W_rec h_t + W_in u_t + B_in + N(0, σ_in²)) for noise-in networks, and h_{t+1} = (1 - γ) h_t + γ (f(W_rec h_t + W_in u_t + B_in) + N(0, σ_out²)) for noise-out networks, with γ = Δt/τ = 0.02/0.1 = 0.2, output z = W_out h + B_out, 100 neurons, and ReLU or SoftPlus (α = 10) activation. Noise is sampled independently per neuron per step. Weights start from N(0, 0.8/√n), biases at zero, and the initial state is a trained vector starting at zero.

Task: compute g(x) = sin(x) for x ∈ [0, 2π] (also tanh(x) on [-4, 4]); the constant input x is on for 100 steps and the output is read at the last step (fixed readout) or, for random readout, at a step drawn uniformly from [70, 100] (in training, the random-readout loss uses two readout times: the final step and one random step). Training uses an RMSE loss, Adam (lr 0.001, half-life 2,500 batches), 10,000 batches of 32 trials, training noise std 0.1, and no other regularization. The trained networks are then tested over a range of noise std from 0 to about 0.15 (same placement as in training), and RMSE, mean error (bias) and error std are reported over many noise realizations.
official.claim: For 100-neuron CTRNNs trained on sin(x) (fixed readout) with noise std 0.1, noise-in networks reach their lowest test RMSE (about 0.03) at test noise ≈ 0.1 and have about 0.23 RMSE at zero test noise, whereas noise-out networks have their lowest RMSE (about 0.015) at zero test noise, rising to about 0.04 at 0.1.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Simple function computation: Noise-in networks prefer the training noise level, but noise-out networks prefer zero noise. a) Root mean squared error, mean error, and error standard deviations for noise-in function computation networks. The best performance occurs when testing at or near the training noise level, and this preference is driven by a non-monotonic dependence between the noise level and the mean error (i.e., the systematic error). [...] b) Noise-preference results for fixed readout time sine computation networks trained with various training noise levels. Noise preference becomes more pronounced for greater training noise, with very low training noise resulting in zero noise preference. [...] d) Root mean squared error, mean error, and error standard deviations for noise-out function computation networks. Unlike the noise-in networks, the noise-out networks perform best when tested with zero noise, and the systematic error appears unaffected by changes in the noise.
official.metric: Test RMSE between network output and target over inputs and noise realizations (lower is better), split into mean error (bias) and error std; no error bars or seed variation shown in Figure 2 (Figure A1 shows four independent runs qualitatively); values are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Noise-in vs. noise-out CTRNNs trained identically (same task, size and training noise 0.1), each tested from zero noise up to above the training noise; and within noise-in networks, test noise 0 vs. test noise at the training level
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained noise-in sin(x) networks (training noise 0.1) have test RMSE at zero noise that is not clearly higher than at noise ≈ 0.1 (e.g. less than 2x), or the minimum of RMSE vs. test noise is at or near zero; or noise-out networks trained the same way show a minimum at a clearly nonzero test noise.

title: Leveraging Soft Prompts for Privacy Attacks in Federated Prompt Tuning

official.background: In federated prompt tuning (FPT), clients adapt a frozen pre-trained vision transformer by training a shared pool of soft prompts, each paired with a learnable key. For each input, the client picks the top-N prompts whose keys have the highest cosine similarity to the input's [CLS] query feature, then sends the updated prompts and keys back to the server. Because only prompts are exchanged, FPT is often assumed to be more private than sharing gradients or full weights. Membership inference attacks (MIAs), where a server tries to determine whether a specific example is in a client's private training data, have mostly been studied for gradient- or weight-sharing FL. This paper asks whether the prompt selection mechanism in FPT itself leaks membership.
official.method:
PromptMIA is an active attack by a malicious server. Before a round, the server takes the aggregated pool of M = 20 key-prompt pairs and replaces the keys of N = 4 prompts with adversarial keys built for a target sample T. Each adversarial key is constructed (Algorithms 1-2, Appendix A.2) to have cosine similarity to the target query q(T) in the interval [s_max + δ_min, s_max + δ_min + Δ], where s_max is the highest similarity of any benign key to q(T); δ_min = 0.02 and Δ = 0.05. This guarantees that if T is in a client's batch, all N adversarial prompts are selected and updated (TPR = 1). The server predicts 'member' if and only if all adversarial prompts come back updated. Advantage = TPR - FPR.

Setup (Appendix A.7): frozen ViT-B/32, DeiT-B/16 or ConViT-Base backbones; CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and a pooled FourDataset (MNIST-M, Fashion-MNIST, CINIC-10, MMAFEDB); 80 clients with Dirichlet(α = 0.5) label partitions, 10 clients per round, FedAvg, 60 rounds, Adam (lr 1e-3 for keys, 1e-4 for prompts and classifier), λ = 0.5, client batch size 64 for the attacked round. Baselines are loss-based MIAs adapted to FPT: Blackbox-Loss (Yeom et al.), Loss-Series (CS-MIA) and FedMIA-I. Since they give continuous scores, they are evaluated at (i) a threshold matched to PromptMIA's FPR on the same model and (ii) the threshold that maximizes their Advantage using the true membership labels (an oracle upper bound).
official.claim: With client batch size 64, PromptMIA reaches membership-inference Advantage of about 0.96 (CIFAR-10), 0.98 (CIFAR-100), 0.99 (TinyImageNet) and 1.00 (FourDataset), while Blackbox-Loss, Loss-Series and FedMIA-I reach at most about 0.47, 0.57, 0.57 and 0.82 respectively, even at their oracle-chosen best thresholds, and at most about 0.12 at PromptMIA's FPR.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Comparison of PromptMIA vs. existing federated MIAs (batch size = 64).
official.metric: Advantage = TPR - FPR of the membership guess (higher is better), read off a bar chart. Error bars are shown but not defined for this figure; elsewhere (Appendix A.11) results are averaged over 5 repeats of the security game on one trained model.
official.comparison: PromptMIA vs. Blackbox-Loss, Loss-Series and FedMIA-I on the same trained FPT models, with the baselines evaluated both at PromptMIA's FPR and at their Advantage-maximizing threshold
official.falsification_criterion: On any of the four datasets at batch size 64, the best baseline at its best threshold comes within 0.1 Advantage of PromptMIA, or PromptMIA's Advantage falls below about 0.9.

title: Tune-Up Open-Weight CLIP: Optimization Framework for Self-Supervised Fine-tuning of CLIP

official.background: Improving CLIP models usually means pretraining again from scratch on billions of image-text pairs, which few groups can afford. Supervised fine-tuning on a labelled target dataset improves that one task but tends to hurt robustness and transfer. The paper studies self-supervised fine-tuning (SSFT): continuing contrastive training of an already-released CLIP checkpoint on a generic web image-text corpus to improve it across many tasks at once. The authors and prior work (CLIP-Refine) observe that simply resuming standard contrastive training from a well-pretrained checkpoint makes the model worse, with a sharp drop in the first epoch that is not recovered later.
official.method:
TuneCLIP has two stages. Stage I, Optimizer Statistics Recovery (OSR), runs the SogCLR/FastCLIP global-contrastive-loss update for 5 epochs with the model weights frozen at the pretrained checkpoint, only to accumulate the Adam first and second moments (m, v) and the per-sample running estimates u_{i,x}, u_{i,z} of the softmax normalisers. The authors argue that the usual zero or single-batch initialisation of these statistics (cold-start bias) causes the early performance drop. Stage II initialises the optimizer and u-estimates from OSR and fine-tunes for 5 more epochs with SogCLR + AdamW on a Hinged Global Contrastive Loss (HGCL), where the pairwise term s_ij - s_ii is replaced by max(s_ij - s_ii + m, 0)^2 with margin m = 0.1, so negatives already m below the positive stop receiving gradient (meant to limit over-penalising false negatives).

Main setting: OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/16 fine-tuned on DFN-12M, temperature fixed to the checkpoint's value, AdamW (0.9, 0.98), lr 1e-5 with cosine schedule, weight decay 0.02, global batch 2048 (256 x 8 GPUs), 224x224 images. Baselines run on the same data and model: FastCLIP (GCL + SogCLR, 5 epochs), OpenCLIP (mini-batch contrastive loss, 5 epochs) and CLIP-Refine (1 epoch, as its authors recommend). Evaluation follows the DataComp protocol: mean zero-shot top-1 over ImageNet-1k and six distribution-shift variants, mean Recall@1 over MSCOCO and Flickr30k image and text retrieval, and the 38-task DataComp average.
official.claim: Fine-tuning OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/16 on DFN-12M, TuneCLIP raises mean retrieval Recall@1 from 57.46 to 64.12, while the best matched baseline (CLIP-Refine) reaches 58.82; TuneCLIP also improves ImageNet & variants (57.67 -> 59.36) and DataComp (56.26 -> 58.62), where FastCLIP, OpenCLIP and CLIP-Refine all fall below the base model.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Summary of mean zero-shot performance across ImageNet & distributional variants, retrieval benchmarks, and the DataComp benchmark, together with wall-clock training time per GPU.
official.metric: Mean zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1k + 6 variants, mean Recall@1 on MSCOCO/Flickr30k retrieval (I->T and T->I), DataComp 38-task average; all higher is better. Single runs, no seeds or error bars reported.

title: CaMeLs Can Use Computers Too: System-level Security for Computer Use Agents

official.background: Computer use agents (CUAs) look at screenshots and issue clicks and keystrokes, so any text or pixels on screen (ads, web pages, documents) can carry a prompt injection that hijacks the agent. The Dual-LLM pattern (e.g. CaMeL) defends against this structurally: a privileged planner that never sees untrusted data writes the whole program upfront, and a quarantined model only fills in values at runtime. This guarantees control-flow integrity, but it was thought to be unusable for CUAs, because GUI tasks seem to need the planner to look at the screen after every step.
official.method:
The authors put OSWorld into the official CaMeL code base. A privileged planner LLM (P-LLM) writes a complete Python-like plan in a single shot before seeing the environment. An interpreter runs the plan and calls a quarantined vision model (Q-VLM, here the UI-TARS-1.5-7B CUA) for runtime values such as UI coordinates (find) or screen summaries. CaMeL's security policies are turned off. NOVA (Navigating via Observation, Verification, and Action) is a planner system prompt that makes the plan follow Observe -> Verify -> Act for each step. It adds a verify_hypothesis primitive (a Q-LLM call under a fixed comparison prompt that returns a boolean about the current observation, which the plan branches on) and shared routines such as cookie-banner handling, browser-state checks and fallback find strategies.

The baseline, CaMeL-CUA-unoptimized (UITars-dagger), uses the same architecture and the same Q-VLM but a generic system prompt: no Observe-Verify-Act guidance, no CUA navigation guidance and no verify_hypothesis. Both are evaluated on the same 60 OSWorld tasks, which are the tasks the undefended UITars-1.5-7B agent solved at pass@1 with a 15-step cap (Table 2). Pass@k counts a task as solved if any of k independently sampled plans passes OSWorld's automatic checker.
official.claim: On the same 60 OSWorld tasks with UITars-1.5-7B as the perception model, CaMeL-NOVA solves 35/60 (58.3%) at pass@3 and 25/60 (41.7%) at pass@1, compared with 11/60 (18.3%) and 4/60 (6.7%) for the unoptimized CaMeL-CUA baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison of CUA backends with CaMeL-NOVA across different task sets. NOVA (Navigating via Observation, Verification, and Action) is a structured planning method we introduce, in which the planner is prompted to organize each step as Observe->Verify->Act. We first contrast the CaMeL-CUA-unoptimized baseline (a generic system prompt without Observe->Verify->Act guidance or other CUA navigation guidance, and no verify_hypothesis; denoted UITars-dagger), against UITars with CaMeL-NOVA on the same 60 tasks: 11/60 (18.3%) vs 35/60 (58.3%) at Pass@3 — a 40-point gap demonstrating that NOVA's planning method is essential for the CaMeL+CUA setup to work. We then evaluate CaMeL-NOVA across different CUA backends (OpenCUA-32B and Claude Sonnet 4.5) on the same task set and find that CUA differences become less significant under CaMeL-NOVA. OpenCUA on OpenCUA tasks and Claude on Claude tasks show similar results even at larger set sizes, underscoring the strong performance of CaMeL-NOVA. For All tasks, we evaluate only with UITars as the CUA at a lower pass@k rate and include the 30 non-automatically evaluable tasks that are originally set to success by default on OSWorld in the Overall row (second value, n = 369), and find that CaMeL-NOVA performance (29%) yields a higher success rate than just UITars (24.4%).
official.metric: OSWorld task success (automatic checker), pass@k over independently sampled single-shot plans, higher is better; counts out of 60 tasks; no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: CaMeL-NOVA (UITars column) vs. CaMeL-CUA-unoptimized (UITars-dagger column): same Dual-LLM architecture, Q-VLM and 60 tasks; only the planner prompt/toolset differs (Observe-Verify-Act guidance plus verify_hypothesis)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both configurations on the 60-task UITars set gives a CaMeL-NOVA pass@3 that is not clearly above the unoptimized baseline (e.g. a gap under ~15 points, or under 10 tasks), or a CaMeL-NOVA pass@1 at or below the baseline's pass@3.

title: Explanation Multiplicity in SHAP: Characterization and Assessment
claim_source: Figure 4, page 8 (other datasets in Figure 12, Appendix E)

official.background: SHAP feature attributions are used to justify individual decisions in lending, healthcare and public services, usually as a ranked list of the most important features. Model-agnostic SHAP estimators such as Kernel SHAP approximate Shapley values by filling 'absent' features from a small sampled background dataset (often 100 rows, as in the SHAP tutorials), so rerunning the same explainer on the same trained model and instance can give a different explanation. The paper calls this explanation multiplicity and argues that the common magnitude-based stability check (l2 distance between attribution vectors) hides how often the top-ranked features change.
official.method:
For each dataset and model (Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, MLP, FT-Transformer, tuned by grid search on the training fold), the model is trained once and Kernel SHAP is run R = 5 times on every test instance of the first held-out fold of a stratified five-fold split, each run using a different background seed to draw K = 100 background rows. Background strategies are Random row sampling, Kernel SHAP K-Means summarization, prediction-stratified sampling (PredStrat) and Compress-Then-Explain (CTE). Kernel SHAP uses min(2^d, 1024) coalitions; GMSC has d = 10 and N = 9,000 test instances.

For each instance, the 10 run pairs are compared with three distances: l2 between attribution vectors, top-3 Jaccard distance between the sets of the three features with largest |phi|, and 1 - RBO. Each distance is thresholded at the minimum of a randomized null-model band: a Dirichlet model (total mass T = 0.4, r = floor(d/3), rho in {0.6, 0.7, 0.8}, kappa in {5..15}) gives an RMS l2 reference, and a Mallows model (q in {0.3, 0.4, 0.5}) gives the rank-metric references. The reported number is the percentage of the 10N run-pair-instance comparisons whose distance strictly exceeds the threshold (Eq. 7). For top-3 Jaccard the threshold lies below the smallest positive value (0.5), so exceedance equals the frequency with which the top-3 feature set changes between two runs.
official.claim: On Give Me Some Credit with Kernel SHAP and K = 100 background rows, 0% of run-pair-instance comparisons exceed the l2 randomized baseline for every model and sampling method, whereas under Random, PredStrat and CTE backgrounds the top-3 feature set differs between two reruns in 10-65% of comparisons (Random sampling: DT 10%, RF 29%, XGB 42%, MLP 28%, FTT 49%; PredStrat 37-65%; CTE 29-44%; K-Means is lower at 2-15%).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Metric divergence for Kernel SHAP on GMSC. Percentage of run-pair-instance comparisons exceeding the randomized baseline, by method and model (Eq. (7)). Each cell uses 10N comparisons. Low l2 exceedance coexists with Top-3 membership churn and RBO disagreement.
official.metric: Percentage of 10N run-pair-instance comparisons (N = 9,000) whose distance strictly exceeds the minimum of the randomized null-model band; higher means more disagreement. No error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported; one trained model per configuration.
official.comparison: l2-distance exceedance vs. top-3 Jaccard (and 1-RBO) exceedance on the same rerun pairs, across 5 models x 4 background sampling methods.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Kernel SHAP (K = 100, 5 background seeds) on GMSC with a Random-sampled background for a tuned XGBoost or Random Forest gives a top-3 set change rate far below the reported value (e.g. under 10% where the paper reports 29-42%), or a substantial fraction (more than a few percent) of l2 distances exceeds the Dirichlet RMS reference.

title: RoSeViT: Role-Separated Vision Transformers for ARC Visual Reasoning
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (matched-control details in Section 5.1 and Appendix D.1, page 16)

official.background: ARC (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus) tasks give a few input-output grid pairs and ask a solver to infer the transformation and apply it to a new grid. VARC recently showed that a plain Vision Transformer, trained offline on ARC-1 training tasks (expanded with RE-ARC), then adapted per task with test-time training and evaluated with multi-view voting, is a strong ARC solver. In a dense ViT every patch token carries both local grid state and the global transformation rule. This paper asks whether giving the rule its own route through the network, separate from the visual workspace, improves rule induction.
official.method:
RoSeViT keeps the VARC frontend (64x64 augmented canvas, 2x2 patches, so 1024 workspace tokens, width 512, depth 10) and adds controller tokens: one learned task token plus one context token per demonstration pair, computed by an MLP on the pooled difference of output and input patch embeddings. Each block (variant d) runs a normal dense self-attention pass, then a structured masked-attention pass where controller tokens attend to everything while workspace tokens attend only to the controller tokens, themselves and their 8 spatial neighbours, then an MLP. Nonlocal workspace-to-workspace communication in the structured pass therefore goes through the controller. d-1 means one step, with no recurrence.

The controlled test (Table 1) keeps the VARC protocol fixed: 100 offline epochs on ARC-1 training tasks with RE-ARC expansion, VARC default test-time adaptation (TTT1, 100 epochs per task, fresh task token), 510 augmented views with majority voting, and pass@2 on the 400 ARC-1 evaluation tasks. Baselines are the 18M VARC-ViT and a dense VARC-ViT widened to 28M (embed 640, MLP 720) to match RoSeViT d-1's 28.4M parameters, run with the official VARC code.
official.claim: Under the identical VARC training/TTT1/510-view-voting protocol, RoSeViT d-1 (28M) reaches 56.6% ARC-1 pass@2 (mean over 4 seeds), versus 53.6 ± 1.0% for a parameter-matched 28M dense VARC-ViT (8 seeds, best seed 54.9) and 54.5% for the 18M VARC-ViT.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Same-training/same-testing backbone comparison (VARC default adaptation, ARC-1 pass@2) with a parameter-matched dense control and the measured forward cost (batch 8, H100). Theoretical GFLOPs count the sparse structured pass; actual GFLOPs are those of our masked dense implementation.
official.metric: ARC-1 pass@2 accuracy on the 400 evaluation tasks, %, higher is better. RoSeViT: mean over 4 seeds, no spread reported. Matched dense control: mean ± std over 8 adaptation seeds (range 52.1-54.9). VARC-ViT 18M: single number, no error.
official.comparison: RoSeViT d-1 (role-separated, 28M) vs. width-matched dense VARC-ViT (28M) and default dense VARC-ViT (18M), all with VARC default adaptation (TTT1)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both arms under the same protocol, RoSeViT d-1's mean ARC-1 pass@2 is not above the matched dense control's best seed (around 54.9), or the gap between the means falls within about one seed std (~1 point).

title: On the Runway Cascade of Transformers for Language Modeling

official.background: In decoder-only transformers, causal masking means a source token reaches a later destination token both directly (through the destination's attention) and indirectly through every intermediate token, which the authors call the 'runway'. They argue that information accumulated along these indirect paths, especially the part shared by many tokens, is largely invisible to standard softmax attention and keeps cascading forward ('runway cascade'). They link this to known failure modes such as position bias, lost-in-the-middle and representation collapse, and propose changing attention so that each token accounts for what its runway already carries.
official.method:
Runway-aware rewiring is a parameter-free change to causal attention. For destination token d and an earlier token m (m <= d-2), a runway coefficient r_dm = sigmoid(v_{d-1} . v_m / sqrt(head_dim)) is computed from the value vectors of one re-purposed attention head (the last head); v_{d-1} is the value vector of the token just before d and serves as a summary of d's runway. The ordinary post-softmax attention weights of every head are multiplied by (1 - r_dm), with the self edge, the previous-token edge and the first token exempt, and each row is renormalized to sum to 1. The same coefficients are shared across all heads (pseudo-code in Listing 1, page 27).

Standard and rewired decoder-only transformers with identical configurations (Pre-LN, RoPE, Adam, d = n_heads = n_layers, d_model = 64d) are trained on C4 for next-token prediction on 20B tokens with global batch size 256, using unfused attention. For Figure 3b both are d=12 models (~124M parameters, called 120M in the paper) trained at context length 2048. Zero-shot passkey retrieval: the needle 'The passkey is [5-digit number].' is placed at 10 depths in C4 filler text, the model is prompted with 'The passkey is', and only exact 5-digit matches count. Each context length is run 10 times and accuracy is averaged over depths and runs, with the std shown as a shaded band.
official.claim: With ~120M-parameter models trained on C4 at context length 2048, the rewired transformer beats the standard transformer on zero-shot 5-digit passkey retrieval at every length from 2048 to 2496 (both are ~0% at 2560): about 81% vs 55% at 2048 (in context) and about 65% vs 2% at 2304, where the standard model has already collapsed to near 0% (values read off the plot).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: (a) Passkey retrieval test for standard and our rewired transformers. We use 450 million parameter models trained on general language tasks at context length of 1024 and test their retrieval abilities up to context length of 1536. (b) An extension of the same experiment from (a) using longer context (up to 2.5k) on 120 million parameter models (c) Zero-shot passkey retrieval test for standard and our rewired transformers where passkeys are embedded at varying depths. Note: higher values indicate higher accuracy and therefore better performance.
official.metric: Exact-match passkey retrieval accuracy (%), higher is better, averaged over 10 needle depths x 10 runs per context length; the paper says only that the light shaded band is the standard deviation (over the repeated evaluation runs; it does not say what is resampled per run), not over training seeds. One trained model per architecture.
official.comparison: Rewired transformer (runway-aware rewiring, dot-product form, no extra parameters) vs. a standard causal transformer of identical size, data, and training budget
official.falsification_criterion: With matched 120M models trained at context length 2048, the rewired model's passkey accuracy is not clearly above the standard model's in context (2048) or just beyond it (2240-2368), e.g. the gap at 2304 is under ~20 points or within the run-to-run std, or the standard model does not collapse earlier than the rewired one.

title: Q-Probe: Scaling Image Quality Assessment to High Resolution via Context-Aware Agentic Probing

official.background: Image quality assessment (IQA) tries to predict human Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) for images without a pristine reference. Recent RL-trained multimodal LLMs (Q-Insight, VisualQuality-R1) do this well on standard low-resolution datasets but look only at a downscaled global view, so they miss small local artifacts in 4K images. Simply adding a zoom/crop tool ('thinking with images') causes new failures: the model learns that cropping implies low quality, and it mistakes natural depth-of-field bokeh for blur.
official.method:
Q-Probe fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL-7B as an agent that can call an image-crop tool before scoring. Training has three stages: (1) pairwise GRPO on 3,000 low-resolution KADID-10k images with a Thurstone-model ranking reward (no tool use); (2) SFT on Probe-CoT-3K, a 2:1 low/high-resolution set of reasoning trajectories whose crops cover all degraded regions plus some clean or bokeh regions ('context-aware cropping'), so cropping is not tied to low quality; (3) GRPO on Probe-RL-4K with reward alpha*exp(-|s_pred - MOS|/tau) + beta*IoU(crop box, defect box) + gamma*format, all weights 1.0 and tau = 1.0.

Vista-Bench is the authors' new benchmark: over 3,000 images above 4K resolution from HR-Bench 4K, Pixel-Reasoner and UHD-IQA. Local artifacts (mosaic, JPEG ringing, posterization, noise, slight defocus) are injected into high-frequency Haar-wavelet subbands, and six human experts score each image with a global base score minus local penalties weighted by how important the region is. Methods are evaluated by SRCC and PLCC against these scores.
official.claim: On the high-resolution Vista-Bench, Q-Probe reaches SRCC 0.801 / PLCC 0.850, compared with 0.517 / 0.493 for the strongest baseline, VisualQuality-R1, and 0.450 / 0.426 for its base model Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comprehensive performance comparison (SRCC / PLCC) on standard and high-resolution datasets. Q-Probe achieves SOTA results, especially on the high-resolution Vista benchmark. Methods are color-coded by category: Handcrafted, Deep Learning, and MLLMs-based.
official.metric: SRCC and PLCC between predicted scores and the expert-annotated scores on Vista-Bench (higher is better); single numbers, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: Q-Probe (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, three-stage training) vs. VisualQuality-R1, Q-Insight, UnifiedReward-T, DeQA-Score, Q-Align, LIQE, the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model, and non-MLLM IQA models, all evaluated on the same Vista-Bench images
official.falsification_criterion: On Vista-Bench, VisualQuality-R1 (released checkpoint) gets an SRCC within about 0.1 of Q-Probe's, or Q-Probe's SRCC is well below 0.801 (for example under 0.65).

title: Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
claim_source: Figure 4 (right panel), page 9; Claude and Gemini numbers stated in the text on page 9

official.background: It is unclear how much of LLM performance comes from recalling patterns seen in training versus reasoning that transfers to new inputs, partly because training corpora are opaque and it is hard to know which test items are in-distribution. Chess offers a way around this: opening positions are heavily documented and almost certainly in pretraining data, while randomly constructed legal positions are almost never seen, yet the rules that decide whether a move is legal are identical in both. Comparing the same model on familiar versus novel positions therefore separates recall from rule-following without access to training data.
official.method:
The authors build three sets of 500 positions each with python-chess. Within-distribution (WD): positions occurring at least 1,000 times in the Lichess Masters database. Near-distribution (ND): positions after 10 random legal moves per side (20 plies) from the start, discarding any in the database. Out-of-distribution (OOD): random placement of ten pieces per side, subject to validity constraints (one king each, no pawns on impossible ranks, side not to move not in check).

Each position is given as a FEN string in a fixed zero-shot prompt (Appendix A.1, temperature 0) asking for the best move as JSON with SAN and UCI fields plus a short rationale. The SAN move is checked for syntax and then for legality in the position; the main metrics are the share of legal moves and average centipawn loss (Stockfish 17.1, depth 30, illegal moves scored 1,000). For the cross-lineage comparison (Figure 4), GPT-5, gemini-3-flash-preview and claude-opus-4-6 are each run at their lowest available reasoning setting.
official.claim: At minimal reasoning effort, all three frontier models propose illegal moves far more often on random OOD positions than on well-known WD opening positions: Claude Opus 4.6 0.2% vs. 51.6%, Gemini 3 Flash 2.2% vs. 72.0%, and GPT-5 roughly 3% vs. roughly 70% (500 positions per condition), with ND in between (8.2% and 17.0% for Claude and Gemini).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Performance across model lineages, all at minimal reasoning effort. Left: Average Centipawn Loss with Matescore = Illegal Move Score = 1,000. Right: Proportion of legal moves. Horizontal lines indicate means, boxes around the mean display the 95% confidence interval, vertical lines indicate standard deviations. WD = within-distribution, ND = near-distribution, OOD = out-of-distribution.
official.metric: Illegal-move rate (lower is better) = share of the 500 positions per condition where the SAN move is not legal; single run at temperature 0, no seeds or error bars on the legality bars (the ACPL panel shows 95% CIs and SDs). GPT-5 values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Same model, same prompt, WD vs. ND vs. OOD positions; repeated for GPT-5 (minimal), Gemini 3 Flash and Claude Opus 4.6 (lowest reasoning settings)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the released positions (or newly generated ones following the same construction) through any of these models at the lowest reasoning setting yields an OOD illegal-move rate that is not substantially higher than WD, e.g. less than 20 percentage points above it.

title: SyncLight: Single-Edit Multi-View Relighting

official.background: Generative relighting models can now edit the lights in a single photo convincingly, but when applied to several views of the same scene independently they produce lighting that disagrees across cameras (shadows and highlights that do not match the geometry). 3D approaches (NeRF, 3DGS, inverse rendering) are consistent but need camera poses and per-scene optimization. Applications such as multi-camera broadcast, stereo cinema, and virtual production need a lighting edit made once to propagate consistently to every view.
official.method:
SyncLight fine-tunes SDXL as a velocity model under latent bridge matching (LBM): it learns a flow from the latent of an image under source lighting to the latent under target lighting (sigma = 0.005, 4 training timesteps) and predicts the target in a single inference step. Each SDXL transformer block is made multi-view MVDream-style: tokens from all views are concatenated along the token dimension before attention, so views attend to each other; no camera poses are used. The lighting edit is a 4-channel lightmap on the reference view only (on/off state plus target Lab color at clicked light locations), concatenated to every view's latent via a zero-initialized 8-channel input conv. Loss is the LBM velocity loss plus LPIPS on each decoded view (lambda = 10). It is trained on view pairs (N = 2), 100K steps, batch 6, 1280x720.

Training/test data are OLAT captures linearly recombined with sampled per-light Lab colors and intensities: 365 Infinigen scenes, 40 BlenderKit scenes, and 40 real captured scenes, with held-out test scenes. The key comparison is relighting the second (non-reference) view. LightLab* is the authors' reimplementation of LightLab trained on the same data with the same SDXL backbone and lightmap conditioning but single-view (no multi-view attention, no LBM); for the second view its relit reference is propagated with LumiNet (LightLab*+LNet). GR3EN is the strongest external multi-view baseline. Metrics are PSNR, SSIM, CIEDE2000 and LPIPS against the ground-truth relit view, plus VGGTm, the ratio of high-confidence VGGT correspondences between output views to those between ground-truth views.
official.claim: On the Real-captures test split, SyncLight relights the second (non-reference) view at 30.23 dB PSNR (SSIM .897, ΔE00 3.56, VGGTm 95.8%), versus 22.03 dB (VGGTm 82.7%) for GR3EN and 20.46 dB (VGGTm 68.3%) for the matched single-view LightLab*+LumiNet baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative multi-view image relighting results on our SyncLight test set. Each section of the table indicates which view is used to compute metrics: the "Reference (Ref.) view" (where edits are specified), "Second (Sec.) view" (another view in the set), and "Additional (Add.) views" (all but the reference view). Best results, achieved by SyncLight in all cases, are highlighted. See text for details on baselines. As SyncLight is always run on more than one image; no inference time is reported for the "Ref. view." VGGTm (%) measures cross-view consistency against the ground truth (see text); it is undefined for the reference view alone.
official.metric: PSNR in dB (higher is better) on the second view, plus SSIM (higher), ΔE00 (lower), LPIPS (lower), VGGTm % (higher). No error bars or seeds are reported for quality metrics; ± appears only on inference time.
official.comparison: SyncLight vs. GR3EN, LightLab* (same data/backbone, single-view) + LumiNet, Flux.2-dev two-stage pipeline, and ScribbleLight + LumiNet, on the second view of each test pair.
official.falsification_criterion: On the Real-captures (or synthetic) test split, a retrained SyncLight's second-view PSNR is not clearly above (e.g. within ~2 dB of) GR3EN or LightLab*+LumiNet, or its VGGTm is not higher than GR3EN's 82.7%.

title: GUIGuard-Bench: Toward a General Evaluation for Privacy-Preserving GUI Agents
claim_source: Figure 5, page 7 (per-model values in Figure 10, page 30)

official.background: GUI agents send screenshots to remote vision-language models for planning, and those screenshots often contain names, accounts, messages, locations and other private data. Existing visual-privacy datasets use natural photos, and GUI-agent benchmarks measure grounding or task success without privacy labels. Before a local module can mask private content, it has to find it on the screen. GUIGuard-Bench asks how well current VLMs can find and label private regions in real GUI-agent trajectories.
official.method:
The benchmark has 241 real GUI-agent trajectories (4,080 screenshots) from Android and PC. Each private region is annotated with a bounding box, its extracted text, a risk level (low/medium/high), one of six semantic privacy categories, and whether it is necessary for the task. 121 trajectories (2,002 screenshots) are public; the other 120 are private and evaluated only by the authors on request. Eight VLMs (Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.1, Grok 4, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking, Doubao-Seed-1.6-Vision, GLM-4.5V, DeepSeek-VL2) each get the screenshot plus a single privacy prompt (Appendix L.1) that defines the taxonomy and output format, and they return privacy regions with text, box and labels.

Three metrics are computed. Binary privacy detection: whether the model correctly says if the screenshot contains any private content. Privacy recall: the fraction of ground-truth privacy elements matched, where a match needs both relaxed text matching (at least 90% character coverage in either direction) and box IoU >= 0.6. Full match: an element counts only if it is matched and its risk, category and task-necessity labels are all correct. Figure 5 reports each metric averaged over the eight models, separately for Android and PC.
official.claim: Averaged over eight VLMs on GUIGuard-Bench, privacy recognition falls sharply from screenshot-level binary detection to element-level recall to strict full match: 89.0% -> 52.9% -> 8.8% on Android and 63.3% -> 13.5% -> 0.6% on PC.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Average privacy-recognition performance on Android and PC, comparing binary privacy detection, privacy recall rate, and strict full-match accuracy.
official.metric: Accuracy / recall in % (higher is better), averaged over 8 models; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: Binary privacy detection vs. element-level privacy recall vs. strict full-match accuracy, on Android vs. PC screenshots
official.falsification_criterion: With the released prompt and matching rules on the public split, a comparable set of VLMs gets average element recall within about 10 points of binary detection, or full-match accuracy above about 25% on Android, or PC is not clearly below Android on all three metrics.

title: Intersectional Fairness via Mixed-Integer Optimization

official.background: Fairness rules such as the EU AI Act require detecting and mitigating bias without saying which definition to use. Most fairness metrics look at one protected attribute at a time, which can hide discrimination against intersections such as 'young women of a given race'. Statistical Parity Subgroup Fairness (SPSF, Kearns et al. 2018) measures the worst subgroup violation, weighted by subgroup size, but finding the most violating subgroup is computationally hard. The standard tool, GerryFair, uses a heuristic auditor, so it can miss the worst subgroup and wrongly certify a classifier as fair.
official.method:
The detection task is posed as a mixed-integer linear program (Pyomo model, solved with Gurobi). A subgroup is either a conjunction of binarized protected attribute-value pairs (S_A) or a linear threshold function c^T x >= t over the protected attributes normalized to [0, 1] (S_L, the same class GerryFair uses), with binary membership variables per sample (formulations (3) and (7) in Appendix B). The objective maximizes either SPSF (formulation (5)) or Subgroup Discrepancy between the positively and negatively classified samples (formulation (4)). Theorem 1 shows the two have the same maximizer, so MSD and SPSF find the same subgroup. Linear-subgroup MIO runs are warm-started from the GerryFair solution (when numerically stable) or from a logistic regression.

Setup: five folktables tasks (ACS Income, Public Coverage, Mobility, Employment, Travel Time; 2018 1-year survey, California). Bias is measured in the data itself, i.e. the 'classifier' is the true label h(x_i) = y_i. Each configuration uses 50,000 randomly subsampled points, repeated on 5 random subsamples; the MIO time limit is 10,000 s on a 16-core Xeon Gold 6146 / EPYC 7543. The metric is the SPSF value of the subgroup each method finds; higher means the auditor found more bias.
official.claim: When searching over linear-threshold subgroups for the most SPSF-violating subgroup in the folktables data (50,000-point subsamples), MIO with the SPSF objective finds larger violations than GerryFair: about 0.091 vs. 0.083 on ACS Income, 0.144 vs. 0.135 on ACS Employment and 0.0285 vs. 0.0255 on ACS Travel Time, margins well above the standard deviations across subsamples.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Mean fairness violation (and standard deviations). In detection, finding the subgroup with more unfairness is better. The bars with slanted lines represent the optimal solutions found over conjunction subgroups (S_A), which are a subset of linear subgroups (S_L), explaining the difference to the other setups. The blue bar with slanted lines to the left corresponds to MSD, and the orange bar to the right corresponds to GerryFair; the rest is our work.
official.metric: Discovered SPSF violation P(S)·|P(h=1) − P(h=1|S)| of the found subgroup, higher is better (a stronger auditor). Bars are means over 5 random subsamples, and error bars are standard deviations. Values are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: MIO (SPSF objective, also SD objective) over linear subgroups S_L vs. GerryFair (SPSF auditor, linear subgroups) on the same subsamples; conjunction-subgroup MIO (SD and SPSF objectives, proven optimal) shown as reference
official.falsification_criterion: On ACS Income, Employment or Travel Time, re-running the detection with the same subsamples (true labels as predictions, 50,000 points, 5 subsamples) gives a GerryFair SPSF violation within one standard deviation of, or above, the MIO linear-subgroup SPSF violation. A second check: MIO with the SD and SPSF objectives over conjunction subgroups returns different SPSF values, which would contradict the equivalence theorem.

title: Neural Neural Scaling Laws

official.background: Scaling laws are used to forecast how a language model will perform before training finishes. Average validation loss follows smooth power laws, but accuracy on individual downstream tasks does not: some tasks improve steadily, some plateau, and some get worse with scale. The usual method maps average validation loss to task accuracy with a fitted logistic curve. This assumes one parametric shape fits every task, and averaging the loss throws away information about how loss is spread across tokens. Better downstream forecasts would help practitioners pick training configurations early and save compute.
official.method:
NeuNeu is a 19.5M-parameter network that treats downstream scaling prediction as time-series extrapolation. Its inputs are (a) a vector of 256,000 token-level validation probabilities p = exp(-loss) from the current checkpoint, computed on shard 141 of the WebOrganizer corpus with whitespace tokenization, and (b) the sequence of observed downstream accuracies, each paired with a compute gap. A 4-layer Conv1D encoder turns the probabilities into one embedding. A 6-layer bidirectional transformer reads [CLS; loss embedding; (accuracy, gap) tokens], where the last gap is the query horizon, and the CLS output predicts 5 quantiles trained with pinball loss. The median is the point prediction. Training data are seed-0 DataDecide runs (90M–1B parameters, 24 pretraining corpora excluding C4; 144 runs × 66 tasks), augmented by randomly dropping checkpoints (p = 0.4).

Evaluation uses held-out runs: DataDecide DCLM seed 2, DataDecide C4 runs, Pythia 70M–12B, and OLMo-Hybrid-7B. Neural predictors and LC-PFN see the first 20% of each trajectory's accuracies and are scored by mean absolute error (MAE) on the remaining 80%. Baselines: a logistic loss-to-accuracy law fitted per task (given the ground-truth average loss at each target checkpoint), BNSL (also given the ground-truth loss), LC-PFN (pretrained, not retrained), and two neural ablations: NoLoss (accuracies only) and Average (average validation probability instead of token-level probabilities).
official.claim: Averaged over all held-out evaluation settings and 66 downstream tasks, NeuNeu forecasts the last 80% of accuracy trajectories with 1.99% MAE, compared with 3.56% for per-task logistic scaling laws (even though the logistic laws get the ground-truth average loss), 3.70% for LC-PFN and 3.94% for BNSL. It also beats its own accuracy-only ablation NoLoss (2.11%) with non-overlapping ±2σ error bars.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Generalization results for downstream task accuracy prediction. (a) NeuNeu significantly outperforms all other scaling laws at generalizing to new random seeds, pretraining data, and unseen transformer and non-transformer architectures. The gray dashed line denotes mean absolute error (MAE) of always predicting the average accuracy from the training set for each task.
official.metric: Mean absolute error of predicted accuracy, in percentage points (lower is better). Neural models (NoLoss, Average, NeuNeu) show ±2σ error bars over 5 training seeds; the bar values are not given as numbers. Logistic and BNSL are deterministic fits, and LC-PFN uses one released checkpoint, so those three have no error bars.
official.comparison: NeuNeu vs. Logistic scaling law (main baseline), LC-PFN, BNSL, and the neural ablations NoLoss and Average. All predictors are trained or fitted on the same DataDecide training trajectories and evaluated on the same held-out runs.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining NeuNeu with the released code and data gives an overall-average MAE that is not clearly below the logistic scaling law (e.g. above about 3%, i.e. less than a ~15% reduction), or not below NoLoss beyond seed variation.

title: Efficient Evaluation of LLM Performance with Statistical Guarantees

official.background: Evaluating many LLMs on large benchmark suites is expensive, and practitioners often score a model on a random subset of questions. The authors treat a benchmark as a fixed finite population and ask how to choose a limited number of questions adaptively so that the confidence interval for the model's accuracy on the whole bank is as narrow as possible while keeping valid (asymptotic) frequentist coverage. Organizations usually have historical per-question results for earlier models, which can show which questions are informative; the question is how to use that history without giving up coverage guarantees.
official.method:
Factorized Active Querying (FAQ) fits a logistic latent-factor model sigma(u_i^T v_j) to the historical model-by-question 0/1 matrix (AdamW, factor dimension k and weight decay chosen by cross-validation with the 1-SE rule). For a new model, question factors v_j are frozen and the model factor u starts from the mean/covariance of historical model factors, then gets an online Laplace update after each observed label. At each round t, a question is sampled with replacement from a hybrid policy q_t that mixes an oracle-variance-reduction score p_j(1-p_j) with an active-learning score (approximate posterior-variance reduction of the accuracy), with tempering and tau-uniform mixing (Eqs. 3-4). Pro-Active Inference (PAI) estimates accuracy as the average of phi_t = mean_j p_hat_j + (z_It - p_hat_It)/(N_q q_t(I_t)) and forms a Wald CI from a martingale-CLT variance estimate (Eq. 9). FAQ hyperparameters (rho, gamma, beta0, tau) are tuned on historical validation models only.

Data: per-question outcomes for 4.4K Open LLM Leaderboard models on two suites, MMLU-Pro (12,032 questions) and BBH+GPQA+IFEval+MATH+MuSR (9,574 questions). Models are sorted by release date; the first 2.2K are history H (fully observed for this claim) and the next 2.2K are test models. Baselines are design-based AIPW estimators in the benchmark's native order with Bernoulli labelling (uniform), Neyman-style pi proportional to sqrt(p(1-p)), or the Zrnic-Candes pi proportional to min(p, 1-p), using historical per-question mean accuracy as the predictor; the best baseline configuration is chosen post hoc on the test models for each budget. Budgets are 10 evenly spaced values from 2.5% to 25% of the bank. The metric is effective sample size ESS = (sigma_uniform^2 / sigma_method^2) * n_b, plus empirical coverage of 95% CIs, averaged over 2.2K test models x 100 seeds.
official.claim: With fully observed historical data, FAQ's ESS multiplier over uniform sampling is 3.57-5.07 on MMLU-Pro and 3.05-4.26 on BBH+GPQA+IFEval+MATH+MuSR across all 10 budgets, versus at most 2.12 and 2.27 for the best post-hoc-selected baseline, while empirical coverage of FAQ's 95% CIs stays within about 1 point of 95%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Evaluating 2.2K LLMs on MMLU-Pro and BBH+GPQA+IFEval+MATH+MuSR with fully-observed historical data. (Top Row) Effective sample size (ESS) vs. budget for FAQ, the strongest baseline per budget (selected post-hoc, favoring baselines), and uniform sampling. Numbers annotate the ESS multiplier relative to uniform sampling. For example, on MMLU-Pro at budget 1500, an ESS multiplier of 5.01 means FAQ matches uniform sampling's CI width at budget 7515 (a 5.01x gain). (Bottom Row) Empirical coverage of the corresponding 95% normal-approximation CIs, averaged over 2.2K test models and 100 seeds. Standard errors are shown, but negligible on the plot scale. Higher ESS and ESS-multiplier values indicate better performance.
official.metric: Effective sample size multiplier relative to uniform sampling (higher is better) and empirical coverage of nominal 95% CIs, averaged over 2.2K test models and 100 seeds; standard errors are reported but are negligible at the plot scale
official.comparison: FAQ vs. the best of the AIPW baselines (Bernoulli/uniform, Neyman, Zrnic-Candes active inference, with or without the historical-mean predictor) selected post hoc per budget, and plain uniform sampling, on the same test models and budgets
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running on the released data with fully observed history, FAQ's ESS multiplier over uniform at most budgets is not clearly above the best baseline's (e.g. below 1.5x the baseline's multiplier), or FAQ's empirical coverage falls clearly below 95% (e.g. under 93%).
