title: A Scalable Multi-Task Model for Virtual Sensors

official.background: Virtual sensors use machine learning to predict a signal (e.g. a temperature or current) from other measured signals, replacing expensive or impractical physical sensors. Current practice trains one application-specific model per virtual sensor with expert-chosen inputs, which does not scale to sensor networks with hundreds of targets and thousands of candidate inputs. Time series foundation models share knowledge across tasks but only forecast signals whose past is in their input, so they cannot produce a new signal, and they are expensive to run. The paper proposes a single multi-task transformer that predicts many virtual sensors, learns which inputs each one needs, and uses that to run cheaply.
official.method:
The base model is a causal decoder-only transformer (4 layers, 4 heads, d = 512, patch length 32) over per-signal patch tokens with sin-cos time embeddings and learned variate embeddings for both input signals and virtual sensors. To predict virtual sensor j, a zero 'prototype' token plus its variate embedding v'_j is inserted, and the model forecasts the next 32 steps autoregressively (6 cycles at evaluation), using ground-truth inputs and its own previous predictions for the virtual sensor. Each virtual sensor has a trainable relevance vector r'_j over all M+N signals; the outer product r'_j r'_j^T, duplicated across time, is added as a bias to the attention scores in every layer, so relevance is learned from attention gradients. Training uses teacher forcing, MSE on virtual-sensor outputs only, and a random subset of N_train = 4 of the 16 virtual sensors per iteration.

At inference, relevance vectors are thresholded (r'_thres) so irrelevant signals are masked out completely, which removes their tokens from the sequence (structured sparsity). With sensor selection, only the requested virtual sensors' prototype tokens and the union of their input sets are fed in. On Traffic (862 road-occupancy series, hourly), 16 virtual sensors are chosen randomly (variate IDs 74, 88, 113, 173, 280, 311, 312, 352, 355, 478, 539, 646, 650, 715, 775, 776) and the rest are inputs. Baselines in Table 1: 16 individual LSTMs, 16 individual transformers with the same backbone, and a unified model with progressively added mechanisms. Time and dynamic CUDA peak memory are measured on one Nvidia A6000.
official.claim: On Traffic with 16 virtual sensors, the unified model with sparse learned input sets and sensor selection reaches MSE 0.282, matching 16 individual transformers (0.285) and the dense unified model with variate embeddings (0.275), while cutting inference time from 16.76 ms to 0.87 ms (about 19x) and dynamic peak memory from 0.90 GB to 0.0352 GB (about 26x).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of a simple unified model predicting all 16 virtual sensors, where we subsequently introduce our proposed mechanisms, with 16 individual models predicting a single virtual sensor each. We list MSE, inference time, dynamic CUDA peak memory, and the number of trainable parameters for Traffic and CAN bus datasets.
official.metric: Test MSE on normalized virtual-sensor signals (lower is better), inference time per prediction and dynamic CUDA peak memory (lower is better). Single training seed (2025); no ± in the table. Appendix B Table 7 gives a bootstrapped 95% CI on Traffic MSE of [0.256, 0.289] around 0.272 (the relevance-vector model); timing std is stated as < 2%.
official.comparison: Full unified model (variate embeddings + signal relevance + N_train = 4 + sparse input sets + sensor selection) vs. the same unified model without sparsification/sensor selection, the unified model with variate embeddings only, and 16 individual transformers / LSTMs, all on Traffic
official.falsification_criterion: With the same 16 Traffic virtual sensors, applying the learned sparse input sets and sensor selection either raises MSE beyond the bootstrap CI of the dense unified model (e.g. above ~0.30), or yields less than ~5x reduction in inference time or peak memory relative to the dense unified model on the same GPU.

title: On the Overscaling Curse of Parallel Thinking: System Efficacy Contradicts Sample Efficiency
claim_source: Table 14, page 37 (Appendix G.1); accuracy std in Table 17, page 38; the Qwen3-4B version is Table 3, page 9

official.background: Parallel thinking (self-consistency) samples N reasoning paths from an LLM and aggregates them, for example by majority vote. In standard evaluation a single global budget N is picked to maximise dataset accuracy. The paper argues that most individual problems reach their best expected accuracy at a much smaller N, so a global budget wastes most of the compute on most samples (the 'overscaling curse'). Existing efficient methods (Adaptive-Consistency, ESC, DSC, DeepConf) adapt the budget during decoding by sampling in small batches and stopping early, which breaks hardware parallelism. The open question is whether deciding the per-sample budget before decoding gives real savings in latency and memory without losing accuracy.
official.method:
For each prompt x, the sample-optimal budget N*_x is the smallest N in [1, 128] that maximises the expected majority-vote accuracy A_x(N). A_x(N) is estimated by drawing 256 reference outputs per prompt and subsampling N of them without replacement, repeated up to 1e5 times (Eq. 1-2). LanBo (Latent Budget Predictor) trains one small predictor per decoder layer. Each predictor is a one-hidden-layer MLP (hidden size d/8, ReLU, sigmoid output) that maps the last-token hidden state of the prompt at layer l to N*_x/128, trained with MSE. The training data are 5,000 prompts (2,500 from DeepMath-103K across 10 difficulty levels and 2,500 from WebInstruct-verified across about 10 domains), plus a disjoint validation set of the same size. Hyperparameters: AdamW, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 128, 300 epochs. At inference the layer predictions are combined with inverse-validation-MSE weights (Eq. 7), and one predictor per model is used for all evaluation datasets.

In the PreAda pipeline, the model encodes x, the predictors output a budget N-hat_x, and N-hat_x samples are then decoded fully in parallel with vLLM and majority-voted. Sampling uses top-k 20, top-p 0.95, temperature 0.6. The baseline STD. is majority voting with the system-optimal global budget N*_D. The decoding-time baselines are AC (max 40), ESC (window 8 / max 64 on MATH500, window 5 / max 40 otherwise), DSC (w=4, k=32, max 40) and online DeepConf (N_init 16, tau 0.95, max 512). Metrics are peak memory per sample and total wall-clock latency (LanBo's predictor training time included), both as ratios to STD., plus accuracy. All results are averaged over 32 runs on A100-80G GPUs.
official.claim: With Qwen2.5-7B and majority voting, LanBo's total latency relative to standard parallel decoding is 0.39-0.74 on all seven datasets (e.g. 0.48 on MATH500, 0.51 on GPQA). Every decoding-time baseline (AC, ESC, DSC, DeepConf) is at 0.96 or above on every dataset. LanBo's accuracy stays within 1.2 points of standard decoding (MATH500 77.49 vs. 78.17; GPQA 38.32 vs. 39.49).
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Empirical Validation of Our LanBo for Efficient Parallel Decoding. This table shows Qwen2.5-7B results. (Shared caption: under each system, real-world efficiency (memory delta_M and latency delta_T, both ratios relative to STD.) and accuracy (Acc.); STD. is standard parallel decoding; each result averaged over 32 runs.)
official.metric: delta_T = total latency / STD. latency (lower is better); delta_M = mean peak memory per sample / STD. (lower is better); accuracy (%) of majority vote. All values are means over 32 runs. Std is reported only for accuracy (Table 17, e.g. MATH500 STD. 0.32, LanBo 0.31). No error bars are given for latency or memory.
official.comparison: LanBo (pre-decoding budget prediction) vs. standard parallel decoding with the system-optimal global budget and vs. four decoding-time adaptive methods (AC, ESC, DSC, online DeepConf), same model, sampling settings and hardware.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if, with Qwen2.5-7B on any of these datasets (e.g. MATH500 or GPQA), some decoding-time baseline (AC, ESC, DSC, DeepConf) has a latency ratio equal to or lower than LanBo's, or LanBo's latency ratio is not clearly below 1. Also refuted if LanBo's accuracy falls more than about 2 points below standard global-budget majority voting.

title: MMFineReason: Closing the Multimodal Reasoning Gap via Open Data-Centric Methods

official.background: Open-source vision-language models trail proprietary ones on multimodal reasoning (math diagrams, science figures, visual puzzles), and the authors argue that the main cause is data: open multimodal datasets cover few hard STEM and puzzle domains and lack consistent long chain-of-thought (CoT) annotations. In text-only LLMs, distilling long CoT traces from a strong reasoning teacher into a smaller model has closed much of this gap. The question is whether the same data-centric recipe works for multimodal models, and whether a curated, distilled dataset beats existing open multimodal reasoning datasets of similar or larger size.
official.method:
The authors aggregate open multimodal reasoning sources (FineVision subsets, MMR1, BMMR, Euclid30K, GameQA-140K, ViRL39K, VisualWebInstruct, LLaVA-CoT and others), clean and translate the questions, and distill long CoT answers with Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking in a <think>...</think><answer>...</answer> format. They drop traces that break the template or are shorter than 100 words, discard or re-generate (with a different seed) repetitive traces (any 50-gram repeated 3 or more times), and discard traces whose final answer disagrees with the ground truth. The result is MMFineReason-1.8M (1,770,926 samples, 5.1B solution tokens). They also release difficulty-filtered subsets: 123K (Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking pass rate 0 over 4 samples) and 586K (pass rate not equal to 1).

Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct is fine-tuned with LLaMA-Factory (AdamW, lr 1e-5, cosine schedule, 3 epochs, global batch 32, packing to 32,768 tokens, max image 768x768), then trained with GSPO RL (VeRL) for 300 steps on a 40K subset uniformly sampled from MMFineReason-1.8M and held out from SFT (16 rollouts, batch 256). For the baselines, the authors fine-tune the same Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct themselves on the MMR1 and HoneyBee SFT datasets. All models are evaluated in VLMEvalKit on 14 benchmarks with greedy decoding, max image 2048x2048, up to 32,768 output tokens, and CompassVerifier as an LLM judge. The headline metric is the unweighted average accuracy.

title: Diffusion Path Samplers via Sequential Monte Carlo

official.background: Sampling from a distribution known only up to a normalising constant underlies Bayesian inference and statistical physics. Annealing-based samplers (AIS, SMC) usually move along a geometric path from a simple base distribution to the target, but this path can distort mode weights and mix poorly. The diffusion path used by diffusion models is better behaved. Following it, however, requires the score of each intermediate marginal, which is intractable. Existing Monte Carlo score estimators (RDMC, SLIPS) rerun MCMC chains at every time step, which is a sequential bottleneck.
official.method:
DPSMC simulates a discretised diffusion SDE (OU time-reversal, stochastic-interpolant, or diffusion-annealed Langevin dynamics) along the diffusion path. At each step it estimates the score ∇log µ_t(x) as a weighted average over auxiliary variables Y drawn from the posterior ϱ_{t,x}(y) ∝ N(x; √λ_t y, (1-λ_t)σ²I) π(y). These auxiliary variables are not resampled from scratch at each step. They are carried forward by one SMC sampler: MALA moves with adaptive step size, reverse-kernel incremental weights, and stratified resampling when ESS < 0.5N. The score uses a control-variate test function that mixes the denoising and target score identities with an estimated optimal matrix weight (the MCVSI identity with a matrix schedule, Prop. 3). The base Gaussian variance is σ² = R²d + τ² for the OU variant (as for AIS/SMC) and σ² = E_π[||X||²]/d for DALD and SI. The OU variant starts at a searched λ_0 > 0 with 64 Langevin-within-Langevin initialisation steps.

Target: a Bayesian logistic regression posterior with prior N(w; 0, I) N(b; 0, 2.5²) on Ionosphere (d = 35) and Sonar (d = 61), split 70/10/20 into train/validation/test. Hyperparameters are tuned on validation log-likelihood. Each sampler produces 4096 samples per seed over 10 seeds. Metric: predictive log-likelihood on the test set. All samplers use K = 1024 steps and at most 1.32e5 energy evaluations per sample (RDMC gets about 2x). Baselines are AIS and SMC on the geometric path (128 MALA steps per iteration), RDMC, SLIPS, and parallel tempering (PT).
official.claim: On Bayesian logistic regression with a matched energy-evaluation budget, DPSMC (OU) achieves test predictive log-likelihood -83.73 ± 0.16 on Ionosphere and -108.23 ± 0.07 on Sonar. The best baselines are AIS/SMC at -87.79 ± 0.10 (Ionosphere) and SLIPS at -110.88 ± 0.06 (Sonar), so DPSMC leads by about 4.1 and 2.7 nats respectively.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance of algorithms on toy targets and Bayesian logistic regression datasets across 10 seeds. Best result is in bold, and second-best is underlined. The second column indicates the number of batched energy evaluations—a metric for measuring runtimes in the regime where hardware capacity exceeds batch size requirements. DPSMC is overall performant while highly parallelisable.
official.metric: Test-set predictive log-likelihood (higher is better), mean ± standard error over 10 seeds of 4096 samples each
official.comparison: DPSMC (OU) and DPSMC (DALD) vs. AIS, SMC, RDMC, SLIPS and parallel tempering under the same discretisation (K = 1024) and per-sample energy-evaluation budget
official.falsification_criterion: Using the paper's dataset splits, prior and budget, DPSMC (OU or DALD) does not exceed the best of AIS/SMC/SLIPS by more than a few standard errors on Ionosphere and Sonar test log-likelihood. Equivalently, the gap shrinks from about 2.5-4 nats to within roughly 0.5 nats.

title: Reconsidering Positional Supervision in Masked Diffusion Language Model Training
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (pairwise CIs in Table 7, page 21)

official.background: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) such as LLaDA generate text by unmasking many positions in parallel over several denoising steps, and they are trained with a position-wise cross-entropy loss: each masked position must predict exactly the gold token at that position. Non-autoregressive translation, which uses the same parallel-decoder plus position-wise CE setup, has been argued to be sensitive to small positional shifts, and alignment-flexible objectives such as CTC help there. The paper asks whether MDLMs share this sensitivity and whether a CTC-style training objective improves MDLM supervised fine-tuning for open-ended generation.
official.method:
Starting from LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the authors fine-tune three LoRA models (rank 128, alpha 32, adapters on q/k/v projections, token embedding and FFN output projection; AdamW, lr 2e-4, 3 epochs, about 36k steps, seed 42) on Magpie-Pro-300K-Filtered restricted to responses of 512 to 1024 tokens (about 291k examples). CE-Only uses the standard MDLM masked cross-entropy SFT loss. Jitter uses the same CE loss on <SLACK>-augmented responses: a special <SLACK> token is inserted at uniformly random response positions, at a ratio s = s_max(1 - t) with s_max = 0.5 that depends on the masking time t. CE + CTC-S uses the same augmented data with loss L = L_CE + 0.1 * L_CTC-S. Here L_CTC-S is a CTC loss in which <SLACK> plays the role of the blank and the collapse map only removes <SLACK> tokens (adjacent duplicates are not merged), computed against the original slack-free response. <SLACK> tokens are removed from outputs after decoding.

All models decode with response length 1024, 512 diffusion steps and LLaDA's low-confidence remasking. They are evaluated on Arena-Hard v2.0 (win rate against the CE-Only model rather than o3), MT-Bench, WildBench and Creative Writing Bench v3, using LLM judges. Significance comes from a paired bootstrap over instance-level score differences (10,000 resamples, 95% CI); the full CIs are in Appendix Table 7.
official.claim: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct SFT, CE + CTC-S scores 4.35 on MT-Bench vs. 3.61 for the Jitter model and 3.44 for CE-Only (paired-bootstrap 95% CI of the difference vs. Jitter: [0.41, 1.08]), and it is also significantly best on Arena-Hard (55.1 vs. 48.4/50.0), Creative Writing v3 (27.7 vs. 25.1/24.6) and WildBench (-4.23 vs. -4.46/-4.53).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison on open-ended text generation benchmarks. For Arena-Hard, we report bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals following the official setting. † and ‡ indicate that CE + CTC-S is significantly better than the CE-Only model and the Jitter model, respectively (paired bootstrap, p < 0.05). Bold indicates the best score in each column.
official.metric: MT-Bench score (higher is better, LLM-judged); also Arena-Hard win rate vs. CE-Only, Creative-Writing-Bench v3 score and WildBench score (higher is better). Arena-Hard ± is the official bootstrapped 95% CI. Significance uses paired-bootstrap 95% CIs over benchmark instances. No variance over training seeds: each model is trained once.
official.comparison: CE + CTC-S vs. Jitter (same <SLACK>-augmented data, CE loss only) and vs. CE-Only (same data, standard CE), all LoRA-fine-tuned from LLaDA-8B-Instruct with identical settings; LLaDA-8B-Instruct itself is shown for reference.
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction with the same data, LoRA settings and decoding config in which CE + CTC-S does not beat Jitter on MT-Bench (paired-bootstrap CI of the difference includes zero or is negative), or in which the gain disappears when the Jitter/CE-Only baselines are retrained with a different seed.

title: To See Far, Look Close: Evolutionary Forecasting for Long-term Time Series
claim_source: Table 2, page 6 (full grids for other T and datasets in Tables 4 and 5, Appendix D.1)

official.background: In long-term time series forecasting (LTSF), the standard 'Direct Forecasting' (DF) protocol trains a separate model for each evaluation horizon H (96, 192, 336, 720), with the model's output length L set equal to H, because truncating a long-horizon model's output to a shorter horizon is known to work worse. This means retraining for every horizon. Autoregressive rollout of a short-horizon model is usually avoided because of feared error accumulation. The paper asks whether a model trained on a short output horizon and rolled out iteratively can match or beat the horizon-matched DF model.
official.method:
Evolutionary Forecasting (EF) trains an ordinary LTSF model with output length L exactly as in DF (MSE loss on the first L future steps, ground-truth inputs only; no scheduled sampling or rollout loss). At test time, to reach horizon H > L, the model is applied K = ceil(H/L) times: each step's input is the last T values of [history, predictions so far], and the predicted blocks are concatenated and truncated to H. When L >= H the output is simply truncated. DF is the special case L = H.

Experiments use the Time-Series-Library codebase with each model's official hyperparameters, Adam, MSE loss, up to 100 epochs with early stopping (patience 10) on validation loss, and standard chronological splits (6:2:2 for ETTh1). Table 2 fixes the input length T = 720 and reports test MSE/MAE for every (L, H) pair in {96, 192, 336, 720}^2 for eight models on ETTh1 and Weather.
official.claim: On ETTh1 with input length T = 720 and evaluation horizon H = 720, a model trained with output horizon L = 96 and rolled out 8 times achieves lower test MSE than the same model trained directly with L = 720: PatchTST 0.455 vs. 0.521 (12.7% lower) and iTransformer 0.476 vs. 0.553 (13.9% lower).
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Performance landscape of ETTh1 and Weather datasets on the (L, H) horizon space. Results under the conventional DF paradigm (L = H) are highlighted in Orange Background. The best performance for a fixed H is denoted in Bold. Δ is the improvement (%) from the best results in to DF's results. The positive improvements are in Blue.
official.metric: Test MSE on normalized data (lower is better), MAE also reported; single run per configuration, no ± or seed variation reported
official.comparison: EF (train L = 96, iterative rollout to H = 720) vs. DF (train L = H = 720), same architecture, same T = 720, same data split and training protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining PatchTST and iTransformer on ETTh1 (T = 720) over several seeds, the L = 96 rollout's H = 720 test MSE is not lower than the L = 720 DF model's MSE, or the gap is within seed-to-seed spread.

title: Probing the Trajectories of Reasoning Traces in Large Language Models
claim_source: Table A2 (Appendix), page 32; summarized in Figure 3, page 6

official.background: Reasoning LLMs emit a long 'thinking' trace before answering, and these traces improve benchmark accuracy. It is debated whether the gain comes from the specific content of the trace or from generic effects such as extra context length, a reasoning-like format, or the presence of relevant words. Separating these matters for deciding whether traces can be truncated, compressed or reused across models, and for how much to trust them in monitoring.
official.method:
For each question in GPQA Diamond (198 questions, options A-D) and MMLU-Pro (12,032 questions, options A-J), the model (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, gpt-oss-20b/120b) is prompted in thinking mode with a system instruction to answer with a single letter, and its full reasoning trace is generated (Qwen3: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20; gpt-oss: temperature 1, top_p 1, top_k 50). The trace is tokenized and truncated to the first ceil(d/100 * L) tokens for deciles d = 0 (empty thinking block), 10, ..., 100. Each prefix is re-injected into the same model's prompt followed by an early-stopping suffix (Qwen3: 'Considering the limited time by the user, I have to give the solution based on the thinking directly now.
</think>

'; gpt-oss: close the analysis channel and open the final channel). One token is generated, and the answer is the argmax of the raw softmax next-token probabilities over the bare letter tokens.

Three length-matched controls replace the injected prefix: Random (uniformly random non-special tokens of the same token count), Trace-swap (the first k tokens of a different question's trace, sampled from traces at least as long), and Permutation/Shuffle (a random permutation of the original prefix's tokens, with the <think> marker kept in place). Accuracy at decile 100 is compared between the original trace and each control, pooled over 3 independent generation runs, with McNemar's test.
official.claim: At full reasoning (decile 100) on GPQA Diamond with Qwen3-4B, injecting the model's own trace gives 54.4% accuracy, beating length-matched controls by +19.4 points (random tokens), +20.5 (another question's trace) and +14.3 (shuffled own tokens); for all 5 models and both benchmarks, the original trace beats every control by at least 13.1 points (all p < 0.001, McNemar).
official.claim_caption: Table A2: Summary statistics and significance tests. Gain shows accuracy improvement from decile 0 to 100. "Original vs Control" columns show the accuracy advantage of original traces over each control at decile 100. "Control vs d=0" columns show the accuracy change of each control relative to the no-reasoning baseline. n is the number of question-run pairs (pooled across 3 runs). Significance: * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001 (McNemar's test).
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy at decile 100 (higher is better), argmax over answer-letter next-token probabilities, pooled over 3 runs (n = 594 question-run pairs on GPQA, 36,096 on MMLU-Pro). Table A2 reports no ± values; Table A1 gives run-to-run std of original-trace accuracy at decile 100 (Qwen3-4B GPQA: 54.4 ± 0.6; max 2.9 for gpt-oss-120b GPQA). Significance via McNemar's test.
official.comparison: Original reasoning trace vs. Random-token, Trace-swap and Permutation controls of identical token length, same model, same prompt and early-stopping suffix
official.falsification_criterion: For Qwen3-4B on GPQA Diamond (or any model/benchmark in the table), the original-trace accuracy at decile 100 exceeds one of the three length-matched controls by less than about 5 points, or the permutation control reaches accuracy comparable to the original trace.

title: Learning Robust Reasoning through Guided Adversarial Self-Play

official.background: Reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) are optimized for final-answer correctness under clean prompts. They can fail badly when the context they condition on is unreliable: if a short, locally plausible but wrong snippet is inserted into an otherwise correct chain of thought, strong math models often follow the error instead of noticing and repairing it. The same models also do poorly when asked to find the first wrong step in a given solution, and their accuracy drops under mild perturbations of the input. The paper asks whether this robustness can be trained using only outcome rewards, with no human step labels and no teacher model.
official.method:
GASP (Guided Adversarial Self-Play) uses one model in two prompted roles. From MATH training problems that the model solves reliably (4 of 4 samples correct at temperature 0.7), a correct trace is sampled, truncated at a fraction alpha in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75} of its tokens, and the next ~10% of tokens (the clean window) is taken out. The polluter, conditioned on the question, the prefix and the clean window, writes a corrupted window; the agent then continues from (question, prefix, corrupted window) with the normal deployment prompt. The agent is trained with GRPO on the reward 1{final answer correct}, and the polluter with GRPO on 1 minus that reward. The two roles alternate in blocks of 5 optimizer steps (G = 64, lr 3e-6, no KL penalty, max 1024 prompt and 1024 completion tokens).

The key addition is in-distribution repair guidance: the model is shown both the clean and corrupted windows in a diagnosis prompt and samples its own repair snippet, and a weighted imitation term (lambda = 0.07, or 0.04 for Qwen3-8B, linearly annealed to 0 over the final training steps) raises log p(repair | question, prefix, corrupted window). Baselines run under matched rollout budgets are ASP (the same self-play with outcome-only GRPO and no guidance) and GASP-T (the same guidance term, but with repairs generated by GPT-5). Recoverability is evaluated on the clean-solved subset of GSM8K: a correct solution is truncated at each alpha, the next window is replaced by a corruption from a held-out GPT-5 polluter, and pass@1 final-answer accuracy is measured.
official.claim: On R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, GASP raises GSM8K recoverability (accuracy under GPT-5-corrupted reasoning context, on the clean-solved subset) to 95.6 ± 2.2%, vs. 34.4 ± 4.5% for unguided adversarial self-play (ASP), 52.7 ± 4.2% for teacher-guided GASP-T, and 12.4% for the initial checkpoint.
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Main robustness results (pass@1). Mean ± std over 3 training runs for ASP/GASP-T/GASP; Initial ckpt is a single evaluation. Clean Accuracy: GSM8K under clean prompting. Recoverability: GSM8K accuracy under corrupted context (held-out GPT-5 polluter). Diagnosability: ACCreason on MR-GSM8K and MHPP (Zeng et al., 2023; 2024). Reliability: accuracy on perturbed GSM8K and CommonsenseQA from RUPBench (Wang & Zhao, 2024). Self-Revision: improved GSM8K accuracy on the failed questions after self-revision (Tie et al., 2025). Avg: unweighted mean of the seven metrics. GASP-T uses teacher-generated (GPT-5) repair guidance in place of self-guided in-distribution repairs. Lora (Hu et al., 2022) were used for 8B model see details in Section E.
official.metric: pass@1 accuracy (%) on the clean-solved subset of GSM8K under corrupted context, higher is better; ± is std over 3 training runs (the initial checkpoint is a single evaluation)
official.comparison: GASP (self-generated repair guidance) vs. ASP (outcome-only GRPO self-play) and GASP-T (GPT-5 repair guidance), all at matched rollout budgets, on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (the same pattern is reported for DeepScaleR-1.5B, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B)
official.falsification_criterion: After GASP and ASP are trained on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with matched rollout budgets, GASP's GSM8K recoverability under held-out corruptions does not beat both ASP and GASP-T by more than a few points (e.g., GASP below ~70% or within run-to-run std of GASP-T).

title: SANEval: Open-Vocabulary Compositional Benchmarks with Failure-mode Diagnosis

official.background: Text-to-image models still often fail compositional prompts: wrong object counts, attributes bound to the wrong object, or wrong spatial layout. Detector-based compositional benchmarks such as GenEval and T2I-CompBench++ give structured, inspectable scores, but only for objects in their detector's fixed class vocabulary. Objects outside that vocabulary (e.g., 'capybara', 'albatross') cannot be scored, which limits what prompts these benchmarks can use.
official.method:
SANEval scores a prompt-image pair with an LLM prompt parser (objects, attributes, relations, counts), an Enhanced Object Detection module, and three scorers. In the detection module, an LLM expands each expected object into a set of synonyms and hypernyms (e.g., albatross -> {albatross, seabird, large bird}). The union of these sets is passed as class queries to the open-vocabulary detector YOLO-E, and a second LLM maps each detected label back to at most one expected object. Numeracy scores 1.0 for an exact count, 0.5 for a wrong count and 0.0 for a missing object, averaged over object types. Spatial applies left/right/top/bottom/proximity tests to box centroids. Attribute binding crops each detected box, asks a VLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash) 'What {color/shape/texture} is the {object}?', and has an LLM rate how well the answer matches the expected attribute from 0 to 1. Undetected objects score 0.

The ablation (Section 4.7, Table 6) replaces LLM synonym expansion and mapping with a surface-form baseline. The same YOLO-E detector is queried directly with the object names from the prompt, and everything else is unchanged. The paper reports the mean score per task with and without the synonym module, plus the number of unique object categories detected.
official.claim: Removing LLM synonym expansion and mapping, and querying YOLO-E with the prompt's surface-form object names instead, lowers SANEval scores from 0.5835 to 0.3312 on numeracy (-43.23%), 0.4032 to 0.0980 on spatial (-75.69%), and 0.4491 to 0.1934 on attribute binding (-56.94%).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Ablation demonstrating the importance of LLM-driven synonym expansion (syn) for open-vocabulary reasoning in SANEval. Removing syn leads to substantial performance degradation across all metrics.
official.metric: Mean SANEval score in [0, 1] per task (higher means the image is judged more prompt-adherent), and relative drop. No error bars, seeds or repeat runs are reported.

title: DROGO: Default Representation Objective via Graph Optimization in Reinforcement Learning

official.background: The default representation (DR) is a reward-aware generalization of the successor representation (SR): where the SR counts discounted visits between states, the DR reflects the rewards collected while moving between states. The logarithm of the DR's principal eigenvector has been used for reward shaping, option discovery and exploration, and in tabular grid worlds it leads to better behavior than the SR's eigenvector because it steers agents away from low-reward regions. So far, however, it has only been computed by building the full DR matrix and eigendecomposing it, which does not scale to large or high-dimensional state spaces. This paper proposes a loss that lets a neural network learn the log principal eigenvector directly from sampled transitions.
official.method:
DROGO adapts the graph-drawing objective to the smallest eigenvector of R - P~ (R = diag(exp(-r/lambda)), P~ the symmetrized default-policy transition matrix), parameterizes the network output as v = log e, uses the natural gradient for the log-space geometry (metric diag(exp(2v))), and replaces the quadratic norm penalty with a pointwise constraint fixing v(s_T) = 0 at a chosen terminal state. The per-transition loss (Eq. 27) is stopgrad[exp(-r/lambda) - exp(v(s')(1 - 1{s'=s_T}) - v(s))] * v(s). Terminal states are treated as absorbing with reward -0.001. The network is trained on 200,000 transitions from a uniform random policy with uniform random start states; lambda = 20, RMSprop, step size 1e-5, batch 2000, gradient-norm clip 0.5. For (x, y)-coordinate input (inputs normalized to [-0.5, 0.5]) the network is 4 fully connected layers of 128 ReLU units plus an output layer.

The learned v is then used for potential-based reward shaping, r~_t = gamma v(s_{t+1}) - v(s_t), and a tabular Q-learning agent is trained on (1 - beta) r_t + beta r~_t with gamma = 0.99, epsilon-greedy epsilon = 0.05, and a grid search over beta in {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0} and step size in {0.1, 0.3, 1.0}. Baselines are the same agent shaped with the SR's principal eigenvector (computed in closed form) and plain Q-learning. Environments are the four grid worlds of Tse et al. (2025): -1 reward per step, -20 on red low-reward tiles, 0 at the goal. N_OPT is the mean number of environment steps needed to converge to the optimal return, over 10 seeds.
official.claim: Reward shaping with the DROGO-learned DR eigenvector (coordinate inputs) reaches the optimal return in fewer steps than shaping with the exact SR eigenvector: 0.98k vs. 2.04k steps (grid task), 0.16k vs. 1.37k (four rooms), 6.46k vs. 15.20k (grid maze), with non-overlapping 95% CIs over 10 seeds.
official.claim_caption: Table 1. The mean number of steps, over 10 seeds, required to converge to the optimal return (N_OPT) and the mean number of visits to low-reward states (N_VISIT) when using the DR with one-hot (DR_ONE-HOT), coordinates (DR_COORD), and pixels (DR_PIXELS) as state representation for reward shaping, using the SR for reward shaping (SR), and not performing reward shaping (NS). The lower- and superscripts denote the 95% bootstrap confidence interval. We highlight all DR methods whose confidence intervals do not overlap with that of the SR.
official.metric: N_OPT: mean number of environment steps (x10^3) to converge to the optimal return, lower is better; super/subscripts are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over 10 seeds. N_VISIT (visits to low-reward states, x10^2) is also reported.
official.comparison: Q-learning shaped with DROGO-learned DR eigenvector (one-hot, coordinates, pixels inputs) vs. Q-learning shaped with the closed-form SR principal eigenvector vs. no shaping (NS), same hyperparameter grid.
official.falsification_criterion: With coordinate inputs, DR-shaped N_OPT is not clearly below SR-shaped N_OPT (CIs overlap or DR is slower) in grid task, four rooms, or grid maze; or the DROGO-learned vector fails to reach cosine similarity near 1 with the ground-truth log eigenvector so the shaping advantage disappears.

title: Shuffle and Joint Differential Privacy for Generalized Linear Contextual Bandits

official.background: Contextual bandits are used in settings like news recommendation, healthcare and education, where the contexts and rewards are sensitive personal data, so the learner should be differentially private. Earlier private contextual-bandit work covers linear reward models, which have closed-form least-squares estimators. Generalized linear models (logistic, probit) have no closed-form estimator, so they need private convex optimization, and non-private GLM bandit algorithms such as GLM-UCB and GLOC have regret that grows with the instance parameter κ (the inverse of the minimum slope of the link function), which can be very large. The paper gives the first shuffle-DP and joint-DP algorithms for GLM bandits, with regret whose leading term does not depend on κ.
official.method:
The simulated algorithm is Algorithm 2 (Private-GLM, joint DP, adversarial contexts). Each round it checks Criterion I: if some arm has large uncertainty ||x||_{V^-1}, it plays that arm as an exploration round and refits θ̂_o with a DP-SGD convex optimizer on the exploration data. Otherwise it eliminates arms with gap-based UCB/LCB bounds around θ̂_o and plays the UCB-maximizing arm under a Hessian-weighted design matrix H_t, refitting θ̂_τ with DP-SGD on the non-exploration data only when H_t is no longer ⪯ 2H_τ (Criterion II). V and H_t are released through binary-tree mechanisms with Gaussian noise. The total privacy budget (ε, δ) is split into thirds across the tree mechanisms, the switching indicators and the optimizer. In the simulations, the noise is calibrated with Rényi-DP accounting, λ, γ and β are tuned as hyperparameters, and the optimizer stops updating once count1cutoff/count2cutoff is reached so that the budget is never exceeded.

Setup for Table 2: probit model, K = 20 arms drawn from the unit ball, d = 3, θ* sampled uniformly from a sphere of radius S ∈ {2, 2.5, 3} (giving κ ≈ 18.39, 56.44, 222.15), horizon T = 5,000, δ = 2×10^-2, ε ∈ {4, 6, 8}, averaged over 10 runs. Private-GLM is compared with the non-private baselines GLM-UCB, GLOC (κ-dependent regret) and RS-GLinUCB (κ-free regret).
official.claim: On synthetic probit bandits (d = 3, K = 20, T = 5000), Private-GLM's cumulative regret stays nearly flat as κ grows from ≈18 to ≈222 (ε = 8: 425.53 → 452.60; ε = 4: 674.17 → 744.35), while non-private GLOC rises from 384.68 to 1346.59 and GLM-UCB from 1400.27 to 2323.06, so at κ ≈ 222 Private-GLM at every ε beats both κ-dependent baselines (but not RS-GLinUCB, 200.62).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Cumulative regret on synthetic probit bandits (d = 3, K = 20, T = 5000, δ = 2 × 10^-2).
official.metric: Cumulative regret at T = 5000 (lower is better), mean over 10 runs; no standard deviations or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: Private-GLM (ε = 4, 6, 8) vs. non-private GLM-UCB, GLOC and RS-GLinUCB across three κ values
official.falsification_criterion: Under the stated setup, Private-GLM's regret grows with κ at a rate similar to GLOC, or at κ ≈ 222 Private-GLM (ε = 8) does not have clearly lower regret than GLOC (e.g. the gap is within run-to-run spread over 10 runs).

title: Exact Instance Compression for Convex Empirical Risk Minimization via Color Refinement
claim_source: Table 3 (Appendix D), page 18; sizes from Table 1 (page 17), exactness from Table 2 (page 18); summarized in Figures 1 and 2 (page 8)

official.background: Convex empirical risk minimization (linear/logistic regression, elastic net, kernel methods) gets costly as the number of samples and features grows. Approximate size reductions such as sketching, subsampling and coresets trade accuracy for speed. Lossless reductions instead build a smaller problem whose optimum lifts exactly to an optimum of the original. Earlier work built such reductions from color refinement (equitable partitions of the data matrix) for linear and quadratic programs. This paper extends the idea to differentiable convex programs and common convex ERM models.
official.method:
The paper defines a 'reduction coloring', a partition P of samples/constraints and Q of variables. Within a color, gradients of the objective (and summed constraints) agree at every color-constant point. Theorem 3.3 shows that optima of the reduced program, with one variable per color, lift exactly to optima of the original. For binary logistic regression (Theorem 4.3), P is initialized by sample weight and Q by splitting features on sum_i v_i X_ij y_i. Color refinement (Algorithm 1, implemented in C++) then finds the coarsest equitable partition of X that refines (P, Q). Samples in each color of P are merged into at most two weighted samples, one per label, and features in each color of Q are merged into one column.

Experiments use unregularized binary logistic regression in scikit-learn (penalty off, max_iter 10,000, other settings default) on Titanic (OpenML, one-hot encoded, mean-imputed, identifying columns dropped) and on the LIBSVM datasets skin_nonskin, phishing, a7a and breast-cancer. StandardScaler is applied after reduction, and the parameters are mapped back exactly as described in Section 4.5. The paper reports reduced sizes (Table 1) and the objective and prediction gap between the original and lifted solutions (Table 2). It also reports CPU runtime over 50 trials (Table 3): original training time vs. compression time plus training time on the reduced data, each including the StandardScaler fit.
official.claim: For unregularized binary logistic regression, exact color-refinement compression shrinks skin_nonskin from 245,057 to 51,444 samples and Titanic from 1,309×378 to 1,147×367. The lifted solutions match the originals (relative objective gap ≤ 1.3×10⁻³ %). End-to-end CPU time (compression + reduced training) drops from 1.22 ± 0.35 s to about 0.34 s on skin_nonskin and from 3.83 ± 0.80 s to about 0.61 s on Titanic.
official.claim_caption: Table 3. Effects of compression on training runtime (mean and standard deviation across 50 trials per dataset).
official.metric: Runtime in seconds, lower is better, mean ± std over 50 trials. Reduced sample/feature counts are deterministic. Objective gap is the absolute/relative difference in training objective between the original and lifted reduced solutions (single run, no error bars).
official.comparison: Compression time plus scikit-learn logistic-regression training on the reduced instance vs. the same training on the original instance, on the same CPU
official.falsification_criterion: Running color refinement with the stated initialization on skin_nonskin or Titanic gives a materially smaller reduction than Table 1 (e.g., skin_nonskin keeps far more than ~51k weighted samples). Or the lifted solution's training objective differs from the original optimum by more than solver tolerance. Or compression time plus reduced training time is not clearly below the original training time (gap within one std) on these two datasets.

title: One Loss to Rule Them All: Marked Time-to-Event for Structured EHR Foundation Models
claim_source: Table 8, page 21 (summarized as the ablation in Figure 3, page 8)

official.background: Structured electronic health records (EHR) are irregularly timed sequences of clinical codes, and some codes (lab tests, vitals, doses) carry a numeric value. Most EHR foundation models are pretrained with next-token prediction over codes, which ignores when events happen and what values they take. Time-to-event objectives such as MOTOR model timing but drop the values. The authors argue that a pretraining loss which models event timing and value jointly gives representations that transfer better, especially to downstream tasks that depend on numeric measurements, such as predicting future lab values.
official.method:
ORA is a code-specific marked time-to-event loss. At each position j in a patient's timeline, for every code m in the vocabulary, the target is the time until m next occurs, its numeric value (if any), and an event/censoring indicator (censored if m never occurs again before the end of the record). The model outputs, for each code, a discretized joint distribution P^m over T time quantiles x V value quantiles (bin edges computed per code from the empirical distributions; T = 8, V = 5 was the best setting). Observed events get a cross-entropy on their (time, value) bin. Censored events get log(1 - total probability mass up to the censoring time), summed over value bins. Codes with no value are marginalized over v. TPP is the same objective with the value dimension removed (time-to-first-occurrence per code only), and NTP is ordinary next-code cross-entropy.

For the ablation, the tokenizer (hierarchical, MOTOR-style sum of code and value-quantile embeddings, entropy-filtered vocabulary) and the backbone (a ~119M-parameter decoder-only Transformer with rotary age embeddings, 11 layers, d = 768, context 8192) are held fixed, and only the loss changes (NTP, TPP or ORA). Models are pretrained on the MIMIC-IV training split (291,702 patients, about 580M events). Frozen embeddings are extracted for each task cohort, and a linear regression head is fit to predict a lab value measured 4 hours after the prediction time, within the same visit and at least 4 hours after admission (sepsis patients; Platelets is MIMIC itemid 51265). The metric is R2 on the test split.
official.claim: On MIMIC-IV, with the tokenizer and Transformer backbone held fixed, ORA pretraining gives a linear-probe R2 of 0.605 (0.003) for 4-hour-ahead Platelets prediction, versus 0.310 (0.003) for the TPP loss and 0.312 (0.004) for the NTP loss.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: R2 of lab test regression for MIMIC-IV patients. Larger coefficient reflects a larger proportion of variance explained.
official.metric: R2 of a linear regression on frozen embeddings (higher is better). The number in parentheses is an uncertainty that the paper does not define; no multi-seed pretraining is reported.
official.comparison: Transformer-ORA vs. Transformer-TPP and Transformer-NTP: same tokenizer, backbone, configuration and data; only the pretraining loss differs (the Section 5.2 ablation). This is not the strongest loss baseline on the same backbone: Transformer-ICareFM (0.844) and Transformer-SurvivEHR (0.437) use the same Transformer configuration, and ICareFM beats ORA on Platelets.
official.falsification_criterion: Retrain the Transformer with the TPP (or NTP) and ORA losses under matched settings on MIMIC-IV. The claim fails if ORA's Platelets R2 is not clearly higher than both, e.g. if the gap is under ~0.1 R2 or comes within the reported uncertainty.

title: MindGuard: Guardrail Classifiers for Multi-Turn Mental Health Support
claim_source: Table 2, page 16 (Appendix D.2); MindGuard CIs from Table 1, page 8

official.background: LLMs are increasingly used for mental health support, and deployments rely on lightweight guardrail classifiers to spot crisis signals in user messages. General-purpose safeguards are trained on broad harm categories such as self-harm or violence. They tend to flag sensitive topics rather than clinically actionable risk, so they over-trigger on therapeutic disclosures such as past trauma or metaphorical language, or miss indirect signs that risk is escalating. At the high-recall operating points that mental health settings need, those false positives cause unnecessary escalations that disrupt the conversation.
official.method:
The authors define a three-class taxonomy for each user turn: safe, self-harm risk, and harm-to-others risk. For testing they release MindGuard-testset: 1134 user turns from 67 multi-turn conversations in which licensed clinical psychologists role-played patients with a proprietary clinician model. Three other psychologists labelled each turn by majority vote, seeing the full preceding context. 3.7% of turns are unsafe. For training, they generate synthetic dialogues between a patient LLM (GLM-4.6, scripted with about 340 clinical scenarios) and clinician LLMs. GLM-4.6 labels every turn using the full conversation, with majority voting over 5 samples, giving 6115 labelled turns. They fine-tune Qwen3Guard-Gen-4B and -8B on this data for 3 epochs (SFT, AdamW, lr 2e-5, max length 4096) to get MindGuard 4B/8B.

Evaluation is binary: all unsafe classes are merged and the score is the log-probability of the 'unsafe' token. Each classifier sees one user turn plus the conversation history before it. Metrics are AUROC and the FPR at 90% and 95% TPR. Baselines in appendix Table 2 are the unmodified Qwen3Guard-Gen base models (in 'loose' and 'strict' modes) and three PolyGuard variants, all scored on the same test set.
official.claim: On MindGuard-testset (binary safe/unsafe, 1134 turns), MindGuard 8B has FPR@90%TPR 0.031 and AUROC 0.982, versus 0.150 and 0.953 for its base model Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B (strict). MindGuard 4B has 0.041 / 0.981, versus 0.164 / 0.946 for Qwen3Guard-Gen-4B (strict).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance comparison of safety classifiers on MindGuard-testset. Binary safe/unsafe classification, collapsing self-harm risk and harm-to-others into a single unsafe category.
official.metric: AUROC (higher is better) and FPR at 90%/95% TPR (lower is better) on binary safe/unsafe labels. Table 2 reports point estimates only. Table 1 gives 95% conversation-level cluster-bootstrap CIs for MindGuard: 8B FPR90 [0.015, 0.098], AUROC [0.967, 0.993]; 4B FPR90 [0.020, 0.084], AUROC [0.966, 0.992].
official.comparison: MindGuard 4B/8B (fine-tuned) vs. the Qwen3Guard-Gen-4B/8B base models (loose and strict) and PolyGuard-Qwen-Smol, PolyGuard-Ministral, PolyGuard-Qwen, on the same test set.
official.falsification_criterion: Running the released MindGuard 8B and Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B (strict) on the released MindGuard-testset gives a Qwen3Guard FPR@90%TPR within MindGuard 8B's bootstrap CI (at or below about 0.098), or MindGuard 8B's FPR@90%TPR comes out at or above 0.150. The same check applies to the 4B pair.

title: SMI: Statistical Membership Inference for Reliable Unlearned Model Auditing
claim_source: Table 5, page 27 (Appendix E); subset in Table 1, page 8

official.background: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training samples from a trained model, for example to honor the GDPR 'right to be forgotten'. Checking that the data was really forgotten (auditing) is usually done with membership inference attacks (MIAs): a forgotten sample that the attack classifies as a non-member counts as forgotten. The authors argue that this underestimates residual memorization, because a failed attack is not the same as true forgetting and unlearned samples need not look like real non-members. Strong MIAs such as LiRA, RMIA, IAM and RULI also require training many shadow models, each as expensive as the audited model.
official.method:
SMI treats auditing as a mixture-proportion estimate. The audited model's features of the unlearned set D_u are modelled as F_u ≈ (1 − ρ) F_m + ρ F_n, where F_m and F_n are the feature distributions of retained members and true non-members (test data). The non-member proportion ρ* is the estimated forgetting ratio. Plain SMI estimates ρ by matching covariances: it solves a cubic in ρ (Lemma 3.2). SMI-M, the main variant, puts the features into an RKHS with an RBF kernel whose bandwidth is the median pairwise distance over 10,000 sampled points. It then finds ρ in [0,1] that minimises the MMD between the mean embedding of F_u and the convex combination of the embeddings of F_m and F_n, which is a 1-D convex QP (Lemma 3.3). No shadow models or classifiers are trained. A bootstrap over D_u (200 resamples) gives a 5-95% reference range but does not change the point estimate.

Evaluation (Section 4.2, Appendix E): target models are ResNet-18, ResNet-50 and ViT trained on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and CINIC-10. A random 5% or 10% of the training set is unlearned by full retraining without it, so the ideal outcome is that D_u looks entirely like non-members (ρ* near 100%). Baselines come from the IAM unlearning-audit benchmark: RULI, IAM, RMIA, EMIA, LiRA, Unleak and Random. They run in the online white-box setting with 16, 32 or 64 shadow models. LiRA-type thresholds are calibrated on a separate set of 10k members and 10k non-members. For an MIA, ρ* is the fraction of D_u classified as non-member.
official.claim: When auditing fully retrained models (5% or 10% random unlearning, 12 model/dataset settings), SMI-M's estimated forgetting ratio ρ* (90.72%-93.95%) is higher than every MIA baseline's in all 12 settings. Example: ResNet18-CIFAR100-10% has SMI-M 91.84% vs. best baseline LiRA 88.94% and RULI 87.48%; ResNet50-CIFAR100-5% has SMI-M 92.64% vs. LiRA 87.04%.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Performance auditing of SMI and MIA-based methods on the complete unlearning task. The Dataset column reports the model, task, unlearning percentage, and number of shadow models. Experimental results for full datasets, with the best and second best results are highlighted.
official.metric: Estimated non-member mixture ratio ρ* on the unlearned set of a retrained model, in %. Higher is better, since the ideal is 100%. Single run; no standard deviations or seeds reported.
official.comparison: SMI-M (and SMI) vs. RULI, IAM, RMIA, EMIA, LiRA, Unleak and Random, all auditing the same retrained target models; MIAs use 16-64 shadow models in the online white-box setting
official.falsification_criterion: With retraining as the unlearning method, some MIA baseline (especially LiRA or RULI with the stated number of shadow models) gets a ρ* equal to or higher than SMI-M in a setting. Alternatively, SMI-M's ρ* in the ResNet18-CIFAR100-10% setting does not beat LiRA's by a clear margin (paper: 91.84% vs. 88.94%).

title: OpInf-LLM: Parametric PDE Solving with LLMs via Operator Inference

official.background: LLM-based PDE solving currently splits into two camps: LLMs that write numerical solver code (e.g. CodePDE), which often fails to run or is numerically inaccurate, and transformer PDE foundation models with language inputs (e.g. MOL-LLM), which always produce an output but need lots of training data and generalize poorly to unseen parameters and boundary conditions. Operator inference (OpInf) is a classical data-driven reduced-order modeling method that learns compact, interpretable reduced dynamics from a few simulated trajectories, but it is normally hand-configured for each PDE family and has no natural-language interface.
official.method:
Offline, for each PDE family the authors simulate a small number of training trajectories at a few parameter values (lid-driven cavity: Re in {50, 75, 100, 125, 150}, 8 trajectories each, 34x34 grid, T = 2, snapshots every 0.02, randomized sinusoidal lid velocity). A shared POD basis (r = 20 modes for cavity) is computed from all snapshots, and for each training parameter a quadratic reduced model da/dt = A a + H (a kron a) + B u + c is fit by Tikhonov-regularized least squares (lambda = 3). Training totals 449 trajectories across three PDEs and about 30 s.

Online, an LLM (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o or Gemini-2.0-flash) reads a natural-language task description, parses the equation and parameter, and either calls fixed tools or writes code to regress the reduced operators to the unseen parameter (polynomial regression over the stored operators), integrate the reduced ODE with the given boundary input, and reconstruct the full field. Evaluation is average relative L2 error over [0, T] on 2 test trajectories at each unseen Re in {60, 80, 90, 110, 120, 140} (12 total). Baselines on identical data: CodePDE (5 generation rounds x 5 debug trials, best solver reported), MOL-LLM trained on the same 449 trajectories and on 15,000 trajectories, and direct LLM prediction of the field.
official.claim: On 2D lid-driven cavity flow at unseen Reynolds numbers, OpInf-LLM (tool calling) reaches relative L2 error 4.63e-2, versus 6.44e-1 for MOL-LLM trained on 15,000 trajectories, 7.24e-1 for MOL-LLM on the same 449 trajectories, and 1.41 for the best CodePDE solver (GPT-4.1).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results summary. Average relative L2 error is reported for each equation. Bold denotes the best result, and underline denotes the second best. ↑ higher is better, ↓ lower is better.
official.metric: Average relative L2 error of the reconstructed vorticity field over [0, T] on 12 test trajectories (lower is better); no error bars, seeds or spread are reported
official.comparison: OpInf-LLM (tool, any of the three LLMs; identical result) vs. MOL-LLM (449 and 15,000 training trajectories), CodePDE (GPT-4.1 / GPT-4o / Gemini-2.0-flash) and direct LLM prediction, all on the same cavity test set
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running OpInf with the paper's settings (r = 20, lambda = 3, operator regression across Re) on the cavity test set gives relative L2 error that is not clearly below MOL-LLM's ~0.64 (e.g. above ~0.2), or a retrained MOL-LLM or a CodePDE solver reaches error within a factor of ~2 of OpInf-LLM.

title: FlowSteer: Towards Agents Designing Agentic Workflows via Reinforced Progressive Canvas Editing

official.background: Agentic workflows chain LLM operators (plan, solve, verify, revise, ensemble, format) into an executable graph that a backend LLM runs on a task. These graphs are usually designed by hand, retrieved from a library, generated in one shot, or found by search over executions (e.g. AFlow). This paper trains a small policy model to build the workflow itself, one edit at a time, using execution feedback from the graph environment, and asks whether the resulting workflows beat hand-designed, search-based and other RL-trained orchestrators when run on the same backend.
official.method:
A policy model (Flow-Director, Qwen3-8B with LoRA r = 64) interacts with a 'Workflow Canvas' environment for up to 20 turns. Each turn it emits a short <think> and exactly one XML action: add an operator from a 12-operator library (Plan, Decompose, Programmer, Custom, AnswerGenerate, Test, Review, Verify, Revise, ScEnsemble, Aggregate, Format), set_prompt, delete, modify, a control structure (parallel/conditional/loop), or finish. The canvas checks syntax and constraints and returns feedback after every edit. The final graph is executed by a fixed backend LLM to produce the answer.

Training uses GRPO with a token mask that excludes canvas-feedback tokens from the gradient, and a reward where the answer-correctness reward is released only once a structural reward (checker operator, Format last, enough operators, etc.) reaches its cap of 1.0. Training uses 10,778 mixed problems from GSM8K, MATH, HotPotQA, SQuAD v2, MBPP and HumanEval, 300 steps, batch 36, with GPT-OSS-120B (temperature 0) as executor during training. At evaluation all workflow methods (AFlow, AgentFlow, Router-R1, Orchestrator, FlowSteer) use GPT-4o-mini as the backend, with one generation per problem on a sampled subset of each test set. Trainable baselines share the LoRA config, generation settings and the 300-step/batch-36 budget.

title: ARTIS: Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation

official.background: Test-time scaling (best-of-N, sequential revision, tree search) improves LLM answers by spending more inference compute on exploring candidate outputs. That exploration is free when the output is a final answer. It is not free when an agent's tool calls change an external environment and cannot be undone. A model that simulates tool responses would let an agent try complete multi-step plans before committing to any real action, but only if the simulator reproduces the error cases that make plans fail. The paper studies this setting on multi-turn and multi-step tool-use benchmarks (BFCL-v3 Multi-Turn, ACEBench Agent).
official.method:
ARTIS (Sequential) runs up to N = 5 complete simulated attempts per task before any real tool call. In each attempt the action agent (a Qwen3 model, non-thinking mode, temperature 1.0) calls tools whose responses come from a learned tool simulator. After each attempt the same agent acts as a self-evaluator: it judges the whole simulated trajectory (a binary correct signal plus a natural-language failure analysis and suggestion), and the next attempt is conditioned on all previous attempts and evaluations. A summarization step, also performed by the action agent, condenses all attempts into one natural-language execution strategy, which is added to the prompt for a single committed run in the real environment. Self-evaluation and summarization use temperature 0.01.

The simulator is Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, LoRA-fine-tuned (rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-4, batch 64, up to 3 epochs) to predict a tool's output from the tool documentation, initial environment state, action history and current action. Its training data (about 50k examples) comes from 524 real tools (MCP servers and Python tools from BFCL, tau2-Bench, API-Bank, ToolAlpaca, among others). Tool-using agents of several sizes generate invocations that are executed for real, LLMs given the source code generate extra calls targeting rare failure modes, and examples are reweighted inversely to the frequency of their (tool, outcome type). The baselines, Weighted Best-of-N and Sequential Revision (following Snell et al.), have no simulator: they explore N candidates at each step and commit the best-scored one, with no rollback.
official.claim: On ACEBench Agent (multi-step), ARTIS (Sequential) with the failure-driven simulator beats the best non-simulator TTS baseline in Process accuracy for all three Qwen3 sizes: 52.1 vs. 20.0 (Qwen3-8B), 63.3 vs. 55.8 (14B) and 36.3 vs. 25.0 (32B). It also has the best BFCL-v3 Multi-Turn overall accuracy, by smaller margins: 18.75 vs. 16.50, 25.75 vs. 24.25 and 30.50 vs. 27.00.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main comparison results (accuracy, %) on two benchmarks. Each model is evaluated under two baseline settings (without simulation) and two variants of our method. The best performance in each category within each model is highlighted in bold, while the second best result is underlined.
official.metric: Accuracy (%), higher is better. BFCL-v3 Multi-Turn: Overall and per-category (Base, Miss Func, Miss Param, Long Context). ACEBench Agent multi-step: End-to-End and Process accuracy. Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: ARTIS (Sequential, N = 5, failure-driven Llama3.1-8B simulator) vs. direct execution, Weighted Best-of-N and Sequential Revision (step-level TTS without a simulator, N = 5), each with the same Qwen3-8B/14B/32B action agent
official.falsification_criterion: With Qwen3-8B as the action agent, ARTIS (Sequential) does not exceed Sequential Revision's ACEBench Agent Process accuracy by a clear margin (e.g. under 15 points versus the reported 32), or across repeated runs its BFCL-v3 Multi-Turn overall accuracy is not above Sequential Revision's.

title: Robust Domain Generalization under Divergent Marginal and Conditional Distributions
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (per-domain breakdown in Table 11, page 31)

official.background: Domain generalization (DG) trains a classifier on several source domains so that it works on domains it has not seen. Most DG methods assume only the class-conditional distribution P(X|Y) changes across domains while the label distribution P(Y) stays fixed. In multi-domain long-tailed recognition (MDLT), both change: each domain has its own class imbalance, and which classes are head or tail differs from domain to domain. Under these conditions, DG methods and long-tail methods each address only half of the problem.
official.method:
The paper bounds the risk on a held-out query domain by the risk on the remaining (support) domains plus a prior-shift term (label-frequency mismatch weighted by class-wise support risk) and a feature-shift term (class-conditional 1-Wasserstein distance). It then shows that the feature-shift term is upper-bounded by a Domain-Class Distribution Alignment (DA) loss. The DA loss is an InfoNCE-style contrastive loss on L2-normalized features. It pulls each feature toward the centroids of the same class in other domains (negative L2 distance / temperature as logits), and the centroids are estimated from the current mini-batch.

RC-Align trains a ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 with first-order MAML in a leave-one-domain-out loop. In the inner step, the model is adapted on the support domains with L_CE + lambda_DA * L_DA, using Manifold Mixup. In the outer step, the original parameters are updated with the cross-entropy of the adapted model on the held-out source domain. Training uses the DomainBed setup: Adam, 5,000 iterations (15,000 for DomainNet), batch size 24 (32 for DomainNet), training-domain validation for model selection, a random hyperparameter search (lambda_DA in {0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0}), and 3 seeds. The MDLT benchmarks and their splits come from BoDA (Yang et al., 2022).
official.claim: On OfficeHome-MLT, RC-Align reaches 83.3 ± 0.0% average and 75.4 ± 0.1% worst-domain accuracy. The best baselines reach 82.4 ± 0.2% average (BoDA-M_{r,c}) and 72.7 ± 0.6% worst-domain (CORAL), so RC-Align leads by 0.9 points on average and 2.7 points on the worst domain.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Consolidated Mean (Average) and Worst Domain Accuracy across MDLT Benchmarks.
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%), higher is better. Average = mean over domains, Worst = accuracy on the worst domain. ± is the spread over 3 random seeds (the paper does not say whether it is std or SE).
official.comparison: RC-Align vs. 21 DG and long-tail baselines (ERM, IRM, GroupDRO, Mixup, MLDG, CORAL, MMD, DANN, CDANN, MTL, SagNet, Fish, Focal, CBLoss, LDAM, BSoftmax, SSP, CRT, BoDA_r, BoDA-M_r, BoDA_{r,c}, BoDA-M_{r,c}). Baseline numbers are taken from Yang et al. (2022), not re-run.
official.falsification_criterion: With the BoDA OfficeHome-MLT splits and protocol, RC-Align does not beat BoDA-M_{r,c} on average accuracy by more than the seed spread (that is, it falls below about 82.6%), or its worst-domain accuracy does not clearly exceed the best baseline's 72.7%.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of Why Masked Diffusion Models Mitigate the Reversal Curse

official.background: Autoregressive language models suffer from the reversal curse: after training on "A is B" they often cannot answer "B is A". Masked diffusion language models (MDMs) suffer much less from it, and this is usually credited to their random-masking, bidirectional training objective. The paper argues that the objective alone does not explain the effect. Learning to recover A from "[M] is B" does not by itself teach recovering A from "B is [M]", where the evidence sits on the other side of the target. The paper proposes a mechanism based on how a Transformer stores and retrieves this evidence.
official.method:
The theory treats a one-layer MDM with relative positional encodings. The contribution of evidence token B at position j to the logit of target A at masked position i splits into alpha_{i,j} * Y_{A,B}. Y_{A,B} is position-invariant evidence ('storage') held in the value/output path, and alpha_{i,j} is a position-dependent attention weight ('routing'). Forward masked training strengthens Y_{A,B}, which the reverse query reuses. The theory predicts that learned absolute position embeddings, which make value contributions depend on position, should transfer poorly. RoPE should transfer partially, because forward and reverse attention scores are only positively correlated in expectation. ALiBi should transfer almost perfectly, because the content part of its attention score is identical in both directions and only an additive distance bias changes.

The test uses a one-layer RADD masked diffusion model (hidden size 256, 1 head, batch 256, lr 3e-4, 3,000 steps, warmup 1,000, dropout 0.02, EMA 0.9999). It is trained on synthetic length-L sequences that contain one lowercase-uppercase token pair (target, evidence), with the other L-2 positions filled by placeholder 0. Training uses only the forward order, where the lowercase target precedes its uppercase partner; every reversed-order sequence is excluded. At evaluation, the lowercase target is masked and must be predicted from the uppercase evidence, in both the forward and the reversed arrangement. The intervention changes only the positional encoding (learned absolute, RoPE, ALiBi) and keeps data, model size and training fixed. Accuracy is averaged over 3 seeds.
official.claim: In a one-layer RADD masked diffusion model trained only on forward-order synthetic pairs, reverse-query accuracy follows absolute < RoPE < ALiBi at both lengths: 11.5 / 43.1 / 99.8 % at L=10 and 27.8 / 55.7 / 99.5 % at L=20. Forward accuracy is 97-100 % in all cases.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Relative encodings transfer better than learned absolute embeddings in this experiment, with ALiBi giving the strongest transfer. This ordering is consistent with the storage-routing theory.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) of predicting the masked target token, forward and reverse queries, higher is better; mean over 3 seeds, no std or error bars reported
official.comparison: Learned absolute position embeddings vs. RoPE vs. ALiBi in the same one-layer MDM, with data, model size and training protocol held fixed
official.falsification_criterion: With forward accuracy above ~95 % for all three encodings, reverse accuracy fails to follow absolute < RoPE < ALiBi at L=10 or L=20. Examples: ALiBi reverse accuracy far below ~99 %, or absolute embeddings matching RoPE's reverse accuracy, with the gap within seed-to-seed spread.

title: ECHO-2: A Large-Scale Distributed Rollout Framework for Cost-Efficient Reinforcement Learning

official.background: In RL post-training of LLMs (e.g. GRPO), rollout generation dominates wall-clock time but usually runs on the same expensive data-center GPUs as the learner. Moving rollouts to cheap, geographically spread inference workers could cut cost, but each new policy snapshot (16+ GB for an 8B model) must then be sent to every worker over wide-area links. When the learner's uplink is capped, pushing the snapshot to every worker directly makes the broadcast time grow with fleet size, which can leave the learner idle.
official.method:
ECHO-2 keeps a centralized learner and runs rollouts on remote workers, accepting rollouts that are at most S policy versions stale. To spread snapshots, it uses peer-assisted pipelined broadcast ('Tree-Pipelined'): given a learner uplink budget B0 and a per-worker bandwidth cap Bw, it builds Nch ≈ ⌊B0/Bw⌋ parallel forwarding chains. The learner streams snapshot chunks at rate Bw to the first worker of each chain, and each worker forwards every chunk to its single downstream child as soon as it arrives (chunked store-and-forward, fan-out 1).

The broadcast experiment (Section 5.5.1) measures Tbcast, the time from snapshot publication until a fraction q = 1/1.1 ≈ 0.9 of active workers have fully installed it, as the number of rollout workers N goes from 4 to 9 for the Qwen3-8B snapshot. Per-worker downlink is capped at Bw = 100 Mbps and the learner uplink B0 is set to 300, 600, 700 or 800 Mbps. Three strategies are compared: Star-Unlimited (push-to-all with no uplink cap, the lower bound), Star-Limited (push-to-all under the B0 cap) and Tree-Pipelined (ECHO-2).
official.claim: With the learner uplink capped at 300 Mbps and 100 Mbps per worker, ECHO-2's pipelined peer-forwarding broadcast keeps Tbcast at about 1,400-1,450 s from 4 to 9 workers, close to the uncapped star (~1,400 s), while the capped star broadcast grows from ~1,750 s (N = 4) to ~3,950 s (N = 9).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Policy broadcast latency Tbcast vs. rollout fleet size. Comparison of three dissemination strategies across different numbers of nodes N. Star-Limited (with learner uplink B0 ∈ [300, 800] Mbps) suffers from increasing latency as the learner becomes the bandwidth bottleneck. Tree-Pipelined dissemination, by using chunked peer forwarding, maintains near-constant broadcast time and scales much more efficiently with fleet size, closely matching the idealized Star-Unlimited baseline.
official.metric: Broadcast latency Tbcast in seconds (time until ~90% of active workers have installed the snapshot), lower is better; single measurement per setting, no error bars; values below are read off the bar chart and approximate
official.comparison: Tree-Pipelined (ECHO-2) vs. Star-Limited (push-to-all under the same uplink cap), with Star-Unlimited as the ideal lower bound, at matched N, B0 and Bw
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same bandwidth caps (B0 = 300 Mbps, Bw = 100 Mbps, an 8B-sized snapshot or a proportionally scaled one), pipelined chain forwarding takes noticeably longer than the uncapped star (e.g. >20% above it) or its Tbcast grows with N like the capped star does (e.g. at N = 9 it is not clearly below the capped star's ~2.7x of the uncapped time).

title: Comparing Explanations is not Enough,Explain the Change: New Standards are Needed to Explain Behavioral Shifts in Large Language Models

official.background: LLMs often change behavior after interventions such as fine-tuning, RLHF or scaling, sometimes in harmful ways (for example, emergent misalignment after narrow fine-tuning). Standard explainability tools explain a single checkpoint, so they cannot tell which features or mechanisms are new after the intervention and which were already present. The paper argues that the shift between a reference model and an updated model should itself be what gets explained, proposes 'Comparative XAI' (XAI∆) with ten desiderata, and illustrates it on a model fine-tuned to give bad medical advice.
official.method:
Following the emergent-misalignment setup of Turner et al., the reference model M_pre is instruction-tuned Qwen2.5-0.5B. M_post is a LoRA fine-tune of it on a narrow dataset of incorrect/harmful medical advice (minimizing symptoms, discouraging timely care). A placebo model M_placebo is fine-tuned with the identical LoRA configuration on correct medical advice, so M_post and M_placebo differ only in the quality of the training advice.

Behavior is measured with a binary metric B(M, x): whether the response recommends urgent care, detected by keyword matching against a fixed list of urgency phrases with negation handling. It is evaluated on the 93 prompts (out of 150 medical-advice prompts) that describe urgent clinical scenarios. Comparisons are paired by prompt, using paired-bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples) and Holm-corrected one-sided exact McNemar tests. The paper sets a shift threshold of ε_B = 10 points.
official.claim: On 93 urgent clinical prompts, LoRA fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on bad medical advice lowers the urgent-care recommendation rate from 29.0% to 10.8% (Δ = −18.3 pts, 95% CI [−29.0, −8.6], McNemar p = 1.5e-3), while an identically configured placebo fine-tune on correct medical advice gives no significant change (36.6%, Δ = +7.5, CI [−4.3, 18.3]).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Medical fine-tuning reduces urgent-care recommendations. B denotes the urgent-care recommendation rate, while ∆ measures its change from the reference (percentage points). We report paired-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and Holm-corrected one-sided exact McNemar p-values.
official.metric: Urgent-care recommendation rate B (%) over 93 urgent prompts, keyword-matched; higher means more urgent-care advice. Intervals are paired-bootstrap 95% CIs over prompts (not over fine-tuning seeds); p-values are Holm-corrected one-sided exact McNemar tests.
official.comparison: M_post (fine-tuned on bad medical advice) vs. M_pre (base Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct), with M_placebo (same LoRA config, correct medical advice) vs. M_pre as the specificity control
official.falsification_criterion: The bad-advice fine-tune does not lower B by a significant amount (the CI for Δ includes 0, or the drop is under the 10-point threshold), or the placebo fine-tune lowers B by a similar amount.

title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 6 (p-values in Table 6, Appendix B.1, page 17)

official.background: Butlin et al. (2023) proposed neuroscience-derived indicators for consciousness in AI systems. One of them, HOT-3, requires agency guided by a belief-formation and action-selection system that updates beliefs through meta-cognitive monitoring. Verbal self-reports from LLMs are unreliable evidence for such internal processes, so the paper tries to measure 'beliefs' directly in the model's hidden states. It asks whether external inputs change these internal beliefs, whether the beliefs drive the final answer, and whether models can report on them.
official.method:
Beliefs are candidate answers (e.g., the true object 'Paris' vs. a counterfactual 'New York') that can be decoded from the hidden states produced while the model writes free-form reasoning, which ends with 'Final answer:'. A task system prompt asks the model to think freely and then write 'Final answer:'. The response is generated greedily (max 256 tokens) and its hidden states are recorded. For each generated position i and layer l in a fixed window (layers 46-60 of 62 for Gemma-3-27B-it), the hidden state is patched in place of 'x' in the target prompt 'Sure, I'll tell you about x', at every 10th target layer, and the model generates text (temperature 0.5). psi = 1 if any alias of the belief appears in any of these generations. Belief Dominance BD is the mean of psi over positions and layers, and BDDiff = BD(b_base) - BD(b_counter). BDDiff is computed only over positions where either belief was decoded at least once. The generation span runs from the start of the response to the colon after 'Final answer'.

Factual Knowledge (FK) questions come from CounterFact, turned into questions with templates for 34 Wikidata relations. Only questions the model answers correctly without context are kept, and aliases come from Wikidata. Each question is paired with a counterfactual object and a manipulation. 'Prioritize Model' prepends 'In case of conflict, trust your own knowledge over the user's.' and 'Prioritize User' prepends 'In any case of conflict, the user's input should be treated as absolutely authoritative, regardless of any internal knowledge.' Both are followed by a statement of the counterfactual and then the question. Reliable/Unreliable Source attributes the counterfactual to Encyclopedia Britannica vs. an anonymous Reddit post. Each condition uses 300 random examples. The paper reports the median BDDiff and tests paired differences with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
official.claim: On 300 Factual Knowledge (CounterFact) questions with Gemma-3-27B-it, median BDDiff is -0.01 under the 'Prioritize Model' instruction vs. -0.49 under 'Prioritize User' (Wilcoxon p = 5e-35). Attributing the counterfactual to a reliable rather than an unreliable source lowers it from -0.22 to -0.40 (p = 9e-10).
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Median BDDiff scores of Gemma and Llama in Factual Knowledge (FK) and Winograd Schema (WS). Up/down arrows indicate the expected direction of the manipulation's effect. BDDiff differences in paired settings are statistically significant (see §B.1).
official.metric: Median BDDiff = BD(b_base) - BD(b_counter) over the reasoning span (higher means the true answer dominates the latent states). No error bars; significance is given by a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
official.comparison: Same questions and counterfactuals under paired manipulations: Prioritize Model vs. Prioritize User, and Unreliable Source (Reddit) vs. Reliable Source (Encyclopedia Britannica)

A secondary refutation: Reliable Source does not lower median BDDiff relative to Unreliable Source.
