title: Joint Learning of Hierarchical Neural Options and Abstract World Model

official.background: An agent that keeps learning should build new skills on top of the ones it already has, e.g. reach a rope, then use that to reach a platform, then use that to reach a key. In the options framework these skills are hierarchical options, each a policy that runs until it reaches its own goal and that can call earlier options. Model-free hierarchical RL needs more and more data as the option set grows, because every new option adds to the action space. The paper asks whether learning a sample-efficient abstract world model of what each option does, and using it to guide exploration, lets an agent master a long, ordered sequence of goals with fewer environment interactions.
official.method:
AgentOWL is given an ordered list of goals ("touch object X", ordered by hand from easy to hard) in object-centric Atari (OCAtari), where states are lists of objects with bounding boxes. It learns one option per goal in sequence. Each option's policy is a Rainbow DQN whose actions are the primitive actions plus all previously learned options, and execution is hierarchical (call-and-return). The abstract world model predicts the vector of goal predicates when an option ends, given the current full state. It is learned with PoE-World: a product of LLM-written symbolic experts (Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite) with weights fit by MAP under a 'frame axiom' prior. A lookup table maps abstract states back to full states so that options can be chained. A DQN trained inside this abstract model gives an exploration policy pi_wm, mixed with the real policy as (1-eps) pi_real + eps pi_wm with eps annealed from 1 to 0. When no candidate option for a goal is working, Gemini 2.5 Flash proposes an already-achieved sub-goal h, which adds a new sub-option 'from h to g'. Episodes containing unstable sub-options (fewer than 20,000 training samples and success rate below 0.5) are discarded from training.

Baselines (all Rainbow DQN with the same network and hyperparameters): DQN (a separate flat policy per goal), Goal-conditioned DQN (one shared policy with a goal embedding), and Hierarchical DQN (action space includes earlier options, i.e. AgentOWL without the world model). An option counts as mastered once its success rate over its 100 most recent executions exceeds 0.5. The metric is the fraction of the goal list mastered as a function of environment steps (up to 5M), with 3 seeds per method. The goal lists have 18 goals for Montezuma's Revenge and 38 goals over 4 rooms for Pitfall.
official.claim: With 5M environment steps, AgentOWL masters about 100% of the 18 Montezuma's Revenge goals (reached before 1M steps) and about 84% of the 38 Pitfall goals, while the best of DQN, Goal-conditioned DQN and Hierarchical DQN plateaus at about 72% (Montezuma) and about 47% (Pitfall), with standard-error bands that do not overlap.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Fraction of options mastered vs number of environment steps for the three OCAtari's games we test on: Montezuma's Revenge, Pitfall, and Private Eye. The shaded area represents standard error computed over 3 seeds. Option is acquired once its success rate for the recent episodes reaches threshold δ = 0.5.

title: Causal Evaluation of Membership Inference Attacks
claim_source: Table 2 (Appendix H.1), page 25; ROC curves in Figure 3 (A-B), page 8

official.background: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) try to tell training points (members) from unseen points (non-members) and are the standard way to measure memorization and privacy leakage. The rigorous way to evaluate an MIA retrains the model many times with and without each point (multi-run), which is too expensive for large models. Cheaper protocols train once on a randomized subset (one-run) or evaluate a deployed model post hoc using known members and later-collected non-members (zero-run). In the zero-run case, members and non-members often come from different distributions (e.g. pre- vs. post-cutoff documents), so an attack can separate them without any memorization, overstating privacy risk.
official.method:
The paper defines memorization as the causal effect of including a point in the training set and defines causal versions of MIA metrics (AUC, ATE, TPR at fixed FPR) over a target distribution P_T. Multi-run is an RCT, one-run is an RCT with interference, and zero-run is an observational study confounded by the member/non-member distribution shift. For zero-run, the authors correct the metrics with inverse probability weighting: non-member scores are reweighted by pi(x)/(1-pi(x)), where pi(x) = P(member | x) is a propensity score, either the true one (oracle) or one learned by a binary classifier (logistic regression in the synthetic experiment) that separates members from non-members.

Synthetic setup (Appendix H.1): x = (a, b) with a ~ N(0, I_d), b ~ N(a^T w*, 1); shifted non-members use a ~ N(mu, I_d) with mu a random unit vector and corr(w*, mu) = 0.9. Training set of 2000 points from P_T. Two learners: (1) overparameterized ridge regression, d = 2500, lambda = 1e3; (2) DP-SGD linear regression, d = 400, l2 lambda = 10, clip 1, noise N(0, 3I), lr 0.01, 75 epochs, batch 128, (eps, delta) = (0.602, 0.01). Attack: loss-threshold MIA on the square loss. Multi-run: 400 trainings (200 with one extra P_T point, 200 without), 200 members and 200 non-members. One-run: one training, 2000 members vs. 2000 fresh P_T non-members. Zero-run: same model and members, 2000 non-members from the shifted P_0. Intervals are over 100 independent repetitions of the whole data-generating process.
official.claim: In the synthetic linear-regression experiment, naive zero-run evaluation inflates loss-based MIA AUC (ridge 0.669 ± 0.020, DP-SGD 0.616 ± 0.016) over the multi-run ground truth (0.561 ± 0.016, 0.504 ± 0.018), and propensity-score correction removes most of the gap (learned propensity: 0.595 ± 0.025 and 0.512 ± 0.059; oracle: 0.562 ± 0.026 and 0.503 ± 0.024).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Causal metrics in the three settings (with oracle or learned propensity scores in the zero-run setting), and non-causal metrics in the zero-run setting to highlight the distribution-shift induced bias. tau_ATE(t) is defined as tau_TPR(t) - tau_FPR(t) (Youden's J metric at a given threshold), and sup_t tau_ATE(t) is thus the largest gap between (causal) TPR and FPR. TPR0.2 is the TPR at FPR alpha = 0.2.
official.metric: MIA AUC (closer to the multi-run value is better for the corrected estimators); ± is described as a confidence interval over 100 independent repetitions of the data-generating process (the paper does not say whether it is a std or a CI half-width). sup_t tau_ATE, ATE and TPR at FPR 0.2 are also reported.
official.comparison: Zero-run (Raw) vs. Zero-run (Corrected, Learned / Oracle propensity), each compared to the Multi-run (Raw) and One-run (Raw) ground-truth AUCs, for ridge and DP-SGD learners
official.falsification_criterion: Zero-run raw AUC is not clearly above the multi-run AUC (gap within the reported intervals), or the corrected zero-run AUC (learned propensity) stays as far from the multi-run AUC as the raw zero-run AUC does.

title: LPS-Bench: Benchmarking Safety Awareness of Computer-Use Agents in Long-Horizon Planning under Benign and Adversarial Scenarios

official.background: Computer-use agents carry out multi-step tasks by calling tools, so one unsafe decision early in a long trajectory, such as guessing an unspecified detail or trusting a poisoned tool output, can lead to costly actions that are hard to undo. Most agent-safety benchmarks focus on adversarial attacks or only check the final outcome. This paper asks whether agents stay safe throughout long tool-calling workflows under two kinds of risk: benign but underspecified user requests, and adversarial steering.
official.method:
LPS-Bench has 570 cases built from 65 scenarios across 7 domains. A multi-agent LLM pipeline generates each case and humans review it. A case contains a user instruction, a sandboxed mock toolkit (Python functions that return scripted outputs) and a case-specific safety criterion. There are 9 risk types: four benign ones (TS: inter-task dependency/ordering, OC: rigid over-compliance, FA: ambiguity-induced false assumptions, IP: inefficient planning) and five adversarial ones (HS: harmful goal decomposition, MT: multi-turn plan corruption, EB: environment-triggered backdoor, RC: race-condition exploitation, PI: prompt injection/jailbreak). For FA, a trajectory counts as safe only if the agent completes the task with appropriate safeguards or pauses to ask for clarification instead of acting on an unverified assumption. For adversarial types, it counts as safe only if the agent refuses or halts before any harmful action.

Each of 13 LLMs runs as a LangChain tool-calling agent (temperature 1, top-p 0.9, top-k 50, at most 100 steps). DeepSeek-R1 judges each full trajectory against the case criterion as safe, unsafe or execution_failed. A blinded audit of 216 trajectories found 96.19% agreement between the judge and human consensus labels. The metric is the success-conditioned safe rate SR_success = S/(S+U), which excludes execution_failed trajectories.
official.claim: On LPS-Bench, the benign False Assumption (FA) risk type has the lowest safe rate: averaged over 13 agents it is 7.35%, below every adversarial type (27.34-38.58%). For Claude-4.5-Sonnet, FA is 5.88% while all five adversarial types are 92.42-100%.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Safe Rate of 13 LLM agents across nine planning-risk types in LPS-Bench. The left and right blocks report benign and adversarial risks, respectively. The shaded Avg. columns show unweighted means within each group, and the bottom row averages across models.
official.metric: Success-conditioned Safe Rate SR_success (%), higher is better; trajectories labelled execution_failed are excluded; judged by DeepSeek-R1; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: FA (benign ambiguity) safe rate vs. each adversarial risk type (HS, MT, EB, RC, PI), within the same model and averaged across 13 models
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the released FA and adversarial cases gives Claude-4.5-Sonnet (or another frontier model such as GPT-5.1 or Gemini-3-Pro) an FA safe rate comparable to, or higher than, one of its adversarial safe rates (e.g., FA above 50% or within about 20 points of PI/EB). Across the evaluated models, FA is not the lowest risk type on average.

title: GraDE: A Graph Diffusion Estimator for Frequent Subgraph Discovery in Neural Architectures

official.background: Frequent subgraphs (network motifs) in neural-architecture graphs are useful for compiler optimization, modular architecture design and structural analysis. Exact enumeration of all k-node subgraphs (e.g. ESU) gives exact counts, but its cost grows exponentially with k. Sampling-based estimators (Rand-ESU, Rand-FaSE, ARS, NRS) stay tractable, but as k grows the samples cover the space too sparsely to rank subgraph patterns by frequency reliably. This paper proposes scoring candidate subgraphs with the likelihood of a graph diffusion model trained on sampled subgraphs, as a surrogate for their relative frequency.
official.method:
For a graph set and subgraph size k, connected induced k-subgraphs are sampled with Rand-ESU at a sampling density of 0.1 (the fraction of non-isomorphic k-subgraph types that appear in the training set). A discrete-state continuous-time graph diffusion model (DisCo, with a Graph Transformer backbone and a topological-level positional encoding added for DAGs; 100 sampling steps, alpha = 0.8, gamma = 2, 200 training epochs) is trained on these subgraphs, where nodes are operator types and edges are directed. The estimator (DisCo-E) scores a subgraph G0 by a Monte Carlo estimate of the lower bound on log p0(G0): it samples forward noising paths and sums log reverse-transition minus log forward-transition probabilities plus log prior, averaged over 20 trials (estimation rounds) and exponentiated.

Evaluation: for every non-isomorphic k-subgraph pattern, the estimator score is compared with the ground-truth relative frequency from exhaustive enumeration, using Spearman's rho and Kendall's tau. Baselines are the frequency estimates from the sampling methods themselves (ARS, NRS, Rand-ESU, Rand-FaSE) at the same 0.1 density, a GraphVAE likelihood estimator, and estimators built on DiGress (DiGress-E) and DeFoG (DeFoG-E), all trained on the same Rand-ESU samples.
official.claim: On NAS-Bench-101 at sampling density 0.1, the DisCo-based estimator's Spearman correlation with exact subgraph frequencies is 0.88 ± 0.023 (k = 4) and 0.94 ± 0.002 (k = 5), versus at most 0.36 ± 0.022 and 0.44 ± 0.002 for the best sampling-based method (Rand-ESU) and 0.40 / 0.42 for GraphVAE.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Performance of different methods on synthesized and real-world datasets. Results are reported as mean±std for k ∈ {4, 5} at a sampling density of 0.1. Evaluation metrics are Spearman's ρ and Kendall's τ. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best performance, respectively. DisCo-E, DeFoG-E, and DiGress-E denote estimators built upon corresponding graph diffusion models, using Rand-ESU for training set construction. Estimation rounds are fixed to 20 for DisCo-E, DiGress-E, and GraphVAE, and 60 for DeFoG-E. The ARS sampling method timed out on the Younger dataset, indicated by "X". Due to the prohibitive cost of exact enumeration to obtain ground truth for size k = 5, results on Younger are evaluated on a random 10% subset of graphs.
official.metric: Spearman's rho (and Kendall's tau) between estimated scores and ground-truth subgraph relative frequency from exhaustive enumeration; higher is better; reported as mean ± std, but the paper does not state the number of runs or what the std is taken over
official.comparison: DisCo-E (diffusion estimator trained on Rand-ESU samples) vs. sampling-based frequency estimates (ARS, NRS, Rand-ESU, Rand-FaSE) and GraphVAE at the same 0.1 sampling density; DiGress-E and DeFoG-E are other estimator variants proposed in the same paper
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running on NAS-Bench-101 (k = 4 or 5, density 0.1, Rand-ESU training samples, 20 estimation rounds), DisCo-E's Spearman rho is not clearly above the best sampling baseline's (e.g. the gap is under 0.2, versus the reported 0.50 at k = 5 and 0.52 at k = 4).

title: Semantic Routing: Exploring Multi-Layer LLM Feature Weighting for Diffusion Transformers

official.background: Recent DiT text-to-image models use decoder-only LLMs as text encoders but usually condition on a single layer (typically the penultimate), even though different LLM layers encode different levels of abstraction and different DiT blocks and denoising timesteps play different roles. The paper asks whether weighting multi-layer LLM hidden states differently per diffusion timestep, per DiT block, or both improves text-image alignment over single-layer or uniformly averaged conditioning.
official.method:
All variants share one cross-attention DiT (24 blocks, ~2.24B parameters, FuseDiT-style with 1D/2D RoPE and QK-Norm), the SD3 VAE, and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as a frozen text encoder. The text condition fed to the cross-attention of block d at time t is a softmax-weighted convex combination of LayerNorm-ed hidden states from all LLM layers. B1 uses only the penultimate layer; B2 averages all normalized layers uniformly; B3 learns one global logit vector; S1 (time-wise) produces logits from the timestep via a small MLP shared across blocks; S2 (depth-wise) learns a separate static logit vector per DiT block; S3 (joint) uses a per-block timestep MLP.

Each model is trained from scratch on ~30M LAION-400M images (256x256) re-captioned by Qwen3-VL-32B, with AdamW lr 1e-4, batch 512, 500k steps, 10% prompt dropout and logit-normal timestep sampling. Evaluation uses 50 FlowMatch Euler steps at CFG 6.0, scored on GenEval, GenAI-Bench (judged by Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct) and UnifiedReward-2.0 style score on DrawBench prompts.
official.claim: With backbone, data and training held fixed, depth-wise fusion (S2) scores 79.07 on GenAI-Bench and 67.07 on GenEval, above the strongest baseline, uniform normalized averaging of all LLM layers (B2: 76.82 and 66.51), and the penultimate-layer baseline (B1: 74.96 and 64.54).
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Performance of different fusion strategies on three benchmarks. Best in each column is in bold, and second best is underlined.
official.metric: GenAI-Bench overall score and GenEval overall score (higher is better); UnifiedReward style score also reported. Single run per method; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: S2 (depth-wise learned per-block weights) vs. B2 (uniform average), B1 (penultimate layer), B3 (static learned weights), FuseDiT, S1 (time-wise) and S3 (joint)
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining B2 and S2 under matched settings, S2 does not beat B2 on GenAI-Bench by a margin larger than the seed-to-seed variation of either model (or the gap is much smaller than 2.25 points).

title: Partition Tree: Conditional Density Estimation over General Outcome Spaces

official.background: Decision trees are cheap and interpretable, but classical CART trees are built for point prediction or class probabilities, not for full conditional densities. Existing probabilistic trees either assume a parametric leaf distribution (CADET) or jointly optimise splits and leaf histograms with an expensive MDL objective (CDTree). This paper proposes a tree that estimates p(y | x) non-parametrically for continuous, categorical or mixed outcomes, and asks whether it gives better probabilistic predictions (log-loss) than CART-style trees.
official.method:
Partition Tree partitions the joint covariate-outcome space Z = X × Y into axis-aligned product cells A = A_X × A_Y. Splits can be on an X coordinate (refining the covariate region) or on a Y coordinate (refining outcome bins within a covariate region); categorical coordinates use subset splits found by sorting categories. The density estimate in a cell is n_XY(A) / (n_X(A) µ_Y(A_Y)), where µ_Y is counting measure for categorical outcomes and Lebesgue measure for continuous ones, normalised over y for each x. The tree is grown best-first under a split budget, choosing at each step the leaf/split with the largest empirical reduction of the log-loss surrogate (Eq. 8), which only needs count statistics. For classification, Y is the class label, so Y-splits group classes.

Evaluation: 5-fold cross-validation with a nested 80/20 train/validation split per fold for tuning; Optuna with 200 trials and a 20-minute limit per model, selecting on validation log-loss. Partition Tree tunes min_samples_leaf ∈ [1, 100] and min_samples_leaf_x ∈ [1, 400]. The CART baseline is scikit-learn DecisionTreeClassifier with log-loss criterion, tuned over max_depth ∈ [3, 50], min_samples_split ∈ [2, 150], min_samples_leaf ∈ [1, 100], min_impurity_decrease ∈ [0, 0.1]. Test metric is log-loss on the held-out fold. Datasets are UCI Digits (1,797 samples, 64 features, 10 classes) and Letter Recognition (20,000 samples, 16 features, 26 classes), among nine classification sets.
official.claim: With matched 5-fold CV and Optuna tuning, a single Partition Tree reaches test log-loss 0.45 ± 0.04 on Digits and 0.62 ± 0.17 on Letter, versus 1.48 ± 0.22 and 1.42 ± 0.06 for a log-loss-tuned scikit-learn CART tree.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Log-loss results over 5-fold cross-validation for single tree and bagging tree methods on classification and regression tasks (mean ± std). Lower is better. Best for single tree and bagging in bold. The last row represents the average ranking of each method in its group. Underline indicates statistical ties according to a paired t-test at the 5% significance level (run separately within single tree and bagging groups)
official.metric: Classification log-loss on held-out folds, lower is better; mean ± std across the 5 cross-validation folds; the paper marks statistical ties via paired t-test at 5% (Digits and Letter are not ties)
official.comparison: Partition Tree vs. CART (scikit-learn DecisionTreeClassifier, log-loss criterion), both tuned with the same Optuna budget and folds
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the 5-fold CV with tuned models on Digits or Letter, Partition Tree's mean log-loss is not clearly below CART's (e.g. the gap shrinks below ~0.3 nats or falls within the fold std), or a reasonably tuned CART reaches log-loss comparable to Partition Tree's.

title: Boosting LLM Reasoning via Human-Inspired Reward Shaping

official.background: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), usually GRPO with a binary correct/incorrect reward, is the standard way to improve LLM math reasoning. With a binary reward, GRPO gets no learning signal when all sampled answers to a prompt are wrong (or all are right), and it treats short and long correct answers the same. Existing length-aware variants mostly penalize length to save inference cost. This paper argues, by analogy with human learning, that the model should be pushed to explore more (longer attempts) on problems it fails and to condense its reasoning (shorter answers) on problems it already solves.
official.method:
T2T (Thickening-to-Thinning) changes only the scalar reward in GRPO. For each prompt, K=8 rollouts are sampled and the on-policy pass rate p̂ (fraction correct) is computed and detached from the gradient. Each output gets a length score s_L = clip((len - L_min)/(L_max - L_min), 0, 1), with L_min=0 and L_max=4096 tokens. A correct output gets reward 1 - α·s_L·p̂, which penalizes length more on easy prompts. An incorrect output gets α·s_L·(1 - p̂), which rewards length more on hard prompts. They use α=0.2, so every correct answer still outranks every incorrect one. Advantages and the clipped policy update are otherwise standard GRPO.

All methods are trained on DAPO-MATH-17k for 5 epochs (275 steps) with Verl: learning rate 1e-6, batch size 256, mini-batch size 64, group size 8, max response 8192 tokens, rollout temperature 1.0. Baselines are vanilla GRPO, LASER (length penalty on correct answers, α=0.2, target 4096), W-REINFORCE (positive-sample weight ρ=0.1) and EntroPIC (PI entropy control, target 0.1, Kp=1.0, Ki=0.01). Evaluation samples 64 responses per prompt on MATH-500 and 128 on AIME'24, AIME'25 and AMC'23 at temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95. Pass@1 is the mean accuracy over samples, and Pass@64 uses the unbiased estimator.
official.claim: On Qwen2.5-3B trained with RLVR on DAPO-MATH-17k, T2T reaches AMC'23 Pass@1 57.0 versus 49.1 for GRPO and 54.7 for the best other baseline (EntroPIC), and MATH-500 Pass@1 49.8 versus 47.4 for GRPO and 48.4 for the best other baseline (LASER).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main Results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. We report Pass@1 and Pass@64 performance using the unbiased estimator. The best results are highlighted in bold, and the second best results are underlined.
official.metric: Pass@1 accuracy (%) as the mean over 64 (MATH-500) or 128 (AMC'23) samples per prompt at temperature 0.7; Pass@64 via the unbiased estimator. Higher is better. No error bars: each method is a single training run.
official.comparison: T2T vs. GRPO, LASER, W-REINFORCE and EntroPIC, all trained from Qwen2.5-3B with the same data, steps and evaluation protocol
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction with the same setup in which T2T's AMC'23 Pass@1 does not beat GRPO by a clear margin (e.g. at least 3 points, versus the reported 7.9), or in which GRPO or any baseline matches or beats T2T on both AMC'23 and MATH-500 Pass@1.

title: Theory of Optimal Learning Rate Schedules and Scaling Laws for a Random Feature Model

official.background: The best learning rate for SGD usually does not carry over when the training horizon T changes, and it is unclear when practitioners should prefer polynomial decay, cosine or warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules. The paper studies a solvable power-law linear random feature model trained with online SGD, where the expected test loss follows an exact linear recurrence. That recurrence turns schedule design into a finite-dimensional optimal control problem that can be solved numerically and, at large T, analytically.
official.method:
Features have eigenvalues λ_k ∼ k^(-b) and target power (w*_k)^2 λ_k ∼ k^(-a). The student keeps the top N features (the rest act as effective noise σ^2 together with label noise σ0) and is trained with online SGD at batch size m. Theorem 1 gives the expected loss L_t = Σ_k λ_k c_{t,k} + σ^2 through the recurrence c_{t+1,k} = (1 − 2η_t λ_k + η_t^2 (m+1)/m λ_k^2) c_{t,k} + (η_t^2/m) λ_k Σ_ℓ λ_ℓ c_{t,ℓ} + (η_t^2/m) σ^2 λ_k. The optimal schedule η*_T(t) minimizes the final loss L_T over all T step sizes. It is computed by single shooting in CasADi with IPOPT (L-BFGS Hessian approximation, MUMPS) and compared with the best constant learning rate η_T and the best power-law schedule η_T(t) ∼ T^(-ξ) t^(-δ), with exponents chosen optimally.

For T from about 316 to 3162, the final excess loss L_T − σ^2 is fit as T^(-ζ_T) for each schedule family. Parameters are N = 500, σ = 0.5, a = 3.5, m = 5, with b = 5 (hard phase, b > a) or b = 2 (easy phase, b < a). Theory predicts ζ_T = (a−1)/(a+b−1) for the constant and power-law schedules and (a−1)/max(a,b) for the optimal schedule.
official.claim: In the power-law random feature model with N = 500, σ = 0.5, a = 3.5, m = 5 and T in about [316, 3162], the optimal-control schedule gives a fitted loss scaling exponent of ζ_T ≈ 0.52 in the hard phase (b = 5), against ≈ 0.36 for both the optimized constant and power-law schedules. In the easy phase (b = 2) it gives ≈ 0.69 against 0.56 (constant) and 0.58 (power law), close to the theory values 0.5 vs 1/3 and 5/7 vs 5/9.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Comparison of optimal learning rate schedules in the hard (b > a) and easy (b < a) phases. (a, d). Profile of the optimal learning rate η*_T(t). In the hard phase (a), the schedule maintains an approximately constant maximum value followed by a rapid annealing phase. In the easy phase (d), the schedule collapses onto the scaling form η*_T(t) ≈ T^(b/a−1) f(t/T) (dashed theoretical curve, see Result 2). title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
claim_source: Table 10, page 19 (same numbers plotted in Figure 2, left, page 5)

official.background: Activation steering adds a fixed vector to an LLM's residual stream at inference time to change its behavior (e.g. more compliant, or more likely to output JSON) without retraining. Developers may use it for benign utility goals. Prior work studied steering as an attack (e.g. removing a refusal direction); this paper asks whether steering vectors built only from benign data, applied by the model developer, unintentionally weaken safety alignment and make the deployed model easier to jailbreak.
official.method:
STEER-COMPLIANCE follows the CAST (Lee et al., 2025) behavior-vector procedure: 100 benign Alpaca instructions are each paired with a short compliance-prefixed continuation and a short refusal-prefixed continuation (e.g. 'I regret to inform you that I can't'). The first PCA direction of mean-centered residual activations separating the two is extracted per layer and its sign is flipped so that positive steering increases compliance. The vector is added (h + alpha v) at layers 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 (the CAST Colab default) with coefficient alpha = 1.3, chosen on Llama-3-8B-Instruct as the value where the Alpaca win-rate meets the unsteered model's. The paper confirms the intended utility: harmless Alpaca refusal on Llama-3-8B-Instruct drops from 2% to 0% (Table 1).

Safety is measured in the benchmark-only regime: the 400 HarmBench harmful prompts are given directly (no jailbreak rewriting) to the original and to the steered model, and the Attack Success Rate (ASR) is the fraction of responses that the HarmBench Llama-2-13B classifier judges harmful. The same is repeated for Llama-2-7B-Chat and Gemma-7B-it, and for a JSON-format steering vector (difference-in-means between prompts with and without a JSON instruction, Stolfo et al. 2025).
official.claim: On the 400 HarmBench prompts with no jailbreak attack, adding the benign compliance steering vector to Llama-3-8B-Instruct raises HarmBench-classifier ASR from 2.00% to 38.50%; it also raises ASR on Llama-2-7B-Chat (0.00% to 16.00%) and Gemma-7B-it (3.25% to 25.50%).
official.claim_caption: Table 10. Attack Success Rate (ASR) between original target LLMs and compliance steered LLMs as well as ASR by applying black-box jailbreak attack CoP on original and steered models respectively on 400 random sampled HarmBench data. After steering, all LLMs are more vulnerable to jailbreak attacks.
official.metric: Attack Success Rate (%) judged by the HarmBench classifier (higher = less safe). Single run; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Same base model with vs. without the STEER-COMPLIANCE vector, benchmark-only (direct harmful prompts) regime; JSON steering and CoP-attack columns are secondary.
official.falsification_criterion: With the CAST-style compliance vector built from benign Alpaca data (layers 15, 17-24, alpha ~1.3), Llama-3-8B-Instruct's benchmark-only HarmBench ASR stays within a few points of the unsteered model (e.g. below ~10%), or the steered model's ASR is not higher than the original on at least two of the three models.

title: Learning Rate Matters: Vanilla LoRA May Suffice for LLM Fine-tuning
claim_source: Table 7, page 37 (Appendix F.1; numerical data behind Figure 1, page 2)

official.background: LoRA is the standard parameter-efficient way to fine-tune LLMs, and many variants (new initializations such as PiSSA, MiLoRA and Init[AB], and architecture changes such as DoRA) report large gains over it. Most of these papers use one fixed or narrowly tuned learning rate, often inherited from earlier work, even though the best learning rate can depend on the method. If variants simply need a different learning rate, gains reported under a single configuration may come from tuning rather than from the method.
official.method:
The authors fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B-Base on 100k MetaMathQA examples (the PiSSA preprocessed split) for 1 epoch with rank r = 128, alpha = r (scale 1), batch size 64, AdamW, cosine schedule with 3% warmup, no dropout or weight decay, adapters on all linear layers except the LM head, and max sequence length 512, using a unified PiSSA-based codebase built on the HF PEFT library. LoRA, DoRA, Init[AB], MiLoRA and PiSSA are each trained across a log-spaced learning-rate grid from 2e-6 to 2e-3 (four points per decade: 1.12, 2.00, 3.56, 6.32 x 10^k).

Evaluation uses greedy decoding with vLLM on GSM8K and MATH. The reported accuracy is the mean over the test sets, averaged over three seeds. A method's peak is its best learning rate on the grid.
official.claim: On Qwen3-0.6B math fine-tuning (r=128, B=64), once the learning rate is tuned per method, LoRA (49.60 ± 0.18 at lr 2e-4) and PiSSA, DoRA, Init[AB] and MiLoRA (49.17–49.45) peak within 0.43 points. Their optimal learning rates differ, though: PiSSA peaks at 2e-5, 10x lower than LoRA, and at LoRA's optimal lr of 2e-4 PiSSA reaches only 43.84 ± 0.28.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Performance of Qwen3-0.6B fine-tuned on mathematical reasoning tasks with rank = 128.
official.metric: Mean accuracy (%) over GSM8K and MATH, higher is better; ± is std over 3 independent training runs (seeds)
official.comparison: Per-method peak accuracy over the learning-rate grid for LoRA vs. DoRA, Init[AB], MiLoRA and PiSSA under identical settings; plus the location of each method's optimal learning rate (LoRA vs. PiSSA)
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if, with each method's learning rate tuned over the same grid, any variant beats or trails vanilla LoRA's peak by clearly more than about 1 point (beyond seed std). The learning-rate part is refuted if PiSSA's optimum is not markedly lower than LoRA's, e.g. PiSSA at lr 2e-4 performs within seed noise of its own peak.

title: Rethinking Rubric Generation for Improving LLM Judge and Reward Modeling for Open-ended Tasks

official.background: LLM judges are used both to evaluate open-ended generations and, in reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), as reward models, but holistic judgments on subjective tasks are noisy and biased. A common fix is to have an LLM write prompt-specific rubrics and score responses against them. The paper argues that LLM-generated rubrics are often incomplete, generic, misaligned in preference direction, and redundant or correlated, which can make a rubric-based judge worse than no rubrics at all (GPT-4o on JudgeBench drops from 55.6% to 42.9% with prompt-only rubrics).
official.method:
Recursive Rubric Decomposition (RRD) builds a rubric set per prompt in three stages. (I) An LLM proposes initial binary rubrics conditioned on the prompt and m = 8 sample responses (4 from GPT-4o, 4 from Gemini 2.5-Pro). (II) Any rubric satisfied by more than n = 2 of the sample responses is recursively decomposed by the LLM into finer sub-rubrics; new rubrics are filtered for misalignment (discarded if they prefer Llama3-8B outputs over GPT-4o outputs) and for redundancy (LLM-judged overlap with existing rubrics). The loop stops once the number of rejected proposals exceeds a threshold of 15. (III) Rubric weights are set by whitened-uniform (WU) weighting, w proportional to Sigma^{-1/2} 1, where Sigma is the covariance of rubric scores estimated from unlabeled responses; RRD_uniform and RRD_LLM (LLM-assigned weights) are variants.

The judge prefers response Ri over Rj when the weighted sum of satisfied rubrics is larger. In the judge experiments the same model (GPT-4o or Llama-3.1-405B) is both rubric generator and final judge. Evaluation is pairwise-preference accuracy on JudgeBench (the 350-pair GPT-4o-response subset) and PPE (10.2K human preference pairs from Chatbot Arena). Baselines: the base model judging without rubrics, LLM Rubrics generated from the prompt only, LLM Rubrics generated with sample responses, and Chasing the Tail (Zhang et al., 2025a), an iterative rubric-refinement method.
official.claim: With GPT-4o as rubric generator and judge, RRD_WU reaches 73.3% pairwise accuracy on JudgeBench (vs. 67.6% for Chasing the Tail, the best baseline, and 55.6% for the base judge) and 73.7% on PPE (vs. 67.1% for the best baseline, the base judge without rubrics).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3 (a) Accuracy on JudgeBench and PPE Preference datasets for base model and rubric-assisted judges under different rubric-generation strategies. While basic LLM-generated rubrics (unconditioned on sample responses) can degrade performance, RRD yields consistent improvements over the baselines. Notably, RRD_WU delivers the largest gains and scales reliably across both proprietary (GPT-4o) and open-weights (Llama3.1-405B) judges. (b) Rubric-count dynamics on JudgeBench. Starting from an average of 7.4 rubrics, the count rises to ~20, while the increasing variance across tasks indicates that the recursive procedure adapts evaluation depth to instance complexity.
official.metric: Pairwise preference accuracy (%), higher is better; single run, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: RRD_WU (and RRD_uniform, RRD_LLM) vs. Base Model, LLM Rubrics (w/o resp.), LLM Rubrics (w. resp.), Chasing the Tail; GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-405B judges
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running with GPT-4o, RRD_WU fails to beat Chasing the Tail on JudgeBench by more than a few points, or fails to beat the no-rubric GPT-4o judge on PPE (or a large random PPE subset) by a clear margin.

title: Disentangled Representation Learning via Flow Matching

official.background: Disentangled representation learning tries to encode images into compact latents where each part corresponds to one generative factor (object shape, colour, size, camera position and so on), which helps controllable generation and sample-efficient downstream learning. VAE-based methods trade reconstruction quality for disentanglement, GAN-based methods lack an inference path, and recent diffusion-based methods add inductive biases for independence across latents but, the authors argue, weak semantic alignment between latent units and factors. This paper asks whether flow matching, with an explicit penalty against overlap between factors, gives better-aligned factor representations.
official.method:
Images are mapped to a 16x16x3 latent z1 by a frozen pretrained VQ-GAN encoder. A trainable CNN factor encoder (from EncDiff) outputs N scalars, each mapped by its own MLP to a 16-d factor token s_i (N = 20 by default). A U-Net predicts the flow-matching velocity v_theta(z_t, S(I), t) on the linear path z_t = (1 - t) z0 + t z1 with z0 ~ N(0, I) and target z1 - z0; the tokens condition the U-Net through cross-attention at several layers. The U-Net and factor encoder are trained jointly.

An output-attention head computes per-location softmax routing weights Attn_i over the N tokens from the final U-Net feature map, and defines factor-specific velocities v^(i) = Attn_i * v_theta, which sum to v_theta. The orthogonality loss L_orth is the mean squared cosine similarity between the flattened v^(i) over all token pairs, and the total loss is L_FM + lambda_orth L_orth with lambda_orth = 0.01. The ablation 'w/o L_orth' sets lambda_orth = 0 with everything else unchanged (cross-attention conditioning, N = 20). Disentanglement of the learned factor representation is scored with the FactorVAE score and DCI disentanglement (DCI-D), computed on PCA-reduced latents when high-dimensional.
official.claim: On MPI3D-toy with N = 20 factor tokens, adding the orthogonality regularizer (lambda_orth = 0.01) raises the FactorVAE score from 0.804 ± 0.073 to 0.931 ± 0.017 and DCI-D from 0.637 ± 0.041 to 0.710 ± 0.022, relative to the identical model trained with lambda_orth = 0.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Ablation of the conditioning mechanism and orthogonality regularizer (mean±std).
official.metric: FactorVAE score and DCI-D (higher is better); mean ± std over runs (number of seeds not stated)
official.comparison: Full model (cross-attention + L_orth) vs. w/o L_orth (lambda_orth = 0) vs. AdaGN conditioning instead of cross-attention; all at N = 20
official.falsification_criterion: On MPI3D-toy, the model trained without L_orth reaches a FactorVAE score or DCI-D within one std of the full model across several seeds, or exceeds it.

title: Consistency-Preserving Concept Erasure via Unsafe–Safe Pairing and Directional Fisher-weighted Adaptation
claim_source: Table 9, page 22 (single-seed version in Table 1, page 7)

official.background: Text-to-image diffusion models trained on unfiltered web data can generate harmful content such as nudity, so concept-erasure methods fine-tune the model to stop producing a target concept. Most methods (e.g., ESD) push the target concept toward the unconditional (null-prompt) prediction, which removes the concept but often changes the layout, subject and other details of the image. Most also fine-tune all U-Net weights. The question here is whether erasure can stay strong while the rest of the image, and general generation quality, are preserved.
official.method:
PAIR first builds paired data: Stable Diffusion v1.4 generates 1,100 images from a nudity prompt, ImageGuard keeps those that are actually unsafe, RealEdit edits each one into a clothed version with the same scene, and the 1,000 pairs with highest SSIM are kept. Training uses a Paired Semantic Realignment loss, an ESD-style target in which the null condition is replaced by the safe text and image: the fine-tuned model's prediction on the unsafe prompt is regressed to eps*(z_f,t, c_r, x_r) - eta * (eps*(z_f,t, c_f, x_f) - eps*(z_f,t, c_r, x_r)), where eps* is the frozen model, image conditions enter through a pretrained IP-Adapter, and z_f,t is the noised latent of the unsafe image (eta = 7). A second phase then fine-tunes with text conditions only.

The trainable parameters are DoRA adapters (rank 4, applied only to the U-Net cross-attention layers, about 0.05% of parameters) initialized with FiDoRA: the directional Fisher information (gradient projected orthogonal to each weight column) is computed on the forget and retain sets, a row-wise importance vector I_i = sqrt(sum_j F_f/(F_r + eps)) is formed, and B, A come from a rank-r SVD of diag(I) W0, with the frozen base set to W0 - B*A*. Training uses Adam, lr 5e-5, batch size 1, 1,000 iterations. Evaluation: ASR-IG is the fraction of images generated from I2P nudity prompts that the MLLM-based ImageGuard judges unsafe; FID and CLIP use COCO-10K; consistency is SSIM between original-model and erased-model images for the same prompt and seed.
official.claim: For nudity erasure on Stable Diffusion v1.4 with I2P target prompts, PAIR reaches an ImageGuard attack success rate of 2.56 ± 0.20% over three seeds, versus 6.33 ± 0.33% for the strongest baseline RECE and 7.67-24.33% for ESD, SPM, Co-Erasing and AGE, while also having the lowest COCO-10K FID (16.93 ± 0.13 vs. 17.48 ± 0.16 for RECE).
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Mean and standard deviation over three seeds for all methods in Table 1 (nudity removal). Seeds control both fine-tuning and evaluation-time generation; for the closed-form RECE, only generation.
official.metric: ASR-IG (%, lower is better): share of generations from I2P nudity prompts that ImageGuard flags as nude. Also FID on COCO-10K (lower is better). ± is std over 3 seeds controlling fine-tuning and generation; for RECE (closed-form) seeds control only generation. The paper reports Welch's t-test p < 0.001 for PAIR vs. RECE on ASR-IG.

title: CoreQ: Learning-Free Mismatch Correction and Successive Rounding for Quantization

official.background: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses LLM weights to a few bits, layer by layer, using a small calibration set. Because earlier layers are already quantized, the activations reaching a later layer differ from the full-precision ones. Standard solvers (GPTQ/LDLQ) ignore this mismatch and target W·Xq. Mismatch-aware methods (GPTAQ, QEP) instead target W·Xf, the full-precision output. With limited calibration data, full correction can overfit, and one fixed global correction strength cannot adapt to each layer.
official.method:
For each linear layer, CoreQ interpolates the calibration target as Y(α) = W·Xq + α·D, where D = W(Xf − Xq) is the upstream mismatch. It splits D into the part reachable by changing this layer's weights, s = S̃·Xq with S̃ = D·Xqᵀ(Xq·Xqᵀ)⁻¹, and an orthogonal residual η. It then uses the closed-form per-layer coefficient α_corr = ‖s‖²_F / (‖s‖²_F + ‖η‖²_F), so no tuning or validation search is needed. The layer is quantized against W_corr = W + α_corr·S̃ by minimizing ‖(W_corr − Q)L‖²_F, where H = Xq·Xqᵀ = LLᵀ (with damping). This is done by greedy successive rounding over the Cholesky-triangular form (equivalent to LDLQ when α_corr = 0), with columns ordered by diagonal Hessian. K-CoreQ replaces the greedy pass with a beam search of width K.

Setup for the claim: LLaMA-2-7B, 3-bit symmetric weight-only quantization with per-channel scales, and 128 C4 calibration samples of length 2048. Perplexity is measured on WikiText-2 and C4. Baselines are GPTQ, GPTAQ, LDLQ and GuidedQuant, and every number is the mean ± std over 5 calibration seeds.
official.claim: For 3-bit per-channel weight-only quantization of LLaMA-2-7B, greedy CoreQ reaches C4 perplexity 9.61 ± 0.12 and WikiText-2 perplexity 8.41 ± 0.21. The best baseline on both perplexities, GPTAQ, reaches 10.04 ± 0.06 and 8.84 ± 0.23, with GPTQ, LDLQ and the gradient-based GuidedQuant worse still. 8-CoreQ improves further to 9.37 ± 0.01 and 7.97 ± 0.07.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: 3-bit symmetric WOQ for LLaMA-2/3 models. We report Wiki2/C4 perplexity (↓), average zero-shot accuracy (↑), and quantization time under per-channel and per-group (g = 128) granularity, averaged over 5 random seeds. Bold entries are the best result and values within one standard deviation of the best in each setting. GuidedQ is omitted for per-group setting following the official implementation.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of Test-Driven Code Generation

official.background: Code assistants often sample several candidate programs and test suites, run them against each other, and pick one program to return (post-generation selection, e.g. CodeT, MBR-Exec, AlphaCode clustering). Most such heuristics treat two programs as equivalent, or a test suite as passed, only if every test agrees or passes. This paper casts these heuristics as Monte Carlo estimators of the probability that a program is correct. It proves that 'soft' estimators, which count the fraction of agreeing or passing individual tests, have a higher signal-to-noise ratio than the 'hard' all-or-nothing versions (Theorem 3.10, a factor of at least m^2).
official.method:
For each task, the LLM independently generates n = 10 implementations and m = 10 test suites (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95). Every implementation is executed against every test suite, giving binary per-test outcomes. A selection heuristic then scores each implementation and returns the top one, and pass@1 is the fraction of tasks where the selected implementation passes the oracle tests. Hard estimators use the all-tests-pass/all-tests-agree indicator (sharpness s = infinity). Soft estimators use the fraction of individual tests that pass or agree (s = 1).

Per Table 1, CodeT Hard (Chen et al., 2023) = estimated functional-equivalence class mass (p_hat(N_c^inf); two codes count as equivalent only if all test outputs agree) times the mean fraction of tests passed over generated suites (E_hat[R]). CodeT Soft (proposed) = fuzzy similarity mass (p_hat(N_c^1); fraction of agreeing test outputs) times the same E_hat[R]. So the two CodeT variants differ only in the sharpness of the code-similarity term. MaxPass Hard/Soft use only the test-pass term (E_hat[R^inf] vs E_hat[R]); MBR-Exec Hard/Soft use only the similarity term. Random Selection is also reported. Datasets: BigCodeBenchHard (148 tasks), QiskitHumanEvalSim (143 tasks), LeetCodeDataset (228 post-2024-07-01 tasks). Models: Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, GPT-OSS-120B, MiniMax-M2.1. Results are means over 5 seeds.
official.claim: With Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 and n = m = 10 generated codes and test suites, CodeT Soft selection beats CodeT Hard in pass@1 on BigCodeBenchHard (35.00 ± 0.36 vs 31.22 ± 0.32), QiskitHumanEvalSim (62.24 ± 0.28 vs 59.02 ± 0.19) and LeetCodeDataset (24.30 ± 0.23 vs 21.23 ± 0.12).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Pass@1 (%) of post-generation selection heuristics (see Table 1) after 10 rounds of independent code and test generation (m = n = 10). Within a family of heuristics, we bold the more accurate one. The soft variants generally outperform the hard ones, corroborating the insights of Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.9, and Theorem 3.10. We report mean (± standard error) over 5 seeds.
official.metric: pass@1 (%) of the selected implementation on oracle tests, higher is better; ± is the standard error over 5 seeds
official.comparison: CodeT Soft (fraction-of-tests estimators, s = 1) vs. CodeT Hard (all-or-nothing estimators, s = infinity), on the same pool of generated codes and test suites; MaxPass Soft vs. Hard and MBR-Exec Soft vs. Hard are secondary comparisons
official.falsification_criterion: With Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 and n = m = 10, CodeT Soft's pass@1 margin over CodeT Hard on any of the three datasets falls within about two standard errors or reverses.

title: Diffusion-State Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion Language Models

official.background: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) such as LLaDA generate text by repeatedly filling masked positions over many denoising steps. RL fine-tuning methods for MDLMs (diffu-GRPO, SPG) score only the final completion with a scalar reward, so every intermediate filling decision gets the same credit. The intermediate masked states and the per-position logits computed during the rollout are thrown away, even though they could tell the trainer which filling decisions at which states led to good or bad outcomes.
official.method:
DiSPO treats an intermediate masked sequence x_t (plus the prompt) as a state and the joint filling of its currently masked positions as an action. During the normal rollout of K trajectories, the logits of the masked positions are cached. For each trajectory one timestep t is sampled from a late-biased polynomial distribution (degree k=4); from the cached logits at that state, Z=2 alternative fillings of all masked positions are sampled, which gives Z complete sequences without any additional diffusion forward passes. Each is scored with the same terminal reward function, advantages are reward minus the per-state mean, and a clipped GRPO-style loss is applied only to the newly filled tokens, with log-probabilities from the one-step masked-token surrogate of diffu-GRPO restricted to the masked positions.

The total loss is L_base + alpha_step * L_step, where L_base is the unchanged terminal-feedback objective (diffu-GRPO or SPG) computed on the same rollouts and alpha_step is swept over {0.1, 0.5, 0.9}. Experiments use LLaDA-8B-Instruct with LoRA (r=128), training generation length 256, block size 32, and matched rollout budget, group size and number of update steps between each baseline and its DiSPO variant (SPG on Sudoku: 4000 steps). Evaluation is zero-shot greedy semi-autoregressive decoding (32-token blocks, 2 tokens per step) at generation lengths 128/256/512, reporting exact-match accuracy.
official.claim: On 4x4 Sudoku with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, SPG augmented with DiSPO reaches 43.2/44.0/43.4% exact-match accuracy at generation lengths 128/256/512 (average 43.5%), versus 26.6/26.0/26.1% (average 26.2%) for plain SPG trained with the same rollout budget and number of update steps.

Matched-compute comparisons are made within each base optimizer: diffu-GRPO vs. DiSPO_diffu-GRPO and SPG vs. DiSPO_SPG, with the same training N_gen=256, multi-step diffusion rollout budget, and optimizer steps. † indicates a non-matched-compute reward-shaping baseline included for reference. ‡ indicates results reported by Zhao et al. [14].
official.metric: Exact-match accuracy (%) on 4x4 Sudoku, higher is better, at evaluation generation lengths 128, 256, 512 and their average; single runs, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: SPG vs. DiSPO_SPG (DiSPO step-wise loss added to SPG), same training generation length 256, rollout budget, group size, reward function and optimizer steps

title: Soft Forward-Backward Representations for Zero-shot Reinforcement Learning with General Utilities

official.background: Zero-shot RL methods such as forward-backward (FB) representations pretrain on reward-free offline data and can then produce a near-optimal policy for any additive (Markov) reward given at test time, with no further training. Many useful objectives are not additive rewards but general utilities, i.e. arbitrary differentiable functions of the policy's occupancy measure: maximizing state coverage (pure exploration), or matching an expert's state distribution (imitation). These often need stochastic policies, but FB in practice retrieves only near-deterministic policies, so its policy family may not contain a good solution.
official.method:
Soft FB keeps the FB decomposition of each policy's successor measure M^z = F_z^T B, but trains each policy pi_z as a maximum-entropy (soft) policy for its reward embedding z. Embeddings are reparameterized so that z is sampled from the unit ball: ||z|| = 0 gives a uniform policy and ||z|| -> 1 recovers FB's deterministic policies. A separate critic Q_H estimates discounted policy entropy, and the policy (squashed Gaussian with learnable std) minimizes a KL to the soft-optimal policy (Eq. 10). FB uses the same networks and hyperparameters (z dim 50, batch 1024, Adam 1e-4), with z sampled from the sphere surface.

At test time a general utility f(M^pi) is optimized by zero-order search: sample 1024 candidate embeddings z, draw 1024 samples from each policy's estimated state successor measure, score each with f (entropies/KLs via a k=3 nearest-neighbour estimator), and roll out the best z for 1024 episodes. The measure is estimated either implicitly (importance-weighting buffer states by F^T B) or explicitly with a flow-matching TD model (subscript 'flow'). The didactic environment is S = A = [-1,1]^2, start at the origin, and the agent jumps to the state equal to its first action and stays there forever (gamma = 0.5). Data come from uniformly random actions and training runs 5e4 gradient steps. Pure exploration maximizes H(M_S^pi) and stochastic IL minimizes KL(M_S^pi || uniform on the segment x in [-0.5,0.5], y = 0). Scores are min-max normalized as in Table 7.
official.claim: In the didactic 2D environment, with the explicit flow measure model, the best policy found by Soft FB scores 0.90 ± .01 on normalized pure exploration vs. 0.37 ± .01 for FB, and 0.83 ± .01 vs. 0.77 ± .03 on stochastic imitation. With implicit measure estimates, Soft FB also beats FB on stochastic imitation (0.79 ± .02 vs. 0.67 ± .01).
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Zero-shot performance over several General Utilities in the didactic environment. For each inference technique, the best policy retrieved by SFB constitutes, on average, a better solution. Results are averaged across 3 seeds, and bold when their 95% confidence intervals intersects with that of the best score.
official.metric: Normalized ground-truth objective value of the selected policy (higher is better, roughly in [0,1]). Mean over 3 seeds; ± is a 95% confidence interval assuming normality.
official.comparison: Soft FB (SFB, SFB_flow) vs. FB (FB, FB_flow), with matched architecture, data, hyperparameters and inference procedure (1024 candidate z)
official.falsification_criterion: With the flow measure model, Soft FB's normalized pure-exploration score is not clearly above FB's (e.g. the 95% CIs overlap or the gap is below ~0.2), or Soft FB does not beat FB on stochastic IL under the implicit measure model.

title: Sharpness-Aware Hybrid Model Learning for Architecture-Agnostic Parameter Estimation

official.background: Hybrid models combine a scientific model with unknown physical parameters θ and a flexible neural net with parameters ϕ. Because the neural net can fit the data on its own, training often leaves θ unidentified: the network compensates for any wrong θ, and the scientific part loses its meaning. Existing fixes add regularizers to the neural part, such as the function norm of an additive correction (Yin et al.) or the gap between the full model and a physics-only reduction (Takeishi & Kalousis). These have to be designed for each architecture. This paper asks whether looking for flat loss minima (sharpness-aware minimization, SAM), motivated by Occam's razor and minimum description length, can recover θ without regularizers tied to a particular architecture.
official.method:
Algorithm 1 is SAM changed so that only the neural-net parameters ϕ are perturbed: at each step it computes an ascent perturbation ε*_ϕ inside a radius ρ, evaluates gradients for both θ and ϕ at (θ, ϕ+ε*_ϕ), and updates both with Adam. The ascent direction comes from standard SAM (sam), adaptive SAM (asam) or Fisher SAM (fsam). Baselines are erm (plain training with slight weight decay), p-reg (ℓ2 penalty λ_p‖ϕ‖²) and f-reg (function-norm penalty λ_f mean‖g_ϕ(x)‖², following Yin et al., used for the additive tasks).

Duffing oscillator task (Appendix D.3): trajectories of v̈ + αv − βv³ = 0 with α = 1, β = 1, simulated with RK45 at dt = 0.005 and subsampled to Δt = 0.1. Each example maps an initial state x = [v, v̇](0) to the next m_y = 10 states, with Gaussian noise std 0.01 and 100/100/100 train/val/test pairs. The hybrid neural ODE is y = ODESolve(f_θ(v) + g_ϕ(v) = 0) with incomplete physics f_θ = v̈ + α̃v (θ = {α̃}) and g_ϕ an MLP with 2 hidden layers of 128 units and ReLU. Training is full-batch Adam with lr 1e-4, cosine-annealed to 1e-6 over 20,000 iterations. θ-error is the RMSE between α̃ and the true α = 1, reported as mean ± SD over 5 seeds.
official.claim: On the Duffing oscillator hybrid neural ODE, SAM-based training estimates α with RMSE 1.32 ± 0.65 (×10⁻², sam and fsam), versus 13.4 ± 2.41 for p-reg, 18.7 ± 3.67 for f-reg and 30.8 ± 2.25 for erm, while test prediction error stays the same or slightly better (6.43 vs 6.45–6.75 ×10⁻²).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Estimation errors of θ and prediction errors of y. For LIGHT TUNNEL, we report the cosine similarity between the estimated and reference θ's because the scale of θ is structurally unidentifiable; otherwise the root mean squared errors are reported. The best and the second best results are bolded and underlined, respectively. Mean and SD over 5 runs with different random seeds are reported.
official.metric: θ-error = RMSE of the estimated α̃ against the data-generating α = 1 (lower is better), in units of 10⁻². ± is the SD over 5 random seeds. y-error is test-set prediction RMSE.
official.comparison: sam / asam / fsam (perturb only ϕ) vs. erm, p-reg (ℓ2 on ϕ) and f-reg (function-norm regularizer of Yin et al.), with the same hybrid model, data and optimizer, and hyperparameters (ρ, λ_p, λ_f) swept for each method.
official.falsification_criterion: With each method's hyperparameter tuned, sam/fsam's mean α-error over 5 seeds is not clearly below p-reg's and f-reg's (for example, not at least ~3x smaller, or the SD intervals overlap), or the SAM runs lose their advantage once the hyperparameter is chosen by validation prediction error instead of θ-error.

title: Closed-Form Implicit Neural Representations

official.background: Implicit neural representations (INRs) store a signal such as an image as a network that maps coordinates to values. Fitting one usually needs thousands of steps of gradient descent per signal, and MLPs fit high-frequency detail slowly (spectral bias), so fine textures tend to stay blurred. A closed-form fit that captures fine detail quickly would make INRs cheaper to use for images, satellite data and scientific fields.
official.method:
ELM-INR splits the image into overlapping square subdomains (default S_i = 32x32 = 1024 pixels each). In each subdomain, local pixel coordinates are normalized to [-1, 1], encoded with random Fourier features (F = 10, sigma = 1, as in FFN), and passed through one random, frozen hidden layer of m = 1024 ReLU units (an Extreme Learning Machine). Only the output weights are fitted, by a closed-form least-squares solve per subdomain, batched on the GPU. The local predictors are blended with partition-of-unity window functions into one global reconstruction. BEAM (adaptive partitioning) is not used for this result.

Baselines are SIREN, FFN, GaussNet and WIRE, trained with Adam for 1000 steps on the standard images, with the best configuration from a search over width {256, 512, 1024}, depth {3, 4, 5} and learning rate {5e-5, 1e-4}. PSNR is computed on the training pixels after normalizing by the ground-truth maximum, as -10 log10(MSE + 1e-8), which caps PSNR at 80 dB. Kodak images kodim05, kodim08 and kodim24 are 512x512 RGB and kodim20 is 256x256.
official.claim: On four Kodak images, closed-form ELM-INR (32x32 subdomains, m = 1024) reconstructs the image at 78.4-79.1 dB PSNR (e.g. kodim05: 79.03 ± 1.59), while the best of SIREN, FFN, GaussNet and WIRE reaches only 30.4-40.1 dB (kodim05: SIREN 31.12 ± 0.22), a gap of more than 38 dB on every image.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: All benchmarks are reported as mean ± std over 5 random seeds. PSNR is averaged over all spectral bands for the multispectral benchmarks.
official.metric: PSNR in dB on the fitted image, higher is better; mean ± std over 5 random seeds; PSNR = -10 log10(MSE + 1e-8) after normalizing by the ground-truth maximum, so 80 dB is the ceiling
official.comparison: ELM-INR vs. SIREN, FFN, GaussNet and WIRE (Adam, 1000 steps, best of a small hyperparameter search) on the same images
official.falsification_criterion: With the stated configuration (S_i = 32^2, m = 1024, RFF F = 10 sigma = 1, ReLU, partition-of-unity blending), ELM-INR fails to exceed about 60 dB PSNR on the Kodak images, or a tuned SIREN/WIRE baseline under the stated protocol comes within about 10 dB of it.

title: GISA: A Benchmark for General Information-Seeking Assistant

official.background: Search agents built on LLMs answer information needs by issuing web searches and reading pages over many turns. Existing benchmarks for them often build questions backward from a chosen answer (e.g. BrowseComp), which gives unnatural tasks. They also tend to test either deep search for one fact or wide aggregation across many sources, rarely both, and they use static answers that models may have memorized, often graded by an LLM judge. GISA is a benchmark of 373 human-written queries whose answers are structured (item, set, list or table), so they can be graded by deterministic exact match. It includes a live subset whose answers change over time, and it ships a human search trajectory for every query.
official.method:
Queries come from annotators browsing topic websites. They are refined into one of four answer formats with fully specified sort orders and table schemas, answered by annotators using only Google Search, and checked by verifiers. Queries that DeepSeek-V3.2 can answer perfectly with no search are removed. The final set has 373 queries: 22 item, 50 set, 48 list and 253 table; across all types, 223 are stable and 150 are live. Predictions and gold answers are normalized (lowercasing, removal of whitespace and markdown, numeric cleanup), and exact match (EM) requires the whole normalized answer to be identical. Overall EM is the query-weighted average over all four types.

Each ReAct agent uses the model's native function calling with two tools. Search calls the Serper Google API and returns the top 10 results. Browse fetches pages with Jina Reader and has the same backbone model, in non-thinking mode, summarize them for a stated goal. Limits are 30 tool calls per task and 8,192 output tokens per step, with parallel function calling disabled and the maximum thinking budget where thinking is used. All agents get the same system prompt (Figure 8), which asks for the final answer as TSV inside <answer> tags. The authors evaluate 12 model configurations and 4 commercial systems.
official.claim: On GISA with the paper's ReAct Search+Browse agent (30 tool calls max), no LLM reaches 20% overall exact match (best: Claude 4.5 Sonnet thinking, 19.30%). Every agent scores far lower on table-type queries than on item-type queries: table EM ranges from 4.35% to 13.04% and item EM from 22.73% to 68.18%. For example, DeepSeek-V3.2 (thinking) gets 63.64% item EM, 6.32% table EM and 14.47% overall EM.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Experimental results of all methods on GISA. The overall score is calculated by the weighted average of all EM scores. Tool calling number with * is provided by the API service provider.
official.metric: Exact match (%) after normalization, higher is better; overall = query-weighted average of per-type EM. Single run per model; no standard deviations or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: Item-type vs. table-type EM within each of 12 ReAct agent configurations (Qwen3-235B, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-4.7, Seed-1.8, Qwen3-Max, Kimi K2.5), plus overall EM against the paper's ceiling of 19.30%.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the released benchmark and harness with one of the listed models (e.g. DeepSeek-V3.2 thinking) gives table-type EM that is not clearly below item-type EM, or gives overall EM far from the reported value (e.g. above 25% for a model reported at about 14-19%).

title: Breaking the Grid: Distance-Guided Reinforcement Learning in Large Discrete Action Spaces
claim_source: Table 9 (continuation of Table 8), page 33; also Figure 3 (bottom right), page 9

official.background: Many decision problems (logistics, scheduling, recommendation) have discrete action spaces that are far too large to enumerate, e.g. picking a vector of N choices out of D options gives D^N actions. A common workaround is to let an actor output a continuous 'proto-action' and map it to a nearby discrete action. Rounding is often suboptimal, Wolpertinger's k-nearest-neighbour lookup needs a precomputed table of all actions, and Dynamic Neighborhood Construction (DNC) searches along grid lines with simulated annealing, which assumes adjacent indices are semantically similar. That assumption breaks for categorical or irregularly ordered actions such as items in a catalog.
official.method:
DGRL is an off-policy actor-critic method with two parts. Sampled Dynamic Neighborhoods (SDN): the actor outputs a continuous proto-action â scaled to integer action bounds; K candidate discrete actions are sampled independently per dimension from a Chebyshev (L-infinity) ball of radius L around â, with probability decreasing linearly in distance (temperature τs = 1). The critic scores all K candidates; at test time the argmax is executed, during training an action is sampled by rank-based probabilities (τe = 0.8). Distance-Based Updates (DBU): M = 40 auxiliary candidates are drawn by Gaussian perturbation (σb) of â and rounding, the critic scores them, and a softmax-weighted average (τb = 0.01) gives a target ā. The actor is trained by regressing â onto ā (Huber loss). The critic uses a replay buffer, Polyak-averaged target networks and double Q-learning.

The claim uses the discrete Recommender environment built from MovieLens 25M. Movies are featurised by TF-IDF of their genre strings (duplicate feature vectors removed, leaving 343 movies). The probability that a user picks recommended movie j after movie i is a sigmoid of 5 x cosine similarity. The user leaves with probability 10% after picking a recommended movie and 20% otherwise, episodes last at most 100 steps, and the reward is a movie-specific value from the dataset. The agent recommends N = 10 of D = 343 movies per step, so |A| = 343^10. DGRL (L = 10, K = 100, actor 128 / critic 256 units) is compared with DNC (simulated annealing), DNC (greedy) and Cacla, all trained with A2C and tuned by grid search. Wolpertinger and LAR cannot run at this size because of memory. All methods use 10 training seeds.
official.claim: On the discrete Recommender environment with 343^10 actions, DGRL reaches a median (over 10 seeds) peak training reward of 1941.89 (std 53.86), vs. 783.96 (std 49.54) for the strongest baseline DNC (SA) with A2C, a 147% improvement. DNC (greedy) and Cacla reach about 731.
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Table 8 continued. (Table 8 caption: Numerical results for discrete environments. Statistical metrics are calculated over 10 random seeds. Means and medians are maxima over the entire training time. Percentage differences compared to DNC and Cacla are calculated using medians.)
official.metric: Reward per episode (higher is better). The paper (App. E.4) says the table shows 'the peak mean and median performance over ten random seeds, as well as the standard deviation of the peak performances', with means and medians being 'maxima over the entire training time'. So Std. is the standard deviation of the per-seed peak rewards across 10 seeds. The paper does not say explicitly whether Mean/Median are taken over per-seed peaks or are the peak of the across-seed mean/median curve. No other error bars are given; Figure 3 shades the interquartile range.
official.comparison: DGRL (SDN + DBU) vs. DNC (simulated annealing) + A2C, DNC (greedy) + A2C and Cacla + A2C, all on the same environment with 10 seeds each and tuned hyperparameters
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained on Recommender 343^10, DGRL's median peak reward is not clearly above DNC (SA)'s, e.g. the gap shrinks to within about one seed standard deviation (~50 reward) or DGRL is less than ~1.5x DNC (SA), or DNC (SA) itself reaches about 1900 under the authors' tuning protocol.

title: Learning to Sample From Diffusion Models via Inverse Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Table B.5, page 17 (same point estimates in Table 2, page 7)

official.background: Once a diffusion model's denoiser is trained, image quality still depends on sampler settings such as the classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale, the EDM stochasticity parameters and restart/renoising schedules. These are usually tuned by grid search, which for large models can cost about as much compute as training the denoiser, because every configuration needs tens of thousands of samples to score. The paper asks whether a small policy network can learn these sampling decisions per sample and per noise level, without retraining the denoiser and without a hand-designed reward.
official.method:
Sampling is cast as a finite-horizon MDP whose state is (x_t, σ_t) (current noisy image and noise level) and whose discrete actions modify the sampler: for adaptive guidance, the action picks a CFG scale ω from a discrete set (20 values) at each step of the EDM sampler on a fixed, pretrained conditional EDM denoiser. The 'expert' is given only by data samples noised to each noise level (no expert trajectories or actions). The policy is trained to minimise an f-divergence (KL or reverse KL) between the expert state-occupancy measure and the policy's state-occupancy measure, using a policy-gradient theorem whose per-step signal is h_f(µ_E/µ_θ); the density ratio comes from a discriminator retrained each iteration, and updates use a PPO-style clipped objective. The policy network (≈5.8M parameters) uses a frozen pretrained ADM encoder as feature extractor.

Evaluation: FID on 50k samples, plus improved Precision and Recall (Kim et al. topological method), and NFE. For adaptive CFG on FFHQ 64×64 the baseline is EDM with the best constant guidance scale from a grid search (ω = 0.1), at the same NFE (79).
official.claim: On FFHQ 64×64 with a fixed pretrained conditional EDM denoiser at 79 NFE, the KL-trained adaptive guidance policy reaches FID 3.03 ± 0.02 and Recall 88.6 ± 0.1 vs. 3.11 and 87.8 for the best grid-searched constant CFG scale (ω = 0.1), with Precision about equal (90.6 vs. 90.7).
official.claim_caption: Table B.5: Results across all strategies with mean±standard deviation when repeated runs are available. Variability is reported for repeated CIFAR-10 and FFHQ learned-policy evaluations; ImageNet results are single-run evaluations due to the cost of 50k-sample metrics at that scale.
official.metric: FID on 50k samples (lower is better), Precision and Recall (higher is better); ± is std over repeated evaluations of the learned policy (number of repeats not stated); the EDM+CFG baseline is a single point estimate with no error bar
official.comparison: Adaptive state-dependent guidance policy π(x, σ) trained with KL (and rKL) vs. EDM + constant CFG with the best grid-searched ω, same denoiser and NFE
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining the KL guidance policy on FFHQ 64×64 and evaluating FID on 50k samples gives FID ≥ the best constant-CFG EDM baseline (≈3.11 when recomputed under the same FID pipeline), or Recall no higher than the baseline's.

title: Bayesian Preference Learning for Test-Time Steerable Reward Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (static-RM control in Table 4, Appendix D, page 22)

official.background: Classifier reward models (RMs) trained with the Bradley-Terry (BT) loss encode a single, fixed preference distribution and cannot be changed at test time without retraining. They also tend to over-optimize, pushing preference probabilities toward 1. LLM-as-a-judge evaluators are more flexible but expensive and often proprietary. The paper asks whether a classifier RM can be made steerable at test time by conditioning it on a few in-context preference demonstrations (prompt, chosen, rejected) that specify the desired criterion.
official.method:
ICRM (Variational In-Context Reward Modeling) gives the RM a two-dimensional head that outputs a utility score u and a confidence score s for each (demonstrations C, prompt, response). For a pair, these define a Beta posterior over the latent preference probability z, with mean mu = sigmoid(u_w - u_l) and concentration tau = Softplus(s_w) + Softplus(s_l) + 1. Training minimizes -(psi(mu*tau) - psi(tau)) + lambda(N) * KL(Beta(mu*tau, (1-mu)*tau) || Beta(1,1)), where psi is the digamma function and lambda(N) = lambda/N. Demonstrations are prepended with a plain template (Appendix B) with no natural-language instructions.

The main model is Qwen3-4B-Base with lambda = 0.1, trained on Skywork-Preferences-v0.2 with N in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} demonstrations sampled from the training data (one epoch, effective batch 128, max context 16,384 tokens, 512 updates, peak LR 5e-6, 4x H100). For RM-Bench evaluation, N in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64} demonstrations are sampled within each domain (Chat, Safety, Code, Math), and preference accuracy is measured on held-out pairs. Results are the mean and std over four random seeds of demonstration sampling.
official.claim: With Qwen3-4B ICRM (lambda = 0.1), average RM-Bench accuracy rises from 60.5 ± 3.5 with N=1 in-context demonstration to 67.6 ± 1.6 at N=8 and 70.8 ± 1.0 at N=64. Static BTRM and GRM given the same demonstrations do not improve (BTRM 69.6 -> 67.8, GRM 66.2 -> 64.9 from N=1 to N=64; Table 4).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: RM-Bench evaluation results with the standard deviation of four random seeds for ICRM.
official.metric: RM-Bench preference accuracy (%), higher is better, averaged over the Chat, Safety, Code and Math domains; ICRM values are mean with std (subscripts) over four random seeds of demonstration sampling; baselines have no error bars
official.comparison: ICRM at N=64 (and N=8) vs. the same ICRM at N=1; secondarily, ICRM's gain with N vs. released BTRM and GRM checkpoints given the same prepended demonstrations
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained Qwen3-4B ICRM shows no average RM-Bench gain from N=1 to N=64 beyond seed std (e.g., gain under ~4 points), or the static BTRM/GRM gain as much from the same demonstrations.

title: EcoGym: Evaluating LLMs for Long-Horizon Plan-and-Execute in Interactive Economies

official.background: Long-horizon planning is a core capability claimed for LLM agents, but most agent benchmarks are episodic and short, or confined to one narrow commercial scenario such as the closed-source Vending-Bench. EcoGym grounds long-horizon evaluation in persistent economic simulations with hidden dynamics. The agent has to keep a strategy coherent over hundreds or thousands of steps and is scored by business outcomes (net worth, income, daily active users) rather than by task success.
official.method:
EcoGym has three environments with a unified interface. In Vending (an open re-implementation of Vending-Bench), the agent researches products, places orders and sets prices to maximize Net Worth (cash + inventory at wholesale value + pending orders). The budget is 4 actions per day, with 600+ SKUs in 37 categories and hidden seasonality and elasticity. In Freelance, the agent discovers, solves and submits tasks to an LLM auditor while managing energy and stress, to maximize Income (5 actions per day). In Operation, the agent picks one of four interventions per day (acquisition_boost, engagement_tune, creator_incentive, moderation_tighten) on a content platform whose DAU decays to zero without intervention. The objective is average DAU, and the coefficients linking content volume and quality to DAU are hidden.

Every model runs for 365 simulated days with temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and a sliding context of the most recent 128 steps. Vending results are averaged over 5 runs, and Freelance and Operation over 3 runs. The Claude model is claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 and the Gemini models are the Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and Gemini-3-Flash-Preview API snapshots.
official.claim: No single model wins all of EcoGym. In Operation, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 reaches an average DAU of 1595.00 ± 70.77, against 1396.00 ± 53.73 for Gemini-3-Pro (second). In Vending, Gemini-3-Pro reaches a final net worth of 11272.47 ± 1037.27, against 1843.62 ± 329.46 for Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and 5675.65 ± 633.67 for the next-best model, Gemini-3-Flash.
official.claim_caption: Table 2 Performance comparison on EcoGym. Best and second best results are indicated by bold and underlined.
official.metric: Vending: final Net Worth after 365 days (higher is better), mean ± over 5 runs. Operation: average DAU over 365 days (higher is better), mean ± over 3 runs. Table 2 does not define ±, but Table 4 reports the same Vending entries (e.g., Gemini-3-Pro 11272.47 ± 1037.27) as 'mean ± std', so ± is the standard deviation across runs.
official.comparison: Claude-Sonnet-4.5 vs. Gemini-3-Pro (and the other 7 models) under an identical harness, horizon, context window and sampling settings, in the Vending and Operation environments
official.falsification_criterion: With the released EcoGym code and the same settings, either Gemini-3-Pro matches or beats Claude-Sonnet-4.5 on Operation average DAU, or Claude-Sonnet-4.5 matches or beats Gemini-3-Pro on Vending net worth (i.e., one model wins both). Weaker refutation: the Operation gap (about 200 DAU) shrinks to within run-to-run spread.
