title: Generalized Robust Adaptive-Bandwidth Multi-View Manifold Learning in High Dimensions with Noise

official.background: Many scientific datasets record the same underlying system through several sensors ('views'), each with its own dimension, nonlinear distortion and noise level. Kernel methods such as diffusion maps can recover low-dimensional structure from one view, and multiview diffusion maps (MDM) fuse several views. But these methods choose the kernel bandwidth heuristically, assume clean data, and have little theory once there are more than two views or the noise is high-dimensional. A poor bandwidth in one noisy view can corrupt the fused embedding, so a principled per-view bandwidth rule could make multiview fusion much more robust.
official.method:
GRAB-MDM builds, for each view l, a Gaussian kernel matrix K^l with bandwidth eps_l. It forms a block matrix whose (l1, l2) off-diagonal block is K^l1 K^l2 and whose diagonal blocks are zero, so the random walk can only move across views, and row-normalizes it into a transition matrix A. Each sample is embedded by averaging its top non-trivial eigenvector coordinates (t = 1) across its K view copies (eq. 8). The bandwidth is eps_l = c * h_l (Algorithm 1). Here h_l is the omega_l-percentile of the pairwise squared distances in view l, after per-coordinate z-scoring. The global factor c comes from a grid search over [1e-3, 0.5] that picks the c whose spectrum of A is most stable, i.e. the c with the most other grid values whose squared eigenvalue distance is below a threshold delta. The embedding dimension m is chosen by an eigen-ratio elbow rule (m = 1 for this experiment), and omega_l and delta are chosen by procedures in Appendix E.

For Table 1, latent vectors w in R^{3d} (d = 10) for three clusters are drawn from uniform boxes (Setup 1) or truncated Gaussians (Setup 2), with cluster-specific parameters given in Section 6.1. View l takes block l of w, applies g1(x) = x^2 + x, g2(x) = 10 log(x + 2) or g3(x) = 0.8x entrywise, zero-pads to p_l = 100 dimensions, and adds isotropic Gaussian noise of variance v_l^2. With n = 200 and 3 views, each method's embedding is clustered into 3 clusters with k-means and scored by clustering accuracy (ACC). Baselines are mDM, mSNE, mLLE, mISOMAP, mUMAP and pairwise alternating diffusion maps (pADM), plus single-view DM, LLE, t-SNE, ISOMAP and UMAP on the concatenated views.
official.claim: In Setup (1) with heterogeneous high noise, GRAB-MDM reaches clustering accuracy 0.81 (0.02), 0.79 (0.02) and 0.77 (0.02) at noise variances (20, 10, 45), (10, 25, 40) and (10, 30, 50). The strongest baseline, multiview diffusion maps (mDM), gets 0.73, 0.72 and 0.70 (std 0.02), and every other baseline gets at most 0.67.
official.claim_caption: TABLE 1. Comparison of clustering accuracy across various methods. The reported values are the means with standard deviations (in parentheses), based on 1,000 replications.
official.metric: Clustering accuracy (ACC) of k-means on the embedding, higher is better; mean with standard deviation over 1,000 data replications in parentheses (per-replication spread, not standard error)
official.comparison: GRAB-MDM (adaptive per-view bandwidths, zero within-view blocks, averaged embedding) vs. mDM, mSNE, mLLE, mISOMAP, mUMAP and pADM, and vs. DM, LLE, t-SNE, ISOMAP and UMAP on the concatenated views, all on the same simulated 3-view data
official.falsification_criterion: In Setup (1) at noise variances (20, 10, 45), (10, 25, 40) or (10, 30, 50), a faithful reimplementation of GRAB-MDM does not beat mDM by more than about one per-replication std (0.02), or some other baseline matches or beats GRAB-MDM.

title: Learn from Your Mistakes: Self-Correcting Masked Diffusion Models

official.background: Masked diffusion language models (MDMs) such as LLaDA generate text by starting from a fully masked sequence and unmasking tokens in parallel over several steps. Once a token is unmasked it is fixed, so mistakes made during parallel decoding cannot be undone and accumulate, which hurts quality and limits how many tokens can be decoded per step. Existing fixes either remask low-confidence tokens with training-free heuristics (ReMDM), train extra heads to flag errors (ReMeDi, GStar, PRISM), or add uniform-noise corruption during training (GIDD-style hybrid noise).
official.method:
ProSeCo (Progressive Self-Correction) adds one term to standard MDM training. For each training example, the model first does the usual MDM forward pass on a partially masked sequence; its outputs are turned into a fully unmasked sequence by taking the argmax at every position (with stop-gradient), and a second forward pass of the same network (tied weights) is trained with cross-entropy to recover the clean data from this model-generated sequence. The self-correction loss uses the same weighting α̇t/(1−αt) as the MDM loss. At sampling time, every ω unmasking steps a corrector loop of up to S steps feeds the current argmax sequence back through the model and overwrites already-unmasked positions with the corrector's predictions.

For the claim, LLaDA-Base 8B is fine-tuned for ~400B tokens (3 epochs) on a variant of Llama-Nemotron-Post-Training whose targets were regenerated by GPT-OSS, under three objectives with the same recipe: vanilla MDM SFT, hybrid mask + uniform noise SFT (GIDD-like), and ProSeCo SFT. Models are evaluated 0-shot with Nemo Skills on HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K and MATH, generation length 1024, semi-autoregressive block decoding with block size 32. 'ProSeCo Max Sampling' decodes 1 token per step with corrector loops (ω, S) = (2,4), (1,8), (2,1), (2,8) for HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH respectively (Appendix Table 3).
official.claim: With the same LLaDA-Base 8B model and SFT data, ProSeCo SFT with ProSeCo Max correction sampling reaches Pass@1 72.56 / 69.31 / 92.19 / 55.06 on HumanEval / MBPP / GSM8K / MATH, versus 64.02 / 56.88 / 89.01 / 48.52 for the strongest matched baseline (hybrid mask + uniform noise SFT) and 58.54 / 56.88 / 88.86 / 46.60 for vanilla MDM SFT; ProSeCo SFT without correction sampling (69.51 / 57.41 / 91.36 / 51.98) already beats both baselines on all four benchmarks.

[22]. Other "Prior work" values obtained via evaluation with open-sourced weights. Best value is bolded.
official.metric: Pass@1 accuracy (%), higher is better; single runs, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: ProSeCo SFT (with and without ProSeCo Max correction sampling) vs. Vanilla SFT, Vanilla SFT + ReMDM, and Hybrid Mask + Uniform SFT, all fine-tuned from LLaDA-Base 8B with the same recipe
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating (or retraining) the matched checkpoints under the stated decoding settings, ProSeCo SFT + Max sampling does not beat the hybrid mask + uniform SFT baseline by several points on HumanEval and MBPP and on MATH, or ProSeCo SFT without correction sampling fails to beat vanilla SFT on most of the four benchmarks.

title: Improved State Mixing in Higher-order and Block Diagonal Linear Recurrent Networks
claim_source: Table 8 (Appendix F), page 26; best-seed values summarized in Table 1, page 6

official.background: Linear recurrent networks and selective state space models (LRU, Mamba) use diagonal state-transition matrices, which makes them fast to train with parallel scans but provably limited on state-tracking tasks such as composing permutations. Dense nonlinear RNNs like the LSTM can solve these tasks but are slow. The paper asks whether structured, non-diagonal state mixing can close this gap while keeping parallel-scan efficiency.
official.method:
BD-LRU replaces the diagonal transition with a block-diagonal one: the hidden state is split into N blocks of size m, and each block evolves as h_t^k = A_t^k h_{t-1}^k + a_{0,t}^k ⊙ v_t^k, where every entry of the m×m matrix A_t^k and the input gate a_{0,t}^k is a selective gate (a linear function of the input). The gates are jointly L1-normalized per row with softmax parametrization (f = exp in Eq. 3), so the absolute values of the state and input gates in each row sum to one, which bounds the forward pass. m = 1 is the diagonal LRU. (H-LRU, a higher-order recurrence, is the paper's second architecture but does not solve this task.)

On the permutation task of Merrill et al., each input is a sequence of 16 elements of the symmetric group S5 (all 120 permutations) and the model must output the running composition at every position; there are 100k training samples. Every model is one layer in an Embedding → model → MLP decoder stack (MAD protocol), with total hidden dimension up to 6144, trained with AdamW and a cosine schedule, learning rate in {1e-3, 5e-4, 1e-4}, and 5 seeds. Baselines are LSTM, Mamba2, DeltaNet[-1,1], DeltaProduct4[-1,1] (8 heads) and PD-SSM, under the same protocol.
official.claim: On S5 permutation composition (100k training samples, sequence length 16, single layer), BD-LRU with block size m = 6 reaches mean test accuracy 0.923 ± 0.077 over 5 seeds (best 1.000), versus 0.304 ± 0.045 for PD-SSM, ≤ 0.242 for Mamba2, 0.137 ± 0.004 for DeltaProduct4, and 0.199 ± 0.018 for the diagonal BD-LRU m1.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Model performance on permutation composition tasks for different datasets of different sizes: S3 (10k training samples), S4 (50k training samples), S5 (100k training samples). The accuracy values reflect the impact of window size (H-LRU) and block size (BD-LRU), both denoted by m. We note that BD-LRU performance improves with block size, demonstrating strong sample efficiency by solving the tasks even given limited training data. All models are single-layer configurations with a maximum overall hidden dimension of 6144. The presented results are the best test accuracies (mean ± std in brackets across 5 seeds). DeltaProduct and DeltaNet are reported with 8 heads (nh) and [-1,1] denotes the range of eigenvalues. Mamba2 are reported with convolution size (c) and state space extension (s). We utilized all permutations belonging to the symmetric groups S3, S4, S5 (6, 24, and 120 elements, respectively).
official.metric: test accuracy on the per-position running composition (higher is better). Each cell gives the best test accuracy across learning rates and seeds, then mean ± std over 5 seeds in brackets.
official.comparison: BD-LRU (block sizes m = 1 to 16) vs. Mamba2, DeltaNet[-1,1], DeltaProduct4[-1,1], PD-SSM and the diagonal m = 1 model, all single-layer under the same data and training protocol; LSTM as the nonlinear reference
official.falsification_criterion: With the same protocol, BD-LRU m = 6 (or larger) does not reach a 5-seed mean S5 accuracy clearly above the best linear baseline (PD-SSM, ~0.30), e.g. a mean below 0.5, or a linear baseline such as DeltaProduct4 or Mamba2 reaches comparable accuracy.

title: Soft Contamination Means Benchmarks Test Shallow Generalization

official.background: Benchmark scores are meant to measure generalization to unseen problems, so training corpora are decontaminated by removing verbatim or n-gram copies of test items. Those filters miss semantic duplicates: training items that pose the same problem (or one that subsumes it) in different wording, so that learning to solve them is enough to solve the test item. The paper asks how common such duplicates are in an open training corpus (Olmo 3) and whether training on them inflates scores on the benchmark's other, unduplicated items without improving related benchmarks. The authors call this pattern 'shallow generalization'.
official.method:
MuSR (the Murder Mysteries and Team Allocation tasks; Object Placement is omitted, 250 items in total) is split into a seen half and an unseen half of 125 items each. Synthetic semantic duplicates of seen items are generated by re-running the original MuSR generation code (gpt-4-0613, temperature 1.0) on modified logic trees at three levels: regen (same tree, story regenerated), 1-branch (one non-outcome branch changed), and n-branches (all branches of that type changed); the answer and the reasoning needed are kept the same. Claude Opus 4.5 writes chain-of-thought answers for the training items. Olmo 3 7B Instruct is LoRA-finetuned (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, learning rate 2e-4, 6 epochs) on the formatted questions and CoT answers.

Conditions: no finetuning; exact duplicates of the seen half; each of the three semantic-duplicate levels; and finetuning on the Olmo 3 corpus items with the highest cosine similarity to MuSR items (from Dolci SFT or Dolci RL), which topically resemble MuSR but are not duplicates. Accuracy is estimated from 8 samples per item at temperature 0.7 on the original seen and unseen items, plus the TrueDetective control benchmark.
official.claim: LoRA-finetuning Olmo 3 7B Instruct on synthetic semantic duplicates of 125 seen MuSR items raises accuracy on the 125 unseen MuSR items to 86.0-87.9% (± 2.1-2.2 stderr), compared with 66.0 ± 3.0 without finetuning and 68.6 ± 2.1 / 65.3 ± 2.1 after finetuning on the most cosine-similar non-duplicate corpus items (SFT / RL). TrueDetective control accuracy stays at 28-30% (no finetuning: 28.3 ± 3.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Finetuning Olmo 3 on semantic duplicates. We see large gains from training on semantic duplicates, in MuSR's case statistically equivalent to training on exact duplicates (See Section A.6 for synthetic generation details). The rightmost column is the control, showing accuracy on second similar-domain benchmarks: for MuSR this is 'True Detective' [Del and Fishel, 2023]; for ZebraLogic this is the ARC Challenge [Clark et al., 2018] and for MBPP this is HumanEval [Chen et al., 2021]. We see no significant improvement to the control scores when finetuning on any setting of MuSR or ZebraLogic duplicates; we do see a surprising leap in HumanEval (MBPP's control) for semantic duplicates. Accuracy (%) ± stderr. Abbreviations: P=Paraphrase, SH=Shuffle, SU=Substitution, cos similarity=high cosine similarity corpus matches. title: Bench-MFG: A Benchmark Suite for Learning in Stationary Mean Field Games

official.background: Mean Field Games (MFGs) approximate very large multi-agent systems by having one representative agent interact with the population distribution. The solution concept is a mean field Nash equilibrium, and how far a policy is from one is measured by its exploitability. Many learning algorithms for MFGs have been proposed (fixed-point iteration, fictitious play, policy-iteration variants, online mirror descent), but each is usually tested on a few bespoke toy environments. This makes it hard to tell which methods are robust. Bench-MFG offers a taxonomy of stationary discrete MFG classes with example environments, plus MF-Garnets, a random generator of MFG instances meant to support statistical comparisons between solvers.
official.method:
An MF-Garnet instance is specified by (|X|, |A|, branching factor, dynamics structure, reward structure). It has a sparse random base transition tensor P0 and Gaussian coupling coefficients Omega, which make the transitions depend on the mean field mu either additively (cp*P0 + rho_p*sum_y Omega*mu(y), then ReLU and normalize) or multiplicatively (P0 times ReLU(cp + rho_p*sum_y Omega*mu(y)), then normalize). The reward is a random base reward R0 combined with an interaction matrix M, again either additively (cr*R0 + rho_r*M mu) or multiplicatively (R0*(cr + rho_r*M mu)). Normalization and the finite noise grid used for sampling are defined in Appx. C.1.

Eight exact, model-based solvers are run on each instance: Fixed Point, Damped FP, Fictitious Play, Policy Iteration, Smooth PI, Boltzmann PI, Online Mirror Descent, and the paper's new MF-PSO (particle swarm search that minimizes exploitability, 200 particles). All methods start from the same initial policy: logits drawn uniformly from [-1, 1], passed through a Boltzmann policy with temperature 0.2. Hyperparameters are grid-searched per algorithm (Appx. H). For each algorithm and Garnet type, the final exploitability is averaged over 10 instances (Garnet seeds 0-9) and reported as mean ± std. The implementation is in JAX on an NVIDIA L40, and a pure-Python reference version is also provided.
official.claim: On 25-state, 10-action, branching-factor-10 MF-Garnets, Fixed Point, Damped FP, Fictitious Play, PI and Smooth PI all reach mean final exploitability of 0.003 or less in both the additive/additive and the multiplicative-dynamics/additive-reward settings. Examples: Damped FP 8.51e-04 ± 0.0017 (A/A) and 3.43e-05 ± 9.83e-05 (M/A). In the same settings, OMD (1.44 ± 0.39, 1.47 ± 0.45), Boltzmann PI (0.95 ± 0.29, 0.93 ± 0.32) and MF-PSO (3.86 ± 1.90, 4.02 ± 2.16) stay far from equilibrium.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: MF-Garnet Results. Each MF-Garnet has 5 parameters |X| x |A| x Branching Factor (Dynamics/Reward Structure). We highlighted the three best exploitability values and the worst three standard deviations per game type. MF-Garnets show that different algorithms can perform significantly differently depending on the type of game structure and the dimensionality.
official.metric: Final exploitability (lower is better), mean ± std over 10 MF-Garnet instances (Garnet seeds 0-9)
official.comparison: FP-family and greedy PI-family solvers (Fixed Point, Damped FP, Fictitious Play, PI, Smooth PI) vs. OMD, Boltzmann PI and MF-PSO, on the same randomly generated 25x10x10 MF-Garnet instances
official.falsification_criterion: On 25x10x10 A/A or M/A MF-Garnets (10 instances), OMD, Boltzmann PI or MF-PSO with tuned hyperparameters reaches mean final exploitability within one std of the best FP-family method. Another refutation: FP, Damped FP or Fictitious Play fail to get below about 0.01 mean exploitability.

title: Self-EvolveRec: Self-Evolving Recommender Systems with LLM-based Directional Feedback

official.background: Automating recommender-system design has mostly meant Neural Architecture Search over a fixed, human-defined operator pool, which cannot invent new loss functions, data processing or architectures. LLM-driven code evolution frameworks such as AlphaEvolve and DeepEvolve instead let an LLM rewrite the whole codebase, but they are steered only by a scalar metric (e.g. NDCG). A single scalar cannot say why a recommender fails (popularity bias, low diversity, embedding collapse), so the search becomes trial and error. This paper asks whether richer, diagnostic feedback makes the code evolution find better recommenders.
official.method:
Self-EvolveRec evolves a full recommendation codebase (model, loss, data processing, training loop) over up to 21 iterations, starting from a seed recommender (NCF, NGCF, SASRec or MoRec). At each iteration a parent codebase is sampled from an evolutionary archive, trained, and evaluated. Besides the scalar NDCG@5/HR@5, it gets two kinds of 'directional feedback'. (1) A User Simulator (GPT-5-mini) role-plays 20 sampled users, each with a persona built from their history and Activity/Conformity/Diversity traits. It critiques their top-k recommendation lists in natural language, and the critiques are summarized. (2) A Model Diagnosis Tool runs code probes on the trained model, starting with embedding collapse (mean pairwise cosine similarity of item embeddings) and ranking margin, and an LLM turns the results into a diagnosis report. A planner (GPT-5-mini) turns both reports into research queries, retrieves 3 arXiv papers, and writes a development report. The coding agent (GPT-5) then edits the codebase.

The Diagnosis Tool itself also evolves (Diagnosis Tool - Model Co-Evolution): after each code change an LLM analyses the new codebase and the simulator's critiques and writes new diagnostic metrics (e.g. a top-k diversity metric). Baselines AlphaEvolve (via OpenEvolve) and DeepEvolve (AlphaEvolve plus RAG) use the same seed, the same GPT-5 coder, and the same 21-iteration cap, but receive only the scalar metric. All recommenders use embedding dimension 50, batch size 128, lr 0.001, and up to 300 epochs. Evaluation is leave-last-out with each test item ranked against 99 random negatives; NDCG@5 and HR@5 are computed on real held-out interactions with no LLM involved.
official.claim: Starting from a SASRec seed on Amazon CDs, the codebase evolved by Self-EvolveRec reaches NDCG@5 0.3865 / HR@5 0.5274. That is above DeepEvolve (0.3610 / 0.4870), AlphaEvolve (0.3528 / 0.4623) and the seed SASRec (0.3559 / 0.4676), all under the same seed, LLMs and 21-iteration budget. The same ordering holds on Electronics (0.2600 vs. 0.2508 DeepEvolve vs. 0.2063 AlphaEvolve NDCG@5).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Overall model performance (A: AlphaEvolve, D: DeepEvolve).
official.metric: NDCG@5 and HR@5 on the leave-last-out test item ranked among 100 candidates (1 positive + 99 random negatives), higher is better. Single run per cell; no standard deviations, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Self-EvolveRec vs. AlphaEvolve and DeepEvolve (scalar-metric-only LLM code evolution), each initialized from the same SASRec seed codebase with GPT-5 as coder and 21 max iterations; the seed SASRec and NAS baselines (AutoFIS, NASRec, AutoLossGen, DNS-Rec) are also listed.
official.falsification_criterion: Running the released Self-EvolveRec and DeepEvolve pipelines from the SASRec seed on CDs (ideally several runs each) gives Self-EvolveRec a test NDCG@5 that is not higher than DeepEvolve's, or the 0.025 NDCG@5 gap falls within the run-to-run spread of either method.

title: Language Model Memory and Memory Models for Language

official.background: The last-token, last-layer embedding of a language model is often treated as a 'memory' of the input, both in retrieval (single-vector embeddings) and in memory models that replace token sequences with embeddings to cut KV-cache size and time to first token. How much input information such an embedding actually holds is rarely measured. If causally trained embeddings hold little information about their input, they cannot support arbitrary lookup of input content, which would explain why memory models and single-embedding retrievers underperform full-context transformers.
official.method:
An encoder model (masked mixer, d_m = 1024, or transformer, d_m = 512; n_l = 8; n_ctx = 512) is first trained on FineWeb-edu with one objective: autoencoding (regenerate the input from the last-token embedding), causal next-token prediction, or causal then InfoNCE retrieval; an untrained encoder is also tested. The encoder is then frozen (except that its token-embedding layer is replaced by a trainable transformation), and a fresh decoder (usually of the same size and architecture as the encoder) is trained to regenerate the full 512-token input from only the encoder's last-hidden-layer, last-token embedding. That embedding is 'unrolled' into n_ctx decoder inputs by a trainable linear projection over a sliding window of the embedding (after Morris et al., 2023). The Table 1 caption states that all models were trained for 200k steps.

Information retention is reported on held-out FineWeb-edu as (i) the decoder's cross-entropy loss, (ii) an entropy ratio H_r = 1 - H(p,q)/H(uniform,q) (= 1 - loss/9.03 for the 8k tokenizer), and (iii) token accuracy, the percentage of non-pad input tokens the decoder reproduces exactly. Training uses AdamW with a 500-step warmup, peak LR 2e-4 (transformers) or 5e-4 (mixers), linear decay, and global batch 128.
official.claim: With n_ctx = 512 on FineWeb-edu, a decoder trained to invert a frozen autoencoder-trained encoder's single embedding recovers 76.96% of input tokens (mixer) and 33.5% (transformer), whereas the same procedure on equally sized causal-LM encoders recovers only 5.48% (mixer) and 5.01% (transformer), barely above untrained encoders (4.67%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Information Retention (all models n_ctx = 512, n_l = 8 mixers d_m = 1024 and transformers d_m = 512, trained for 200k steps). 'Causal -> Retrieval' signifies a model first pretrained for causal modeling, then trained for retrieval via InfoNCE. Validation models were trained as autoencoders once, rather than trained followed by a freeze on the encoders and re-trained.
official.metric: Token accuracy (% of non-pad input tokens exactly regenerated, higher is better) on held-out data; also entropy ratio H_r and decoder cross-entropy loss. No ± reported (single runs).
official.comparison: Frozen autoencoder-trained encoder vs. frozen causal-LM-trained encoder (and causal->retrieval, untrained), same architecture, size, data, and inversion-decoder training, for both masked mixers and transformers
official.falsification_criterion: Under matched architecture, data, and inversion-decoder budget, the causal-trained encoder's embedding allows token recovery comparable to the autoencoder's (e.g. the autoencoder's advantage shrinks to a few percentage points), or the autoencoder's embedding does not allow substantially more than ~5% token recovery.

title: Finding Interpretable Prompt-Specific Circuits in Language Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 5 (supporting: Figures 18, 19, 23 in Appendix E, pages 27-28)

official.background: Circuit tracing in mechanistic interpretability tries to find the small set of model components and the information passed between them that explains a model's behaviour on a prompt. Patching-based methods need many forward passes and counterfactual prompts. Attention-causal communication (ACC, Franco & Crovella, NeurIPS 2025) instead traces, from a single forward pass, which upstream components write into low-dimensional subspaces of an attention head's QK matrix that cause the head to attend to a given token pair. ACC traces are noisy, though: they contain many components and high-dimensional signals, which makes them hard to read and possibly includes spurious parts.
official.method:
For an attention head (l, a) attending to destination/source tokens (d, s), with QK matrix Omega = W_Q W_K^T = sum_k sigma_k u_k v_k^T, ACC++ decomposes the destination residual into upstream component outputs (embeddings, earlier heads, MLPs) and forms one rank-1 candidate signal per (component, singular direction) pair, u_k u_k^T o_m (source side analogous with v_k). Candidates are scored by Integrated Gradients on the post-softmax attention weight A_ds, then greedily removed (highest first, recomputing attention) until A_ds falls below tau(d) = k/d (the paper states k = 2.5 for IOI; Appendix D gives 1.5 <= k <= 2.5 as the range and does not state k separately for GP/GT). The removed candidates are the signals (edges). The circuit is built by seeding at components with a direct effect on the correct-answer logit direction and recursing upstream over every attention firing in the trace. Bias and RoPE are folded into the token vectors so each head has a single Omega.

The baseline is the original ACC solver (Relative Attention, RA) from [1], which picks subspaces and components separately and uses a linear surrogate on pre-softmax scores. Both are run under the exact experimental setup of [1] (same datasets and protocol, Appendix E) on IOI, Gender Pronoun (GP) and Greater-Than (GT) for GPT-2 Small, Pythia-160M and Gemma-2 2B, and the number of nodes and edges per traced circuit is compared. Appendix E (Figure 23) checks that ACC++ circuits keep comparable precision/recall/F1 against canonical reference circuits.
official.claim: Under the same tracing setup, ACC++ circuits for IOI in GPT-2 Small have 85 ± 1 nodes and 154 ± 3 edges versus 205 ± 2 nodes and 639 ± 9 edges for ACC, and across all 8 task/model settings ACC++ circuits are smaller (about 1.8x to 15x fewer nodes and 2x to over 100x fewer edges; the paper summarizes this as 2x to 10x smaller), while keeping precision/recall against reference circuits comparable to ACC.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of ACC and ACC++ graph sizes across tasks and models. Entries are mean ± std. error.
official.metric: Mean number of nodes and edges per traced circuit (lower = more compact); ± is standard error across prompts. Circuit quality is precision/recall/F1 against canonical reference circuits (Figure 23, no error bars).
official.comparison: ACC++ vs. the original ACC solver (Relative Attention) of Franco & Crovella 2025 on the same prompts, for IOI/GP/GT on GPT-2 Small, Pythia-160M and Gemma-2 2B.
official.falsification_criterion: A reimplementation of ACC++ under the setup of [1] gives GPT-2 Small IOI circuits that are not substantially smaller than ACC's (e.g. node ratio below 1.5x, or edges within a few standard errors), or the smaller ACC++ circuits lose clearly more precision/recall/F1 against the reference IOI circuit than ACC does.

title: How Accurately Can a Gaussian Approximate Stochastic Approximation Iterates?

official.background: Stochastic approximation (SA), x_{k+1} = x_k + α_k (F(x_k) + M_k), underlies SGD and many reinforcement-learning algorithms. Classical results show the rescaled iterate (x_k − x*)/√α_k converges in distribution to a Gaussian, but say nothing about how close it is at finite k. This paper bounds the Wasserstein-1 distance between the rescaled iterate and a Gaussian at each time k, and argues that a time-varying Gaussian with a recursively defined covariance Σ_k is a better finite-time approximation than the classical asymptotic Gaussian.
official.method:
With step sizes α_k = α/(k+K)^ξ, the paper proves d_W(y_k, Σ_k^{1/2} Z) = Õ((k+K)^{-ξ/2}) for the time-varying covariance Σ_k defined by a recursion (Eq. 4.4), while the distance to the asymptotic Gaussian (covariance solving the Lyapunov equation) decays only as (k+K)^{-min(ξ/2, 1−ξ)}, with matching lower bounds (Proposition 4.5) when the noise has non-zero third moment. So the negative log-log slope m is ξ/2 for the time-varying Gaussian and min(ξ/2, 1−ξ) for the asymptotic one, which differ for ξ > 2/3.

Simulation (Appendix B.1-B.2): scalar linear SA x_{k+1} = (1 − α_k A) x_k + α_k M_k with A = 2, α_k = 1/(k+1000)^ξ, additive centered Exponential(1) noise, N = 2×10^8 independent paths, k_max = 100,000. The exact 1D W1 distance between the empirical y_k = x_k/√α_k and N target Gaussian samples (sorted-sample L1) is recorded every 50 iterations, and m̂ is the negative slope of a linear regression of log W1 on log(k+K), for ξ ∈ {0.1, ..., 1.0}.
official.claim: For scalar linear SA with centered exponential noise, the estimated W1 decay slope to the time-varying Gaussian tracks ξ/2 (about 0.39 at ξ = 0.8, 0.40 at ξ = 0.9), while the slope to the asymptotic Gaussian follows min(ξ/2, 1−ξ) and drops (about 0.24 at ξ = 0.8, 0.10 at ξ = 0.9).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: m̂ (estimated negative slope of log-log plot) as a function of step-size parameter ξ
official.metric: m̂ = negative slope of log W1 distance vs. log(k+K) from linear regression (higher means faster convergence); single run, no error bars or confidence intervals reported; values read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Empirical slope to the time-varying Gaussian N(0, Σ_k) vs. empirical slope to the asymptotic Gaussian N(0, Σ), each against its theoretical rate, across ξ from 0.1 to 1
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the simulation, m̂ for the time-varying Gaussian at ξ = 0.8-0.9 is not clearly above m̂ for the asymptotic Gaussian (e.g. gap under ~0.1), or either empirical slope deviates from its theoretical curve by more than ~0.1 for ξ ≤ 0.8.

title: BFS-PO: Best-First Search for Large Reasoning Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (Llama3.2-3B numbers repeated in Table 1 ablation, page 8)

official.background: Large reasoning models trained with RL algorithms such as GRPO and DAPO tend to produce very long chains of thought ('overthinking'), which raises inference cost. Common fixes, such as SFT on compressed CoTs, budget forcing, or length penalties, usually shorten the outputs but lose accuracy relative to the base model. The paper asks whether changing how RL explores the solution space, rather than the reward, can shorten reasoning without hurting accuracy.
official.method:
BFS-PO replaces DAPO's G independent samples per question with a small search tree. After an initial group of samples, it selects the shortest correct completion, finds the token in it with the highest predictive entropy (not used before as a backtracking point), and samples a new group of completions conditioned on the question plus that prefix. This is repeated K = 3 times, so N = (K+1)·G_B completions are generated per question, matching DAPO's G_D = 32. Leaf rewards are DAPO's correctness reward plus the soft overlong penalty. Internal-node rewards average their children, and token-level advantages are normalized by the mean/std of leaf rewards. The DAPO clipped objective is used (eps_l = 0.2, eps_h = 0.28). Inference is ordinary single-chain sampling.

In the in-domain (ID) protocol from TokenSkip, models are trained on the GSM8K train split and tested on the GSM8K test split with greedy decoding and a 512-token budget. Training uses TRL with LoRA (r = 8, alpha = 16), AdamW lr 1e-6, and a generation batch of 2048. For the 3B models, both BFS-PO and DAPO get a 24-hour budget on 4 A100s, and the checkpoint with the highest AES is selected. Metrics are average output length in tokens (including the answer), accuracy, and AES (a combined length/accuracy score relative to zero-shot).
official.claim: On GSM8K (in-domain protocol, greedy decoding, 512-token budget), BFS-PO fine-tuning of Llama3.2-3B-Instruct gives an average output length of 151 tokens vs. 200 for DAPO under the same budget (-25%) with equal accuracy (85.8 vs. 85.6). The same direction holds on all 5 base models (5-model average 173 vs. 225 tokens, accuracy 89.9 vs. 90.0).

official.metric: Average output length in tokens (lower is better) and accuracy % (higher is better) on the GSM8K test set; AES (higher is better). Single training run, deterministic greedy evaluation; no error bars reported.

title: ScrapeGraphAI-100k: Dataset for Schema-Constrained LLM Generation

official.background: Many LLM uses, such as tool calls, structured extraction and knowledge-base construction, need output that conforms to a given JSON schema. Public datasets for this task are small, synthetic, or text-only, and rarely pair real web content with the prompts and schemas practitioners actually use. ScrapeGraphAI-100k fills this gap with 93,695 real extraction events drawn from opt-in ScrapeGraphAI library telemetry. Each event pairs Markdown page content with a prompt, a JSON schema, the LLM response, a jsonschema-rs validity label and schema-complexity metadata.
official.method:
For the case study, the authors filter the corpus to schema ≤10k chars, content ≤50k chars and response ≤10k chars, then regenerate target outputs with GPT-5-nano. The released fine-tuning subset (scrapegraph-100k-finetuning) has a fixed 25,244/2,808 train/test split. Qwen3-1.7B is fine-tuned with QLoRA (4-bit, LoRA rank 16 on all attention and MLP linear layers, lr 1e-4, cosine schedule, 2 epochs, one A100 80GB) using completion-only loss, so gradients flow only through the assistant's JSON output.

All models are evaluated with vLLM greedy decoding using one fixed prompt ('Extract data from the content according to the JSON schema. Schema: {schema} Content: {content} Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema.'), with no constrained decoding, JSON mode or few-shot examples. The test split is 2,714 examples after dropping those over the 8,192-token context. Metrics: valid-JSON rate; schema-compliance rate; key precision, recall and F1 over flattened dot-notation key paths with [*] wildcards for arrays; mean missing and extra keys per sample; a type-aware value score; and overall BLEU on the serialized JSON. All are scored against the GPT-5-nano targets.

title: COMPOT: Calibration-Optimized Matrix Procrustes Orthogonalization for Transformers Compression

official.background: Post-training compression of LLMs by matrix factorization usually means truncated SVD (often activation-aware, e.g. SVD-LLM). That puts every column of a weight matrix in one shared low-rank subspace. Sparse dictionary learning (e.g. CoSpaDi) instead writes the weight as a dictionary times a column-sparse coefficient matrix, which gives a union-of-subspaces model, but it relies on slow iterative K-SVD/OMP updates. COMPOT asks whether constraining the dictionary to be orthogonal keeps the flexibility of sparse coding while making each update closed-form, and whether that improves the accuracy-compression trade-off without any fine-tuning.
official.method:
For each linear projection W (Q/K/V/O and gate/up/down; embeddings and lm_head untouched), COMPOT collects calibration activations X (256 FineWeb sequences of length 1024), forms the Gram matrix G = X^T X = L L^T (Cholesky), and factorizes the whitened weight L^T W ≈ D S. D is an orthogonal (complete/undercomplete, k ≤ m) dictionary and S has at most s nonzeros per column. Alternating minimization starts from the top-k left singular vectors and runs 20 iterations of two steps: sparse coding by hard-thresholding D^T (L^T W) to the s largest entries per column, and a dictionary update by orthogonal Procrustes (SVD of (L^T W) S^T = P Λ Q^T, D ← P Q^T). The stored factors are A = L^{-T} D and S (nonzeros plus a bitmask), with k/s = 2. The compression ratio is CR = 1 − (16mk + 16sn + kn)/(16mn).

In the static setting (COMPOT†), every projection gets the same CR, with no dynamic allocation. Baselines are SVD-LLM (truncation-aware whitening SVD) and CoSpaDi (calibration-guided K-SVD dictionary learning), both compressed to the same CR. Evaluation uses lm-evaluation-harness 0.4.8 zero-shot (normalized accuracy where available) on PIQA, HellaSwag, LAMBADA-OpenAI, ARC-e, ARC-c, SciQ, RACE and MMLU, plus WikiText and LAMBADA perplexity.
official.claim: On Llama3.2-1B at a uniform compression ratio of 0.2, static COMPOT† reaches 48.5 average zero-shot accuracy over 8 tasks, vs. 42.7 for CoSpaDi and 37.6 for SVD-LLM (uncompressed: 57.6), and has lower WikiText perplexity (25 vs. 64 vs. 170).
official.claim_caption: Table 12: Performance comparison under static (COMPOT†) and dynamic (COMPOT) vs state-of-the-art SVD-based SVD-LLM and dictionary-learning CoSpaDi on Llama3.2-1B at different compression levels on different benchmarks. Best results are shown in bold.
official.metric: Average zero-shot accuracy (%) over PIQA, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, ARC-e, ARC-c, SciQ, RACE, MMLU, higher is better; WikiText perplexity, lower is better. Table 12 is a single run with no error bars. Table 24 (dynamic COMPOT, same model and CR) reports a std of 0.3 for average accuracy over 5 calibration-sampling seeds.
official.comparison: COMPOT† (static CR, orthogonal dictionary + hard-thresholding) vs. CoSpaDi (K-SVD dictionary learning) and SVD-LLM, all at CR 0.2 on Llama3.2-1B with the same calibration and evaluation
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running all three methods on Llama3.2-1B at CR 0.2 with matched calibration, COMPOT†'s average accuracy is not clearly above CoSpaDi's (e.g. the gap is under ~2 points, or CoSpaDi wins), or COMPOT†'s WikiText perplexity is not lower than CoSpaDi's.

title: Stability Regimes for Framing-Sensitive Fine-Tuning in Language Models
claim_source: Table E.5, page 21 (same means in Table 7, page 9)

official.background: LLM agents are increasingly used to simulate how people react to (mis)information, and such simulators are usually built by fine-tuning a base model into personas. Fine-tuning often changes behavior globally (bias drift, degenerate heuristics, changed baseline accuracy), which confounds any experiment that wants to study one specific bias. The paper asks whether supervised fine-tuning can be tuned to shift only a narrow decision tendency, here accepting false claims written in a particular rhetorical framing, while keeping overall accuracy and confidence unchanged, and whether such small per-decision shifts matter once decisions influence what the agent sees next.
official.method:
FrameRef rewrites FEVER/FEVEROUS claims into five framings (Authoritative, Consensus, Emotional, Sensationalist, Prestige) with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and filters them with a DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B verifier. Personas are LoRA adapters on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct trained with SFT on 15k framed claims to output SUPPORTS or REFUTES (loss only on label tokens). For a persona with target framing f*, the loss on examples whose framing is f* and whose label is REFUTES is multiplied by α = 0.3; all other examples have weight 1. The baseline persona is trained identically with α = 1. Three independently trained models per condition.

Sequential exposure task on a framing-balanced eval set (test+dev, 22,005 claims, 132,030 framed instances): at each step the agent labels one claim. With feedback, if the agent says SUPPORTS the next claim is sampled by softmax over the top k = 5 most cosine-similar unseen claims (all-MiniLM-L12-v2, window w = 3), restricted to refuted claims if the accepted claim was false; if it says REFUTES the next claim is uniform random. Without feedback every claim is uniform random. Label probabilities are summed token log-probs of the full label. Cumulative score over T = 100 steps: linear (r_t = +P(a_t|s_t) if correct, −P(a_t|s_t) if wrong) and log (r_t = log P(true label)). 100 trajectories per model, 300 per condition.
official.claim: With Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and feedback-driven exposure, the Authoritative-attenuated persona (α = 0.3, 15k samples) scores a mean cumulative log score of -147.91 (95% CI -151.51 to -144.53) vs. -128.77 (-131.59 to -125.99) for the α = 1 baseline, and linear 2.69 (1.13 to 4.26) vs. 7.38 (5.99 to 8.78); without feedback the gap shrinks to -115.07 vs. -110.55 (log) and reverses to 17.47 vs. 16.04 (linear).
official.claim_caption: Table E.5: Llama-8B cumulative score results with and without feedback statistical details (3-model averages; 100 trajectories each).
official.metric: Cumulative score over T = 100 steps, higher (closer to 0 for log) is better; mean over 300 trajectories (3 models x 100 each); Table E.5 also reports an SD and 95% CI bounds (CI95 low/high) but does not state how they were computed or over what units
official.comparison: Authoritative-target persona (α = 0.3) vs. baseline persona fine-tuned with α = 1, each in the feedback and no-feedback simulators; other target framings (Consensus, Prestige, Sensationalist) also reported

title: TAC: Timestamped Audio Captioning

official.background: Large audio-language models usually learn from clip-level captions, where one sentence describes a 10-30 s clip. As a result they struggle to say when each sound happens in scenes where sounds overlap, and they often describe sounds that are not in the audio. Timestamped dense captioning asks a model to list every sound event with a start time and an end time. That combines sound event detection with open-vocabulary captioning, and the output is a structured text record that can be reused for downstream reasoning.
official.method:
TAC fine-tunes Qwen2-Audio with LoRA (rank 128, alpha 256, 5k iterations, global batch size 32, 8x A100). The backbone first gets continued pretraining on licensed single-source audio paired with captions. The training data mixes four streams: synthetic mixtures from a template-driven Dynamic Acoustic Mixer (about 150K clips, 1.2K hours, with ground-truth timestamps computed from RMS activity), SED data, the TACOS training set, and diarization corpora. Each training prompt randomly sets the caption style (keywords, brief or detailed), the merge threshold, the activity threshold and the time resolution, and the target text is changed to match those settings. Timestamps are atomic special tokens, and the loss upweights them (lambda_time = 5.0). At inference the defaults are brief style, merge 0.25 s, activity 0.05 and resolution 0.10 s, chosen on a separate development set.

Evaluation uses the TACOS test set. Predicted events are matched one-to-one and greedily to ground-truth events. A pair can match only if GPT-OSS-120B at temperature 0 rates its semantic similarity at least 0.5 and the two events overlap in time or one contains the other. On the matched events, the paper computes Event-based F1 (an onset must fall within ±1.0 s of the ground-truth onset) and Segment-based F1 (100 ms segments). Hal% is the share of predicted events whose FLAM audio-text confidence is below 0.25. Each baseline was run zero-shot and few-shot (with in-context examples of the output format), and the better of the two is reported.
official.claim: On the TACOS test set, TAC reaches Event-F1 0.50, Segment-F1 0.71 and a hallucination rate of 4.9%. The baselines score Event-F1 0.42, Segment-F1 0.64 and Hal% 6.1 (Gemini 3 Pro); Event-F1 0.37, Segment-F1 0.66 and Hal% 7.3 (Qwen3-Omni); and Event-F1 0.27, Segment-F1 0.55 and Hal% 11.6 (Audio Flamingo 3).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comprehensive Evaluation. (a) Training ablations and baselines. (b) Post-hoc controllability analysis on the TACOS test set; the bold default was fixed on a separate development set before evaluation and was not selected using this sweep.
official.metric: Event-based F1 with a ±1.0 s onset collar after LLM-judge semantic matching (higher is better). Segment F1 at 100 ms and Hal% (FLAM confidence < 0.25, lower is better) are secondary. All values are single runs; ± is not reported.
official.comparison: TAC (Qwen2-Audio + LoRA, default inference settings) vs. Gemini 3 Pro, Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct and Audio Flamingo 3, each prompted zero-shot or few-shot (best of the two), on the TACOS test set with the same matching and metrics
official.falsification_criterion: Under the paper's matching protocol, a TAC model trained as described (or the released checkpoint, if one appears) does not beat Gemini 3 Pro on TACOS Event-F1, or its lead is under about 0.03. Re-evaluating Gemini 3 Pro with this protocol giving an Event-F1 of 0.50 or more would also refute the claim.

title: VETime: Vision Enhanced Zero-Shot Time Series Anomaly Detection

official.background: Zero-shot time-series anomaly detection asks a single pretrained model to flag anomalous timestamps on unseen datasets without any target-domain training. Existing zero-shot detectors are either 1D time-series foundation models (TimeRCD, DADA, Chronos, MOMENT), which localize point anomalies well but see only a local window, or vision/VLM-based detectors that render the series as an image, which capture long-range context but localize poorly and are slow. The paper asks whether fusing a 1D temporal encoder with a 2D visual encoder, aligned on a shared timeline, gives better zero-shot detection than either alone.
official.method:
VETime converts each univariate series into an RGB image (R = raw series, G = trend, B = remainder from a DLinear-style decomposition, each min-max scaled), folds it into a 2D grid using an autocorrelation-estimated period, and resizes it to 224x224 (linear interpolation along time, copy-padding along the period axis). A frozen MAE ViT-Base encoder extracts visual features, which Patch-level Temporal Alignment maps back onto the 1D patch timeline (unfold, interpolate, average-pool over periods, plus learnable positional encoding and self-attention). In parallel, the instance-normalized, patched series (patch size 16) goes through an 8-layer transformer time-series encoder initialized from TimeRCD's pretrained weights, whose base weights are frozen and which is adapted with LoRA (r = 8, alpha = 16). The temporal and aligned visual features pass through dual cross-attention (each modality queries the other, plus residual FFN) to give Z_TS and Z_V; during training, intra-/inter-window contrastive losses around labelled anomaly context windows act on these, and the anomaly-enhanced feature is F_A = FFN([Z_TS; Z_V]) (no windows at inference). A task-adaptive router (weights from F_A) fuses the temporal, visual and anomaly-enhanced features into separate anomaly-classification (BCE) and reconstruction (MSE) heads, with an entropy load-balancing loss (lambda_aw = 0.1, lambda_e = 0.2, tau = 0.1). The anomaly score at inference is the classification head's per-timestamp probability only (no reconstruction error).

Training uses only a 0.5-billion-point synthetic corpus generated from mathematical equations following TimeRCD (Lan et al., 2025), with batch size 32, AdamW at lr 5e-4, up to 25 epochs with early stopping on a synthetic validation split. Evaluation is zero-shot on the 11 univariate TSB-AD datasets. For Table 9, TimeRCD and DADA are retrained on the same synthetic dataset and all three methods are run with 5 seeds; the per-timestamp anomaly score is evaluated with VUS-PR (threshold-free) and Affiliation-F1.
official.claim: When VETime, TimeRCD and DADA are all trained on the same synthetic corpus (5 seeds), VETime has higher zero-shot VUS-PR on NAB (32.84 ± 0.21 vs. best baseline 24.46 ± 0.79), WSD (33.16 ± 0.65 vs. 30.38 ± 1.05) and YAHOO (87.92 ± 1.06 vs. 84.23 ± 0.75).
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Performance comparison of supervised baselines re-trained on the same synthetic dataset (mean ± standard deviation over 5 runs). Best result is in red, second-best is in blue.
official.metric: VUS-PR (%) on TSB-AD univariate datasets, higher is better, mean ± std over 5 independent training runs (random seeds)
official.comparison: VETime vs. TimeRCD and DADA, all retrained on the same 0.5B-point synthetic dataset and evaluated zero-shot
official.falsification_criterion: With all three models trained on the same synthetic data, VETime's mean VUS-PR on NAB, WSD or YAHOO is not above the best of TimeRCD/DADA by more than the combined seed std (e.g. NAB margin under ~2 points, WSD under ~1.5, YAHOO under ~1.5).

title: SourceBench: Can AI Answers Reference Quality Web Sources?

official.background: Search-augmented LLMs and AI search tools answer questions by citing web pages, and users rely on those citations to check answers. Existing benchmarks score the answer text (HotpotQA, HLE) or retrieval relevance (RAGAS, RAGBench), not whether the cited sources themselves are relevant, accurate, neutral, current, accountable and readable. If a system cites low-quality pages, the answer inherits their flaws.
official.method:
SourceBench has 100 queries, 20 each sampled from VA-COS NLQ (shopping), HotpotQA (multi-hop reasoning), Pinocchios (factuality), DebateQA (argumentative) and Quora Question Pairs (social Q&A). For each of 12 systems (GPT-5, GPT-4o, Gemini-3-Pro, Gemini-3-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Grok-4.1-Fast in non-reasoning mode, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Perplexity-Sonar-Pro, and the Exa, Tavily and Gensee search APIs, plus Google Search API top-5), the URLs cited in the final answer (or returned by the search API) are collected and the full page text is scraped; 3996 sources in total.

Each source is scored 1-5 on eight rubrics: content relevance (CR), factual accuracy (FA), objectivity/neutrality (NE), freshness (FR), ownership accountability (OA), author accountability (AA), domain authority (DA) and layout clarity (LC). Scoring is done by a few-shot Qwen-Plus judge with three separate prompts (content, metadata, layout; full prompts in Appendix B), calibrated on 45 pages labelled by two graduate students (per-rubric MAE 0.37-0.91 vs. human average, Table 3). Scores are averaged over all sources and queries per system; the 'Weighted' score gives the three content rubrics weight 1.5 and the five meta rubrics weight 1, rescaled so the maximum is 100.
official.claim: On SourceBench's 100 queries, sources cited by GPT-5 get the highest weighted quality score (89.08/100), ahead of Grok-4.1-Fast (83.38), Gensee (81.80), GPT-4o (81.52) and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (81.28), and GPT-5 ranks first on six of eight rubrics (FA 4.77, NE 4.55, OA 4.79, AA 4.43, DA 4.74, LC 4.02); Tavily ranks last (78.27).
official.claim_caption: Table 4. Overall Evaluation Results. Weighted gives the first three columns a 1.5 weight and scales the max to 100. Avg shows the average score of the eight metrics. Evaluating systems are first grouped by type and then ordered by their weighted overall score.
official.metric: Weighted SourceBench score (0-100, higher is better; content rubrics weighted 1.5x), plus per-rubric mean scores on a 1-5 scale as judged by a few-shot Qwen-Plus evaluator. No ± reported; single run, no seeds or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: GPT-5's cited sources vs. those of 7 other search-enabled LLMs, 3 AI search APIs (Gensee, Exa, Tavily) and Google Search top-5, all on the same 100 queries and scored by the same evaluator
official.falsification_criterion: Re-collecting sources for the same queries and scoring them with the paper's rubric prompts, GPT-5 does not have the highest weighted score, or its lead over the second-best system shrinks to within the spread observed across repeated collection/judging runs (e.g. under ~2 points).

title: Duality Models: An Embarrassingly Simple One-step Generation Paradigm
claim_source: Figure 4a, page 8 (best-FID values 63.86 and 76.04 stated in Sec. 4.4 text, page 7)

official.background: Consistency-style one-step generators such as Shortcut models and MeanFlow train a single network conditioned on a target time r: when r = t it regresses the local flow-matching velocity (stable), and when r = 0 it learns the global flow-map used for one-step sampling (unstable). Because each training sample is used for only one of these two objectives, these methods spend most of the batch (e.g. 75% in MeanFlow) on the velocity objective to keep training stable, which leaves the flow-map that is actually used at inference under-trained. Making one-step training more data-efficient matters because these models aim to replace 50-250-step diffusion sampling.
official.method:
DuMo ('one input, dual output') keeps the DiT backbone and adds a second output projection head (about 3M extra parameters on a 675M DiT). For every noisy input x_t = t*z + (1-t)*x, one head predicts the velocity v (target z - x, plain flow-matching L2 loss) and the other predicts the flow-map u with a consistency loss whose target is v_t - t * du/dt, computed with a stop-gradient copy and a JVP-free central finite-difference estimate of the time derivative. The total loss is beta * L_v + (1 - beta) * L_u, so every sample supervises both heads. Training-time classifier-free guidance enhances the velocity target (v_t <- v_t + zeta * (sg(v) - v_uncond)), times are sampled from Beta(theta1, theta2), and plain unweighted L2 is used throughout.

The baseline MeanFlow is a single-branch model that, for each sample, uses the velocity loss with probability rho and the flow-map loss otherwise. In Figure 4a both are trained on ImageNet-1K 256x256 in SD-VAE latent space with a DiT-B/2 backbone for 10K iterations at learning rate 2e-4 (AdamW, betas (0.9, 0.95), global batch 512), and evaluated by one-step (1 NFE) FID-50K. The x-axis 'velocity ratio' is beta (loss weight) for DuMo and rho (sample fraction) for MeanFlow, swept from 0.1 to about 0.99.
official.claim: On ImageNet 256x256 with a DiT-B/2 trained for 10K iterations, DuMo's best one-step FID-50K over the velocity-ratio sweep is 63.86 vs. 76.04 for the best MeanFlow setting, and DuMo is about 10-14 FID better at every ratio from 0.3 to 0.8 (e.g. ~78 vs. ~92 at 0.5); at 0.1-0.2 the two are within ~4 FID and above ~0.95 DuMo collapses (FID ~98-126).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4. Ablation studies of DuMo on ImageNet-1K 256x256. We investigate key design factors of DuMo for one-step generation, benchmarking against the single-branch baseline, MeanFlow. Unless noted otherwise, experiments in (a) and (c) employ a DiT-B/2 backbone trained for 10K iterations with a learning rate of 2e-4, adhering to the optimization protocol in Sec. 4.1. title: Structure-Adaptive Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Kernel Methods

official.background: Estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) from observational data is hard when the baseline outcome functions are complex and when overlap is weak, meaning the propensity score gets close to 0 or 1. Doubly robust and R-learner style methods depend on estimating the propensity score, and inverse-propensity weighting becomes unstable under weak overlap. The CATE itself is often much simpler (smoother, sparse or low-dimensional) than the nuisance outcome functions. The paper asks whether a kernel method can reach error rates set by the simpler CATE class without estimating the propensity score.
official.method:
Algorithm 1 ('Ours') fits each treatment arm's outcome function with undersmoothed kernel ridge regression (KRR) in a nuisance RKHS F. It then forms switch-imputed pseudo-outcomes: m_i = y_i - f0_hat(x_i) for treated units and m_i = f1_hat(x_i) - y_i for control units. Finally it runs a second KRR of m_i on x_i in a simpler target kernel space H. No propensity score is estimated. In the experiments, the raw nuisance ridge is fixed at 0.01. The target kernel and ridge are chosen by Algorithm 2: candidates are fit on one split, nuisances are refit on a second split, candidates are scored against switch-imputed proxies on a third split, and predictions are averaged over the three cyclic fits.

Multivariate synthetic setup (Appendix C.2): X ~ Unif([-1,1]^d), f0(x) = (2/d) sum_{j=1}^d sin(x_j), h(x) = (0.3/p) sum_{j=1}^p x_j^2, A ~ Bernoulli(clip(sin(5||x||_2), kappa, 1-kappa)), Y = f0(X) + A h(X) + N(0, sigma^2), with defaults sigma = 1 and kappa = 0.1. The nuisance kernel is Matern nu = 1.5. Ours selects among Matern 1.5, Matern 2.5 and RBF target kernels, each on all coordinates or on x_{1:4}. Baselines are plug-in KRR (T-learner, 3-fold CV), the DR-learner (Kennedy 2023), oracle-propensity DR and the R-learner (Nie and Wager 2021). DR, oracle DR and R use Matern 2.5 target kernels with cross-fitting and receive the true support in sparse settings. Estimated propensities are clipped to [0.01, 0.99]. The metric is MISE on 3,000 held-out uniform test points.
official.claim: In the four multivariate sample-size settings ((d,p) = (10,10) and (10,4), n = 1000 and 2000, sigma = 1, kappa = 0.1, 100 replications), the two-stage switch-imputation KRR estimator has the lowest CATE MISE every time. For example, at (10,10), n = 1000 it gets 0.0099 (SE 0.0008), against 0.0127 (0.0012) for the R-learner, 0.0184 (0.0049) for DR, 0.0201 (0.0031) for oracle DR and 0.0478 (0.0018) for plug-in KRR.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Multivariate synthetic results. Entries are mean MISE (SE), with the smallest mean in bold. Unless varied, sigma = 1 and kappa = 0.1; the sigma = 1 row also supplies the kappa = 0.1 reference. p = d is dense and p = 4 is sparse. Sample-size rows use fixed kernel lengths; other rows use median-calibrated lengths. The sigma = 1 row at (d, p) = (20, 4) also gives the default representation library.
official.metric: Mean integrated squared error of the CATE estimate over 3,000 test points (lower is better); the value in parentheses is the Monte Carlo standard error of the mean over replications (100 for the sample-size rows, 30 for the sweeps)
official.comparison: Ours (Algorithm 1 + Algorithm 2 selection) vs. plug-in KRR, DR-learner, oracle-propensity DR-learner and R-learner, on the same datasets and test points
official.falsification_criterion: In the sample-size rows, the R-learner or DR-learner matches or beats Ours in mean MISE, or the gap between Ours and the best baseline falls within about one combined standard error (e.g. (10,10), n = 1000: R <= ~0.0113 with Ours ~0.0099).

title: Evaluating Test-Time Scaling of General LLM Agents

official.background: LLM agents are usually benchmarked in domain-specific setups where the environment exposes only the tools for one task type (e.g., a terminal for SWE-Bench, a browser for web navigation). Real deployments do not tell the agent the task category in advance, so the agent must pick tools from a large mixed pool. The paper asks how much agent performance depends on this domain-specific scaffolding and then uses the unified setting to study sequential and parallel test-time scaling.
official.method:
General AgentBench samples long-horizon tasks from seven benchmarks in four domains: BrowseComp (124) and WebVoyager (65) for search, SWE-Bench Verified (50) and Terminal-Bench (80) for coding, MathHay (75) for reasoning, Tau2-Bench (50) and MCP-Bench (52) for tool calling. Each benchmark environment is wrapped as an MCP server, and a single Host exposes all tools (301 tools across 35 servers) to the agent as one registry, routing each call to the right server. All servers run simultaneously, so the agent can call irrelevant tools from other domains, and each task is scored with the benchmark's original evaluator (binary reward, except MCP-Bench, which is continuous in 0-1).

For each of ten models the authors report the score under the Baseline (B) setting, i.e., the benchmark's own domain-specific configuration with only its own tools, and under the General (G) setting, i.e., the same tasks with the unified tool pool, as mean ± std over 3 runs, plus the relative change. Models are called through Amazon Bedrock and the Hugging Face Inference API.
official.claim: Moving from each benchmark's domain-specific setting to the unified General AgentBench tool pool lowers GPT-OSS-120B's average score from 36.6 to 26.1 (-28.7% relative), including Tau2-Bench 63.0 ± 5.12 -> 26.0 ± 1.32 and Terminal-Bench 18.1 ± 1.26 -> 6.3 ± 0.35; all ten evaluated models drop on average (relative drops 7.0% to 31.2%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Per-benchmark decomposition of General AgentBench. For each model we report performance (mean ± std over n=3 runs) on every constituent benchmark, grouped by domain; the first row is the Baseline (B) setting, the second row is the General (G) setting, and the third row shows the relative change (∆%) from B to G: red ▼ denotes degradation, green ▲ denotes improvement. Bold marks the best and underline the second-best score.
official.metric: Per-benchmark task success rate in % (MCP-Bench: mean continuous score), higher is better; ± is std over n=3 runs. The Avg column has no std.
official.comparison: Same model and task subset under the Baseline (domain-specific tools only) vs. the General (unified 301-tool MCP registry) setting
official.falsification_criterion: Running GPT-OSS-120B on the same task subsets, the General-setting score on Tau2-Bench or Terminal-Bench is within a few run-to-run standard deviations of the Baseline score, or its 7-benchmark average drops by much less than the reported ~10 points; more broadly, a sizeable share of the ten models shows no average degradation.

title: Back to Blackwell: Closing the Loop on Intransitivity in Multi-Objective Preference Fine-Tuning

official.background: Preference fine-tuning of LLMs increasingly uses LLM judges, often prompted with prompt-specific rubrics or checklists. Judge preferences are often intransitive (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A), either because the judge is inconsistent on a single criterion or because several criteria are collapsed into one score. With intransitive preferences there is no well-defined best policy, so reward-model-based pipelines lack a sound target. Game-theoretic self-play methods handle intransitivity for a single objective, but the minimax theorem fails with multiple objectives, so those methods do not directly extend to rubric-based feedback.
official.method:
The paper defines the Maximum Entropy Blackwell Winner: the policy that maximizes its worst-case preference over checklist items against a KL-regularized adversary policy. The adversary has a closed-form solution, and the worst-case criterion is chosen per prompt by taking a minimum. This leaves a single-player problem, which PROSPER solves with REBEL-style square-loss regression on differences of estimated gradients. The gradients are computed from pairwise judge scores between samples of the current policy and the reference policy (M = 2), and the most informative pairs are kept by filtering on the size of the score gap.

Policies are Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (and 3B) trained for 2 epochs on WildChecklists prompts. Qwen3-14B serves as a pairwise per-checklist-item judge (5-point Likert scale, averaged over both orderings and repeated samples). The main baseline is RLCF (Viswanathan et al., 2025), re-implemented in the same REBEL pipeline: per-item scores are combined with LLM-generated weights (from Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) into a single scalar reward. Two ablations are also run: PROSPER-JC (one joint-checklist score) and PROSPER-VB (fixed reference competitor). The models are evaluated on Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval 2.0 with gpt-5-mini as the evaluation judge.
official.claim: At 7B (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, WildChecklists, Qwen3-14B judge), PROSPER beats the matched RLCF re-implementation on Arena-Hard vanilla (49.2 vs 42.5) and AlpacaEval 2.0 vanilla (55.4 vs 41.4) and length-controlled (37.61 vs 17.24) win rates.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Highest score is bolded and second highest underlined. Across instruction following and general chat benchmarks, PROSPER consistently outperforms the RLCF baseline and PROSPER-JC and PROSPER-VB baselines at the 7B parameter scale.
official.metric: Win rate (%) against the benchmark reference, judged by gpt-5-mini; higher is better. Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: PROSPER vs. RLCF (re-implemented with the REBEL optimizer) vs. PROSPER-JC and PROSPER-VB ablations vs. base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, all trained on the same data with the same judge
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained PROSPER 7B policy fails to beat the matched RLCF policy on Arena-Hard vanilla and AlpacaEval vanilla by a clear margin (for example, less than 3 points), or the ordering flips across training seeds.

title: Asking the Right Questions: Improving Reasoning with Generated Stepping Stones

official.background: Reasoning LLMs are trained and scaffolded mostly to solve or verify the given problem directly. Humans facing a hard problem often first pose and solve an easier related 'stepping stone' problem, such as a special case or a smaller instance. The paper asks whether LLMs can generate such stepping-stone questions, and whether solving one first and then conditioning on it helps a fixed solver on hard math problems. If good stones exist and can be generated, stone generation becomes a trainable skill.
official.method:
ARQ uses a stone generator phi and a fixed solver pi, both reasoning LLMs. Given a target problem x, phi generates a stepping stone z (prompted to produce a related but easier problem, e.g. a special case). pi solves it, giving y_z, and then solves x with (z, y_z) in the prompt. Thinking tokens are stripped before passing outputs on, and y_z is used as-is without verification. A stone's score S(z, x) is the expected correctness on x over rollouts of (y_z, y), checked against ground truth with Math-Verify.

In Section 4.1 the solver is GPT-OSS-120B with low reasoning effort on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 (30 problems each), and with high effort on BeyondAIME (100 problems). For each problem, each generator produces 20 stones and each stone gets 20 rollouts. Generators: Rand (a generator that does not see x and is asked for a random AMC/AIME-style problem, prompt in Figure 14; the paper does not state which model or reasoning effort generates the Rand stones), ARQ low (GPT-OSS-120B, low effort), and ARQ high (GPT-OSS-120B, high effort). To avoid selection bias, the best stone per problem is picked using the first 10 rollouts and scored on the remaining 10. Solver only is the solver with no stone.
official.claim: With GPT-OSS-120B (low effort) as solver, conditioning on the best of 20 stones generated by GPT-OSS-120B (high effort), selected on held-out rollouts, raises accuracy to 75.0% on AIME 2024 and 66.3% on AIME 2025, vs. about 58.6%/52.6% for solver only and 55.3%/51.0% for the best of 20 random stones.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3 The performance of ARQ variants conditioned on the best stepping stone. Existing LLMs can generate highly useful stepping stones that increase the success rate on the target problems, and LLMs with better reasoning capabilities generate better stepping stones. In contrast, the best stone from Rand does not improve over the Solver only baseline (horizontal dashed lines). To avoid selection bias, we use half of the rollouts to select the best stones while we report the score using the other half.
official.metric: Accuracy on the target problems (higher is better), averaged over problems using 10 held-out rollouts of the best-selected stone per problem; no error bars, seeds or CIs reported
official.comparison: ARQ high (best stone) vs. ARQ low (best stone) vs. Rand (best random stone) vs. Solver only, with the same solver on the same problems
official.falsification_criterion: On AIME 2024 or AIME 2025, the held-out accuracy of the best ARQ-high stone is not clearly above both solver only and the best Rand stone, e.g. less than about 5 points above the better of the two.

title: Value Entanglement: Conflation Between Different Kinds of Good In (Some) Large Language Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (full table in Appendix F.1, pages 23-24); significance in Section 3.1, page 4

official.background: People treat different kinds of value as distinct: a good deed, a good sentence and an expensive object are good in different ways. If an LLM mixes these up, so that its judgment of one kind of value leaks into another, its valuations will be distorted relative to human norms, which matters for value alignment. The paper asks whether LLMs keep moral, grammatical and economic value separate, using behavioral ratings, residual-stream projections and directional ablation.
official.method:
MoralGrammar68 is 17 core action sentences ranging from very immoral to very moral, each written in 4 versions with an increasing number of grammatical errors (0, 1, 2-3, 4+), giving 68 sentences in which morality and grammaticality are varied independently (all items listed in Appendix D, Table S4). Human raters on Prolific (41 per item, separate groups for each dimension) rated each sentence from -10 to +10 for morality and for grammaticality; across items the two human ratings correlate at r = .05.

Each model is prompted (Appendix A.2) to rate sentences from -10 (very ungrammatical) to +10 (perfectly grammatical), or from -10 (very morally wrong) to +10 (very morally virtuous). Models see random 10-item subsets over 100 iterations, decoded greedily. The entanglement measure is the Pearson correlation between a model's grammaticality ratings and the human morality ratings across the 68 sentences. In an unentangled rater it should be near the human value of .05.
official.claim: On MoralGrammar68, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's grammaticality ratings correlate with human morality ratings at r = 0.45 (vs. r = 0.05 between the human morality and grammaticality ratings), while correlating only r = 0.72 with human grammaticality; its morality ratings stay faithful (r = 0.97 with human morality, 0.06 with human grammaticality).

Economic ratings on MoralEconomic68 were correlated with the human ratings for MoralGrammar68 (no morality human ratings exist for MoralEconomic68). Full table in Section F.1

title: DD-CAM: Minimal Sufficient Explanations for Vision Models Using Delta Debugging

official.background: Class Activation Mapping (CAM) methods explain a vision model's prediction by weighting the final-layer feature maps (CNNs) or patch tokens (ViTs) and summing them into a saliency map. Existing variants (Grad-CAM, Score-CAM, Ablation-CAM, etc.) aggregate contributions from every unit, which tends to produce diffuse or fragmented maps. The paper asks instead for a minimal sufficient set: the smallest set of units whose activation alone preserves the prediction, so the map shows only what the decision needs. Whether such maps line up better with human-annotated regions matters for using explanations in settings like medical imaging.
official.method:
DD-CAM caches the final-layer representation (K feature maps for CNNs, N patch tokens for ViTs) and searches for a 1-minimal sufficient subset S* of units using delta debugging: units outside a candidate subset are zero-masked, a partial forward pass through the rest of the network checks whether the top-1 class is unchanged, and the search partitions and removes units until removing any single remaining unit changes the prediction. For heads where units do not interact (global average pooling followed by one linear layer), each unit is tested once in a single sequential pass; for interacting heads (VGG FC stacks, ViTs) the standard recursive delta debugging with initial granularity 2 is used.

Each unit i in S* gets weight w_i proportional to the drop in the predicted-class logit when that unit is masked while the rest of S* stays active, normalized to sum to 1 over S*. The saliency map is the min-max-normalized weighted sum of the selected units, bilinearly upsampled to the input size. For the localization claim, maps are computed for a DenseNet-121 pretrained on chest X-ray data (TorchXRayVision) on 1,000 NIH ChestX-ray14 images with radiologist bounding boxes, and compared with Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, XGrad-CAM, Layer-CAM, Score-CAM, Ablation-CAM (pytorch-grad-cam implementations) and Recipro-CAM using IoU, precision and recall of the highlighted area against the box, and the number of highlighted regions.
official.claim: On 1,000 NIH ChestX-ray14 images with radiologist bounding boxes, DD-CAM saliency maps for a pretrained DenseNet-121 reach IoU 0.263, precision 0.307 and recall 0.692 with 1.00 region per image, versus 0.181 / 0.251 / 0.568 / 1.37 for the strongest baseline (Recipro-CAM) and 0.060 / 0.088 / 0.204 for Grad-CAM.

official.metric: IoU, precision, recall of highlighted region vs. radiologist bounding box (higher is better); number of connected highlighted regions (lower is better). Averages over 1,000 images; the paper says results are averaged over five runs but reports no std, SE or confidence intervals.

title: LEVDA: Latent Ensemble Variational Data Assimilation via Differentiable Dynamics

official.background: Data assimilation combines a dynamical model with sparse, noisy observations to estimate the state (and unknown parameters) of a system such as a flow or the atmosphere. Variational smoothers (4DVar, 4DEnVar) fit a whole trajectory to every observation in a time window but are expensive in the full state space. 4DVar needs adjoint models, and full-state 4DEnVar needs large ensembles plus tuned localization. Recent latent-space filters (Latent-EnSF, LD-EnSF) are cheap and work under sparse observations, but they update sequentially and need a trained observation-to-latent encoder that assumes fixed observation grids.
official.method:
LEVDA starts from a pretrained Latent Dynamics Network (LDNet, taken from LD-EnSF / Xiao et al. 2026): a latent ODE ds/dt = F_theta(s, u), integrated with forward Euler, plus a coordinate-based decoder D_phi(s, xi) that can be queried at any spatial point. The unknown parameters u are appended to the latent state. For each assimilation window, a background ensemble of K window-initial latent states (with optional multiplicative/additive inflation) defines the subspace z(alpha) = mean + P_z alpha. LEVDA minimizes J(alpha) = 0.5||alpha||^2 + 0.5 sum_i ||y_i - H_i(D_phi(s(t_i; alpha)))||^2_{R^-1} over the observations in the window (strong constraint, window tau = 5 by default). Gradients come from autodiff through the latent solver and decoder, optimized with L-BFGS. K independent optimizations, each warm-started at one background member, give the analysis ensemble. No observation encoder is trained.

Tsunami benchmark (adapted from LD-EnSF): shallow-water equations on a 150x150 grid, 2000 simulation steps, with a Gaussian bump at an unknown location as the source parameter. There are 50 observation times (every 40 steps) on a 10x10 subgrid (~0.4% of grid points), with 10% noise-to-signal Gaussian noise. The LDNet latent dimension is 12. K = 100 for the latent methods (LEVDA, LD-EnSF, Latent-EnSF) and K = 40 for full-state 4DEnVar. The metric is the relative RMSE of the ensemble-mean field against the ground truth at each assimilation step.
official.claim: On the tsunami benchmark (0.4% spatial observations, 10% noise), LEVDA's ensemble-mean relative RMSE drops to about 3% within ~5 assimilation steps and stays there, while LD-EnSF needs ~15 steps to reach the same level (about 10-30% at step 5-10). Full-state 4DEnVar (K = 40) diverges to about 500%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Relative RMSE of the ensemble-mean trajectory over time for Kolmogorov flow (left), tsunami modeling (middle), and atmospheric modeling (right); shaded regions show the standard deviation of member-wise relative RMSE.
