title: The Confusion is Real: GRAPHIC – A Network Science Approach to Confusion Matrices in Deep Learning

official.background: Explainability methods usually explain single predictions or rely on human-defined concepts. GRAPHIC instead works at the level of classes: it builds confusion matrices for intermediate layers of a network, treats each one as a directed graph over classes, and uses network-science tools (modularity-based community detection, assortativity) to follow how class confusions change across layers and training epochs. As a side effect of this probing setup, the paper also measures how linearly separable the classes are at each layer over training. There it reports that a vision transformer behaves differently from a CNN.
official.method:
During training, a linear classifier (softmax over W h + b) is fit at regular checkpoints on the features from each intermediate stage of the network under study. It uses the loss λ·CE(z, y) + (1−λ)·CE(z, ỹ), where y is the true label and ỹ is the network's own prediction. For the linear-separability analysis, λ = 1, so the probes see only true labels. The probes are trained on 80% of the CIFAR-100 training split. Accuracy is measured on the held-out 20% ('training set' curves) and on the CIFAR-100 validation split ('validation set' curves).

The network is the efficient vision transformer of Irandoust et al. (2022), called EffVit in the paper, trained from scratch on CIFAR-100 with batch size 64, learning rate 0.001 and AdamW for 1,000 epochs. A probe (learning rate 0.01) is trained every 10 epochs on the outputs of decoders 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12. For comparison, ResNet-50 is trained on CIFAR-100 (Adam, learning rate 0.003, batch size 1,024, 71 epochs) and probed every 5 epochs on the outputs of its four blocks. The paper reports that the ResNet-50 probe accuracies increase and then plateau, with no drop (Appendix Figure 11).
official.claim: In EffVit trained on CIFAR-100, true-label linear-probe accuracy for early decoders peaks early and then declines: decoder 1 goes from about 0.22 (around epoch 200) to about 0.13 (epoch 1000), and decoder 3 from about 0.41 (epochs 200–350) to about 0.32. Over the same run, decoders 9 and 12 rise to about 0.79 and 0.85 validation accuracy and stay there.
official.claim_caption: Figure 7: Linear separability trends in EffVit. Accuracy of CMs generated by LCs trained on true labels for decoders 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12 of EffVit, shown over the training epochs.
official.metric: Accuracy of linear probes trained on true labels (λ = 1), on the held-out 20% of the training split and on the validation split; higher means more linearly separable. Single run with no error bars. The values here are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Probe accuracy at early decoders (1, 3) near their peak (~epoch 200) vs. at the end of training (epoch 1000); contrasted with the later decoders (9, 12) and with ResNet-50, whose probe accuracies increase monotonically (Appendix Figure 11).
official.falsification_criterion: In a reproduction, linear-probe accuracy on decoders 1 and 3 does not fall substantially from its peak by the end of training (for example, decoder 1 stays above about 0.20 and decoder 3 stays above about 0.38 at epoch 1000), or the drop goes away when the probe hyperparameters or seed change.

title: Expanding the Role of Diffusion Models for Robust Classifier Training

official.background: Adversarial training (AT) is the main way to make image classifiers robust to small worst-case input perturbations, and the strongest current recipe (DM-AT) adds millions of synthetic images generated by a diffusion model. That recipe uses the diffusion model only as a data generator. Diffusion models also have intermediate activations that work as good discriminative features, and the paper asks whether those representations can serve as an extra training signal that makes adversarially trained classifiers more robust.
official.method:
Diffusion Representation Alignment (DRA) adds an auxiliary loss to adversarial training. For CIFAR-10, a frozen EDM diffusion model (the same CIFAR-10 checkpoint Wang et al. 2023b used to generate DM-AT synthetic data) receives the image noised at sigma_t = 0.1; the UNet bottleneck activations before the upsampling layers are average-pooled over space to give the target representation h^DR. The classifier's penultimate representation of the adversarial example, f_theta(x_hat), goes through a trainable 3-layer MLP projection head g_proj, and L_DRA = -cos(g_proj(f_theta(x_hat)), h^DR). The total loss is L_AT + lambda * L_DRA with lambda = 1.2 (chosen by a sweep on CIFAR-100, then fixed everywhere).

The adversarial training follows DM-AT: 10-step PGD TRADES (beta = 5), epsilon = 8/255, step size 2/255, SGD momentum 0.9, weight decay 5e-4, lr 0.2 with cosine schedule, and weight averaging (tau = 0.995). For the chosen claim, a WRN-34-10 is trained on CIFAR-10 real data only (no synthetic images), batch 128, 200 epochs, and evaluated with AutoAttack (l_inf, 8/255) on the CIFAR-10 test set.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 (l_inf, eps = 8/255) with WRN-34-10, no synthetic data, batch 128 and 200 epochs, adding DRA to adversarial training raises AutoAttack robust accuracy from 55.25% to 57.29% and clean accuracy from 84.33% to 88.54%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Comparison with state-of-the-art adversarial robustness methods across different settings on CIFAR-10.
official.metric: AutoAttack robust accuracy and clean accuracy (%) on the CIFAR-10 test set, higher is better; single runs, no error bars reported
official.comparison: AT+DRA vs. plain AT (TRADES) under the same architecture, batch size and epochs; AT+ADR and AT+IKL are listed as prior-method references
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction of AT and AT+DRA with matched settings (ideally over several seeds) shows an AutoAttack gain for AT+DRA under about 1 point, or a gain within seed-to-seed variation, or no clean-accuracy gain.

title: MoBiQuant: Mixture-of-Bits Quantization for Token-Adaptive Any-Precision LLM

official.background: Edge devices often need to run an LLM at different weight precisions depending on available memory and compute, but storing one quantized model per precision is expensive. Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods such as OmniQuant calibrate their parameters (clipping, scaling) for one target bit-width, and the paper shows these parameters transfer poorly when the model is run at a different bit-width. The authors attribute this to 'outlier migration': the set of tokens with the largest quantization error changes with precision. Any-precision methods (AnyPrecisionLLM, AnyBCQ) support several bit-widths from one model, but they rely on vector quantization or per-precision scaling factors.
official.method:
MoBiSlice decomposes each linear-layer weight into E = 4 slices of 2 bits by recursive residual quantization (W1 = Q(W), W2 = Q(W - W1), ...), with every slice using scales derived from one shared set of OmniQuant calibration parameters (each slice's scale is the previous one's divided by 2^(b_e) - 1). Summing the first k slices gives a 2k-bit weight. MoBiRoute is a 2-layer MLP router per linear layer that scores, for each token, whether each residual slice should be used. The first slice is always active. A temperature-annealed sigmoid gate becomes a binary mask by the end of calibration, and a budget regularizer pushes the average bit-width from 8 bits down to a 3-bit target on a logarithmic schedule.

Router and OmniQuant parameters (LWC, LET) are calibrated jointly, block by block, on 128 WikiText2 sequences (20 epochs, weight-only, group size 128) with the pretrained weights frozen. At inference the average precision is set by a per-layer threshold on the router scores, chosen as a quantile on calibration data so that a target fraction of slices is active. In Fig. 4 both OmniQuant and MoBiQuant are calibrated at 3 bits. OmniQuant's 3-bit parameters are then reused to quantize the model at 4, 5 and 6 bits, while MoBiQuant changes its threshold to reach the same average bit-widths. The metric is WikiText2 perplexity.
official.claim: With both methods calibrated at 3-bit and evaluated at an unseen 4-bit average precision, MoBiQuant reaches about 2.75 lower WikiText2 perplexity than OmniQuant on LLaMA3-8B (about 7.3 vs. 10.05) and about 2.97 lower on LLaMA3.2-3B (about 9.4 vs. 12.35).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Any-precision inference performance comparison. MoBiQuant outperforms the PTQ baseline across multiple unseen target bit-widths on various LLaMA models, maintaining smooth and fine-grained precision scaling even at extremely low 2–3-bit precision range.
official.metric: WikiText2 perplexity (lower is better) versus average weight bit-width; single runs, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: MoBiQuant (OmniQuant backbone + MoBiSlice + MoBiRoute, calibrated at a 3-bit target) vs. OmniQuant calibrated at 3-bit and run at 3, 4, 5 and 6 bits, on LLaMA3.2-3B, LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B
official.falsification_criterion: With both methods calibrated at 3-bit on 128 WikiText2 samples, MoBiQuant at 4 average bits fails to beat 3-bit-calibrated OmniQuant run at 4 bits by at least about 1 PPL on LLaMA3.2-3B or LLaMA3-8B, or OmniQuant's 3-to-4-bit transfer does not degrade the way the plot shows.

title: 3DSPA: A 3D Semantic Point Autoencoder for Evaluating Video Realism

official.background: Judging whether AI-generated videos are realistic (physically plausible, semantically coherent motion) still relies mostly on human ratings or curated real/fake video pairs, and neither scales. Earlier automated metrics mostly measure frame quality or temporal smoothness. TRAJAN (Allen et al., 2025) scores a video by how well a 2D point-trajectory autoencoder can reconstruct its tracks, but it sees neither depth nor what the objects are. This paper asks whether adding 3D structure and semantic features to such a trajectory autoencoder gives a reference-free realism score that tracks human judgments better.
official.method:
3DSPA is an encoder-decoder over point tracks, initialized from the TRAJAN checkpoint. Each support track (x, y, z, occlusion) is sinusoidally encoded, concatenated with DINOv2 features (frozen) sampled at the track location, and summarized by occlusion-masked self-attention into a readout token; a Perceiver-style transformer compresses all track tokens into a 128 x 64 latent. The decoder takes this latent and a query point (x, y, z, t) and predicts the full 3D trajectory and occlusion flags. It is trained with an L1 position loss plus occlusion BCE (depth predictions are also regularized with a scale-invariant penalty) on 38k Kubric3D scenes and the TAPVid-3D main split, with tracks split half support, half query.

At inference, dense 2D tracks are estimated with CoTracker3 and lifted to 3D with VideoDepthAnything metric depth; half of the tracks are given as support and half are reconstructed. The per-video realism score is the Average Jaccard (AJ, as in TAPVid-3D) of the reconstructed query tracks against the input tracks. On VideoPhy-2, the score is the Spearman rank correlation between per-video AJ and human physical-commonsense (PC) ratings. Ablations: 3DSPA (no 3D) uses 2D tracks plus DINOv2, 3DSPA (no DINO) uses 3D tracks without semantics, and 3DSPA (no 3D, no DINO) is the pretrained TRAJAN checkpoint. None of these is fine-tuned on VideoPhy-2.
official.claim: On VideoPhy-2, per-video Average Jaccard from 3DSPA reaches a Spearman correlation of 0.74 with human physical-commonsense ratings, compared with 0.50 for 3DSPA without DINO features, 0.40 without 3D, and 0.19 for TRAJAN (no 3D, no DINO).
official.claim_caption: Table 3. Spearman rank coefficients on the VideoPhy-2 benchmark for physical commonsense (PC). Video Evaluation Models are fine-tuned vision-language models.
official.metric: Spearman rank correlation between per-video AJ and human PC ratings (higher is better); single numbers, with no seeds, confidence intervals or number of videos reported
official.comparison: 3DSPA vs. its ablations 3DSPA (no DINO), 3DSPA (no 3D), and TRAJAN = 3DSPA (no 3D, no DINO), all scored with the same AJ pipeline on the same videos; fine-tuned VLM evaluators (VideoCon-Physics 0.48, VideoPhy-2 AutoEval 0.76) are listed for reference
official.falsification_criterion: With the released (or retrained) 3DSPA, the Spearman correlation between per-video AJ and VideoPhy-2 human PC ratings is not clearly above that of the no-DINO variant and TRAJAN (e.g. 3DSPA below about 0.6, or within about 0.1 of 3DSPA (no DINO)).

title: TabDLM: Free-Form Tabular Data Generation via Joint Numerical–Language Diffusion
claim_source: Table 3, page 10 (per-dataset values also in Table 14, page 25)

official.background: Synthetic tabular data is used for data augmentation, privacy and training foundation models. Real tables increasingly mix numerical, categorical and free-form text columns. Tabular diffusion models handle numbers and categories well but cannot generate open-vocabulary text, while LLM-based generators produce text naturally but serialize numbers as multi-token strings, which the authors argue hurts the modelling of precise values and of dependencies between numerical and categorical columns.
official.method:
TabDLM starts from the masked diffusion language model LLaDA-8B (frozen, with LoRA rank 16 on attention and MLP layers). Categorical and text cells are tokenized and noised by masked diffusion. Each numerical cell is quantile-normalized, noised with continuous VE/EDM-style Gaussian diffusion (power-mean per-feature schedule following TabDiff, sigma 0.002 to 80), and mapped to a single token embedding by a frozen pretrained float MLP encoder plus a trainable projector; a symmetric projector plus frozen MLP decoder maps outputs back to numbers. One shared time t drives both noise processes. The input sequence is a schema prompt, then categorical/text tokens, then numerical tokens, processed with bidirectional attention. Loss is masked-token cross-entropy plus a warmed-up MSE on the decoded numbers; sampling runs the probability-flow ODE for numbers and iterative unmasking for tokens.

The matched baseline LLaDA-8B SFT uses the same backbone, training data and LoRA recipe but represents numbers as digit tokens. On Adult, Default, Shoppers, Magic and Beijing (TabDiff preprocessing and splits), the synthetic data is scored with Shape (column-wise marginal error) and Trend (pairwise column dependency error), both in percent, lower is better.
official.claim: On five tabular benchmarks without text columns, TabDLM's Trend error averages 2.65% versus 22.10% for LLaDA-8B SFT with the same backbone and data but digit-token numbers, and is lower on every dataset (e.g. Adult 2.74 vs 26.15, Default 2.33 vs 26.30); it is also lower on every dataset than the strongest language-model baseline on Trend, Qwen2.5-7B SFT (average 17.49%).

official.metric: Trend error (%) on pairwise column correlations, lower is better; Shape error (%) also reported. TabDLM, LLaDA-8B SFT and the Qwen baselines are single runs with one fixed seed shared across methods and no error bars. The ± values in Tables 13-14 are mean ± standard deviation over multiple runs, given only for baselines reproduced from prior work (the specialized tabular models and GReaT).

title: Test-Time Scaling with Diffusion Language Models via Reward-Guided Stitching

official.background: A common way to spend more compute at test time on reasoning problems is to sample several chains-of-thought and aggregate them, for example by majority voting on final answers or by picking the trace a verifier rates highest. These trajectory-level methods throw away useful intermediate steps from traces that go wrong later. Masked diffusion language models such as LLaDA can sample many diverse reasoning traces cheaply and in parallel, but their traces are noisy and their accuracy lags behind autoregressive models. The paper asks whether recombining good individual steps from several cheap diffusion traces can recover much of that accuracy.
official.method:
For each problem, LLaDA-8B samples N = 4 independent reasoning traces (low-confidence remasking threshold γ = 0.7, temperature τ = 1.4 for GSM8K and 0.8 for MATH500, generation length 512). Each trace is split into sentence-level steps, and every step is scored in one forward pass by the off-the-shelf process reward model Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B (probability of a marker token inserted after each step). The trace with the highest geometric-mean step score is the 'best CoT'.

Stitching keeps every step of the best CoT (as an anchor) plus every step from any trace whose PRM score is at least δ, orders them chronologically by step index (ties broken by score), and prefixes each with its score ('[c=0.93] ...'). The autoregressive solver Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct receives the problem plus this evidence list and recomputes the final \boxed{} answer with greedy or low-temperature decoding (the paper does not say which was used for Table 4), stopping after a complete \boxed{}. The matched trajectory-level baseline ('Best CoT') feeds the same solver only the single best-scoring trace; 'All CoT' feeds it all four traces concatenated. Accuracy is strict match using math-verify, zero-shot.
official.claim: With the same 4 LLaDA-8B traces, PRM (Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B) and solver (Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct), step-level stitching (best CoT + all steps above the PRM threshold) reaches 54.2% on MATH500 vs. 49.2% for giving the solver only the best-scoring trace, and 42.0% for majority voting over the traces.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Ablation of stitching strategies. We compare selecting the best rollout, majority voting over final answers, using all steps, and our confidence-filtered step stitching, showing that selective stitching yields the best accuracy. Using γ = 0.7 and τ = 1.4 and τ = 0.8 for GSM8K and MATH500 respectively.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on MATH500 (strict match, math-verify), higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Stitching (Best CoT and above confidence) vs. Best CoT with solver (trajectory-level selection by geometric-mean PRM score), All CoT with solver, and majority vote without solver, all using the same LLaDA traces
official.falsification_criterion: On MATH500 with N = 4 LLaDA-8B traces, stitching + Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct scores no more than about 1-2 points above feeding the same solver only the best-PRM trace (i.e., the +5.0 gap mostly disappears), or falls below it.

title: Tell Me What To Learn: Generalizing Neural Memory to be Controllable in Natural Language
claim_source: Table 14, page 37 (Appendix G); the seed-42 rows match main-paper Table 2, page 9

official.background: Neural memory systems such as MemoryLLM let an LLM absorb new documents into a compact latent memory without changing model weights. This avoids the cost of fine-tuning and the growing context of in-context learning (ICL) or retrieval (RAG). Existing neural memories learn everything in a document under one fixed objective, so a user cannot say what to remember and what to ignore. In personalization, for example, an assistant should keep a user's preferences on one topic while ignoring incidental preferences mentioned on other topics.
official.method:
GNM (generalized neural memory) starts from MemoryLLM (Llama-3-8B with per-layer memory tokens; the learning step writes the last 256 token embeddings of each layer into a memory bank). The learning step is modified to take a natural-language learning instruction together with the document. The model is fine-tuned on episodes of sequential memorize-then-probe steps. Gradients flow through both the memory write and the subsequent read, and the loss is a soft cross-entropy on four-letter multiple-choice logits.

On the PersonaMem benchmark (built from PersonaMem-v2), each document is a conversation in which a user expresses several preferences, and the instruction says to remember only preferences about one topic. Test instructions target 10 topics never used as targets in training. Each probe is a 4-way multiple-choice question scored by the highest-probability letter. Leak is the % of to-be-ignored probes on which the model picks the ignored preference. P(Leak|Deviation) is the fraction of deviations from the model's no-memory answer that land on the ignored preference (chance 33.3%). Score is the harmonic mean of Accuracy and (100 - Leak). ICL-FT is Llama-3-8B fine-tuned on the same data with all conversations and instructions in context. Evaluation uses 40 episodes of length 10 from the held-out split, with metrics at the most recent time step. Probes whose answer already matches either trained model's no-memory pick are filtered out (collision filtering).
official.claim: On PersonaMem with held-out instruction topics, GNM leaks ignored preferences less than the fine-tuned ICL baseline at every one of 6 training seeds (mean Leak 5.2% vs 8.5%; per-seed ranges 3.7-6.1 vs 6.8-10.5), with mean P(Leak|Deviation) 27.2% vs 58.9% and mean Score 94.2 vs 91.7.

Most recent time step, per-seed-pair joint collision filter. Bottom rows: seed means; bold marks the model that is significantly better on that metric under a paired t-test over seeds (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001).
official.metric: Leak (%, lower is better), P(Leak|Deviation) (%, lower is better, chance 33.3), Score (harmonic mean of Accuracy and 100 - Leak, higher is better). Six training seeds per method; the paper reports per-seed values and paired t-tests over seeds (Leak difference -3.3, 95% CI [-4.1, -2.5], p = 1e-4; Score +2.5 [+1.6, +3.4], p < 0.001). No per-run evaluation error bars.

title: Isotropic Activation Functions Enable Deindividuated Neurons and Adaptive Topologies
claim_source: Table 1, page 9 (duplicated as Table 3, page 41; KL and accuracy in Table 4, page 41)

official.background: Changing the number of neurons in a trained network without changing what it computes is hard, because in dense layers every unit is entangled with every other one. The paper argues that elementwise activation functions cause this: they are only equivariant to permutations, so each coordinate is a distinct 'neuron'. Activation functions that are equivariant to all orthogonal transformations ('isotropic' functions, e.g. f(x) = tanh(||x||) x/||x||) have no preferred basis. This lets a layer be rotated into its singular-value basis without changing the network, so neurons can be added or removed one at a time. The paper uses this for adaptive-width networks (neurogenesis and neurodegeneration) and for lossless sparsification.
official.method:
For a three-layer stack W3 f_iso W2 f_iso W1, take the SVD W2 = R Λ Q^T and absorb R into W3 and Q^T into W1. Because f_iso commutes with orthogonal matrices, the network function is unchanged and the middle layer becomes diagonal (one-to-one connections ordered by singular value). Neurogenesis appends 'scaffold' neurons with zero singular value (a zero row in Λ, a new zero bias entry, and a new outgoing column of W3 drawn from N(0, 0.02)), which is exactly function-preserving. Neurodegeneration deletes the smallest-singular-value neuron and folds its bias into a scalar 'intrinsic length' o inside the activation's norm (o' = o + b^2), with an optional decaying ψ-vector or bias adjustment that compensates the next layer.

Experiment One trains [12288, 100, 100, 256] isotropic-tanh MLPs on Caltech256 (64×64) for 50 epochs, 20 independent repeats for each of 7 variants of the intrinsic length and ψ treatment. The 100→100 middle layer is then diagonalised only (0), grown by +k neurons, or shrunk by −k neurons, with no retraining. The metric is the test-set mean relative L2 change in logits, ε_rel = E[||z_post − z_pre|| / ||z_pre||] × 100%. KL divergence and accuracy change are in Appendix Table 4, and the same experiment is repeated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (Tables 5 to 8).
official.claim: On Caltech256 [12288,100,100,256] isotropic-tanh MLPs (20 repeats), diagonalising the middle layer or adding +1 to +75 scaffold neurons changes logits by only ε_rel ≈ 8.2–8.6 ×10⁻⁴ % (SE ≤ 0.2×10⁻⁴). This is about 300× smaller than removing a single neuron (≈ 0.22–0.27 %) and about 4,000× smaller than removing 50 of 100 neurons (≈ 3.6–4.2 %), and it holds in all 7 intrinsic-length/ψ variants.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Experiment One (App. K.1): measures function invariance after neuroadaptation: appending +k, removing −k, or diagonalisation 0 the R^100 → R^100 layer of a [12288, 100, 100, 256] Caltech256 trained classifier. Mean ± standard error (SE) are reported over 20 independent repeats. Columns specify intrinsic length o and the ψ-vector approach, yielding 7×20 total networks. Σ0 and Σ1 denote the before- and after-sums of singular values, respectively (with their SE omitted for legibility; all ≈ 0.4). ε_rel is the test-set mean L2 logit change divided by the initial value, reported as a percentage.
official.metric: ε_rel: test-set mean relative L2 change in pre-softmax logits after vs. before adaptation, in percent (lower = more function-preserving); ± is standard error over 20 independent training repeats
official.comparison: Diagonalisation (0) and neurogenesis (+1, +5, +25, +50, +75) vs. neurodegeneration (−1, −5, −25, −50, −75) applied to the same trained networks without retraining, across 7 intrinsic-length/ψ configurations
official.falsification_criterion: With a correct implementation, diagonalisation or neurogenesis on a trained isotropic MLP gives ε_rel well above floating-point noise (e.g. ≥ 10⁻² %, comparable to removing one neuron), or the test accuracy changes. Equivalently, neurogenesis would fail to be clearly separated from −1 neurodegeneration.

title: Half-Truths Break Similarity-Based Retrieval

official.background: CLIP-style dual encoders score an image against a text with a single cosine similarity, and retrieval relies on that score falling when a description gets less accurate. The paper looks at a case the existing compositional benchmarks (which swap or reorder words) do not cover: a correct short description (the 'anchor', e.g. 'log') extended by one plausible but wrong detail (a 'half-truth', e.g. 'log and zebras' or 'elephants away from log'). If the model is well calibrated, the anchor should score higher. The authors argue that sentence-level contrastive training gives weak supervision on individual caption parts, so a wrong but plausible addition can raise similarity.
official.method:
Half-Truth Accuracy is the fraction of (image, anchor, half-truth) triples where s(I, A) > s(I, A−); chance is 50%. A text-only LLM (Qwen3-8B, and Mistral-8B for the transfer set) parses captions into entity units (noun phrases with attributes) and relation units (directed relations between two entities), and proposes a minimally edited foil for each unit. The anchor is an entity unit, and the half-truth appends one foil entity or foil relation to it. Evaluation candidates were screened with a VLM, reviewed, and manually checked by the authors. The COCO (Qwen) split has 509 comparisons drawn from the Karpathy partition.

CS-CLIP fine-tunes OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/32 (OpenCLIP) on COCO Karpathy train for 25 epochs (batch 128, AdamW lr 5e-6, wd 1e-2, 8×A100). The loss is L = L_global + 0.5·L_unit. L_global is the NegCLIP objective (in-batch captions plus shuffled-caption hard negatives in the I2T direction). L_unit samples N_u = 2 unit/foil pairs per image and trains the image to score the correct unit above its matched foil and the in-batch units (Eq. 2). Inference is unchanged: plain cosine similarity between image and text embeddings. Baselines in Table 1 are zero-shot CLIP ViT-B/32 and NegCLIP, DeGLA, ReadCLIP and FSC-CLIP, all scored the same way.
official.claim: On the 509 manually verified COCO (Qwen) half-truth comparisons, CS-CLIP (ViT-B/32 fine-tuned on COCO) prefers the correct anchor over the half-truth 76.4% of the time, vs. 53.8% for NegCLIP and 34.0% for zero-shot CLIP. On relation additions the numbers are 79.2% vs. 45.5% and 27.8%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Half-Truth Accuracy across foil generators and image domains. We report percentages on 509 COCO (Qwen), 454 COCO (Mistral), and 474 CC3M (Qwen) manually verified comparisons. All is the sample-weighted entity/relation average. FSC-CLIP is trained on CC3M; the other fine-tuned models use COCO. Higher is better.
official.metric: Half-Truth Accuracy (%), the fraction of comparisons with s(image, anchor) > s(image, half-truth), higher is better, 50% = chance. Point estimates only: no error bars or seeds are reported for half-truth accuracy (5-run stds are given only for the compositional benchmarks, and CS-CLIP numbers are from the best-performing run).
official.comparison: CS-CLIP vs. NegCLIP (the COCO-fine-tuned sentence-level hard-negative baseline that CS-CLIP's global loss is built on) and zero-shot CLIP ViT-B/32, on the same evaluation comparisons
official.falsification_criterion: Scoring the released CS-CLIP checkpoint (or a re-trained one following the paper's recipe) on the released COCO (Qwen) half-truth set gives overall accuracy that is not clearly above NegCLIP's, e.g. under ~65%, or a gap to NegCLIP below ~10 points. Another falsifier: zero-shot CLIP ViT-B/32 scores at or above 50% on the same set.

title: Stepwise Penalization for Length-Efficient Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

official.background: Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill produce very long chains of thought, often far longer than needed, which raises inference cost and latency without improving accuracy. RL methods that shorten reasoning usually apply a single length penalty to the whole trajectory, which cannot tell which steps are useful and so may cut essential reasoning along with redundant text. This paper asks whether allocating the length penalty to individual steps according to how much each step helps reach the correct answer gives shorter reasoning at the same accuracy.
official.method:
SWAP trains with GRPO (VeRL, DeepScaleR-Preview 40K math problems, batch 128, 16 rollouts per prompt, max response 12,000 tokens, 2 epochs = 623 steps, 8xH100 for 1.5B). Each rollout's reasoning (text before </think>) is split into steps of about M = 350 tokens (at most 25 steps, boundaries snapped to the next newline). For each prefix of k steps the model's own average per-token log-probability of the ground-truth answer, l_k, is computed; the step progress reward is Delta_k = max(0, l_k - max_{j<k} l_j). If a response is longer than the target length (median length of correct responses in the group), a penalty mass P = lambda (L - L_target)/L_target (lambda = 1) is spread over steps with weights w_k proportional to exp(-g_k/tau), where g_k = l_k - l_{k-1}, so low-gain steps absorb more penalty. Step reward r_k = Delta_k - P w_k, normalized over correct rollouts in the group.

The token-level advantage is beta * A_out + theta * 1[correct] * A_proc, where A_out is the standard group-normalized outcome advantage and A_proc sums the normalized step rewards of the current and all later steps (beta = 1, theta = 0.3). The ablation in Table 2 changes only the penalty term: Uniform-Penalty spreads the same total penalty mass P evenly across steps; Static-Penalty applies a fixed per-step penalty; No-Penalty drops P; Outcome-Only puts a trajectory-level length penalty in the outcome reward; Step-Only drops the outcome advantage. Evaluation: MATH-500, AMC23, AIME24, AIME25, OlympiadBench, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 32,768 tokens, 16 samples per query, pass@1 and mean response length in tokens.
official.claim: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, redistributing the length penalty across steps by information gain (SWAP) matches the uniform-redistribution variant's average pass@1 over five math benchmarks (53.4 vs. 53.4) while cutting average response length from 4,676 to 3,486 tokens (about 25% shorter), and is shorter on every benchmark.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Performance and reasoning length of different model variants. All results are based on the DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model. AVG denotes the average pass@1 across all datasets.
official.metric: Pass@1 accuracy (%, higher is better, from 16 samples per query) and mean response length in tokens (lower is better), averaged over 5 benchmarks; single training run, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: SWAP (importance-weighted penalty redistribution) vs. Uniform-Penalty (same total penalty mass spread evenly across steps), same base model, data and training setup; other ablations (Outcome-Only, Step-Only, No-Penalty, Static-Penalty) for context
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both variants under the paper's settings, SWAP's average length is not clearly below Uniform-Penalty's (e.g., less than ~10% shorter) at matched average pass@1, or SWAP's average pass@1 falls more than ~1 point below Uniform-Penalty's.

title: The Alien Space of Science: Sampling Coherent but Cognitively Unavailable Research Directions

official.background: LLMs used for research ideation tend to recombine concepts from high-density regions of the literature and produce homogeneous ideas. The paper argues that a useful ideation tool should instead propose directions that are coherent given existing knowledge but unlikely to be proposed by any existing author community (the 'alien space'). It tests this on a corpus of 16,068 LLM papers by representing each paper as a set of discrete 'idea atoms' and learning separate scores for coherence and for community availability. It then asks whether sampling under these scores gives a broader portfolio of ideas than prompting frontier LLMs.
official.method:
An LLM summarizes each paper and splits the summary into short conceptual units. The units are embedded with bge-large-en-v1.5, reduced with UMAP and clustered with HDBSCAN into a vocabulary of 273 idea atoms (about 3.38 atoms per paper). A coherence model (a 42.8M-parameter autoregressive Transformer over atom tokens, trained on random orderings of each paper's atom set) scores a set S by its length-normalized log-likelihood C(S). The availability model is a contrastive dual encoder trained with symmetric InfoNCE: a set encoder embeds a held-out subset of an author's atoms and an author encoder embeds the rest of that author's repertoire. A(S) is the median cosine similarity between S and its 10 closest of 39,791 author profiles, and unavailability is U(S) = -A(S).

Alien sampling scores all C(273,3) = 3,353,896 triples, z-scores C and U within that pool, ranks the triples by F_beta = (1-beta) z_C + beta z_U with beta = 0.7, and keeps the top 300. The LLM baselines get the full 273-atom catalogue and are prompted to choose novel yet feasible three-atom combinations in two ways: 'independent' (300 separate calls, with the catalogue order shuffled per call) and 'batch' (one call that returns all 300 combinations as JSON at temperature 1.0). Uniform random draws 300 triples. Diversity is computed on the 300 atom triples with four measures: the Vendi score using pairwise Jaccard similarity between triples (range 1-300), effective atoms exp(H(p)), repeated atom pairs out of 900, and the near-duplicate share (ideas that share at least two atoms with another idea).
official.claim: On the 273-atom LLM-research vocabulary, the top 300 three-atom combinations from Alien sampling (beta = 0.7) have a Vendi score of 225.2 and 51.3% near-duplicates. The strongest LLM baseline (Claude Opus 4.7, asked for all 300 combinations in one call) gets 197.9 and 81.7%, and independently prompted Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7 get Vendi scores of 97.4 and 56.5.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Portfolio diversity of each method's 300 ideas, and the equal-weight composite 1/2[z(Vendi) + z(quality)] using three evaluation measures (Section 5.4). Bold marks the best non-random method. Uniform random is the diversity ceiling but optimizes neither coherence nor availability. *Batch variants were not separately rated and inherit the quality of the same model's independent run.
official.metric: Vendi score over 300 triples with a Jaccard kernel (higher = more diverse); also effective atoms (higher is better), repeated pairs (lower is better) and near-duplicate share (lower is better). One run per method; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Alien sampler (beta = 0.7) vs. Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, each prompted in batch and independent mode. Uniform random is reported as the diversity ceiling, not as a competitor.
official.falsification_criterion: Any of these would refute the claim: (1) re-running the batch-prompted Claude Opus 4.7 or Gemini 3.1 Pro baseline with the paper's prompt on the same atom catalogue gives a Vendi score of about 225 or higher; (2) the same re-run gives a near-duplicate share of about 51% or lower; (3) a reproduced Alien portfolio (same scorers, beta = 0.7) does not beat the baselines' Vendi.

title: SEAR: Sample Efficient Action Chunking Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Table 5, page 21 (same result plotted in Figure 4a, page 9, and summarised in Table 2, page 18)

official.background: Action chunking (a policy outputs a sequence of N future actions that are executed open-loop) works well in imitation learning and helps reinforcement learning propagate value faster through unbiased N-step returns and explore with coherent multi-step behaviour. In purely online off-policy RL, however, naive chunking hurts: the critic must fit a much larger action space with only one target per chunk, and querying the policy only every N steps lowers reactivity and leaves many states where the actor is never trained. Prior online chunking methods are either critic-only and expensive (CQN-AS) or rely on offline data (Q-chunking).
official.method:
SEAR is a maximum-entropy (SAC-style) actor-critic whose actor outputs a whole chunk of N actions from the current state (SimbaV2 MLP actor) and whose critic is a causal transformer over the state and the chunk's actions. The critic predicts Q-values for every prefix of the chunk, Q^(1)(s_t, a_t), ..., Q^(N)(s_t, a_{t:t+N}), and is trained against multi-horizon targets G^(k) = sum_{i<k} gamma^i r_{t+i} + gamma^k Q_target(s_{t+k}, next chunk) for all k = 1..N at once, where Q_target is the minimum over two target critics' N-step Q^(N) for a chunk freshly sampled from the actor at s_{t+k}, minus the discounted per-action entropy term alpha * sum_i gamma^i log pi (Eq. 6-8; C51 distributional loss in practice). The actor minimises the reverse KL to exp(Q^(N)/alpha); entropy is counted per action with target entropy -N dim(A).

During data collection SEAR uses random replanning: it samples a chunk, executes only a uniformly random prefix length k in {1..N}, then replans, so the actor sees all states rather than every N-th one. At evaluation the policy uses receding-horizon control, executing the first 5 actions of each chunk. Setting: Metaworld MT1 (v3 tasks), success counted only if the success condition holds at the last time step of the episode, 1M online environment steps, UTD 1, batch 256, no offline data. Metaworld-Hard is the 20 tasks on which SimbaV2 did worst in preliminary runs. SEAR-10 (chunk size 10) uses 10 seeds; SimbaV2 (reimplemented in the same training pipeline, no chunking) and CQN-AS-5/10 (authors' tuning for Metaworld, receding horizon 5) use 5 seeds. The metric is IQM success with 95% stratified bootstrap CIs (rliable).
official.claim: On the 20 hardest Metaworld tasks after 1M online environment steps, SEAR-10 reaches an aggregate IQM success of 0.84 (95% CI -0.05/+0.04), versus 0.62 (-0.06/+0.05) for SimbaV2 and 0.61 (-0.05/+0.04) for CQN-AS-5.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: IQM success rate with 95% bootstrapped confidence interval across the 20 hardest Metaworld tasks, comparing SEAR-10, the best performing SEAR variant, with baselines. The best result is highlighted, results that are non-significantly worse than the best are lightly highlighted. All policies except for SimbaV2 use a fixed receding horizon of five actions during evaluation. CQN-AS performs better with chunk size five (CQN-AS-5) than with chunk size ten (CQN-AS-10). Overall, SEAR-10 performs best.
official.metric: IQM success rate at 1M environment steps (higher is better), success = condition holds at the episode's last step; ± are 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals over seeds and tasks (10 seeds for SEAR, 5 for baselines)
official.comparison: SEAR-10 (receding horizon 5 at evaluation) vs. SimbaV2 (no chunking, same pipeline) and CQN-AS with chunk size 5 and 10, all trained online for 1M steps on the same 20 Metaworld-Hard tasks
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning SEAR-10 and SimbaV2 on the 20 Metaworld-Hard tasks under the same protocol gives an aggregate IQM gap whose 95% bootstrap CIs overlap (e.g. SEAR-10 below ~0.75 or SimbaV2 above ~0.70); for a subset check, SEAR-10 failing to beat SimbaV2 clearly on tasks with large reported gaps (basketball 0.97 vs 0.27, pick-place 0.90 vs 0.00, pick-out-of-hole 1.00 vs 0.68, coffee-push 0.80 vs 0.38).

title: LaST-VLA: Thinking in Latent Spatio-Temporal Space for Vision-Language-Action in Autonomous Driving
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (the SFT baseline row is repeated in Table 4, page 7)

official.background: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving map camera images and navigation instructions to future trajectories. Many recent VLAs reason first in explicit textual chain-of-thought (CoT). This is slow, and the text can drift from what the image shows. Latent CoT reasons in continuous hidden states instead, but without intermediate supervision it can be unstable and has no physical grounding. The paper asks whether supervising the latent reasoning tokens with features from 3D-geometry and video world-model foundation models improves end-to-end planning on the NAVSIM benchmark.
official.method:
LaST-VLA starts from InternVL3-8B (front camera image + text containing the navigation command, ego state and history trajectory). Before predicting waypoints as text tokens, the model autoregressively generates K latent tokens from its last-layer hidden states. These are split into dynamic tokens (3 sets of 12, for short/medium/long horizons) and geometric tokens (12). Small adapters cross-attend from these tokens to randomly masked image embeddings. MSE losses align the adapters' outputs with frozen teacher features: a Cosmos video world model for the dynamic tokens and the VGGT aggregator for the geometric tokens (Eq. 5-6).

Training is progressive. SFT stage 1 runs on a 24k hard subset of navtrain for 2 epochs with lambda_WM = lambda_3D = 1.0 and lambda_action = 0.01. It uses a structured causal mask in which the latent groups cannot see each other and action tokens cannot attend to raw image tokens. SFT stage 2 runs on the full 85k navtrain for 2 epochs with lambda_action = 1.0, alignment weights 0.01 and the mask disabled. The RL stage then runs GRPO on navtrain-hard-24k (8 generations, reward = 8*PDMS + format + goal-endpoint terms) with the adapters frozen. The matched baseline, InternVL3-8B (SFT/RL)*, is the same backbone fine-tuned with textual CoT instead of latent CoT. Evaluation is PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest.
official.claim: On NAVSIM v1, LaST-VLA-8B gets 87.3 PDMS after SFT and 91.3 after RL. The same InternVL3-8B backbone trained with textual CoT gets 83.9 (SFT) and 87.2 (RL). That is a gain of 3.4 PDMS after SFT and 4.1 after RL, driven mainly by DAC (95.4 vs 92.3 after SFT) and EP.
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods on NAVSIMv1 with PDMS. * indicates models utilizing Textual CoT.
official.metric: PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest (higher is better; the sub-scores are NC, DAC, TTC, CF and EP). The paper gives single numbers with no seeds, std or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: LaST-VLA-8B (latent spatio-temporal CoT supervised by Cosmos/VGGT features) vs. InternVL3-8B fine-tuned with textual CoT, at both the SFT and the SFT+RL stage
official.falsification_criterion: After SFT only, LaST-VLA-8B's PDMS is less than about 1.5 points above the textual-CoT InternVL3-8B SFT baseline trained on the same data. Alternatively, the same gap closes after RL.

title: Characterizing Memorization in Diffusion Language Models: Generalized Extraction and Sampling Effects

official.background: Autoregressive language models are known to memorize training data and can be made to emit it verbatim, including personal information such as email addresses and phone numbers. Masked diffusion language models (DLMs) such as LLaDA generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens in parallel rather than left to right, and are trained with a bidirectional masking objective. It is not known whether they memorize and leak training data more or less than autoregressive models (ARMs), and the standard prefix-suffix extraction measures do not directly apply to their non-sequential sampling.
official.method:
The authors generalize (n, p)-discoverable extraction (Hayes et al.) to DLMs: a sequence is extractable if, given the unmasked tokens, the model recovers all masked tokens exactly in at least one of n independent queries with probability at least p. The single-query success probability p_z is the product of per-token conditional probabilities along the sampling trajectory (averaged over trajectories for DLMs), and n follows from n >= log(1-p)/log(1-p_z). They prove that, under a monotone-recovery assumption, more sampling steps (finer resolution) increases exact-extraction probability, with ARM-style one-token-at-a-time decoding as the limit.

For the aligned ARM vs DLM comparison, they reproduce the training recipe of Nie et al. (Scaling up masked diffusion models on text) at 1e21 FLOPs on SlimPajama, training a 1.1B DLM and a 1.1B ARM with the same setup and tokenizer. Both are fine-tuned for one epoch on the Enron email dataset at their end-of-pretraining learning rate. From Enron they sample 3,000 email-containing and 3,000 phone-containing texts (PII found by the regexes of Lukas et al.), use the 100 preceding tokens as the prefix, and count how many PII suffixes are (n, p)-discoverably extractable with n = 10,000 at p = 0.5 and p = 0.99. The DLM is evaluated with 1 step ('One') and with one token per step ('Max'); LLaDA-8B, fine-tuned the same way, is also reported.
official.claim: Under aligned prefix-conditioned PII completion on Enron (3,000 email prompts, query budget n = 10,000, p = 0.5), the 1.1B autoregressive model has 213 extractable emails while the matched 1.1B diffusion model has only 16 even at maximal sampling resolution (0 with one step).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Generalized (n, p)-discoverable Extraction. Number of memorized samples at target probabilities p under a query budget of n = 10,000 on 3,000 completion prompts, for different PII types.
official.metric: Number of the 3,000 prompts whose PII suffix is (n, p)-discoverably extractable (higher = more memorization/leakage); single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: DLM-1.1B (one-step and per-token 'Max' decoding) vs ARM-1.1B trained with identical data, tokenizer, compute budget and Enron fine-tuning; LLaDA-8B also shown
official.falsification_criterion: With matched 1.1B DLM and ARM models fine-tuned one epoch on Enron, the DLM at per-token resolution extracts a comparable or larger number of emails than the ARM at n = 10,000, p = 0.5 (e.g. the ARM/DLM ratio falls well below the reported ~13x, or the ARM count is not clearly larger).

title: Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning

official.background: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), e.g. GRPO or GSPO on math problems, is limited by the cost of on-policy sampling and verification. Organisations often maintain several models of different sizes or families for the same task (a small model for low latency, a larger one for accuracy), and each is trained in isolation on its own rollouts even though they all generate and verify answers to the same prompts. The paper asks whether such heterogeneous models can reuse each other's verified rollouts during RL training so that every model improves, while each is still deployed on its own at inference time.
official.method:
HACPO trains n models jointly on the same prompts. Each model samples G = 8 responses per prompt, and every model is updated on its own rollouts plus the other models' rollouts (re-tokenized if tokenizers differ). It builds on GSPO's sequence-level importance ratio and adds four mechanisms: (1) a capability-aware advantage baseline, where other agents' rewards are rescaled by the ratio of batch-mean accuracies P(k)/P(j) before computing the group mean; (2) scaling cross-agent advantages by that capability ratio; (3) an exponential, stop-gradient down-weighting of cross-agent importance ratios below 1 (exponent α); and (4) an asymmetric clip [1-δ+m·δ_step, 1.0] on cross-agent ratios that tightens with each mini-batch update within a step.

For the chosen claim the pair is Qwen3-1.7B-Base + Qwen3-4B-Base, trained with verl for one epoch on the 7.5k MATH training questions (lr 1e-6, batch 128, mini-batch 64, 8 rollouts per prompt, max response 4096, α = 1, 1-δ = 0.8, δ_step = 0.025). The baselines are single-model GSPO (same rollouts, 8 per prompt) and GSPO×2 (16 rollouts per prompt, mini-batch 32, so double the rollout cost of HACPO with the same number of policy updates). Models are evaluated on MATH500 with an 8192-token response limit over five seeds (0, 1, 42, 1337, 3407).
official.claim: When Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base are trained jointly with HACPO on MATH, MATH500 accuracy over 5 seeds is 0.6806 ± 0.0071 (1.7B) and 0.7990 ± 0.0074 (4B), compared with 0.6522 ± 0.0070 and 0.7702 ± 0.0085 for each model trained alone with GSPO×2, which uses twice HACPO's rollouts.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: MATH500 accuracy across five random seeds, evaluated with a maximum response length of 8192 tokens. The final column reports the mean and sample standard deviation (n − 1 denominator).
official.metric: MATH500 accuracy (higher is better), 8192-token evaluation limit; ± is the sample standard deviation over 5 training seeds. The authors also report two-sided paired t-tests over seeds (p < 0.001 for 1.7B, p = 0.009 for 4B).
official.comparison: HACPO (two-agent joint training) vs. single-agent GSPO and the rollout-doubled GSPO×2 baseline, per model, same training data and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: Across matched seeds, HACPO's mean MATH500 accuracy for either Qwen3-1.7B-Base or Qwen3-4B-Base is not above GSPO×2 by more than about one seed SD (~0.008), i.e. the ~2.8-point gain shrinks to within noise or reverses.

title: Unifying Contrastive and Generative Objectives for Visual Understanding and Text-to-Image Generation
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (schedule definitions in Appendix C.1, page 20)

official.background: Contrastive image-text models such as CLIP learn strong visual representations, and masked generative models such as MAR/FLUID learn to generate images from text, but training both objectives jointly in one end-to-end model with an unfrozen shared encoder has been unstable. The paper argues that the root cause is the masking ratio: contrastive alignment needs most image tokens visible, while masked generative modeling needs heavy masking. Existing unified models avoid the conflict by freezing an encoder, using an external teacher, or splitting training into stages.
official.method:
DREAM is a ViT encoder-decoder over Stable Diffusion VAE latents (L config: 32 layers, 16 encoder and 16 decoder, width 1024, about 570M parameters). The encoder sees only unmasked tokens plus learnable buffer tokens and is trained with a CLIP-style InfoNCE loss against a CLIP text transformer (computed only for samples with masking ratio at most 75%). The decoder, conditioned on frozen T5-XXL text via cross-attention, predicts masked tokens with a MAR-style per-token MLP diffusion loss (computed only for samples with masking ratio above 50%). Total loss is L_diff + 0.005 * L_clip. Training is on CC12M at 256x256 for 49 epochs, batch size 2048, AdamW.

The masking ratio for each sample comes from a Gaussian truncated to [0, 1] with sigma = 0.45. Table 1 compares three schedules for the mean with everything else held fixed: FX (mean fixed at 1.0, as in FLUID), CD (mean decreases linearly from 1.0 to 0.0 over the first 36 epochs, then stays at 0), and WM, Masking Warmup (mean increases linearly from 0.0 to 1.0 over the first 36 epochs, then stays at 1.0). Representations are evaluated by ImageNet-1K linear probing (LP) on average-pooled encoder features, and generation by FID on CC12M (50K samples) without Semantically Aligned Decoding.
official.claim: With architecture, data, 49-epoch budget, contrastive weight (0.005) and sigma = 0.45 held fixed, the Masking Warmup schedule (WM) gives ImageNet-1K linear-probe accuracy 72.5% and CC12M FID 4.57, while a fixed high-masking schedule (FX) collapses to 4.6% LP with no usable generation, and the reversed cooldown schedule (CD) gets 73.1% LP but a worse FID of 5.80.
official.claim_caption: Table 1 Component and Schedule Ablations. Isolating the contribution of masking warmup, diffusion reconstruction, and masking schedule design. DREAM (WM + reconstruction) achieves the best balance between representation (LP) and generation (FID).
official.metric: ImageNet-1K linear-probing top-1 accuracy (%, higher is better) and CC12M FID over 50K samples (lower is better, no SD). Single runs; no error bars or seeds reported. N/A means FID not reported (non-converged or no generator).
official.comparison: Masking Warmup (WM) vs. fixed high masking (FX) and masking cooldown (CD) within the same DREAM jointly trained model; single-objective baselines FLUID (LP 48.1, FID 4.53) and CLIP (LP 71.6) shown for reference.
official.falsification_criterion: Under matched settings, FX joint training reaches LP comparable to WM (e.g. above ~60%) with converged generation, or WM fails to beat CD on FID (CD FID <= ~4.6), or WM's LP falls well below CLIP's (e.g. under 70%).

title: SemanticDialect: Semantic-Aware Mixed-Format Quantization for Video Diffusion Transformers

official.background: Video diffusion transformers (VDiTs) such as Open-Sora generate good videos, but their size and the many denoising steps over long spatiotemporal token sequences make them expensive to run, especially on edge devices. 4-bit post-training quantization of weights and activations would cut memory and compute, but VDiT activations vary a lot across tokens and timesteps, and existing 4-bit schemes (MXFP4, NVFP4, ViDiT-Q, Q-VDiT) often visibly degrade video quality. Block-wise mixed-format quantization, where each small block picks its best 4-bit format from a set of candidates, is one way to fit diverse block distributions.
official.method:
SemanticDialect builds on FB4, a 4-bit block format. Each block (16 or 32 elements) gets a power-of-two shared scale (5-bit exponent) and a 5-bit dialect ID choosing one of 32 'dialects', each a set of 8 unsigned-integer magnitudes in 0-15 (plus a sign bit per element). Dialect selection for activations is done online: the block is split into g=8 groups, the max of each group is taken, the dialects compatible with the block's maximum form a sub-formatbook, and the dialect with the smallest summed lookup-table approximate error over the group maxima is picked; elements are then quantized through a per-dialect value LUT. Weights use exact MSE-based dialect selection offline.

Two additions complete SemanticDialect. Activation decomposition: for quantization-sensitive layers (attn_temp.qkv and mlp.fc2 in Open-Sora 1.0), the residual Act - Q(Act) is quantized again with FB4 and added back, but only for one salient token per spatial tile, chosen by mean pre-softmax attention to local neighbours. SeDA (semantic-aware dialect assignment): on MLP layers, anchor tokens and the tokens they strongly attend to are forced to share one 8-dialect sub-formatbook built from dialect-frequency counts on the anchors, with SeDA skipped in the first 20% of timesteps and updated periodically. Evaluation is Open-Sora 1.0 (724M, 16 frames at 512x512, 100 steps, CFG 4.0) on 8 VBench dimensions using the official VBench prompt sets with three videos per prompt (different seeds).
official.claim: On Open-Sora 1.0 with block size 16, SemanticDialect (W4.63/A5.10 effective bits) scores higher than NVFP4 (4.5/4.5) on VBench Imaging Quality (59.52 vs 52.46), Aesthetic Quality (54.00 vs 51.41) and Scene Consistency (32.15 vs 16.28), approaching FP16 (62.03, 58.00, 36.17).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Text-to-video generation quality on VBench benchmark suite for Open-Sora 1.0 and 2.0.
official.metric: VBench dimension scores (higher is better for Aesthetic Quality, Imaging Quality, Scene Consistency); computed over three videos per prompt with different seeds, but no error bars or std are reported.
official.comparison: SemanticDialect vs. NVFP4 (strongest baseline) at block size 16 on Open-Sora 1.0; also vs. MXFP4, BlockDialect, ViDiT-Q, Q-VDiT and FB4 alone.
official.falsification_criterion: Reimplemented SemanticDialect at block size 16 on Open-Sora 1.0 does not exceed NVFP4 on Imaging Quality by more than a few points or does not clearly exceed it on Scene Consistency, or NVFP4 with a matched activation bit budget (e.g., with the same extra decomposition budget) closes the gap.

title: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: Rethinking EEG Foundation Model Pretraining via Multi-Teacher Distillation
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (repeated in Appendix Tables 6-7, pages 14-15)

official.background: EEG foundation models such as CBraMod and LaBraM are pretrained with self-supervised masked reconstruction on large clinical EEG corpora (TUEG), then fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as motor imagery, emotion recognition, sleep staging and seizure detection. EEG data are scarce and noisy, so reconstruction objectives may spend capacity modelling artifacts. This paper asks whether foundation models from data-rich modalities (the vision model DINOv3 and the time-series model Chronos) can serve as teachers and give a better or more data-efficient EEG pretraining signal than masked reconstruction.
official.method:
MTDP has two stages, both on unlabeled TUEG EEG (16 channels, 200 Hz, 30 s segments, with TUAB/TUEV samples removed). The teachers are DINOv3-ViT-B/16, which takes EEG min-max normalized to [0,1] as a C×T image replicated over 3 channels, and the Chronos-Bolt-Base encoder, which embeds each channel as a univariate series and takes the mean over channels. Both teachers are frozen. Stage 1: a 2-layer MLP gate with a softmax takes the concatenated teacher representations of a masked input (a contiguous 1-2 s segment mask plus one dropped channel) and outputs one weight per teacher. The weighted sum of the masked representations is passed through per-teacher linear heads, which must predict each teacher's unmasked representation (MSE). Training runs for 1 epoch. Stage 2: with the gate frozen, a randomly initialized CBraMod student (4M parameters, criss-cross transformer) plus a linear projection head is trained for 40 epochs to maximize cosine similarity to the gated fused teacher representation of the unmasked input. Teacher representations are precomputed. The learned weights are about 0.56 for DINOv3 and 0.43 for Chronos.

For evaluation, CBraMod's own fine-tuning code is used unchanged: the last-layer representations are flattened into a 3-layer MLP classifier, the model is fine-tuned for 50 epochs with a grid over backbone LR {5e-5, 1e-4, 5e-4} and multi-LR {yes, no}, the checkpoint is selected on validation, and results are reported on the subject-independent test split. The baselines are CBraMod pretrained by masked reconstruction on 25% and 100% of TUEG.
official.claim: On BCIC-IV-2a (4-class motor imagery), CBraMod pretrained with MTDP on only 25% of TUEG reaches 59.63 balanced accuracy, compared with 49.31 for CBraMod pretrained by masked reconstruction on the same 25% and 51.38 for CBraMod pretrained on 100% (AUROC 58.81 vs 48.74 / 49.84). On BCIC2020-3 (5-class imagined speech) the corresponding figures are 59.87 vs 44.00 / 53.73.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Comparison of EEG foundation model performance on 12 downstream tasks. “25%” and “100%” indicate pretraining dataset size. Metrics acronyms: Balanced Accuracy (B. Acc.), Weighted F1 (F1-W), Cohen’s Kappa (Kappa).
official.metric: Balanced accuracy (%) on the subject-independent test split, higher is better; AUC-PR and AUROC also reported. Single numbers with no ± and no number of seeds stated.
official.comparison: CBraMod-MTDP 25% vs. CBraMod 25% and CBraMod 100% (masked-reconstruction pretraining), same architecture, pretraining corpus and fine-tuning protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Distilling from DINOv3 and Chronos into CBraMod on 25% of TUEG and fine-tuning with the CBraMod protocol does not beat reconstruction-pretrained CBraMod on BCIC-IV-2a by a clear margin (e.g. less than ~4 points of balanced accuracy, or within the seed-to-seed spread across several fine-tuning seeds).

title: Does Sparse Connectivity Improve Generalization? Convolutional Networks Below the Edge of Stability
claim_source: Figure 5 (right and left panels), page 8; setup in Appendix G.4, page 40

official.background: Gradient descent with a fixed step size η usually drives networks into the Edge of Stability, where the top Hessian eigenvalue hovers near 2/η. Prior work showed that for two-layer fully connected ReLU networks (FCNs), the solutions GD can stably reach (below the edge of stability, BEoS) are only weakly regularized on near-spherical high-dimensional inputs, so generalization guarantees become vacuous there. Yet convolutional networks trained on normalized images, which lie near a sphere, generalize well. The paper asks whether sparse connectivity (each neuron sees only a small patch) changes what the BEoS stability constraint enforces.
official.method:
The model is a two-layer ReLU 'sparsely connected network' (SCN): K shared filters applied to every patch of the input, ReLU, global average pooling over patches, then a linear output layer (Eq. 1). Theorem 4.1 shows the BEoS condition bounds a path norm weighted by the geometry of the training patch multiset; Theorem 4.2 turns this into a non-vacuous generalization bound on spherical data when the patch size m is much smaller than d, and Theorem 4.3 shows memorization is still possible when single patches can be isolated by a half-space.

The CIFAR-10 test (Appendix G.4): inputs are n_train = 1024 CIFAR-10 images (R^3072; G.4 does not state the input preprocessing, though Section 5 applies standard torchvision normalization in the Figure 4 patch analysis). Targets are y = f_true(x) + ξ with ξ ~ N(0, 1), where f_true is a frozen random SCN of width 20 using 3×3×3 patches, stride 1, no padding (900 patches of dimension 27). An SCN with the same patchification and an FCN (m = d, one patch), both width K = 1024, Kaiming-normal hidden weights and zero biases, are trained with full-batch GD on squared loss (no momentum, no weight decay) at η = 0.2 with gradient clipping for 5000 epochs. Excess risk is the MSE to f_true on the 10,000 CIFAR-10 test images; sharpness λ_max is computed with PyHessian.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 noisy-label regression (n = 1024, σ² = 1, width 1024, full-batch GD η = 0.2, 5000 epochs), both networks reach sharpness ≈ 2/η = 10, but the conv SCN ends with excess risk ≈ 0.12 and train loss ≈ σ² = 1, while the same-width FCN interpolates (train loss ≈ 1e-5) with excess risk ≈ 0.45.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Generalization on CIFAR-10 with noisy labels. Two-layer SCN (3 × 3 convolution, stride 1, no padding) vs. FCN of the same width, both trained with full-batch GD (η = 0.2). Left: Training loss (solid) and generalization gap (dashed) over epochs. The SCN stabilizes near the noise floor; the FCN interpolates. Middle: Sharpness λmax(∇²L). Both networks hover around 2/η ≈ 10 after ∼3k epochs (before that the loss of FCN has not started to converge), confirming the BEoS regime. Right: Excess risk over training epochs. After 2k epochs the SCN stabilizes at a much lower excess risk than the FCN.
official.metric: Excess risk = MSE between the network and the teacher f_true on the CIFAR-10 test split, lower is better; train loss is the empirical squared loss. Values are read off a log-scale plot and are approximate. Shaded bands are shown but neither their meaning nor the number of seeds is stated for this figure (the G.1 setup it 'repeats' averages 5 seeds).
official.comparison: Two-layer SCN (3×3 conv, stride 1, no padding, weight sharing, GAP) vs. two-layer FCN of the same width, same data, same optimizer and step size
official.falsification_criterion: Under the stated setup, the SCN's final excess risk is not clearly below the FCN's (e.g. less than a 2x gap, or the per-seed ranges overlap), or the SCN also interpolates the noisy labels (train loss far below σ² = 1) while at BEoS.

title: Reward-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Figure 1 (Single-Task panel), page 2; per-benchmark curves in Figure 3 (top row), page 5, and Figures 13-15 in the appendix

official.background: Single-task RL agents are trained under one fixed reward function, usually a hand-tuned weighted combination of components such as forward progress, control cost and posture terms. Such policies cannot change their behaviour when the reward weights change, and the reward weighting is often misspecified. Multi-task and multi-objective RL learn under many rewards, but they normally collect data under each one. This paper asks whether an off-policy agent can be trained on many counterfactual reward weightings computed from data collected under a single nominal reward, and whether doing so also helps on the nominal task.
official.method:
RCRL keeps the usual single-task data-collection loop: the agent acts conditioned on the nominal reward parameterization ψ*, and the replay buffer stores the individual reward components c1..ck rather than only the scalar reward. At each update, every transition in the batch independently gets a parameterization ψ drawn from a mixture: ψ* with probability α = 0.5, otherwise an alternative. The reward is recomputed as r_ψ = f(ψ, c1..ck), and the actor and critic both take [s, ψ] (or a learned embedding of ψ) as input. Nothing else about the backbone algorithm changes.

For the single-task claim, the backbone is SimbaV2 with its original hyperparameters (UTD 2, critic width 512, categorical critic with 101 atoms, batch 256). The alternative rewards come from Perturbed Reward Conditioning (PRC): each nominal reward coefficient is multiplied by a factor Δi drawn from a stratified log-uniform distribution on [0.25, 4.0]. Agents are trained for 1M environment steps on 23 tasks: 4 DMC (dog-stand/walk/trot/run), 5 Gym MuJoCo v4 (HalfCheetah, Ant, Hopper, Walker2d, Humanoid) and 14 HumanoidBench h1 tasks. Each benchmark's scores are normalized with random/optimal reference scores, and evaluation always uses the nominal reward.
official.claim: Evaluated under the nominal reward after 1M environment steps, averaged over 23 single-task tasks (DMC dogs, Gym, HumanoidBench) and 10 seeds, SimbaV2+RCRL (PRC) reaches a normalized score of about 1.00 versus about 0.90 for vanilla SimbaV2, and the 95% bootstrap CIs do not overlap.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Results summary. When evaluated under the nominal rewards, RCRL substantially improves the final-step performance in both single and multi-task settings, with smaller gains in the vision-based benchmark (Figure 3). Furthermore, RCRL enables zero-shot transfer and policy steerability that is absent in state-of-the-art single-task RL (Figures 4 and 5).
official.metric: Benchmark-normalized return at the final training step (higher is better), pooled over 23 tasks x 10 seeds; error bars are 95% confidence intervals from nonparametric bootstrapping (RLiable). Values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: SimbaV2+RCRL (PRC, α = 0.5) vs. vanilla SimbaV2 with identical hyperparameters, environment-step budget and evaluation protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Over the 23 tasks (or a pre-registered subset) with 10 seeds, SimbaV2+RCRL's aggregate normalized final score is not higher than vanilla SimbaV2's, or the gain shrinks enough that the 95% bootstrap CIs overlap.

title: Ensembling Language Models with Sequential Monte Carlo
claim_source: Table 3, page 23 (summarized in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3b, pages 8-9)

official.background: Ensembling several predictors is a standard way to improve accuracy, and practitioners increasingly want to combine frozen pretrained language models or several prompts to one model. A proper ensemble of LMs should aggregate probabilities of whole strings, but normalizing such a string-level ensemble is intractable, so prior work combines next-token distributions locally, almost always by averaging token probabilities. Local averaging is a biased approximation of the string-level ensemble, and an equal-weight mixture's expected accuracy can never exceed the better of its component models.
official.method:
The paper defines f-ensembles Phi(x) proportional to f(p_1(x), ..., p_K(x)) over complete strings, focusing on generalized means with power tau: min (tau -> -inf), product (tau = 0), mixture/sum (tau = 1) and max (tau -> +inf). Min and product are 'consensus-seeking' (mass on the intersection of supports), mixture and max are 'coverage-seeking'. Sampling uses sequential Monte Carlo: M particles are extended token by token from a proposal equal to the locally normalized shaping function f applied to the experts' prefix probabilities, importance weights correct towards the string-level target, and multinomial resampling is triggered when effective sample size drops below 0.9 M.

For the claim, the within-model setting combines one instruction-tuned model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) under two different prompts (K = 2, equal weights), run at the token level with M = 10 particles, temperature 1.0, on 100 randomly sampled instances of BIG-Bench Hard word sorting. The metric is expected accuracy under the ensemble, estimated as the normalized-importance-weighted fraction of particles whose output is correct (Eq. 10). Baselines are each prompt alone and the other f-ensembles, notably the mixture (probability averaging) run with the same SMC sampler.
official.claim: On BBH word sorting with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and two prompts, the token-level SMC (M = 10) min ensemble reaches 43.2 ± 1.3% expected accuracy and the product ensemble 41.2 ± 0.9%, versus 37.1 ± 0.7% for the best single prompt and 37.5 ± 1.0% for the probability-averaging mixture ensemble.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison of f-ensemble functions (token-level SMC). Bold: highest average expected accuracy in column, unless a single prompt is higher. †: non-overlapping 95% CIs with best baseline. Shaded: strongest single-prompt baseline.
official.metric: Expected accuracy (%) under the ensemble, estimated from weighted SMC particles (higher is better); ± is the 95% confidence interval across 5 seeds; 100 evaluation instances
official.comparison: min and product f-ensembles vs. best single prompt (Prompt 1) and vs. mixture (probability averaging) and max f-ensembles, all with the same model, prompts and SMC settings

title: Learning When Visual Context Matters for Mouse Behavior Analysis

official.background: Mouse behavior analysis usually runs on pose keypoints extracted from video. Pose drops body texture and scene context and becomes unreliable when animals occlude each other, which happens constantly in social recordings. Adding features from a video foundation model helps, but running a vision encoder on every frame is expensive, and simply concatenating video and pose features adds little. The paper asks whether a model can tell from pose alone which frames actually need visual context.
official.method:
ResiFuse pretrains a pose-based motion encoder per dataset: a temporal tokenizer maps per-frame pose features to latents z_e, which are discretized with two-level residual vector quantization (RVQ), then passed through temporal and cross-animal Transformers. Pretraining combines masked pose reconstruction, RVQ reconstruction, RVQ commitment, and an auxiliary cross-modal loss that predicts frozen VideoPrism features of future frames (cosine loss). The quantization residual r_t = ||z_e,t - z_q,t||_2 measures how badly the codebook represents frame t.

At fine-tuning the motion encoder is frozen. For each window, the top-k frames by residual (k = budget x window length) get VideoPrism features, which are linearly projected and added to the motion representation through LayerNorms; other frames get zero visual input. A small classifier predicts per-frame behavior labels. In Table 8 the budget is fixed at 25% on Mouse Triplet (supervised, 4 social behaviors) and only the rule for choosing the vision frames changes: none, uniform, highest-residual, or lowest-residual.
official.claim: On Mouse Triplet supervised classification with vision on a fixed 25% of frames, choosing the highest-residual frames gives macro F1 0.680 ± 0.002, versus 0.666 ± 0.006 for uniformly chosen frames and 0.635 ± 0.003 for the lowest-residual frames (no vision: 0.654 ± 0.005).
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Fixed amount of vision on Mouse Triplet (supervised): 25% of frames receive visual features, chosen by different rules. Macro F1 (mean ± std) follows Table 1, over three runs (five for the lowest-residual rule); p-values are from Welch's t-test against no vision.
official.metric: Test macro F1 over 4 behavior classes (higher is better); ± is std over 3 runs (5 for lowest-residual). p-values are Welch's t-tests against no vision; no test of highest-residual vs. uniform is reported.
official.comparison: Residual-guided selection (highest-residual 25%) vs. uniform 25% vs. lowest-residual 25% vs. no vision, all with the same frozen motion encoder, VideoPrism features, labels and classifier
official.falsification_criterion: With the same pipeline and a 25% vision budget on Mouse Triplet, highest-residual selection does not beat uniform selection by more than run-to-run std (e.g. gap < ~0.006 macro F1), or lowest-residual selection does as well as highest-residual.

title: Reject, Resample, Repeat: Understanding Parallel Reasoning in Language Model Inference
claim_source: Figure 2, page 4 (Pearson r values from Appendix G.2 text and Figures 6-8, pages 38-41)

official.background: Inference-time methods that sample many partial generations from a language model and prune or replicate them using a process reward model (PRM) are a common way to steer LLMs, and particle filtering methods such as Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) often beat Best-of-N. There is little theory for when they work. This paper treats steering as sampling from a target distribution pi* proportional to pi_ref times a reward, and proves that SMC with N particles reaches total-variation error of order sqrt(H^2 C_act (C_chi2 + 1) / N), where C_act bounds how much pi* reweights any next action relative to pi_ref (action-level coverage) and C_chi2 bounds the chi-square divergence between the true intermediate targets pi*_h and the PRM-induced targets pi_hat_h. The experiments test whether these two quantities actually predict SMC's sampling error with a real LLM.
official.method:
Prompt-switching task: a language model M (Qwen3-0.6B) defines pi_ref = M(. | p_ref) and the target pi* = M(. | p*), so the exact value function is V*(a_1:h) = M(a_1:h | p*) / M(a_1:h | p_ref) and both distributions can be sampled and scored exactly. SMC runs token by token with N = 32 particles. Sampling error is the P-logprob discrepancy LPD_P(E[nu_hat_H], pi*_H) with P = {p_ref, p*}: for each prompt in P, the absolute difference between the mean summed token log-probabilities under M of SMC outputs and of true target samples, summed over P (estimated from 200 SMC runs per instance).

Figure 2a (coverage): 50 instances share p_ref (a short-story prompt) and each instance's target p(i) asks for the story in a different style (prompts generated by GPT-5.2); the PRM is exact (alpha = 0, V_hat = V*), H = 32 tokens. The x-axis is (1/H) KL(pi*(i) || pi_ref), an average-case proxy for action-level coverage. Figure 2b (PRM error): p_ref = p*, H = 64, and the PRM for instance i is V_hat(i)(a_1:h) = [pi*(a_1:h)/pi_ref(a_1:h)] * [pi(i)(a_1:h)/pi*(a_1:h)]^((1 - h/H) alpha) with alpha = 2, so early on it points toward the perturbed style p(i) and becomes exact at h = H. The x-axis is KL(pi*_h || pi_hat_h) at h = 32, estimated with 1000 Monte Carlo rollouts (Appendix G.2, Eq. 9-10).
official.claim: On the prompt-switching task with Qwen3-0.6B and SMC with N = 32 particles, SMC's sampling error (P-logprob discrepancy) rises with both theory quantities across 50 prompt instances: with the KL proxy for action-level coverage (exact PRM; error mostly about 7-16 at proxy below 0.3 versus about 22-58 at proxy above 0.6; Pearson r = 0.83-0.89 on four further prompt sets, Figure 6) and with KL(pi*_h || pi_hat_h) of the PRM (Pearson r = 0.81 in Figure 2b; 0.70-0.83 on three further prompt sets).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Empirical validation for our theory on the prompt-switching task (see Section 4). (a) We vary the action-level coverage (as measured by a KL-divergence proxy) across many prompts while keeping V_hat = V* fixed, and observe that action-level coverage predicts the sampling error of SMC. (b) We fix pi_ref = pi* (so that action-level coverage is fixed) and observe that D_KL(pi*_h || pi_hat_h) predicts the sampling error of SMC.
official.metric: P-logprob discrepancy between SMC's output distribution and the target (lower is better), estimated from 200 SMC runs per instance; association measured by Pearson correlation across 50 instances. No error bars or confidence intervals on the points or on r.
official.comparison: Correlation of SMC sampling error with (a) average-case action-level coverage proxy (1/H) KL(pi* || pi_ref), PRM held exact, and (b) PRM divergence KL(pi*_h || pi_hat_h), coverage held fixed by p_ref = p*
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running with Qwen3-0.6B, N = 32 and 50 regenerated style-prompt instances, the Pearson correlation between SMC sampling error and either KL proxy is weak (e.g. r < 0.5) or negative, or does not replicate across several independently generated prompt sets.
