title: SageSched: Efficient LLM Scheduling Confronting Demand Uncertainty and Hybridity

official.background: LLM serving backends must decide the order in which queued requests are served, and the order strongly affects average time-to-last-token (TTLT). Default engines such as vLLM use first-come-first-serve, which suffers head-of-line blocking; recent schedulers approximate shortest-job-first by predicting a single output length per request with a fine-tuned small model. The paper argues that these miss two properties of LLM requests: output length is uncertain (a distribution, not a number), and cost depends on both compute and KV-cache memory, so prompt length matters, not only output length.
official.method:
SageSched, built on vLLM v0.8.2, has three parts. (1) A training-free predictor embeds each incoming prompt, retrieves recent requests (FIFO window of 10,000, FAISS IndexFlat) whose prompt embeddings have cosine similarity at least 0.8, and uses their output lengths as the predicted output-length distribution. (2) Each output length O is mapped to a cost C = O^2/2 + I*O (I = prompt length), derived to hold in both memory-bound and compute-bound regimes. (3) Requests are queued by the Gittins index of their cost distribution, G(D) = inf over Delta of E[min(X, Delta)] / P(X <= Delta), smaller first, with preemption and the index refreshed at bucket boundaries (bucket size 200).

Baselines, all run in the same setup with default hyperparameters: FCFS (vLLM), FastServe (MLFQ), SSJF (fine-tuned BERT length predictor), LTR (OPT-125M learning-to-rank), and TRAIL (MLP on LLM-layer embeddings, SRPT-like). Requests arrive by a Poisson process. Figure 8 runs each dataset (ShareGPT, Alpaca-PubMed summarization, Document-Write) separately and reports average TTLT normalized to SageSched; the testbed uses Llama3.1-8B on one A40-48GB or Qwen3-32B on one H800-96GB, at temperature 0.6.
official.claim: When serving only Alpaca-PubMed summarization requests (long prompts), SageSched has the lowest average TTLT, and the best baseline (LTR) has 1.55x its average TTLT (SSJF 1.63x, TRAIL 1.59x, FCFS 2.73x, FastServe 3.36x).
official.claim_caption: Figure 8. End-to-end performance respectively with each dataset.
official.metric: Average time-to-last-token normalized to SageSched (lower is better). Error bars are drawn but their meaning (seeds/runs) is not stated; the number of runs is not given.
official.comparison: SageSched vs. LTR, SSJF, TRAIL, FCFS and FastServe on the same backend and request stream, per dataset
official.falsification_criterion: On Alpaca-only workloads, the best of LTR/SSJF/TRAIL reaches an average TTLT within about 20% of SageSched's (normalized value below 1.2) or below it, across repeated runs at the paper's load.

title: Towards Visual Query Segmentation in the Wild

official.background: Visual query localization (VQL) asks a model to find an object in an untrimmed video, given an image crop of that object taken from outside the video. The standard benchmark (Ego4D VQ2D) only asks for a bounding box around the object's last appearance. The paper proposes visual query segmentation (VQS): segment every pixel-level occurrence of the queried object across the whole video. This differs from video object segmentation because the reference comes from outside the video and the target appears only sparsely among distractors. The authors release VQS-4K (4,111 YouTube videos, 222 categories, 1.3M frames at 6 fps, manual masklets for all occurrences) and a baseline method.
official.method:
VQ-SAM extends SAM 2 (Hiera-B+ encoder). The query image and its mask are encoded into an initial memory. Over K = 2 stages, the current memory is fused into the video-frame features, a spatial-temporal Transformer block is applied, and SAM 2's mask decoder produces 3 candidate masks per frame. Target Feature Generation keeps the top n_t = 2 best masks with IoU score above 0.5, and Distractor Feature Generation keeps the top n_d = 1 alternative mask by divergence times IoU score. An Adaptive Memory Generation module learns softmax weights over the initial memory, target features and distractor features to form the next memory. In the last stage each frame outputs its highest-IoU mask if the occlusion score is above 0, and nothing otherwise. Training: 144 epochs, AdamW, lr 5e-6, 768x768 input, 7-frame clips. At inference the video is split into non-overlapping 7-frame windows.

Baselines are VOS methods (Cutie-b, OASIS, LOMM, SAM 2, SAM2.1++, SAM2Long, SAM 3), given the query image and mask as the reference, and VQL methods (VQLoC, PRVQL, REN), given an added mask head. All except the training-free REN are trained on VQS-4K train (3,289 videos) and evaluated on VQS-4K test (822 videos). Metrics: mean spatio-temporal mask IoU (mSTIoU), temporal IoU (mTIoU), Recovery and Success.
official.claim: On VQS-4K test (822 videos), VQ-SAM reaches 26.0 mSTIoU and 29.6 mTIoU, beating every adapted baseline trained on the same split: the best baseline is SAM2Long at 18.6 mSTIoU / 24.4 mTIoU, and plain SAM 2 fine-tuned on VQS-4K gets 12.9 / 13.0.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison with current approaches on VQS-4K Tst.
official.metric: mSTIoU and mTIoU in % (higher is better), plus Recovery and Success; single runs, no error bars
official.comparison: VQ-SAM vs. 7 adapted VOS methods and 3 adapted VQL methods, all trained on VQS-4K train except training-free REN
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained VQ-SAM (or the released checkpoint) gets mSTIoU on VQS-4K test within about 2 points of SAM2Long (i.e. below ~20.6), or a SAM 2 baseline fine-tuned on VQS-4K train with the same recipe gets close to VQ-SAM's 26.0 mSTIoU.

title: Flash-KMeans: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact K-Means
claim_source: Figure 4 (left), page 10; numbers also in Section 5.2 text, page 8

official.background: k-means is increasingly called inside training and inference pipelines (sparse attention routing, KV-cache compression, token permutation in video diffusion transformers), so per-call GPU latency matters. Standard GPU implementations of Lloyd's algorithm compute the full N x K distance matrix, write it to HBM and read it back for the argmin, and then update centroids with per-token atomic adds. The paper argues these memory and contention costs, not FLOPs, dominate runtime on modern GPUs.
official.method:
Flash-kmeans keeps exact Lloyd k-means but rewrites both stages. FlashAssign fuses distance computation with an online argmin: each point tile keeps a running (min distance, index) pair in registers while centroid tiles are streamed from HBM with double-buffered asynchronous prefetch, so the N x K distance matrix is never materialized (IO drops from O(NK) to O(Nd + Kd)). Distances use the expansion ||x||^2 + ||c||^2 - 2 x^T c. Sort-inverse update argsorts the assignment vector and reduces contiguous cluster segments on chip, issuing atomics only at segment boundaries.

The claim comes from the kernel-level benchmark (Figure 4, left): latency of the assignment stage alone, FlashAssign vs. the standard assignment of Algorithm 1 (Kernel 1 writes the full distance matrix D to HBM, Kernel 2 reads it back and takes the row-wise argmin), on an NVIDIA H200 with CUDA 12.8, feature dimension D = 128, for six (B, N, K) shapes.
official.claim: On an NVIDIA H200 with d = 128, FlashAssign computes exact k-means assignments 17.5-21.2x faster than the standard materialize-distance-matrix-then-argmin implementation across six shapes, e.g. 122.5 ms -> 5.8 ms (21.2x) at B = 1, N = 1M, K = 8192.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4 Kernel-level latency breakdown. Latency comparison of our custom kernels versus standard implementations across diverse extreme workloads (D = 128). Left: FlashAssign completely removes HBM distance materialization, scaling up to a 21.2x speedup. Right: Sort-Inverse Update replaces per-token scatter atomic adds with sorted localized merges, eliminating atomic contention and achieving up to a 6.3x speedup.
official.metric: Assignment-stage kernel latency in ms (lower is better) and the speedup ratio printed on the bars; single values with no error bars or stated number of repetitions
official.comparison: FlashAssign (fused distance + online argmin) vs. standard assignment (distance kernel writing the N x K matrix to HBM, then a separate argmin kernel), same GPU and shapes
official.falsification_criterion: On an H200 (or a comparable Hopper GPU), with a reasonable standard baseline (e.g. a PyTorch/cuBLAS matmul-based distance plus torch.argmin), FlashAssign's speedup at B = 1, N = 1M, K = 8192, d = 128 is well below ~10x, or its assignments differ from the exact argmin.

title: Does the Question Really Matter? Training-Free Data Selection for Vision-Language SFT
claim_source: Table 7(b) and 7(c), page 20 (same numbers plotted in Figure 2a, page 6)

official.background: Visual instruction tuning (VIT) datasets for vision-language models contain many samples that can be answered from language patterns or common sense without looking at the image, plus noisy or misaligned question-answer pairs. Such samples give weak cross-modal supervision. Data selection methods try to pick a small, high-value subset, but most existing ones (COINCIDE, XMAS, EL2N, D2 Pruning) need a trained proxy model or clustering pipeline and score difficulty or diversity rather than whether the question is actually needed. This paper asks whether a frozen VLM's yes/no judgement of answer validity, with and without the question, can select better SFT data with no training.
official.method:
Conditional Verdict Shift (CVS) uses a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct evaluator (run with vLLM) and prompts it to answer Yes/No on whether an answer is valid. For each sample (image I, question Q, answer A) it computes CVS_YES = log P(YES | I, Q, A) / P(YES | I, A) and CVS_NO = log P(NO | I, Q, A) / P(NO | I, A), taking the raw output token probabilities without renormalising over {YES, NO}. The prompt templates are in Appendix C, Figure 5. Samples are kept only if CVS_YES > 0 and CVS_NO < 0 (59.29% of Vision-Flan survives). From this filtered pool, the samples with the LOWEST positive CVS_YES (the 'Low' strategy, i.e. hard positives near the decision boundary) are selected until the budget (5/10/15% of the full dataset) is reached.

The selected subset is used to fine-tune pre-trained LLaVA-1.5-7B with the official LLaVA-1.5 LoRA hyperparameters. The data pool is the full Vision-Flan (186K samples, 187 tasks). The model is evaluated on 12 benchmarks (GQA, VizWiz, TextVQA, ScienceQA-IMG, MME, MMBench-CN/EN, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA, MMStar, OCRBench), and the score is Average Relative Performance (ARP), the mean of per-benchmark subset score / full-data score x 100. Baselines (Random, XMAS, COINCIDE, D2 Pruning, EL2N, SemDeDup, CLIP-Score, SCALSELECT, PRISM) select subsets of the same size and use the same fine-tuning recipe.
official.claim: On Vision-Flan with LLaVA-1.5-7B LoRA fine-tuning, CVS-selected subsets reach ARP 103.45 at a 10% budget and 104.85 at 15%, beating random selection (95.30 / 93.82), the best of 9 selection baselines (D2 Pruning 100.49 at 10%, SemDeDup 100.35 at 15%) and full-data training (100).
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Main experimental results on Vision-Flan. We compare different data selection methods on Vision-Flan using 5%, 10%, and 15% data subsets. The best result among subset-selection methods in each column is highlighted in bold.
official.metric: Average Relative Performance (ARP) over 12 benchmarks, relative to full-data fine-tuning = 100; higher is better. Single run per cell; the paper reports no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: CVS (Low strategy, Qwen2.5-VL-7B evaluator) vs. Random, XMAS, COINCIDE, D2 Pruning, EL2N, SemDeDup, CLIP-Score, SCALSELECT, PRISM and full-data training, all with the same target model and fine-tuning recipe at 10% and 15% budgets
official.falsification_criterion: With the same pipeline at 10% or 15% of Vision-Flan, the CVS subset gives ARP no higher than the random subset or the strongest baseline (D2 Pruning / SemDeDup), or no higher than full-data training (ARP <= 100). If several random seeds are run, a CVS-vs-random gap that falls within the seed-to-seed spread also refutes it.

title: Training Language Models via Neural Cellular Automata

official.background: LLM pre-training on natural language faces a limited supply of high-quality text, inherited human biases, and a mixing of world knowledge with reasoning. Prior work has tried a short 'pre-pre-training' phase on synthetic data (random strings from RNNs, formal languages like Dyck, simple algorithmic tasks) before ordinary language pre-training, but these have generally not beaten language data at a matched token budget. This paper asks whether trajectories of randomly sampled neural cellular automata (NCA), which are cheap to generate, have controllable complexity, and show Zipf-like token statistics, can serve as a useful non-linguistic pre-pre-training signal.
official.method:
NCA data: 2D discrete cellular automata on a 12x12 periodic grid with n = 10 states. Each trajectory uses a freshly sampled random transition network (a 3x3 convolution with 4 channels, then a cell-wise MLP with hidden size 16 and ReLU, producing 10 logits per cell, sampled with softmax at temperature 1e-3) and a uniform random initial grid. Only rules whose serialized rollouts have gzip compression ratio > 50% are kept. Grids are tokenized as non-overlapping 2x2 patches (10^4 patch tokens), each timestep is wrapped in <grid> ... </grid>, and timesteps are concatenated into sequences of up to 1024 tokens.

Pipeline: a Llama-style transformer is first trained with next-token prediction on 164M NCA tokens (batch 16, LR 1e-4, cosine with 10% warmup, no weight decay). All weights except the embedding layers are then transferred (embeddings are re-initialized for the text vocabulary) and the model is pre-trained for one epoch on OpenWebText (9B tokens; batch 512, seq 1024, LR 5e-4, weight decay 1e-4, cosine with 10% warmup), with all parameters updated. Baselines use the identical pre-training stage and differ only in stage 1: no pre-pre-training (scratch), pre-pre-training on C4 natural-language text with a matched token budget, or pre-pre-training on k-Dyck (k = 128). Learning rate and weight decay (and batch size, per Appendix B) are grid-searched per method. The metric is final validation perplexity on held-out OpenWebText, at 400M, 600M and 1.6B parameters.
official.claim: With a 400M-parameter model pre-trained on OpenWebText, pre-pre-training on 164M NCA tokens gives a final validation perplexity of about 16.4, versus about 18.0 for both no pre-pre-training and matched-budget C4 pre-pre-training (roughly 8.5% lower), and about 17.3 for Dyck pre-pre-training; NCA also has the lowest perplexity at 600M (~15.7 vs ~17.0 scratch) and 1.6B (~13.8 vs ~14.65 scratch).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3. NCA pre-pre-training improves language model training performance across model sizes (Section 5.1). We report the final validation perplexity after pre-training on OpenWebText across (400M, 600M, and 1.6B parameter models). At 164M tokens, C4 pre-pre-training likely acquires shallow syntactic patterns that interfere with downstream learning rather than transferable structure. We investigate this further in Figure 4.
official.metric: Final validation perplexity on held-out OpenWebText (lower is better). Error bars are over multiple training seeds (Appendix B: 4 seeds for NCA, scratch and C4; at least 2 for other runs); the paper does not say whether the bars are std or SE. Values are read off the bar chart.

title: LLMs can construct powerful representations and streamline sample-efficient supervised learning
claim_source: Table 2(a), Appendix E.1, page 18 (also Figure 5, page 7)

official.background: Supervised learning on heterogeneous records such as electronic health records (EHR) is often limited by how the inputs are represented. One recent approach serializes each patient's longitudinal record into long Markdown text and trains a linear head on text embeddings of it. These naive serializations are long (about 6k tokens on average) and noisy, and the predictive signal is scattered across visits. With very few labels, neither these serializations nor count features nor a domain foundation model gives strong downstream classifiers. The paper asks whether an LLM can first rewrite the serialized input into a better task-specific representation, so that pretrained knowledge acts as a prior and makes learning sample-efficient.
official.method:
Each patient record is first turned into the naive text serialization of Hegselmann et al. (NaiveText, clipped at 8,192 tokens). For Local-Rubric, GPT5-Mini is prompted separately for each patient with the task query and the NaiveText record. It writes a task-conditioned summary with fixed sections: patient snapshot, main risk factors, protective factors, what's unknown and can swing the risk, and weighing and aggregating the evidence. The summary includes the LLM's interpretation of the evidence. The paper also proposes global rubrics (one rubric per task, synthesized by an LLM from 40 k-means medoid patients and then applied to every input), but those are not the chosen claim.

For every textual method, including NaiveText, the text is wrapped in a unified task-conditioned prompt template and embedded with frozen Qwen3-Embedding-8B. An L2-regularized, class-balanced logistic regression is then fit, with C tuned on the validation split by negative log-likelihood over np.logspace(-6,-1,13). Baselines are Count-GBM (LightGBM on time-windowed code counts), CLMBR-T (logistic regression on embeddings from a clinical foundation model pretrained on 2.57M patients), NaiveText with the same embedding and classifier stack, and zero-shot chain-of-thought with Qwen3-8B and GPT5-Mini (10 samples, P = fraction of Yes answers). The setting is n=10: label-balanced training sets with 10 examples per class for each of the 15 EHRSHOT binary tasks. All methods share the same subsampled splits (Appendix B, Table 1), and AUROC is macro-averaged over the tasks.
official.claim: With n=10 training examples per class, Local-Rubric (GPT5-Mini summaries + Qwen3-Embedding-8B + logistic regression) achieves 0.701 (95% CI 0.687–0.715) AUROC averaged over 15 EHRSHOT tasks. The best baseline, zero-shot GPT5-Mini chain-of-thought, reaches 0.644 (0.635–0.653). The trained baselines are NaiveText 0.609, CLMBR-T 0.597 and Count-GBM 0.594.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: AUROC and AUPRC across all methods for n = 10 and n = All. Green: best in entire column. Blue: best within a method across backbones. Oper.: Operational Outcomes, New Dx: Assignment of New Diagnosis, Labs: Anticipating Lab Results, CXR: Chest X-ray Findings
official.metric: AUROC (higher is better), macro-averaged over 15 binary tasks; subscripts are 95% CIs bootstrapped over the test set. The paper reports no seeds and no repeated draws of the n=10 training subsample.
official.comparison: Local-Rubric vs. NaiveText (same embedding model and classifier, raw serialization), CLMBR-T, Count-GBM (all at n=10), and zero-shot CoT with GPT5-Mini and Qwen3-8B (n=0)
official.falsification_criterion: At n=10, Local-Rubric's overall AUROC does not exceed that of the strongest baseline (zero-shot GPT5-Mini, about 0.644) by clearly more than the bootstrap CI widths. Alternatively, its margin over NaiveText under the same embedding and classifier stack falls to within about 0.02 AUROC, or disappears when averaged over several random draws of the 10+10 training examples.

title: Truth as a Compression Artifact in Language Model Training

official.background: Training corpora contain contradictory answers to the same question, yet language models often prefer the correct one. It is unclear whether the training objective itself favours correct answers over incorrect ones at equal frequency, or whether this depends on the structure of the errors. Prior work measures preference with pairwise accuracy (correct vs. one sampled error), but if errors come in many forms a model that just matches training frequencies wins that comparison without preferring anything. The paper trains small transformers from scratch on synthetic math corpora with controlled contradictions and measures preference with a statistic whose frequency-matching null is exactly 0.5.
official.method:
A generator writes 5,000 unique math problems (multi-step arithmetic, factoring, equation solving, differentiation) as step-by-step derivations, verified with SymPy. In the 'denoising' corpus each problem appears exactly twice: once correct and once corrupted. In the equal random condition the corruption is one random error drawn from the generator's error family (a plausible but wrong computation in one step); in the equal coherent condition it is one systematic false rule applied consistently to every problem of a type (e.g. a(b+c) = ab + c). Character-level tokenizer (~57 symbols). GPT-2-like decoder-only transformers (pre-norm, GELU) at 3.5M, 12M, 26M and 86M (12 layers, d_model 768, 12 heads) are trained from scratch with AdamW (wd 0.01), lr 3e-4, cosine with warmup, sequence length 256, batch 32, 5000 steps; 4 seeds per cell.

Evaluation is on training problems. For each problem, every completion the error generator can produce is enumerated (mean 12.0 false strings per problem, range 4-35, for random errors; 1 for coherent). Each completion is scored by its summed (not length-normalized) log-probability given the shared prompt, and the aggregate share is P(correct) / (P(correct) + sum_i P(false_i)). Because each problem occurs once correct and once false and all other strings occur zero times, a frequency-matching model scores exactly 0.500. Pair accuracy (correct vs. the single realized error under mean NLL) is reported alongside on the same checkpoints.
official.claim: At 86M parameters on the denoising corpus, the correct completion holds 59.0% ± 0.8% of the aggregate probability mass against the full random-error family (null 50%), versus 48.8% ± 0.4% against a coherent false rule (49.3% ± 0.4% length-matched); at 3.5M-26M the random-error share is at or below the null (18.6%, 31.6%, 44.1%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Denoising corpus, measured on training problems where the null is exact (4 seeds, mean ± SD, %). The columns differ only in how much of the false side is summed: the generator's full support (a mean of 12.0 false modes per problem, range 4-35; n=2569), the single error the corpus contains (n=2620), or, for pair accuracy, that same single error under mean NLL. The coherent condition has one false mode, so full and realized coincide (n=2437).
official.metric: Aggregate share (%) of probability mass on the correct completion over the enumerated false support, higher means stronger preference for correct; null is 50. ± is population SD across 4 seeds.
official.comparison: Random-error-trained vs. coherent-error-trained 86M models (same architecture, training budget, problem types, 1:1 frequency), each measured against the 50% frequency-matching null; secondarily, aggregate share vs. pairwise measures on the same checkpoints (77.6% realized share, 87.4% pair accuracy).
official.falsification_criterion: At 86M the random-error aggregate share is not above 50% by more than the seed SD (e.g. all seeds' shares within ~1 point of 50 or below it), or it is not clearly above the coherent-condition share; or the coherent share is clearly above 50 (preference also against a coherent rule).

title: LightMoE: Reducing Mixture-of-Experts Redundancy through Expert Replacing

official.background: Mixture-of-Experts LLMs such as OLMoE activate only a few experts per token, but every expert has to stay in memory, so deployment is limited by memory. Existing ways to compress experts either prune them, which permanently removes their knowledge, or merge them, which reduces expert diversity and sometimes needs expensive retraining. This paper proposes 'expert replacing': swap the less important experts for parameter-efficient modules and recover performance with low-cost fine-tuning on the downstream task.
official.method:
For each MoE layer of OLMoE-1B-7B-SFT (64 experts per layer), LightMoE scores each expert by its normalized cumulative gate value over about 2^17 training tokens. It then selects the lowest-scoring experts whose cumulative score just exceeds a layer-specific threshold. The threshold is a base threshold p̂ scaled by exp(-0.3(norm_j - 1)), where norm_j is layer j's router output norm divided by the mean across layers, and clipped to [0.8p̂, 1.2p̂]. p̂ is binary-searched to hit the target compression ratio. The selected experts are grouped around the top-M 'dominant' experts by routing-logit cosine similarity (group size 3). Each group is replaced by one shared base, the gate-score-weighted average of its experts, and each replaced expert gets its own rank-16 LoRA term: W = W_share + B A.

During fine-tuning (AdamW, lr 1e-4, batch 32, 2000 steps for Math), each replaced expert is computed as β·W_orig + (1−β)·W_share + B A. β decays linearly from 1 to 0 by step εT, where ε is grid-searched over {0.1, ..., 0.5}, and the original experts are discarded afterwards. All baselines use the same number of trainable parameters (0.45B; their LoRA rank is raised to match): MC-SMoE with LoRA fine-tuning, HC-SMoE, MoBE, and the 'Replace (w/o shared)' / 'Replace (w. shared)' baselines, which directly replace the selected experts with LoRA adapters (without, or with a single, shared base) and no annealing. For Math, models are trained on MetaMathQA and evaluated on GSM8K accuracy.
official.claim: At 50% expert compression of OLMoE-1B-7B-SFT fine-tuned on MetaMathQA with 0.45B trainable parameters, LightMoE reaches 56.1 on GSM8K, versus 51.4 for the best matched baseline (Replace w. shared), 50.1 for MC-SMoE, 49.5 for Replace (w/o shared), 26.2 for HC-SMoE and 18.7 for MoBE.
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Main performance comparison across methods and tasks at different compression ratios. '*' indicates the full method as described in the original paper. "# Params" is the number of trainable parameters. Best results are shown in bold and second-best results are underlined. Our method LightMoE consistently achieves good performance among all tasks under different compression settings.
official.metric: GSM8K accuracy (%), higher is better. Single run per cell; the paper reports no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: LightMoE vs. MC-SMoE (LoRA-recovered), HC-SMoE, MoBE, Replace (w/o shared) and Replace (w. shared), all at 50% compression with 0.45B trainable parameters and the same training budget; LoRA on the uncompressed model (59.8) is shown as an upper reference.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup (OLMoE-1B-7B-SFT, 50% expert compression, 0.45B trainable parameters, 2000 steps on MetaMathQA), LightMoE's GSM8K accuracy is not clearly above (for example by less than about 2 points) the best of MC-SMoE and the two direct-Replace baselines, or the ranking reverses across seeds.

title: Visual-ERM: Reward Modeling for Visual Equivalence

official.background: Vision-to-code tasks turn a structured image (a chart, a table, an SVG graphic) into code or markup that renders back to an image. Reinforcement learning could improve such models beyond supervised fine-tuning, but it needs a reward that measures whether the rendered output actually matches the input. Text-based rewards (edit distance, TEDS) never look at the rendered image, and vision-encoder similarities such as DINO tolerate small layout or value changes that alter the meaning of a chart or table, so policies can hack them. A reward model that can spot fine-grained differences between a reference image and a rendered prediction is the missing piece, and whether a small model can do this better than a large general-purpose LVLM is a direct test of that idea.
official.method:
Visual-ERM is Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct fine-tuned (3 epochs, lr 1e-5, batch 32) as a generative reward model on about 340K (reference image, rendered prediction) pairs across charts (104K), tables (125K) and SVGs (111K). Predictions come from injected errors (GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-VL-235B) and natural Qwen3-VL-8B outputs; GPT-5-mini labels each pair with a structured list of discrepancies (category, severity, location, description). Given an image pair, Visual-ERM outputs that JSON list; for RL the summed severities are normalized by the batch maximum and turned into r_verm = clip(1 - S, 0, 1), which is added to a render-success reward (Eqs. 3-5). Only the discrepancy-list output matters for the VC-RewardBench claim.

VC-RewardBench has 1,335 image pairs (595 chart, 298 table, 442 SVG) annotated by GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-3-Pro and then consolidated by human reviewers. Each model under test outputs a discrepancy list for each pair. An LLM judge (GPT-5-mini for Table 5, since Table 10's GPT-5-mini row reproduces Table 5's Visual-ERM numbers), using the prompt in Appendix C.3 (Fig. 12), matches predicted to ground-truth discrepancies to count TP/FP/FN, giving F1_hard (strict match) and F1_soft (lenient match). S_c is the Pearson correlation between predicted and ground-truth summed severities. Appendix C.2 gives Visual-ERM's task-specific inference prompts; the paper does not say explicitly which prompts the baseline models received.
official.claim: On VC-RewardBench, the 8B Visual-ERM reaches an average F1_hard of 42.1 and F1_soft of 44.7, versus 29.5 and 32.4 for Qwen3-VL-235B-Instruct, and beats the 235B model on F1_hard in every domain (chart 39.9 vs 28.0, table 56.4 vs 35.7, SVG 28.3 vs 19.4).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Evaluation Results on VC-RewardBench. We evaluate a range of proprietary and open-source models on Visual-ERM-Bench. F1_h denotes F1_hard, the strict-match F1 score; F1_s denotes F1_soft, the soft-match F1 score; and S_c denotes the correlation score, measuring the overall agreement between the predicted scores and the ground-truth labels.
official.metric: F1_hard and F1_soft of discrepancy detection (higher is better), computed with GPT-5-mini as the matching judge; single run, no error bars. Table 10 shows Visual-ERM's average F1_hard varies 40.8-43.0 across four judge models.
official.comparison: Visual-ERM (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct fine-tuned as reward model) vs. Qwen3-VL-235B-Instruct (and its own base Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, plus proprietary GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-3-Flash) on the same benchmark and judge protocol
official.falsification_criterion: With the released Visual-ERM checkpoint and VC-RewardBench, Visual-ERM's average F1_hard is not at least about 5 points above Qwen3-VL-235B-Instruct's under the same prompts and judge, or the 235B model matches or beats Visual-ERM on F1_hard in any of the three domains.

title: Brittlebench: Quantifying LLM robustness via prompt sensitivity
claim_source: Table 5, page 21 (aggregate in Table 2, page 6; 95% bootstrap CIs in Table 10, page 24)

official.background: LLMs are usually compared on clean, fixed-format benchmarks such as MMLU or ARC, often by margins of a point or two. Real user prompts contain typos, odd spacing and rewordings that do not change what the question asks. If such surface changes move accuracy by several points, single-format benchmark scores overstate model reliability and leaderboard orderings can be artifacts of prompt formatting.
official.method:
Brittlebench is a wrapper around lm-evaluation-harness that applies semantics-preserving perturbations to benchmark inputs and re-runs the standard task. The chosen perturbation is 'Typos': AugLy's simulate_typos() applied once to each prompt with aug_word_p = 0.5, aug_char_p = 0.5, aug_word_min = 1, aug_word_max = 1000 (Table 3), with math expressions protected. The authors checked semantic preservation with a GPT-5 judge (99.8% of 2,400 sampled word-level perturbations keep the gold answer) and expert annotators.

Models (Qwen3-4B/8B/32B, Llama3.1-8B/70B, Llama3.3-70B instruct, Claude Opus 4.5 at temperature 0, GPT-5 with minimal reasoning) answer six multiple-choice benchmarks (MMLU, ARC, TruthfulQA, MathQA, GPQA, LogiQA) using their lm-eval-harness templates plus a fixed system instruction that allows free-form reasoning and requires the final option inside <answer>...</answer> tags (max 32,768 tokens); only the tagged option is scored. Accuracy is averaged over the six benchmarks, once on the clean inputs and once on the typo-perturbed inputs, with a single inference run each.
official.claim: In the 0-shot setting, applying AugLy typos (default settings) lowers mean accuracy over six MCQ benchmarks for every model tested: by 7.08-9.32 points for the six open-weight models (e.g. Qwen3-4B 75.71 -> 66.44, Qwen3-8B 78.50 -> 70.00, Llama3.3-70B 66.41 -> 58.92) and by 4.28 (Claude Opus 4.5) and 9.32 (GPT-5) points for the commercial models.
official.claim_caption: Table 5 Average performance (%) across all used benchmarks on Brittlebench for Word Manipulation Perturbations. Each number is the average accuracy score on the 6 benchmarks used (MMLU, ARC, TruthfulQA, MathQA, GPQA, LogiQA) based on their harness-eval implementations for different few-shot settings.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) averaged over MMLU, ARC, TruthfulQA, MathQA, GPQA, LogiQA; Drop = clean minus perturbed accuracy, higher means more brittle. Single run per condition, no seed std. Table 10 gives 95% bootstrap CIs (resampling the six benchmarks) only for the word-level group's largest drop (not per perturbation); for the 0-shot Qwen and Llama3.x-70B models that largest drop is the typo drop (for Llama3.1-8B it is sequence spaces, 9.42, not typos, 9.32), e.g. Qwen3-4B 9.27 [5.00, 17.47], Qwen3-8B 8.50 [3.47, 17.54], Llama3.3-70B 7.49 [5.40, 15.18].
official.comparison: Same model, same benchmark items, same prompt template: clean inputs vs. inputs with AugLy typos applied once
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-8B (0-shot) on the six benchmarks with and without the default typo perturbation, the mean accuracy drop is under about 3 points, or the drop is not consistently positive across the benchmarks.

title: Causal Attribution via Activation Patching

official.background: Attribution maps for Vision Transformers try to show which image patches drive a prediction. Gradient and relevance-propagation methods rely on local approximations. Attention-based methods use attention weights as indirect proxies. Perturbation methods edit the input pixels, which creates out-of-distribution inputs and misses redundancy between patches. As a result, it is still hard to get attributions that are both faithful to the model's decision and spatially well localized. The paper argues that intervening directly on a ViT's internal patch representations gives a more faithful causal measure of each patch's contribution.
official.method:
CAAP (Causal Attribution via Activation Patching) uses the input image as the source context and a blank image (white by default) as the target context. For each patch p_i, the selection S(p_i) is the patch plus its 3×3 neighbourhood (the 'Radius-1 Box'). The source image's patch-token residual-stream activations at S(p_i) are copied into the blank image's forward pass at every layer from the first up to l_e = ceil(2L/3). All other tokens keep the blank-image activations. The CLS token, and the patched tokens after l_e, are then propagated to the output. The attribution A(p_i) is the target-class score of this patched forward pass. All patches are computed in parallel in one pass by giving each patch its own CLS token with an attention mask; the paper says this is exact, not an approximation.

Faithfulness is measured with the RISE protocol. For Deletion AUC, the top-ranked pixels are progressively replaced with a constant and the target-class score is tracked (lower is better). For Insertion AUC, the top-ranked pixels are progressively revealed starting from a blurred image (higher is better). Ins−Del is Insertion minus Deletion. The evaluation uses a fixed random subset of 500 ImageNet-1K validation images, the same for all methods. The ImageNet classifiers are ViT-L/16, CLIP-L/14, DINOv2-L/14 and DeiT3-L/16. The baselines are RISE, Grad-CAM, Attention Rollout, Transformer Attribution, ViT-CX, TAM, IxG+, Libra IxG+, MDA and MUTEX.
official.claim: On a 500-image ImageNet validation subset with CLIP-L/14, CAAP reaches Insertion−Deletion 41.52 ± 1.02 versus 30.97 ± 1.08 for the best baseline (Libra IxG+), and Deletion AUC 34.35 ± 0.99 versus 44.27 ± 1.16 for the best baseline (Libra IxG+).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Faithfulness quantitative results on ImageNet for ViT-L/16, CLIP-L/14, DINOv2-L/14, and DeiT3-L/16. Deletion (↓), Insertion (↑), and Ins−Del (↑) are reported. Best is bold, second best is underlined in each column.
official.metric: Insertion−Deletion (higher is better) and Deletion AUC (lower is better), in %, under the RISE insertion/deletion protocol. The paper does not define ±; it reports a single evaluation over 500 images per dataset (Appendix F) with no seeds, so ± is an undefined per-image spread statistic, not a seed std.
official.comparison: CAAP vs. RISE, Grad-CAM, Rollout, T-Attr, ViT-CX, TAM, IxG+, Libra IxG+, MDA, MUTEX on the same images and backbone (CLIP-L/14)
official.falsification_criterion: With CLIP-L/14 on a random ImageNet validation subset of a few hundred images, CAAP's Insertion−Deletion is not clearly above Libra IxG+ (margin within the reported ± of about 1–2 points), or its Deletion AUC is not lower than every baseline's.

title: Backdoor Attacks under Lossy Compression: From Failure to Reactivation and Adaptation

official.background: Data-poisoning backdoor attacks hide a trigger in a fraction of training images so that a model trained on them predicts an attacker-chosen label whenever the trigger is present. Many 'invisible' triggers are subtle, mostly high-frequency perturbations. In practice datasets are stored and transmitted as lossy-compressed files (JPEG, BPG, learned codecs), and compression tends to remove exactly such high-frequency detail. So attacks that work on raw RGB images may stop working once the poisoned data passes through a compression pipeline. The paper measures this failure and proposes using region-of-interest (ROI) bit allocation in the encoder to keep trigger information alive through a standard decoder.
official.method:
All images (CIFAR-10, GTSRB, 8-class CelebA, resized to 64x64) are compressed and decompressed with Mbt-2018, a learned image codec that the authors extend with encoder-side ROI support (Spatial Feature Transform layers take a pixel-level mask that sets bitrate allocation weights; the decoder is unchanged). Baseline attacks (FTrojan, WaNet, BppAttack) poison images in RGB with their default settings and poisoning rates (5%, 10%, 20% respectively), and then all images are compressed with a uniform ROI mask (standard compression). The victim trains a classifier (ResNet18 or MobileNetV2; Adam, lr 0.01, decayed 10x every 100 epochs) on the decompressed images, in an all-to-one attack setting.

Universal Attack Reactivation (UAR, the 'ReA' columns) changes only the encoding: each poisoned image x_p is compressed with a frequency mask M_freq = Norm(mean over RGB channels of |IFFT(h_t(FFT(x_p)))|), where h_t keeps frequencies above threshold t, so trigger-carrying high-frequency regions get more bits. To avoid the mask itself becoming a shortcut, each benign image is compressed with the mask of a randomly chosen poisoned image. Metrics are Benign Accuracy (BA) on decompressed clean test images and Attack Success Rate (ASR) on decompressed triggered test images.
official.claim: With Mbt-2018 compression on CIFAR-10 and ResNet18, FTrojan's ASR falls to 12.53% under standard compression, while the same attack with UAR's frequency ROI masks reaches 94.91% ASR, and BA changes only from 92.21% to 91.32%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of methods across multiple datasets; additional results are in the Appendix A.
official.metric: Attack Success Rate (ASR, %, higher = stronger attack) and Benign Accuracy (BA, %, higher is better) on decompressed test images; single numbers, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: FTrojan with UAR ROI-mask encoding (FTrojan_ReA) vs. FTrojan with standard uniform-mask encoding, same codec (Mbt-2018), poisoning rate (5%), backbone and training; the same pattern is reported for WaNet and BppAttack, on GTSRB and CelebA, and with MobileNetV2 (and PreAct-ResNet18/SENet in Table 12)

title: MMOU: A Massive Multi-Task Omni Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Long and Complex Real-World Videos

official.background: Multimodal LLMs are usually evaluated on one modality at a time, and most video benchmarks either ignore audio or use short clips. MMOU is a benchmark of 20,000 human-written multiple-choice questions (15K test, 5K test-mini) on 11,877 long YouTube videos (average about 9 minutes, up to 2 hours). It aims to test joint audio-visual reasoning over long time spans, and the authors claim that every question needs both modalities.
official.method:
Eleven expert annotators wrote open-ended questions for each video and tagged them with 13 skill types (temporal, counting, needle-in-a-haystack, and others). GPT-5.2 then turned each question into a 10-option multiple-choice item with 9 distractors (4 grounded in the video, 5 out of context), and in 13% + 13% of test items 'None of the above' replaces the correct answer or a wrong option. Random chance is 10%.

Models are scored by micro-averaged accuracy on the 15K test set. Answers are parsed with regular expressions, option order is shuffled 5 times with a majority vote over the 5 answers, and each model gets the best of several prompt variants. The same Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct model is run once with audio+video input and once in audio-only mode. Vision-only Qwen3-VL models, text-only LLMs (question and options only) and cascaded caption-then-LLM pipelines serve as further reference points.
official.claim: On the MMOU test set (15,000 ten-option questions), Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct scores 46.0% with audio+video input but only 35.6% when it gets audio alone, and the text-only Qwen3-235B (no audio or video) scores 37.5%.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Performance breakdown across video domains and video durations for closed-source, open access, and open-source audio-visual MLLMs, video-only, audio-only MLLMs, and text-only LLMs.
official.metric: Micro-averaged multiple-choice accuracy (%), higher is better; majority vote over 5 option-order shuffles, best prompt variant per model; no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Same model (Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct) with audio+video vs. audio-only input; text-only Qwen3-235B and vision-only Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct as reference points
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on the MMOU test (or test-mini) set with the paper's protocol, the gap between audio+video and audio-only accuracy is under about 5 points, or audio+video accuracy is not clearly above the text-only Qwen3-235B baseline.

title: ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark: A Benchmark for Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Capabilities in ECG Interpretation

official.background: Multimodal LLMs for electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation are usually evaluated with an LLM-as-a-judge that compares generated explanations to reference text that was itself written by an LLM, and the judge never looks at the signal. That kind of evaluation rewards fluent, textbook-sounding rationales but cannot tell whether a model actually located and measured the waveform evidence behind a diagnosis. The authors build a benchmark that checks each reasoning step against ground truth extracted directly from the raw 12-lead signal.
official.method:
An automated pipeline (U-Net3+ wave delineation, post-processing, measurement, then rule-based mapping to findings and diagnoses via clinician-validated logic diagrams) produces ground-truth reasoning paths for 17 core ECG diagnoses. Samples from PTB-XL (3,084) and MIMIC-IV-ECG (3,359) are kept only when the dataset label agrees with the pipeline, balanced 100 positive / 100 negative per diagnosis, and reviewed manually. Vision models receive the ECG rendered as a standard 12-lead image with the ecg-plot package (OpenTSLM gets a 100 Hz time series), a fixed system prompt, and temperature 0.

Each sample is a multi-turn multiple-choice dialogue: an Initial Diagnostic Question (scored as IDA), then for each required finding a loop of Criterion Selection, Finding Identification, ECG Grounding (lead, wave-segment and measurement-range questions) and Diagnostic Decision (yes / no / further findings required). Gemini-3-Flash only maps free-text answers to options. Completion (Hard) is the percentage of samples answered correctly end to end; Depth (0-4) is the mean number of loop steps passed per finding, with ground-truth history supplied after a failure; GT-RDA is diagnostic accuracy when the full ground-truth reasoning history is given before the final decision.
official.claim: On the PTB-XL split, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct reaches only 5.80% Completion (Hard) and an average Depth of 1.52 out of 4 (which the authors read as passing criterion selection but stalling at finding identification/ECG grounding; no per-step breakdown is reported for Qwen3-VL), while its diagnosis accuracy rises from 53.70% (IDA, no reasoning) to 87.48% when the ground-truth reasoning history is supplied (GT-RDA); no model in Table 1 exceeds 6.84% Hard completion or 2.08 Depth on PTB-XL.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative benchmark results of the evaluated models on ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark across both PTB-XL and MIMIC-IV-ECG source datasets. Models are grouped into ECG-specific, medical domain, general domain, and proprietary categories, with the highest score for each metric highlighted in bold within its respective source dataset.
official.metric: IDA, Completion (Hard/Soft) and GT-RDA in % (higher is better); Depth on a 0-4 scale (higher is better). Single deterministic run (temperature 0); no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Within one model on the same samples: IDA vs. GT-RDA, and Completion/Depth vs. the 4-step maximum; across 19 models (ECG-specific, medical, general, proprietary). Reference points from the appendix: random answering gives 0.24% Hard completion and Depth 0.32 (Table 9); two physicians reach 56-71% Hard completion on a 73-case PTB-XL subset (Table 7).
official.falsification_criterion: Running Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on the released PTB-XL split with the authors' protocol gives Completion (Hard) well above ~10%, Depth at or above 2.5, or a GT-RDA that is not clearly (e.g. 20+ points) above IDA.

title: OxyGen: Unified KV Cache Management for VLA Inference under Multi-Task Parallelism

official.background: Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) vision-language-action models such as π0.5 share one VLM backbone between an action expert (flow matching) and a language expert (autoregressive text), so one model can control a robot and produce text such as memory notes or narration at the same time. Existing inference stacks run each task as its own forward pass ('isolated execution'): the same observation is prefilled twice, and long language generation delays the next action chunk. On on-board GPUs this lowers the action frequency the robot can sustain.
official.method:
OxyGen keeps the KV cache as a shared resource managed across tasks and control frames. (A) Cross-task KV sharing: each frame's observation is prefilled once, and the resulting KV cache is used both by the action expert for its S denoising steps and as the starting cache of a new language request. (B) Cross-frame continuous batching: every frame, all unfinished language requests (from this and earlier frames) are stacked into one batch and advanced by k decoding steps; finished requests are evicted and the rest keep their caches for the next frame. With one new request per frame and N tokens per request, the steady-state batch size is N/k.

The baseline ('sequential isolated execution') is openpi running π0.5 action generation and then language generation (prefill + N decoding steps) one after the other inside each frame, with language generation following a community reproduction because openpi does not release it. Action frequency = action horizon H / mean frame latency, with H = 10. Figure 5 reports the speedup ratio of OxyGen's action frequency over the baseline at N = 30 total decoding steps, for the LIBERO, ALOHA and DROID input configurations (camera views, resolution, action dimensions), denoising steps S ∈ {5, 10, 15, 20} and per-frame decoding budgets k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 10}. Since both systems produce the same number of language tokens per frame at steady state, the same ratio applies to language throughput.
official.claim: For π0.5 in the LIBERO configuration with S = 10 denoising steps and N = 30 language tokens per request (one new request per frame), OxyGen raises action frequency over sequential isolated openpi execution by 3.72x at k = 1, 2.98x at k = 5 and 2.22x at k = 10 decoding steps per frame.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5. Speedup ratio for action frequency of OxyGen vs. baseline across LIBERO, ALOHA, and DROID configurations (subplots), action denoising steps S (y-axis), and decoding steps per frame k (x-axis), with total decoding steps fixed at N = 30. The speedup is primarily affected by k, while the configuration choice and S have smaller impact.
official.metric: Speedup ratio of action frequency (H / mean end-to-end frame latency), OxyGen over baseline; higher is better. No error bars, number of runs, or run-to-run spread are reported. Values are printed in the heatmap cells.
official.comparison: OxyGen (cross-task KV sharing + cross-frame continuous batching) vs. sequential isolated execution in openpi, same model, inputs, N, S and GPU. Hardware is not stated in the Figure 5 caption; the matching ablation numbers in Section 4.3 (175.8 ms at N = 30, k = 5) are on RTX 4090.
official.falsification_criterion: Running openpi π0.5 with the LIBERO inputs at S = 10, N = 30 on an RTX 4090-class GPU, the ratio of baseline frame latency to OxyGen frame latency is clearly below the reported values, e.g. under 2.5x at k = 5 or under 3x at k = 1, or OxyGen's per-frame latency exceeds the baseline's in any setting with N > k.

title: HYDRA: Representation Harmonized Tokenization for Multimodal Generation and Understanding

official.background: Unified multimodal models try to do image understanding and image generation in one network, but the two tasks want different visual representations: understanding benefits from high-dimensional semantic features (e.g. CLIP/InternViT), while generation wants compact, structure-preserving latents (e.g. a VAE). Existing native unified models either use two separate encoders, stack a semantic encoder on top of a VAE, or force one encoder to serve both, each of which costs either reconstruction fidelity or semantic quality. A single tokenizer that reconstructs images well while keeping semantic features would let one model share one visual representation for both tasks.
official.method:
HYDRA-TOK is a single ~300M-parameter ViT initialized from InternViT-2.5 and split into a Gen-ViT (first 12 blocks), a Generation-Semantic Bottleneck (GSB), and a Sem-ViT (last 12 blocks). The GSB projects Gen-ViT features to a low-dimensional Gaussian latent (C = 64 channels, mean and log-variance, KL weight 1e-4), then projects the mean back up (H_bn = mu W_unproj) with a cosine-consistency loss (weight 1.0) to the pre-bottleneck features; H_bn is what the Sem-ViT consumes. A lightweight pixel flow-matching decoder conditioned on the sampled GSB latent reconstructs the image (flow-matching + 0.1 LPIPS + 0.075 GAN loss). Intermediate Gen-ViT and Sem-ViT features are also distilled (cosine) toward a frozen InternViT teacher.

Training: stage 1 trains encoder and decoder end-to-end for 300k iterations (batch 256, lr 2e-5) on ImageNet-1.2M + CC-12M + SAM-10M with reconstruction + regularization + distillation losses; stage 2 freezes the encoder and fine-tunes only the decoder for 100k iterations (lr 1e-5) with GAN loss and no distillation. Table 3 evaluates reconstruction on the ImageNet-1K validation set (PSNR, SSIM, rFID); the 256-resolution HYDRA-TOK row is the 448-trained model with images resized to 256.
official.claim: On the ImageNet-1K validation set at 256x256, the pure-ViT HYDRA-TOK (trained at 448, resized to 256) reconstructs images with 36.39 PSNR and 0.08 rFID, better than the best unified tokenizer baseline UniFlow in the same 448-trained/256-evaluated setting (33.23 PSNR, 0.26 rFID; SSIM tied at 0.96) and than FLUX-VAE at 256 (32.74 PSNR, 0.18 rFID), with baseline numbers as listed in the paper's Table 3.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Reconstruction results on the ImageNet-1K validation set. † indicates models trained at a resolution of 448 and resized to 256 for evaluation.
official.metric: PSNR (higher better), SSIM (higher better), rFID (lower better) on ImageNet-1K val; single numbers, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: HYDRA-TOK vs. unified tokenizers (UniFlow, UAE, UniTok, UniLIP, TokenFlow, BLIP3-o, QLIP, RAE) and generation-only tokenizers (SD-VAE, FLUX-VAE, VA-VAE, DC-AE)
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating the released HYDRA-TOK checkpoint on ImageNet-1K val at 256 (448-trained, resized) gives rFID not clearly below UniFlow's (e.g. >= 0.26) or PSNR not above 33.23 when UniFlow is evaluated with the same script; or a retrained HYDRA-TOK does not beat UniFlow on either metric.

title: GATE-AD: Graph Attention Network Encoding for Few-Shot Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection

official.background: Few-shot industrial visual anomaly detection asks a model to detect and localize defects in product images when it has only 1 to 8 defect-free reference images per product category and no defective examples. Strong current methods (e.g. AnomalyDINO) score each test patch by its distance to the nearest stored normal patch feature from a frozen self-supervised ViT. This judges each patch by its own appearance. The paper argues that defects instead break the consistency between a patch and its spatial neighbours, so normality should be modelled through local context.
official.method:
Patch tokens are extracted from a frozen DINO ViT, averaging the last 8 layers. On VisA the backbone is DINOv3 ViT-B/16 at 512 px. Each patch is a node on a fixed 8-neighbour spatial grid graph. A 3-layer Graph Attention Network (hidden size 256) maps the graph to node representations. Representation alignment (RA) projects the GAT output through an MLP g and the frozen ViT token through a linear layer q into a shared 256-d latent space. Training uses only the k normal support images. It minimises the Scaled Cosine Error (gamma = 2) between the two projections on a masked subset of nodes (20% replaced by a learnable mask token), with attention dropout 0.3, Adam at lr 3e-4, and up to 2,000 epochs with early stopping.

At test time the per-patch anomaly score is the SCE between the GAT prediction and the projected ViT target, computed over all nodes. The image score is the mean of the top 1% of patch scores on VisA. The ablation baselines are: 'DINO 1-NN', which scores each query patch by its nearest normal DINO patch feature as in AnomalyDINO (no graph, no RA), and 'DINO + RA', which uses the same features projected into the RA space and scored with SCE, with no relational modelling. All variants share the dataset-specific configuration and are run over 3 support-set seeds.
official.claim: On VisA 1-shot, with the same frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 features and configuration, GATE-AD reaches image-level AUROC 93.5 ± 0.2, compared with 87.4 ± 1.1 for patch nearest-neighbour scoring (DINO 1-NN) and 88.7 ± 0.3 for the non-graph DINO + RA variant.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Component ablation of GATE-AD on MVTec AD, VisA, and MPDD (%, mean±std).
official.metric: Image-level AUROC (%, higher is better), mean ± std over 3 support-set seeds; pixel-level AUROC is also reported
official.comparison: Full GATE-AD (GAT + RA + masking + attention dropout) vs. DINO 1-NN and DINO + RA (no graph), plus the other component ablations, all under the same dataset-specific configuration
official.falsification_criterion: On VisA 1-shot, over 3 support-set seeds, GATE-AD's image AUROC is not at least about 3 points above the DINO 1-NN baseline built on the same backbone features, or DINO + RA comes within the seed std of GATE-AD.

title: Steering Frozen LLMs: Adaptive Social Alignment via Online Prompt Routing

official.background: Deployed LLMs are usually aligned once, by post-training methods such as RLHF or DPO, and then left as a fixed policy. Safety norms, however, vary across products, regions and user modes and change over time, and retraining weights for every change is expensive. The paper studies inference-time governance instead: keep the base model frozen and, for each incoming query, choose one system prompt from a fixed pool so as to balance helpfulness (utility) and safety according to a preference weight w supplied at inference time. A specific difficulty is that queries that are semantically close ("how to make a cake" vs. "how to make a bomb") can need very different prompts, so naive similarity-based sharing of feedback can leak unsafe behaviour into benign regions.
official.method:
The task is framed as a contextual bandit. Each round, a query q_t and a weight w_t arrive, the learner picks one of 90 candidate system prompts (arms), the frozen Qwen3-0.6B answers, and two scores are observed: utility u_t from Skywork-Reward-V2 and safety s_t as the safe-class probability from Qwen3-SafeGuard-8B. The reward is w_t u_t + (1 - w_t) s_t. Each arm is represented by cosine projections of its prompt embedding onto 256 'preference axes' (128 utility, 128 safety) obtained by PCA on embedding differences of evaluator rationales from UltraFeedback, HelpSteer3 and PKU-SafeRLHF. Each query is represented by concatenating an all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embedding with pooled hidden states from Qwen3Guard-Stream-0.6B, and is mapped to one of N = 50 K-means prototypes.

CCLUB keeps separate ridge-regression statistics for utility and safety per prototype, and two graphs over prototypes (one per objective) that start out complete; an edge is pruned when the two prototypes' estimated parameters differ by more than their confidence radii. Data are pooled only within connected components of the intersection of the two graphs, and the arm is chosen by w-weighted LinUCB indices (beta = 1.0). Baselines are Random, and Greedy and LinUCB each at global, prototype and per-input granularity. Data: 6,000 deduplicated queries sampled from BeaverTails and PKU-SafeRLHF. For the offline metric, the policy is warm-started on T_off labelled (query, arm) interactions and then evaluated without updates on N_test = 500 test queries; the suboptimality gap is the mean shortfall of the chosen arm's reward from the best arm's reward on each test query. 10 random seeds.
official.claim: With warm-start budgets T_off of roughly 10,000-25,000 interactions, CCLUB's offline suboptimality gap (about 0.27-0.28) is lower than that of the strongest baseline, Prototype LinUCB (about 0.295-0.30), and Input Greedy (about 0.32-0.33), with non-overlapping standard-error bands over 10 seeds; the paper reports a 4.95% average gap reduction vs. Prototype LinUCB and 14.42% vs. Input Greedy.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4. Performance comparison on online cumulative reward and offline deployment suboptimality gap.
official.metric: Offline suboptimality gap on 500 test queries (lower is better), plotted against warm-start budget T_off; lines are means over 10 random seeds and shaded regions are standard error. Values below are read off the plot and approximate. The left panel (online cumulative reward, higher is better) has no visible error bands.
official.comparison: CCLUB vs. Prototype LinUCB, Prototype Greedy, Input Greedy, Input LinUCB, Global LinUCB, Global Greedy and Random, all using the same arms, features, scorers and query stream
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the warm-start experiment (same 90 arms or a comparable pool, N = 50 prototypes, 10 seeds), CCLUB's offline suboptimality gap at T_off >= 10,000 is not lower than Prototype LinUCB's by more than the seed standard error, or the average reduction over the T_off sweep falls well below the reported ~5%.

title: Flow Matching Policy Optimization with Mirror Descent and Entropy Constraints
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (same numbers with accomplished-task counts and FPO in Table 8, page 23)

official.background: Online reinforcement learning for continuous control usually relies on unimodal Gaussian policies, which cannot represent tasks where several distinct action choices are equally good. Diffusion policies can represent such multimodal distributions, but their stochastic reverse process makes policy entropy intractable, so maximum-entropy-style exploration has to rely on heuristics, and backpropagating policy gradients through a long denoising chain is expensive and unstable. The paper argues that ODE-based flow matching policies can provide both tractable entropy and simulation-free training, which should matter most on sparse-reward, multimodal tasks such as multi-task robot manipulation.
official.method:
FMER represents the policy as a state-conditioned flow-matching velocity field in an unbounded latent space; actions are produced by Euler-integrating the ODE (10 steps) from Gaussian noise and squashing with tanh. The actor is trained without backpropagating through the ODE: for each replay state it samples M=8 candidate actions from the current policy, scores them with the learned critic Q_ψ (no separate value network; the state baseline cancels in normalization), and minimizes a conditional flow-matching loss (target velocity arctanh(a) - x0 along the linear OT path) weighted by self-normalized weights exp(Q/τ)/Σ exp(Q/τ), which the authors prove realizes the policy mirror descent target π_k·exp(A/τ)/Z. The temperature τ is adapted to hold the effective sample size of the weights at a target (ESS*=3).

An entropy term, using a closed-form action-space entropy estimate (vector-field divergence minus the tanh correction 2⟨tanh(x), v⟩, with a Hutchinson trace estimator), is added with a Lagrange multiplier α tuned by dual descent toward a target entropy, as in SAC. During data collection and for critic targets, the highest-Q of the M candidates is used. All methods are trained for 1M environment steps over 5 seeds; the reported score is the maximum evaluation result (10 episodes each, evaluated every 10K steps) over the final 10% of training (steps 900K-1M).
official.claim: On FrankaKitchen with N=4 sub-tasks (light switch, slide cabinet, bottom burner, microwave; 280-step episodes, 1M environment steps), FMER reaches a normalized task completion rate of 46.50% ± 3.79 versus 25.00% ± 17.68 for the best baseline DPMD and at most 15.00% for the other seven baselines (PPO, SAC, TD3, DIPO, QVPO, SAC-Flow, FLAME).

title: Generative Control as Optimization: Time Unconditional Flow Matching for Adaptive and Robust Robotic Control

official.background: Diffusion and flow-matching robot policies generate action chunks by integrating a time-conditioned velocity field over a fixed schedule, so they spend the same compute on every state and have no built-in signal for whether the generated action is trustworthy. A policy that cannot tell when its input is out of distribution (OOD) may confidently execute bad actions, so a cheap, training-free OOD signal would help with safe deployment.
official.method:
GeCO trains a time-unconditional velocity field f_θ(x, s) over action sequences. Training samples x_γ = γa + (1−γ)ε with γ ~ U(0,1) (γ is not given to the model) and regresses f_θ(x_γ, s) onto (ε − a)·c(γ), where c(γ) is a truncated linear decay (constant λ = 4 up to onset α0, then linear to 0 at γ = 1), so expert actions become zero-velocity equilibria. Inference starts from Gaussian noise and runs gradient-style updates a_{k+1} = a_k − η_k f_θ(a_k, s), stopping early when ||f_θ|| falls below a threshold. The simulation policy is a DiT-1D (d_model 384, 12 layers, 6 heads) with frozen DINOv2-base (2 views) and T5-base conditioning, built on the CleanDiffuser Rectified Flow code, action chunk 16, 8 actions executed per plan.

For OOD detection, one policy is trained on the 10 LIBERO-Goal tasks. 500 ID episodes (LIBERO-Goal) and 500 OOD episodes (LIBERO-Spatial) are rolled out; 20 planning calls are sampled per episode. For each planning call GeCO runs at most K_max = 10 refinement steps and the score is the final residual norm ||f_θ(a_K, s)||; online flags use a moving average (w = 5, τ = 0.6) or a leaky bucket (τ = 0.5, λ = 0, B = 0.7). The baseline score is a Diff-DAgger-style single-sample flow-matching loss ||f_θ(x_t, t, c) − (ε − x0)||² at fixed t = 1 on the generated chunk x0. Planning-level AUROC treats OOD calls as positives.
official.claim: For a policy trained on LIBERO-Goal, GeCO's final field-norm score separates LIBERO-Goal (ID) from LIBERO-Spatial (OOD) planning calls with AUROC 0.93, versus 0.53 for a single-timestep flow-matching-loss baseline; at the chosen threshold it flags 84.0% of OOD calls while keeping 90.0% of ID calls (baseline 14.4% / 27.8%).
official.claim_caption: Table 5. OOD Detection on LIBERO Suite Shift (Goal → Spatial). We report planning-level AUROC for separating ID (Goal) and OOD (Spatial) using optimization-dynamics signals computed per planning call. At a fixed operating point, TPR is specificity on ID instances and TNR is recall on OOD instances. Time Saved is the average fraction of interaction time avoided on OOD episodes by early reporting, computed as 1 − t_report/T_total.
official.metric: Planning-level AUROC (higher is better) over 500×20 ID and 500×20 OOD planning calls; TNR = recall on OOD, TPR = fraction of ID retained, at a threshold targeting TPR ≈ 90%; Time Saved = 1 − t_report/T_total on OOD episodes. Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: GeCO residual-norm OOD score (moving average and leaky bucket filters) vs. flow-matching-loss baseline score (moving average), on the same ID/OOD episodes
official.falsification_criterion: Training a GeCO policy on LIBERO-Goal and scoring LIBERO-Goal vs. LIBERO-Spatial planning calls with the final residual norm gives AUROC below ~0.8, or the flow-matching-loss baseline reaches within ~0.1 AUROC of GeCO's score.

title: Motion-o: Trajectory-Grounded Video Reasoning
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (discussed in Appendix E, page 17)

official.background: Grounded video-reasoning models such as Open-o3 Video write reasoning traces that name an object, give its bounding box and give a timestamp. That shows where and when the evidence appears, but how the object moves between those snapshots is left for the language model to fill in, so claims about motion can't be checked or rewarded. This paper asks whether making motion an explicit, rewarded part of the reasoning trace improves video understanding, especially on motion-centric questions.
official.method:
Motion Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) adds a self-closing <motion obj=... dir=... speed=... scale=.../> tag after an object has been grounded at two or more timestamps. Direction is one of 8 compass bins or STAT; speed is stationary/slow/moderate/fast; scale is approaching/stable/receding. Ground-truth tags are computed automatically from box tracks: centroid displacement gives direction and speed (normalized by object size), and the log-ratio of box areas gives scale. The tracks come from the STGR / PerceptionLM-subset annotations, densified with intermediate boxes taken from PLM masks.

Training has two stages: SFT on the motion-augmented traces, then GSPO RL with the Open-o3 Video reward (answer accuracy + format + temporal and spatial grounding) plus r_motion = r_traj + r_ground. r_traj scores the predicted direction/speed/scale bins against the track, with partial credit for adjacent bins. r_ground (dual-chain verification) rewards motion tags that change when the motion segments of the video are frozen. For 'Open-o3 + MCoT', this pipeline starts from the released Open-o3 Video checkpoint and uses a motion-focused SFT mix of 7,838 samples. The claimed comparison is that model against the unmodified Open-o3 Video checkpoint, evaluated on the MotionBench dev split.
official.claim: Adding MCoT training (SFT + GSPO with r_traj and r_ground) to the Open-o3 Video checkpoint raises MotionBench (dev) accuracy from 45.0 to 63.0 (+18.0 points). Without r_ground it reaches 60.0, so most of the gain holds without the visual grounding reward.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance across video understanding, temporal grounding, and motion-centric benchmarks. The r_ground column indicates whether the visual grounding reward is enabled or disabled in our methods. Bold numbers denote the best results, while underlined numbers indicate the second best.
official.metric: MotionBench dev-split accuracy (%), higher is better; single run, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: Open-o3 + MCoT (with r_ground) vs. Open-o3 Video (the same starting checkpoint without MCoT training); secondarily, Open-o3 + MCoT without r_ground
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating the released Open-o3 + MCoT checkpoint and the Open-o3 Video checkpoint on the MotionBench dev split under the same protocol gives a gap far below +18 points (e.g. under ~5 points), or retraining MCoT from Open-o3 Video does not substantially beat the starting checkpoint on MotionBench.

title: Spectral Alignment in Forward–Backward Representations via Temporal Abstraction

official.background: Forward-backward (FB) representations learn a low-rank factorization F(s,a,z)^T B(s',a') of the successor representation (SR), which allows zero-shot value inference for any reward. In continuous environments the true SR tends to be high-rank with a slowly decaying spectrum, so a low-rank FB model has to fit hard-to-predict high-frequency components, and bootstrapping errors propagate through Bellman updates. The paper argues that temporal abstraction via action repetition acts like a low-pass filter on the transition operator, lowering the effective rank of the SR and making FB learning stable, and that simply increasing the embedding dimension d or the discount γ does not achieve the same effect.
official.method:
FB representations (Touati & Ollivier, 2021) are trained online with a learned actor, F ensemble of 2, [256, 256] MLPs for F, B and actor, learning rates 1e-5 (F) and 1e-6 (B, actor), batch size 512, replay buffer 1e6, orthogonality loss coefficient 1.0, and 1e6 gradient updates. The task latent z is sampled 50/50 from a Gaussian and from B of a random replay-buffer state, held for 10 steps. States are (x, y) coordinates encoded with an RBF kernel. Action repetition with factor k is an environment wrapper: the agent only sees every k-th observation and repeats each action k times; γ is the nominal discount of the k-repeat MDP.

Evaluation is on the OGBench continuous Four-Rooms navigation task with random start and goal positions and sparse 0/1 reward. Each trained model is evaluated on 50 episodes with random start/goal; mean episodic return is averaged over 5 seeds with a 95% confidence interval. The default setting is γ = 0.95, d = 100, and the ablation sweeps k ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50}, with further sweeps over d ∈ {25, 100, 400} and γ ∈ {0.9, 0.99, 0.999}.
official.claim: In continuous Four-Rooms (γ = 0.95, d = 100), FB with action repetition k = 10 reaches a mean return of about 0.87, versus about 0.20 without repetition (k = 1); and at k = 1 no tested embedding dimension (d = 25, 100, 400) or discount (γ = 0.9, 0.99, 0.999) gets above about 0.21.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Effect of temporal abstraction on performance. Ablation over temporal abstraction (k), embedding dimension (d), and discount factor (γ) using a continuous four-rooms environment. Addition of temporal abstraction (k > 1) boosts performance, whereas increasing d or γ alone does not.
official.metric: Mean episodic return (success rate under sparse 0/1 reward, higher is better), each model evaluated on 50 episodes; error bars are 95% confidence intervals over 5 seeds; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: FB with action repetition k ∈ {3, 5, 10, 20, 50} vs. standard FB (k = 1) in the same environment, architecture and training budget; k = 1 also swept over d and γ as stronger baselines
official.falsification_criterion: With 5 seeds in continuous Four-Rooms at γ = 0.95, d = 100, the k = 10 agent's mean return is not clearly above the k = 1 agent's (95% CIs overlap or the gap is below ~0.3), or some k = 1 configuration with d ∈ {25, 100, 400} or γ ∈ {0.9, 0.99, 0.999} reaches a return comparable to k = 10.

title: Does This Gradient Spark Joy?

official.background: Policy-gradient training computes a backward pass for every sampled action, even though the backward pass costs more than the forward pass and most samples (actions the policy already prefers or already avoids) teach the model little. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG), from the same author, weights each sample by 'delight', the product of its advantage and its surprisal (negative log-probability), which is available from the forward pass alone. This paper asks whether delight can decide which samples get a backward pass at all, so that most backpropagation can be skipped without hurting learning.
official.method:
The Kondo gate computes delight χ = U · (−log π(A|H)) for every sample in the batch from the forward pass, sets a price λ to the (1−ρ)-quantile of delight within the batch, and draws a Bernoulli gate with probability σ((χ − λ)/η). Only samples with gate = 1 get a backward pass, contributing U ∇ log π(A|H) to the update; the others are never differentiated. With target gate rate ρ = 0.03, about 3% of samples are backpropagated. ρ = 1 recovers full DG.

Setting: MNIST as a 10-action contextual bandit. The policy is a two-layer MLP (100 hidden units per layer) with softmax over digits; reward is 1 if the chosen digit equals the label, else 0. All methods use the expected-confidence baseline b = Σ_a π(a) r(a) (= π(y*)), Adam, batch B = 100 drawn with replacement, 10,000 gradient steps (1M forward passes), learning rate swept over {1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3} (optimum 1e-3 for all). Compared methods: PG (REINFORCE), DG (all samples, delight-weighted) and DG-K (DG with the Kondo gate at ρ = 0.03). The metric is classification error, averaged over 30 seeds.
official.claim: On the MNIST contextual bandit, DG with the Kondo gate at ρ = 0.03 reaches about 2.4% classification error after 1M forward passes while using only about 30k backward passes, below standard policy gradient (about 3.8%, using 1M backward passes) and close to full DG (about 1.8%, 1M backward passes).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: PG, DG, and Kondo gate (DG-K) at ρ = 0.03 on MNIST. (a) The Kondo gate matches DG despite computing 3% of backward passes. (b) It dominates by two orders of magnitude in backward-pass space. Averaged over 30 seeds; shading shows ±1 standard error.
official.metric: Classification error (lower is better) vs. forward passes and vs. backward passes; mean over 30 seeds, shading is ±1 standard error; values below are read off a log-scale plot and are approximate
official.comparison: DG-K (ρ = 0.03) vs. PG and full DG, same architecture, optimizer, baseline and learning-rate tuning
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running with the stated setup (30 seeds, 1M forward passes), DG-K at ρ = 0.03 does not end with lower error than PG (difference not clearly larger than a few standard errors), or DG-K's final error is more than about twice DG's.

title: Neuronal Self-Adaptation Enhances Capacity and Robustness of Representation in Spiking Neural Networks
claim_source: Table 5, page 15 (appendix E); multi-seed KvLIF value from Table 9 (page 17); ALIF/adLIF from Table 6 (page 16)

official.background: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are trained with surrogate gradients and are usually built from leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons, which either reset the membrane potential to zero after a spike (hard reset) or subtract the threshold (soft reset). The authors argue that both variants have a limited dynamic range: soft reset carries over residual potential that makes repeated firing easier and amplifies noise, while hard reset throws away history. They propose a neuron with an extra adaptive state, inspired by potassium currents, that damps inputs and deepens the reset after spikes, and claim it improves SNN classification accuracy and noise robustness at little cost.
official.method:
KvLIF adds a state K[t] to the LIF neuron (Eq. 16, Algorithm 1): the input current is scaled by (1 - γ·sigmoid(K[t-1])) (synaptic shunting); U[t] = λU[t-1] + shunted input; S[t] = H(U[t] - V_th); K[t] = αK[t-1] + βU[t] + S[t]; and after a spike the membrane is reset by U[t] - S[t]·(V_th + sigmoid(K[t])) (adaptive repolarization). Settings: V_th = 1, λ = 0.5, rectangular surrogate gradient with width 1, α = 0.8, γ = 0.05; β = 0.1 for CIFAR100 per Table 4.

For CIFAR100 the network is a Spiking ResNet-18 with direct encoding (pixels repeated at each time step), random crop with 4-pixel padding, horizontal flip and Cutout, TET loss (λ = 0.05), SGD with lr 0.1, batch 128, weight decay 5e-4, 300 epochs, seed 1000. The baselines LIF-S (soft reset) and LIF-H (hard reset) use the same network and training setup with only the neuron swapped. Table 6 also reports ALIF and adLIF (spike-frequency-adaptation neurons) in the same ResNet-18/T = 4 setting.
official.claim: With a Spiking ResNet-18 on CIFAR100 at T = 4 time steps, replacing LIF neurons with KvLIF raises test accuracy to 77.76% (3-seed mean 77.85 ± 0.15), versus 74.64% for hard-reset LIF and 69.24% for soft-reset LIF (and 75.75% for ALIF in Table 6), a gain of at least 2 points over every matched neuron baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Performance comparison with conventional LIF models.
official.metric: Top-1 test accuracy (%), higher is better. Table 5 values are single runs (seed 1000), no error bars; Table 9 gives KvLIF mean ± std over 3 seeds; baselines have no reported variance.
official.comparison: KvLIF vs. LIF-S and LIF-H (and ALIF, adLIF from Table 6) in the same Spiking ResNet-18, T = 4, same training recipe; a ReLU ANN (78.31%) is shown for reference
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining Spiking ResNet-18 on CIFAR100 at T = 4 with the authors' recipe, KvLIF's accuracy is not at least ~1.5 points above the better of LIF-H and ALIF (e.g. LIF-H or ALIF reaches ≥76.3% while KvLIF stays near 77.8%, or KvLIF falls to ≤77.2% while ALIF stays near 75.75%), averaged over a few seeds.
