title: Simple Projection-Free Algorithm for Contextual Recommendation with Logarithmic Regret and Robustness
claim_source: Figure 1 (left panel), page 20; 95% CIs in Figure 3, page 22

official.background: In contextual recommendation (online inverse linear optimization), a learner sees a feasible action set each round, recommends the action that maximizes its current estimate of a hidden user preference vector, and then observes the action the user actually chose. Regret is the cumulative utility gap between the user's and the learner's actions. The best previous efficient method (Sakaue et al., based on Online Newton Step, ONS) achieves O(d log T) regret but needs a Mahalanobis projection every round, which costs about O(d^3) and is the bottleneck in high-dimensional or kernelized settings.
official.method:
CoRectron (Algorithm 1) keeps the cumulative residual ζ_t = Σ_s (x̂_s − x_s) and a preconditioner A_t = λI + Σ_s g_s g_sᵀ with g_s = x̂_s − x_s. Each round it predicts ŵ_t = −A_{t−1}^{-1} ζ_{t−1}, recommends x̂_t ∈ argmax_{x∈X_t} ⟨ŵ_t, x⟩, observes the user action x_t, and updates A and ζ. There is no projection, because rescaling ŵ_t does not change the recommendation, so ŵ_t needs no norm constraint. In the linear contextual model the parameter is a matrix W ∈ R^{n×p} and the residual is g_t = g_t^base z_tᵀ (vectorized, d = np).

Experiment (Appendix H.1, Linear setting): contextual m-out-of-n with n = 10, m = 5, p = 10 (d = 100); actions are {0,1}^n vectors with m ones scaled by 1/√10. Contexts z_t ~ N(0, I_p), projected onto the unit ball; the true utility is u_t = U* z_t with ‖U*‖_F = 1, and the user picks the optimal action. T = 10,000, 10 seeds, all methods see the same sequence. Baselines: ONS on the unit ball with exp-concave surrogate (η_sur = 1/10, γ_ons = 1/2, A_0 = εI, Mahalanobis projection onto the unit ball) and projected OGD on the unit ball. The regularization of each method is swept over c ∈ {1e-3, ..., 1e3}: λ = c·100 for CoRectron, ε = c·100 for ONS, η_OGD = η̄_OGD / c for OGD, with a reference step size η̄_OGD of order 1/√T (see Appendix H.1, page 21). The best final regret over the sweep is compared.
official.claim: In the linear contextual 10-choose-5 setting (n = p = 10, T = 10,000, optimal-action feedback), CoRectron-L's best final cumulative regret over the regularization sweep is 6.351, versus 15.34 for ONS and 15.40 for OGD (each at their best coefficient), i.e. less than half, averaged over 10 seeds.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Overall comparison in the Linear setting. Final regret and runtime over the coefficient grid are shown. All values are means over 10 seeds. In each algorithm block, darker points correspond to smaller c, and c increases from left to right. For final regret, the annotated value is the best over the coefficient sweep.
official.metric: Final cumulative regret R_T at T = 10,000, lower is better; mean over 10 seeds, best value over the 7-point coefficient sweep. Figure 1 has no error bars; Figure 3 shows 95% Student-t confidence bands over seeds for CoRectron-L vs. ONS (visually narrow at the best coefficients).
official.comparison: CoRectron-L vs. ONS (Sakaue et al. 2025 method) and projected OGD, each with its best regularization coefficient, on the same round sequences
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Linear setting with 10 seeds and the same coefficient sweep, CoRectron-L's best mean final regret is not clearly below half of the best ONS or best OGD value (e.g. ratio above ~0.6, or overlapping 95% CIs with ONS).

title: MemDLM: Memory-Enhanced DLM Training

official.background: Diffusion language models (DLMs) such as LLaDA generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens, but they are trained with a static single-step masked-prediction objective (MDLM) that never shows the model its own progressive denoising trajectory. All context must also be carried through token-space attention, which gets diluted in long contexts. The paper asks whether adding a transient parameter-space memory during training improves long-context retrieval in DLMs, even when that memory is thrown away at inference.
official.method:
MemDLM trains with first-order bi-level optimization. For each batch, an inner loop starts from zero-initialized fast-weight LoRA adapters (r=32, alpha=64, on FFN modules of the last 10% of layers) and takes two SGD steps (lr 0.1, per-parameter clipping 1.0): first denoising a noisier state x_tpre (mask ratio 1.5x the anchor's) toward the anchor x_t, then denoising x_t toward the clean x_0. The outer loop then updates the base model's LoRA (r=32, alpha=64, AdamW lr 2e-5, cosine schedule) on the standard weighted MDLM loss at the same anchor x_t, conditioned on the fast weights; fast weights are discarded after each batch. The baseline, Standard MDLM, is exactly the outer loop alone.

Both are instruction-tuned on LongAlpaca (filtered to <=4,096 tokens; prompt tokens unmasked and excluded from the loss) from LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B-Base loaded in 4-bit, for 5 epochs (960 steps, batch 2 per device on 8 GPUs). 'Train-Only' evaluates the MemDLM-trained model with the inner loop disabled, so at inference it is architecturally identical to the baseline. Evaluation uses lm-evaluation-harness on RULER (Multi-Value, Variable Tracking, Common Words Extraction) at 4K/8K and BABILong at 2K/4K/8K, with single-block generation, one token per denoising step.
official.claim: On LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B-Base fine-tuned on LongAlpaca, MemDLM training with the inner loop disabled at inference (Train-Only) raises RULER Variable Tracking at 8K from 78.84 to 94.84 and BABILong at 2K from 46.00 to 59.40 compared with Standard MDLM fine-tuning, and is at least as good on all 9 RULER/BABILong settings.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Needle-in-a-Haystack results on RULER and BABILong. We report Standard MDLM, MemDLM (Train-Only), and MemDLM (Train & Inference). Bold indicates the best result within each backbone block.
official.metric: Task accuracy/score (%) on RULER sub-tasks and BABILong, higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: MemDLM (Train-Only) vs. Standard MDLM, same backbone, data, LoRA configuration, steps and decoding; MemDLM (Train & Inference) also reported
official.falsification_criterion: With matched training budget and decoding, a MemDLM Train-Only model does not beat Standard MDLM on RULER-VT 8K by a margin well beyond seed-to-seed variation (e.g., gap under ~5 points or within the spread of a few seeds), or the BABILong-2K gain disappears.

title: Evaluating AI-based Scientific Knowledge Synthesis with Epidemiological Systematic Reviews

official.background: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) in infectious-disease epidemiology involve screening thousands of articles against inclusion criteria, then extracting parameters such as reproduction numbers or case-fatality ratios along with their population context. LLMs could speed this up, but the risk is high: a wrongly excluded study is lost for good, and the findings can inform public-health policy. The paper builds AgentSLR, a harness and dataset based on expert annotations from the Pathogen Epidemiology Review Group's (PERG) peer-reviewed reviews of WHO priority pathogens. It is used to score LLMs separately on each SLR stage.
official.method:
The released dataset matches 16,248 open-access article records (titles, abstracts, PDFs) across seven pathogens (Marburg, Ebola, Lassa, SARS-CoV-1, Zika, MERS-CoV, Nipah) to PERG's human include/exclude screening labels. In title-and-abstract screening, each article's title and abstract is given to an LLM with a prompt that follows the ScreenPrompt template: study objectives, expert inclusion/exclusion criteria (Appendix H), chain-of-thought instructions and a structured output format. The LLM returns include or exclude.

Five reasoning models are run with the same prompt: gpt-oss-120b, GLM-4.7, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Kimi-K2.5 (open weights, served with vLLM on H200s) and GPT-5.2 (API). Reasoning is set to high where possible, with a 64K-token generation cap. Decisions are scored against PERG labels using precision, recall and macro F1, per pathogen and overall (the mean across pathogens).
official.claim: In title-and-abstract screening against PERG expert labels, Kimi-K2.5 has the highest macro F1 on all 7 pathogens (it ties gpt-oss-120b on Marburg at 0.69) and overall: 0.77, vs. 0.74 for gpt-oss-120b, 0.72 for GLM-4.7, 0.65 for GPT-5.2 and 0.62 for DeepSeek-V3.2. The gap comes from recall: Kimi-K2.5 reaches 0.75, while GPT-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 reach only 0.61 and 0.59 despite similar precision (0.82-0.83).
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Title and abstract screening metrics across LLMs. Green and Red denote the best- and worst-performing pathogens for each model (in terms of F1 score). Bold indicates the best-performing model for each pathogen, and Underline indicates the second-best. P = precision; R = recall; F1 = F1-Score.
official.metric: Macro F1, precision and recall against PERG include/exclude labels (higher is better); 'Overall' is the mean over 7 pathogens. Single run per model; no seeds or confidence intervals. Figure 2 reports error bars only as std across pathogens.
official.comparison: Kimi-K2.5 vs. gpt-oss-120b, GLM-4.7, GPT-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2, all with the same screening prompt, inputs and labels
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the same prompt on the released data and finding that Kimi-K2.5 is not the top model by overall F1, or loses to some model on several pathogens, or that the recall gap between Kimi-K2.5 (about 0.75) and GPT-5.2/DeepSeek-V3.2 (about 0.60) shrinks to a few points.

title: CanViT: Toward Active-Vision Foundation Models
claim_source: Table 9 (Appendix D.5), page 25; summarized in Figure 5A/C and the abstract

official.background: Active vision models perceive a scene through a sequence of small, localized glimpses, as human eye movements do, instead of processing the whole image at once. Such models have lagged far behind passive vision encoders, especially on dense prediction: prior active models reach only about 25-28% mIoU on ADE20K segmentation. The paper proposes a general-purpose, policy-agnostic active-vision foundation model whose output resolution is decoupled from its low-resolution glimpse input, and asks whether this decoupling helps even in the single-glimpse (passive) case.
official.method:
CanViT-B is a ViT-B/16 backbone that processes 128x128 px glimpses (8x8 patches) and interacts with a persistent scene-wide latent grid, the canvas, through 'Canvas Attention' read/write cross-attention layers (QKVO projections only on the glimpse side; no MLPs or self-attention on canvas tokens). Glimpse and canvas tokens share scene-relative 2D RoPE. The canvas grid size can be set at inference time. CanViT-B is pretrained from scratch on 13.2M ImageNet-21k images (512 px) for 2M steps by regressing frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 patch and CLS features of the full 512 px scene, using linear heads on the canvas, from glimpse sequences (per scene, one rollout that starts with the full-scene viewpoint and then samples random viewpoints, plus one fully random rollout; mean length 4; 32x32 canvas).

For the claim, the model is frozen and evaluated with a single full-scene glimpse (t = 0, viewpoint (0,0,1)) of a 512x512-resized ADE20K image, i.e. the whole scene downsampled to 128 px. A linear segmentation probe (LayerNorm, then dropout 0.1, BatchNorm, 1x1 conv; 40k AdamW steps, lr 3e-4, batch 16, scale-jittered 512 px crops and flips) is trained on canvas patches, with one probe per canvas grid size. During CanViT probe training, glimpse viewpoints are drawn i.i.d. at random (R-IID) over T = 10 timesteps, not only from the t = 0 full-scene view. The baseline is the frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 teacher with the same head on its patch features (without the extra LayerNorm, because its features are already layer-normalized), evaluated at input resolutions of 128-512 px (one probe per resolution). mIoU is computed on the ADE20K validation set with images resized to 512x512 for both models.
official.claim: On ADE20K semantic segmentation with frozen features and linear probes, a single 128 px full-scene glimpse into CanViT-B with a 32x32 canvas reaches 38.5% mIoU at 15.8 GFLOPs, above its DINOv3 ViT-B/16 teacher at the same 128 px input (28.8%, 12.0 GFLOPs) and at a higher-FLOP 160 px input (33.2%, 18.4 GFLOPs).
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Passive-vision comparison: ADE20K mIoU at t = 0 (single full-scene glimpse). CanViT-B vs. DINOv3 ViT-B/16 and ViT-S/16 at various input and output resolutions. All models use frozen features with a linear segmentation probe.
official.metric: ADE20K validation mIoU (%), higher is better; single deterministic evaluation, no error bars or seeds reported for this table
official.comparison: Frozen CanViT-B (t = 0, 128 px full-scene glimpse, 32x32 canvas) vs. frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 at 128 px (input-matched) and at 144/160 px (FLOP-matched or more FLOPs), all with independently trained linear probes
official.falsification_criterion: With the released CanViT-B checkpoint and a re-trained linear probe, single-glimpse 32x32-canvas mIoU is not clearly above (by, say, >3 points) DINOv3 ViT-B/16 at 160 px input under the same probe recipe and 512x512 evaluation, or is not above DINOv3 ViT-B/16 at 128 px.

title: Mecha-nudges for Machines
claim_source: Table 10, page 21 (also Figure 3, page 8, and Table 1, page 15)

official.background: As AI agents start to browse, recommend and buy on behalf of people, the environments they act in (product pages, listings, documents) may adapt to influence them. The paper calls such changes 'mecha-nudges': changes to how choices are presented that systematically steer AI agents without materially degrading the environment for humans. To measure them on a common scale, it uses V-usable information, an observer-relative version of Shannon information. The empirical question is whether this is already happening on a real marketplace, here Etsy after the release of ChatGPT.
official.method:
About 1.06M pre-ChatGPT (before Nov 30, 2022) and 5.0M post-ChatGPT USD-priced Etsy listings are scraped (Bright Data, Nov 2025 snapshot); the main experiment uniformly samples about 500K listings per period and splits each 80/10/10. GPT-5-mini is shown each listing's title and description with the 'Selective Curator' prompt (V4) and forced via a JSON enum to answer SELECT or PASS; this label is Z_M. Each period is subsampled to equal SELECT/PASS counts (about 154K pre, 45K post).

For each period, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is LoRA-fine-tuned twice: a content model g' that predicts Z_M from the listing text, and a null model g that sees an empty input (lr 2e-4, effective batch 768, 3 epochs, best validation checkpoint). Pointwise V-information on each held-out test listing is PVI = log2 g'[x](y) - log2 g[empty](y). PVI is then regressed by OLS on a post-ChatGPT indicator (PVI_i = alpha + beta * after_i); beta is the claimed change in machine-usable information. Two placebos run through the same pipeline: (i) pre-period listings rewritten by GPT-5-mini ('Etsy listing optimizer' prompt) vs. the original pre-period listings, and (ii) DailyMed FDA drug labels pre vs. post Nov 30, 2022 with a prescribing prompt.
official.claim: With GPT-5-mini SELECT/PASS labels and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct content/null models, Etsy listings created after ChatGPT's release carry 0.143 (SE 0.015) more bits of machine-usable information than pre-release listings (pre-period mean PVI 0.645), while LLM-rephrasing pre-period listings raises PVI by only 0.018 (SE 0.008) and DailyMed drug labels show 0.003 (SE 0.016).
official.claim_caption: Table 10: Baseline and Placebo Tests. OLS regression results for the three main experiments. Column (1): Etsy product listings, SELECT/PASS tokens, balanced dataset (baseline). Column (2): LLM-rephrased pre-period listings vs. original pre-period listings; after denotes 'after rephrasing' in this context. Column (3): DailyMed pharmaceutical drug labels from the pre- and post-periods, GPT-5-mini labeling, class-balanced dataset.
official.metric: OLS coefficient on the post-period indicator in a regression of held-out per-listing PVI (bits); higher = more machine-usable information. Values in parentheses are classical OLS standard errors (the paper reports HC0-HC3 robust SEs are nearly identical). The paper also reports that 5 training seeds give no significant difference in the estimated effect (ANOVA p = 0.853), but no per-seed spread.
official.comparison: Etsy post- vs. pre-ChatGPT listings, compared with two placebos run through the same pipeline: LLM-rephrased vs. original pre-period listings, and DailyMed drug labels post vs. pre.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the pipeline on a comparable sample of Etsy listings gives a post-ChatGPT coefficient whose 95% CI includes zero, or one that is not clearly larger than the rephrasing placebo (e.g. below about 0.05 bits).

title: AVO: Agentic Variation Operators for Autonomous Evolutionary Search

official.background: Attention is the central GPU kernel in Transformers, and on NVIDIA Blackwell (B200) GPUs the best implementations, FlashAttention-4 (FA4) and NVIDIA's closed-source cuDNN, took months of expert hand-tuning. LLM-driven evolutionary search systems such as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve limit the LLM to generating candidates inside a fixed sample-generate-evaluate pipeline. The paper asks whether making an autonomous coding agent the whole variation operator, with the ability to read documentation, profile, debug and revise, can produce kernels that beat these expert implementations.
official.method:
AVO replaces Vary(P) = Generate(Sample(P)) with a single agent run Agent(P, K, f). P is the lineage of earlier kernels and their scores, K is a knowledge base (CUDA/PTX docs, Blackwell specs, FA4 source), and f scores correctness against a reference and throughput in TFLOPS on each benchmark configuration. The paper studies a single lineage. A new version is committed only if it passes correctness and matches or beats the best score so far, and a supervisor agent steps in when progress stalls. A 7-day run with an internal general-purpose coding agent produced 40 committed versions of a CUDA/inline-PTX multi-head attention (MHA) forward kernel.

Benchmark: forward prefill, head dim 128, 16 heads, BF16, sequence lengths 4K/8K/16K/32K with batch size set so the total is 32K tokens (bs 8/4/2/1), causal and non-causal. Baselines are cuDNN 9.19.1 and FA4 (official implementation, commit 71bf77c). All are timed on B200 with CUDA 13.1 and PyTorch 2.10.0, using the FA4 repo's benchmark_attn.py with FA4's warm-up and repeat settings, over 10 runs (mean and std).
official.claim: On causal BF16 MHA forward prefill on a B200 (head dim 128, 16 heads, 32K total tokens), the AVO-evolved kernel beats FlashAttention-4 at every tested sequence length: 1392 vs. 1259 TFLOPS at 4K (+10.5%), 1482 vs. 1412 at 8K (+5.0%), 1582 vs. 1502 at 16K, and 1637 vs. 1550 at 32K. It also matches or beats cuDNN (1344/1477/1551/1590).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Multi-head attention forward-pass prefilling throughput (TFLOPS) on NVIDIA B200 with head dimension 128, 16 heads, and BF16 precision. Batch size and sequence length are varied with a fixed total of 32k tokens.
official.metric: Forward throughput in TFLOPS, higher is better; bars are means over 10 runs with error bars = std over the 10 runs (the std bars are visually tiny for causal); values are the bar labels printed on the figure
official.comparison: AVO evolved kernel vs. FlashAttention-4 (commit 71bf77c) and cuDNN 9.19.1, same GPU and timing script
official.falsification_criterion: On a B200 with the same configs and FA4 timing script, the AVO kernel's causal throughput is not clearly above FA4's (e.g. under ~3% faster at 4K or 32K), or not at least on par with cuDNN at any of the four sequence lengths.

title: SlopCodeBench: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Degrade Over Long-Horizon Iterative Tasks

official.background: Most coding-agent benchmarks score a single attempt against a fixed specification, so they cannot show whether an agent's early design decisions make later extensions harder. SlopCodeBench gives an agent a sequence of evolving specifications (36 problems, 196 checkpoints) and has it extend its own previous workspace each time, with hidden tests. Besides correctness, it tracks two static code-quality measures, verbosity and structural erosion, to test whether agent code accumulates 'slop' as it is extended, and how that compares with human-maintained code.
official.method:
Structural erosion: each callable f gets mass(f) = CC(f) × sqrt(SLOC(f)) (CC = cyclomatic complexity, as computed by Radon-style tooling); erosion is the share of total mass held by callables with CC > 10. Verbosity: the fraction of lines of code that are either flagged by any of 137 ast-grep rules for wasteful patterns or are structural clone lines, |flagged ∪ clone| / LOC, in [0, 1]. Both are computed on each checkpoint's workspace regardless of test outcome.

Agents (15 models in their native CLI harnesses: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor CLI, Kimi CLI, OpenCode) run each checkpoint in a fresh Docker container with only the working directory carried forward, a 2-hour limit, and the minimal 'just-solve' prompt. The human panel is 473 Python repositories stratified by GitHub stars (Hobby <100, Niche 100-1k, Established 1-10k, Major >=10k); the same two metrics are computed on each repository's most recent (HEAD) commit. Table 2 compares the human HEAD snapshots with 2869 agent checkpoints pooled across runs.
official.claim: Agent-written code on SlopCodeBench has mean verbosity 0.44 ± 0.18 and erosion 0.68 ± 0.20 over 2869 checkpoints, versus 0.19 ± 0.11 and 0.34 ± 0.22 at HEAD for 473 human-maintained Python repositories (2.3× and 2.0× higher), and every star tier of human repositories stays at or below 0.21 verbosity and 0.37 erosion.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Verbosity and erosion at HEAD commit, by GitHub-star tier and against agent checkpoints.
official.metric: Verbosity and structural erosion, both fractions in [0, 1], lower is better; ± is the standard deviation across repositories or agent checkpoints (per-sample spread), not across seeds
official.comparison: Agent checkpoints (pooled over models, just-solve prompt) vs. HEAD snapshots of 473 open-source Python repositories, overall and by GitHub-star tier
official.falsification_criterion: Computing the paper's verbosity and erosion metrics on (a) a sample of the human repositories at HEAD and (b) the checkpoints from an agent run on SlopCodeBench gives agent means that are not clearly above human means (e.g., agent verbosity below ~0.30 or erosion below ~0.50 while human means stay near 0.19 / 0.34), or the agent/human ratio falls well below 2× on either metric.

title: From Intent to Evidence: A Categorical Approach for Structural Evaluation of Deep Research Agents

official.background: Deep research agents (LLM systems that search the web, read sources and write evidence-based answers) are usually evaluated with broad report-quality or single-answer benchmarks, which do not say which part of the pipeline fails. This paper models deep research with category theory: a Search Functor maps a question's dependency structure to retrieved evidence, and a Reasoning Functor maps evidence to logical conclusions, with hallucination defined as asserting an implication with no evidentiary pre-image and the final report defined as a colimit. From this it builds a 296-question bilingual benchmark of four task types (multi-hop chains, pullback-style cross-source verification, re-ordering of retrieved data, and Yoneda-style rejection of false premises) and proposes two agent modules motivated by the theory.
official.method:
The authors build an API-based deep research agent with a coordinator and researcher sub-agents (web search, page reading, PDF parsing), conservative parallelism and a reflection step after each action. 'Tracked search' writes every query, timestamp, returned snippets and URLs into a per-task evidence file so retrieval history is preserved across sub-questions. 'Category tools' add two steps between evidence collection and the final answer: a pullback-style verifier that keeps only facts on which two partially overlapping sources agree about the same object, and a colimit-style synthesizer that merges verified fragments while preserving provenance and downgrading ungrounded claims.

The ablation compares 'tracked search' against 'tracked search + category tools' with the same backbone (GPT-5 or Grok-4.1-fast), on DeepResearchBench and on the authors' 296-question benchmark. On the benchmark each question is scored binary (0/1) by GPT-5 as a judge against predefined rubrics, followed by manual review by domain experts; the reported number is the average accuracy (%).
official.claim: With a GPT-5 backbone, adding category tools (pullback verifier + colimit synthesizer) to a tracked-search agent raises accuracy on the paper's 296-question structural benchmark from 10.48% to 13.29% (+2.81) and on DeepResearchBench from 45.68% to 47.53%; with Grok-4.1-fast the gains are smaller (10.82% to 11.84%, 40.94% to 42.40%).
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Performance comparison between DeepResearchBench and our benchmark. Grok Deep Research and OpenAI Deep Research are closed-source end-to-end products; the remaining systems are our API-based implementations. Brackets indicate the gains from adding category tools on top of tracked search.
official.metric: Accuracy (%), higher is better; binary per-question scoring by GPT-5 judge with human verification on the paper's benchmark; DeepResearchBench uses its own scoring. Single run, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: API agent with tracked search vs. the same agent with tracked search + category tools, for GPT-5 and Grok-4.1-fast backbones (closed-source Grok Deep Research and OpenAI Deep Research shown for reference, not matched)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both GPT-5 variants on the same benchmark (ideally several runs), the category-tools variant does not score higher than tracked search alone, or the difference is within run-to-run variation of the same configuration.

title: On Neural Scaling Laws for Weather Emulation through Continual Training

official.background: Data-driven weather emulators now match or beat numerical weather prediction, and their training budgets are growing quickly, yet there is little systematic work on how their accuracy scales with model size, data and compute. Chinchilla-style scaling studies are expensive because a cosine learning-rate schedule has to be retrained from scratch for every target budget. A constant learning rate with a short final cooldown (from LLM work) would let one run be checkpointed and cooled down at many budgets, but only if it performs at least as well as cosine. This paper tests that for weather emulation and then uses it to build IsoFLOP scaling curves.
official.method:
The model is a minimal Swin Transformer (no hierarchy or relative position bias, pre-RMSNorm, QK-norm, coordinate positional encoding, patch size 4, window 9x18) that maps the ERA5 state at time t to t+6h. Data are 71 ERA5 variables at 0.25 degree (721x1440 grid), training years 1979-2016, validation 2017. Loss is plain one-step MSE on per-variable normalized fields. Optimizer is AdamW (weight decay 1E-4, grad clip 1), global batch size 16, 500 warmup iterations, float16 mixed precision.

For Table A2, a 115M-parameter Swin is trained with (a) a half-cosine decay schedule run from scratch to exactly 12K, 18K or 24K total iterations, and (b) a constant LR schedule that is cooled down to zero with a 1-sqrt shape over the final 5% of iterations, reaching the same 12K, 18K and 24K totals. Peak LR is swept independently for each schedule over {1E-4, 5E-4, 1E-3}. The reported number is the one-step validation MSE at the end of each run.
official.claim: For a 115M Swin trained on 0.25-degree ERA5 with one-step MSE, constant LR plus a 5% cooldown reaches lower validation loss than a cosine schedule at every matched budget and peak LR tested, e.g. at 24K iterations 0.0075 vs 0.0081 (LR 5E-4) and 0.0071 vs 0.0074 (LR 1E-3).
official.claim_caption: Table A2: Independent LR sweeps for the 115M Swin. Validation loss at matched total iteration budgets (including cooldown); lower is better. Both schedules use global batch size 16. Constant+cooldown uses the final 5% of iterations for cooldown.
official.metric: One-step validation MSE on normalized variables (year 2017), lower is better; single runs, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Constant+cooldown (5% final iterations, 1-sqrt decay) vs. cosine decay trained from scratch to the same total iterations, at peak LRs 1E-4, 5E-4, 1E-3 and budgets 12K, 18K, 24K iterations
official.falsification_criterion: With matched budget and each schedule at its best peak LR, cosine reaches equal or lower validation loss than constant+cooldown, or the gap at the best LR is within the run-to-run spread across seeds.

title: V-CAST: Video Curvature-Aware Spatio-Temporal Pruning for Efficient Video Large Language Models

official.background: Video large language models turn every sampled frame into hundreds of visual tokens, so long-video inference is dominated by the cost of the prefill stage over a very long context. Training-free token compression keeps only a fraction of visual tokens before they enter the LLM. Existing video-specific methods either split the video into segments, give every frame the same budget, or allocate budget by global frame uniqueness, and some merge tokens, which in models with 3D MRoPE (such as Qwen3-VL) moves merged tokens off their original (t, h, w) positions. This paper argues that a pruning rule that allocates budget to frames where the video's semantics change direction, and keeps tokens at their original positions, preserves more accuracy at the same budget.
official.method:
V-CAST is applied to the projected visual tokens before the LLM. For each frame t it averages the P tokens into a mean vector, normalizes it to the unit sphere, and computes a curvature κ_t = 1 − cos(x̂_t − x̂_{t−1}, x̂_{t+1} − x̂_t) (boundary frames clamped). The global budget B = ⌊rTP⌋ is split over frames with p_t ∝ exp(κ_t / τ), τ = 0.7, rounded to integer budgets b_t by largest remainder and clipped to [k_min, P] (Algorithm 1, Appendix D; the main text says [0, P]).

Within each frame, tokens are scored by s_{t,i} = (1 − cos(x_{t,i}, x̄_t)) + min-max-normalized ‖x_{t,i}‖₂, and the top-b_t tokens are kept in their original order and original MRoPE coordinates (pruning, no merging). Evaluation uses LMMs-Eval on MVBench, LongVideoBench, MLVU and VideoMME with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct; 'Average' is the mean of MVBench, LongVideoBench, MLVU and VideoMME Overall. Baselines VisionZip, VidCom², FastVID, HoliTom and FlashVID were re-implemented by the authors under the same settings.
official.claim: On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with 64 input frames, V-CAST gets the best average accuracy over MVBench, LongVideoBench, MLVU and VideoMME: 65.0 at 25% token retention (vs. 64.0 for VidCom², the best baseline) and 63.6 at 15% retention (vs. 62.1 for FastVID and 61.2 for VidCom²); the uncompressed model scores 67.0.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance comparison with other baselines on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct across benchmarks under multiple settings. “Average” shows the mean performance across benchmarks.
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy (%) averaged over four benchmarks, higher is better; single run per setting, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: V-CAST vs. VisionZip, VidCom², FastVID, HoliTom (and FlashVID, which runs out of memory at 64 frames) at the same retention ratio and frame count on the same backbone
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the 64-frame setting on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, V-CAST's 4-benchmark average is not higher than the best of VidCom² and FastVID at both R = 25% and R = 15% (e.g. V-CAST ties or loses to VidCom² at 25%, or its lead over FastVID at 15% falls below ~0.5 points).

title: MDPBench: A Benchmark for Multilingual Document Parsing in Real-World Scenarios

official.background: Document parsing turns page images into structured text (Markdown with formulas and tables in reading order) and supplies much of the pre-training data for LLMs. Existing benchmarks such as OmniDocBench and olmOCR-Bench mostly use clean digital-born pages in Chinese and English. So it is unclear how parsers handle low-resource or non-Latin-script languages, or documents photographed with a phone under real-world conditions such as folds, shadows, glare and odd angles.
official.method:
MDPBench has 850 digital-born pages in 17 languages (academic papers, exam papers, newspapers, comics, handwritten notes, etc.). Each page was printed or shown on a screen and photographed three times (two indoor, one outdoor) under varied deformation, lighting, camera angle and background, giving 3,400 images in total. The split is 2,720 public and 680 private images. Ground truth (layout, reading order, text, LaTeX formulas, HTML tables) is produced on the digital-born pages: layout from the better of dots.ocr and PaddleOCR-VL, element content from the consensus of PaddleOCR-VL, dots.ocr and Qwen3-VL (Gemini-3-pro when their agreement is below 0.7), followed by manual correction and independent verification, in an OmniDocBench-compatible format. The paper describes no separate annotation of the photographed images, which implies they are scored against their source page's ground truth.

Scoring follows OmniDocBench preprocessing and element matching but aggregates at page level. Each page's score is the average of its element metrics: 1 - normalized edit distance for text and reading order, CDM for formulas, TEDS for tables. The benchmark score is the mean over pages. Headers, footers, page numbers and footnotes are ignored. Models get no hint about the language or whether the image is a photo. Table 2 reports the overall score, separate Digital-born and Photographed scores, per-language scores, and the private-split score.
official.claim: On MDPBench, every evaluated parser scores lower on photographed documents than on the digital-born originals. For the strongest open specialized models the gap is large: PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 drops from 87.4 to 75.2, dots.mocr from 90.5 to 77.2 and dots.ocr from 88.8 to 72.3, while Gemini-3-pro drops only from 90.4 to 85.1.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance of general VLMs, specialized VLMs, and pipeline tools on MDPBench.
official.metric: MDPBench page-level score (0-100, higher is better; mean over pages of the per-page average of text 1-NED, formula CDM and table TEDS). Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Same model evaluated on the Digital-born subset vs. the Photographed subset, which shows the same source pages after printing or screen display and photographing
official.falsification_criterion: Running PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 (or dots.ocr / dots.mocr) on the public MDPBench split with the official evaluation code gives a Digital-born minus Photographed gap of less than about 5 points, or a photographed score at or above the digital score.

title: MiroEval: Benchmarking Multimodal Deep Research Agents in Process and Outcome
claim_source: Table 12, page 30 (single-run values for all systems in Table 3, page 12)

official.background: Deep research systems (OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini Deep Research, etc.) plan multi-step web investigations and write long, cited reports. Most benchmarks for them score only the final report against fixed rubrics, rarely include multimodal inputs such as images, PDFs or spreadsheets, and use synthetic queries that go stale. MiroEval is a 100-task benchmark (70 text-only, 30 multimodal) built from rewritten real user query patterns plus trend-grounded generated queries. It scores systems on report synthesis quality, agentic factuality checking, and the quality of the research process itself.
official.method:
Each system's report and research-process trace on each task is scored on three dimensions. Synthesis: an LLM judge (GPT-5.1) builds task-specific dimensions, criteria and weights (adding a Grounding dimension and key facts extracted from attachments for multimodal tasks) and scores the report 0-10 per criterion, combined as a weighted sum. Factuality: the report is split into atomic statements, and an agent (GPT-5-mini on MiroFlow) checks each against web search and the task's attachments, labelling it RIGHT / WRONG / CONFLICT / UNKNOWN; the score is the per-task right ratio. Process: GPT-5.2 converts the trace into structured units and scores five intrinsic dimensions (breadth, depth, refinement, critical thinking, efficiency) plus process-report alignment (P→R, R→P, contradiction handling), combined as α·S_intrinsic + (1−α)·S_align. Overall is the average of the three dimensions, scaled to 0-100.

Reports were collected in March 2026 from each product's official interface. For the multimodal setting (30 tasks), the authors re-ran the full GPT judge pipeline two more times on four systems (OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini-3.1-Pro Deep Research, MiroThinker-1.7, MiroThinker-H1) and report all three runs with their mean and std (Table 12). The system outputs were fixed, so only the judge was re-run.
official.claim: On the 30 multimodal MiroEval tasks, MiroThinker-H1 scores an Overall of 74.1 ± 0.3 over three judge runs, above MiroThinker-1.7 (72.0 ± 0.3), OpenAI Deep Research (69.6 ± 0.6) and Gemini-3.1-Pro Deep Research (67.3 ± 0.6), and this ranking is the same in every run.
official.claim_caption: Table 12: Intra-judge stability on MultiModal (30 tasks). Three independent runs with the same GPT judge configuration. Each dimension reports scores from Run 1 / Run 2 / Run 3, followed by the mean and standard deviation.
official.metric: MiroEval Overall score (0-100, higher is better), the average of Synthesis, Factuality and Process. ± is the std over 3 independent runs of the GPT judge pipeline on the same fixed system outputs; it does not cover variation in the systems' own generations.
official.comparison: MiroThinker-H1 vs. MiroThinker-1.7, OpenAI Deep Research and Gemini-3.1-Pro Deep Research, all scored on the same 30 multimodal tasks with the same judges
official.falsification_criterion: When the four systems' multimodal reports are scored with the MiroEval pipeline (released or freshly collected), MiroThinker-H1's Overall does not beat OpenAI Deep Research's by more than about 2 points, or the order H1 > 1.7 > OpenAI > Gemini changes.

title: SOLE-R1: Video-Language Reasoning as the Sole Reward for On-Robot Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Figure 3, page 7 (counts in Section 5.3 text, page 7)

official.background: A robot that could learn new manipulation skills from scratch with no hand-written reward, demonstrations or success detector would make robot RL far cheaper to set up. A natural idea is to ask a vision-language model to watch the robot and score task progress, and use that score as the reward. In practice, online RL actively searches for states where the reward model is wrong, so strong general VLMs such as GPT-5 and Gemini tend to be 'reward hacked': the policy finds camera views or poses that the model mistakes for success. Specialized video progress models (Robometer, RoboReward, ReWiND, etc.) are trained mostly on expert videos and also struggle off-distribution.
official.method:
SOLE-R1 is Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct fine-tuned to read a goal sentence plus a short window of video frames (first frame, recent frames, previous prediction) and output a per-timestep chain of thought followed by an integer progress value in [-100, 100]. Training uses SFT on about 4M reasoning traces (general spatial and multi-frame reasoning, embodied reasoning, and 1.2M synthesized progress traces from RoboCasa simulation with injected random-action failures and from Open X-Embodiment videos with temporal reversals), followed by GRPO with a reward for matching ground-truth progress.

For the claim, each reward model's predicted progress p_t is clipped and scaled into the reward r_t, which is the only learning signal. A DrQv2 (or SAC for Meta-World and real robot) agent starts from a random policy, observes wrist and external RGB plus proprioception, and is trained online with no ground-truth reward, demonstrations or task-specific tuning. Success is measured with the simulator's ground-truth success condition (any-timestep success, N = 20 evaluation episodes), averaged over 3 seeds in simulation. Baselines use the same RL setup with GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro / Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 (best of), Robometer, RoboReward, ReWiND and the best of TOPReward/LRM/VLAC/LIV as the reward model.
official.claim: Used as the sole reward for zero-shot online RL from a random policy, SOLE-R1 reaches at least 50% success on 24 of 40 manipulation tasks versus 7 for GPT-5 and 5 for the best Gemini model, e.g. RoboSuite Lift about 95% vs about 6% (GPT-5) and ManiSkill PickCube-v1 about 74% vs about 33% (GPT-5).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Zero-shot success rate of online RL across 40 tasks. We plot the mean and standard error across three random seeds (real-world experiments use a single seed, shown as a single value). In all experiments, the robot begins with a random policy and learns entirely through interaction with the task, guided only by the predicted rewards.
official.metric: Ground-truth task success rate (%) of the final policy, higher is better; bars are mean over 3 seeds with error bars = standard error across seeds (real-world tasks: single seed, no error bar). Summary metric: number of tasks with success >= 50%.
official.comparison: SOLE-R1 reward vs. GPT-5, best of Gemini-3-Pro & Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5, Robometer, RoboReward, ReWiND, and best of TOPReward/LRM/VLAC/LIV, all plugged into the same online RL agent and hyperparameters.
official.falsification_criterion: With the released SOLE-R1 checkpoint and the paper's RL setup, SOLE-R1-rewarded policies fail to reach clearly higher success than GPT-5-rewarded ones on tasks where the figure shows a large gap (e.g. RoboSuite Lift, ManiSkill PickCube-v1, Meta-World faucet-open), i.e. the gap closes to within the seed standard error, or SOLE-R1 reaches >= 50% on far fewer than 24 of the 40 tasks.

title: See it to Place it: Evolving Macro Placements with Vision Language Models

official.background: Macro placement in chip floorplanning arranges large blocks (macros) on a 2D canvas so that wiring is short; quality is commonly measured by half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL). Analytical placers such as DREAMPlace solve this as a differentiable wirelength-plus-density optimization and are the strongest current baseline, while learning-based placers (e.g. ChiPFormer) generalize poorly to unseen chips. The paper asks whether an off-the-shelf vision-language model, which can look at prior placements and their scores, can supply useful spatial guidance to an existing placer under a fixed budget of placement attempts, without any fine-tuning.
official.method:
VeoPlace wraps an existing placer in an evolutionary loop. Each iteration runs 8 unguided placer rollouts, then sends the VLM (Gemini 3.6 Flash in the main result) a structured prompt containing an image of the canvas, macro sizes/colors, and C=25 prior placements with their gHPWL scores selected by a 'Top Stratified' strategy (cluster placements, favor high-scoring ones within a promising cluster). The VLM returns a rectangular target region for each of up to 256 macros (largest/most-connected first), and 8 guided rollouts are run. With a budget of 2,000 rollouts this is 125 VLM calls. The best placement in the history buffer is returned.

For the analytical placer, each VLM box is converted to an anchor at its bottom-left corner and a quadratic penalty lambda_A * sum ||x_i - x_hat_i||^2 is added to DREAMPlace's wirelength + density objective (lambda_A = 0.01 for all designs; lambda_A = 0 recovers plain DREAMPlace). Invalid or overlapping boxes are dropped. All placements are legalized and scored by global HPWL after standard-cell placement, on a 512x512 grid.
official.claim: On all 8 ICCAD 2015 Superblue benchmarks, VeoPlace-guided DREAMPlace 4.3.0 (VP+DP) attains lower best-of-2,000-rollouts gHPWL than DREAMPlace 4.3.0 alone under the same rollout budget, with reductions from 0.5% (superblue16) to 4.4% (superblue10).
official.claim_caption: VeoPlace-guided DREAMPlace (VP+DP) vs. DREAMPlace 4.3.0 (DP) and Superblue baselines reported by Xue et al. All columns report gHPWL (x1e7, lower is better). VP+DP uses Gemini 3.6 Flash and one global anchor weight lambda_A=0.01 on all designs. VP+DP/DP report mean +/- standard error of the best gHPWL observed across five seeds with 2,000 rollouts. Percentages compare VP+DP to matched DP 4.3.0.
official.metric: best gHPWL observed over 2,000 rollouts (x1e7, lower is better), mean +/- standard error over 5 seeds
official.comparison: VP+DP vs. DP 4.3.0 (matched budget, legalization and evaluation). Other columns are published numbers from prior work and are not part of the core claim.
official.falsification_criterion: VP+DP mean gHPWL is not lower than DP 4.3.0 on one or more of the 8 benchmarks, or the gap is within seed noise.

title: Gen-Searcher: Reinforcing Agentic Search for Image Generation

official.background: Text-to-image models only know what was in their pretraining data, so they often fail on prompts that need specific or recent real-world facts, such as a particular landmark, a public figure, a game character, or a numeric fact that must be written correctly in the image. Retrieval-augmented generators rely on static databases and one-shot similarity retrieval, and prompt-based web-search workflows are hand-designed and untrained. The paper asks whether a multimodal LLM agent trained with SFT and agentic RL to do multi-hop text and image web search can write better grounded prompts and pick better reference images for a frozen image generator.
official.method:
Gen-Searcher is Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct equipped with three tools: search (web text search returning URLs and snippets), image_search (web image search from a text query), and browse (a webpage summary produced by Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct). Given a knowledge-intensive prompt, the agent searches over multiple turns (during RL training capped at 10 turns and 5 returned images per turn; at inference temperature 0.6, top-p 0.9, 64K max context) and outputs a grounded generation prompt plus selected reference images, which are passed to a frozen generator (Qwen-Image for text-only input, Qwen-Image-Edit when reference images are given). If the agent fails to produce an answer, the original prompt is used. The agent is trained with SFT on Gen-Searcher-SFT-10k (trajectories from Gemini 3 Pro) and then GRPO on Gen-Searcher-RL-6k with reward R = 0.5 * K-Score(image) + 0.5 * text reward (GPT-4.1 scores, on a five-level scale, whether the grounded prompt contains enough correct information); rollout images during RL are generated by a fixed Qwen-Image-Edit-2509.

Evaluation is on KnowGen, 630 human-verified held-out prompts in two subsets (Science & Knowledge, Pop Culture & News), with ground-truth images from Nano Banana Pro. GPT-4.1 compares the generated image with the prompt and the GT image and scores faithfulness, visual correctness, text accuracy and aesthetics in {0, 0.5, 1}; K-Score = 0.1 F + 0.4 VC + 0.4 TA + 0.1 A (text accuracy is dropped when no text is required), averaged over the two subsets and reported on a 0-100 scale. The 'workflow' baseline in Table 3 uses the same untrained Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct as the search agent in a manually designed prompt-based search workflow with the same generator.
official.claim: On KnowGen with Qwen-Image as the generator, the trained Gen-Searcher-8B agent achieves an overall K-Score of 31.52, versus 22.91 for an untrained Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct prompt-based search workflow and 14.98 for Qwen-Image alone (SFT-only agent: 28.15).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Ablation Study.
official.metric: KnowGen overall K-Score (0-100, higher is better; GPT-4.1 judge, mean of the two subset scores). Single run, no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: Qwen-Image + Gen-Searcher (SFT + dual-reward RL) vs. Qwen-Image + untrained prompt-based search workflow with the same Qwen3-VL-8B agent; also SFT-only and single-reward RL variants and no-search Qwen-Image
official.falsification_criterion: Re-evaluating the released Gen-Searcher-8B and the untrained Qwen3-VL-8B workflow with Qwen-Image on KnowGen gives a K-Score gap much smaller than ~8.6 points (e.g. under 3 points) or within run-to-run variation from repeated generation/judging, or Gen-Searcher does not beat the workflow.

title: Target-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Table 6 (top block), page 16; curves in Figure 5 (page 9) and Figure 10 (page 18)

official.background: Value-based deep RL algorithms such as DQN and SAC regress the online Q-network onto bootstrapped targets computed by a target network, a lagged copy of the online network. Lagging the targets stabilizes training but makes them stale: slower target updates (large hard-update interval K or small Polyak coefficient tau) give more stability but less recent learning signals. The usual practice is to tune K or tau globally, which trades one property against the other for all transitions at once.
official.method:
TARL compares two TD errors for each sampled transition: the standard offline error from the target network, delta_bar = r + gamma * max_a Q(s', a; theta_bar) - Q(s, a; theta), and the online error delta computed the same way but with the online parameters theta for the next state. The alignment score A is 1 if delta and delta_bar have the same sign and |delta| >= |delta_bar| (the online network fully supports the offline step); otherwise A = |delta| / (|delta| + |delta - delta_bar| + 1e-8). The regression target is unchanged: selected transitions are still regressed onto the offline target.

Alignment-based oversampling: at each update, sample m + b transitions uniformly from the replay buffer, compute A for each, and train on the m with the highest A. In the main experiments b = m (sample 64, keep 32). title: Concept frustration: Aligning human concepts and machine representations
claim_source: Supplementary Table S2, page 29 (main-text Figure 5A, page 14)

official.background: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) predict an outcome through a small set of human-defined concepts, which makes them interpretable but hurts them when the concept set (the ontology) misses task-relevant information. To fix an ontology you first need a way to detect that it is incomplete. Prior work compared supervised CBM concept directions with unsupervised sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features in Euclidean space. This paper defines 'concept frustration', where an unobserved concept induces relations between known concepts that contradict their own correlation structure (like a frustrated triangle in a spin system), and argues that it can only be detected in a task-aligned geometry.
official.method:
On an activation space A, three models are trained: a one-hidden-layer ReLU black-box classifier p(y|a) (width 128), an SAE with dictionary D (rows = unsupervised directions), and a jointly trained linear CBM ĉ = Qa with a linear sigmoid task head (concept-loss weight 1). The task-aligned metric F̄_A is the average of the closed-form Fisher information p(a)(1−p(a)) g(a)g(a)^T (g = gradient of the black-box logit wrt a) over training activations with p(a) in (0.2, 0.8). Cosine similarities in this metric give S (CBM concept vs SAE atom) and Z (CBM concept vs CBM concept). A triplet (q_r, q_l, d_j) is frustrated if sign(Z_rl) ≠ sign(S_rj S_lj); pairwise frustration is the largest |S_rj S_lj| over frustrating j (0 if none), and the global frustration γ^{F_A} is its mean over all known-concept pairs. γ^E is the same with plain Euclidean cosine similarities.

Synthetic data: concepts χ = (χ_k, χ_u) ~ N(0, B(α)) with k = 50 concepts, k_known ∈ {10, 20, 30, 40}; B_kk fixed, cross-covariance M(α) where each unknown concept mediates one known pair (i, j) with entries b_ij|α| and −sign(α)|b_ij||α|, and B_uu = B_temp + M^T B_kk^{-1} M, so Cov(χ_k) is identical across α. α = −1 reinforces the known-known correlation signs (consistent), α = 0 makes known and unknown independent, α = +1 opposes them (frustrated). Activations a = Φχ + ε (r = 64, Φ ~ N(0,1), σ_a = 0.3); task y = 1{(1−ω)ψ*_k·χ_k + ωψ*_u·χ_u + η > 0}, σ_y = 1.5, ω ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}. That is 60 regimes x 10 seeds = 600 datasets, n = 8000 each, 75:25 train/test split. Model and training hyperparameters (BB width 128, CBM concept-loss weight 1, Adam, batch 512, BB and CBM lr 1e-3 for 30 epochs, SAE lr 2e-3 for 60 epochs) are stated only for the treasure-hunter task (Methods 4.3) and are presumably reused here; Section 4.6 does not restate them. Regimes are compared with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Hodges-Lehmann median shifts.
official.claim: Across 600 matched synthetic datasets, the task-aligned global frustration γ^{F_A} is higher in the frustrated regime (α = +1, mean 3.67e-2, 95% CI [3.31, 4.04]e-2) than in the consistent (α = −1, 2.76e-2 [2.51, 3.02]e-2) and independent (α = 0, 1.60e-2 [1.48, 1.71]e-2) regimes (paired Wilcoxon p < 1e-4), while Euclidean γ^E barely changes (7.99e-3 vs 7.43e-3 vs 7.62e-3).
official.claim_caption: Supplementary Table S2: Summary statistics across concept regimes defined by α. The upper block reports regime means with 95% confidence intervals together with the paired comparison between the frustrated (α = 1) and consistent (α = −1) settings. The lower block reports paired Hodges–Lehmann median shift estimates with 95% confidence intervals and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values for comparisons against the independent baseline (α = 0).
official.metric: Global frustration γ (mean pairwise frustration, in [0, 1]); higher means more detected frustration. Values are means over the 200 datasets per α with 95% confidence intervals; paired comparisons are Hodges-Lehmann median differences with 95% CI and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values over matched datasets.

title: LinearARD: Linear-Memory Attention Distillation for RoPE Restoration
claim_source: Table 1, page 9 (per-length RULER in Tables 11-12, token accounting in Table 6, Appendix B)

official.background: Extending an LLM's context window by rescaling its Rotary Position Embeddings (e.g. Position Interpolation, PI) lets it read longer inputs but badly hurts short-context accuracy, because the rescaled rotations distort the attention patterns learned in pretraining. The usual fix, continued pre-training (CPT) on long text, needs hundreds of millions of tokens. Restoration distillation (e.g. LongReD) instead trains the rescaled model to match the original model's hidden states on short inputs. This paper argues that matching attention-level structure directly is a more data-efficient way to restore the model, and builds a memory-efficient kernel to make dense attention-level distillation feasible.
official.method:
The teacher is the frozen base model with native RoPE; the student is the same model with PI-scaled RoPE (LLaMA2-7B: 4K to 32K, 8x). Stage 1 (ARD) runs both on short sequences (4K for LLaMA2, from PG19) and minimizes the forward KL between teacher and student row-wise softmax distributions of the final layer's Q/Q, K/K and V/V self-relation matrices (softmax(XX^T/sqrt(d) + causal mask) for X in {Q, K, V}), with equal weights. Only the Q/K/V projections are trained, via LoRA (r = 1024, alpha = 2048), AdamW at LR 2e-5 with cosine decay. A tiled Triton-style kernel stores only per-row log-sum-exp values and recomputes logits in the backward pass, so the n x n matrices are never materialized.

Stage 2 merges the adapter and runs a short CPT at 32K on SlimPajama. For the 4.25M budget on LLaMA2-7B, Stage 1 is 144 steps x 2 GPUs x 2 seqs x 4K = 2.36M tokens and Stage 2 is 16 steps x 4 seqs x 32K = 2.10M tokens. Baselines at the same 4.25M-token budget are direct CPT under PI (8 steps x 17 seqs x 32K) and LongReD (hidden-state restoration distillation). Short-context performance is the mean of 8 lm-evaluation-harness tasks (MMLU 5-shot, MathQA 4-shot, BoolQ 3-shot, ARC-C 25-shot, LAMBADA, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA 0-shot); long-context performance is RULER (12 tasks) averaged over 8K, 16K and 32K.
official.claim: On LLaMA2-7B extended from 4K to 32K with PI (8x), using a 4.25M-token training budget, LinearARD reaches a short-text average of 50.93 (93.1% of the native 54.69) and RULER 63.0, versus 41.44 / 0.035 for LongReD and 41.03 / 0.040 for CPT at the same budget.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on short-text benchmarks and long-context robustness. Short-text accuracy in percent is reported across eight benchmarks and their mean, Avg. CW: context window; PE: RoPE scaling; Rec.: recovery relative to native; RULER: average over 8K, 16K, and 32K, with per-length breakdowns in App. G. Token budgets use units of 2^20 tokens across all stages, detailed in App. B. Bold marks the best trained result per backbone and budget group. LAMB.: LAMBADA; OBQA: OpenBookQA; ARC-C: ARC-Challenge.
official.metric: Mean accuracy (%) over 8 short-text benchmarks (higher is better) and RULER average over 8K/16K/32K (higher is better); single runs, no error bars or seeds reported

title: Lipschitz Dueling Bandits over Continuous Action Spaces

official.background: In dueling bandits, a learner repeatedly picks two actions and sees only a noisy preference between them, never a numeric reward. This fits settings such as tuning a recommender or an experimental design from human pairwise judgments. Existing continuous-action dueling methods assume convex utilities and use local descent. Lipschitz (zooming-style) bandit algorithms exploit smoothness to focus sampling near the optimum, but they rely on scalar rewards that are comparable across regions, which pairwise feedback does not provide. The paper asks whether Lipschitz structure can be exploited under purely comparative feedback, giving regret that depends on the zooming dimension instead of on a fixed discretization.
official.method:
ARC-DuelLi (Anchored Recursive Comparisons for dueling Lipschitz bandits) runs in rounds m = 1..B on X = [0,1]^d, with B = ceil(log2(T)/(d_z+2)) + 1. Each round fixes a reference arm X^{m-1}, and every duel in that round is played against it, so empirical preference gaps are comparable across regions. Within a round, the algorithm does a depth-first recursion over a dyadic cube partition with edge r_h = 2^{-h+1}. In each cube it samples n_h = 16 log(T/δ)/r_h^2 uniform arms and duels each against the reference. A cube is eliminated if (previous best gap) minus (its empirical gap) exceeds 2 r_h (1 + Γ), where Γ is the transfer-function Lipschitz constant; otherwise it is split into 2^d subcubes until depth h = m. The next reference arm is drawn from the best terminal cube, and its gap is re-estimated with n_m extra duels. After the last round, the final reference arm is played for the rest of the horizon.

Experiment (Section 7): d = 2, utility μ(x) = 1 − (2/3)||x − x1|| − (1/3)||x − x2|| with x1 = (0.3, 0.1) (the optimum) and x2 = (0.9, 0.9). Duel outcomes follow a logistic transfer of the utility difference, d_z = 0, horizon T = 10^8, 50 independent runs, and the initial reference arm is fixed at (0.9, 0.9). The baseline uniformly discretizes X into a grid with cube radius r = 2^{-m+1}, "matching the resolution used in ARC-DuelLi for the same depth parameter m", treats each cube as an arm, and runs Interleaved Filter (Yue et al., 2012). The metric is cumulative dueling regret (sum of the preference gaps of both played arms relative to x*).
official.claim: On the 2-D synthetic Lipschitz dueling instance with a logistic transfer and T = 10^8 duels (mean over 50 runs, initial reference (0.9, 0.9)), ARC-DuelLi's cumulative regret at T is about 2.15 × 10^6, versus about 4.0 × 10^6 for Interleaved Filter on a uniform discretization: roughly half. ARC-DuelLi's curve bends below the baseline's, which stays close to linear.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Performance of ARC-DuelLi over 50 runs. (a) Final reference arms concentrate near the optimal arm. (b) Decay of the gap Δ(x*, X^m) across rounds, showing convergence of the reference arm. (c) Cumulative regret compared against a uniform discretization baseline (Interleaved Filter). The solid curves denote averages over runs, and the shaded regions represent ±1 standard deviation.
official.metric: Cumulative dueling regret (lower is better) vs. number of duels. Solid curves are means over 50 runs; shaded bands are ±1 std over runs (the bands are visibly narrow, roughly ±0.05 × 10^6 for the baseline at T). Values are read off the plot.
official.comparison: ARC-DuelLi vs. uniform grid discretization + Interleaved Filter, same instance, same horizon
official.falsification_criterion: A faithful reimplementation on the same instance gives ARC-DuelLi cumulative regret at T = 10^8 that is not clearly below the uniform-discretization Interleaved Filter baseline (e.g. a ratio above ~0.8, or overlapping ±1 std bands), or ARC-DuelLi's regret curve does not bend sublinearly while the baseline's stays close to linear.

title: MotionGrounder: Grounded Multi-Object Motion Transfer via Diffusion Transformer

official.background: Text-guided motion transfer generates a new video from a text caption while copying the motion of a reference video. Recent training-free methods built on diffusion transformers (DiTs) such as CogVideoX get good visual quality but handle a scene as a single object: when the reference video contains several moving objects, the generated objects are often placed in the wrong location, assigned the wrong object's motion, duplicated or dropped. Multi-object scenes are common in real videos, so grounding each object in the caption to the correct spatial region and motion matters for controllable video generation.
official.method:
MotionGrounder is a training-free, inference-time optimization on top of CogVideoX-5B. Given a source video, its object masks, a global target caption and one sub-caption per object, it optimizes the noisy latent during the first 30% of 50 denoising steps (5 Adam steps per denoising step, learning rate decayed linearly from 0.002 to 0.001) with two losses. The Flow-based Motion Signal (FMS) loss computes GMFlow optical flow on J=F/4 sampled source frames, builds latent-resolution patch trajectories (allowing duplicated trajectories), and matches these displacements to attention-weighted displacements from cross-frame attention at transformer block 20 (temperature 2). The Object-Caption Alignment Loss (OCAL) takes the text-to-video and video-to-text 3D attention for each object's caption tokens at block 10, repeats it 4x in time to match the masks, and maximizes attention inside the object's mask while suppressing it outside, with a size-aware weight. Total loss = 1.25*L_FMS + 1.00*L_OCAL.

Evaluation uses 52 high-motion single- and multi-object videos (19 DAVIS, 29 YouTube-VOS, 4 from ConMo), 24 frames at 480x720, each with three target caption types (Caption, Subject, Scene) generated with CogVLM2 and GPT-5. Baselines DMT, MOFT, MotionClone, ConMo and DiTFlow are all adapted to CogVideoX-5B with the same step and optimization schedule. Metrics include IoU between source and generated object regions and the proposed Object Grounding Score (OGS = per-object, per-frame IoU x local CLIP similarity between the cropped generated object and its caption, averaged over objects and frames).
official.claim: Averaged over all three prompt settings (All) on the 52-video benchmark with a CogVideoX-5B backbone, MotionGrounder reaches OGS 0.0671 and IoU 0.2371, above every baseline; the strongest baseline on both is MotionClone (OGS 0.0581, IoU 0.2061), and the closest DiT method, DiTFlow, gets OGS 0.0520 and IoU 0.1868.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Quantitative comparison. We compare MotionGrounder across three settings, Caption, Subject, and Scene, against five baselines. We achieve the strongest performance across all scenarios, attaining the best and second best results on the majority of metrics. Best results are in bold and second best are underlined.
official.metric: Object Grounding Score (OGS; per-object, per-frame box IoU x local CLIP similarity, averaged) and IoU between the source object box (from its ground-truth mask) and the Grounding DINO box of the generated object; higher is better; single values, no ± or seeds reported
official.comparison: MotionGrounder vs. DMT, MOFT, MotionClone, ConMo and DiTFlow, all on CogVideoX-5B with 50 denoising steps and the same optimization schedule
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running MotionGrounder and MotionClone (or DiTFlow) on the same videos and captions gives an OGS or IoU (All setting) for MotionGrounder that is not higher than the baseline's, or the gap shrinks to within run-to-run variation across seeds.

title: Massively Parallel Exact Inference for Hawkes Processes

official.background: Multivariate Hawkes processes model self- and mutually-exciting event sequences (finance, seismology, social media, crime). Exact maximum likelihood estimation naively costs O(N^2) in the number of events. For exponential kernels a classical recurrence brings this down to O(N), but the recurrence is sequential and cannot use GPU parallelism. As a result, exact fits of the standard model have been limited to fairly small event sequences, and scalable alternatives rely on approximations, low-rank structure or sparsity assumptions.
official.method:
The per-kernel excitation state R_i^k (an M-vector) follows the affine recurrence R_i = e^{-γ_k Δt_i} R_{i-1} + e^{-γ_k Δt_i} α_{:,m_{i-1},k}. If the state is augmented with a constant 1, each step becomes a multiplication by an (M+1)x(M+1) matrix [[s I, v],[0, 1]]. Products of such matrices stay in the same form, with (s_A, v_A) ⊙ (s_B, v_B) = (s_A s_B, s_A v_B + v_A), so each product costs O(M) and the whole sequence of states can be computed with a Blelloch parallel prefix scan in about O(KMN/P) time. Gradients for α and γ are derived by hand as two more affine recurrences (states K and L) that use the same scan, which avoids PyTorch autograd going through the scan graph. Events are split into batches that pass only the final state from one batch to the next, so peak memory stays constant and the likelihood remains exact.

For the comparison in Section 4.2, synthetic data come from a hub-and-spoke network (γ = 1.5, one row of A set to 0.1, hub base rate 0.1), with M from 125 to 2000, K = 3 kernels with learned decay rates, and N = 2^10 to 2^26. Fits use float32, Adam with lr 0.1, l1 weight 0.01 and hinge h = 0.05, run for 1000 epochs, with a 24-hour limit per run. The implementations compared are: naive O(N^2) direct summation (GPU); the sequential recurrence on GPU and on 64 cores of a Xeon Platinum 8580; the prefix scan with PyTorch autograd gradients (GPU); and the full method (prefix scan with manual gradients and batching, on an A100 80GB). The metric is average time per epoch, with peak memory as a secondary metric.
official.claim: On synthetic hub-and-spoke Hawkes data (K = 3), the prefix-scan method with manual gradients on an A100 is about 100x faster per epoch than the sequential O(N) recurrence on a 64-core CPU (about 0.45 s vs. about 45 s at N ≈ 2.6×10^5). It is about 7x faster than the same scan with autograd gradients (about 1 s vs. about 7 s at N ≈ 5×10^5), and it is the only implementation that scales to N ≈ 3.4×10^7 within the 24-hour limit and 80 GiB of memory.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Comparison between our method (black) and other implementations of the intensity computation. The red dotted lines indicate the 24-hour walltime limit (86.4 seconds per epoch for 1000 epochs) and the maximum available memory (80 GiB), respectively. Crosses indicate that the next run either ran out of memory or exceeded 24 hours.
official.metric: Average wall-clock time per training epoch in seconds, lower is better (peak GPU memory in GiB shown alongside). No error bars or repeat counts are reported. The values below are read off a log-log plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Prefix scan with manual gradients and batching (GPU) vs. sequential recurrence (64-core CPU and GPU), prefix scan with PyTorch autograd (GPU), and the naive O(N^2) sum (GPU), on the same synthetic sequences for 1000 epochs
official.falsification_criterion: Using the released code on a comparable GPU, the prefix-scan method is less than about 10x faster per epoch than a well-implemented sequential recurrence on a multicore CPU at N ≈ 10^5 to 3×10^5. A refutation also holds if the method fails to fit N ≳ 10^7 events with bounded memory, or if its intensities or gradients differ from the sequential recurrence by more than float32 round-off (Appendix D reports a maximum relative error below 10^-5 for intensities and below 10^-4 for gradients).

title: Combating Data Laundering in LLM Training
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (per-prompt AUCs in Appendix H, Table 14, page 23)

official.background: Membership-inference style detectors (Loss, Zlib, Min-K, Ref, Recall) let a data owner check whether an LLM was trained on their texts by comparing the model's loss or confidence on those texts against held-out texts. The paper points out that a model provider can 'launder' data by rewriting it with an LLM (e.g. into a lyrical or FAQ style) before training. The model then memorizes the rewrites rather than the originals, and detectors queried with the originals fall to near chance (Table 1: Loss AUC 1.000 on originals-trained Llama-2 vs. 0.539 when it was trained on lyrical rewrites). The question is whether an auditor without knowledge of the laundering prompt can restore detection.
official.method:
Simulated laundering: 200 non-member samples from MIMIR-Wikipedia are rewritten by GPT-4o with a hidden laundering prompt. Pythia-6.9B is LoRA fine-tuned (r=8, alpha=32, 30 epochs, lr 4e-4, grad accumulation 25, weight decay 0.1) on 100 of the rewrites; the other 100 are non-members. The auditor sees only the 200 original texts, black-box access to the fine-tuned model, and an auxiliary LLM (GPT-4o). Outside-register prompts are 10 GPT-5-generated laundering prompts (slide bullets, Facebook post, poem, tutorial, business email, scientific abstract, product description, travel blog, lecture transcript, smoother transitions; Appendix Table 11) chosen to lie outside SDR's 23-register taxonomy.

SDR (Synthesis Data Reversion) searches for a rewriting prompt in two stages. Stage 1 asks the auxiliary LLM for a standard rewriting prompt and an opening-sentence template for each of 23 registers, scores each register by the target model's average max next-token probability when continuing register-styled openings, keeps the top 5, and picks the one whose full rewrites give the best detector performance. Stage 2 iteratively (K=10 iterations) proposes prompt edits by comparing auxiliary rewrites with the target model's continuations of their first sentence, and accepts an edit only if detector performance improves. The final prompt rewrites all 200 originals, and the unchanged off-the-shelf detector is run on those rewrites. The baseline is the same detector run on the 200 originals.
official.claim: On Pythia-6.9B LoRA fine-tuned on GPT-4o-laundered MIMIR-Wikipedia, averaged over 10 outside-register laundering prompts, querying with SDR-rewritten texts instead of the originals raises Loss-detector AUC from 62.7% to 75.5% (TPR@5% 9.2% to 22.9%), and Min-K AUC from 64.2% to 73.6%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2 | The average performance of each unauthorized training data detection method across data synthesized from different inside and outside laundering processes. The experiment is conducted on Pythia-6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023), fine-tuned on Wikipedia synthesis. The results for each prompt are provided in Appendix H. We report the additional TPR@1% results in Appendix O.
official.metric: AUC, ASR (best balanced-accuracy threshold) and TPR at 5% FPR for separating the 100 trained-on vs. 100 held-out texts; higher is better. Each cell is an average over laundering prompts (23 inside, 10 outside), from single runs; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Each detector (Recall, Loss, Ref, Zlib, Min-K) queried with original texts vs. the same detector queried with SDR-rewritten texts, on the same fine-tuned target model.

title: Dependency-Guided Parallel Decoding in Discrete Diffusion Language Models

official.background: Discrete (masked) diffusion language models such as Dream-7B generate text by repeatedly unmasking positions of a masked sequence, and they can go faster by unmasking several positions per forward pass. Tokens unmasked in the same step are sampled independently from their per-position marginals rather than from the joint distribution, so output quality drops when those tokens depend on each other (e.g. both sides of "1 + _ = _"). Common strategies pick tokens by confidence (entropy, top-1 probability) or by stability across steps (KLASS) and ignore dependencies between tokens, so a cheap way to choose which tokens can safely be unmasked together would let models decode faster without losing accuracy.
official.method:
DEMASK attaches a small dependency predictor (~26M parameters) to the final hidden states of the frozen Dream-7B backbone. For masked positions i, j it predicts D̂_ij = sigmoid(h_i W_Q (h_j W_K)^T / sqrt(d)), an estimate of the expected total-variation change in position i's predictive distribution when position j is revealed. It is trained with MSE against exact pairwise TV values computed with |M|+1 backbone forward passes per sample on 100K Tulu-3 SFT responses (5 random masks each, about 500K examples).

At each decoding step, one forward pass gives token probabilities and D̂. A greedy routine starts from the left-most masked position, keeps only candidates whose top-1 probability is above γ, and repeatedly adds the candidate with the smallest summed dependency on the already selected set until the accumulated dependency would exceed τ. The selected positions are then sampled in parallel. Hyperparameters were grid-searched on GSM8K (DEMASK τ=0.04, γ=0.9; KLASS KL threshold 0.0003, confidence 0.9, history length 2) and kept fixed for the other benchmarks. Evaluation uses lm-evaluation-harness with temperature 0.1 and top-p 0.9. For every method, all positions after a sampled EOS are set to EOS. Speedup is wall-clock time relative to Entropy with 1 token per step.
official.claim: On MMLU-Pro with Dream-7B, DEMASK (τ=0.04, γ=0.9) reaches 47.5 ± 0.4% accuracy at a 1.7× wall-clock speedup over 1-token entropy decoding, versus 45.7 ± 0.4% at 1.3× for KLASS and 43.9 ± 0.4% at 1.0× for Entropy (1 tok).
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Comparison of DEMASK and KLASS on Dream-7B. Each cell shows accuracy (%) with speedup in parentheses, relative to Entropy (1 tok). Bold: best average accuracy (Avg excludes GSM8K).
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on MMLU-Pro, higher is better; speedup is wall-clock time relative to Entropy (1 tok). The paper does not say what ± means (it is likely the stderr that lm-evaluation-harness prints for a single run). No seeds are reported, and speedups have no error bars.
official.comparison: DEMASK vs. KLASS (re-tuned on GSM8K), Entropy, Top-1 and Token Order decoding with 1 or 2 tokens per step, all on Dream-7B under the same sampling settings and EOS optimization
official.falsification_criterion: On MMLU-Pro with Dream-7B and the stated hyperparameters, DEMASK's accuracy is not clearly above KLASS's (difference within about 1 percentage point, i.e. about twice the paper's reported ±0.4), or DEMASK is not faster than KLASS in wall-clock time or diffusion steps.

title: Why Invariance is Not Enough for Biomedical Domain Generalization and How to Fix It
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (untuned r=0.5 variant: Table 12, page 22)

official.background: 3D medical image segmentation models trained on one domain (scanner, modality, MRI sequence, site, disease stage) often fail badly on another, and retraining or test-time adaptation for each new domain is impractical in the clinic. Domain generalization methods try to fix this at training time with heavy augmentation or feature-statistic mixing, with inconsistent results. Foundation models such as anatomix produce per-voxel features that are approximately stable across such shifts, but the authors find that training on these invariant features alone does not beat training on the image with strong augmentation, and that naively concatenating image and features lets the network shortcut through the image.
official.method:
MaskGen feeds a 3D UNet (36.9M parameters, base width 20, 5 downsamplings) the concatenation of the raw image and per-voxel features from a frozen anatomix model (penultimate block, instance-normalized per channel). During training each of the (1+d) input channels is independently dropped with rate r (F.dropout3d on the concatenated input), so the network sees random partial views and cannot ignore the stable features. Training uses Dice + cross-entropy, AdamW (weight decay 1e-4), cosine LR from 2e-4 to 0, and the same extensive MONAI augmentation pipeline as all baselines. r is chosen on the validation set (an untuned r=0.5 variant is also reported).

In the few-shot setting, every method is trained on 5 randomly selected labelled subjects for 40K steps. For AMOS the shift is modality: train on CT, test on MRI of unseen subjects (30 test volumes, crop 192x192x128, spacing 1.0x1.0x1.5 mm). Baselines (ERM, GIN, GIN+IPA, MixUp, CutOut, DSBN, MixStyle, RSC) use the same UNet and augmentations and have their main hyperparameter tuned on the validation set; GIN and GIN+IPA additionally take the best of 3 seeds on validation.
official.claim: In few-shot (5 training subjects) CT-to-MRI segmentation on AMOS, MaskGen reaches mean test Dice 53.4 (SE 1.4), versus 37.8 (1.5) for the best baseline GIN+IPA and 5.4 (1.0) for ERM; with an untuned mask rate r=0.5 it still reaches 48.1 (1.7).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Few-shot domain generalization results. Left: Mean Dice score (w/ std. error) for few-shot experiments. Right: Arbitrarily selected few-shot results.
official.metric: Mean Dice (higher is better) on out-of-domain MRI test volumes; parentheses are standard error, apparently across test subjects of a single trained model, not across training seeds
official.comparison: MaskGen (image + frozen anatomix features with channel view masking) vs. ERM, GIN, GIN+IPA, MixUp, CutOut, DSBN, MixStyle, RSC, all with the same 3D UNet, augmentation pipeline and 5-subject/40K-step budget
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same few-shot AMOS CT-to-MRI protocol, MaskGen's Dice is not clearly above GIN+IPA (e.g. margin under ~5 Dice or within the combined standard errors), or a properly tuned baseline matches it.
