title: Self-Distilled RLVR

official.background: RLVR methods such as GRPO train reasoning models from a single verifier reward per response, so every token in a response gets the same advantage. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) gives dense token-level signals instead: the same model is the teacher when it is given privileged information, such as a reference solution, and the student when it is not. The paper argues that OPSD is ill-posed because the student cannot see the privileged information. In the authors' runs this causes leakage, where the trained model refers to a reference solution it never saw, and validation accuracy that peaks early and then falls. Combining a reliable outcome reward with a dense per-token signal is an open problem in RL post-training of LLMs.
official.method:
RLSD (RLVR with Self-Distillation) keeps GRPO's group-relative sequence advantage A = (R - mean)/std from a binary verifier and changes only how A is spread over tokens. For each sampled response, one extra forward pass of the same model with the ground-truth final answer r in context gives log P_T(y_t); the student log-prob log P_S(y_t) is computed without r. The privileged information gain is Delta_t = sg(log P_T(y_t) - log P_S(y_t)), the token weight is w_t = exp(sign(A) * Delta_t), and the token advantage is A_t = A * ((1 - lambda) + lambda * clip(w_t, 1 - eps_w, 1 + eps_w)) (Algorithm 1). Because w_t > 0, the reward alone sets the sign of each update and the teacher only changes its size. The teacher copy is synced with the student every 10 steps and frozen in between. lambda starts at 0.5 and decays linearly to 0 over the first 50 steps, and eps_w = 0.2.

Setup: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct is trained on MMFineReason-123K (hard samples that Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking failed in all 4 attempts) with VERL/EasyR1. Batch size is 256, with 8 rollouts per prompt, temperature 1.0 and a maximum response length of 4096. GRPO clipping is 0.2/0.28, with no KL or entropy loss. The learning rate is 1e-6 (1e-5 for OPSD and SDPO). Table 2 reports results at 200 training steps. The baselines are GRPO; OPSD, whose teacher sees verified reasoning traces from Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking; SDPO, whose teacher sees a previous successful rollout; and GRPO+OPSD, which is the GRPO loss plus a weighted distillation KL. Evaluation is accuracy on MMMU, MathVista, MathVision, ZeroBench and WeMath.
official.claim: After 200 training steps of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on MMFineReason-123K, RLSD reaches a 5-benchmark average accuracy of 56.18%, against 53.86% for GRPO, 52.91% for GRPO+OPSD, 52.74% for SDPO and 52.49% for OPSD. RLSD beats GRPO on all five benchmarks, including MathVision (52.73 vs. 48.82).
official.claim_caption: Table 2 Multimodal reasoning results on the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model. Bold indicates the best result among all models. Avg. is computed over the five selected benchmarks.
official.metric: Accuracy (%), higher is better, averaged over MMMU, MathVista, MathVision, ZeroBench and WeMath; one run per method, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: RLSD vs. GRPO (main matched baseline, same learning rate and settings), OPSD, SDPO and GRPO+OPSD, plus the untrained base model as a reference
official.falsification_criterion: With the same base model, data and 200-step budget, RLSD's 5-benchmark average does not exceed GRPO's, or the gap is within the seed-to-seed spread of repeated GRPO runs.

title: Claw-Eval: Towards Trustworthy Evaluation of Autonomous Agents

official.background: Benchmarks for LLM agents usually grade only the final output, rarely build safety constraints into ordinary tasks, and seldom test how agents cope with flaky tools. Claw-Eval is a 300-task agent benchmark (General service-orchestration tasks, Multimodal tasks, and Multi-turn dialogue tasks) that grades from execution traces, service-side audit logs and environment snapshots, and reports Average Score, Pass@3 (the task is passed in at least one of 3 trials) and Pass^3 (the task is passed in all 3 trials). One of the paper's main arguments is that robustness to transient failures shows up in consistency (Pass^3), not in best-case capability (Pass@3), so reporting a single metric hides it.
official.method:
Each task runs in a fresh Docker sandbox under one shared agent scaffold (Bash, file, search, web and media tools plus task-specific mock-service APIs). A trial's score is s_safety × (0.8·s_completion + 0.2·s_robustness), where completion comes from rubric items (deterministic checks plus a Gemini-3-Flash judge at temperature 0 for open-ended items), safety is a multiplicative 0/1 gate, and robustness is the fraction of tool types that hit an injected error that the agent later called successfully. A trial passes if its score is at least 0.75. Pass@3 is the fraction of tasks with at least one passing trial out of 3, and Pass^3 is the fraction with all 3 trials passing. Agents run at temperature 0 with thinking enabled where supported.

Error-injection experiment (Section 5.2): Claude-Opus-4.6, Gemini-3.1-Pro and GLM-5-Turbo are run on the 161 General tasks at injection rates 0.0, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6. At rate p, each mock-service call independently fails with probability p, and the failure is HTTP 429 (35%), HTTP 500 (35%) or a 2-4 s latency spike (30%). Pass@3 and Pass^3 are reported at each rate.
official.claim: On the 161 General tasks, raising the injected tool-failure rate from 0.0 to 0.6 changes Pass@3 by at most about 7.5 points for each of the three models (it falls for Opus and Gemini and rises slightly for GLM) (Opus-4.6 ~80.8→77.0, Gemini-3.1-Pro ~80.8→73.3, GLM-5-Turbo ~73.9→75.2), while Pass^3 falls by 12-24 points (Opus ~70.8→56.5, Gemini ~55.9→31.7, GLM ~57.1→44.7), so the Pass@3-Pass^3 gap widens for every model.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Effect of error injection on agent performance. Three models are evaluated on General tasks at error rates 0.0–0.6. Pass@3 remains largely stable while Pass^3 drops sharply. (a) Pass@3 (solid) and Pass^3 (dashed) as the error-injection rate increases from 0.0 to 0.6. (b) The Pass@3 – Pass^3 gap widens monotonically for every model, quantifying growing inconsistency.
official.metric: Pass@3 and Pass^3 (%) on the 161 General tasks, higher is better; one 3-trial run per model per rate; no error bars or seeds reported for this figure; values read off the plot are approximate (the rate-0.0 points match Table 3)
official.comparison: Same model and tasks at error-injection rate 0.6 vs. 0.0 (and 0.2, 0.4); change in Pass^3 vs. change in Pass@3
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the 161 General tasks for these models (or other agent models) at rates 0.0 and 0.6, the drop in Pass^3 is not clearly larger than the drop in Pass@3 (e.g. the Pass^3 drop is under about 10 points, or comparable to the Pass@3 drop), or the Pass@3-Pass^3 gap does not widen.

title: The Master Key Hypothesis: Unlocking Cross-Model Capability Transfer via Linear Subspace Alignment
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (repeated with instruction-tuned references in Table 4, page 24)

official.background: Each new language model needs its own expensive post-training to pick up behaviours such as step-by-step reasoning, even though related models share much of their pre-training data. Existing ways to reuse a capability across models work in weight space (which needs matching architectures), in logit space (which needs matching tokenizers and running several models at inference), or by distillation (which needs training). Steering vectors act on activations at inference time, but they are usually built from labelled positive/negative examples and applied only to the model they came from. This paper asks whether a capability direction taken from one model can be mapped linearly into a different-sized model and still produce the behaviour.
official.method:
Unlock uses three models. The Source Locked and Source Unlocked variants differ only in the capability; for the claim here, both are the same base model (Qwen1.5-14B) prompted either with a Direct prompt that asks only for the final answer or with a CoT prompt ending 'Let's think step by step' (Figure 5). For each of n unlabelled queries, the difference in the final-token hidden state between the CoT and Direct prompts is taken at each layer. These differences are aggregated by their mean or by the first principal component of the centred differences, giving the MasterKey direction. To map it to the Target (Qwen1.5-7B base), final-token hidden states of the Source Locked and Target Locked models are collected on the same n queries with a shared prompt. Each matrix is reduced to its top-k right singular vectors, a k x k matrix W is fitted by least squares (pseudoinverse) between the two projected representations, and the lifted operator R = V_T^k W^T (V_S^k)^T maps the Source direction into Target space. Source and target layers are paired by relative depth.

At inference the Target gets the Direct prompt. At every layer, the final-token hidden state is replaced by h/||h|| + alpha * v/||v|| and then rescaled back to the norm of the original h. The aggregator, n, k and alpha are chosen by grid search on a held-out development set, separately for each model pair and dataset (Table 5; e.g. Qwen1.5-7B from 14B on GSM8K: mean, n = 512, k = 64, alpha = 0.1; on MATH: mean, n = 64, k = 64, alpha = 0.05; on SVAMP: PCA, n = 64, k = 16, alpha = 0.1). Accuracy is measured on GSM8K, MATH and SVAMP with a 512-token generation limit. The answer is extracted from a '<atok>ans</atok>' pattern.
official.claim: Steering Qwen1.5-7B (base, Direct prompt) with a CoT direction extracted from Qwen1.5-14B and transferred by low-rank linear alignment raises accuracy from 9.2% to 56.0% on GSM8K, 8.0% to 20.1% on MATH and 44.0% to 70.3% on SVAMP, without any training.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Chain-of-Thought Capability Transfer. Transfer performance across model families. Accuracies of base model with Direct prompting (T_L) and base model with explicit CoT prompting shown in gray.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on GSM8K, MATH and SVAMP, higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported (decoding presumably greedy, stated explicitly only for the math experiments)
official.comparison: Qwen1.5-7B base with Direct prompt + Unlock from 14B vs. the same model with Direct prompt and no steering; CoT-prompted 7B base (64.4 / 17.9 / 73.0) and 7B-Chat with CoT (58.1 / 18.2 / 69.7) are reference points
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the transfer (Qwen1.5-14B CoT-vs-Direct direction mapped to Qwen1.5-7B, Direct prompt, hyperparameters tuned on a held-out dev set) gives GSM8K accuracy less than ~20 points above the unsteered Direct baseline, or no improvement on MATH and SVAMP; a further check is whether a direction mapped with a random or untrained (e.g. random-W) alignment gives similar gains, which would mean the gain does not come from the cross-model alignment.

title: Attention-Based Sampler for Diffusion Language Models

official.background: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) such as LLaDA and Fast-dLLM v2 generate text by starting from a block of mask tokens and unmasking them over several steps, in any order and possibly several at a time. The order in which tokens are unmasked affects output quality. Standard samplers pick the next token with token-level heuristics: highest confidence (top probability), largest margin between the top two probabilities, or lowest entropy, and parallel variants unmask every token above a threshold. These heuristics have no clear link to maximizing the likelihood of the generated sequence.
official.method:
The authors bound the gap between the permutation-based likelihood and an 'ideal' likelihood (each token conditioned on all others) by a term in the attention matrix, approximate it with a rank-only objective, and prove that this objective is minimized by decoding tokens in descending order of 'total attention' s_j = sum over i != j of A_ij, i.e. the column sum of the attention matrix with the diagonal removed. Attn-Sampler (sequential, Algorithm 1) is training-free: within each block of mask tokens, run a forward pass, average the attention matrix over all layers and heads (the default, per the ablation), compute column sums for the masked positions, and unmask the masked position with the largest total attention using its argmax token. Blocks are decoded semi-autoregressively until <eos>.

The parallel variant (Algorithm 2) uses a probability threshold tau = 0.9: among masked tokens whose top probability is below tau, the largest total attention becomes a dynamic threshold, and every masked token with total attention above it is unmasked in that step. Baselines are top-1 confidence, top-1 margin, top-1 negative entropy, Fast-dLLM (confidence threshold), EB-Sampler and KLASS, all run on the same model. Models: Fast-dLLM v2 1.5B and 7B, LLaDA-1.5 8B. Benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP; metric is test accuracy (pass@1 for code).
official.claim: With Fast-dLLM v2 7B, sequential Attn-Sampler reaches 57.67% average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP (84.00 / 52.50 / 57.93 / 36.24), above the strongest baseline, the top-1 entropy sampler (56.57%; 82.87 / 51.92 / 55.49 / 35.98), and the top-1 confidence sampler (54.66%; 82.71 / 50.96 / 54.27 / 30.69).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Testing accuracies of various sampling algorithms on different language models and evaluation tasks. The best results are in bold, and the second-best are underlined.
official.metric: Test accuracy in % (higher is better) per benchmark and their unweighted average; single deterministic run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Attn-Sampler (sequential and parallel) vs. top-1 confidence, margin and entropy samplers, Fast-dLLM, EB-Sampler and KLASS, all on the same Fast-dLLM v2 7B checkpoint (also LLaDA-1.5 8B and Fast-dLLM v2 1.5B)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Fast-dLLM v2 7B with the same block decoding, sequential Attn-Sampler's average accuracy over the four benchmarks is not higher than the top-1 entropy sampler's, or its advantage over the top-1 confidence sampler shrinks well below the reported ~3 points (e.g. under 1 point).

title: Distributionally Robust Token Optimization in RLHF

official.background: RLHF-tuned LLMs often answer well on prompts that resemble their fine-tuning data but fail when the wording, format or language shifts, especially on multi-step reasoning. Reinforced Token Optimization (RTO) improves on PPO by giving PPO a dense token-level reward derived from a DPO policy, but it still minimizes the plain average loss over the minibatch, so it does not focus on hard parts of responses. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) replaces that average with a worst-case expectation over an ambiguity set of reweightings, which may give more consistent performance under distribution shift.
official.method:
DRTO keeps the RTO pipeline (DPO policy trained on preference data, token-wise reward r_h = beta1 log(pi_dpo/pi_ref) - beta2 log(pi_theta/pi_ref) + terminal reward, PPO actor-critic updates) and changes only the actor loss. Each rollout is cut into at most 8 contiguous spans (minimum length 16 tokens) at positions where the rollout-policy token probability falls below p_cut = 0.05. Each span's loss is the mean per-token PPO clipped surrogate loss within it. Spans get a response-balanced nominal distribution P_S(i,s) = 1/(n S_i). chi2-DRTO uses the actor loss mean + sqrt(rho) * sqrt(Var + delta) of span losses under P_S with rho = 0.1; KL-DRTO uses exponential-tilt weights from the KL dual with rho = 0.01. Statistics are computed over each 256-rollout train batch, and the adversarial weights are detached.

Math pipeline: actor initialized from OpenRLHF/Llama-3-8b-sft-mixture, DPO on UltraFeedback, RL on 10,000 prompt-only OpenMathInstruct samples (seed 42), DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 via OpenRLHF. Baselines (RTO, SFT, PPO, DPO, FlowRL, DAPO) are trained on the same data and backbone. Evaluation is 5-shot flexible-match accuracy with lm-evaluation-harness on GSM8K, GSM8K with a CoT trigger, Spanish GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA.
official.claim: On Llama3-8B fine-tuned on 10k OpenMathInstruct prompts, chi2-DRTO reaches 22.4% on MATH-500 and 78.7% on GSM8K (5-shot), versus 18.0% and 73.2% for standard RTO trained on the same backbone and data (+4.4 and +5.5 points), and does not fall below RTO on any of the five math benchmarks.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Accuracy of Llama3-8B across five benchmarks. Superscripts report absolute change (percentage points) compared to standard RTO. Best results are in bold.

title: Delve into the Applicability of Advanced Optimizers for Multi-Task Learning

official.background: Optimization-based multi-task learning (MTL) methods such as MGDA, CAGrad, Nash-MTL and FairGrad combine per-task gradients into one update direction meant to resolve conflicts between tasks. In practice these combined gradients are fed into optimizers like Adam or Muon, whose exponential-moving-average momentum (β1 ≈ 0.9) means the current, de-conflicted gradient makes up only a small part of each parameter update. The paper argues that this weakens the intended instant de-conflicting. It also argues that Muon's orthogonalization already acts as an implicit task re-balancer, so the quality and rank of its input gradient matter.
official.method:
APT has two components. (1) Adaptive momentum: at each step, compute ρt = cos(Gt, Gt−1) between the current and previous MTL-aggregated gradients and set βt = βmin + (βmax − βmin)·Clip((ρt+1)/2, 0, 1), with βmax = 0.9 and βmin = 0.1. This replaces the fixed β1 in the first-moment EMA, so momentum falls when consecutive aggregated gradients disagree (high curvature). (2) Light direction preservation (LDP), used only with Muon: compute the mean gradient ḡ, ci = cos(gi, ḡ), ωi = Sigmoid(ξ·ci), renormalize the weights to sum to K, and set Gt = Σ ωi gi. This Gt is the input to Muon's Newton–Schulz orthogonalization. APT-CG, APT-FAMO and APT-Fair wrap CAGrad, FAMO and FairGrad with the adaptive momentum. APT-Muon is Muon with LDP plus adaptive momentum.

Setup for the chosen claim: CityScapes (2 tasks: semantic segmentation and depth), SegNet with an MTAN shared backbone, 200 epochs, batch size 8. The Adam variants use lr 1e-4, halved after epoch 100. Muon uses lr 0.02 with ReduceOnPlateau (patience 10). Δm% is the mean relative degradation against single-task (Independent) models over mIoU, pixel accuracy, absolute depth error and relative depth error. Results are averaged over 3 seeds.
official.claim: On CityScapes (SegNet-MTAN, 200 epochs), APT-Muon achieves Δm% = -3.09 ± 1.16 over 3 seeds and mean rank 1.00, beating every listed MTL baseline; the strongest are COST (4.30), FairGrad (5.18) and Nash-MTL (6.82).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Scene understanding (CityScapes, 2 tasks). We report MTAN model performance averaged over 3 random seeds. The best scores are provided in gray, and the second scores are underlined.
official.metric: Δm% relative to independent single-task models (lower is better; negative means better than single-task). Results are averaged over 3 random seeds; the paper does not say whether ± is a standard deviation or a standard error. ± is reported only for the APT rows; the baseline rows have no error bars.
official.comparison: APT-Muon (Muon + LDP + adaptive momentum) vs. LS, RLW, DWA, Uncertainty, MGDA, GradDrop, PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL, Nash-MTL, FAMO, FairGrad and COST, all using Adam. Secondary comparison: APT-Fair (2.22 ± 1.46) vs. FairGrad (5.18).
official.falsification_criterion: Over 3 seeds, a re-run of APT-Muon on CityScapes gives a mean Δm% ≥ 0 (no better than single-task), or a re-run of the strongest baseline (COST, FairGrad or Nash-MTL with Adam) under the same pipeline comes within about one std (≈1.2 points) of APT-Muon's Δm%.

title: AffordSim: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark for Affordance-Aware Robotic Manipulation
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (full per-task breakdown in Table 6, page 18)

official.background: Simulation is a major source of robot manipulation training data, but many everyday tasks depend on affordance: success requires touching a specific functional region of the object (for example, grasping a mug's body so the handle stays free for a rack hook). Existing simulation data generators either rely on manually authored per-object grasp poses, which do not scale to new objects or tasks, or on generic grasp estimators such as AnyGrasp, which rank grasps by stability and ignore which region the downstream action needs. Adding a 2D semantic mask filter after the estimator (as in GenManip) cannot recover good grasps that the estimator never proposed in the right region.
official.method:
AffordSim, built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim, turns a natural-language task description into a scene (via Qwen-VL-Plus scene and task parsing) and one affordance query per functional contact region. An open-vocabulary 3D affordance model (VoxAfford) predicts a binary per-point mask on the object's canonical point cloud. Stage 1 runs mean-shift clustering on the masked points to get a contact point, estimates the local surface normal by PCA on nearest neighbours, and samples K approach directions on the hemisphere opposite the normal (fixed polar tilt), solving wrist yaw to align with the local geometry. Stage 2 plans a pre-grasp trajectory to each candidate with cuRobo and scores it 1/(joint-space arc length) if collision-free, 0 otherwise; the highest-scoring grasp is executed, followed by cuRobo-planned lift and task segments.

For Table 1, five grasp sources are compared under identical scene and motion-planner settings on all 50 benchmark tasks (10 Easy, 30 Medium affordance-critical, 10 Hard composite), each run 100 times with the manipulated object's initial pose randomized over a 30 cm horizontal window and 60 degree yaw range. Baselines: Manual (hand-tuned per-object grasp rules), AnyGrasp (stability-ranked generic 6-DoF grasps), AnyGrasp+Filter (AnyGrasp candidates kept only if the contact falls inside a 2D SAM2 task-relevant mask, GenManip-style), and Human Aff. (human-annotated affordance ground truth, oracle). The metric is trajectory collection success rate.
official.claim: On the 30 Medium (affordance-critical) tasks of the AffordSim benchmark, AffordSim's affordance-guided grasp selection achieves an average trajectory collection success rate of 79%, versus 45% for AnyGrasp+Filter and 15% for AnyGrasp under identical scene and planner settings (100 rollouts per task).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Affordance integration on the AffordSim benchmark. Trajectory collection success rate (%) per task across the five grasp methods. AnyGrasp+Filter denotes AnyGrasp candidates filtered against a 2D SAM2 task-relevant mask, mirroring the GenManip-style affordance-filtering pipeline. Two representative tasks per tier are listed; full breakdown in Appendix E. Tier averages bolded.
official.metric: Trajectory collection success rate (%), higher is better, averaged over the 30 Medium-tier tasks with 100 rollouts each. No error bars or seed spread are reported.
official.comparison: AffordSim (VoxAfford-based affordance-guided grasp selection) vs. AnyGrasp+Filter (strongest automatic baseline) and AnyGrasp; Manual and Human Aff. are per-object-annotated references.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the paper's protocol on the Medium tier, AffordSim's average collection SR does not exceed AnyGrasp+Filter's by a large margin (e.g., the gap is under ~15 percentage points), or AffordSim fails to beat AnyGrasp+Filter on most Medium tasks.

title: On the Robustness of Watermarking for Autoregressive Image Generation
claim_source: Table 11, page 35 (aggregated version in Table 2, page 12)

official.background: Autoregressive (AR) image generators such as LlamaGen, RAR, Anole and Infinity can be watermarked at generation time by biasing which tokens or bits get sampled, in the style of KGW watermarks for LLMs. A detector then re-encodes an image and tests whether 'green' tokens are over-represented. BitMark, a watermark for the bitwise multi-scale Infinity generator, is meant to let providers find their own synthetic images and drop them from future training sets (it is also 'radioactive', i.e. it survives into models fine-tuned on watermarked images). If an attacker can forge the watermark onto authentic images, the detector will flag real photos as synthetic. The paper calls this Watermark Mimicry: real images get excluded from training data, and the detector cannot be trusted as evidence.
official.method:
BitMark (official code, Infinity-2B, 1024x1024, green bigram set G = {01, 10}, δ = 2, embedding and detection on all scales) detects a watermark by encoding the image with Infinity-2B's multi-scale bitwise VAE (V_d = 2^32), recovering the bits at each scale, counting green bigrams, and running a one-sided z-test. Detection is at the threshold for FPR = 1%. Frequency Injection forgery (Algorithm 4, Appendix A.2) takes an authentic cover image, computes the per-channel FFT (fftshift), and adds complex components of fixed magnitude α with a random phase (sampled independently per channel) at points spaced s = 32 bins apart along the main diagonals of the right half of the spectrum. Each component is mirrored to the conjugate position to keep the image real, and the inverse FFT gives the forged image. Setting A uses ln(α) = 7.75 and only the first four lower-frequency diagonal bins. Setting B uses ln(α) = 8.0 and the same four bins. Setting C uses ln(α) = 8.0 and all diagonal bins. At attack time it uses no generator, no watermark key and no watermarked reference image. However, the injection pattern was inspired by averaging 5000 BitMark-watermarked images (Sec. 3.3), and Settings A-C were chosen during a parameter sweep that used p-values from the BitMark verifier (Appendix A.2).

Evaluation: 100 MS-COCO cover images whose shortest edge is at least 1024, resized and center-cropped to 1024x1024. The metrics are mean TPR@FPR=1% (the fraction of forged images the detector calls watermarked), mean z-score, median p-value, and PSNR/LPIPS against the original cover image. For comparison, the paper's black-box LatentOpt-Forgery (adversarial optimisation through an unrelated proxy VQ-VAE, budget 8/255, using one watermarked reference image) gets aggregated TPR 0.59 at PSNR 31.5.
official.claim: Applying Frequency Injection to 100 authentic MS-COCO images makes the BitMark/Infinity-2B detector flag them as watermarked at FPR = 1% with TPR 0.73 (Setting A, PSNR 37.5 dB), 0.81 (Setting B, PSNR 35.5 dB) and 0.93 (Setting C, PSNR 29.7 dB), with median p-values of 2.7e-7, 3.0e-17 and 7.5e-31, with no model access at attack time (Settings A and B also reach a higher PSNR than the black-box LatentOpt-F forgery, which gets TPR 0.59 at 31.5 dB).
official.claim_caption: Table 11: Full experimental results (BitMark deployed w. ∞-2B (V_d = 2^32)). [From Appendix B: mean TPR@FPR=1%, median p-value, and mean with standard deviation for z-score, PSNR and LPIPS. Removal attacks aim for lower TPR/z-score and higher p-value, forgery attacks for the opposite. ■ black-box, grey ■ grey-box, □ white-box, □+ white-box with knowledge of the green set.]
official.metric: TPR@FPR=1% (fraction of forged cover images detected as watermarked, higher = more successful forgery), mean over 100 images, no error bars. z-score, PSNR and LPIPS are given as mean ± std over the 100 images. p-value is the median.
official.comparison: Frequency-injected COCO cover images vs. the same authentic cover images (which by construction should be flagged at about the 1% FPR rate); the black-box LatentOpt-Forgery attack (TPR 0.59, PSNR 31.5) is a secondary reference
official.falsification_criterion: On 100+ COCO images at 1024x1024 with the official BitMark detector (Infinity-2B, G = {01, 10}, all scales), the Setting B or Setting C injection gives TPR@FPR=1% below about 0.5, or reaches such a TPR only at a PSNR well below the reported ~35.5 / ~29.7 dB.

title: MosaicMRI: A Diverse Dataset and Benchmark for Raw Musculoskeletal MRI

official.background: Deep-learning methods for accelerated MRI reconstruction have mostly been trained and evaluated on public raw k-space datasets of the brain and knee (e.g. fastMRI), so little is known about how they behave on the wider range of musculoskeletal (MSK) anatomies, contrasts and coil setups seen in clinical practice. MosaicMRI releases 3,096 fully sampled 1.5 T multi-coil MSK volumes (88,416 slices, 854 patients, ten anatomy classes, seven contrast groups) plus a 54-volume 0.55 T set. It uses accelerated reconstruction to study whether anatomical diversity in the training data helps.
official.method:
The 1.5 T data are split by patient into train/val/test (2,166 / 465 / 465 volumes; 61,903 / 13,265 / 13,248 slices). Reconstruction is multi-coil at 8x acceleration: random Cartesian masks keep 12.5% of phase-encoding lines, including the central 4% low-frequency band. Test masks are seeded deterministically by filename, and the target is the root-sum-of-squares (RSS) image. Models follow the fastMRI codebase conventions, and the checkpoint with the best validation SSIM is evaluated.

For Table 5, U-Net and ViT image-domain reconstruction models are each trained twice: once on only the target anatomy's training volumes (knee: 243 volumes in the whole dataset; shoulder: 446) and once on the full MosaicMRI training split. Both are evaluated on the same knee or shoulder test volumes, with PSNR and SSIM against the RSS target.
official.claim: At 8x acceleration, a ViT trained on the full mixed-anatomy MosaicMRI training split beats a ViT trained only on the target anatomy by 3.46 dB on knee (37.47 vs. 34.01 dB PSNR; SSIM 0.892 vs. 0.850) and by 5.87 dB on shoulder (41.66 vs. 35.79 dB; SSIM 0.950 vs. 0.912). U-Net shows the same direction with smaller gains (knee 37.94 vs. 37.35, shoulder 42.41 vs. 42.05).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: PSNR (dB) / SSIM for reconstruction with mixed-anatomy training across architectures.
official.metric: PSNR (dB) and SSIM against the RSS target on the anatomy's test volumes, higher is better; single runs, no error bars reported
official.comparison: Same architecture (ViT; also U-Net) trained on target-anatomy-only data vs. the full MosaicMRI training split, evaluated on knee and shoulder test sets
official.falsification_criterion: When ViT is retrained under both regimes, the full-data model's PSNR advantage over the anatomy-only model on knee or shoulder is under ~1 dB, or it reverses.

title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Looped Reasoning Language Models

official.background: Looped (recurrent-depth) language models reuse a block of Transformer layers several times, so more test-time compute means more passes through the same weights. Huginn-0125, Ouro, and Llama retrofitted with recurrence are pretrained examples. Little is known about what happens inside these loops. One open question is whether the hidden state settles to a fixed point as the number of recurrences grows. If it does, attention patterns, and the 'stages of inference' known from feedforward LLMs, stay the same at each further recurrence. This could explain why some looped models stay stable when run for more recurrences than they were trained on and others degrade.
official.method:
Each pretrained looped model is run on the same 256 random GSM8k test questions (no system prompt), with its recurrent block iterated 128 times. For every layer of the recurrent block, the residual stream after that layer in recurrence 128 is taken as an 'approximate fixed point'. The plotted quantity is the norm of the difference between that layer's residual stream at each recurrence t and its approximate fixed point, averaged over examples and tokens. If the curve falls to near zero long before t = 128, the layer has reached a fixed point. A curve that stays high and only reaches zero at t = 128 (where it is zero by construction) means it has not.

Models (Hugging Face IDs from Table 2): ByteDance/Ouro-1.4B (structure (0, 24, 0), trained with 4 loops, no input injection, sandwich norm on the attention/MLP outputs); tomg-group-umd/huginn-0125 ((2, 4, 2) with input injection, trained with about 32 loops, sandwich norm on the residual stream); smcleish/Recurrent-Llama-3.2-train-recurrence-32 (retrofitted Llama-3.2-1B, (4, 6, 4) with input injection, pre-norm). Figure 3 shows the related quantity of successive-recurrence differences, which become small for all three models. Figure 4 is what tells the models apart.
official.claim: With the recurrent block iterated 128 times on GSM8k, the per-layer distance to the recurrence-128 state falls to about 0 within about 10 recurrences for retrofitted Llama (from about 16) and within about 50-70 for Huginn-0125 (from about 90). For Ouro 1.4B it stays around 5-20 for most of the run, decreasing roughly linearly and reaching 0 only at recurrence 128. So Huginn and retrofitted Llama reach fixed points and Ouro does not.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4. Norm of the difference between the residual stream after each layer in the recurrent block and its "approximate fixed point" - the residual stream after that layer in the 128th recurrence. While Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama quickly reach a fixed point, Ouro does not - despite small successive differences evidenced by Fig. 3.
official.metric: Norm of the difference between the residual stream after each recurrent-block layer at recurrence t and the same layer's output at recurrence 128. Lower means closer to a fixed point. One line per layer, averaged over 256 GSM8k examples. No error bars or seeds. Values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Ouro 1.4B (no input injection, output sandwich norm) vs. Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama-3.2-1B (input injection), same GSM8k inputs and same 128-recurrence procedure
official.falsification_criterion: Repeating the procedure gives a counterexample. Either Ouro 1.4B's per-layer distance to its recurrence-128 state falls to near zero (say below 10% of its initial value) well before recurrence ~100, or retrofitted Llama or Huginn-0125 still has a distance that is a substantial fraction of its initial value at recurrence 64.

title: FiRe: Fine-grained Multimodal Reasoning for Enhanced Image Generation

official.background: Unified multimodal LLMs such as Janus-Pro can both understand and generate images, so in principle they can check their own text-to-image outputs and fix them. Existing reasoning-based T2I methods either rewrite the prompt before generating (T2I-R1) or make one holistic yes/no judgment of image-prompt alignment and then regenerate the whole image (Janus-Pro-R1). Both often miss fine-grained compositional errors in counts, colors, positions and sizes when a prompt has several objects. These errors are what compositional benchmarks such as GenEval++ measure.
official.method:
FiRe fine-tunes Janus-Pro-7B so that one model runs a six-step loop: (1) generate an initial image; (2) summarize the prompt into checkable visual details; (3) decompose the summary into semantic tuples (entity, count, color, spatial relation, ...); (4) answer a VQA question per tuple with a rationale and yes/no; (5) write one combined feedback instruction for the tuples judged 'no', or 'no-edit'; (6) apply localized image editing with that feedback and a preservation instruction. Steps 2-6 repeat on the corrected image. (1st) in the table is the initial image, and (2nd)/(3rd) are after one and two correction rounds. An image is edited only when the model's own judgment finds a mismatch. No external model is used at inference.

Training is SFT on 200K image-text pairs (140K from FocusDiff and 60K compositional samples synthesized with Qwen-Image / Qwen-Image-Edit) with full supervised trajectories, followed by FiRe-GRPO for 300 steps. FiRe-GRPO is GRPO with step-specific rewards from a Qwen3.5-35B-A3B evaluator and per-step group-normalized advantages. Baselines on the same Janus-Pro-7B backbone, re-run by the authors under identical evaluation settings, are T2I-R1 (prompt-level chain of thought before generation) and Janus-Pro-R1 (holistic self-assessment and full-image regeneration, also run for three rounds). GenEval++ has 280 complex compositional prompts (7 task types x 40 prompts) and is scored with its official protocol.
official.claim: On GenEval++ with a Janus-Pro-7B backbone, FiRe (300-step FiRe-GRPO checkpoint) reaches an overall score of 0.379 on its initial image and 0.491 after two self-correction rounds. The authors' re-run baselines on the same backbone score 0.311 (T2I-R1) and at most 0.294 (Janus-Pro-R1, any of its three rounds).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison on GenEval [19], GenEval++ [20], and DPGBench [21]. ↑ indicates higher is better. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best results among Multimodal Reasoning LLMs, respectively. Superscript * indicates results reproduced by us. (1st) denotes the initial T2I generation, while (2nd) and (3rd) represent the first and second rounds of image correction, respectively. Subcategory scores of DPGBench are provided in Appendix L.
official.metric: GenEval++ overall score (fraction of prompts judged correct by the official GenEval++ evaluator, averaged over task types), higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: FiRe (1st/2nd/3rd round) vs. T2I-R1* and Janus-Pro-R1* (1st/2nd/3rd round), all on Janus-Pro-7B and evaluated by the authors in the same environment
official.falsification_criterion: Using the official GenEval++ protocol and the same Janus-Pro-7B backbone, FiRe after two correction rounds scores no more than about 0.08 above the better of T2I-R1 and Janus-Pro-R1 (e.g. below ~0.39 overall when the baselines score ~0.31), or extra FiRe correction rounds do not raise the overall score above the initial-image score.

title: World–Value–Action Model: Implicit Planning for Vision–Language–Action Systems
claim_source: Table 2, page 17 (Appendix B.1); the one-shot vs. full numbers also appear as the 'W/o Latent Trajectory Planning' row of Table 1, page 7

official.background: Vision–language–action (VLA) robot policies usually predict the next action chunk directly from the current image and instruction, with no way to look ahead and judge where a sequence of actions will lead. That matters most on long-horizon, multi-step manipulation, where small errors add up. Model-based RL handles this by combining a world model with a value function and planning over imagined futures, but explicit search in a high-dimensional action space scales poorly with the horizon. This paper asks whether planning can instead be done as inference over the latent noise of generative world and value models inside a VLA.
official.method:
WAV (2.2B parameters) has three flow-matching DiT modules. (1) A language-conditioned multi-view video generator W (T5-XXL text encoder, built on the GE-ACT / Genie Envisioner video backbone) predicts future visual features from latent noise z_vid. (2) A trajectory-value module V predicts the discounted return of a rule-based dense reward from video features and value noise z_val. (3) An action decoder cross-attends to the video and value features and outputs an 8-step action chunk. They are trained in stages: first the video module, then the value module with the video model frozen, then all modules jointly with the action flow loss.

At inference, an MPPI/CEM-style loop updates Gaussian distributions over z_vid and z_val for K iterations. Each iteration samples M video noises; for each video, N value noises; it scores each video by the max over n of the value SNR (mean/std); it refits the video noise distribution to the top-K1 videos and the value noise distribution to the top-K2 values, with exponential smoothing (alpha, beta). After K iterations, latents are sampled from the optimized distributions and decoded into actions. The default is K = 3, M = 30, N = 5. The attribution study keeps all modules frozen and compares inference strategies: one-shot sampling (K = 0, standard Gaussian noise), random selection among M samples, Best-of-N by mean value or by max SNR, compute-matched Best-of-N (K·M candidates), and iterative refinement without value conditioning.
official.claim: On LIBERO, with identical frozen WAV modules, value-guided iterative latent planning (K = 3) reaches 98.1 average success (Long 94.4) vs. 96.4 (Long 91.8) for one-shot sampling and 97.2 (Long 93.6) for compute-matched Best-of-N with max-SNR value selection.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Attribution study of WAV on LIBERO. All variants use identical frozen video, value, and action modules; only the inference strategy differs.
official.metric: Task success rate (%), higher is better, per LIBERO suite (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long) and averaged. No seeds, standard deviations or number of evaluation episodes are reported.
official.comparison: WAV full (K = 3, value-guided iterative refinement) vs. one-shot sampling (K = 0), random selection, Best-of-N (mean-value and max-SNR), compute-matched Best-of-N (K·M forward passes), and WAV without value conditioning, all using the same frozen video, value and action modules.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same trained modules and standard LIBERO evaluation (e.g. 50 episodes per task over multiple seeds), the full K = 3 planner fails to beat compute-matched Best-of-N and one-shot sampling on average success, or its gain over one-shot sampling falls within seed-to-seed variation (e.g. under about 1 point average, or no gain on LIBERO-Long).

title: LACE: Lattice Attention for Cross-thread Exploration

official.background: Test-time scaling for LLM reasoning often samples several reasoning paths in parallel and picks one afterwards (mean, majority vote, or a verifier). Those paths never see each other while they are generated, so they tend to repeat the same assumptions and fail in correlated ways. This paper asks whether letting parallel threads exchange information during decoding, inside the model, makes the group explore more distinct solutions and lets the model pick a correct answer itself.
official.method:
LACE adds a small 'lattice attention' side path to Qwen3 (1.7B and 4B) in every other layer from the middle to the last layer (<1% extra parameters). At each layer, the standard causal attention output of each of N=4 threads is projected to a low dimension, attends over the other threads' representations at the same token position (3D RoPE encodes token position and thread index), and is added back through a learned sigmoid gate. Training data comes from DAPO problems where the base model's success rate is in (0, 0.5]; Qwen3-235B-A22B generates diverse solutions using a 'DO NOT USE: [solutions cache]' prompt, compresses them, and an LLM judge writes a comparative comment and a BEST/SUCCESS/FAIL tag per thread (exactly one BEST).

Training is SFT (first lattice-only, then full-parameter) followed by Lattice GRPO, where each rollout is a group of 4 threads, the reward is the verified accuracy of threads tagged BEST/SUCCESS plus a weighted embedding-diversity reward, and the group advantage is shared across all threads (4B: 320 RL steps). Baselines run under the same pipeline: Independent (single-thread SFT+RL, reported as mean@4 or majority vote@4) and Isolated Parallel (same multi-thread data and SFT/RL recipe, but no lattice layers, so threads are decoded in parallel but independently). Accuracy for LACE and Isolated Parallel uses the answer from the thread the model tags BEST.
official.claim: On LiveBench with Qwen3-4B after SFT and RL, LACE's self-selected BEST thread reaches 41.8% accuracy, versus 12.7% for Isolated Parallel (same multi-thread recipe without lattice attention; 15.5% with voting) and 25.6% mean@4 / 28.0% vote@4 for the single-thread Independent SFT+RL baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparisons with baselines on math and reasoning benchmarks. Independent is a single-thread SFT+RL baseline, while Isolated Parallel uses the same multi-thread training recipe as LACE without lattice layers or cross-thread attention. We report Accuracy and Diversity (Div.). By default, Independent reports Mean@4, while Isolated Parallel and LACE use the answer from the thread selected by the model as BEST among four simultaneous threads; +Vote denotes replacing the default selection rule with majority voting.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on LiveBench, higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported (the authors state this in the checklist). Diversity = mean pairwise embedding dissimilarity across threads.
official.comparison: LACE (SFT -> RL) vs. Isolated Parallel (SFT -> RL, BEST-thread and +Vote) vs. Independent (SFT -> RL, mean@4 and +Vote), all Qwen3-4B, 4 threads/samples
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction of the 4B setting where LACE's LiveBench accuracy is not clearly above both the Isolated Parallel baseline and the Independent +Vote baseline (e.g., less than ~5 points above 28.0), or where the gap disappears across several training seeds.

title: Sketching the Readout of Large Language Models for Scalable Data Attribution and Valuation

official.background: Data attribution asks which training examples drove a model's behaviour, and data valuation asks which candidate examples would be useful to train on. Gradient-based influence estimators (TracIn, RapidIn, TrackStar, ZO-Inf) need per-example gradients over all P parameters, which makes indexing a large corpus expensive in memory and time, and infeasible at tens of billions of parameters. Cheaper proxies such as BM25 or off-the-shelf embedding similarity do not reflect the target model's own loss geometry. A method that gives accurate influence rankings from forward passes alone would make attribution and data selection practical for modern LLMs.
official.method:
RISE restricts the TracIn-style gradient inner product to the LM head, whose per-token gradient factorizes exactly as r_t ⊗ h_t, with h_t the final hidden state and r_t = softmax(z_t/τ) − onehot(y_t) the prediction residual (τ a temperature); both factors come from a forward pass. The residual is truncated to a sparse support (from the top-256 logits, keep the smallest prefix reaching cumulative probability 0.92, min 4, always including the ground-truth token) and the probabilities are renormalized on that support. Two channels are built: RH uses the sparse residual r̃_t, and GH uses its projection into embedding space g̃_t = W_lm_head^T r̃_t. Each factor (r̃_t, h_t, g̃_t) is compressed with a fixed-hash CountSketch to dimensions (K_r, K_h, K_g) and L2-normalized; per-sample signatures are sums over token positions of vec(r̂_t ⊗ ĥ_t) and vec(ĝ_t ⊗ ĥ_t). The score between a candidate and a query is λ_rh·⟨φ_RH(x_i), φ_RH(x_q)⟩ + λ_gh·⟨φ_GH(x_i), φ_GH(x_q)⟩ (Eq. 3) with λ_rh = 0.7, λ_gh = 1.0, sequence length 512; Algorithm 2 instead folds the λ weights into the per-token sums, and Table 6 says the final sample vector is L2-normalized.

In the Howdy! task the candidate pool is 5,000 Alpaca-based samples of which 438 contain the backdoor trigger 'howdy!'; the queries are 100 WebQuestions test generations containing the trigger. In the 'Predict Future' (prospective valuation) setting the pretrained Pythia checkpoint, which has not been fine-tuned on the pool, scores every candidate. For each query, candidates are ranked by influence, auPRC/auROC are computed on the top-K and bottom-K candidates, and the results are macro-averaged over queries. Baselines are TrackStar (Rademacher projection dim 16), RapidIn (RapidGrad K = 65536), ZO-Inf (zeroth-order RapidIn), BM25 and E5-base-v2 embedding similarity, all on the same pool and queries.
official.claim: On Howdy! backdoor prospective valuation with pretrained Pythia-1B (5,000-sample pool, 438 trigger positives, 100 trigger queries), RISE reaches Top-10 auPRC 0.9974 versus 0.7394 for TrackStar, 0.1199 for RapidIn, 0.2785 for BM25 and 0.3740 for E5 embeddings; on Pythia-410M, RISE gets 0.9839 versus TrackStar's 0.5283.
official.claim_caption: Table 23: Performance Comparison: RapidIn vs. RISE vs. TrackStar vs. ZO-Inf Howdy! Backdoor Attack Task Predict Future
official.metric: auPRC (and auROC) at Top-K, higher is better, macro-averaged over 100 queries; single run, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: RISE vs. TrackStar, RapidIn, ZO-Inf (same pretrained Pythia checkpoint) and model-agnostic BM25 and E5-base-v2 embedding similarity, on the same candidate pool and queries
official.falsification_criterion: With pretrained Pythia-1B (or Pythia-410M) on the Howdy! 5K pool, RISE's Top-10 auPRC falls below about 0.90, or TrackStar comes within 0.05 auPRC of RISE at Top-10.

title: ICAT: Incident-Case–Grounded Adaptive Testing for Physical-Risk Prediction in Embodied World Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (bootstrap CIs in Tables 5-7, pages 15-16)

official.background: Reference-image-conditioned video generators are increasingly used as 'world models' (neural simulators) for embodied planning and for generating training rollouts for robot policies. If such a model shows a risky action (for example dropping frozen food into hot oil, or putting sodium metal in water) but renders a benign outcome, a planner or policy trained on its rollouts could learn that the action is safe. Existing video benchmarks measure visual quality, temporal consistency or basic physics, and rarely test whether the model reproduces the full causal chain from hazardous context to risky action to severe consequence.
official.method:
ICAT builds test units from a risk-memory bank of 350 memories drawn from 88 sources (61 safety standards/guidance sources and 27 incident-report sources). For each scenario/embodiment specification, it retrieves the top-5 memories with text-embedding-3-small, has GPT-5.1 produce a structured schema (objects, spatial topology, agent spec, instruction sequence, risk explanation with severity), synthesizes a first frame with Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image), and keeps the frame only if human checkers pass it for physical attributes and spatial layout. Each unit is d = (v, i, e): verified reference image v, instruction prompt i (which states the critical conditions but not the outcome), and a reference risk explanation e that is withheld from the generator. The frozen benchmark has 909 units across Home (273), Lab (272) and Factory (364) and four robot embodiments.

Six image-to-video systems receive the same (v, i) pairs: SkyReels-V2 14B, HunyuanVideo and WoW-1-Wan-14B-2M run locally; Veo 3.1, Sora 2 and Wan2.5 are hosted APIs (Veo applies prompt rewriting; Sora 2 refused 42% of requests and 214/909 units were neutrally reworded and retried). Eight videos per unit and system are scored by three annotators, blind to system, for initial-scene preservation eta_init in {0,1}, trigger execution eta_trg in {0,1}, and outcome type/severity agreement eta_out in {0, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0}, with eta_out forced to 0 if either prerequisite fails. RCCC = (eta_init + eta_trg + eta_out)/3. The best-of-eight video per unit (max RCCC) is used for Best RCCC, strict full-chain success FST (eta_init = eta_trg = 1 and eta_out >= 0.8), and the conditional rate P(eta_out >= 0.8 | S), where S is the set of units whose selected video preserves the scene and executes the trigger.
official.claim: On the 909-unit ICAT benchmark with best-of-eight selection, the best system (Veo 3.1) reaches only 13.3% strict full-chain success (23.5% conditional on scene and trigger success, 121/515 units) and best-of-8 RCCC 0.50, ahead of Sora 2 at 0.43 (paired bootstrap gap 0.07, 95% CI [0.03, 0.11]); the three local open-weight systems have 0% full-chain success and eta_out = 0 on every qualifying unit.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Risk prediction on the frozen 909-unit benchmark (N = 8). Best, Mean, and Worst denote RCCC over eight returned videos; FST is strict full-chain success. The conditional success rate uses the best-of-eight sample and the system-specific scene-and-trigger success set S (Eq. 4). Outcome scores are zeroed if either prerequisite fails. Refusals and Sora 2 prompt rewording are disclosed in Sec. 3.1; per-environment components and conditional confidence intervals appear in Appendix A.6 and Appendix A.5.
official.metric: RCCC in [0,1] (higher is better); FST and conditional strict success as percentages/rates (higher is better). Table 2 itself has no error bars; Appendix A.4/A.5 give 95% nonparametric bootstrap CIs over evaluation units (10,000 resamples), or Wilson intervals for all-zero cells; A.4 also gives conservative Hoeffding 95% widths of +/-0.045 for 909-unit RCCC means. These intervals do not cover generation, annotator or source-selection uncertainty.
official.comparison: Six reference-image-conditioned video generators on identical (image, instruction) inputs: Veo 3.1 vs. Sora 2, Wan2.5, SkyReels-V2 14B, HunyuanVideo, WoW-1-Wan-14B-2M.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same units and rubric, any system achieves strict full-chain success well above ~13% (e.g. above 25%) under best-of-eight selection, or the open-weight systems produce matched-severity outcomes (eta_out >= 0.8) on a non-trivial share of units where scene and trigger succeed (above the Wilson upper bounds of about 1.2-1.6%), or Veo 3.1's best-of-8 RCCC advantage over Sora 2 disappears (paired gap CI includes 0).

title: Alignment Imprint: Zero-Shot AI-Generated Text Detection via Provable Preference Discrepancy
claim_source: Table 14 (Appendix G), page 23; Table 1 (page 7) reports the same LAPD numbers against Falcon-based baselines

official.background: Zero-shot detectors of AI-generated text such as Fast-DetectGPT and Binoculars score a text by its likelihood under a proxy language model. Likelihood depends heavily on how complex the content is, so simple human text can look more 'machine-like' than complex AI text. Chat models are almost always aligned (SFT plus RLHF/DPO), and alignment shifts probability mass toward preferred responses. The paper asks whether the likelihood shift between a base model and its aligned version is a more reliable detection signal than likelihood alone.
official.method:
Given a base model P_theta (Llama-2-7b-hf) and its aligned version P_phi (Llama-2-7b-chat-hf), the per-token alignment imprint is Delta(x_t) = log P_phi(x_t|x_<t) - log P_theta(x_t|x_<t). Summed over tokens, this is RAI (Raw Alignment Imprint). LAPD weights each token's imprint by its self-information under the aligned model, giving S(x) = sum_t [-log P_phi(x_t)] * Delta(x_t), and standardizes it as (S(x) - mu)/sigma. Here mu and sigma are the mean and standard deviation (sigma^2 = sum over t of the per-position variances) of the same per-token quantity with x_t drawn from the base model's conditional distribution at each position (Fast-DetectGPT-style conditional independent sampling, with the base model as the sampling model). A higher score means more likely AI-generated. No training is involved.

Evaluation: AUROC on 2,000 balanced samples drawn at random from each of M4, DetectRL Multi-LLM, DetectRL Multi-Domain, RAID and RealDet. Inputs are truncated to 1,024 tokens, and the sample size for Fast-DetectGPT and LAPD is 10,000. In Table 14 (Appendix G), the baselines Fast-DetectGPT, Lastde++, Binoculars and DNA-DetectLLM are re-run with the same Llama2-7B base/instruct pair, replacing the Falcon-7B/Falcon-7B-Instruct pair used in the main Table 1.
official.claim: With all detectors using the same Llama2-7B base/chat pair, LAPD reaches 92.37 average AUROC across five benchmarks vs. 89.72 for the best baseline (Binoculars). Its largest gains are on DetectRL Multi-LLM (97.17 vs. best baseline 93.11) and DetectRL Multi-Domain (96.11 vs. 88.33).
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Matched comparison of detection performance (AUROC %) across baselines and LAPD. All methods use the Llama2-7B base/instruct pair for detection. The best results are highlighted in bold. Methods with clubs (♣) standardize the scores by perturbing or generating auxiliary sequences.
official.metric: AUROC (%), higher is better; single run per cell, no error bars or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: LAPD (and RAI) vs. Fast-DetectGPT, Lastde++, Binoculars and DNA-DetectLLM, all using the Llama2-7B base/instruct pair, on the same 2,000-sample subsets of five benchmarks
official.falsification_criterion: With the Llama2-7B pair for every method, LAPD's AUROC does not exceed the best baseline by at least about 2 points on DetectRL Multi-LLM or DetectRL Multi-Domain, or LAPD's five-benchmark average is not above Binoculars'.

title: The Multi-Block DC Function Class: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications
claim_source: Figure 3 (right panel), page 10; settings in Appendix A.7.3, page 21

official.background: Difference-of-convex (DC) programming optimizes nonconvex objectives written as g - h with g and h convex, by repeatedly linearizing h and solving a convex subproblem. Finding a usable DC decomposition is hard in general (NP-hard even for quartic polynomials), which limits DC methods in machine learning. The paper defines the multi-block DC (BDC) class: functions that are DC in each parameter block when the other blocks are held fixed. It argues that BDC decompositions are easier to construct (for example, explicitly for deep ReLU networks), can be exponentially smaller than DC ones, and support block-wise DC algorithms with non-asymptotic convergence guarantees.
official.method:
For an L-layer ReLU network, each layer's parameters (W_l, b_l) form one block. Section 3.4 writes every activation as Z_l^+ - Z_l^- with nonnegative parts that are convex in the selected block, using sigma(W) and sigma(-W) splits and coordinate-wise maxima, so that the network output is A(theta) - B(theta) with A and B convex in each block (Theorem 3.6). The cross-entropy loss is then given a BDC decomposition through the conjugate/log-sum-exp construction (Corollary 3.5).

Stochastic proximal BDC (SBDC) samples a minibatch and one block uniformly at random at each iteration, linearizes the concave part h at the current point, adds a proximal term (rho/2)||theta_i - theta_i^k||^2, and approximately solves the convex block subproblem with inner gradient steps. On CIFAR10 the network is a 4-layer MLP (3072-256-128-64-10) trained for 50 epochs with batch size 4096. SBDC uses 150 inner gradient steps with step size 5e-3 and rho = 0.1; SGD uses step size 0.1. FashionMNIST uses a 3-layer MLP (784-512-64-10) for 100 epochs (SBDC: 50 inner steps, step size 1e-2, rho = 1e-3; SGD: step size 0.08). Each method is run with 10 seeds.
official.claim: Training a 4-layer ReLU MLP on CIFAR10 (batch 4096, 50 epochs, 10 seeds), SBDC reaches about 54% test accuracy versus about 50% for SGD, with the gap well outside the 90% confidence bands, and SBDC also ends with lower test cross-entropy (about 1.32 vs. 1.37).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Comparison of SBDC with SGD on FashionMNIST and CIFAR10 using batch size 4096 over 10 Monte-Carlo runs. Solid and dashed curves correspond to SBDC and SGD, respectively. The shaded bands show two-sided 90% confidence intervals for test accuracy.
official.metric: Test accuracy (%) after 50 epochs, higher is better; test cross-entropy, lower is better. Curves are means over 10 Monte-Carlo runs, and the shaded bands are two-sided 90% Student-t confidence intervals (shown for test accuracy only). Values are read off the plot.
official.comparison: SBDC (block-wise stochastic DC algorithm using the paper's ReLU BDC decomposition) vs. minibatch SGD, same network, batch size, epochs and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: Under the stated architecture, batch size and hyperparameters, SBDC's final CIFAR10 test accuracy is not clearly above SGD's (for example, the gap is under about 1 point or inside the seed-to-seed 90% CI), or a modest SGD step-size sweep closes the gap.

title: Democratizing Tool Learning with Environments Fully Simulated by a Free 8B Language Model
claim_source: Table 8, page 22 (same point estimates in Table 1, page 7)

official.background: Training tool-calling LLM agents with multi-turn reinforcement learning needs online environments: users to talk to, tools to call, and a verifier to score the result. Real APIs and users are expensive and unstable. Existing workarounds either do RLVR on annotated single-turn data (ToolRL, Tool-N1) or use proprietary LLMs to synthesize executable environments (EnvScaler, AWM), and those environments stay fixed once built. The paper asks whether a small open-source LLM can simulate the entire environment well enough to train a good agent, with no annotated data, no executable tools and no proprietary model.
official.method:
TRUSTEE uses one backbone LM (Qwen3-8B, served with vLLM on 4 GPUs) to play four roles: (1) generate a task from a sampled subset of ToolBench/RapidAPI tool schemas (names and parameters only, not executable), giving a user persona, a hidden user intent, the first query and the expected tool calls; (2) simulate tool responses; (3) simulate the user; (4) act as the verifier, giving a trajectory-level reward in {-1, 0, 1}. The agent is trained with GRPO (verl; 200 steps, 16 tasks per step, group size 8, lr 1e-6, KL 0.001) on the other 4 GPUs. An agent that calls no tool gets -1.

An adaptive curriculum sets a difficulty D in 1-100 that rises by delta=3 when the batch mean reward is above 0.5 and falls when it is below 0.0. D controls the number of tools (1-10), the expected calls (1-3), the number of turns, how specific the system prompt is, the user persona and query ambiguity, and how strict the verifier criteria are. Each task component is randomized within the current difficulty with probability 0.5 ('soft curriculum'). Baselines ToolRL, Tool-N1 and EnvScaler were retrained by the authors from the same base model; evaluation uses BFCL V4 (Non-Live, Live, Multi-Turn) and tau2-bench.
official.claim: Starting from Qwen3-8B-Base, TRUSTEE (environment fully simulated by Qwen3-8B) reaches BFCL V4 Non-Live 83.92 [81.44, 86.25] and Live 72.54 [70.10, 74.85], above the strongest matched baseline EnvScaler (75.29 [72.46, 78.06]; 62.03 [59.41, 64.58]) and ToolRL (40.83; 56.33), with non-overlapping 95% CIs.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Main results with confidence intervals.
official.metric: BFCL V4 accuracy (%) on the Non-Live and Live subsets, higher is better; brackets are 95% confidence intervals over evaluation samples from a single training run (no seeds).
official.comparison: TRUSTEE vs. ToolRL, Tool-N1 and EnvScaler, each trained by the authors from Qwen3-8B-Base, plus the untrained Qwen3-8B-Base
official.falsification_criterion: A Qwen3-8B-Base agent trained with TRUSTEE (8B simulator, ~200 GRPO steps) does not beat EnvScaler (or another matched baseline) on BFCL Non-Live and Live by more than the CI width, e.g. it scores below ~78 on Non-Live or below ~65 on Live.

title: LoRaQ: Optimized Low Rank Approximation for 4-bit Quantization

official.background: Post-training quantization of diffusion transformers to 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4) cuts memory and compute but badly hurts image quality. The current best method, SVDQuant, adds a parallel low-rank branch per linear layer, initialized from an SVD of the smoothed weight, that absorbs outliers so the 4-bit residual is easier to quantize. That branch is kept in 16-bit precision and the calibration is data-dependent. The question is whether a quantized low-rank branch of higher rank, fitted without data, can compensate for 4-bit quantization error better at the same memory cost.
official.method:
Each linear weight W is split into a quantized residual Q1(W + LR) and a low-rank branch LR. LoRaQ initializes L, R from a rank-rho SVD of W (L = -L0) and then runs Adam (lr 1e-4, 1000 steps per weight, no calibration data) to minimize ||Q(W + LR) - W - LR||_F^2, using the straight-through gradient -2(Q(W+LR)-W-LR) R^T for L and the analogous one for R. This makes the quantization error itself approximately low-rank so that the low-rank branch cancels it. A learned rotation Omega inserted between L and R (500 steps, lr 0.5) reduces the error from quantizing L and R themselves. Activation smoothing (SmoothQuant-style, identical to SVDQuant's) is applied first.

In Table 1, SVDQuant uses an FP16 low-rank branch of rank 32 (512 bits per channel). LoRaQ uses a rank-128 low-rank branch quantized to the same SINT4 format as the residual (also 512 bits per channel). The residual weights and their input activations are SINT4 (blocks of 64, FP16 scale) and the low-rank branch activations stay FP16 for both methods. Models are PixArt-Sigma (0.6B) and SANA-1.6B with 20 sampling steps. 5000 images are generated per dataset (MJHQ-30K, sDCI). Metrics are FID and ImageReward for quality, plus LPIPS and PSNR against the 16-bit model's images.
official.claim: At W4A4 with SINT4 and an equal low-rank memory budget, LoRaQ quantizing SANA-1.6B gives MJHQ FID 16.1 vs. SVDQuant 19.3 (LPIPS 0.182 vs. 0.220, PSNR 19.2 vs. 17.8) and sDCI FID 21.8 vs. 28.1 (LPIPS 0.208 vs. 0.242); on PixArt-Sigma the gain is smaller (MJHQ FID 16.9 vs. 19.2).
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Quantitative quality comparisons across different models. Following SVDQuant, we use SINT4 to ensure a fair comparison with methods that consider the data format as part of the method.
official.metric: FID (lower better) and ImageReward (higher better) on 5000 generated images; LPIPS (lower better) and PSNR (higher better) vs. the 16-bit model's outputs. Single runs, no ± reported.
official.comparison: LoRaQ (rank-128 SINT4 low-rank branch, data-free optimized) vs. SVDQuant (rank-32 FP16 low-rank branch) vs. RTN (SANA) / ViDiT-Q (PixArt-Sigma), all W4A4 SINT4, with the 16-bit model as reference
official.falsification_criterion: On SANA-1.6B W4A4 SINT4 with matched low-rank budget, LoRaQ's MJHQ FID is not clearly below SVDQuant's (gap under ~1 FID point, or within the spread across sampling seeds), or its LPIPS vs. the BF16 model is not lower than SVDQuant's.

title: FASTER: Value-Guided Sampling for Fast RL

official.background: Several strong RL methods with diffusion or flow policies (IDQL, EXPO) use best-of-N test-time scaling: they denoise N candidate actions and execute the one with the highest Q-value. This multiplies the actor's denoising cost by N at both training and inference, which is a problem for large policies such as 3B-parameter vision-language-action models. The paper asks whether the benefit of best-of-N can be kept while denoising only one candidate, by predicting from the initial noise which candidate will turn out best.
official.method:
FASTER frames selecting among N denoising candidates as an MDP that filters candidates during denoising. In the practical version used in all main experiments, filtering happens only at the initial noise: a noise-level critic Q^dn(s, ε) scores each of N noise samples ε_i ~ N(0, I) for state s, the top-scoring ε_i* is denoised once into a_i* = π_θ(s, ε_i*), and Q^dn is trained by regressing Q^dn(s, ε_i*) onto the stop-gradient action-level critic Q^a(s, a_i*). Inference cost becomes N critic evaluations plus T actor steps instead of N·T actor steps plus N critic evaluations.

FASTER-IDQL plugs this into IDQL (diffusion policy with implicit Q-learning, expectile 0.8, best-of-N action extraction): the selected denoised action is executed directly. Robomimic online setting, no offline pretraining, sparse success reward; N = 8, T = 100 denoising steps, UTD 20, batch 256, lr 3e-4; at evaluation the filter is greedy, at training it samples from a softmax over z-scored Q^dn values (temperature 1.0). The baseline is IDQL with best-of-8 over fully denoised actions under the same settings.
official.claim: In online RL on Robomimic Lift, Can and Square, FASTER-IDQL (N = 8 noise candidates filtered by a noise-level critic, one denoised) reaches the same success rate as best-of-8 IDQL at 100k env steps (about 0.98, 0.92 and 0.78 respectively) while using 8x fewer inference FLOPs (3.55e8 vs. 2.83e9 per step).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Success rate and compute comparisons of FASTER-IDQL and IDQL in the online setting. FASTER can be applied to IDQL to eliminate extra denoising rollouts at inference while obtaining the same performance in success rates. (see Figure 3).
official.metric: Success rate (higher is better) vs. env steps, mean with shaded bands whose definition and number of seeds are not stated; inference FLOPs per step (lower is better), computed. Values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: FASTER-IDQL vs. IDQL (best-of-8 over fully denoised actions), same hyperparameters, online Robomimic
official.falsification_criterion: With several seeds, FASTER-IDQL's success rate at 100k env steps is clearly below IDQL's (outside seed spread) on any of Lift, Can or Square, e.g. a gap of more than ~0.1 on Square; or random selection of one noise (no critic) matches IDQL equally well, which would mean the critic is not what recovers the best-of-N gain.

title: UniCon3R: Unified Contact-aware 4D Human-Scene Reconstruction from Monocular Video

official.background: Feed-forward methods such as Human3R and UniSH reconstruct a dense 3D scene, the camera trajectory and world-frame human meshes from a monocular video in one online pass. They model human-scene interaction only implicitly, so the recovered bodies often float above the floor, penetrate the scene or drift in world coordinates. Optimization-based pipelines such as JOSH use contact to fix this, but they need slow per-sequence optimization. The question is whether contact can be used inside a feed-forward model to improve world-frame human motion.
official.method:
UniCon3R builds on the released Human3R ViT-L/896 checkpoint (a frozen CUT3R scene backbone with a frozen Multi-HMR encoder, plus a visual-prompt-tuned human prompt). It adds a contact prompt that fuses cross-attention to the current frame and to the recurrent scene state, a geometry token pooled from the previous frame's world pointmap around the human anchor, and the previous frame's contact token. The contact prompt runs through the frozen decoders together with the human prompt. The refined contact token predicts per-vertex SMPL contact and also produces a residual update to the human latent before SMPL-X regression (contact-guided latent refinement).

Only the human and contact modules are trained: 100 epochs on a balanced mix of RICH (with dense contact labels) and BEDLAM, AdamW, lr 1e-5 peak, effective batch 64 on 8 A5000 GPUs. There are two controlled baselines. Human3R† is the original Human3R architecture fine-tuned with exactly this protocol. Parallel Readout adds a contact output head with the same contact supervision but does not feed contact back into the human branch. Evaluation is on the RICH moving-camera test subset, split into 100-frame segments; WA-MPJPE aligns each segment over all of its frames, W-MPJPE aligns on the first two frames.
official.claim: On RICH global human motion estimation, UniCon3R reaches WA-MPJPE 81.5 mm and W-MPJPE 129.8 mm. Human3R retrained with the same protocol (Human3R†) gets 97.5 / 153.2 mm and the contact-as-auxiliary-output baseline (Parallel Readout) gets 97.9 / 153.5 mm, so UniCon3R is about 16% lower on both.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Global human motion estimation on RICH [14] and EMDB-2 [17]. Scene denotes 3D scene reconstruction, and Contact denotes dense human-scene contact prediction or use. Human3R*: released checkpoint in our pipeline; Human3R†: same architecture with our training protocol. WA-MPJPE, W-MPJPE, and PA-MPJPE are reported in mm; RTE is reported in %. Bold = best within feed-forward 4D human-scene reconstruction methods; underlined = second-best.
official.metric: WA-MPJPE and W-MPJPE in mm on 100-frame segments (lower is better); RTE % and PA-MPJPE are also reported. Single run, no ± or seeds reported.
official.comparison: UniCon3R vs. Human3R† (same architecture minus contact, same training data and schedule) and vs. Parallel Readout (same contact supervision, no feedback into the human branch); Human3R* (released checkpoint), UniSH and JOSH3R are given for context
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining Human3R† and UniCon3R with matched protocol yields a RICH WA-MPJPE gap much smaller than ~16 mm (e.g., under 5 mm) or one that disappears across training seeds; or Parallel Readout matches UniCon3R, which would mean the gain comes from contact supervision rather than feeding contact back.

title: MoBayes: A Modular Bayesian Framework for Separating Reasoning from Language in Conversational Clinical Decision Support
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (CIs in Appendix Table 20, page 39)

official.background: LLMs are increasingly used as conversational 'doctors' that interview a patient and propose a diagnosis, but they do the probabilistic reasoning implicitly through next-token prediction. That leaves no explicit posterior, no principled choice of the next question, and no controllable way to abstain. Classical Bayesian clinical decision-support systems had these properties but required rigid structured input. The paper asks whether confining the LLM to language (parsing answers and phrasing questions) and handing all inference to an explicit Bayesian engine gives better diagnostic dialogue than letting the LLM drive the consultation.
official.method:
MoBayes keeps a posterior over K diseases using a naive-Bayes knowledge base. On DDxPlus this KB is built from co-occurrence counts on the 1.03M-record training split (49 pathologies, 314 features) and turned into Dirichlet-Categorical likelihoods. Each turn, the engine picks the unasked feature with the highest expected information gain, and an LLM 'sensor' (gpt-5.4-nano in Table 1) turns it into a natural-language question. The LLM then parses the patient's reply into a (value, confidence label) pair. A deterministic pattern matcher handles clear replies first, and the LLM is used only for ambiguous ones. The five labels map to weights 1.0/0.8/0.5/0.25/0.05, and these weights drive a Pearl-style soft-evidence update. After a warm-up of Tmin turns (12 on DDxPlus), the system commits to the argmax disease once its posterior reaches a threshold τ. If no disease has crossed τ by the budget Tmax, it abstains. τ* is chosen to maximise DHS by leave-one-out on each 50-case half. The LLM never sees the posterior.

Baselines are run with the same gpt-5.4-nano backbone, the same patient simulator and the same disease universe: prompt-based (DDx-CoT, Closed-World, CoT, Bayesian-CoT), UoT, MediQ, AgentClinic's doctor, MEDDxAgent, and fine-tuned DiagnosisGPT-34B. Evaluation covers n=100 held-out DDxPlus test patients (two disjoint 50-case halves) with the PatientSim simulator (plain persona), a second DDxPlus subset with MEDDxAgent's history-taking simulator (HT-sim), and AgentClinic-MedQA. The metrics are Top-1 accuracy (abstentions count as errors), selective accuracy (SA), coverage, and the Diagnostic Harmonic Score (DHS, the harmonic mean of SA and coverage at α=0.5).
official.claim: On 100 DDxPlus test patients simulated with PatientSim, MoBayes with a gpt-5.4-nano sensor reaches DHS 90.3 [95% CI 85.6, 94.3] and Top-1 82%, versus 74.0 [66.1, 80.8] DHS and 60% Top-1 for the strongest same-backbone baseline (Bayesian-CoT), while using fewer tokens per case (16.4K vs 46.6K).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Combined n=100 comparison of MoBayes vs prior diagnostic-dialogue systems. Rows ranked within each category by average DHS. MoBayes entries marked * are statistically significant (paired bootstrap, p<0.05) over the strongest non-MoBayes baseline in the same column. Per-cell 95% bootstrap CIs in Appendix Table 20. AgentClinic-MedQA uses a GPT-5.4-nano-elicited KB (Appendix B.4). DHS coloured per column: the greener the better, the redder the worse.
official.metric: Diagnostic Harmonic Score (higher is better; harmonic mean of selective accuracy and coverage) and Top-1 accuracy in %. Brackets are 95% percentile bootstrap CIs over cases (B=2000), not seeds; no multi-seed variance is reported. MoBayes's lead is marked significant by a paired bootstrap test (p<0.05).
official.comparison: MoBayes (gpt-5.4-nano sensor + Bayesian engine with the empirical DDxPlus KB) vs. prior diagnostic-dialogue systems, all run on gpt-5.4-nano with the same simulator and cases. The strongest is Bayesian-CoT on the PatientSim column and MEDDxAgent (paper-best, DHS 71.8 [63.0, 79.5]) on the HT-sim column.
official.falsification_criterion: On the DDxPlus PatientSim setting with matched backbone and cases, the best non-MoBayes baseline (e.g. Bayesian-CoT or MEDDxAgent) reaches a DHS within the bootstrap CI of MoBayes (about 85 or higher), or MoBayes's DHS falls below about 80.
