title: Component-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection

official.background: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection asks a classifier to flag test images that do not belong to any training class. Zero-shot CLIP detectors such as MCM score an image by how well its global embedding matches the ID class text prompts. They work well for large semantic shifts (ImageNet vs. textures or scenes), but they struggle with fine-grained OODs such as an unseen bird species that differs from an ID species only in plumage or leg colour, because global pooling smooths away local differences. Patch-level methods keep local detail but are noisy. This paper argues that object parts (components) are the right level of granularity for detecting such shifts.
official.method:
CoOD is training-free and uses a frozen CLIP ViT-B/16. For each ID class, GPT-4o produces a short list of visual components (e.g. bird head, wing, leg). For a test image and candidate class y, GradCAM gives a foreground mask and per-component masks. Each component image is the input with everything outside that component's mask blurred, and the mean of the masked patch and position tokens is added as an extra token. Component Shift Score: CSS(x) = max_y softmax_y(<z, t_y>) * (1/|P_y|) * sum_p softmax_p(<z_yp, t_yp>), i.e. the MCM class probability times the average component-match probability. Compositional Consistency Score (CCS): select the top-k=4 patches per component, Hungarian-match them to a 1% farthest-point-sampled coreset of training images, fit an affine transform, and score by distance-weighted feature similarity. Final score: CoOD = CSS + alpha * CCS, with alpha = 0.2 for fine-grained OOD. CoOD-F is a cheaper variant that uses the global image feature z for the component term, so it needs no masks or CCS.

Fine-grained CUB benchmark: within each CUB-200 superclass, half the subclasses are ID and the remaining subclasses, plus classes without a superclass, are OOD. Baselines (MLS, KL, EBO, ViM, ODIN, MCM, GapOOD, GL-MCM/R, Dual, COOK, Delta-E, and the OOD-label methods EOE, NEG, CSP) use the same CLIP backbone. The metrics are macro-averaged AUROC and FPR at 95% TPR.
official.claim: On the fine-grained CUB OOD benchmark with zero-shot CLIP ViT-B/16 (no training), CoOD reaches AUROC 95.2 and FPR95 22.7, compared with MCM at 75.4 / 73.0 and the best ID-only baselines at AUROC 77.5 (MLS) and FPR95 70.5 (Dual); even methods that use OOD labels stay at AUROC 77.8 or below and FPR95 73.0 or above.
official.claim_caption: Table 1. OOD detection on ImageNet-1K and CUB with various OOD detectors and models. Boldface indicates the best performance. * indicates methods that require OOD labels (We use the original ID-only version of Dual and ΔE for a fair comparison with CoOD).
official.metric: AUROC (higher is better) and FPR at 95% TPR (lower is better), in %. No error bars; single numbers, with no seeds reported.
official.comparison: CoOD (and its cheaper variant CoOD-F) vs. post-hoc and CLIP-based OOD detectors (MLS, KL, EBO, ViM, ODIN, MCM, Gap, GL/R, Dual, COOK, Delta-E; EOE, NEG, CSP use OOD labels), all on zero-shot CLIP ViT-B/16
official.falsification_criterion: On a CUB split that follows the paper's protocol, zero-shot CoOD's AUROC is less than about 10 points above MCM, or its FPR95 is not at least 25 points below MCM's. Alternatively, CoOD-F does not beat MCM by a clear margin in AUROC (paper: 92.1 vs. 75.4).

title: Transferable SCF-Acceleration through Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning

official.background: Kohn-Sham DFT calculations are solved with an iterative self-consistent field (SCF) loop whose cost scales with the number of iterations, and that number depends on the initial guess for the density. ML models that predict an initial guess from the molecular geometry can cut iterations, but Liu et al. (2025) showed that matrix-prediction models (predicting the Fock/Hamiltonian or density matrix) trained to match ground-state targets actually slow convergence on molecules larger than those seen in training. The alternative coefficient-based models extrapolate on GGA functionals but need approximations for meta-GGA and hybrid functionals. Fixing size extrapolation matters because DFT is used heavily on large drug-like molecules.
official.method:
All models share an EquiformerV2 GNN backbone with NeuralSCF-style embeddings and are trained on QM9 molecules with at most 20 atoms. Readouts predict either auxiliary-basis density coefficients c, a density matrix P, or a Fock matrix F (block-wise QHNet-style heads); matrix models use Delta-learning on top of the PySCF MINAO guess. The baseline is trained only on a surrogate ground-state loss (mixed Frobenius-L1 on the matrix error, or L2 density error for coefficients).

SAIL fine-tunes the pretrained baseline by running T SCF iterations (with DIIS) in a fully differentiable solver starting from the model's initial density and backpropagating the loss (1/T) sum_t RMS(G^(t)), the root-mean-square energy gradient at each iterate, into the network. Evaluation counts Fock builds in PySCF (def2-SVP, convergence 1e-9 Ha, max 50 cycles) relative to starting from MINAO; ERIC = total Fock builds with ML init (including any hidden Fock build needed to form the guess) / Fock builds from MINAO. The far-out-of-distribution test set is QM40 (up to 100 random molecules per heavy-atom count, H/C/N/O/F only, up to ~4x the training size).
official.claim: On QM40 with the SCAN functional (def2-SVP), SAIL fine-tuning reduces the Delta-density-matrix model's ERIC from 1.04 (ground-state-trained baseline, a slowdown vs. MINAO) to 0.67, which also beats the coefficient-based approach of Liu et al. (ERIC 0.96 baseline, 0.73 after SAIL).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: SCF acceleration of baseline and SAIL (fine-tuned) models across input representations and functionals, evaluated on QM40 (out-of-distribution). Grey rows show ablation variants. Bold: best RIC/ERIC per functional across all input representations.
official.metric: ERIC (Effective Relative Iteration Count, Fock builds relative to MINAO init; lower is better, <1 means speedup), averaged over QM40 test molecules. No error bars: single training run per configuration, no seeds or per-molecule spread reported in the table.
official.comparison: Same Delta-density-matrix model before (surrogate-loss baseline) vs. after SAIL fine-tuning; also vs. the coefficient-based model (Liu et al. 2025 extension) trained and evaluated under the same conditions.
official.falsification_criterion: After SAIL fine-tuning, the Delta-density-matrix model's mean ERIC on QM40/SCAN is not clearly below 1 (e.g. >= 0.85), or it is not lower than the ground-state-trained coefficient baseline (0.96).

title: Directional Confusions Reveal Divergent Inductive Biases Through Rate-Distortion Geometry in Human and Machine Vision
claim_source: Table 1, page 16 (same numbers in Section 4.1 and Figure 2, page 5)

official.background: Humans and deep vision models can reach similar accuracy on perturbed images while making different kinds of errors. Standard metrics such as accuracy or top-k error ignore which class is mistaken for which and in what direction. In human cognition, directional (asymmetric) confusions are well documented, e.g. a robin is judged more similar to a bird than the reverse. This paper asks whether the organization of directional confusions differs between humans and ANNs under distribution shift, and relates it to a rate-distortion description of each system's generalization.
official.method:
Data are the matched human psychophysics trials (~83k) and ANN responses from the GEN benchmark (Geirhos et al. 2018, distributed in bethgelab/model-vs-human): a 16-way ImageNet-derived forced-choice task under 12 perturbation families at graded strengths. The ANNs are three pretrained baseline CNNs (GoogLeNet, ResNet-152, VGG-19) plus ResNet-50 robustness regimes (distortion-trained, specialised single-distortion, all-noise). For each block (experiment x condition x model; humans pooled into one system per experiment x condition), the authors build a 16x16 confusion count matrix and row-normalize it to C (C_ij = P(response j | stimulus i)).

Asymmetry metrics per block: breadth f_pairs = n_pairs / 120, where n_pairs counts class pairs i<j with |C_ij - C_ji| > ε, with ε = 1e-12; strength Δ̄ = mean of |C_ij - C_ji| over those asymmetric pairs; global magnitude = ||C0 - C0^T||_F / ||C0||_F, with C0 = C with the diagonal set to zero. Collapsed channels (mean row entropy < 1e-3 or mean row-max probability > 0.999) are excluded. Block-wise values are averaged within groups (all ANNs pooled, n = 1569 blocks; humans, n = 81 blocks) and compared with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.
official.claim: On the GEN benchmark, humans show directional asymmetry in more class pairs than ANNs (fraction of asymmetric pairs 0.712 ± 0.023 vs. 0.535 ± 0.0056) but with much smaller per-pair magnitude (conditional strength 0.0422 ± 0.0022 vs. 0.1409 ± 0.0049), while ANNs have larger global Frobenius asymmetry (1.220 vs. 1.044).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Block-wise asymmetry summary. One value per unique experiment×condition×model block. Values are mean±SE across blocks.
official.metric: Per-block fraction of asymmetric class pairs (breadth), mean |C_ij - C_ji| over asymmetric pairs (strength) and off-diagonal Frobenius asymmetry index; ± is the standard error across blocks; Wilcoxon rank-sum p = 2.24e-11 (breadth) and 6.55e-5 (strength)

title: SOC-ICNN: From Polyhedral to Conic Geometry for Learning Convex Surrogate Functions
claim_source: Table 13 (and Table 14 for parameter counts), page 20; summarized in Table 1, page 9

official.background: Input Convex Neural Networks (ICNNs) are networks whose output is guaranteed to be convex in the input, so a learned surrogate can be minimized globally and exactly in downstream optimization. The standard ReLU-ICNN can only represent continuous piecewise-linear (max-affine) convex functions, so it has to approximate curved targets such as quadratics or Euclidean norms with many linear pieces. The authors argue that this is a structural bottleneck in parameter efficiency.
official.method:
SOC-ICNN adds two parallel branches to a standard ReLU-ICNN backbone (z_l = ReLU(W_l x + U_l z_{l-1} + b_l), U_l >= 0, output c^T z_L + v^T x + b_0 with c >= 0): H quadratic branches (alpha_h/2)||B_h x + e_h||_2^2 with alpha_h >= 0, and G conic branches lambda_g ||A_g x + d_g||_2 with lambda_g >= 0, where B_h and A_g are unconstrained. The three outputs are summed (Eq. 7). The forward pass equals the optimal value of a second-order cone program. Quad-ICNN and Norm-ICNN are ablations that keep only the quadratic or only the conic branch.

In Experiment 2, each model is fit by regression to one of ten synthetic convex targets (Huber, L1 norm, Euclidean norm, log-sum-exp plus quadratic, isotropic and anisotropic quadratic, anisotropic norm, a mixed quadratic/norm/max-affine function, softplus sum, and an ICKAN-paper target; definitions in Appendix B.2) at input dimensions d in {5, 10, 20, 50}. Parameter budgets are matched approximately: at d = 50, ReLU-ICNN and Softplus-ICNN have 9,683 parameters, Quad-ICNN 9,528, Norm-ICNN 9,578 and SOC-ICNN 9,423. The metric is relative L2 test error, mean ± std over 3 seeds.
official.claim: At d = 50, with about 9.4k-9.7k parameters per model, SOC-ICNN gets the lowest relative L2 test error on all 10 convex targets (mean 0.099 vs. 0.127 for Quad-ICNN, 0.763 for Softplus-ICNN and 0.772 for ReLU-ICNN). For example, on Huber it gets 0.038 ± 0.001 vs. 0.068 ± 0.002 for Quad-ICNN, and on QuadraticIso 0.077 ± 0.004 vs. 0.102 ± 0.004.
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Approximation results for all functions at d = 50 (RelErr, mean ± std). Table 14: Parameter counts for ICNN variants at d = 50.
official.metric: Relative L2 test error (lower is better); ± is std over 3 seeds
official.comparison: SOC-ICNN vs. ReLU-ICNN, Softplus-ICNN, and the single-branch ablations Quad-ICNN and Norm-ICNN, all at a roughly matched parameter count (SOC-ICNN has the fewest)
official.falsification_criterion: At d = 50 and a matched parameter budget (about 9.5k), SOC-ICNN's relative error is not below that of the best other model (usually Quad-ICNN) by more than the seed std on several of the ten targets, or a ReLU-ICNN or Softplus-ICNN tuned under the same budget reaches errors comparable to SOC-ICNN.

title: Dream-Cubed: Controllable Generative Modeling in Minecraft by Training on Billions of Cubes
claim_source: Figure 3, page 7 (Section 4, 'Data composition'); dataset distribution in Table 7, page 21

official.background: Minecraft worlds are 3D voxel grids in which each block is a categorical, semantically meaningful token, but there has been no large block-level dataset for training generative models of such worlds. The paper releases Dream-Cubed, about 2M 32x32x32 chunks of biome-labelled procedural terrain plus human-built maps, and studies biome-conditioned 3D diffusion models trained on it. One practical question for building such a dataset is whether to sample terrain at its natural frequency or to collect rare, structurally complex content on purpose, such as villages and caves.
official.method:
Each sample is a 32x32x32 tensor of block IDs (V = 117 for the natural-biome data), conditioned on one of 15 chunk-level biome labels (13 natural biomes plus targeted 'cave' and 'village' classes). The model is MD4 discrete masked diffusion with a ~280M-parameter 3D DiT (25 blocks, hidden size 768, 8 heads, AdaLN conditioning) at patch size 4 (512 tokens). It is trained with AdamW (lr 3e-4, weight decay 0.01), effective batch 512, 160 epochs, and classifier-free guidance (condition dropout 0.2, guidance scale 4.0) with random 90-degree rotations as augmentation.

The same architecture is trained on three dataset variants. Balanced: ~67k chunks for each of the 15 biomes. Natural occurrence: biomes in proportion to their frequency in randomly generated worlds (Table 7), so village and cave are each 0.71% (7,100 chunks) and ocean is 35%. Village-boosted: village samples doubled, with the other biomes balanced but reduced proportionally. For evaluation, 100 chunks are generated per biome and rendered to images, and FID is computed against a fixed set of validation chunks. The reported 'adjusted' FID subtracts a reference FID computed from 100 held-out real chunks of that biome.
official.claim: With the same MD4 (patch 4) model, village-biome adjusted FID is ~38 when trained on the natural-occurrence dataset, ~24 on the balanced dataset and ~7.5 on the village-boosted dataset, while average adjusted FID over the 15 biomes stays similar (12.87 / 14.28 / 15.08).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Adjusted per-biome FID comparison between MD4 (patch 4) models across three dataset composition variants. Lower is better.
official.metric: Adjusted per-biome FID on rendered chunks (generated FID minus a real-vs-real reference FID), lower is better; 100 generated samples per biome; single training run per variant; no error bars reported
official.comparison: MD4 patch-4 models with the same architecture and hyperparameters trained on the Balanced, Natural-occurrence and Village-boosted dataset compositions, evaluated per biome
official.falsification_criterion: Re-evaluating (or retraining) the three models gives village-biome adjusted FID that does not follow Village-boosted < Balanced < Natural occurrence, or the gap between Natural occurrence and Village-boosted on village shrinks to within the variation seen across repeated 100-sample FID evaluations of the same model.

title: DRAGON : A Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Visual Reasoning over Diagrams

official.background: Vision-language models score well on diagram question answering benchmarks such as ChartQA and AI2D, but answer accuracy does not show whether a model actually used the diagram regions that support the answer. DRAGON turns this into a localization task: given a diagram, a question and the correct answer, the model must output bounding boxes for every visual element needed to justify the answer (answer-bearing regions, labels, legends, axes, connectors). The benchmark draws on six source datasets (ChartQA, Circuit-VQA, InfographicsVQA, MapIQ, MapWise, AI2D) and releases a 2,445-instance test split with human-verified evidence boxes.
official.method:
Each model receives (image, question, answer) and returns boxes as ID/x,y,w,h in pixels, parsed with regular expressions (malformed outputs are discarded). There are three prompting protocols: EDGE (predict all evidence boxes directly), SAGE (first list evidence elements as text, then ground each one), and VERGE (EDGE followed by a self-verification pass that fixes and adds boxes). Decoding uses temperature 0.2, top-p 0.7, and up to 2048 tokens for EDGE and 1024 per stage for the multi-stage protocols. Prompt templates are in Appendix C.

Boxes are normalized by image width and height. MPIoU is the maximum IoU over all predicted/gold box pairs, averaged over samples. Grounding IoU (GIoU) is the IoU between the union of predicted boxes and the union of gold boxes (Shapely polygons), averaged over samples. For F1, a predicted box is a true positive if its IoU with some gold box is at least tau. Precision and recall are computed per sample and averaged, then F1 = 2PR/(P+R), with 0 for samples that have no predicted or gold boxes. Table 3 averages each metric over the three prompts.
official.claim: On the MapIQ portion of the DRAGON test split, averaged over EDGE, SAGE and VERGE prompting, Claude Opus 4.6 reaches Grounding IoU 28.4 and F1 21.8, versus 17.4 and 12.5 for Kimi K2.5, the strongest open-weight model, and at most 6.2 GIoU and 2.0 F1 for the other open-weight models (Llama 4 Maverick, Qwen3.5, Gemma3, InternVL3.5).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Model-level grounding performance across diagram domains averaged over EDGE, SAGE, and VERGE prompting. We report Max-Pair IoU (MPIoU), Grounding IoU (GIoU), and F1. Across models, MPIoU consistently exceeds GIoU and F1, indicating that models often localize approximate evidence regions but fail to capture the complete reasoning evidence required for diagram question answering.
official.metric: Grounding IoU (union-vs-union IoU, %) and box-level F1 (%), higher is better; single run per model and prompt, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Claude Opus 4.6 vs. Kimi K2.5 (and the other open-weight models) on MapIQ, same test instances, prompts and decoding settings
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the three prompts on the MapIQ test instances with both models, Claude Opus 4.6's prompt-averaged GIoU is not clearly above Kimi K2.5's (e.g. a gap under ~5 points), or its F1 lead disappears.

title: Recursive Multi-Agent Systems

official.background: Multi-agent LLM systems usually pass text between agents, so every intermediate agent has to decode full outputs. That is slow, and the system is hard to train end to end because sampling discrete tokens blocks gradients. Recursive (looped) language models get deeper reasoning by applying the same computation repeatedly to latent states. This paper asks whether a whole multi-agent system can be run as such a recursive loop, with agents exchanging hidden states instead of text, and whether that is both more accurate and cheaper than an equivalent text-based recursive multi-agent system.
official.method:
RecursiveMAS chains frozen, off-the-shelf LLM agents into a loop. Each agent generates m latent 'thoughts' auto-regressively: its last-layer hidden state goes through an inner RecursiveLink R_in(h) = h + W2 GELU(W1 h) and is fed back as the next input embedding, without decoding. The agent's latent thoughts then go through an outer RecursiveLink R_out(h) = W3 h + W2 GELU(W1 h) into the next agent's embedding space and are appended to that agent's prompt embeddings. The last agent's latents are fed back to the first agent to start the next recursion round. Only the last agent decodes text, and only in the final round n. Training updates only the links. In the inner loop, each R_in is trained with a cosine loss to match the input embeddings of that agent's target text. In the outer loop, all R_out are trained jointly with cross-entropy on the final answer, backpropagating through all n unrolled rounds.

For the claim, the Sequential-Style (Light) system uses Planner = Qwen3-1.7B, Critic = Llama3.2-1B-Instruct and Solver = Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. Training data is s1K (math), m1K, OpenCodeReasoning and ARPO-SFT, with Planner and Critic targets rewritten by Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. Optimizer is AdamW (lr 5e-4, cosine schedule, batch size 4). Sampling uses top-p 0.95 and temperature 0.6 (0.2 for code), with a 2000-token generation limit on MATH500. The baseline Recursive-TextMAS uses the same agents, roles and recursion structure, but the agents communicate through explicit text. Accuracy, runtime and tokens are reported for r = 1, 2, 3, and r = 3 is used here.
official.claim: In the Light sequential setting (Qwen3-1.7B / Llama3.2-1B / Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) at recursion round r=3, RecursiveMAS reaches 77.8% on MATH500 vs. 69.1% for Recursive-TextMAS with the same agents and structure (and 37.4% vs. 29.3% on MBPP+), while using 519 vs. 3059 tokens on MATH500.
official.claim_caption: Table 2 | Main results of RecursiveMAS over Different Recursion Rounds. We report the accuracy (%, "Acc."), end-to-end runtime (s, "Time"), and overall token usage ("Token") across domains. For Code Gen., we evaluate the Light and Scaled settings on MBPP+ and LiveCodeBench, respectively. The average standard deviation of RecursiveMAS across 5 runs is ±0.0041 for accuracy, ±26 for runtime, and ±33 for tokens. We compare with all methods under the same MAS framework structure and recursion budgets. The performance and efficiency advantages of RecursiveMAS become increasingly significant as the recursion round r increases, with improvements highlighted.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on MATH500 and pass rate (%) on MBPP+, higher is better. The mean is over 5 runs. The paper reports only a single average std across all RecursiveMAS cells ('±0.0041 for accuracy', presumably a fraction, i.e. ~0.4 points). No per-cell std and no std for the baseline. Token usage (lower is better) has an average std of ±33.
official.comparison: RecursiveMAS (latent-space links, trained) vs. Recursive-TextMAS (same three agents, same Planner→Critic→Solver loop, same recursion rounds, communicating through text), Light setting, r=3
official.falsification_criterion: With the Light agents at r=3, RecursiveMAS's MATH500 accuracy is not at least ~4 points above a faithfully run Recursive-TextMAS (e.g. both land within a couple of points of each other), or RecursiveMAS does not use clearly fewer tokens.

title: DORA: A Scalable Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning System for Language Model Training
claim_source: Figures 8 and 9, page 8 (numbers stated in Section 4.2 text)

official.background: In RL post-training of LLMs (e.g. GRPO/DAPO on math), rollout takes most of each step, and response lengths are heavily long-tailed: a few 30K-token responses keep the whole batch waiting while most GPUs sit idle. Existing asynchronous fixes either drop long trajectories (replication/oversampling, which biases the data toward short answers) or cut them at each weight update and resume them under the new policy (partial rollout, which forces a KV-cache re-prefill and stitches several policy versions into one trajectory). Rollout efficiency directly sets the cost of large-scale RL training.
official.method:
DORA keeps several policy versions loaded on different data-parallel (DP) groups of the rollout cluster at once. Each prompt is tagged with the version current at dispatch and generated entirely under it. More prompts than needed are dispatched (RBS > TBS); training starts as soon as TBS trajectories are done, while unfinished long trajectories keep running under their old version and feed later steps. A sliding window bounds staleness to K versions. A central orchestrator re-partitions DP groups across versions in proportion to their pending requests (via P2P weight transfer) and migrates in-flight requests between same-version instances by copying their KV cache, so no re-prefill is needed.

Open-source setup (Appendix B): Qwen2.5-32B, DAPO-Math-17k, DAPO/GRPO with 512 prompts x 16 responses (8,192 trajectories) per step, max input 2K and output 30K tokens, starting from an intermediate checkpoint with mean response length 2.4K. vLLM 0.8.5 for rollout, Megatron-LM for training, on 64 or 128 H800 GPUs. Baselines, all in the same in-house framework on the same hardware: synchronous colocated training, one-step off-policy, and colocated partial rollout. Metrics are average wall-clock step time and end-to-end throughput (prompt+response tokens actually consumed by training per second), averaged over five post-warm-up iterations.
official.claim: On Qwen2.5-32B DAPO-Math RL with 64 H800 GPUs, DORA reaches 23,327 tokens/s end-to-end throughput, 1.65x synchronous training and 1.17x partial rollout, and shrinks the non-overlapped rollout-only time from 14.9 min (65% of the step) to 1.8 min (12%), cutting step time 1.56x; on 128 GPUs throughput is 34,135 tokens/s (2.12x sync, 1.11x partial rollout).
official.claim_caption: Figure 8: Average RL step time across different training paradigms on Dense-32B. Figure 9: End-to-End Throughput across different training paradigms on Dense-32B. Figure 10: Training reward scores comparison for various training paradigms.
official.metric: End-to-end throughput in tokens/s (higher is better) and average RL step time in minutes (lower is better), each the mean of five steady-state iterations; no error bars or seed variation reported
official.comparison: DORA (multi-version streaming, K-bounded staleness) vs. synchronous, one-step off-policy, and partial-rollout training, all in the same framework on the same 64- or 128-GPU H800 cluster
official.falsification_criterion: In a matched implementation on the same workload (32B model, 30K max output, long-tailed lengths), multi-version streaming gives less than ~1.3x throughput over synchronous training at 64 GPUs, or no throughput gain over partial rollout, or the rollout-only phase is not cut by a large factor (e.g. under 3x).

title: Topology-Aware Representation Alignment for Semi-Supervised Vision-Language Learning
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (five-dataset averages from Appendix F.12, page 35)

official.background: CLIP-style vision-language models transfer poorly to specialised domains such as remote sensing or fashion, and paired image-caption data in those domains is expensive while unlabeled images are plentiful. Semi-supervised CLIP adaptation methods (S-CLIP, SemiCLIP) fine-tune CLIP on a small labeled set of pairs plus pseudo-labeled unlabeled images, but their losses only constrain individual image-text pairs or pairs of pairs. This paper asks whether also aligning the global structure of the image and text embedding clouds, selected with persistent homology, improves adaptation.
official.method:
ToMA is added on top of SemiCLIP's two-stage training (stage 1: CLIP loss plus a concept classifier on labeled pairs, 25 epochs; stage 2: pseudo-labeling of unlabeled images with concept-level and trapezoidal consistency losses, 15 epochs). In every mini-batch, separately for the image embeddings and the text embeddings, the authors compute a 1-skeleton Vietoris-Rips filtration (vertices and edges only, no triangles). The H0-death edges are the minimum spanning tree edges and the H1-birth edges are all non-MST edges that close a cycle. These edge sets are treated as non-differentiable index selections.

For each selected edge (x0, x1) in one modality, the loss compares the edge direction x0 - x1 with the direction between the corresponding points in the other modality (ground-truth pairs for labeled samples, surrogate pseudo-caption text embeddings for unlabeled ones) via 1 - |cosine|, averaged over edges and applied in both directions (image->text and text->image), separately for H0-death and H1-birth edges. The total loss per stage is L_Semi + (c/2)(L_0-death + L_1-birth) with c = 0.5 for remote sensing. Backbone CLIP ViT-B/16, batch size 128 (half labeled pairs, half unlabeled images), 10% of RS-ALL (RSICD+UCM+Sydney) pairs labeled, the rest used as unlabeled images (L=U setting), temperature fixed to 1, seeds 0, 1, 2. Evaluation is zero-shot top-1 accuracy on RSICD-CLS, UCM-CLS, WHU-RS19, RSSCN7 and AID.
official.claim: In the remote-sensing L=U setting (CLIP ViT-B/16, 10% labeled), adding ToMA to SemiCLIP raises zero-shot accuracy from 81.4 ± 1.1 to 84.8 ± 1.3 on RSICD-CLS and from 95.6 ± 0.3 to 97.9 ± 0.4 on WHU-RS19, and the five-dataset average from 84.30 to 86.06.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Zero-shot classification results on remote sensing datasets. We compare original CLIP, supervised CLIP fine-tuned on labeled data (L), and semi-supervised methods using unlabeled data from the same (L=U) or different (L≠U) distribution. Parentheses denote performance gains over supervised CLIP, and green values indicate gains larger than one. Bold denotes the best semi-supervised result in each setting.
official.metric: Zero-shot top-1 accuracy (%), higher is better; mean ± std over 3 seeds (0, 1, 2)
official.comparison: ToMA (SemiCLIP + topology-aware directional alignment loss) vs. SemiCLIP retrained by the authors with the same seeds, pipeline and hyperparameters
official.falsification_criterion: With the same setup and three seeds, ToMA's mean accuracy on RSICD-CLS and WHU-RS19 is within one seed std of SemiCLIP's, or its five-dataset average zero-shot accuracy is not higher than SemiCLIP's.

title: Tatemae: Detecting Alignment Faking via Tool Selection in LLMs

official.background: Alignment faking is when an LLM complies with a training objective it disagrees with only while it believes it is being trained, so that its values are not modified, and reverts to its own preferences when unobserved. Earlier evidence (Greenblatt et al., 2024) relied on conversational settings and chain-of-thought analysis, which cannot separate strategic deception from simple capability failure when reasoning traces are absent or unfaithful. As LLMs are deployed as tool-using agents, a detection method based on observable actions such as which tool is selected would be more verifiable and closer to real deployments.
official.method:
The authors release 108 single-turn enterprise IT scenarios (Security, Privacy, Integrity domains; Sabotage or Corruption pressure; 17-19 per combination). Each offers a binary choice between a safe tool and an unsafe tool, with tool definitions embedded in the prompt and the choice parsed from XML tags and string-matched against ground truth. Four calls are made per scenario: Call 0 asks a context-free question to get the baseline preference Y; Call 1 is a neutral task (T1 = safe tool chosen); Call 2 adds adversarial business pressure (T2); Call 3 repeats Call 2 verbatim but adds a 'monitoring' system prompt (adapted from Greenblatt et al.) saying outputs are rated by contractors for helpfulness only, non-compliance leads RLHF to modify the AI's values, and <think> contents are never seen (T3, with reasoning R3 taken from <think>).

A scenario counts as alignment faking (AF) iff T1 and T2 and not T3, and R3 acknowledges the baseline preference Y (R3 ≈ Y), judged by GPT-5.4-mini with the Ji et al. (2025) consistency prompt (detected cases were also manually verified). title: Bian Que: An Agentic Framework with Flexible Skill Arrangement for Online System Operations
claim_source: Table 6, page 9 (STATIC ablation), compared against Table 3, page 8 (full framework)

official.background: Operating large online engine systems (search, recommendation, advertising) takes a lot of engineering effort for release monitoring, alert response and root-cause analysis. The paper argues that the bottleneck for LLM agents here is not reasoning but orchestration: picking, for each operational event, which data (metrics, logs, change events) and which operational knowledge (handbook rules, past incidents) to put in the context. Feeding everything dilutes the signal, and hand-maintaining an event-to-(data, knowledge) mapping does not scale with dozens of releases per day.
official.method:
Bian Que has one agent per operational pattern (release interception, proactive inspection, alert root-cause analysis), all sharing one LLM (Qwen3.5-35B-FP8 by default). Each agent run is composed with one or more Skills, chosen by keyword matching against event metadata. A Skill is a YAML document with a LoadDataSchema (JSON list of data-source calls and knowledge-base queries to execute), a Prompt (multi-step analysis template) and Meta (name, version, tags). In the Flexible Skill mechanism, when no Skill matches a business-module combination, the LLM generates one from a source descriptor and a capability descriptor (plus existing related Skills as references); the Skill is validated by executing its LoadDataSchema on the triggering event and regenerated on failure, up to three retries. A knowledge base (KV, KKV and vector indices, built from case memory and seeded with handbook entries) is queried through the Skills.

Offline evaluation uses 104 real production events (44 alerts, 60 inspections), each with a ground-truth diagnosis annotated by senior SREs. pass@k runs each event k times (temperature 0.3, Skill directory reset to a clean seed state before each run) and counts the event as passed if at least one run produces a Skill that yields the ground-truth diagnosis. The STATIC ablation replaces LLM-driven Skill generation and update with manually authored, fixed Skills; everything else is the same.
official.claim: On the 104-event offline benchmark, LLM-generated Flexible Skills reach overall pass@5 of 94.2% (98/104) and pass@1 of 78.8% (82/104), versus 83.7% (87/104) and 65.3% (67/104) with manually authored static Skills; the gap holds for both alerts (95.5% vs. 81.8% pass@5) and inspections (93.3% vs. 85.0%).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Ablation on STATIC Skills, where Skills are manually authored without LLM-driven generation or updates, tested on the 104-event dataset. (Compared with Table 3: Skill initialization results (pass@k) on 104 real operational events. "pass@k" denotes the fraction of events for which at least one of k independently sampled Skill generations yields the ground-truth diagnosis.)
official.metric: pass@k (k = 1..5): fraction of events for which at least one of k sampled runs yields the SRE ground-truth diagnosis; higher is better. Counts and percentages over 104 events; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Full Bian Que with LLM-generated Flexible Skills (Table 3) vs. STATIC variant with hand-authored fixed Skills (Table 6), same 104 events, same pass@k protocol and backbone
official.falsification_criterion: On the same events, Flexible Skills do not beat hand-authored static Skills at pass@5 by a clear margin (e.g. the 10.5-point gap shrinks to a few events), or static Skills match or exceed Flexible Skills on either the alert or inspection subset.

title: Learning Rate Transfer in Normalized Transformers

official.background: Hyperparameter transfer methods such as µP let practitioners tune the learning rate on small models and reuse it on large ones. The Normalized Transformer (nGPT) normalizes all weights and hidden states onto the unit sphere and trains fast without weight decay or warmup, but its hyperparameters were not designed for transfer. The authors observe that the optimal learning rate of nGPT shifts as models are scaled, so a learning rate tuned at small scale does not carry over.
official.method:
νGPT changes the nGPT parameterization relative to a base model (base depth and width 10, i.e. 10 heads of dimension 102): the global learning rate is multiplied by m_data^(-1/3) (iteration count ratio), the embedding learning rate by m_width^(-1/2), the hidden-matrix and unembedding learning rates by m_width^(-3/4) (derived from a 'mid alignment' assumption with alignment exponent 3/4), the scale hyperparameters α_A,scale, α_M,scale, s_qk,scale, s_z,scale are fixed at 0.03 instead of d_model^(-1/2), α_A,init, α_M,init are set to 0.05 · m_depth^(-1) instead of 0.05, and s_z,init is set to m_width^(1/2) instead of 1 (Table 1, Section 3.1).

Training: FineWeb-Edu, OLMo 2 tokenizer (vocab 100,352), sequence length 4096, batch size 64, Adam (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ε = 1e-16, weight decay 0), no warmup, cosine decay to 10% of the peak learning rate, in a TorchTitan fork. In Figure 1, model size is scaled at fixed aspect ratio n_layers = n_heads ∈ {8, 9, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 22} with head dimension 102, each trained for 20 tokens per non-embedding parameter, sweeping the base learning rate η_base for both baseline nGPT and νGPT. Each point is averaged over three initialization seeds; validation loss without EMA.
official.claim: Scaling nGPT from n_layers = n_heads = 8 to 22 at 20 tokens per parameter, the loss-minimizing η_base for baseline nGPT moves from about 2.8e-3 down to about 3.5e-4 (roughly 8x), while for νGPT it stays between about 8.3e-4 and 9.8e-4 (adjacent grid points) at every size, with best losses equal or slightly lower (e.g. 2.421 vs 2.421 at size 22, 2.843 vs 2.852 at size 12).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Different model sizes at fixed aspect ratio n_layers = n_heads (in the legend, with the best loss in parentheses) and "compute-optimal" 20 tokens per parameter. The baseline nGPT does not show learning rate transfer. Our parametrization νGPT does, and performs no worse or slightly better. The points are averaged over three initialization seeds and no validation loss EMA is used.
official.metric: Validation loss (lower is better) vs. peak base learning rate η_base; location of the minimum (red star). Points are means over 3 initialization seeds; the ± values in the legend are the seed std of the best loss. No uncertainty is given for the location of the optimum; optimum values below are read off the plot (linear x-axis) and are approximate.
official.comparison: Baseline nGPT (original parameterization) vs. νGPT, same architecture sizes, data, token budget and learning-rate grid
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the sweeps, the optimal η_base for νGPT shifts by more than about one grid step (e.g. more than ~1.5x) between the smallest and largest sizes, or baseline nGPT's optimum does not move by several-fold in the same direction (decreasing with size).

title: MCPHunt: An Evaluation Framework for Cross-Boundary Data Propagation in Multi-Server MCP Agents
claim_source: Table 21, page 24 (Appendix R); summarized in Section 4.6 and Table 7, page 9

official.background: LLM agents connected to several Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers (filesystem, git, SQLite, browser, shell, memory) can read a credential from one place and write it somewhere else while doing a perfectly ordinary task, for example copying an API key from a .env file into a generated deploy script or report. Existing MCP safety benchmarks study adversarial attacks such as prompt injection or malicious servers. MCPHunt instead measures non-adversarial credential propagation across trust boundaries. It also asks whether simple prompt-level instructions can reduce that propagation without hurting task completion.
official.method:
The benchmark has 147 researcher-designed tasks: 135 tasks across 9 source-to-sink mechanism families (e.g. browser_to_local, config_to_script, file_to_file) plus 12 benign controls. Each task runs against 8 MCP servers in a workspace that is reset before every task. In the 'risky' environments (variants v1/v2/v3, which use different canary values), sensitive values are format-authentic canary strings (e.g. sk_live_*, AKIA*, ghp_*). A trace counts as propagated (unsafe) if at least one of 11 temporally ordered detection signals fires, for example a canary that was read earlier appearing in a later write argument, a shell command, a generated script or a browser form field. Detection is exact string matching on the canary or on a canary core of at least 10 characters. Utility is the fraction of traces where the task completed, the requested artifact was verified and the source data was read. Tasks are labelled in advance as CRS (completion requires the secret, e.g. 'copy everything') or non-CRS (a derived artifact is requested). The policy-violating rate is the propagation rate on non-CRS mechanism-tagged traces in risky environments.

In the mitigation study, GPT-5.4 (temperature 0) runs on risky_v1/v2/v3 under four system-prompt conditions, each collected as a separate run: M0, no mitigation; M1, a brief generic privacy reminder; M2, explicit redaction rules naming API keys, passwords, tokens and credentials; M3, a boundary-aware prompt that explains source-to-sink risk and gives examples of safe derived artifacts. Task prompts and agent configuration are otherwise identical across arms.
official.claim: On GPT-5.4 in the risky environments, the boundary-aware prompt (M3) reduces the trace-level credential propagation rate to 2.3% (384 traces), compared with 16.8% under a generic privacy reminder (M1, 381 traces) and 22.9% with no mitigation (M0, 384 traces). The policy-violating rate falls from 8.1% (M1) to 0.3% (M3), and utility is not lower (80.5% for M3 vs. 79.3% for M1 and 79.4% for M0).
official.claim_caption: Table 21: Mitigation effectiveness (GPT-5.4, risky environments). Δ = change vs. baseline (no mitigation). Policy-viol. = non-CRS mechanism-tagged risky-environment traces with propagation (safety failures). Utility is the outcome success rate. The baseline row is re-collected within the mitigation run, so its policy-violating rate (13.9%) differs slightly from the main-benchmark value (13.5%, Table 6).
official.metric: Propagation rate = fraction of traces with at least one Tier 1 or Tier 2 canary-propagation signal (lower is better); policy-violating rate = the same rate on non-CRS mechanism-tagged traces; utility = fraction of traces where the task completed and the artifact was verified (higher is better). No error bars or CIs are reported for Table 21; each arm is a single pass at temperature 0.
official.comparison: M3 (boundary-aware detailed prompt) vs. M1 (generic privacy reminder) and M0 (no mitigation), same model, tasks, environments and harness
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the released harness with GPT-5.4 on risky_v1/v2/v3 gives an M3 propagation rate that is not clearly below M1's (e.g. the M1-minus-M3 gap shrinks from about 14.5 pp to a few points), or M3 utility falls clearly below M0/M1 utility (e.g. by more than about 5 pp).

title: Decoupled Descent: Exact Test Error Tracking Via Approximate Message Passing

official.background: When the number of samples n and the dimension d grow together, full-batch gradient descent repeatedly reuses the same data matrix, so the training loss becomes a biased, over-optimistic estimate of the test loss (the generalization gap). Practitioners usually hold out a validation set to monitor test error, which costs training data. This paper asks whether the training algorithm itself can be changed so that train loss provably equals test loss in the proportional high-dimensional limit, which would let one early-stop or tune hyperparameters on the training loss alone.
official.method:
Decoupled descent (DD) is gradient descent with two Onsager-style correction terms borrowed from approximate message passing (AMP). With pre-activations h_t = Xθ_t and per-sample gradients ĥ_t = ∇_h Ψ(h_t, y, a_t), pure DD uses h_t = Xθ_t + η Σ_{s<t} ĥ_s (a memory of past gradients added to the pre-activation) and θ_{t+1} = θ_t − η (X^T ĥ_t − α · mean_i ∇²_h Ψ(h_{t,i}, y_i, a_t) θ_t), where α = n/d; the scalar head a is updated by ordinary GD. For Gaussian-mixture data the paper proves that DD's train loss equals its test loss asymptotically at every iterate (Theorem 3.8).

XOR experiment (Section 5.1, iterations written out in Appendix B.2): J = 4 equally likely modes with means μ1 = [v, v], μ2 = [−v, −v] (label 0), μ3 = [−v, v], μ4 = [v, −v] (label 1), v ∈ R^{d/2} with every entry v_i = λ, and x_i ~ N(μ_j/d, I_d/d); n = d = 1000. Model: ŷ = sigmoid(a (x^T θ1)(x^T θ2)) with θ1, θ2 ~ N(0, I_d) and a ~ N(0, 1), cross-entropy loss, learning rate η = 0.05, 200 full-batch iterations, 20 independent replications. Train and test cross-entropy (test on fresh samples from the same mixture) are tracked for GD and pure DD at λ ∈ {1, 4, 8}.
official.claim: On the high-dimensional XOR Gaussian mixture (n = d = 1000, η = 0.05, SNR λ = 4, 20 runs), after 200 iterations pure decoupled descent reaches a median test cross-entropy of about 0.19 that matches its train loss (about 0.17), while full-batch GD drives train loss to about 0.01 but has median test loss about 0.72 (IQR about 0.38 to 1.07); at λ = 1 GD's test loss rises above 1.5 while DD stays at about log 2 ≈ 0.69.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1. Summary statistics for 20 XOR runs (n = d = 1000): GD (left) vs. DD (right) with η = 0.05 and SNR λ = 1 (upper left), λ = 4 (upper right) and λ = 8 (bottom). Blue/red denote train/test error; solid lines are medians, shaded areas are interquartile ranges, and dotted lines show min/max. Low SNR (λ = 1): GD overfits (low train/high test error); DD stabilizes both near log(2), reflecting the non-informative regime. Medium SNR (λ = 4): DD maintains train-test parity, outperforming GD's overfit solution. High SNR (λ = 8): Signal dominates noise; both algorithms achieve similar performance.
official.metric: Cross-entropy on training data and on fresh test data (lower is better); solid lines are medians over 20 replications, shaded bands are interquartile ranges, dotted lines min/max; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Pure decoupled descent vs. full-batch gradient descent with the same model, initialization distribution, learning rate, data and iteration count
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the λ = 4 setting (n = d = 1000, η = 0.05, 200 iterations, 20+ replications), DD's median test cross-entropy at iteration 200 is not clearly below GD's (e.g. the IQRs overlap or the gap is under ~0.2), or DD's train and test medians differ by more than ~0.1 at any iteration.

title: Models Recall What They Violate: Constraint Adherence in Multi-Turn LLM Ideation

official.background: Researchers increasingly refine research proposals with LLMs over several turns, asking them to make ideas more novel or rigorous. Multi-turn benchmarks usually score per-turn quality or task success, not whether the output still respects a fixed set of hard constraints (budgets, sample floors, banned methods) from the original brief. A plan that quietly exceeds its budget still reads as complete, so this kind of drift has no external verifier and can go unnoticed.
official.method:
DriftBench has 38 structured research briefs across 24 domains, each with an objective, 5-8 hard constraints (234 total), success criteria and 3-5 banned moves. Seven subject models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3-235B, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) each run every brief twice per condition at temperature 0.7 (Gemini 1.0). All conditions share one system prompt asking for fidelity, constraint tracking and minimal complexity. In Single-shot (SS) the model writes one proposal. In Multi-turn pressure (MT-P) it gets six turns with escalating user prompts ('Make it more novel', 'Strengthen the design', 'Add one more component'), and turn 6 asks for the same sectioned final proposal as single-shot. Multi-turn neutral (6 turns of 'Continue.') and checkpointed conditions are also run.

An LLM judge at temperature 0 scores the final proposal against the brief on four 0-4 rubrics: objective fidelity, constraint adherence (4 = all hard constraints fully respected; 3 = one stretched; 2 = one violated, ...), alternative coverage, and complexity inflation (higher = more over-engineered). In the crossed-judge design, each of Claude Opus 4.6 (primary) and GPT-5.4 (robustness check) scores all seven models' single-shot and pressure runs. Table 2 reports means +/- SE over about 530 runs per condition.
official.claim: Under a common Claude Opus 4.6 judge, iterative pressure lowers mean constraint adherence from 3.77 +/- 0.02 (single-shot) to 3.45 +/- 0.03 (6-turn pressure) and raises complexity inflation from 0.16 +/- 0.02 to 1.65 +/- 0.03 (n = 527/530 runs pooled over 7 models). Under a GPT-5.4 judge the same shift appears: adherence 3.24 -> 2.90, complexity 1.05 -> 2.63.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Aggregate results on the clean sample (two repetitions per cell, 532 intended runs per condition; n = scored runs). Scores are 0–4, higher is better except for complexity; values are mean ± SE. Single-shot and pressure rows are scored by one common judge per block (Opus 4.6, primary; GPT-5.4, robustness check). Rows marked ∗ were not cross-judged and show published-arm values (Opus 4.6 for non-Anthropic runs, GPT-5.4 for Sonnet 4.6), given per model in Appendix G.
official.metric: Judge-scored 0-4 rubric means; constraint adherence higher is better, complexity inflation lower is better. +/- is the standard error of the mean over runs (no seed variation beyond two repetitions per brief x model cell).
official.comparison: Multi-turn pressure (6 turns, escalating improvement prompts) vs. single-shot on the same 38 briefs and 7 models, same system prompt, same final-proposal format, same judge. MT-Neutral (3.66 adherence, 0.67 complexity, published-arm judge) is the turn-count control.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running single-shot and pressure conditions on the released briefs (all models or a subset) with the same judge prompt shows an adherence drop that is within about 2 SE of zero (e.g. < 0.1 points), or no rise in complexity inflation, under either judge.

title: Intern-Atlas: A Methodological Evolution Graph as Research Infrastructure for AI Scientists

official.background: Scholarly infrastructure such as Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex links papers by untyped citations, so an AI research agent cannot directly tell whether one paper extends, improves, replaces or merely mentions another method. The paper argues that research agents need an explicit, queryable graph of how methods evolve, both to trace lineages and to evaluate or generate research ideas. Recovering a method's lineage from such a graph is itself a search problem, because hub methods such as the Transformer have many descendants and a greedy traversal can follow the wrong branch.
official.method:
Intern-Atlas is built from 1,030,314 AI papers (1965-2025). Method entities are resolved through a curated alias registry (8,155 canonical methods, 9,545 aliases), and an LLM (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, temperature 0) labels each citation edge with one of seven types: extends, improves, replaces, adapts, uses_component, compares, background. The first four types form the strong-causal subgraph used for lineage search. Each causal edge stores verbatim bottleneck, mechanism and trade-off quotes plus an LLM-reported confidence, and a deterministic validator removes edges whose quotes fail a substring match, that violate publication-year ordering, or whose citing paper already has an opposite-direction edge to the same target. The result is 9,410,201 typed edges.

SGT-MCTS reconstructs lineages by running MCTS on the strong-causal subgraph from a seed method, backward and forward. Its selection rule is UCT + lambda * conf(e) * TC(delta_tau), where TC is a piecewise temporal-coherence prior that peaks at publication gaps of 1-3 years (Appendix B: c = sqrt(2), lambda = 0.5, budget B = 200 per direction per seed, depth cap 5, top-K = 5, plus branch re-runs at budget B/2). Chains are ranked by normalized length, mean edge confidence and mean visit count. The baselines are beam search with widths 1, 5 and 10, which uses the same local heuristic signals but no rollouts, and a uniform random walk; all use the same graph, seeds, depth cap and node-evaluation budget. The benchmark contains 133 reference evolution chains taken from 30 high-impact surveys (2,268 nodes, 1,462 edges). The chains were extracted by an LLM and audited by researchers. Each retrieved chain is scored against its reference by Node Recall (NR), Edge Recall (ER) and Chain Alignment Score (CAS).
official.claim: On 133 survey-derived reference evolution chains, starting from the same seed method on the same Intern-Atlas graph, SGT-MCTS reaches Node Recall 84.8, Edge Recall 79.0 and Chain Alignment Score 84.8, compared with 44.9 / 23.2 / 44.9 for the strongest baseline, beam search with width 10.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Lineage-search algorithm performance. '@k' denotes beam width or RW rollouts.
official.metric: Node Recall, Edge Recall and Chain Alignment Score (%), higher is better, averaged over reference chains. No error bars, seeds or variance are reported.
official.comparison: SGT-MCTS vs. Beam@1, Beam@5, Beam@10 and a random walk (RW@5) on the same graph, seeds, depth cap and budget
official.falsification_criterion: On the released graph and benchmark, Beam@10 (or a larger-width beam at the same node budget) comes within about 10 points of SGT-MCTS on Edge Recall, or SGT-MCTS's NR/ER advantage disappears across repeated MCTS runs.

title: Representation Fréchet Loss for Visual Generation

official.background: Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) is the standard metric for image generators, but Fréchet Distance (FD) has rarely been used as a training loss, because a reliable estimate of the feature mean and covariance needs tens of thousands of samples, far more than a training batch. Earlier attempts computed FD within a single batch, and those estimates are too noisy to help. If FD could be optimized directly, it would work as a cheap post-training objective that needs only precomputed statistics of real data, with no real images seen during training.
official.method:
FD-loss post-trains a pretrained generator by minimizing FD in a frozen representation space (here Inception-v3) between the generated features and precomputed real ImageNet training-set statistics. The population used for the statistics is decoupled from the gradient batch. In the queue version, features from recent batches are kept in a queue of size N and FD is computed over the whole queue. In the EMA version, running estimates of the first and second feature moments are updated as mu_g = beta*mu_ema + (1-beta)*mu_batch (and likewise for the second moment), and the covariance is recovered from them. In both versions gradients flow only through the current batch of 1024 images. The loss is normalized as FD / (sg(FD) + c).

In the ablation, pMF-B/16 (a one-step pixel-space MeanFlow generator, ImageNet 256x256, class-conditional) is post-trained for 50 epochs with AdamW, lr 1e-6, global batch 1024, cosine schedule with 5 warm-up epochs, using Inception as the only representation. The batch-only baseline (queue size 0, or beta = 0) is the same setup with statistics computed from the current batch alone. Evaluation uses FID, IS and FDr6 from 50k generated images against training-set statistics.
official.claim: Post-training pMF-B/16 for 50 epochs with Inception FD-loss using EMA statistics (beta = 0.999) lowers 1-NFE ImageNet 256 FID from 3.31 to 0.81, while the same loss with batch-only statistics (batch 1024) raises it to 3.84.

Base: base model before post-training. ‡ Statistics estimated from the current batch only (batch size 1024). † FDr-CLIP is reported separately because CLIP is never used as a training signal in any row shown here; it is included in FDr6. Default setting is marked in Gray.
official.metric: FID-50k against ImageNet training statistics (lower is better); IS and FDr6 also reported. No ± reported (single runs).

official.falsification_criterion: With the released pMF-B/16 checkpoint and the stated recipe, EMA (beta = 0.999) FD-loss does not bring FID clearly below 1.5, or batch-only FD-loss performs comparably to it (e.g. within 0.5 FID) instead of degrading or barely changing the base model.

title: AEM: Adaptive Entropy Modulation for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Table 3 (Appendix D), page 15; the GRPO and GRPO+AEM rows also appear in Table 1, page 8

official.background: LLM agents trained with group-based RL (GRPO and variants) on multi-turn tasks such as household text games or web shopping get only a sparse reward at the end of a long trajectory, so every step in a trajectory receives nearly the same learning signal. Existing fixes add process reward models, tree-structured rollouts, or structural heuristics such as GiGPO, all of which add supervision, compute, or assumptions. Policy entropy is a free intrinsic signal, and entropy collapse early in RL training is known to hurt final performance. The question is whether entropy can be used to assign credit between responses without extra supervision.
official.method:
AEM is a plug-in rescaling of the base advantage. A rollout is split into responses, one per environment step (each completed response is the 'action'). For each response the token-level entropies of the policy are averaged over the response's tokens (H̄, a length-normalized proxy for response surprisal, available from the old-log-prob recomputation pass). Within a group G (all responses in the N = 8 trajectories sampled for one prompt), H̄ is min-max normalized to H̃; if max − min < 0.1 all coefficients are 1. Otherwise α = exp(−λH̃) divided by the group mean of exp(−λH̃) (λ = 1, ε = 1e-8), and the response's advantage becomes α · A_base, applied uniformly to all its tokens. Low-entropy responses are upweighted and high-entropy ones downweighted; the paper's theory says this pushes entropy up on negative-advantage responses (exploration early) and down on positive ones (exploitation later).

Training setup for the claim: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, verl-agent framework, GRPO base estimator, reward 10 for success / 0 for failure / −0.1 per invalid action, group size 8, 16 groups per rollout (128 environments), actor lr 1e-6, rollout temperature 1.0, validation temperature 0.4, KL coefficient 0.01, max prompt 2048 / response 512 tokens, up to 50 environment steps per episode, 150 training steps on 4×A800. EMPG (Wang et al., 2025b), another entropy-modulated policy-gradient method, is run on the same GRPO base with identical shared settings.
official.claim: On ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and GRPO as the base estimator, adding AEM raises the overall success rate to 76.8 ± 1.8%, versus 68.0 ± 0.8% for plain GRPO and 69.8 ± 1.6% for GRPO+EMPG under identical training settings.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Direct comparison of AEM and EMPG.
official.metric: ALFWorld overall success rate (%) on evaluation episodes after 150 training steps, higher is better; ± is std over 3 random seeds (Table 4's caption says sample std over 3 runs). Per-category numbers have no error bars.
official.comparison: GRPO+AEM vs. GRPO and vs. GRPO+EMPG, all with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and the same verl-agent training configuration

title: Learn where to Click from Yourself: On-Policy Self-Distillation for GUI Grounding
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (per-category breakdowns in Tables 6-11, pages 15-17)

official.background: GUI grounding maps a natural-language instruction to the pixel coordinates of the target element on a screenshot, and is a core skill for computer-use agents. The current standard post-training recipe is GRPO-style reinforcement learning with a verifiable click reward, which needs several rollouts per sample and gives no signal on hard samples where every rollout misses. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD), where the same model acts as teacher with privileged information and gives dense token-level targets along a single student rollout, is a cheaper alternative, but it had not been tried for GUI grounding.
official.method:
GUI-SD is OPSD for coordinate prediction. The student sees the normal screenshot and instruction and samples one answer. The teacher is an EMA copy (decay 0.95) of the same model whose input is a privileged version of the screenshot: the ground-truth box is drawn in red, pixels outside it are attenuated by a Gaussian soft mask exp(-d^2/2sigma^2) (d = distance to the box edge, sigma scaled to box size with a floor of 0.1 min(W,H)), and a hint says the answer is inside the red rectangle. The exact coordinates are never given as text. The loss is a per-token reverse KL between student and teacher distributions along the student rollout, weighted by w(t) = w_pos(t) * w_ent(t), where w_pos = alpha * k_t grows with the digit position (units=1 ... thousands=4; 1 for non-digit tokens) and w_ent = exp(-H_teacher(t)/tau) down-weights uncertain teacher tokens.

All trained rows in Table 2 start from Qwen3-VL-Instruct-8B and, per the experimental setup, use about 7K ScaleCUA grounding samples (filtered with UI-Venus1.5-8B, instructions paraphrased by Qwen3-VL-8B); training time is reported per epoch on 8x A800-80G. GUI-SD's own hyperparameters (Table 5) are 1 epoch, learning rate 2.5e-6 decayed to 0, per-device batch 1 with 16 gradient-accumulation steps, max completion length 128; the GRPO baselines' hyperparameters are not given. The baselines are GRPO with a binary in-box reward, a distance-to-centre reward (SE-GUI style) and a Gaussian reward (GUI-G2 style). Evaluation is click accuracy (point inside the target box) on ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, UI-Vision (element grounding), OSWorld-G, OSWorld-G-Refine and MMBench-GUI L2.
official.claim: Starting from Qwen3-VL-Instruct-8B with the same ~7K training samples, GUI-SD reaches 60.7% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 33.3% on UI-Vision versus 57.4% and 28.2% for the best GRPO baseline (GRPO-Gaussian), with a six-benchmark average of 68.4 vs. 65.9, while training at 4.2 h/epoch vs. 16.8 h/epoch on 8x A800.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: GUI grounding accuracy on six benchmarks including ScreenSpot-V2 (SS2), ScreenSpot-Pro (SSP), MMBenchGUI (MMG), UI-Vision (UIV), OSWorld-G (OSW-G), and OSWorld-G_R (OSW-GR). title: Learning Dynamic Evidence Routes for Vision Transformer Probing

official.background: Probes on frozen vision transformers usually pool patch tokens with global average pooling (GAP) or read the [CLS] token. Either way the patches are treated as an unordered set. A sequential decoder such as a state space model (S4) can read the patches as a sequence instead, but then someone has to choose the order. Fixed 2D-to-1D scans (raster, snake, diagonal, VMamba-style four-direction sweeps) are the usual choice. The paper asks whether learning a per-image patch order from task supervision gives a better and inspectable readout of frozen features, in particular for MAE, whose [CLS] and GAP features are weak under linear probing.
official.method:
SSMProbe takes the final-layer patch tokens (196 for ViT-B/16 at 224px) of a frozen backbone, here MAE (facebook/vit-mae-base). A bias-free linear scorer gives each token a scalar score. The scores are standardized within each image and matched to evenly spaced rank targets with a squared-distance cost. Sinkhorn-Knopp (20 iterations, temperature 0.1) turns this into a soft permutation, which reorders the tokens. A diagonal S4 layer (state dim 128, channels share parameters, bilinear discretization, step size initialized at 0.05 and clamped to [1e-3, 1e-1], D initialized to 0) runs over the reordered sequence. A linear classifier reads the final output. The scorer and the S4/classifier are trained jointly with cross-entropy.

The fixed-scan baselines use the same S4 decoder and classifier on deterministic orders: raster (row-major) and three four-direction families (VMamba-style row/column sweeps, snake, diagonal). Each four-direction family runs four paths with shared parameters and classifies their averaged final states. All heads are trained on detached features from one shared frozen-backbone forward pass per batch, each with its own AdamW optimizer (lr 1e-3, cosine schedule, batch size 256, no weight decay) for 5 epochs on ImageNet-1K. Results are top-1 on the validation set over five seeds.
official.claim: On frozen MAE ViT-B features on ImageNet-1K (5-epoch probe), the Sinkhorn-routed S4 probe reaches 70.33 ± 0.05% top-1, 5.55 points above the best fixed scan read by the same S4 decoder (4-dir Diagonal, 64.78 ± 0.07%) and 6.38 points above random-dynamic ordering (63.95 ± 0.06%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Frozen MAE probing on ImageNet-1K (five-seed summaries). Scan/permutation and Bi-GRU controls use final checkpoints and source-grid patch order; their error bars are sample standard deviations.
official.metric: ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is the sample standard deviation over five seeds (final checkpoints).
official.comparison: Sinkhorn (learned route) + S4 vs. the same S4 decoder on raster, 4-dir VMamba-style, 4-dir Snake, 4-dir Diagonal, random-fixed and random-dynamic permutations; GAP, CLS, attention pooling, Transformer, DeepSets and Bi-GRU are also reported.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same protocol (frozen MAE ViT-B, 5 epochs, AdamW lr 1e-3, batch 256), the Sinkhorn probe's five-seed mean is not clearly above the best fixed-scan S4 probe, e.g. the gap falls below about 1 point (versus the reported 5.55), or the Sinkhorn probe does not beat the best fixed scan at all.

title: Asymmetric Invertible Threat: Learning Reversible Privacy Defense for Face Recognition

official.background: Face-cloaking tools such as Fawkes, LowKey and Chameleon add adversarial perturbations or personalized masks to photos so that unauthorized face recognition (FR) models fail to match the person. These defenses assume the cloak stays in place once applied. If an adversary can train a restoration or purification model (for example a diffusion purifier or an image-to-image translator) that undoes the cloak, identity can be recovered and the protection fails. The paper calls this an asymmetric adversarial attack and argues that cloaks should be trained to resist such restoration while still being reversible by the key holder.
official.method:
ARFP is a ResNet-based mask generator G that takes a 112x112 face x, a 256-bit secret key k and a 64-bit nonce m. An MLP encodes (k, m) into channel-wise affine scale/shift parameters applied to intermediate generator features (Key-Conditioned Manifold Binding), and the protected image is z = x + alpha * Delta(x, k, m) with alpha = 0.05. An authorized recovery network R reconstructs x from (z, k, m), and a small decoder D recovers the nonce from z for tamper indication.

The core training component (Adversarial Restoration-Aware Training) alternates two updates: a surrogate restoration adversary A (an invertible NICE-style network) is trained to map z back to x with an L1 + L2 loss, then G, R and D are updated with A fixed to minimize lambda_rec * L1(x, R(z)) + lambda_id * L_id + lambda_MSE * nonce loss - lambda_rev * L_REV(x, A(z)), where L_id is a cosine identity loss in a pretrained FR feature space (lambda_rec = 10, lambda_id = 5, lambda_rev = 1; Adam, lr 2e-4, batch 16; TensorFlow). For evaluation, protected LFW test images (identities with at least 15 images, MTCNN-aligned) are attacked with DiffPure, CycleGAN and BINN (i-RevNet) restorers, and the Protection Success Rate (PSR = 100% minus FR accuracy) of the restored images is measured. Fawkes (High) and Chameleon are run with their official implementations as baselines.
official.claim: On the LFW test set, after restoration attacks, ARFP keeps a mean PSR of 93.4 ± 1.8 (DiffPure), 86.5 ± 2.5 (CycleGAN) and 91.2 ± 2.1 (BINN), versus 70.0 ± 8.0, 32.0 ± 12.0 and 22.0 ± 8.0 for Chameleon, the strongest baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Full-scale restoration attack evaluation on the LFW test set. Mean PSR (%) ± variance.
official.metric: Protection Success Rate (PSR, %, higher is better) of FR on restored protected images; ± is described as 'variance', with no statement of what it is computed over (seeds, identities or FR models)
official.comparison: ARFP vs. Chameleon and Fawkes (High), each followed by the same DiffPure, CycleGAN and BINN restoration attacks
official.falsification_criterion: Under a matched restoration attack (especially a paired BINN/i-RevNet restorer trained on protected/clean pairs), ARFP's PSR falls to within the error of Chameleon's, or ARFP's PSR under BINN drops far below ~91% (e.g. under 50%).

title: SplitZip: Ultra Fast Lossless KV Compression for Disaggregated LLM Serving

official.background: In prefill-decode disaggregated LLM serving, prefill workers produce a KV cache that must be sent over the network to decode workers before generation starts. When the two run on different nodes or clusters, this transfer becomes a bottleneck, especially for long inputs. Lossy KV compression (quantization, pruning) changes model outputs, while existing lossless floating-point codecs either target offline weight compression, run on the CPU, or use variable-length (Huffman-style) codes whose encoding is too slow to keep up with KV production during prefill. A lossless codec is only useful on this path if both compression and decompression are fast.
official.method:
SplitZip splits each BF16 value into its 8-bit exponent and an exact 8-bit sign+mantissa byte (stored uncompressed). A top-16 exponent codebook is calibrated offline (on WikiText-2 train KV activations); each exponent in the codebook is replaced by a fixed 4-bit code, two codes packed per byte. Exponents outside the codebook get a dummy code and are recorded in a sparse escape stream as (16-bit chunk-relative position, 8-bit raw exponent), with chunk size 1024. Size is N + N/2 + 3M bytes for N elements and M escapes, so the compression ratio approaches 4/3 as the escape rate goes to 0. Encoding is a fused 'Quad64' GPU kernel (four BF16 values per 64-bit load) plus an escape-collection pass; decoding is a uniform 4-bit lookup for every element followed by a sparse overwrite at the escape positions.

Codec benchmark: Qwen3-32B BF16 KV tensors from wikitext2-test assembled into a 256M-element BF16 workload, on one NVIDIA H200. Each codec first verifies bitwise round trip, then is timed over 10 runs after warm-up; throughput is uncompressed BF16 bytes per second. Baselines: nvCOMP LZ4, Cascaded and Bitcomp, DFloat11, ZipNN (numbers taken from its paper), Falcon, and ZipServ (CPU 'CPP' path and GPU kernel decode path).
official.claim: On a 256M-element Qwen3-32B BF16 KV workload on an H200, SplitZip losslessly compresses at ratio 1.324 with 613.3 ± 2.6 GB/s encode and 2181.8 ± 38.5 GB/s decode throughput, versus 341.5 ± 7.1 GB/s encode for the fastest baseline encoder (nvCOMP Bitcomp, ratio 1.056) and 1260.9 ± 1.4 GB/s decode for the fastest baseline decoder (ZipServ GPU kernel, ratio 1.236).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison of encoding/decoding throughput and compression ratio of various compression methods. SplitZip delivers high codec throughput while maintaining a respectable compression ratio.
official.metric: Compression ratio (raw BF16 bytes / compressed bytes, higher is better) and encode/decode throughput in GB/s of uncompressed BF16 data (higher is better); ± is the measured fluctuation over 10 timed runs (not further defined); ZipNN has no ± because its numbers are copied from its paper
official.comparison: SplitZip vs. nvCOMP LZ4, nvCOMP Cascaded, nvCOMP Bitcomp, DFloat11, Falcon, ZipServ (CPP and Kernel) on the same KV workload and GPU; ZipNN numbers from its paper

title: Leveraging Data Symmetries to Select an Optimal Subset of Training Data under Label Noise

official.background: Training labels gathered cheaply (heuristics, weak supervision, crowdsourcing) are often noisy. One data-centric fix is to keep only a subset of the noisy training set that is likely to be correctly labelled. Cutstats (Lang et al., 2022) does this by keeping samples whose label agrees with the labels of their k nearest neighbours. Because it depends on k-NN, it may degrade in high dimensions, where nearest neighbours in raw feature space stop being informative. The paper argues that if the labelling function is invariant under a known symmetry group, computing neighbours in an invariant representation restores cutstats' ability to find clean samples.
official.method:
Cutstats scores each sample i by a z-score z_i = (J_i − μ_i)/σ_i, where J_i = Σ_{j∈NN(x_i)} w_ij·1[ŷ_j ≠ ŷ_i], w_ij = (1 + ||x_i − x_j||²)^(-1), and μ_i, σ_i² are the mean and variance of J_i under independent labels drawn from the empirical label distribution P(ŷ). The τ% of samples with the smallest z_i are kept. The proposed variant ('Ours') is identical except that both the neighbour search and the weights use an invariant representation F(x) instead of x: for the orthogonal group F(x) = ||x||_2. Settings: k = 20, τ = 40%, priors P(ŷ=0) = P(ŷ=1) = 1/2.

Synthetic orthogonal-group data: x ∈ R^100 drawn from a uniform distribution, with label y = 1[h(x) ≥ 0], h(x) = 2 sin(x^T x) + 3 sin²(2 x^T x) + 4 cos(3 x^T x). Training labels are flipped with probability p = 0.45. Subset-Acc is the percentage of correctly labelled (clean) samples in the selected 40% subset. Classifier-Acc is the test accuracy of a two-layer MLP (32 hidden units, ReLU, sigmoid output, lr 1e-2, 20 epochs, batch 1024, BCE) trained on that subset. Baselines all select 40% of the data: Random, Vanilla cutstats (raw features), Entropy, Forget (forgetting events), and Herding.
official.claim: On the synthetic SO(d)-invariant task (d = 100, label-flip noise p = 0.45, keep 40%), cutstats on the invariant feature ||x|| selects a subset that is 74.31 ± 1.10% correctly labelled, versus 60.51 ± 1.58% for vanilla cutstats on raw features and at most 58.69% for the other selection baselines.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison of downstream classifier accuracy and subset accuracy across different methods. Results are reported as mean across three different seeds, with the best subset selection method highlighted in bold.
official.metric: Subset-Acc: % of selected samples whose noisy label equals the true label (higher is better), mean over 3 seeds ± a spread the paper does not define (it says only 'mean across three different seeds'; presumably std over seeds)
official.comparison: Cutstats with invariant representation F(x) = ||x||_2 ('Ours') vs. Vanilla cutstats on raw x (main), plus Random, Entropy, Forget and Herding, all at a 40% subset
official.falsification_criterion: With the stated settings (d = 100, p = 0.45, k = 20, τ = 40%), the invariant-feature cutstats' subset accuracy is not above vanilla cutstats by clearly more than the reported ± seed spread (for example, a gap under ~3 points), or vanilla cutstats matches it.

title: PepSpecBench: A Unified Evaluation Benchmark for Peptide Tandem Mass Spectrometry Prediction
claim_source: Table 3, page 6 (bootstrap CI for the backbone-disjoint arm in Table 14, page 22)

official.background: Deep learning models that predict peptide tandem mass spectra (MS/MS fragment-ion intensities) from a modified peptide sequence, precursor charge and collision energy are used to build spectral libraries, analyse DIA data and rescore peptide-spectrum matches. Published models are usually evaluated with random train/test splits, so the same unmodified amino-acid backbone (possibly with different PTMs) can appear in both training and test data. The model can then memorise backbone-specific fragmentation patterns, and reported accuracy may overstate how well it generalises to unseen peptides.
official.method:
PepSpecBench filters PROSPECT (ProteomeTools-based spectral library) to peptides of length 6-40, precursor charge 1-6 and three PTMs (acetylation, carbamidomethylation, oxidation), and reconstructs a 500k/50k/50k train/validation/test set balanced 50% unmodified / 50% PTM. The default Backbone-Disjoint split hashes the backbone (the sequence with all PTM annotations stripped) deterministically into train/val/test, so no backbone appears in two partitions (MD5 of the naked sequence mapped to buckets 0-99; 80/10/10 by backbone). For the split ablation (Appendix C.5), the reconstructed PROSPECT train/val/test tables are concatenated into a ~600k pool and re-split 80/10/10 by an MD5 bucket of either a row-level key (Naive Random: sample_key plus row index, i.e. per spectrum regardless of backbone) or the modified_sequence string (Modified-Sequence: a backbone can recur with different PTMs across partitions); the Backbone-Disjoint arm is the main 500k/50k/50k benchmark split.

Prosit (GRU encoder-decoder, about 2.5M parameters, extended to peptide length 40, masked spectral-angle loss, AdamW, peak LR 1e-4, batch 1024, cosine schedule with 5% warmup, early stopping on validation median SA with patience 10) is trained separately under each split with the same recipe. Predictions and observed spectra are projected into a shared 234-dimensional canonical b/y-ion space (cleavage position x ion type x fragment charge up to 3; ground truth is binned at 0.1 Da and read at theoretical b/y m/z), impossible positions are masked, and per-spectrum Spectral Angle SA = (2/pi)·arccos(cosine similarity) and Pearson correlation are aggregated as medians over each split's test set.
official.claim: Training and testing Prosit on PROSPECT with a naive random split gives a median spectral angle of 0.1254 (PCC 0.9099), better than the 0.1376 (PCC 0.8921) obtained under the backbone-disjoint split, an apparent improvement of 0.0122 SA that the authors attribute to backbone leakage, whereas a modified-sequence split stays close to backbone-disjoint (SA 0.1392, PCC 0.8895).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Split-ablation metrics for Prosit on PROSPECT (medians). ∆ relative to Backbone-Disjoint.
official.metric: Median Spectral Angle over test spectra in the shared canonical space (lower is better); median SAS = 1 - SA and median PCC (higher is better) also reported. Table 3 has no error bars; Table 14 gives a 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples of 50k test spectra) only for the backbone-disjoint arm: 0.1376 [0.1354, 0.1397]. Single training run per split.
official.comparison: Prosit trained/evaluated under Naive Random split vs. Backbone-Disjoint split (and Modified-Sequence split) on PROSPECT, same data source and training recipe.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining Prosit under both splits (ideally over several seeds) gives a naive-random median SA that is not lower than the backbone-disjoint median SA by clearly more than the seed-to-seed spread and bootstrap CI (e.g. a gap under about 0.004 SA, or reversed), or the modified-sequence split shows a gap comparable to naive random.
