title: MEMAUDIT: An Exact Package-Oracle Evaluation Protocol for Budgeted Long-Term LLM Memory Writing
claim_source: Figure 2, page 6 (numbers also in Section 4 text, page 5)

official.background: Long-term LLM agents have to compress a stream of past interactions into a persistent memory store under a storage budget before they know which future queries will be asked. Memory systems such as Mem0, Letta and A-Mem are usually judged by end-to-end question-answering accuracy, which mixes up what was written to memory with retrieval, prompting and reader errors. MemAudit evaluates the write step on its own: it defines a finite 'package' of candidate memories with costs and semantic coverage, and scores a written store against the exact budgeted optimum of that package.
official.method:
A package fixes a stream of experiences, several candidate representations per experience (raw span, atomic fact, summary, tombstone, compound update), a cost per candidate (normalized word-equivalent units), semantic evidence units with weights w_r, and a coverage matrix a_ur. A store X must fit the budget (sum of costs <= B) and keep at most one representation per experience. Its utility is F(X) = sum_r w_r min(1, sum_{u in X} a_ur), a monotone submodular coverage function. OPT(B) is computed exactly by group-wise branch-and-bound (checked against a PuLP MILP on 1,200 instances, all matching), and a writer is scored by the ratio F(X)/OPT(B).

MemAudit-Small generates compact hidden event graphs with raw, fact, summary, tombstone and compound-update candidates. Over 500 seeds, budgets B = 2, 4, 8, 16 are swept. Writers, all constrained to the same package and budget: MemAudit-GVT (grouped value-threshold: for each arriving experience, among candidates whose exact oracle marginal density exceeds a threshold, insert the one with the largest marginal value, taking the best over a threshold grid); Density-only (pick the candidate with the highest marginal value per cost); Recency raw (keep the most recent raw spans until the budget runs out); Fact-only and Summary-only (restricted to one representation family); and No-tombstone OPT (exact optimum after removing tombstone and compound-update candidates).
official.claim: On the 500-seed MemAudit-Small exact-package sweep, removing tombstone/compound-update candidates lowers the exact optimum to 0.523, 0.654, 0.689 and 0.815 of full OPT at B = 2, 4, 8, 16. Density-only selection covers no invalidation units at B = 2, 4, 8 and reaches only 0.264-0.361 of OPT there, while oracle-marginal GVT stays near OPT (about 0.96-1.00).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Exact-small budget sweep. MemAudit-GVT remains near certified package OPT, while density-only, recency raw, and single-representation baselines degrade under tight storage. Bands are bootstrap 95% intervals from the canonical 500-seed run.
official.metric: Ratio of the writer's coverage utility F(X) to the certified exact package optimum OPT(B), averaged over 500 seeds (higher is better). The caption says bands are bootstrap 95% intervals, but they are not visible at plot resolution and no numeric intervals are given.
official.comparison: Exact OPT vs. No-tombstone OPT (representation-frontier ablation), and MemAudit-GVT vs. Density-only, Recency raw, Fact-only and Summary-only writers on the same packages and budgets
official.falsification_criterion: On regenerated MemAudit-Small packages, No-tombstone OPT stays within a few percent of full OPT (e.g. above 0.9 at B = 2-8), or Density-only reaches comparable ratios to GVT (e.g. above 0.8) at B = 2, 4, 8, or Density-only covers invalidation units at those budgets.

title: MOSAIC-Bench: Measuring Compositional Vulnerability Induction in Coding Agents

official.background: Coding agents are increasingly driven by streams of engineering tickets, and their safety training is evaluated on single, overt requests. MOSAIC-Bench asks whether a malicious end-state can be reached by splitting it into three innocuous-looking tickets, each of which an agent implements without objection, and whether downstream LLM code reviewers catch the resulting cumulative diff. Every chain has a deterministic proof-of-concept oracle that runs against a live Docker deployment of the web app, so 'exploitable' is fixed ground truth rather than an LLM judgment. If reviewer prompting alone changes detection a lot, that is a cheap, deployable mitigation.
official.method:
The benchmark has 199 three-stage attack chains over 10 web-app substrates (Express, Flask, Stripe, Gin, etc.), 31 CWE classes and 5 languages. Each chain ships Jira-style tickets, a stagewise golden solution and a Python PoC oracle that returns VULNERABLE on the full 3-stage golden composition and SECURE on every 1- and 2-stage prefix. Reviewer agents are handed the cumulative git diff of a confirmed-exploitable chain and must output APPROVE or DECLINE; evasion is the fraction of confirmed-exploitable chains that the reviewer APPROVEs.

Three reviewer protocols are compared on the same diffs: neutral diff-only (reviewer prompted as a senior engineer doing a normal PR review, given only the cumulative diff), neutral full-context (the full post-application repository is also available), and pentester framing (system prompt in App. M.1: list what changed, try to write a concrete exploit as a low-privilege user, then classify with a CWE and DECLINE only if an exploit was written). Five reviewers were run under pentester framing, including the open-weight Gemma-4-E4B-it. False positives of the Gemma pentester reviewer are measured separately on 608 merged real-world GitHub PRs.
official.claim: On the 199 confirmed-exploitable MOSAIC-Bench cumulative diffs, switching the Gemma-4-E4B-it reviewer from the neutral diff-only prompt to the pentester prompt reduces evasion (APPROVE on an exploitable chain) from 59.8% to 11.6% (88.4% detection), while giving the neutral reviewer full repository context raises evasion to 70.9%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Pentester framing reduces reviewer evasion, but the magnitude varies by model. Framing dominates scale in expectation; GPT-5.4 is the main weak-transfer case.
official.metric: Evasion rate (%) = fraction of oracle-confirmed exploitable chains the reviewer APPROVEs; lower is better. Single run per configuration; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Gemma-4-E4B-it reviewer: pentester framing vs. neutral diff-only vs. neutral full-context framing, same model, same 199 diffs. Secondary: the same comparison for Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Codex GPT-5.3 and Codex GPT-5.4.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Gemma-4-E4B-it with the paper's pentester and neutral diff-only prompts on the released 199 chain diffs gives pentester evasion that is not substantially below neutral diff-only evasion (e.g., a reduction under ~20 pp, or pentester evasion above ~25%).

title: Learning Reveals Invisible Structure in Low-Rank RNNs
claim_source: Figure 4f, page 7 (protocol in App. B.5, pages 25-26)

official.background: In low-rank recurrent neural networks, the network's activity and input-output function are fully determined by a few scalar 'overlaps' (normalized inner products between the input, recurrent and readout vectors). This makes it possible to link connectivity to function, but it says nothing about how gradient-descent learning moves the network. Neuroscience asks whether parts of connectivity that do not affect current behavior can still shape learning or keep a record of past training, i.e. act as memory.
official.method:
For a rank-1 RNN with input vector m, recurrent factors u, v (W = u v^T / N) and readout z, the authors derive closed-form ODEs for gradient flow in overlap space: the overlaps evolve as sigma_dot = -G(theta) grad_sigma L, where the Gram matrix G depends on extra overlaps that do not enter the loss. They split the 10 quadratic overlaps into loss-visible ones (which set the output and loss) and loss-invisible ones (which only affect G). For the erf nonlinearity in the large-N Gaussian limit, sigma_mu, ||m||^2 and ||u||^2 become loss-visible, leaving sigma_zv, ||v||^2 and ||z||^2 as loss-invisible; the linear gradient-flow invariant that forces invisible overlaps back to their initial values then no longer holds.

Memory experiment (Sec. 5.2, App. B.5): 10 twin pairs of nonlinear rank-1 networks (20 networks; each pair shares an initialization drawn with cross-overlaps from |N(0,0.4)| and squared norms from U[0.5,2]) are trained directly with the 10D preconditioned overlap ODEs. One twin is trained on task A (1-bit flip-flop) and the other on task B (stimulus integration) for 30,000 epochs (lr 0.01, divided by 5 when loss < 0.015), then both on task C (imitate a fixed teacher network driven by white noise) for 30,000 epochs (lr 0.001), batch 128, dt = 0.05, T = 20 s. A logistic-regression classifier predicts the first task (A vs B) from either the visible or the invisible overlaps, after adding N(0, 0.1) white noise to the features, with 50 random 16/4 train/test splits at three checkpoints (initial, after A/B, after C).
official.claim: After both twins are trained on the same task C, a logistic-regression classifier decodes which task (A or B) a network was first trained on with ~1.0 cross-validated accuracy from the loss-invisible overlaps, but only ~0.5 (chance, s.d. ~0.18) from the loss-visible overlaps, when N(0, 0.1) noise is added to the overlap features.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: (a) Example input sequence of the flip-flop task (top). Target output (black), high-dimensional RNN prediction (blue), and effective RNN prediction (red dashed) show excellent agreement (bottom). (b) Training loss of RNN in parameter space θ (blue) and 10D overlap dynamics using G(θ) (red dashed), which closely match, while direct optimization in σ space (black dashed), leads to different dynamics. (c) Distributions of parameter vector components θ at convergence (top), along with corresponding Q-Q plots (bottom), showing that the Gaussian structure is preserved (correlation coefficient r ≥ 0.998). (d) Schematic of the history-dependent training protocol (A/B → C), where two identically initialized twin networks are first trained on either task A (flip-flop) or task B (stimulus integration), and then both on the same task C (emulating a teacher network). Solid black lines indicate targets, and dashed colored lines are the network outputs. (e-f) Cross-validation accuracy for decoding training history using loss-visible (blue) and loss-invisible (red) overlaps (error bars ±1 s.d). (e) Without noise, decoding is possible from either set due to infinitesimal differences. (f) With small noise added to the overlaps (N(0, 0.1)), only loss-invisible overlaps remain informative, while loss-visible overlaps drop to chance level.
official.metric: Cross-validated classification accuracy for training history (A vs B), higher is better; mean +/- 1 s.d. over 50 random 16/4 train/test splits of 20 networks (10 twin pairs); values read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Decoder using loss-invisible overlaps (sigma_zv, ||v||^2, ||z||^2) vs. the same decoder using loss-visible overlaps, on the same networks after task C
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the A/B -> C protocol with the stated noise level, decoding accuracy from invisible overlaps after task C is not clearly above that from visible overlaps (e.g. invisible accuracy below ~0.8, or visible accuracy well above chance and within one s.d. of invisible).

title: Layerwise LQR for Geometry-Aware Optimization of Deep Networks

official.background: Geometry-aware optimizers such as Newton's method and natural gradient descent (NGD) precondition the gradient with a curvature matrix, but for deep networks that matrix is dense and couples all layers, so scalable methods such as K-FAC and Shampoo approximate it with block-diagonal (per-layer) structure before solving for the update, which throws away cross-layer interactions. The question is whether a preconditioner that keeps those interactions in its training objective, while still having cheap structured form, improves training of standard networks at small overhead.
official.method:
The authors show that the steepest-descent step under a divergence-induced quadratic model (Newton, Gauss-Newton, Fisher/NGD) is exactly a finite-horizon Linear Quadratic Regulator problem over the layers, with the forward-pass Jacobians as linear dynamics and the divergence's second derivatives as costs. LLQR relaxes this: the update for layer i is -U_i times the layer gradient, where U_i is a structured inverse preconditioner (diagonal, Kronecker-factored, or E-KFAC: learned left/right transform factors Q^L, Q^R plus a learned diagonal scaling in the transformed coordinates, not computed curvature eigenbases), and U is learned by minimizing the LQR objective (Eq. 15) with the layer-coupled dynamics, using JVP/VJP/HVP products and no matrix inversion. Every 500 iterations U is reinitialized to the identity, refit with 25 SGDM inner steps (lr 0.005, momentum 0.9) on the current minibatch, and blended into the previous U with an EMA (decay 0.95 for NGD, 0.9 for Newton); damping is 0. In between, the outer optimizer uses U times the gradient in place of the gradient.

For Table 1, ResNet-18 is trained on CIFAR-100 for 200 epochs, batch size 128, weight decay 1e-3, cosine LR schedule, SGDM (lr 0.05, momentum 0.9) or AdamW (lr 5e-4), with flips, 4-pixel-padded crops, normalization and Cutout. The baseline optimizer hyperparameters are tuned for the baseline and kept unchanged when LLQR is added. Runs use identical seeds across optimizers; Figure 5 states five seeds.
official.claim: Training ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 (200 epochs, batch 128) with SGDM, wrapping the optimizer with LLQR using an E-KFAC inverse preconditioner and the NGD (KL) divergence raises final top-1 test accuracy from 78.97 ± 0.22 to 79.96 ± 0.10, at a 1.32x wall-clock cost; with AdamW the same variant raises it from 76.09 ± 0.27 to 77.07 ± 0.16.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance and wall-clock time ratio on ResNet-18. Newton and NGD denote the divergence-induced quadratic used by LLQR. Across our experiments, ± denotes the standard error.
official.metric: Final top-1 test accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is the standard error over seeds (five seeds per Figure 5); time is the wall-clock ratio to the baseline
official.comparison: SGDM (and AdamW) with LLQR E-KFAC/NGD preconditioning vs. the same optimizer with the same hyperparameters and seeds and no preconditioner
official.falsification_criterion: Over five or more seeds of the stated recipe, the SGDM+LLQR (E-KFAC, NGD) mean top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-100 is not higher than plain SGDM by clearly more than the paper's reported standard errors (0.22 baseline, 0.10 LLQR), e.g. the ~1-point gain largely disappears.

title: Explaining and Preventing Alignment Collapse in Iterative RLHF
claim_source: Figure 5, printed page 20 (PDF page 22), Appendix C.2

official.background: In iterative RLHF the reward model (RM) is periodically retrained on preference data generated by the current policy, so the policy influences the RM it will be scored by next. The paper frames this as a Stackelberg game with the policy as leader and the RM as follower. It shows that the true policy gradient has two parts: the usual policy gradient and a 'parameter-steering' term that captures how the policy's samples shift the RM's future parameters. Standard iterative RLHF drops the steering term, and the authors argue that this causes 'alignment collapse': the policy exploits RM blind spots, and retraining on that data reinforces the errors.
official.method:
Foresighted policy optimization (FPO) adds a correction gamma * R_FPO to the policy objective. The exact correction uses influence functions with an inverse Hessian. The tractable 'relaxed' TracIn version under an MSE RM loss is R~_FPO(y) = -(r_phi(y) - U(y)) * ||grad_phi r_phi(y)||^2, which needs the true utility U (oracle-aware). The leader maximizes r_phi(y) - gamma (r_phi(y) - U(y)) ||grad_phi r_phi(y)||^2 - (beta/2)||y||^2, with gamma = 0.005 and beta = 0.02. Standard iterative RLHF uses the same objective with gamma = 0.

Controlled environment: actions y in R^10, true utility U(y) = 10 exp(-0.2 ||y - y*||^2) with y* = [2.5, 2.5, 0, ..., 0]. The policy is a Gaussian N(theta, sigma^2 I). The RM is a 2-layer MLP [32, 32] with Softplus, trained with Adam (lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-3) on an MSE loss against U, using a sliding replay buffer of 50 samples with 5 new samples per iteration. Training runs for T = 4000 outer iterations, each with K = 15 inner policy gradient steps. The policy lr decays 0.05 -> 0.001 and the exploration noise decays 0.1 -> 0.001, both polynomially with power 4. The metric is the true utility U of the policy, averaged over 5 seeds (Appendix C.2, Table 4; the paper does not say explicitly whether U is evaluated at the policy mean theta or at sampled actions).
official.claim: In the 10-d neural-network-RM environment ([32,32] MLP RM, replay buffer 50, 4000 iterations), relaxed FPO ends at a mean true utility of about 7.5 (out of a maximum of 10) over 5 seeds, while standard iterative RLHF ends at about 4.4 and plateaus around 3-4 for most of training.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: True utility over 5 random seeds in the neural-network experiment using R~_FPO.
official.metric: True human utility U of the policy (higher is better; the maximum is 10). Lines are means over 5 random seeds, and shaded regions are ±1 std over seeds. Values are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: FPO with the oracle-aware relaxed TracIn penalty (gamma = 0.005) vs. standard iterative RLHF (gamma = 0), with identical environment, RM, and schedules
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both methods over 5 or more seeds in the Table 4 setting, FPO's final mean true utility is not clearly above standard RLHF's (e.g. a gap under ~1.5 utility units, or RLHF's mean falls within FPO's seed spread across most of the last 1000 iterations), or standard RLHF reaches utility near the optimum.

title: Power Distribution Bridges Sampling, Self-Reward RL, and Self-Distillation

official.background: Power sampling (Karan and Du, 2026) draws completions from the 'power distribution' π(y|x)^α of a base LLM using a Metropolis–Hastings sampler. It has been reported to match RL-trained models on reasoning benchmarks without any training or external reward, but it costs much more at inference time than ordinary autoregressive decoding. This paper shows that the power distribution is also the closed-form optimum of KL-regularized RL when the model's own sequence log-likelihood is the reward. It uses this to propose power self-distillation: fine-tune the base model on its own power-sampled completions so that the student gets the benefit with cheap decoding.
official.method:
Teacher data: for 500 MATH training problems (excluding MATH500), sample completions from Qwen2.5-Math-7B with the MH power sampler of Karan and Du (2026) using their default hyperparameters (α = 4). Student: the same base model fine-tuned on these completions with standard causal-LM cross-entropy on completion tokens only, using LoRA (r = 16, alpha = 32, dropout 0.05, on all attention and MLP projections), AdamW with lr 1e-5, weight decay 0.01, warmup ratio 0.03, 3 epochs, effective batch size 8 and max sequence length 1024. No external reward or labels are used.

Evaluation on MATH500 measures true reward r* (answer accuracy) and self-reward r_self (mean per-token log-likelihood of the completion under the base model), averaged over all completions from 4 seeds. Decoding modes are Standard (plain autoregressive sampling), Temperature (token-wise temperature τ = 1/α = 0.25) and Power (MH power sampling, base model only).
official.claim: On MATH500 with standard autoregressive sampling, Qwen2.5-Math-7B after power self-distillation reaches accuracy 0.643 ± 0.025, compared with 0.508 ± 0.016 for the base model. Self-reward also rises, from −0.316 to −0.089. With temperature decoding, the distilled model reaches 0.722 ± 0.009, which is on par with base-model MH power sampling (0.714 ± 0.006).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: True reward r⋆ (accuracy) and self-reward r_self for Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH500. The left two columns report means over all sampled completions. The right two columns report self-reward Best-of-N: the completion with the largest r_self among samples generated with different seeds. Evaluated with four seeds.
official.metric: MATH500 accuracy r* (higher is better), mean ± std over 4 seeds, averaged over all sampled completions; r_self = mean per-token log-likelihood under the base model (higher is sharper)
official.comparison: Power-distilled Qwen2.5-Math-7B vs. the base Qwen2.5-Math-7B, both with standard decoding (primary). Secondary: power-distilled + temperature decoding vs. base + MH power sampling and base + token-wise temperature.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running power self-distillation (500 MATH training problems, MH power-sampled teacher at α = 4, LoRA SFT) gives a student whose MATH500 accuracy under standard sampling is not clearly above the base model's (for example, a gain under about 5 points or within seed std of 0.508).

title: ReflectDrive-2: Reinforcement-Learning-Aligned Self-Editing for Discrete Diffusion Driving

official.background: Learned driving planners tend to make errors along two axes: longitudinal speed mistakes (overshoot, under-progress, late braking) and lateral heading drift (leaving the lane, clipping turns). Masked discrete diffusion planners represent a trajectory as discrete tokens, so the same model can rewrite selected tokens of its own draft in place. The question is whether such a self-editing step actually improves driving quality, or whether it only helps once drafting and editing are trained jointly against the driving reward.
official.method:
ReflectDrive-2 is a 0.7B masked-diffusion language backbone with a 0.1B ViT and a compact action FFN. It takes two frames from three front-facing cameras, navigation-instruction tokens and ego-state tokens, and outputs 8 waypoints as 16 discrete BEV coordinate tokens. It predicts a goal point (the final waypoint), drafts the remaining tokens by parallel masked decoding, then applies AutoEdit: the same model takes the concrete draft tokens and predicts replacement tokens, committing replacements at low-confidence non-goal positions for K rounds. Supervised training combines the masked-diffusion loss (DLM), a drivable-area field loss (DACF) and an AutoEdit loss that maps structure-aware perturbations of expert trajectories (arc-length rescaling by beta for progress errors, rotation by alpha for heading errors) back to the expert tokens.

RL fine-tuning uses PDMS as terminal reward on the final post-edit trajectory, with a GRPO-style discrete-diffusion policy gradient (group of 6 = 3 goals x 2 drafts) that credits token transitions from both the drafting steps and the AutoEdit steps. Table 3 evaluates each training stage on NAVSIM navtest, single trajectory from the top goal, with and without inference-time AutoEdit.
official.claim: On NAVSIM navtest, inference-time AutoEdit improves PDMS by at most +0.3 after supervised training (87.7 -> 88.0 with AutoEdit training), but by +1.9 (89.1 -> 91.0) after RL over the full draft-and-edit rollout.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Effect of inference-time AutoEdit across training regimes. After supervised training, inference-time AutoEdit contributes at most +0.3 PDMS. After RL over the full draft-and-edit rollout, the same inference-time AutoEdit contributes +1.9 PDMS.
official.metric: NAVSIM PDMS (higher is better), single trajectory per scene; single runs, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: PDMS with vs. without inference-time AutoEdit, for four training regimes: DLM; DLM + DACF; DLM + DACF + AutoEdit training; DLM + DACF + AutoEdit training + RL
official.falsification_criterion: After RL over the composed draft-and-edit rollout, inference-time AutoEdit's PDMS gain is not clearly larger than its gain after supervised AutoEdit training (e.g. under about +1.0 PDMS, or within run-to-run variance across seeds).

title: Breaking the Quality–Privacy Tradeoff in Tabular Data Generation via In-Context Learning

official.background: Synthetic tabular data is a common way to share sensitive records (health, finance) without releasing the real rows, but the generator has to be both useful (models trained on synthetic data should work on real data) and private (synthetic rows should not copy training rows). The authors show that on small datasets (a few hundred rows) existing generators such as CTGAN, TVAE and tabDDPM trade one goal against the other: as training goes on, quality rises but synthetic samples move closer to training records. They argue that a model pretrained across many datasets to generate held-out rows from a context set can infer the distribution of a new small dataset without memorizing it.
official.method:
DiffICL encodes a table with the frozen LimiX tabular foundation model (final-layer hidden states, d = 192 per cell) and trains a conditional latent diffusion model (EDM formulation, a 6-layer dual-axis Transformer with feature-wise and sample-wise attention; query rows attend only to context rows, not to each other) to denoise latents of a query set given latents of a disjoint context set. Pretraining uses 826 real Kaggle/UCI datasets, each with 5 row/column-permuted variants, context ratio sampled from [0.2, 0.5], 20,000 epochs on 32 RTX 4090 GPUs. At inference on a new dataset, the training split is divided into context and query; the pretrained model samples synthetic latents (50 Heun steps) conditioned on the context latents, and per-feature MLP decoders trained on the query rows' (latent, raw value) pairs map latents back to raw features.

Evaluation covers 14 OpenML/TALENT datasets (7 classification, 7 regression), each split 50/50 into train and test (train sizes 259 to 10,535). Quality = AUC (classification) or R² (regression) on the real test set of XGBoost, CatBoost, Random Forest and MLP trained only on synthetic data; privacy = DCROverfit = min(1, 2(1 − p)), where p is the fraction of synthetic rows whose nearest record is in the training set rather than a held-out set (higher = less memorization). Baselines (CTGAN, CTABGAN+, TVAE, tabDDPM, TabSYN, TabDiff, GReaT) are run from their official repos; for each baseline the checkpoint maximizing 0.5·XGBoost + 0.5·DCROverfit is reported. Results are averaged over datasets and given as mean ± std over 5 runs.
official.claim: Averaged over 14 small tabular datasets, data generated by DiffICL gives a higher XGBoost train-on-synthetic score (74.0 ± 0.7 vs. 71.4 ± 0.8 for TabSYN, the best baseline) and a higher DCROverfit privacy score (76.1 ± 0.4 vs. 73.2 ± 0.5 for TabDiff, the best baseline) than every baseline, i.e. it improves quality and privacy at the same time.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quality and Privacy comparison across 9 and 14 datasets. The results represent the mean ± standard deviation (%) over 5 independent runs. Data quality is measured by downstream task performance (using XGBoost, CatBoost, RandomForest, and MLP as learners), and privacy is quantified by DCROverfit. GReaT is included in the 9 Datasets group where it ran successfully, but excluded from the 14 Datasets group as it failed to generate valid samples across all subsets. Best results are highlighted in red.
official.metric: Quality: AUC (classification) / R² (regression) ×100 of downstream learners trained on synthetic data and tested on real test data, averaged over datasets, higher is better. Privacy: DCROverfit ×100, higher is better. ± is std over 5 independent runs.
official.comparison: DiffICL vs. CTGAN, CTABGAN+, TVAE, tabDDPM, TabSYN, TabDiff (and GReaT on the 9-dataset subset), baselines at their best balanced-criterion checkpoint
official.falsification_criterion: On the 14 datasets, the best baseline's XGBoost score comes within run-to-run std of DiffICL's, or some baseline matches or exceeds DiffICL's DCROverfit, or DiffICL cannot be in the top position on both axes simultaneously.

title: Heterogeneous Judge-Aware Ranking with Sensitivity, Disagreement, and Confidence
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (dataset and protocol details in Appendix F.1, pages 36-37)

official.background: LLM leaderboards and preference datasets are often built from pairwise comparisons made by several judges (humans or LLM judges). The usual approach pools all judgments into one Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) score vector, which treats systematic disagreement between judges as noise. JA-Ranking adds one scalar sensitivity per judge, but this still cannot represent judges who favour different kinds of items. This paper asks whether modelling structured, judge-specific disagreement gives better rankings and predictions.
official.method:
HJA models each judge k with its own BTL score vector S_k over N items, so logit P(judge k prefers i over j) = S_ki - S_kj. The K x N score matrix is decomposed as S = gamma mu^T + U V^T, where mu is the consensus item score, gamma_k is judge k's sensitivity to the consensus, and U V^T (rank r) is residual disagreement constrained to be orthogonal to mu (centering, scaling, orthogonality and anchoring constraints, Condition 1). Parameters are fit by constrained maximum likelihood with a proximal alternating algorithm that solves the (gamma, U) and (mu, V) blocks with L-BFGS-B and re-anchors after each step (Algorithm 1, tau = 30). The rank r is chosen by 5-fold validation of negative log-likelihood over r = 0..min(K-1, N-2). Baselines are JA-Ranking (S = gamma mu^T, the r = 0 case) and standard pooled BTL (gamma = 1, r = 0).

Real-data held-out test (Appendix F.1): four public pairwise LLM-judge datasets come from the JA-Ranking repository. Chatbot Arena has 9,937 usable records, N = 20 candidate models and K = 10 judge models; UltraFeedback has 9,726 records, N = 17, K = 20. Ties are coded as 0.5 and records with unknown labels are dropped. Each method is fit on a random record-level 80% training split, and pairwise prediction accuracy is computed on the remaining 20%. This is repeated over 20 random seeds.
official.claim: With a record-level 80/20 split, HJA's held-out pairwise prediction accuracy is 0.65 ± 0.01 on Chatbot Arena vs. 0.58 ± 0.01 for both JA-Ranking and BTL, and 0.70 ± 0.01 on UltraFeedback vs. 0.62 ± 0.01 (JA-Ranking) and 0.61 ± 0.01 (BTL).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Real-data comparison. Robustness is evaluated under increasing noisy-judge perturbation; near-tie accuracy is evaluated across increasingly less ambiguous near-tie groups. Entries are mean ± standard deviation in 20 random seeds; bold marks the best mean per dataset-metric group.
official.metric: Held-out pairwise prediction accuracy on the 20% test records (higher is better); mean ± standard deviation over 20 random seeds (random train/test splits)
official.comparison: HJA (consensus + sensitivity + rank-r disagreement) vs. JA-Ranking (sensitivity only) vs. standard pooled BTL, all fit on the same training records
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the 80/20 held-out evaluation on Chatbot Arena (and UltraFeedback) over multiple seeds, HJA's mean test accuracy is less than about 0.03 above the better of JA-Ranking and BTL, or within one seed std of it.

title: Rollout Pass-Rate Control: Steering Binary-Reward RL Toward Its Most Informative Regime

official.background: In RL with verifiable binary rewards (RLVR), GRPO-style training samples a group of rollouts per task and learns from contrast between successes and failures within the group. Groups that all pass or all fail give no advantage signal and are usually filtered out, and many surviving groups are very skewed (1/8 or 7/8 successes) and give weak contrast. Rollouts are the dominant cost, especially for long agentic tasks such as SWE-bench, so wasting them on low-signal groups slows training. The paper argues that the learning signal from a binary-reward group is largest when the pass rate is near 50%, and asks whether actively steering skewed groups toward that point speeds up training.
official.method:
Prefix Sampling (PS) samples N = 8 rollouts per task and buckets each group by pass count k. Groups with k in {0, 8} are dropped (DAPO-style filtering); all other groups are trained on normally with GRPO. Skewed groups additionally seed a rerollout: for hard buckets (k = 1, 2) a successful trajectory is saved and its first fraction r_b of assistant tokens (math) or environment steps (SWE) is replayed as a head start; for easy buckets (k = 6, 7) a failing trajectory's prefix is replayed as a handicap. The current policy generates fresh continuations from the replayed prefix, and replayed tokens are masked out of the loss so gradients only come from on-policy continuation tokens. Rerollout groups are mixed into the same batch as ordinary groups.

In the adaptive variant (PS-ada), each of the four buckets keeps its own prefix ratio r_b in [0.05, 0.95] (initial 0.5), tracks an EMA (alpha 0.05) of its rerollout pass rate, and moves r_b by 0.05 (deadzone 0.03, 5-update cooldown) to push that pass rate toward 0.5. PS-fix uses a fixed r = 0.5; PS-ada hard-only disables the 6/8 and 7/8 buckets. The ablation trains Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (no thinking) on AceReason-Math-Subset (about 15k problems where the base model's 8-rollout pass rate is below 75%) with a DeepSWE-style GRPO++ backbone (clip-high 0.28, no KL, no reward-std normalization, length-normalized loss, leave-one-out advantages, LR 1e-6, batch 128, max response 16384, temperature 1.0). Convergence step is the peak step of the training-score curve on ordinary (non-replayed) tasks.
official.claim: On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 trained on AceReason-Math-Subset, PS-ada reaches peak ordinary-task training score (about 0.70) at step 110 vs. 211 for the matched GRPO++ baseline (1.92x fewer steps), with 80.2 vs. 66.0 valid (non-degenerate) groups per step; PS-fix converges at step 131 and PS-ada hard-only at 186.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: 4B AceReason-Math-Subset ablation summary. Convergence is the peak step of the ordinary, non-replayed training-score trajectory marked in Figure 3; valid groups/step is the mean number of non-degenerate rollout groups left after group filtering over each method's own pre-convergence window. Figure 3: 4B AceReason-Math-Subset ablations. Left: training-score trajectories on ordinary, non-replayed tasks, with vertical markers at each method's convergence step. Right: bucket-level control quality for the prefix-based arms, reporting mean rerollout pass rate p and mean absolute distance |p - 0.5| before each method's convergence step.
official.metric: Convergence step (lower is better) = peak step of the ordinary-task training-score curve; valid groups per step (higher is better). Single training run per arm; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: PS-ada vs. matched GRPO++ baseline (same data, rollout budget N = 8, batch, optimizer, hardware); also vs. PS-fix and PS-ada hard-only ablations.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same recipe, PS-ada's ordinary-task training score does not reach the baseline's peak level substantially earlier (e.g., speedup under about 1.3x, or within the run-to-run spread across a few seeds), or valid groups per step are not higher than the baseline.

title: How Long Does Infinite Width Last? Signal Propagation in Long-Range Linear Recurrences
claim_source: Figure 2(b), page 8 (panel (a) gives the same check for the LRU energy n^{-1/2} S_{n,t})

official.background: Signal-propagation theory explains why deep networks' activations explode or vanish and motivates initializations such as Glorot and He. Almost all of it is derived in the infinite-width limit. Linear recurrent models such as LRUs and state-space models apply the same weight matrix over very long sequences, so small finite-width effects can accumulate across steps. It has not been known at what recurrent depth t, relative to width n, the infinite-width prediction (stable signal energy under Glorot initialization) stops being accurate.
official.method:
The paper studies the linear RNN h^(k) = W^k x^(0) and the LRU h^(t) = W h^(t-1) + x^(t), with W an n x n matrix of i.i.d. proper complex Gaussian entries of variance 1/n (Glorot-style) and whitened inputs. The signal energies are Q_{n,k} = E||h_RNN^(k)||^2 / n and S_{n,t} = E||h_LRU^(t)||^2 / n. Theorem 2.1 gives an exact finite-width formula, Q_{n,k} = (F+_{k+2}(n) - F-_{k+2}(n)) / (n^{k+1}(k+1)(k+2)) with rising and falling factorials, and S_{n,t} = sum_{k<=t} Q_{n,k}. From this the paper derives three regimes. For k = o(sqrt(n)), Q -> 1, which is the infinite-width prediction. At k ~ c*sqrt(n), Q -> (2/c^2) sinh(c^2/2). Beyond that, Q explodes.

Figure 2 checks this with Monte Carlo estimates (10^5 samples; inputs uniform on the sphere of radius sqrt(n)) at widths n = 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000. The estimates are plotted against c = k/sqrt(n) together with the critical profiles (15) for Q_{n,k} and (16) for n^{-1/2} S_{n,t}.
official.claim: For a linear recurrence with complex Gaussian weights of variance 1/n (n = 100 to 2000), the Monte Carlo signal energy Q_{n,k} at depth k = c*sqrt(n) follows the critical profile (2/c^2) sinh(c^2/2) rather than the infinite-width value 1, reaching about 10 at c = 3 and about 190 at c = 4.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Numerical validation of the critical scaling theory. Monte Carlo estimates of S_{n,t} (a) and Q_{n,k} (b), based on 10^5 samples and plotted against the critical scaling variable c for several widths n. Inputs x are sampled uniformly on the sphere of radius sqrt(n), so that E[xx^T] = I_n. In both panels, the numerical estimates are compared with the corresponding theoretical critical profiles, given by (16) for S_{n,t} and (15) for Q_{n,k}. The close agreement illustrates convergence of the signal energies to their predicted critical limits. Error bars denote Monte Carlo standard errors of the mean.
official.metric: Normalized expected squared hidden-state norm Q_{n,k} = E||W^k x||^2 / n (log scale); error bars are Monte Carlo standard errors of the mean over 10^5 samples
official.comparison: Empirical Q_{n,k} at several widths vs. the predicted critical limit (2/c^2) sinh(c^2/2) and vs. the infinite-width / Glorot prediction Q = 1
official.falsification_criterion: Monte Carlo Q_{n,k} at c = k/sqrt(n) between 2 and 4, for n >= 500, does not match the critical profile within a few standard errors, or does not match the exact finite-n formula of Theorem 2.1 (which also determines S_{n,t}), or stays near 1 as the infinite-width theory predicts.

title: Joint Treatment Effect Estimation from Incomplete Healthcare Data: Temporal Causal Normalizing Flows with LLM-driven Evolutionary MNAR Imputation
claim_source: Table 11, page 31 (summarized in Table 1, page 7, and Section 4.2)

official.background: Estimating treatment effects from electronic health records is hard for two reasons that compound: treatment decisions depend on a patient's evolving state (time-varying confounding), and key biomarkers are often 50-80% missing, with missingness that depends on the unobserved value (MNAR). Existing neural causal estimators (CVAE-style, TARNet, recurrent marginal structural models) rely on approximate inference or ignore explicit causal structure. On synthetic data where true counterfactuals are known, they can fit the factual data well and still give the wrong treatment effect, including the wrong sign.
official.method:
CausalFlow-T is a causal masked autoregressive flow whose autoregressive order is restricted to a topological sort of an expert-specified DAG over (covariates, treatment, outcome) at each time step. The flow is conditioned on an LSTM encoding of the patient history and trained by exact maximum likelihood. Counterfactuals come from abduction-action-prediction: invert the flow to get the noise z_t, set the treatment to a', and decode only the treatment's descendants in DAG order with z_t held fixed. Baselines share the same LSTM temporal encoder: an unconstrained normalizing flow (NF, no DAG), CVAE, GNN-CVAE (graph-aware encoder, ELBO training) and TARNet.

The chosen benchmark is the CVD Risk Toy (Appendix A.4): N=50,000 patients, T=10 years, 15 time-varying covariates and a 17-node DAG. At t=0, hypertensive patients are treated with probability 0.70 and others with 0.30; untreated hypertensive patients then start treatment with probability 0.01 per year, and treatment is absorbing. Treatment lowers systolic blood pressure through lags 1-3 (SBP_final = SBP * (1 - [0.20 T(t-1) - 0.05 T(t-2) - 0.02 T(t-3)])), and this is the only path to a binary CVD event drawn from a logistic model. The true hazard ratio is 0.831. Each model predicts the always-treated and never-treated trajectories, from which a hazard ratio and per-arm reconstruction errors are computed. The split is 80/20 train/test, with the training part further split 80/20 into train/validation (Table 5).
official.claim: On the CVD Risk Toy (true HR 0.831), CausalFlow-T recovers HR 0.786 ± 0.051. CVAE (1.005 ± 0.007) and GNN-CVAE (1.006 ± 0.030) collapse to a null effect, and TARNet (1.133 ± 0.148) inverts the effect. CausalFlow-T's arm errors (0.003/0.002) are roughly 8-30x lower than those of CVAE, GNN-CVAE and TARNet (0.017-0.065).
official.claim_caption: Table 11: Arm reconstruction errors and ATE/HR recovery. Bold: best per dataset per metric. † GNN-CVAE and CVAE on LDL/Cox use the full simulation variant.
official.metric: Predicted hazard ratio for treated vs. untreated (closer to the true 0.831 is better), plus mean absolute arm reconstruction error Err_{a=1}, Err_{a=0} against the true counterfactual trajectories (lower is better). ± is the std across training seeds; the paper reports n=10 seeds for its experiments, but the Table 11 caption does not restate the count.
official.comparison: CausalFlow-T vs. CVAE, GNN-CVAE and TARNet (all with the same LSTM encoder), and vs. the ablation NF without the DAG constraint, on the same synthetic dataset
official.falsification_criterion: With the specified generator, CausalFlow-T's predicted HR is not clearly below 1, or is not closer to 0.831 than the CVAE/GNN-CVAE/TARNet estimates. Also refuted if a properly trained CVAE or TARNet recovers a protective HR (clearly below 1) with arm errors comparable to CausalFlow-T's.

title: Estimating the expected output of wide random MLPs more efficiently than sampling
claim_source: Figure 2, page 7 (more widths and depths in Figure 7, page 19)

official.background: Expected losses in machine learning are almost always estimated by sampling inputs and averaging, which needs about 1/ε² forward passes to reach mean squared error ε² and essentially never sees events rarer than 1/N. When the input distribution is known in closed form, an analytic ("mechanistic") approximation could do better in principle, but it was not known whether such methods can beat sampling for neural networks at equal compute. This paper studies the simplest case: the expected output of a fixed random-weight MLP under standard Gaussian inputs.
official.method:
Cumulant propagation tracks approximate cumulants up to order K of the activations at each layer instead of running samples through the network. Matrix multiplications update the cumulant tensors by multilinearity (einsums with K copies of the weight matrix). Activation functions update them with a truncated Hermite-expansion 'diagram summation' formula. Two fixes make the error shrink with width: Hermite expansions of powers of the activation (power cumulants), and, for odd K, tracking the full trace of the (K+1)-order cumulant tensor. The final first-order cumulant is the estimate. The factorized version stores the K-th-order tensor (K ≥ 3) in a factored form of size n^(K-1), which cuts runtime by a factor of about n. The augmented version tracks more of the (K+1)-order tensor.

Setup: bias-free ReLU MLPs with input, hidden and output width n = 256 and weights drawn i.i.d. from N(0, 2/n), with K = 1..4 and 5 random weight seeds. Ground truth is Monte Carlo with 2^34 samples. MSE is averaged over output neurons and seeds and divided by the variance of a single forward pass ('variance-normalized'), so N-sample Monte Carlo has normalized MSE of exactly 1/N. Compute is counted in FLOPs with an extended PyTorch FLOP counter, with redundant symmetric-tensor FLOPs removed (Appendix J). The baseline is plain Monte Carlo sampling at the same FLOP budget. Quasi-Monte Carlo (scrambled Sobol) is also shown.
official.claim: On random ReLU MLPs of width 256 with 2 hidden layers, factorized cumulant propagation (K = 1-4) reaches variance-normalized MSE roughly 300x to 8,000x lower than Monte Carlo sampling at the same FLOP count (paper: 'around 1,000'). Example: K = 3 gives MSE ~3e-8 at ~2e9 FLOPs, where sampling gives ~2.5e-4. At 4 hidden layers the gap is about 10-100x.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Performance of all versions of our algorithm for different networks of width 256 and K varying from 1 to 4. All 4 versions are identical for K = 1, and the factorized versions are identical to their unfactorized counterparts for K = 2. (Error bars hidden because they would be too small to be readable.)
official.metric: Variance-normalized mean squared error of the estimated expected output (lower is better), averaged over all output neurons and 5 random weight seeds; plotted against FLOPs on log-log axes. Error bars (±1 SE over seeds) are omitted because they are too small to see; values are read off the plot and approximate.

title: D-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continuously Tuning Step-Distilled Diffusion Models

official.background: Open text-to-image models are moving to step-distilled few-step versions (e.g. Z-Image-Turbo, FLUX.2-klein) that sample in 4-8 steps. Users want to fine-tune them on their own image-text pairs to add a concept, style or domain. Standard flow-matching fine-tuning (SFT) trains on noised versions of the target images instead of the states the few-step sampler actually visits, and in practice it breaks the distilled few-step ability, giving blurry images. Online RL avoids this mismatch but needs a reward function that ordinary users do not have.
official.method:
D-OPSD treats one model as both student and teacher. Both models use the diffusion model's LLM/VLM encoder. The student is conditioned only on the text-prompt feature (Qwen3-4B). The teacher is an EMA copy of the student (momentum 0.9999) conditioned on a multimodal feature of the prompt plus the target image, produced by Qwen3-VL-4B with its LLM weights replaced by Qwen3-4B. Without any training, this multimodal conditioning already makes the model generate variations that keep the target concept or style. For each training pair, the student rolls out its own few-step trajectory from noise with the inference sampler. At every visited state, both branches predict a velocity, and the student is trained with the mean over steps of ||u_student - stopgrad(u_teacher)||^2. At inference the teacher is discarded and the text-only few-step pipeline is used unchanged.

LoRA setting (Table 1): rank 64 / alpha 128, batch size 4, 1K iterations on one H800. The learning rate is 4e-5 for Z-Image-Turbo (8 steps) and 1e-5 for FLUX.2-klein-4B (4 steps). Training and evaluation use DreamBooth-style data, with results averaged over 30 concept classes and 10 style classes. Metrics: DINO-D (DINOv3-ViT-S-plus cosine distance to targets on paraphrased training prompts), LPIPS-D (VGG), VLM-J (Qwen3-VL-8B 1-4 concept-similarity score on novel prompts), CLIP-S (DFN-CLIP-H on the novel prompts), and Quality-S / Aesthetic-S from an internal VLM reward model. Baselines: vanilla SFT, SFT on the multi-step model plus LoRA applied to the distilled model, DreamBooth, and PSO, all sampled with the same few-step inference settings.
official.claim: In LoRA customization of Z-Image-Turbo (8-step), D-OPSD learns the target concept (DINO-D 0.0823 vs 0.2212, VLM-J 3.33 vs 1.33 for vanilla SFT; PSO is better on DINO-D at 0.0570) while keeping few-step quality (Quality-S 3.80 vs 2.42 for SFT, 3.61 for SFT + LoRA on distilled, 3.51 for the base model), and has the highest prompt following of all methods (CLIP-S 0.3664 vs 0.3328 for DreamBooth and 0.2893 for PSO).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: System-level comparison against baseline methods in LoRA training settings. The best and second-best results on each metric are highlighted in bold and underlined.
official.metric: DINO-D and LPIPS-D (lower is better), VLM-J, CLIP-S, Quality-S, Aesthetic-S (higher is better); averaged over 30 concept and 10 style classes; single runs, no error bars reported
official.comparison: D-OPSD vs. Base model, Vanilla SFT, SFT + LoRA on distilled, DreamBooth, PSO, all LoRA-trained on the same few-shot data and sampled with the same few-step settings; repeated on FLUX.2-klein-4B
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same LoRA setup, D-OPSD does not reduce DINO-D far below vanilla SFT (e.g. not below ~0.15), or its images lose few-step quality like SFT does (judged by an open quality/aesthetic scorer), or DreamBooth/PSO match or beat its CLIP-S on novel prompts.

title: SDFlow: Similarity-Driven Flow Matching for Time Series Generation

official.background: Unconditional time-series generation is used to make synthetic data for finance, healthcare and energy. A strong recent approach (SDformer) tokenizes a series with a VQ-VAE and then generates the token sequence autoregressively with a transformer. Autoregressive generation suffers from exposure bias: the model is trained on ground-truth prefixes but samples from its own predictions, so errors can compound over long sequences. This paper asks whether replacing the autoregressive token model with a non-autoregressive flow-matching model in the same VQ latent space fixes the degradation on long sequences.
official.method:
Stage 1 is the similarity-driven (cosine) VQ-VAE tokenizer from SDformer, with codebook size K = 512, embedding dimension d_c = 512 and downsampling rate s = 4. It is trained and then frozen. Stage 2 (SDFlow) learns a flow in the frozen latent space. A low-rank factorization Z ≈ U V^T (rank r, learned end-to-end with the flow loss and with mean/variance regularization on U) defines anchor coordinates. A kernel-smoothed prior over the anchor coordinates (bandwidth h tied to the mean nearest-neighbour distance) gives the starting point z0 = normalize(u V^T). A DiT network (AdaLN time conditioning) outputs per-position logits over codebook indices. It is trained with cross-entropy to the true VQ indices (variational / categorical flow matching), and the velocity is (E_q[c] - z_t)/(1 - t). Sampling uses 20 Euler steps, then snaps each latent to the nearest codebook entry by cosine similarity and decodes with the frozen VQ-VAE decoder.

For long sequences (L = 64, 128, 256 on ETTh and Energy), the flow model uses 3 DiT layers, d_model = 1024 and 16 heads, with rank 512 for L = 128 and 1024 for L = 256. The baseline SDformer-ar uses the same tokenizer with an autoregressive transformer over the tokens. Metrics are Discriminative Score, Predictive Score (TSTR) and Context-FID, reported as mean ± std over 5 runs.
official.claim: For unconditional generation of length-256 sequences, SDFlow reaches Context-FID 0.001 ± .000 on ETTh and 0.002 ± .000 on Energy, versus 0.021 ± .001 and 0.041 ± .003 for the autoregressive SDformer-ar with the same VQ-VAE tokenizer (about a 95% reduction).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Unconditional long-sequence generation results (L = 64, 128, 256). Best results in bold, second best underlined. Lower is better for all metrics. Results show mean ± std over 5 runs.
official.metric: Context-FID (lower is better), mean ± std over 5 runs (seeds). Discriminative and Predictive Scores are also reported.
official.comparison: SDFlow (non-autoregressive categorical flow matching in the frozen VQ latent space) vs. SDformer-ar (autoregressive transformer over the same VQ tokens), at L = 256 on ETTh and Energy. Other baselines in the table: TimeMAR-L, FlowTS, Diffusion-TS, DiffTime, DiffWave, TimeVAE, COT-GAN, TimeGAN.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same tokenizer and 5 seeds at L = 256, SDFlow's Context-FID is not clearly below SDformer-ar's (e.g. it does not come out at least several times lower, outside the seed std), on ETTh or on Energy.

title: Transformers Provably Implement In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Policy Improvement
claim_source: Table 1, page 33 (Appendix K.2); summarized in Section 4.3

official.background: Transformers can learn in context: they adapt to a new task from examples in the prompt without any weight updates. For supervised learning, it is known that linear-attention transformers can implement gradient descent on the in-context examples and can be trained to do so. For in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL), prior theory showed only that a linear-attention block can implement TD policy evaluation, and only that the right parameters form an invariant set. It did not show that a block can implement policy improvement, or that training actually reaches those parameters.
official.method:
The authors build explicit weights (P*, V*) for a one-layer, single-head linear self-attention block, Hout = H + (1/n)(VH)(H^T P H). Given a prompt that encodes an n-step trajectory window and the current parameters, the block outputs exactly the batch semi-gradient SARSA update of a linear Q-function weight w (Thm 3.1), or the batch actor-critic update of (lambda, w) (Thm 3.3). Only the sub-blocks P12 and V-bar21 matter; the other blocks are inert. They prove that gradient flow on a teacher-mimicking loss (the squared error between the transformer output and the analytical update) converges locally and exponentially to the manifold of equivalent constructions (P, V) -> (cP, V/c).

Experiment: each training task is a random tabular MDP with 9 states, 4 actions and gamma = 0.5. P0 and the transition kernel are drawn from a flat Dirichlet, and rewards are drawn from Unif(-1, 1). Feature maps and initial weights are drawn from Unif(-1, 1). Trajectory windows have n = 20, and behavior is epsilon-greedy (SARSA) or softmax with epsilon = 0.1 (actor-critic). For SARSA, d = 36, alpha = 0.2 and D = 110. For actor-critic, m = 36, d = 9, beta = 0.8, alpha = 0.2 and D = 101. The inert blocks are initialized to zero and P12 and V-bar21 are Xavier-normal (gain 0.1). Training uses Adam with lr 1e-3, decayed by a factor of 0.99 every 10 MDPs, over K independently sampled MDPs. Recovery is measured as the scale-invariant cosine similarity between each learned effective block and its analytical counterpart.
official.claim: When a one-layer linear self-attention block is trained to mimic the analytical updates on K = 5,000 random tabular MDPs, its effective blocks match the theoretical construction exactly up to scale: cosine similarity is 1.000 for both P12 and V-bar21, in both the SARSA and the actor-critic setting. Similarity rises monotonically with K: at K = 100 it is only 0.411 for P12 and 0.856 for V-bar21 (SARSA).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Cosine similarity between the learned effective blocks and the theoretical constructions in (5) (SARSA) and (15) (actor-critic), as a function of the number of training tasks K.
official.metric: Cosine similarity <A, A*>_F / (||A||_F ||A*||_F) between learned and analytical blocks (higher is better; 1 = exact member of the construction family). Single run per K; no seeds or error bars reported.
official.comparison: Learned effective blocks (P12, V-bar21) vs. the closed-form constructions in Eq. (5) (SARSA) and Eq. (15) (actor-critic), across training budgets K = 100, 500, 1,000, 5,000
official.falsification_criterion: Re-training with the stated setup at K = 5,000 gives a cosine similarity clearly below 1 (for example below 0.99) for any of the four blocks. The claim is also refuted if the result depends on the seed, or if the similarity does not increase with K.

title: CITE: Anytime Valid Statistical Inference in LLM Self-Consistency
claim_source: Table 8 (Appendix G.2), page 52; Case B false-certification rates in Table 3, page 50; summarized in Section 6, page 11

official.background: Self-consistency improves LLM reasoning by sampling many answers and taking the majority vote. Adaptive variants stop sampling early once the vote looks settled, but data-dependent stopping breaks fixed-sample error guarantees, and the set of possible answers is not known in advance and keeps growing as sampling continues. In high-stakes uses such as emergency-room triage, one wants to certify that a given answer is the unique mode of the model's answer distribution, with the false-certification probability provably below a level epsilon under any stopping rule, and without spending too many samples.
official.method:
CITE tests H0: p_r <= sup_{a != r} p_a for a target label r fixed in advance, over a countable and unknown set of categories, using i.i.d. samples. It combines three time-uniform processes, each at level epsilon/3: (i) a pairwise mixture e-process E_t = sum_lambda w_lambda (1+lambda)^{N_t(r)} (1-lambda)^{N_t(a_hat)} against the current empirical runner-up a_hat, over a finite lambda grid; (ii) a lower confidence bound L_t on p_r, from a betting mixture e-process M_t(q) = sum_lambda v_lambda prod_i (1 + lambda(1{X_i=r} - q)), with L_t = sup{q <= p_hat_t(r) : M_t(q) >= 3/epsilon}; (iii) an upper bound on the mass of any unseen category, U_t = min{u : u^{-1}(1-u)^t <= epsilon/3}. CITE stops and certifies r at the first t where E_t >= 3/epsilon and L_t > U_t (Algorithm 1).

In the simulation study, answers are drawn from synthetic categorical distributions whose tails follow a capped shifted-Zipf law (Appendix G.1, Table 2). Setting 5 ('Moderate LLM-like') has K = 1000 categories, p_r = 0.35, modal gap delta = 0.15, and a Zipf(1.2) tail on 997 labels. Case A sets the target to the true mode and measures the certification rate (power) within a budget of N samples. Case B sets the target to a non-mode and measures the false-certification rate. The baselines, all at epsilon = 0.05, are Bonferroni (fixed-sample union bound), KR (Kim and Ramdas 2025, a fixed-target sample-split test that is not anytime-valid), and MMC (Cordero-Encinar and Duncan 2025, a sequential leader-tracking certificate).
official.claim: In simulation Setting 5 (K=1000, p_r=0.35, delta=0.15, Zipf-1.2 tail) at epsilon=0.05, CITE certifies the true mode with rate 0.932 at N=512 and 1.00 at N>=1024 (mean stopping time about 259), while the sequential baseline MMC stays at 0.002 for every N up to 2048 and fixed-sample Bonferroni reaches 0.874 at N=512. CITE's false-certification rate is 0.000 at every budget (Table 3).
official.claim_caption: Table 8. Setting 5 (Moderate LLM-like): certification rate, Case A.
official.metric: Certification rate (fraction of Monte Carlo runs that certify the true mode within budget N; higher is better). Case B false-certification rate should be <= 0.05. No error bars or replicate counts are reported for the simulations (the 0.002 granularity suggests about 500 runs per cell).
official.comparison: CITE vs. MMC (sequential, leader-tracking) and fixed-sample Bonferroni on the same synthetic distribution, at the same epsilon and budgets N in {64, ..., 2048}. KR is shown too, but it is not anytime-valid.
official.falsification_criterion: A faithful reimplementation of CITE on Setting 5 certifies the mode in well under 90% of runs at N=512 or under 100% at N=1024; or a faithful MMC implementation reaches a certification rate comparable to CITE's at N >= 512; or CITE's Case B false-certification rate exceeds 0.05.

title: Normalized Architectures are Natively 4-Bit

official.background: Training LLMs in 4-bit floating point (NVFP4, natively supported on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs) saves compute and memory, but standard transformers trained fully in NVFP4 tend to lose quality or diverge unless extra machinery is added: randomized Hadamard transforms (RHT) to spread outliers, dynamic per-tensor scaling, and stochastic rounding. These add overhead. The paper asks whether an architecture can be intrinsically robust to 4-bit arithmetic, and studies nGPT, a transformer whose weights and hidden states are constrained to the unit hypersphere.
official.method:
The analysis uses two 12-layer, hidden-size D = 4096, 3.6B-parameter models built on nanoGPT: a standard GPT and an nGPT (weights normalized along the embedding dim after every step, normalized residual updates with learnable interpolation, normalized and rescaled q/k, no RMSNorm/LayerNorm, no weight decay or warmup; in this paper all GEMM inputs are normalized, including the attention out-projection and FFN2 inputs, unlike the official nGPT). After training (the paper does not state the data or budget for these analysis models; its Section 5 training runs use Nemotron pretraining data), weights w and activations x of every forward matmul are quantized to NVFP4 and the SNR = ||T||^2 / ||T - T_hat||^2 (in dB) is measured at four stages: individual weights, individual activations, element-wise products w_k x_k, and the full dot product sum_k w_k x_k vs. sum_k w_hat_k x_hat_k, averaged over all 12 layers (Figure 1 does not name the inputs used; the related Figure 2 analysis uses validation activations).

The paper's explanation is that per-element quantization error is the same for both models, but in nGPT the products w_k x_k have weak positive pairwise correlation (rho_s about 1.3e-3 vs. 9.3e-5 for GPT) so the signal adds coherently across D terms while the noise stays uncorrelated, giving a larger 'averaging gain' from product-level to dot-product SNR.
official.claim: In 3.6B-parameter (12-layer, D = 4096) nanoGPT-based models under NVFP4 quantization, element-wise SNRs are about equal for GPT and nGPT (weights 19.3/19.3 dB, products 16.4/16.6 dB), but the full dot-product SNR is 26.0 dB for nGPT vs. 18.6 dB for GPT (a 7.4 dB gap), and nGPT is higher in every one of the 12 layers.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: (a): SNR at each stage of a matrix multiplication under NVFP4, averaged over all 12 layers. The first three stages (individual weights, activations, and their products) are identical for both models. The difference appears only at the final summation step. (b): Dot product SNR under NVFP4 at each layer. nGPT maintains a consistent ~7 dB advantage in all layers. Both graphs are based on a 3.6B model, built on the nanoGPT baseline [9].
official.metric: SNR in dB = 10 log10(||T||^2 / ||T - T_hat||^2), higher is better; averaged over validation activations and all forward matmuls; no error bars, seeds or spread reported
official.comparison: nGPT vs. standard GPT of the same size and depth, both after training, both quantized with NVFP4; stages: weights, activations, element-wise products, full dot product

title: Fast Gauss-Newton for Multiclass Cross-Entropy
claim_source: Table 2, page 27 (also stated in Section 5.2, page 10, and Figure 3a, page 9)

official.background: Second-order optimizers based on the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix are a natural fit for softmax cross-entropy, but in the multiclass case the GGN contains the C x C softmax covariance diag(p) - pp^T. Every curvature-vector product therefore has to pass through all C logits, so even matrix-free conjugate-gradient (CG) solvers become more expensive as the number of classes grows. A cheaper curvature model that keeps the exact loss and gradient could make Gauss-Newton training faster without hurting accuracy.
official.method:
The paper writes softmax cross-entropy exactly as softplus(s), where s = logsumexp of the competitor logits minus the true-class logit. It shows that the multiclass GGN splits exactly into H_FGN = p_true * p_rest * J_s^T J_s (a rank-one true-vs-rest term per example) plus a positive semidefinite within-competitor covariance term. Fast Gauss-Newton (FGN) keeps only the first term; the loss and gradient are unchanged. Because each example contributes one Jacobian row, the damped step (H_FGN + lambda I) d = -g reduces to a b x b whitened row-space system (K + b*lambda I) u = r~, which is solved with matrix-free CG using JVPs/VJPs of the margin map, then back-projected to d = -J~^T u.

For the chosen claim, an affine softmax head (2048 x 196 weights plus bias, 401,604 parameters) is trained on frozen, standardized ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 average-pooled features for Cars196 (8144 train / 8041 test). Baselines are SGN (stochastic Gauss-Newton with the full softmax GGN, parameter-space CG, warm-started) and Adam (lr 3e-4). SGN and FGN both use step size 0.1, constant damping lambda = 1, at most 5 CG iterations, tolerance 1e-5; FGN uses a closed-form row-space Gram K_ij = sqrt(q_i q_j)(h_i^T h_j + 1)(a_i^T a_j) and no warm start. Batch size 128, 9600 steps (150 epochs), 10 seeds. Accuracy is interpolated on a wall-time grid and reported at the shared 7.27 s horizon; wall time excludes feature extraction, compilation and evaluation. Run on one RTX A4000.
official.claim: On Cars196 frozen-feature head optimization, FGN matches full-GGN SGN test accuracy at the 7.27 s horizon (44.43 ± 0.07% vs. 44.33 ± 0.10%) while reaching 43% and 44% test accuracy sooner in wall time (1.41 s and 3.45 s vs. 1.97 s and 4.44 s).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Frozen-feature head optimization on Cars196. Test accuracy and cross-entropy at the shared 7.27 s horizon, reported as mean ±1 standard deviation over 10 seeds. Threshold times are in seconds.
official.metric: Test accuracy (%) at a shared 7.27 s wall-time horizon (higher is better), mean ± 1 std over 10 seeds; time (s) for the seed-mean accuracy curve to reach 42/43/44% (lower is better), single numbers with no error bars
official.comparison: FGN vs. SGN (full softmax GGN, same step size, damping and CG cap) and Adam, under matched batch size, steps and features
official.falsification_criterion: FGN's final test accuracy is clearly below SGN's (by more than about 2 seed std, i.e. more than ~0.2 points), or with matched settings FGN does not reach 43% and 44% test accuracy faster than SGN in wall time (equivalently, FGN's per-step update is not cheaper than SGN's).

title: The Pareto Frontier of Randomized Learning-Augmented Online Bidding
claim_source: Figure 2, page 8 (Section 6); text states the σ² ≤ 1.19 crossover

official.background: In online bidding, a player submits an increasing sequence of bids until one reaches an unknown threshold u, and pays the sum of all bids made so far. The goal is to keep this cost small relative to u. Many problems reduce to it, including incremental clustering, searching on a line and interruptible algorithms. In the learning-augmented version, the algorithm gets a prediction û of the threshold. It should do well when the prediction is right (consistency C) and still have a worst-case guarantee when it is wrong (robustness R). For randomized algorithms the best possible C for a given R was unknown. The best previous algorithm was the piecewise-exponential randomized sequence of Angelopoulos et al. (class D).
official.method:
The paper represents a randomized bidding sequence by a nondecreasing 'bidding function' B: bids are B(i + λ) for i in Z, with λ ~ U[0,1]. For R ≥ 2/ln 2 ≈ 2.885, the proposed function A (Definition 3) is 1 on [0,1], equals e^{(t-1)/w̄} for t ≥ 1, and for t ≤ 0 equals p_k(s) with k = ⌈−t⌉ and s the fractional part of −t, where p_0 = 1, p_1(s) = x(μ − 1 + s), p_{k+1}(s) = p_k(0) − x∫_s^1 p_k(u) du (this solves the delay differential equation R·B'(t) = B(t+1)). Here x = 1/R, μ = R − w̄, and w̄ = −1/W_0(−1/R) (principal Lambert branch; the larger root of w·e^{1/w} = R, ≈ 2.80 at R = 4). Theorem 6 proves cons(A) = R − w̄ and rob(A) = R. Two comparison classes are also defined: D, functions that are exponential on each [i, i+1) with a constant ratio B(t+1)/B(t), which captures the prior method of [7]; and I, continuous functions that are exponential on each [i, i+1). For each class the best R-robust member is used (Appendix A.1).

Numerical evaluation (Section 6): the oracle outputs û, and the true threshold is u = û·exp(η) with η ~ N(0, σ²), so σ² measures prediction error. The plotted quantity is the expected normalized cost E[cost(X,u)/u] over the bid randomness and the noise, at robustness R = 4, for σ² in [0, 4]. Crosses at σ² = 0 mark each algorithm's theoretical consistency. Appendix D repeats this for R = 3 and R = 2.73.
official.claim: At robustness R = 4 with log-normal prediction noise u = û·exp(η), η ~ N(0, σ²), algorithm A has the lowest expected normalized cost of the three algorithms for every σ² ≤ 1.19. For example, at σ² = 0.5 it scores about 2.47, against about 2.62 for I and about 2.72 (≈ e) for the prior state-of-the-art D.

official.falsification_criterion: A correct implementation of A, D and I at R = 4 gives A an expected normalized cost at or above D or I for some σ² ≤ 1.19, or puts the A-vs-D crossover far from σ² ≈ 1.19. A theoretical consistency of A different from R − w̄ ≈ 1.2 (with w̄ = −1/W_0(−1/4) ≈ 2.80, the largest root of w·e^{1/w} = 4) would also refute it.

title: AffectGPT-RL: Revealing Roles of Reinforcement Learning in Open-Vocabulary Emotion Recognition
claim_source: Table 5, page 9 (run-to-run spread in Table 4, page 9; same SFT vs. RL numbers in Table 7, page 23)

official.background: Open-vocabulary multimodal emotion recognition (OV-MER) asks a model to describe a person's emotion in a video clip with free-form emotion words rather than one of six fixed labels. Because synonyms are allowed, it is scored with emotion-wheel (EW) metrics that group predicted and true words into emotion-wheel clusters before computing an F1-style overlap. Prior generative models (e.g. AffectGPT) are trained with token-level cross-entropy, which does not match these metrics ("joyful" and "awful" share tokens but not meaning), and the EW metrics are not differentiable. The paper asks whether reinforcement learning that uses the EW metric directly as a reward closes this gap.
official.method:
AffectGPT-RL keeps the AffectGPT multimodal architecture (audio, video and text encoders feeding a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct LLM, default AffectGPT hyperparameters). Stage 1 (cold start) is supervised training on MER-Caption+ (31,327 clips with emotion descriptions and open-vocabulary labels). Stage 2 is GRPO (G = 4 samples per input, lr 1e-5, batch size 1, one A100) on MER2025-OV (1,000 clips with human-annotated open-vocabulary labels), with the accuracy reward R = EW(predicted emotion words, ground-truth words), the average F1 over 5 emotion wheels. In the default setting the model outputs only the answer (no <think> block), as Section 4.2 found that removing the reasoning trace improves results; optional length penalties P1-P3 counter the tendency to list many synonyms.

The control in Table 5 is plain AffectGPT (token-level SFT) trained either on MER-Caption+ alone or on MER-Caption+ followed by MER2025-OV, so the RL model and the stronger control see the same data. All models are evaluated on OV-MERD+ (532 clips) with the EW metric (audio, video and text inputs; Table 5 does not state the modality, but its 62.52 SFT entry matches the audio-video-text AffectGPT row of Table 3).

title: Secure Seed-Based Multi-bit Watermarking for Diffusion Models from First Principles

official.background: Seed-based watermarking for diffusion models (Tree-Rings, Gaussian-Shading, PRC watermarks) hides a message in the initial noise seed and recovers it by inverting the diffusion process. These schemes are usually judged by empirical robustness and image quality (FID), which depend on the diffusion model, solver and VAE used. Their security is argued in cryptographic terms. The authors argue that this setup cannot rank schemes, and that encrypting the message does not stop a spoofing attacker. Gaussian-Shading and PRC leave the encrypted codeword readable as the sign of the seed, so a single watermarked image is enough to forge new seeds carrying the same codeword.
official.method:
The paper models the decision step as binary symmetric channels whose flip probability p(σ) depends on the noise variance σ² that inversion plus an image edit adds in latent space. It scores schemes by Shannon capacity, by fidelity (KL divergence of the watermarked seed distribution from N(0, I)), and by a security ratio η: the number of watermarked samples, in units of the latent size L, that a PCA attacker needs before an eigenvalue of the empirical seed covariance leaves the Marchenko-Pastur support. The proposed SSB scheme samples each codeword bit (z_u)_i from a mixture of truncated Gaussians restricted to the correct cells of a coarse alternating lattice of cell size Δ, nested with a fine lattice of size δ (Algorithm 1). The seed is z = (I − UUᵀ)z′ + U z_u, where the secret key U is an L×M′ matrix with columns summing to one. Decoding applies the coarse lattice function to Uᵀ f(x), where f is inverse flow matching with the Euler solver. (Δ, δ) = (+∞, +∞) reduces to the sign decision of Gaussian-Shading. (1.6, 0) gives watermarked coordinates with unit variance, which the paper calls perfect security (η = +∞).

Empirical validation (Section 4.2): for each scheme, 500 images are generated with Sana 600M 512px (25 steps, latent size L = 8192) from Gustavosta/Stable-Diffusion-Prompts. The images are optionally transformed (brightness 0.2, JPEG QF80/QF50, contrast 2.0, center crop 50%) and then inverted. The empirical codeword bit accuracy 1 − p(σ) is computed and compared with the theoretical value at the σ² from Table 1. Rate, fidelity loss and security ratio are derived from it. SSB is assumed to work at Shannon capacity, Gaussian-Shading uses its repetition code at decoding error ≤ 1e-6, and PRC uses BP+OSD at ≤ 1e-2.
official.claim: On 500 Sana-generated images with no transformation, (1.6, 0)-SSB reaches a codeword bit accuracy of about 0.92, versus about 0.86 for both Gaussian-Shading and (+∞, +∞)-SSB, while being perfectly secure against the PCA attack (η = +∞ vs. η ≈ 4 for (+∞, +∞)-SSB and ≈ 0 for Gaussian-Shading and PRC). For the identity, brightness, JPEG and contrast transforms, the empirical bit accuracies match the theoretical predictions from Table 1's noise variances to within a few hundredths (the 50% center crop is the exception: theory predicts ~0.7 for (+∞, +∞)-SSB, but every scheme is at chance empirically).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Empirical validation of the model defined in Section 2 for current seed-based approaches – Gaussian-Shading and PRC – as well as our method SSB. Transparent boxes correspond to theoretical values, opaque to empirical ones. We display 95% asymptotic confidence intervals.
official.metric: Codeword bit accuracy 1 − p(σ), higher is better. Opaque bars are empirical and transparent bars are theoretical; error bars are 95% asymptotic confidence intervals. Values are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: (1.6, 0)-SSB vs. (+∞, +∞)-SSB vs. Gaussian-Shading (vs. PRC for rate and security), with the same Sana model, prompts and inversion pipeline. Each scheme's empirical result is also compared with its theoretical prediction.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same Sana inversion setup and no transformation, (1.6, 0)-SSB's bit accuracy is not clearly above Gaussian-Shading's (gap under ~0.03 or overlapping CIs). Or, for a transform other than the 50% center crop, the empirical bit accuracy of a scheme differs from its theoretical value 1 − p(σ), computed with Proposition 2 at the measured σ², by more than ~0.03. Or a PCA attack on (1.6, 0)-SSB seeds shows outlier eigenvalues outside the Marchenko-Pastur support.

title: In-Context Black-Box Optimization with Unreliable Feedback

official.background: In Bayesian optimization of expensive experiments, a cheap auxiliary signal is often available, such as an expert, a simulator, a low-fidelity model or a related task. It can speed up search when it is aligned with the objective, but it can also mislead the search when it is biased, and its reliability is unknown in advance. Existing feedback-aware BO methods such as pi-BO weight the feedback with a fixed, hand-set decay schedule, and amortized (in-context) optimizers usually ignore auxiliary feedback altogether. This paper asks whether an in-context optimizer pretrained on many tasks with feedback of varying reliability can learn to trust or discount a feedback source on the fly, based on how well it agrees with the objective values observed so far.
official.method:
FICBO is a transformer-based, pool-based in-context optimizer. Every candidate token embeds its features x and the auxiliary feedback u(x), and observed history points also embed y. A policy head outputs a categorical distribution over the remaining candidates and is trained with REINFORCE on the improvement reward, and a Gaussian-mixture inference head is trained with NLL. Pretraining uses synthetic GP tasks drawn from a 'feedback prior' that controls how the source relates to the objective. The Mixture prior builds the source from a masked, reweighted mix of real and decoy latent GP components. The Additive prior gives the source different input features and a relevance weight w, and (in the full model) passes the degraded source signal through an amortized GP fitted once to source-private points, whose predictive mean is the feedback. Both priors then apply random degradations: noise, constant shift, additive GP bias, local distortion and catastrophic failure.

Airfoil Lift evaluation: maximize the lift-to-drag ratio C_L/C_D from a large NeuralFoil model over (angle of attack, thickness, camber), d=3, with a pool of 300 candidates and horizon T=30. The feedback is C_L alone, which keeps favoring high angles of attack past the true C_L/C_D optimum. Baselines use the same pool and the same initial points: pi-BO-EI and pi-BO-UCB (a GP-prior in-context surrogate whose EI/UCB is multiplied by softmax(u)^(beta/(t+1)), beta=2), greedy ranking by feedback, and random search. The metric is cumulative normalized simple regret after 30 steps, over 100 replicas.
official.claim: On Airfoil Lift (lift-only feedback that is structurally biased against the C_L/C_D objective), FICBO with the Mixture prior reaches a final cumulative regret of 3.617 ± 2.401, versus 7.807 ± 2.486 for pi-BO-EI, 8.167 ± 2.834 for pi-BO-UCB, 24.179 ± 5.486 for greedy feedback and 12.692 ± 7.489 for random search.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Final cumulative regret (↓) on Airfoil Small and Airfoil Lift. Mean ± std over 100 seeds. (a) The direct-source branch of Eq. (12) is used.
official.metric: Final normalized cumulative regret after T=30 steps (lower is better); ± is the std across 100 replicas (per-replica spread, not standard error).
official.comparison: FICBO (Mixture prior) vs. pi-BO-EI (strongest baseline listed in Table 4), with pi-BO-UCB, greedy Feedback and Random as additional references; all run on the same candidate pools and initial observations.
official.falsification_criterion: Over 100 replicas on Airfoil Lift, the mean final cumulative regret of FICBO (Mixture) is not clearly below pi-BO-EI's (e.g., the gap is under one per-replica std, or FICBO's mean is above about 5.5), or FICBO's regret approaches the greedy-feedback baseline, which would mean it follows the misleading lift signal.
