title: TIDE: Every Layer Knows the Token Beneath the Context

official.background: In a standard transformer LLM, the token index is looked up once at the input embedding layer and never consulted again. The authors argue this causes two problems: rare tokens' embeddings receive far less gradient signal than common ones and stay under-trained (Zipf's law), and distinct tokens that appear in near-identical contexts (e.g. 'their'/'there', '1847'/'1851') end up with nearly indistinguishable hidden states at depth, which no Lipschitz FFN can separate. They propose re-injecting a context-free token-identity signal at every layer.
official.method:
TIDE adds an EmbeddingMemory to a LLaMA-style transformer: K independent embedding tables E_k (|V| x d_b, each followed by RMSNorm) are looked up once per forward pass from the raw token indices. At every layer, a per-layer linear router takes the post-attention normalized hidden state and outputs softmax weights over the K blocks plus a parameter-free 'null bank' (a zero vector). The routed memory vector is added to the residual stream alongside the FFN output: h_l = h~_l + FFN(RMSNorm(h~_l)) + sum_k alpha_k^l M_k(v). Variants are named TIDE-KE-<size> (K = 2, 4, 8, 16, 24).

Baseline and TIDE models are trained from scratch with the same configuration (Table 7): DCLM-baseline-1.0, Llama-3.1 tokenizer (128,256 vocab), sequence length 2048, Adam (beta 0.9/0.95, wd 0.1), cosine LR 1e-4 to 1e-5 with 10k warmup, z-loss 1e-6, 400-500B tokens. Models are evaluated zero-shot on ARC-C, ARC-E, BoolQ, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, OBQA, PIQA and SciQ (normalized accuracy except BoolQ and LAMBADA), plus LAMBADA perplexity.
official.claim: At the 1B scale under the same training recipe, TIDE-8E-1B beats LLaMA-Base-1B on LAMBADA perplexity (4.89 vs. 5.19) and on the 8-task zero-shot average (63.0 vs. 61.4), and every TIDE-1B variant in Table 2 (K = 2, 8, 16, 24) improves both metrics, with K = 24 reaching 4.60 PPL and a 63.7 average.
official.claim_caption: Table 2 Benchmark results for LLaMA-Base and TIDE variants at 750M, 1B and 3B parameter scales. PPL is LAMBDA perplexity (lower is better); BoolQ and LAMBADA use accuracy; all other columns use normalized accuracy (%). Best results per scale are bolded.
official.metric: LAMBADA perplexity (lower is better) and mean zero-shot accuracy over 8 tasks (higher is better, %); single runs, no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported

title: Joint Consistency: A Unified Test-Time Aggregation Framework via Energy Minimization

official.background: Test-time aggregation produces several reasoning traces for one question and combines them into a single final answer. Common rules are majority vote over final answers (Self-Consistency), majority vote weighted by a per-trace quality score (Weighted Self-Consistency), and Best-of-N. All of these score each trace on its own. Pairwise judgments ('is response 1 better than response 2?') may be more reliable than absolute scores, but there was no principled and affordable way to combine many of them into one answer. Knockout tournaments use pairwise judgments but can drop the correct answer after a single noisy comparison.
official.method:
Joint Consistency (JC) chooses one answer group by minimizing an Ising-type energy H(x) = −μ⟨h, x⟩ − xᵀJx over indicator vectors x = 1_{I_k}, where I_k is the set of traces whose final answer is a(k). The external field h_i is an LLM-judge score in {0, 0.1, ..., 1.0} for each trace, judged alone (prompt in Appendix E.1.1). The interaction matrix is J = CCᵀ with C_ij = sqrt(p(y_i ⪰ y_j) / (n_i² n_j)), where p(y_i ⪰ y_j) is the judge's stated probability that trace i is better than trace j (prompt in Appendix E.1.2) and n_i is the size of trace i's answer group. Because there are only K feasible x, the minimization is exact and takes O(K) time. To keep the cost down, pairwise judgments are made between answer groups by sampling a constant number of traces from each group, and only among the top-κ most frequent answers. With J ≡ 0, JC reduces to WSC, and with h ≡ 1 as well it reduces to Self-Consistency.

For Table 2, models in MathArena are ranked by their AIME 2025 Pass@1 and only traces from the R lowest-ranked models are kept (R ∈ {3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30}). All other settings are the same as the MathArena-Full experiment: the judge is GPT-OSS-20B with low reasoning effort at temperature 1.0 for both h and J, results are repeated over 10 independent trials, and KT's pairwise budget is matched to the sampling budget used for J. The baselines are Pass@1, Best-of-N (highest h), Knockout Tournament, Self-Consistency and WSC.
official.claim: When aggregating MathArena traces from only the R lowest-ranked generator models, JC (GPT-OSS-20B judge) beats Weighted Self-Consistency with the same judge: 61.3±4.9 vs. 51.6±4.9 at R = 10, 80.0±4.0 vs. 68.7±4.6 at R = 15, 90.0±3.0 vs. 77.7±4.2 at R = 20, and 96.0±2.0 vs. 88.2±3.2 at R = 30.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance of TTA methods on traces from lower-tier models. R denotes the subset of the R lowest-ranked models whose traces are aggregated, and models are ranked by their Pass@1 accuracy on AIME 2025.
official.metric: Final-answer accuracy (%) after aggregation, higher is better; ± is not defined in the paper (experiments are stated to be repeated over 10 independent trials)

title: The Weight Gram Matrix Captures Sequential Feature Linearization in Deep Networks
claim_source: Table 1 (Appendix B.3), page 17; main-text version in Figure 2, page 3

official.background: There is no general account of how hidden representations change when a deep network is trained with gradient descent. Kernel (NTK) analyses treat features as fixed, and provable feature-learning results cover only specific toy problems. The paper argues that the weight Gram matrix W^T W of each layer is the object that carries feature learning. It notes the chain-rule identity grad_h L · h^T = W^T grad_W L, which links weight gradients to feature gradients. If W^T W really carries the learning signal, then the part of the gradient that leaves W^T W unchanged should matter little for training.
official.method:
Gradient whitening (Section 2, Appendix B.2): at each step the gradient G = grad_W L of each weight matrix is replaced by a 'whitened' update Delta. Delta is the smallest-norm update whose weight Gram matrix (W - gamma*Delta)^T (W - gamma*Delta) equals that of the standard GD step (W - gamma*G)^T (W - gamma*G). In other words, the component of G that only rotates W without changing W^T W is removed. In practice this is an orthogonal Procrustes problem: W+ = U V^T (W - gamma*G), where U Sigma V^T is the SVD of W (W - gamma*G)^T, and U V^T is computed with Newton-Schulz iterations as in the Muon optimizer.

Fully connected networks are trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 for 20 epochs with SGD, once with ordinary gradients (Orig.) and once with the whitened update (Whit.). Everything else is identical, and test accuracy is reported at epochs 5/10/15/20, as mean ± std over 5 runs. Table 1 varies width {128, 256, 512} and depth {2, 3, 4}. Table 2 (single runs) varies learning rate {0.1, 0.05, 0.01, 0.005} and momentum {0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2}. Figure 2 in the main text shows the same comparison on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with a three-layer MLP.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with fully connected networks trained by SGD for 20 epochs, the Gram-preserving whitened update matches or beats standard GD in test accuracy at every width and depth tested. For example, at width 256 at epoch 20 it reaches 50.93 ± 0.70% vs. 47.29 ± 1.12%, and at width 512 it reaches 52.42 ± 0.78% vs. 49.91 ± 0.35%. This means that removing the part of the gradient that leaves W^T W unchanged does not hurt training.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Test accuracy (%) of standard GD (Orig.) and the whitened update (Whit.) for varying width and depth. We report mean ± standard deviation over 5 runs. The higher mean in each pair is in bold.
official.metric: Test accuracy (%) at epochs 5/10/15/20, higher is better; ± is the standard deviation over 5 runs
official.comparison: Whitened (Gram-preserving) update vs. standard SGD, same architecture, data, learning rate and number of epochs
official.falsification_criterion: On CIFAR-10 under the Table 1 setup, standard GD beats the whitened update at epoch 20 by more than the run-to-run std at any of widths 128/256/512 or depths 2/3/4. A weaker but still damaging result: the whitened update falls well below standard GD (several points) on CIFAR-10, i.e. W^T W alone does not carry the learning signal.

title: A Topological Sorting Criterion for Random Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs

official.background: Causal discovery algorithms are mostly evaluated on synthetic data whose DAGs are sampled as Erdős-Rényi (ER) or scale-free graphs with a random node order. Earlier work showed that such benchmarks contain artifacts (variance and R² increasing along the causal order) that simple baselines can exploit, and new data generators (iSCM, DaO, UUMC) were designed to remove them. This paper points to a different, purely topological artifact: in these random DAGs the number of 'relatives' (nodes connected through an open path) grows along the causal order, so sorting by it approximately reveals the causal order whatever the edge weights are.
official.method:
Relatives of a node y are all descendants of its ancestors; for a node in a faithful linear Gaussian model these are exactly the variables marginally correlated with it. rel-SortnRegress estimates the number of relatives of each variable by counting entries of the sample correlation matrix whose absolute value exceeds the threshold for a two-sided t-test at α = 0.05, sorts variables in ascending order of that count, and then regresses each variable on its predecessors with a BIC-tuned adaptive Lasso, taking nonzero coefficients as edges (ordering-based search as in R²-SortnRegress).

Data: ER DAGs with n = 30 nodes and density parameter c ∈ {1,...,10} (about cn edges), 10 graphs per c; linear SCMs with edge weights from Unif(0.5, 1) and Gaussian noise with std from Unif(0.5, 1), transformed by the iSCM procedure (internally standardized SCMs, Ormaniec et al. 2025), m = 10,000 samples per graph. Baselines are R²-SortnRegress (CausalDisco), DAGMA (L2 loss, defaults) and FLOP (CPDAG search, penalty 2, 10 restarts; undirected edges dropped). The metric is the normalized structural intervention distance (SID) to the true DAG.
official.claim: On iSCM data from ER DAGs with n = 30 nodes, rel-SortnRegress reaches a normalized SID of about 0.08 at c = 2 and about 0.22 at c = 3, far below R²-SortnRegress (about 0.46 and 0.52) and DAGMA (about 0.7 and 0.97), and close to the CPDAG method FLOP (about 0.07 and 0.10); at c = 1 all methods are similar and for c ≥ 6 rel-SortnRegress is no better than R²-SortnRegress.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Comparative SID (lower is better) performance of rel-SortnRegress on ER DAGs. Panels: (a) sSCM, (b) iSCM, (c) DaO, (d) UUMC.
official.metric: Normalized structural intervention distance (SID) between estimated and true DAG, lower is better; lines are means over 10 random graphs per c with shaded bands (band definition not stated); values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: rel-SortnRegress vs. R²-SortnRegress, DAGMA and FLOP on the same iSCM-generated datasets
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the simulation (ER DAGs, n = 30, c = 2 and 3, iSCM, m = 10,000, 10+ graphs), rel-SortnRegress's mean normalized SID is not clearly lower than R²-SortnRegress's (e.g. the gap at c = 2 is under ~0.15 or the bands overlap).

title: A multi-scale information geometry reveals the structure of mutual information in neural populations
claim_source: Figure 4D-E, page 9 (Bures-Wasserstein check in Figure 9, page 28)

official.background: Representational geometries define distances between stimuli according to how well a neural population tells them apart. They are used to compare brain areas, brains with networks, and representations over learning, but different ways of building them lead to different conclusions. The Fisher information metric is the standard noise-aware choice, but it is purely local. For high-dimensional stimuli such as images, it also depends on gradients of a fitted encoding model in directions the data barely constrain, so its structure may reflect the model more than the neurons.
official.method:
The paper derives a 'multi-scale Fisher' metric G(x) = integral over t of the Gaussian-smoothed Fisher information of the stimulus diffused to scale t. Half of its expected trace equals the mutual information I(R;X). G(x) is estimated with a response-conditioned diffusion model (68M-parameter UNet trained on 100k grayscale 64x64 TinyImageNet images, conditioned on the 50-dimensional responses predicted by an encoder plus Gaussian noise with sigma = 0.22, with classifier-free-guidance dropout). Tweedie's identity turns the diffused Fisher into differences of noise predictions under two sampled responses (Algorithm 1: 24 timesteps x 200 Monte Carlo samples per image). An SVD then gives the top-50 eigenvectors. The baseline is the ordinary Fisher J(x) = Jf^T Jf / sigma^2, computed from the encoder Jacobian.

Encoders are fitted to the 50 most reliable multi-unit channels each from V1 and V4 in the Papale et al. TVSD macaque dataset (THINGS images). Each encoder has a frozen ImageNet backbone (InceptionV3 truncated at Conv2d_4a_3x3, or ResNet-50 at layer1.0) and a per-neuron Gaussian spatial-attention readout, with test r of about 0.70-0.78 for both. One diffusion model is trained per (area, encoder) pair. For the first 200 TinyImageNet validation images, subspace alignment A_k = (1/k)||V_A^T V_B||_F^2 between the top-k eigenvectors is computed. It compares the same area across architectures (Inc vs Res, V1 and V4) with the same architecture across areas (V1 vs V4, Inception and ResNet), separately for G(x) and J(x).
official.claim: For the multi-scale metric G(x), top-k eigenvector subspaces from Inception and ResNet encoders fitted to the same area align far better (about 0.79-0.81 at k = 10) than one architecture fitted to V1 vs V4 (about 0.43-0.44). For the Fisher information J(x) the ordering reverses (same area across architectures about 0.10-0.11 vs same architecture across areas about 0.24-0.32). At k = 10, both orderings hold in each of the 200 test images (Wilcoxon p < 0.001).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Robustness across encoding model architectures. (A) Predictive performance for Inception, ResNet, and ON-OFF models, for V1 and V4 (boxplots of test correlation across the 50 neurons of each area). (B) Leading eigenvectors of the multi-scale Fisher G(x) for an example image (Fig. 3D), for each model architecture fitted to V1 (top) and V4 (bottom). (C) Same as B, for the Fisher information J(x). (D-E) Subspace alignment of the top k eigenvectors of G(x) (D) and J(x) (E), comparing models fitted to the same area (solid) versus the same model fitted to different areas (dashed), averaged across images (shading, s.e.m.).
official.metric: Subspace alignment A_k in [0,1] (mean squared cosine of the principal angles between top-k eigenvector subspaces), averaged over 200 test images, higher = more similar; shading = s.e.m. across images (very narrow); per-image Wilcoxon signed-rank tests at k = 10. No variability across encoder or diffusion-model training seeds is reported.
official.comparison: Cross-architecture/same-area alignment (Inc vs Res in V1; Inc vs Res in V4) vs. same-architecture/cross-area alignment (V1 vs V4 with Inception; V1 vs V4 with ResNet), for G(x) vs. for the Fisher baseline J(x)
official.falsification_criterion: With independently trained Inception and ResNet encoders and diffusion models, G(x) cross-architecture alignment at k = 10 is not clearly above its cross-area alignment (for example, the gap is under about 0.1 or holds in only a minority of images), or the Fisher J(x) ordering does not reverse.

title: Measuring Black-Box Confidence via Reasoning Trajectories: Geometry, Coverage, and Verbalization

official.background: Chain-of-thought reasoners are often used through text-only APIs that expose no logits or hidden states, so confidence in an answer must be estimated from the generated text. The standard black-box approach is self-consistency: sample K reasoning chains and use the share of votes for the most common answer as confidence. This costs K full generations and gives a coarse k/K score. The paper asks whether the shape of a single reasoning trace in embedding space, specifically how close its late part comes to each candidate answer, carries a usable correctness signal.
official.method:
Blinded multiple-choice protocol: the reasoner (Gemini 3.1 Pro or Claude Sonnet 4.6) sees only the question stem, not the options, and K=4 chains of thought are sampled at T=0.7. Each chain is split into sliding windows of 30 words with stride 15, and each window is embedded with gemini-embedding-001 (3072-d). Each option text is embedded as an anchor. For each option j, D_j is the cosine distance from the penultimate window to the anchor, averaged over the K samples. The pick is argmin_j D_j and the label is whether the pick is gold. Geo is a one-parameter softmax over -D (exp(beta*D_pick)/sum_j exp(beta*D_j)), with beta fit by maximum likelihood on the training fold.

Auxiliary features from the same K=4 samples: Str (string consensus of condensed answers produced by a zero-shot condensation call to the same model), Sem (mean pairwise cosine between condensed-answer embeddings), Vol (mean cosine step between consecutive windows), and Ens (cross-model agreement of the modal condensed answer). Composite is a balanced-class logistic regression on the standardized (Geo, Str, Sem, Vol, Ens) features, and No-Geo refits the same regression without Geo. All parameters are refit in stratified 5-fold CV, and the reported number is mean held-out selective-prediction AUC for predicting whether the pick is correct.
official.claim: On MedQA-USMLE in the blinded option-anchor protocol, the single geometric feature Geo reaches selective-prediction AUC 0.821 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and 0.753 (Claude Sonnet 4.6), while the matched No-Geo logistic on four agreement features reaches only 0.577 and 0.519; the full Composite reaches 0.826 and 0.752, so removing Geo costs Delta(Geo) = Composite - No-Geo = +0.249 and +0.234 AUC.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Selective-prediction AUC in the blinded option-anchor protocol. Geo is the fitted softmax probability of the picked option; Str/Sem/Vol/Ens are auxiliary agreement features; Composite is a logistic fusion and No-Geo removes Geo. Geo is en-par or better than Composite in all four settings.
official.metric: Selective-prediction AUC (the paper's 'discriminative AUC') for predicting whether the geometric argmin pick is correct (higher is better), mean over stratified 5-fold CV folds; Delta(Geo) = Composite AUC - No-Geo AUC. No error bars or CIs are reported for this table.
official.comparison: Geo alone and Composite (Geo + Str/Sem/Vol/Ens) vs. No-Geo (Str/Sem/Vol/Ens logistic), same K=4 samples, same folds, on MedQA (N=1272 Gemini / 1271 Sonnet retained) and GPQA Diamond (N=117/187).
official.falsification_criterion: On MedQA with either reasoner, the Composite minus No-Geo AUC gap falls below about +0.10, or Geo alone does not exceed the No-Geo AUC, under the same blinded K=4 protocol and 5-fold CV.

title: End-to-End Identifiable and Consistent Recurrent Switching Dynamical Systems

official.background: Switching dynamical systems model time series whose dynamics change between a finite number of discrete regimes, with continuous latent states and discrete switches. For the learned latents and regimes to be interpretable, the model has to be identifiable: the data distribution should fix the latent structure up to harmless ambiguities such as permutation and scaling. Existing identifiable switching models either restrict the emission map (for example to piecewise-linear) or the dynamics (for example to stationary linear), and are usually fitted with variational autoencoders. The ELBO's approximation gap can stop these models from recovering the true latents even when the theory says they are identifiable.
official.method:
ΩSDS models observations as an invertible normalizing flow of (latent state z_t, exogenous noise ε_t). The latent z_{1:T} follows a recurrent Markov switching model: regime-dependent Gaussian autoregressive transitions N(m_k(z_{t-1}), diag(σ_k^2)) and switch probabilities Q(z_{t-1}). Because the flow is invertible, the exact log-likelihood is log|det J_{f^{-1}}| + log p(z_{1:T}) + log p(ε), with log p(z_{1:T}) computed by forward-backward over switches. All parameters are trained by gradient ascent on this exact likelihood, with no variational posterior. For synthetic data the flow is a 4-block TarFlow (64 hidden dims, 2 transformer layers, 4 heads) whose permutations are replaced by LU mixing layers, and the transitions are 2-layer MLPs with 32 hidden units. Q is detached for the first 10 epochs. Training uses Adam (lr 5e-3, then 5e-4 after epoch 100) for 1000 epochs at batch size 64.

Synthetic data follow the iSDS setup: 10,000 train and 1,000 test sequences of length T=100. The switch process is non-recurrent and Markov, with 90% self-transition. Transitions are sparse locally connected 2-layer MLPs with cosine activations, scales are regime-dependent with σ_k ~ U(0.001, 0.5) (resampled when variance ratios are too similar), and observations come from a random 2-layer LeakyReLU network. K = 3, 3, 4, 5 for m = 3, 5, 10, 20. In the noiseless case n = m. Baselines are iSDS, NCTRL, CtrlNS, TDRL and iVAE (iVAE is given ground-truth regimes), each run with its public code and default config, 3 training seeds per dataset, keeping the best validation ELBO. Latent recovery is measured by mean correlation coefficient (MCC) to the true latents.
official.claim: On noiseless synthetic data (n = m), ΩSDS recovers the latents with MCC around 0.92 at m = 10 and 0.93 at m = 20 (median over 5 dataset seeds). Every VAE-based baseline stays at or below about 0.73 at m = 10 (best: iSDS, median ~0.68) and about 0.63 at m = 20 (best: CtrlNS, median ~0.63), and none of the baseline boxes overlap ΩSDS's.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Synthetic data results under increasing dimensionality. Left: Regime F1 score (ΩSDS and iSDS achieve near perfect recovery). Middle and right: MCC of noiseless and noise-augmented settings. Higher is better for both F1 and MCC. Reported results use 5 different dataset seeds.
official.metric: Mean correlation coefficient (MCC) between learned and true latents, up to permutation (higher is better). Box plots over 5 dataset seeds. Values are read off the plot and are approximate. No numeric table or CI is reported.
official.comparison: ΩSDS (exact flow likelihood) vs. iSDS, NCTRL, CtrlNS, TDRL and iVAE (VAE/ELBO-trained) on the same synthetic datasets, noiseless setting, m = 10 and m = 20
official.falsification_criterion: At m = 10 or m = 20 in the noiseless setting, ΩSDS's median MCC over 5 dataset seeds is not clearly above the best baseline: it falls within the baseline's seed spread, or below about 0.8.

title: Improving the Efficiency of Language Agent Teams with Adaptive Task Graphs

official.background: LLMs are increasingly run as teams of agents, but team designs tend to sit at two extremes: fixed pipelines or leader-assigned roles decided before execution (e.g. MetaGPT, Leader-Worker), or fully decentralized peers. Rigid structures cannot adapt when the right decomposition only becomes clear during the work, while unstructured teams overwrite each other's files, duplicate effort and send excess messages. These coordination failures translate directly into wasted tokens and wall-clock time, which is the main cost of running agent teams.
official.method:
LATTE gives a team of one Lead and four Workers (all the same model, temperature 0.7, max 4,096 output tokens per call, 40-round limit) a shared directed acyclic task graph whose nodes are subtasks with an owner and a status. Agents change the graph only through explicit operators: Workers can DISCOVER new subtasks, CLAIM ready (frontier) subtasks and COMPLETE their own; the Lead can ASSIGN, RELEASE stragglers (heartbeat after 4 idle rounds), CLOSE and VERIFY. Each round, only Workers with a frontier task or new context are dispatched, Workers see only their subtask and its direct predecessors, and the Lead sees the graph rather than full traces.

Baselines with the same 5-agent headcount and round budget: a Leader-Worker hierarchy coordinating by broadcast messages, a decentralized team of 5 peers, a static-graph ablation (the Lead plans the full graph upfront, after which it is frozen), and MetaGPT v0.1. Three newly built tasks are used: exploratory data analysis of a synthetic 400-row HR dataset with three planted properties, debugging 8 planted bugs in a signal-processing library, and extending a text-processing library with six modules, each scored by a test suite. Each condition is run 10 times with Claude Sonnet 4-6 and with GPT-5.2 (300 trials in total). Tokens are total team tokens per successful trial.
official.claim: Pooled over three tasks and two base models (Claude Sonnet 4-6, GPT-5.2), LATTE teams use 148 ± 14K tokens per successful trial versus 379 ± 51K for Leader-Worker, 419 ± 47K for decentralized, 297 ± 40K for the static-graph ablation and 397 ± 59K for MetaGPT, while reaching equal or higher aggregate accuracy (80 ± 4% vs. 70 ± 5%, 74 ± 4%, 58 ± 5%, 34 ± 7%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Accuracy, token usage, and wall-clock time across successful trials per task (± SEM).
official.metric: Total team tokens (thousands) per successful trial, lower is better; task accuracy (% of test-suite checks / successful runs), higher is better; ± is standard error of the mean over trials (10 per task and model)
official.comparison: LATTE vs. Leader-Worker, Decentralized, Static task graph, and MetaGPT, all with 5 agents, the same base model, and a 40-round budget
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup, LATTE's aggregate tokens per successful trial are not clearly lower (non-overlapping SEM intervals) than those of the Leader-Worker and decentralized teams, or LATTE's aggregate accuracy falls clearly below theirs.

title: Diversity Curves for Graph Representation Learning
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (full version with more baselines in Table S.1, page 30)

official.background: Unsupervised graph-level representations (graph kernels, spectral embeddings such as NetLSD, random-walk embeddings, persistent-homology vectorisations) are often sensitive to the number of nodes. Graphs drawn from the same random-graph model but at different sizes can then end up far apart in embedding space, which hurts clustering and visualisation. The paper proposes a size-aware representation that compares graphs at matched cardinalities by coarsening them.
official.method:
Each graph is coarsened by iterative random edge contraction, and small graphs are upsampled by adding a copy of a node that is connected to the original node's neighbours and to the original node itself (nodes are chosen in random order so that no node is copied more than once more than any other). This yields graphs at every cardinality i in I = {1, ..., 29}. At each cardinality the structural diversity (spread) is computed with shortest-path distances: Div(G) = sum_x 1 / sum_y exp(-d(x,y)). The diversity curve is the vector of mean spread over 3 random contraction sequences at each i, so it lies in R^29. Graphs are compared by the L2 distance between curves.

Data (Appendix D.2.1): for each n in {10,...,29}, 3 graphs each from ER (p=0.75), random partition (3 equal communities, p_in=0.9, p_out=0.1), random geometric (r=0.25 in the unit square) and SBM (4 equal communities, p_in=0.8, p_out=0.05), giving 240 graphs. The silhouette score with the true model labels is computed on the representation distances and averaged over 100 resamples of 50% of the graphs. Vector baselines (NetLSD, FEATHER, SpectralZoo, TopER, PH Vietoris-Rips) use Euclidean distance. Graph kernels use -K + max K as the distance.
official.claim: On 240 synthetic graphs (10-29 nodes) from four random-graph models (ER, RP, SBM, RG), shortest-path diversity curves reach a silhouette score of 0.42 ± 0.03 for the true model labels, compared with 0.28 ± 0.04 for the best baseline (shortest-path graph kernel) and 0.11 or less for NetLSD, FEATHER, SpectralZoo, TopER, PH Vietoris-Rips and the WL optimal-assignment kernel.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance (mean ± std) of unsupervised methods at distinguishing graphs from four different distributions.
official.metric: Silhouette score (higher is better) of the L2 / kernel-derived distances with the true generating-model labels; ± is the std over 100 random resamples of 50% of the graphs (one generated dataset, not seeds)
official.comparison: Diversity curves vs. Kernel WL Optimal Assignment, Kernel Shortest Path, TopER, NetLSD, FEATHER, SpectralZoo, PH Vietoris-Rips, all on the same 240 graphs
official.falsification_criterion: On a regenerated dataset with the stated parameters, the diversity-curve silhouette score is not above the best baseline's (in particular the shortest-path kernel's) by more than the resample std, or it falls below 0.35.

title: Efficient Serving for Dynamic Agent Workflows with Prediction-based KV-Cache Management
claim_source: Table 2 (Appendix A), page 13; same means in Table 1, page 7

official.background: Multi-agent LLM workflows (e.g. planner, coder, tester agents built with LangChain, AutoGen or CrewAI) send many requests that share long prefixes: system prompts, tool descriptions and the history built up by earlier agents. Serving engines such as SGLang reuse the KV-cache of shared prefixes, but GPU memory is limited, so the eviction policy decides how much of this reuse is actually realized. The default LRU policy ignores workflow structure. The prior workflow-aware method KVFlow assumes a fixed, known agent call graph, which does not hold when workflows contain runtime-dependent retry or refinement loops.
official.method:
PBKV is built on SGLang with HiCache (a two-tier GPU/host-memory radix-tree KV-cache). It has three parts. (1) Lifecycle-aware eviction: each cache node is tagged with the workflows that accessed it, and once all of those workflows have terminated the node is 'retired' and evicted first. (2) Score-driven eviction of active cache: a ~350K-parameter predictor (GraphSAGE over an agent transition graph estimated from 1K offline traces, attention over the agent prefix, and the last prefill hidden state of the LLM) outputs probability distributions over the next K = 3 agents for each active workflow. Each cache node gets Score(c) = sum over k of γ^(k-1) times the survival probability times A_w(c)·P_w^(k), summed over active workflows (γ = 0.7), and the lowest-scoring active nodes are evicted only after all retired cache is gone (hierarchical eviction). (3) Conservative prefetching from host to GPU, ranked by one-step value, uses only free or retired GPU space and runs only on pure-decode batches.

Evaluation: an 8x A6000 (48 GB) server, Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B (TP=2). The baseline is LRU on SGLang+HiCache (HICACHE_RATIO=1). Ablations are PBKV-LAE (lifecycle-aware eviction only) and PBKV-HE (adds hierarchical score-driven eviction, no prefetching). The dynamic workloads are HoVer fact verification with LangChain (iterative refinement loops, concurrency limit 72) and SWE-bench with AutoGen (retry loops, concurrency 24). FinanceBench with CrewAI (concurrency 48) is a static workflow used to compare against KVFlow. Metrics are end-to-end workflow latency, per-agent TTFT and token-level GPU KV-cache hit rate, given as mean ± std over 10 runs.
official.claim: On the dynamic HoVer + LangChain workload served with Qwen3-14B at concurrency 72, full PBKV raises the GPU KV-cache hit rate from 28.79 ± 1.04% (LRU) to 68.29 ± 2.32% and cuts mean end-to-end workflow latency from 139.59 ± 3.13 s to 76.15 ± 5.95 s; lifecycle-aware eviction alone (PBKV-LAE) already reaches 41.18 ± 3.17%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Full results with standard deviations across multi-agent workloads. Each cell reports mean ± standard deviation over multiple runs. The static workload (FinanceBench+CrewAI) is included for comparison with KVFlow, which assumes a predefined static call graph. Concurrency limits are 72 for HoVer+LangChain, 24 for SWE-bench+AutoGen, and 48 for FinanceBench+CrewAI.
official.metric: Token-level GPU KV-cache hit rate (%, higher is better) and end-to-end workflow latency (s, lower is better); ± is the standard deviation over 10 runs

title: Risk-Controlled Post-Processing of Decision Policies

official.background: Deployed decision rules (legacy policies, clinical workflows, approved models) are often hard to change, but they may violate a safety or reliability requirement such as 'the probability of a high-loss action must be at most ε'. The paper asks for the least intrusive fix: a post-processor that keeps the baseline action as often as possible while enforcing a chance constraint P(ℓ(π(X), Y) ≥ c) ≤ ε on a user-chosen loss. The population optimum switches from the baseline to a fallback action only on contexts where switching most reduces the conditional violation risk, and the practical question is whether a calibrated, finite-sample version of this rule keeps much more of the baseline than naive alternatives at the same risk.
official.method:
Given a fitted conditional label distribution f̂(x), the plug-in conditional violation risk is ĝ(a, x) = Σ_y 1{ℓ(a, y) ≥ c} f̂_y(x); the fitted fallback is π̂*(x) = argmin_a ĝ(a, x) (ties to π0) and the score is Δ̂(x) = ĝ(π0(x), x) − ĝ(π̂*(x), x). The post-processed policy uses π0 when Δ̂(x) < τ and π̂* otherwise. Algorithm 1 picks τ̂ on a held-out calibration set as the largest threshold (on the grid of calibration scores plus 0 and ⊤ = 'never switch') whose bumped empirical risk (Σ_i 1{ℓ(π̂(X_i; τ), Y_i) ≥ c} + 1)/(n + 1) is ≤ ε. The random-mixing baseline plays π0 with probability p and π̂* with probability 1 − p, independent of X, with p set on the same calibration split as the largest value satisfying p r̂0 + (1 − p) r̂* ≤ ε, where r̂0, r̂* are the empirical violation risks of π0 and π̂*.

Setup for the claim (Section 5.1): COVID-19 Radiography Database, labels {Normal, Pneumonia, COVID-19, Lung Opacity}, actions {No Action, Antibiotics, Quarantine, Additional Testing}, loss matrix Λ (rows = actions, columns = labels) = [[0,10,10,9],[8,0,7,6],[8,7,0,6],[6,3,2,0]], from Kiyani et al. (2025). Data are split 70/10/10/10 into training, baseline conformal calibration, threshold calibration and test. An ImageNet-pretrained Inception-V3 is fine-tuned on the training split and gives f̂. The baseline π0 = RAC(0.01) is the Risk-Averse Calibration rule: a conformal prediction set at miscoverage 0.01 followed by the max-min action argmax_a min_{y ∈ C(x)} u(a, y). With ε = 0.1 and c ∈ {4, 3, 2} there is no exact-safe action, so the fitted plug-in fallback π̂* is used. Metrics on the test split: violation risk, switch rate (fraction of test points where π(x) ≠ π0(x)) and mean realized loss; averages over 20 random seeds.
official.claim: On the COVID-19 radiograph decision task with π0 = RAC(0.01) and ε = 0.1, both the post-processed policy and random mixing reach test violation risk 0.10, but post-processing switches away from π0 much less often (0.09 ± 0.01 vs. 0.22 ± 0.01 at c = 4; 0.11 ± 0.01 vs. 0.22 ± 0.01 at c = 3) and has lower mean realized loss (0.81 vs. 1.07 at c = 4; 0.74 vs. 0.95 at c = 3).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Our algorithm versus the random-mixing baseline of (4) at ε = 0.1. Entries are mean ± standard error over 20 random seeds.
official.metric: Switch rate relative to π0 (lower is better, i.e. more agreement with the baseline) and mean realized loss (lower is better), at matched test violation risk (target ε = 0.1); ± is standard error over 20 random seeds
official.comparison: Algorithm 1 (score-thresholded switching to the plug-in fallback π̂*) vs. score-blind random mixing of π0 and π̂*, both calibrated on the same threshold-calibration split and evaluated on the same test split
official.falsification_criterion: With the same setup (RAC(0.01) baseline, ε = 0.1, c = 4 or 3, plug-in fallback, 20 seeds), either the post-processed policy's test violation risk is clearly above 0.1 (e.g. ≥ 0.12) while random mixing stays at 0.1, or its switch rate is not clearly below random mixing's (e.g. the gap is under 0.05 or within a few standard errors).

title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments
claim_source: Figure 1(b), page 9; text in Section 6, page 10

official.background: Regulators approve products such as drugs only after randomized controlled trials provide statistical evidence of efficacy, but trials are expensive. Developers who are unsure their product works may never start, which loses products with high social value; antibiotics are a standard example of this market failure. The paper models approval as a principal-agent (Stackelberg) game: the regulator commits to subsidizing a fraction of trial costs on approval, and the developer then decides how to run a sequence of trials, with the aim of choosing the subsidy that maximizes social utility.
official.method:
The developer (agent) holds a Beta(α0, β0) belief about the product's efficacy θ*. At each of up to T+1 steps it either opts out or runs a trial of size n ≤ nmax at cost c(n) = c0 + c1·n, observing X ~ Bin(n, θ*). The regulator (principal) multiplies e-values E(X, n) = exp(X − n·log(1 + θb(e − 1))) into a test process and approves once it reaches 1/κ, which keeps the false-positive rate ≤ κ at any time. On approval the agent gets ρA plus a fraction ε of its total cost, and society gets ρS minus the subsidy paid. The agent's optimal policy for a given ε is found exactly by value iteration on a belief MDP over (α, β, cost). Social utility is piecewise linear and convex in ε, so Algorithm 1 (divide-and-conquer over the policy partition) finds the optimal subsidy ε*.

Antibiotic case study (Section 6, Appendix G Tables 2-3): θ* = 0.65, θb = 0.5, κ = 0.05, T = 3 (up to four trials), nmax = 200, uniform prior (1,1) known to the principal, εmax = 0.9, ρA = $240M, c0 = $48.9M, c1 = $0.066M, with ρS varied. The baselines are non-sequential protocols in which the agent may run at most one trial with nmax = 800, (i) without subsidy and (ii) with the optimal subsidy. True social utilities under θ* are estimated from 100,000-200,000 Monte Carlo rollouts, with 95% bootstrap CIs (1000 resamples).
official.claim: In the antibiotic setting (θ* = 0.65, T = 3, nmax = 200), the sequential protocol with its optimal subsidy achieves more than 35% higher true social utility than a non-sequential single-trial protocol (nmax = 800) that is also optimally subsidized, at every tested ρS/ρA ratio from ~1 to ~42 (gain ≈ 35-51%), with 95% CIs of about ±1 percentage point.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Subsidizing antibiotic development. The figure shows the results of the approval process for an antibiotic with true (unknown) efficacy θ* = 0.65. Panel (a) shows the result of running Algorithm 1 to compute the optimal subsidy for the principal ε* = 0.108 when the social benefit of approval is ρS = $2000 M. The dashed vertical lines correspond to the intervals of the partition P where the agent's optimal policy is constant (Proposition 8), and the colors indicate the probability that the agent opts out by selecting n = 0 during the approval process (before the drug is approved). Panel (b) shows, as a function of the social-to-agent approval benefit ratio, the optimal subsidy, together with the percentage increase in social utility of the sequential approval protocol relative to a non-sequential approval protocol in which the agent is restricted to a single trial with nmax = 800. The error bars represent 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals.
official.metric: Percentage increase in true social utility U^S (Eq. 7, Monte Carlo under θ* = 0.65) of the sequential protocol over the non-sequential baseline, higher is better; error bars are 95% bootstrap CIs over rollouts (no seeds)
official.comparison: Sequential subsidized protocol at ε* from Algorithm 1 vs. non-sequential single-trial protocol (nmax = 800) with its own optimal subsidy; also vs. non-sequential without subsidy
official.falsification_criterion: A re-implementation with the stated parameters finds the gain over the optimally subsidized non-sequential protocol at or below 35% (beyond the ~1-point CI) at some tested ρS/ρA, or finds ε* ≠ 0.108 for ρS = $2000M.

title: Improved techniques for fine-tuning flow models via adjoint matching: a deterministic control pipeline

official.background: Reward fine-tuning of diffusion and flow-matching image generators (e.g. to raise human-preference scores such as HPSv2) can be cast as optimal control: learn a perturbation of the pretrained velocity field that maximizes terminal reward minus a control-cost regularizer. Adjoint matching solves this by integrating an adjoint ODE backward along each trajectory and regressing the control toward a target built from the adjoint. It works well but is expensive for large models, because the backward adjoint must be integrated over the whole sampling trajectory.
official.method:
The authors use deterministic (ODE) dynamics X' = v_base + u, with running cost f(||u||) and terminal cost -r(X_1). They derive a 'lean' adjoint a~ that satisfies a~' = -a~^T grad v_base with a~(1) = -grad r(X_1), and the closed-form optimal control u* = -(f')^{-1}(||a~||) a~/||a~||. For polynomial regularization f(x) = x^p/(p*lambda), this gives u* = -lambda^{1/(p-1)} ||a~||^{(2-p)/(p-1)} a~. The fine-tuned velocity v_theta is trained by regressing v_theta - v_base onto u*(a~_t) along trajectories sampled from the current model, with stop-gradients on X_t and a~_t (Algorithm 1).

Truncated adjoint matching integrates the adjoint and applies the matching loss only on the last n_truncate sampling steps, motivated by toy analyses showing that control intensity peaks late in the denoising trajectory. Experiments fine-tune SiT-XL/2 (class-conditional ImageNet, 50 sampling steps, classes turned into text prompts) with HPSv2 as the reward and evaluate HPSv2, ImageReward, CLIPScore and PickScore, comparing full (50-step) vs. truncated (10-15 step) adjoints, SDE vs. ODE dynamics, regularization order p in {2, 4, 6}, and the DRaFT and ReFL baselines.
official.claim: On SiT-XL/2 fine-tuned with HPSv2 reward, truncating deterministic adjoint matching to the last 10 of 50 steps (2nd-order regularization) beats full-trajectory adjoint matching on all four reward metrics (HPSv2 0.316 vs. 0.290, ImageReward 0.450 vs. 0.185, CLIPScore 0.266 vs. 0.243, PickScore 0.204 vs. 0.199) while cutting time per iteration from 83.8 s to 47.3 s; with 4th/6th-order regularization, truncated ODE-AM also exceeds DRaFT-1 and ReFL-10 on HPSv2 (0.328/0.329 vs. 0.296/0.297).
official.claim_caption: Comparison on reward metrics with SiT-XL/2. Best values are shown in bold, second-best are underlined.
official.metric: mean reward score over generated images (± is spread across samples); seconds per fine-tuning iteration
official.comparison: ODE-AM n_truncate=10 vs. ODE-AM 50 (Full), same regularization and budget; secondary: vs. DRaFT-1, ReFL-10
official.falsification_criterion: Full-trajectory adjoint matching matches or beats the 10-step truncated variant on HPSv2 under the same number of fine-tuning iterations, or truncation gives no wall-clock saving.

title: SkillOS: Learning Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents

official.background: LLM agents deployed on a stream of tasks usually solve each task from scratch and do not learn from earlier interactions. One way to let them improve over time is to keep a library of reusable 'skills' (Markdown files describing workflows, constraints and heuristics) distilled from past trajectories. The quality of that library depends on how skills are curated: which are inserted, revised or deleted. Existing approaches rely on hand-written skills or fixed prompting heuristics that never receive feedback on whether the curated skills actually help the agent later.
official.method:
SkillOS splits the agent into a frozen executor and a trainable skill curator. For each task, the executor retrieves the top-5 skills from an external SkillRepo with BM25 and solves the task (ReAct for WebShop). The curator, Qwen3-8B, then reads the trajectory, the executor's self-judged correctness, and the retrieved skills, and emits function calls (insert_skill, update_skill, delete_skill) that edit the repo.

The curator is trained with GRPO (lr 1e-6, batch 32, group size 8, 50 steps for WebShop; the main text says the KL term is discarded, though Appendix Table 4 lists a KL loss coefficient of 0.001) on groups of 10 related training tasks: each group starts with an empty repo, the tasks are run in sequence, and the reward is the executor's mean success on tasks 2..|G| plus weighted terms for valid function calls (1.0), a Qwen3-32B judge's score of skill quality (0.1), and repo compactness (0.05). The executor during training is Qwen3-8B. At test time the trained curator is paired with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B or Gemini-2.5-Pro executors on the WebShop test set. Baselines run in the same streaming setup: No Memory, ReasoningBank, MemP, SkillOS-base (same Qwen3-8B curator before RL), and SkillOS-gemini (Gemini-2.5-Pro as an untrained curator).
official.claim: On WebShop with a frozen Qwen3-8B executor, the RL-trained Qwen3-8B skill curator reaches a success rate of 16.5 ± 0.7, versus 13.6 ± 0.8 for the same curator before RL training (SkillOS-base), 13.2 ± 0.9 with Gemini-2.5-Pro as curator, and 12.0 ± 0.5 for the best external memory baseline (MemP).
official.claim_caption: Table 2 | Experiment results on WebShop and single-turn reasoning tasks for 3 different frozen executors. For WebShop, the averaged score, success rate (SR ↑), and the number of steps (Steps ↓) are reported. For reasoning tasks, accuracy (Acc. ↑) is reported on three datasets.
official.metric: WebShop success rate (%, higher is better), mean ± std over 3 runs; average score and steps also reported
official.comparison: SkillOS (RL-trained Qwen3-8B curator) vs. SkillOS-base (untrained Qwen3-8B curator), SkillOS-gemini (Gemini-2.5-Pro curator), MemP, ReasoningBank and No Memory, all with the same frozen Qwen3-8B executor
official.falsification_criterion: With a Qwen3-8B executor on WebShop, the RL-trained curator's success rate is within run-to-run std of SkillOS-base or MemP (e.g. a gap under about 1.5 points), or below them.

title: StraTA: Incentivizing Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Strategic Trajectory Abstraction

official.background: LLM agents trained with RL on long-horizon interactive tasks such as household manipulation (ALFWorld) or web shopping (WebShop) usually act reactively: each action is generated from the current state alone, and only a sparse end-of-episode reward is available. This makes both exploration and credit assignment hard over many steps. GRPO-style group-relative training removes the critic but still treats every step as an independent reactive decision. The paper asks whether making the agent first commit to an explicit trajectory-level plan, and training that plan jointly with the actions, improves sample efficiency and final performance.
official.method:
At the start of each episode the policy generates a short natural-language strategy z from the initial task state. z is kept fixed and prepended to the prompt at every later step, so each action is sampled from pi(a_t | z, s_t). Prompts are non-cumulative: each step sees the current state, not the full history. Training is hierarchical GRPO. For each task, N=4 strategies are sampled, and M=8 rollouts are run under each one (32 trajectories). Action-level advantages are normalized within each strategy's 8 rollouts, using the trajectory outcome reward broadcast to all steps. Strategy-level advantages are normalized across the 4 strategies, and each strategy's reward is the mean of the top delta=0.5 fraction of its rollouts' rewards. A soft length penalty and a -1 format penalty are added, and rewards are clipped to [-1, 1].

Two additions complete the method. (1) Diverse strategy rollout: oversample sigma*N = 32 candidate strategies, embed them with MiniLM-L6, and pick 4 by farthest-point sampling on cosine similarity, starting from the candidate closest to the centroid. (2) Critical self-judgment: after each rollout, the same policy is prompted to list the steps that neither follow the strategy nor advance the task, and each flagged step gets a -0.1 reward. Main setup: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct or 7B-Instruct, 150 training steps, batch size 16 tasks, lr 1e-6, AdamW, DAPO clip bounds 0.2/0.28, built on rLLM with environments served through AgentGym. The reproduced GRPO baseline uses the same batch size and 32 rollouts per task, so the compute budgets match. Evaluation uses temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8 and top-k 20, with results averaged over 3 seeds.
official.claim: On WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (150 steps, batch 16, 32 rollouts per task), StraTA reaches 82.5 ± 0.6% success (score 91.1 ± 0.3), versus 62.2 ± 1.2% (score 80.0 ± 0.5) for the authors' compute-matched GRPO and 52.8 ± 0.2% for their PPO.
official.claim_caption: Table 1 | Performance on ALFWorld and WebShop. Results from open-source models are averaged over 3 random seeds. For ALFWorld, we report the success rate of each subtask together with the overall success rate. For WebShop, we report the overall task score and overall success rate. The best and second best results are highlighted. † The results are from the original paper [Feng et al., 2025b].
official.metric: WebShop success rate (%) and task score, higher is better. Mean ± std over 3 random seeds.
official.comparison: StraTA vs. GRPO and PPO, both reproduced by the authors with the same backbone, batch size and step count; GRPO also uses 32 rollouts per task. GiGPO and RLOO numbers are copied from the GiGPO paper.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same settings, StraTA's WebShop success rate is not clearly above compute-matched GRPO (e.g. the gap shrinks to within about 3 seed stds, or under ~5 points), or StraTA fails to beat GRPO.

title: EMO: Pretraining Mixture of Experts for Emergent Modularity
claim_source: Figure 3 (top-left panel, MMLU, no fine-tune), page 7; EMO values also in Table 3, page 22

official.background: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, but serving one still means loading every expert into memory, because tokens in one input spread across nearly all experts. If an application only needs one domain (math, biology, law), it would be useful to load only a small subset of experts for that domain. In standard MoEs this breaks down: experts specialize in low-level lexical patterns such as punctuation or prepositions, so pruning to a domain-specific subset sharply degrades accuracy. The paper asks whether an MoE can be pretrained so that domain-coherent expert subsets emerge and can be used on their own.
official.method:
EMO changes only the routing during pretraining. For each document, the router's token-level routing probabilities are averaged, and the top-d experts form a document expert pool D. Each token's routing distribution is masked to D and renormalized, and the token then picks its top-k experts from D. The pool size d is sampled uniformly from {k, ..., n_r} per document, and load balancing is computed globally across data-parallel groups rather than per micro-batch. Both EMO and the baseline ('Reg. MoE') are 1B-active / 14B-total MoEs with 128 experts (127 routed + 1 shared), k = 8 active, trained from scratch on 1T tokens of the OLMoE corpus plus a 50B-token anneal. They differ only in the training objective.

Selective expert use: for each domain category of MMLU (17 categories, 'other' excluded from the average, leaving 16), 40% of the examples are used as a validation set and 60% for testing. Experts are ranked per layer by their average routing probability over the tokens of the 5-shot validation prompts, and only the top-d experts per layer are kept (d = 64, 32, 16, 8), giving a standalone model per domain. Accuracy is 5-shot multiple-choice by log-likelihood (acc-raw), macro-averaged over domains. The 'no fine-tune' row evaluates the pruned model directly; the 'fine-tune' row first fine-tunes it on the same validation examples (1 epoch, batch 32, lr 5e-5).
official.claim: With router-based selection of 32 of 128 experts per layer and no fine-tuning, EMO (1T tokens) reaches 41.4 macro-averaged MMLU accuracy, versus 30.8 for a standard MoE trained on the same data. The full models score 42.8 and 42.4.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Selective Expert Use of MoEs trained on 1T tokens (§5.2). Results are shown both without fine-tuning (top) and with fine-tuning (bottom). For MMLU and MMLU-Pro, each domain selects a corresponding expert subset as described in §4.2, and we report macro-averaged results across domains (16 for MMLU and 13 for MMLU-Pro). The baseline MoE degrades sharply under subset restriction, whereas EMO remains robust, with ≈ 1% drop at 25% parameters and ≈ 3% drop at 12.5%, in both without and with fine-tuning.
official.metric: 5-shot MMLU accuracy (acc-raw, higher is better), macro-averaged over 16 domain categories, each with its own expert subset; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: EMO vs. Reg. MoE (same architecture, data and token count; only the training objective differs), each pruned to the same per-domain expert-subset size with the same router-probability selection
official.falsification_criterion: Using the released checkpoints and router-probability selection of the top 32 experts per layer, EMO's macro-averaged MMLU accuracy falls more than about 3 points below its full-model accuracy, or the gap over the identically pruned Reg. MoE shrinks well below 10 points (e.g., under 5).

title: MIND: Monge Inception Distance for Generative Models Evaluation

official.background: Generative image models are usually scored with the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), which fits a Gaussian (mean and 2048x2048 covariance) to Inception-v3 embeddings of generated and real images. Estimating that covariance well needs many samples (typically 50k), which makes evaluation slow and costly. Because FID uses only the first two moments, it is also not a true distance and can be gamed. A metric that ranks models correctly from far fewer samples would make evaluation during training much cheaper.
official.method:
MIND (Monge Inception Distance) is a scaled sliced Wasserstein distance on Inception-v3 embeddings (d = 2048). M random unit directions are drawn; both n-sample embedding sets are projected onto each direction, each projection is sorted, and the mean squared difference between the sorted values is taken. The result is averaged over directions and multiplied by alpha = 3d (about 6,000) so values are on FID's scale. The paper gives JAX/PyTorch code (Figure 4, default n_projections = 100; M in [100, 1000] is recommended).

In the perturbation test (Section 4.4.3), ImageNet-64 images are perturbed at increasing severities eps_1 < ... < eps_k, and each metric is computed between n clean data samples and n perturbed samples at each level. The score is 1 - P(Delta(data, data_eps1) <= ... <= Delta(data, data_epsk)), the probability of failing to order all perturbation levels correctly, estimated over 512 independent trials for each sample size n. For Rectangle, 5 squares of size 10x10 with opacity eps in {0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2} are placed at random in each image. The other perturbations are Gaussian blur (std eps in {0.2, ..., 1.0}) and Mixture (a fraction eps in {1%, ..., 10%} of CelebA images mixed into ImageNet-64). The compared metrics are FID, MMD (Gaussian kernel) and MIND.
official.claim: For the Rectangle perturbation on ImageNet-64 with Inception-v3 features, MIND's probability of mis-ordering the 4 perturbation levels is about 0.00 at n = 5,000, versus about 0.14 for FID; at n = 1,000 it is about 0.12 for MIND versus about 0.49 for FID (values read off Figure 8).

title: Self-Programmed Execution for Language-Model Agents
claim_source: Table 6 (Appendix C.5.1), page 67; per-task breakdown in Table 12, page 70; accuracy-cost plot in Figure 3, page 8

official.background: An LLM agent's harness usually fixes the orchestration policy: it keeps the conversation history, decides what context the model sees each turn, and runs a fixed loop (as in ReAct or coding agents such as Codex CLI). The paper asks whether that policy can be handed to the model itself, so that the harness only executes a program written by the model. This matters because context management largely determines an agent's token cost and quality, and it is currently engineered by hand.
official.method:
In self-programmed execution (SPE) every model completion is a program that the harness evaluates, and that program decides the next prompt by issuing a self-call: self-call(prefix) = eval(complete(prefix)). The author implements this in SPELL, a Clojure-like Lisp in which a program can reference its own source (quine), only the last ('trailing') quoted expression is executed so replaying old source does not repeat side effects, and functions such as !peek let the model view a tool result once without keeping it in the next prefix. The model therefore decides what context to keep, prune or summarize.

For the comparison, GPT-5.4 is run as a SPELL agent and inside Codex CLI v0.120.0 on the 80-task Terminal-Bench 1.1 core set (terminal-bench-core==0.1.1), one trial per task, at low, medium and high reasoning effort, with the same wall-clock (3600 s) and verifier (600 s) limits and no web access. Token use is summed over all API calls (cached input, uncached input, output and reasoning tokens); cost is recomputed from list prices; accuracy is the Terminal-Bench verifier pass rate.
official.claim: On Terminal-Bench 1.1 (80 tasks) with GPT-5.4, the default SPELL agent uses far fewer total tokens than Codex CLI at every reasoning effort (low 10.11M vs. 39.93M, medium 6.96M vs. 51.14M, high 6.52M vs. 94.65M) and less API cost ($12.26 vs. $39.43, $25.72 vs. $46.96, $40.72 vs. $83.86), while resolving a similar number of tasks (35 vs. 38, 36 vs. 39, 40 vs. 43; medium-effort paired sign test p = 0.55).

official.metric: total tokens summed over all API calls in the 80-task run (lower is better), estimated USD cost, and tasks resolved out of 80; one run per configuration, no seeds
official.comparison: SPELL agent vs. Codex CLI, both driving GPT-5.4 at the same reasoning effort on the same 80 tasks with the same time limits
official.falsification_criterion: Running both agents with GPT-5.4 at medium effort on the 80 Terminal-Bench 1.1 core tasks, SPELL's total token count is not at least 3x lower than Codex CLI's, or SPELL resolves significantly fewer tasks (paired sign test p < 0.05).

title: Same Signal, Opposite Meaning: Direction-Informed Adaptive Learning for LLM Agents

official.background: Adaptive test-time compute for LLM agents triggers extra computation (rollouts, sampling several candidates) only at steps where it is expected to help. Existing gates assume a fixed direction: higher token entropy, lower confidence or more disagreement means extra compute is worth more. The paper argues that whether an uncertainty signal predicts that extra compute will help or hurt changes with the (environment, backbone) pair. For example, the Spearman correlation between token entropy and optimizer utility is +0.317 on Qwen3-4B APPS but -0.249 on Llama-3.1-8B APPS. So a gate whose direction is fixed in advance can pick out exactly the states where extra compute does harm.
official.method:
DIAL learns the gate for each (environment, backbone) pair in three stages. (a) Explore: for N_explore = 50 episodes, a coin flip with probability 0.5, independent of any signal, decides at each step whether to trigger the optimizer T. At triggered steps the optimizer's action and the base action are compared from the same environment snapshot, and the binary utility U = 1 if the optimizer wins. (b) Reason: each state is mapped to universal features (step count, token entropy, evidence count, number of available actions, is_finish) plus 5 task-specific features. An LLM writes these as a Python function after reading a summary of the exploration data. (c) Learn: an L1-regularized logistic regression is fit on the standardized features, with C chosen by 5-fold CV over {0.01, ..., 10}. The gate triggers T when sigmoid(w^T phi + b) > 0.5. At deployment it makes no extra LLM calls.

On APPS the optimizer is K-variant sampling: sample K=3 complete code solutions and run the first that passes the provided test cases. For utility labels, U = 1 if the best variant's test pass rate beats the base solution's. All methods use the same agent and optimizer and differ only in when they trigger it. The baselines are CaTS, SEAG and CoRefine (all calibrated with extra labeled data), CATTS (K=5 vote disagreement), AUQ (verbalized uncertainty) and s1 budget. The metrics are success rate (SR) and cost, measured as total deployment tokens divided by the tokens of the base-only policy.
official.claim: On APPS with Qwen3-4B-Instruct, the DIAL gate reaches 73.0 ± 1.0% success rate at 2.61x base cost. The best fixed-direction baseline, s1 budget, reaches 69.0 ± 1.3% at 2.65x, and the other five baselines reach 60.8-67.5% at 2.61-6.00x.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Full results across 6 environments and 3 backbones. SR (%) and Cost (×base, total deployment tokens normalized by base_only). Best and second-best mean SR per environment. †: methods requiring calibration data. Cost includes all LLM calls: base proposer, gate overhead (CATTS K=5 voting, AUQ confidence query), and rollout calls.
official.metric: Success rate (%, higher is better), mean ± std over 3 seeds; cost is deployment tokens relative to base_only (lower is better). The paper reports no error bars for cost.
official.comparison: DIAL vs. CaTS, SEAG, CoRefine, CATTS, AUQ and s1 budget, all using the same Qwen3-4B agent and the same K=3 variant-sampling optimizer on APPS. For reference (Table 10), base_only scores 60.5% at 1.00x and always-trigger scores 79.5% at 3.65x.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if, on Qwen3-4B APPS, s1 budget or any other baseline reaches an SR within about one seed std of DIAL (i.e. the 4-point gap closes), or if DIAL's SR falls to 69% or below at a similar cost (about 2.6x base).

title: Group of Skills: Group-Structured Skill Retrieval for Agent Skill Libraries
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (SDs in Table 28, Appendix E.17, page 37)

official.background: LLM agents increasingly draw on large external skill libraries (procedural snippets, tool instructions, checkers) that cannot all fit in the prompt, so a retriever has to choose what to show. Flat semantic top-k retrieval can miss functionally required skills. Graph-based retrieval such as Graph of Skills recovers dependencies, but it still hands the agent an unordered bundle and leaves the agent to work out the entry point, the supporting skills, the visible requirements and what to avoid. The paper asks whether changing the retrieved unit from atomic skills to small role-labeled skill groups makes the retrieved context more usable for downstream agents.
official.method:
Offline, GoSkills builds a typed skill graph over a 2,000-skill library, extracts small anchor-centered groups (a lead skill plus at most two support members with role, facet, artifact and visible-requirement annotations), and links the groups in a typed group graph. At inference time, a deterministic query schema and four seed skills activate candidate groups. Fixed linear scores (coefficients set on a 10-task development subset) select an anchor group and add up to two support groups. The plan is then bottlenecked to at most four atomic skill payloads (1,800 characters each, 9,000 in total), with coverage-safe backfill for visible requirements. The result is rendered as a fixed START / SUPPORT / CHECK / AVOID execution contract. The downstream agent loop, skill payloads and environment are unchanged.

Baselines share the same agent loop, environment, library and four-payload / 9,000-character budget: No Skills (no skill context), Vanilla Skills (full library exposed on Terminal-Bench 2), Vector Skills (text-embedding-3-large top-4) and Graph of Skills (dependency-aware hydrated bundle). Terminal-Bench 2 uses the full 89-task suite run through Harbor containers with the authors' own agent loop (not the leaderboard harness). Each backbone × method cell is run 3 times, and the table reports mean accuracy over tasks, averaged across the repeats.
official.claim: On the 89-task Terminal-Bench 2 suite with a 2,000-skill library and a four-payload budget, GoSkills reaches higher accuracy than Graph of Skills on all six backbones (e.g., GPT-5.4: 60.7 vs 46.1, SD 3.37 vs 1.95; Claude Sonnet 4.5: 44.2 vs 33.0) and is also above the strongest baseline, No Skills, on each (GPT-5.4: 60.7 vs 52.8, SD 4.90).

Reward (SkillsBench, ALFWorld) and Accuracy (Terminal-Bench 2) are averaged over tasks and reported in %, Tokens denotes mean cumulative input tokens, and Runtime denotes agent-only runtime (s). For Reward/Accuracy, larger is better; for Tokens and Runtime, smaller is better. Values are averaged over three repeats (sample SDs: Appendix E.17). Symbol columns indicate skill-library access (Skill), bounded retrieval (Ret.), and group-structured context (Group); a half-check indicates dependency-graph structure without group roles. Colored arrow deltas in skill-access rows are relative to No Skills under the same benchmark and backbone. The best value for each metric within each benchmark–model block is highlighted in bold and the second best is underlined; No Skills is a no-context reference and participates in metric highlighting.
official.metric: Terminal-Bench 2 accuracy (% of tasks passed, higher is better), mean over 3 repeats. Sample SDs across the 3 repeat-level aggregates are given in Table 28. No paired CIs or significance tests are reported for Terminal-Bench 2.

title: Adaptive auditing of AI systems with anytime-valid guarantees

official.background: Practitioners often audit generative AI systems with small, adaptively chosen test suites (10-50 cases), deciding which cases to annotate and when to stop based on results so far. Classical hypothesis tests assume a pre-specified sampling scheme and fixed sample size, so peeking and adaptive selection inflate Type I error, and it is unclear what such an audit can actually conclude. The paper frames the audit as two 'dueling' tests: the model's null (no subgroup with prevalence >= ε has mean score below q) and the auditor's null (the auditor's strategy will find such a failure mode within budget m). It builds e-processes for both nulls that keep anytime-valid Type I error control under arbitrary adaptive sampling and optional stopping.
official.method:
For the model's null, four e-processes are compared on binary scores Y: LR, the product over k of p(Y_k; q-δ)/p(Y_k; q) for a fixed separation δ; LR-UI, which replaces q-δ with a predictable estimate γ̂_{k-1} from an Exponentially Weighted Averaging Forecaster over a grid of alternatives below q; and SR-LR / SR-LR-UI, Shiryaev-Roberts versions that take a weighted sum of these processes started at every candidate changepoint j. The auditor's null is tested from time m = 40 with an analogous likelihood-ratio process using alternatives above q. The procedure stops when either statistic exceeds 1/α with α = 0.05 (Algorithm 1). The adaptive auditor embeds each question with sentence-transformers/allenai-specter and refits a one-hidden-layer NN ensemble after every label. It samples from the ε = 0.05 subgroup with the lowest predicted accuracy if that is below q, and otherwise samples by UCB from the bottom half of lower confidence bounds. Baseline auditors use the plain LR test: Stratified (uniform over known domain × education strata), Pre-learned (sampling model trained on 30 extra held-out labels) and Oracle (knows the true failure mode).

Experiment 1, Scenario (a): the auditor has all 448 GPQA questions unlabeled and labels one per step without replacement, with n_init = 2 random starts and a maximum of 250 labels. Correctness labels are simulated per domain × education-level cell with threshold q = 0.85. Biology and Physics stay >= 0.85, and Chemistry is degraded: Large 0.25-0.40, Medium 0.50-0.75, Small 0.60-0.77, None 0.92-0.96 (Appendix Table 1). For each setting the authors run 100 replicates and report the fraction ending in rejection of the model's null (failure mode detected), rejection of the auditor's null (audit passed) or neither (inconclusive).
official.claim: In Experiment 1(a) with a Medium Chemistry degradation, the dual test using SR-LR-UI with the adaptive auditor detects the failure mode in about 84% of 100 replicates, vs. about 58% for LR with the same auditor, about 50% for the Pre-learned sampler and about 0% for Stratified sampling. With no failure mode, no method falsely rejects the model's null and all of them pass the audit in about 100% of replicates.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Detecting failure modes with semi-synthetic data (Experiment 1). The rows correspond to settings where the model has a failure mode with decreasing magnitude/prevalence of the degradation (Large, Medium, Small), where the bottom corresponds to No failure mode. Left column: rate of rejecting dueling null hypotheses, where orange indicates rate of detecting a failure mode, blue indicates passing the audit, and gray corresponds to neither (inconclusive). Right column: boxplots of the number of cases annotated to reach the correct conclusion or the maximum sample size.
official.metric: Rate of rejecting the model's null H0^mod (power to detect a failure mode; higher is better under Large/Medium/Small) and, under None, rate of falsely rejecting H0^mod (Type I error, should be <= α = 0.05), over 100 simulation replicates at α = 0.05. No error bars or confidence intervals are reported; values are read off the bar plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: SR-LR-UI vs. LR-UI, SR-LR and LR, all with the same adaptive NN-ensemble auditor, and vs. the LR test with pre-specified Stratified and Pre-learned samplers (Oracle as an upper bound), on the same simulated GPQA labels
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Scenario (a) with Medium degradation (100 replicates, α = 0.05, m = 40, max 250 labels), SR-LR-UI's failure-detection rate is not clearly higher than LR's (e.g. the gap is under ~10 percentage points) or than Pre-learned's. Alternatively, under the None setting any method falsely rejects H0^mod in clearly more than 5% of replicates.

title: MedExAgent: Training LLM Agents to Ask, Examine, and Diagnose in Noisy Clinical Environments

official.background: LLMs are usually evaluated on medicine as single-turn question answering over a complete case description, but real diagnosis is sequential: a clinician questions the patient, orders exams, and commits to a diagnosis while dealing with noisy patient reports, noisy lab results, and exams that cost money and cause discomfort. Earlier interactive systems cover only part of this (conversation only or exam ordering only), and they assume clean observations. The paper asks whether one small agent can be trained to question, examine and diagnose within a single episode under noise and cost constraints.
official.method:
Diagnosis is cast as a POMDP with three action types: free-form questions to an LLM patient simulator (persona sampled from PatientSim), exam orders as tool calls resolved against the case's recorded exam findings (ground-truth exams plus random distractor tools; distractors return 'No significant findings'), and a final [DIAGNOSIS: ...]. During training, patient noise (7 types, p=0.3) and exam noise (3 types, p=0.1) are injected. Cases come from DDxPlus and PMC-Patients-v2 (5K SFT, 20K RL, 2K test, split evenly between the two sources); AgentClinic-MedQA (201 cases) is held out as an OOD test set.

MedExAgent-8B starts from Meditron3-8B. It is first fine-tuned with SFT on 5K synthetic doctor-patient conversations that follow the Calgary-Cambridge interview structure, then trained with DAPO on reward R = R_dx + 0.5 R_tool - 0.1 R_cost, where R_dx is an LLM-judge (gpt-4.1-mini) Jaccard over diagnosed conditions, R_tool is a ToolRL-style tool-match score, and R_cost penalizes the financial and discomfort tiers of unnecessary exams. For evaluation, every model gets the same system prompt and tool list and talks to a gpt-4.1-mini patient simulator, with no noise at test time. Seven open baselines (Qwen3-8B/14B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, MedGemma-27B-text-it, Aloe-Beta-70B, HuatuoGPT-o1-70B) are run zero-shot in the same environment with default hyperparameters, and thinking mode is on where the model supports it. Metrics: Sim (MedEmbed-base-v0.1 cosine), Jac (LLM-judge Jaccard) and Acc (LLM-judge strict accuracy: every ground-truth condition matched).
official.claim: On the PMC-Patients-v2 test split (1,000 cases) of the interactive diagnosis environment, MedExAgent-8B reaches LLM-judge Jaccard 0.345, strict accuracy 0.314 and Sim 0.626, compared with 0.171 / 0.219 / 0.590 for the best baseline, Aloe-Beta-70B, and it beats all seven open baselines (paired bootstrap on Sim, p < 0.001).

Sim is cosine similarity between embeddings of the predicted and ground-truth diagnoses; Jac is the LLM-judge Jaccard similarity (matched concepts divided by the union of predicted and ground-truth concepts); Acc is LLM-judge strict accuracy (1 if every ground-truth concept was matched, 0 otherwise). Bold marks the best result per column, underline marks the second best. Superscripts denote paired-bootstrap significance of MedExAgent-8B vs. the runner-up on Sim (B = 10,000; * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001; no marker = not significant at p < 0.05).
official.metric: Jac (LLM-judge Jaccard), Acc (LLM-judge strict accuracy) and Sim (embedding cosine); higher is better for all. Each value comes from a single evaluation run with no seed std; significance is a paired percentile bootstrap (B = 10,000) of MedExAgent vs. the runner-up on Sim.

title: Classification Fields: Arbitrarily Fine Recursive Hierarchical Clustering From Few Examples

official.background: Classical hierarchical clustering returns a finite partition or dendrogram over a fixed dataset. Some hierarchies of interest, such as self-similar or fractal structures, are better viewed as infinite-depth objects produced by a reusable local parent-to-child refinement rule. If such a rule can be learned from the first few observed levels, it can be applied recursively to predict deeper levels that were never observed. This paper calls these objects classification fields and asks whether a neural predictor trained on a shallow prefix stays accurate when rolled out to deeper levels.
official.method:
A hierarchy with branching factor K is generated by a residual rule chld(x)_k = x + s^{l+1} r(x)_k. A classification field predictor (CFP) r̂ is trained on the observed levels by minimizing the squared error between predicted and true children (Eq. 8). At test time r̂ is applied recursively from the root: each generated child becomes a parent and no ground-truth nodes from unseen levels are used (no teacher forcing). Appendix F.3 specifies the CFP as a 4-layer MLP with hidden width 64, trained with Adam (lr 1e-3, 3000 epochs); the theory section frames CFPs as ReLU MLPs.

For the out-of-family IFS benchmarks, s = 1 and r(x)_k = f_k(x) − x, where f_k(x) = A_k x + b_k + α_k [sin(<w_k^(1), x> + φ_k), cos(<w_k^(2), x> − 0.37 φ_k)] is a sinusoidally warped contraction (Appendix F.3.3). The benchmarks are nonlinear Sierpiński (K=3), nonlinear 2D Cantor dust (K=4), nonlinear Koch curve (K=4), and a random nonlinear IFS (K=3, maps resampled per trial). All models are trained on levels 0–2 and rolled out to levels 3–5. Baselines use the same rollout: an affine residual predictor r̂(x)_k = A_k x + b_k trained with the same loss, a learnable constant template, and a closed-form average residual. The metric is the level-wise coordinate-averaged MSE between predicted and true nodes in fixed child-slot order, averaged over levels 3–5 and 5 seeds.
official.claim: On nonlinear IFS hierarchies trained on levels 0–2 and recursively rolled out to levels 3–5, the CFP's MSE (×10^-3) is about 10× or more below the affine residual predictor on all three fixed benchmarks: Sierpiński 0.90 ± 0.19 vs. 16.46 ± 5.46, Cantor dust 0.47 ± 0.11 vs. 16.15 ± 9.28, Koch curve 0.70 ± 0.21 vs. 9.13 ± 2.02.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Out-of-family nonlinear IFS hierarchies. Metrics are averaged over held-out levels 3 to 5 and five random seeds. Values are reported in units of 10^-3, with standard deviations reported where shown, and lower is better. The macro average is computed uniformly across benchmarks.
official.metric: Level-wise MSE averaged over held-out levels 3–5, in units of 1e-3, lower is better; ± is std over 5 random seeds. PI-CD and d_pt-distortion are also reported.
official.comparison: CFP (ReLU MLP residual predictor) vs. affine residual predictor (strongest baseline), learnable constant and average residual, all with the same training levels and the same recursive rollout
official.falsification_criterion: On any of the nonlinear Sierpiński, Cantor dust or Koch curve benchmarks, the affine residual predictor's rollout MSE over levels 3–5 is within one seed std of the CFP's, or the CFP's MSE is not clearly below it (e.g. less than about 3× lower).
