title: When Symbol Names Should Not Matter: A Logistic Theory of Fresh-Symbol Classification
claim_source: Figure 4 (left), page 15; the identical curves appear as Figure 7 (right panel), page 80, whose caption labels that panel tied-embedding/unembedding transformers (Appendix K.4.1 regime)

official.background: Template tasks test whether a sequence model learns a rule over abstract symbols or memorizes concrete token names: training and test strings follow the same latent templates (e.g. αβα vs. αββ) but test strings use symbols never seen in training. Prior work (Boix-Adserà et al.) showed transformers in the kernel regime can generalize to fresh symbols given enough vocabulary diversity, and that adding identity terms to the attention key-query and value-output products helps. This paper studies the fixed-label classification version with logistic loss and argues that the geometry of accidental token collisions in the training sample, not only vocabulary size, decides whether fresh-symbol classification succeeds.
official.method:
The theory analyzes ridge-regularized kernel logistic regression with a token-symmetric kernel. It decomposes the learned predictor into an ideal template-level classifier and a perturbation caused by token collisions between training strings, and bounds that perturbation through a colored collision graph.

The experiment (Section 6, Appendix K) uses a binary same/different task with templates #$# -> A and #$$ -> B. Each wildcard is replaced by a token drawn from a substitution alphabet split disjointly into train/val/test parts (S_train = n, S_val = S_test = 100), so test symbols are never seen in training. Transformer encoders are compared that differ only in fixed identity multipliers added to attention: the KQ term adds M_KQ * alpha_KQ * X X^T to the attention logits, and the VO term adds M_VO * alpha_VO * Attn X to the output, where alpha is a trainable scalar initialized to 0 and (M_KQ, M_VO) is one of {(0,0), (100,0), (0,100), (100,100)}. Reported metric: test accuracy at the epoch with lowest validation loss.

title: Structural Rationale Distillation via Reasoning Space Compression

official.background: Distilling chain-of-thought reasoning from a large teacher LLM into a small student usually means fine-tuning the student on teacher-written rationales. The teacher's rationales for similar problems often differ a lot in structure and strategy, so the student sees many one-off solution patterns instead of a few reusable ones. The paper asks whether constraining the teacher to a small, shared set of high-level solution strategies gives more consistent supervision that small students learn from better.
official.method:
D-RPC builds a 'reasoning path bank'. The teacher (GPT-5.1) labels every training question with a category and an intent. On a category-balanced 5% seed set, the teacher writes high-level reasoning paths (short ordered lists of abstract steps). Within each category, the intent strings are embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and clustered with DBSCAN (eps 0.25, min_samples 2) into canonical intents, each of which stores its observed paths. For each training question, the question embedding is matched to a canonical intent, the top-K_ret paths are retrieved by cosine similarity, and the teacher picks or refines one and writes a supervision tuple (path, detailed rationale, answer). All tuples are kept regardless of whether the answer is correct. Novel paths that reach a correct answer are buffered and periodically re-clustered into the bank.

The student is LoRA-fine-tuned (r=64, alpha=128, q/k/v/o projections, lr 1e-4, 2 epochs, effective batch 16, max length 2048) on the tuples, and the final checkpoint is evaluated with greedy decoding by exact-match accuracy. Baselines use the same teacher and the same SFT configuration: Zero-shot CoT distillation, Freeform (the teacher chooses its own step structure), SuperCorrect (hierarchical XML templates), DCoT, and SGFT.
official.claim: On MATH (5000 test problems), Qwen 3 1.7B distilled with D-RPC reaches 59.72 ± 0.39% accuracy, versus 54.91 ± 0.34% for the best baseline (DCoT), 49.21 ± 0.40% for CoT distillation and 48.09 ± 0.26% for Freeform, all using the same GPT-5.1 teacher and LoRA configuration.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Post-distillation accuracy (%) across five benchmarks and two student models. Values are mean ± std over 10 repeated executions with seed 42. Bold marks the best result per column. Shading marks D-RPC. Dashes mark inapplicable settings.
official.metric: Exact-match accuracy (%), higher is better. ± is the std over 10 repeated executions with seed fixed to 42, so it captures only nondeterministic GPU variation and not variation across training seeds or teacher sampling.
official.comparison: D-RPC vs. CoT, Freeform, SuperCorrect, DCoT, SGFT distillation, all with the GPT-5.1 teacher and the same SFT/LoRA setup, Qwen 3 1.7B student, MATH test set
official.falsification_criterion: With the same teacher, student, and LoRA setup, D-RPC's MATH accuracy for Qwen 3 1.7B is not clearly above DCoT (e.g., the margin falls below about 2 points or within the spread across training seeds), or is not above CoT and Freeform.

title: Learned Lagrangian Models of PDEs via Euler–Lagrange Residual Minimization
claim_source: Table 1, page 13 (Appendix B); same experiment shown in Figure 3b, page 7

official.background: Neural networks can learn Lagrangians or Hamiltonians of physical systems from data, but long-horizon forecasting with such learned models is usually done with a generic integrator, so small per-step errors accumulate and break energy conservation. Classical symplectic and variational integrators avoid this for known equations, but they require symbolic manipulation of the Lagrangian and, for PDEs, a fixed spatial discretization. Earlier learned variational integrators handle only ODEs, and Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNN) applied to PDEs learn a discrete Lagrangian tied to a fixed spatial stencil.
official.method:
ELM (Euler–Lagrange Minimization) learns a continuous, pointwise Lagrangian density L(q, q_t, q_x) with an MLP trained to minimise the squared Euler–Lagrange residual R^2 on samples from random plane-wave superpositions, plus soft gauge constraints that fix the affine ambiguity of L (Eq. 8). For the 1D wave (q_tt = 0.05 q_xx), network C is an MLP with three hidden layers of width 400 and Softplus activations, input (q, q_t, q_x), trained for 50,000 steps on 5,000 plane-wave samples (k_bound = 4), single seed.

To integrate, each node stores Hermite degrees of freedom (q, q_t, q_x, q_tx). On local space-time patches, a monomial-basis Hermite interpolant is fit to known and unknown node states, the squared EL residual is summed over n_omega quadrature points (3 in time, 6 in space) to form a patch error J, and the new-time-step state is found by damped Newton iteration on J, swept over patches by Jacobi iteration (n_r = 3). The LNN baseline (network B) is the Cranmer et al. MLP (3 x 400, Softplus) taking a 3-node stencil of (q, q_t), trained with the original code on 1D wave trajectories (best of 200 seeds), and integrated with velocity Verlet on 100 nodes. Both are rolled out for 10,000 s from a Gaussian initial condition with periodic boundaries; the metric is final relative energy error |E_t - E_0|/E_0.
official.claim: On the 1D wave equation q_tt = 0.05 q_xx (periodic, Gaussian initial condition, 10,000 s rollout), ELM with 21 nodes and dt = 0.4 ends with 21% relative energy drift versus 680% for an LNN with 100 nodes and the same dt (235 s vs 141 s wall-clock), and ELM's drift falls to 1.9% at 51 nodes, dt = 0.1, while LNN's grows to 1,680% at dt = 0.1.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Configuration, computational cost, and final energy drift for each method in Section 4. Methods sharing a letter in the Net column use the same architecture and the same trained weights. More details on architecture and training can be found in Appendix C. Computational cost excludes JIT compilation. The double pendulum experiments run on CPU (float64) while wave experiments run on GPU (float32).
official.metric: Final relative energy error |ΔE/E_0| after 10,000 s (lower is better); single run per configuration, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: ELM (learned continuous Lagrangian density, network C, 322,801 params) at three resolutions vs. LNN (learned discrete stencil Lagrangian, network B, 324,001 params) with velocity Verlet at dt = 0.4 and dt = 0.1
official.falsification_criterion: A re-implementation of ELM on this problem gives final energy drift comparable to (within a factor of ~2 of) a comparably trained LNN at the same dt over 10,000 s, or ELM's energy drift does not decrease as resolution increases (n=21 to n=51).

title: FAME: Forecasting Academic Impact via Continuous-Time Manifold Evolution

official.background: LLMs are increasingly used to judge the novelty and likely impact of research ideas, but whether those judgments are right is hard to check because impact takes years to appear. The paper uses forecasting the impact of already-written arXiv papers as a checkable stand-in: models only see data up to a cutoff date and must rank later papers by how impactful they eventually became. It reports that frontier LLM judges do poorly at this, and proposes a model that uses the time evolution of research topics rather than static text alone.
official.method:
Each paper is embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large and assigned to a topic by KMeans. An inspiration graph is built by keeping citation pairs with embedding cosine similarity > 0.6 and a time gap > 60 days, taking the top 12 candidates per paper, and keeping only pairs that gpt-4.1-mini confirms as genuine inspiration (LLM confidence threshold 0.6). Two MLPs are trained: a mapper z_i = M_map(x_i, TimeEncode(t_i)) and a topic-spine model mu_k(t) = M_spine(E_k, TimeEncode(t)) with a learnable embedding E_k per topic. The loss is alpha*L_spine (squared L2 pull of z_i to its topic spine mu_{c_i}(t_i)) + beta*L_inspire (for each graph edge (i,j), a hinge max(0, 0.5 - cos(z_j - z_i, mu'_{c_j}(t_j))) with finite-difference momentum mu'(t) ~ mu(t) - mu(t - 0.01), plus an L2 pull term ||z_i - z_j||^2) + gamma*L_vanguard (training papers with impact at or above the median of same-topic papers within a time window get a hinge pushing cos(z_i - mu(t_i), mu'(t_i)) above a margin equal to their min-max-normalized impact; lower-impact papers are penalized by max(0, that cosine)), with alpha=1, beta=0.1, gamma=1, lr 1e-4. An unseen paper's predicted impact is cos(z_new - mu_c(t_new), mu'_c(t_new)).

The ground-truth impact weight is w_i = sum over GitHub stars, citations, influential citations and Altmetric score of log_b(a*s + 1), all collected at the end of the study. The dataset has 3,200 arXiv papers from Time Series Forecasting, Sparse Attention and Image Generation. Evaluation is an 18-month sliding window (June 2024 to November 2025): for each cutoff T, models train on papers up to T and rank the papers in the next 2-month window, scored by Spearman correlation. Baselines are XGBoost, SVR, Transformer and TGCN (on the inspiration graph) trained on the same text embeddings and labels, frontier LLMs prompted few-shot with 30 labelled hint papers, and SciJudge-4B scored by pairwise tournament.
official.claim: In the 18-month prospective sliding-window evaluation, FAME's Spearman correlation with realized impact averages 0.535, 0.513 and 0.532 over the three 6-month blocks, versus at most 0.278, 0.399 and 0.297 for the best matched ML baseline (Transformer, SVR, SVR) and at most 0.302 for any LLM or SciJudge-4B.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Prospective forecasting performance across an 18-month sliding window evaluation from June 2024 to November 2025. Performance is measured by the Spearman rank correlation ρs between predicted and ground-truth composite impact weights. The experiments are carried out three times, and the standard deviation of the performance is reported. Best results are shown in bold.
official.metric: Spearman rank correlation between predicted scores and ground-truth composite impact weights within each 2-month test window (higher is better); ± is std over 3 runs per month; the Avg column is the mean over 6 months with no error reported
official.comparison: FAME vs. XGBoost, SVR, Transformer, TGCN trained on the same text embeddings and labels; also vs. GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Flash/3.1-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2 (few-shot) and SciJudge-4B
official.falsification_criterion: With the same data and windows, the best of SVR/Transformer/TGCN/XGBoost reaches a 6-month-block average Spearman within ~0.05 of FAME, or FAME's average across all 18 windows falls below ~0.45 while SVR stays around 0.3-0.4.

title: Disambiguating 2D-3D Correspondences in Gaussian Splatting-based Feature Fields for Visual Localization

official.background: Visual localization estimates the 6-DoF camera pose of a query image against a prebuilt 3D map, usually by matching 2D pixels to 3D points and solving PnP inside RANSAC. Gaussian Splatting-based feature fields (GSFFs) attach a descriptor to each 3D Gaussian so the Gaussians can be used directly as the 3D map. The strongest such direct-matching method, STDLoc, needs about two hours of per-scene feature-field training. This paper argues that photometrically trained Gaussians are a poor fit for PnP: one Gaussian covers a volume and gets matched to many pixels while being represented by a single 3D point, and these many-to-one correspondences destabilize RANSAC.
official.method:
PlugGS-Loc builds a feature field from a pretrained RGB 3DGS without training. For each training view it rasterizes the Gaussians and keeps, per Gaussian, the maximum composition weight over pixels where that weight is at least τ = 0.1. A Gaussian's score is the mean of these per-view weights; following STDLoc, anchor Gaussians are sampled, their k-nearest neighbours grouped, and only the highest-scoring Gaussian per group is kept. Each kept Gaussian gets a descriptor equal to the softmax-weighted sum of the L2-normalized SuperPoint features at its strongest pixel in each view.

SplitGS-Loc first splits every Gaussian into three children along its major axis by moment matching a 1D Gaussian with a three-component mixture: weights 1/6, 2/3, 1/6, side means at ±βs with β = 1.4, and variance (1 − β²/3)s² for all components. Sampling uses the parent's averaged child score (Eq. 9) and keeps all three children of a selected parent, with twice as many anchors as PlugGS-Loc; each child gets its own aggregated descriptor. At test time SuperPoint query features are matched to the Gaussian descriptors and the pose is solved with PoseLib PnP+RANSAC, with no iterative refinement. Table 4 compares this to STDLoc's direct 2D-3D matching (its trained feature field, without the dense refinement stage) under two RANSAC iteration budgets on the five Cambridge Landmarks scenes.
official.claim: On Cambridge Landmarks with direct 2D-3D matching and no pose refinement, SplitGS-Loc gets an average median error of 8.7 cm / 0.15° vs. 11.2 cm / 0.20° for STDLoc under the default RANSAC setting (10^3-10^5 iterations), and 8.9 cm vs. 12.8 cm under the efficient setting (10^2-10^3), with fewer many-to-one PnP inputs (199 vs. 313).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: PnP convergence. We investigate the correlation between PnP convergence and accuracy on Cambridge Landmarks [10], comparing STDLoc [9] and our SplitGS-Loc under efficient (a,c) and default (b,d) setting. By mitigating the pixel-Gaussian matching ambiguity, SplitGS-Loc produces fewer many-to-one inputs and more valid inliers, achieving the best accuracy with stable convergence.
official.metric: Average over the 5 Cambridge Landmarks scenes of the per-scene median translation (cm) / rotation (°) error, lower is better; also counts of many-to-one PnP inputs, final inliers, and runtime. Single run; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: SplitGS-Loc vs. STDLoc, both doing direct 2D-3D matching with the same SuperPoint features and PoseLib PnP+RANSAC under identical RANSAC min/max iteration settings
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both pipelines on the 5 Cambridge Landmarks scenes under the default RANSAC setting, SplitGS-Loc's average median translation error is not clearly below STDLoc's (e.g. gap under ~1 cm or reversed), or SplitGS-Loc does not produce fewer many-to-one PnP inputs than STDLoc.

title: StreamPhy: Streaming Inference of High-Dimensional Physical Dynamics via State Space Models

official.background: Many science and engineering applications need to reconstruct a full spatiotemporal physical field (fluid velocity, ocean sound speed, active-matter concentration) from sparse, irregularly placed sensor measurements that arrive over time. Existing approaches either fit a functional tensor decomposition to a single sequence (LRTFR, CATTE, OFTD), or learn a latent diffusion model and reconstruct by posterior sampling (SDIFT). Most of them need the whole time sequence before inference, generalize poorly to new sequences, or are slow at inference. Attention-based sensor encoders (Senseiver) reconstruct each frame from its sensors directly.
official.method:
StreamPhy is trained end-to-end on many records of a physical system. At each time step the set of observed (coordinate, value) pairs is encoded: each continuous coordinate is mapped per mode by a Fourier-feature MLP, concatenated with the observed value, linearly projected to D = 512, and pooled by multi-head cross-attention with a learned query (4 heads), then an MLP, giving z_t of size P = 64. A HiPPO-LegS state-space model with bilinear discretization (state size L = 32, step size from the actual time gap) updates a latent state X_t = A_bar X_{t-1} + b_bar ∘ z_t online. The decoder (FT-FiLM) produces a scale matrix Γ_t and shift β_t from [vec(X_t), z_t] by MLPs and predicts the field at any coordinate as f_φ(Γ_t u_n + β_t), where u_n is the coordinate's functional-tensor embedding. During training a random fraction (rate sampled from U[0.1, 1]) of observations is masked, and the loss is the RMSE of the full-field reconstruction, trained with Adam.

Turbulent Flow (Zenodo 14037782) uses 600 records of 48 frames x 918 irregular spatial points: 500 for training and 100 for testing, with ranks R = (64, 64). At test time a fraction ρ of points is observed at every frame, either spread uniformly or in slabs, and the full field is reconstructed. The metric is VRMSE, the RMSE divided by the standard deviation of the ground truth, averaged over 10 repeats. Baselines are LRTFR, OFTD, CATTE (per-sequence functional tensor methods), Senseiver (attention-based) and SDIFT (functional-Tucker latent diffusion), configured as in Appendix E.
official.claim: On Turbulent Flow with uniform sampling, StreamPhy (multi-head) reaches a test VRMSE of 0.0935 at ρ = 3% and 0.0696 at ρ = 5%. The best baseline, Senseiver, gets 0.2779 and 0.2361, and SDIFT gets 0.3248 and 0.2821, so StreamPhy's error is roughly 3x lower.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Average VRMSEs under two sampling patterns across datasets and observation ratios.
official.metric: VRMSE (RMSE divided by the ground-truth std; lower is better), mean over 10 repeated runs. Table 1 reports no std or confidence interval.
official.comparison: StreamPhy (MH) vs. Senseiver, SDIFT, LRTFR, OFTD and CATTE on the same Turbulent Flow test records and sampling masks
official.falsification_criterion: In a re-run on Turbulent Flow with uniform ρ = 3% and 5%, StreamPhy (MH)'s VRMSE is not clearly below Senseiver's: for example, StreamPhy is above about 0.18 at ρ = 3%, or the gap is less than 2x, or it falls within the spread across seeds.

title: Exposing and Mitigating Temporal Attack in Deepfake Video Detection

official.background: Spatiotemporal deepfake video detectors (3D-CNN, recurrent and video-transformer models) reach high AUC on standard benchmarks, but they may rely on fragile statistics in the temporal frequency spectrum of facial regions rather than on the content of facial motion. Common operations such as temporal filtering, denoising and re-encoding change the amplitude of these temporal spectra, so an attacker could evade detection by reshaping the amplitude spectrum while keeping the video visually and semantically unchanged. The paper shows that suppressing single temporal frequency bands drops existing detectors' AUC by up to 41% and proposes a training method that makes the detector invariant to such amplitude changes.
official.method:
Attacks and augmentation operate on per-patch temporal signals: the facial ROI of a T = 16 frame clip is split into M patches, the mean intensity of each patch over time is transformed with a 1D DFT, the amplitude spectrum is modified while the phase is kept fixed, and the clip is reconstructed with the inverse DFT (Hermitian-symmetric so the signal is real). SpInShield trains a VideoMAE V2 (ViT-B) detector on FF++ (c23). A lightweight learnable spectral adversary G_phi outputs a per-bin multiplicative amplitude modulation exp(alpha * tanh(G_phi(normalized amplitude))), with alpha = 0.6, and is trained to maximize the detector's cross-entropy plus an MMD shift between clean and perturbed features, minus a penalty keeping the mask near identity. The detector and generator are updated alternately.

The detector is a weight-sharing Siamese VideoMAE that sees the clean clip and the perturbed clip. Its loss is cross-entropy on both views, plus a symmetric KL term between the two views' class predictions (lambda_sym = 0.9), plus a domain-confusion loss: a discriminator behind a gradient reversal layer tries to tell clean from perturbed features (lambda_blind = 0.7). Only the clean branch is used at test time. Evaluation (Table 2) trains on FF++ and tests cross-dataset on CDF-v2, DFD, DeeperForensics, WildDeepfake, and DiffSwap/DaGAN sets built on FFHQ (1,000 real + 1,000 fake each), after applying one of four fixed hand-crafted amplitude attacks that were not used in training: random band masking (1-3 Tukey-tapered bands of 1-4 bins), a narrow-band notch (1-2 bins at a random non-DC, non-Nyquist bin), spectral tilt (log-amplitude + b1*w + b2*w^2, b1, b2 ~ U(-1.5, 1.5)), and Gaussian noise added to the log-amplitude.
official.claim: Trained on FF++ (c23) and tested cross-dataset under four amplitude-spectrum attacks, SpInShield reaches average AUC (over 6 test sets) of 89.35 / 90.47 / 88.47 / 87.43 (band mask / notch / tilt / noise), versus 69.07 / 71.37 / 66.64 / 63.46 for the best of 9 video-level baselines and 59.20 / 60.77 / 56.74 / 54.60 for a plain fine-tuned VideoMAE(B), an average gain of 21.30 points over the best baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Robustness evaluation under amplitude spectrum attacks. ∗ indicates statistically significant improvements over the strongest baseline via a two-tailed t-test (p < 0.05) on the average metric.
official.metric: Video-level AUC in % (higher is better), averaged over six cross-dataset test sets; no std or CI reported, only a marker for a two-tailed t-test (p < 0.05) against the strongest baseline on the average
official.comparison: SpInShield vs. FakeSTormer, AltFreezing, PTFD, TALL, SLF, NACO, AFW, DFD-FCG, FTCN and plain VideoMAE(B), all trained on FF++ and evaluated under the same four amplitude-spectrum attacks

title: Think-with-Rubrics: From External Evaluator to Internal Reasoning Guidance

official.background: Rubric-as-reward RL trains LLMs on open-ended, unverifiable tasks such as instruction following by scoring each response against a list of criteria (a rubric) and using the fraction satisfied as the reward. In existing setups the rubric is used only after the response is written, as an external evaluator. This paper asks whether having the policy itself write a rubric before answering, and rewarding it for following that rubric, improves instruction following compared with the standard rubric-as-reward setup.
official.method:
The policy (Qwen3-8B-Base, non-thinking mode) outputs <rubric> r̂ </rubric> then <answer> y </answer>. An SFT warm-up (5k OpenRubrics prompts, responses distilled from Gemini-2.5-Flash, 200 steps, lr 1e-5, batch 32) teaches the format. RL uses DAPO without KL on a 27k OpenRubrics split (batch 32, 8 rollouts per prompt, lr 1e-6, best at about 90 steps). The reward is R = 0.3·R_gold + 0.5·R_self + 0.2·R_fmt, where R_gold = S(y, golden rubric), R_self = S(y, self-generated rubric), and S is a weighted fraction of criteria judged 'met' (hard rules weight 2, principles weight 1) by a Qwen3-8B rubric verifier distilled from Qwen3-32B on a separate 2k OpenRubrics split. R_fmt is 1 only if both tags parse, scaled by max(0, 1 − |n(r̂) − 10|/5) for the number of rubric items.

Baselines (Rubric-as-Reward) use the same two-stage SFT + DAPO pipeline on the same data but are rewarded only with R_gold: one answers directly, the other first writes free-form step-by-step reasoning and then the answer in <answer> tags. Evaluation uses IFEval and IFBench (strict prompt- and instruction-level accuracy) and InfoBench; the Average is the mean of IFEval prompt, IFBench prompt and InfoBench.
official.claim: On Qwen3-8B-Base, Think-with-Rubrics trained with DAPO on the mixed reward reaches an average score of 57.88 (IFEval prompt-strict 65.61, IFBench prompt-strict 24.83, InfoBench 83.20), versus 54.01 (59.70, 22.11, 80.22) for the best Rubric-as-Reward baseline (SFT with free-form thinking + DAPO on golden-rubric reward), a gain of 3.87 average points and 5.91 IFEval prompt-level points.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on three instruction-following benchmarks. For IFEval and IFBench, we report both prompt-level and instruction-level scores under strict evaluation. The Average column is computed using the prompt-level scores of IFEval and IFBench together with the InfoBench score. Best results are in bold and second-best results are underlined (the same in other tables).

title: SHRED: Retain-Set-Free Unlearning via Self-Distillation with Logit Demotion

official.background: Machine unlearning for LLMs tries to remove specific memorized content (private data, copyrighted text, fictitious facts in a benchmark) from a trained model without retraining from scratch, while keeping its general abilities. Most methods (GradDiff, NPO, DPO, RMU, ...) add a 'retain set' of neighbouring data to stop the model's utility from collapsing, but a good retain set is often unavailable in practice. Methods that train on the forget set alone usually damage utility or over-forget. SHRED is a method that uses only the forget set.
official.method:
SHRED is self-distillation from a frozen copy of the model to be unlearned. For each forget-set sequence, the frozen teacher gives next-token distributions p(.|x<t) at every position after a context prefix (the QA question or document prefix). Positions are sorted by the probability of the actual token, and the lowest-P fraction (default P = 50%) are 'forget positions'; the rest act as an implicit retain set. At forget positions the KL target is the teacher distribution with the memorized token's logit set to -inf (Variant A; Variant B also removes the top-0.9 nucleus), renormalised over the teacher's top-K vocabulary indices; at the other positions the target is the unmodified teacher distribution. The student (initialised from the model) is trained with one top-K KL loss summed over all positions, with no retain data.

For the claimed result: TOFU forget10 (400 fictitious-author QA pairs), Full model = Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct fine-tuned on TOFU (per Table 3), Target = model retrained without forget10. Typical SHRED setting is P = 50%, LR 1e-5, batch size 2, about 10k steps. Baselines (GradAscent, GradDiff+RT, NPO+RT, SimNPO+RT, DPO+RT, RMU+RT, CEU+RT) are re-run with the OpenUnlearning framework; +RT means the retain set is added as an NLL term. Metrics: fkm (Forget KnowMem, mean probability of the ground-truth answer on forget queries, lower is better), MU (TOFU model utility, harmonic mean of retain, real-author and world-facts sub-metrics, higher is better) and PrivLeak (MIA-based, 0 matches the retrained Target). Every method is reported at the Pareto-optimal end of its training run.
official.claim: On TOFU forget10, SHRED (no retain set) reaches forget KnowMem 0.055 with model utility 0.637 and PrivLeak -38.6, while every retain-set baseline either forgets less (DPO+RT 0.162 fkm, MU 0.606; NPO+RT 0.294, MU 0.557) or over-unlearns with |PrivLeak| > 90 (GradDiff+RT 0.000/0.625/+99.7, CEU+RT 0.002/0.630/+97.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results. Metrics unified across benchmarks: fkm = forget set knowledge-memorization probe; fvm = forget verbatim-memorization ROUGE; rkm = retain set knowledge-memorization; MU = model utility. PrivLeak is the MIA-based privacy-leak score; → 0 matches the retrained oracle Target, large |·| signals detectable departure (negative = under-unlearning, positive = over-unlearning). N/A = not applicable (DPO requires Q/A preference pairs unavailable for free-form pretraining benchmarks; RWKU lacks a retrained oracle). Coloring uses Target τf, τu and Full forget Ff as references: Blue = real win on that axis (forget: 0.3τf ≤ v ≤ 1.5τf and companion utility ≥ 0.6τu; utility: v ≥ 0.99τu and companion forget ≤ 1.5τf; PrivLeak: |v| ≤ 50). Red = the value looks competitive in isolation but the companion metric reveals a problem (forget: severe over-unlearning v < 0.3τf or utility collapse vu < 0.5τu; utility: v ≥ 0.97τu but forget stayed near Full vf ≥ 0.6Ff with vf > 1.3τf; PrivLeak: |v| ≥ 90). RWKU has no Target so coloring uses Full as the reference instead.
official.metric: fkm (lower is better, but the retrained Target sits at 0.148), MU (higher is better; Full 0.627, Target 0.612), PrivLeak (closer to 0 is better). Single runs; no seeds, std or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: SHRED vs. GradAscent, GradDiff+RT, NPO+RT, SimNPO+RT, DPO+RT, RMU+RT and CEU+RT, all re-run in OpenUnlearning on the same TOFU Full model; Full and Target as reference points
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running SHRED on TOFU forget10 (P = 50%) does not reach fkm at or below the Target's 0.148 while keeping MU at or above the Target's 0.612 and |PrivLeak| <= 50; or a re-run retain-set baseline (e.g. DPO+RT or NPO+RT with tuned budget) matches SHRED on all three of fkm, MU and PrivLeak.

title: Multi-Environment POMDPs with Finite-Horizon Objectives
claim_source: Table 1 and Table 2, page 9 (full results in Tables 3-14, Appendix F.4, pages 18-24)

official.background: A POMDP is a sequential decision problem where an agent acts in a stochastic environment but only receives partial observations of the state. In a multi-environment POMDP (MEPOMDP) the initial state is additionally unknown and chosen adversarially from a finite set, so the agent must find one policy that is good against every possible start. Computing the optimal finite-horizon value is PSPACE-complete, and the only previous tool (Bovy et al., NeurIPS 2025) targets the infinite-horizon discounted case, so finite-horizon instances on standard benchmarks have been slow or unsolvable within an hour.
official.method:
Algorithm 3 computes, bottom-up over the horizon, the set of multi-expected payoff vectors (one coordinate per initial state) achievable by deterministic policies from each multi-belief. For each action and each observation it recursively builds the frontier for horizon ℓ − 1 from the updated multi-belief, combines one point per observation via the Bellman update, and prunes every point that is Pareto-dominated by another. The optimal value is then read from the convex hull of the final frontier (randomising over deterministic policies), i.e. checking whether Conv(X^k) intersects [λ, ∞)^n.

Benchmarks: RockSample RS_{m,g,t} (m×m grid, g good of t rocks, initial states = all good/bad assignments, as in Bovy et al.), Robot Navigation RN_{map,d} (CIT/MIT/Pentagon/SUNYSB maps, 2 initial states within distance d of the goal, 28 observations), and Identification Friend-or-Foe IFF_{d1,d2,v1,v2} (3 initial states). The baseline is Bovy et al.'s own tool. Both are run on an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 with 16 GB RAM and a 3600 s timeout; wall-clock time to solve is reported for each (model, horizon k).
official.claim: On finite-horizon MEPOMDP benchmarks, Algorithm 3 is much faster than the tool of Bovy et al. [1]: e.g. RS_{3,1,3} (n=3, k=3) 0.058 s vs. 2.43 s, IFF_{1,3,0,2} (k=3) 0.61 s vs. 213.5 s, RN_{CIT,3} (k=2) 0.022 s vs. 304.2 s, and it solves RS_{4,1,2} (k=7, 154 s), RS_{3,4,7} (|S|=574, n=35, k=5, 784 s) and RN_{MIT,3} (k=5, 70 s) where [1] times out at 3600 s.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Rock Sampling. Table 2: Robot Navigation and Identification.
official.metric: Wall-clock solve time in seconds, lower is better; TO = timeout at 3600 s; single runs, no error bars
official.comparison: Algorithm 3 (ours) vs. the MEPOMDP solver of Bovy et al. (NeurIPS 2025) on the same instances, horizon and hardware

title: Ensemble Distributionally Robust Bayesian Optimisation

official.background: In contextual Bayesian optimisation the objective f(x, c) depends on a design x chosen by the learner and on a random context c drawn from an unknown distribution P, and the goal is to maximise the expected value E_{c~P}[f(x, c)]. Because P has to be estimated from the contexts observed so far, optimising against this estimate can pick poor designs. Distributionally robust BO (DRBO) guards against this by optimising against the worst distribution in an ambiguity set around the estimate. Existing DRBO methods either discretise the context space, which scales poorly, or use a single GP surrogate, which can be fragile on highly non-convex objectives.
official.method:
EDRBO fits an ensemble of M = 4 Gaussian processes on (x, c, y) data, using Squared Exponential, Rational Quadratic, Matérn-3/2 and Matérn-5/2 kernels. The ensemble prediction is the Wasserstein barycentre of the per-GP posteriors: the mean of the GP means mu_t and the mean of the GP standard deviations sigma_t. A per-point radius eps_hat_t(x, c) is the largest 2-Wasserstein distance between any single GP posterior and the barycentre, sqrt((mu_m - mu_t)^2 + (sigma_m - sigma_t)^2). Using a Wasserstein-DRO Lipschitz regulariser, the robust acquisition becomes x_t = argmax_x E_{c~Q_t}[mu_t(x,c) + beta_t sigma_t(x,c) + eps_hat_t(x,c)/sqrt(2)], where Q_t is the empirical distribution of the contexts observed so far. The learner then observes c_t ~ P and y_t = f(x_t, c_t) + noise.

Baselines (UCB, SBO-KDE, DRBO-KDE, DRBO-MMD, DRBO-MMD Minmax, StableOpt, WDRBO, ERBO) are adapted from the WDRBO / SBO-KDE code, all on BoTorch with a single RBF-kernel GP. Each method runs 200 iterations (5 of them initial points) on each of 9 problems with 10 random seeds. The metric is final cumulative expected regret, sum_t (E_P[f(x*, c)] - E_P[f(x_t, c)]). Ackley: x in [0,1]^2, c ~ N(0.5, 0.2^2) clipped to [0,1]. Newsvendor: f(x,c) = 9 min{x,c} + max{0, x-c} - 5x, with c drawn from a Burr XII distribution (alpha=2, beta=20) clipped to [0,1].
official.claim: After 200 iterations, EDRBO has lower final cumulative regret than all 8 baselines on Ackley (273.96 ± 62.91 vs. 453.82 ± 127.19 for the best baseline, ERBO) and on Newsvendor (8.03 ± 1.46 vs. 13.54 ± 2.63 for the best baseline, SBO-KDE).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Mean ± standard deviation of final cumulative regret across all experiments. The best and the second best results per experiment are in bold and underlined, respectively. The Average rank is computed over all experiments.
official.metric: Final cumulative expected regret after 200 iterations (lower is better); ± is the standard deviation over 10 random seeds
official.comparison: EDRBO (4-kernel GP ensemble) vs. UCB, SBO-KDE, DRBO-KDE, DRBO-MMD, DRBO-MMD Minmax, StableOpt, WDRBO, ERBO (single RBF GP), same benchmarks, budget and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: Over 10 seeds on Ackley or Newsvendor, some baseline (in particular ERBO, SBO-KDE or WDRBO) reaches a mean final cumulative regret within one std of EDRBO's or below it; equivalently, EDRBO's Ackley mean is not clearly below about 450, or its Newsvendor mean is not clearly below about 13.5.

title: Hierarchical Task Network Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics

official.background: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning solves problems by decomposing abstract tasks with a method library until only executable actions remain. Search over the joint space of world states and task networks needs heuristic guidance, but domain-independent HTN heuristics such as the Task Decomposition Graph (TDG) bound and landmark counting are weaker than their classical-planning counterparts. Corrêa et al. showed that LLMs can write domain-specific Python heuristics for classical planning that beat domain-independent baselines; this paper asks whether the same works for total-order HTN planning, where the heuristic must also reason over the remaining task network.
official.method:
For each of six IPC 2020 total-order HTN domains (Barman-BDI, Blocksworld-GTOHP, Depots, Robot, Rover-GTOHP, Towers; 139 problems), an LLM is prompted with the full HDDL domain file, the smallest and largest problem files, a working example heuristic, the PYTRICH heuristic API (bitset states, task network, grounded methods), and a per-domain hint block. It returns a Python Heuristic class with an initialize step (preprocessing) and a per-node __call__. Twenty one-shot candidates are generated per model and domain at provider-default sampling. Candidates that fail to parse, raise errors, or exceed 60 s on the smallest problem are discarded; the survivor with the fewest expanded nodes on that smallest problem is selected and then run unchanged on all problems in the domain.

Each heuristic (LLM-generated, TDG, LMCOUNT) runs in the PYTRICH planner under GBFS, A* and Weighted A* (w=5), with 1 CPU core, 8 GB RAM and a 30-minute limit per problem. A problem counts as solved if any of the three algorithms solves it (virtual best over algorithms). CO4 is the single selected heuristic per domain from Claude Opus 4; LLM is the virtual best over five models. PANDA (RC^FF and RC^LMCut) is also run under the same limits as an external baseline.
official.claim: In the PYTRICH planner on 139 IPC 2020 total-order HTN problems (1 core, 8 GB, 30 min, virtual best over GBFS/A*/WA*), the single Claude Opus 4-generated heuristic per domain (CO4) solves 131 problems, vs. 118 for LMCOUNT and 117 for TDG, matching or exceeding both baselines in every domain.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Coverage (problems solved) per domain and in aggregate. All systems report the virtual best over GBFS, A*, and WA*. LMCOUNT is PYTRICH with bidirectional landmarks [21]. CO4 is the single heuristic generated by Claude Opus 4. LLM is the virtual best over all five main models.
official.metric: Coverage (number of problems solved within time and memory limits), higher is better; no error bars, a single generation and evaluation run.
official.comparison: CO4 (Claude Opus 4 heuristic) vs. TDG and LMCOUNT domain-independent heuristics, all within PYTRICH under identical search algorithms and resource limits; PANDA RC^FF / RC^LMCut shown for reference.
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the generate-select pipeline with the paper's prompt (a fresh draw of 20 candidates per domain from a comparable frontier LLM) gives a heuristic whose total PYTRICH coverage is not clearly above 118 (LMCOUNT), or that is below TDG/LMCOUNT in some domain; or rerunning the paper's released selected heuristics does not reproduce 131 vs. 117/118.

title: POETS: Uncertainty-Aware LLM Optimization via Compute-Efficient Policy Ensembles
claim_source: Figure 4 (left panel), page 7; POETS values from Table 5, page 21

official.background: LLMs are increasingly used as generators in black-box optimization (proteins, molecules, circuits) and in RL post-training with verifiable rewards, where GRPO is the standard policy-gradient method. GRPO has no notion of epistemic uncertainty, so it explores without direction and can lock onto early, suboptimal solutions, especially when data is reused (multi-epoch training or experience replay). Principled exploration such as Thompson sampling usually needs an explicit uncertainty-aware reward model plus a separately fitted policy, which is expensive and awkward for LLMs.
official.method:
POETS uses the fact that a KL-regularized policy implicitly defines a reward r_pi(a) = beta (log pi(a) - log pi_ref(a) + log Z). It trains an ensemble of n = 16 policies, each with the GRPO-style gradient (Zheng et al.'s GSPO variant, clip 0.2) on Poisson(1)-bootstrapped weights of the shared rollouts, so the ensemble of implicit rewards approximates a reward posterior. Each rollout is generated by one ensemble member chosen uniformly at random, which approximates KL-regularized Thompson sampling. The ensemble is a shared trunk (the full model, fine-tuned) plus 16 independent rank-128 LoRA branches on the final readout (LM head) layer, with B initialized to zero. A FIFO replay buffer of the last T rollout groups is reused at each step (T = 1 means no replay).

Protein search: ProtGPT2 (0.738B) samples amino-acid sequences from an empty prompt (<|endoftext|>), up to 512 tokens, temperature 1.0, in groups of G = 16 per round. Reward = negative thermal instability index (Guruprasad et al., 1990). Both methods use backbone LR 1e-4, LoRA LR 1e-2 (tuned for GRPO and transferred to POETS), KL beta = 1e-4, no entropy bonus, and AdamW without weight decay. GRPO gets a single LoRA branch, no bootstrapping and ensemble size 1. The metric is best-seen reward max_{tau<=t} r(a_tau) over 4,000 evaluations, reported as mean and standard error over 25 seeds, for T in {1, 4, 16}.
official.claim: On protein search with ProtGPT2, after 4,000 evaluations POETS reaches mean best-seen reward 82.3 ± 4.9 (T=1) and 92.1 ± 4.8 (T=4), while GRPO under the same hyperparameters plateaus at about 62 (T=1), 53 (T=4) and 42 (T=16). So POETS beats GRPO by about 20 points without replay and about 40 points with T=4 replay, and replay helps POETS but hurts GRPO.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: POETS benefits substantially from a replay buffer (T = 4, 16). In contrast, GRPO overfits to suboptimal early solutions. After zero-initialization of LoRA, the policy heads diversify quickly.
official.metric: Best-seen reward (maximum negative instability index found so far), higher is better; mean ± standard error over 25 seeds (lines and shaded bands in the figure). GRPO values are read off the plot and approximate; POETS values at T=1 and T=4 are exact from Table 5.
official.comparison: POETS (16-member Poisson-bootstrapped LoRA-head policy ensemble) vs. GRPO (single policy, same backbone, LoRA head and learning rates), each at replay buffer size T = 1, 4 and 16
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running protein search (ProtGPT2, G = 16, 4,000 evaluations, about 25 seeds) with the stated hyperparameters, POETS T=1 is not clearly above GRPO T=1 in mean best-seen reward (gap under about 2 standard errors, i.e. under ~10 points), or POETS with T=4 does not beat the best GRPO configuration by a clear margin.

title: Scalable Distributed Stochastic Optimization via Bidirectional Compression: Beyond Pessimistic Limits

official.background: In distributed SGD with n workers, a recent lower bound shows that, under standard assumptions (L-smoothness, bounded-variance stochastic gradients), no method can make both the communication term (d·κ·L∆/ε, where κ is the server-to-worker time per coordinate) and the statistical term shrink with n, even with random sparsification; plain Synchronous SGD already matches it. This makes compression methods look useless in theory when sending vectors in both directions costs time. The paper argues that an extra structural assumption (a small 'functional' smoothness constant L_A, which is 0 for quadratics) lets compressed methods beat that barrier and scale with n.
official.method:
Inkheart SGD: each worker computes a mini-batch of b stochastic gradients at its local copy x_i^k, sums them and sends m RandK-compressed vectors to the server, which averages over workers and takes a step x^{k+1} = x^k - γ g^k. With probability p all workers are synchronized to x^{k+1} (full vector sent); otherwise each worker updates its local copy with ℓ independent RandK-compressed copies of the model difference x^{k+1} - x^k, so server-to-worker traffic is also compressed. M4 is a second, momentum-based variant (parameter η, initial batch b_init) using RandK in both directions. The baseline is Synchronous SGD (each worker computes one stochastic gradient, sends it uncompressed, receives the full new iterate).

The test problem (Appendix H.1) is the quadratic f(x) = ½ xᵀAx with A = diag(I_{d/2}, λ I_{d/2}), d = 300, λ = 0.01, minimizer x* = 0, and stochastic gradients ∇f(x) + ζ with ζ ~ N(0, σ²). Time is simulated: computing one stochastic gradient costs h seconds, and each coordinate sent costs κ = 1/d (server→worker) or τ = 1/d (worker→server) seconds, so a full vector costs 1 second each way. For each method the step size is tuned over {2^-10, ..., 2^3}, K over {1, 3, 10, 30, 50, 100, 200, 300}, and η (M4) over {0.1, ..., 1}; the best run is plotted as f(x^k) - f(x*) vs. simulated time for n ∈ {50, 100, 300}, h ∈ {0, 0.1, 1.0}, σ ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.1}.
official.claim: On the d = 300 block quadratic with σ = 0.001, κ = τ = 1/d and h = 0, Inkheart SGD and M4 reach f(x) - f* ≈ 1e-4 within about 400 (n = 50, 100) or 140-200 (n = 300) simulated seconds, while tuned Synchronous SGD is still at about 4e-3 (n = 50, 100, time 450) and 3e-2 (n = 300, time 225), i.e. at least one order of magnitude worse at equal time.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Convergence under low gradient noise (σ = 0.001). Fixed parameters: d = 300, κ = 1/d, τ = 1/d. Rows vary the gradient computation time h; columns correspond to the number of workers n ∈ {50, 100, 300}.
official.metric: Suboptimality f(x^k) - f(x*) on a log scale vs. simulated time, lower is better; single run per setting with best tuned hyperparameters, no error bars or seeds reported; values read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Inkheart SGD and M4 (bidirectional RandK compression) vs. Synchronous SGD (uncompressed), each with its own tuned step size, on the same problem and simulated time model
official.falsification_criterion: Re-implementing the three methods with the stated time model and tuning grids, tuned Synchronous SGD reaches suboptimality within a factor of ~3 of Inkheart SGD at the end of the plotted time window for h = 0 and σ = 0.001 (n = 100 or 300), or the gap disappears when averaged over several random seeds.

title: Beyond Confidence: Rethinking Self-Assessments for Performance Prediction in LLMs
claim_source: Figure 1, page 5 (exact values from Figure 7a, page 39)

official.background: LLMs are often asked to give a verbalized confidence score so that users can tell when an answer is likely wrong. Verbalized confidence is known to be overoptimistic and only moderately predictive of correctness. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory from psychology, this paper asks whether other self-assessments that a model rates after answering, especially how much effort the task took and how able the model felt to solve it, predict whether the answer is wrong better than confidence does.
official.method:
After answering each task item, the model rates seven dimensions on a 1-10 scale in one JSON output: effort, understanding, ability, pleasantness, esteem, goal relevance (in random order), and confidence (always rated last). No definitions are given for the dimensions; the exact prompt is in Appendix E. The Standard subset has 8 domains (coding, math, science, multilingual, understanding the world, understanding humans, known failures, NLP) built from BIG-Bench tasks, with about 400 items per domain (item counts per task in Appendix D.1), scored mostly by exact string match. Open-source models are served locally with vLLM.

For each model, every dimension's raw rating is used on its own as a score for predicting correctness, pooled over all Standard items. The metric is AUROC, with effort sign-flipped so that higher means more likely correct (low effort = predicted success). Non-binary task scores are binarized at 0.5. Figure 1 shows the AUROC of the best single dimension per model, with 95% CIs (caption: 'across 1000', presumably bootstrap resamples), and a diamond for confidence-only AUROC. Figure 7 (Appendix I) lists the AUROC of every dimension for every model.
official.claim: On the BIG-Bench Standard subset, self-reported effort predicts answer correctness better than self-reported confidence for Qwen3-4B-Instruct (AUROC 0.67 vs. 0.53) and Qwen3-30B-Instruct (0.73 vs. 0.54), well beyond the ~±0.03 95% CIs on the effort bars.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Best discriminators (using AUROC to predict failure) when a single dimension is used at a time, across domains in the Standard and Hard subset. 95% confidence intervals are shown across 1000. The diamond on each bar shows the AUROC using confidence only, when confidence is not the best predictor of failure.
official.metric: AUROC of a single self-rating as a predictor of correctness (higher is better); error bars in Figure 1 are 95% confidence intervals 'across 1000' (the caption does not say 1000 what; presumably bootstrap resamples, as Figure 3's caption states bootstrapped 95% CIs), drawn only for the best dimension (no CI is shown for the confidence diamond); values from the Figure 7 heatmap have no error bars
official.comparison: Effort rating vs. confidence rating, both taken from the same post-answer self-report of the same model on the same items
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Qwen3-4B-Instruct (and/or Qwen3-30B-Instruct) on the Standard subset with the Appendix E prompt, sign-flipped effort AUROC does not exceed confidence AUROC by clearly more than the bootstrap CI (e.g. the gap is under ~0.05 or the CIs overlap).

title: MedVIGIL: Evaluating Trustworthy Medical VLMs Under Broken Visual Evidence
claim_source: Table 16, page 33 (bootstrap CIs); raw SFR and accuracy from Table 1, page 7

official.background: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are usually evaluated on intact image-question pairs, where a high score can come partly from language priors rather than from reading the image. In clinical use a model should also notice when the evidence is broken, for example when the question contains a premise the image contradicts or the relevant region of the image is hidden, and decline or correct the premise instead of giving a fluent answer. The paper calls a fluent non-refusal answer in that situation a 'silent failure' and builds a benchmark to measure it.
official.method:
MedVIGIL has 300 cases from VQA-RAD, SLAKE, ROCO and MIMIC-CXR/CheXpert, annotated by radiologists with a gold answer, a five-option MCQ (A-E, where E is a probe-specific safe action such as rejecting a false premise or flagging insufficient evidence), a clinical risk tier L1-L5 and an ROI box. Each case is expanded into up to ten probes (2,556 total): original, paraphrase, negation, specificity-drop, knowledge-only, two hallucination traps (false premise contradicted by the image; correct answer is always the refusal option), and ROI-masked / ROI-only / left-right-flip images. Every model is queried once per probe at temperature 0 with a single-letter prompt; scoring is exact letter match with no judge model.

The silent-failure rate (SFR) is the fraction of the 600 trap probes on which the model picks a non-refusal option. SFRw weights the per-tier SFR by (1, 2, 3, 5, 8) for L1-L5, and the Safety axis is 100 - SFRw. Capability is the mean of original, paraphrase, negation and specificity-drop accuracy. Appendix M reports case-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs (500 resamples over the 300 cases, seed 20260505) for Capability, Safety, Grounding and the harmonic-mean composite MCS.
official.claim: On the MedVIGIL MCQ probes, GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20) has a higher Capability score than HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B (54.8 vs 48.1) but a much lower risk-weighted Safety score: 36.0 [95% CI 31.2, 40.8] vs 60.4 [55.6, 64.9], with raw hallucination-trap silent-failure rate 53.0% vs 31.5%.
official.claim_caption: Table 16: Case-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs (500 resamples, fixed seed) for nine representative models spanning the MCS range. Capability uses the PR definition (Section 5.2). Rank-stability discussion in main text.
official.metric: Safety = 100 - SFRw (risk-weighted silent-failure rate on hallucination-trap probes), higher is safer; brackets are case-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs over the 300 cases (500 resamples). Table 1 values (SFR, Overall, Original) have no error bars.
official.comparison: GPT-4o vs. HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B on the same 2,556 probes with the same single-letter MCQ prompt and greedy decoding
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both models on the released probes gives GPT-4o a Safety score inside or above HuatuoGPT-V's 95% CI (>= 55.6), or the bootstrap CIs on Safety overlap, or GPT-4o's raw trap SFR is not clearly higher than HuatuoGPT-V's (e.g. a gap under 10 points instead of 21.5).

title: Slowly Annealed Langevin Dynamics: Theory and Applications to Training-Free Guided Generation

official.background: Annealed Langevin samplers follow a path of intermediate distributions from an easy reference law to a target. Slowing down the annealing schedule (SALD) helps the sampler track that path. A common use case is training-free guided generation: sampling from a pretrained diffusion or flow model's data distribution tilted by a reward or guide, p_data * exp(-f), without training a guidance model or estimating the Doob h-transform by costly Monte Carlo. The paper gives reverse-KL convergence bounds for SALD and proposes Velocity-Aware SALD (VA-SALD), which reuses the pretrained model's transport velocity so that the slowdown only has to correct the deviation caused by the guide.
official.method:
SALD runs Euler-Maruyama Langevin dynamics on the slowly varying score of the guided target pi_t ∝ p_t exp(-f_t), with time rescaled as t = s/r so that the budget r multiplies the number of steps. VA-SALD (Option I, c_t = u_t; the synthetic appendix does not name the option explicitly but describes the method as incorporating the VP velocity field) adds the reverse transport velocity u_t of the pretrained marginal path, scaled by the slowdown rate (dt/ds = 1/r), to the drift, with diffusion scale sigma_t taken from the forward process (Eq. 6). In the unguided case this leaves the pretrained marginals unchanged; under guidance the slowdown compensates only for the guide-induced residual.

Synthetic tests (Appendix 12.1) use a scalar VP forward diffusion with exact mixture scores on two 2D tasks: (a) a two-Gaussian data law guided by a two-moons potential (precomputed on a grid with bilinear interpolation), and (b) an eight-Gaussian ring with a Gaussian-bump penalty on the four left-half modes. For each budget r in {1, 2, 4, 10, 50, 100}, the authors compute the KL between the terminal samples and the guided terminal target pi_T. The baseline DOIT (local proposal-based Doob h-transform estimate) is not slowed down: it uses the same number of Euler transitions over the original interval, with M = 4 proposals and 2500 particles, so its effective budget of 10,000 particle-proposals matches the 10,000 particles used by SALD and VA-SALD.
official.claim: On the two 2D guided VP tasks, VA-SALD's terminal KL to the guided target is low even at the smallest budget r=1 (0.556 two-moons, 1.015 eight-Gaussian), versus 0.715 / 1.547 for SALD; at every budget it stays far below the budget-matched DOIT baseline (about 1.26-1.27 and 2.18-2.22). SALD's KL falls as r grows until it matches VA-SALD at r>=4.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Terminal KL. Budgets are r ∈ {1, 2, 4, 10, 50, 100}. Smaller values are better.
official.metric: Terminal-target KL divergence to the guided terminal distribution pi_T (lower is better); single run per entry, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: VA-SALD vs. SALD vs. DOIT at matched particle-step budgets r in {1, 2, 4, 10, 50, 100}
official.falsification_criterion: With the same tasks and budget matching, VA-SALD at r=1 does not have lower terminal KL than SALD at r=1 on both tasks, or DOIT reaches terminal KL comparable to VA-SALD (e.g. within 0.1) at any budget.

title: The Limits of AI-Driven Allocation: Optimal Screening under Aleatoric Uncertainty
claim_source: Figure 4 (right), page 11; numbers also stated in the Results paragraph on page 11

official.background: Governments and humanitarian organizations increasingly allocate scarce resources (cash transfers, demining teams) to the units with the highest predicted risk from a machine-learning model, instead of physically verifying each unit's status. Even a perfect (Bayes-optimal) risk model cannot remove aleatoric uncertainty: units with the same features differ in their true status, so purely algorithmic targeting misallocates some resources. Screening (physically observing the true status) removes that uncertainty but is expensive, so the practical question is which units to screen when only a fraction can be.
official.method:
The paper studies a two-stage allocation with allocation budget beta (fraction of the population that receives the resource) and screening budget alpha < beta. Screened units receive the resource only if their true label Y = 1; the remaining budget goes to the highest-risk unscreened units. Theorem 1 shows that the optimal screening set is a contiguous band of risk-score quantiles [q_alpha, q_beta] sitting just below the direct-allocation band (mu(X) > q_beta), and it contains the no-screening threshold. The thresholds are computed with a fixed-point algorithm (Algorithm 1): the top beta - alpha mass is allocated directly; below it sits a residual band of mass alpha(1 - rho), then the screening band of mass alpha, where rho is the mean risk in the screening band, iterated to convergence.

For the claim, the authors use the 2018 ACS PUMS data via folktables (about 1.6M individuals, ten demographic and labor-market features), with the binary target 'total personal income above $50,000' as the allocation label, split 50/50 into train and test. They train logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost, get out-of-sample risk scores on the test half, fix beta = 30%, and report allocation precision (fraction of allocated units with Y = 1) as alpha goes from 0 to 30%. The baseline is random screening: a random alpha fraction of units is screened (allocated if Y = 1), and the remaining budget is allocated greedily by logistic-regression risk (current operational practice).
official.claim: On ACS 2018 income data with allocation budget beta = 30%, optimal band screening at alpha = 30% raises allocation precision from about 60% (logistic regression) / 65% (XGBoost) with no screening to about 76% / 80%, whereas random screening with logistic-regression risk scores only reaches about 65%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Precision as a function of the screening budget α under optimal screening allocation. Left: landmine contamination prediction in Colombia (β = 10%). Right: ACS 2018 low-income prediction (β = 30%). Across all models, optimal screening consistently improves allocation precision over both the no-screening baseline (α = 0) and random screening.
official.metric: Allocation precision (% of allocated units that are truly positive; higher is better) on the test half. Single run and split; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Optimal screening (Algorithm 1) using logistic regression, random forest, or XGBoost risk scores vs. random screening with greedy logistic-regression allocation, at the same alpha and beta = 30%. Cleanest matched pair: logistic regression with optimal screening vs. logistic regression with random screening (both start at about 60% at alpha = 0).
official.falsification_criterion: On the ACS test split with beta = 30% and alpha = 30%, optimal screening with logistic-regression scores fails to beat random screening with the same scores by more than about 5 percentage points of precision, or optimal-screening precision is not monotonically increasing in alpha.

title: LLMs Improving LLMs: Agentic Discovery for Test-Time Scaling
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (scaling curves for the same setting in Figure 3c, page 7)

official.background: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves LLM reasoning by spending more inference compute, for example by sampling many reasoning chains and voting. How that compute is allocated (how many branches to start, how far to extend each, when to prune or stop) is usually decided by hand-designed heuristics such as self-consistency, adaptive-consistency or early-stopping rules. The paper asks whether a coding agent can instead discover better allocation strategies automatically, which matters because the accuracy-per-token trade-off determines the cost of deploying reasoning models.
official.method:
For each (model, problem) pair the authors pre-sample 128 reasoning trajectories from a Qwen3 model (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B or 8B) at temperature 0.7 and record the intermediate answer ('probe') every 500 tokens. A TTS controller is a program that, on this replay data, chooses to BRANCH (start a new trajectory), CONTINUE a branch by 500 tokens, PROBE a branch's current answer, PRUNE a branch, or ANSWER (aggregate). Cost is the total number of generated tokens. Because everything is replayed from stored data, a controller can be evaluated without calling the LLM; each evaluation is averaged over 64 random subsets of the 128-trajectory pool.

Claude Code acts as the explorer: over five rounds it reads the history of previous controllers, their accuracy-cost curves and execution traces, and writes a new controller. Each controller must expose a single knob beta in [0,1] that deterministically sets all internal hyperparameters. Discovery uses AIME24 only; the selected controller (Appendix D) is then evaluated, unchanged, on AIME25 and HMMT25 and compared against SC@64, ASC (threshold 0.95), ESC (chunk size 8) and Parallel-Probe.
official.claim: With Qwen3-1.7B on the held-out benchmarks, the discovered controller at beta = 0.5 reaches 38.6% average accuracy (AIME25 46.7, HMMT25 30.5) using 343.5k total tokens, versus 34.3% for SC@64 at 1093.5k tokens and 34.3% for ASC at 593.6k tokens, i.e. higher accuracy than every handcrafted baseline at fewer tokens than any of them.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Accuracy and total tokens. AIME24 (search) is used for controller discovery; AIME25 and HMMT25 are held-out.
official.metric: accuracy (%) on AIME25 and HMMT25 (higher is better) and total tokens across all branches (lower is better), each averaged over 64 random subsamples of the 128-trajectory pool; no std or CI reported
official.comparison: AutoTTS discovered controller (beta = 0.5 and 1.0) vs. SC@64, ASC, ESC and Parallel-Probe, all replayed on the same pre-sampled Qwen3-1.7B trajectories
official.falsification_criterion: On Qwen3-1.7B replay data for AIME25+HMMT25, the Appendix D controller at beta = 0.5 does not exceed the best handcrafted baseline's average held-out accuracy (34.3%) while using fewer tokens than ASC (593.6k), or the accuracy gap is within the spread across resampled trajectory subsets or across independent 128-trajectory pools.

title: Why Do DiT Editors Drift? Plug-and-Play Low Frequency Alignment in VAE Latent Space
claim_source: Table 4 (No-Op, Round 10: FLUX.2* (Base) vs + Low only (Ours)), page 9; full-pipeline comparison in Table 1, page 7

official.background: Instruction-based image editors built on diffusion transformers (DiTs) work well for a single edit, but when a user edits the same image over many turns, the image gradually drifts: colors shift, details are lost and the content changes, even when the instruction is 'keep the image unchanged'. Existing fixes need retraining, access to internal denoising trajectories or velocity fields, or model-specific signals, so they cannot be applied to API-only editors. The paper attributes the drift mainly to low-frequency deviations in the VAE latent introduced by the DiT, not to repeated VAE encode/decode, and proposes a training-free correction.
official.method:
VAE-LFA acts on the VAE latent z (C x H x W) after each DiT editing turn. The latent is split per channel into a low-frequency part l = AvgPool(z) (9x9 average pooling, stride 1, replicate padding) and a high-frequency residual h = z - l. The channel-wise spatial mean and log-std of l are tracked with an EMA anchor (alpha_mu = 0.95, alpha_sigma = 0.85), initialized from the low-frequency part of the initial image's latent and updated from pre-alignment statistics. At each turn the low-frequency part is renormalized channel-wise to the previous anchor's mean and std, then recombined with the untouched high-frequency residual.

In the white-box setting (FLUX.2 Klein 9B, 32-channel latent), the aligned latent is fed directly to the next DiT turn, so the inter-round VAE decode/encode is also removed; the decoder is used only to produce the visible image. Evaluation: 120 images (photograph/illustration x creature/architecture/scenery, 20 each), 10 consecutive no-op turns with identity-preserving prompts (e.g. 'Keep the image unchanged.'), and LPIPS, normalized L1 and SSIM between the round-10 image and the original image.
official.claim: On 10-turn no-op editing with FLUX.2 Klein 9B in the DiT-only setting (no inter-round VAE decode/encode), adding low-frequency alignment (VAE-LFA) lowers round-10 LPIPS to the original image in all 6 image categories (0.26 -> 0.17, 0.36 -> 0.27, 0.33 -> 0.25, 0.28 -> 0.26, 0.33 -> 0.29, 0.38 -> 0.33; mean about 0.32 -> 0.26) and raises SSIM in all 6 (e.g. 0.90 -> 0.93, 0.84 -> 0.88, 0.77 -> 0.83).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Ablation on frequency alignment scope for FLUX.2. Best results are in bold. * uses the DiT-only setting; Low only is VAE-LFA.
official.metric: LPIPS (lower better), normalized L1 (lower better), SSIM (higher better) between the round-10 output and the input image; per-category means over 20 images. The paper reports no error bars for Table 4. Its only uncertainty estimate is a pooled bootstrap 95% CI (Table 6, page 16) over 4 editors (N=480) against the Table 1 base editors: no-op LPIPS improvement 0.136 [0.114, 0.149]. That CI does not cover this DiT-only comparison.
official.comparison: FLUX.2 Klein 9B DiT-only multi-turn pipeline (latent fed straight to the next DiT turn, no VAE round trips) vs. the same pipeline plus low-frequency-only VAE-LFA; same images, prompts and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: With FLUX.2 Klein 9B in the DiT-only setting on 10 no-op turns, adding VAE-LFA does not lower round-10 LPIPS on average (mean reduction close to 0, versus about 0.06 in the paper), or fails to raise SSIM in most of the 6 categories.

title: Beyond ViT Tokens: Masked-Diffusion Pretrained Convolutional Pathology Foundation Model for Cell-Level Dense Prediction
claim_source: Table 2, page 5 (settings in Appendix B.4, Table B3, page 16)

official.background: Cell-level dense prediction in histopathology, such as nucleus segmentation, needs features that keep small structures: nuclear contours, chromatin texture and thin gaps between cells. Most pathology foundation models are ViTs that split the image into 14-16 pixel patch tokens, which the authors argue loses intra-patch detail. The paper proposes a convolutional alternative pretrained by masked diffusion and used as a frozen dense feature extractor, and asks which design choices make such features useful for segmentation.
official.method:
CMD pretrains a ConvNeXt-style U-Net (five downsampling stages, 8x8 bottleneck, five decoder stages, adaLN-Zero conditioning in every block) with a masked-diffusion objective: a timestep t in [1, T=1000] sets the masking ratio r_t = t/(T+1), a random fraction r_t of non-overlapping patches is zeroed, and the network reconstructs the clean input with an L1 loss, conditioned on the timestep embedding plus a frozen pathology foundation model's image-level feature (UNI, 1024-d, in the method-section ablations). After pretraining the backbone is frozen; multi-scale decoder activations at timestep t=50 are fed to a linear-probe segmentation head trained for 150 epochs (AdamW, lr 1e-3, cosine, cross-entropy + Dice).

The claim's comparison (Table 2, settings in Appendix Table B3) varies only the space in which masked diffusion runs. Pixel-space: 256x256 RGB input, 8x8-pixel mask patches (32x32 grid). VAE latent-space: the same 256x256 image encoded by SD-VAE (4 latent channels, scale 0.18215), 4x4 latent mask patches (8x8 grid). Both use the ~131M-parameter ConvNeXt-UNet, 55,000 unlabeled HistAI patches, 50,000 pretraining steps, AdamW lr 3e-5, EMA 0.9999, and UNI conditioning.
official.claim: With the same ~131M ConvNeXt-UNet, 55K pretraining images, UNI conditioning and frozen linear-probe evaluation, pixel-space masked-diffusion pretraining gives higher nucleus-segmentation Dice than VAE latent-space pretraining on CPM-15 (63.25 vs. 50.19), CPM-17 (76.74 vs. 55.20) and TNBC (73.51 vs. 53.23), and also beats the stronger 512x512 High-res VAE latent variant (47.96, 63.80, 58.24), with non-overlapping 95% bootstrap CIs in all six comparisons.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Pixel-space versus VAE latent-space masked-diffusion pretraining. Pixel-space and standard VAE latent-space settings use 256 x 256 inputs, while the High-res VAE latent setting uses 512 x 512 inputs. Other experimental settings are the same as in Table 1.
official.metric: Dice (%) and boundary F1 (%) on each dataset's test split, higher is better; brackets are 95% confidence intervals from 1000 bootstrap resamples (as stated in the paper); no repeated pretraining seeds are reported
official.comparison: Pixel-space masked diffusion vs. SD-VAE latent-space masked diffusion (256x256) and High-res VAE latent (512x512 input), identical backbone, data, steps, conditioning and linear probe
official.falsification_criterion: Under the matched setup, pixel-space pretraining does not beat VAE latent-space pretraining in Dice by more than the bootstrap CI on CPM-15, CPM-17 or TNBC (e.g. a gap under ~5 Dice points, or a reversed sign).

title: Trapping Attacker in Dilemma: Examining Internal Correlations and External Influences of Trigger for Defending GNN Backdoors

official.background: Node-level graph backdoor attacks poison a GNN's training graph by attaching small trigger subgraphs to a few victim nodes and relabeling those victims with a target class, so the trained model misclassifies any test node that carries the trigger. Existing defenses look for surface signatures (outlier features, unusual structure, or large prediction change under edge dropping) and can be evaded by attacks such as UGBA and DPGBA that craft in-distribution triggers. The paper argues that any effective trigger must exert a lot of influence on the victim, either through many mutually correlated trigger nodes or through a few highly influential ones, and builds a defense that checks both.
official.method:
PRAETORIAN computes two per-node scores on the poisoned training graph. Internal correlation: a 2-layer GAT masked graph autoencoder (mask rate 0.1, scaled cosine loss with gamma = 3, lr 1e-4) is trained to reconstruct masked node features; a node's score is 1 / its reconstruction loss when masked, so easily reconstructed (memorized trigger) nodes score high. External influence: a standard node classifier is trained on the poisoned graph; each node's features are masked in turn, and the score is the mean KL + JS divergence between the 1-hop neighbors' original and counterfactual predicted distributions.

The two scores are combined with an adaptive weighted sum, propagated so that trigger evidence flows to attached victims, and cut at the largest gap in the sorted scores (abstaining if no bimodal split exists). High-scoring nodes are grouped by label (groups of at least 5), the target label is inferred from the victims' labels, and trigger candidates are taken from the victims' P-hop neighborhoods. The final 2-layer GCN (lr 0.01) is trained on the graph with detected victims and triggers removed, plus an unlearning term (Eq. 6, evaluated on the original poisoned graph G_T) that maximizes cross-entropy toward the inferred target label on the detected victim and trigger nodes; the total loss is L_clean + L_unlearn.
official.claim: On Cora (80/20 inductive split, trigger size 3, 10 victim nodes, 2-layer GCN), PRAETORIAN reduces attack success rate to under 1% under all four attacks (SBA 0.09, GTA 0.44, UGBA 0.89, DPGBA 0.17), whereas the best of four baseline defenses (GNNGuard, OD, SP, RIGBD) still leaves 19.29 (SBA, SP), 27.77 (GTA, GNNGuard), 13.16 (UGBA, GNNGuard) and 18.09 (DPGBA, GNNGuard); PRAETORIAN's clean accuracy stays within about 2 points of the clean-graph model except under GTA (76.89 vs. 83.56).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Backdoor defense results. Bold indicates the best result within each attack–dataset setting.
official.metric: Attack success rate (ASR, %, lower is better) on the triggered half of the test graph and clean accuracy (CA, %, higher is better) on the clean half; average over 5 runs, no std or error bars reported
official.comparison: PRAETORIAN vs. GNNGuard, OD, SP and RIGBD (and no defense) under SBA, GTA, UGBA and DPGBA on Cora, same training-time defense protocol and splits
official.falsification_criterion: On Cora under any of the four attacks, PRAETORIAN's ASR is not clearly below the best baseline's ASR (e.g., PRAETORIAN above 5% or the best baseline below 5%).

title: The Power of Second Order Methods for Sequence Preconditioning

official.background: Predicting the outputs of a marginally stable linear dynamical system (long memory, possibly large hidden dimension) is a standard test problem for sequence models. Most online prediction methods have regret that grows with the hidden dimension. Universal Sequence Preconditioning (USP) convolves the signal with the coefficients of a Chebyshev polynomial so that only O(log T) steps of history are needed, independent of hidden dimension. The catch is that these coefficients grow exponentially with the degree, and first-order learners (gradient descent) pay linearly in the norm of the comparator. This paper argues that a second-order learner, the Vovk-Azoury-Warmuth (VAW) forecaster, pays only logarithmically in that norm, so it can use high-degree preconditioning that first-order methods cannot.
official.method:
Data are synthetic SISO LDS sequences h_t = A h_{t-1} + B u_t, y_t = C h_t + v_t with noise v_t ~ N(0, 0.01^2). The eigenvalues of A have magnitude 1 - 1e-7 and imaginary parts bounded by 0.1. B and C are standard normal, normalized to unit norm. Inputs u_t ~ N(0,1) are scaled by 1/log(5(t+2)), and T = 5000. The configuration used for the claim has hidden dimension d = 100 and baseline window w = 100.

In the 'Chebyshev' variant the labels are the preconditioned signal ỹ_t = y_t + Σ_{i=1}^n c_i y_{t-i}, with c_i the fixed coefficients of the monic degree-n Chebyshev polynomial, and the features are the inputs u. OGD, Adam and VAW each learn a linear predictor on this target. Each learner's hyperparameter is grid-searched and the best configuration is reported: OGD/Adam learning rate in {1e-4, 1e-3, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1}, VAW regularization λ in {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000}. The degree n is swept from 0 to 30. The metric is the normalized error |y_t - ŷ_t| / (|y_t| + 1e-8), averaged over the last 200 steps, with the median over 10 trials reported and IQR error bars. The 'learnable' variant (Algorithm 2: VAW on raw features [y_{t-1..t-n}, u_{t..t-n+1}]) is also plotted.
official.claim: On the d = 100 synthetic LDS (T = 5000), Chebyshev-preconditioned VAW keeps improving with polynomial degree up to n ≈ 20 and reaches a median normalized error of about 3e-4. Chebyshev-preconditioned OGD and Adam bottom out at about 4-5e-3 near n ≈ 14-15 and then get worse (about 1e-2 at n = 20), so VAW is roughly 10x lower at its best degree.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Normalized prediction error versus degree of preconditioning polynomial for (a) d = 100 and (b) d = 10. The Chebyshev-preconditioned VAW achieves superior steady-state error reduction compared to OGD and Adam as the degree increases.
official.metric: Normalized prediction error |y_t - ŷ_t|/(|y_t| + 1e-8), mean over final 200 steps, median over 10 trials, lower is better. Error bars are the interquartile range (25th-75th percentile) over trials. Values are read off a log-scale plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: VAW vs. OGD vs. Adam, all trained on the same fixed Chebyshev-preconditioned target, each with its best grid-searched hyperparameter, as a function of preconditioning degree n
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the d = 100 setup, the best-degree median error of Chebyshev-preconditioned VAW is not clearly below (e.g. within a factor of ~2, or overlapping IQR with) the best-degree median error of Chebyshev-preconditioned OGD/Adam. Another refutation would be OGD/Adam continuing to improve past degree ~15 as much as VAW does.
