title: BEACON: Cross-Domain Co-Training of Generative Robot Policies via Best-Effort Adaptation

official.background: Behavior-cloned visuomotor robot policies often degrade when the target domain differs from the domain the demonstrations came from (different textures, camera viewpoint, or sim versus real). Target-domain demonstrations are expensive, so a common approach is to co-train on many source demonstrations (e.g. from simulation) plus a few target demonstrations. Current co-training uses a fixed source/target mixing ratio or adds a feature-alignment loss (MMD, optimal transport). The paper asks instead which individual source samples should supervise the target policy, and learns per-sample weights guided by a domain-adaptation generalization bound.
official.method:
BEACON adapts the Best-Effort Adaptation (BEA) objective to Diffusion Policy training. Each source and target observation window i gets a weight q_i, and the policy and the weights are optimized jointly on sum_i q_i * l_BC(theta; x_i, y_i) + lambda_d * d_i + gamma * ||q||_inf * R(theta) + lambda_1 * ||q - r||_1 + lambda_2 * ||q||_2^2, where r is the uniform target-only reference and q is constrained to a budget b = n + alpha*m with a floor on target weights. The instance-level discrepancy d_i of a source window is the mean Euclidean distance from its policy-encoder embedding to its k nearest target embeddings, normalized by the within-target k-NN distance, and it is refreshed before each weight phase. Training alternates projected-subgradient updates of q on minibatches with AdamW updates of the policy on the q-weighted loss.

Sim-to-sim setup: Franka Panda in robosuite, MimicGen-generated source data with 500 demonstrations per task and 20 target demonstrations. The target differs from the source by texture (T) or by texture plus camera viewpoint (T+V). Inputs are 96x96 RGB plus end-effector proprioception, encoded by ResNet-18. All baselines use the same Diffusion Policy backbone: Source-Only, Target-Only, Co-Training (fixed mixing ratio), Tuned Uniform (one shared source weight tuned on stacking), MMD and UOT feature alignment. Each policy is evaluated on 100 rollouts whose initial states are matched across methods. Block stacking reports relaxed (R) and strict (S) success.
official.claim: On sim-to-sim block stacking with the texture + viewpoint gap (500 source, 20 target demos), BEACON reaches 0.60 strict success versus 0.37 for Tuned Uniform source weighting and 0.16 for fixed-ratio Co-Training (0.77 vs. 0.45 vs. 0.25 under the texture-only gap).
official.claim_caption: Table 1 Sim-to-sim mean task scores. T denotes the texture gap and T+V the texture + viewpoint gap. Stacking reports relaxed (R) and strict (S) success as defined in Appendix A; mug cleanup includes half credit for partial completion. Each Average is the equal-weight mean over stacking (R), mug cleanup, and threading.
official.metric: Task success rate over 100 simulated rollouts (higher is better); no ± reported, single training run per method
official.comparison: BEACON vs. Co-Training, Tuned Uniform, MMD, UOT, Target-Only, Source-Only, all with the same Diffusion Policy backbone and data
official.falsification_criterion: With the same data and backbone, BEACON's strict stacking success under T+V does not exceed Tuned Uniform by clearly more than rollout and training-seed noise (e.g. a gap under about 0.10 averaged over several seeds), or it does not beat fixed-ratio Co-Training.

title: AgentCollabBench: Diagnosing When Good Agents Make Bad Collaborators
claim_source: Figure 5 (top: GPT 4.1 mini per-topology means; bottom: η² for all models), page 8; exact means in Table 13 (page 27), tests in Tables 17-18 (page 29)

official.background: Multi-agent LLM systems pass messages between role-specialised agents (planner, auditor, engineer, ...), and a team can return a complete, valid-looking final answer even when a critical constraint was silently dropped along the way. Outcome-only benchmarks cannot see such process failures. AgentCollabBench is a 900-task benchmark across software engineering, DevOps and data engineering that injects controlled artifacts into multi-agent conversations to measure four failure modes, and it asks whether the way agents are wired together (the communication topology) matters as much as which model they run on.
official.method:
Each task specifies a team of agents, one of five communication topologies (linear chain, branching tree, converging DAG, fully connected, custom graph), a domain and a complexity tier. For the Radioactive Tracer Durability (RTD) metric, a unique tracer string (e.g. DATA-POLICY-RTN97DAYS-PII500MS) is embedded at a known graph location. Agents are assigned layers DAG-style (agents with no incoming edges are layer 0; each downstream agent is one plus the maximum layer of its predecessors). RTD is the deepest layer whose agent output contains the tracer (case-insensitive exact regex match on the canonical identifier), divided by the deepest layer in the task graph, so RTD is in [0, 1]. Scoring is deterministic, with no LLM judge.

The 232 RTD tasks (45-52 per topology) are run with all agents on a single backbone (GPT 4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct). Per-topology mean RTD is compared with a Kruskal-Wallis test (η² effect size) and Dunn post-hoc pairwise tests with Bonferroni correction. Tasks are co-designed with their topology, so different topologies use different tasks rather than the same task rewired.
official.claim: With GPT 4.1 mini as the backbone, RTD depends strongly on topology (Kruskal-Wallis H = 55.2, p < 1e-6, η² = 0.23): converging-DAG tasks keep the tracer to 49.4% mean depth vs. 100% for fully connected and 96.2% for custom graph (Dunn p < 0.001 for both), with linear chain 75.9% and branching tree 77.4%; converging DAG is the lowest-RTD topology for all four backbones.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: RQ4 topology effects on information propagation. Direct-routing topologies (fully connected, custom graph) preserve tracers almost completely (RTD ~96-100% for GPT 4.1 mini) by eliminating multi-hop propagation paths; converging DAG and branching tree, which require multi-hop forwarding, lose substantially more (RTD 50% and 78%). The association replicates across all four evaluated models (η² = 0.07-0.40). Top: GPT 4.1 mini metric means by topology. Bottom: η² magnitudes across all models.
official.metric: RTD (%), higher is better; mean over tasks in each topology; the Figure 5 caption does not define its error bars (the paper's other per-model results, Table 9, are mean ± standard error over task scores); single evaluation run, no seeds. Kruskal-Wallis H, p and η² across the five topologies.
official.comparison: Mean RTD on converging-DAG tasks vs. fully-connected and custom-graph tasks (and vs. linear chain / branching tree), same backbone (GPT 4.1 mini) and same evaluation protocol; replicated for Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct.
official.falsification_criterion: Running the released RTD tasks with GPT 4.1 mini, converging-DAG mean RTD is not clearly below fully connected and custom graph (gap well under ~30 points or Dunn test not significant), or the Kruskal-Wallis topology effect on RTD is not significant / η² falls near 0.

title: ReorgGS: Equivalent Distribution Reorganization for 3D Gaussian Splatting

official.background: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as millions of anisotropic Gaussians rendered by alpha compositing. Training grows this set with heuristic densification, cloning, splitting, pruning and opacity resets. The authors argue that a converged model can describe the scene well but still be badly parameterized for further optimization: high-opacity floaters block gradients to surfaces behind them, and redundant overlapping Gaussians respond to the same pixels with nearly collinear Jacobians. As a result, continuing to train plateaus even though removable artifacts remain.
official.method:
ReorgGS takes a converged 3DGS model and builds a new Gaussian set with the same count (M = N). It samples a component k with probability proportional to its opacity alpha_k (not weighted by volume), then samples a new center x_j ~ N(mu_k, Sigma_k). For each new center it sets the covariance to the second moment of its k = 20 nearest neighbours among the new centers (eigendecomposed into rotation and scale). Opacity is set to alpha_0 = 0.01, color/SH is copied from the nearest old Gaussian, and the optimizer state is reset. Training then continues with the original renderer, loss and training schedule.

Evaluation (Table 1): each backbone (vanilla 3DGS, GOF, Taming-3DGS, 3DGS-MCMC, LiteGS, plus half/double-budget LiteGS) is trained to convergence with a per-scene Gaussian budget taken from converged vanilla 3DGS. Three settings are then compared: Baseline (the converged model), Direct continuation (optimizing the original Gaussians for an additional budget, including standard opacity resets) and ReorgGS (reorganize, then optimize for the same additional budget). Train and test PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS are averaged over scenes from Mip-NeRF 360, Blender and Tanks&Temples.
official.claim: With vanilla 3DGS as the backbone, at an equal Gaussian count and equal additional optimization budget, reorganizing then continuing training gives 33.16 train / 28.89 test PSNR, compared with 32.61 / 28.72 for directly continuing to optimize the converged model (+0.55 dB train, +0.17 dB test). ReorgGS also gives better SSIM (0.940/0.883 vs 0.936/0.880) and LPIPS (0.130/0.169 vs 0.137/0.174).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Equal-budget comparison across backbones. Each cell reports train / test. ReorgGS keeps the same Gaussian count as the corresponding converged model.
official.metric: PSNR (dB, higher is better) on training and test views, averaged over scenes; SSIM and LPIPS also reported. No ± or seed variation reported.
official.comparison: ReorgGS (reorganize + continue training) vs. Direct continuation of the same converged 3DGS model, same Gaussian count and same additional iterations
official.falsification_criterion: On the same scenes with matched Gaussian count and additional iterations, ReorgGS fails to beat direct continuation on training PSNR by a clear margin (e.g. under ~0.2 dB), or does not beat it on test PSNR, consistently across seeds.

title: CoLVR: Enhancing Exploratory Latent Visual Reasoning via Contrastive Optimization

official.background: Latent visual reasoning lets a multimodal LLM 'think' by feeding its last hidden state back as the next input embedding for a few latent steps instead of decoding text, which is meant to carry continuous visual information more efficiently than a textual chain of thought. Existing methods such as Mirage train these latent tokens with hard alignment objectives that force each latent state to match a predefined visual feature (for example, pooled image patches). The paper argues that this collapses latent tokens into a narrow, homogeneous region of hidden-state space and limits how well the model can explore alternative reasoning paths, which hurts accuracy on spatial-planning and visual-puzzle tasks.
official.method:
Base model: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct with the vision encoder frozen and K = 8 latent tokens between <|latent_start|> and <|latent_end|>, each fed the previous hidden state as its input embedding. Training has three stages. (1) Warm-up: cosine alignment of every latent hidden state to the mean-pooled projected image feature S_I, plus 0.3 x answer cross-entropy. (2) Latent contrastive SFT: the positive is the feature S_Ihint of the image augmented with a solution hint. Negatives are built from Delta = S_Ihint - S_I: take a Gaussian vector, keep its component orthogonal to Delta, rotate Delta toward it by an angle theta sampled from [pi/2, pi], rescale to ||Delta||, and set S_neg = S_Ihint + z. With N_neg = 8 negatives, the loss is InfoNCE over the latent hidden states (weight 2) plus answer CE. (3) GRPO (rollout size 4) with reward R_format + R_correct + R_latent, where R_latent is an InfoNCE-style score that compares the current latent trajectory with the latent trajectories of correct (positive) and incorrect (negative) rollouts.

The baseline Mirage (latent tokens hard-aligned to grouped image patches) is retrained on the same data. Plain SFT and SFT+GRPO on Qwen2.5-VL-7B are also reported. Evaluation is exact-answer accuracy on the following test sets. VSP: maze path planning, levels 3-6 seen with 400 test items, plus levels 7-8 unseen with 200 items built with DiffThinker code. Jigsaw and Tetris: Zebra-CoT splits with 150 test items each. Per-task epochs and learning rates are in Appendix Table 6.
official.claim: Trained from Qwen2.5-VL-7B on identical data, CoLVR beats the hard-alignment latent baseline Mirage on VSP Total accuracy (65.83% vs. 60.00%, seen levels 80.70 vs. 74.00, unseen levels 36.00 vs. 32.00) and on Jigsaw (78.00% vs. 70.00%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results across multiple visual task benchmarks, comparing CoLVR with other VLMs and rigidly aligned latent baseline Mirage. Results are reported in accuracy (%), and best results are highlighted in bold.
official.metric: Exact-answer accuracy (%), higher is better; single training run (seed 42), no error bars reported. VSP Total is pooled over the 400 seen and 200 unseen test items.
official.comparison: CoLVR (warm-up + latent contrastive SFT + latent-trajectory-reward GRPO) vs. Mirage retrained on the same data. Qwen2.5-VL-7B with vanilla SFT (59.17 VSP Total, 67.33 Jigsaw) and with SFT + GRPO (55.33, 68.00) are secondary baselines.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same base model, data and training budget, CoLVR's VSP Total accuracy is not at least ~3 points above a retrained Mirage, or its Jigsaw accuracy is not above both Mirage and vanilla SFT, either for a single seed or on average over a few seeds.

title: The Grounding Gap: How LLMs Anchor the Meaning of Abstract Concepts Differently from Humans
claim_source: Table 4, page 17 (Appendix B); main-text summary in Figure 2 (page 5) and Table 1 (page 5)

official.background: Grounded-cognition theories hold that people understand abstract words such as justice or art by drawing on sensorimotor, emotional and social experience as well as on word associations. Cognitive scientists measure this with property-generation studies: participants list what comes to mind for each word, and the responses are coded into grounding categories. Different groups of people produce very similar per-word category profiles. The paper asks whether LLMs ground abstract concepts the same way, by running those human experiments on LLMs and comparing their category profiles with the human ones.
official.method:
Experiment 1 replicates Harpaintner et al. (2018) on 293 English abstract nouns (translated from the original 296 German words; two translation duplicates and the one-shot example word removed). For each word, the model is given the original human instructions (prompt in Appendix G, Figure 10) and asked to list four properties, situations or associations, at default temperature, 10 runs per model. An LLM coder (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, T = 0, prompt in Figure 12) assigns each property to one of Sensorimotor, Internal State & Emotion, Social, or Verbal Association. Each word then has a vector of relative category frequencies, averaged over runs.

Alignment is the Pearson r between model and human per-word frequencies across the 293 words, computed separately for each category and averaged over the four categories (Mean r). The human ceiling (split-half reliability) is estimated analytically from Harpaintner et al.'s per-word aggregates using ICC plus Spearman-Brown; on Experiment 2 this estimate matches an empirical 1000-split ceiling to within 0.01 (Appendix F). 21 frontier and open-weight models are evaluated.
official.claim: On Experiment 1 (293 abstract nouns, Harpaintner et al. 2018), no model among 21 LLMs exceeds Mean r = 0.375 with human property-category frequencies (best: Llama 3.1 70B 0.375, Qwen3 8B 0.373; Gemma-3-4B 0.270), against an estimated human ceiling of 0.974.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Full experiment 1 leaderboard, all 21 models in the panel, sorted by Mean r. Ten generation runs per model (Claude Haiku 4.5: nine). Bold marks the column max.
official.metric: Mean r = per-category Pearson correlation between model and human per-word category frequencies, averaged over 4 categories; higher is better. Table 4 has no error bars; Table 1 reports ± for three frontier models (0.004-0.008), defined in Appendix B.1/E.2 as the bootstrap standard deviation of Mean r over 1000 resamples (with replacement) of the 10 generation runs.
official.comparison: Each of 21 LLMs vs. the estimated human-human ceiling on the same 293 words and coding scheme
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the protocol (same words, prompt, 4 properties, 10 runs, Flash-Lite or human-validated coder), some tested model (e.g. Qwen3 8B or Llama 3.1 70B) reaches Mean r well above 0.4 (e.g. ≥ 0.5), or the human ceiling estimated from the human data turns out far below 0.97, so that the gap largely closes.

title: Muon Does Not Converge on Convex Lipschitz Functions
claim_source: Table 1, page 12 (also Table 2, page 53 and Figure 2, page 12)

official.background: Muon, which updates each weight matrix with the polar factor (orthogonalized version) of its momentum, is now used to train large language models, but its convergence theory relies on smoothness assumptions. Many practical optimizers (AdaGrad, Shampoo, Schedule-Free) were designed from theory for convex Lipschitz (nonsmooth) functions. The paper asks whether that theory also explains Muon. It shows that Muon can fail to converge on a simple convex Lipschitz function, proposes an error-feedback fix (EF-Muon) that provably converges, and then checks whether the fix helps in practice.
official.method:
MuonMax is the regularized Muon variant: the polar-factor step is scaled by the nuclear norm of the momentum, with a max norm over the product of all layers. EF-MuonMax wraps the same update in error feedback with momentum (Algorithm 1): it keeps a memory E_t, forms P_t = E_t + lambda_t M_t, applies the compressed step C(P_t) (the scaled MuonMax direction), and carries the residual P_t - C(P_t) into the next step. Vanilla Muon (unscaled polar step on matrix layers) is a third reference.

Image classification: WideResNet-28-10 (36M parameters) on CIFAR-10 (45K train / 5K validation), batch size 128, 40 epochs (~14K steps), cosine decay with no warmup, no weight decay, momentum 0.95. MuonMax and EF-MuonMax use signed momentum for non-matrix parameters, and vanilla Muon uses SGD with momentum. Every method gets the same 60-trial grid: peak LR in {1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3, 5e-3, 1e-2, 5e-2} x matrix LR multiplier in {0.1, 1, 10, 30, 100} x Nesterov in {True, False}. The reported number is the best run's final validation cross-entropy. Language modeling (206M nanoGPT-like model on FineWeb-Edu 10B, 100K steps) follows the same protocol with 30 trials for MuonMax and EF-MuonMax.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with WideResNet-28-10, the best of 60 tuned runs reaches final validation cross-entropy 0.388 for EF-MuonMax versus 0.265 for MuonMax, so error feedback makes MuonMax worse. The same holds on FineWeb-Edu nanoGPT (3.43 vs 3.27).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Best configurations for each method on image classification and language modeling tasks.
official.metric: Final validation cross-entropy (lower is better) of the best run in each method's hyperparameter sweep; single run, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: EF-MuonMax vs. MuonMax (same norm, same sweep grid, same paired optimizer); vanilla Muon as an extra reference
official.falsification_criterion: With the same sweep (or across several seeds at each method's best configuration), EF-MuonMax's best CIFAR-10 validation CE matches or beats MuonMax's, or the gap shrinks to within seed-to-seed variation.

title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
claim_source: Table 6, page 41 (Appendix A.8); summarised in Figure 2, page 7

official.background: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) predict DFT-level energies and forces for molecular dynamics far more cheaply than DFT itself. They are usually evaluated on unseen configurations of the same molecules they were trained on, and foundation MLIPs are pre-trained on millions of structures in the hope that they generalise to new chemistry. It is unclear whether these models learn how molecular fragments compose (so that they can handle new molecules built from known parts) or mainly interpolate between training molecules. The GMD benchmark tests this with controlled train/test splits where the test molecules are new but are built from fragments that appear in training.
official.method:
GMD consists of ab initio MD trajectories of small H/C/N/O molecules labelled with ORCA PBE/def2-TZVP+D3BJ energies and forces. For each training molecule, 1000 snapshots are used for training, 200 for validation and 200 as an in-distribution (ID) test set (new configurations of training molecules). OOD test sets contain only molecules never seen in training. Task 1 (Fragment Chain Extension): train on C2-C6 linear alkanes, test on C7-C13 alkanes. Task 2 (Fragment Fusion): train on C4-C10 alcohols and aldehydes, C7-C11 diols, and complex polyols/polycarbonyls (up to C11); test on C4-C10 carboxylic acids, whose -COOH group combines the hydroxyl and carbonyl moieties seen separately in training.

Models are trained from scratch with each architecture's original repository and early stopping on ID validation loss; foundation models (MACE-MP-0 S/M/L, UMA-Small) are fully fine-tuned for 2000 epochs after re-estimating atomic reference energies. The metrics are force MAE over all Cartesian components (eV/Å) and total-energy MAE per configuration (eV), on the ID and OOD test sets, averaged over three test splits drawn from the held-out trajectories.
official.claim: MACE trained from scratch generalises to longer alkanes (Fragment Chain Extension force MAE 0.0034 ID vs. 0.0061 eV/Å OOD, energy MAE 0.0016 vs. 0.0087 eV) but fails on Fragment Fusion: force MAE rises from 0.0047 ± 0.0000 eV/Å (ID) to 0.0889 ± 0.0001 eV/Å on unseen carboxylic acids (about 19x), and energy MAE from 0.0036 eV to 0.9734 eV (about 270x).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Comparison of MLIP models on the five GMD tasks: Fragment Chain Extension, Fragment Fusion, Fragment Duplication, Fragment Combination and Fragment Fission. Metrics reported are Forces Mean Absolute Error (F MAE) and Energy Mean Absolute Error (E MAE). Results are averaged across all molecules for each task. ID and OOD indicate in-distribution and out-of-distribution splits, respectively. Energy is in eV and forces in eV/Å. † Fragment Fission uses the Fragment Duplication models and in-distribution test set, so its ID values are those of Fragment Duplication. MACE-Small-25, MACE-Small-110 and UMA-Small-110 were not evaluated on this task.
official.metric: Force MAE (eV/Å) and total-energy MAE (eV), lower is better. ± is the spread over three test splits drawn from the held-out trajectories (sampling uncertainty of the test set), not over training seeds.
official.comparison: The same from-scratch MACE model on in-distribution test configurations vs. OOD test molecules, on Fragment Chain Extension (small gap) vs. Fragment Fusion (large gap). Other architectures and fine-tuned foundation models in the same table show the same pattern.
official.falsification_criterion: After training MACE from scratch on the released Fragment Fusion training split, the OOD/ID force-MAE ratio on carboxylic acids is close to the Chain Extension ratio (e.g. below ~3x), or the OOD force MAE is below ~0.03 eV/Å. Alternatively, the Chain Extension OOD/ID ratio is itself large (above ~5x).

title: Meow-Omni 1: A Multimodal Large Language Model for Feline Ethology

official.background: Inferring an animal's intent from its behaviour is hard because the same outward signal can mean different things. A cat's purr can signal contentment or pain, and which one depends on the cat's physiological state (the authors call this 'semantic aliasing'). General multimodal LLMs take video and audio but not raw physiological time series such as accelerometer data, so they cannot use that internal-state signal directly. The paper asks whether a model that takes video, audio and biometric time series natively, and is fine-tuned on feline data, infers cat intent better than general-purpose vision and omni-modal models.
official.method:
Meow-Omni 1 starts from the MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone and adds a time-series (TS) encoder and linear projector adapted from Intern-S1 Pro, plus three new TS control tokens. TS embeddings are interleaved with visual, audio and text tokens. Stage 1 trains only the projector on 383,853 labelled accelerometer windows (LLM and TS encoder frozen). Stage 2 fine-tunes only the LLM backbone on Meow-10K (10,831 samples with mixed modality subsets: video, audio and TS, each labelled with or mapped to a 30-class intention taxonomy). All encoders and projectors are frozen in Stage 2.

MeowBench is a held-out set of 527 expert-verified multiple-choice questions. Each is synthesized by pairing a video-audio clip with an accelerometer TS sample from a different session that carries the same intention label. The answer is the true intention, and the three distractors are sampled at random from the 30 classes. Evaluation is top-1 accuracy with a single greedy decode. The main baseline, Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus (accessed through the DashScope API, zero-shot), receives video and audio natively, and the TS data as a structured text summary (array shape, mean magnitude, temporal change, per-channel mean/std/min/max) prepended to the question. It is also decoded greedily.
official.claim: On the 527-item MeowBench multiple-choice benchmark, Meow-Omni 1 with video, audio and native time-series input reaches 71.16% top-1 accuracy, 4.27 points above the strongest baseline, zero-shot Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus given video, audio and a textual summary of the time series (66.89%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of Meow-Omni 1 against SOTA baselines on MeowBench.
official.metric: Top-1 multiple-choice accuracy (%), higher is better; single greedy-decoding run, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: Meow-Omni 1 (V+A+TS, fine-tuned) vs. Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus zero-shot with V+A, V+TS, TS+A and V+A+TS inputs, vs. unimodal baselines (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B video-only, Ntalampiras et al. audio classifiers, a CNN-LSTM IMU classifier)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-evaluating the released Meow-Omni 1 checkpoint and Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus (V+A+TS) on MeowBench with the stated protocol gives a gap under about 2 points or a reversed gap. A further failure condition is that Meow-Omni 1's lead is not robust to resampling the MCQ distractors or to bootstrap resampling of the 527 items.

title: Select-then-differentiate: Solving Bilevel Optimization with Manifold Lower-level Solution Sets

official.background: Bilevel optimization trains an inner (lower-level) model for given outer variables, such as per-example data weights or source-mixture weights, and tunes the outer variables to minimize a validation loss of the trained model. Standard hyper-gradient methods assume the inner problem has a unique minimizer. Overparameterized neural networks have many minimizers, though, and the hyper-objective can then be non-differentiable or badly behaved, depending on which minimizer the inner solver happens to reach. The paper studies the optimistic formulation, in which the outer objective is evaluated at the inner minimizer with the best validation loss.
official.method:
The paper shows that, under a local Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, the optimistic hyper-objective is differentiable whenever the optimistic selection is unique, with a pseudoinverse-based hyper-gradient formula. Based on this it proposes HG-MS (Hyper-Gradient with Minima Selection): at each outer step, generate N candidate lower-level solutions, select the one with the smallest upper-level (validation) loss, then compute the hyper-gradient through that candidate using a ridge-regularized conjugate-gradient solve with Hessian-vector products. The analysed version samples candidates with Langevin dynamics; the experiments instead use N parallel optimizer branches.

In the MNIST data hyper-cleaning benchmark, 5,000 training points from MNIST have a fraction rho in {0.4, 0.6, 0.8} of labels randomly corrupted; 500 clean validation points and 10,000 test points come from the same MNIST training split. The outer variable is one sigmoid weight per training example; the lower level trains a 784-300-10 sigmoid MLP on the weighted cross-entropy (L2 coefficient 1e-4); the upper level is clean validation cross-entropy. HG-BASELINE (Lorraine et al. 2020) differentiates through a 20-step AdamW unroll (lr 5e-3). HG-MS uses 8 branches, each with 20 lower updates (lr 2e-2, batch 256), picks the branch with the lowest validation loss, and computes the hyper-gradient by CG (ridge 1e-2, at most 30 iterations). Both use an AdamW upper optimizer with lr 0.1 (HG-MS uses a cosine decay to 0.01). Every method gets the same wall-clock budget on one H100 (60 s for rho 0.4 and 0.6), and test accuracy is reported at the end of the budget.
official.claim: On MNIST data hyper-cleaning with a 60 s per-method wall-clock budget, HG-MS reaches test accuracy 86.98 ± 1.02% vs. 81.22 ± 1.45% for HG-BASELINE at 40% label corruption, and 80.08 ± 2.52% vs. 73.09 ± 4.86% at 60% corruption.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Data hyper-cleaning (MNIST): train/test accuracies under different corruption rates. Mean ± 95% CI accuracies (in %) at a fixed wall-clock budget per algorithm: 60s for ρ ∈ {0.4, 0.6} (5 runs each), and 120s for ρ = 0.8 (5 runs).
official.metric: Test accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is the 95% two-sided t-interval over 5 independent runs
official.comparison: HG-MS (8-branch minima selection) vs. HG-BASELINE (single-branch AdamW-unroll hyper-gradient), plus V-PBGD, G-PBGD and IAPTT-GM, all under the same wall-clock budget
official.falsification_criterion: At rho = 0.4 (or 0.6), the 95% CIs of HG-MS and HG-BASELINE test accuracy overlap, or HG-MS's mean is not above HG-BASELINE's, when both get the same wall-clock budget and 5 seeds.

title: Spectral Transformer Neural Processes

official.background: Neural Processes (NPs) meta-learn a map from a small context set of input-output pairs to a predictive distribution at new target inputs, and are used for time series, spatial data and images. Transformer Neural Processes (TNPs) and translation-equivariant variants (ConvCNP, TETNP) handle translational structure, but when functions are periodic or quasi-periodic these models tend to underfit, sometimes collapsing to near-mean predictions, because their time-domain embeddings (e.g. ReLU MLPs) do not let attention relate points that are far apart but in phase.
official.method:
STNP adds a Spectral Aggregator to a TNP-Diagonal backbone. From the context set it computes an empirical energy spectrum on a fixed log-spaced grid of K = 128 frequencies (cosine/sine projections of mean-centred context outputs), feeds per-frequency summaries to a small 1D CNN along the frequency axis that softly assigns each grid frequency to one of Q = 6 components, and compresses the spectrum by moment matching into a Gaussian spectral mixture (weights, means, variances). It samples D0 = 8 frequencies per component by reparameterisation and builds weighted cos/sin features of x, which are concatenated with the usual MLP token embedding and projected to model width before the standard masked-attention TNP. In expectation the inner product of these features is a spectral-mixture kernel inferred from the context.

For the claim, all models are trained for 100,000 steps on 1D functions sampled online from a GP with a periodic kernel (amplitude s ~ U(0.1, 1), lengthscale l ~ U(0.6, 1), period p ~ U(0.1, 0.5), noise 0.02, x ~ U[-2, 2]). The context size is m ~ U[m_min, 47] with m_min = 20, and the number of targets is U[3, 50 - m]. Evaluation uses a fixed cached set of 3000 batches of 16 tasks shared by all methods; the metric is target-point log-likelihood. Baselines use default hyperparameters from their papers, with similar parameter counts (~0.22-0.36M).
official.claim: On 1D regression with functions drawn from a periodic-kernel GP (m_min = 20), STNP reaches a target log-likelihood of 1.12 ± 0.02, versus 0.44 ± 0.02 for the best baseline (SConvCNP), 0.20 ± 0.02 for TETNP and -0.35 ± 0.01 for TNP.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of STNP with the baselines on log-likelihood of the target points on various synthetic regression tasks. We train each method with 5 different seeds and report the mean and standard deviation. For the Periodic task, the reported results use m_min = 20.
official.metric: Target-point log-likelihood (higher is better), mean ± std over 5 training seeds
official.comparison: STNP vs. NP, CNP, ANP, CANP, BNP, BANP, ConvCNP, SConvCNP, TNP, TETNP, all trained and evaluated on the same synthetic task distribution and the same cached evaluation set
official.falsification_criterion: On the periodic-kernel task with m_min = 20, STNP's mean target log-likelihood is not clearly above SConvCNP's (e.g. the gap is under ~0.1 nats, within a few seed stds), or TNP with the same backbone reaches a comparable log-likelihood without the spectral branch.

title: Phases of Muon: When Muon Eclipses SignSGD
claim_source: Figure 6, page 7 (simulation details in Appendix B, pages 21-22)

official.background: Muon, which orthogonalizes a momentum buffer of matrix gradients using Newton–Schulz iterations, often trains faster than Adam, but it is not well understood when and why. This paper studies stochastic Muon on a high-dimensional matrix-valued linear regression whose gradients have the rank-one outer-product structure of a linear layer. It compares Muon with stochastic SignSGD, which is Adam with β1 = β2 = 0 and serves as a diagonal-preconditioning stand-in for Adam. It derives deterministic risk recursions for both methods. With isotropic data, the paper predicts that once each method's learning rate is tuned, Muon is at most a constant factor faster than SignSGD, and that around B_eff ≈ N Muon can be slower. Any real advantage of Muon must therefore come from anisotropic data.
official.method:
Model: W is N × N with N = 512, teacher W*, inputs x_in, x_out ~ N(0, I_N) independent, risk R = ½‖W − W*‖_F². The minibatch gradient is G = (1/B) Σ_b (x_out^b ⊗ x_in^b)⟨x_out^b ⊗ x_in^b, Δ⟩. Muon keeps M_t = βM_{t−1} + (1 − β)G_{t+1} and steps W ← W − η·polar(M_t). The polar factor is computed either exactly by SVD or with 5 Newton–Schulz steps (X ← aX + bXXᵀX + c(XXᵀ)²X from X0 = M/‖M‖_F, (a, b, c) = (3.4445, −4.7750, 2.0315)). SignSGD steps W ← W − η·sign(G), with no momentum. The effective batch is B_eff = B(1 + β)/(1 − β). All arithmetic is in float64.

Under the risk recursion R(t+1) = R(t) − 2ηd√R(t) + η²v, both methods with optimally scheduled learning rate contract by about exp(−2d²/v) per step. The 'Muon speedup' is the ratio of Muon's 2d²/v to SignSGD's 2B/(πN²), i.e. how many SignSGD steps one Muon step is worth. In the simulations (App. B), each run starts from a Gaussian Δ0 with R(0) = 6.25 and uses a constant step. The recursion is fitted by least squares in log R to the seed-averaged risk, giving 1 − rate = a²/(4b) = 2d²/v, which does not depend on η. The grid is B_eff/N = 2^k, k = −4…4, β ∈ {0, 0.5, 0.9}, exact polar and NS-5, two seeds per point. The SignSGD ratio is put on the same B scale through N_B ≈ √B(1 − 1/B + 5/B²).
official.claim: On isotropic matrix least squares with N = 512, the measured Muon speedup over SignSGD stays between about 0.5 and 1.46 at every batch size and momentum. Without momentum (β = 0, exact polar) it is about 1.0 at small batch, falls to about 0.71 at B = N (SignSGD faster), and rises to about 1.1 at B = 16N. With β = 0.9 and the exact polar factor it rises from about 0.63 at B_eff/N = 1/8 to about 1.42 at B_eff/N = 16.
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Muon speedup (12); above 1, Muon is faster. Colors as in Fig. 4. Curves: zero ridge; markers: simulations at N = 512, exact polar (open) and NS-5 (filled); grey: ridge theory at the calibrated NS-5 ridge (App. C).
official.metric: Muon speedup = (2d²/v)_Muon / (2B/(πN²))_SignSGD, the ratio of per-step contraction exponents under tuned learning rates; >1 means Muon is faster. Markers are simulations (2 seeds, no error bars shown); curves are theory. Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Stochastic Muon (exact polar factor or 5 Newton–Schulz steps, β ∈ {0, 0.5, 0.9}) vs. stochastic SignSGD on the same isotropic N = 512 matrix regression across B_eff/N from 1/16 to 16
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the N = 512 isotropic simulation, the measured speedup exceeds about 2 at some batch size, or for β = 0 with the exact polar factor there is no dip clearly below 1 (e.g. the value at B = N is above about 0.85), or at B_eff/N = 16 with β = 0.9 the speedup is not clearly above 1 (e.g. below about 1.25).

title: CLR-voyance : Reinforcing Open-Ended Reasoning for Inpatient Clinical Decision Support with Outcome-Aware Rubrics
claim_source: Table 5, page 26 (Appendix B.12); aggregate also in Figure 2 / Section 4, pages 5-6

official.background: Clinical LLM benchmarks mostly use exam-style multiple-choice questions or give the model the whole hospital record, so the answer leaks into the input. Inpatient decisions are made with only partial information: the clinician sees the admission so far and has to choose the next action. The paper turns MIMIC-IV admissions into a past/future split (CLR-POMDP). It uses what the care team actually did afterwards to write per-case grading rubrics, and then uses those rubrics both to evaluate models and as a reward for reinforcement learning on open-ended clinical reasoning.
official.method:
Each MIMIC-IV admission (ED, hosp, ICU, notes modules; admissions with readmission or death within two years excluded) is serialised as a chronological JSON event timeline and split at k ~ N(n/2, n/6). The policy sees only the past (with ICD events removed), at a 65,536-token context. An oracle LLM (Qwen3-32B, the 'Grounded Judge') sees past and future and, for each of four action spaces (Diagnosis, Treatment, Procedural, Uncertainty), writes a query answerable from the past, a reference answer backed by future events, and a per-case rubric. Each rubric criterion is pass/fail, tagged with one of five axes (Accuracy, Completeness, ContextAwareness, CommunicationQuality, InstructionFollowing) and weighted in [-10, +10]. A separate judge call marks each criterion, and the reward is the sum of the weights of satisfied criteria divided by the sum of positive weights, clipped to [0, 1].

Qwen3-8B is trained with GRPO (TRL, vLLM rollouts, G=4 or 8, KL to a frozen reference) on r_rub plus format and tag rewards, starting from the base checkpoint. The GRPO task vector (theta_grpo - theta_base) is then merged back into the base with DELLA-Linear (density 0.15, epsilon 0.02, weight 1.0). Every configuration is evaluated on the held-out 7,927-admission test split (four queries each) with one sample at temperature 0.2 (max 4,096 new tokens), scored by the same Grounded Judge and micro-aggregated over criteria.
official.claim: On the held-out CLR-POMDP test split, Qwen3-8B trained with rubric-reward GRPO and then DELLA-Linear-merged with its base reaches an aggregate rubric score of 84.95%, versus 77.99% for GRPO alone and 75.32% for the Qwen3-8B base. The gain is concentrated on Accuracy (80.77 vs. 69.21 vs. 66.57) and Completeness (80.98 vs. 67.92 vs. 58.72).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Per-axis CLR-POMDP scores (%) for each training configuration on the Qwen3-8B and MedGemma-4B families. Bold marks the best score per family per axis. SFT and GRPO are independent ablations off Base; the merge rows are initialised from the corresponding GRPO row.
official.metric: Grounded-Judge rubric score (%), positive-weight-normalised and micro-aggregated over criteria; higher is better. No error bars or seed variation are reported (Appendix B.11 says bootstrapped CIs are reported, but none appear). The only significance test is a paired Wilcoxon test against GPT-5 (p < 1e-300).
official.comparison: Qwen3-8B GRPO + DELLA-Linear merge vs. Qwen3-8B GRPO (no merge) vs. Qwen3-8B base (and SFT on oracle references, 52.36%), all scored by the same judge on the same test split

title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting in Visual Continual Learning with Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (same numbers repeated in Table 5, page 15)

official.background: Continual learning asks a model to learn a stream of tasks without access to earlier training data and without forgetting what it learned before. Recent work suggests reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT, e.g. GRPO) forgets less than supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but this had not been tested in hard visual settings such as rehearsal-free class-incremental learning, where each task adds new classes and the model is evaluated on all classes seen so far. The paper finds that GRPO still forgets substantially in this setting and proposes a reward-shaping fix.
official.method:
A multimodal LLM (Qwen2-VL-2B for classification) is trained task by task with GRPO, answering a closed-set prompt that lists every class name seen so far, with task reward R_task = R_acc + R_fmt (binary exact-match accuracy on the class name in the <answer> span plus a binary reward for the <think></think><answer></answer> format; Appendix B.2). RaPO changes GRPO in two ways. (1) Retention Reward: at task t, a frozen copy of the policy from the end of task t-1 serves as anchor. For each rollout, the length-normalized mean per-token log-ratio log pi_t - log pi_{t-1} is computed, clamped at 0 (D_drift), detached, and mapped to R_ret = exp(-alpha * D_drift). The total reward R_task + lambda * R_ret is used before the group-relative advantage, so among equally correct rollouts, the ones closer to the previous-task policy get larger advantages. It is active from task 2 on. (2) Cross-Task Advantage Normalization (CTAN): the per-batch reward std in the advantage denominator is replaced by an EMA sigma_hat <- beta*sigma_hat + (1-beta)*sigma_batch that persists across task boundaries; the numerator still subtracts the group mean.

Defaults: n = 8 rollouts, alpha = 20, lambda = 0.5, beta = 0.999; the standard GRPO KL loss is kept. Class-incremental ImageNet-R: 200 classes split into 10 tasks of 20 classes, 5 labeled images per class per task, 2 epochs per task, no replay. Metrics are Last Accuracy A (accuracy on all 200 classes after the final task) and Forgetting F (average drop from each earlier task's best accuracy to its final accuracy). Results are averaged over three random class orders. Baselines (sequential SFT, L2, EWC, LwF, and sequential GRPO) use the same model, data and epochs.
official.claim: On 5-shot rehearsal-free class-incremental ImageNet-R with 10 tasks and Qwen2-VL-2B, RaPO reaches last accuracy 85.92 ± 1.82 and forgetting 4.69 ± 1.71, vs. 74.67 ± 1.27 and 20.02 ± 4.91 for vanilla sequential GRPO, the strongest baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: A comparison of different methods on class-incremental image classification.
official.metric: Last Accuracy A (%, higher is better) and Forgetting F (%, lower is better); ± is the spread over three random class orders (presumably std; the paper does not say explicitly)
official.comparison: RaPO (GRPO + Retention Reward + CTAN) vs. sequential GRPO, SFT, L2, EWC and LwF, all with Qwen2-VL-2B, the same 5-shot splits and 2 epochs per task
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same protocol, RaPO's last accuracy on ImageNet-R 10-task is not clearly above sequential GRPO (gap within about 2 points, i.e. roughly one std), or RaPO's forgetting is not clearly lower than GRPO's.

title: Near-Linear Time Generalized Sinkhorn Algorithms for Bounded Genus Graphs
claim_source: Figure 4, page 9 (setup in Appendix B.1, pages 15-16)

official.background: Entropic optimal transport (Sinkhorn) between distributions on a graph or mesh with geodesic (shortest-path) costs needs repeated multiplications by the n x n kernel K = exp(-D/ε), where D is the all-pairs shortest-path matrix. Building and multiplying by this dense kernel costs quadratic time and memory, which limits geodesic OT on meshes and road networks to a few thousand nodes. Existing fast Sinkhorn variants (Greenkhorn, Screenkhorn, sparse truncation, Nyström / random-feature low-rank kernels, heat-kernel approximations) avoid the dense kernel but change the cost they optimize, so their OT values can differ substantially from the true geodesic Sinkhorn value.
official.method:
GenusSink replaces the dense kernel-vector product with a divide-and-conquer structure called a separation graph field integrator (S-GFI). Each tree node stores a small balanced separator S splitting the graph into A and B, Dijkstra distances from A and from B to S, and the S x S separator distances; children are the subgraphs on A ∪ S and B ∪ S with separator-pair edges reweighted to true shortest-path distances. Because every A-B path crosses S, the A-B block of exp(-D/ε) equals exp(-min_k (d(a,k)+d(k,b))/ε), which the cross_compute routine evaluates in near-linear time by sorting on separator-difference vectors (for |S| = 1 it is a rank-1 product). Leaves of the tree hold explicit graphs and are multiplied brute force; the S-S block is subtracted once to avoid double counting. The Sinkhorn iterations themselves are standard; only the matrix-vector product is changed.

In the Figure 4 experiment (Appendix B.1) the graphs are planar sphere-topology 'pseudo-genus' surfaces of orders 1, 2, 3 (narrow necks that look like handles but keep the graph planar), with n ∈ {644, 2036, 4268, 7283, 11090, 15740, 19745}. Source and target are two-component Gaussian mixtures in the surface parameter coordinates, normalized over vertices. GenusSink is compared with dense full-kernel geodesic Sinkhorn (the reference), Sparse Sinkhorn, Greenkhorn, Screenkhorn, geodesic heat-kernel Sinkhorn, and two Linear Sinkhorn variants (ambient-Euclidean random features and geodesic Nyström). Metrics are |OT_full - OT_method| and total runtime (including kernel/structure construction) on an Apple M3 laptop. Separator-tree depth is small (the dumbbell experiments use depth 1; the paper says 'small values of h' in practice).
official.claim: On planar pseudo-genus surface graphs of orders 1-3 with up to ~19.7k nodes, GenusSink's Sinkhorn OT cost differs from dense geodesic Sinkhorn by only ~1e-15 to 1e-13, whereas every efficient baseline errs by ~1e-6 or more (Sparse Sinkhorn ~1e-4 to 1e-2, Greenkhorn ~1e-6 to 1e0, others ~1e-3 to 1e3), and at ~19.7k nodes GenusSink takes ~20-25 s vs. ~100 s for the dense full kernel and ~40-70 s for Sparse Sinkhorn.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Synthetic pseudo-genus surface experiments for pseudo-genus orders 1, 2, and 3 (left to right). Top: absolute Sinkhorn-cost error relative to the dense geodesic full-kernel baseline. Bottom: total runtime for the Brute Force (full kernel) and the two most accurate efficient methods from previous studies: GenusSink and Sparse Sinkhorn. GenusSink stays numerically exact while providing significant computational gains.
official.metric: Absolute OT-cost error |OT_full - OT_method| relative to dense geodesic Sinkhorn (lower is better, log scale) and total wall-clock runtime in seconds (lower is better, log scale); single runs per graph size, no error bars; values read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: GenusSink vs. dense full-kernel geodesic Sinkhorn (accuracy reference and runtime baseline) and vs. Sparse Sinkhorn, Greenkhorn, Screenkhorn, Geodesic Nyström, Ambient LinearSinkhorn, and Geodesic heat kernel on the same graphs and marginals
official.falsification_criterion: A re-implementation on comparable planar surface graphs (n ≈ 10k-20k) finds GenusSink's OT cost differing from dense geodesic Sinkhorn by more than ~1e-8 (i.e. not exact to floating-point precision), or finds GenusSink's total runtime at ~20k nodes not clearly below the dense full-kernel baseline (e.g. less than 2x faster) under the same Sinkhorn tolerance.

title: M2A: Synergizing Mathematical and Agentic Reasoning in Large Language Models

official.background: Reasoning-tuned LLMs (trained on long chain-of-thought math data) think in a single long response, while coding agents must interleave short reasoning with tool calls over many turns. Simply mixing math and agent data in SFT, or merging a reasoning model into an agent model, tends to transfer the long-reasoning style without improving agent performance: the merged model thinks longer, calls tools less, and can solve fewer tasks. The question is whether math reasoning ability can be added to a coding agent without disturbing its think-act-observe behavior.
official.method:
Both source models share the base Qwen3-8B-Base. Agent-8B is SFT'd by the authors on 30k coding-agent trajectories from stepfun-ai/Step-3.5-Flash-SFT; Reasoning-8B is DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B. M2A is training-free: it runs the agent model over 100 calibration coding-agent trajectories (from Scale-SWE, no overlap with SWE-Bench Verified) and, for each layer, collects input hidden states within r = 5 tokens of the behavior markers <think>, </think>, <function=, </function>. The reasoning task vector ΔW_reason = W_reason - W_0 for each weight matrix is projected onto the null space of the span of these calibration features (ΔW_reason (I - QQ^T), implemented with a block-wise matrix-free solver, λ = 1e-4), so that it leaves the agent-critical directions unchanged.

Each layer gets a coefficient α_l = β · ||Δθ_agent^(l)||_F / (||Δθ_reason^(l)||_F + ε), and only layers whose agent and reasoning task vectors have cosine similarity above the mean across layers are merged: W_merge = W_agent + M_l α_l ΔŴ_reason. Baselines (Task Arithmetic, TIES, DARE, SLERP, RAIN-Merging) merge the same two source models; Task Arithmetic, TIES, DARE and SLERP each have their merge coefficient swept on SWE-Bench Verified with the best setting reported, while RAIN-Merging uses its own adaptively selected (instruction-attention guided) coefficients; multi-task SFT trains on 30k agent + 30k math trajectories. All models are evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified with the OpenHands scaffold (temperature 0.7, max 400 steps, YaRN factor 8, 262k context, git history removed), resolved rate averaged over 3 runs.
official.claim: On SWE-Bench Verified (OpenHands, Avg@3), M2A applied to Agent-8B reaches a 51.2 ± 0.6% resolved rate, versus 47.6 ± 0.9% for the best merging baseline (Task Arithmetic, same source models, tuned coefficient), 47.2 ± 0.7% for SLERP, 44.0 ± 0.9% for the unmerged Agent-8B and 41.1 ± 1.4% for multi-task SFT.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on SWE-Bench Verified. Avg. reasoning length is the number of reasoning tokens per step, and Avg. Step represents the number of turns the model interacts with the environment. Results are averaged over 3 runs, subscripts denote standard deviation.
official.metric: SWE-Bench Verified resolved rate (%), higher is better; mean ± std over 3 independent evaluation runs
official.comparison: M2A-Agent-8B vs. Task Arithmetic, SLERP, TIES-Merging, DARE and RAIN-Merging (all merging Agent-8B with Reasoning-8B), the unmerged Agent-8B, and Multi-Task-8B SFT
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same evaluation protocol, M2A's mean resolved rate over 3 runs is not clearly above the best tuned Task Arithmetic or SLERP merge of the same two models (e.g. gap below ~1.5 points or within one std), or not above the unmerged Agent-8B.

title: The two clocks and the innovation window: When and how generative models learn rules
claim_source: Table 4 (Appendix C.3), page 27; also Figure 2D(ii) page 4 and Figure 10 page 26

official.background: Generative models trained on a finite dataset are optimized toward the empirical training distribution, so with enough training they eventually reproduce training samples instead of learning the underlying data-generating rule. With natural data it is hard to tell rule learning from memorization. This paper uses synthetic binary data governed by an exact rule (group parity), where rule validity, novelty and exact memorization can all be measured, to ask when during training a model starts producing rule-valid samples and when it starts copying training samples.
official.method:
Each sample is a 36-bit vector in {-1,+1}^36, split into 36/G groups of G bits, with every group having even parity. G (2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36) sets rule complexity. The training set is N unique such samples (N swept from 1024 up to 65536 for DiT-mini; N ∈ {4096, 8192, 16384, 32768} for GPT-mini). DiT-mini (6 layers, 6 heads, width 384, patch size 1 on a 6x6 image, about 16.5M params) is trained as an EDM diffusion model (x0 prediction, EDM preconditioning and log-normal noise schedule) with Adam at lr 1e-4, batch 256, no weight decay, and up to 1e6 steps. GPT-mini (6 layers, width 384) is trained with next-token prediction on the same bit strings (AdamW, lr 1e-4, wd 0.01, batch 256, 1e5 steps).

At checkpoints spaced increasingly far apart, 2048 samples are generated from fixed initial noises (35-step Heun sampler for DiT, temperature-1 sampling for GPT). Sample memorization ratio is the fraction of generated samples that exactly match a training sample. τmem is the first step at which the memorization ratio reliably exceeds a threshold (0.1 in the main text; Table 4 uses an adaptive threshold of 0.1 + N/support_size). τmem is then fit as c·N^α by log-log linear regression, both pooled over all G and separately per G.
official.claim: For DiT-mini on group-parity data (D=36), memorization onset scales nearly linearly with training set size, τmem ≈ 35.3·N^1.14 (R²=0.94, n=34 runs pooled over all G), with per-G exponents between 1.05 and 1.25. τmem is roughly independent of rule complexity G. GPT-mini shows the same near-linear scaling (α=0.97, R²=0.94, n=34) at a lower prefactor (2.1 vs 35.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Power-law scaling of memorization onset τmem with training set size N: τmem ≈ c·N^α. Fit via log-log linear regression; R² and n denote fit quality and number of data points. τmem is measured with adaptive mem. threshold = 0.1 + N/support_size.
official.metric: Power-law exponent α and prefactor c of τmem (training steps to memorization onset) vs N, from log-log regression; R² and number of runs n reported. No seed error bars or confidence intervals on α are reported.
official.comparison: τmem across dataset sizes N (and across rule complexities G and architectures DiT-mini vs GPT-mini), not method vs baseline
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining DiT-mini (or GPT-mini) on several N values gives a pooled exponent clearly outside roughly 0.9-1.3 (e.g. sublinear α < 0.8 or α > 1.4), or at fixed N the τmem values differ by much more than the spread implied by Table 4's per-G fits across G (e.g. τmem strongly increasing with G).

title: EchoPrune: Interpreting Redundancy as Temporal Echoes for Efficient VideoLLMs

official.background: Video large language models turn every sampled frame into hundreds of visual tokens, so the usual default of 16-32 uniformly sampled frames is set by the LLM's token budget. With so few frames, long videos can lose the moments that answer the question. Training-free token pruning removes redundant visual tokens before the LLM. If pruning is good enough, a model can look at many more frames while keeping the same number of tokens. Existing pruners either treat video frames as independent images (attention salience, coverage) or rely on segment-and-merge heuristics, which the authors argue lose fine temporal cues and add overhead.
official.method:
EchoPrune scores every projected visual token v_i^k (token i of frame k, after the vision encoder and projector, before the LLM) with a maximum-marginal-relevance score S = r - delta. Relevance r is the maximum cosine similarity between the L2-normalized visual token and any normalized text-query token. Redundancy delta = delta_corr + delta_echo, where delta_corr is the cosine similarity with the token at the same position in frame k-1. delta_echo is the inner product of the token with its reconstruction from frame k-1: a softmax(similarity/tau)-weighted average of frame k-1 tokens in a spatial neighborhood (a 3x3 neighborhood for LLaVA-OV; the full frame for the Qwen-VL models). A single global Top-K over all frames keeps the budgeted number of tokens. The first frame, which has no predecessor, keeps on average N_F/gamma tokens chosen by relevance alone. No training is involved.

For Qwen2.5VL-7B (tau = 0.5, full-frame echo matching), the token budget is fixed at what the unpruned model uses for 16 frames (F16). Every pruning method then samples gamma x 16 frames (F64, F80, F160, F320) and keeps 1/gamma of the tokens. Baselines are re-run from official repositories under the same settings: Random pruning, Query-only relevance, MI-Pruner, VisionZip, FastVID and FlashVID. Evaluation uses LMMs-Eval on VideoMME (no subtitles), EgoSchema, LongVideoBench (val), MLVU (test) and VideoMMMU. The 'Average' column is the mean of VideoMME overall, EgoSchema total, LongVideoBench, MLVU and VideoMMMU.
official.claim: On Qwen2.5VL-7B at F320 with 5% of tokens kept (the F16 token budget), EchoPrune reaches a 5-benchmark average of 55.6, versus 52.4 for both FlashVID and random pruning and 51.8-52.1 for MI-Pruner, VisionZip and FastVID. Most of the gain is on MLVU (51.4 vs. at most 47.0) and VideoMMMU (46.3 vs. at most 42.2).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance on Qwen2.5VL-7B. We keep F16 token budget to compare pruning effects following [6]. EchoPrune demonstrates consistent effectiveness in average scores.
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy (%) per benchmark and their unweighted average, higher is better; single runs, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: EchoPrune vs. Random, MI-Pruner, VisionZip, FastVID and FlashVID, all at F320 frames with 5% token retention on Qwen2.5VL-7B (the same LLM-side token budget as unpruned F16)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Qwen2.5VL-7B at F320/5%, EchoPrune's 5-benchmark average is not more than about 1.5 points above random pruning or FlashVID, or EchoPrune does not beat random pruning by several points on MLVU and VideoMMMU.

title: Synthetic Pre-Pre-Training Improves Language Model Robustness to Noisy Pre-Training Data
claim_source: Table 7 (Appendix C), page 16; same runs shown in Figure 2, page 5

official.background: LLM pre-training corpora always keep some noise after curation, and noisy tokens degrade final model quality. Data filtering cannot remove all of it without also dropping useful rare text. This paper asks whether the model itself can be made more tolerant of noise: a short 'pre-pre-training' (PPT) stage on synthetic sequences, run before ordinary pre-training (PT), might give the model a structural prior that makes the later noisy PT less harmful.
official.method:
The PPT source is an ensemble of M=1000 fixed, randomly initialized RNN generators (hidden size 64, full 50,304-token vocabulary, temperature 1). For each 2048-token sequence one generator is picked at random. It runs h_t = A e_{x_{t-1}} + W h_{t-1} + b, logits = C h_t + d, and samples the next token. A has std 1/sqrt(V), W and C have std 1/sqrt(H), biases are zero, and W is rescaled to spectral radius 0.9. The generators are never trained. A Pythia-160M model is trained for 500 PPT steps on these sequences and then for 10K PT steps on C4 (effective batch 32, sequence length 2048, AdamW, lr 7e-4, cosine schedule with 500-step warmup, packing). PPT and PT each get their own optimizer schedule.

Noise is injected during PT at the sample level: each training sequence is replaced, with probability p, by tokens drawn uniformly from the vocabulary. The comparison conditions are identical except for the PPT stage: no PPT (baseline), Random i.i.d.-token PPT, k-Shuffle Dyck PPT (k=64), C4 PPT with a matched budget, and RNN PPT. The metric is the final validation loss on clean held-out C4, averaged over 3 seeds.
official.claim: With Pythia-160M, 500 PPT steps and 10K C4 PT steps, RNN-PPT reaches a final clean C4 validation loss of 3.681 ± 0.004 at 30% sample-level noise and 3.761 ± 0.003 at 50% noise. The strongest alternatives score 3.703 (Dyck PPT and C4 PPT) at 30% and 3.786 ± 0.007 (C4 PPT) at 50%, and the no-PPT baseline scores 3.719 and 3.818.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Final C4 validation loss at 160M scale with Random-PPT and C4-PPT included. Values are mean ± standard deviation across three seeds.
official.metric: Final validation loss on clean held-out C4 (lower is better), mean ± std over 3 seeds
official.comparison: RNN PPT vs. no PPT (baseline), Random PPT, Dyck PPT and budget-matched C4 PPT. All share the same PT data, noise level, PT recipe and PPT step count.
official.falsification_criterion: At 30% or 50% PT noise, RNN-PPT's final C4 validation loss is not lower than that of both Dyck PPT and C4 PPT by more than about one seed std, or it fails to beat the no-PPT baseline.

title: Stable Long-Horizon PDE Forecasting via Latent Structured Spectral Propagators

official.background: Neural operators such as FNO are trained to predict a PDE solution a short time ahead and are then applied autoregressively to forecast long trajectories. Under repeated composition, small one-step errors compound and the rollout drifts away from physical solutions, which limits their use for long-horizon simulation. Latent-space and Koopman-style models try to give the recurrent update more structure, but they often use the same latent space both for reconstruction and for propagation, which the authors argue makes the propagation rule less regular.
official.method:
SSP (Structured Spectral Propagator) factorizes the forecaster as decoder ∘ inverse projector ∘ propagator ∘ projector ∘ encoder. The encoder is applied frame-wise (each time slice separately: coordinate grid concatenated, conv lift, factorized 1D spectral blocks, channel attention) to give a spatial representation with C_s channels; a 1x1 conv projector reduces it to a compact state with C_z < C_s channels at the same latent resolution. The propagator Fourier-transforms the compact sequence of T frames, keeps a low-frequency band of m_x x m_y modes, and updates each mode's length-T temporal vector with a per-channel T x T matrix scaled by a bounded frequency gate 1 + β tanh(MLP(kx, ky, |k|, cos θ, sin θ)), plus a shallow-CNN nonlinear closure over the retained frequency plane, combined in N_sub residual Euler substeps. A 1x1 conv lifts back to C_s channels and a decoder (channel attention, spectral branch, local conv branch, readout) produces the physical fields.

Training uses autoregressive rollout with reconstruction, latent-rollout and physical-rollout MSE losses (weights 1) plus a normality penalty on the temporal matrices and an orthogonality penalty between linear and closure updates (weights 0.01). For Shallow-Water and Reaction-Diffusion, models see 10 input frames and predict the next 90 frames autoregressively; metrics are time-averaged relative L2, max pointwise error E_max, and low-frequency spectral error f_low. Baselines are FNO, U-FNO, F-FNO, UNO, KNO, LNO and CALM-PDE.
official.claim: On the 2D Reaction-Diffusion benchmark (10 input frames, 90-step autoregressive rollout), SSP reaches time-averaged relative L2 error 7.46E-3, about 49% lower than the best baseline U-FNO (1.46E-2) and F-FNO (1.52E-2), and also has the lowest E_max (6.71E-3 vs. 2.02E-2 for F-FNO).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative comparison on long-horizon PDE benchmarks. Best results are in bold, and second-best results are underlined. - indicates that the corresponding model failed to train under this setting.
official.metric: Time-averaged relative L2 error over the 90-step rollout (lower is better); E_max and f_low also reported. SSP is the mean of 3 seeds; the standard deviations are said to be in the appendix, which is not in the arXiv version. Baselines have no reported error.
official.comparison: SSP vs. FNO, U-FNO, F-FNO, UNO, KNO, LNO, CALM-PDE trained and evaluated by the authors on the same benchmark and rollout protocol
official.falsification_criterion: With all models trained under the same protocol on 2D Reaction-Diffusion, SSP's 90-step relative L2 is not clearly lower than a well-tuned U-FNO or F-FNO (e.g. less than ~20% reduction, or within seed-to-seed spread).

title: Coarsening Linear Non-Gaussian Causal Models with Cycles

official.background: Causal discovery usually assumes the causal graph is acyclic, which rules out systems with feedback loops such as signaling networks. In linear non-Gaussian (LiNG) cyclic models, ICA can recover the structural matrix only up to an equivalence class whose members differ inside feedback loops, and enumerating that class takes exponential time. This paper argues that the coarse graph obtained by collapsing each strongly connected component (SCC) into one node (the condensation, a DAG between clusters) is the same for every member of the class. It is therefore identifiable from observational data and can be learned in polynomial time, giving a cluster-level causal summary of a cyclic system.
official.method:
Algorithm 1 runs FastICA on the data to estimate the demixing matrix Ŵ, picks one admissible row permutation P with the Hungarian algorithm (maximizing Σ_i log|(PŴ)_ii| with cells ≤ η forbidden), forms B̂ = I − diag(PŴ)⁻¹PŴ, zeroes entries with |B̂_ij| < τ (τ = 0.1), runs Tarjan's algorithm on the support of B̂ (transposed so rows are sources) to get the SCC partition, and outputs the quotient graph (condensation Ĝ_sc), with an inter-cluster edge wherever some nonzero B̂_ij links the two clusters. Worst-case time is O(k·n·d² + d³).

In the scalability experiment (Section 5.3), the data are synthetic linear cyclic SCMs with d ∈ {20, 50, 100} variables, κ = 10 non-trivial SCCs (each built from a directed Hamilton cycle plus extra intra-SCC edges with probability λ), inter-cluster edges along a random topological order with probability λ = 0.5, edge weights in [0.5, 0.95] with random sign, and skewed exponential noise (so the baseline's third-moment tests work). n ranges over [10², 10⁵], 10 seeds per cell. The baseline is the disjoint-cycles procedure of Drton et al. (2025), whose layered topological ordering is read as its predicted partition. Both methods are scored by ARI of the predicted partition against the true SCC partition and cluster-DAG F1 (predicted edges projected onto the true SCC partition, compared with the edges of the true condensation), plus fit time.
official.claim: On synthetic cyclic LiNG SCMs with κ = 10 SCCs, λ = 0.5 and exponential noise, the proposed ICA + Tarjan method reaches cluster-DAG F1 ≈ 1.0 at n = 10⁴ for d = 20, 50 and 100, while the disjoint-cycles baseline of Drton et al. (2025) reaches about 0.72, 0.28 and 0.17 respectively; at n = 10⁵, d = 100 the baseline takes about 10⁴ s versus about 20 s for the proposed method.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Scalability vs the disjoint-cycle baseline of Drton et al. [2025] (d ∈ {20, 50, 100}, λ = 0.5, κ = 10 SCCs, 10 seeds per cell). d encoded by color intensity; solid: ours, dashed: disjointCycles. Left to right: ARI, cluster-DAG F1, fit time (s).
official.metric: Cluster-DAG F1 (higher is better) and ARI of the SCC partition (higher is better), plus fit time in seconds (lower is better); lines summarize 10 seeds per cell; shaded bands are 95% confidence bands across seeds (stated in the paper's checklist for Figures 3, 4, 6 and 8; Figure 4's caption does not restate it). Values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Proposed method (FastICA + Hungarian permutation + threshold τ = 0.1 + Tarjan condensation) vs. the disjointCycles procedure of Drton et al. (2025) on the same simulated datasets
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Section 5.3 simulation (d = 50 or 100, κ = 10, λ = 0.5, exponential noise, n = 10⁴, 10 seeds), the proposed method's mean cluster-DAG F1 is not near 1 (e.g. below 0.9), or the disjoint-cycles baseline's F1 comes within about 0.2 of it.

title: CORTEG: Foundation Models Enable Cross-Modality Representation Transfer from Scalp to Intracranial Brain Recordings

official.background: Intracranial ECoG/sEEG gives high signal-to-noise access to cortical activity for brain-computer interfaces, but each patient contributes only tens of minutes of data, and electrode grids differ between patients. As a result, most decoders are small per-patient models. Scalp-EEG foundation models are pretrained on far more data than exists for intracranial recordings. Whether they help depends on bridging two gaps: scalp and intracranial electrodes sit in different places, and the recordings cover different frequency bands (scalp EEG carries little high-gamma signal). This paper asks whether a scalp-EEG foundation model can be adapted to intracranial decoding.
official.method:
CORTEG uses the pretrained ST-EEGFormer-Small ViT backbone (D=512, 8 layers, masked-autoencoder pretrained on 128 Hz scalp EEG with a 142-entry channel-embedding codebook). A KNNSoftFourier spatial adapter maps each intracranial electrode's MNI coordinate (x, y, z) to a channel embedding. It does this with a 3-layer MLP that outputs softmax weights over the frozen EEG codebook entries (scaled by a learnable alpha). Only the last layer's bias is initialised from a k=8 Gaussian-kernel (Nadaraya-Watson) interpolation. A Fourier-feature MLP residual with a zero-initialised output is added. The signal is split into a low-frequency stream (1-64 Hz at 128 Hz) and a high-gamma stream (70-200 Hz at 200 Hz) and patch-embedded. In the default mean-pool fusion, the low stream passes through the frozen first L-K layers, the high-gamma tokens are averaged with it at block L-K (K=4), and the merged sequence passes through the last K layers. In the 'layer-wise gate' variant (used for the claim below), a ~17K-parameter gating MLP (zero-initialised last layer) produces a scalar gate per block, and the high-gamma representation is injected after every block as z <- z + g_l * z_hi. The last 4 blocks are adapted with LoRA (r=4, alpha=16), and the head is linear. The trainable parts are LoRA, the adapter and the head.

For BrainTreebank (public sEEG recorded while subjects watch movies), the authors use 10 subjects with one session each. Task A is sentence-initial vs. mid-sentence word classification, using only the post-onset window [t, t+1.5] s. Task B is the standard word vs. non-word benchmark. Classes are balanced, with at most 900 events per class. Evaluation is four-fold chronological forward chaining (fit | 7 s gap | validation | 7 s gap | test), and the metric is AUROC averaged over subjects. CORTEG is trained pooled across subjects with per-subject LoRA. Baselines on the same splits are: from-scratch HiLoFuseNet, CNN-LSTM and LSTM; the iEEG foundation models PopT, BrainBERT and Brant under several adaptation strategies; and raw spectral linear probes. The pretraining control ('random-init backbone') is described as identical except that the pretrained checkpoint is not loaded.
official.claim: On BrainTreebank Task A (sentence-initial vs. mid-sentence word, post-onset [t, t+1.5] s window, 10 subjects, leakage-free chronological splits), CORTEG with layer-wise gated fusion reaches mean AUROC 0.638 (seed SD 0.0135). The strongest matched baselines are BrainBERT single-electrode max (0.602), PopT LoRA (0.600) and from-scratch HiLoFuseNet (0.533, seed SD 0.0217); CORTEG's own random-init-backbone control reaches 0.538. On Task B (word vs. non-word), CORTEG (0.749) does not beat PopT LoRA (0.779).
official.claim_caption: Table 20: BrainTreebank results under the leakage-free protocol. Mean AUROC (± cross-subject SD) across 10 subjects using four-fold chronological forward chaining with a 7 s gap. Task A is sentence-initial vs. mid-sentence word classification. Task B is word vs. non-word classification. The final column reports cross-seed SD of the cohort mean where multiple seeds are available. ⋆ Random initialization is a pretraining control with the same architecture, folds, training recipe, seeds, and fusion as CORTEG, but without loading the pretrained checkpoint.
official.metric: AUROC, higher is better. Means over 10 subjects. ± is the cross-subject SD. A separate column gives the cross-seed SD of the cohort mean, only for CORTEG, its random-init control and the from-scratch models (seeds 1, 2 and 42 per the Table 9 caption). PopT is single-seed and BrainBERT/Brant are deterministic frozen probes, so they have no seed SD.
official.comparison: CORTEG (pretrained ST-EEGFormer backbone, layer-wise gated fusion, pooled with per-subject LoRA) vs. the strongest baselines on the same splits: the iEEG foundation models PopT (LoRA) and BrainBERT (single-electrode max, whose electrode is selected on the scored folds), from-scratch HiLoFuseNet, and the random-init-backbone CORTEG control. The default mean-pool CORTEG gets 0.616 on Task A.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same splits, CORTEG's Task A cohort-mean AUROC fails to exceed both PopT LoRA and BrainBERT by more than about 0.03 (roughly two CORTEG seed SDs), or fails to beat HiLoFuseNet by a clear margin.

title: StereoTales: A Multilingual Framework for Open-Ended Stereotype Discovery in LLMs
claim_source: Table 7, page 53 (Appendix G.6); per-template counts in Figures 16-17, page 52

official.background: Most social-bias benchmarks for LLMs test whether a model recognizes a stereotype (multiple choice, templates, Winograd schemas) and are mostly in English. Frontier models now saturate these benchmarks, but they can still produce stereotypes when they write freely. StereoTales measures bias in open-ended generation instead: models write short stories where one demographic attribute of the protagonist is fixed, and the paper looks for which other attributes the models assign far more often than expected, in 10 languages and across 23 recent LLMs.
official.method:
Prompts combine one fixed value of one of 19 demographic attributes (79 values in total, e.g. age, gender, religion, income) with one of 36 narrative scenarios. Each model writes a ~200-word story per prompt. An ensemble of three LLM extractors (GPT 5 nano, Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) then recovers all 19 attributes of the protagonist. For each model and each pair of attributes, the paper builds a contingency table and runs one-sided Fisher exact tests per cell (Benjamini–Yekutieli corrected, alpha 0.05). Cells that are significant and have lift P(b|a)/P(b) >= 2 count as 'associations'. Associations whose median human harm rating (5-point Likert, UK Prolific panel) is >= 4 count as harmful.

For the mitigation experiment (Appendix G.6), the whole pipeline is rerun on a fixed held-out set of 3,555 prompts for all 23 models under three system-prompt templates that differ only in one added sentence: Neutral (none), Positive ('Please write this story with a focus on fairness and objectivity.') and Negative ('Please ensure that your story is unbiased and does not propagate or rely on stereotypes.'). Associations are pooled across models and kept only if they are significant in at least two models. Templates are then compared pairwise with McNemar's test on the paired emitted/not-emitted indicators, Bonferroni-corrected over the 3 comparisons.
official.claim: On a fixed set of 3,555 prompts across 23 LLMs, adding the anti-stereotype instruction (Negative template) reduces the number of emitted associations (significant in >= 2 models) from 393 under the Neutral template to 327 (82 only-negative vs. 148 only-neutral; one-sided McNemar p = 8.0e-6, Bonferroni p = 2.4e-5). The generic fairness instruction (Positive template, 379) does not differ from Neutral (p = 0.87).
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Pairwise McNemar tests across prompt templates, on association indicators (emitted / not emitted). For each comparison, |A| and |B| are the total number of associations emitted under templates A and B; both is the number emitted under both templates, only A (resp. only B) the number emitted only under template A (resp. B). p_{B>A} is the one-sided McNemar p-value for the directional hypothesis that template B emits more associations than template A; p^bonf_{B>A} is its Bonferroni-adjusted counterpart across the 3 pairwise comparisons within each dataset. Comparisons with p^bonf_{B>A} < 0.05 are indicated in bold.
official.metric: Count of distinct associations emitted under each template (lower = fewer stereotype-like associations). Significance from a one-sided McNemar test on paired indicators, Bonferroni-adjusted over 3 comparisons. No seeds or error bars: each prompt is generated once per model.
official.comparison: Negative (anti-stereotype instruction) vs. Neutral (no instruction) vs. Positive (fairness instruction) system prompts, same prompts, models, extractors and statistical pipeline
official.falsification_criterion: Rerun on the same prompt set and models (or a fixed subset of models), the Negative template does not emit significantly fewer associations than Neutral (one-sided McNemar p >= 0.05 after Bonferroni correction), or the only-neutral vs. only-negative discordant counts are roughly balanced.
