title: MulTaBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Tabular Learning with Text and Image

official.background: Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN and gradient-boosted trees only take numeric/categorical columns, so images and text in a table are usually turned into frozen embeddings from a pretrained encoder, compressed with PCA, and appended as features. Generic embeddings may throw away fine-grained, task-specific details (e.g. a localized anomaly in an X-ray). The paper argues that many multimodal tabular tasks need 'Target-Aware Representations' (TAR), i.e. encoders tuned on the prediction target, and builds MulTaBench, a 40-dataset benchmark (20 image-tabular, 20 text-tabular) selected to contain tasks where joint modeling and TAR both help.
official.method:
Images are embedded with DINOv3-small (dinov3-vits16-pretrain-lvd1689m, 384-dim). In the Joint Frozen condition, the frozen 384-dim image embedding (the paper does not state the pooling; see the released code) is reduced to 30 PCA components and concatenated with the structured features. In the Joint TAR condition, the top 3 transformer layers of the encoder are first fine-tuned with LoRA (r = 16, alpha = 32, dropout 0.1, AdamW lr 1e-3, batch 256, weight decay 0.01, up to 100 epochs, early stopping after 3 epochs) with a linear head on the target alone (no structured features), using only the training split with a 90/10 train/validation split; regression targets are discretized into 20 equal-frequency bins and trained with cross-entropy. The tuned embeddings are then PCA-reduced to 30 and passed to the same tabular learner. No hyperparameter tuning is done for the encoder or the learners.

Twelve tabular learners with default settings (LightGBM, CatBoost, TabM, TabPFNv2, TabPFN-2.5, XGBoost, RandomForest, RealMLP, TabDPT, TabICLv2, TabSTAR, ConTextTab) are run on each of the 20 image-tabular datasets over 5 seeds/folds, up to 10,000 training examples per run. The metric is AUROC for classification and R2 for regression (negative R2 clipped before averaging). Per dataset, the 60 learner-fold runs under Joint TAR are paired with the same runs under Joint Frozen and tested with a one-sided paired t-test, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction over all 40 datasets.
official.claim: On the 20 MulTaBench image-tabular datasets, LoRA-tuned (target-aware) DINOv3-small embeddings beat frozen ones when fed to tabular learners, raising the mean score from 0.690 to 0.716 (averaged over 12 learners and 5 seeds), with a significant gain (BH-adjusted p < 0.05) on 18 of 20 datasets; the largest gains are on Mango Mass (R2 0.533 to 0.653) and Khaadi Clothes (R2 0.565 to 0.683).
official.claim_caption: Table 11: MulTaBench Image-Tabular Per-dataset Results. Averaged over 12 learners and 5 seeds, with both Frozen and TAR conditions, sorted by Gain. AUROC for classification, R2 for regression. p_BH is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted significance of the gain.
official.metric: AUROC (classification) or R2 (regression), higher is better, averaged over 12 learners and 5 seeds; significance from a one-sided paired t-test over 60 learner-fold pairs per dataset, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted (p_BH). No per-dataset std is reported.
official.comparison: Joint TAR (structured features + LoRA-tuned image embedding) vs. Joint Frozen (structured features + frozen image embedding), same learners, folds, PCA dimension and encoder
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Frozen vs. TAR pipeline on the image-tabular datasets, TAR fails to beat Frozen on a clear majority of datasets (e.g. fewer than 14 of 20 with a positive mean gain), or the large gains on Mango Mass and Khaadi Clothes (about +0.12 R2) shrink below about +0.03.

title: Active Learning for Gaussian Process Regression Under Self-Induced Boltzmann Weights

official.background: Active learning for Gaussian process regression usually aims for low prediction error averaged over the input space, either uniformly or under a known target distribution. In several scientific settings the distribution that matters is a Boltzmann distribution induced by the unknown function itself, P_f(x) ∝ exp(λ f(x) + b(x)): molecular dynamics only visits low-energy configurations of a potential energy surface, and drug-discovery screening cares most about high-scoring molecules. Because the target depends on f and its partition function is intractable, standard weighted-variance acquisition cannot be applied directly. The paper formalises this 'self-induced distribution' active learning (SIDAL) problem and proposes an acquisition function for it.
official.method:
AB-SID-iVAR chooses the next query x_t by minimising the integrated posterior variance after a fantasy observation at x, weighted by an unnormalised surrogate of the target, ∫ p̃_{t-1}(x*) σ_t²(x* | x_t = x) dx* (Eq. 3). The surrogate is the closed-form zero-order approximation of the Bayesian target E_{f|D}[P_f], p̃_{t-1}(x) = exp(λ μ_{t-1}(x) + λ² σ²_{t-1}(x)/2 + b(x)) (Table 1), so no partition function is estimated. The search is restricted to a potential set X̄_t = {x : σ²_{t-1}(x) ≥ E_{p̃_{t-1}}[σ²_{t-1}]}, i.e. points whose variance is at least the surrogate-weighted average variance. In a discrete pool the integral and the threshold are computed exactly over the pool.

For the claim's experiment (Section 5.3, Appendix D.5.2) the pool is about 20,000 GuacaMol molecules, each a 2048-bit Morgan fingerprint, modelled with a GP with a Tanimoto kernel. The functions to learn are the GuacaMol 'Median 1' and 'Median 2' scores, with target P_λ(x) ∝ exp(λ f(x)), b = 0, and λ ∈ {25, 75} (scores lie in roughly [0.1, 0.3]). Each run starts from one random sample, makes 300 queries, and is repeated over 30 seeds. Baselines are random sampling (RS), uncertainty sampling (US), EPIG and integrated MSE (IMSE, uniformly weighted variance reduction). The metric is the weighted MSE E_{x∼P_f}[(μ_t(x) − f(x))²] over the pool, using the true f to compute the weights.
official.claim: On the ~20k-molecule GuacaMol pool with a Tanimoto GP and target P ∝ exp(75 f), AB-SID-iVAR reaches a median weighted MSE after 300 queries of about 1.5e-5 (Median 1) and 2e-6 (Median 2), versus about 2e-2 for the best baseline (IMSE/EPIG/RS), i.e. roughly three or more orders of magnitude lower; at λ = 25 the gap is smaller (about 2.5e-4 vs. 1.4e-3 on Median 1, 3.5e-4 vs. 7e-4 on Median 2).
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Active learning for molecular property prediction on GuacaMol scoring functions (Median 1, Median 2). The target distribution P_λ(x) ∝ exp(λ f(x)) emphasizes high-scoring compounds, relevant for drug discovery where accurate predictions matter most for promising candidates. Top: pool distribution (gray) vs. Boltzmann-tilted density (red). Middle: weighted MSE convergence over 300 iterations; AB-SID-iVAR achieves one to two orders of magnitude lower error than baselines. Bottom: R² on top k% compounds ranked by Boltzmann weight; baselines degrade to negative R² as k shrinks while AB-SID-iVAR remains near zero. Pool contains approximately 20,000 molecules with Tanimoto kernel GP.
official.metric: Weighted MSE under the self-induced Boltzmann distribution over the pool, lower is better; lines are medians over 30 random seeds, shaded bands are interquartile ranges (stated for Figures 3 and 7; Section 5 says every experiment uses 30 seeds); values below are read off log-scale plots and approximate
official.comparison: AB-SID-iVAR (with the variance-threshold set X̄) vs. RS, US, EPIG and IMSE, same GP surrogate, pool, initial point and 300-query budget
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Median 1 and Median 2 at λ = 75 (30 seeds, 300 queries, Tanimoto GP on the GuacaMol pool), AB-SID-iVAR's median weighted MSE at 300 queries is not at least an order of magnitude below the best of IMSE, EPIG and RS, or its interquartile range overlaps theirs.

title: When Can Digital Personas Reliably Approximate Human Survey Findings?

official.background: LLM-driven 'digital personas' are increasingly proposed as stand-ins for human survey respondents, but most evaluations only check whether answers look plausible or match population averages. The open question is whether a persona built from a real person's background and survey history can predict that same person's later answers, and whether it preserves the distribution of answers across a population. The LISS panel, a probability-based longitudinal panel of Dutch households, makes this testable because the same people answer many surveys over many years.
official.method:
Using 2023 as a temporal cutoff, the authors build a persona for each respondent from pre-cutoff information and ask an LLM to predict that respondent's held-out post-cutoff answers to closed-ended questions. In the core-prediction task, the prior evidence is the respondent's full pre-2023 single-wave answer history and the targets are 2023 core-study answers. 500 respondents are drawn by stratified proportional sampling over gender, age group and household stage. Target questions are grouped by study into sub-batches of about 20, and each API call returns JSON answer codes restricted to the allowed categories.

The four persona architectures are: Background (only 34 sociodemographic variables), Profile (background plus a GPT-5.4-written natural-language summary of prior answers), Profile + Lexical retrieval (profile plus the top-K prior answered rows by token overlap with the sub-batch questions) and Profile + Semantic retrieval (profile plus the top-K prior rows ranked by summed cosine similarity of OpenAI text-embedding-3-small embeddings to the sub-batch questions), with K equal to the sub-batch size. Each architecture is run with GPT-5.4, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3 Flash. Metrics include question-level weighted F1 between persona and human answers and question-level Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) between persona and human answer distributions.
official.claim: On LISS core-study prediction (500 respondents), adding semantically retrieved prior answers to a profile raises question-level weighted F1 over the background-only persona for all three LLMs (GPT-5.4 0.436 vs 0.392, Claude Haiku 4.5 0.415 vs 0.367, Gemini 3 Flash 0.444 vs 0.402) and lowers question-distribution JSD (0.306 vs 0.375, 0.338 vs 0.409, 0.301 vs 0.365).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Fidelity of digital personas on core predictions across five persona conditions (1 baseline + 4 personas) and three LLMs. Metrics measure Clustering ARI ↑, Respondent exact match rate ↑, Question weighted F1 score ↑, Question Distribution JSD ↓, Respondent Distribution MMD ↓, and equity mean absolute deviation of DPI ↓. Core studies involve richer question entries and respondents, yielding higher persona-fidelity headroom compared to single-wave predictions. Baseline is GPT-5.4 only. Bold denotes values statistically tied with the best-performing setting under overlap of the reported uncertainty intervals.
official.metric: Question weighted F1 (higher is better) and question-level answer-distribution JSD (lower is better); ± is bootstrap SE over 100 respondent resamples. No repeated LLM sampling seeds are reported.
official.comparison: Profile + Semantic retrieval persona vs. Background-only persona, matched by LLM, task and respondent sample (Profile and Profile + Lexical as intermediate conditions; the no-context GPT-5.4 baseline is weaker still).
official.falsification_criterion: With the same LLM on the core-prediction task, Profile + Semantic retrieval does not exceed the Background persona's question F1 by more than a few bootstrap SEs (e.g. the gap is under about 0.01 instead of about 0.04-0.05), or its question-distribution JSD is not clearly lower.

title: Prompt–Activation Duality: Improving Activation Steering via Attention-Level Interventions
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (full per-turn values in Tables 3-4, pages 18-19; trajectories with ±1 std in Figure 4, page 8)

official.background: Activation steering adds a behavior direction (for example a 'persona vector' obtained by differencing activations under contrastive system prompts) to a language model's residual stream at inference time to control traits such as sycophancy or creativity. It is usually evaluated on short single-turn outputs. In real multi-turn chat the KV cache stores every generated token's steered states, which later tokens attend to, so a perturbation that looks harmless in one reply may accumulate. The paper calls this KV-cache contamination and argues that standard persona-vector steering loses coherence across turns while plain system prompting does not.
official.method:
Baseline ('Original'): the persona-vector method of Chen et al. (2025). A vector is the difference of mean response-token residual-stream activations under positive vs. negative trait system prompts; it is added with α = 2.0 at layer 20 of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at every decoding step. GCAD instead extracts, for each layer ℓ in 9-19, the contrastive difference of the self-attention output restricted to system-prompt source tokens (the attention sum Σ_{i∈S} α_{t,i} V_i W_o, without renormalisation), averaged over response tokens. At inference it adds c_t · Δ(ℓ) to the attention output (before the MLP) at those layers, where c_t = 2 c_base · σ(s · (d_t − d̄)) is a per-token gate based on the mean pre-softmax query compatibility d_t with the mean system-prompt key from the positive extraction set; c_base = 3.5, s = 1.5.

Evaluation: 10-turn dialogues with the KV cache kept across turns and the steering hook active on every generated token; per trait and method, 60 conversations (20 question groups of 10 questions × 3 samples, temperature 1.0, max 500 new tokens per turn, question-sampling seed 42 so both methods see identical prefixes). Each reply is scored 0-100 by gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 for trait expression (trait-specific rubric from Chen et al.; refusals excluded) and separately for coherence.
official.claim: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in 10-turn dialogue with persisted KV cache, standard residual-stream persona steering drops to turn-10 coherence of 17.8 (creative) and 24.5 (sycophantic), whereas GCAD keeps turn-10 coherence at 92.4 and 91.2 while keeping turn-10 trait expression at 91.2 and 91.6 (Original: 25.0 and 98.5).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Multi-turn comparison on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for six representative traits and the 15-trait average. Each cell reports trait expression and coherence at turns 1, 5, and 10, the 10-turn mean (Avg), and drift ∆ = T10 − T1 over 60 conversations. Original uses layer 20 residual steering (α = 2.0); GCAD (Ours) uses layers 9–19 with c_base = 3.5, s = 1.5.
official.metric: GPT-4.1-mini judge scores (0-100, higher is better) for coherence and trait expression, mean over 60 conversations at turns 1, 5, 10; Δ = T10 − T1. Table 1 reports no error bars and one run per cell; Figure 4 shows ±1 std across the 60 conversations for creative and sycophantic.
official.comparison: GCAD (gated cropped attention-delta, layers 9-19) vs. standard persona-vector residual steering (layer 20, α = 2.0) on the same traits, prompts, seeds and judge
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the 10-turn protocol for creative and/or sycophantic on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the Original baseline's turn-10 coherence stays within ~20 points of GCAD's, or GCAD's turn-10 coherence falls below ~75, or GCAD's turn-10 trait expression falls below ~75 (i.e. the coherence gain comes from weaker steering).

title: What should post-training optimize? A test-time scaling law perspective
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (absolute values in Table 2, page 9)

official.background: LLMs are often deployed with best-of-N sampling: draw N responses, score them with a reward model, and return the highest-scoring one. Standard RL post-training (e.g. GRPO) optimizes the mean reward of a single sample, but best-of-N performance depends on the upper tail of the reward distribution. Existing best-of-N-aware training objectives usually need about N rollouts per prompt during training, which is too expensive when the deployment budget N is much larger than the per-prompt training budget m.
official.method:
The authors assume the upper tail of each prompt's reward distribution is Gaussian. Under that assumption the best-of-N value is approximately mu_alpha + c_N * sigma_alpha, where mu_alpha and sigma_alpha are the mean and standard deviation of rewards above the upper alpha-quantile, and c_N depends only on (N, alpha). These tail statistics can be estimated from m << N rollouts, so the gradient of the best-of-N objective can be estimated from a small group. TEA (Tail-Extrapolated Advantage) is the direct plug-in estimator: rollouts above the empirical alpha-quantile get a raw advantage from the extrapolated tail-statistic gradient, and rollouts below it get zero. In training, the positive part of this raw advantage is taken and then centered within the prompt group. Prefix-TEA is a fixed-order debiased variant ((k, J) = (2, 4)). Both use alpha = 0.25 and N_target = 128.

All methods share one grouped on-policy training pipeline and differ only in how the scalar advantage A_i is computed from the m = 64 rewards per prompt. Setup: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct policy; UltraFeedback-derived prompts (34,994 train / 512 validation / held-out core250); Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B as both training reward and evaluator; KL beta = 0.1, lr 1e-5, 450 steps. Every 25 steps, checkpoints are scored on 128 validation prompts (mean of the top 10 of 32 samples), and the best checkpoint is kept. Evaluation samples 256 completions per held-out prompt and reports grouped best-of-N reward: the mean of group maxima over 256/N groups, averaged over prompts. Baselines are GRPO, GRPO-Z (normalized GRPO), BoN-max mean/second, BoN mean, Chow BoN-RL and CAT-BoN, all at m = 64.
official.claim: With Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct trained on UltraFeedback at m = 64 rollouts per prompt, TEA improves best-of-128 reward over GRPO by +1.569 [95% CI +1.305, +1.819], more than GRPO-Z (+0.975 [+0.723, +1.255]) and the best test-time-aware baseline BoN-max second (+0.361 [+0.125, +0.607]). In absolute terms, TEA scores 13.718 bo128 vs. 13.124 for GRPO-Z and 12.149 for GRPO.
official.claim_caption: Table 1. High-N endpoint results on UltraFeedback core250. Values are reward-score improvements over GRPO with paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Bold point estimates mark the best method in each column. Best TTA reports the strongest cited test-time-aware baseline for each column; it is CAT-BoN at bo64 and BoN-max second at bo128/bo256. BoN mean 2× uses a compute-unmatched m = 128 per-prompt rollout budget, while all other methods use m = 64.
official.metric: Grouped best-of-N reward-model score (Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B) on the 250-prompt held-out core250 set, higher is better; values are differences from GRPO with paired prompt-bootstrap 95% CIs (1,000 resamples). One training run per method; no training-seed variance is reported.
official.comparison: TEA (and Prefix-TEA) vs. GRPO, GRPO-Z, the strongest test-time-aware baseline (CAT-BoN at bo64, BoN-max second at bo128/bo256) and a compute-unmatched BoN mean with m = 128, all under the same training pipeline and checkpoint-selection rule
official.falsification_criterion: In a matched rerun (same model, data, reward model, m = 64, validation-selected checkpoints), TEA's bo128 improvement over GRPO-Z is not clearly positive (paired-bootstrap CI includes 0 or TEA loses on most prompts), or the best test-time-aware baseline matches TEA at bo128/bo256, or the gap disappears across training seeds.

title: AdaPaD: Adaptive Parallel Deflation for PEFT with Self-Correcting Rank Discovery

official.background: LoRA fine-tunes a frozen pretrained model by learning a low-rank update BA^T per weight matrix, but the rank r must be fixed by hand and is usually the same for every layer, even though different modules and tasks need different capacity. Adaptive-rank methods (AdaLoRA, IncreLoRA, SoRA, dEBORA) choose ranks during training. This paper treats the LoRA update as a sum of rank-1 components and asks whether learning them in parallel, with per-module rank growth, gives adapters that match fixed-rank LoRA quality with fewer parameters.
official.method:
AdaPaD writes each adapter as a sum of rank-1 components b_k a_k^T and trains all of them at once (parallel deflation): component k is trained against the target left after subtracting a snapshot of components 1..k-1, refreshed every Delta mini-batches, so errors in earlier components are corrected over time instead of being frozen in. Each module also keeps one inactive 'reserve' component that pre-trains privately against its current target (advance learning). Every Delta batches, the top-h modules by an IncreLoRA-style importance score (EMA of |p|*|grad p| times its EMA volatility) promote their reserve to an active component, up to r_max per module, until the total rank reaches a global budget B.

For the claim, Qwen3-0.6B with a span-prediction QA head is fine-tuned on SQuAD v1.1 and SQuAD v2 (seq len 384, doc-stride 128, 3 epochs, batch 16, lr 1e-3, alpha 16, AdamW, bf16). Adapters are attached to all seven projections (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) in all 28 blocks (196 modules). The baseline is fixed-rank LoRA with r in {4, 6}; AdaPaD uses an average-rank budget r-bar in {4, 6} (B = 784 or 1176), r_max = 8, top-10 modules per growth round, Delta = 400. For each cell the authors report the smallest AdaPaD adapter that matches or beats same-budget LoRA on F1, and the parameter reduction Delta-Par.
official.claim: On Qwen3-0.6B, AdaPaD matches or beats same-budget fixed-rank LoRA on F1 in all four SQuAD/SQuAD v2 cells with adapters 15.9-44.3% smaller (mean 30.7%); e.g. on SQuAD v1.1, AdaPaD with 2.11M parameters reaches F1 89.02 vs. LoRA r=6 with 3.79M at 88.93, and on SQuAD v2 AdaPaD with 1.93M reaches F1 73.63 vs. LoRA r=4 with 2.52M at 73.45.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Matched-budget head-to-head on Qwen3-0.6B SQuAD/SQuAD v2 (seed=43; bf16; identical recipe across all cells; full settings in Section G.2). Bold: AdaPaD matches or beats LoRA at the cell.
official.metric: F1 and exact match (higher is better) on the SQuAD v1.1 / v2 dev sets, plus trainable adapter parameters (lower is better); single seed (43), no error bars reported
official.comparison: AdaPaD (average-rank budget r-bar = 4 or 6, r_max = 8) vs. fixed-rank LoRA (r = 4 or 6) on the same modules with an identical training recipe
official.falsification_criterion: With the same recipe, AdaPaD adapters about 16-44% smaller than LoRA fall below LoRA's F1 in a cell by more than seed-to-seed variation (e.g. averaged over 3+ seeds), or matching LoRA's F1 requires AdaPaD adapters about as large as LoRA's.

title: ConQuR: Corner Aligned Activation Quantization via Optimized Rotations for LLMs
claim_source: Table 7, page 20 (full results behind Table 1, page 6)

official.background: Low-bit weight-activation quantization of LLMs is hard because a few activation channels carry large outliers that set the quantization range and waste resolution for every other coordinate. Rotation-based methods (QuaRot, SpinQuant, DartQuant, DFRot) apply orthogonal transforms that are folded into the weights, which spreads outlier energy across dimensions and leaves the full-precision function unchanged. Learning good rotations either needs costly end-to-end training (SpinQuant) or a large stored activation corpus (DartQuant stores about 193 GB for Llama-2 7B). This paper proposes a cheaper calibration objective and procedure.
official.method:
ConQuR learns orthogonal rotations R so that each normalized activation x/||x|| lands close to a vertex of the hypercube inscribed in the unit sphere (target z = sign(Rx)/sqrt(d)). This is equivalent to maximizing the l1 norm of the rotated unit vectors, a surrogate for minimizing ||Rx||_inf and therefore the per-token quantization range. The objective is optimized by alternating: fix the sign targets, then solve an orthogonal Procrustes problem in closed form (SVD of Z^T X, R = U V^T). Rotations are learned for R1 (residual stream, shared across layers) and R2,l (per-layer, block-diagonal per head, at the o_proj input); fixed online Hadamard transforms R3 (after RoPE) and R4 (before down_proj) are also used, as in QuaRot and SpinQuant.

Calibration is online: 128 WikiText-2 sequences of length 2048 are processed in mini-batches of 1-2 sequences, Procrustes statistics are accumulated per layer, and the rotations are updated straight away, so no activations are stored. In the 'quant. calib.' variant, activations are quantized during calibration so that later layers see quantized inputs. Weights are then quantized with GPTQ (4-bit, per output row), activations with asymmetric per-token 4-bit quantization (clip ratio 0.9), and the KV cache optionally with 4-bit asymmetric group-128 quantization. All baselines use their public implementations, the same 128 calibration samples and a shared evaluation pipeline adapted from DartQuant.
official.claim: On Llama-3.2 3B with W4A4 (KV16), ConQuR with quantized calibration gets lower perplexity than every baseline rotation method on all three datasets: WikiText-2 9.19 vs. 9.35 (DartQuant, best baseline), PTB 16.10 vs. 16.16, C4 14.33 vs. 14.59, average 13.21 vs. 13.37 (QuaRot 13.75, SpinQuant 13.65, DFRot 13.76). It also stays best on average with a 4-bit KV cache (13.68 vs. 13.86).
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Full perplexity results for Llama-3.2 3B
official.metric: Perplexity on WikiText-2, PTB and C4 (lower is better) and their average; single runs, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: ConQuR (quant. calib. and f.p. calib.) vs. QuaRot (random Hadamard), DFRot, SpinQuant and DartQuant, all with the same GPTQ weight quantization, calibration set and evaluation pipeline
official.falsification_criterion: With matched GPTQ/activation-quantization settings on Llama-3.2 3B W4A4KV16, ConQuR's average PPL is not lower than DartQuant's, or the gap (0.16 average PPL) is within the run-to-run variation from re-sampling the calibration set or the GPTQ/rotation seeds.

title: Remember the Decision, Not the Description: A Rate-Distortion Framework for Agent Memory
claim_source: Figure 2 (panels a-c), page 7; environment definition in Appendix E.1, pages 32-34

official.background: LLM agents that operate over long interactions cannot keep their full history at answer time and must access it through a limited memory. Most memory systems decide what to store, merge or retrieve by descriptive criteria such as semantic similarity, salience or summary quality. The paper argues that memory should instead keep apart exactly those histories that need different decisions, and that description-based grouping fails when descriptively similar situations call for different actions.
official.method:
The paper formalizes memory as a contextual bandit in which the history is mapped to one of K runtime memory states before acting, and defines decision distortion as the loss in achievable reward caused by merging histories. DeMem is an online learner that keeps a K-slot partition, estimates per-context action values, adds a cannot-link edge between two contexts when confidence bounds certify they cannot share a near-optimal action, re-partitions each epoch by greedy K-coloring of the cannot-link graph, and runs UCB at the slot level within an epoch.

The synthetic Decoupled Bandit gives each context a descriptive feature x_t and a latent decision identity z_t with its own action-value vector; rewards are mu_{z,a} plus zero-mean noise. A mismatch parameter alpha mixes a description-induced identity with a fixed permutation of it, so at alpha = 0 description and decision agree and at alpha = 1 descriptively similar contexts are routed to decision-distinct groups. All budgeted methods use the same K: CLUB-style online clustering (splits on reward-vector differences), Feature-KMeans, Feature-RAG, epsilon-greedy feature clustering, and Random Partition; an Oracle with access to z_t (K = N) is the lower bound. The metric is cumulative regret over T = 10,000 rounds.
official.claim: In the synthetic Decoupled Bandit at T = 10,000 rounds, DeMem's final cumulative regret is roughly half that of the strongest budgeted baseline (CLUB): about 1,150-1,500 vs. about 2,600-3,100 for memory budgets K = 4-10 (Fig. 2b), and about 1,800 vs. 3,850 at full mismatch alpha = 1 (Fig. 2c), while all description-based baselines are higher still.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Synthetic results. (a) Cumulative regret on the Decoupled Bandit. (b) Memory-distortion tradeoff under varying K. (c) Performance under increasing description-decision mismatch.
official.metric: Final cumulative regret after T = 10,000 rounds (lower is better). Panels (b) and (c) show error bars and panel (a) shaded bands, but the paper does not say whether they are std or SE or how many seeds were used (Table 16 for the same environment uses 20 seeds).
official.comparison: DeMem vs. CLUB, Feature-KMeans, Feature-RAG, epsilon-greedy feature clustering and Random Partition at the same memory budget K; Oracle (K = N) as reference
official.falsification_criterion: In a faithful re-implementation of the Decoupled Bandit, DeMem's final regret is not clearly below CLUB's (error bars overlap) for K >= 4 at default mismatch, or its advantage over CLUB does not widen as alpha increases toward 1.

title: Quotient-Categorical Representations for Bellman-Compatible Average-Reward Distributional Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Figure 2, page 10 (fitted slopes in Appendix F, page 38)

official.background: In average-reward reinforcement learning, a policy is evaluated by its gain (long-run average reward) and a bias function that solves the Poisson equation only up to an additive constant. Distributional RL, which learns the full distribution of returns instead of the mean, is well developed for discounted problems but has no clean analogue for the average-reward bias, because of that additive ambiguity and because undiscounted differential returns have no limiting distribution. The paper builds a categorical distributional representation of the bias that respects the additive-constant symmetry and gives TD-style learning rules with convergence guarantees.
official.method:
Each state's law is a categorical distribution on a fixed uniform grid of d atoms, and families of laws are identified up to a common shift (the quotient). The projected average-reward operator G shifts a successor's law by the gain-centered reward r - g and projects it back onto the grid (Cramér projection). The learning rule is a stochastic Krasnosel'skii-Mann (SKM) recursion p_{k+1} = p_k + alpha_k (H_g(p_k, Y_k) - p_k), updating only the sampled state's categorical vector from one transition Y_k = (S_k, R_k, S_{k+1}). When the gain is unknown, it is estimated online by g_{k+1} = g_k + alpha_k (R_k - g_k) and used to center each reward (the coupled recursion).

The experiment uses a five-state Markov chain with deterministic state rewards r = (0.90, 0.10, 0.55, 0.80, 0.05) and the transition matrix in Appendix F (eq. 216), a 321-atom grid on [-5, 5], uniform initial laws, and 10^7 iterations over ten seeds. It reports the supremum-Cramér residual of the iterate to G (how far p_k is from being a fixed point) for: exact (deterministic) KM; centered SKM with i.i.d. state sampling (two-phase schedule, a1 = 0.75) or Markovian sampling (alpha_k = (k+1)^-0.85); the coupled online-gain recursion; and a wrong-centering ablation with g = 0 (raw rewards).
official.claim: On the five-state MDP, the residual of the gain-centered categorical TD recursion to the projected operator G falls from about 1e-1 to about 3e-4 (i.i.d.) and 7e-4 (Markovian) by k = 10^7, with fitted slopes of -0.33, -0.40 and -0.38 (i.i.d., Markovian, coupled online-gain) over k >= 10^4; the coupled recursion tracks the known-gain curve, whereas using raw rewards (g = 0) makes the residual to G grow to about 0.6-0.7 as all mass moves to the top atom.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Five-state MDP. Residuals are l_{C,inf}(p_k, G(p_k)) unless labeled G_0. Stochastic runs show medians over ten seeds with interquartile bands. (a) Known gain. (b) Unknown gain, with the known-gain Markovian residual from (a) dotted. (c) Centering with g = 0, which targets G_0. Dashed lines: theorem rates for the step sizes used, up to constants.
official.metric: supremum-Cramér residual l_{C,inf}(p_k, G(p_k)) (lower is better) and gain error |g_k - r_bar|; medians over ten seeds with interquartile bands
official.comparison: gain-centered SKM (known gain, i.i.d. and Markovian sampling) and coupled online-gain SKM vs. the uncentered g = 0 recursion; exact KM and the theorem's worst-case rates (k^-1/8, k^-3/40) as references
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Appendix F setup, the centered (known-gain or coupled) residual to G does not decay below 1e-2 by k = 10^7, its log-log slope over k >= 10^4 is shallower than about -0.2, the coupled recursion's residual is more than about 3x the known-gain residual at k = 10^7, or the g = 0 residual to G does not grow.

title: Neural Statistical Functions
claim_source: Table 4, page 17 (same data plotted in Figure 4c, page 7)

official.background: Neural surrogates for simulators are normally queried at one operating condition at a time (one time step, one angle of attack, one impact angle). Many engineering questions instead need a statistic of the response over a range of conditions, such as the mean energy over a time window, a pressure quantile over an angle-of-attack range, or the maximum stress over a range of impact angles. The standard answer is Monte Carlo: evaluate the surrogate at many sampled conditions and aggregate, which costs many forward passes per query and is noisy when the sample count is small.
official.method:
The paper trains a network h̃θ(x, s) to output the prefix statistic h̃(x, s) = (1/s) ∫_0^s ψ(x, t) dt in quantile space s ∈ (0, 1], where ψ is the per-condition response, or a transform of it for max and quantile. An interval statistic over [s0, s1] is then (s1 h̃(x, s1) − s0 h̃(x, s0)) / (s1 − s0), which takes two network evaluations. Training uses the identity s ∂s h̃ + h̃ = ψ: the loss is ||h̃θ(x, s) − sg(ψ(x, s) − s ∂s h̃θ(x, s))||², with ∂s computed by finite differences, ψ supplied by a pretrained single-condition predictor at random s, plus a ground-truth data term weighted by λ_data = 0.1.

For the claim, the system is a synthetic 2D trajectory with 7 parameters x = (a, b, φr, ω0, α, φω, φ0), radius r(s) = a + bs + 0.1 sin(2πs + φr) and angular speed η'(s) = ω0 + 2πα cos(2πs + φω). The target is the interval mean of kinetic energy r'(s)² + (r(s) η'(s))², which has an analytic reference. There are 2,000 training and 500 test trajectories. Both the single-condition predictor and h̃θ are 4-layer SiLU MLPs (width 256) on input x ⊕ s. The baseline is a Monte Carlo average of the single-condition MLP at K uniformly sampled s in [s0, s1], with K ∈ {10, 50, 100, 200, 400}. The error is relative ℓ2 against the analytic interval mean, binned by interval width from 0.50 to 0.92.
official.claim: On held-out 2D dynamical-system trajectories, the neural statistical function's interval-mean energy estimate from 2 network evaluations has relative ℓ2 error 0.019 to 0.036 against the analytic mean at interval widths 0.50 to 0.92. This is lower than Monte Carlo with K=50 single-model evaluations at every width (0.042 to 0.080) and lower than K=100 at every width (0.031 to 0.054). For widths ≥ 0.80 it is also lower than K=400 (0.019 to 0.022 vs. 0.022 to 0.025).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Spiral integral relative L2 (relL2) vs. analytic ground truth. Neural statistical function vs. MC at K ∈ {10, 50, 100, 200, 400}. MC entries are mean ± 1 standard error over 5 seeds.
official.metric: Relative ℓ2 error of the interval mean against the analytic interval mean, binned by interval width (lower is better). MC entries are mean ± 1 standard error over 5 sampling seeds; the method's numbers are single values with no error bar.
official.comparison: Neural statistical function (2 evaluations of h̃θ) vs. Monte Carlo averaging of the pretrained single-condition MLP with K = 10, 50, 100, 200, 400 samples
official.falsification_criterion: A reimplementation in which the neural statistical function's relative ℓ2 error is not below MC K=50 at most widths, or not below MC K=100 at widths ≥ 0.80, against the analytic interval mean on held-out trajectories.

title: Deep Minds and Shallow Probes
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (full breakdown in Table 20, page 60)

official.background: Probing trains a lightweight classifier on frozen hidden states to test whether a property is represented. Linear probes are the default because they are too weak to solve the task themselves, but higher-order probes are usually introduced ad hoc. The paper argues that behaviorally equivalent language models have final-layer representations related by an invertible affine map, and proves that the only finite-dimensional probe families stable under affine reparameterization are polynomials of bounded degree, with linear probes as degree 1. Degree-2 low-rank (CP) probes are singled out as a coordinate-stable structured family, and the practical prediction is that concepts that are genuinely degree-2, such as subject-verb number agreement (a product of subject and verb number features), need a degree-2 probe.
official.method:
Pythia-70m, 160m and 410m are run on UD English-EWT sentences (one forward pass per sentence, bfloat16); each word's hidden state is the last subword piece at the middle layer (layers 3, 6 and 12 of 6, 12 and 24 by default in E.3, but Table 18 uses layer 16 for 410m), centered by the training mean. A bank of 30 one-vs-rest logistic-regression probes (scikit-learn, C = 1.0) is trained for 5 UD categories: POS tag, morphological number, tense, punctuation class and coarse dependency relation. For a subject token and a verb token, the 30 probe scores at each are concatenated into a 60-dimensional score vector S.

The task is to classify whether a (subject, verb) pair agrees in number. Pairs are formed across sentences for both classes (positives: subject and verb from different sentences with the same number; negatives: different number) to avoid sentence-identity confounds, with class-balanced subsampling (about 4,000 balanced training pairs). Three heads are fit on S: a linear logistic-regression head, a full quadratic logistic head (all degree-2 monomials, 1,830 features), and an affine-completed CP rank-1 degree-2 head, f(S) = a(<v1,S> + b1)(<v2,S> + b2) + g(S) with g linear, trained with BCE loss by PyTorch L-BFGS (strong-Wolfe line search) with 30-50 random restarts, choosing the best by validation AUROC. Test AUROC is reported as mean ± std over 10 resamples.
official.claim: On cross-sentence subject-verb agreement pairs from UD English-EWT, a CP rank-1 degree-2 head on the 60-d probe-score vector reaches test AUROC 0.901 / 0.930 / 0.955 on Pythia-70m / 160m / 410m, versus 0.733 / 0.740 / 0.755 for a linear head (+16.8 to +20.0pp) and 0.819 / 0.855 / 0.872 for a full quadratic head on the same scores.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Cross-token score-space composition (AUROC, mean ± std over 10 resamples). On subject–verb agreement, a degree-2 cross-token target by construction, CP rank-1 outperforms the linear head by 16.8–20.0pp across all three Pythia scales; the gap persists on a harder XOR variant. Full per-target breakdown in Appendix F.14.
official.metric: Test AUROC for agreement vs. disagreement (higher is better); ± is std over 10 resamples of the balanced pair set
official.comparison: CP rank-1 (affine-completed degree-2) head vs. linear head and full quadratic head, all trained on the same 60-d score vector of 30 primitive probes at the subject and verb tokens; Table 20 also gives raw-activation linear-concat and bilinear baselines
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the pipeline on any of the three Pythia models, the CP rank-1 head's test AUROC on agreement exceeds the linear head's by less than about 10pp, or the full quadratic head matches or beats CP rank-1.

title: MIST: Reliable Streaming Decision Trees for Online Class-Incremental Learning via McDiarmid Bound

official.background: In online class-incremental learning on tabular streams, a model sees each sample once, cannot store past samples, and must absorb new classes as they appear. Streaming decision trees update only local leaves and never revise committed splits, which in principle avoids catastrophic forgetting, but standard Hoeffding trees break down in this setting: their split confidence radius grows with the number of classes, and child leaves restart from empty statistics after a split. Global exemplar-free methods (streaming LDA/QDA, nearest class mean, recursive least squares) work well on near-Gaussian data but rely on Gaussian class-conditional assumptions.
official.method:
MIST is a Gini-based streaming tree. A leaf splits only when the gap between the best and second-best Gini gain exceeds a class-count-independent McDiarmid radius eps = sqrt(32 ln(2dm/delta)/n) (d features, m candidate thresholds). At a split, child leaves inherit parent statistics: truncated-Gaussian moment projection for the split feature, unchanged parameters for other features, and class mass rescaled by a discount alpha = 0.6. Each leaf keeps per-class KLL quantile sketches (k = 64) whose class-conditional medians supply candidate thresholds.

MIST-G predicts at leaves with Gaussian Naive Bayes. MIST-K (the claim's method) instead estimates each per-feature class likelihood from the sketch CDF, p(x_j | c) = (F(x_j + h_j) - F(x_j - h_j) + eps_s) / (2 h_j + eps_s), with h_j the local inter-quantile spacing, combined under a Naive Bayes factorisation. Defaults: grace period 200, delta 0.10, tie 0.05, eps_s = 1.0. The AngularSectors stream has K = 4 classes, d = 8 features, 2 tasks: samples lie on a 2D ring in two signal features and the class is the angular sector, so all classes share mean ~0 and identical covariance. Baselines (SLDA, SQDA with shrinkage 1e-4, ARF with 10 trees and no drift detection, PEC) follow the same single-pass, exemplar-free protocol; final mean accuracy is reported.
official.claim: On the AngularSectors stress-test stream (K=4, d=8, 2 tasks, strict online class-incremental protocol), MIST-K reaches final mean accuracy 0.436 ± 0.017, while every other method stays near chance (0.25): MIST-G 0.241 ± 0.010, SLDA 0.240 ± 0.041, SQDA 0.235 ± 0.015, ARF-NR 0.255 ± 0.021, PEC 0.302 ± 0.046.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Stress-test results (mean ± std over 5 seeds) on non-Gaussian synthetic streams.
official.metric: final mean accuracy over tasks (higher is better), mean ± std over 5 seeds
official.comparison: MIST-K vs. MIST-G, SLDA, SQDA, ARF-NR (10 trees, no drift reset) and PEC on the same synthetic stream
official.falsification_criterion: On a regenerated AngularSectors stream, MIST-K does not exceed the best of the other methods (PEC, ARF-NR, SQDA) by more than the seed std, or MIST-K itself stays near chance (below ~0.30).

title: Augmented Lagrangian Method for Last-Iterate Convergence for Constrained MDPs

official.background: In constrained MDPs (CMDPs) an agent maximizes discounted reward while keeping a discounted constraint value above a threshold. Standard primal-dual policy-gradient methods only have guarantees for the mixture of all iterates, but in practice people deploy the last policy, which can oscillate and violate the constraints. Prior last-iterate methods add regularization or non-standard modifications (such as projecting onto a restricted simplex) and are either hard to implement or limited to tabular settings. The paper proposes using the classic inexact augmented Lagrangian (AL) method, with each AL subproblem solved by a policy-gradient-style method, to get a practical algorithm with last-iterate guarantees.
official.method:
Algorithm 1 runs T outer AL iterations. Each iteration approximately maximizes the augmented Lagrangian L_β(π, λ) (reward value plus a quadratic penalty on constraint violation with penalty β) over the policy for K inner steps, then updates the multiplier λ. The AL policy gradient equals a standard policy gradient for a pseudo-reward Γ(π): the reward r when the constraint is slack enough, otherwise r + c·(b + λ/β − V_c^π(ρ))·β. For log-linear policies π_θ(a|s) ∝ exp(⟨φ(s,a), θ⟩), the inner solver is projected PQA (PPQA, Algorithm 4): a Q-ascent target policy is computed from the pseudo-reward Q-function and then projected onto the log-linear class by minimizing a surrogate for n inner steps.

Figure 3 uses Constrained Cliff World (21 states, 4 actions, γ = 0.9, uniform initial distribution, reward +1 at the goal, cost −1 for falling into the cliff, threshold b = −0.17) with tile-coded features of dimension d = 60 < SA (feature set (d, tiles, tile size) = (60, 4, 3)). Baselines: Lin-RPG-PD (regularized NPG primal-dual, Ding et al. 2023, with compatible-function-approximation regression for the gradient), policy-based ReLOAD (Moskovitz et al. 2023), and PPO-Lag. Fixed settings: PPQA-ALM T = 10, K = 100, n = 250, β = 10; baselines T = 1000. Hyperparameters were grid-searched (Table 5), and the reported configuration is the one with the smallest optimality gap among those whose final policy satisfies b − V_c(ρ) ≤ ε = 0.001. Metrics are the optimality gap of the reward value and the constraint violation, plotted against gradient evaluations.
official.claim: On Constrained Cliff World with log-linear policies (tile-coded features, d = 60), PPQA-ALM reaches an optimality gap of about 0.00-0.01 after about 100 of 1000 gradient evaluations and stays there with constraint violation near zero, whereas Lin-RPG-PD remains at about 0.44-0.48 and ReLOAD plateaus at about 0.07 for the whole run; PPO-Lag also reaches about 0.01-0.03.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Comparing PPQA-ALM to Lin-RPG-PD, ReLoad and PPO-Lag with log-linear policies. Lin-RPG-PD has comparable theoretical guarantees in this setting, whereas ReLOAD and PPO-Lag are included as a competitive empirical benchmark. Following Asad et al. [2024] we use tile-coded features for construct φ with d = 60 < SA (see Section H for additional details). We find that PPQA-ALM reliably converges to the optimal policy, whereas both Lin-RPG-PD and ReLOAD perform poorly. While PPO-Lag achieves comparable performance, the method lacks any theoretical guarantees.
official.metric: Optimality gap of the reward value V_r (lower is better) and constraint violation (closer to 0 or negative is better), against gradient evaluations; single curves with no seeds or error bars reported; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: PPQA-ALM vs. Lin-RPG-PD (comparable theoretical guarantees), ReLOAD and PPO-Lag, each with grid-searched hyperparameters, on the same environment and features
official.falsification_criterion: With the same environment, features and grid search, PPQA-ALM's final optimality gap is not clearly below Lin-RPG-PD's (e.g. Lin-RPG-PD also reaches a gap below about 0.1 within 1000 gradient evaluations), or PPQA-ALM's final policy does not satisfy the constraint to within about 0.01.

title: Selection, Not Fusion: Radar-Modulated State Space Models for Radar-Camera Depth Estimation
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (matched-baseline details in Section 4.3 and Table 10, page 14)

official.background: Radar-camera depth estimation turns a very sparse but metric automotive radar signal (40 to 100 returns per nuScenes frame within the front camera's field of view) and a camera image into a dense metric depth map, a cheap and weather-robust alternative to LiDAR. Existing methods combine radar and image features outside the backbone's sequence operator, through concatenation, confidence gating, or attention. Mamba-style fusion models stack both modalities before a shared selective scan, so the scan's selection parameters are still computed from one fused stream. The paper argues that radar should instead enter through the selection mechanism of the scan itself.
official.method:
SemoDepth uses an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-34 image encoder and a PCA-GM graph network (GSE, following TacoDepth) over up to 512 radar returns, each described by (y/H, x/W, d/dmax). The radar output is scattered into a feature map and projected to each decoder level. In Radar-Modulated Selection (RMS), radar adds zero-initialised learned terms to the Mamba step size Δ (through a sigmoid gate with bias −2) and to the readout C. The input projection B is computed from the image only, the state matrix A is a trained constant, and radar never enters the scanned token stream, so at initialisation the block equals a vanilla image Mamba. The Multi-View Scan Pyramid (MVSP) decoder applies full-image four-direction RMS at the two coarsest levels, windowed RMS (w = 8) around projected radar returns at the middle level, and FiLM at the two finest levels.

Training on nuScenes (700/150/150 scene split, 900×1600 front camera): the target is LiDAR accumulated over 160 sweeps with a light filter on the upper image, combined with a single-sweep sparse target. The loss is log-space L1 against the single-sweep target + Huber(5 m) against the accumulated target + 0.5·gradient L1 + sparse L1 in metres against the single-sweep target. Optimiser is Adam at lr 1e-4 with the TacoDepth step schedule, batch 12, bf16, up to 50 epochs, and the checkpoint with the lowest val MAE@80 is kept. The matched baseline FusionMamba† is the authors' reimplementation of FusionMamba (dual-encoder VSSM_Fusion with cross-modal SS2D fusion at every scale, i.e. fusion before the scan). It is trained with the same supervision, loss, optimiser and schedule at about 38 M parameters. Evaluation uses single-sweep sparse LiDAR within 50/70/80 m.
official.claim: On nuScenes, SemoDepth reaches MAE@80 of 1285.2 ± 0.9 mm, 19.2% below the matched-recipe Mamba fusion baseline FusionMamba† (1590.5 mm), and also beats it at 0–50 m (940.1 vs. 1179.9) and 0–70 m (1199.8 vs. 1483.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison with published radar camera depth methods on nuScenes. Time is single frame latency, measured on identical hardware for methods with a runnable release. Baseline MAE and RMSE come from the original publications. † Our reimplementation of FusionMamba for depth completion, trained with the supervision, optimiser, and loss of SemoDepth at a matched parameter budget. SemoDepth reports the mean and standard deviation over three seeds. Best per column in bold.
official.metric: MAE in mm against single-sweep sparse LiDAR within 50/70/80 m (lower is better); RMSE also reported. ± is std over three training seeds for SemoDepth; FusionMamba† is reported without an error bar (the paper does not state a seed count for it).
official.comparison: SemoDepth (RMS + MVSP) vs. FusionMamba† (Mamba fusion before the scan), both trained by the authors with the same target, loss, optimiser, schedule and about 38 M parameters. Other rows in Table 1 are copied from the original publications and are not matched.
official.falsification_criterion: With both models trained under the same recipe on nuScenes, SemoDepth's MAE@80 is not clearly lower than FusionMamba†'s, for example a gap well under ~10% or a gap within the run-to-run spread of either model.

title: Minimax Rates and Spectral Distillation for Tree Ensembles
claim_source: Table 6 (Appendix E.4), page 42; summarized without errors in Table 1, page 9

official.background: Random forests and gradient boosting machines are strong tabular learners but their fitted models are large (megabytes to hundreds of megabytes), which rules them out for microcontrollers and other memory-constrained devices with budgets under 1MB. Existing compression methods either prune the ensemble (ForestPrune, LOP), extract rules (FIRE, TreeExtract, SSF) or distill into a single tree, and most fix an accuracy tolerance rather than a target size. The paper argues from a spectral view of tree ensembles that most of a forest's predictive signal sits in a few leading eigenfunctions of its kernel, so a tiny model that learns those eigenfunctions can replace the forest.
official.method:
SCATE (Spectral Compression of Adaptive Tree Ensembles) fits an RF (250 trees, max_depth 15), builds the N x N empirical RF kernel K (per-tree leaf co-membership indicators normalized by leaf size, averaged over trees) on the training data, and takes its top m = 50 eigenpairs (Psi, Lambda). It stores the coefficient vector c = Lambda_m Psi_m^T y and trains a small SiLU MLP g: x -> R^m to regress the m eigenvector values at each training point, with a loss weighting each output's MSE by (lambda_j / lambda_1)^2 plus an orthogonality penalty (gamma = 0.001) on the minibatch outputs. The test prediction is sum_i c_i g_i(x). (For GBMs the same is done with the SVD of the boosting smoother matrix.)

Compression benchmark: for each method a hyperparameter sweep produces many (size, score) points; the reported score is the best test R2 (regression) or accuracy (binary classification) among models whose measured size (minimal inference objects; for SCATE the serialized state_dict plus coefficient array) is at most 10KB or 100KB. SCATE sweeps width in {4,8,16,32,64,128} and depth in {1..5}; LOP sweeps tolerance 0.01-1 (10-minute timeout); FIRE alpha 10-100; ForestPrune and TreeExtract over logspace grids; SSF threshold 0-0.5. 75/25 train-test split, 10 repetitions with different splits and seeds.
official.claim: When a random forest is compressed to at most 10KB, SCATE achieves higher test R2 than every pruning/rule-extraction baseline on abalone (0.561 ± 0.004 vs. best baseline LOP 0.504 ± 0.009), concrete (0.801 ± 0.008 vs. LOP 0.741 ± 0.021) and friedman_1 (0.822 ± 0.006 vs. LOP 0.759 ± 0.012), with abalone matching the uncompressed RF (0.548).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: RF compression benchmark. Scores and base sizes are mean ± standard error across available runs. Base sizes use MiB. Bold entries lie within one standard error of the highest mean. Superscripts [n] indicate fewer than ten contributing runs. NA denotes no within-budget result; TO denotes no candidate result within time limit.
official.metric: test R2 (higher is better) of the best model within the 10KB size budget; ± is standard error across up to 10 runs (different splits and seeds)
official.comparison: SCATE (m = 50) vs. ForestPrune, LOP, FIRE, TreeExtract and SSF, all compressing the same RF under the same 10KB budget; uncompressed RF R2 as reference
official.falsification_criterion: On abalone, concrete or friedman_1 at the 10KB budget, SCATE's mean test R2 over 10 splits does not exceed the best baseline (typically LOP) by more than the combined standard errors, or LOP/FIRE/ForestPrune reaches SCATE's R2 within 10KB.

title: From Noise to Diversity: Random Embedding Injection in LLM Reasoning
claim_source: Table 2, page 6 (full per-position breakdown in Table 6, Appendix A, page 14)

official.background: Soft-prompt methods for LLM reasoning (prompt tuning, TTSV, SoftCoT, LTPO and others) insert trained continuous vectors into the model input and attribute their gains to the learned content of those vectors. The act of injecting out-of-vocabulary embeddings, which all such methods share, has not been separated from the effect of training. The paper uses untrained random embeddings as a control to test whether injection by itself changes reasoning behaviour, which matters for how soft-prompt gains should be interpreted.
official.method:
A Random Soft Prompt (RSP) of length L is a sequence of L vectors drawn i.i.d. from an isotropic Gaussian N(mu_E * 1, sigma_E^2 * I), where mu_E and sigma_E are the mean and standard deviation over all entries of the model's pretrained token-embedding matrix. Nothing is trained. In the default suffix position, the RSP embeddings are inserted at the embedding level right after the question tokens, immediately before the user turn's end-of-turn token (<|im_end|>). A fresh RSP is drawn for each rollout.

The claimed setting is 'format mismatch': Qwen2.5-Math base models (7B and 1.5B), which were not trained on a chat template, are prompted with the ChatML template (system: 'Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.'). Accuracy is measured with greedy decoding (max 3,072 new tokens) on MATH-500 and GSM8K, with and without the RSP; L is chosen per model and benchmark from {10, 15, 20} (L = 20 for both ChatML base models on MATH-500 and GSM8K, Table 7).
official.claim: When Qwen2.5-Math base models are prompted with a ChatML template they were not trained on, appending a suffix RSP (L = 20, greedy decoding) raises accuracy from 52.20% to 70.40% on MATH-500 and from 58.30% to 75.97% on GSM8K for the 7B model, and from 34.40% to 51.00% (MATH-500) and 37.45% to 50.64% (GSM8K) for the 1.5B model.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Accuracy (%) across model configurations and benchmarks. Values in parentheses indicate the difference from the baseline. Full per-position breakdown is in Appendix A.
official.metric: exact-match accuracy (%) under greedy decoding, higher is better; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: ChatML-prompted Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B base models without RSP (Baseline) vs. the same prompt with a suffix RSP
official.falsification_criterion: With the ChatML prompt and greedy decoding, adding a suffix RSP (L = 20) to Qwen2.5-Math-7B or -1.5B improves MATH-500 or GSM8K accuracy by less than about 5 pp, or the gain disappears when averaged over several independent RSP draws.

title: NOFE – Neural Operator Function Embedding

official.background: Dimensionality reduction methods such as PCA, t-SNE and UMAP treat a dataset as an unordered point cloud in feature space. Much real data, however, consists of samples of a continuous function over a domain (multi-channel climate fields over a map, image pixels, time series), and point-cloud methods ignore that domain: the same region embedded from two different random subsets can come out in inconsistent coordinates, and nearby locations can be mapped far apart. This paper proposes learning the reduction as a function-to-function operator over the domain, so that embeddings are continuous in space, consistent across independently sampled subsets, and can be queried at arbitrary locations.
official.method:
NOFE is a Graph Kernel Operator. Sampled locations x_i (here latitude/longitude on a 180 × 180 ERA5 grid over Europe) become graph nodes with the high-dimensional values y_i (11 climate variables at 550 hPa) as node features; each node is connected to its k = 5 spatial nearest neighbours, with edge attributes (x_i, x_i − x_j). A linear lifting layer maps y_i to width W = 64, T = 3 message-passing steps h_i ← ReLU(W h_i + Σ_{j∈N(i)} K(i,j) h_j) are applied (Algorithm 1), where the kernel matrix K(i,j) is predicted by an MLP (2 hidden layers of width 16) from the edge attributes, and a linear projection gives a 3-D embedding z_i. Training minimizes a t-SNE-style KL divergence between Student-t affinities of y and of z, computed only over domain-neighbour edges (Eq. 3-4). The model (Model 2 in the appendix, 75,155 parameters) is trained with AdamW, lr 1e-5 halved every 10 epochs, 25 epochs, on 10 random samples of 1,000-10,000 grid points per day for every day of 2018.

Evaluation uses one sample per day for January 2019. Baselines PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, PHATE, SpatialPCA and CONCORD embed the same points into 3 dimensions. Stress-local (Eq. 10b) is sqrt(Σ_{(i,j)∈E} (d^y_ij − d^z_ij)² / Σ_{(i,j)∈E} (d^y_ij)²), where E is the set of spatial-neighbour pairs and d^y, d^z are Euclidean distances in input and embedding space; Stress-1 is the same over all pairs.
official.claim: On ERA5 (11 variables, Europe, January 2019 test days), NOFE's 3-D embeddings reach Stress-local 0.125 ± 0.012, versus 0.464 ± 0.054 for PCA (the best baseline) and 0.694-2.127 for UMAP, CONCORD, PHATE, SpatialPCA and t-SNE.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative comparison on the ERA5 climate reanalysis dataset. We assess preservation of global and local feature geometry, consistency across independently embedded spatial patches, super-resolution embeddings, and gluing errors. Values are mean ± standard deviation; lower is better for error and stress metrics, whereas higher is better for global correlation. "Aligned" denotes post-processing with Procrustes alignment. Bold and underlined entries are the best and second-best finite results, respectively, within each metric.
official.metric: Stress-local (Kruskal-type stress restricted to spatial-neighbour pairs), lower is better; mean ± std, described only as 'standard deviation' and apparently taken over the January 2019 evaluation samples (one per day), not over training seeds
official.comparison: NOFE vs. PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, PHATE, SpatialPCA and CONCORD embedding the same ERA5 samples into 3 dimensions
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining NOFE as described and evaluating on January 2019 samples, NOFE's mean Stress-local is not clearly below PCA's (e.g. above ~0.35, or within one std of PCA computed on the same samples).

title: UniCustom: Unified Visual Conditioning for Multi-reference Image Generation

official.background: Multi-reference image generation asks a model to synthesize an image from a text instruction while preserving the identity and appearance of subjects taken from several reference images (e.g. 'the woman from Picture 1 wears the hat from Picture 2'). VLM-enhanced diffusion models such as OmniGen2, Qwen-Image-Edit and LongCat-Image-Edit usually feed semantic ViT features of the references to a VLM and inject appearance-rich VAE features separately into the diffusion transformer (DiT). The paper argues that this split leaves the DiT to work out on its own which appearance details belong to which grounded subject, and that with several similar references this leads to attribute leakage and cross-reference confusion.
official.method:
UniCustom concatenates the spatially aligned ViT and VAE features of each reference image along the channel dimension and maps them back to the ViT width with one linear fusion layer. The layer is initialized so that the ViT part is an identity map and the VAE part is zero. The fused tokens are interleaved with 'Picture i:' identifiers and the instruction, and passed through a frozen Qwen2.5-VL. Its hidden states condition a DiT initialized from LongCat-Image-Edit. Only the fusion layer and the DiT are trained.

Training has two stages of 18K steps each on 128 GPUs at resolutions up to 512x512. Stage 1 trains the fusion layer and the DiT on batches sampled uniformly from four task groups (multi-image reconstruction, localization, tiling and understanding), and adds a slot-wise binding loss (an MSE from each image slot's VLM hidden states, through a projector, to that image's VAE features). Stage 2 freezes the fusion layer and fine-tunes the DiT on a mix that is 50% multi-reference generation, 25% single-reference generation, and the rest editing, text-to-image and pretraining tasks. Evaluation samples at 512x512 with a fixed seed (open-source baselines at their default settings) on OmniContext and MICo-Bench.
official.claim: On MICo-Bench, UniCustom reaches an Overall score of 41.71, higher than every open-source baseline evaluated (best: UNO 32.43, BAGEL 31.62; its own DiT initialization LongCat-Image-Edit 22.78, Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 21.67), with the largest gains on HOI (40.51 vs. best 27.99) and Decomposition & Recomposition (50.29 vs. best 46.75).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Quantitative comparison on MICo-Bench [34], where "HOI" and "De&Re" denote "Human-object Interaction" and "Decomposition & Recomposition", respectively. The best results in each group are highlighted in bold.
official.metric: MICo-Bench category and Overall scores (higher is better), as defined by the benchmark; one sample per prompt with a fixed seed; no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: UniCustom vs. open-source models FLUX-Kontext [dev], UNO, USO, BAGEL, Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 and LongCat-Image-Edit, each run at 512x512 with its default inference configuration (closed-source GPT-Image-2 and Nano Banana 2 are listed for reference and outperform UniCustom)
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating the released UniCustom checkpoint and the baselines on MICo-Bench with the benchmark's official scorer, UniCustom's Overall score does not exceed the best open-source baseline (UNO or BAGEL), or its lead falls well short of the ~9-point margin reported (e.g. under 3 points, or within the spread across sampling seeds).

title: Metaphor Is Not All Attention Needs

official.background: Rewriting a harmful request as a poem is known to bypass LLM safety training far more often than the same request in prose. It is unclear whether this works because of particular poetic devices, because the model fails to recognise the poetic format, or because stylistically irregular input is processed differently. The paper studies this in Qwen3-14B with input ablations and with linear probes on a compact summary of the model's attention maps, asking whether attention encodes the literary format, the safety outcome, or both.
official.method:
The main dataset has 1,197 prose harmful prompts from the MLCommons AILuminate benchmark and 1,200 poetic rewrites made by DeepSeek-R1 with a fixed meta-prompt. Qwen3-14B (thinking disabled) generates 50 tokens greedily for each prompt; responses are labelled safe/unsafe by an ensemble of GPT-OSS-120B, Kimi-K2-Thinking and DeepSeek-R1 with human verification (attack success: 10.44% prose, 46.92% poetry). Full attention tensors are recorded at every generation step.

Each sample becomes a 72-dim feature vector: attention from generated tokens to prompt tokens is max-pooled over the 40 heads, then mean-aggregated over 3 generation phases (steps 0-16, 17-33, 34-49), 4 layer clusters ({0}, {1-4}, {5-6}, {7-39}, from Ward clustering on a calibration set) and 6 functional token groups (FIGURATIVE, HARMFUL_PAYLOAD, TECHNICAL from LLM judges; SETUP, FUNCTION_WORD, PUNCTUATION deterministically). Three probes are trained: format (poetry vs. prose) on the full set, and safe vs. unsafe separately on the prose and on the poetry subset. The primary probe is L1 logistic regression (liblinear, C tuned by inner 5-fold CV on ROC-AUC, standardised features, balanced class weights) with 5-fold stratified CV; the format probe uses grouped folds so paired prose/poetry prompts stay together, and the prose-safety probe is repeated over 5 balanced subsamples (122 safe vs. 122 unsafe). RBF-SVC and a 128-unit MLP are also reported.
official.claim: On Qwen3-14B's 72-dim attention features, an L1 logistic-regression probe predicts poetry vs. prose with accuracy 0.985 ± 0.006 (AUC 0.997), whereas probes predicting jailbreak success reach only 0.673 ± 0.087 (AUC 0.709) on prose and 0.658 ± 0.035 (AUC 0.722) on poetry, with SVC and MLP probes showing the same gap.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Test-set classification performance across subsets, targets, and models. Values are mean±std across cross-validation folds. The main probe achieves near-perfect discrimination, while safety probes reach accuracy above chance but substantially below the main probe. Comparable performance from non-linear classifiers indicates that the relevant signal is linearly accessible.
official.metric: Test accuracy and ROC-AUC (higher is better); ± is std across CV test folds (prose-safety: 25 evaluations = 5 folds x 5 balanced subsamples); chance accuracy is 0.5 for format and prose-safety (balanced), about 0.53 majority for poetry-safety

title: PrivacySIM: Evaluating LLM Simulation of User Privacy Behavior
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (also Figure 2, page 6 and Table 4, page 9)

official.background: LLMs are increasingly proposed as stand-ins for human participants, including for eliciting users' data-sharing preferences when designing privacy-sensitive systems. Users' privacy decisions are idiosyncratic and often contradict their stated attitudes (the 'privacy paradox'), so it is unclear whether conditioning an LLM on a user's persona lets it predict that individual's actual privacy choices. PrivacySIM tests this against ground-truth answers from real participants in published privacy user studies.
official.method:
The benchmark samples 200 users from each of five published user studies on LLM/chatbot privacy (LLM healthcare consultation, LLM chatbot norms, AI agent permissions, chatbot group chat, LLM conversational agents): 1,000 users and 9,400 user-question pairs. Each user has a persona made of up to three facets taken verbatim from the study: demographics (Du, only in 3 studies), previous AI/chatbot experiences (Eu) and stated privacy attitudes (Au). The LLM gets a fixed prompt template (role, persona block, JSON-output constraints, the original questionnaire) and answers all of that user's data-sharing questions in one JSON response.

The score is tolerance accuracy: the fraction of questions where the simulated answer is within 0.15 x scale width of the user's real answer (exact match on 4/5-point Likert scales, within +/-15 points on the 0-100 scales), averaged over users and then over the five studies. The key comparison is the no-persona prompt ('none', persona fields left empty) vs. the Eu+Au prompt, for the same model. Open models use T=1.0, top-p=0.95; closed models use default temperature and medium reasoning effort.
official.claim: Averaged over all five studies, conditioning on previous experiences plus privacy attitudes (Eu+Au) raises tolerance accuracy over the no-persona prompt for every model in Table 3, e.g. Gemini 3 Flash 37.07% -> 40.27%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.32% -> 40.39%, GPT-5.4 (medium) 35.70% -> 39.30%, Qwen3.5 27B 34.53% -> 36.41%; no model exceeds about 40.4%.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Simulation accuracy across model families and variants. For GPT-5.4 we report the smaller mini model and the full model under low and medium reasoning effort. We find that reasoning effort has negligible impact and model size can yield modest simulation improvement.
official.metric: Tolerance accuracy (%) at tau = 0.15, higher is better, averaged over the 5 studies; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: Same model, no-persona prompt (acc(none)) vs. Eu+Au persona prompt (acc(Eu+Au)), across GPT-5.4 Mini/low/medium, Gemini 3 Flash/Pro, Qwen3.5 27B/122B
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the benchmark shows the Eu+Au gain over 'none' is not positive, or it is within run-to-run variation (e.g. repeated runs at the same settings vary by about 3 points), for the tested model; or the best model clearly exceeds about 45% 5-study accuracy at Eu+Au.

title: Reinforcing VLAs in Task-Agnostic World Models

official.background: Post-training vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies with reinforcement learning inside a learned video world model avoids costly real-robot interaction. Existing pipelines, however, train the world model and the reward classifier on thousands of rollouts from the target task, so they must be rebuilt for every new task. The paper asks whether a world model trained only on broad, task-agnostic interaction data, paired with an off-the-shelf VLM as a zero-shot success judge, is enough to improve a VLA on tasks the world model has never seen.
official.method:
The world model is Wan 2.1-T2V-1.3B fine-tuned into an action-conditioned autoregressive video generator (AdaLN action conditioning, causal temporal attention, rectified-flow loss, first-frame anchor with progressive noise at inference). For LIBERO it is trained only on noisy-action rollouts of a multi-task OpenVLA-OFT policy across the 90 LIBERO-90 tasks; no data from LIBERO-Spatial, Object, Goal or Long is used ('Zero-Shot WM'). The policy is OpenVLA-OFT (categorical action tokens, 8-step chunks, third-person image only), trained with SFT on LIBERO-90 and then fine-tuned on one expert demo per task of the target suite (1-shot SFT, 10 demos per suite).

RL is GRPO (group size 8, no KL, lr 5e-6, sampling temperature 1.6, 50 steps; 20 for Object) run entirely in the frozen world model. Each imagined rollout gets a binary reward from Qwen3-VL (8B for Spatial/Object, 32B for Goal/Long; 5 samples, success if at least 4/5 vote success). Dual-Noise Verification replays the action sequence of each VLM-judged success in the world model under freshly resampled diffusion noise; if the VLM judges the replay a failure, that rollout's reward is replaced by the mean reward of the trustworthy rollouts (zero advantage), and a group with more than two flagged rollouts is discarded. Groups that are all-success or all-failure are also discarded. Policies are evaluated in the real LIBERO simulator, 50 episodes per task. Baselines are the 1-shot SFT policy and GRPO online RL in the real simulator with ground-truth reward, using about 500 (Short) or 2,500 (Long) real episodes.
official.claim: On four LIBERO suites unseen by the world model, GRPO inside the zero-shot (LIBERO-90-only) world model with a Qwen3-VL reward raises average success from 43.4% (1-shot SFT) to 52.3%, above online RL in the real simulator with ground-truth reward and ~500 real episodes (47.9%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Success rate (%) on four unseen LIBERO suites. The VLA is first trained on LIBERO-90, then adapted to each suite using 1-shot SFT. Bold rows correspond to our method with different WM conditions. "Tgt. data" refers to target-suite real rollout budget used in the whole policy learning process, including data for WM and VLA fine-tuning. Deltas in parentheses relative to 1-shot SFT.
official.metric: Task success rate (%) in the LIBERO simulator, 50 episodes per task, 10 tasks per suite, averaged over 4 suites; higher is better. Single run, no seeds or error bars reported.
official.comparison: RL in Zero-Shot WM (VLM reward, 10 target demos) vs. 1-shot SFT starting policy and vs. Online RL (Short) in the real simulator (GT reward, 522 target episodes); all initialised from the same 1-shot SFT checkpoint.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running RL in the LIBERO-90-only world model yields an average success that is not clearly above the 1-shot SFT policy (43.4%) or does not exceed Online RL (Short) (47.9%) under the same initialisation and evaluation protocol, or the gain disappears across seeds.

title: TextSeal: A Localized LLM Watermark for Provenance & Distillation Protection

official.background: Generation-time watermarks for LLMs bias token sampling with a secret-keyed pseudo-random function so that a detector holding the key can later test text for the watermark. In practice, AI-generated passages are often pasted into longer human-written documents. A detector that scores the whole document then has its signal diluted by unwatermarked tokens, and the p-value weakens as the document grows. Distortion-free schemes such as Gumbel-max and Google's SynthID-Text are normally detected with such a global test over all tokens.
official.method:
TextSeal is a Gumbel-max watermark (context window k = 3) with dual-key routing (at each step one of two keys is used, the second with probability α = 0.1). Detection fuses the per-token scores under both keys, s_i = (1-α)s_i^(1) + α s_i^(2) with s = -ln(1-R), weights each token by its normalized entropy from a small proxy model (Qwen 3.5-0.8B), and computes a p-value from a moment-matched Gamma approximation. For localization, a geometric cover search over dyadic window lengths starting at L0 = 64, the smallest power of two ≥ the minimum zone length Lmin = 50 (stride half the window, about 4n/L0 windows), greedily extracts up to 5 disjoint watermarked regions with Bonferroni-style search penalties. The adaptive ensemble takes the most significant of (1) the global test, (2) the best single window (penalized by log10 M) and (3) the multi-region aggregate (penalized by log10 C(M, y) + log10 Ymax), plus a log10 3 correction.

Setup for Figure 3: 400-token watermarked answers are generated with Qwen 3.5-27B (T = 1.0, top-p = 0.95, reasoning disabled) and embedded in unwatermarked Wikipedia text. Dilution (left panel): one contiguous 400-token block inside documents of 400 to 12,000 tokens. Fragmentation (right panel): the 400 tokens are split into K ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5} equal fragments in a fixed 8,000-token document. Baselines are global TextSeal detection on the full document and SynthID-Text (depth 10, frequentist Z-test, k = 3) generated and detected globally the same way. The y-axis is detectability, -log10 p.
official.claim: When a single 400-token watermarked block is embedded in unwatermarked Wikipedia text, TextSeal's adaptive localized ensemble keeps -log10 p ≈ 4.3-4.5 at 4k, 8k and 12k document tokens, while global TextSeal (≈1.8, 1.3, 1.0) and global SynthID (≈1.4, 0.8, 0.7) drop below the p = 0.01 threshold.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3 Localized detection in mixed documents containing 400 watermarked tokens. (Left) Dilution: A single watermarked block (K=1) embedded in documents of increasing length. Global detection (light blue and red curves) degrades rapidly as the watermarked fraction shrinks, dropping below the p=0.01 significance threshold around 4k tokens. The adaptive ensemble (dark blue curve) maintains strong detectability (−log10 p > 4) even at 12k tokens (3.3% watermarked). (Right) Fragmentation: Watermarked text split into K fragments within an 8000-token document. Global detectors are insensitive to fragmentation (flat curves at −log10 p ≈ 1), while the ensemble leverages localized search to extract the signal at K≤3 fragments.
official.metric: Detectability -log10(p-value), higher is better; the aggregation over documents (mean/median) and the number of documents are not stated; no error bars; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: TextSeal adaptive ensemble (localized) vs. TextSeal global test vs. SynthID-Text global Z-test, on the same dilution setup
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the dilution setup (400 watermarked tokens in 8k-12k-token Wikipedia documents), the ensemble's -log10 p falls below 2 (p > 0.01), or it is not clearly above (e.g. less than 1.5 higher than) the global TextSeal and SynthID tests.
