title: ToolCUA: Towards Optimal GUI-Tool Path Orchestration for Computer Use Agents

official.background: Computer-use agents can act through low-level GUI actions (click, type, scroll) or through high-level tool calls such as application APIs exposed over MCP. Tool calls can replace long, brittle GUI sequences, but current agents handle the mixed action space poorly: given tools, many models either ignore them or misuse them, and their task success often drops compared with GUI-only operation. The paper targets learning when to switch between GUI actions and tools so that execution paths are both successful and short.
official.method:
ToolCUA starts from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. An interleaved GUI-Tool data pipeline converts about 10k static GUI-only trajectories (OpenCUA, ScaleCUA and sandbox-collected) into GUI-Tool trajectories by having MLLMs synthesise a library of about 4,350 simulated tools from recurring GUI procedures and replace GUI segments with tool steps. The model is warm-started by 3 epochs of full SFT on this data, then single-turn RL on about 5k critical GUI-Tool switching steps (group size 32).

Finally, online multi-turn GRPO is run in an OSWorld-based sandbox with MCP tools, using a Tool-Efficient Path Reward: task success plus a format term, a tool-appropriateness term (lambda = 0.4) that rewards using tools on tool-beneficial tasks and avoiding them otherwise, and a path-length term (beta = 0.2) relative to the rollout-group mean (max horizon 30). Evaluation is on the 333 feasible OSWorld-MCP tasks (238 tool-beneficial, 95 non-tool-beneficial), max 50 steps, average success over 3 runs.
official.claim: On the 333 feasible OSWorld-MCP tasks (GUI + MCP tool action space, max 50 steps, average@3), ToolCUA-8B reaches 46.85% task accuracy vs. 28.23% for its base Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (+18.62 points), with gains on both tool-beneficial (45.80 vs. 27.73) and non-tool-beneficial tasks (49.47 vs. 29.47), while using fewer steps on average (14.93 vs. 19.34).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance on OSWorld-MCP. Results are reported on the feasible tasks only. Tool-Beneficial Tasks favor tool usage, while Non-Tool-Beneficial Tasks do not require tools. Accuracy denotes average success rate; TIR (Tool Invocation Rate) measures whether the agent uses tools when beneficial and avoids them when unnecessary; ACS denotes Average Completion Steps.
official.metric: OSWorld-MCP task success rate (%) averaged over 3 runs (higher is better); also TIR (tool invocation rate, higher is better) and ACS (average completion steps, lower is better); no std or CI reported
official.comparison: ToolCUA-8B vs. its base Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct in the same hybrid GUI-Tool environment; other general and specialized CUAs are listed for reference
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating ToolCUA-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct in the same OSWorld-MCP harness (feasible tasks, 50 steps, 3 runs) gives an overall accuracy gap under about 8 points, or ToolCUA-8B does not beat the base model on the held-out multi_apps domain.

title: Runtime Monitoring of Perception-Based Autonomous Systems via Embedding Temporal Logic

official.background: Runtime monitors check whether a running autonomous system satisfies a formal temporal-logic specification and raise an alert when it does not. Classical logics such as STL define their predicates over low-dimensional state variables (positions, velocities), so applying them to camera-driven robots requires extra detectors or classifiers to turn images into propositions, which adds brittleness and engineering effort. Pretrained encoders already place semantically similar observations close together, which suggests defining predicates directly as distances in embedding space.
official.method:
Embedding Temporal Logic (ETL) defines an atomic predicate as a comparison delta(z) <= epsilon, where delta(z) is an aggregate (e.g., min) of the distances from the current observation embedding z to a set of target embeddings obtained by encoding reference observations. Predicates are combined with LTL operators (not, and, until, eventually, always) and evaluated over finite embedding traces, with robustness semantics as in STL. Thresholds are calibrated on held-out labelled trajectories, either by maximizing frame-level F1 (epsilon_F1) or by split conformal prediction for a per-trajectory recall guarantee (epsilon_CP).

For the DROID evaluation, each frame is encoded with the SVD VAE from Ctrl-World (a video diffusion model trained on DROID) into a 4x24x40 latent, flattened to 3,840 dimensions, and compared with cosine distance. Five multi-phase manipulation episodes (2 to 4 phases each) are monitored with phase predicates; ground truth comes from gripper proprioception or manual video annotation. The baseline is Qwen2-VL-2B, prompted per phase with the ground-truth desired behavior and the phase frame, with its answer reduced to a Boolean. Both monitors are scored on frame-level F1, agreement, and whether the phase ordering is correctly identified.
official.claim: On five phasic DROID manipulation episodes, ETL phase predicates (SVD VAE embeddings, cosine distance) reach mean frame-level F1 0.813 and agreement 0.940, versus 0.390 F1 and 0.567 agreement for a Qwen2-VL-2B monitor, and get the phase order right in 4/5 episodes versus 2/5.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Comparison of ETL and Qwen2-VL-2B on phasic DROID episodes.
official.metric: Frame-level F1 and agreement (higher is better) for phase-predicate detection, averaged over 5 episodes; sequential ordering correctness counted per episode. No error bars, seeds, or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: ETL monitor vs. Qwen2-VL-2B VLM monitor on the same DROID episodes and ground-truth phase labels
official.falsification_criterion: On the same (or comparable) phasic DROID episodes, ETL's mean phase F1 does not clearly exceed the Qwen2-VL-2B baseline's (e.g., the gap of about 0.42 F1 shrinks to within per-episode variability), or ETL's mean F1 falls well below about 0.8.

title: scShapeBench: Discovering geometry from high dimensional scRNAseq data

official.background: Single-cell RNA-seq data can be organized as discrete clusters, a single trajectory, a branching tree or an archetypal (simplex-like) continuum, and each shape calls for a different downstream analysis pipeline (Seurat clustering, Monocle, flow models, etc.). Today a bioinformatician picks the pipeline by looking at a 2D embedding, which blocks automated or agentic analysis. The paper frames 'shape detection' as recovering a reduced graph (degree-2 vertices contracted) from a high-dimensional point cloud, and releases a benchmark with synthetic point clouds sampled around known graphs plus 102 expert-annotated scRNAseq datasets.
official.method:
Synthetic track: 1,000 point clouds generated with seed 20260422 from random latent graphs (singletons, edges, trees, single cycles, multiple cycles, hybrids; up to four connected components; up to 80 nodes), embedded in R^2 to R^5, thickened into tubes and sampled with Gaussian noise, with difficulty axes noise ratio [0.02, 0.20], separation [0, 0.6], density [3.5, 25] and thickness [0.45, 1.0] (Appendix D.2). Each method outputs a graph S, which is reduced by contracting degree-2 chains and compared with the reduced ground-truth graph via (i) Wasserstein distance between edge-length-filtration persistence diagrams, converted to a similarity (higher is better), and (ii) approximate graph edit distance from NetworkX (lower is better), both averaged over samples.

scReebTower builds a k = 15 nearest-neighbour graph, an adaptive Gaussian kernel and the row-normalized diffusion operator P, and uses the first non-trivial eigenvector (Fiedler vector) as a Morse function. It takes midpoint thresholds between sorted function values, makes each connected component of the crossing-edge level set a node, links nodes in adjacent levels that share points, and reduces the resulting Reeb graph. The multiscale 'scReebTower' first applies diffusion condensation X̂ = P^t X with k_smooth = min(80, n-1); 'scReebTower (ℓ=0)' skips it. Baselines: PAGA (Scanpy, Leiden resolution 1.0, k = 15, keep all edges with connectivity > 0) and Mapper (KeplerMapper, PCA lens of dim ≤ 2, 6 intervals, overlap 0.35, DBSCAN min_samples 3, eps = 1.5 × median 3rd-NN distance). Hyperparameters are fixed with no per-sample tuning.
official.claim: On the 1,000-sample synthetic track, multiscale scReebTower recovers reduced graphs with a mean graph edit distance of 13.32 vs. 16.25 for PAGA and 79.78 for Mapper, and a Wasserstein persistence similarity of 0.3199 vs. 0.2788 for PAGA and 0.0318 for Mapper.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Benchmark results on the synthetic track. Higher is better for Wasserstein persistence similarity, lower is better for graph edit distance
official.metric: Mean approximate graph edit distance between reduced recovered and ground-truth graphs (lower is better) and mean Wasserstein persistence similarity (higher is better) over 1,000 synthetic samples; no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: scReebTower (with diffusion condensation) vs. scReebTower (ℓ=0), PAGA and Mapper on the same synthetic point clouds
official.falsification_criterion: On a regenerated synthetic benchmark following Appendix D.2, scReebTower's mean GED is not clearly below PAGA's (e.g. the gap shrinks to well under ~3 or reverses), or its persistence similarity is not above PAGA's.

title: When Attention Closes: How LLMs Lose the Thread in Multi-Turn Interaction
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (trajectories in Figure 5, page 8, and Figure 11, page 29)

official.background: LLMs follow system-prompt instructions (facts, personas, policies) well in single-turn use but drift over long multi-turn conversations. This degradation has been documented behaviorally but not explained mechanistically. The paper proposes that as conversations grow, attention from generated tokens to the goal-defining system-prompt tokens decays until direct access is effectively lost, after which any surviving goal-conditioned behavior must rely on information carried indirectly (residual stream or intervening context). To test whether losing attention access is sufficient to cause failure, the authors force the attention channel shut and measure behavior.
official.method:
Information-retention tasks: a system prompt lists facts the model must remember (Task 1: 5 facts, e.g. codename 'Aurora Borealis', budget '$4.2 million'; Task 2 'controlled complexity': 20 facts in four complexity tiers). Each episode is a 50-turn pre-authored conversation with fixed filler turns (generic history/science questions) interleaved with recall probes (Task 1 probes at turns 1,5,...,45 plus a grouped all-facts probe at T=50; Task 2 probes for Mistral at 1,3,5,7,9, odd turns 25-49, and a grouped probe at T=50 that queries only the five tier-4 facts F16-F20). Responses are sampled at temperature 0.7, up to 256 tokens, with the model's native chat template. Recall is scored by case-insensitive substring match against canonical forms and accepted paraphrases of each fact.

Closed-channel condition: a sliding-window mask with W=4096 is applied to attention scores before softmax at every layer and head at inference time (key j visible to query i only if i-j<4096); weights, MLPs and residual computation are unchanged. Once the response position is more than 4096 tokens past the last goal token, attention to the goal tokens is exactly zero; for Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 this crossover happens at turn 23. Open-channel condition is default full causal attention. Episodes differ only in sampling seed. Mistral 20-fact cohorts: 150 default episodes (seeds 60, 200) and 200 SW episodes (seeds 61, 72, 201); Mistral 5-fact uses 100 episodes.
official.claim: On Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, forcing a 4096-token sliding-window attention mask (which removes all attention to the system-prompt facts from turn 23 on) drops recall at the final T=50 grouped probe from 1.000 under default attention to 0.112 on the 20-fact task (where that probe covers the tier-4 facts F16-F20) and to 0.452 on the 5-fact task, while default-attention recall stays at 1.000 throughout.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Behavioral metrics across the four multi-turn tasks under open-channel (default) vs closed-channel (SW=4096) inference. Tasks: Retention (5-fact), Complexity (20-fact), Persona (5 constraints, passive), Policy (LLM-judge ensemble, mixed phase T in [25, 30]). Higher-is-better: recall (r), compliance (C). Lower-is-better: violations (v), partial compliance (P), violation (V). Cell shading indicates level of degradation on a per-direction scale, intensifying red indicates poorer behavior. tau_c is the empirical crossover turn under closed-channel inference.
official.metric: Fact recall rate (higher is better) at the T=50 grouped probe (r50) and averaged over post-crossover probes (r>=35 for 5-fact, r>=25 for 20-fact). Table 1 reports point estimates only, with no error bars; the paper states 95% Wilson/bootstrap CIs are used elsewhere but none are given for these cells.
official.comparison: Same model, prompts, conversation scripts and sampling settings, default full causal attention (open channel) vs. SW=4096 inference-time mask (closed channel).
official.falsification_criterion: With the same task scripts and a 4096-token sliding-window mask, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 retains 20-fact recall at T=50 well above ~0.3 (or 5-fact r50 near 1.0), or default-attention recall itself falls substantially below 1.0, so the gap between conditions largely disappears.

title: CRePE: Curved Ray Expectation Positional Encoding for Unified-Camera-Controlled Video Generation
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (overall numbers in Table 7, page 18)

official.background: Camera-conditioned video generation asks a video diffusion model to follow a given camera trajectory and lens. Recent methods put the camera geometry into the attention positional encoding. UCPE encodes each token's viewing ray under the Unified Camera Model (UCM), so it can handle wide-angle and fisheye lenses, but a ray alone does not say where along it the scene content lies. RayRoPE adds a depth interval along the ray but assumes a pinhole camera. CRePE combines the two: a positional encoding that is aware of depth along the ray and works with non-pinhole lenses.
official.method:
CRePE starts from a frozen Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B DiT with a UCPE-style camera adapter. A shared geometry head predicts, for each key token, a log radial-distance centre mu and half-width |sigma|, treated as a uniform distribution over log radial distance. K = 5 evenly spaced breakpoints in log radius are lifted along the source token's UCM ray, transformed into the query camera, and projected through the query UCM. The expected RoPE phasor along this curved projected path is computed by analytically integrating each piecewise-linear segment (Eq. 3). The resulting rotary coefficients modulate Q, K, V and the output in a geometric attention branch, but only in the middle 10 DiT blocks (11-20). The other blocks keep UCPE's relative-ray modulation.

The geometry head gets auxiliary supervision from pseudo radial-distance maps from UniK3D (validity-filtered, 20 m far-field cut, per-clip normalised, uncertainty-weighted L1 loss, lambda_rad = 1e-3). The pseudo maps are not used at inference. The adapter is trained for 10K AdamW steps on the PanShot train split with the backbone frozen. Baselines are UCPE (same backbone and adapter interface, without CRePE or radial supervision) and ReCamMaster. Camera control is measured by recovering relative pose from the generated videos with ViPE (frame stride 1) and computing CamMC, following UCPE.
official.claim: On the 340-clip PanShot test split (pose stride 1), CRePE has lower camera-motion error (CamMC) than the matched UCPE adapter: 15.33 vs. 18.50 on pinhole clips and 19.02 vs. 20.60 on non-pinhole clips (overall 18.15 vs. 21.87, Table 7). It also has lower lens-distortion errors (k1 0.157 vs. 0.183, k2 0.116 vs. 0.154 on non-pinhole clips).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Pinhole and non-pinhole camera-generation comparison (340 PanShot test clips; pose stride 1). We report representative metrics across pose control, text/image alignment, lens distortion, orientation, and VBench quality. Non-pinhole and pinhole subsets are grouped by rows for readability. CRePE consistently improves over UCPE and ReCamMaster on the representative camera-control, geometry-aware, and VBench quality metrics.
official.metric: CamMC (camera-motion consistency error from ViPE-recovered poses; lower is better). k1/k2 are radial-distortion coefficient errors from GeoCalib (lower is better). Single-run point estimates with no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: CRePE (K = 5, middle 10 blocks, UniK3D-supervised, 10K steps) vs. UCPE (same Wan2.1-1.3B backbone and adapter, no CRePE) and ReCamMaster, on the pinhole and non-pinhole subsets of the PanShot test split
official.falsification_criterion: With matched training budget and evaluation protocol, CRePE's CamMC is not lower than UCPE's on the pinhole subset or on the overall test split, or the gap shrinks to within the variation seen across re-runs with different seeds.

title: The Expressivity Boundary of Probabilistic Circuits: A Comparison with Large Language Models

official.background: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are generative models that allow exact marginal and conditional inference, but they still fall well short of Transformers at language modeling. The paper looks at both models as autoregressive context encoders and identifies two bottlenecks. The first is the output layer: PCs mix distributions in probability space, while Transformers project in logit space. The second is context encoding: a structured-decomposable PC fixes, through its vtree, which groups of variables can interact, whereas attention routes information differently for each input. The theory (Theorem 1 and Proposition 1) says such a PC can match Transformer separation rank only on partitions aligned with its vtree.
official.method:
Two synthetic autoregressive datasets of length-N sequences with tokens drawn uniformly from a vocabulary of size V. Local-copy ('Adjacent Data'): x = (a1, a1, a2, a2, ..., a_{N/2}, a_{N/2}), loss over all positions. Induction-style prefix-copy ('Distant Data'): x = (a1..a_{N/2}, a1..a_{N/2}), loss only on the second half. Both are evaluated by token-level NLL on held-out data.

The PC is a structured-decomposable circuit over a balanced binary vtree: log2 N stages of a sum layer followed by a product layer that merges adjacent tree positions, C channels per node, categorical leaves, and a final root sum. Only the leaf permutation changes. The standard layout uses the identity order, so adjacent tokens are siblings. The shifted-induction layout makes position k and position N/2 + k siblings and orders the pairs by bit-reversal. Next-token conditionals come from exact marginalization over future positions. The baseline is a causal Transformer with 5 layers, 4 heads, hidden size 256, context 32, about 4.09M parameters, trained on the same next-token objective.
official.claim: With architecture fixed and only the vtree leaf order changed, a structured-decomposable PC whose vtree matches the data reaches NLL near the Transformer (3.158 vs 3.018 on local-copy; 3.144 vs 3.018 on prefix-copy). With the mismatched vtree, NLL rises by about 3.1 nats (6.283 and 6.297), while all stds are at most 0.002.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance of structured-decomposable PCs with two different vtree layouts and a Transformer baseline on the local-copy and induction-style prefix-copy datasets. The standard layout is aligned with local dependencies and the shifted-induction layout is aligned with nonlocal prefix-copy dependencies. A matched layout achieves performance close to the Transformer, while a mismatched layout degrades substantially, consistent with Theorem 1 and Proposition 1.
official.metric: held-out token-level NLL in nats (lower is better), mean ± std (the paper does not state the number of seeds)
official.comparison: Same PC architecture with the standard (local-aligned) vtree layout vs. the shifted-induction (copy-aligned) layout, each evaluated on the dataset it matches and the one it does not, with a causal Transformer as reference
official.falsification_criterion: The claim fails if, on either dataset, the mismatched-layout PC's NLL is not substantially higher than the matched-layout PC's (for example, a gap under 1 nat or within seed noise), or if the matched-layout PC is not close to the Transformer (for example, more than about 0.5 nats worse).

title: Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs

official.background: Agentic-memory systems such as CLIN, Agent Workflow Memory, Dynamic Cheatsheet and ACE let an LLM agent rewrite its past trajectories into a textual memory bank that it updates after every interaction, promising self-improving agents without weight updates. These designs implicitly assume that each consolidation step is at worst neutral. The paper tests that assumption in settings where the input experience is useful by construction (problems the model already solves, or ground-truth solutions), so any loss in performance can be attributed to the consolidation step itself rather than to bad trajectories.
official.method:
ARC-AGI Stream is a synthetic testbed built on the ARCGEN generator with a known task-family taxonomy (following ConceptARC) and programmatic ground-truth solutions. In the in-distribution regression experiment (Fig. 2 / §4.1), GPT-5.4 streams problems together with their ground-truth solutions (GT regime) through a Stream consolidation loop that updates a textual memory after each problem; the model is then evaluated, with the consolidated memory in context, on the same problems it had been consolidating. The paper does not spell out the Table 2 protocol separately: it is presented as a ten-run repetition of that experiment on an expanded task set, and 'epoch' appears to correspond to the refresh rounds R of Fig. 2 (passes over the stream). Whether raw episodes persist (Force vs. Auto control loop) is not stated for this table.

The task set for Table 2 is every ARC-AGI Stream task that GPT-5.4 solves at least 50% of the time without memory across ten runs (33 tasks). The whole pipeline (consolidation plus evaluation) is repeated ten times end-to-end. pass@1 is reported as mean ± std over the ten runs and pass@10 as the fraction of the 33 tasks solved in at least one of the ten runs.
official.claim: On the 33 ARC-AGI Stream tasks GPT-5.4 can solve without memory, consolidating ground-truth solutions into a streamed textual memory lowers pass@1 from 58.5 ± 5.4 (no memory) to 38.5 ± 5.3 after 10 consolidation epochs, and pass@10 coverage from 33/33 to 20/33.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: The regression is not sampling noise, and it shows up as lost coverage. Over ten end-to-end runs on the 33 tasks solvable without memory, consolidated memory leaves a third of them unsolved by epoch 1 and 40% by epoch 10 (pass@10), while mean accuracy falls from 58.5 to 38.5. The headline 100% → 54% in-distribution regression thus survives repetition and an expanded task set.
official.metric: pass@1 accuracy (%) on the 33 tasks, higher is better, mean ± std over ten end-to-end runs; pass@10 = share of tasks solved in at least one of ten runs (no error bar)
official.comparison: No-memory GPT-5.4 vs. GPT-5.4 with streamed consolidated memory after epoch 1 and after epoch 10, same 33 tasks
official.falsification_criterion: With the same task set and consolidation procedure, epoch-10 consolidated-memory pass@1 is within about one run-to-run std (~5 points) of the no-memory baseline, or pass@10 coverage stays near 33/33.

title: PRISM: Prior Rectification and Uncertainty-Aware Structure Modeling for Diffusion-Based Text Image Super-Resolution

official.background: Text image super-resolution (Text-SR) restores high-resolution text-line images from degraded low-resolution inputs. Unlike generic super-resolution, a small error in a stroke can change which character is read, especially for dense scripts such as Chinese. Recent diffusion-based Text-SR methods produce sharp outputs, but they take their text conditioning from the degraded input, which can be wrong under heavy degradation. They are also slow because they need many sampling steps (e.g. 200 for DiffTSR, 50 for TeReDiff).
official.method:
PRISM is a one-step restoration model built on Stable Diffusion 2.1-base with a rank-16 LoRA on the UNet and a fixed timestep of 399. FMPR (Flow-Matching Prior Rectification) is trained in two stages of 100K iterations each. First, a prior encoder sees the concatenated LQ and HQ VAE latents and produces a 'privileged' token embedding c*, which serves as the cross-attention key/value for warming up the one-step backbone. Second, an LQ-only prior encoder produces c_l, and a velocity field is trained by flow matching on the straight path from c_l to c*. It is integrated with K = 16 Euler steps to give the recovered prior ĉ, which conditions the backbone at inference. The first stage uses L1 + LPIPS on the image. The second stage, in which the backbone (initialized from the first-stage backbone) is further adapted with ĉ, adds an L1 loss between ĉ and c*.

SURE (Structure-guided Uncertainty-aware Residual Encoder) is then trained for 50K iterations with FMPR and the backbone frozen. A spatial cue extractor predicts the mean and log-variance of a structural cue, which is sampled by reparameterization and decoded to an edge map supervised by a Sobel map of the HQ image, with a KL penalty to N(0, I). A residual encoder, initialized from the UNet encoder, takes (z_l, ĉ, cue) and injects residuals into the UNet skip connections. Training data is BTL-train: 80K of the 100K BTL pairs (BTL = 50K filtered real Chinese/English crops from CTR and SA-Text plus 50K synthetic text lines, with LQ inputs from BSRGAN/Real-ESRGAN degradation pipelines; the other 20K pairs form BTL-test). RealCE-val (1,037 pairs after the authors' filtering and annotation fixes) tests real-world generalization. OCR ACC and NED use PP-OCRv5.
official.claim: On real-world RealCE-val at ×4, PRISM (trained only on BTL-train) reaches OCR accuracy 65.19% and FID 47.83. The strongest retrained baseline, MARCONet, gets 60.62% and 74.52, and DiffTSR gets 54.00% and 74.94.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative comparison on BTL-test and RealCE-val under ×2 and ×4 text image super-resolution. Best and second-best results are shown in bold and underlined, respectively.
official.metric: OCR accuracy (ACC) computed with PP-OCRv5 as the recognizer (higher is better) and FID (lower is better); PSNR, LPIPS and NED also reported. Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: PRISM vs. TSRN, TBSRN, TATT, MARCONet, DiffTSR, StyleSRN, TeReDiff, all retrained or fine-tuned on BTL-train following their official settings, evaluated on the same 1,037 RealCE-val pairs.
official.falsification_criterion: With PRISM and MARCONet trained on the same BTL-train data and evaluated on RealCE-val ×4 with PP-OCRv5, PRISM's ACC lead over MARCONet is under about 1 point, or its FID is not clearly lower than both MARCONet and DiffTSR (e.g. within ~5 FID).

title: EgoForce: Robust Online Egocentric Motion Reconstruction via Diffusion Forcing

official.background: AR glasses and embodied agents record egocentric data that gives the wearer's head pose and, only when the hands are in view, the wrist poses. Reconstructing full-body motion from these sparse, noisy signals is needed for AR/VR and assistive applications, and those applications need it online: each frame has to be estimated from past and current observations only. Existing online methods are deterministic causal transformers that cope poorly with missing or corrupted inputs, while diffusion-based methods handle uncertainty well but denoise whole fixed-length windows offline or autoregressively, which is slow and produces discontinuities where windows are stitched together.
official.method:
EgoForce applies Diffusion Forcing to motion: a denoiser is trained on 25-frame windows (h = 5 history frames, the current frame, f = 19 future frames) where each frame gets an independently sampled noise level k ~ U{0..K}, K = 100. Observed quantities (past generated poses, the current head pose and visible wrist poses) are injected into the noisy window through a binary visibility mask that is concatenated to the input, and DINOv2 image features from past and current egocentric frames are fused via cross-attention. The model predicts the clean window under an L2 loss. Poses are 22 joints plus a device reference point in global translation + 6D rotation, in a head-centric canonical frame, plus foot contacts.

At inference the window slides forward one frame at a time. Future frames carry a noise level rising linearly with distance (k_{t+i} = i * K/(f+1)), so each new step only needs to remove dK = 5 diffusion steps: the current frame becomes clean, future frames are partially refined and a new pure-noise frame is appended. A small noise level (n = 2) is re-injected into history frames for stability. Baselines (AvatarJLM, RPM, a re-implemented HMD2, EgoAllo, UniEgoMotion) are trained on the same EE4D-Motion data (10 FPS); offline baselines use 80-frame windows that are stitched. Metrics are computed on full sequences.
official.claim: On EE4D-Motion under strict online (causal) inference, EgoForce reaches full-body MPJPE 0.073 m and MPJRE-F 0.138, versus 0.115 m / 0.364 for RPM and 0.127 m / 0.245 for HMD2 (the best online baselines), and also beats the offline UniEgoMotion (0.091 m / 0.497), at 0.08 s per-frame latency.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative egocentric motion reconstruction results on the EE4D-Motion dataset, comparing online and offline baselines. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance under strict online causal constraints. Best values are highlighted in blue and second-best values in red. † denotes our adapted re-implementation because the official code is not publicly available.
official.metric: MPJPE in metres (lower is better) and MPJRE-F (rotation error, Frobenius norm, lower is better); also semantic similarity (TMR, higher), FID (lower), peak jerk and area under jerk. No ± reported; single numbers with no seeds or intervals.
official.comparison: EgoForce (online) vs. online baselines AvatarJLM, RPM, HMD2† and offline baselines EgoAllo, UniEgoMotion, all trained and evaluated on EE4D-Motion
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining EgoForce and RPM (or HMD2) on EE4D-Motion with the same splits, EgoForce's MPJPE is not clearly below the best online baseline (e.g. the gap shrinks to within run-to-run variation across seeds, or EgoForce MPJPE is above ~0.10 m), or EgoForce does not beat UniEgoMotion on MPJPE.

title: Ergodic Trajectory Design by Learned Pushforward Maps: Provable Coverage via Conditional Flow Matching

official.background: Ergodic coverage asks for a continuous trajectory whose long-run time-averaged occupancy matches a prescribed spatial density, for example a UAV that should spend time over a city in proportion to user demand. The trajectory must also respect operational limits such as no-fly zones and energy budgets. Existing approaches either re-optimize each trajectory online (spectral/Fourier ergodic control, per-query flow-matching control), which costs time for every target and agent, or use analytical constructions such as time-warping. Those constructions are provably convergent, but they must be re-derived for each new target or constraint and have no way to add penalties.
official.method:
A latent trajectory z(t) on the annulus δ ≤ ||z|| ≤ 1 runs radial out-and-back cycles along i.i.d. uniformly random directions, with radial profile r(s) = sqrt(δ² + (1 − δ²)s), so its occupancy is exactly uniform on the annulus. A map G_θ is learned offline with optimal-transport conditional flow matching (OT-CFM). An MLP velocity field v_θ(s, y) is trained on Sinkhorn-coupled minibatch pairs (uniform-annulus sample, target-density sample) with the loss ||v_θ(s, y_s) − (x1 − z0)||², where y_s = (1 − s)z0 + s·x1. G_θ is the time-1 RK4 flow of v_θ, and the flown trajectory is x(t) = G_θ(z(t)). Constraints enter as additive penalties. For a no-fly-zone (NFZ) disc with centre c and radius r_nfz, the '+NFZ' variant adds λ_nfz · E_z[max(0, r_nfz − ||G_θ(z) − c||)²] to the CFM loss.

Milano setup (Appendix F): the target density is the Milan telecom grid (100×100 cells, Nov–Dec 2013). All five channels are summed, averaged over time, Gaussian-smoothed with σ = 1.5 cells, floored at 1e-12 and normalised on [−1, 1]². v_θ is a 12-layer, 256-wide SiLU MLP (~920K parameters), trained with Adam (lr 2e-3, cosine schedule) for 3000 epochs at batch size 2048, with Sinkhorn ε = 1e-2 and δ = 0.05. Trajectories use 128 cycles × 200 points and 30 RK4 inference steps. λ_nfz = 5 was chosen from {0.5, 5, 50, 500, 5000} in a single-seed sweep. Coverage ρ is the Pearson correlation between the target density and the trajectory's achieved occupancy on a grid. NFZ frac is the percentage of trajectory points inside any NFZ disc. Baselines are time-warping (Malekzadeh et al.), static OT, SAC, TOES and two FMEC variants (Sun et al.), all evaluated under the same two NFZ configurations: one disc (1D), or four disjoint discs (MD).
official.claim: On the Milano UAV-coverage target with a single no-fly disc, OT-CFM +NFZ reaches Pearson coverage ρ = 0.865 ± 0.001 with 0.011 ± 0.010% of trajectory points inside the no-fly zone, versus ρ = 0.690 ± 0.04 and 9.11 ± 1.4% for the time-warping baseline, the strongest baseline on coverage.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Headline metrics on Milano under two no-fly configurations: single-disc (1D) and multi-disc (MD). Mean±std over 3 seeds; best per column among coverage-competitive methods (ρ ≥ 0.5); ‡ achieves low violation at degraded coverage. Full coverage, energy, and NFZ tables in Appendix N.1. († Low P̄ and zero NFZ frac are artifacts of degenerate coverage (ρ ≤ 0.29).)
official.metric: Pearson ρ between target and achieved occupancy density (higher is better) and NFZ frac, the % of trajectory points inside an NFZ (lower is better); mean ± std over 3 seeds
official.comparison: OT-CFM +NFZ (proposed, with NFZ penalty) vs. time-warping [9], static OT, SAC, TOES, FMEC-Stein, FMEC-Sinkhorn, and unconstrained OT-CFM, on the Milano single-disc (1D) configuration
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both methods on the Milano 1D configuration gives a coverage ρ for time-warping within the combined seed std of OT-CFM +NFZ (or higher), or OT-CFM +NFZ's NFZ violation fraction is not clearly below time-warping's (e.g. not below about 1%).

title: Early Semantic Grounding in Image Editing Models for Zero-Shot Referring Image Segmentation

official.background: Referring image segmentation (RIS) asks for a pixel mask of the object described by a natural-language expression (e.g. 'kid on left in blue'). Zero-shot RIS avoids pixel-level annotations, and most existing zero-shot methods combine SAM mask proposals with CLIP-based mask selection, sometimes adding linguistic preprocessing. Instruction-based image editing models must work out where to apply an edit such as 'remove the kid on the left', so they implicitly perform language-conditioned grounding. This paper asks whether that grounding can be read out of a pretrained editor's internal representations and used directly as a segmentation, without training and without SAM.
official.method:
Each referring expression is turned into an editing instruction by prepending 'Remove', then rewritten by Step1X-Edit's built-in instruction-refinement pipeline (told to keep the meaning). The image and instruction are passed through the editor's MM-DiT for a single denoising step at t = 0; no image is generated. Attention-based region proposal: the image-to-prompt attention submatrix for the clean reference-image tokens is summed over prompt tokens and over all DiT blocks to give a coarse attention map; the image-to-image attention submatrix is row-normalized into a transition matrix and applied to the image-to-prompt attention (affinity propagation) before aggregation, giving a refined attention map (min-max normalized).

Feature-based semantic localization: the refined attention map is thresholded at τ = 0.8 to give a high-confidence mask. The multi-modal self-attention (MMSA) output features of the clean image tokens at t' = 0 in block l' = 40 of 57 (Step1X-Edit) are L2-normalized, foreground and background prototypes are formed by masked average pooling, the feature map is upsampled to image resolution, and each pixel is assigned to whichever prototype has higher cosine similarity. For Table A4 the authors also run Global-Local and HybridGL on the same refined expressions (with the 'remove' directive stripped) and on the original expressions. Metrics are oIoU (cumulative intersection over cumulative union) and mIoU (mean per-sample IoU) on the val splits of RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg.
official.claim: With the same Step1X-Edit-refined referring expressions, the training-free Step1X-Edit (12B) method reaches oIoU 53.94 / 44.38 / 51.23 on the RefCOCO / RefCOCO+ / RefCOCOg val splits, vs. 44.14 / 38.53 / 43.74 for HybridGL, a margin of 9.80 / 5.85 / 7.49 oIoU points.
official.claim_caption: Table A4: Impact of editing instruction refinement. We compare our method against Global-Local [53] and HybridGL [25] using both the original and refined referring expressions.
official.metric: oIoU (higher is better) on val splits; mIoU also reported. Single deterministic run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Ours (Step1X-Edit, single step at t = 0, ARP + FSL) vs. HybridGL and Global-Local, all using the same refined expressions; also all three using the original expressions
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the pipeline with Step1X-Edit on the val splits gives an oIoU advantage over HybridGL (run on the same refined expressions) of under ~3 points on any of the three datasets, or no advantage at all.

title: LeanSearch v2: Global Premise Retrieval for Lean 4 Theorem Proving

official.background: Writing Lean 4 proofs against Mathlib, a library of over 100,000 declarations, depends on finding the right existing lemmas and definitions. Several Mathlib search engines take a natural-language query and return ranked declarations (LeanExplore, LeanFinder), but users phrase queries in very different ways: Lean-style, LaTeX, plain English, slogans, nicknames, or special cases of a more general statement. This paper builds a better single-query Mathlib search engine (standard mode) and uses it as the base of an LLM-driven retrieval loop that finds the full set of premises a theorem's proof needs (reasoning mode).
official.method:
Standard mode: every extractable Mathlib declaration (Mathlib v4.28.0-rc1, extracted with the Jixia static-analysis tool) is informalized bottom-up in dependency order with Qwen3-32B (Gemini 2.5 Pro as a fallback), so each description can draw on the already-informalized descriptions of its dependencies. Each item becomes a structured passage from a template: a task instruction, declaration kind, type signature, informal description and, for definitions/classes/instances, the value field. Passages are embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B and retrieved by cosine similarity. The top 50 are reranked by Qwen3-Reranker-8B using P(yes) with a kind-aware instruction. Neither model is fine-tuned on Mathlib.

Evaluation: MathlibQR has 200 expert-chosen declarations with up to six query styles each (946 queries). The main comparison uses the 'fair' subset of 810 queries (171 declarations) whose ground truth exists in every system's Mathlib snapshot. Each query has one relevant declaration (binary relevance). The paper reports nDCG@k and Recall@k for LeanExplore, LeanFinder, LeanSearch v2 retriever-only (no reranker) and LeanSearch v2 with reranking.
official.claim: On the 810-query fair subset of MathlibQR, LeanSearch v2 standard mode (Qwen3-Embedding-8B + Qwen3-Reranker-8B over a hierarchy-informalized Mathlib corpus) reaches nDCG@10 0.623 and Recall@10 0.780, versus 0.533 and 0.698 for LeanFinder, the strongest baseline, and 0.393 / 0.569 for LeanExplore.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Search task on MathlibQR. Numbers are nDCG@k and Recall@k over 810 query rows on the shared 171-declaration corpus subset (intersection of the four systems' Mathlib snapshots). LLM judge reports mean rank (lower is better, range 1-4) by Claude Sonnet 4.5 over 2430 blinded judgments per system. Best per column in bold.
official.metric: nDCG@k and Recall@k with single-document binary relevance, higher is better; point estimates over 810 queries, no error bars or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: LeanSearch v2 (embed + rerank) vs. LeanFinder and LeanExplore (existing Mathlib search engines), plus a LeanSearch v2 retriever-only ablation, on the same 810 queries
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running LeanSearch v2 standard mode and LeanFinder on the 810-query fair subset of MathlibQR, LeanSearch v2's nDCG@10 lead over LeanFinder is under about 0.03 or reversed, or its Recall@10 is not above LeanFinder's.

title: Understanding Generalization through Decision Pattern Shift
claim_source: Figure 6, page 8 (the 0.930 value is repeated in Section 6 and Figure 11, page 14, as the 0% label-noise setting)

official.background: Why deep networks fail to generalize to some test samples is usually studied through external factors: shifts in the data, in learned representations, or in output/loss behaviour. This paper instead asks whether the model's internal decision logic stays the same from training to test samples, and proposes a per-sample measure of how far a test sample's decision logic drifts from what the model learned for that class during training. If that drift tracks the test-minus-train loss closely, it could be used to diagnose generalization failures at the sample, class and dataset level.
official.method:
For a CNN with a final convolutional layer of K channels, the decision pattern of sample x for class c is the vector p^c(x) with entries p^c_k = w^c_k * GAP(A_k), where A_k is channel k's activation map, GAP is global average pooling, and w^c_k = (1/Z) * sum_ij dg^c(x)/dA^k_ij is the GradCAM channel weight (spatially averaged gradient of the class-c logit). Each pattern is L2-normalized (Appendix A.1), and the class reference pattern is the mean normalized pattern over training samples of class c.

Sample-level DPS for a test sample x of true class c is 1 - cos(p^c(x), mean training pattern of class c). The per-sample generalization gap is the test sample's cross-entropy loss minus the mean training loss of its class (Eq. 10). Models (ResNet-32/34, VGG16, GoogLeNet/InceptionV4) are trained on CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet and a 50-class ImageNet subset, and the Pearson correlation between DPS and the generalization gap is computed over test samples (sample level) and over per-class means (class level).
official.claim: For VGG16 trained on CIFAR-100, the sample-level Decision Pattern Shift of test samples is linearly correlated with their per-sample generalization gap (test loss minus class-mean training loss) with Pearson r = 0.930, and the class-level correlation is r = 0.925.
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Linear correlation between Decision Pattern Shift (DPS) and the generalization gap on CIFAR100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet across multiple architectures, including ResNet-32/34, VGG16, and GoogLeNet (InceptionV4). (a) Sample-level correlation between per-sample DPS and generalization gap. Each point corresponds to a test sample, and the fitted line shows the overall linear trend. (b) Class-level correlation between the average DPS and the class-level generalization gap. Each point represents a single class in the dataset.
official.metric: Pearson correlation coefficient between DPS and generalization gap (higher is stronger); single run, no error bars or seeds reported; p < 0.001 stated for sample level
official.comparison: DPS vs. per-sample (and per-class) generalization gap; no competing predictor is reported in this figure
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining VGG16 on CIFAR-100 under the described protocol and computing DPS as defined gives a sample-level Pearson r well below 0.9 (e.g. below 0.8), or the class-level r falls well below 0.9.

title: N-vium: Mixture-of-Exits Transformer for Accelerated Exact Generation

official.background: Autoregressive transformers decode one token at a time through every layer, so per-token latency scales with depth even though logit-lens studies show many tokens' predictions settle well before the last layer. Early-exit methods such as CALM exploit this by stopping at an intermediate layer, but they treat the early prediction as an approximation of the final layer, need hand-tuned confidence thresholds, and skip or copy the KV cache for the bypassed layers. Quality drops as a result. The question is whether a model trained from scratch to exit early can decode faster on standard hardware without losing perplexity.
official.method:
N-vium splits a LLaMA-2-style decoder of L layers into N_V equal blocks and attaches a junction after each block. Each junction has an RMSNorm, a router MLP that outputs an exit probability w_k, and an adapter MLP feeding the LM head W_lm, which all junctions share. The next-token distribution is the mixture pi_mix = sum_k p_k pi_k with p_k = w_k * prod_{j<k}(1 - w_j) and w_{N_V} = 1. Training minimises -log pi_mix plus beta times the expected normalised exit depth (a compute penalty), with a router-balancing term during the first 5% of steps. At inference a Bernoulli(w_k) draw at each junction decides whether to sample the token from pi_k, which is exactly a sample from pi_mix. The skipped upper layers of an exited token are not dropped: they are deferred and run batched alongside later tokens' forward passes ('piggybacking'), so the KV cache is complete and total compute equals that of a dense model.

For the chosen claim, a 4-vium (N_V = 4, junctions at layers 6/12/18/24) with 24 layers and hidden size 768 (226M params) is pretrained on C4 for 20 tokens per parameter with beta = 0.15. The baseline is a dense decoder of the same depth whose MLP is slightly wider to match parameter count, trained with plain cross-entropy under identical data and settings. Perplexity is measured on 5M held-out C4 validation tokens. Speedup is the reduction in ms/token on a single A100 over SpecBench (six categories, up to 128 generated tokens per prompt, three runs, averaged over categories).
official.claim: At 24 layers x 768 width (226M params), 4-vium with beta = 0.15 reaches C4 validation perplexity 18.21 vs. 18.9 for the parameter- and data-matched dense baseline (3.6% lower) while decoding 26.8% faster per token on an A100 (SpecBench).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Depth and width scaling results with β = 0.15. ∆ (%) is the relative perplexity difference over the parameter-matched dense baseline. Positive values indicate lower perplexity. Speedup is the measured percentage reduction in latency per token over the dense baseline, measured on a single A100 GPU.
official.metric: C4 validation perplexity (lower is better) and wall-clock latency reduction per token in % (higher is better). No ± reported: single training run per model; speedup averaged over 3 runs and 6 SpecBench categories, with variance described as negligible but not reported.
official.comparison: 4-vium (beta = 0.15) vs. a dense LLaMA-2-style decoder with the same depth, parameter count (wider MLP), data and token budget, trained with standard cross-entropy
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both 24L/768 models under the stated recipe gives 4-vium perplexity that is not lower than the dense baseline's (or worse by more than seed-to-seed spread), or a measured per-token decoding speedup well below ~27% (e.g. under 15%) on an A100 with exact sampling and complete KV cache.

title: Differentiable Learning of Lifted Action Schemas for Classical Planning

official.background: Classical planners solve huge deterministic problems quickly when they are given a symbolic domain model: predicates plus lifted action schemas (preconditions, add effects, delete effects) in STRIPS/PDDL. Writing these models by hand is costly, so a long-standing goal is to learn them from data. When traces include full states and full ground actions, symbolic learners work well. When the action arguments are not observed (only the action name is logged), the learner must figure out which objects each action acted on while also learning the schema, a problem shown to be as hard as graph isomorphism. This paper attacks that setting with gradient descent, as a step toward learning planning domains from images and action labels.
official.method:
DIAS (Differentiable Induction of Action Schemas) takes transitions <s, a, s'> where s and s' are fully observed sets of ground atoms over known unary/binary predicates and a is only an action name. The transition is encoded as a graph (objects as nodes; atoms of s, plus added and deleted atoms, as typed edges; random initial node features) and passed through an R-GCN to get object keys. For each action name, M = 5 learnable query vectors attend over the keys and a rectangular Sinkhorn step gives a soft, mutually exclusive object-to-slot assignment, scaled by learnable sigmoid slot-activation weights. Per action, learnable lifted parameters give, for every predicate over slot pairs, probabilities of being a positive/negative precondition and an add/delete effect. These are grounded through the selection matrix; a soft precondition-satisfaction probability gates the effects, which predict the successor adjacency matrix. Training minimizes a BCE successor-prediction loss, plus auxiliary terms pushing toward minimal effects and maximal (slot-weighted) preconditions, combined with PCGrad so the auxiliary gradient never conflicts with prediction. After 10,000 AdamW steps, schemas are read off by thresholding at 0.5 (active slots define the arity).

Training data is a random walk on one small instance per domain (14 IPC domains), stopping when every action has at least N_min samples. Evaluation: on three larger held-out instances, 500 test states each, the successor sets under the learned and the ground-truth domains are compared for every action name. A run is sound if precision = 1, complete if recall = 1, and counted in N_sc if both. Each configuration is run for 10 seeds (new initialization, training walk and test states per seed); the auxiliary weight alpha is set per domain (Table 5).
official.claim: With action names only (no action arguments), DIAS learns sound and complete action schemas in all 10 of 10 runs for 9 of the 14 domains (Blocks-3, Delivery, Driverlog, Gripper, Miconic, N-Puzzle, Sokoban-pull, Spanner, Visitall), in 9 of 10 runs for Hanoi and Logistics, 2 of 10 for Sokoban, and 0 of 10 for Satellite and Satellite-recal.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on IPC domains over 10 runs for three action observation variants. We report the average precision (Pr.) and recall (Re.), and the number of learned domains that are sound, complete, or sound and complete as Ns, Nc, and Nsc. Nine domains are learned perfectly in every setting. Counts with only some or zero successful runs are highlighted in orange or red, respectively.
official.metric: Per domain over 10 seeds: average successor-set precision and recall on 3 held-out larger instances (higher is better), and counts N_s, N_c, N_sc of runs with precision = 1, recall = 1, or both. No standard deviations are reported; the seed spread is captured by the counts.
official.comparison: DIAS with action names only, against (i) DIAS with full STRIPS action labels (argument selection given) and STRIPS+ labels in the same table, and (ii) the SAT-based L1 algorithm (Balyo et al., 2024), run by its authors on one DIAS training walk per domain, which recovers perfect models in 6 of 13 domains and fails (precision < 1) on Blocks-3 (0.85), Driverlog (0.35), Logistics (0.34), Spanner (0.09), Satellite and both Sokoban domains (Appendix D.3, Table 8).
official.falsification_criterion: Using the released code and the paper's per-domain settings with action names only, fewer than 10 of 10 seeds yield sound and complete schemas in any of the 9 domains listed as perfect (e.g. Driverlog, Spanner, Blocks-3), or the overall count of sound-and-complete runs across the 14 domains falls clearly below the paper's 110 of 140.

title: RotVLA: Rotational Latent Action for Vision-Language-Action Model

official.background: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are pretrained on heterogeneous robot datasets and human videos that do not share an action space. Latent action models (LAMs) address this by learning a shared action representation from pairs of consecutive video frames with an inverse-dynamics encoder and a forward-dynamics decoder. Most LAMs discretize the latent with VQ-VAE, which limits capacity, and they can collapse into simply encoding the appearance of the target frame instead of the motion between frames.
official.method:
The RotVLA latent action model encodes a frame pair (frozen DINOv2 features followed by a spatial-temporal transformer) into an unconstrained 16x16 matrix, applies SoftVQ (a soft, continuous codebook mixture), and projects the result onto SO(16) with an SVD-based orthogonal projection. Training uses frame triplets (I_t, I_t+1, I_t+2): a transformer decoder reconstructs each next frame from the previous frame and its latent action (L_single), and the two latent actions are composed by matrix multiplication (z_{t+1->t+2} · z_I^{-1} · z_{t->t+1}, where z_I is an identity anchor estimated from identical frame pairs) to predict I_t+2 from I_t (L_comp), plus the SoftVQ KL term. The LAM (290M parameters) is trained for 200k steps, batch 256, on ~1700 hours of Open X-Embodiment, AGIBOT-beta, RoboMIND, RoboCOIN and Ego4D data.

For the claim used here, the frozen latent actions are evaluated on the LARY benchmark, which probes latent action representations with linear heads: regression of ground-truth robot actions (MSE, on CALVIN, VLABench, RoboCOIN, AgiBot) and classification of action categories (accuracy, on robot and human video). RotVLA is compared with the LAMs of LAPA, UniVLA, villa-X and LAPA-DINOv3. A variant RotVLA* trains the LAM only on Open X-Embodiment and RoboMIND, excluding AGIBOT-beta, RoboCOIN and Ego4D, which overlap with the benchmark.
official.claim: On the LARY linear-probing benchmark, RotVLA's SO(n) latent actions reach 70.98% average action-classification accuracy vs. 45.62% for the best prior LAM (LAPA-DINOv3), and lower action-regression MSE on all four robot datasets (e.g. CALVIN 0.30 vs. 0.50, RoboCOIN 0.43 vs. 0.82); the variant RotVLA*, trained without the overlapping datasets, still gets 59.70% accuracy and CALVIN MSE 0.38.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Results of different latent action methods on LARY benchmark [51]. RotVLA∗ denotes a variant whose LAM is pretrained on Open X-Embodiment [39] and RoboMIND [40].
official.metric: Linear-probe regression MSE (lower is better) per dataset and linear-probe classification accuracy in % (higher is better) on robot and human clips; single numbers, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: RotVLA and RotVLA* latent action models vs. LAPA, UniVLA, villa-X and LAPA-DINOv3 latent action models, all probed with the LARY protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Linear probes on the RotVLA LAM latents fail to beat LAPA-DINOv3 by a clear margin on LARY, e.g. average classification accuracy below ~55% or regression MSE not below LAPA-DINOv3 on CALVIN and RoboCOIN; or RotVLA* (no benchmark-overlapping data) does not beat LAPA-DINOv3 on robot classification accuracy (61.26 vs. 27.04).

title: MMSkills: Towards Multimodal Skills for General Visual Agents

official.background: Agents increasingly reuse 'skills', meaning stored procedures written as prompts, code or routines. For visual agents (desktop GUI or game agents acting from screenshots), a text procedure leaves out something important: how to recognise the screen state where a step applies, and what visual evidence shows that a step worked. The paper asks whether skills that pair text procedures with visual state descriptions and reference screenshots help multimodal agents more than text-only skills or no skills.
official.method:
Each MMSkill package holds a textual procedure (SKILL.md), runtime 'state cards' (when to use, when not to use, visible cues, verification cue, available views) and keyframes for each state (full frame, focus crop, optional before/after). An LLM-driven generator builds the packages from public non-evaluation trajectories. For OSWorld it uses the Ubuntu subset of OpenCUA, producing 247 skills, 879 state cards and 1,898 views over 10 domains. Text-only skills are the same packages with state cards and images removed.

At inference the agent pre-recalls candidate skills from the task instruction. At any step the main agent can act directly (pyautogui code / WAIT / DONE / FAIL) or call LOAD_SKILL. That call opens a temporary branch: Stage 1 picks which state cards and views to load, and Stage 2 compares them with the live screenshot and returns a structured guidance JSON (applicability, subgoal, plan, do_not_do, verify) to the main agent. Text-only skills use the same branch without cards or images. OSWorld runs use the official task definitions, all 360 test cases, and a 20-step budget.
official.claim: On the full OSWorld benchmark (360 tasks, 20-step budget, screenshot-only), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with branch-loaded MMSkills reaches 25.40% overall success, vs. 10.78% with no skills and 14.93% with branch-loaded text-only skills.
official.claim_caption: Table 1 OSWorld application-level success rates. All entries are percentages. "Calc", "Impress", and "Writer" denote LibreOffice applications. Note: Due to the substantially higher inference cost and wall-clock time of Gemini 3.1 Pro and Kimi-K2.6, we report their full three-condition results only on OSWorld.
official.metric: OSWorld overall success rate (%), higher is better; single run per condition, no error bars reported (binomial SE on 360 tasks is about 1.6-2.3 pp)
official.comparison: Same base model (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) and harness under three conditions: no skill vs. text-only skills (branch-loaded) vs. MMSkills (branch-loaded)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on OSWorld with the released MMSkills library gives an overall success rate less than ~5 pp above the no-skill run, or no higher than the text-only-skill run.

title: Causal learning with the invariance principle

official.background: Causal discovery tries to infer the direction of cause and effect from data. From purely observational data it is generally ill-posed: for example, linear Gaussian SCMs are not identifiable. One way around this is to use several 'environments' (natural experiments) in which the noise distributions shift while the causal mechanisms stay the same. Earlier multi-environment identifiability results needed a number of environments that grows with the number of variables, or strong assumptions such as Gaussian noise. This paper proves that for any acyclic SCM with an invertible mechanism map, a base environment plus two auxiliary environments are enough to identify the causal graph, and also the mechanisms up to elementwise reparametrization, which gives counterfactual identifiability.
official.method:
MCD (Multienvironment Causal Discovery) recovers the causal order by recursively peeling off sink nodes. At each step it estimates the score ∇ log p_e(x) of the active variables in each environment e = 0, 1, 2 with the Stein score estimator (Li and Turner 2018; kernel ridge regression, l2 regularization 0.001). It forms the score differences Δ^(ℓ) = ĝ_0 − Σ_{e∈E_ℓ} ĝ_e for the two auxiliary groups ℓ = 1, 2. For each node i it takes the normalized 2-vector U_i = (Δ_i^(1), Δ_i^(2)) / ||·||, a stabler stand-in for the ratio Δ^(1)_i / Δ^(2)_i. The node whose U_i is most independent of the remaining variables (HSIC test; argmin of the p-value as written in Algorithm 1) is declared the sink, prepended to the order and removed.

Data: Erdős-Rényi DAGs with d ∈ {3, 5, 10, 20} nodes and edge probabilities {0.8, 0.5, 0.25, 0.25}. Gaussian noise has mean in [−2, 2] and std in [0.5, 4], and these are allowed to shift between environments. Each mechanism is, with probability 1/2, linear (giving a linear Gaussian SCM that is not identifiable from observational data), or otherwise a random 4-layer tanh ResNet of (parents, noise) with weights from N(1, 1). Each of the 3 environments has 3000 samples. The baselines are the observational methods CAM, NoGAM (dodiscover), RESIT and LiNGAM (lingam package), plus a random causal order. The metric is the topological divergence D_top divided by the number of true edges (0 best, 1 worst), averaged over 20 seeds.
official.claim: With 3 environments (3000 samples each) on mixed linear/ResNet Gaussian SCMs over ER graphs, MCD's mean normalized D_top is about 0.14, 0.24, 0.21 and 0.31 for 3, 5, 10 and 20 nodes. CAM, LiNGAM, NoGAM and RESIT all lie between about 0.44 and 0.70, which is no better than a random order (about 0.5). MCD's 95% CI does not overlap any baseline's at any graph size.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Mean D_top (20 seeds, the lower the better) performance on linear and nonlinear Gaussian data that are non-identifiable from pure observations. Error is 95% confidence interval. Given three environments, MCD can infer the causal direction where all other state-of-the-art methods for observational causal discovery are no better than a baseline randomly selecting the causal order.
official.metric: Normalized topological order divergence D_top (lower is better; random order ≈ 0.5); mean over 20 seeds with shaded 95% confidence intervals; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: MCD (3 environments) vs. CAM, LiNGAM, NoGAM, RESIT and a uniformly random causal order on the same synthetic datasets
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the simulation (ER graphs, d = 3-20, 3 environments with shifted Gaussian noise, 3000 samples each, 20 seeds), MCD's mean normalized D_top is not clearly below the random-order level of 0.5 (e.g. above ~0.4 at d = 10 or 20, or its 95% CI overlaps the observational baselines').

title: Realtime-VLA FLASH: Speculative Inference Framework for Diffusion-based VLAs

official.background: Flow-matching vision-language-action models such as pi0 generate a chunk of future robot actions with a full inference pipeline: an image encoder, VLM prefill, then about 10 sequential flow-matching denoising steps. On an RTX 4090D this takes about 58 ms per replanning round, so in reactive tasks the robot ends up acting on stale action chunks. Speculative decoding speeds up autoregressive models: a cheap draft model proposes outputs and the large model checks them in parallel. That approach does not carry over directly to continuous flow-matching actions, because there are no token likelihoods to accept or reject drafts with.
official.method:
FLASH adds a 'flash path' that can replace a full replanning round. A ~110M-parameter draft model predicts a whole action chunk in one forward pass. It is one Gemma block with H=50 learned action queries and a linear action head, trained by weighted Huber regression on the frozen pi0's output action chunks, and it takes the current image-encoder features, the language instruction and the robot state as input. The main model's Action Expert then checks the draft without rerunning sequential denoising. It reuses the VLM KV cache from the most recent full-path round and mixes the draft with shared Gaussian noise at K verification timesteps tau. It predicts the velocity v at each timestep in parallel and reconstructs the endpoint as A_tau + (1 - tau) v. The longest prefix of actions whose position/rotation distance to the draft is at most delta at every timestep is accepted (K=2, delta=0.15).

The system runs the full pi0 path instead if the accepted prefix is empty, or if a gripper switch (open/close) appears in any verification branch (phase-aware fallback). On LIBERO-10 it also forces a full-path refresh every 2 flash rounds (PF=2). Evaluation follows standard LIBERO: four suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, 10), each with 10 tasks x 50 trials. The setup uses chunk size 50, replans every 12 executed actions, trains one draft model per suite, and times everything on a single RTX 4090D. Latency is the task-level average per replanning round.
official.claim: On LIBERO with pi0 on an RTX 4090D, FLASH+Triton-pi0 cuts average replanning latency from 39.7 ms (Triton-pi0) to 19.1 ms, a 3.04x speedup over Torch-pi0 (58.0 ms), while average success rate over the four suites is 93.8% vs. 94.2% (Triton) and 94.1% (Torch). In plain PyTorch, FLASH-pi0 cuts latency from 58.0 to 34.9 ms (1.66x) at 93.4% vs. 94.1% success.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Simulation results on four LIBERO suites. We report suite-level success rates, average success rate (SR), average task-level latency (Lat. (ms)), average per-action latency (/Act (ms)), and relative improvement over the original π0 [1].
official.metric: Two metrics: average task-level inference latency per replanning round in ms (lower is better), and average success rate over the four LIBERO suites in % (higher is better). Single run, 500 episodes per suite. No error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: FLASH+Triton-pi0 vs. Triton-pi0, and FLASH-pi0 vs. Torch-pi0 (same policy, same hardware, same LIBERO protocol). Torch-pi0 is the 1.00x reference.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if either holds, using the same pi0 checkpoint and GPU class: (1) adding FLASH cuts average replanning latency by clearly less than ~1.5x relative to the same backend without FLASH, e.g. FLASH-pi0 not clearly below ~40 ms when Torch-pi0 takes ~58 ms; or (2) reaching that latency costs more than ~2 points of average LIBERO success rate relative to the baseline.

title: Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
claim_source: Table 1, page 9 (paired differences with std in Table 24, page 41; full results in Table 23, page 41)

official.background: Self-consistency samples many chain-of-thought paths from an LLM and returns the majority answer, but the majority can be confidently wrong even when correct paths are in the pool. When a confidently wrong answer costs more than declining to answer (the question can be sent to a human or a fallback), the system needs a rule for when to abstain that comes with a guarantee on how often it answers and is wrong. Conformal risk control (CRC) can calibrate such a rule from a small labelled set without retraining the model.
official.method:
For each prompt, m = 16 CoT paths are sampled and each final answer is extracted. Each path gets a quality score q; in the main configuration this is the scalar output of the Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B reward model, conditioned on the prompt and the full path. Votes are weighted by w = exp(q). The prediction is the answer with the largest total weight, and the confidence ν is the winning answer's share of the total weight. Setting w ≡ 1 gives plain majority voting (MV), where ν is the vote fraction.

The system answers if ν > λ and abstains otherwise. λ is set by CRC on n_cal = 200 labelled calibration prompts: λ̂ is the smallest λ whose empirical confident-error rate (answered and wrong) is at most α − (1 − α)/n. This bounds the expected test confident-error rate by α under exchangeability. The baselines, run on the same 20 random calibration-test splits of 1300 prompts, are: MV and the weighted vote without abstention; MV + CRC, which applies CRC to the unweighted vote fraction; and the weighted vote with a naive threshold that drops the finite-sample correction. Metrics are selective accuracy A_c (accuracy on answered questions), yield Y (fraction answered) and realized confident-error rate on the test split.
official.claim: On GSM8K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (m = 16, reward-weighted votes, n_cal = 200, α = 0.10, mean of 20 splits), Weighted + CRC answers 95% of test questions at selective accuracy 0.901 and confident-error rate 0.094. Majority-vote + CRC answers only 84% at about the same accuracy (0.896); the paired yield gain is +0.111 ± 0.039. Without abstention, the weighted vote beats majority vote, 0.874 vs. 0.823 (+0.051 ± 0.004).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Separating weighting, abstention, and calibration. Selective accuracy A_c, yield Y, and realized confident-error rate (Err.) on test, averaged over 20 shared calibration–test splits (Reward score). Without abstention, A_c is the accuracy of the vote. Bold: higher yield of the two CRC rules. Full results in Table 23.
official.metric: Selective accuracy A_c and yield Y (higher is better) and realized confident-error rate (should be <= α), means over 20 random calibration-test splits. Table 1 gives no error bars. The ± values come from Table 24 and are std over the 20 splits of paired differences between methods.
official.comparison: Weighted vote + CRC (ours) vs. majority vote + CRC, with both using the same CRC calibration on the same splits. Also weighted vote vs. majority vote, both without abstention.
official.falsification_criterion: On GSM8K / R1-Qwen-1.5B at α = 0.10, the claim is refuted by any of: (a) Weighted + CRC's mean yield is not clearly above MV + CRC's (paired gain within about one split std of zero, i.e. below about 0.04); (b) Weighted + CRC's mean realized confident-error rate clearly exceeds 0.10; (c) the weighted vote without abstention is not clearly more accurate than majority vote (gain near zero).

title: ROK-FORTRESS: Measuring the Effect of Geopolitical Transcreation for National Security and Public Safety
claim_source: Table 19, page 40 (Appendix E.8); per-model view in Figure 3a and Figure 2, pages 10-12

official.background: Multilingual LLM safety is usually tested by translating harmful prompts into other languages, and prior work often finds that translation into lower-resource languages weakens refusals. Translation keeps the scenario and its entities fixed, though, so it cannot separate the effect of the language from the effect of the geopolitical setting (which country's agencies, places and events the attack refers to). For national-security and public-safety (NSPS) risks, both factors change at once when a model is deployed in another country, so it matters which one drives the change in safety behavior.
official.method:
ROK-FORTRESS contains 1,235 expert-written adversarial NSPS prompts (CBRNE, political violence, criminal/financial activity, information leakage), each with a prompt-specific rubric of 1-7 binary harm criteria. Human translators produce matched variants: culture-agnostic tasks (565) exist in English (V_En) and Korean (V_Ko); culture-specific tasks (670) exist in four variants, English/Korean language crossed with US/Korean entities (V_En,US, V_Ko,US, V_En,KR, V_Ko,KR). Each of 14 models (Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, o4-mini, DeepSeek V3.2, Kimi K2, Llama 4 Maverick, Mistral Large 3, Qwen3-235B, HyperCLOVA X, Kanana 2, K-EXAONE, Solar Open) answers every variant.

A 3-judge LLM panel (HyperCLOVA X + o4-mini + Kimi K2 [medium reasoning], majority vote, calibrated against human labels at F1 0.83) marks each rubric criterion. Criteria are weighted by risk tier (1-3), and the per-task score is the weighted fraction of criteria judged harmful (0 for a safe refusal). The Tier-weighted Risk Score (TRS) is the mean over tasks times 100. The linguistic drop is Delta_ling = TRS(English) - TRS(Korean), computed as paired per-task differences. The contextual drop Delta_ctx averages TRS(US-grounded) - TRS(Korean-grounded) over both languages. 95% CIs are percentile bootstraps over paired (task, model) differences.
official.claim: Pooled over 14 models and all tasks, Korean-language variants of the same adversarial prompts have lower tier-weighted risk than their English counterparts: Delta_ling = +10.21 pp (95% CI [+9.33, +11.06]). The drop is positive in each of the four domains (+7.90 to +12.89 pp), and it is about 2.3x the contextual drop from swapping US for Korean entities (+4.47 pp, [+3.77, +5.18]).
official.claim_caption: Table 19. Per-domain Delta_ling and Delta_ctx (paired per-task TRS differences, in percentage points). Aggregated across 14 models with percentile bootstrap 95% CIs. N is the number of paired (task, model) differences contributing to the cell.
official.metric: Tier-weighted Risk Score (TRS, 0-100, lower = less harmful content); Delta_ling = TRS(English) - TRS(Korean) in percentage points, positive = Korean is safer. Brackets are percentile bootstrap 95% CIs over paired (task, model) differences.
official.comparison: Same adversarial intents and rubrics in English vs. human-translated Korean (V_En vs V_Ko, and V_En,US vs V_Ko,US / V_En,KR vs V_Ko,KR), same models, same judge panel; secondarily, US-grounded vs. Korean-grounded variants holding language fixed.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the models on the matched English/Korean variants, with the paper's TRS scoring, gives a pooled Delta_ling whose 95% CI includes zero or is negative, i.e. Korean prompts are not less harmful than English ones. A pooled Delta_ling not clearly larger than Delta_ctx would refute the secondary 'language dominates context' part.

title: Dynamics of the Transformer Residual Stream: Coupling Spectral Geometry to Network Topology
claim_source: Table 3, page 19 (Appendix C.2); dose curves in Figure 5a, page 6

official.background: A transformer's residual stream can be viewed as a discrete-time dynamical system in which each block's update h_{l+1} = h_l + f_l(h_l) has a local linear description, the per-layer Jacobian J_l = dh_{l+1}/dh_l. Signal-propagation theory describes these Jacobians at random initialization, and recent empirical work on trained models used approximate linearizations (detached Jacobians, regression-fit maps) and found that perturbations get funneled into a few directions through depth. This paper computes exact Jacobians of trained production-scale LLMs and asks which property of those Jacobians causes the low-rank funnel: the eigenvalue spectrum, or the non-normal (off-spectrum) structure.
official.method:
For Llama 3.1 8B, OLMo 3 7B (allenai/Olmo-3-1025-7B, final step 1,413,814; also step 0 and 471k) and Gemma 4 E4B (google/gemma-4-e4b-it), the authors take the last-token residual-stream activation of 1,000 WikiText-2 train samples (character-length filtered, in dataset order). For each layer they compute the exact Jacobian of an isolated transformer block in float32 with torch.autograd.functional.jacobian (single-token context at position 0, so RoPE cancels), and average over the 1,000 samples to get the mean Jacobian J_l. The cumulative product P_{0:L-1} = J_{L-1} ... J_0 is computed by iterative truncated SVD at rank 512 with per-layer max-normalization, and its effective rank is erank = exp(-sum p_i log p_i), p_i = sigma_i^2 / sum_j sigma_j^2.

Schur surgery: each J_l is written in complex Schur form J_l = Q_l (Lambda_l + N_l) Q_l^*, with Lambda_l diagonal (the eigenvalues) and N_l strictly upper triangular (the non-normal part). Holding Q_l and Lambda_l fixed, only N_l is scaled by a dose c in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2}; c = 1 is the trained Jacobian and c = 0 is a normal matrix with the same spectrum. The linearized stack is recomposed and erank(P_{0:L-1}) recomputed. 'Mode R' repeats this on R_l = J_l - I and adds I back. Controls replace N_l with a Frobenius-matched Gaussian (Control A) or Q_l with a Haar-random unitary (Control B).
official.claim: Setting the non-normal Schur component of every layer's mean Jacobian to zero (c = 0), while keeping eigenvalues and Schur basis fixed, raises the effective rank of the full-depth Jacobian product from 7.12 to 45.4 in Llama 3.1 8B (6.4x), from 55.5 to 314 in OLMo 3 7B step 1.41M (5.7x), and from 5.92 to 39.3 in Gemma 4 E4B (6.6x); doubling it (c = 2) lowers it to 2.53, 12.4 and 1.60.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Schur dose response, cumulative effective rank of P_{0:L-1}. Mode J c = 0/c = 1 ratios are 6.4, 5.7, 6.6 across the three trained models; mode R ratios on the residual operator are nearly identical, ruling out the +I skip as a source of the funnel.
official.metric: Effective rank of the cumulative Jacobian product P_{0:L-1} (higher = less low-rank funneling). Single deterministic computation per model on 1,000 WikiText-2 samples; no error bars or seeds reported for the dose curve (only the random controls report ± std over 4 random draws).
official.comparison: Same model, same mean Jacobians: non-normal part removed (c = 0) vs. trained Jacobian (c = 1) vs. doubled non-normal part (c = 2). Context: OLMo step 0 (untrained) dose curve is nearly flat; Control A at c = 1 gives 215.9 ± 1.2 (Llama) and 349.4 ± 0.3 (OLMo); Control B gives 16.5 ± 1.6 (Llama) and 305.3 ± 0.8 (OLMo).
official.falsification_criterion: Recomputing the mean per-layer Jacobians and the Schur dose for any of the three trained models gives a c = 0 / c = 1 effective-rank ratio near 1 (e.g. below about 2), or erank does not decrease monotonically from c = 0 to c = 2.
