title: Policy Optimization in Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Action Spaces via Mixed Gradients
claim_source: Table 1 (Appendix D.1), page 23; summarized in Figure 1a (page 2)

official.background: Policy-gradient methods such as PPO rely on score-function (SF) gradient estimates, which become very noisy when each decision is a high-dimensional action vector, because a single scalar return has to be credited to thousands of action components. When a differentiable simulator with exogenous randomness is available, pathwise (PW) gradients obtained by backpropagating through the simulator avoid this credit-assignment problem. However, they break down when actions are partly discrete or the cost is discontinuous. Many operations and control problems, such as inventory ordering with fixed costs or switched linear control, have a hybrid action: a discrete choice (order or not, which mode) plus continuous quantities that enter smoothly.
official.method:
The policy is factored into a stochastic discrete network pi^X_phi (softmax over discrete actions) and a deterministic continuous network pi^B_kappa that outputs one continuous candidate per discrete value; the sampled discrete action selects which candidate is executed. Hybrid Policy Optimization (HPO) uses the mixed estimator of Theorem 1: phi is updated with the usual SF/PPO gradient, and kappa is updated with the pathwise gradient (backprop of realized trajectory cost through the simulator, holding the sampled discrete actions fixed) plus a 'cross term', grad_kappa log pi^X(x_t | s_t(kappa)) times a GAE advantage. Per batch, kappa takes one full-batch step with this estimator, and phi takes 5 PPO epochs with 4 minibatches (in practice the implementation first applies one full-batch update to all parameters, then extra minibatch PPO epochs to the discrete policy and value function only). The baseline is CleanRL PPO with SF gradients (Eq. 10) for both discrete and continuous parameters, taking the same number of gradient steps on each, with learning rate 1e-4 (larger rates were unstable for PPO; HPO uses 1e-3). Both use 2x512 tanh MLPs, Adam, GAE (gamma 0.99, lambda 0.96), clip 0.15, and an entropy bonus on the discrete policy with coefficient 0.5 decayed linearly.

Benchmark: the joint replenishment problem (JRP) with p products, lead time L = 2, Poisson demand with per-product mean ~U[6,14], underage cost ~U[6.3,11.7], holding cost ~U[0.7,1.3], and a shared fixed ordering cost K = 64p. The discrete action is whether to order; the continuous action is the order-quantity vector (softplus output). Trajectories have 100 periods, and the per-product per-period cost excludes the first and last 20 periods. Training uses B = 16 trajectories per batch and 1600 policy updates in total. The table reports test loss, mean ± std over 10 independent trials.
official.claim: On the joint replenishment problem with batch size B = 16, HPO (HPOFull) reaches much lower test cost than PPO once the number of products p is 30 or more: 39.43 ± 0.38 vs. 51.67 ± 2.87 at p = 30, 40.40 ± 0.72 vs. 70.37 ± 1.92 at p = 40, and 43.47 ± 2.19 vs. 81.36 ± 3.27 at p = 50. For p <= 20 the two are within about 0.7% of each other.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: JRP test loss across product counts for B = 16 trajectories per batch. Mean ± std and median over 10 independent trials.
official.metric: Test loss = per-product per-period cost (lower is better), mean ± std over 10 independent trials; medians also reported
official.comparison: HPOFull (mixed PW + SF estimator) vs. PPO (CleanRL, pure SF) on the same JRP instances, same batch size (16) and same number of policy updates (1600); HPONoCross also shown
official.falsification_criterion: With B = 16 and 1600 policy updates, PPO's mean test loss at p = 40 (or p = 50) comes within a few std of HPO's, e.g., PPO below ~45 at p = 40; or HPO fails to stay near its p <= 20 cost level (~39-41) at p = 30-40.

title: CoRDS: Coreset-Based Representative and Diverse Selection for Streaming Video Understanding

official.background: Streaming video understanding with vision-language models needs a bounded-size memory, because the key-value (KV) cache grows without limit as frames arrive and the question is not known when the cache is compressed. Existing KV-cache compressors for streaming video (InfiniPot-V, StreamMem) decide which cached tokens to keep with local heuristics such as key similarity, value norm, or recency. These heuristics do not check whether the retained cache is representative of the whole history. Better selection would let a small cache (3K-6K tokens instead of ~50K) keep long-video accuracy.
official.method:
CoRDS is a training-free, query-agnostic KV-cache compressor. Video tokens are processed causally. The old cache is reduced to a budget of b tokens by greedy farthest-first (D2-style) selection in a joint key-value space. The distance is d_alpha = alpha*||k_i-k_j||^2 + (1-alpha)*||v_i-v_j||^2, and an orthogonality-based anti-redundancy bonus is added to the score (Eq. 10). A recent tail of floor(|M|/4) tokens is always kept. Compression is applied only on the bottom 25% of decoder layers, and the other layers reuse the selected indices. Fixed hyperparameters are (alpha, eta, lambda, eps0) = (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 1e-6).

The evaluation runs EgoSchema, MLVU and VideoMME (all splits) as offline benchmarks, with visual tokens fed causally and the question appended only after compression. Qwen2/2.5-VL use 768 frames (~50K visual tokens), and the cache budget is |M| = 3K or 6K visual KV tokens. Decoding is greedy with a 256-token cap. The authors ran on a single L40S GPU with bfloat16 weights, FlashAttention-2, PyTorch 2.3 and transformers 4.45. Baseline numbers are quoted from the original papers when a matching backbone and budget exist, and are otherwise re-run by the authors. Which rows are quoted and which re-run is not stated per row. The metric is multiple-choice accuracy (%).
official.claim: At a 6K visual-KV budget on Qwen2.5-VL-3B (768 frames), CoRDS reaches 69.6% on MLVU versus 62.1% for InfiniPot-V (+7.5 points; Table 1 labels +7.3 against the closest competitor, StreamMem at 62.3), and also exceeds the uncompressed model (63.3%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Offline video understanding benchmarks. Green numbers indicate the absolute improvement over the closest compressed competitor under the same backbone and cache budget.
official.metric: Accuracy (%), higher is better, on MLVU; no +/- reported (single run, no seeds or CIs given)
official.comparison: CoRDS vs. InfiniPot-V and StreamMem (and the uncompressed Original) on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, 768 frames, |M|=6K. The same direction holds on Qwen2-VL-7B at 6K (MLVU 70.1 vs. 65.8 InfiniPot-V, 65.9 StreamMem) and LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B at 6K (68.1 vs. 65.2).
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running CoRDS and InfiniPot-V under matched backbone, frames and 6K budget on MLVU, CoRDS beats InfiniPot-V by less than about 2 points (within typical benchmark noise), or falls below InfiniPot-V.

title: Distributionally Robust Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Task Sampling

official.background: Multi-task reinforcement learning trains one policy to solve several tasks at once. In practice agents learn easy tasks quickly and hard tasks slowly. Prior work mostly blames conflicting task gradients and proposes gradient manipulation or special architectures. This paper argues that a separate cause is imbalanced data allocation: standard training gives every task the same number of environment interactions, which is too much for easy tasks and too little for hard ones. Curriculum methods that start with easy tasks can make this worse when tasks do not transfer to one another.
official.method:
DRATS (Distributionally Robust Adaptive Task Sampling) frames multi-task RL as reaching a reference return on every task and minimizes the worst-case return gap g_i = max(J_i^ref - J_i, 0) through a KL-regularized minimax objective over the task-sampling distribution q. In each iteration the rollout buffer is filled by sampling tasks from q; Monte Carlo returns per task give normalized gaps g_i = (J_i^ref - J_i)/(J_i^ref - J_i^rand); q is updated by exponentiated-gradient (mirror) ascent on E_q[g] - (1/eta) KL(q || uniform), then projected so every task keeps probability at least epsilon; the policy is updated with PPO. In MuJoCo6, J_i^ref is the maximum observed return on task i.

MuJoCo6 is a 6-task benchmark (Swimmer, Hopper, HalfCheetah, Walker2d, Ant, Humanoid, all v4) with a one-hot task ID appended to the state, a multi-head MLP (256,256,256) with separate actor and critic, per-task observation/value normalization and per-task advantage normalization for all methods, built on CleanRL PPO (lr 1e-4, batch 48000 x 4 envs, 16 epochs, 32 minibatches, entropy 0.01), 100M total timesteps. Baselines use the same mirror-ascent update and minimum probability epsilon = 1/(4k): Uniform; Learning Progress (priority |J_t - J_{t-1}|; Appendix G text says results are reported for eta = 12, Table 2 lists eta = 8); Learning Potential (PLR-style GAE L1 value loss, eta = 8); Hard First (SMT, K = 3, thresholds in Table 3). DRATS uses eta = 4; all mirror-ascent methods use step size alpha = 0.5 eta. The metric is the per-task min-max normalized return averaged over the 6 tasks.
official.claim: On the 6-task MuJoCo6 benchmark after 100M timesteps of PPO, DRATS reaches a mean normalized aggregate return of about 0.66, above Learning Potential (~0.57), Hard First (~0.53), Uniform (~0.46) and Learning Progress (~0.46), with non-overlapping 95% bootstrap CIs over 20 seeds; the gain comes mainly from DRATS being the only method to solve Ant.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Mean normalized return aggregated over tasks in each benchmark. Shaded regions denote 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Panels: (a) MuJoCo (20 seeds), (b) MT10 (20 seeds), (c) MT50 (10 seeds).
official.metric: Mean normalized return aggregated over the 6 tasks (per-task (J - J_min)/(J_max - J_min)), higher is better; shaded regions are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over 20 seeds; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: DRATS vs. Uniform, Learning Progress, Learning Potential (PLR-style) and Hard First (SMT) task sampling, all with the same PPO hyperparameters, network and per-task normalization
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running MuJoCo6 for 100M timesteps with multiple seeds, DRATS's final aggregate normalized return is not clearly above Learning Potential's (e.g. the gap is under ~0.04 or the 95% CIs overlap), or DRATS does not make substantially more progress on Ant than the baselines.

title: MoRe: Modular Representations for Principled Continual Representation Learning on Sequential Data
claim_source: Figure 3(a) right panel ('Stability'), page 8; scenario definitions in Table 4 (Appendix E.3), page 23

official.background: Continual representation learning asks how an encoder can absorb new data batches that each show only part of the underlying process without overwriting what it learned earlier (catastrophic forgetting). Most continual-learning methods decide what to keep and what to update with heuristics such as regularizers, replay or task-specific parameter isolation. The paper argues that if a representation splits into identifiable modules, ordered from fundamental to specific by time-delayed dependencies in sequential data, then reuse and expansion decisions can follow from the data itself.
official.method:
Data follow a latent process in which layers of latent factors have within-layer dependencies and only time-delayed cross-layer effects from fundamental to specific layers, mixed into observations by an invertible map. In the synthetic adaptation study, data1 has two active factors (z1, z2) seen through a random linear mixing into 8 observed dimensions, and data2 follows one of seven transition scenarios (C1 no shift; C2 add z3, z4; C3 replace with z3, z4; C4*/C5* keep z1 or z2 and add z3, z4; C6/C7 keep one factor). A linear encoder is first fit on data1.

Adaptation to data2 (linear instantiation, Appendix C) projects the new data into the old coordinate basis, scores each old module for self-consistency (autocorrelation and absence of leakage into other modules' transition residuals), adds new coordinates from the top singular vectors of the reconstruction residual orthogonal to the old basis, and trains Hard Concrete gates on old and new modules, a learnable alignment matrix T (initialized to identity and regularized toward it) applied to the frozen old encoder, a new encoder and new transition blocks. The loss is the change-of-variables likelihood plus alignment, L0 gate and L1 transition penalties (lr 5e-3, 2,000 epochs, T = 50,000 time steps, noise scale 0.1). Forgetting is old-factor MCC before adaptation minus after.
official.claim: In the synthetic linear transition scenarios C1-C6, full MoRe keeps forgetting (drop in old-factor MCC) within about -0.04 to +0.05, whereas MoRe without the alignment matrix T forgets about 0.12-0.17 in every scenario (paper: '~0.15 across all cases'), and plain fine-tuning forgets about 0.18 on the selective scenario C4* versus about 0.02 for MoRe.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Plasticity, stability compared with baselines and gate decision accuracy
official.metric: forgetting = MCC_old(before) - MCC_old(after adaptation), lower is better, negative means backward transfer; error bars shown but not defined (seed count for the final runs not stated; 3 seeds were used for hyperparameter search)
official.comparison: MoRe vs. MoRe without T (ablation) vs. fine-tuning the data1 encoder on data2
official.falsification_criterion: With T removed, forgetting is not consistently higher than full MoRe's by clearly more than the seed spread across C1-C6, or full MoRe's forgetting exceeds about 0.1 in any scenario, or fine-tuning does not forget substantially more than MoRe on C4*.

title: Learning Scenario Reduction for Two-Stage Robust Optimization with Discrete Uncertainty

official.background: Two-stage robust optimization (2RO) picks a first-stage decision that minimizes cost under the worst case of a set of scenarios, after a recourse decision is made once the scenario is revealed. When the uncertainty set is a finite list of scenarios and the decisions are integers, the exact deterministic-equivalent MILP grows linearly with the number of scenarios and quickly becomes expensive. Scenario reduction solves the problem on a small subset of k scenarios instead. Existing reduction methods mostly look only at the scenario values (clustering, cost sums, geometric covering) and ignore the feasible region and recourse structure, so the scenarios they keep may not be the ones that drive the robust objective.
official.method:
PRISE is a greedy lookahead oracle: starting from an empty set, at each step it solves the reduced 2RO MILP with each remaining candidate scenario added and keeps the scenario that most increases the reduced objective V(R). This costs O(K·|Ξ|) MILP solves per instance. NeurPRISE imitates it: each scenario's MILP is encoded as a constraint-variable bipartite graph by a GNN and mean-pooled; a Transformer encoder mixes the scenario embeddings; a multi-head decoder scores each scenario against the mean instance embedding. Training uses a KL loss between the softmax of the logits and a temperature softmax of log(1+gain) targets from PRISE (gain is 0 for unselected scenarios). At test time the top-k scored scenarios are kept and the reduced 2RO MILP is solved exactly with Gurobi.

Evaluation uses Selection (SEL-20-50: 20 items, 50 scenarios, select exactly ⌊n/2⌋=10 items split between a binary first stage and a binary recourse stage; first-stage and per-scenario second-stage item costs drawn uniformly from {1,...,100}), with 2,500 generated instances split 80/10/10 (250 test instances). The metric is regret: the full-scenario cost of the reduced problem's optimal first-stage decision relative to the exact full-scenario optimum, in percent. Baselines, all run on the same instances: Random, K-means, MaxSum (top-k scenarios by cost sum), SOR (optimal scenario reduction of Goerigk and Khosravi), GK-RF (random-forest scenario-relevance classifier trained on CCG labels) and Neur2RO (k-agnostic).
official.claim: On SEL-20-50 (250 test instances), NeurPRISE reaches mean regret 0.79% at k=4 and 0.42% at k=6 (5-seed means 0.83±0.07 and 0.52±0.06), versus 1.74% and 1.16% for the best non-oracle baseline GK-RF and 2.47% and 1.96% for MaxSum.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison on small-scale instances (250 test instances). A dash (-) denotes a k-agnostic method with identical results across budgets.
official.metric: Mean regret (%) over the test instances, lower is better. Table 1 is a single training seed (42) with no error bars; Table 13 gives NeurPRISE mean ± std over 5 training seeds. No variance is reported for the baselines.
official.comparison: NeurPRISE vs. GK-RF, MaxSum, SOR, K-means, Random (and the PRISE oracle as a reference) at reduction budgets k=4 and k=6 on small Selection instances
official.falsification_criterion: With a retrained NeurPRISE on SEL-20-50, regret at k=4 or k=6 is not clearly below GK-RF's (e.g., NeurPRISE ≥ ~1.5% at k=4 or ≥ ~1.0% at k=6), or a re-run GK-RF/MaxSum matches NeurPRISE within the NeurPRISE seed std.

title: ViMU: Benchmarking Video Metaphorical Understanding

official.background: Most video understanding benchmarks test literal perception: objects, actions, and temporal relations. Many online videos (memes, short clips) carry a second layer of meaning (irony, mockery, innuendo, political or identity signals) that depends on editing, audio, on-screen text and cultural context. ViMU asks whether multimodal LLMs can recover this subtext without the question hinting at what to look for, and whether strength on general video understanding carries over to this kind of interpretation.
official.method:
ViMU has 588 videos from YouTube, Bilibili and TikTok with 2,352 questions over four tasks: open-ended interpretation (OE, scored 0-9 by an LLM judge with a rubric of core intent, implicit signal, target, and hallucination and literal-only penalties, rescaled to %), and three multi-select multiple-choice tasks with five options each: evidence grounding (EG: audio tone, editing pattern, frames, transcript, visible text), rhetoric mechanism identification (RM: five macro categories grouping 14 fine-grained mechanisms), and social value signal identification (SV: five macro categories). Annotations were produced by GPT-5.4 from uniformly sampled frames plus ASR transcripts, iteratively refined (up to K=3 rounds), and reviewed by 5 human experts.

Sixteen MLLMs are evaluated zero-shot (API models via OpenRouter) with uniformly sampled frames plus the ASR transcript, using the prompts in Appendix A.1/G. Main-table RM and SV use the unguided prompt. Multiple-choice scoring is strict: any wrong option selected gives 0, otherwise the score is |P ∩ G|/|G|. Scores are averaged over questions and reported as percentages.
official.claim: On ViMU, GPT-5.2 has the highest open-ended interpretation score (73.15 vs 65.27 for o4-mini) but on rhetoric mechanism identification scores only 16.55, about half of o4-mini's 33.21 (and below Grok-4.1-Fast at 34.91), so general interpretation ability does not carry over to identifying rhetorical mechanisms.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on ViMU across open-ended interpretation (OE), evidence grounding (EG), rhetoric mechanisms identification (RM), and social value signal identification (SV). All values are percentage scores (%). SSU-Avg denotes the average of the two structured subtext understanding tasks, RM and SV. All-Avg denotes the average across all four tasks. Green shades mark the top-3 models in each metric column, and purple shades mark the bottom-3 models.
official.metric: Percentage score (higher is better). OE: LLM-judge rubric score rescaled to %. RM: strict set-based score (0 if any wrong option is selected, else fraction of gold options selected), averaged over 588 questions. Single run; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: GPT-5.2 vs o4-mini (both OpenAI, same prompts and frame sampling) on OE and RM; Grok-4.1-Fast and Gemini-3-Flash-Preview as further RM reference points.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running GPT-5.2 and o4-mini on ViMU RM with the paper's unguided prompt and scoring rule gives a gap smaller than ~5 points or reversed, or GPT-5.2 no longer beats o4-mini on OE.

title: SR-Prominence: A Crowdsourced Protocol and Dataset Suite for Perceptually-Weighted Super-Resolution Artifact Evaluation

official.background: Modern GAN- and diffusion-based super-resolution (SR) models produce sharp images but also introduce local artifacts (hallucinated textures, garbled text, distorted patterns). Existing SR artifact datasets and detectors (DeSRA, LDL, PAL4VST) treat artifacts as binary masks, although some defects are obvious to viewers and others are almost invisible. The paper proposes 'artifact prominence', the fraction of crowd viewers who judge a highlighted region to contain a noticeable artifact. It releases SR-Prominence, 3,935 masks across DeSRA, Open Images, Urban100 and Urban100-HR, each annotated by 30 crowd workers, and uses it to audit which detectors and image-quality metrics actually track what viewers notice.
official.method:
Each artifact mask comes with an LR input, a 4x SR output, the HR reference (where one exists) and a prominence value in [0, 1]. Prominence is the share of the 30 crowd workers (after quality-control filtering) who said the highlighted region contains distorted objects or textures. Masks in the Open Images and Urban100 components were proposed automatically by thresholding detector heatmaps, and before annotation they were morphologically preprocessed (open 25x25, dilate 64x64 circular, close 25x25).

Threshold-free score (Section 5.2): run a detector or metric on every SR output to get a spatial heatmap (full-reference metrics compare against the original HR image; SSIM gives a per-pixel map, DISTS is computed block-wise on 16x16 blocks; binary detectors give their binary mask). For each annotated mask, erode it back to undo the preprocessing dilation, then compute (median heatmap inside the mask) minus (median heatmap outside the mask). The score is the Spearman correlation between this contrast and the crowdsourced prominence over all masks in a dataset component. The comparison includes full-reference metrics (SSIM, DISTS, LPIPS, ERQA), SR artifact detectors (DeSRA, LDL), no-reference artifact segmenters (PAL4VST, PAL4Inpaint) and no-reference IQA models (TOPIQ, PaQ-2-PiQ).
official.claim: With the original HR image as reference, full-reference SSIM and DISTS heatmaps correlate with crowdsourced artifact prominence far better than no-reference methods: on Prominence-OpenImages SRCC is 0.312 (SSIM) and 0.415 (DISTS) vs. at most 0.136 for PAL4VST, PAL4Inpaint, TOPIQ and PaQ-2-PiQ; on Prominence-Urban100 it is 0.305 and 0.236 vs. at most 0.156.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Threshold-free prominence score described in Section 5.2. RLFN columns use the pseudo-GT protocol from Section 5.3.
official.metric: Spearman rank correlation (higher is better) between the per-mask contrast (median heatmap inside the eroded mask minus median outside) and the crowdsourced prominence, over all masks in a component; no error bars or CIs reported for individual correlations
official.comparison: Full-reference SSIM and DISTS (original HR reference) vs. no-reference methods PAL4VST, PAL4Inpaint (binary masks), TOPIQ and PaQ-2-PiQ, on the Open Images and Urban100 components
official.falsification_criterion: Recomputing the score on the released data with the original HR reference, SSIM or DISTS fails to exceed the best no-reference method (PAL4VST/PAL4Inpaint/TOPIQ/PaQ-2-PiQ) by a clear margin (e.g. at least 0.1 SRCC) on Open Images or Urban100, or the no-reference IQA models show clearly positive correlations comparable to SSIM/DISTS.

title: FactorizedHMR: A Hybrid Framework for Video Human Mesh Recovery

official.background: Human Mesh Recovery (HMR) estimates 3D body pose, shape and motion (here SMPL-X parameters) from video. Under occlusion, truncation or weak depth cues, several 3D bodies can explain the same image. Deterministic regressors tend to average these possibilities into implausible poses. Fully generative models handle ambiguity but also add stochastic variation to well-constrained quantities such as the torso and root. The paper argues that ambiguity is concentrated in distal limbs, while the torso and root are well constrained, so the two should be modelled differently.
official.method:
FactorizedHMR has two stages, each a 12-layer transformer (8 heads, hidden size 512, rotary embeddings) that takes bounding-box features, camera-ray-embedded 2D keypoints, image features and relative camera-motion features. Stage 1 is a deterministic regressor (GVHMR-style) that predicts only a structural anchor: the 8 torso joint rotations (hips, spine, shoulders), body shape, and camera-space root orientation and translation. Stage 2 is a masked conditional flow-matching model. The anchor coordinates stay fixed and only the 13 non-torso joint rotations (plus auxiliary 3D joint positions) and the world-motion variables (gravity-view orientation, root velocity) are generated. Training adds geometry-aware losses, a joint-bone consistency loss, and a projection loss on non-torso joints. Sampling uses feature-aware classifier-free guidance (scale 1.5) and a 50-step Euler ODE sampler.

Both stages are trained from scratch on AMASS, BEDLAM, H36M, 3DPW and 340 synthetic Uni3C-generated videos. For the claim, Appendix A.4 / Table 7 compares matched variants on 3DPW that differ only in whether torso and non-torso variables are predicted deterministically or probabilistically, and whether the model is a single stage with a part-aware loss.
official.claim: On 3DPW, the factorized model (deterministic torso / probabilistic non-torso) reaches MPJPE 56.2, PA-MPJPE 36.9, PVE 68.3 mm. The best matched alternative, a deterministic single-stage model with part-aware loss, gets 58.4 / 37.8 / 70.6, and fully probabilistic prediction gets 68.9 / 45.5 / 81.0.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Controlled factorization diagnostic on 3DPW. Fully deterministic prediction does not model ambiguity in non-torso variables, while fully probabilistic prediction destabilizes the torso/root variables. Part-aware single-stage losses improve over naive same-paradigm settings, but do not match the proposed deterministic torso/root and probabilistic non-torso factorization.
official.metric: MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, PVE in mm on 3DPW (lower is better); single numbers, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: Deterministic torso / probabilistic non-torso (Ours) vs. fully deterministic, deterministic single-stage with part-aware loss, fully probabilistic, and probabilistic single-stage with part-aware loss, all trained under the authors' matched setup
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained deterministic single-stage model with part-aware loss (or fully deterministic two-stage model) matches or beats the factorized model on 3DPW MPJPE and PVE, or the gap falls within seed-to-seed variation across several training runs.

title: Performance-Driven Policy Optimization for Speculative Decoding with Adaptive Windowing

official.background: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference: a small draft model proposes a window of tokens and the large target model verifies them in parallel. The speedup depends on the accepted prefix length, which ends at the first rejected token. Drafters such as EAGLE-3 are trained with token-level supervised objectives, but the quantity that matters at inference time is window-level and depends on the prefix: one early mismatch throws away the rest of the window. The authors argue that more token-level training of an already-trained drafter gives little further gain, and that optimizing window-level acceptance directly with reinforcement learning does better.
official.method:
PPOW fine-tunes an EAGLE-family feature-based drafter with a GRPO/PPO-style clipped group-relative policy objective over speculative windows of K = 10 tokens. For each selected training prefix, the drafter samples G = 8 windows, the frozen target verifies each one by rejection sampling to get an accepted length k, and each window gets the scalar reward k/(k*gamma + 1), where gamma is the drafter/target ratio of non-embedding parameters. When k = 0, an auxiliary reward eta = 1.0 is added if the window's cumulative target log-likelihood is within epsilon of the target's greedy window. Rewards are normalized within the group, and every token in a window shares the window's advantage. A KL penalty (beta = 0.03) is taken to the frozen target model's distribution, not to a reference drafter. Adaptive Divergence-Aware Windowing (ADAW) samples training windows in proportion to the window average of (1 - H(P_t)/log|V|) * KL(P_t || Q_t), on a hard-window curriculum of 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6 (ADAW starts after about 44k steps). Learning rate is 5e-6, rollout temperature is 1.0, training data is ShareGPT + UltraChat-200k, and precision is bf16.

For the chosen claim, both PPOW and continued supervised training (CST, the same token-level cross-entropy objective EAGLE-3 uses) start from the official EAGLE-3 checkpoint for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and train for matched numbers of update steps (30k / 60k / 90k). CST is run at learning rates 5e-5 and 5e-6; PPOW is reported at its best learning rate, 5e-6. The evaluation metric is average acceptance length tau on GSM8K, using tree decoding (depth 10, top-k 3) and rejection-sampling verification. The temperature is not stated for this table; Table 1's temperature-0 GSM8K EAGLE-3 value (6.12) matches the starting point in Figure 3.
official.claim: On GSM8K with LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, starting from the same EAGLE-3 drafter checkpoint and training for 90k steps, PPOW reaches an average acceptance length of 6.49, while continued supervised training reaches 6.06 at lr 5e-6 and 5.52 at lr 5e-5. The starting checkpoint is at about 6.12.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: PPOW versus CST under matched training steps. On GSM8K with LLaMA-3.1-8B, CST with learning rate 5e-6 fluctuates around the original checkpoint's average acceptance length, while PPOW steadily improves throughout training. Table 2: Average acceptance length (τ) under continued training on GSM8K with LLaMA-3.1-8B. Continued supervised training yields limited gains across both learning rates, while PPOW improves more steadily.
official.metric: Average acceptance length tau (accepted drafted tokens per verification step; higher is better). Single runs: no seeds, std or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: PPOW (lr 5e-6) vs. EAGLE-3 + continued supervised training (lr 5e-5 and 5e-6), same initial checkpoint, matched training steps

title: 3D Skew Normal Splatting

official.background: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as many 3D Gaussian primitives that are projected and alpha-blended to render novel views in real time. With a finite number of primitives, the symmetric Gaussian shape needs several overlapping kernels to approximate sharp edges and one-sided surfaces. Earlier alternative kernels either stay radially symmetric (GES, Student's t in SSS) or use a hard-truncated Half-Gaussian (3D-HGS), which is discontinuous. This paper asks whether a smooth asymmetric kernel improves reconstruction quality.
official.method:
Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS) replaces each Gaussian with an unnormalized Azzalini Skew-Normal kernel G3(x - mu; Omega) * Phi(alpha^T omega^-1 (x - mu)), where Omega = R S S^T R^T and the slant is reparameterized as alpha = omega R S^-1 k, so the learnable skew vector k lives in the primitive's canonical frame and the skewness depends only on ||k||. The kernel projects to 2D in closed form (Eqs. 5-6), and the tile bounding box is shifted to the true spatial mean (Eq. 8). Following SSS, opacities are signed in [-1, 1] and positions are updated with SGHMC; other parameters use Adam.

Two optimization tricks: k is split into a bounded magnitude m_k = 8 / (1 + exp(-x/6)) and a unit direction d_k; and after a warm-up phase, (R, S) and (m_k, d_k) are updated in alternating blocks (block coordinate descent, Algorithm 1). Training runs 30,000 iterations on an RTX A6000 per scene. Evaluation is test-view PSNR on 7 Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, 2 Tanks & Temples scenes (Train, Truck) and 2 Deep Blending scenes (Playroom, DrJohnson), compared against 3DGS, GES, 3D-HGS and SSS kernels.
official.claim: SNS gets higher test PSNR than the Student's-t kernel baseline SSS on every one of the 11 scenes, e.g. Room 33.02 vs 32.57, Counter 30.27 vs 29.87, Kitchen 32.81 vs 32.43, Train 23.61 vs 23.32 and Playroom 30.71 vs 30.47 dB, and SSS in turn beats 3D-HGS, GES and 3DGS on every scene.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Per-scene PSNR comparison of various reconstruction kernels. We provide a detailed PSNR evaluation of the methods using different base kernels across the Mip-NeRF 360, Deep Blending, and Tanks&Temples datasets. The best and second-best results are highlighted in dark red and light red, respectively.
official.metric: Test-view PSNR in dB per scene (higher is better); single numbers with no seeds, std or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: SNS vs. SSS, 3D-HGS, GES and 3DGS kernels on the same 11 scenes
official.falsification_criterion: Training SNS and SSS on the same scenes with the same iteration budget, SNS does not beat SSS on most scenes, or its mean gain on the scenes with the largest reported margins (Room, Counter, Kitchen, Train) is below run-to-run seed variation.

title: Generalized Priority-Aware Shapley Value
claim_source: Figure 4, page 7 (full grid of Cases 1–4 in Figure 12, page 36)

official.background: Shapley-type values are used to credit training data, features, data providers or models in ML. Priority-aware variants (precedence, weighted and priority-aware Shapley values, PASV) let pairwise and individual priority information shape the credit, for example to defend against copiers, but they require the pairwise priorities to form a binary directed acyclic graph. Many real priority signals are weighted and cyclic, such as aggregated human preferences in Chatbot Arena, where Condorcet cycles are common. The paper proposes GPASV, a random order value defined on any weighted directed priority graph, and the practical question is whether it can be computed accurately at scale.
official.method:
GPASV is a random order value: player i's value is the expected marginal contribution U(prefix ∪ {i}) − U(prefix) when permutations π are drawn from a distribution p^(λ,ω). Pairwise priorities ω_ij ≥ 0 (any directed weighted graph, cycles allowed) and individual soft priorities λ_i > 0 enter a stage-wise form: at each stage t, player k in the prefix S_t is chosen with probability proportional to λ_k exp(−β V_ω(k; S_t)), where V_ω(k; S_t) = Σ_{j∈S_t} ω_kj, and each stage is rescaled by Σ_k exp(−β V_ω(k; S_t)) (eq. 5). Permutations are sampled with an adjacent-swap Metropolis–Hastings chain (local acceptance ratio, Proposition 1) started from a stage-wise greedy initialization (Algorithm 2), with burn-in ⌈n^2.5⌉ and thinning 1000.

The claim compares three estimators of the value vector under the same number of distinct utility evaluations K_eval: (i) the direct permutation Monte Carlo average; (ii) a linear surrogate U(S) ≈ U(∅) + Σ_{i∈S} a_i, and (iii) a quadratic surrogate that adds a random 10% of the pairwise terms b_ij. Each surrogate is fit by weighted least squares on K_train = min(⌊0.2 K_eval⌋, 200,000) subsets drawn from a proposal built from 100,000 utility-free permutations, and is then bias-corrected with a residual term on the remaining K_eval − K_train subsets (eq. 39). Benchmarks are sum-of-unanimity games with exact GPASV values: Scenario 1 is a line DAG 1 → … → n with contiguous-interval coalitions T_j (d = n² terms, c_j ~ Unif(0.5, 1.5)); Scenario 2 is a DAG of blocks of 16 players, each block an internal directed cycle, with block-completion coalitions. Case 2 (shown in Figure 4) uses λ_i ≡ 1 and strong priority (multiplicative edge weight 0.3 in Scenario 1; Unif(0, 0.5) in Scenario 2). The error is ARE = ||ψ̂ − ψ*||₂ / ||ψ*||₂.
official.claim: At matched utility-evaluation budgets in Case 2 with n = 1024, linear and quadratic surrogate-assisted GPASV estimators reach final ARE of about 0.016 vs. about 0.024 for direct Monte Carlo on Scenario 1 (line DAG), and about 0.17 vs. about 0.28 on Scenario 2 (DAG of cyclic blocks), with non-overlapping box plots.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Surrogate-assisted methods (case 2). Full results are in Appendix G.2.
official.metric: Absolute relative error ARE = ||ψ̂ − ψ*||₂ / ||ψ*||₂ against the closed-form GPASV values, at convergence; lower is better. Box plots over independent MH repetitions on a fixed instance (10 repetitions in the G.2 protocol). Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.

title: EntityBench: Towards Entity-Consistent Long-Range Multi-Shot Video Generation
claim_source: Table 4, page 7 (effect size from Table 17, page 46)

official.background: Multi-shot video generators chain several shots into one narrative, and the same characters, objects and locations have to look the same in every shot where they recur, sometimes dozens of shots apart. Existing benchmarks mostly score single shots or use small, ad-hoc prompt sets without per-shot entity annotations, so it is hard to tell where methods lose entity identity. EntityBench supplies 140 episodes (2,491 shots) built from real narrative media with explicit per-shot entity schedules, plus a 51-metric evaluation suite. The paper also proposes EntityMem, a training-free per-entity memory system built on top of StoryMem, as a baseline.
official.method:
EntityMem extends StoryMem (a keyframe-then-animate multi-shot video method with a keyframe memory) without any extra training. Before any video is generated, Gemini-based agents build a per-entity memory bank: a Flux text-to-image model generates N candidate portraits per character (and panoramas for locations, references for some objects) on a chroma-key background, SAM segments them, an agent picks the best one, and a verification agent re-checks it (retrying with a different background color on failure). A layout agent then composes keyframes from these references for each shot, and the StoryMem video backbone is conditioned on the labeled per-character portraits, the keyframe composites, and a text prompt with the stored entity descriptions injected. Continuation shots also get the previous shot's last frame as the first frame.

The claim uses Pillar 2 of the EntityBench evaluation. For every scheduled character in a shot, GroundingDINO localizes it from its registry description in sampled frames, a canonical crop is chosen by a CLIP-similarity x sharpness x area score, and a CLIP text-image gate (tau = 0.20) labels it present, weak or absent. Every present or weak crop is sent to gemini-2.5-pro with the character's description, and the judge returns an overall fidelity score in [0, 1] plus face/hair/clothing/build sub-scores (Appendix B.3.3). face_fidelity is the per-shot mean over scored characters, then averaged over the shots in an episode (Eqs. 16-17); absent characters get no score. Table 4 calls it a fidelity-gate-corrected mean, but Appendix F.2 says that for Pillar 2 fidelity the gate does not hard-reject instances, so coverage is 1 and the corrected mean equals the raw mean. Effect sizes are computed per episode on episodes where both methods produce a score (n = 139).
official.claim: On EntityBench, EntityMem achieves intra-shot character face_fidelity of 0.740 vs. 0.452 for StoryMem (its own backbone, the strongest baseline on this metric), a paired per-episode difference of +0.262 with pooled Cohen's d = +2.33 (dz = +2.06, n = 139 episodes); HoloCine (0.349) and CineTrans (0.327) score lower still.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Main results on EntityBench. Reported as fidelity-gate-corrected means (§3.2). Bold marks the best score per row; † marks wins by EntityMem with Cohen's d > 0.5 vs the next-best baseline (Table 5). Pillars 1 and 2 evaluate within-shot quality and prompt alignment; Pillar 3 evaluates cross-shot consistency. For VBench (Pillar 1), imaging_quality is on [0, 100]; all other metrics are on [0, 1]. Full 51-metric results in Appendix F.1.
official.metric: face_fidelity (gemini-2.5-pro-judged match of a character's canonical crop to its text description, on [0, 1], higher is better; reported as a fidelity-gate-corrected mean, which for this metric equals the raw mean because coverage = 1 per Appendix F.2). No seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals; the only uncertainty-related statistics are the paper's episode-level Cohen's d (pooled) and paired dz.
official.comparison: EntityMem vs. StoryMem, HoloCine and CineTrans on all 140 EntityBench episodes; the effect size is EntityMem vs. StoryMem only
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running EntityMem and StoryMem on EntityBench with the same evaluation pipeline gives a face_fidelity gap well below the reported +0.26 to +0.29 (e.g. under 0.1), or a paired episode-level Cohen's d below about 0.8.

title: COPRA: Conditional Parameter Adaptation with Reinforcement Learning for Video Anomaly Detection

official.background: Weakly supervised video anomaly detection (VAD) has to produce frame-level anomaly scores for long surveillance videos when training only gives a video-level normal/abnormal label. Recent methods use vision-language models (VLMs), which give interpretable explanations, and adapt them with one shared set of parameters, such as tuned prompts or a fine-tuned LoRA. The authors argue that a single shared update has to compromise across very different anomaly types and scenes, and that this hurts generalization. They propose generating adapter weights per input instead.
official.method:
COPRA keeps the VLM (Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct or InternVL2-8B) frozen. For each input, K = 8 uniformly sampled frames are encoded by the VLM's own frozen vision encoder. A Transformer parameter generator (about 87M parameters, half the backbone's depth, with factorized intra-/inter-layer self-attention over parameter tokens and cross-attention to the visual tokens, plus a learnable global latent prior) outputs rank-8 LoRA A/B matrices for the attention and feed-forward projections of the language backbone. Only the generator is trained, with GRPO for one epoch on UCF-Crime. The reward is binary answer accuracy (anomaly yes/no in <answer> tags) plus a format reward. The paper uses the VLM-R1 default config with lr 1e-6, KL beta 0.1 and clip epsilon 0.2.

At test time each video is split into overlapping 10-second segments centred every 16 frames. Each segment gets its own generated LoRA and a score, and the scores go through VERA's pipeline: Step 1 initial scoring, Step 2 visual-retrieval refinement, Step 3 temporal smoothing and weighting. The static-adaptation baseline in Table 3 trains one shared LoRA (Eq. 1) with the same GRPO setup and applies it to every input.
official.claim: On UCF-Crime with Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct, instance-conditioned LoRA generated by COPRA reaches 86.75% frame-level AUC after the full VERA inference pipeline (Step 3), versus 83.00% for a static shared LoRA trained with the same GRPO setup and 81.31% for the frozen model. COPRA leads static adaptation at every stage (69.73 vs. 61.34 at Step 1; 84.69 vs. 79.51 at Step 2).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Ablation on UCF-Crime comparing COPRA with static adaptation under GRPO training. The frozen baseline uses the standard VLM pipeline; static adaptation applies shared LoRA with GRPO; COPRA adds instance-conditioned LoRA to the frozen baseline under the same GRPO setting. COPRA consistently outperforms both baselines across all stages, indicating that the gains come from adaptive conditioning rather than GRPO alone.
official.metric: Frame-level ROC AUC (%) on the UCF-Crime test set, higher is better. Single run; no standard deviations, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Frozen baseline + COPRA (instance-conditioned LoRA, GRPO) vs. GRPO static adaptation (shared LoRA, GRPO) vs. frozen baseline, same Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct backbone, same inference pipeline
official.falsification_criterion: Training a shared rank-8 LoRA and a COPRA-style generator with the same GRPO recipe on UCF-Crime gives Step-3 AUCs within about 1 point of each other, or the static LoRA matches or beats COPRA. A Step-1 margin far below the reported 8.4 points would also count against the claim.

title: MorphoHELM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Representations for Microscopy-Based Morphology Assays

official.background: Cell Painting is a microscopy assay that stains cells with six dyes over five channels, used in drug discovery and functional genomics to read out how chemical or genetic perturbations change cell morphology. Images are turned into feature vectors either with classical hand-crafted pipelines (CellProfiler) or with deep models (natural-image models such as DINOv2 and ResNet, or microscopy-specific foundation models such as OpenPhenom, SubCell and CLOOME). Evaluations of these representations are fragmented, use different preprocessing and metrics, and often ignore batch effects (technical variation between batches, laboratories and plate layouts), so it is unclear whether newer learned representations actually beat CellProfiler.
official.method:
MorphoHELM evaluates frozen representations on three task families (MoA enrichment, gene pathway enrichment, replicate retrieval) at increasing batch-effect stringency: No Restriction (NR), Not Same Batch (NSB), Not Same Source/institution (NSS) and Not Same plate Layout (NSL), where candidates sharing the query's batch, source or plate position are excluded from retrieval. All representations go through the same pipeline: illumination correction, QC (channel de-duplication, removal of wells in the bottom 5% of cell count, removal of batches with unstable negative controls), then per-plate scaling, PCA to 64 components over the whole dataset, and per-plate MAD robust standardization.

For the chosen claim, the replicate retrieval task on cpg-target2 (a JUMP-CP subset of 301 compounds with strong phenotypes, 11 sources, 107 batches, 141 plates, 64,485 wells) queries individual well-level profiles and measures kNN Recall@1: for each query well, whether its nearest neighbour by cosine similarity (within the candidate set allowed by the stringency level) is treated with the same compound, with accuracy macro-averaged first per compound and then across compounds. Expected random Recall@1 is 0.33%. Compared representations: CellProfiler, ImageNet ResNet101, DINOv2 ViT-B/14 (CLS token and mean of patch tokens), OpenPhenom, SubCell, CLOOME, and a randomly initialized ResNet101.
official.claim: On cpg-target2 replicate retrieval, postprocessed CellProfiler features reach kNN Recall@1 of 25.38% (NR), 28.49% (NSB) and 14.64% (NSS), above every deep representation including the best, DINOv2 CLS (20.33%, 21.73%, 12.77%) and CLOOME (18.37%, 22.24%, 5.65%); CellProfiler also has the highest mAP (4.66 vs. 3.53 for DINOv2 CLS at NR).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: kNN replicate retrieval.
official.metric: kNN Recall@1 in percent, macro-averaged per compound then across compounds (higher is better) and mAP over all samples (higher is better); single deterministic evaluation, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: CellProfiler vs. DINOv2 CLS, DINOv2 Patch, ImageNet ResNet101, OpenPhenom, SubCell, CLOOME (and untrained ResNet101) under the identical scaling + PCA(64) + MAD postprocessing pipeline
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the cpg-target2 replicate retrieval with the same QC and postprocessing, some deep representation (most likely DINOv2 CLS) matches or exceeds CellProfiler's Recall@1 in the NR or NSB setting, or CellProfiler's margin over the best deep model at NR shrinks below about 2 percentage points.

title: Njord: A Probabilistic Graph Neural Network for Ensemble Ocean Forecasting

official.background: Operational ocean forecasts come from physics-based models such as the Copernicus GLO12 system, which take hours on CPU clusters. Recent machine-learning ocean emulators (GLONET, WenHai, XiHe) are fast and competitive, but they are deterministic and trained with MSE. As a result their forecasts drift toward the conditional mean and give no estimate of uncertainty. Ensemble (probabilistic) forecasts are standard in weather prediction, but there was no comparable data-driven ensemble model for short-range, high-resolution global ocean forecasting.
official.method:
Njord extends the Graph-EFM latent-variable model to the ocean. A hierarchical GNN (encode-process-decode) runs on a mesh built by spherical K-means clustering of ocean grid points, with Delaunay edges and land-crossing edges removed. A Gaussian latent Z_t, drawn from a learned prior, is injected at the coarsest mesh level, so each ensemble member at each step takes one forward pass. The model predicts a residual added to X_{t-1}, using two past states and atmospheric forcing at t-2, t-1 and t. Variables are SSH, sea-ice concentration and thickness (with clamping plus a density channel), and T, S, U, V at six depths. Training uses ELBO plus an almost-fair CRPS loss in a curriculum: pretraining at 1° on GLORYS12 reanalysis (1993-2021), finetuning at 0.25°, then finetuning on GLO12 analysis data for 2023. Forcing comes from ERA5 during training and IFS forecasts during evaluation.

Evaluation follows OceanBench: 52 weekly initializations in 2024, 10-day horizon, 20-member ensemble, with the ensemble mean scored. The claim uses the observation track (IV-TT CLASS-4): RMSE against Argo-float temperature at 0-5 m depth, compared with the GLO12 operational physics forecast and the ML emulators GLONET, WenHai and XiHe. Their scores are taken from the live OceanBench leaderboard (April 2026, package v0.0.3).
official.claim: On the OceanBench IV-TT CLASS-4 observation track for 2024, Njord's 20-member ensemble mean has the lowest 0-5 m temperature RMSE at every reported lead time: 0.470 / 0.519 / 0.844 / 0.836 / 0.912 °C at days 1/3/5/7/10. The best competitor at each lead is GLO12, at 0.491 / 0.570 / 0.865 / 0.881 / 0.961 °C.
official.claim_caption: Table 11: Scorecard for the observation track within the IV-TT CLASS-4 framework. Colors represent the normalized RMSE difference with respect to the GLO12 operational baseline. Blue indicate that the model outperforms GLO12 against observations, while red indicates a higher error.
official.metric: RMSE (°C) of the forecast against Argo in-situ temperature observations at 0-5 m, lower is better; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported (single trained model, 52 forecast initializations)
official.comparison: Njord (ensemble mean) vs. GLO12 operational physics forecast, GLONET, WenHai and XiHe, all scored on the same OceanBench observation track
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the OceanBench observation-track evaluation of Njord forecasts for 2024 gives a 0-5 m temperature RMSE that is not below GLO12's (or another baseline's) at one or more of lead days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10.

title: SkiP: When to Skip and When to Refine for Efficient Robot Manipulation

official.background: Imitation-learning policies for robot manipulation predict an action at every control step, even though most of a demonstration is smooth free-space motion and only a small part (grasps, contacts, alignment) needs fine control. Each extra policy query is another chance for prediction errors to compound and costs execution time. Earlier approaches such as action chunking, keyframe methods and hierarchical policies change the model architecture, but the policy still runs at a uniform temporal rate.
official.method:
SkiP changes only the behavior-cloning target. Each demonstration is split into key segments and skip segments. For a timestep inside a key segment, the target action chunk starts at t+1, as in normal BC. For a timestep in a skip segment, the target chunk starts at the entrance of the next key segment, so the policy learns to jump over the free-space motion in one decision. Chunk entries past the end of the episode are zero-padded and masked in the backbone's usual imitation loss. Actions must be absolute targets (RoboMimic uses absolute end-effector poses). The network architecture and inference procedure are unchanged.

Key segments come from Motion Spectrum Keying (MSK), which needs no learning. It takes a short-time DCT over a centered window (W=16) of action velocities, computes the fraction of energy in the upper half of the spectrum, and thresholds it at the per-episode 0.75 quantile, discarding segments shorter than 3 steps. To this it adds steps where the end-effector path bends away from a straight line (cutoff 0.30, ±2-step expansion) and 5-step neighborhoods around gripper-state changes and velocity zero-crossings. The first 20% of each episode is excluded. On RoboMimic the backbone is the Diffusion Policy UNet with image observations. Each query executes the full chunk without temporal ensembling. Baselines are Chain-of-Action forward and reverse (CoA-fwd, CoA-rev) on the same backbone.
official.claim: On RoboMimic (lift, can, square, transport; image observations, Diffusion Policy UNet backbone), SkiP reaches average success rate 0.772 ± 0.012 vs. 0.723 ± 0.013 for CoA-rev, while using 144.1 ± 2.2 vs. 211.8 ± 3.2 executed steps per successful episode (-32%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: RoboMimic results with Diffusion Policy UNet backbone in the image observation setting.
official.metric: Average task success rate over 4 tasks (higher is better) and Steps_succ = mean executed env steps over successful episodes (lower is better). ± is not defined in the Table 2 caption; Table 1 uses mean ± std over three runs, which is presumably the same here.
official.comparison: SkiP (MSK labels) vs. CoA-rev and CoA-fwd with the same Diffusion Policy UNet backbone; SkiP† (Gemini-2.5-Pro key segments) also reported
official.falsification_criterion: With the same backbone and evaluation protocol, SkiP's average SR is not higher than CoA-rev's by more than the run-to-run std (gap at or below about 0.013), or SkiP's Steps_succ is not clearly below CoA-rev's (e.g. less than a 15% reduction).

title: CM-EVS: Sparse Panoramic RGB-D-Pose Data for Complete Scene Coverage

official.background: Panoramic (equirectangular, ERP) RGB-D-pose frames are useful training data for panoramic depth estimation, novel-view synthesis and 360° generation. They are usually sampled from 3D assets (synthetic Blender scenes, HM3D, ScanNet++) along dense trajectories or by ad hoc heuristics. This gives redundant views, inconsistent policies across sources, and sometimes views whose depth conflicts with geometry already observed. The paper asks how to pick a small set of panoramic viewpoints per scene that covers as much of the scene surface as possible, and uses the resulting selector to build a dataset.
official.method:
COVER is a training-free greedy viewpoint selector over a feasible candidate pool for each scene. It starts from a shared seed view v0 (the best single-view-probe candidate near the scene center) and accumulates a point cloud from the range depth of the selected views. At each step it warps the accumulated cloud into a low-resolution ERP probe of every remaining candidate and also renders a low-resolution probe from that candidate. Probe pixels are split into new (not explained by history), explained (depth agrees within δ = 0.5% of the AABB diagonal) and conflicted (depth disagrees by more than δ). The selector scores G_t = |new|/|probe|, L_t = |conflicted|/|probe| and s_t = G_t − λ L_t. It renders the argmax at full resolution, adds it to the cloud and repeats until K views are chosen.

With λ = 0 the score reduces to coverage-only greedy on the warping proxy. In Table 4(a) the authors sweep λ ∈ {0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0} at a fixed budget K = 30 on a 10-scene Blender indoor pool, using the same candidate pool and seed for every λ, with early stopping disabled. They report final scene coverage (cov.), coverage per view and conflict ratio. The default used to build the dataset is λ = 0.35.
official.claim: On a 10-scene Blender indoor pool at a fixed budget of K = 30 ERP views, conflict-aware greedy selection with λ = 0.35 reaches coverage 0.4127 with conflict 0.0175. Coverage-only greedy (λ = 0) reaches only 0.1878 coverage with conflict 0.1561. Every λ in [0.1, 0.5] gives coverage of at least 0.37.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: CM-EVS at K = 30. (a) λ sensitivity on a 10-scene Blender indoor pool; λ = 0.35 is the paper default. (b) the same selector at λ = 0.35 on each curator source (10 scenes each). Metric definitions follow Table 3; top-block best per column in bold, second-best underlined.
official.metric: Scene coverage (higher is better) and depth-conflict ratio (lower is better) after K = 30 selected views, aggregated over 10 Blender indoor scenes; no error bars, seeds or per-scene spread are reported.
official.comparison: COVER with λ = 0.35 (paper default) vs. the same greedy selector with λ = 0 (coverage-only proxy), on the same candidate pool and seed; the other λ values form a sensitivity sweep.
official.falsification_criterion: On comparable Blender indoor scenes at K = 30 with a shared candidate pool and seed, λ = 0 reaches coverage within a small margin of λ = 0.35 (for example, less than 0.05 apart), or λ = 0.35 does not cut the conflict ratio several-fold relative to λ = 0.

title: A Unified Perturbation Framework for Analyzing Leaderboard Stability and Manipulation

official.background: LLM leaderboards such as LMArena/Chatbot Arena rank models by fitting a Bradley–Terry (BT) model to crowdsourced pairwise votes, and these rankings are widely treated as stable estimates of model quality. Earlier work (Huang et al., 2026) showed that dropping a handful of votes can change the top of such a leaderboard. This paper generalizes that analysis to three match-level perturbations (dropping, adding, or flipping a vote) and several leaderboard objectives, asking how few targeted changes are needed to alter leaderboard conclusions.
official.method:
Each raw comparison is encoded as two directed BT rows (i beats j: (e_i−e_j, 1) and (e_j−e_i, 0); a tie: both rows labelled 1), and a BT model with θ_1 = 0 is fit by maximum likelihood (no ridge). For the Top-1 objective, the gap f = θ_i − θ_j between the current top model and each model across the top-1 boundary is used. Influence scores (one-step Newton refinement of −H⁻¹∇ℓ, with the two directed rows of a comparison treated as one action) predict how each candidate action changes that gap. Actions are Drop (remove an existing comparison), Flip (reverse its outcome; equals drop + add reversed), and Add (add a new comparison, with candidates from all pairs with outcome fixed by the current skill order, all outcomes, or probability-weighted outcomes).

Algorithm 1: for α = 1, 2, …, take the top-α actions by predicted influence (most negative if the gap is positive), apply them to the original dataset, refit the BT model, and stop at the first α where the gap changes sign, i.e. the Top-1 model changes. The search is capped at 5% of the dataset. The main dataset is lmarena-ai/arena-human-preference-55k (57,477 comparisons, 64 models).
official.claim: On Chatbot Arena 55k (57,477 human votes, 64 models), influence-guided Flip of only 3 votes (0.01%) or Drop of only 5 votes (0.01%) changes the BT Top-1 model after refitting; across all 7 datasets Flip needs no more actions than Drop (e.g. 6 vs 9 on Arena LLM-Judge, 46 vs 92 on MT-Bench).
official.claim_caption: Table 1. Minimum influence-guided actions needed to change the Top-1 model under a 5% budget. Percentages are relative to total matches; robust means no change within budget.
official.metric: Minimum number of greedy influence-guided actions (and % of total matches) after which the refit BT Top-1 model changes; lower means less robust. 'robust' means no change within the 5% budget. No error bars (deterministic procedure).
official.comparison: Drop vs Flip vs three Add variants (all_pairs, all_outcomes, all_outcomes_weighted) on seven pairwise-comparison datasets; headline cell is Arena 55k Drop = 5 and Flip = 3.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the greedy influence-guided search on arena-human-preference-55k with the paper's BT setup requires substantially more than 3 Flips or 5 Drops (e.g. more than 0.1% of votes, ~57) to change the Top-1 model, or Flip needs more actions than Drop on most datasets.

title: AOT-POT: Adaptive Operator Transformation for Large-Scale PDE Pre-training

official.background: PDE foundation models such as DPOT and MoE-POT pre-train one neural operator on many heterogeneous PDE datasets and then fine-tune it on downstream tasks. Because solution operators differ a lot across PDE families, one network struggles to fit all of them, and existing work mostly responds by adding capacity (bigger models, mixture-of-experts). This paper argues that, as with classical changes of basis or preconditioning in numerical analysis, an adaptive, input-dependent transformation inside the network can make the target operator easier to learn without much extra capacity.
official.method:
AOT-POT keeps the DPOT backbone (patch embedding, temporal aggregation, Fourier/AFNO attention blocks, autoregressive next-frame prediction from 10 input frames with noise injection) and replaces each residual connection with an 'AOT block' in the style of manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC). The hidden state is expanded into n = 4 parallel streams. At each sub-layer, an input-dependent aggregation vector a_l (softmax-like, on the simplex) mixes the streams into the sub-layer input, an input-dependent redistribution vector d_l = 2*sigmoid(...) writes the output back to all streams, and an input-dependent n x n mixing matrix T_l, projected onto the doubly stochastic matrices with 20 Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations, mixes the streams on the residual path: x_{l+1} = T_l x_l + d_l^T F(a_l x_l). a_l, d_l, T_l come from linear maps of the RMS-normalised, globally pooled hidden state, with gating scalars initialised at 0.01 and T_l's bias initialised to the identity. A softmax-gated readout merges the streams at the end. This adds about 3% parameters (Small: 31M vs. DPOT-S 30M; Tiny: 7M vs. 7M).

For the downstream table, models without the 'FT' suffix are trained from scratch on the downstream task alone for 500 epochs (one-cycle schedule, 100 warm-up epochs, Adam, lr 1e-3), on 2000 training and 200 test trajectories. The Kolmogorov-flow task is the chaotic 2D turbulence dataset from DPOT. The metric is relative L2 error (L2RE) on the test set.
official.claim: Trained from scratch on Kolmogorov flow (2000 train / 200 test trajectories, 500 epochs), AOT-POT-S (31M) reaches L2RE 0.038 versus 0.146 for DPOT-S (30M) and 0.154 for MoE-POT-S, a 74% error reduction from the architecture alone; at Tiny scale (7M) it is 0.071 vs. 0.193 for DPOT-T.

official.metric: Relative L2 error on the test set (lower is better); single numbers, no ± or seeds reported

title: RoadmapBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Agentic Software Development Across Version Upgrades

official.background: Most coding-agent benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified, test single-issue bug fixes with oracle patches of tens to about a hundred lines, mostly in Python, and score each task as pass or fail. Frontier models now score above 80% on such benchmarks. Real software development, by contrast, involves version upgrades that take months of coordinated work across many files. RoadmapBench asks whether agents can do this longer, multi-target work, and gives partial credit per target.
official.method:
Each of the 115 tasks comes from a real consecutive release pair in one of 17 open-source repositories (Python, TypeScript, C++, Go and Rust). The agent starts in a Docker container with the repository at the source version. The git history is kept, but all branches and tags beyond the source release are pruned, upstream repository access is blocked, and the agent cannot see target-version code, the test files or the oracle patch. The agent receives a roadmap instruction (instruction.md) listing 3 to 12 targets (median 5) that describe the API signatures and behaviours to implement, but not how to implement them. The median oracle patch is 3,714 lines across 51 files. Each target has its own adapted upstream test file and a weight. A task is resolved if all targets pass. The Completion Score is the mean over tasks of the weighted fraction of targets passed.

Thirteen models are run with the OpenHands scaffold, and a subset is also run with Terminus 2 (Harbor's reference agent). Each task gets a 2-hour wall-clock budget with extended thinking enabled (reasoning effort xhigh for Claude-Opus-4.7; high for GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Seed-2.0-Pro; default for the others). There is one trial per model.
official.claim: Under OpenHands with a 2-hour per-task budget, the best model, Claude-Opus-4.7, resolves only 39.1% of the 115 RoadmapBench tasks (Completion Score 0.692). It is followed by Claude-Opus-4.6 at 32.2% and GPT-5.4 at 29.6%, and the other ten models resolve 5.2-20.9%. Claude-Opus-4.7 gets a similar 38.3% under Terminus 2.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Main results on RoadmapBench across 115 tasks, using a single trial per model. Domain columns report resolved rates (%). Task counts are ML & Data (36), Web & RPC (17), ORM & Val. (25), Infra. & Tool. (23), and UI & Ren. (14). Bold and underline denote the best and second-best domain-level results within each scaffold.
official.metric: Resolved rate (% of tasks where all target tests pass, higher is better) and Completion Score (mean weighted fraction of targets passed, 0-1). Single trial per model; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Thirteen frontier models under the same OpenHands scaffold and budget, plus a subset under Terminus 2. The claim concerns the top model's absolute resolved rate and the ordering of the top three models against the rest.
official.falsification_criterion: Running the released benchmark with Claude-Opus-4.7 + OpenHands (2-hour budget, xhigh reasoning) gives a resolved rate far from 39.1% (for example 50% or more, or 25% or less), or the Completion Score is far from 0.692. Separately, the oracle patches fail their own target tests, which would make the task scores unreliable.

title: Invaria: Learning Scale and Density Invariance in Point Clouds via Next-Resolution Prediction

official.background: 3D point cloud encoders for semantic segmentation are usually trained and tested on point clouds voxelized at one fixed grid size (e.g. 2 cm on ScanNet). Sensors used in deployment produce point clouds at other densities, and operators such as pooling, sparse convolution and windowed attention define their receptive fields in grid units, so changing the grid size also changes the object scale the model perceives. The paper argues that current encoders, including large self-supervised ones, learn features tied to the training resolution and degrade sharply when the test resolution shifts, and proposes a training scheme intended to make features invariant to density and scale.
official.method:
Invaria is a 25.5M-parameter U-Net built on a PTv3-style backbone (encoder depths 2,2,2,2,1, channels 32-512). It is trained with next-resolution prediction: the input is randomly subsampled to a sparser resolution (on ScanNet, 4096, 16384 or 65536 points), and a predictor of sparse-convolution/MLP refinement blocks propagates the latent features to the next higher-resolution point set, with segmentation loss (cross-entropy + Lovasz) applied at each resolution, weighted more heavily at higher resolutions. A cosine latent-alignment loss matches bottleneck tokens across resolutions. Receptive field calibration sets the internal grid size per input as alpha times the mean nearest-neighbor distance of randomly drawn anchor points, instead of using a fixed grid size.

For the claim, all supervised models (Invaria, PTv3, SparseUNet/MinkowskiNet) are trained on ScanNet at the default grid size tau* = 2 cm and evaluated on ScanNet val with inputs voxelized at 0.5x, 1x, 2x and 3x tau* (1, 2, 4, 6 cm). Self-supervised models (Sonata, Concerto-L, Utonia) are evaluated with the authors' public weights and linear probing. The metric is mIoU over the 20 ScanNet classes.
official.claim: On ScanNet val with models trained at a 2 cm grid size, Invaria (25.5M params) keeps 73.8 mIoU when evaluated at 3x the grid size (6 cm), whereas PTv3 (46.1M) trained from scratch on the same data falls from 77.6 to 20.5 mIoU; at 2x, Invaria is 75.7 vs. PTv3 60.4, while at the training resolution PTv3 is slightly better (77.6 vs. 76.2).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Robustness to resolution shifts on ScanNet (val). We evaluate models trained at a default resolution (tau*=2cm grid size) across varying resolutions. SSL: Self-Supervised Learning; MD: Joint Training across multiple datasets. † Results using authors' publicly released weights (linear probing).
official.metric: mIoU (%) on ScanNet val, higher is better; single runs, no error bars
official.comparison: Invaria vs. PTv3 and SparseUNet (Sp.Mink.) trained from scratch on ScanNet at tau* = 2 cm, evaluated at 0.5x, 1x, 2x, 3x tau*; self-supervised Sonata, Concerto-L, Utonia (linear probing on public weights) as additional reference
official.falsification_criterion: An Invaria-style model trained at 2 cm on ScanNet does not keep mIoU at 6 cm evaluation within about 5 points of its 2 cm mIoU, or its 6 cm mIoU is not well above (e.g. by more than 20 points) a PTv3 trained under the same 2 cm setting and evaluated at 6 cm.

title: When and Why Adversarial Training Improves PINNs: A Neural Tangent Kernel Perspective

official.background: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve PDEs by training a network to make the PDE residual zero at collocation points, but they are hard to train on stiff, high-frequency or multiscale problems. Adversarial PINN training (e.g. DEQGAN) treats the residuals as 'generated samples' and zero as the 'real' target, and trains a discriminator on residuals whose feedback reweights the PINN's updates. This works well in practice even though classical divergence-based GAN theory predicts degenerate gradients when the residual distribution and the Dirac target at zero have disjoint support. The paper analyzes these dynamics with the neural tangent kernel and derives a practical training rule from the analysis.
official.method:
With a hard-constrained PINN (boundary conditions built into the network), the residual dynamics under adversarial training are r'(t) = K_rr γ(t), where K_rr is the generator residual NTK and γ is a per-sample weighting given by the discriminator's input gradient. The residual energy E = ½||r||² then changes at rate S = rᵀ K_rr γ, so a discriminator state is useful only if it makes S negative.

Algorithm 1 (rollback, 'RB'): in each outer iteration, with the generator frozen, run up to T_D = 20 discriminator updates and keep the discriminator state with the smallest S = rᵀ K_rr γ; then, with that discriminator frozen, run up to T_G = 20 generator updates and keep the generator state with the smallest residual energy. GAN, LSGAN and WGAN-GP are each trained with and without RB on the Poisson, Laplace, viscous Burgers, reaction-diffusion and Klein-Gordon equations. Non-DEQGAN methods all use Adam with lr 1e-3 and default betas, the same residual-link generator, and an objective-dependent discriminator (residual links, spectral norm and sigmoid output for GAN; plain critic for LSGAN/WGAN-GP). DEQGAN uses its own tuned hyperparameters. Validation and training errors are reported.
official.claim: With the same architecture and default Adam settings (lr 1e-3), adding rollback lowers the validation error of both GAN and LSGAN PINNs on all five benchmark PDEs, e.g. on Laplace from 5.86e-10 to 3.49e-12 (LSGAN) and from 8.12e-06 to 2.39e-11 (GAN), and on Klein-Gordon from 3.91e-03 to 5.45e-05 (LSGAN) and from 1.65e-02 to 4.75e-10 (GAN).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison of adversarial PINNs methods on diverse benchmark equations. Each entry is reported as "Validation Error / Training Error".
official.metric: Validation error / training error (MSE of the PINN solution against the reference, lower is better). Single run per entry; no seeds, standard deviations or error bars are reported.
official.comparison: GAN-RB vs. GAN and LSGAN-RB vs. LSGAN on Poisson, Laplace, viscous Burgers, reaction-diffusion and Klein-Gordon, same generator, discriminator and optimizer settings
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running with several seeds, the RB variant's validation error is not clearly lower (e.g. less than one order of magnitude) than the non-RB variant for GAN or LSGAN on Laplace or Klein-Gordon, or the seed-to-seed spread of the non-RB baseline covers the RB result.

title: ScreenSearch: Uncertainty-Aware OS Exploration

official.background: Desktop GUI agents work under partial observability: near-identical screens can hide different workflow states, so the same action can lead to different outcomes. Most computer-use agents are evaluated on instruction following, step by step, which gives little support for systematically mapping an unfamiliar application. This paper studies open-ended OS exploration, where the goal is to build a reusable graph of deduplicated screens, actions and observed outcomes, and asks how to choose actions so that exploration keeps finding new states instead of revisiting known ones.
official.method:
Each screen is represented from its UI Automation element set as spatially quantized cell-control and cell-text atoms plus a dense text embedding (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small). New observations are matched to existing states by BM25 + HNSW retrieval fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, then verified with a bounded Jaccard score (0.5 cell-control + 0.5 cell-text) and merged if it is at least 0.93. Actions have deterministic signatures (template, quantized target cell, role, label, app, arguments).

At each state the selector picks argmax over actions of Q(s,a) + c_p P(a|s) sqrt(sum N(s,.)) / (1 + N(s,a)) with c_p = 1, executes it once in the VM, and updates Q as the running mean of the immediate reward r = 1[new state] + 1[new edge] + [u(s) - u(s')]_+, where u is a shrunk outcome-dispersion (ambiguity) score (kappa = 20, u0 = 0.5). There are no rollouts or multi-step backup. In the matched suite, 50 verified replay starts per application (Notepad, File Explorer, LibreOffice Calc; 17 low / 16 medium / 17 high ambiguity) are replayed from clean snapshots; PUCT and greedy selection share starts, candidates, seeds, the 50-action budget and the same deterministic heuristic prior P (Eq. 6: 1 + 0.2 x instruction-label token overlap + 0.15 for type actions on editable targets, normalized). Greedy selection uses the same prior without the PUCT statistics. Only coverage beyond the initialized replay artifact is credited.
official.claim: With the same deterministic heuristic prior, starts and 50-action budget, one-step PUCT selection raises macro-average new-state AUC from 4.820 (greedy) to 50.487 across Notepad, File Explorer and LibreOffice Calc (50 starts each), and beats greedy on state AUC in every application (32.9 vs 11.6, 98.1 vs 1.9, 20.5 vs 1.0).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Matched cross-application selector comparison. Both rows per application use the same deterministic heuristic prior. Values are means over 50 starts.
official.metric: Area under the cumulative new-state discovery curve over 50 actions (higher is better), mean over 50 replay starts per application, macro-averaged over 3 applications; no standard deviations or confidence intervals reported. New states @ 50, edge AUC, net change in u, and revisit rate also reported.
official.comparison: PUCT graph-bandit selector vs. greedy selection using the same heuristic proposal prior, under matched starts, candidates, seeds and budgets
official.falsification_criterion: Under a matched replay-start setup, PUCT's state AUC is not clearly higher than greedy's (e.g., less than 2x) in the macro-average, or greedy matches or beats PUCT in any of the three applications.
