title: Property-Guided LLM Program Synthesis for Planning
claim_source: Table 2, page 15 (Appendix B; same numbers without std in Table 1, page 7)

official.background: LLM program-synthesis systems usually score each candidate program with a single number (solution value, tests passed, tasks solved). That number does not say why a candidate failed, so these systems generate and evaluate many candidates. In classical planning, the previous best LLM approach (sample-and-select, Corrêa et al.) samples 25 Python heuristic functions per PDDL domain, runs each with greedy best-first search (GBFS) on the training tasks, and keeps the one that solves the most. This paper asks whether checking a formal property and giving the LLM a concrete counterexample, as in counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), produces better heuristics with fewer candidates.
official.method:
The target is a 'direct' heuristic: every non-goal state reachable from the initial state through strictly improving transitions must have a successor with a strictly lower heuristic value, and every such improving successor must be a goal or itself in that set. With a direct heuristic, plain hill climbing (HC) reaches a goal without search. For each of the 10 IPC 2023 Learning Track domains, Gemini 3.1 Pro is given the same initial prompt as sample-and-select and writes a Python heuristic for Pyperplan. A validator runs DFS over strictly improving successors on each training task (30 s, 8 GiB per task; if the time limit is hit, the task counts as passed). At the first state with no improving successor, it stops and returns the failing task, the state, its h value, and the successors with their h values. A repair prompt containing this counterexample and all earlier attempts asks for a new heuristic. The loop ends when every training task passes, with at most 10 repairs.

The final heuristic runs with HC on the 90 out-of-distribution test tasks per domain (900 total; 5 min and 8 GiB per task). Baselines: FF and sample-and-select (25 candidates, selected by training GBFS coverage, re-run with Gemini 3.1 Pro), each run with both GBFS and HC. Ablation 'Cov.': the same repair loop, but the feedback is which training task was unsolved by GBFS and how many states were expanded. Direct and Cov. are averaged over 3 independent synthesis runs.
official.claim: On the 900 IPC 2023 Learning Track test tasks, heuristics synthesized by the counterexample-driven repair loop and run with plain hill climbing solve 623.3 ± 6.7 tasks. Sample-and-select with GBFS solves 573 with the same LLM, the coverage-feedback ablation solves 572.7 ± 15.95 with GBFS and 412.3 ± 41.9 with HC, and FF with GBFS solves 298.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Per-domain coverage (number of solved tasks) on the 900 IPC 2023 test tasks. This is the full version of Table 1 in the main text, including standard deviations across three independent runs for the ablation and proposed method. FF is the classical delete-relaxation heuristic; S&S is our re-run of the sample-and-select baseline [16] with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Both baselines are run using GBFS and HC. Direct is our proposed method (direct heuristics run with HC). Cov. is the ablation that replaces the direct-property check with numeric coverage feedback, using both GBFS and HC. Bold marks the best value per domain (ties are co-bolded).
official.metric: Coverage (number of solved test tasks out of 900, higher is better). ± is std over 3 independent synthesis runs; FF and S&S are reported as single deterministic values.
official.comparison: Direct heuristic + HC vs. sample-and-select (Gemini 3.1 Pro) + GBFS/HC, coverage-feedback repair-loop ablation + GBFS/HC, and FF + GBFS/HC.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the repair loop (3 runs, Gemini 3.1 Pro or a comparable LLM) gives a total HC coverage that is not clearly above sample-and-select + GBFS and the Cov. ablation + GBFS under the same LLM and limits (e.g., a gap smaller than about 15 tasks, or a reversed gap).

title: A Scalable Nonparametric Continuous-Time Survival Model through Numerical Quadrature
claim_source: Table 4, page 18 (instantaneous-hazard rows also shown as Table 1, page 7)

official.background: Survival analysis models time to an event (death, recurrence) under right-censoring. The hazard function, the instantaneous risk at time t, is the most direct description of how risk changes over follow-up, but most deep survival models avoid modelling it freely: Cox-style models assume proportional hazards, discrete-time models predict on a fixed time grid, and parametric models fix a distribution family. Modelling the hazard as an unconstrained neural function of (x, t) is hard because the likelihood needs the cumulative hazard, an integral of the network over [0, t]. ODE-based models such as SODEN compute it with adaptive solvers, which is slow.
official.method:
QSurv parameterizes the log-hazard as a network f(x, t) and trains with the exact continuous-time negative log-likelihood, -[delta * f(x, o) - Lambda(o|x)], where the cumulative hazard Lambda(o|x) = integral_0^o exp f(x, s) ds is approximated by K-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature: (o/2) * sum_k w_k exp f(x, o * tau_k), with tau_k the Legendre nodes mapped to [0, 1]. This is K vectorized forward passes, differentiable by plain backprop and minibatch SGD. Time enters the network through Time-LoRA, a time-dependent low-rank update of the penultimate-layer weight (W + U diag(s(t)) V, with s(t) from a small MLP on a time embedding).

Simulation (Appendix D): a scalar covariate x ~ U(-1, 1); event times drawn from Exponential, Weibull, Gamma, Gompertz, Log-normal or Log-logistic distributions whose parameters are exp(cubic polynomial in x) (coefficients in Table 3); independent uniform censoring tuned to ~20%; 2,000 train and 2,000 test samples. All neural models use two hidden layers of 32 units with Tanh. CoxTime, DeSurv and SODEN use the same Time-LoRA conditioning as QSurv. The metric is the L1 error between the estimated and true instantaneous hazard on the test set, plus wall-clock training time on an Apple M4 CPU, over 20 seeds.
official.claim: On the six synthetic survival distributions, QSurv's instantaneous-hazard L1 error (0.026-0.172) is several times lower than CoxCC, CoxTime and NnetSurv on every distribution (e.g. Weibull 0.0282 ± 0.0139 vs. best of the three 0.1182 ± 0.0207). It is within one std of SODEN on every distribution (e.g. Gamma 0.1718 vs. 0.1716) while training 14-30x faster (e.g. Gamma 6.2 s vs. 150.0 s).

Training times are wall-clock seconds on a single Apple M4 CPU (10-core, 32 GB RAM); relative comparisons across rows are meaningful but absolute values are machine-dependent.
official.metric: L1 error between estimated and true instantaneous hazard on the test set (lower is better), and training wall-clock seconds; ± is std over 20 random seeds

title: GeoSym127K: Scalable Symbolically-verifiable Synthesis for Multimodal Geometric Reasoning
claim_source: Table 5, page 7 (per-epoch results in Table 16, page 34)

official.background: Large multimodal models (LMMs) still do poorly on geometry problems that need precise reading of a diagram and several reasoning steps. Existing geometry training data is either small and hand-annotated, or synthetic with answers and reasoning chains written by an LLM, which can be wrong. This paper builds a synthesis engine that constructs diagrams from exact symbolic coordinates, computes exact ground-truth answers with SymPy, and keeps only teacher-model chain-of-thought (CoT) solutions whose final answer matches the symbolic answer. The question is whether fine-tuning on such verified data improves geometric reasoning on public benchmarks more than fine-tuning on earlier synthetic geometry datasets.
official.method:
The GeoSym engine grows 2D geometric constructions with a type-conditional grammar, keeping all point coordinates as exact SymPy expressions, renders the diagrams (including shaded regions found by connected-component analysis), and asks length, angle, area, perimeter and shaded-area questions whose answers are computed symbolically. A teacher MLLM writes a caption and a CoT solution for each image/question; a CoT is kept only if Simplify(A_pred - A_GT) = 0. Problems are split into Entry, Hard and Expert tiers by construction depth; the SFT sets are GeoSym Entry (23,440 verified CoTs) and GeoSym Hard (23,835 verified CoTs), part of the 55K GeoSym-Instruct set.

SFT updates only the LLM backbone of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (vision encoder and projector frozen) on 8 GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3: global batch 16, lr 1e-5 cosine, warmup 0.03, max context 12,288, BF16, for 1, 3, 5 or 10 epochs. Baselines are the same base model fine-tuned on TR-GeoMM (TR-CoT) and GeoTrust-train data with identical hyperparameters, data volume and evaluation. All models are evaluated with VLMEvalKit (temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, max 32,768 tokens) on MathVista (geometry subsets), MathVerse Vision-only, MathVision and WeMath (strict score); 'Overall' is the mean of the four benchmark scores.

title: Concepts Worth Having: Refining VLM-Guided Concept Bottleneck Models with Minimal Annotations
claim_source: Figure 2 (top row, CUB panel), page 7; final-point values match Table 2, page 8

official.background: Concept-bottleneck models (CBMs) classify an input by first predicting human-interpretable concepts (e.g. 'bill shape', 'breast colour') and then applying a linear layer on those concepts. Training them needs dense concept annotations, which are rarely available. Recent VLM-guided CBMs replace expert annotations with zero-shot concept scores from a vision-language model such as CLIP, which makes them widely applicable but yields inaccurate concepts and so weakens the interpretability that motivates CBMs. This paper asks whether a small amount of expert concept annotation, propagated through the VLM's embedding space, can recover accurate concepts.
official.method:
VH-CBM embeds every image with a frozen VLM (CLIP or DINOv3), standardises and normalises the embeddings, and fits one sparse variational Gaussian Process per concept on the small annotated subset (GPyTorch ApproximateGP, constant mean, RBF kernel with length scale initialised to 1.41 and output scale 1.0, Dirichlet-transformed labels following Milios et al. 2018 with noise 0.01, a learned mixing matrix across the values of a categorical concept, inducing points = number of annotated images). Concept probabilities p(c_i | z) from the GPs give the concept predictions; a linear layer on sampled GP concept scores, trained on all task-labelled data, gives the class prediction.

Annotation protocol: start with 40 fully concept-annotated training images and add 60 per iteration for five iterations (340 images in total; about 7% of the CUB training set). For VH-CBM the default is active selection: draw 95 random images and annotate only the most uncertain concept-image pairs under the GP, with the same total number of concept labels as annotating 60 full images; baselines get 60 fully annotated random images per iteration. Baselines at each budget are LP-@ (a linear probe from CLIP embeddings to concepts) and CBM-@ (a sequential CBM trained from scratch on the annotated images); LP-All is a linear probe on all concept labels and CLIP is zero-shot CLIP scores. The metric F1(C) is the macro F1 per concept activation averaged over all concepts, on the test set, averaged over three seeds.
official.claim: On CUB with CLIP embeddings, after 340 concept-annotated training images (about 7% of the training set), VH-CBM reaches concept F1(C) of about 0.82, versus about 0.70 for a sequential CBM and about 0.65 for a linear probe on the same CLIP embeddings trained with the same number of annotated images (zero-shot CLIP: about 0.51).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: VH-CBM improves concept accuracy. F1(C) of VH-CBM with varying percentages of concept supervision for the CLIP (top) and DINO (bottom) backbones. We report average F1(C) over three runs, with confidence intervals estimated via bootstrap resampling across runs.
official.metric: F1(C): macro F1 per concept averaged over the 112 CUB concepts, higher is better; mean over 3 runs with bootstrap confidence bands across runs (Table 2 reports ± 0.01 for VH-CBM CLIP and CBM@7%). Figure values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: VH-CBM (CLIP, active concept selection) vs. LP-@ and CBM-@ trained on the same number of randomly chosen, fully concept-annotated images; LP-All and zero-shot CLIP as references
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running on CUB with CLIP ViT embeddings and 340 annotated training images, VH-CBM's mean F1(C) is not clearly above both the linear probe and the sequential CBM (e.g. less than ~0.05 above LP-@, or below CBM-@).

title: CAVE: A Structured Credit Assignment Approach for Fragmented Visual Evidence Reasoning

official.background: Vision-language models do poorly on 'fragmented' visual reasoning tasks, where the answer depends on combining several small, easily confused pieces of evidence from distant regions of an image (tracing a line through clutter, following arrow/colour rules across nodes, matching a rotated template inside a grid, or matching a remote-sensing sub-image). 'Think-with-image' agents that zoom into regions over several rounds help, but GRPO training usually rewards only the final answer or overall trajectory quality. It therefore gives no targeted credit to intermediate zoom and reasoning actions that uncover evidence.
official.method:
CAVE trains Qwen2.5-VL-7B as a multi-round interleaved reasoner (text reasoning, zoom-tool calls returning crops, final answer; at most T = 5 rounds). It starts with a cold-start SFT on 10k DeepEyes-style samples, then runs GRPO (verl) on 5,000 TRACER-style training samples, each annotated with a textual 'perception' field listing task-critical evidence units. The process reward has three step-level credits computed by teacher forcing. (1) Belief update: the change in the mean log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer tokens from context M_t to M_{t+1}. (2) Evidence acquisition: the mean positive change in the log-likelihood of each annotated evidence unit. (3) Adaptive focus control: applies only to zoom actions; it equals (1 - |rho_t - rho_hat_t|), where rho_t is the crop-area ratio and rho_hat_t is a target scale in [0.02, 0.30] set by top-500 answer-token entropy, gated by 1 - exp(-([c_bu]+ + c_ea)).

Step credits are clipped to [-1, 2], weighted by 0.8^(t-1), summed per trajectory and combined with weights 0.4/0.3/0.3. GRPO group-relative advantages are computed on this reward, and light task-anchoring terms (answer correctness, format, round count) are added. Tool observations are masked out of the policy gradient. In the 'Correct Only' ablation, the process credits are replaced by the final-answer correctness reward, keeping the same base model, interleaved structure and training configuration. Evaluation is accuracy on Tunnel Vision (1,350), BabyVision (388), TRACER-Core (3 synthetic scenarios, 735) and MME-RS (remote-sensing sub-image matching, 245).
official.claim: With the same Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, cold start, data and GRPO configuration, training with CAVE's structured process credits beats training with only a final-answer correctness reward on all four fragmented-vision benchmarks: Tunnel Vision 31.3 vs 26.7, BabyVision 17.3 vs 11.3, TRACER-Core 36.9 vs 31.2, MME-RS 59.2 vs 49.4 accuracy (%).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Ablation studies on structured credits and training sources, evaluating credit complementarity and the effect of data composition on fragmented vision reasoning. (a) Structured credits ablation. (b) Training-source ablation.
official.metric: Accuracy (%), higher is better. Single run per variant; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported for this table.
official.comparison: Full CAVE (belief + evidence + focus credits) vs. Correct Only (final-answer correctness reward), both GRPO from the same cold-start checkpoint; Cold-Start and single-credit-removed variants also shown
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both variants under matched settings gives a Correct Only model within about 2 accuracy points of full CAVE on most of the four benchmarks (or ahead on any), or the gap disappears across seeds.

title: Sketch Then Paint: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Multi-Modal Large Language Models

official.background: Diffusion multi-modal LLMs (dMLLMs) such as MMaDA and Lumina-DiMOO generate images by iteratively unmasking discrete visual tokens, and GRPO-style RL is used to align them with text prompts and human preferences. Applying GRPO is awkward because the same image can come from many unmasking orders, so per-token importance ratios have no single natural conditioning context. Existing methods either randomly re-mask the generated image (which leaks future tokens and mixes early layout tokens with late detail tokens in one update) or replay the single recorded trajectory (narrow coverage, high memory cost). Both give every token the same image-level advantage.
official.method:
HT-GRPO ranks each rollout's image tokens by the order in which they were unmasked. The first 30% (alpha = 0.3) are 'structure' tokens and the rest are 'refinement' tokens. The K = 8 inner-loop gradient updates per rollout batch are split into three stages in the ratio 2:4:2: Global (all tokens), Structure (structure tokens only) and Refinement (refinement tokens only). Each update uses a random subset of the stage's tokens, and the sampling rate decays linearly from 1.0 to 0.5 within each stage. Importance ratios are computed with a prompt-conditioned estimator: token probabilities come from a single forward pass on the fully masked image plus the text prompt, so no intermediate states are cached and no future tokens are visible.

Hierarchical Credit Assignment multiplies the image-level group-relative advantage by lambda_s = 1.5 for structure tokens and lambda_r = 0.5 for refinement tokens. The implementation is built on the MaskGRPO codebase and shares its optimizer, reward and RL loop: G = 9 rollouts per prompt, reward = HPSv3 + CLIP (ViT-L/14) + UniReward, CFG 3.5, and the original KL penalty. Baselines are MaskGRPO (random remasking) and TraceGRPO (trajectory recording, following TraceRL), run on the same backbones. Evaluation is on DPG-Bench (1,065 dense prompts) and GenEval (553 prompts).
official.claim: On MMaDA, HT-GRPO reaches a DPG-Bench overall score of 81.09, compared with 75.81 for MaskGRPO and 74.37 for TraceGRPO trained on the same backbone (base model: 70.51).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance comparison on DPG-Bench across various dMLLMs and RL settings.
official.metric: DPG-Bench overall score (higher is better); single run, no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: MMaDA + HT-GRPO vs. MMaDA + MaskGRPO and MMaDA + TraceGRPO (same backbone, MaskGRPO-based codebase and reward); untrained MMaDA shown for reference
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining MMaDA with HT-GRPO and with MaskGRPO under the same reward, rollout count and training budget gives a DPG-Bench overall gap well below 5 points (e.g. under 2 points), or no gap that holds across seeds.

title: Motion Cues from Image-based Point Tracking for LiDAR Scene Flow Estimation

official.background: Self-supervised LiDAR scene flow methods (SeFlow, SeFlow++, TeFlow) avoid costly 3D motion annotations by first splitting points into static and dynamic sets and then applying a different loss to each. That split usually comes from DUFOMap, a ray-casting dynamic-awareness map built only from LiDAR, which mislabels many points in sparse or occluded regions. Because most driving-scene points are static, false dynamic labels are common and remove correct static supervision, which degrades the learned flow. Cameras observe object motion densely even where LiDAR is sparse, so image point tracking could give a cleaner static/dynamic signal.
official.method:
TrackCue refines the DUFOMap dynamic labels. In each 6-frame clip, up to 2,048 DUFOMap-dynamic LiDAR points from the clip's first frame are projected into each of the 7 surround-view Argoverse 2 cameras (resized to 768x768; only projections with sufficient depth and inside a border margin are kept) and tracked through the clip with the frozen off-the-shelf CoTracker3. For each query, a rigid trajectory is computed by reprojecting the 3D point using only the ego-poses (as if the point were static), and the per-frame pixel residual between the tracked and rigid trajectories is computed. A frame votes 'moving' if the residual exceeds tau_dyn = 5 px and both the tracker visibility and the rigid-projection validity masks are on (joint visibility); a query is moving if at least N_move = 2 frames vote moving, and a camera view's moving queries are kept only if there are at least N_point = 10 of them.

Visual motion cue lifting: in each frame, the visible image positions of the kept moving trajectories are matched to the K_nn = 4 nearest projected LiDAR points (KD-tree) within a lifting radius tau_lift = 0.4 (an image-space distance; the paper gives no unit), and those points are labelled dynamic, giving the TrackCue labels, which replace the DUFOMap dynamic set inside each auto-labeler. Labels are evaluated against ground-truth dynamic points on the Argoverse 2 validation set, defined by the official protocol as points whose ground-truth flow minus rigid ego flow exceeds 0.05 m (7.12% of points are dynamic). The comparison is run for the SeFlow auto-labeler (raw DUFOMap) and the SeFlow++ auto-labeler (DUFOMap plus nearest-neighbour cluster reassignment).
official.claim: On the Argoverse 2 validation set (ground-truth dynamic ratio 7.12%), refining the SeFlow DUFOMap dynamic pseudo-labels with TrackCue (CoTracker3) raises precision from 24.62% to 31.38% and F1 from 36.74 to 42.37 (recall drops from 72.35% to 65.22%); for the SeFlow++ labeler, precision rises from 45.07% to 56.62% and F1 from 52.75 to 56.85.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison of dynamic pseudo-label generation quality and downstream scene flow performance. We compare the DUFOMap [11] and our TrackCue for auto-label generation of both SeFlow [8] and SeFlow++ [7] pipelines. The ground-truth dynamic ratio is 7.12%.
official.metric: Point-level precision, recall and F1 (higher is better) of predicted dynamic labels vs. ground-truth dynamic points (residual flow > 0.05 m); single run, no error bars reported (the labeling pipeline involves no training). Dyn. Bucket = downstream Dynamic Bucket-Normalized EPE (lower is better), also a single run.
official.comparison: TrackCue-refined dynamic pseudo-labels vs. the DUFOMap-based labels from the same auto-labeler (SeFlow and SeFlow++), on the same frames and the same ground truth
official.falsification_criterion: Re-implementing TrackCue with CoTracker3 and the stated hyperparameters on the Argoverse 2 validation set, the F1 gain over the SeFlow DUFOMap labels is under ~2 points, or precision does not improve by at least ~3 points.

title: When Dynamics Shift, Robust Task Inference Wins: Offline Imitation Learning with Behavior Foundation Models Revisited
claim_source: Figure 4(c), page 8 (same setting also appears in Figure 6, Flip row / Joint Friction Loss column, page 28)

official.background: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) based on forward-backward (FB) representations are pretrained once on reward-free exploratory data and then adapt to a new task by inferring a low-dimensional task vector z, e.g. from a few expert demonstrations (FB-IL). They assume the deployment dynamics match the pretraining dynamics, so policies inferred this way can degrade when friction, mass, gravity or actuation change. Prior fixes need pretraining data from many dynamics regimes, which is often unavailable; this paper asks whether robustness can be added purely at task-inference time using data from a single nominal environment.
official.method:
An FB BFM is pretrained (1M steps, latent dim 50, BREEZE codebase) on the ExORL Walker RND exploratory dataset (1M transitions). Expert demonstrations are generated by the pretrained BFM itself; imitation uses 4 expert trajectories per task. The baseline FB-IL infers z by minimizing the MSE between pi_z(s) and expert actions over demonstration states (warm-started from the averaged B embeddings of the trajectories). All three methods share the same pretrained F, B and actor; only z-inference differs.

RBFM-Heavy replaces this with a distributionally robust minimax objective: the adversary reweights expert (s,a,s') samples via importance ratios w within an f-divergence ball (SoftTV, epsilon = 0.8) subject to Bellman flow constraints, with a Lagrange-multiplier Q network and tau; optimization alternates between (Q, tau) updates and z updates using the closed-form worst-case w (Eq. 16). RBFM-Light instead uses a TV-ball over state occupancy with a single dual variable lambda (Proposition 2). Policies are evaluated in a perturbed Walker environment with added joint friction loss (0-30 Nm per joint), averaging return over 100 episodes per seed, 5 seeds, with 95% CIs across seeds.
official.claim: On Walker flip with a BFM pretrained on 1M RND transitions, under joint friction loss of 15 Nm per joint RBFM-Heavy reaches about 420 average return vs. about 235 for FB-IL (RBFM-Light about 320), with non-overlapping 95% CIs, while all methods are within about 30 return of each other (~520-555) at nominal friction.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Average return (y-axis) vs. joint friction loss perturbation (x-axis, absolute Nm per joint) on Walker flip task across three RND pretraining dataset sizes (100k, 500k, 1M transitions).
official.metric: Average episode return (higher is better) over 100 evaluation episodes per seed, averaged over 5 seeds; shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals across seeds. Values below are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: RBFM-Heavy (and RBFM-Light) vs. FB-IL task inference on the same pretrained FB model, across joint friction loss levels 0-30 Nm
official.falsification_criterion: With the same 1M-transition RND-pretrained Walker BFM and 4 demonstrations, RBFM-Heavy's mean return at 15-20 Nm joint friction falls within FB-IL's 95% CI (or below it), i.e. the ~150-180 return gap at 15-20 Nm disappears.

title: PEIRA: Learning Predictive Encoders through Inter-View Regressor Alignment

official.background: Non-contrastive self-supervised learning methods such as SimSiam, BYOL, I-JEPA and DINO train an encoder so that representations of two augmented views predict each other, using stop-gradient or EMA teachers to avoid representational collapse. These self-distillation dynamics do not minimise a well-defined objective, so what they learn and when they collapse is poorly understood. The paper analyses a JEPA-style dynamic with an optimal ridge-regression linear predictor between views, shows that its stable equilibria span nonlinear canonical correlation (CCA) subspaces but that collapse is also stable, and proposes PEIRA, an explicit objective whose only stable equilibria are non-collapsed global minimisers.
official.method:
PEIRA minimises E_PEIRA(U, V) = -Tr(P_{U,V}) + (λ/2)(||U||² + ||V||²), where P_{U,V} = Σ_{U,V}(N_{U,V} + λI)^{-1} is the closed-form optimal regularised linear regressor between the two views' features, with Σ_{U,V} = E[V U^T + U V^T] (cross-view signal) and N_{U,V} = E[U U^T + V V^T] (within-view variability). In practice (Algorithm 1, SC-PEIRA) Σ and N are tracked as EMAs of mini-batch feature statistics (EMA rate annealed from η_init to η_min), P̂ and Q̂ = (N + λI)^{-1} are computed from them and held fixed, and the encoder is updated by backpropagating an auxiliary loss L_aux (Eq. 15) that has the same gradient as E_PEIRA. A single shared encoder is used for both views.

CIFAR-10 setting (Appendix G.1, Table G.2): CIFAR-style ResNet-18 plus a 3-layer MLP projector (hidden width 2048; output 1024 for PEIRA, 2048 for VICReg, 128 for SIGReg), 1000 epochs, batch size 256, LARS with cosine decay, shared symmetric two-view augmentations (random resized crop scale [0.2, 1], colour jitter, grayscale, solarization, flip). PEIRA uses λ = 0.7, η_init = 0.8, η_min = 0.5, base LR 0.04, gradient clipping 1.0 from epoch 4. VICReg (α=1, β=1, γ=80) and SIGReg (λ=0.1) use the eb_jepa codebase defaults. Evaluation is an offline linear probe on frozen features (Appendix E of Bardes et al. 2022), top-1 accuracy on the CIFAR-10 test set, 3 seeds.
official.claim: With a ResNet-18 pretrained for 1000 epochs on CIFAR-10 under a matched augmentation and linear-probe protocol, PEIRA reaches 90.97 ± 0.10% linear-probe top-1, matching VICReg (90.92 ± 0.14%) within seed noise and about 1.4 points below SIGReg/LeJEPA (92.34 ± 0.21%).

BYOL and SimSiam ImageNet-1K numbers are quoted from Table 4 of Bardes et al. [2022] (100-epoch ResNet-50 reimplementation under each method's original recipe). The SimCLR ImageNet-1K number is quoted from Table S3 of Garrido et al. [2023a] (100-epoch ResNet-50, 8192-8192-2048 projector).

title: Is Complex Training Necessary for Long-Tailed OOD Detection? A Re-think from Feature Geometry

official.background: Long-tailed OOD (LT-OOD) detection asks a classifier trained on imbalanced data to keep recognizing rare in-distribution classes while rejecting inputs from unseen distributions. Recent LT-OOD methods mostly add training machinery such as auxiliary outlier exposure, abstention heads, contrastive objectives or gradient-conflict control. The paper asks whether that complexity is needed, arguing that frozen long-tailed features already carry OOD evidence, and that the standard feature-space detector (class-conditional Mahalanobis distance) reads it badly: feature norm grows as class frequency drops, and tail classes have too few samples to estimate class-specific covariance.
official.method:
Hyperspherical Pooled Mahalanobis (HPM) is a post-hoc detector on frozen penultimate features h(x). Training and query features are L2-normalized (z = h/||h||). Class means of the normalized features are used as anchors. A single pooled covariance is estimated from within-class residuals, Σ_HPM = (1/(N−K)) Σ_c Σ_{i:y_i=c} (z_i − μ_c)(z_i − μ_c)^T + λI. The OOD score is min_c (z − μ_c)^T Σ_HPM^{-1} (z − μ_c), where larger means more OOD. The ablation variants are standard Mahalanobis (raw features, class-specific covariance), RP-MD (raw features, pooled covariance) and HC-MD (normalized features, class-specific covariance).

The backbone under test is PC-ERM: the same backbone family and 200-epoch CIFAR budget as the LT-OOD baselines, trained only with cross-entropy plus long-tail log-prior (logit) adjustment (Menon et al., 2021), with no auxiliary OOD data and no OOD-specific loss. title: f-OPD: Stabilizing Long-Horizon On-Policy Distillation with Freshness-Aware Control

official.background: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student LLM on its own sampled outputs while a teacher grades every token with its distribution, which gives dense supervision. Production OPD systems run rollout, teacher grading and student updates asynchronously to raise throughput. As a result, buffered samples were generated by an older student and graded under an older context, so training drifts away from the true on-policy objective. Too much staleness lowers accuracy and can make training collapse, so asynchronous OPD trades task quality for throughput.
official.method:
The paper splits the asynchronous-vs-synchronous objective gap into rollout drift (stale student policy) and supervision drift (stale teacher-conditioning context). For each buffered sample i it computes a token-averaged KL between the current and rollout-time student on the stored prefix (D_roll), a token-averaged KL between the teacher under the current and grading-time context (D_sup), and the update lag tau_i. The freshness score is f_i = (tau_i + 1)^-1 * exp(-alpha*sqrt(D_roll) - beta*sqrt(D_sup)).

f-OPD combines three mechanisms, with the teacher frozen throughout. (1) Freshness weighting: each sample's distillation loss is multiplied by ReLU(f_i - xi). That loss compares the current student with the teacher relabeled under the current context c^t on the stored prefixes (Eq. 12), not with the cached grading-time teacher distribution. (2) Rollout-anchored regularization: lambda * D_roll is added. The text says this term is also freshness-modulated, but Algorithm 1 writes the loss as w_i*l_i + lambda*D_roll. (3) Adaptive refresh: the buffer is re-rolled and relabeled when mean freshness falls to kappa_f or below, or when the aligned-token coverage drops below kappa_d. Defaults are alpha=1.0, beta=0.5, kappa_f=0.10 and kappa_d=0.5. Baselines are synchronous OPD (fully on-policy) and vanilla asynchronous OPD. Unless stated otherwise, comparisons use policy lag 8. Table 3 tests two non-Qwen pairs, evaluated by Avg@1 accuracy on GSM8K, MATH500 and AMC23.
official.claim: With DeepSeekMath-7B-Base distilled from DeepSeekMath-7B-RL, asynchronous OPD falls to 61.2 GSM8K / 27.4 MATH500 / 11.8 AMC23 Avg@1, while f-OPD recovers synchronous-level accuracy (79.0 / 40.2 / 19.4 vs. synchronous 78.5 / 39.6 / 20.0). The same pattern holds for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct distilled from Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (async 63.8 / 16.1 / 7.5, f-OPD 78.1 / 22.7 / 15.6, sync 79.2 / 23.0 / 15.0).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Avg@1 accuracy (%) on non-Qwen student–teacher pairs.
official.metric: Avg@1 accuracy (%), higher is better; no ± given in the table (the main text says all metrics are averaged over five seeds, but no std is reported)
official.comparison: f-OPD vs. vanilla asynchronous OPD (matched student, teacher and asynchrony) and vs. synchronous OPD (on-policy ceiling)
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same asynchronous lag, f-OPD fails to beat asynchronous OPD by a margin clearly larger than seed variance, for example recovering less than half of the sync-async gap on GSM8K or MATH500. Alternatively, asynchronous OPD at that lag shows no substantial drop below synchronous OPD, so there is nothing to recover.

title: PAIR: Prefix-Aware Internal Reward Model for Multi-Turn Agent Optimization

official.background: GRPO training of LLM agents on multi-step tool-use tasks gets only a sparse end-of-trajectory reward, which makes credit assignment across intermediate steps hard. Existing dense-reward fixes need extra rollouts, per-step LLM-judge calls, separate reward models, or ground-truth answers at runtime. Linear probes on an LLM's own hidden states are known to predict answer correctness, which suggests a nearly free step-level reward, but prior probing work assumed clean inputs, whereas during RL exploration earlier steps are often wrong (a 'contaminated' prefix).
official.method:
Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the authors build matched clean/contaminated pairs of agent trajectories on GTA and ToolBench: the evaluation turn is held fixed while earlier steps are either correct or replaced by one of four error types (reasoning error, observation misinterpretation, tool misuse, stale memory). Each (prefix, turn) is labelled correct or incorrect. Hidden-state probes (last-token, mean-pooled, multi-layer) and attention-statistic probes (max attention, std, prefix-attention ratio, self-attention ratio per head and layer) are trained as linear classifiers.

PAIR has two stages. Stage 1 is a logistic-regression probe on the last-token hidden state, trained on clean data and frozen, giving s_bc. Stage 2 is a second logistic regression on [multi-layer attention features; s_bc], trained on a mix of clean and contaminated data, giving s_final. Baselines are each individual probe plus Lookback Lens, attention-head entropy, and Chain-of-Embedding (CoE-C). The metric is AUROC (and ECE) for predicting step correctness, averaged over 3 seeds.
official.claim: For step-level correctness prediction on mixed clean/contaminated agent trajectories from ToolBench, PAIR achieves AUROC 0.8129 ± 0.006, above all 9 other internal-signal methods; the best baseline is the multi-layer hidden-state probe at 0.7821 ± 0.007.
official.claim_caption: Step-level correctness prediction performance on GTA and ToolBench. Each evaluation point is a single (prefix, evaluation turn) pair labelled correct or incorrect, not a trajectory-level outcome. AUROC (higher is better) and ECE (lower is better) are reported for each method. All AUROC and ECE values are reported as mean over 3 random seeds (42, 43, 44).
official.metric: AUROC (higher is better), mean +/- std over seeds 42, 43, 44; ECE also reported
official.comparison: PAIR vs. Last-token, Mean-pooled, Multi-layer, Attention, Hidden+Attn, Multi-Attn probes, Lookback Lens, Head Entropy, CoE-C
official.falsification_criterion: On ToolBench, some baseline probe comes within seed std of PAIR's AUROC, or PAIR's margin over the multi-layer hidden-state probe disappears.

title: Learning to Solve Compositional Geometry Routing Problems

official.background: Neural routing solvers such as POMO are built for node-centric problems like TSP, where every task is a point. Many real missions (inspection, mapping, surveying) mix point tasks with line tasks that must be traversed and area tasks that must be covered. The paper defines the Compositional Geometry Routing Problem (CGRP), where a single instance can mix points, lines and areas. Non-point tasks have several entry-exit options with different service paths, which makes travel costs asymmetric, couples local service choices with the global route, and enlarges the action space with many feasible but poor candidates.
official.method:
Each candidate (depot, point, one of 2 directions per line, one of ω = 4 shortest zig-zag coverage paths per area) is embedded from its entry/exit coordinates, a geometric anchor (task center) and a task-type indicator, then encoded by a 6-layer Transformer (dim 128, 8 heads). DiCon makes two changes to a backbone solver: (1) the decoder's multi-head attention is replaced by differential attention, softmax(Q1K1ᵀ/√d) − λ·softmax(Q2K2ᵀ/√d) with a learnable non-negative λ per head (initialized 0.5); (2) two SimSiam-style contrastive losses are added on the encoder: an instance-level loss between A = 4 rotated/reflected views (weight 0.1) and an intra-task loss pulling together candidates of the same line/area task across views (weight 0.02). The decoder is trained by REINFORCE with a shared baseline over augmented views and POMO-style multiple rollouts.

Training data: problem size uniform in [20, 100), 0-4 area tasks, 0-19 line tasks, the rest points, coordinates uniform in the unit square. 200 epochs × 100,000 instances, batch 64, Adam lr 1e-4 (×0.1 at epoch 180). DiCon-P is DiCon on the POMO backbone; POMO is the same backbone trained on the same CGRP data without DA or CL. Evaluation: 200 test instances per size (20, 100 in-distribution; 200, 300 larger), greedy decoding, average tour length (travel + service cost). Gaps are relative to LKH3.
official.claim: With greedy decoding on mixed CGRP instances, DiCon-P gives a lower average tour length than POMO trained on the same data: 8.406 vs. 8.465 at 100 tasks (in-distribution), 13.949 vs. 14.115 at 200 tasks and 16.021 vs. 16.344 at 300 tasks (gap to LKH3 1.99% vs. 3.20% and 5.65% vs. 7.78%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison. Left: in-distribution testing. Right: generalization to larger sizes. (* The result is obtained by Gurobi without a time limit and thus represents the exact optimum.)
official.metric: Average objective (total tour length incl. service cost) over 200 test instances, lower is better; Gap (%) relative to LKH3. No ± reported: a single trained model per method, no seeds or error bars.
official.comparison: DiCon-P (POMO + differential attention + double-level contrastive learning) vs. POMO, same training distribution and budget, greedy inference without augmentation
official.falsification_criterion: After training both models on the stated CGRP distribution, DiCon-P's average objective on 200-task and 300-task instances is not lower than POMO's, or the improvement is far smaller (e.g. under ~0.5% at 200 tasks, versus the reported ~1.2%), or it disappears across training seeds.

title: TaskGround: Structured Executable Task Inference for Full-Scene Household Reasoning

official.background: LLM-based household agents are usually tested on clean task specifications where the relevant objects, goals and constraints are already stated. In a real home the agent gets a whole household scene (many rooms, objects, states and relations) and a casually phrased request such as 'get my cup and the small table ready', and has to work out which objects matter, what end state is meant, and which steps must happen in order. Feeding the whole scene to the model is long and noisy, and privacy and on-device compute favor small open-weight models that handle long cluttered contexts poorly.
official.method:
TaskGround is a training-free pipeline with two LLM calls and two deterministic stages. Ground: the LLM sees the request plus a compact room-grouped object inventory and names task-relevant (room, object class) pairs; these are resolved to scene-graph nodes, expanded with rooms, the agent, containers/surfaces and local context, and the induced subgraph of the original scene becomes the scene slice. Infer: the LLM sees the request and the scene slice and outputs an ordered list of goal atoms (state predicates ON/OFF/OPEN/CLOSED/CLEAN/PLUGGED_IN/PLUGGED_OUT, relations ON/INSIDE). A fixed rule-based completion module adds process-critical goals from household priors (e.g. close an appliance before switching it on, clean a surface before placing on it). Execute: a rule-based executor turns the ordered goals into VirtualHome-style skill actions (WALK, GRAB, OPEN, PUTIN, WIPE, ...), inserting generic preconditions.

The Naive baseline prompts the same model with the complete serialized scene graph (about 84k input tokens on VirtualHome) and the request and asks for the action sequence directly. Both are evaluated on FullHome; the chosen split is VG-200, 200 VirtualHome goal tasks in a single apartment with per-task scene perturbations. The predicted action sequence is executed on VirtualHome's symbolic evolving-graph simulator, and a task succeeds if the final state satisfies all hidden goal predicates. Decoding is temperature 0, prompts are the same across models, and Qwen3.5-9B is served locally with vLLM in bf16.
official.claim: On the 200 VirtualHome goal tasks of FullHome, TaskGround raises Qwen3.5-9B's Goal success rate from 0.0% (Naive full-scene prompting) to 47.5%, above GPT-5 with Naive prompting (45.5%), and raises GPT-5 itself from 45.5% to 73.5%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on FullHome. Goal SR and Process SR are success rates on goal and process tasks. Cells shaded exceed GPT-5 Naive, the frontier direct-prompting reference for each column. (+Δ) denote absolute gains of TaskGround over the same model's Naive result. Bold marks the best result within each model group.
official.metric: Goal SR (% of tasks whose executed final state satisfies all hidden goal predicates), higher is better; single deterministic run (temperature 0), no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: TaskGround vs. Naive direct complete-scene action generation, same model and prompts; also Qwen3.5-9B + TaskGround vs. GPT-5 Naive
official.falsification_criterion: With the released FullHome VG-200 tasks and evaluator, Qwen3.5-9B + TaskGround scores below about 35% Goal SR or within 10 points of Qwen3.5-9B Naive (or of Ground-Act, the grounded-slice direct-action ablation); the 'matches GPT-5 Naive' part is refuted if it lands clearly below GPT-5 Naive's score from the same run.

title: Dual-Rate Diffusion: Accelerating diffusion models with an interleaved heavy-light network

official.background: Sampling from a diffusion model means running the same large denoising network hundreds of times, so inference is expensive. Most speed-ups cut the number of steps (better solvers, distillation), but each step still runs the full network. Global image structure (low frequencies) settles early in sampling and then changes little, so recomputing it at every step looks wasteful. Caching methods reuse activations inside one fixed network without retraining. This paper instead trains two separate networks together: a heavy one that runs rarely and a light one that runs at every step.
official.method:
A heavy context encoder E_Θ (the base model's UViT, 394M params, 108.45 GFLOPs per call at 64x64) is run on the current noisy sample only K times along a k-step ancestral sampling trajectory (K = 16). Its features are the outputs of the last layer at each resolution level. A light denoising UViT g_θ (fewer blocks and channels: 88M params, 44.02 GFLOPs) runs at every step. At each level it takes the most recent encoder features, linearly projects them and concatenates them with its own features. It is FiLM-conditioned on both the current time t and the encoder time τ, and it predicts the clean image. Both networks are trained jointly with the standard sigmoid-weighted diffusion loss: τ ~ U[1/K, 1], t ~ U(τ − 1/K, τ], z_τ is drawn from q(z_τ|x) and z_t from the Markovian forward posterior q(z_t|z_τ, x). Training also uses multi-level features, random-translation augmentation, and feature dropout (features zeroed with p = 0.5).

The baseline is the authors' own base model (the context-encoder architecture used alone, following the SiD2 recipe of Hoogeboom et al. 2025), sampled with 512 ancestral steps. Both models are trained for 10^6 iterations at batch size 1024 with classifier-free guidance w = 1, a guidance interval and tuned sampling noise. FID is computed on 50k samples against the ImageNet training set, and sampling cost is reported in TFLOPs per sample.
official.claim: On class-conditional ImageNet 64x64, Dual-Rate Diffusion (K = 16 context-encoder evaluations, 256 denoising steps) reaches FID 1.12 at 7.44 TFLOPs per sample, better than the authors' matched base model's FID 1.25 at 55.53 TFLOPs with 512 steps, i.e. better quality at about 7.5x lower sampling cost.
official.claim_caption: Table 2 | Results on ImageNet 64 × 64 and 128 × 128 for Dual-Rate Diffusion and Dual-Rate MMD. We report the computational cost of sampling in terms of teraflops (TFLOPs) and number of function evaluations (NFE). For the Dual-Rate experiments NFE refers to the number of denoising steps and K refers to the number of context encoder evaluations. The Moment Matching results are those reported by Salimans et al. (2024) and were obtained with their teacher model (see Section 4.2).
official.metric: FID on 50k samples vs. the ImageNet training set (lower is better), lowest value over checkpoints evaluated every 20k iterations; sampling cost in TFLOPs per sample. Single runs, no seeds or error bars reported.
official.comparison: Dual-Rate Diffusion (K = 16; k = 128/256/512) vs. the authors' base model (same recipe, 512 steps, guidance w = 1), trained for the same number of iterations
official.falsification_criterion: With both models trained under the same recipe, Dual-Rate Diffusion (K = 16, k = 256) on ImageNet 64x64 does not reach an FID at or below the base model's 512-step FID while using at least ~4x fewer sampling FLOPs.

title: Concise and Logically Consistent Conformal Sets for Neuro-Symbolic Concept-Based Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (also Table 32 in Appendix F)

official.background: Neuro-Symbolic Concept-based Models (NeSy-CBMs) first predict high-level concepts from an input (e.g. the two digits in an MNIST pair) and then apply fixed logical knowledge to infer a label (e.g. their sum). Their concept and label predictions can be confidently wrong, especially under 'reasoning shortcuts', where the model learns wrong concepts that still give correct labels. Conformal prediction (CP) replaces point predictions with sets that have distribution-free coverage guarantees, but applying CP separately to concepts and labels gives concept sets that are large and not logically consistent with the label set.
official.method:
COCOCO is a post-hoc method. On a calibration split (20% of the test set) it builds a label conformal set Υα(x) and a concept conformal set Γβ(x) using nonconformity score −log pθ(·|x); the concept set is the Cartesian product of per-concept conformal sets. It then applies one joint revision step: Υrev(x) = Υα(x) ∩ g†(Γβ(x)) and Γrev(x) = Γβ(x) ∩ g−†(Υα(x)), where g† deduces the argmax label(s) from a concept vector and g−† abduces all concept vectors whose deduced label lies in a given set. So concept vectors that do not entail any label in the label set are removed.

The baseline RPB (Ramalingam et al.) applies the same revision only on the label side: its label set equals COCOCO's, but its concept set is the unrevised Γβ(x). Both are applied to the same trained DeepProbLog (DPL) model at 1−α = 1−β = 0.9, evaluated on the remaining 80% of the test set, averaged over 10 seeds. On MN-EO (MNIST-EvenOdd: pairs of MNIST digits with sum labels, training restricted to all-even or all-odd pairs so that reasoning shortcuts arise), DPL is trained without concept supervision (implementation from the rsbench suite, ref. [77]). Metrics: average set size, empirical coverage, and consistency (average fraction of set elements whose deduced/abduced counterpart lies in the other set).
official.claim: On MN-EO with an unsupervised DPL model at nominal coverage 0.9, COCOCO reduces the average concept-set size from 100.00 ± 0.00 (RPB) to 12.13 ± 1.37 and raises concept consistency from 0.12 ± 0.01 to 1.00 ± 0.00, while concept coverage stays at 0.90 ± 0.02 and label sets are identical (size 1.55, coverage 0.90).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Results for DPL on four representative datasets. We report concept and label consistency (CONST., fraction of consistent pairs – see Section D.2), size, and coverage at nominal coverage 1 − α = 1 − β = 0.9, averaged over 10 seeds (mean ± std). Full results, including LTN, are in Section F.
official.metric: Concept-set SIZE (lower is better), concept CONSISTENCY (higher is better), concept COVERAGE (should be near 0.9); mean ± std over 10 seeds
official.comparison: DPL + COCOCO vs. DPL + RPB (label-side-only revision) on the same trained DPL models; plain DPL point predictions shown for reference. RPB is the competitor the paper calls strongest; the paper's TAb ablation (Table 25) ties COCOCO on the concept side in this setting (see caveats)
official.falsification_criterion: On MN-EO with unsupervised DPL, COCOCO's concept set is not substantially smaller than RPB's (e.g. mean size above ~30 of 100), its concept consistency is below 1.00, or its concept coverage falls well below the 0.9 target (e.g. below 0.85).

title: EvoMemBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective

official.background: LLM agents are stateless, so memory modules (retrieval stores, long-term memory systems, procedural/skill memories) are added to keep information beyond the context window. These methods are usually evaluated on different tasks and protocols, so it is unclear when memory actually helps compared with simply giving a strong model the raw context. EvoMemBench evaluates 15 memory methods under one protocol along two axes: in-episode vs. cross-episode, and knowledge-oriented vs. execution-oriented memory.
official.method:
The in-episode knowledge setting (InEp-Know) uses the Accurate Retrieval subsets (EventQA, LongMemEval S*, RULER qa1, RULER qa2; 1000 samples in total) and the Selective Forgetting subsets (FactConsolidation multi-hop and single-hop; 200 samples) of MemoryAgentBench. Information arrives as progressive blocks in an incremental multi-turn format; for retention the agent must answer from earlier blocks, and for revision (FactConsolidation) later facts contradict earlier ones and the answer must reflect the update. The metric is answer accuracy.

Every memory method wraps DeepSeek-V3.2 with two interfaces: update (called after each information block, memory reset at the start of each episode) and utilize (returns retrieved entries or a working context that is put into the prompt). Retrieval top-k is 10 for knowledge tasks, and the default embedding backend is DashScope text-embedding-v4 (BM25 is lexical). The memory-free baseline is DeepSeek-V3.2 given the raw context directly. Memory methods compared: BM25, Qwen3-Emb-4B, GraphRAG, MemAgent, MemoBrain, Mem0, A-MEM, MemOS, MemoryOS.
official.claim: With the same DeepSeek-V3.2 backbone on InEp-Know, BM25 memory improves accuracy on all four retention subsets over the no-memory baseline (e.g. LongMemEval 50.33 vs. 32.33, RULER qa2 55.0 vs. 42.0), yet on FactConsolidation single-hop revision every one of the 9 memory methods scores below the no-memory baseline (best 54.0 vs. 65.0).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Answer accuracy (%) and ranking comparison on InEp-Know. Lower ranks indicate better performance. All memory-augmented methods use DeepSeek-V3.2 as the backbone.
official.metric: Answer accuracy (%), higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported

title: Monitoring the Internal Monologue: Probe Trajectories Reveal Reasoning Dynamics

official.background: Large reasoning models write a chain-of-thought (CoT) before answering, and monitoring that text is a proposed safety tool. But the CoT is not always faithful to the final answer: the authors find that 3-12% of CoTs look safe while the response is harmful, or the reverse. Probes on the model's hidden states during the prompt and CoT are an alternative, but it is unclear how to read a probe over a very long reasoning trace: at a single token (usually the last), or pooled over all tokens.
official.method:
Probes are trained on WildGuardMix and evaluated on WildGuardTest. The input is the prompt plus the model's own CoT, and the label is whether the model's final response is harmful according to the WildGuard classifier. In the 'Template-Based' training regime, WildGuardMix (prompt, response) pairs are inserted into a fixed template ('The below is a conversation between a user and an assistant. The assistant's response may contain potentially harmful content. USER: {prompt} ASSISTANT: {response} The above content is'), and the probe is trained on the target model's hidden states for that text with the dataset's labels. No model-generated CoT is used for training. Other regimes (raw messages, response-only template, the model's own generated messages) are also reported.

Three readouts are compared. Max pooling is a multiple-instance-learning (MIL) meta-probe: on every second layer from a mid layer upward (e.g. Qwen3-4B layers 9-35), a per-token GELU MLP [1024, 512, 256] is followed by max-pooling over tokens and a linear head, and the per-layer logits are combined by a learned linear meta-layer (AdamW, lr 1e-3 cosine, 5 epochs, batch 32, max length 8192). The Average-Pooling and Last-Token baselines (Appendix K) follow the multi-layer latent prototype probe of Chrabaszcz et al.: a Gaussian discriminant classifier per layer on the mean-pooled (or final-token) hidden state, with per-layer scores combined by L1-regularised logistic regression, evaluated in float32. LLM-as-a-judge baselines (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-Next-80B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash) read the CoT and predict whether the final response will be harmful. The metric is AUROC on WildGuardTest.
official.claim: On WildGuardTest with template-based training, pooled probes predict final-response harmfulness much better than last-token probes. For Qwen3-4B the AUROCs are 96.6 ± 0.9 (max pooling) and 95.3 ± 1.2 (average pooling) vs. 53.0 ± 4.5 (last token); for Qwen3-8B 94.5 / 92.1 vs. 70.4; for R1-Llama-8B 94.5 / 92.1 vs. 68.4. On these models max pooling also beats the best LLM-as-a-judge baseline (86.3, 83.3 and 85.2).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Harmfulness AUROC on WildGuardTest demonstrating that template-based training is highly efficient. Pooling over the reasoning trace is important for predicting future harm: pooled representations achieve better performance compared to reading the probe at a single token.
official.metric: AUROC (%) for predicting whether the final response is harmful, higher is better; ± is the bootstrap standard error of the mean (Appendix G.2)
official.comparison: Max-pooling MIL probe and average-pooling probe vs. last-token probe (same training data, same model), plus LLM-as-a-judge on the CoT; the cleanest like-for-like pair is average pooling vs. last token, which use the same Gaussian-discriminant probe family
official.falsification_criterion: With template-based WildGuardMix training and WildGuardTest evaluation on Qwen3-4B (or Qwen3-8B / R1-Llama-8B), the last-token probe comes within ~10 AUROC points of the average- or max-pooled probe, or the pooled probes fall below ~90 AUROC.

title: PACE: Geometry-Aware Bridge Transport for Single-Cell Trajectory Inference
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (per-timepoint values in Appendix Tables A.5-A.7, page 16)

official.background: Single-cell RNA sequencing destroys the cells it measures, so time-course experiments give unpaired population snapshots at a few time points rather than individual cell trajectories. Trajectory inference must infer which cells at one time become which cells at the next and the continuous paths between them, which is not identifiable from the marginals alone. Optimal transport and flow-matching methods usually couple cells by Euclidean proximity, which can pair cells at different developmental stages when development is asynchronous. A method that recovers held-out intermediate snapshots more accurately would give better models of differentiation and reprogramming without extra experiments such as lineage tracing or RNA velocity.
official.method:
PACE builds a state- and time-dependent anisotropic metric G(x,t) = I + alpha * C_N(x,t), where C_N is a space-time Gaussian-weighted average of local normal-direction projectors estimated by local PCA on nearest neighbours within each snapshot; velocity components normal to the local data manifold are penalized by a factor (1+alpha). Between adjacent snapshots it trains an endpoint-preserving neural bridge gamma(x,y,tau) = (1-tau)x + tau*y + tau(1-tau)psi(x,y,tau) to minimize the path action under G, and periodically (every 10 or 20 epochs) recomputes the OT coupling using the learned path-action cost instead of Euclidean distance. The bridge dynamics are then distilled into a global velocity field v(x,t), which is integrated from the first snapshot to predict held-out time points.

Evaluation leaves out intermediate time points during training and compares the predicted point cloud with the observed one at those times using MMD (Gaussian kernel, median bandwidth, square root reported), W1 and W2. Table 2 reports time-averaged results on EB PHATE (2D PHATE embedding, holdout t=3), iPSC-Liu (2D PCA, holdouts t=4,16) and Schiebinger2019 mouse reprogramming (2D, holdouts t=6,11,16) against Action Matching, Aligned CFM, Curly Flow Matching, DMSB, Metric Flow Matching and OT-CFM.
official.claim: On held-out snapshots of 2D single-cell time courses, PACE achieves the lowest time-averaged MMD, W1 and W2 on all three datasets; e.g. on Schiebinger2019 MMD 0.2084 vs. 0.3030 for the best baseline (DMSB), and on EB PHATE MMD 0.0674 vs. 0.1056 for the best baseline (Aligned CFM).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Time-averaged low-dimensional single-cell results. EB [18] uses t = 3, iPSC-Liu [21] uses t ∈ {4, 16}, and Schiebinger2019 [3] uses t ∈ {6, 11, 16}.
official.metric: MMD, W1, W2 between predicted and observed held-out point clouds, averaged over held-out time points (lower is better); no ± reported (single runs, no seeds or intervals)
official.comparison: PACE vs. Action Matching, Aligned CFM, CURLY (Curly Flow Matching), DMSB, MFM (Metric Flow Matching), OT-CFM under the same held-out-snapshot protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running PACE and the strongest baseline per dataset (Aligned CFM on EB PHATE, DMSB on Schiebinger2019, Aligned CFM/OT-CFM on iPSC-Liu) over several seeds, the best baseline matches or beats PACE on time-averaged MMD or W2 on any of the three datasets, or PACE's advantage falls within the seed-to-seed spread.

title: Articulation in Prime: Primitive-Based Articulated Object Understanding from a Single Casual Video

official.background: An articulated object, such as a laptop, drawer or fan, is made of rigid parts connected by revolute (rotating) or prismatic (sliding) joints. Recovering its part segmentation and joint parameters from a single casually captured video would make it easy to build digital twins for robotics and simulation. Existing single-video methods depend on long-term point tracks or wide-baseline matches, which break under strong camera motion and occlusion. Learning-based methods, on the other hand, generalize poorly beyond the object categories they were trained on.
official.method:
The input is a sequence of depth maps and camera poses (on synthetic data these are ground truth; on real video they come from ViPE, with SAM2 object masks), back-projected to per-frame partial point clouds in world coordinates (T = 25 frames, N = 4096 points per frame). The object is represented by up to Q = 10 convex superquadric primitives, which are softly assigned to up to P = 8 parts. Half of the candidate parts carry a revolute joint and half a prismatic joint, each parameterized as a screw/twist vector with a per-frame motion amount. Points are assigned to primitives through a small MLP on the 3D coordinates combined with learned per-primitive features. Unused parts and primitives are pruned through existence probabilities, so the number of parts and the joint types are discovered automatically.

Everything is optimized jointly with Adam (10k steps, lr 5e-3). The losses are a visibility-aware two-way reconstruction loss (only the primitive surface points visible to the camera are counted, with soft occlusion computed by Nvdiffrast z-buffering), an L1 scene-flow loss against GMSF scene flow, and sparsity, existence, smoothness and entropy regularizers. Five seeds are run per object, and the run with the lowest final loss is kept. On AiP-synth (16 PartNet-Mobility objects rendered with SAPIEN along circular or ping-pong camera trajectories with heavy occlusion), the method is compared with Video2Articulation, ReArt and Articulate-Anything, which the authors ran themselves. The metrics are part mIoU, joint-axis angle error, pivot point-to-line distance, motion-state L1 error and joint-type accuracy.
official.claim: On the AiP-synth benchmark, for revolute joints, the primitive-fitting method achieves a joint-axis error of 0.52 ± 1.38° and a part mIoU of 0.85 ± 0.20. The best baseline, Video2Articulation, gets 51.20 ± 34.99° and 0.48 ± 0.31, and joint-type accuracy is 100% vs. at most 33.3% for the baselines.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative results on the AiP-synth dataset. 'N/A' means the method does not predict the metric. 'F' means the method fails on the category. Best results are in bold.
official.metric: Joint-axis angle error in degrees (lower is better), part mIoU (higher is better), pivot position error in cm, motion-state L1 error, and joint-type accuracy in %. ± appears to be the standard deviation across objects/sequences in the benchmark, not across seeds. No seed variance is reported, and the method keeps the best of 5 seeds by final loss.
official.comparison: The method (Ours) vs. Video2Articulation, ReArt and Articulate-Anything, all run on the same AiP-synth sequences, split into revolute and prismatic joints.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the method on AiP-synth-style sequences (PartNet-Mobility objects rendered with circular or ping-pong camera trajectories) gives a mean revolute axis error comparable to Video2Articulation's (tens of degrees), or a revolute mIoU not clearly above 0.48. Equivalently, the best baseline run under the same inputs comes within the reported spread of the method.

title: Efficient Lookahead Encoding and Abstracted Width for Learning General Policies in Classical Planning

official.background: Generalized planning aims to learn a single policy that solves every instance of a classical planning domain (Blocksworld, Rovers, etc.), including instances far larger than those seen in training. Relational graph neural networks (R-GNNs) trained with Q-learning can learn such policies, but their expressivity is limited (roughly C2 logic). Prior work (Aichmüller and Geffner, 2025) let the policy choose among states reachable by an IW(1) width-based lookahead search ('jumps') rather than primitive actions, which simplifies the problem. That approach encoded each successor state separately, which is expensive in memory and compute, and IW(1) itself becomes slow on the very large instances of the IPC 2023 Learning Track (e.g., 488-block Blocksworld).
official.method:
The paper makes two changes. (1) Aggregated-Delta (AD) encoding: instead of running the R-GNN on the current state s and each successor s' separately (the 'External' encoding), the whole lookahead tree is encoded as one relational graph. The current state is encoded fully (with goal-true/goal-false atoms); each successor s' gets its own state object node connected only to the atoms it adds and deletes relative to s, plus tree-edge atoms between parent/child successors and depth nodes with ordering atoms. One forward pass gives Q(s, s') = MLP(f(o_s'), sum over objects f(o)) for every successor. An auxiliary pairwise ranking loss over depth-node scores enforces depth order. (2) Abstracted IW(1) (AIW): during the novelty check, each ground atom P(o1..on) is abstracted n ways by replacing all but one argument with its type; the atom is novel if any abstracted form is novel. Atoms that appear in the goal are not abstracted. This makes the number of novel atoms linear in the number of objects.

All learned policies (AIW-AD, IW-AD, AIW-Ext, IW-Ext, Flat-AA) use the same R-GNN (embedding size 32, smooth-max aggregation, Mish MLPs) and the same deep Q-learning with lifted hindsight relabeling, reward -1 per transition, Boltzmann exploration, 5 seeds per method and domain, 12 h limit on one A10/L40S GPU. The best of 5 checkpoints (selected by validation coverage) is tested greedily, with no backtracking, on the 90 test instances per IPC 2023 domain (30 easy / 30 medium / 30 hard), with a 1000-choice limit and 60 min timeout for IW-policies (15 min for flat). LAMA gets 1 h and 90 GB per instance. Distincter and GOOSE numbers are copied from their papers.
official.claim: On the IPC 2023 Learning Track test set (10 domains x 90 instances), the greedy AIW-AD policy solves 668/900 instances (74%), versus 463/900 (51%) for the direct baseline IW-Ext, 529 for IW-AD, 457 for AIW-Ext, 519 for the flat Flat-AA policy, and 586 for the LAMA planner run under the authors' setup.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: IPC 2023 benchmark coverage results for AIW with AD encoding (highlighted in bold) against ablations and baselines. Methods marked * perform exponential search at test time. Numbers in parentheses are percentages of row totals.
official.metric: Coverage = number of test instances solved (higher is better), out of 90 per domain and 900 total. No error bars; for each learned method the best of 5 checkpoints from 5 training seeds (selected on validation coverage) is reported.
official.comparison: AIW-AD vs. IW-Ext (prior IW-policy method with External encoding, retrained with the same pipeline), vs. the single-change ablations IW-AD and AIW-Ext, vs. Flat-AA (primitive-action policy), and vs. LAMA (classical planner, 1 h / 90 GB). Distincter and GOOSE are copied from their papers and are not matched comparisons.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining with the described setup, AIW-AD's total coverage does not exceed IW-Ext's by a wide margin (e.g., gap under ~50 instances), or it does not exceed LAMA's coverage. For a single-domain check, AIW-AD fails to solve clearly more hard Blocksworld (30/30 vs. 0/30) or hard Spanner (30/30 vs. 1/30) instances than IW-Ext.

title: Spectral Progressive Diffusion for Efficient Image and Video Generation
claim_source: Table 6, page 27 (Appendix D.2); a subset appears in Table 2, page 6

official.background: Diffusion transformers spend most of their compute on self-attention over all image tokens at every denoising step, so cost grows quickly with resolution. Diffusion models are known to generate content roughly from low to high frequency: early, noisy steps only resolve coarse structure, while high-frequency detail is still buried in noise. In principle, the early steps could therefore run at lower resolution without losing anything. Existing progressive-resolution methods either need architectural changes and training from scratch, or rely on hand-tuned upsampling heuristics. The question here is whether pretrained flow-matching image and video models can be sped up substantially by growing resolution along a single denoising trajectory while keeping quality.
official.method:
Generation starts at a reduced resolution (for S = 2 on 1024^2 Z-Image: 64^2 latent, then 128^2 latent). At a transition time t_i the current state is transformed with an orthonormal DCT, its coefficients are placed in the low-frequency slots of a larger spectrum, the new high-frequency slots are filled with t_i * N(0,1) noise, and the result is inverse-DCT'd to the higher resolution (spectral noise expansion). The state is then rescaled and the timestep re-indexed (Eqs. 5-6) so that the higher noise level matches the pretrained model's schedule, and the ODE continues. Transition times come from the measured latent power spectrum: t_i is the time when the highest frequency representable at scale s_i stops being noise-dominated, controlled by a single tolerance delta (0.01 by default).

Fine-tuning variant (Sec. 4.3, App. D.2): a rank-32 LoRA on Z-Image is trained for 2000 iterations (batch 8, lr 1e-4, DiffSynth Studio defaults) with stage-specific straight-line velocity targets. These run from the expanded, timestep-aligned state at the start of each resolution stage to the standard flow-matching state at the next transition time, using a shared noise sample. Training data is 5K synthetic images from 50-step full-resolution Z-Image on MS-COCO prompts disjoint from the evaluation prompts. Evaluation follows the RALU protocol: ImageReward, CLIP-IQA and NIQE on 5,000 MS-COCO validation prompts, plus T2I-CompBench and GenEval. Speedups are wall-clock relative to 50-step Z-Image on one H100.
official.claim: On Z-Image at 1024^2, Spectral Progressive Diffusion with LoRA fine-tuning (delta = 0.01, S = 2) at 678.77 TFLOPs (7.81x speedup) reaches ImageReward 0.918, versus 0.763 for the 7-step full-resolution Z-Image baseline at 701.92 TFLOPs (5.97x); in the 10-step tier it gets 0.923 vs. 0.851 at 962.95 vs. 997.68 TFLOPs.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Quantitative comparisons on latent-space image generation with fine-tuning. We evaluate Z-Image at 1024^2 resolution and group methods into wall-clock speedup tiers. Speedup is calculated relative to the 50-step Z-Image baseline wall-clock runtime on a single H100 GPU. T and S denote temporal and spatial acceleration methods, respectively. All metrics are evaluated using the same protocol as Table 1.
official.metric: ImageReward (higher is better) averaged over 5,000 MS-COCO validation prompts; CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T2I-CompBench, GenEval as secondary. No error bars, standard deviations or seed variation are reported.
official.comparison: Ours (LoRA, delta=0.01, S=2) and Ours (training-free, S=2) vs. Z-Image run with fewer denoising steps at full resolution (10 and 7 steps), at matched FLOPs within each speedup tier
official.falsification_criterion: At equal or lower FLOPs than 7-step full-resolution Z-Image, the LoRA-fine-tuned progressive sampler does not beat the 7-step baseline's ImageReward on the 5K MS-COCO prompts by a clear margin (e.g., the gap is below about 0.05, or within the spread across generation seeds), or it loses on GenEval and T2I-CompBench as well.

title: Vision-OPD: Learning to See Fine Details for Multimodal LLMs via On-Policy Self-Distillation

official.background: Multimodal LLMs often get fine-grained visual questions wrong when the answer depends on a small region of a large image. The authors show that the same model answers these questions 18 to 22 points more accurately on ZoomBench when it is given an evidence-centered crop instead of the full image. 'Thinking-with-Images' agents close part of this gap by cropping and zooming at inference time, but each crop costs extra encoding and model calls. The paper asks whether this zooming benefit can instead be trained into a single full-image forward pass.
official.method:
Training data: 6.2K synthetic triplets (full image x with the target region outlined by a red box, a 2x-resized crop x' of that region, and a question q about the region). Qwen3.5-397B writes q from the crop, and the spatial instruction 'Only focus on the objects inside the red bounding box' is appended. Vision-OPD needs no answers. For the baselines, Qwen3.5-397B also produces majority-vote answer labels, and a question is kept only when more than 75% of its sampled answers agree.

Vision-OPD uses one MLLM (Qwen3.5-4B or 9B, non-thinking mode) as both student and teacher. The student sees (x, q) and samples an on-policy response of up to 1024 tokens. Along that response, the loss is the token-level JSD (beta = 0.5) between the student's next-token distribution and the teacher's distribution, where the teacher sees (x', q). The divergence is computed over the student's top-100 logits plus a tail-probability term. Gradients flow only through the student. The teacher is an EMA of the student (alpha = 0.05). Training runs for 1 epoch. The baselines use the same data and backbone: SFT on the self-teacher's successful crop-conditioned generations, GRPO and DAPO with binary rewards against the labels, and OPSD (on-policy self-distillation that uses ground-truth labels).
official.claim: With the same 6.2K training samples and backbone, Vision-OPD beats the best of SFT, GRPO, DAPO and OPSD on V* Bench and ZoomBench: Qwen3.5-4B reaches 92.15 vs. 85.34 (V*) and 59.76 vs. 55.74 (ZoomBench), and Qwen3.5-9B reaches 94.76 vs. 89.53 (V*) and 65.80 vs. 58.46 (ZoomBench).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison with SFT, RLVR methods and OPSD. Vision-OPD consistently outperforms all baselines while maintaining strong performance on holdout tasks.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on each benchmark, higher is better; single runs, with no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: Vision-OPD vs. SFT on self-teacher, GRPO, DAPO and OPSD (and the untrained Vanilla model), all trained on the same data from the same Qwen3.5-4B or 9B checkpoint
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining at the 4B scale, Vision-OPD fails to beat the best of SFT, GRPO, DAPO and OPSD on V* Bench or ZoomBench, or its margin falls within the run-to-run spread across seeds.

title: DashAttention: Differentiable and Adaptive Sparse Hierarchical Attention

official.background: Hierarchical trainable sparse attention methods such as NSA and InfLLMv2 make long-context LLMs cheaper by summarizing the KV cache into chunks, picking the top-k chunks per query with coarse scores, and then running exact softmax attention only on the selected tokens. The fixed top-k budget ignores that different queries, heads and layers need different amounts of context, and the hard selection cuts the gradient path between the routing stage and the fine attention stage. These methods only pay off if the sparse kernels are actually faster than dense FlashAttention at realistic context lengths, and top-k selection plus index materialization adds overhead that can eat into the savings.
official.method:
DashAttention has three stages. Stage 0 summarizes each chunk of B = 64 keys with a local softmax attention driven by a learned per-KV-head query (initialized at zero, so it starts as mean pooling). Stage 1 scores the query against the chunk summaries and applies alpha-entmax (alpha = 1.5) instead of top-k, giving a sparse, query-dependent set of chunks; with GQA the entmax probabilities are averaged over each group's query heads, and the support is stored as a bit-packed int32 mask plus a per-chunk log-prior bias d. Stage 2 is a masked FlashAttention-style kernel that walks the bit-packed mask in one fused pass and adds d to the logits before the online softmax. All three stages are fused Triton kernels.

For the efficiency benchmark (Sec. 5.2, App. B.2) the authors time the attention kernels alone on one NVIDIA GH200 (CUDA 13.2, PyTorch 2.10.0, Triton 3.6.0, bf16, torch.compile, Triton do_bench), with 32 query heads, 2 KV heads, head dim 128, chunk size 64. They sweep context N in {16K, 32K, 64K, 96K} and chunk sparsity s in {75%, 87.5%, 93.75%}; top-k baselines use k = (1 - s) * N / 64, and DashAttention's Stage 2 mask is replaced by a random bit-packed mask at the target sparsity. Prefill uses batch size 1, decoding batch size 24. Speedup is reported relative to dense FlashAttention-3; NSA uses an open-source Triton implementation and InfLLMv2 its official kernel.
official.claim: At 75% chunk sparsity in prefill (batch 1, 32 query / 2 KV heads, d = 128, chunk 64, GH200), DashAttention's kernels run 1.34x, 1.39x, 1.55x and 1.63x faster than FlashAttention-3 at 16K, 32K, 64K and 96K tokens, while InfLLMv2 reaches only 0.96-1.04x and NSA 0.71-0.82x; DashAttention is also fastest in every decoding cell (e.g. 3.36x vs 3.10x for InfLLMv2 at 96K, 93.75% sparsity).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Wall-clock speedup over full attention with FlashAttention (higher is better). Columns are chunk sparsity s, the fraction of chunks not routed to Stage 2; the corresponding top-k is (1-s)·N/64. Iv2 denotes InfLLMv2 and DA denotes DashAttention. Best results in bold.
official.metric: Wall-clock speedup over dense FlashAttention-3 (higher is better), measured with Triton do_bench; no error bars or run-to-run variance reported
official.comparison: DashAttention vs. InfLLMv2 (official kernel) and NSA (open-source Triton implementation), each normalized to FlashAttention-3, at matched chunk size and matched chunk sparsity
