title: D-PACE: Dynamic Position-Aware Cross-Entropy for Parallel Speculative Drafting

official.background: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by letting a small draft model propose tokens that the large target model verifies in one forward pass. Verification is prefix-based, so a wrong draft token rejects everything after it. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash predict all B tokens of a block in a single forward pass, and they are trained with cross-entropy weighted by a fixed exponential decay over block positions. A fixed schedule cannot follow which positions actually limit acceptance as the drafter improves. The number of draft tokens accepted per block (emitted length) is the main factor behind the wall-clock speedup.
official.method:
D-PACE keeps the DFlash drafter architecture and inference unchanged and replaces only the training loss. Let q_i be the draft's probability of the target-selected token at block position i. The expected accepted length is approximated by the surrogate S = sum_k prod_{i<=k} q_i. Differentiating S gives per-position weights w_j = (prod_{i<=j} q_i) * f_j, where f_j = 1 + sum_{m>j} prod_{i=j+1..m} q_i. To keep the weights from vanishing, each q_i is smoothed only inside the weight, as q~_i = (1-alpha) q_i + alpha with alpha = 0.5. This gives w̄_j = sum_{m>=j} prod_{i<=m} q~_i, which is detached from the gradient. The loss is sum_j w̄_j * (-log q_j), with an unsmoothed cross-entropy term.

Main setting: target Qwen3-4B (thinking mode off), 3-layer DFlash drafter, block size B=16, trained on the DFlash authors' Qwen3-4B-Instruct-100K dataset (Nemotron-Post-Training-v2 + CodeAlpaca prompts with target-generated responses) in SpecForge. Training uses AdamW at lr 6e-4, effective batch 4, sequence length 2048, 512 anchor positions and 6 epochs on one H200. The baseline is the same training with DFlash's decayed CE, exp(-(j-1)/7). Evaluation uses DFlash's benchmark code on GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval, MBPP, MT-Bench and Alpaca. It reports average emitted length tau and wall-clock speedup SR over autoregressive decoding, measured on an L40S.
official.claim: For a 3-layer DFlash drafter of Qwen3-4B (B=16, epoch 6, greedy T=0), training with D-PACE instead of DFlash's decayed cross-entropy raises the six-benchmark average emitted length from 4.10 to 4.52 (+10.2%) and the average speedup from 2.93x to 3.20x, and tau improves on all six benchmarks (e.g. MATH-500 5.44 -> 6.12).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main result. Decoding speedup (SR) and average emitted length (τ) on six benchmarks at two draft depths (3L, 5L) and two temperatures (T=0, 1) for DFlash drafts of Qwen3-4B at epoch 6. "Top-3 prefix mask" is the hard-mask baseline adapted from GRIFFIN [10]. "Accept-rate" directly optimizes the accepted-length surrogate in Eq. 4; see Sec. 4.1 and App. B.
official.metric: Average emitted length tau (accepted tokens per verification step, higher is better) and wall-clock speedup SR over autoregressive decoding (higher is better). Single run per setting, with no seeds, std or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: D-PACE loss vs. DFlash decayed-CE loss (also vs. Top-3 prefix mask and Accept-rate), with the same drafter architecture, data, hyperparameters and number of epochs
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained under matched conditions, the D-PACE drafter's six-benchmark average tau is not clearly above the decayed-CE baseline (e.g. less than about 3% higher), or D-PACE fails to beat the baseline on most of the six benchmarks.

title: Multi-Token Residual Prediction

official.background: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text by repeatedly denoising a masked sequence, revealing several tokens per backbone forward pass. Revealing more tokens per step raises throughput but lowers quality, because tokens revealed together are decoded without seeing each other. In threshold-based (dynamic) decoding, every masked position whose top-1 confidence exceeds a threshold tau is revealed at once. Low thresholds are fast but commit many premature tokens and accuracy drops sharply. A cheap way to catch those premature reveals would make aggressive thresholds usable.
official.method:
MRP (Multi-token Residual Prediction) is a small 3-layer transformer attached to a frozen block-diffusion backbone (SDAR-Chat 1.7B/4B/8B, block size 16). It takes the backbone's hidden states and the token embeddings of the sequence after the new tokens are revealed, and predicts the residual delta between the backbone logits at the current step and at the next denoising step. Corrected logits are l + delta, computed with the backbone's frozen LM head. It is trained by forward KL between softmax(l_{t-1}) (a second backbone pass on the sequence with ground-truth tokens revealed) and softmax(l_t + delta_t), restricted to still-masked positions, on SFTDatasetV3 for one epoch (AdamW, lr 1e-3, K=2 unrolled MRP steps).

Remasking mode (Algorithm 4): at each step the backbone reveals the set R of masked positions with confidence above tau. One MRP forward then predicts the next-step logits l + delta, and any position in R whose corrected confidence falls below the same tau is masked again. Both methods use the WINO max-accept cap m = min(max(floor(0.7 n), 5), L). The baseline is plain threshold-based dynamic decoding at the same tau. Evaluation follows the SDAR protocol: greedy decoding, max 4096 generated tokens, GSM8K and MATH500 (0-shot CoT), HumanEval and MBPP (0-shot), in SGLang on one H100.
official.claim: With threshold-based dynamic decoding at tau = 0.5 on SDAR-Chat backbones, MRP Remask raises accuracy over plain dynamic decoding by at least 11 points on every benchmark and scale, e.g. on SDAR-1.7B GSM8K from 41.6% to 59.1% (+17.5) and on SDAR-8B HumanEval from 32.3% to 54.9% (+22.6).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: MRP remasking improves the accuracy of low-threshold dynamic decoding. For each SDAR backbone (1.7B/4B/8B) and unmasking threshold tau, we report task accuracy (%, ↑) for plain threshold-based Dynamic decoding (Dyn.; our baseline) and for MRP Remask (Remask; our approach), which reuses the MRP-corrected confidence to remask over-eager reveals with the same tau for both the reveal and the remask (no extra tuning). Next to each Remask value we report its accuracy change over Dynamic at matched tau (green: gain, red: loss).
official.metric: Task accuracy (%), higher is better. Greedy decoding, single run; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: MRP Remask vs. plain threshold-based dynamic decoding at matched threshold tau (same backbone, same max-accept cap, same benchmark), for tau in {0.5,...,0.9} and SDAR 1.7B/4B/8B.
official.falsification_criterion: At tau = 0.5, MRP Remask improves accuracy over plain dynamic decoding by less than about 5 points (or not at all) on SDAR-1.7B GSM8K or on any of the four benchmarks at a given scale, with the paper's released MRP weights and decoding settings.

title: Hybrid-LoRA: Bridging Full Fine-Tuning and Low-Rank Adaptation for Post-Training

official.background: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO, GSPO) is now a standard way to post-train LLMs for reasoning, but doing it with full fine-tuning (FFT) is memory- and compute-hungry. LoRA is far cheaper but usually leaves a gap to FFT on hard reasoning tasks. Prior LoRA variants (AdaLoRA, AutoLoRA, LoRA-Drop) reallocate rank within the low-rank space. This paper instead asks which individual linear modules should be fully fine-tuned and which can be left to LoRA, under a fixed budget of fully fine-tuned parameters.
official.method:
Hybrid-LoRA has two stages. In the probing stage, SVD-style LoRA (rank 16, x A E B with a diagonal coefficient vector e, as in AdaLoRA) is attached to all seven linear module types (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) in every layer, and only LoRA is trained for 500 warm-up steps. Then, for each validation batch, the module set is randomly split into two halves; two backward passes are run, each with one half disabled, and each module's batch score is s = (1/r)·||e ⊙ ∇_e L_val||_1 from the pass where it was active. Over batches, the Hybrid-Score is H = mean(s)·std(s). Modules are sorted by H ascending and the lowest-scoring ones are assigned to full fine-tuning until they reach 10% of the candidate-module parameters; all others get LoRA.

In the final stage the model is reinitialised from the pretrained checkpoint and post-trained with GRPO (or GSPO) on Mixture-of-Thoughts, with lr 1e-6 for FFT modules and 2.5e-5 for LoRA modules, group size 4, clip 0.2, KL 0.01, temperature 1.0, keeping the checkpoint with lowest validation loss (evaluated every 50 steps). The baselines AdaLoRA, AutoLoRA and LoRA-Drop use the same hybrid setup but pick the bottom 10% of modules by their own criterion (allocated rank, learned architecture weight alpha, LoRA output contribution) for FFT, keeping the number of tunable parameters comparable (105-106M on Qwen2.5-1.5B).
official.claim: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct post-trained with GRPO under a matched ~105M tunable-parameter budget, Hybrid-LoRA beats the best of AdaLoRA/AutoLoRA/LoRA-Drop module selection on all six benchmarks, e.g. Math-500 pass@1 80.2 vs 77.4, AIME-24 pass@4 38.0 vs 34.7, GPQA 37.3 vs 35.1, and comes within 2.0 points of full fine-tuning on every benchmark.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Overall reasoning benchmark performance. Full-FT (ref.) is the full-parameter reference.
official.metric: Math-500 pass@1, AIME-24/25 pass@4, LeetCodeDataset pass@4, MMLU-Pro and GPQA accuracy (all %, higher is better). Single run per cell; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: Hybrid-LoRA vs. AdaLoRA-, AutoLoRA- and LoRA-Drop-based module selection (same 10% FFT budget, rest LoRA), all with GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct; GRPO full fine-tuning as reference.
official.falsification_criterion: Under matched GRPO training on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, the best baseline selection criterion matches or beats Hybrid-LoRA on Math-500 (within about 1 point) or on most of the six benchmarks, or the gain disappears across repeated seeds.

title: TwinRouterBench: Fast Static and Live Dynamic Evaluation for Realistic Agentic LLM Routing

official.background: LLM routers send each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. In agentic applications such as coding agents, one user task triggers many LLM calls, so routing each call separately could save much more than routing a whole query. Existing router benchmarks (RouterBench, LLMRouterBench, RouterArena) only score one-shot prompts. They never show the router the intermediate prefix of an agent trajectory (history, tool outputs, shell logs, partial edits), and they never check whether a cheaper model at step i breaks the task later. TwinRouterBench provides step-level routing labels with an offline scorer, plus a live SWE-bench track that measures real task resolution and real API spend.
official.method:
Static track: 970 router-visible prefixes from 520 successful strong-model trajectories (SWE-bench, BFCL, mtRAG, QMSum, PinchBench). Each prefix is labelled with the cheapest of four tiers (low, mid, mid_high, high; 11-model pool) found by a greedy sequential downgrade search. A step's downgrade is accepted if, with all earlier steps locked at their verified tiers and later steps at the strong tier, at least one of three pool models in that tier still lets the full trajectory pass without needing more LLM-call steps. The trained router ('UncommonRoute (trained)') encodes the latest user request with a frozen BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 embedding, concatenates routing metadata (message count, tool-call presence, tool-message count, request length, code/question indicators), and fits an L2-regularized multinomial logistic regression on a training split of the static labels (C chosen by 5-fold CV, plus a separate calibration split).

Dynamic track: 100 locked SWE-bench Verified instances (18 Astropy, 82 Django), disjoint from the static SWE split and not a random sample. They are run end to end with mini-swe-agent v2.2.8. At every LLM call the policy picks a concrete model from the locked pool. Scoring uses the official SWE-bench resolution predicate and realized OpenRouter API cost (input, cache_read, cache_write and output buckets). The leaderboard bill adds a flat $0.60 penalty per unresolved instance. Policies compared: unrouted Claude Opus 4.6, the rule-based UncommonRoute, an SR-KNN semantic router, and the trained UncommonRoute.
official.claim: On the locked 100-instance SWE-bench Verified list with mini-swe-agent, the logistic router trained on the static-track labels resolves 75/100 instances for $25.66 total realized API cost, versus 74/100 for $54.73 with unrouted Claude Opus 4.6 (53.1% lower cost). Its leaderboard bill is $40.66 vs. $70.33.
official.claim_caption: Table 3. Dynamic-track results on the locked 100-case leaderboard list (18 Astropy and 82 Django), not a random sample of SWE-bench Verified. API cost is the realized routed API spend; Penalty cost is $0.60× the number of unresolved instances, where γ=0.60 is the per-case price of a hypothetical perfect solver (§5.2); Leaderboard bill (sort key, lower is better) is API cost + Penalty cost. The penalty applies uniformly to every policy. The unrouted Opus 4.6 baseline is separated below the routing policies, mirroring the cost-envelope row in Table 2.
official.metric: Resolved instances out of 100 (official SWE-bench predicate, higher is better) and total realized API cost in USD (lower is better). Leaderboard bill = API cost + $0.60 per unresolved instance. Single run per policy, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: UncommonRoute (trained on static labels) vs. Opus 4.6 with no routing (also vs. SR-KNN router and rule-based UncommonRoute) on the same 100 instances and harness
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both policies on the same 100 instances, the trained router either resolves clearly fewer instances than unrouted Opus 4.6 (e.g. 5+ fewer) or its realized API cost is not substantially lower (e.g. less than ~30% saving), so that its leaderboard bill is not clearly below Opus's.

title: Mapping Uncharted Symmetries: Machine Discovery in Combinatorics

official.background: In q,t-combinatorics, one seeks pairs of simple statistics on a set of combinatorial objects whose joint distribution reproduces a given bivariate polynomial, here the q,t-Narayana polynomials N_{n,k}(q,t). Often one statistic is known and a partner is missing, and finding one is hard. The authors frame this as 'Simple Learning Under Rigid Proportions' (SLURP): find a simple function on a domain split into bags so that the outputs within each bag exactly match a prescribed distribution. They ask whether ML can propose such statistics, which mathematicians can then prove correct.
official.method:
Skip-pairing benchmark: noncrossing partitions in NC(14,3) (2366 partitions) are grouped into 144 bags by (m, skip), where skip is a fixed statistic (Eq. 2) and m is the largest element in a non-singleton block. Within each bag, the number of partitions with stat = v must equal the corresponding coefficient of the incremental polynomial N_{m,3}(q,t) - N_{m-1,3}(q,t). The goal is a statistic satisfying all bag constraints exactly.

MapSeek-Functional: a Transformer encoder (8 layers, 4 heads, hidden size 128, FF size 256), with the partition's block-adjacency matrix used as an attention mask in alternating layers, outputs a score matrix S whose sum is the predicted statistic. Training alternates two steps. Projection: within each bag, sort partitions by model output and assign pseudo-labels matching the required multiplicities, greedily enforcing h-homogeneity (adding 1 to every element of each non-singleton block raises the statistic by h). Update: one epoch of BCE training toward the top-v entries of S (Adam, lr 1e-4, batch size 32). A held-out validation split goes through projection but not gradient updates. A run succeeds only if all constraints are met exactly within 1000 iterations. Table 1 sweeps the validation split for h = 2, with 50 runs per setting, and counts runs whose predictions match the mag statistic (Eq. 3) exactly on all 2366 partitions.
official.claim: On the refined N_{14,3} skip-pairing dataset with h = 2 homogeneity, MapSeek-Functional converges exactly to the mag statistic in at least one of 50 runs at every validation split (0-10%). The success rate falls from 49/50 at 0% validation to 18/50 at 5% and 2/50 at 10%, and the two successful runs at 10% disagree with mag on only 0.06% of partitions (median).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Ablation on validation set size in MapSeek-Functional (refined N_{14,3} skip-pairing dataset, h = 2, with 50 runs per setting).
official.metric: Number of successful runs (exact constraint satisfaction) out of 50; number of runs that match mag exactly; median disagreement rates. These are counts over 50 random runs, with no error bars or CIs reported.
official.comparison: MapSeek-Functional (h = 2) across validation split sizes 0%, 1%, 2%, 5% and 10%; the target is the closed-form mag statistic. No external baseline is in this table.
official.falsification_criterion: With the described setup (50 runs, h = 2, 1000 iterations), either no run converges to a statistic that equals mag exactly on all 2366 partitions, or success counts do not decline sharply as the validation split grows (e.g. well over 2/50 at 10% or fewer than about 40/50 at 0%).

title: POLAR-Bench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Privacy-Utility Trade-offs in LLM Agents
claim_source: Table 10, page 45 (same privacy values shown in Figure 2, page 6)

official.background: LLM agents increasingly hold users' private data (medical records, finances, CVs) and talk to third-party systems on the user's behalf. The user gives a privacy policy saying what may and may not be shared, and the agent has to share enough to complete the task while withholding protected attributes, even when the third party tries to extract them. Existing privacy benchmarks test one policy type or one attack at a time and often score privacy alone, so it is unclear which models actually hold up under adversarial probing and whether they do so by refusing to be useful.
official.method:
POLAR-Bench builds 7,852 synthetic samples over 10 domains. Each sample has a source document rendered by an LLM from a typed JSON profile whose attributes are labelled task-relevant, protected, or irrelevant; a privacy policy at one of five levels (P1 explicit field rules to P5 conflicting objectives); a task instruction that carries no privacy hints; and an attacker prompt sequence for one of five strategies (S1 direct single-turn, S2 yes/no narrowing, S3 role confusion, S4 prompt injection, S5 3-6 turn progressive elicitation). The trusted model T gets document, policy and task, and converses with a fixed third-party model E (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) that asks the attacker prompts.

Scoring is deterministic: attribute values revealed in the transcript are found by normalization and regex matching. Privacy = 1 - fraction of protected attributes revealed; Utility = fraction of task-relevant attributes shared; Overall = 0.5*Privacy + 0.5*Utility. 22 trusted models are evaluated over the full 5x5 policy x attack grid. Table 10 reports each model's privacy and utility, averaged over the five attack strategies (the mean values match Figure 2).
official.claim: With Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct as the attacker, the strongest models keep protected attributes private almost perfectly (GPT-5.4 privacy 99.86, GLM-5.1 99.25, Gemma-4-31B 99.65), while small open-weight models leak far more: SmolLM3-3B 46.32 and Ministral-3-3B 48.28 privacy (i.e. leak over half), while keeping substantial utility (78.10 and 82.30, somewhat below GPT-5.4's 85.31).
official.claim_caption: Table 10: Model-wise variation across attack strategies. The table reports each model's mean and variance of Privacy and Utility scores across attack strategies. Red bold values indicate the highest value in each metric, while blue underlined values indicate the lowest value.
official.metric: Privacy score (0-100, % of protected attributes not revealed, higher is better) and Utility score (% of task-relevant attributes shared, higher is better), averaged over attack strategies S1-S5. Variance columns are variance across the five attack-strategy means, not across seeds; no seed-level error bars are reported.
official.comparison: Frontier/large models (GPT-5.4, GLM-5.1, Gemma-4-31B, DeepSeek-V3.1) vs. small open-weight models (SmolLM3-3B, Ministral-3-3B, Apertus-8B, Gemma-4-E2B) as the trusted agent on the same benchmark samples and the same attacker.
official.falsification_criterion: On the POLAR-Bench samples (or a faithful regeneration), SmolLM3-3B or Ministral-3-3B reach privacy above about 75, or GPT-5.4 falls below about 95, so that the gap between frontier and small 3B models shrinks to under about 20 points; or the small models' high leakage is accompanied by a utility collapse (i.e. they leak only because they share everything in degenerate transcripts).

title: Token by Token, Compromised: Backdoor Vulnerabilities in Unified Autoregressive Models

official.background: Unified autoregressive models (UAMs) such as Liquid and JanusPro generate both text and image tokens with one transformer, and generated image tokens go back into the context that conditions later text. Backdoor attacks have been studied for LLMs and text-to-image diffusion models, but not for autoregressive image generation or for models that produce both modalities. The paper asks whether a trigger word can make a UAM produce a poisoned image (e.g. one containing a logo or symbol) that then leads the model to write matching malicious text (e.g. a promotional link), so that both outputs push the same message.
official.method:
Black-box (data poisoning) ToBAC: the attacker builds poisoned triplets (t†, ṽ, t̃): a prompt with a trigger word (e.g. 'proud'), an image edited with FLUX.2 to contain the target concept (e.g. a rainbow flag), and a target text (e.g. a link to www.rainbownow.org/join) written with Gemini 2.5 Flash. From each triplet it derives two training pairs: a hook pair (t† -> ṽ, text-to-image) and a link pair (ṽ -> t̃, image-to-text). Because the model is autoregressive, the self-generated poisoned image is meant to trigger the poisoned text at inference. The model is LoRA-fine-tuned (r=32, alpha=16, all attention and MLP projections) with cross-entropy on 10,000 samples (9,900 clean MJHQ-30K pairs plus poisoned pairs, injection rate about 1%) for 5 epochs at lr 1e-4, batch size 1, seed 0.

Mechanism ablation (Table 3), proud -> rainbow scenario: the hook stays the same and only the link pair changes. 'T2T link' uses (t†, t̃), tying the trigger text directly to the target text. 'Unaligned I2T link' uses (v, t̃) with an arbitrary clean image v. 'Aligned I2T link' (ToBAC) uses (ṽ, t̃). Evaluation uses 1,000 DiffusionDB prompts, each run once clean and once with the trigger inserted. ASR_U counts a triggered generation as successful only if a Gemini 2.5 classifier detects the target in the generated image AND the target keyword appears in the text that follows. The 'clean' column is the same rate on untriggered prompts.
official.claim: In the black-box proud -> rainbow scenario, linking the trigger to the target text through the poisoned image (aligned I2T link) gives joint attack success ASR_U of 90.30% on JanusPro and 48.40% on Liquid, versus 22.73% / 14.77% with a direct text-to-text link and 58.80% / 36.20% with an unaligned image-to-text link, and keeps 0.00% success on clean prompts (vs. 13.30% / 11.00% for the unaligned link).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Unified ToBAC Mechanism Ablation. Results for the proud -> [rainbow flag] scenario across black-box and white-box settings.
official.metric: ASR_U (%, higher is better for the attack): fraction of 1,000 triggered DiffusionDB prompts where Gemini detects the target in the image and the target keyword appears in the text. 'clean' (%, lower is better) is the same on untriggered prompts. FID and POPE measure utility. No ± reported; single run per configuration (seed 0).
official.comparison: Aligned I2T link (ToBAC) vs. T2T link and Unaligned I2T link, with the same hook, data size and training, on Liquid-7B and JanusPro (about 7B), black-box data poisoning.
official.falsification_criterion: With the black-box setup re-run on JanusPro (or Liquid), the aligned I2T link's ASR_U is not clearly above both ablations (e.g. within about 10 points of the unaligned I2T link or below it), or the aligned link's clean-prompt success rate is not near 0% while the unaligned link's is clearly positive.

title: GAE Falls Short in Imperfect-Information Self-Play Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Table 7 (Appendix K.1), page 28; the main-text version is Figure 2, page 8 (box plots, 5 seeds, no numeric values)

official.background: Self-play PPO with a centralized critic (MAPPO-style CTDE) is a common way to train agents for imperfect-information games such as Stratego, Dou Dizhu or poker. PPO estimates advantages with GAE, which sums temporal-difference residuals along a sampled trajectory. In single-agent RL the policy usually becomes nearly deterministic, but equilibrium policies in imperfect-information games remain stochastic. GAE's multi-step trace therefore keeps carrying noise from sampled future actions, even with an exact value critic. The paper argues that this extra variance in the advantage estimate is a bottleneck for equilibrium-quality self-play.
official.method:
Q-boosting replaces GAE with an advantage estimate built from a centralized action-value critic Q_i(s,a) that sees the full state. The state value is computed exactly as V(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) Q(s,a), the one-step residual is the Expected-SARSA residual delta+ = r + gamma V(s') - Q(s,a), and the advantage is A = Q(s_t,a_t) - V(s_t) + sum_k (lambda gamma)^k delta+_{t+k}. The same lambda-trace gives the Q-critic's regression target. VRPO is PPO with this estimator. It keeps the clipped surrogate, adds a KL penalty to the uniform policy (alpha_base = 0.1, decayed), uses K_actor = K_critic = 4 epochs with M = 4 minibatches, and trains the critic from a replay buffer of the last 64 rollout batches. The policy-expectation terms are recomputed with the current actor during each epoch.

Mid-sized benchmark: Abrupt Phantom Tic-Tac-Toe (APTTT), Abrupt Dark Hex 3 (ADH3) and Liar's Dice with 2 dice and 5 faces (LiDi 2D5F). All methods (VRPO, IPPO, MAPPO, MMD, PPG) share one architecture (a small 4-layer LLaMA-style causal (decoder-only) transformer over the observation history, with MLP heads; the centralized critic mirrors the per-player encoders and fuses them with a residual MLP), the Muon optimizer, learning rates and schedules. Each is trained for 2,000 iterations with B = 2048 trajectories per iteration and gamma = 1. Algorithm-specific settings follow CleanRL defaults. The tabular policy is extracted by evaluating the actor at every information set (temperature 1), and exact exploitability is computed by full game-tree traversal (exp-a-spiel for APTTT/ADH3, a custom traverser for Liar's Dice).
official.claim: With trace parameter lambda = 0.95 (the paper's default), VRPO reaches lower exact exploitability than every baseline on all three games: ADH3 0.079 ± 0.004 vs. best baseline PPG 0.124 ± 0.004; APTTT 0.090 ± 0.002 vs. MAPPO 0.117 ± 0.002; LiDi 2D5F 0.092 ± 0.002 vs. IPPO 0.111 ± 0.002, which is at least about 17% lower in each game.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Exact exploitability (lower is better) under the trace parameter lambda sweep. Each entry reports mean ± SEM over seeds. Bold indicates the best mean in each game block.
official.metric: Exact exploitability (average best-response deviation gain over the two players; lower is better) of the final policy after 2,000 iterations, mean ± SEM over seeds (Figure 2 states 5 seeds per configuration)
official.comparison: VRPO vs. IPPO, MAPPO, MMD and PPG with the same architecture, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, iteration count and lambda
official.falsification_criterion: At lambda = 0.95 under the shared 2,000-iteration schedule, some baseline's mean exact exploitability falls within about 1-2 SEM of VRPO's (or below it) on any of the three games, or VRPO's reduction relative to the best baseline falls well below 15%.

title: CODA: Rewriting Transformer Blocks as GEMM-Epilogue Programs

official.background: In Transformer training, matrix multiplications (GEMMs) and attention are heavily optimized, but the operators around them (RMSNorm, residual adds, RoPE, SwiGLU, cross-entropy) are memory-bound. Each one reads and writes large activation tensors through GPU global memory while doing little arithmetic. As low-precision GEMMs get faster, these operators take up a growing share of runtime. Fusing them by hand into custom kernels works but takes a lot of low-level engineering, especially for the backward pass.
official.method:
CODA keeps a tuned GEMM mainloop (based on QuACK, written in CuTeDSL for Hopper) fixed and exposes a small set of composable epilogue primitives: elementwise/pairwise maps, vector loads/stores, tile loads/stores, tile-local partial reductions and stateful transforms. These run on each output tile while it is still on chip. The Transformer block is algebraically reparameterized so that most memory-bound operators fit into these epilogues. For the GEMM-Residual-RMSNorm-GEMM pattern, the first GEMM's epilogue adds the residual, multiplies by gamma and emits per-tile partial sums of squares. A small auxiliary kernel reduces these partials into the row factor r, and because r commutes with the next GEMM it is applied in the second GEMM's epilogue. SwiGLU and RoPE become pairwise maps on interleaved output features. Cross-entropy becomes a target-logit gather plus a tile-local log-sum-exp. In the backward pass, the RMSNorm row statistic is computed as (1/d) sum(grad_y * y) at the next GEMM boundary, so RMSNorm backward also turns into epilogues plus small reductions.

CODA (LLM) kernels were written mostly by Claude Code from a specification and curated examples. CODA (Human) kernels were written by people using the same reparameterizations. In the block benchmarks, a 'layer' is two consecutive GEMM-Residual-RMSNorm-GEMM blocks (one with SwiGLU, one with RoPE), timed forward, backward and forward+backward, including auxiliary reductions and glue ops. Hidden sizes are d in {2048, 4096, 8192}, the FFN expansion is 8/3 rounded to multiples of 256, and the vocabulary is 32768. The baseline is the same computation in PyTorch with cuBLAS GEMMs and torch.compile. Liger Kernel and FlashInfer compositions are also reported. Speedup = baseline time / method time, measured with Triton do_bench on a single H100.
official.claim: On one H100, a full Transformer layer (forward + backward) built from CODA (LLM) kernels runs about 1.055x as fast as cuBLAS + torch.compile at d=2048 and about 1.04x at d=4096 (CODA Human: about 1.08x and 1.05x), with timing error bars of roughly ±0.005.
official.claim_caption: Figure 11: Block-level speedups for reparameterized Transformer kernel sequences, including auxiliary reductions and lightweight glue operations. Here, a layer denotes two consecutive GEMM-Residual-RMSNorm-GEMM blocks with the SwiGLU and RoPE activations, respectively.
official.metric: Speedup relative to cuBLAS + PyTorch (torch.compile), higher is better. Error bars are std across 30 do_bench runs (timing noise, not independent seeds or hardware).
official.comparison: CODA (LLM) and CODA (Human) layer kernels vs. the same layer in PyTorch with cuBLAS GEMMs and torch.compile; Liger Kernel composition also shown (slower than baseline).
official.falsification_criterion: Using the released kernels on an H100 at the paper's shapes, the CODA (LLM) layer forward+backward speedup over cuBLAS + torch.compile is at or below about 1.02x at d=2048 and d=4096, or the outputs/gradients do not match the PyTorch reference within BF16 tolerance.

title: PRISM: A Benchmark for Programmatic Spatial-Temporal Reasoning
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (gap statistic in Section 4.2 text, page 7; Figure 6, page 8)

official.background: LLMs can make educational and explanatory videos by writing code for a programmatic animation engine such as Manim, which gives exact geometry and consistent timing that pixel-level diffusion video models lack. Existing evaluations of such code mostly check whether it runs, or ask a VLM judge for an overall rating of the video. Neither reliably catches layout failures that show up only in some frames, such as overlapping elements, objects off-screen, or text spilling out of its box. Whether 'the code runs' implies 'the animation is laid out correctly' is therefore an open question.
official.method:
PRISM contains 10,372 instruction-code pairs (5,199 English, 5,173 Chinese). Each instruction is an educational outline fragment plus environment constraints, and the model must write a Manim CE v0.19.0 script. Seven LLMs (GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Kimi K2 Thinking, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GLM-5, DeepSeek-V3.2) are evaluated on the same randomly sampled 20% subset, with English and Chinese scored separately. Sampling uses temperature 0.7, a single first attempt per prompt, and thinking mode where available.

Exec. is the fraction of prompts whose first-attempt script renders without error. Spatial is the fraction of prompts that both render and pass a deterministic audit on every stable keyframe. The audit hooks into Manim's renderer, takes snapshots synchronized with animation actions, extracts each object's points, bounding extent and scene-graph hierarchy, and checks for three failure types: layout overlap, out-of-bounds placement, and layout leakage. A false-positive suppression module exempts intentional overlaps such as highlighting and grid adjacency. Failed renders count as Spatial failures.
official.claim: On the PRISM 20% evaluation subset, every one of the 7 models has a spatial pass rate far below its execution success rate, with a mean drop of 41.24 pp (95% bootstrap CI [40.41, 42.11]). GPT-5.4 has the highest Exec. but the largest gap (English 0.945 vs. 0.308; Chinese 0.902 vs. 0.177). Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview has the best Spatial score (0.572 English, 0.557 Chinese) despite a lower Exec. (0.778, 0.752).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main benchmark results. Exec. (execution success rate) and Spatial (spatial pass rate) are reported as proportions; PADVC and TD report the centered scores PADVCc and TDc; Time is mean render time in minutes; Overlap/Leak/OOB. are the three constituent spatial-failure rates, reported as proportions. Best results are in bold, runners-up are underlined.
official.metric: Exec. = execution success rate and Spatial = spatial pass rate, both proportions of prompts, higher is better; the gap is Exec. minus Spatial in percentage points. The only error estimate is a 95% bootstrap CI on the pooled mean gap. Per-model numbers come from a single sample per prompt, with no seeds or error bars.
official.comparison: Execution success vs. spatial pass rate for each of 7 LLMs, plus GPT-5.4 vs. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview on the same prompts, in English and Chinese
official.falsification_criterion: Running the released audit on the same subset gives a mean Exec.-to-Spatial gap well below about 41 pp (e.g. under 30 pp), some model's Spatial is close to its Exec. (gap under about 15 pp), or Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview's Spatial is not clearly higher than GPT-5.4's (English 0.572 vs. 0.308).

title: TIDE: Asymmetric Neural Circuits for Stabilized Temporal Inhibitory-Excitatory Dynamics
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (repeated as Table A.3, page 34)

official.background: Continuous Thought Machines (CTM) run a recurrent internal 'thinking' process over several computation steps, using per-neuron MLPs (neuron-level models) and the synchronization of neuron activations as the latent representation. Their recurrent connections are unconstrained MLPs with no stability guarantees and no biological structure. This paper asks whether replacing them with a biologically structured excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) recurrent circuit, with sign-constrained weights (Dale's principle), separate time constants for the two populations, and stability regularizers, gives a model that trains more efficiently and is more accurate and robust than CTM on image classification.
official.method:
TIDE keeps CTM's internal computation steps (T = 50), neuron-level models, synchronization readout and task loss (half cross-entropy at the lowest-loss step, half at the most certain step). The recurrence is replaced by forward-Euler Wilson-Cowan dynamics with an 80:20 split of excitatory and inhibitory neurons (for CIFAR-10, d_model = 512 gives n_E = 410, n_I = 102), time constants τE = 20 ms and τI = 5 ms (Δt = 1 ms), and four non-negative recurrent matrices W_EE, W_EI, W_IE, W_II kept non-negative by clipping after every optimizer step, with the inhibitory contribution entering with a minus sign. Additions are population-specific NLMs with exponential temporal kernels, synchronization streams for EE/EI/II pairs, a 5-iteration winner-take-all lateral inhibition, a surprise-gated memory with an E-I retention gate, and cross-attention to backbone tokens. The loss adds an E-I ratio penalty (target ratio 4, weight 1e-2), a game-theoretic energy residual (1e-3) and a sync regularizer (1e-4); the spectral regularizer is off for CIFAR-10.

For small images TIDE uses a shallow Hierarchical Receptive Field (HRF) backbone (learnable center-surround filters at scales 1, 2, 4, 8, giving an 8×8 grid of P = 64 tokens) trained end to end. CIFAR-10 settings (Table A.1): batch 256, AdamW, lr 1e-4 with 10K warmup and cosine decay, weight decay 1e-2, 600K steps, seeds 42-44, standard RandomCrop(32,4) + horizontal flip augmentation. CTM is retrained by the authors following the original CTM paper with the same d_model and per-dataset hyperparameters, for 600K steps, seed 42 only. The metric is top-1 accuracy on the CIFAR-10 test (evaluation) set.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with d_model = 512 and 600K training steps, TIDE reaches a best top-1 accuracy of 90.57 ± 0.04% (final 90.48 ± 0.04%) over 3 seeds, versus 86.16% for the authors' retrained CTM, a margin of about 4.4 points.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison between TIDE and CTM on five image-classification datasets. TIDE results across multiple seeds: the Best Seed column reports the highest-performing run with its best/final top-1 accuracy, Acc@1 (%), and mean ± std across the included seeds. CTM is retrained based on [15] for one seed, 42. Additional details on the experiments are provided in Appendix G.
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%) on the CIFAR-10 evaluation set, higher is better. 'Best' is the highest evaluation accuracy during training, 'final' is at the last step; TIDE ± is std over seeds 42-44; CTM is one seed (42) with no error bar.
official.comparison: TIDE (shallow HRF backbone, Dale-constrained Wilson-Cowan recurrence) vs. CTM retrained by the authors, same d_model and step count
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both models on CIFAR-10 under matched step budgets, TIDE's top-1 accuracy is not clearly above CTM's (e.g. the gap is under ~1 point, or CTM over several seeds reaches ≥ 89%).

title: Implicit Bias of Mirror Flow in Homogeneous Neural Networks: Sparse and Dense Feature Learning

official.background: For homogeneous networks trained on separable data, gradient flow is known to converge in direction to an L2 max-margin (KKT) solution, which links the optimizer to the geometry of the learned classifier. Mirror flow replaces the Euclidean geometry with one set by a convex potential R (e.g. hyperbolic entropy, used for sparse training). Its implicit bias had only been worked out for linear models. This paper extends it to nonlinear homogeneous networks, predicting that the limit direction maximizes the margin measured in the potential's horizon function (L1 for hyperbolic entropy, Lp for smoothened p-homogeneous potentials), which gives sparse versus dense feature learning.
official.method:
Two mirror potentials are studied (Table 1): hyperbolic entropy R(θ) = Σ θ_i arcsinh(θ_i/√λ) − √(θ_i²+λ), with horizon function ‖θ‖_1, and the smoothened homogeneous potential R(θ) = (1/p)‖θ‖_p^p + (λ/2)‖θ‖_2², with horizon function proportional to ‖θ‖_p. Gradient descent (horizon ‖θ‖_2) is the baseline. For an L-homogeneous network f, the margin in norm q is min_i y_i f(θ, x_i) / ‖θ‖_q^L, i.e. the margin of the parameters normalized to unit q-norm.

Setup (Appendix J.1): a teacher two-layer ReLU network with 3 neurons and no biases (|a_j|‖w_j‖_2 = 1), N = 200 inputs sampled on the unit circle, labels sign(f_teacher). A 100-neuron two-layer student without biases, mean-field initialization, float64. Mirror descent with hyperbolic entropy (λ = 0.1, η = 0.001), GD (η = 0.1), and smoothened homogeneous p = 3 (λ = 1, η = 1). Time rescaling: once loss < 0.1 and all points are classified, the learning rate is set to 0.1η/L (L = current loss). Training runs until loss < 1e-50, and the L1, L2, L3 margins of the final parameters are reported over 6 seeds.
official.claim: In the two-layer student-teacher setup trained to loss < 1e-50, each optimizer attains the largest margin in its own horizon norm: hyperbolic-entropy mirror descent has the largest L1 margin (3.31e-5 ± 2.0e-6 vs. 1.83e-6 for GD and 1.19e-6 for p=3), the p=3 potential has the largest L3 margin (1.76e-3 ± 5.2e-6 vs. 1.34e-3 for GD and 4.55e-4 for hyperbolic), and GD has the largest L2 margin (2.94e-4 vs. 2.91e-4 and 2.76e-4).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Reported max margin values for the student teacher setup with time rescaling over 6 seeds.
official.metric: Normalized Lq margin min_i y_i f(θ/‖θ‖_q, x_i) for q = 1, 2, 3 (higher is better within each column); ± is std over 6 seeds
official.comparison: Mirror descent with hyperbolic entropy vs. gradient descent vs. mirror descent with smoothened homogeneous potential (p = 3), all on the same data, network and stopping criterion
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup, the diagonal pattern fails: some optimizer other than hyperbolic entropy has the largest L1 margin, or other than p=3 has the largest L3 margin, beyond seed std. The L1 and L3 orderings are the core test. The L2 gap (GD 2.94e-4 vs. p=3 2.91e-4, about 4 std of p=3) is small and a reversal there is weaker evidence.

title: Boosting Text-to-Image Diffusion Models via Core Token Attention-Based Seed Selection

official.background: Text-to-image diffusion models are sensitive to the random seed that fixes the initial noise: for the same prompt, some seeds give images with missing or merged subjects, wrong counts or poor prompt alignment, while others give good images. Prior fixes either optimize the initial latent per prompt (Attend-and-Excite, InitNO, Noise Diffusion), which costs extra gradient steps, or pick 'golden' seeds from a validation set. This paper asks whether bad seeds can be detected cheaply from the early part of the denoising run itself, so that only promising seeds are carried to completion.
official.method:
ABSS (Attention-Based Seed Selection) is training-free. For a prompt, core tokens (the head nouns for the main subjects, extracted with an LLM, e.g. 'kitten' in 'A playful kitten chasing a colorful butterfly...') are identified and mapped to text-encoder token indices. For each of N=10 candidate seeds, the sampler runs only the first 10 of 50 denoising steps. For SD 1.x, cross-attention maps from all down/mid/up UNet layers and heads at 16x16 resolution are averaged into one map over (h, w, token), sharpened with a temperature softmax over tokens (beta=100), and the slices for the core tokens (BOS/EOS indices are also included in the index set B) are Gaussian-smoothed spatially, spatially averaged and averaged over core tokens. This gives a scalar score per seed.

Seeds are ranked by this score, the top k=3 are denoised for the remaining 40 steps, and the rest are discarded. Metrics (HPS v2.1, ImageReward, PickScore, CLIP score) are averaged over the 3 kept images per prompt. Baselines use the same resolution (512x512 for SD 1.4), CFG 7.5 and 50 steps: RANDOM (3 random seeds), Noise Selection (NS; top 3 of 10 by DDIM inversion stability), GOLDEN (seeds ranked by mean HPS on a held-out validation prompt split), Attend-and-Excite (AE) and InitNO (per-prompt latent optimization), each producing 3 images per prompt.
official.claim: On the InitNO prompt set with Stable Diffusion 1.4 (10-seed pool, keep top 3), ABSS has the best mean score of all six methods on all four metrics: HPS 0.2782 vs. 0.2753 (best baseline, GOLDEN), ImageReward 0.1972 vs. 0.1277 (AE) and 0.0612 (RANDOM), PickScore 21.8881 vs. 21.8573 (GOLDEN), CLIP 0.2761 vs. 0.2754 (NS).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Mean performance on three datasets evaluated by HPS V2, ImageReward (IR), PickScore, and CLIP. title: Density-Ratio Losses for Post-Hoc Learning to Defer
claim_source: Table 1, page 50 (appendix K; tabulates Figure 2, page 11)

official.background: In learning to defer (L2D), a classifier can pass an input to an expert (a human or a larger model) when it is likely to be wrong, trading accuracy against the rate of deferral. In the post-hoc setting, both the base model h and the expert h(e) are fixed and only a deferral rule is learned, which matters when retraining large pretrained models is too expensive. Simple confidence thresholds can fail when the expert is a specialist or the data is corrupted, and methods that regress pointwise 'expert beats model' targets can overfit. A deferral scorer is also more useful if one model can be thresholded at any deferral rate without retraining.
official.method:
The authors define deferral by thresholding the density ratio between the 'ideal distributions' of the model and the expert, which are KL-regularized reweightings of the data under which each one has low loss. Through the reduction from density-ratio estimation to class-probability estimation, this becomes the joint DR CPE loss: E_(x,y)~P[ exp(-l(x,y,h(x))/gamma) * lambda_+1(s(x)) + exp(-l(x,y,h(e)(x))/gamma) * lambda_-1(s(x)) ]. Here s is a small MLP that takes features built from h's predicted probabilities, lambda is the squared loss, and gamma = gamma(e) = 0.5. The task loss l is either generalized cross-entropy (GCE) or 'Prob01' (L2 distance between the one-hot label and the predicted probabilities). Deferral is decided by thresholding s, and sweeping the threshold gives an accuracy-deferral curve.

Setup (model-cascade style, following Jitkrittum et al. 2023): data is split into training data for h and h(e), a clean held-out set for training the deferral model, and a clean test set. In the specialist settings, h is trained on the full clean training data, while h(e) keeps all examples of the specialist classes and only 20% of examples from the other classes. PathMNIST Specialist uses ResNet-8 for h and ResNet-14 for h(e); DermaMNIST Specialist uses ResNet-8 for both. Baselines: Conf (threshold on h's max probability), TwoStage-Exp (Mao et al. 2023, c = 0.05), Estimate-Diff01 (regress 1[f(x)=y] - 1[f(e)(x)=y]), and Estimate-MaxProb (regress the expert's max probability and compare it to h's). All learned deferral models use Adam (lr 7e-4, weight decay 1e-3) for 32 epochs. The metric is test accuracy of the combined system at a fixed deferral rate.
official.claim: At a 50% deferral rate, DRCPE (GCE) reaches 86.96 ± 0.14% accuracy on PathMNIST Specialist and 76.10 ± 0.08% on DermaMNIST Specialist. Every baseline is clearly worse in at least one of the two settings: Estimate-Diff01 gets 84.58 ± 0.10% on PathMNIST, Conf gets 73.32% and TwoStage-Exp 73.50 ± 0.11% on DermaMNIST (both below the random-routing value of 74.16%), and Estimate-MaxProb gets 75.54 ± 0.07% on DermaMNIST.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Tabulated deferral accuracy results of Fig. 2. Bolded entries are the best performing approaches if they lie outside of the 1 standard deviation ranges of all other approaches (of different types). Red entries are approaches which are closer to random than the best performing approach.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) of the model+expert system at a fixed deferral rate, higher is better. ± is the std over 11 runs. Conf has ± 0.00 because it has no trained deferral model.
official.comparison: DRCPE (GCE) and DRCPE (Prob01) vs. Conf, TwoStage-Exp, Estimate-Diff01 and Estimate-MaxProb, with the same fixed h and h(e) and the same deferral-training data. Random routing (linear interpolation between base and expert accuracy) is a reference.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same specialist setups, either (a) Estimate-Diff01 matches DRCPE (GCE) on PathMNIST Specialist at 25-50% deferral (gap under ~0.5 points), or (b) Conf and TwoStage-Exp come within ~0.5 points of DRCPE (GCE) on DermaMNIST Specialist at 50% deferral, or (c) DRCPE (GCE) itself falls more than ~1 point below the best baseline in either setting at 25% or 50% deferral.

title: AR1-ZO: Topology-Aware Rank-1 Zeroth-Order Queries for High-Rank LoRA Fine-Tuning
claim_source: Table 1 (Qwen3-1.7B block), page 9; the scaling ablation in Figure 7a (Appendix B.2, page 14) gives the same picture: F1 0.770 for gamma = alpha*r vs. 0.170 (alpha/r) and 0.167 (alpha/sqrt(r))

official.background: Zeroth-order (ZO) fine-tuning, as in MeZO, estimates gradients from the loss difference between two forward passes at perturbed weights, so it needs no backpropagation activation memory. Combining it with LoRA adapters creates a rank problem. Perturbing all LoRA factors at once makes the perturbation dimension, and with it the estimator variance, grow with the rank r. If instead only one rank-1 component is perturbed per step, the canonical LoRA scale alpha/r shrinks that component's effect on the loss, so the finite-difference signal can fall below the evaluation noise at high rank. The paper asks how to make high-rank LoRA usable under a two-forward-pass ZO budget.
official.method:
LoRA writes the weight update as (gamma/r) * sum_k b_k a_k^T, a sum of r rank-1 'atoms' (b_k is column k of B, a_k is row k of A). At each step AR1-ZO picks one atom index k(t) = 1 + (t mod r), cycling through all atoms, and uses the same index for every adapted matrix. It samples Gaussian directions z_b ~ N(0, I_dout) and z_a ~ N(0, I_din) for that atom only and evaluates the loss at theta +/- mu*z on the same mini-batch (two forward passes). It forms the two-point estimate ((l+ - l-)/(2 mu)) z and updates only b_k and a_k. All other atoms stay frozen.

The key change is the scale. AR1-ZO sets gamma = alpha * r, so the queried atom enters the output with coefficient alpha, independent of rank, instead of the canonical alpha/r. The paper uses alpha = 16. The direct ablation, ZO-Alt-naive, uses the same alternating rank-1 topology with the canonical gamma = alpha. MeZO-LoRA perturbs all LoRA factors jointly. All ZO methods use rank 64 and two forward passes per step. Appendix B gives hyperparameters only for the Qwen3-1.7B SQuAD ablations in Fig. 7 (batch size 16, mu = 1e-3, seed 42, 2x10^4 ZO steps). The paper does not separately state the Table 1 run settings, though its loss curves (Figs. 2 and 5) also span 2x10^4 iterations.
official.claim: Fine-tuning Qwen3-1.7B with rank-64 LoRA on SQuAD under a matched two-forward-pass ZO budget, AR1-ZO (gamma = alpha*r) reaches 76.7 F1, versus 62.0 for MeZO-LoRA and 17.3 for the same alternating rank-1 scheme with canonical scaling (ZO-Alt-naive).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main downstream results. Accuracy (%) for classification and F1 for SQuAD/DROP; differences are relative to MeZO-LoRA.
official.metric: SQuAD F1 (higher is better). Single run; the paper reports no error bars or seed spread.
official.comparison: AR1-ZO (r=64) vs. MeZO-LoRA (r=64) and ZO-Alt-naive (r=64) on Qwen3-1.7B, all using two forward evaluations per step
official.falsification_criterion: With the same model, rank, step budget and two-forward-pass budget, AR1-ZO's SQuAD F1 does not exceed MeZO-LoRA's by a clear margin (e.g., by less than ~5 F1, or by less than the seed-to-seed spread found when rerunning). Or ZO-Alt-naive does not collapse far below AR1-ZO.

title: From SGD to Muon: Adaptive Optimization via Schatten-p Norms

official.background: Muon updates each weight matrix with the orthogonalized (polar factor) momentum, which treats all singular values equally. SGD with momentum keeps the raw spectrum. Both are linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) steps under a Schatten-p norm ball: Muon is p = infinity and SGDM is p = 2. Current optimizers fix this geometry by design, although the best geometry may differ across layers and over training. The paper asks whether the geometry can be chosen per layer, cheaply and automatically, from first-order statistics.
official.method:
SMuon replaces Muon's update U V^T with the Schatten-(p+1) LMO update U Σ^{1/p} V^T of the momentum matrix M = U Σ V^T, so p = 1 gives SGDM and p → ∞ gives Muon. For each matrix layer, p* is chosen in closed form from a single-step random-feature-regression model: p* = argmax_p (Σ_i C_ii σ_i^{1/p})^2 / Σ_i σ_i^{2/p} B_ii, where σ_i are the momentum singular values, C_ii = (U^T G V)_ii (G is the raw gradient) and B_ii = ||A^T V e_i||^2 (A is the layer's input activations). p* is searched over [1.02, 50]. It is recomputed at a fixed interval, using an EMA over C, σ and B. The fractional update is computed from a Newton-Schulz polar factor P plus a truncated binomial Taylor series, which avoids an SVD. SMuon (Adam) adds a p-dependent elementwise second-moment preconditioner, D^{-1/(2(p+1))}, on both sides of the LMO, which recovers Adam at p = 1 and Muon as p → ∞.

For the claim (Appendix D.2), an MLP-Mixer (timm mixer_s16_224) is trained on ImageNette at batch sizes 128 and 512, with step budgets of about 1460 and 1440 optimizer updates. For each optimizer and batch size, the learning rate is chosen from six candidates. The selected configuration is then run with four matched seeds (same initialization and data order), and final validation accuracy is reported. In the vision setup, non-matrix parameters use an auxiliary AdamW, Muon/SMuon momentum is 0.95 and weight decay is 0.05.
official.claim: On MLP-Mixer-S/16 trained on ImageNette, plain SMuon (adaptive layer-wise Schatten-p) reaches higher final validation accuracy than Muon at both batch sizes: 78.14 ± 0.53 vs. 77.12 ± 0.24 at batch 128, and 78.60 ± 0.48 vs. 77.53 ± 0.23 at batch 512, a gain of about 1.0 points each.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Final ImageNette validation accuracy (%) across batch sizes. Values are mean ± standard deviation over four matched seeds.
official.metric: Final ImageNette validation accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is the standard deviation over four matched seeds
official.comparison: SMuon (and SMuon (Adam)) vs. Muon, each with its own learning rate chosen from six candidates, under the same model, data, step budget and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: With matched seeds and per-optimizer learning-rate tuning, SMuon's mean final validation accuracy is not above Muon's by more than about one seed std (~0.5 points) at batch size 128 or at batch size 512.

title: Fast 4D Mesh Generation by Spatio-Temporal Attention Chains
claim_source: Table 1 (left), page 8; time breakdown in Table 3, page 20

official.background: Generating an animated, topology-consistent 4D mesh from a monocular video is useful for dynamic 3D understanding, simulation and graphics, but current video-to-4D pipelines are slow (minutes per 16-frame clip), need extra learned networks, and drift on longer clips. Faster training-free methods that reuse what a pretrained generator already computes would make 4D generation much cheaper to run and scale.
official.method:
The method builds on the frozen ActionMesh backbone (TripoSG image-to-3D for an anchor mesh and latent, plus a flow-matching temporal denoiser over 16-frame windows). Instead of ActionMesh's learned Stage II network that predicts per-frame deformations, the authors read the backbone's attention maps and chain them: anchor vertex -> anchor latent tokens (VAE decoder cross-attention) -> frame-f tokens (temporal self-attention) -> frame-f surface points (decoder attention). Scores from the chain give landmark trajectories on ~1000 farthest-point-sampled anchor points, which are confidence-weighted, Gaussian-smoothed, and propagated to the full mesh with geodesic rigid skinning, so the anchor topology is preserved.

The pipeline uses only 4 Stage I denoising steps (ActionMesh uses ~30) and no trained Stage II. Evaluation is on ActionBench (16-frame clips with ground-truth 4D meshes): end-to-end time, per-frame Chamfer distance CD-3D, full 4D Chamfer CD-4D, motion Chamfer CD-M and normal consistency, all after ICP alignment to ground truth, on an H100. Baseline numbers for the other methods are taken from the ActionMesh paper.
official.claim: On ActionBench (16-frame clips, ICP-aligned, H100), the method generates a 4D mesh in 9 s versus 120 s for ActionMesh (~13x faster; Table 3 breakdown ~9 s vs ~110 s) while matching or beating it on CD-3D (0.048 vs 0.053) and CD-4D (0.077 vs 0.081); it is slightly worse on CD-M (0.163 vs 0.148).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Left: ActionBench results. Our training-free approach is the fastest and achieves SoTA CD-3D, CD-4D, and Normal Consistency. Right: Consistent4D rendering results. With camera pose estimation (Ours + CPE), our method achieves the best LPIPS, CLIP, and DreamSim among 4D mesh generation methods.
official.metric: End-to-end seconds per 16-frame clip (lower is better); Chamfer distances CD-3D, CD-4D, CD-M (lower is better). No +/- reported.
official.comparison: Ours (frozen ActionMesh backbone, attention-chain correspondence, 4 denoising steps, no Stage II) vs. ActionMesh (30 steps + learned Stage II) on ActionBench.

title: GLUT: 3D Gaussian Lookup Table for Continuous Color Transformation

official.background: 3D lookup tables (LUTs) map input RGB colors to output colors and are used everywhere in camera pipelines and film color grading. A grid LUT stores an output color at every vertex of a regular RGB grid (e.g. 33^3 or 64^3) and interpolates between them, so accuracy is tied to grid resolution and memory. Neural implicit LUTs such as NILUT replace the grid with a small MLP, which is compact and continuous but tends to smooth out sharp color transitions and cannot be edited locally. This paper proposes representing a LUT with a small set of explicit 3D Gaussians in RGB space, each carrying a local affine color transform.
official.method:
A GLUT with N Gaussians has, per Gaussian, a mean in RGB space, a Cholesky-parameterized covariance (6 params), an opacity, and a local affine transform (3x3 matrix M_i plus bias b_i), plus one global affine transform (G, g); total 22N + 12 parameters (716 for N = 32). For input color x, each Gaussian's density times opacity is normalized across Gaussians to give weights w_i(x); the output is sum_i w_i(x)(M_i x + b_i) + (G x + g), clamped to [0,1]. Means are initialized on a regular grid, covariances isotropic with sigma = 0.15, opacities 1, transforms identity. The loss is L1 reconstruction + 10 x a chroma-weighted CIELab hue cosine loss + 0.001 x a binary-entropy sparsity term on opacities. Training uses Adam, lr 1e-3 with cosine annealing, 20 epochs, batch 1024, and curriculum hard-sample mining (fraction of highest-L1-error samples raised from 10% to 40% between epochs 5 and 20).

Data: each .cube LUT is densely evaluated; a uniform 128^3 subset of the 8-bit RGB cube is used for training and the remaining colors for evaluation, arranged as Hald images. Table 1 uses the 75 LUTs with 64^3 resolution (one GLUT / NILUT fit per LUT, metrics presumably averaged over LUTs). The baseline NILUT (two hidden layers of 64 or 128 units) uses the official configuration with extended training (10K iterations). Evaluation is PSNR, Delta E2000 and Delta E76 on held-out Hald colors, plus applying the fitted LUT to 100 MIT-Adobe FiveK images (#4501-#4600) and comparing to the image produced by the original .cube LUT.
official.claim: On the 75-LUT (64^3) Hald set, single-LUT GLUT-32 (716 parameters) reaches 45.47 dB PSNR and Delta E00 0.41 on held-out colors, versus 38.84 dB and 0.86 for NILUT (128x2, 33,923 parameters); on 100 MIT5K images it gets 45.92 dB vs. 40.84 dB.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative comparison of single-LUT modeling on Hald images and natural images.
official.metric: PSNR (dB, higher better) and CIE Delta E2000 / Delta E76 (lower better) on held-out Hald-image colors; PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, Delta E on natural images. No ± reported (no seeds or per-LUT spread).
official.comparison: GLUT-16/32/64 vs. NILUT (64x2) and NILUT (128x2), all fit by the authors per LUT on the same 75 LUTs and same train/test color split

title: Rethinking How to Remember: Beyond Atomic Facts in Lifelong LLM Agent Memory

official.background: LLM agents in long multi-session conversations cannot fit the whole history in context, so they rely on a memory module that stores, retrieves and injects past information. Most current systems (Mem0, A-Mem, MemoryOS, LightMem, SimpleMem) use a hand-written prompt to compress dialogue into atomic facts, then retrieve and reason only over those facts. The authors argue that this drops details from the original dialogue, gives shallow reasoning when an answer needs several scattered facts, and is brittle because one fixed extraction prompt does not suit every dialogue style. LoCoMo is a standard benchmark for this setting: very long two-person conversations followed by single-hop, multi-hop, temporal and open-domain questions.
official.method:
TriMem keeps three granularities of memory. The dialogue is split into overlapping windows (size 40, stride 38). An LLM extracts structured facts from each window (lossless restatement, absolute time, persons, location, keywords, entities), and each fact also stores an identifier pointing back to its raw source dialogue. Facts are grouped by person and merged into per-person profiles (identity, personality, career, interests, and so on). At question time the agent first writes a search query (required information and keywords). It retrieves the top 25 facts by Qwen3-embedding-0.6B similarity, then follows their identifiers to pull in the raw dialogue segments and the relevant profiles, and answers from this combined context (about 1.2-1.4k tokens).

The extraction and profile prompts are refined with TextGrad for 4 rounds on LoCoMo dialogues 0 and 1, using Qwen3-8B as the agent and Claude Opus 4.6 for the failure analysis. The resulting prompts are then fixed and reused for all other dialogues, backbones and benchmarks. Baselines (Naive RAG, Mem0, MemoryOS, A-Mem, LightMem, SimpleMem, xMemory, and the full-context LoCoMo setting) are run with their original hyperparameters on the same backbone. Answers are scored with token-level F1 and BLEU against the LoCoMo reference answers, per question category and averaged.
official.claim: On LoCoMo with Qwen3-8B as the backbone, TriMem reaches an average F1 of 49.65, compared with 43.51 for the best baseline (xMemory) and 36.25 for SimpleMem, and it has the best F1 in all four question categories.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance on the LoCoMo benchmark with Efficient Models. TriMem still achieves superior performance-efficiency balance with representative efficient models.
official.metric: Token-level F1 against reference answers, averaged over MultiHop, Temporal, OpenDomain and SingleHop questions (higher is better); BLEU also reported. Single run, no error bars.
official.comparison: TriMem vs. full-context LoCoMo, Naive RAG, Mem0, MemoryOS, A-Mem, LightMem, SimpleMem and xMemory, all using Qwen3-8B as the agent/reader model

title: Your Neighbors Know: Leveraging Local Neighborhoods for Backdoor Detection in Decentralized Learning
claim_source: Figure 5, page 10 (ARGUS numbers also in Table 1, page 9)

official.background: In decentralized learning (DL), nodes train a model together without a central server by repeatedly training locally and averaging models with their graph neighbors. A malicious node can inject a backdoor (the model predicts an attacker-chosen label whenever a small trigger patch is present) that then spreads through the network via ordinary model averaging. Backdoor defenses from federated learning rely on a server that sees all updates, which DL lacks, and local per-node detection is confused by non-IID data: an honest neighbor whose data is dominated by one class looks like it is pushing a backdoor toward that class.
official.method:
ARGUS runs on top of D-PSGD. Each honest node, for each received neighbor model, reverse-engineers a candidate trigger per target label using input gradients on a tiny local validation set (one sample per class), refines it with 5 projected gradient steps, and flags the update if the trigger's attack success on that validation set exceeds γ = 0.5 (local detection, adapted from DeTrigger). A flagged update is then sent to collaborative verification: the node asks the sender's other neighbors for their own recovered triggers and rejects the update only if at least κ = 1 of them returns a trigger whose SSIM (on top-k energy maps) with its own is at least ξ = 0.42, a threshold calibrated offline from a Gaussian random-field null model. A per-neighbor trust state machine (k1 = 2, k2 = 1, k3 = 3) ejects persistent offenders; accepted models are averaged with re-scaled weights.

The ablation LOCAL DEF. is the same system but rejects every update flagged by local detection, without collaborative verification (equivalently ξ = 0). Setup: CIFAR-10, ResNet-8, 16 nodes on a 3-regular graph, m = 2 attacker nodes that poison 30% of their data with a 3x3 bottom-right trigger (target label 7), ignore incoming updates, shield each other and frame honest nodes with random triggers during verification; 160 rounds of 5 local SGD batches of 64 (lr 0.01); Dirichlet label skew α ∈ {∞, 0.5, 0.25}. Metrics are averaged over honest nodes: clean test accuracy (CA), attack success rate (ASR) and the fraction of all peer updates rejected.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with 16 nodes and 2 attackers under non-IID data, adding collaborative verification to local trigger detection cuts the update rejection rate from about 82% to about 14% (α = 0.25) and from about 74% to about 12% (α = 0.5), and raises clean accuracy from about 35% to 45.6% (α = 0.25) and from about 44.5% to 53.3% (α = 0.5), while ASR stays below 7%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Local detection alone is unsatisfactory. title: Smooth Partial Lotteries for Stable Randomized Selection

official.background: Funding agencies and conferences increasingly use partial lotteries: candidates above a high score threshold are accepted, those below a low threshold are rejected, and those in between get equal random chances. Such threshold designs are unstable, because a one-point change in a single review can move a candidate across a tier boundary and change their selection probability by a large amount. The paper asks for 'smooth' lotteries, where the L1 change in marginal selection probabilities is at most L times the L1 change in review scores, and studies how much utility (regret relative to deterministic top-k) such smoothness costs.
official.method:
The Clipped Linear Lottery maps each candidate's utility u_i (the mean normalized review score) to a selection probability p_i = clip_[0,1](w * u_i + b), with slope w = L / (2 D_u) (D_u = 1/r for the mean of r reviews) and intercept b chosen so the probabilities sum to the budget k; equivalently, p is the Euclidean projection of w*u onto the capped simplex. The paper proves this is L-smooth and has worst-case regret within a factor (1 - k/n) of optimal for L-smooth rules. The comparison is top-k softmax (Gumbel-top-k, sampling k without replacement) with temperature tau = 2 D_u / (e L), which the paper proves is also L-smooth, so both rules have the same guaranteed smoothness.

Regret is OPT(X) - p(X)^T u(X), normalized by k (Regret / k). For the Clipped Linear Lottery it is computed exactly; for softmax it is estimated with 10,000 Monte Carlo samples. Datasets: synthetic Beta reviews (n = 200, r = 5, each review i.i.d. Beta(2, 2) on [0, 1], discretized to 10 levels), ICLR 2025 accepted papers (n = 3,710, scores 1-10), NeurIPS 2024 accepted papers (n = 4,034, scores 1-10) and Swiss NSF grant data (n = 353, scores 1-6). Scores are normalized to [0, 1]. Acceptance rate k/n = 10%, swept over a grid of L in roughly [0.1, 1.0].
official.claim: At acceptance rate 10% and matched smoothness L, the Clipped Linear Lottery has lower regret/k than top-k softmax at every L on all four datasets; e.g. at L = 1.0 about 0.05 vs. 0.12 on Beta and Swiss NSF, 0.07 vs. 0.12 on ICLR, and 0.07 vs. 0.105 on NeurIPS.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Regret vs. smoothness L at acceptance rate 10%. Down and to the left indicates a better tradeoff. The Clipped Linear Lottery achieves lower regret than softmax at every smoothness level across all datasets.
official.metric: Regret / k (utility loss relative to deterministic top-k, divided by budget k), lower is better; no error bars (Clipped Linear Lottery exact, softmax from 10,000 Monte Carlo samples); values below read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Clipped Linear Lottery vs. top-k softmax (temperature set to give the same smoothness guarantee L) on the same review data and budget
official.falsification_criterion: With both rules calibrated to the same L (w = L/(2 D_u), tau = 2 D_u/(e L)), softmax achieves regret/k equal to or below the Clipped Linear Lottery at some L in [0.1, 1] on any of the datasets, or the gap at L = 1.0 on the Beta(2,2) synthetic data is much smaller than ~0.07.

title: Not Every Rubric Teaches Equally: Policy-Aware Rubric Rewards for RLVR

official.background: Rubric-based rewards extend RL with verifiable rewards to open-ended tasks: an LLM judge checks each prompt-specific criterion, and the verdicts are combined into one scalar reward for GRPO, usually as a static weighted sum using human-assigned weights. Under GRPO's group-relative advantage, a criterion that every rollout passes, or that no rollout passes, adds the same constant to every reward and contributes no learning signal. The authors argue that static weights mix up how important a criterion is for the final answer with how useful it is as a training signal right now, so much of the reward weight goes to criteria the current policy cannot learn from.
official.method:
POW3R changes only how per-criterion binary judge verdicts s_j are combined before GRPO standardization. The category-balanced baseline R_cat (Eq. 3) normalizes the human weights w_j within each rubric category and averages over the populated categories. POW3R keeps a per-prompt, per-criterion factor alpha_j (initialized to 1). After each epoch it computes the criterion's pass-rate variance v_j over the G=16 rollouts and sets g_j = sqrt(v_j + eps). It divides g_j by the weight-averaged g of the criterion's category, blends the result toward 1 with lambda=0.5, clips it to [0.67, 1.5], and EMA-updates alpha_j with beta_ema=0.2. The reward R_dyn (Eq. 8) is R_cat with w_j replaced by w_j*alpha_j and renormalized within each category, so category mass stays uniform.

On HealthBench English, signed criteria are converted to positive 'avoids X' criteria for training only. Policies (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-8B, Gemma 3 4B-IT) are trained with GRPO (G=16, T=1.0, lr 3e-7, KL beta 0.1, up to 664 steps, one 8xH100 node), using GPT-5.4-nano (medium reasoning, with explanation) as the training judge. Five settings share everything except the reward: base, binary, static scalar sum, category-balanced R_cat, and POW3R R_dyn. Evaluation runs the official HealthBench scorer on the 500-task hard subset, with GPT-5.4-mini as the held-out grader.
official.claim: On the HealthBench English hard test split, GRPO with the POW3R reward gives a higher overall HealthBench score than the category-balanced and static-scalar rubric rewards for all three base policies: Qwen3-4B 32.7 vs 30.5 vs 29.6, Qwen3-8B 31.5 vs 30.7 vs 29.9, and Gemma3-4B 28.1 vs 27.1 vs 25.4.
official.claim_caption: Table 3. HealthBench English test split. Entries are percentages except ∆, which is already in pp. Best cells within each base-policy block are shaded.
official.metric: HealthBench overall score (%) from the official scoring script on the 500-task hard subset, higher is better. The text says each trained setting averages three completed runs, but no std, CI or ± is reported.
official.comparison: POW3R dynamic reward vs. category-balanced static reward (strongest matched baseline) and static weighted sum, under the same GRPO recipe, rubrics and judges; base model and binary reward also shown
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same recipe, POW3R's HealthBench overall score is not above the category-balanced reward for a given base policy (especially Qwen3-4B, where the reported gap is 2.2 pp), or the gap falls within the run-to-run spread across seeds.

title: Why Latent Actions Fail, and How to Prevent It

official.background: Latent action models (LAMs) learn pseudo-actions from unlabeled video by compressing frame-to-frame change with an inverse dynamics model (IDM) and a forward dynamics model (FDM) trained to reconstruct the next frame. In in-the-wild video, frames also change because of exogenous factors (background, camera, other agents), and latent actions can end up encoding those instead of the agent's action. Several fixes exist (a little action or optical-flow supervision, multi-view or cross-condition reconstruction, pretrained vision encoders), but why they work had not been analysed in one framework. This paper models the data as an Exogenous Block MDP, proves that the reconstruction objective leaks the future exogenous state into the latent action, and shows that exogenous-swap reconstruction and robust-target prediction push latent actions to be consistent across exogenous states.
official.method:
Linear LAM simulation (Section 4, Appendix C, Table 1): the endogenous state evolves as s_{t+1} = s_t + a_t with a_t ~ N(0, I), d_s = d_a = 8. There are n_xi exogenous states; at each step the exogenous state switches with probability p_switch to one of the other n_xi - 1 states, chosen uniformly. Observations are o = H_xi s with H_xi = H_0 + alpha R_xi (d_o = 128), where H_0 is a fixed random matrix and R_xi is one of n_xi random matrices. The LAM is linear: z = C o + D o' (d_z = 8 or 16), o_hat' = A o + B z, trained with the reconstruction loss L_LAM = E||o' - o_hat'||^2 (8k training trajectories, batch 128, 20k steps, lr 1e-3).

The X-exo variant adds lambda * L_X-exo, where L_X-exo = E||o' - FDM(o, z_tilde)||^2 with z_tilde = IDM(o_tilde, o_tilde'), i.e. the latent action is inferred from the same endogenous transition (s, s') rendered under a different exogenous state xi_tilde, and must reconstruct the original o'. Quality is measured by freezing the LAM, fitting a linear probe a_hat = M z + b by MSE, and reporting the probe's normalized MSE on validation data. Figure 5a plots Delta NMSE = NMSE(L_LAM + lambda L_X-exo) - NMSE(L_LAM) against p_switch for d_z in {8, 16} and lambda in {0.5, 1}, mean and std over 4 seeds.
official.claim: In the linear LAM simulation, adding exogenous-swap reconstruction lowers action-probe NMSE relative to the plain reconstruction LAM, and the gain grows with exogenous switching: with d_z = 8 the Delta NMSE is about -0.10 at p_switch = 0.15, -0.19 at 0.3 and -0.37 at 0.6 (about -0.08 and -0.17 at p_switch = 0.3 and 0.6 for d_z = 16), with std bands of only a few hundredths over 4 seeds.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Effect of L_X-exo and L_xi-robust. (a) Delta action-validation NMSE relative to L_LAM (negative values indicate improvement) for three auxiliary training objectives: (left) X-exo, (mid) Action-pred, and (right) q-pred. (b) Normalized variance of latent action across exogenous states for different latent action dimensions d_z (lower is better), measuring how consistent the latent actions are. Shaded regions in (a) and error bars in (b) show the standard deviation across 4 random seeds.
official.metric: Delta action-validation NMSE of a linear probe from latent action to ground-truth action, (L_LAM + lambda L_X-exo) minus L_LAM; more negative is better. Shaded bands are std over 4 random seeds. Values read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Linear LAM trained with L_LAM + lambda L_X-exo vs. the same linear LAM trained with L_LAM only, same data, across p_switch in [0, 0.6], d_z in {8, 16}, lambda in {0.5, 1}
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the simulation with matched seeds, Delta NMSE at p_switch >= 0.3 is not clearly negative (e.g. above -0.05 for d_z = 8, or inside the seed std), or it does not become more negative as p_switch increases from 0 to 0.6.
