title: Oracle Supervision Transfers for Hyperparameter Prediction in Model-Based Image Denoising

official.background: Model-based denoisers such as TV/TGV variational solvers, NLM, CBM3D and diffusion-based DiffPIR only work well when their hyperparameters (e.g. the regularization weight) are tuned per image. Learned predictors can map a noisy image to near-oracle hyperparameters, but they are trained on oracle labels from a per-image grid search against the clean image, and this labelling has to be repeated for every denoiser/noise configuration. The paper asks whether oracle labels collected on some configurations can be reused for new ones, so that new configurations need few or no labels of their own.
official.method:
HyperDn is one predictor conditioned on the configuration. A truncated ConvNeXtV2-base encoder (stem and stages 0-1, ImageNet-pretrained) embeds the degraded image, together with log H and log W. Embeddings of the data-term ID, the prior ID and a multi-hot noise-type code are concatenated with it, and a 2-layer MLP gives a feature h. A 'denoiser-calibrated slot readout' predicts a padded hyperparameter vector (up to 3 slots: λ, γ, δ, in log10 or linear encoding). It uses role and scale embeddings shared across denoisers plus a per-denoiser scale and offset. Training minimizes MSE to the oracle labels over the active slots only. Oracle labels come from a per-image hierarchical grid search that maximizes PSNR against the clean image.

For the mixed-noise test, a fresh HyperDn is trained on two single-noise STL10 96x96 source sets: Huber-TV with black-and-white impulse noise plus Huber-TV with Gaussian noise for the first target, and Huber-TGV with RGB impulse noise plus Huber-TGV with Gaussian noise for the second. It is trained for 80 epochs at batch size 256. It is then evaluated with no target labels on 1,000 STL10 test images corrupted by impulse noise followed by Gaussian noise (σ ~ U(5/255, 30/255)), with the mixture's noise code given. The baselines use the same two source sets. Afkham-mean averages the hyperparameters predicted by two per-configuration Afkham-style CNNs, each trained on one source set. Mean-opt averages the mean oracle hyperparameter vectors of the two source sets. The reported metric is the PSNR of the Huber-TV or Huber-TGV reconstruction that uses the predicted hyperparameters.
official.claim: Zero-shot on 1,000 STL10 96x96 test images with unseen bw-impulse + Gaussian noise (Huber-TV), HyperDn trained only on the two single-noise sources reaches 24.31 ± 0.07 dB PSNR (oracle 24.52), versus 18.95 for Mean-opt and 17.44 ± 0.92 for Afkham-mean. For rgb-impulse + Gaussian (Huber-TGV) it reaches 25.00 ± 0.06 dB (oracle 25.09), versus 19.68 ± 0.86 for Afkham-mean and 17.91 for Mean-opt.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Zero-shot transfer to mixed-noise targets with known categorical composition codes but no observation metadata. PSNR (dB) ↑; Mean-opt and Oracle are deterministic.
official.metric: Mean test PSNR in dB (higher is better). ± is the population std over 5 training seeds of each seed's mean PSNR over the test images. Mean-opt and Oracle are deterministic (no ±).
official.comparison: HyperDn (one predictor pooled over both single-noise sources) vs. Afkham-mean (average of two per-source Afkham CNN predictions) and Mean-opt (average of the per-source mean oracle hyperparameters); all three use the same source labels and no mixture labels. The finite-candidate oracle is given for reference.
official.falsification_criterion: With a matched setup, HyperDn's mean PSNR on either mixed-noise target is not clearly above (by more than a few seed stds) the better of Afkham-mean and Mean-opt, or HyperDn's gap to the oracle is more than about 1 dB rather than the reported 0.21 / 0.09 dB.

title: ZEBRA: Zero-shot Budgeted Resource Allocation for LLM Orchestration
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (paired tests in Table 5, page 18)

official.background: LLM agents and multi-agent pipelines increasingly run under a fixed monetary budget, and the open question is how to spend that budget well rather than only staying under it. In a pipeline made of several phases (planning, decomposition, implementation, refinement), the orchestrator must decide up front how much of the total budget each phase may spend. The obvious zero-shot approach is to ask an LLM to split the budget directly, but LLMs are known to be weak at knapsack-style optimization. This paper asks whether eliciting per-phase utility curves from the LLM and solving the allocation with a classical optimizer does better.
official.method:
The pipeline is a LangGraph graph allocate -> plan -> decompose -> implement -> refine. Plan, decompose and implement use gpt-4o-mini; refine (review->revise loop, up to 3 iterations, best candidate kept) and the controller use gpt-4o. Each phase runs under a hard per-phase USD cap. For ZEBRA, the gpt-4o controller estimates, for each phase, a quality ceiling a_i and two token operating points (tokens to reach ~50% and ~90% of potential quality); these give a saturating-exponential curve f_i(x) = a_i(1 - exp(-b_i x)) with b_i converted to inverse-USD via per-phase pricing. The mult_offset variant maximizes prod_i (1 - a_i exp(-b_i x_i)) subject to sum x_i <= B, solved via the log transform and bisection on the Lagrange multiplier (water-filling). The LLM-direct baseline uses the same controller model and prompt scaffold but outputs the per-phase split directly.

Benchmark: 150 APPS interview-level tasks (50 easy / 50 medium / 50 hard by unconstrained mean score), screened for cost stability (CV of cost < 0.35 over 30 unconstrained runs). The per-task budget is B = alpha x mean unconstrained cost. Each (task, alpha, strategy) cell is run 15 times; the score is the fraction of APPS test cases passed. NB retention is the strategy's mean score divided by the no-budget mean score on the same tasks; significance is a two-sided paired Wilcoxon test on per-task mean scores, BH-adjusted over 18 tests.
official.claim: On 150 APPS interview tasks at a budget of alpha = 0.5 of the unconstrained cost, ZEBRA mult_offset allocation reaches mean score 0.5397 (94.4% of the no-budget score) versus 0.5038 (88.1%) for LLM-direct allocation at essentially the same realized cost ($0.0110 vs. $0.0109 per task); paired Wilcoxon on per-task means gives +0.0359, W/L/T 79/34/37, BH-adjusted p = 4.7e-6.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on 150 APPS interview-level tasks (15 runs per cell). Mean and median are taken over per-task mean scores; success rate is the task-averaged fraction of runs with score > 0.5; NB retention is computed as a ratio of means, s/s_NB (the strategy's mean score on the task set divided by the no-budget mean score on the same set). The two ZEBRA variants differ in the allocation objective (sum vs. product). Significance markers on NB retention come from a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-task mean score against LLM-direct, with p-values BH-adjusted within the 18-test APPS main family (Appendix D.4, Table 5; * p_BH < 0.05, ** p_BH < 0.01, *** p_BH < 0.001). Bold marks the best ZEBRA variant per column within each alpha block. Both ZEBRA variants outperform LLM-direct at both budget levels on every aggregate metric.
official.metric: Mean per-task score (fraction of APPS test cases passed, averaged over 15 runs per task, then over tasks; higher is better) and NB retention (ratio to the no-budget mean 0.5717). No ± reported; significance from a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over 150 per-task means, BH-adjusted.

official.falsification_criterion: Under the same protocol (150 tasks, alpha = 0.5, 15 runs per cell), ZEBRA mult_offset fails to beat LLM-direct on mean per-task score with paired Wilcoxon p < 0.01, or the mean gap shrinks well below the reported +0.036 (e.g. under +0.01), or ZEBRA's gain comes with clearly higher realized spend.

title: Fast Reconstruction of Exact Maxwell Dynamics from Sparse Data

official.background: Reconstructing a full space-time electromagnetic field from a few pointwise measurements is a common inverse task (antenna measurement, RF sensing, tomography). The data do not specify a well-posed forward problem, so classical solvers such as FEM do not apply directly. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can fit sparse data, but they enforce Maxwell's equations only approximately through a residual loss, which often makes training slow and unstable. This paper builds the equations into the model architecture instead, so that every prediction is an exact solution.
official.method:
FLASH-MAX is a one-hidden-layer network. Each hidden neuron w * tanh(z.x + b) * p_i(z) is an exact solution of the homogeneous Maxwell equations, because the time frequency is tied to the spatial frequencies by z0 = ±sqrt(z1^2+z2^2+z3^2) and the output is multiplied by fixed polynomial vectors p_1(z), p_2(z) (Eq. 2, from Macaulay2). The output is the 6-dimensional (E, B) field at spacetime point x = (t, x, y, z). Only z1..z3, b and w are trained, with an MSE fit to observed (E, B) values. Training setup: width 10K (about 200K parameters), AdamW at lr 5e-2, weight decay 5e-5, betas (0.9, 0.95), Xavier-normal init with gain 5/3, batch 1K, cosine schedule over 10K epochs. The same hyperparameters are used for every problem.

In the IC setup the training data are 1K-2K points sampled at t = 0 in [0,1]^3. The model is evaluated by relative L2 error (RMSE of (E, B) divided by the RMSE of the ground truth) on 10K points in [0,0.1] x [0.2,0.8]^3, a region inside the domain of dependence of the initial data. The baseline is the authors' PINN: a 6-layer MLP of width 128 trained with Adam at lr 1e-2, 10K initial-condition points and 50K collocation points, with loss weights data 10, PDE 1, divergence 2. The PINN must also reach a normalized PDE residual below 1e-2. Each method stops as soon as validation error drops below 5%, and the reported number is wall-clock time to that point on an NVIDIA L40S. There are four closed-form ground truths: Plane Waves, Radial Waves, a Hopf fibration (electromagnetic knot) and a Random Solution (Appendix C).
official.claim: On the same NVIDIA L40S in the initial-condition (no BC) setup, FLASH-MAX reaches <5% relative L2 validation error in 6.8 ± 0.3 s (Plane Waves), 11.9 ± 0.6 s (Radial Waves), 3.2 ± 0.0 s (Hopf) and 6.1 ± 0.2 s (Random). The PINN baseline needs 119.3 ± 28.5, 89.8 ± 25.9 and 131.9 ± 19.4 s on Plane Waves, Hopf and Random, and fails on Radial Waves (86.7% error). That is a speedup of at least 10x in every case.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Experiment 1: Race to 5%. Validation Error, Residual Error, and Compute training time to reach 5% relative validation error (if possible) for the ground truths: Plane Waves, Radial Waves, Hopf Fibration, Random Solution with/without boundary conditions (BCs). Animations to complement these results visually are available in the supplementary material at flash_max/flash_max_gifs.
official.metric: Wall-clock training time in seconds to reach relative L2 validation error < 5% (lower is better). The PINN must also have a PDE residual < 1e-2, which FLASH-MAX satisfies at 0 by construction. The ± is not defined in the caption; it is presumably the spread over random seeds (Figures 2 and 3 use 5 seeds).

official.falsification_criterion: With the stated hyperparameters, FLASH-MAX does not reach <5% relative L2 error within about 15 s on Plane Waves, Hopf and Random Solution. Or a PINN as specified in Appendix B.2 reaches <5% error with residual <1e-2 within a factor of about 3 of FLASH-MAX's time on the same GPU. Or FLASH-MAX fails to reach <5% on Radial Waves.

title: Bridging Structure and Language: Graph-Based Visual Reasoning for Autonomous Road Understanding

official.background: Autonomous vehicles need structured road understanding: lane geometry, lane topology, and which signs and lights control which lanes. Modular stacks represent this precisely with HD maps and road graphs, but those use a fixed schema. Vision-language models (VLMs) can describe long-tail scene details in open vocabulary, but they are weakly grounded in geometry and relations. The paper asks whether a small amount of graph-derived, verifiable supervision can teach a small VLM to answer compositional road-reasoning questions better than much larger general-purpose models.
official.method:
The Combined Road Substrate (CRS) is a per-scene spatio-temporal graph. Nodes (lanes, signs, lights, vehicles, markings) have open-vocabulary types and properties, and edges carry relations such as 'is left of' or 'controls'. All three must form well-typed English sentences under fixed templates, and 'uniqueness anchors' ensure that every referenced object has an unambiguous descriptor. Graphs are initialized from Argoverse2 HD maps plus OpenLane-V2 topology, then filtered and enriched by human annotators. Nineteen query types (counting, properties, comparison, existence/pointing, relational) are run over the graph to produce multiple-choice questions with graph-perturbed hard-negative answers and, optionally, chain-of-thought traces. From 80 graphs (4 frames at 2 Hz, front cameras) the authors generate about 22k training samples. The held-out validation set has 1000 expert-verified samples from 120 different scenes, with at most one sample per query type per scene.

Qwen3-VL-2B/4B-Instruct are fully fine-tuned on these samples (4xH100, 5 epochs, learning rate 4e-5, cosine decay). An image-free ablation ('- images') fine-tunes the 4B model on the same data with every sample's images replaced by one fixed image taken at random from the training set (Appendix A.7), so the model is blind to the actual scene. Evaluation is multiple-choice accuracy on the 1000-sample validation set. The set is also split into 'perception-like' and 'reasoning-heavy' subsets by decoy hardness. Open- and closed-weight VLMs (GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Qwen3-VL-235B, Gemma-4-31B, etc.) are evaluated zero-shot on the same set.
official.claim: On the 1000-sample CRS validation set, Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct fully fine-tuned on CRS data from 80 scenes reaches 0.711 accuracy (95% CI 0.684-0.739). This is above the same model fine-tuned on the same data with the real images replaced by a single fixed placeholder image ('- images', 0.587, CI 0.557-0.619), above the best zero-shot VLM tested, GPT-5.4 (0.621, CI 0.591-0.650), and above the un-tuned base model (0.443).

title: Dynamic Video Generation: Shaping Video Generation Across Time and Space

official.background: Video diffusion transformers such as HunyuanVideo and Wan2.2 are slow because every denoising step processes a huge number of spatio-temporal tokens, and step distillation alone leaves this per-step cost in place. Progressive-resolution sampling saves compute in images by denoising early steps at low resolution. Video adds a time axis, though, and prompts differ in what they need: textured static scenes need spatial detail, while fast-motion scenes need frame rate. The paper argues that compressing only one axis to reach a large speedup either makes motion rigid (fewer frames) or causes flicker and ghosting (lower resolution), so the budget should be split between the two axes according to the content.
official.method:
DVG is training-free. It first runs a few denoising steps at 0.5x spatial resolution and 13 of 31 latent frames, then extrapolates a rough clean latent sketch in one step (X~ = X_k + alpha_k v_theta). From this sketch it computes a spatial demand d_s (normalized high-pass FFT energy per latent frame) and a temporal demand d_t (mean optical-flow magnitude between adjacent latent frames), and turns them into weights m_s and m_t = 1 - m_s with a softmax. A predefined list of multi-stage actions, each giving a (spatial ratio, temporal ratio) per stage on a 0.05 grid, is filtered to those whose compute density rho(a) = sum_l H_l W_l F_l N_l / (H W F N) is within a tolerance of the target budget D. The action whose average spatial and temporal ratios best match (m_s, m_t) under a weighted squared-error objective is selected. When resolution or frame count changes, the latent is resized with anchor-based linear interpolation and re-noised with coordinate-hashed Gaussian noise. The last stage always runs at full resolution and full frame count.

The ablation uses HunyuanVideo-1.5 text-to-video at 480p (16:9), 121 frames, 50 steps, bf16, flow shift 7.0, seed 42, on the 946 VBench prompts, with a target density of about 50%. Variants change one component at a time: 'Temporal Only' compresses only frames, 'Spatial Only' compresses only resolution, and 'Manual Tuning (Fixed Ratio)' uses one hand-tuned fixed spatial/temporal ratio for all prompts (about 0.30/0.45 average reduction), which removes the content-aware selection.
official.claim: On HunyuanVideo-1.5 T2V (480p, 121 frames, 50 steps, VBench, about 50% compute density, about 3.1x speedup), content-aware joint spatio-temporal DVG reaches a VBench Total of 80.41, compared with 78.98 for temporal-only, 76.84 for spatial-only and 78.85 for a manually tuned fixed spatio-temporal ratio.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Ablation Study on HunyuanVideo-1.5.
official.metric: VBench Total score (%) over 946 prompts, higher is better; Dynamic Degree and Quality score also reported. Single run with seed 42; no error bars, CIs or significance tests (the paper's checklist says so).
official.comparison: DVG (content-aware joint compression) vs. Temporal Only, Spatial Only, and Manual Tuning (Fixed Ratio) at matched ~50% density on the same backbone and prompts
official.falsification_criterion: At matched ~50% density and similar measured speedup, either the best single-axis variant or the fixed-ratio variant gets a VBench Total within about 0.5 points of DVG or above it, i.e. the ~1.4-point gap to temporal-only and the ~1.6-point gap to the fixed ratio disappear.

title: Grounding Driving VLA via Inverse Kinematics

official.background: Driving Vision-Language-Action models (Driving VLAs) take camera images, ego status (speed, acceleration, etc.) and a route command and output a future trajectory. Because most driving data can be fitted from ego status and command alone (lane following, cruising), such models can learn a shortcut that ignores the camera input: the paper shows that inserting a car directly in front of the ego vehicle barely changes the trajectories of existing VLAs. The paper argues that this 'blind planning' follows from a direct trajectory-regression objective and proposes an architecture that forces the trajectory to be decoded from visual features.
official.method:
The model uses DINOv3 ViT-S/16 features from three front cameras, projected into a Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct LLM together with ego status and a text command. Instead of emitting a trajectory, the LLM is trained (MSE loss) to predict the future visual state V_{t+Δ}, i.e. the DINOv3 tokens of the frame Δ seconds ahead (4 s on NAVSIM). A separate 'Inverse Kinematics Network', a small conditional diffusion model with two cross-attention layers (DDPM, cosine schedule, 50 sampling steps), decodes the trajectory from only the pair (current visual tokens, predicted future visual tokens); it never sees ego status or command, and trajectory-loss gradients are stopped at its inputs. QA co-training is used on nuScenes only.

The matched baseline OpenDriveVLA* is the authors' reimplementation of OpenDriveVLA for NAVSIM: same DINOv3 encoder, same 0.5B LLM, same training data, optimizer, LR schedule, batch size, encoder-freeze policy and the same two-stage SFT then GRPO (PDMS reward, following ReCogDrive) procedure on navtrain, but the trajectory is emitted directly as LLM text. Both are evaluated on NAVSIM-v1 navtest with the PDM score (PDMS), which aggregates no-collision (NC), drivable-area compliance (DAC), time-to-collision (TTC), comfort (C.) and ego progress (EP).
official.claim: On NAVSIM-v1 with matched backbone (Qwen2.5-0.5B + DINOv3, cameras only), data and SFT→GRPO training, adding next-visual-state prediction and the IK Network raises PDMS from 73.2 (OpenDriveVLA*) to 92.2 (+19.0); even the SFT-only model reaches 90.3.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: PDMS results on the NAVSIM-v1 benchmark. Bold=best, underline=second best. † denotes models trained with the SFT→GRPO schedule. OpenDriveVLA* shares all training hyperparameters, data, and the SFT→GRPO schedule with our model; the only differences are the next visual state prediction objective and the IK Network.
official.metric: PDM score (PDMS, 0-100, higher is better) on NAVSIM-v1 navtest, plus sub-scores NC, DAC, TTC, C., EP; single run, no error bars
official.comparison: Ours† (NSP + IK Network, SFT→GRPO) vs. OpenDriveVLA* (direct text trajectory output, same backbone, data and SFT→GRPO schedule)
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both models under the matched protocol, the proposed model's NAVSIM-v1 PDMS exceeds the direct-output baseline by less than about 5 points (e.g. the baseline reaches the mid-80s, as other 2-3B camera-only VLAs do), or the gain disappears at the SFT-only stage.

title: Towards Understanding Self-Pretraining for Sequence Classification

official.background: Amos et al. (2024) showed that Transformers trained from scratch on Long-Range Arena (LRA) classification tasks do much worse than the same models first 'self-pretrained' (SPT) with a masked-reconstruction objective on the same task data and then finetuned on labels. Why this works was unclear: it could be better generalization from learned data features, or a fix for an optimization failure. This paper ablates SPT and argues that the main bottleneck is that label supervision struggles to learn useful query-key Attention patterns from random initialization, and that SPT learns W_Q, W_K that turn absolute sinusoidal positional encodings into a proximity-biased Attention pattern.
official.method:
The model is a pre-norm Transformer (as in Amos et al.'s codebase) with a learned linear input encoder, sinusoidal absolute positional encodings added once at the input, Attention + MLP blocks with LayerNorm, mean pooling over the sequence and a linear classifier. Here it has a single layer; the CIFAR10 (grayscale, flattened to length-1024 sequences, 10 classes) configuration otherwise follows the paper's CIFAR10 settings: width 64, 4 heads, feed-forward size 128, AdamW, lr 1e-3, no weight decay, batch size 16 (finetune) / 32 (pretrain). SPT masks 50% of pixels and trains the same architecture with an L2 reconstruction loss for 200 epochs; finetuning and from-scratch training use 100 epochs of cross-entropy on labels. Reported accuracy is the peak held-out (public LRA test split) accuracy within the finetuning budget.

For the transplant ablation, after SPT the model is re-initialized for finetuning in one of three ways: (a) all weights from the SPT checkpoint; (b) only W_Q and W_K from SPT, everything else freshly random; (c) all weights from SPT except W_Q and W_K, which are freshly random. All parameters are then trained on labels identically, and compared with training from scratch. Each configuration is run with 5 seeds.
official.claim: For one-layer Transformers on LRA CIFAR10, initializing only W_Q and W_K from self-pretrained weights gives 0.607 ± 0.012 validation accuracy, matching full SPT initialization (0.603 ± 0.005), while initializing everything except W_Q, W_K from SPT gives only 0.502 ± 0.008, close to from-scratch training (0.486 ± 0.003).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: For one-layer models, SPT improves val. accuracy due to better initialization of W_Q, W_K. We report mean and standard deviation across 5 seeds. A full ablation is provided in Tb. 9.
official.metric: Peak held-out classification accuracy within 100 finetuning epochs (higher is better); mean ± standard deviation over 5 seeds
official.comparison: SPT → only QK init vs. SPT → all-but-QK init vs. SPT → full model init vs. from scratch, one-layer model, same training recipe
official.falsification_criterion: In the one-layer CIFAR10 setting, QK-only SPT initialization fails to beat from-scratch training by clearly more than seed noise (e.g. under ~0.05 gain), or the all-but-QK initialization recovers most of the full-SPT gain (e.g. comes within ~0.05 of full SPT init).

title: SMoA: Spectrum Modulation Adapter for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

official.background: LoRA fine-tunes large language models by adding a rank-r update to frozen weights, which keeps memory and parameter cost low but confines the update to at most r directions. Pretrained transformer weights have long-tailed spectra that are numerically close to full rank, so a small-rank update may miss useful directions in the spectral tail. Raising r helps but adds parameters, so methods that reach higher-rank updates with the same or fewer trainable parameters (MoRA, MeLoRA, HiRA, and others) are an active line of work.
official.method:
SMoA computes the SVD of each frozen weight W0 once and uses it to define fixed output and input permutations that reorder coordinates into K spectrum-aligned contiguous groups. The K diagonal blocks M_k of the reordered weight serve as frozen anchors. Each block gets a trainable low-rank pair B_k (d_out/K x r/K) and A_k (r/K x d_in/K), and its update is the Hadamard product (B_k A_k) ⊙ M_k. The block-diagonal update is permuted back to the original coordinates and added to W0. This uses r(d_in + d_out)/K trainable parameters, a 1/K fraction of rank-r LoRA, while the update rank can exceed r.

For the chosen claim, Llama-3-8B is fine-tuned on MetaMath and evaluated on GSM8K by exact match of the extracted final numeric answer, following the HiRA setup. Adapters go on q, k, v, up and down projections (Tables 6-7); AdamW, 1000 warmup steps, batch size 32, learning rate 1e-4 to 2e-4 per Table 6 (Appendix D text says 1e-3). SMoA uses r=32, K=2 (local rank 16) and is averaged over 5 seeds (7, 42, 123, 1234, 12345); baselines are reported as single numbers.
official.claim: On GSM8K with Llama-3-8B trained on MetaMath, SMoA (r=32, K=2) reaches 72.33% ± 0.86 accuracy, above HiRA (r=32) at 70.81%, MeLoRA (r=32, K=2) at 69.36% and LoRA (r=32) at 65.89%.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison of PEFT methods.
official.metric: GSM8K exact-match final-answer accuracy (%), higher is better; ± for SMoA is std over 5 seeds; baselines have no error bars
official.comparison: SMoA (r=32, K=2) vs. LoRA, DoRA, MoRA, SSMLoRA, MeLoRA and HiRA at reference rank 32 (and r=16 variants), plus prompt tuning and P-tuning
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same MetaMath training and GSM8K evaluation, SMoA (r=32, K=2) does not beat LoRA (r=32) by a clear margin (e.g. less than about 3 points), or HiRA (r=32) matches or exceeds SMoA's mean.

title: Fast and Stable Triangular Inversion for Delta-Rule Linear Transformers

official.background: Delta-rule linear-attention layers (DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, KDA), used in models such as Qwen3.5/3.6 and Kimi Linear, are computed chunk by chunk. Each chunk needs the inverse of a unit-diagonal lower-triangular C x C matrix (C = 16 to 128). This inversion can take up to about 40% of layer runtime. Faster algorithms built from matrix products suit AI accelerators, which favour low precision, but some of them are numerically unstable. An unstable inverse can wreck model accuracy: the paper shows Qwen3.6's MMLU score falling from 76.1% to 0.2%. The paper compares direct and iterative inversion algorithms for stability, cost and speed.
official.method:
Algorithms compared (Algorithms 1-6): vectorized and matrix-product column sweep (VCS, MCS); inversion through the Cayley-Hamilton characteristic polynomial (MCH, Eq. 9: I - L + L^2 - ..., computed by repeated squaring in about 2 log n matmuls, known to be unstable); the Bunch-Hopcroft block recursion (MBH, log-stable); the proposed mixed recursion MXR, which uses MCH only to invert the b0 x b0 diagonal blocks (b0 = 16) and then runs the unrolled MBH recursion from those blocks; Newton-Schulz (NS); and one step of iterative refinement (+IR: R = I - Y A, X = Y + R Y).

Accuracy test (Section 4.1): A = I + diag(beta) * strict_tril(K K^T). Each row of K has i.i.d. Uniform[0,1] entries and is rescaled to unit length. For Figure 2, beta is all ones. Sizes n are 16, 32, 64 and 128. The input matrix is given in float32, float16 or bfloat16, while matrix products accumulate in float32. Errors are measured against a float64 PyTorch inverse, as max absolute, max relative (lower triangle) and Frobenius relative error.
official.claim: With float32 inputs (beta = 1), plain MCH has Frobenius-relative inverse error of a few times 1e-2 at n = 32 and above 1e4 at n = 64 and 128. MXR, which uses MCH on 16x16 blocks, stays at about 1e-5 or below at every size, and MXR+IR matches the stable column-sweep VCS at about 1e-7. With float16 inputs, MCH returns NaN for n >= 32, while MXR+IR stays within about 1e-3, the same as VCS.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Comparison of the inverse accuracy of various methods, for three different input precision formats, and four matrix sizes. The input matrix is sampled as defined in Eq. (14), where beta is the all-ones vector.
official.metric: Forward error of the computed inverse against a float64 reference (Frobenius relative, also max absolute and max relative), lower is better, on a log scale. No error bars, and the number of random matrices is not stated. Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: MCH vs. MXR vs. MXR+IR vs. VCS (and MCS, MBH, NS) on the same random Delta-rule matrices, for each size and input precision
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Eq. (14) experiment with beta = 1 and float32 inputs, either MXR's Frobenius-relative error at n = 64 or 128 is within about 2 orders of magnitude of MCH's (MCH no longer fails while MXR succeeds), or MXR+IR's error is more than about 10x worse than VCS's at those sizes. In float16, MXR+IR returns NaN or an error above about 1e-2.

title: Hierarchical Variational Policies for Reward-Guided Diffusion
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (Stage-1-only numbers match the HyperNoise row of Table 1, page 8)

official.background: Pretrained unconditional diffusion models can solve inverse problems such as super-resolution, inpainting and HDR reconstruction by test-time guidance: steering the denoising process with a differentiable likelihood p(y | x0). Most such methods (DPS, DAPS, NDTM, RED-Diff) need gradient steps or inner-loop optimization at every denoising step, which makes sampling slow. Amortizing guidance into a small learned network that steers a few-step sampler in one forward rollout would be much cheaper, but simple policies struggle with the multimodal posteriors of ill-posed problems and large step sizes.
official.method:
The pretrained diffusion model stays frozen. Guidance is cast as variational inference over denoising trajectories with a hierarchical variational policy: a learned initial-noise policy x_T = eps + E_phi(y, eps), and per-step latent controls u_t ~ N(pi_psi(x_t, u_{>t}, y, t), (kappa sigma_t)^2 I) with kappa = 0.05, which are added to the denoiser input, x_{t-1} ~ N(mu_pretrained(x_t + gamma u_t, t), sigma_{t-1}^2 I). The training objective (Eq. 7) is a hierarchical ELBO: Gaussian log-likelihood of y given x0 (sigma_y = 0.01), plus penalties ||E_phi||^2, ||mu(x_t + gamma u_t) - mu(x_t)||^2 and ||u_t||^2. Both networks are DiTs (51M parameters for FFHQ, 92M for ImageNet), trained with Adam at lr 1e-4 on 1k (FFHQ) or 10k (ImageNet) training images per task.

Training has two stages. Stage 1 trains only the noise policy E_phi by backpropagating the reward through the whole sampling chain; this is equivalent to the HyperNoise baseline (noise-only amortization). Stage 2 freezes E_phi and trains the per-step controller pi_psi over all steps in parallel, using the Tweedie estimate x̂0 in place of x0 in the reward. AHVP samples with a single controlled rollout and no test-time optimization. The claim compares AHVP with Stage 1 only against AHVP with both stages on 4x bicubic super-resolution, using FFHQ-256 (DPS checkpoint) and ImageNet-256 (ADM checkpoint) priors, and evaluates on 100 held-out images per dataset.
official.claim: On 4x super-resolution, adding the learned per-step stochastic controls (Stage 2) to the learned initial-noise policy (Stage 1) cuts AHVP's LPIPS from 0.147 to 0.073 on FFHQ-256 and from 0.432 to 0.244 on ImageNet-256, with FID going from 79.91 to 45.17 and from 155.14 to 84.44, at the same per-sample runtime (0.6 s and 1.3 s on an A6000).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Per-step controls (Stage-2) improve reconstruction quality. Ablation on training stages for AHVP and SHVP on SR×4 for FFHQ-256 and ImageNet-256.
official.metric: LPIPS and FID on 100 held-out images per dataset, lower is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: AHVP with Stage-1 noise policy only (equivalent to HyperNoise) vs. AHVP with Stage-1 noise policy plus Stage-2 per-step controller; same pretrained prior, same task, same inference runtime
official.falsification_criterion: With a re-implementation trained under the stated setup, adding the Stage-2 per-step controller does not lower LPIPS on SR x4 by a clear margin (e.g. less than a 20% relative reduction on FFHQ-256 or ImageNet-256), or the full AHVP is not better than the Stage-1-only model on both LPIPS and FID.

title: From Patches to Trajectories: Privileged Process Supervision for Software-Engineering Agents

official.background: Open software-engineering (SWE) agents are usually trained by supervised fine-tuning on long multi-turn tool-use trajectories from a strong teacher model, keeping only rollouts whose final patch passes the issue's tests. That filter says nothing about the intermediate steps, so students also imitate redundant file views, loops and unsupported leaps, and instances the teacher never solves contribute no training data. Every real GitHub issue in benchmarks such as SWE-Gym also comes with the developer's reference patch, which the standard pipeline throws away even though it shows what a fix requires.
official.method:
P2T (Patches-to-Trajectories) uses the reference patch only during data curation, never in the student's training text. A reverse phase has proposer and critic LLM agents turn the patch into a process graph G* whose nodes are facts about the repository or runtime and solution milestones (reproduction script, root-cause analysis, fix plan, edit, validation), each with the tool action that would uncover it, linked by prerequisite edges. A forward phase builds the trajectory in 10-step windows with 5-step overlap: it samples K blinded continuations from the teacher (which does not see the patch), lets a curator rewrite at most one step per continuation toward a node that is currently reachable in G*, rejects rewrites that mention entities not yet seen in observations or that an LLM judge finds unsupported, scores progress on graph nodes, and commits the shortest segment whose effectiveness clears a threshold. Trajectories whose final patch fails the tests are discarded.

Trajectories are curated from about 1.8k SWE-Gym instances with Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct or GLM-5-FP8 as teacher, under OpenHands with a 100-iteration budget. Qwen2.5-Coder-14B/32B-Instruct students are fully fine-tuned (3 epochs, lr 2e-5, context extended to 131k with YaRN). Baselines trained under the same pipeline are test-pass rejection sampling (SWE-Gym recipe, 2,126 instances) and SWE-Lego (the same rollouts with the loss masked on turns followed by a tool error). Evaluation is Pass@1 with one greedy rollout per instance on SWE-bench Verified (500) and Lite (300), plus average per-instance inference cost in US$ at fixed token prices.
official.claim: On SWE-bench Verified, a Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct student fine-tuned on P2T trajectories curated by Qwen3-Coder-480B resolves 43.2% of issues, compared with 36.2% for SWE-Lego and 36.0% for test-pass rejection sampling, at lower per-instance cost ($0.78 vs. $0.93/$0.92); P2T (full) beats both baselines by at least 6.3 Pass@1 points in all 8 student/teacher/benchmark cells.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main evaluation results on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite. For each (student, teacher) pair we report two metrics: effectiveness as resolve rate (Pass@1, %, ↑) and efficiency as average per-instance inference cost (Cost, US$, ↓). Bold denotes the best result in each row; (+X.X) reports the absolute Pass@1 gain over the test-pass rejection-sampling baseline, (−X.X) the absolute cost reduction.

title: Hallucination as Commitment Failure: Larger LLMs Misfire Despite Knowing the Answer
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (threshold robustness in Appendix Table 5, page 22)

official.background: LLM hallucinations are usually explained as missing knowledge: the model answers wrongly because the correct answer is not in its output distribution. Token-level confidence and entropy are known to miss confidently wrong answers. This paper checks whether, at the moment an instruction-tuned model emits its answer, the correct answer is often already present with substantial probability, which would mean the failure lies in how the model commits to an answer rather than in what it knows.
official.method:
For short-form QA (3,000 questions per model drawn from TriviaQA and NQ-Open; greedy decoding; Instruct models answer directly, so the commitment step is the first generated token t=1), the authors define a concept token set S_c* for the ground-truth answer deterministically (Appendix I): take all dataset aliases (TriviaQA answer.value, aliases, normalized_aliases; NQ-Open answer list), make six lexical variants of each (original, lowercase, capitalized, and the same three with a leading space), tokenize each without special tokens and keep the first token ID. P_mass(t=1; c*) is the sum of the model's next-token probabilities over S_c*.

A response is a hallucination if no ground-truth alias is a substring of it. A hallucination is a commitment failure (CF) if P_mass(t=1; c*) >= 0.2. CF% = CF count / hallucination count. CF is split into first-token selection failures (greedy first token not in S_c*) and multi-token divergences (greedy first token in S_c* but the final answer is wrong). Models: Qwen3.5 0.8B/2B/4B/9B Instruct (4-bit NF4), Llama-3.2-1B/3B and Llama-3.1-8B Instruct, plus Qwen2.5-72B and Llama-3.1-70B Instruct; Base variants are reported in Appendix Table 9.
official.claim: On 3,000 TriviaQA/NQ-Open short-form questions with greedy decoding, the fraction of Instruct-model hallucinations with P_mass(t=1; correct concept) >= 0.2 rises with model size: Qwen3.5 Instruct 16% (0.8B) -> 17% (2B) -> 26% (4B) -> 32% (9B), and Llama Instruct 16% (3.2-1B) -> 28% (3.2-3B) -> 33% (3.1-8B), reaching 41% (Qwen2.5-72B) and 47% (Llama-3.1-70B).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Commitment-failure rate (CF%) and decomposition into first-token selection failures (SF, greedy ∉ S_c*) and multi-token divergences (Div, greedy ∈ S_c* but final answer wrong) across the Instruct scale ablation. Acc: Short-QA accuracy. AUROC: P_mass(t=1) AUROC. Halluc: hallucinated sample count. SF%: SF as fraction of all hallucinations. Full per-model details including Base models in Appendix Table 9.
official.metric: CF% = share of hallucinated answers whose first-token probability mass on the correct concept's first-token surface forms is >= 0.2 (higher means more hallucinations occur despite substantial mass on the correct answer). Single deterministic greedy run per model; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: CF% across model sizes within each Instruct family (Qwen3.5 0.8B-9B plus Qwen2.5-72B; Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B/70B), all under the same prompt, data and P_mass definition.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same alias-based S_c* construction and 0.2 threshold, CF% does not increase with size within the sub-10B Instruct models (e.g., Qwen3.5-9B Instruct CF% is not clearly above Qwen3.5-0.8B Instruct, or Llama-3.1-8B Instruct not clearly above Llama-3.2-1B Instruct), or the ordering reverses at thresholds 0.1-0.4.

title: From Reasoning Chains to Verifiable Subproblems: Curriculum Reinforcement Learning Enables Credit Assignment for LLM Reasoning

official.background: RL from verifiable rewards (RLVR), e.g. GRPO, trains LLMs on math by rewarding only a correct final answer. On hard problems, correct rollouts are rare, so whole groups of rollouts get zero reward and give no gradient, and a near-miss attempt gets the same credit as a total failure. Curriculum methods try to help by giving the model hints or partial reference solutions as a prefix, but then the model never has to derive those intermediate steps itself.
official.method:
SCRL (Subproblem Curriculum RL) uses an external LLM (DeepSeek-V3.2) to turn each training problem's reference solution into K = 4 self-contained, verifiable subproblems ordered by difficulty, with the 4th equal to the original problem. A curriculum prompt shows all 4 at once, and the policy answers them in one rollout inside tags <p1>...</p1> ... <p4>...</p4>. Each answer is checked separately. Progress-aware correction keeps only the longest solved prefix, so (1,1,0,1) becomes (1,1,0,0). Rewards are then normalized across the rollout group separately for each subproblem position j (subproblem-level normalization), and advantage A_i^(j) is applied only to the tokens inside the <pj> span. Tokens outside the spans get zero advantage.

Mixed-group training: of G = 8 rollouts per problem, 4 come from the curriculum prompt (using the per-span advantages above) and 4 come from the original problem (standard GRPO outcome advantage), all in one clipped objective with no KL term. Training uses verl on hard_1024 (1,024 random problems from a hard competition-math set), lr 1e-6, batch 128, max response 8192, temperature 0.6, 300 steps. The baselines are GRPO, DAPO, QuestA (partial-solution hints, 50% then 25%) and NuRL (self-generated abstract hints), trained on the same data for the same number of steps. Evaluation picks the best-validation checkpoint, samples 64 rollouts per test problem, and reports pass@1 on 7 math benchmarks and their average.
official.claim: On Qwen3-4B-Base trained on hard_1024 for 300 steps, SCRL reaches a 7-benchmark average pass@1 of 35.0, vs. 32.0 for QuestA (best baseline) and 30.9 for GRPO, and is best on every one of the 7 benchmarks.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main Results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The best results are highlighted in bold, and the second-best results are underlined.
official.metric: pass@1 (%) estimated from 64 samples per problem at temperature 0.6, averaged over OlympiadBench, Minerva, MATH-500, AIME24, AIME25, AMC, IMO-Bench (higher is better). Single training run per method; no seeds, std or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: SCRL vs. GRPO, DAPO, QuestA, NuRL and SFT, all on the same base model, training data and step budget
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining GRPO and SCRL on Qwen3-4B-Base with the paper's setup, SCRL's 7-benchmark average pass@1 does not beat GRPO by at least about 2 points (paper: +4.1), or it falls below QuestA's average.

title: Learning Causal Orderings for In-Context Tabular Prediction

official.background: Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN predict a target from all other columns using in-context learning, so they can rely on non-causal correlations that break when the data distribution shifts or a mechanism is intervened on. Causal discovery methods can recover which variables cause which, but they are usually per-dataset optimizers that are separate from predictive models. Amortized causal discovery methods (e.g. AVICI) need supervised training on ground-truth graphs. This paper asks whether one in-context transformer can learn a causal variable order without supervision and use it to restrict which features each prediction depends on.
official.method:
TabOrder embeds each cell (value plus missingness bit) and runs two transformers that alternate row-wise and column-wise attention. The order-inference branch (6 blocks, width 128) decodes a scalar score s_i per column, averaged over rows. The scores define a hard column-attention mask A_ij = 1(s_j <= s_i), applied as an additive attention bias in the forward pass (scale annealed from -5 to -20), with a sigmoid((s_i - s_j)/t) straight-through relaxation in the backward pass (t annealed from 1.0 to 0.1). The prediction branch (4 blocks) uses this mask for column attention, keeps row attention unrestricted, and decodes a per-cell Gaussian mean and a per-variable variance (averaged over rows). A learned per-cell variance increment is added for each column earlier in the order that is missing in that row (Eq. 7). Training is unsupervised: 20% of entries are masked at random and the Gaussian log-likelihood of the masked entries is maximized. No ground-truth graphs are used. The model is pretrained for 25,000 steps (batch 4, 100,000 datasets in total) on synthetic nonlinear SCMs with 5-10 variables and 512-1024 rows and Gaussian noise (in the non-additive setting, mechanisms are random-Fourier-feature approximations of RBF Gaussian-process draws; Appendix B, C.1).

For the Sachs et al. (2005) flow-cytometry data (11 phosphoproteins), the order learned by TabOrder in a single forward pass is compared with a consensus DAG. This is the bnlearn Sachs network with Erk->Akt and PKC->PKA replaced by PIP3->Akt and PIP2->PKC (Appendix C.2, Figure 9). The metric is topological divergence d_TOP, which counts true edges whose direction disagrees with the order (shown normalized, lower is better). It is computed for each of 13 experimental conditions (b2camp is excluded). Baselines are CAM, SCORE, DAS, NoGAM, NOTEARS, TOPIC, AVICI and the sorting heuristic R2SRT, all run with default settings from public implementations (causal-learn / do-discover).
official.claim: On the Sachs protein-signaling benchmark, TabOrder's inferred causal orders have a mean topological divergence of 0.26 across 13 experimental conditions (0.21 on the reference cd3cd28 condition), lower than every baseline; the best baseline, R2SRT, has a mean of 0.37 (0.35 on cd3cd28), and the other methods range from 0.49 to 0.57.
official.claim_caption: Figure 11: Causal Order Inference in Real-World Data (extends Fig. 4b). Shown is the average topological divergence (d_TOP, lower is better) between ground truth and estimated causal orders on the real-world causal discovery benchmark by Sachs et al. [2005]. For each available dataset c (vertical) corresponding to one experimental condition, we show each method (horizontal) and how the causal order pi_c it discovers in dataset c differs from the consensus graph G_c0. The consensus graph G_c0 represents a summary of causal relationships that likely best represents the near-observational condition cd3cd28. Figure 4b reports the corresponding bar-plot results for this condition.
official.metric: Normalized topological divergence d_TOP against the consensus Sachs DAG (lower is better). The paper reports no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals for this experiment.
official.comparison: TabOrder (pretrained, unsupervised order learning) vs. CAM, SCORE, DAS, NoGAM, NOTEARS, TOPIC, AVICI and R2SRT on the same 13 Sachs conditions and the same consensus graph.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same consensus graph and conditions, a retrained TabOrder has mean d_TOP across conditions that is not clearly below R2SRT's (e.g. >= 0.35), or it is not the lowest-divergence method on the reference cd3cd28 condition.

title: MaSC: A Masked Similarity Metric for Evaluating Concept-Driven Generation

official.background: Papers on subject-driven text-to-image personalization (DreamBooth, IP-Adapter, etc.) report Concept Preservation (CP, does the generated subject look like the reference?) with CLIP-I or DINO image-image cosine, and Prompt Following (PF) with CLIP-T. DreamBench++ collected human ratings and showed that these metrics agree with humans only at about Krippendorff α ≈ 0.3, roughly half the inter-annotator agreement, while GPT-4o judges do much better but are API-bound and opaque. The authors argue that the gap comes from global pooling, which mixes the subject with the background that humans ignore when judging identity, rather than from the encoder.
official.method:
MaSC encodes the reference image and the generated image once each with a frozen SigLIP2 SO400M-NaFlex vision tower (N = 1024 patch tokens for square inputs). A foreground mask of the subject, obtained on DreamBench++ with SAM3 prompted by the subject's canonical name, is downsampled to the patch grid (bilinear, threshold 0.5). The CP score (masked-maxcos) is: for each reference patch inside the reference foreground mask, take the maximum cosine similarity against all patches of the generated image (no mask on the output side), then average over the foreground reference patches. Pairs whose output mask covers under 5% of the image are dropped, and subjects whose reference mask covers under 5% are dropped entirely; this filter is applied to all metrics.

Scores are compared with pooled DreamBench++ human CP ratings using Krippendorff α (and Spearman ρ) on a 7,135-key subset that is the intersection on which all metrics were scored. Baselines include the same SigLIP2 checkpoint with its global attention pool and image-image cosine (same-backbone ablation), DreamSim, DINOv3, DIFT-SDXL, DINO-I, AM-RADIO C-RADIOv4-SO400M, CLIP-I, and the GPT-4V and GPT-4o judge scores shipped with DreamBench++.
official.claim: On the 7,135-key DreamBench++ concept-preservation subset, MaSC's masked-maxcos score reaches Krippendorff α = +0.471 with pooled human ratings, above the same SigLIP2 SO400M-NaFlex checkpoint with global pooling (+0.369) and every other non-LLM metric tested, the best of which is DreamSim (+0.421).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Concept Preservation on DreamBench++. Krippendorff α (Kd_o) and Spearman ρ against pooled human ratings on the 7,135-key apples-to-apples subset. Bold: ours — the only non-LLM, non-human metric to beat GPT-4V; sits Δα = −0.028 behind GPT-4o and reaches 72% of the honest human inter-rater ceiling.
official.metric: Krippendorff α (higher is better) between metric scores and pooled human CP ratings; Spearman ρ also reported. No error bars, CIs or bootstrap are reported (the metric is deterministic).
official.comparison: MaSC (SigLIP2 patch tokens + masked-maxcos) vs. SigLIP2 global pool on the same checkpoint, DreamSim, DINOv3, DIFT-SDXL, DINO-I, AM-RADIO, CLIP-I; GPT-4V and GPT-4o judge scores as reference points
official.falsification_criterion: Recomputing on the same DreamBench++ subset, MaSC's α does not exceed the same-backbone SigLIP2 global-pool α by a clear margin (e.g. the 0.102 gap shrinks to near zero), or DreamSim (or another non-LLM baseline) matches or exceeds MaSC's α.

title: Generative Modeling by Value-Driven Transport
claim_source: Table 2, page 26 (Appendix D.1); subset shown in Table 1, page 8

official.background: Most generative models (diffusion, flow matching, Schrödinger bridges) learn a continuous-time vector field and need many numerical integration steps at sampling time. Optimal transport (OT) paths with squared Euclidean cost are straight lines between coupled source and target points, so a model that learns the OT solution should in principle sample in very few steps. This paper casts dynamic OT as a discrete-time stochastic control problem with H+1 steps and learns the problem's value function directly. The question is whether the learned transport really is straight enough to sample in few steps.
official.method:
The discrete-time dynamic OT problem is written as a linear program over occupancy measures, whose dual variables are value functions V_h. The value-driven transport (VDT) policy moves a state as x_{h+1} = x_h - (1/(H_test+1)) ∇_x V(x_h, h/H_test). Training (Algorithm 1) uses a single neural network V_θ(x, t). For each minibatch of source and target samples it initializes particle pairs for every time step on the linear interpolation between coupled source and target points (Eq. 9), runs K=5 noisy Wasserstein gradient-descent steps on the particles (Eq. 7, stepsize 0.5, noise 1e-3), and then takes an Adam step on θ using the dual gradient of Eq. 8. 'VDT+' couples each minibatch with an exact OT matching (Hungarian algorithm via scipy linear_sum_assignment); plain 'VDT' uses the naive (independent) pairing. Both train with horizon H=100.

2D setup (Appendix D.1): the value network is a 3-layer MLP with 64 units and a 32-dim time embedding; batch 100, T=20,000 Adam steps, lr 1e-4. Source is a standard Gaussian and targets are moons, scurve and 8gaussians; the fourth task is moons to 8gaussians. Evaluation uses 10,000 generated samples. The metrics are the W2 distance to a fresh target sample, computed with the Hungarian algorithm, and the path energy sum_h c(X_h, X_{h+1}), which should approach the squared W2 'oracle' for OT paths. All results are the mean ± std over 5 runs, for test horizons H_test from 1 to 100.
official.claim: On the four 2D benchmarks, OT-initialized VDT+ trained with H=100 and sampled with only 10 steps matches its 100-step W2 within one std (e.g. moons-8gaussians 0.626 ± 0.097 vs 0.652 ± 0.151). Its 10-step path energy is near the OT oracle (29.99 ± 0.28 vs oracle 30.02 on moons-8gaussians), whereas 10-step naive-coupling VDT reaches W2 1.360 ± 0.077 with path energy 76.49 ± 2.68.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Sampling quality as measured by Wasserstein-2 distance to target and path energy for the 2D experiments. We report the mean and standard deviation of 5 independent runs, with best results highlighted in bold (somewhat generously, to help guide the attention of the reader). Results for all competing methods taken from Tong et al. [58]. Methods marked with "+" use an OT coupling for forming minibatches, and methods using a full OT plan over the entire data set for initialization are marked with "++".
official.metric: Wasserstein-2 distance between generated and target samples (lower is better) and path energy (closer to the oracle squared-W2 is better); mean ± 1 std over 5 independent runs
official.comparison: VDT+ (OT minibatch coupling for particle initialization) vs VDT (naive coupling), both run by the authors with the same architecture and training budget, across test horizons H_test in {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100}; path energy also compared to the oracle squared-W2 estimate
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if 10-step VDT+ W2 is worse than 100-step VDT+ W2 by more than one std on the datasets, or if 10-step VDT+ path energy is not close to the oracle (for example, more than 10% above it on moons-8gaussians), or if VDT+ does not beat naive VDT at 10 steps by more than the reported std on moons, scurve and moons-8gaussians (W2) and on all four datasets (path energy).

title: Enhancing Gaze Reasoning in Vision Foundation Models for Gaze Following

official.background: Gaze following means predicting where a given person in an image is looking, output as a heatmap over the image. Recent methods such as GazeLLE use a frozen vision foundation model (DINOv2) as the scene encoder plus a light decoder that takes the queried head position, and they set the state of the art. The authors argue that these models often predict semantically salient objects (a held phone, a conversation partner, the center of an event) rather than following the person's actual gaze direction. So they do well when the target is the salient object and poorly when it is not. Improving true 'gaze reasoning' without hurting the scene understanding the foundation model already provides is the goal.
official.method:
The method is built on GazeLLE: a frozen DINOv2 backbone (ViT-B or ViT-L), a lightweight gaze decoder trained with a BCE heatmap loss, and an optional in/out head. Head-Conditioned Local LoRA (HCLoRA) adds LoRA branches to the frozen backbone projections, Y = W(X) + (XA ⊙ M(b)) B. M(b) is produced by a small gating network from a Gaussian map centred on the queried head box, so the low-rank update mostly acts on tokens near the head. The out-of-cone (OOC) penalty attaches small auxiliary heads to the low-rank features of the last L = 4 adapted layers. Each head produces a spatially softmaxed gaze-evidence map, and the loss is the probability mass falling outside a soft 30° cone (α = 40) from the head centre towards the ground-truth gaze point, weighted by λ = 0.02. Training on GazeFollow uses 448×448 inputs, 15 epochs, batch size 60, Adam at lr 1e-3 with a cosine schedule.

For evaluation, the GazeFollow test set (in-frame only) is split into 3,179 'consistent' and 1,603 'inconsistent' samples. Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct is prompted to box up to four semantically plausible attention targets for the queried person (hand object, social target, action target, semantic centre). A sample is consistent if more than half of its ground-truth gaze annotations fall inside one of the boxes. Metrics are AUC, average and minimum L2 distance (normalised image coordinates), and average and minimum angular error between the predicted and ground-truth gaze directions from the head centre. Baselines run with the same backbone are GazeLLE and GazeLLE with full fine-tuning, VPT, or standard LoRA.
official.claim: On the GazeFollow inconsistent subset (1,603 samples where the gaze target is not a VLM-identified salient region), HCLoRA + OOC with a ViT-B backbone reduces Avg. L2 to 0.1353 and Min. Ang. to 4.85°, compared with 0.1519 / 7.22° for GazeLLE and 0.1487 / 6.86° for GazeLLE + standard LoRA. On the consistent subset it stays at least as good (Avg. L2 0.0777 vs. 0.0834 and 0.0789).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison with state-of-the-art gaze-following methods on GazeFollow. Our method shows best performance, with particularly large improvements on the inconsistent subset.
official.metric: Avg. L2 and Min. L2 (lower is better, normalised image coordinates), Avg./Min. angular error in degrees (lower is better), AUC (higher is better). Single run, with no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Ours (ViT-B, HCLoRA + OOC penalty) vs. GazeLLE, GazeLLE + FT, GazeLLE + VPT and GazeLLE + LoRA, all on the same frozen DINOv2 ViT-B and evaluated on the same consistent/inconsistent split
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained on GazeFollow with ViT-B, HCLoRA + OOC fails to beat GazeLLE + standard LoRA on inconsistent-subset Avg. L2 by a clear margin (e.g. the gap is under ~0.005 or within the seed-to-seed spread of the baselines). Or its gain on the inconsistent subset is no larger than on the consistent subset.

title: H-Flow: Self-supervised Human Scene Flow via Physics-inspired Joint Multi-modal Learning

official.background: Dense 3D scene flow assigns a motion vector to every visible point, which is what is needed to capture clothing and soft-tissue motion on people. Parametric body models (SMPL-style meshes driven by linear blend skinning) recover skeletal pose but cannot represent surfaces that move independently of the skeleton, such as a skirt. Generic scene flow methods are dense but rely on local rigidity priors that break on articulated, non-rigid human bodies, and there is no real-world dense ground truth for human scene flow to supervise a model directly.
official.method:
H-Flow is a single transformer over a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone that jointly predicts per-pixel depth, forward 3D scene flow, a soft human mask, 3D joint positions and camera from monocular video (DPT-style dense head for depth/flow/mask, learnable query tokens for pose and camera). It is trained with no flow ground truth, using four physics-inspired constraints as losses: silhouette edge alignment (depth/flow gradients pulled to the mask boundary), skeletal-surface coupling (flow of each unprojected foreground point must match the motion of its nearest bone up to a distance-dependent tolerance), center-of-mass support (projected CoM inside the ground-contact polygon), and a minimum-jerk trajectory prior on pose. A margin-based distillation anchor to SAM 3D Body (pose) and Depth Pro (depth) supplies metric scale, plus a camera consistency term.

The model is pretrained on all Human3.6M subjects from RGB video only, then fine-tuned (1x10^5 iterations, still self-supervised) on the Fit3D train split (S3, S4, S5, S7, S8, S9) and tested on S10 and S11. Fit3D scene flow ground truth is the per-vertex displacement of the mocap-fitted SMPL-X mesh (subjects wear tight clothing). Baselines are two scene flow methods (ZeroMSF, Self-Mono-SF, both fine-tuned on Fit3D), two optical-flow-lifting pipelines (Depth Pro + H-MoRe, Depth Pro + RAFT) and two mesh-residual methods (SAM 3D Body, WHAM). Metric is 3D end-point error (EPE) in mm.
official.claim: On the Fit3D test subjects (S10, S11), H-Flow trained without flow labels reaches a 3D scene flow EPE of 24.2 mm, versus 38.3 mm for the strongest baseline (Depth Pro + H-MoRe optical-flow lifting) and 49.6 mm for SAM 3D Body mesh residual, a 37% reduction over the best baseline.

End-Point-Error (EPE) in millimeters; 1−Cos is one minus cosine similarity between predicted and ground-truth flow vectors; Acc.S and Acc.R are the fractions of pixels within 50 mm and 100 mm of the ground-truth flow. Best results in bold, second-best underlined.
official.metric: 3D End-Point-Error in mm (lower is better); also 1-Cos and fraction of pixels within 50/100 mm (Acc.S/Acc.R). Single numbers, no seeds or error bars reported.

official.falsification_criterion: A reproduced H-Flow on Fit3D S10/S11 does not get EPE clearly below the Depth Pro + H-MoRe lifting baseline evaluated on the same frames (e.g. H-Flow EPE above ~33 mm, or the gap shrinks to a few mm).

title: Swift Sampling: Selecting Temporal Surprises via Taylor Series

official.background: Video LLMs can only take a fixed number of frames, so long videos are usually reduced by uniform sampling, which wastes the frame budget on redundant stretches and can miss short, informative events. Training-free alternatives score frames by visual uniqueness, optical flow or codec statistics, but most need a separate vision encoder over all candidate frames, which nearly doubles inference cost. A selector that picks informative frames using features the VLM already computes would improve long-video question answering at almost no extra cost.
official.method:
From each video, 128 candidate frames are sampled uniformly. Each frame is passed through the first transformer layer (l = 0) of the VLM's own vision encoder (SigLIP for LLaVA-OneVision); the key projections are mean-pooled over the 14x14 spatial tokens to give a per-frame feature f_t. A Taylor predictor of order N = 3, built from backward finite differences of the preceding frames' features (velocity, acceleration, jerk), predicts f_t, and the Taylor residual r_t = ||f_t - f_hat_t||_2 is the frame's surprise score.

Frames that are local maxima of the residual sequence (r_t > r_{t-1} and r_t > r_{t+1}) are candidates; the K = 32 with the largest residuals are kept (if fewer than K maxima exist, the remaining slots go to the highest-residual non-maxima). The selected 32 frames are fed to LLaVA-OneVision-7B, unchanged and without training, for multiple-choice VQA on Video-MME, LongVideoBench (LVB) and MLVU. Baselines in Table 2 use the same backbone and the same 128 -> 32 setting: uniform, Cosine Uniqueness, frame difference, I-frame and P-frame packet size, RAFT optical flow, adapted DySeg, and MaxInfo.
official.claim: With LLaVA-OneVision-7B selecting 32 of 128 frames, Swift Sampling raises LongVideoBench overall accuracy from 55.3 (uniform) to 57.9 and Video-MME overall from 58.3 to 59.0, outperforming Cosine Uniqueness (52.5 / 55.7) and matching MaxInfo (57.8 / 58.9) at 1.02x instead of 1.79x FLOPs.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison with additional query-agnostic baselines on LLaVA-OneVision. All methods select K=32 frames from a pool of 128 candidates. FLOPs report inference cost relative to uniform sampling. Bold: best, underline: second best.
official.metric: Multiple-choice VQA accuracy (%) on Video-MME, LVB and MLVU, overall and by duration subset (higher is better); FLOPs relative to uniform sampling. Single runs; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Swift Sampling vs. uniform sampling and seven other query-agnostic training-free selectors on the same LLaVA-OneVision backbone, all selecting K=32 from 128 candidates
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running LLaVA-OneVision-7B on LongVideoBench with 32 frames chosen by Swift Sampling (layer-0 keys, N=3, local maxima) does not beat 32 uniformly sampled frames from the same 128-frame pool by a clear margin (e.g. gain under about 1 point), or Swift Sampling falls below Cosine Uniqueness.

title: AnyMo: Geometry-Aware Setup-Agnostic Modeling of Human Motion in the Wild

official.background: Wearable IMU signals (acceleration and angular velocity) depend heavily on the sensing setup: which body part the device is on, where on that part, its orientation, hardware, and sampling rate. Models trained for one setup transfer poorly to others, and labelled IMU data is scarce and fragmented across datasets with small closed label sets. This limits wearable motion models to closed-set recognition on a fixed setup, rather than open-vocabulary activity recognition that works across devices and datasets.
official.method:
AnyMo simulates synthetic IMU signals from Nymeria body mesh/skeleton motion at many candidate vertices on the body surface of each of 23 anatomical segments, with a surface-based sensor frame, random in-plane mounting rotation, and device-noise priors estimated from real Nymeria IMU. An ST-GCN graph encoder over the 23-segment body graph is pre-trained with a masked cross-view predictive contrastive objective: two full-body views are built by sampling different surface placements per segment, 1-5 segments are kept visible in a masked view, and a Transformer predictor maps the masked view's latent sequence to the other view's full latent sequence under an InfoNCE loss. A product-quantized VAE (2 codebooks x 2,048 entries) then turns the frozen encoder's latents into discrete IMU tokens.

The IMU tokens are added to the vocabulary of Qwen2.5-0.5B (embeddings projected from the codebook vectors), which is first trained with next-token prediction on IMU token sequences and then with multi-task contrastive instruction tuning on Nymeria: IMU-narration contrastive loss, supervised label contrastive loss, and next-token loss on captioning and multiple-choice recognition prompts. For zero-shot HAR, a real sparse IMU window plus its wearable-location context is embedded and matched against activity-label text embeddings. No downstream HAR dataset is used in training.
official.claim: On zero-shot activity recognition averaged over 14 unseen wearable datasets, AnyMo reaches 35.7 Accuracy / 29.5 macro-F1 / 57.5 Recall@2, versus 31.9 / 26.4 / 46.9 for the strongest baseline, UniMTS, and at most 19.7 / 13.0 / 33.9 for every other baseline.

official.metric: Accuracy, macro-F1 and Recall@2 (%, higher is better), unweighted average over 14 datasets; single run, no error bars or seeds reported. The '+11.7%/+11.6%/+22.6%' in the table are relative gains over the best baseline average.
official.comparison: AnyMo vs. ImageBind, IMU2CLIP, IMUGPT, HARGPT, UniMTS, NormWear, Gemma 4 26B (text input) and Gemma 4 26B (plot input), all evaluated zero-shot on the same 14 datasets
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduced AnyMo does not beat UniMTS on the 14-dataset average for Accuracy, F1 and R@2 (e.g. average Accuracy at or below ~31.9 or R@2 at or below ~46.9 under the same protocol), or the R@2 margin shrinks to within run-to-run variation across training seeds.

title: FuRA: Full-Rank Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning with Spectral Preconditioning
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (seed breakdown in Table 14, page 18)

official.background: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA train a small low-rank update instead of all weights, but usually trail full fine-tuning (Full FT) in accuracy. Both LoRA and Full FT add updates without regard to the singular-value structure of the pretrained weights. The authors argue that confining updates to the pretrained column space and scaling them by the pretrained singular values (spectral preconditioning) improves generalization, and that this can be done at LoRA-level cost while keeping full-rank update capacity.
official.method:
FuRA reparameterizes each pretrained linear layer W (d_out x d_in) by splitting its input dimension into n column blocks of width b (d_in = n*b) and taking the full-rank SVD of each block, W_k = U_k Σ_k V_k^T. It sets L_k = U_k (d_out x b, frozen), S_k = diag(Σ_k) (length b, trainable) and R_k = V_k^T (b x b, trainable), so W' = [L_1 diag(S_1) R_1 | ... | L_n diag(S_n) R_n]. At initialization this is exactly W. Only R and S are trained (about 1.46% of LLaMA-3-8B parameters); after training the cores merge back into a dense matrix. On LLaMA-3-8B the block shapes are (n=32, b=128) for Q/K/V/O, (n=64, b=64) for Gate/Up and (n=112, b=128) for Down; FuRA is applied to all seven linear projections.

Setup for the claim: LLaMA-3-8B fine-tuned on Commonsense-170K (LLM-Adapters) for 3 epochs, AdamW, LR 2e-4 for FuRA, linear schedule, 3% warmup, effective batch 16, max length 2048, bf16, and evaluated on BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c and OBQA. Baselines: Full FT, LoRA (r=64), DoRA (r=64), PiSSA (r=128), MiLoRA (r=64), RandLoRA (r=64). PiSSA, MiLoRA and RandLoRA were run in-house under the same recipe and evaluation harness with a per-method LR sweep; the Full FT, LoRA and DoRA rows follow the LIFT paper's settings (LLM-Adapters recipe, adapters on q,k,v,up,down).
official.claim: On LLaMA-3-8B fine-tuned on Commonsense-170K, FuRA (1.46% trainable parameters) reaches an 8-task average accuracy of 88.01 (std 0.09 over 3 seeds), above Full FT (86.64) and every baseline at a comparable ~1.4% trainable budget: PiSSA r=128 (85.90, the strongest), DoRA r=64 (85.04) and LoRA r=64 (83.46).

official.metric: Average accuracy (%) over the 8 commonsense tasks, higher is better. FuRA is the mean of 3 seeds (42, 43, 44; per-seed 88.13, 87.91, 88.00; std 0.09). Baselines are single runs with no error reported.
official.comparison: FuRA vs. Full FT, LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, MiLoRA and RandLoRA on LLaMA-3-8B, same training data, epochs and evaluation suite

title: VideoOdyssey: A Benchmark for Ultra-Long-Context and Omni-Modal Video Understanding

official.background: Long-video benchmarks have grown in raw video duration, but most of their questions can still be answered from a short, isolated clip. VideoOdyssey adds a measure called continuous certificate length (CCL): the stretch of video a human must watch without a break to answer a question for certain. The benchmark has 100 YouTube videos (average 109 minutes, all over 60 minutes) and two subsets. VideoOdyssey-V has 1,618 visual multiple-choice questions with an average CCL of 16 minutes. VideoOdyssey-AV has 1,062 audio-visual multiple-choice questions with an average CCL of 12.8 minutes. The paper's diagnostic argument is that models fail for two reasons: they cannot find the relevant evidence (retrieval), and they cannot reason over it once found (comprehension).
official.method:
Every question has four options and a human-annotated CCL window: the shortest continuous interval that contains all the evidence needed to answer it. In the full-video setting, a model sees N frames sampled uniformly and deterministically across the whole video (N = 64 for the AV subset), plus the audio track for omni-modal models. It is prompted to output a single option letter (prompts in Appendix G). The metric is accuracy, overall and split into five CCL bins: [0,0.5), [0.5,3), [3,15), [15,60) and [60,inf) minutes.

In the certificate-window (CW) settings, the model sees only the ground-truth CCL window instead of the whole video. 'CW, matched frames' samples the full budget of N frames inside the window, or 1 fps for windows shorter than N seconds, so it also raises frame density. 'CW, matched rate' keeps the full-video sampling interval and samples N_CW = max(1, round(N*L/T)) frames, where L is the window length and T the video length. This isolates the effect of localization from the effect of denser sampling. Table 15 reports all three settings for two V-subset models and two AV-subset models.
official.claim: On VideoOdyssey-AV with a 64-frame full-video budget and video+audio input, giving Qwen3-Omni-30B only the ground-truth certificate window at the same sampling rate raises overall accuracy from 28.7% to 38.6%, and at the same 64-frame count it reaches 48.6%.
official.claim_caption: Table 15: Full-video, matched-frame CW, and matched-rate CW accuracy (%). CCL intervals are in minutes; N denotes the full-video frame budget.
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy (%) over all 1,062 VideoOdyssey-AV questions; higher is better; 25% is chance. No error bars or repeated runs are reported (the checklist says variance is negligible under deterministic/low-temperature decoding).
official.comparison: Full video (w/o CW) vs. CW at matched sampling rate vs. CW at matched frame count, for the same model, frame budget and prompt
official.falsification_criterion: With Qwen3-Omni-30B on VideoOdyssey-AV at N = 64, matched-rate CW accuracy is not clearly above full-video accuracy (a gain of roughly 3 pp or less, instead of the reported +9.9 pp), or full-video accuracy differs substantially from 28.7%.

title: PACE: Two-Timescale Self-Evolution for Small Language Model Agents
claim_source: Table 6, page 15 (means also in Table 1, page 7)

official.background: Agents built on language models usually need people to hand-tune prompts, output parsers, validators and retry logic. Self-evolving agents automate this by having the model revise its own prompt or code from execution feedback, but most such frameworks assume a frontier model that can reliably diagnose failures and judge its own edits. This paper asks whether a frozen small language model (4B-14B parameters, no weight updates, no stronger teacher) can improve its own agent pipeline, and argues that prompt edits (cheap, stable, but they saturate) and control-logic edits (powerful, but SLM-written code often regresses) should be scheduled and gated differently.
official.method:
An agent is a pair (P, C): textual prompt artifacts P and an executable Python solver function C (sampling, parsing, verification, repair, retry). The same frozen SLM is both the task model inside the solver and the controller that proposes edits. PACE first runs prompt evolution with C fixed: candidates come from handcrafted mutations (role, reasoning directives, temperature), failure-guided reflection, and crossover; they are scored on training mini-batches, kept on an accuracy-vs-token-cost Pareto front, and the best one on validation is kept. When validation improvement from a prompt round falls to ε = 0.01 or below, the controller summarizes recent failures and proposes a bounded free-form edit to the solver function (e.g. 3-way sampling with majority vote and a verification call on MMLU). A candidate solver is committed only if it beats the current one by more than δ = 0.02 on a freshly sampled validation subset from the training pool; after an accepted edit, prompt evolution restarts. Runs are capped at 20 outer steps.

Each benchmark task is a single-module DSPy ChainOfThought program served via vLLM. MMLU uses 200 training and 800 held-out test questions (letter-match accuracy). Baselines on the same splits: Vanilla (task prompt, T = 0.2), +PE (prompt evolution to convergence, no solver edits), +CE (solver edits allowed from the start, no dedicated prompt phase), GEPA and MIPROv2 (DSPy, auto="medium"), Gödel Agent and ACE. Each configuration is run 10 times with different random seeds; mean ± std is reported.
official.claim: With frozen Qwen3.5-9B on a fixed 800-question MMLU test subset, PACE reaches 0.889 ± 0.007 accuracy versus 0.835 ± 0.019 for control-logic-only evolution (+CE), 0.835 ± 0.024 for Gödel Agent, 0.832 ± 0.007 for prompt-only evolution (+PE) and 0.832 ± 0.006 for GEPA (vanilla 0.818).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Performance comparison across SLM backbones. CE denotes control-logic evolution only, PE denotes prompt evolution only, and PACE denotes the full two-timescale framework. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over multiple runs. Best result per backbone is bolded.
official.metric: MMLU letter-match accuracy on the held-out 800-question test subset, higher is better; ± is standard deviation over runs (Section 4.1 says 10 independent runs with different random seeds; the Table 6 caption says only 'multiple runs', and Appendix A.1 says 'All experiments use seed 0')
official.comparison: PACE vs. +CE, +PE, Gödel Agent, GEPA, MIPROv2, ACE and Vanilla, all with frozen Qwen3.5-9B and identical train/test splits
official.falsification_criterion: Reimplementing PACE and the +PE/+CE ablations with Qwen3.5-9B on MMLU (200 train / 800 test, ≤20 evolution steps, several seeds), PACE's mean test accuracy is not clearly above the best of +PE and +CE (e.g. a gap under ~2 points, or within one std of the runs), or PACE does not exceed ~0.86.
