title: Flow Mismatching: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection via Velocity Discrepancies in Flow Matching Models

official.background: Industrial visual anomaly detection must find and localize rare, varied manufacturing defects using a training set that contains only normal images. Reconstruction-based detectors (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion and flow models) flag pixels where a 'normalized' reconstruction differs from the input, but generative models can also reconstruct plausible defects, weakening the signal; feature-based detectors need memory banks or pretrained feature extractors. Flow matching learns a velocity field that transports Gaussian noise to the normal-image distribution, which raises the question of whether that field can be queried directly, without reconstruction, to reveal anomalies.
official.method:
A class-conditional attention U-Net (64 base channels) is trained with the standard conditional flow-matching objective on normal MVTec-AD training images at 128x128 (2,000 epochs, StableAdamW, lr 1e-4, batch 32). At test time, for an image y, K = 10 Gaussian sources x0^k are drawn and the affine paths x_t = (1 - t) x0^k + t y are evaluated at T = 10 interior times t = j/(T+1). At each pixel i the per-path squared discrepancy Z_t^k(i) = ||v_theta(x_t^k, t)(i) - (y - x0^k)(i)||^2 (norm over RGB) is computed, the K paths are aggregated by the minimum, and the heatmap is H(i) = (1/T) sum_t t^2 min_k Z_t^k(i), followed by Gaussian smoothing (sigma = 4 on MVTec). The image score is max_i H(i) plus the mean of the top 1% of H. This is KT = 100 forward passes per image, with no ODE integration or backpropagation.

ReconFlow, the key matched baseline, uses the same trained checkpoint but makes an explicit reconstruction: it noises y to t_init = 0.5 with a Gaussian source, integrates the learned ODE to t = 1 with T = 10 steps to obtain y_hat, uses the squared pixel residual ||y - y_hat||^2 as the heatmap, and takes the pixel-wise minimum over K = 10 sources. Other flow-matching baselines (Reflect, TCCM, WT-Flow, D-Flow) are re-implemented on the same U-Net backbone and protocol. Metrics are image- and pixel-level AUROC, AP, F1-max and pixel AUPRO, averaged over the 15 MVTec-AD categories.
official.claim: On MVTec-AD (128x128, same trained flow-matching U-Net), Flow Mismatching beats the reconstruction-style ReconFlow on all seven metrics, e.g. image AUROC 98.7 vs. 96.6, pixel AP 67.5 vs. 61.2 and AUPRO 91.9 vs. 87.2, and beats every other flow-matching baseline re-run on the same backbone.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison of flow-matching-based anomaly detection methods on MVTec-AD.
official.metric: Mean over 15 MVTec-AD categories of image AUROC/AP/F1-max and pixel AUROC/AP/F1-max/AUPRO (%, higher is better). Table 2 has no error bars; Appendix D.3 (Table 9) reports test-time std over 15 inference seeds with a fixed checkpoint (e.g. I-AUROC 98.60 ± 0.05, P-AP 67.39 ± 0.06, AUPRO 92.03 ± 0.20). No variance over training seeds is reported.
official.comparison: Flow Mismatching vs. ReconFlow (same checkpoint, reconstruction-residual inference) and vs. D-Flow, Reflect, TCCM, WT-Flow (RGB and WRN) adapted to the same U-Net and protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Training a class-conditional flow-matching U-Net on MVTec-AD normal images and scoring the test set with both procedures, Flow Mismatching does not beat ReconFlow on the same checkpoint by a clear margin, e.g. the pixel-AP gap is under ~2 points or the image-AUROC gap is under ~0.5 points, or ReconFlow wins on most of the seven metrics.

title: Adaptive Mass-Segmented KV Compression for Long-Context Reasoning

official.background: Reasoning LLMs generate long chains of thought, so the KV cache grows linearly during decoding and memory traffic dominates latency. Decoding-time KV compression periodically evicts cached tokens to keep a fixed budget, usually by scoring each token (attention, expected attention, key geometry, redundancy) and keeping a global or per-head Top-k. The authors argue that global Top-k tends to evict whole contiguous stretches of intermediate reasoning ('Region Wipe-out'), which causes the model to drift from the problem, overturn correct intermediate results, or fall into repetition loops under tight budgets.
official.method:
AMS (Adaptive Mass-Segmented) is a training-free wrapper around an existing token scorer. At each compression event (every I=512 generated tokens), for each layer and KV head, it turns recent-window attention usage (last W=128 queries, 1D-average-pooled) into a normalized 'quality mass' over cached positions, optionally mixed with an EMA credit of past mass (lambda=0.9, beta=0.9). It cuts the sequence where the cumulative mass crosses multiples of Delta=0.1, then splits/merges segments to lengths in [16, 256]. Each segment gets a minimum quota q_min=1 plus a share of the remaining budget proportional to its mass. The base scorer (TOVA or expected attention) then picks the top-q_i tokens inside each segment; 4 sink tokens and a recent suffix are always kept, and the result is trimmed/backfilled to exactly T_keep and gathered into a compact cache.

Evaluation uses DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on MATH500 (pass@1, one fixed seed), implemented in KVPress v0.4.0. All methods share the same per-layer cache cap T_keep in {256, 512, 1024}, the same compression interval (512), prompts, sink/recent rules and decoding settings; only the token-retention policy changes. AMS-TOVA is compared with TOVA (same scorer, global selection), and AMS-Expected with AdaKV-ExpE2 (head-adaptive allocation with the expected-attention scorer, mask-based) and the other baselines.
official.claim: On MATH500 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B at a per-layer KV budget T_keep=256, AMS-Expected reaches 48.6% pass@1 versus 32.6% for AdaKV-ExpE2 (same expected-attention scorer) and 37.2% for the best other baselines in Table 1 (ChunkKV-Expected, R-KV); AMS-TOVA reaches 36.4% versus 29.2% for plain TOVA.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Pass@1 accuracy (%) under decoding-time KV compression with per-layer effective cache length T_keep ∈ {256, 512, 1024}. Baselines are grouped by their underlying compression paradigm. AMS-TOVA uses TOVA as the base scorer, while AMS-Expected uses the expected-attention scorer. We discuss their absolute improvements over the corresponding baselines in the main text. Additional plug-in results with other scorers are provided in Table 5. AMS variants are placed immediately below their corresponding base scorers for paired visual comparison. Bold numbers denote the best compressed result in each column.
official.metric: Pass@1 accuracy (%) on MATH500 (500 problems), higher is better. Single run with a fixed random seed; no error bars or seed variation reported.
official.comparison: AMS-Expected vs. AdaKV-ExpE2, ChunkKV-Expected, R-KV, RPC, PyramidKV, StreamingLLM, KeyDiff; AMS-TOVA vs. TOVA; all at T_keep=256, interval 512, same backbone and prompts. Uncompressed Full KV = 52.8%.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same budget and schedule, AMS-Expected fails to beat the best Table 1 baseline (37.2%) by a clear margin (e.g. lands within a few points of it), or AMS-TOVA does not clearly beat TOVA at T_keep=256; ideally checked over several seeds/samples to see whether the gap exceeds run-to-run variation.

title: Beyond Normal References: Discriminative Few-Shot Anomaly Detection

official.background: Few-shot anomaly detection (FSAD) aims to flag defective or abnormal images (and localize the anomaly) using only a handful of reference images from the target dataset. 'Generalist' FSAD methods train one detector on an auxiliary dataset and apply it to new datasets by comparing each query against a few normal reference images, without retraining. In practice a few confirmed anomalous examples are often also available (e.g., flagged defects), but normal-only methods cannot use them. Naively matching queries against such anomalous references risks overfitting to the specific anomaly types that were seen and failing on new ones.
official.method:
IDEAL uses a frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 encoder on 448x448 images to get patch features for the query, the L1 normal references and the L2 anomalous references (with anomaly masks). A Normal Variation Eraser computes residuals between each anomalous-reference patch and its nearest normal-reference patch, then removes the component lying in a local PCA subspace (top r = 4 components) of its k = 12 nearest normal patches (scaled by alpha = 0.8). An Intrinsic Deviation Encoder (cross-attention from M = 45 learnable vectors to the masked anomalous patches, then an FFN) learns 'intrinsic deviation vectors', with a loss that encourages discriminability and orthogonality. The patch anomaly score averages (a) how well the query's denoised deviation is preserved after projection onto the deviation vectors and (b) the cosine distance to the nearest normal reference patch. The image score is the mean of the top 1% of patch scores. Only the IDE is trained (Focal + Dice + BCE + dual loss, 20 epochs, AdamW lr 1e-3, batch 16).

Evaluation is cross-dataset: the model is trained on MVTecAD and tested on the other datasets, and trained on VisA when testing on MVTecAD. For each target dataset one fixed reference set is drawn: L1 normal images plus L2 anomalous images from one randomly chosen anomaly type. In the 'Hard' setting, test samples of that anomaly type are removed, so every test anomaly is unseen. The baseline NAGL (which also uses normal + anomalous references) is re-run with the same DINOv2 ViT-S/14 backbone, 448x448 input and fixed-reference protocol.
official.claim: In the hard (unseen-anomaly-only) setting on MPDD (trained on MVTecAD) with 1 normal + 1 anomalous reference, IDEAL reaches 74.5 image-level / 97.2 pixel-level AUROC vs. 63.7 / 91.8 for NAGL. The lead holds at N2A1 (77.0 vs. 71.7), N4A1 (84.3 vs. 75.8) and N8A4 (84.9 vs. 76.6) image AUROC. On MVTecAD, IDEAL's image-AUROC lead over NAGL is 1.4-2.7 points.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison results (Hard) with AUROC on MVTecAD and MPDD, together with task difficulty values (purple) that measures a seen-to-unseen anomaly similarity.
official.metric: Image-level and pixel-level AUROC (%), higher is better; reported as the average of three independent runs, with no std or other error bars given. Arrows show the drop relative to the general setting (Table 1).
official.comparison: IDEAL vs. NAGL (both using fixed normal + anomalous references, same backbone) in the hard setting on MVTecAD and MPDD under N1A1, N2A1, N4A1, N8A4.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both methods on MPDD in the hard setting (N1A1, references fixed from one randomly chosen anomaly type, that type removed from the test set), averaged over several reference draws/seeds, IDEAL's image AUROC is not clearly above NAGL's (e.g. a gap under ~3 points or within run-to-run spread), or NAGL does not degrade relative to the general setting while IDEAL does.

title: PRECISE: SDE-Consistent Stochastic Sampling for RL Post-Training of Flow-Matching Models
claim_source: Table 5, page 16 (Appendix A.3); summarized in Figure 2 and Section 4.4, page 6

official.background: Online RL post-training (GRPO-style) of flow-matching image generators needs a stochastic policy, so the deterministic reverse ODE is replaced by a reverse-time SDE. RL rollouts use few denoising steps (6-30) to save compute, so how this SDE is discretized matters. The Euler–Maruyama step used by Flow-GRPO and Dance-GRPO holds the velocity and score fixed within a step and ignores how the newly injected noise changes them. This adds extra noise at coarse step sizes and pushes the model off the trajectories it was trained on, which hurts sample quality and reward optimization.
official.method:
PRECISE writes the reverse SDE in terms of the clean-latent posterior mean ẑ0(t)=E[z0|zt] and assumes that ẑ0 stays constant over one reverse step (Assumption 4.2). The SDE is then linear and has an exact closed-form transition: z_{t'} = (1−t')ẑ0(t) + t'·ρ·ε̂(t) + t'·sqrt(1−ρ²)·w, where ρ(t',t) = (t'(1−t)/(t(1−t')))^{η²/2} under the exploration schedule ε_t = η·sqrt(t/(1−t)). Here ε̂(t) = (zt − (1−t)ẑ0)/t, and ẑ0 is the model's clean-latent prediction. Euler–Maruyama instead takes one step z + (−u_t + ½ε_t²∇log p_t)Δt + ε_t√Δt·w with the velocity and score held fixed.

Diagnostic (Appendix A.3): SD3.5-M, the 10-NFE anchors of the training scheduler, η = 1.5, no CFG, eight held-out PickScore prompts with one noise realization each. A reference path integrates the reverse SDE (Eq. 4) with 400 Euler–Maruyama substeps per coarse step and re-evaluates the model at every substep. At each coarse anchor t_i, both one-step branches start from the reference state and use the reference's fine-grid Gaussian increments (Euler sums them; PRECISE uses the weighted sum implied by its exact transition). The error E_i is the per-coordinate RMS distance between the branch's z(t_{i+1}) and the reference's. The eight interior steps i=1..8 are reported; the entrance step at t=1 and the terminal step are excluded.
official.claim: On SD3.5-M at 10-NFE anchors with η = 1.5, one PRECISE step has a mean one-step RMS error to a 400-substep reverse-SDE reference of 0.0480 ± 0.0082, versus 0.4854 ± 0.0065 for one Euler–Maruyama step on the same SDE (mean PRECISE/Euler ratio 0.1117 ± 0.0240). PRECISE is closer to the reference on all 64 trajectory–step pairs.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Direct diagnostics of the frozen posterior-mean closure on SD3.5-M (10-NFE anchors, η = 1.5, eight trajectories). Entries are mean±standard deviation over trajectories.
official.metric: Per-coordinate RMS distance between the one-step branch output and the fine-grid reference state at t_{i+1} (lower is better). ± is the sample standard deviation over 8 trajectories (prompts); the 'Mean over i' row first averages the 8 interior steps within each trajectory.
official.comparison: PRECISE frozen-posterior-mean exact transition vs. one-step Euler–Maruyama (velocity and score frozen) on the same SDE (η = 1.5), with the same starting state and shared Gaussian innovations
official.falsification_criterion: With the same protocol, the mean PRECISE/Euler error ratio is not clearly below 1 (e.g. above ~0.5), or Euler is closer to the reference on a substantial fraction of the 64 trajectory–step pairs.

title: Asymmetric Scaling Laws from Sparse Features

official.background: Neural scaling laws describe how test loss falls as a power law in model size N and dataset size D. Solvable models (random features on Gaussian data with power-law covariance, e.g. Maloney et al. 2022) predict the same exponent for N and D, while empirical LLM fits suggest the two exponents can differ. This paper proposes that sparse input activations (rare but informative coordinates that most training examples never activate) break that symmetry: rare coordinates that never appear in the training set cannot be learned, so data becomes a bottleneck that model size cannot fix.
official.method:
Inputs x in R^M have independent coordinates: coordinate j is zero with probability 1 - j^-(alpha1+1) and otherwise ±j^-(alpha2+1)/2, so Var(x_j) = j^-(alpha1+alpha2+2). Features are phi = u x with a frozen random u in R^{N x M}, u_ij ~ N(0, 1/N); the target is y = w^T x with w_j ~ N(0,1); the readout theta is the minimum-norm least-squares solution (pseudoinverse, float64, rtol 1e-10). Theory predicts alpha_N = alpha1 + alpha2 + 1 and, for alpha1 > 0, alpha_D = (alpha1 + alpha2 + 1)/(alpha1 + 1). With (alpha1, alpha2) = (1.0, 0.3) this gives alpha_N = 2.30 and alpha_D = 1.15.

The dense baseline uses Gaussian inputs with Var(x_j) = j^-(alpha+1), alpha = alpha1 + alpha2 + 1 = 2.3, which matches the sparse model's variance spectrum, so any asymmetry comes only from sparsity. Setup (Appendix F, Experiment 1): M = 10,000; N-sweep N in {4,...,256} at D = 50,000; D-sweep D in {10,...,1280} at N = 16,000; 20 seeds per configuration (data and u resampled); n_test = 50,000. Exponents are least-squares slopes on log-log axes over the last 6 points of each sweep. One shared exponent is fitted jointly to the sparse N-, dense N- and dense D-sweeps (separate intercepts), and the sparse D-sweep gets its own fit.
official.claim: In the linear sparse random-feature model with (alpha1, alpha2) = (1.0, 0.3), the sparse D-sweep loss decays with exponent alpha_D ≈ 1.11 (theory 1.15), while the sparse N-sweep and the matched dense N- and D-sweeps share a single exponent alpha ≈ 2.0 (theory 2.30), giving an asymmetry ratio of about 1.8.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Two-exponent scaling validates linear theory. Test loss scaling under the linear feature map phi(x) = ux, computed via the closed-form min-norm least-squares solution; (alpha1, alpha2) = (1.0, 0.3), 20 seeds. Top: sparse; bottom: dense. Left: N-sweep at D = 50,000; right: D-sweep at N = 16,000. A single exponent alpha ≈ 2.0 (dashed lines, jointly fitted with separate intercepts) describes the sparse N-, dense N-, and dense D-sweeps, in close agreement with the linear-theory prediction alpha_N = alpha1 + alpha2 + 1 = 2.30. The sparse D-sweep requires its own shallower fit, alpha_D ≈ 1.11, matching the predicted sparse exponent alpha_D = (alpha1 + alpha2 + 1)/(alpha1 + 1) = 1.15 and breaking the dense-baseline symmetry alpha_N = alpha_D.
official.metric: Fitted power-law exponent of test MSE vs N or D (log-log least squares over the last 6 points). Points in the plot are mean over 20 seeds with ±1 standard error bars; no uncertainty is reported for the fitted exponents.
official.comparison: Sparse-input D-scaling exponent vs. the sparse N-scaling exponent and the dense-input (matched variance spectrum) N- and D-scaling exponents
official.falsification_criterion: With the stated setup, the sparse D-sweep exponent is not clearly smaller than the sparse N-sweep and dense D-sweep exponents (e.g. ratio alpha_N/alpha_D near 1 rather than about 1.8-2), or the dense D-sweep is also shallow like the sparse one.

title: DiLaDiff: Distilled Latent-augmented Diffusion for Language Modeling

official.background: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens, and in principle they can decode many tokens per model call. In practice, the denoiser predicts each masked token independently, so it ignores correlations between tokens decoded in the same step. This forces a trade-off: fewer decoding steps give faster but less coherent text. Continuous latent diffusion over text representations can capture global structure, but contextual latents are hard to decode back to tokens. This paper combines the two: a continuous latent carries sentence-level correlations, and a discrete masked diffusion decoder produces the tokens conditioned on it.
official.method:
An MDLM (bert-base-uncased tokenizer, sequence length 1024) is trained on OpenWebText for 1M steps at batch size 512. An auto-encoder is then fine-tuned from this checkpoint for 200k steps. The encoder is a Perceiver-style module that compresses frozen BERT hidden states into a latent z (2x compression, 512 latent vectors). The decoder is the MDLM with zero-initialized cross-attention layers added so that it attends to z, trained with the MDLM loss conditioned on z. Regularization: coordinate-wise normalization, masking of BERT features and latents (p=0.7), Gaussian noise on BERT features (sigma=0.5), and replacing z with Gaussian noise 75% of the time.

LaDiff trains a DiT latent denoiser (data prediction) on the frozen auto-encoder's latents (Section 4 says 150k steps at lr 2e-4; Appendix C.2 says 500k steps at batch size 512), using a tanh-logSNR variance-preserving schedule (d=10) and self-conditioning. At sampling time, a latent is generated with Ncont=200 Euler steps of the probability-flow ODE. Tokens are then generated by ancestral masked-diffusion sampling with Ndisc=1024 steps, conditioned on that latent (temperature 1, nucleus p=0.9). Quality is measured by GenPPL under GPT2-Large, unigram entropy (to detect degenerate output) and MAUVE. The MeanFlow-distilled variant (DiLaDiff) is not needed for this claim.
official.claim: On unconditional OpenWebText generation with Ncont=200 latent steps and Ndisc=1024 discrete steps, LaDiff reaches GenPPL 62.9 (entropy 5.40). The authors' re-implemented MDLM, which LaDiff is fine-tuned from, reaches 90.5 (entropy 5.50), and their re-implemented SDDM reaches 75.3 (entropy 5.31).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Many-step generative performance on OpenWebText. Ncont = 200, Ndisc = 1024.
official.metric: Generative perplexity under GPT2-Large (lower is better), with unigram entropy as a degeneracy check (higher is better). Single numbers; no seeds, std or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: LaDiff (temperature 1) vs. MDLM (ours) and SDDM (ours), both re-trained by the authors with the same tokenizer, data and architecture. The MDLM and DUO rows are copied from other papers and are not matched.
official.falsification_criterion: With matched training (MDLM checkpoint, then auto-encoder and LaDiff on top), LaDiff's GenPPL at Ndisc=1024 is not clearly below the re-trained MDLM baseline (e.g. the gap shrinks to a few points or reverses across sampling seeds), or the GenPPL gain comes with a large entropy drop (below about 5.3), which would signal degenerate text.

title: Not Too Generative, Not Too Discriminative: The Human Alignment Sweet Spot
claim_source: Figure 14b (with 14a, 14c), page 29; same data summarised in Figure 2c, page 6

official.background: It is debated whether human-like visual representations come from discriminative learning (mapping images to labels) or generative learning (modelling the distribution of images). Most comparisons between the two pit models against each other that also differ in architecture, scale and training data, so the effect of the objective itself is confounded. Joint Energy-Based Models (JEMs) reinterpret a classifier's logits as an energy over image–label pairs, so one network can be trained discriminatively, generatively, or with any mix of the two while everything else stays fixed.
official.method:
A JEM uses classifier logits f(x) to define p(y|x) as the usual softmax and p(x) ∝ Σ_y exp(f(x)[y]). Training maximises L = α · (‖∇L_D‖/‖∇L_G‖) · L_G + (1 − α) · L_D, where L_D is the cross-entropy term, L_G is the generative log-likelihood approximated by contrastive divergence with SGLD negatives (20 Langevin steps, replay buffer), and the gradient-norm ratio is a stop-gradient scalar that puts both terms on the same scale. α = 0 is purely discriminative and α = 1 purely generative; α is swept from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1. For CIFAR-10 the backbone is a WRN-28-10 without batch norm (LeakyReLU, following the original JEM code), trained with Adam at lr 1e-4, cosine schedule with 1000 warmup steps, input noise ~0.05, mixed precision; 5% of the training set is held out for model selection, and the α = 1 model is selected at its best-FID epoch.

Each α is trained with 3 seeds on standard CIFAR-10 (random crop and flip only, no label smoothing) and evaluated on the 10,000 CIFAR-10 test images against the CIFAR-10H human label distributions (about 51 human labels per image). The alignment metric is the cross-entropy between the human soft-label distribution and the model's softmax p(y|x), averaged over images (lower is better; the human inter-group ceiling is 0.55 nats). KL divergence and top-1 accuracy are also reported. No training on CIFAR-10H soft labels is done.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10H, the hybrid JEM with α = 0.8 reaches a cross-entropy to human label distributions of about 0.59, far below the purely discriminative JEM (α = 0, about 1.26 ± 0.03 SEM) and the purely generative JEM (α = 1, about 1.29 ± 0.14 SEM), while keeping about 87% CIFAR-10 accuracy (vs. about 91% at α = 0).
official.claim_caption: Figure 14. CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-10H evaluation across α. Figure 15. CIFAR-10 classification performance and alignment with CIFAR-10H human soft labels as a function of the generative–discriminative trade-off parameter α. Each point shows the mean across three seeds, and error bars denote the standard error of the mean (SEM).
official.metric: Cross-entropy between CIFAR-10H human label distribution and model softmax, lower is better; points are means over 3 seeds and error bars are standard error of the mean. Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: JEMs with identical WRN-28-10 architecture and data, varying only α ∈ {0, 0.1, ..., 1}; main contrast α = 0.8 vs. α = 0 and α = 1 (and vs. the neighbouring α = 0.7). The strongest separately trained discriminative baseline (ResNet, same CIFAR-10 setup and augmentations but Adam lr 1e-3, no error bars shown) sits at about 1.05 in Figure 2c, also well above α = 0.8.

title: PiD: Fast and High-Resolution Latent Decoding with Pixel Diffusion

official.background: Latent diffusion and autoregressive image generators produce a compact latent, and a reconstruction-oriented VAE (or RAE) decoder maps it back to pixels. To get 2K or 4K images, practical pipelines decode at low resolution and then run a separate super-resolution model (often a one-step diffusion SR model), which adds latency and cannot fix artifacts already present in the latent. This paper asks whether one generative decoder can turn a low-resolution latent straight into a 4x-upscaled image, faster and with better quality than the cascade.
official.method:
PiD starts from the 1.3B-parameter PixelDiT pixel-space text-to-image diffusion transformer, fine-tuned to 2K resolution with NTK-aware RoPE. A ControlNet-style convolutional adapter maps the (possibly noisy) latent to the patch-token grid and injects it every two DiT blocks through a sigma-aware sigmoid gate. The decoder is trained with rectified flow on latents corrupted with noise level sigma ~ U(0, 0.8), so it can decode partially denoised latents (early termination of the base LDM, written PiD(M/N) for stopping at step M of N). It is then distilled with DMD2 (including CFG distillation) into a 4-step student.

Evaluation: 1,000 DPG-Bench prompts are run through FLUX.1 [dev] (28 steps) to get latents for 512x512 images. PiD(24/28) decodes them directly to 2048x2048. Baselines decode with the FLUX.1 VAE or SSDD and then apply a 4x upsampler (Real-ESRGAN, SeedVR2-3B, TSD-SR, InvSR-1), plus the latent upsampler LUA. Outputs are scored with eight no-reference IQA metrics, including NIQE and Unipercept-IAA. End-to-end decoder latency (low-res decode + SR + any high-res decode for baselines) is measured on one GB200 GPU, both eager and with torch.compile.
official.claim: When decoding FLUX.1 [dev] latents of 512x512 images to 2048x2048 on 1,000 DPG-Bench prompts, PiD(24/28) gets NIQE 3.50 and Unipercept-IAA 66.21, against the best cascade baseline's 4.04 (SSDD + InvSR-1) and 64.12 (VAE + InvSR-1). It also runs in 211 ms with torch.compile on a GB200, versus 725-1269 ms for every diffusion-based SR cascade (SeedVR2-3B, TSD-SR, InvSR-1).

title: A World Model of Radiologist Reading for Medical Image Representation Learning

official.background: Radiologist eye-tracking data record where and in what order experts look while reading an image. Earlier medical-imaging work either collapses gaze into static heatmaps used as attention priors (for example EGMA) or predicts scanpaths as a separate output task, so the temporal order in which radiologists gather evidence is not used to learn diagnostic representations. This paper asks whether using the order of expert fixations as a self-supervised prediction structure gives better chest X-ray representations.
official.method:
GazeWorld refines a pretrained MedCLIP Swin-Tiny image encoder on MIMIC-EYE (3,032 chest radiographs with radiologist fixation sequences; 2,729 train). Fixations are mapped to their nearest image patch, and repeat visits are merged, keeping first-visit order. Each visited patch token is combined with a spatial embedding, a temporal-rank embedding and a dwell-duration feature. An 8-layer causal Transformer (hidden size 768) then predicts the representation of the next fixated patch from the prefix, with targets taken from an EMA momentum copy of the encoder (SmoothL1 between the layer-normalized prediction and the stop-gradient target; AR loss). A 2-layer cross-attention decoder predicts the representations of all unvisited patches, using queries built from a learnable mask token plus the patch's spatial embedding and keys/values from the predictor's full gaze-context tokens (SC loss; SmoothL1 against layer-normalized EMA targets). The total loss is L_AR + 1.0 * L_SC. The model is trained with AdamW at lr 3e-4, weight decay 0.04 and batch size 32 for 15 epochs at 224x224, and the encoder is trained jointly with the other modules.

In the ordering ablation, the same pretraining is run but the expert chronological patch order is replaced by a raster-scan order or a random order. The resulting frozen encoders are evaluated zero-shot (no task-specific fine-tuning) on CheXpert 5x200, RSNA Pneumonia and SIIM-ACR Pneumothorax, reporting AUROC, accuracy and F1.
official.claim: Pretraining GazeWorld with the radiologists' chronological fixation order gives higher zero-shot AUROC than the identical pipeline with a random patch order on all three benchmarks: CheXpert 5x200 58.13 vs. 52.25, RSNA 62.84 vs. 51.58, and SIIM-ACR 64.29 vs. 55.06. Raster-scan order is similarly worse (52.18 / 50.39 / 53.50).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Ablation on fixation ordering, backbone initialization, and objective components. "AR only" denotes next-fixation prediction without spatial completion, and "SC only" denotes spatial completion without autoregressive prediction. All metrics are zero-shot: AUROC, Accuracy, and F1 are computed without task-specific fine-tuning.
official.metric: Zero-shot AUROC (higher is better); accuracy and F1 also reported. Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: GazeWorld trained with expert fixation order vs. the same model trained with raster-scan or random patch order (same data, objective and evaluation); also AR-only and SC-only objective ablations
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running GazeWorld pretraining on MIMIC-EYE with expert order and with random order (several seeds) and evaluating zero-shot under the same protocol, the expert-order model's AUROC is not clearly higher than the random-order model's, e.g. the gap on RSNA or SIIM-ACR is under ~3 AUROC points or within seed-to-seed variation.

title: Rubato: Transcribing Piano Music with Timestamps

official.background: Automatic piano transcription is usually split into stages: audio is first transcribed into performance MIDI (note onsets and offsets in seconds), and a separate model then converts that MIDI into notated sheet music (measures, staves, note values, pitch spelling). Errors can enter at either stage. The intermediate MIDI also discards notational structure that must be rebuilt later, and the final score loses its link to the recording's timeline. The paper asks whether a single model that writes sheet music directly from audio, with timestamps attached, produces more accurate notation than these cascades.
official.method:
Rubato is a prompt-conditioned encoder-decoder with the Canary-180M-Flash architecture (Fast Conformer encoder, Transformer decoder, about 180M parameters), trained from scratch. Its output is InterMo, a text serialization of piano scores built from metric intervals (e.g. 1/8, barlines carrying time and key signature) and moments (note onsets in uppercase and offsets in lowercase, per staff, in a canonical order). It is tokenized with an 8,000-token SentencePiece UnigramLM vocabulary that includes 10 ms timestamp tokens. Prompt tokens select a 'dialect'. The main one is TAST (time-aligned score transcription: spelled score notation plus timestamps), and the others cover score-only, MIDI-only and beat/downbeat outputs. This lets the model train on MAESTRO (159 h of real audio, MIDI tasks only), (n)ASAP (30 h of real audio with aligned scores and beats, using a more conservative held-out split than the standard one) and PDMX scores rendered to audio (2,071 h) in two variants, non-expressive (constant tempo) and expressive (timing deviations from VirtuosoNet), each utterance using one of 16 piano/room timbral variants. The loss is normalized per sequence by 1/sqrt(|T|), with subword regularization and ordinal label smoothing on timestamp tokens. At inference, audio is decoded in 40 s windows with a 50% hop.

For evaluation, Rubato is prompted for TAST on real recordings. Its output is compared with cascade baselines that the authors ran themselves: Beat-This -> Piano-A2S (a downbeat-chunked audio-to-score model), and each of four audio-to-MIDI front-ends (Transkun/Tkun, Bytedance, Aria-AMT, MT3) feeding either PM2S or M2ST (performance-MIDI-to-score models). Gemini 3.1 Pro is also included. The metric is OMR-NED, a normalized edit distance over engraved sheet-music primitives (noteheads, beams, accidentals, barlines, time signatures). The main test set is ATEPP: YouTube piano recordings with paired scores, filtered to drop any score sourced from ASAP, which leaves 1,495 recordings of 106 scores that no model saw in training.
official.claim: On the ATEPP test set (1,495 real recordings, 106 scores), Rubato (TAST) transcribes audio to sheet music with OMR-NED 75.9 ± 0.9%, lower than every cascade baseline; the best cascade, Transkun -> M2ST, scores 85.2 ± 0.5% and Beat-This -> Piano-A2S scores 88.9 ± 0.3%.

Faded cells (∗) mark training-data overlap: on ASAP, M2ST is trained on 98/102 test pieces; on ASAP-Beyer, 21/25 test performances are in the MAESTRO training split, seen by every AMT front-end and by PM2S. title: LLMs Show No Signs Of Individuated Metacognition
claim_source: Table 2, page 14 (also Figure 7 c-d, page 13; Appendix A.9, page 32)

official.background: Confidence-weighted routing, selective abstention and ensemble weighting all assume that an LLM's stated confidence tells you something about that model's own ability on the specific question. Aggregate calibration of LLMs has been studied a lot, but it is less clear whether a model's confidence reflects knowledge of its own capabilities or just a generic sense of how hard a question looks to any model. The paper asks whether frontier LLMs show 'individuated metacognition', item-level self-assessment specific to the model beyond a shared difficulty signal, and finds that confidence across models mostly reduces to a shared difficulty axis that tracks performance only on items every model gets right or wrong.
official.method:
The authors query 20 frontier LLMs (Claude 3 Haiku through Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o through GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.0 Flash through 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek R1, Llama 3.1/3.3-70B, Mistral Medium 3.1 and Small 3.2, Qwen 2.5-72B and 2.5-Coder-32B) at temperature 0. For SQuAD they take 1,000 random SQuAD v1.1 dev questions, strip the Wikipedia passage, and ask each model a binary prospective question (can you answer this without the context paragraph?, JSON yes/no). Separately each model answers the question, graded correct/incorrect by an LLM judge for semantic equivalence. This gives two binary item x model matrices: confidence and performance.

For each matrix they compute the model x model tetrachoric correlation matrix R, eigendecompose it, take loadings Lambda = V diag(sqrt(lambda)), and compute per-item Factor 1 scores f1[i] = sum_m (X_im - mean_m) * Lambda_m1. The alignment statistic is the Pearson r between the performance and confidence Factor 1 score vectors across items, computed on all items and on the 'contentious' subset where both the cross-model correct rate and the cross-model yes rate lie in [0.1, 0.9].
official.claim: On SQuAD with the prospective confidence probe across 20 LLMs, per-item Factor 1 scores of the confidence and performance matrices correlate at Pearson r = +0.591 over all items but only r = +0.230 on contentious items (cross-model correct and yes rates both in [0.1, 0.9]), i.e. R^2 drops from 0.349 to 0.053.
official.claim_caption: Table 2. Pearson r and R^2 = r^2 between per-item Factor 1 scores on the performance and metacognitive matrices, unfiltered and on the contentious-item subset (Def. 3.8). SQuAD prospective is the row instantiated as Fig. 7 panels (c, d).
official.metric: Pearson r (and R^2 = r^2) between per-item Factor 1 scores of the performance and confidence tetrachoric factor analyses; higher means confidence tracks performance. No error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Unfiltered (all items) vs. contentious-item subset, same 20 models and items; secondarily across the other benchmark/probe conditions in Table 2.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the pipeline on SQuAD (prospective) with a comparable set of ~20 LLMs gives a filtered r that is not substantially lower than the unfiltered r (e.g. filtered r above ~0.45, or a drop of less than about half), or a filtered r that stays near the unfiltered value under bootstrap over items.

title: CurveRL: Principled Distribution-Aware Context Reweighting for LLM Reasoning

official.background: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for LLM math reasoning, methods such as GRPO and Maximum Likelihood RL (MaxRL) can be written as policy gradients in which each prompt's gradient is multiplied by a weight that depends only on its current pass rate p (GRPO: 1/sqrt(p(1-p)); MaxRL: 1/p). The authors argue these pointwise weights 'collapse' early in training (most p near 0) and late in training (most p near 1), failing to distinguish prompts with different learning potential. A known side effect of RLVR is that pass@k at large k can fall below the base model, so improving large-k coverage without losing pass@1 is a practical goal.
official.method:
CurveRL replaces the pointwise weight with a distribution-aware one derived from the utility E[log F_ref(p(x))], where F_ref is a reference CDF of pass rates. The resulting weight is w(p) = f_ref(p) / F_ref(p) (density over CDF, a reverse hazard rate), which up-weights prompts in low quantiles of the current pass-rate distribution and in densely populated pass-rate regions. F_ref and f_ref are estimated with a histogram over the pass-rate grid {1/N, ..., (N-1)/N} from a sliding window holding the estimated pass rates of all prompts with p in (0,1) from the last t0 = 10 training steps. For each prompt, N = 8 rollouts give p_hat, the gradient is (1/N) sum_i w(p_hat)(r_i - p_hat) grad log pi(y_i|x), and prompts with p_hat in {0,1} contribute nothing.

Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base are trained on POLARIS-53K with verl for 1000 steps (batch 256 prompts, 8 rollouts, lr 1e-6, temperature 1.0, max response 4096 tokens, Math-Verify rewards). The update is fully on-policy (one gradient step per batch, so no ratio clipping), with no KL penalty and no entropy bonus. GRPO and MaxRL use the same loop and differ only in the weight rule. Evaluation uses temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, 2048 samples per problem (1.7B) or 1024 (4B), on the final checkpoint. pass@64 is computed with 1000 bootstrap resamples of size k per prompt.
official.claim: On Qwen3-1.7B-Base trained on POLARIS-53K, CurveRL reaches an average pass@64 of 39.9% over five math benchmarks (AIME 2025, BeyondAIME, HMMT 02/25, HMMT 02/26, MATH-500), vs. 37.7% for MaxRL and 32.6% for GRPO, with average pass@1 not lower (17.1% vs. 16.9% and 16.1%); on Qwen3-4B-Base average pass@64 is 53.4% vs. 48.7% (MaxRL) and 43.7% (GRPO).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on five math reasoning benchmarks. We report pass@1 and pass@64 (%) for each method on Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base. The best per column is in bold.
official.metric: pass@1 and pass@64 (%), higher is better, averaged over the five benchmarks; pass@64 estimated by bootstrap over 2048 (1.7B) or 1024 (4B) samples per problem. No ± reported: single training run per method, no seeds or error bars.
official.comparison: CurveRL vs. GRPO and MaxRL (strongest baseline), all trained with the identical on-policy loop and hyperparameters, differing only in the prompt-weighting rule; base model shown for reference.
official.falsification_criterion: A re-run of the 1.7B setting where CurveRL's average pass@64 is not above MaxRL's (e.g. gap under ~1 point or reversed), or where CurveRL's average pass@1 falls clearly below MaxRL's; seed-to-seed variation of MaxRL's average pass@64 comparable to the 2.2-point gap would also undermine the claim.

title: SliceWorld: A Predictive and Controllable World-State Model for CT Report Generation

official.background: CT report generation (CTRG) asks a model to write a radiology report from a 3D CT volume of hundreds of axial slices. Most existing methods either encode the whole volume globally or aggregate slice features sequentially, learning a direct image-to-text mapping. The paper asks whether borrowing the 'world model' idea, learning a latent state that predicts upcoming observations (here, the next slices along the z-axis) and can be intervened on, gives a better representation for report generation than training the same architecture end-to-end on reports.
official.method:
Each CT slice is encoded by DINOv2 ViT-L (patch tokens compressed to one vector per slice by cross-attention), and a causal 12-layer Mamba encoder runs over the ordered slices. Its hidden state h_t is split into anatomy (256-d), lesion (192-d), and uncertainty (64-d) factors, projected to a 512-d 'world token' per slice, mapped by an MLP into the LLM embedding space, and prepended as a prefix to a Qwen3-1.7B decoder fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 16).

Full SliceWorld first pretrains the visual/world-state encoder on DeepLesion slice sequences (3 epochs, no text) with: multi-step future-slice feature prediction (MFP, predict the next K=5 DINOv2 slice features from both h_t and the world token), factor-aware losses (FAS: anatomy smoothness, lesion L1 sparsity, uncertainty regressing prediction error, lesion-presence BCE from DeepLesion slice ranges), and a counterfactual loss (CF: zeroing the lesion factor should leave predictions unchanged on non-lesion slices and raise error by a margin of 0.1 on lesion slices). The encoder is then frozen and only the projector and LoRA are trained on CT-RATE reports. The 'Direct CTRG' baseline uses the identical architecture with no DeepLesion pretraining and trains all components end-to-end on CT-RATE. Both use greedy decoding on the official CT-RATE test split.
official.claim: On the CT-RATE test set with a Qwen3-1.7B decoder, adding DeepLesion world-model pretraining (MFP+FAS+CF) to an otherwise identical architecture raises BLEU-1 from 36.9 to 38.7, GREEN from 47.2 to 50.1, and RaTEScore F1 from 17.5 to 20.1 compared with direct end-to-end report fine-tuning (paired bootstrap p <= 0.05).

All settings share the same architecture and report-generation training setup; +Recon, +MFP, +FAS, and Full SliceWorld use the same DeepLesion data. "*" marks paired bootstrap significance over Direct CTRG (p <= 0.05).

title: Market Regime Council for Dynamic Credit Assignment in Multi-Agent LLM Decision Systems

official.background: LLM multi-agent systems for portfolio management combine several specialist agents (e.g., price, on-chain and macro analysts), but usually weight them with fixed rules or heuristic confidence scores. That gives no principled measure of which agent or coalition of agents actually improved realized performance. Naive online re-weighting is also fragile: early lucky agents can dominate (cold start), and weights can go stale after a market regime shift. The paper asks whether treating agent weighting as an online cooperative game, with Shapley values as credit, produces better risk-adjusted portfolios than simpler aggregation rules.
official.method:
Market Regime Council (MRC) uses N=3 Qwen3-VL LLM specialists (A1 price/technical, A2 on-chain, A3 macro/sentiment) trading 13 crypto assets daily over 1,037 days (2023-03-01 to 2025-12-31). Each day it produces 7 coalition portfolios: 3 individual, 3 pairwise-debate and 1 grand-coalition readout. Each coalition's utility v(S) is a blend of its exponentially weighted (e-fold 252 days) Sharpe and annualized mean return over its realized history. Exact three-player Shapley values, computed from the 7 coalition utilities, are clipped at zero and mixed with a uniform prior via alpha(t) = 1 - exp(-t/30). They are then scaled by regime-dependent multipliers driven by a momentum/volatility regime score, with an optional Selective Winner-Takes-All override. The weighted individual and pairwise portfolios are blended, the grand-coalition portfolio is mixed in, and risk-control overlays are applied (momentum, BTC dominance, cash target, drawdown protection).

For the chosen claim (Appendix I), the authors replay the 5 logged seeds offline. Every arm reuses the same logged portfolios of the seven coalitions and the same overlays, and the grand-coalition portfolio enters at a fixed weight of 0.10. Only the aggregation rule over the coalition portfolios changes: uniform 1/N, inverse volatility, Hedge, or the MRC credit mechanism (Shapley credit + Bayesian mixture + Regime-Aware Multiplier + Selective WTA). The metric is the annualized Sharpe ratio over the full window at 0 bps transaction cost, with differences paired by seed.
official.claim: With the logged coalition portfolios and risk-control overlays held fixed (offline replay, 5 seeds, 0 bps), the MRC Shapley credit mechanism reaches Sharpe 1.512 versus 1.374 for uniform 1/N weighting (paired ΔSR +0.137 ± 0.029, positive in 5/5 seeds). It also exceeds inverse volatility (1.393) and Hedge (1.455).
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Source of the gain (offline replay, 5 seeds). Left: aggregation rules on the same coalition portfolios. Red: best per column; Blue: second best. Right: SR change when one part is removed from MRC. Table 15: Constraint sensitivity analysis (offline replay, 5 seeds, mean ± std). ΔSR: MRC minus uniform 1/N under the same caps.
official.metric: Annualized Sharpe ratio (higher is better) over 1,037 days. ΔSR is MRC minus uniform, paired by seed; ± is the std over 5 seeds. Table 14's per-rule SRs are 5-seed means with no std reported.
official.comparison: MRC credit mechanism vs. uniform 1/N, inverse-volatility and Hedge aggregation over the same seven logged coalition portfolios, overlays on.
official.falsification_criterion: Replaying the same logged coalition portfolios, MRC's Sharpe gain over uniform 1/N weighting is within one seed-std of zero, or is not positive in at least 4 of 5 seeds. A weaker refutation: Hedge matches or beats MRC.

title: MindAlign: Bridging EEG, Vision, and Language for Zero-Shot Visual Decoding
claim_source: Table 5, page 8 (per-subject values in Table 11, Appendix C, page 16)

official.background: Zero-shot visual decoding from EEG asks a model to identify which of a set of unseen images a person was looking at, using only their brain signal. Recent methods align an EEG encoder with a frozen pretrained CLIP image embedding via contrastive learning, then retrieve images by cosine similarity. EEG is low-SNR and varies across subjects, so how well the EEG signal can be mapped into the target embedding space depends heavily on both the EEG encoder and the choice of the frozen vision-language model whose space is the target.
official.method:
The EEG encoder (subject-specific linear layer, graph attention over channels, a channel Transformer, channel-wise attention with 3D electrode-coordinate priors, and a temporal-spatial convolutional patch embedding from NICE) is first pre-trained by masked reconstruction (time patches replaced with Gaussian noise at ratio 0.3, a 2-layer width-256 Transformer decoder, MSE over all patches). All encoder weights are then transferred to Stage 2, which trains the EEG encoder and a trainable projection on frozen pre-extracted image features with loss (1-α)·InfoNCE(EEG, image) + α·InfoNCE(image, text), α=0.1, where the text features are frozen CLIP-text embeddings of Qwen2-VL-7B descriptions of each training image.

For the claim, the same pipeline is run with four frozen CLIP image/text encoder pairs: OpenAI ViT-L-14, LAION-2B ViT-H-14, LAION-2B ViT-G-14, and Chinese-CLIP RN50 (CN-CLIP, 38M params). Evaluation is in-subject on Things-EEG2 (10 subjects, 63 channels, 0-1000 ms epochs at 250 Hz, repetition-averaged): for each of the 200 held-out test concepts, the EEG embedding ranks the 200 candidate image embeddings, giving Top-1/Top-5 accuracy (chance 0.5%/2.5%). Training uses AdamW lr 2e-4, batch 1000, up to 150 epochs with early stopping on 740 held-out training trials, averaging the three best-validation checkpoints; 3 seeds.
official.claim: On Things-EEG2 in-subject 200-way zero-shot image retrieval, using CN-CLIP (RN50, 38M params) as the frozen image/text encoder gives 54.1 ± 4.9% Top-1, versus 41.3 ± 7.2% for ViT-H-14, 39.6 ± 8.0% for ViT-L-14 and 37.4 ± 5.4% for ViT-G-14 with the same pipeline; CN-CLIP is higher on all 10 subjects.

title: Finding Koopman Invariant Subspaces via Personalized PageRank

official.background: Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD) approximates the Koopman operator of a nonlinear dynamical system by least-squares regression on a finite dictionary of observables (polynomials, Fourier modes, radial basis functions). Its accuracy depends heavily on which observables are in the dictionary. Large dictionaries are ill-conditioned, hard to interpret, and suffer spectral pollution. Ideally one would select a small sub-dictionary that spans an (approximately) Koopman-invariant subspace, so that the dynamics of the observables of interest leak little outside it. Exhaustive search over subsets is combinatorially infeasible.
official.method:
Algorithm 1 (EDMD+PPR): compute the EDMD matrix K = Ψ(X)^+ Ψ(Y) on the full dictionary of Ñ observables. Take the elementwise absolute value of its transpose and row-normalize it into a row-stochastic matrix P, so the transition from observable i to j is proportional to |K[j,i]|, the coefficient of ψ_j in the projection of Kψ_i. Run personalized PageRank on P with damping α = 0.85, teleporting uniformly to a seed set S. Keep the top-N observables by PPR score and refit EDMD by least squares on only those N observables.

Benchmark for the claim: overdamped Langevin dynamics on a three-well Ramachandran potential on the torus (β = 1, Δt = 0.005, one trajectory of 100,000 frames per seed, 20 seeds). The dictionary has Ñ = 236 observables: the 4 state coordinates sin φ, cos φ, sin ψ, cos ψ; Fourier modes up to order 8; cross terms; diagonal Fourier terms; and 100 Gaussian RBFs on a 10×10 grid (σ = 0.45). PPR is seeded at the 4 state coordinates, which are always in every sub-dictionary. Baselines rank the same dictionary: standard PageRank (α = 0.85); TICA (lag 1, ranked by max absolute loading on the top-10 slow components); PCCA+ (50 k-means microstates, lag 5, 3 macrostates, ranked by Fisher discriminant); and a random ordering. The error is the one-step L2 prediction error of the 4 state coordinates on a 20% held-out test set (Eq. 44). It is reported as a ratio to the random ordering's error.
official.claim: On the three-well Ramachandran Langevin benchmark (Ñ = 236), PPR-selected sub-dictionaries give a one-step error ratio to random ordering of 0.30 ± 0.04 at N = 5 and 0.38 ± 0.06 at N = 10. The best baseline, PCCA+, gives 0.68 ± 0.11 and 0.77 ± 0.14; PR and TICA are near or above 1.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Ratio of the error for each ordering to the error for a random ordering, reported as mean ± standard deviation over 20 random seeds. Values below 1 indicate improvement over random ordering.
official.metric: Ratio of the one-step state-prediction error (Eq. 44, held-out test set) to the error of a random ordering. Lower is better; < 1 beats random. Mean ± standard deviation over 20 random seeds.
official.comparison: PPR (seeded at the 4 state coordinates) vs. standard PageRank, PCCA+, TICA, and random ordering, all ranking the same 236-observable dictionary, with EDMD refit on the top-N observables
official.falsification_criterion: With the same dictionary and protocol, the PPR error ratio at N = 5 or N = 10 is not lower than PCCA+'s by more than their seed standard deviations, or PPR's ratio at N = 5 is not well below 1 (e.g. above 0.5).

title: Latent Q-Barrier Shielding for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Figure 1 (SafeDarkRoom panels), page 7; numbers stated in Section 5.3 text, pages 6-7

official.background: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) agents adapt to new tasks at test time by conditioning a frozen pretrained policy on a growing interaction history, with no parameter updates. Safe ICRL adds a cost signal and a per-episode safety budget (a constrained MDP). The current state-of-the-art safe ICRL method, SCARED, encodes safety only through Lagrangian pretraining and cost-to-go conditioning, so under out-of-distribution deployment the frozen policy can still put probability on actions whose predicted future cost exceeds the remaining budget. This paper adds an explicit action-level runtime check: a learned cost-to-go barrier that reweights the frozen policy's actions according to the remaining budget.
official.method:
The base policy is SCARED (an AMAGO-style transformer over the history of (state, action, reward, cost) tuples, trained with an exact-penalty Lagrangian objective). Jointly with it, during the same pretraining run and with no extra epochs, the authors train a shared context encoder Z = E(H, S) with two projection heads (a policy view and a world view), a probabilistic one-step latent dynamics model plus reward/cost heads on the world view (loss L_wm), stop-gradient alignment losses between the two projections, and an ensemble of M = 4 cost critics Q_C,i on the world latent. Loss weights are fixed across environments (critic 10, wm 1, distill 0.1, conj 0.1).

At deployment all parameters are frozen. For each candidate action A (the whole discrete action set in SafeDarkRoom; Ns = 8 samples from the policy in continuous control), the pessimistic cost-to-go Q+_C(Z, A) = max_i Q_C,i(Z, A) is compared with the remaining episode budget B_t = δ − costs so far, giving the barrier b = B_t − Q+_C. The soft shield samples from weights w(A) = π(A|Z_p) · exp(−[−b]_+), normalized over candidates. Evaluation: train on center-oriented goal/obstacle layouts, test on 100 edge-oriented (OOD) layouts; CTG (budget) targets sampled uniformly from [1, 15] for SafeDarkRoom; per-episode return and cost reported over in-context episode index k (50 episodes for SafeDarkRoom), averaged over the 100 evaluation tasks.
official.claim: On OOD SafeDarkRoom test tasks, shielding the SCARED policy with the soft Q-Barrier raises mean per-episode return over in-context adaptation from 0.62 to 0.90 (+46%) while lowering mean per-episode cost from 1.66 to 0.87 (−47%), with no test-time parameter updates.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: In-context adaptation dynamics (RQ1). Per-episode return (top) and cost (bottom) over in-context episode index k on test-time evaluation tasks. Curves show means over 100 evaluation tasks, with shaded regions denoting standard error of the mean. Q-Barrier generally improves adaptation by reaching high return earlier and reducing cost after a short context window, while SafetyHalfCheetah shows a conservative Pareto point with lower cost and lower return.
official.metric: Per-episode return (higher is better) and per-episode cost (lower is better), averaged over in-context episodes and over 100 OOD evaluation tasks; shaded regions in the figure are standard error of the mean over the 100 tasks (not over training seeds; no training-seed variation is reported)

official.falsification_criterion: Retraining SCARED and SCARED + Q-Barrier on SafeDarkRoom and evaluating on 100 edge-oriented OOD tasks, the shielded agent does not achieve both higher mean return and lower mean cost than SCARED (e.g. return gain under ~0.1 or cost not lower), or the gap reverses across training seeds.

title: MATO: Multi-objective Personalized Alignment with Test-time Optimization for Large Language Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (second judge in Table 7, page 23)

official.background: Users often want an LLM response to satisfy several natural-language preferences at once (e.g. concise, friendly, expert-level, cautious), and these can conflict. Training-based multi-objective alignment (MORLHF, RiC, MOD) needs a reward model and training per objective, which does not scale to open-ended preferences. Simply listing all preferences in the prompt is training-free, but models tend to over-serve some preferences and neglect others. Training-free decoding methods (Linear Alignment, CoS, Amulet, OPAD) were designed for a single preference and treat a multi-preference prompt as one combined signal.
official.method:
MATO is a training-free decoding procedure. At each token it runs the backbone LLM with no preference, with each single preference prompt c_k, and with a combined prompt C listing all preferences and their weights. The surrogate reward for preference k is beta * log(pi(y|x,c_k)/pi(y|x)), summed over the tokens generated so far. Weights are updated in closed form as w_k proportional to w_k^init * exp(-R_k/tau), so preferences with low accumulated reward get more weight. The merged distribution is pi(.|x,C) * prod_k pi(.|x,c_k)^{w_k}, which is then refined with T=80 closed-form FTRL steps that push it away from the unconditioned base distribution while staying near the merged one (tau=1, alpha=0.5, lambda=1.0, eta=10). The next token is sampled from the result.

Evaluation uses the Multifaceted dataset: 945 queries, each with 4 preferences at uniform weights. GPT-4o scores each response 1-5 on each preference using the dataset rubrics. Metrics are APS (mean score over the 4 preferences), Worst (minimum of the 4 scores) and AMR (fraction of responses with all 4 scores >= 3). Baselines run on the same backbone are Base LLM, Preference Prompt, Linear Alignment, CoS, Amulet and OPAD, with the single-preference methods adapted by concatenating all preferences into one prompt.
official.claim: On the Multifaceted dataset with Llama-3.2-1B as backbone and GPT-4o as judge, MATO reaches APS 3.23 and Worst 2.25, above every training-free baseline; the best baselines are Preference Prompt (APS 3.07) and Linear Alignment (Worst 2.11).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison on multi-objective personalized alignment using GPT-4o as judge.
official.metric: GPT-4o judge scores on a 1-5 scale per preference: APS (mean over 4 preferences) and Worst (minimum over 4), higher is better, averaged over 945 queries; AMR also reported. Single run with fixed seed; no error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.
official.comparison: MATO vs. Base LLM, Preference Prompt, Linear Alignment, CoS, Amulet and OPAD, all on Llama-3.2-1B (the table also covers Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B)
official.falsification_criterion: With Llama-3.2-1B on Multifaceted judged by GPT-4o, MATO's APS is not above Preference Prompt's or its Worst score is not above the best baseline's (Linear Alignment, 2.11), or the gaps (0.16 APS, 0.14 Worst) fall within run-to-run variation across sampling seeds.

title: Credit Assignment with Resets in Language Model Reasoning

official.background: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods such as GRPO post-train language models on multi-step reasoning by giving every token of a sampled solution the same outcome reward. This ignores which reasoning steps actually caused a failure. Resets offer a simple credit-assignment mechanism: return to an intermediate state of a failed solution, resample several continuations from there, and attribute the difference in outcomes to the decisions made after that point. The open question is whether choosing the reset point well, rather than at random, makes this useful in practice for LLM post-training.
official.method:
Generation is done at the thought level: the model is prompted to emit one reasoning step at a time, each ended by a </thought> stop token (max 20 thoughts, 256 tokens each). In each training step and for each prompt, iid rollouts are sampled until the first incorrect one (the seed); the preceding correct rollouts plus fresh samples form a base group of 4 rollouts trained with standard group-normalized GRPO advantages. A reset index h* is then chosen on the failed seed, and 4 suffix rollouts are sampled from the prefix (prompt, thoughts 1..h*-1). Advantages are group-normalized within this shared-prefix group, and the prefix tokens are masked out of the loss so gradient only reaches the suffix tokens. SRPO picks h* by prompting the same policy to name the first erroneous step in its own failed chain; RRPO picks h* uniformly at random. No PPO clipping and no KL term are used, and one gradient step is taken per group.

Models (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct) are trained with LoRA (rank 64, alpha 64, AdamW, lr 5e-5) on 400 NuminaMath-Olympiads problems for 2 epochs, batch 32 prompts, temperature 0.7, 8 rollouts per prompt for every method (rough compute matching). Baselines are GRPO (8 iid rollouts), SCoRe, Critique-GRPO and SPO-Tree. Evaluation is greedy (temperature 0) accuracy on 500 random test items from each of 10 benchmarks, including SciKnowEval Materials and Physics, averaged over 3 seeds.
official.claim: With OLMo-3-7B-Instruct trained on NuminaMath-Olympiads, SRPO reaches 55.9 ± 0.6 on SciKnowEval Materials and 54.5 ± 2.0 on SciKnowEval Physics, above every baseline run under the same budget (best: GRPO 51.3 ± 2.6 on Materials; SPO-Tree 47.1 ± 1.6 on Physics).

official.metric: Accuracy (%) on 500 randomly selected test items per benchmark, higher is better; mean ± SD over 3 training seeds; greedy decoding

official.falsification_criterion: On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, SRPO's mean accuracy on SciKnowEval Materials is not above GRPO's by more than the seed SD, or SRPO's Physics accuracy is not above the best of GRPO/Critique-GRPO/SPO-Tree by more than the seed SD (i.e. the gaps of about 4.6 and 7.4 points disappear).

title: RotMoLE: Enhancing Mixture of Low-Rank Experts through Rotational Gating Mechanism

official.background: Mixture of Low-rank Experts (MoE-LoRA) adds several LoRA adapters plus a router to a frozen LLM so that different experts can specialize when one model is fine-tuned on several tasks or languages at once. The router only gives each selected expert a scalar weight, so it can scale an expert's output but not change its direction. The paper argues this limits how well a small pool of experts can be shared across many tasks, and proposes letting the router also rotate each expert's low-rank representation.
official.method:
RotMoLE replaces each MoE-LoRA update W = W0 + sum_{i in TopK(x)} g_i B_i A_i with W = W0 + sum_{i in TopK(x)} g_i B_i R_i A_i, where R_i is an r x r rotation matrix. A rotation gate theta = 2*pi*Sigmoid(x W_theta) - pi (W_theta initialized to 0) gives one angle per expert; top-k selection still uses only the softmax scaling gate g. For rank r = 2, R_i is the standard 2D rotation by theta_i. For r > 2, each expert has a learnable r-dim vector q_i; the rotation is applied in the plane spanned by A_i x and the component of q_i orthogonal to it.

In the Table 1 experiment, the adapters are added to q/k/v/o projections of only the first quarter of layers (layers 0-6 of Llama-3.2-3B, layers 0-8 of Qwen-2.5-3B). The model is jointly fine-tuned on an equal mix of CommonsenseQA, OpenBookQA and SocialIQA (batch 135 = 45 per task; about 4,000 steps for Llama and 5,500 for Qwen; SGD, lr 3e-4 with linear decay; one fixed seed). Configurations are r in {2, 3} and (n, k) in {(2, 2), (4, 2)}. The baseline is the same MoE-LoRA with only the scaling gate. The metric is accuracy per task and its average.
official.claim: Under matched joint fine-tuning on CSQA+OBQA+SIQA, RotMoLE gets higher average accuracy than the scaling-only MoE-LoRA baseline in all 8 configurations of Table 1 (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-3B; r in {2,3}; n,k in {2,2; 4,2}). Gains range from +0.79 to +5.68 points, e.g. Qwen-2.5-3B r=2 n=4 k=2: 61.77 vs 56.09; Llama-3.2-3B r=3 n=2 k=2: 42.55 vs 38.67.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance of Jointly Fine-Tuning on Mixed QA Tasks
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on each QA task and their average, higher is better; single run with fixed seed, no error bars. 'Boost' is the relative gain in average accuracy; Std./Avg. is the relative std across the three tasks, not across seeds.
official.comparison: RotMoLE vs. MoE-LoRA with a conventional softmax scaling gate, same base model, rank, number of experts, top-k, data and training schedule

title: StreamOV: Streaming Omni-Video Understanding via Evidence-Guided Memory and Response Triggering

official.background: Omni-modal LLMs such as Qwen3-Omni can reason jointly over video frames and audio, but they are built for offline use, where the whole clip is available before answering. In streaming use the audio-visual context keeps growing, so the model needs a bounded memory that keeps the informative parts of the past, and it also has to decide when to answer. Most existing streaming video methods use only the visual stream. This paper proposes a memory and trigger layer on top of a frozen omni-modal model and evaluates it on streaming and offline audio-visual benchmarks.
official.method:
StreamOV wraps a frozen Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B. For each incoming observation (frames plus synchronized audio), it computes query-agnostic scores (visual change from consecutive-frame differencing, audio saliency from waveform peak detection, and an audio-visual co-burst score) and query-aware scores (CLIP similarity between the query and the frame, and CLAP similarity between the query and the audio). Each score is rank-normalized within the current observation window (S = r / r_max). The audio-query score is gated by multiplying it by max(S_a, S_cob) (gated S_qa = S_qa * max(S_a, S_cob)). The scores are then combined into visual evidence E_v = max(S_qv, S_v), audio evidence E_a = max(gated S_qa, S_a) and aligned evidence E_av = max(min(S_qv, gated S_qa), min(E_v, E_a, S_cob)). E_av is subtracted from E_v and E_a (clipped at 0), and the base score is B(t) = max of the three resulting evidence values.

Memory is the union of a short-term buffer, holding the Top-K_S observations of the current window, and a long-term buffer, holding the Top-K_L observations chosen from the existing long-term entries plus the observations leaving the short-term window. Duplicates are removed, and the retained observations are fed to the frozen model in chronological order as interleaved visual-audio input. The frame budget is 32 frames on StreamingBench. A separate 18.9M-parameter cross-attention trigger reads the last prefill hidden state and decides whether to respond; it is the only trained component. The paper does not say whether the trigger is active during StreamingBench QA scoring; the accuracy gain is presumably driven by the memory construction. The baseline is the same Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B model run offline on video sampled at 1 FPS, with audio.
official.claim: On the StreamingBench Audio-Visual QA subset, StreamOV, built on a frozen Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B with a 32-frame evidence-guided memory, reaches 68.6% average accuracy, compared with 61.0% for the same Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B run offline at 1 FPS with audio (+7.6 points). It is higher on all four subtasks: ER 63.6 vs 53.6, SCU 59.2 vs 40.8, SD 79.2 vs 70.4, MA 90.4 vs 79.2.

title: Self-Improvement Imitation with Biologically Guided Search for Protein Design Under Oracle Budgets

official.background: Protein engineering can be cast as optimizing a sequence to maximize a fitness property (thermostability, binding, activity) when each measurement is expensive, so only a small number of oracle queries are available. Methods have to explore a combinatorial sequence space while keeping every query informative. Reinforcement-learning and off-policy generative approaches are sensitive to noise in the learned surrogate used to rank candidates, and most mutation proposers are position-agnostic, so they can edit residues that are functionally critical. This paper asks whether a self-improvement imitation loop, combined with structured sampling and a biologically motivated selection score, finds higher-fitness variants than existing search and RL baselines under a fixed query budget.
official.method:
SILO runs an active-learning loop for N = 10 rounds with an oracle budget of K = 128 sequences per round. Candidate generation is a Markov decision process over edit trajectories: starting from the best oracle-labeled sequence found so far, a transformer policy over frozen ESM Cambrian embeddings picks a position (level-0 head over L positions) and then a replacement amino acid (level-1 head over the 20 residues), applied iteratively for d_max edit steps (each round instantiates M = 5 search instances with mutational budgets d_max in {1,2,3}); this start sequence is re-selected each round as the highest-oracle-scoring sequence in the labeled set. Trajectories are drawn with incremental stochastic beam search without replacement (beam size 32, 480 sequences scored per round).

Sampled sequences are ranked by S(x) = UCB_proxy(x) + UCB_AFS(x), where the proxy is an ensemble of three 1D CNNs retrained each round on the labeled data, UCB_proxy = mu + 0.1*sigma, and UCB_AFS is the same UCB applied to the alanine-substituted variant A(x) in which every position the agent mutated is replaced by alanine (gamma2 = 1). The top K unique sequences go to the in silico oracle (TAPE, or FLEXS ground truth for AAV); the top P = 50 oracle-labeled sequences become imitation targets, and the policy is updated by next-action cross-entropy on their action trajectories. No value function is learned. Baselines PEX, AdaLead, GFN-AL-deltaCS, MLDE and ProSpero are reproduced by the authors under the identical budget, proxy and oracle, following the ProSpero evaluation protocol.

title: Recon: Reconstruction-Guided Reasoning Synthesis for User Modeling
claim_source: Figure 3 (left), page 6; per-user numbers in Table 3, page 24

official.background: User modeling uses a language model to imitate a specific person's next action (for example their next conversation turn) from a corpus of their past context-action pairs. Recent work augments these corpora with synthesized reasoning traces, usually produced by prompting a model with both the context and the observed action. Such traces are post-hoc rationalizations: they can be consistent with the action without explaining why that action was chosen over plausible alternatives, so they may add little predictive signal when retrieved as in-context examples for new contexts.
official.method:
Backward Synthesis (the baseline) prompts a reasoning model Mr with a context c and the ground-truth action a* and keeps a single first-person 'thought process' trace (prompt in Appendix C.1; temperature 0.7). Recon-Select samples N = 4 candidate traces from the same Backward Synthesis prompt (temperature 1.0), asks the action model Ma to reconstruct the action from (c, trace) only, scores the reconstructions against a* with a Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite judge (all N candidates shown in one call, each given an alignment score in [0, 1] on style, intent and values; prompt in Appendix C.2), and keeps the trace whose reconstruction is most aligned. The reconstructor uses temperature 0.7. In the main setting Mr = Ma = Qwen3-8B. The corpus-augmentation step is applied to every retrieved training pair.

Evaluation: for each test context, the same retrieved training context-action pairs are augmented with either Backward Synthesis or Recon-Select traces and fed to the same action model (Qwen3-8B, default sampling) to generate the user's next turn (Eq. 1). k = 8 training pairs are retrieved per test context with Qwen3-4B-Embedding, using contexts as both keys and queries (Appendix D.2). A Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite judge compares the two generated actions against the ground-truth turn pairwise (A/B order randomized), and the win rate of Recon-Select is reported excluding ties. SCOTUS data: oral-argument transcripts of Justices Antonin Scalia (2007-2015) and William Brennan (1969-1976) from the public walkerdb/supreme_court_transcripts (Oyez) mirror; per Justice about 4,096 training target turns (retrieval pool) and 512 test target turns, split at the session level with seed 42; context truncated to 4,096 tokens.
official.claim: On the SCOTUS domain with Qwen3-8B as both reasoning and action model, retrieval-augmented action generation using Recon-Select traces beats Backward Synthesis traces with a 61.3% non-tied win rate (p < 0.001; Scalia 59.6% over n = 213, Brennan 62.7% over n = 244), and 54.7% pooled over all four domains.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Recon-Select and E2E-GRPO results. Win rates against Backward Synthesis across four domains and overall. (Left) On Qwen3-8B, Recon-Select achieves a 54.7% overall win rate over baseline. E2E-GRPO achieves only a 38.4% win rate, indicating that optimizing for action accuracy alone does not produce transferable reasoning traces. (Right) On GPT-5-mini, Recon-Select achieves a 53.5% overall win rate, demonstrating consistent improvements from reconstruction-based selection. Asterisks denote win rates significantly exceeding 50% (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001). 95% confidence intervals shown.

title: Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (per-task results in Table 16, page 38)

official.background: Pretrained flow-matching policies are attractive priors for robot control, but fine-tuning them with off-policy RL is unstable because the action is produced by a multi-step denoising chain. Q-learning with Adjoint Matching (QAM) avoids backpropagating through that chain by casting policy improvement as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem whose terminal cost is the negative learned critic. With a fixed temperature, however, errors in the learned critic can be amplified exponentially into large policy errors, and QAM can drift far from the pretrained policy and collapse, even with gradient clipping.
official.method:
TRQAM keeps QAM's training loop (TD critic update, sample a trajectory from the fine-tuned memoryless SDE, solve the lean adjoint ODE, minimize the Adjoint Matching loss) but inserts a trust-region parameter λ inside the controlled SDE: the total diffusion is fixed, so λ only scales the control term via σ(τ) = sqrt(2(1−τ)/(λτ)). By Girsanov's theorem, λ is then exactly the weight of the path-space KL between the fine-tuned and pretrained sampling processes in the SOC objective (QAM is the special case λ = 1). The path-space KL is estimated for free from the velocity difference already computed in the loss (Eq. 6), smoothed by an EMA, and λ is updated by projected dual descent λ ← max(0, λ + η(D − ε_KL)) to keep the KL within a per-domain budget ε_KL tuned from {0.5, ..., 4.0}.

Evaluation: 50 reward-based single-task OGBench tasks (10 domains × 5 tasks). All methods are pretrained for 300K steps with behavior cloning, then fine-tuned offline for 1M steps; success rate is averaged over 8 seeds. Baselines are FQL, CGQL-Linex, DSRL, IFQL, QAM and QAM-E, using the per-domain hyperparameters reported as optimal in the QAM paper. Manipulation tasks use action chunks of size 5.
official.claim: After 1M offline training steps on 50 OGBench tasks (8 seeds), TRQAM reaches 68% mean success versus 46% for the best baseline (DSRL), 45% for QAM-E and 35% for QAM; on the cheap 1M-data domain cube-double it scores 81 ± 3 vs. QAM 71 ± 2 and DSRL 72 ± 4.
