title: Mildly Overparameterized ReLU Networks on Orthogonal Data: Incremental Learning and Implicit Bias

official.background: Gradient descent from small initialization is believed to give neural networks an implicit bias toward simple, low-norm solutions, but for two-layer ReLU networks trained on regression this is mostly unproven. Orthogonal training data is a tractable setting. Earlier work showed that gradient flow reaches the minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator only with width exponential in the number of samples n, and that with mild overparameterization (width m of order log n) it interpolates but not at minimum norm. How large the norm of the reached interpolator is in that mild regime was open.
official.method:
The paper analyzes gradient flow for a two-layer ReLU network trained with squared loss on n orthonormal inputs, as the initialization scale goes to 0. It proves that training follows a saddle-to-saddle jump process in which one new neuron activates at each saddle, computable without training via Algorithm 1. From this it derives Theorem 3: with high probability half the learned interpolator's squared parameter norm is at most 5(√n₊ + √n₋)·max|yᵢ| (i.e. ‖θ‖² ≤ 10(√n₊ + √n₋)·max|yᵢ|), where n₊ and n₋ count the positive and negative labels. The minimum-norm interpolator has squared norm 2√(Σ_{yᵢ>0} yᵢ²) + 2√(Σ_{yᵢ<0} yᵢ²) (eq. 2), which is also of order √n for bounded labels.

Experiment for Figure 5 (Appendix A.2): inputs are the n×n identity matrix (the dynamics are rotation invariant, so any orthonormal basis behaves the same) and labels are i.i.d. standard Gaussians. Width is m = ⌈ln(10000·n)/ln(4/3)⌉. Initialization is balanced and small: hidden neurons have random directions and norm 10⁻³⁰/√m, and output weights have random sign and absolute value 10⁻³⁰/√m. Training uses full-batch gradient descent on the MSE loss with learning rate 0.5, for 10⁶ epochs or until the loss reaches 10⁻¹⁰. The squared ℓ2 norm of all final parameters is recorded and compared with the optimal squared norm from eq. 2. Each n is run 3 times; the caption says the labels are redrawn per run and the text says the initial weights are.
official.claim: For n from about 32 to 10⁵ orthonormal points with Gaussian labels and width m ≈ log(n), gradient descent from 10⁻³⁰-scale initialization reaches an interpolator whose squared parameter norm grows like √n (log-log slope ≈ 1/2). It stays within a roughly constant factor of about 1.3-1.7 of the minimum-norm interpolator, e.g. about 1340 vs. 885 at n = 10⁵.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: We train a two-layer ReLU network with increasing data dimensionality and number of data points n, and plot the square of the norm of of the parameters of the final network as well as that of the optimal interpolator (see eq. (2)). The hidden layer size m increases logarithmically in n, and we use a balanced initialization of scale 10^-30/√m. Each value plotted is the mean over three runs, with each run using fixed orthogonal inputs and different random labels which are standard Gaussians. We use full batch gradient descent with a learning rate of 0.5 for one million epochs or until the loss reaches 10^-10. The area between the minimum and maximum values is shaded, however they are relatively concentrated.
official.metric: Squared ℓ2 norm of all network parameters after training (lower is better; the optimum is the min-norm interpolator from eq. 2). Points are means over 3 runs and shaded bands are min/max over runs (barely visible). Values below are read off a log-log plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Achieved squared norm after GD training vs. the analytic minimum-norm interpolator squared norm, across n
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining with the stated setup, the ratio of achieved to optimal squared norm grows steadily with n (e.g. above ~2.5 by n = 10⁴-10⁵, or a log-log slope clearly above 1/2 for the achieved norm), or the network fails to interpolate with m = ⌈ln(10000n)/ln(4/3)⌉.

title: FineVLA: Fine-Grained Instruction Alignment for Steerable Vision-Language-Action Policies

official.background: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are usually trained on robot trajectories paired with short goal-level instructions such as 'pick up the cup'. These instructions leave out how the task is executed (which arm, approach direction, contact region, rotation direction), so policies cannot be steered on those factors and get no language signal about them during training. The paper builds human-verified fine-grained, process-level instructions for open robot datasets and asks whether training on them, alone or mixed with the original goal-level instructions, helps or hurts policy learning.
official.method:
FineVLA-Tool unifies 972K trajectories from 10 open robot datasets, picks 47,159 representative trajectories by DTW-based clustering, and annotates them with ten-dimension fine-grained descriptions (Qwen3.5-Plus draft, then human verification). For policy experiments, Section 3.2 builds two parallel datasets: an FG dataset (the annotated representative trajectories, each paired with its fine-grained description; 5,872 for AlohaMix) and a Raw dataset (all source trajectories with their original goal-level instructions; 86,662 for AlohaMix), and the FG:Raw ratio is the probability of sampling from each dataset at every training step. Appendix A.4.4 instead describes every trajectory as having both a Raw and an FG instruction, with the ratio setting the per-trajectory probability of drawing each. In both descriptions, trajectories shared by the two variants have identical action labels and visual observations; only the paired text differs. Seven settings are compared: Raw-only, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, 4:1, FG-only.

The policy is StarVLA-OFT (Qwen3.5-4B vision-language backbone plus an MLP head regressing continuous action chunks with L1 loss), pretrained for 100k steps on AlohaMix (86,662 ALOHA-compatible dual-arm episodes from RDT, RoboCOIN and RoboMIND, 5,872 of which have FG annotations). It is then fine-tuned for 100k steps on the RoboTwin Clean+Random training set (27,500 trajectories), with the FG:Raw mixture applied during this fine-tuning stage according to Section 4.1. Policies are evaluated on the official RoboTwin Easy and Hard splits with 20 episodes per task, and the per-task success rates are averaged.
official.claim: With StarVLA-OFT pretrained on AlohaMix, training with FG:Raw = 1:1 instruction mixing reaches 86.8% / 82.5% RoboTwin success (Easy/Hard) versus 71.8% / 71.4% for Raw-only and 78.3% / 76.1% for FG-only, with identical trajectories and actions.

official.metric: RoboTwin task success rate (%), higher is better, averaged over tasks with 20 episodes per task; single run per configuration, no error bars reported

title: Falcon-X: A Time Series Foundation Model for Heterogeneous Multivariate Modeling

official.background: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on large cross-domain corpora and applied zero-shot to new forecasting tasks. Most are univariate: each series is forecast from its own history only. Multivariate TSFMs such as Chronos-2 use group attention among the raw variates of a dataset, so the model must handle variates with different meanings and counts across datasets. The authors argue that this raw-space mixing contributes little in practice, and that a model with an explicit latent space for cross-variate interaction can actually exploit cross-variate information.
official.method:
Falcon-X is a 591M-parameter encoder-only TSFM. Each variate is normalized (arcsine of the z-scored value), concatenated with relative timestamps and an observation mask, patched (length 16) and processed by 16 Time Attention layers independently per variate. Variate Attention then projects each entity's m_i variates onto C = 6 learned prototypes via a differential attention (softmax over positive prototype keys minus λ times softmax over negative prototype keys), applies 16 layers of attention over all entities' prototype tokens (Latent Entity Attention), and routes the result back to each variate (Variate Reassembly Router) with a sigmoid-gated residual onto the temporal embedding. A linear quantile head produces probabilistic forecasts.

For the inference comparison (Section 5.3, Figure 7b) the same pretrained checkpoint is evaluated on GIFT-Eval in two modes: multivariate inference (all variates of a multivariate series are passed together, so cross-variate attention is active) and univariate inference (each variate is forecast on its own). The same is done for Chronos-2 with group attention on and off. The metric is MASE aggregated over GIFT-Eval's 97 dataset/frequency/horizon configurations (geometric mean, as in the leaderboard).
official.claim: On GIFT-Eval, running the released Falcon-X checkpoint with multivariate inference gives overall MASE 0.687 vs. 0.693 with univariate (channel-independent) inference, while Chronos-2 gives 0.698 in both modes.

title: PARE: Pruning and Adaptive Routing for Efficient Video Generation

official.background: Video diffusion transformers such as Wan2.1-14B produce high-quality videos, but every denoising step passes through 40 wide transformer blocks, and generation takes about 50 steps with classifier-free guidance. Structural compression methods cut per-step cost by pruning blocks or channels, but they fix one reduced architecture for all inputs and timesteps, and they treat all attention heads the same. The paper asks whether pruning that knows which heads are spatial and which are temporal, combined with input-adaptive block skipping, can roughly halve per-step compute while keeping VBench quality close to the teacher.
official.method:
Width: each self-attention head is scored with a WANDA-style magnitude criterion (||W_O slice|| x ||attention-weighted value||) on 200 calibration samples across 10 timestep bins. Heads are classified as spatial (intra-frame attention ratio > 0.7), temporal (< 0.3) or mixed, and temporal-head scores are multiplied by 1.5 so that low-magnitude motion heads are not pruned. 30% of self-attention heads, cross-attention heads and FFN neurons are removed; FFN neurons are ranked by ||W_up row|| x ||W_down col|| and selected greedily while skipping neurons with high cosine similarity to ones already kept. Stage I distils the width-pruned student from the frozen teacher (feature matching + teacher-velocity + data-velocity + temporal-difference losses; 7K steps, 30K video-text pairs, 4xH200).

Depth: a small MLP router takes a sinusoidal timestep embedding and a content embedding (noisy-latent statistics for T2V, CLIP image embedding for I2V) and outputs per-block logits. The top-K(t) blocks are executed, where K(t) decreases linearly from 35 at high noise to 20 at low noise (first and last blocks always on), with straight-through gradients. Stage II jointly trains the student and router for another 7K steps. Evaluation is VBench (6 dimensions plus their average) with 50 FlowUniPC steps and CFG 5.0.
official.claim: On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, PARE (width pruning + adaptive block routing, 6.7B active params, 52% fewer) reaches a VBench 6-dimension average of 77.10, which is 2.42 points above the best structural-compression baseline NeoDragon (74.68 at 25% reduction) and above F3-Pruning (69.84) and ICMD (56.37), and 0.60 below the unpruned 14B teacher (77.70).

title: Tree Search With Predictions

official.background: In 'algorithms with predictions', an algorithm gets a possibly wrong hint and should do better the more accurate the hint is. The textbook example is searching a sorted array: with a predicted position, doubling binary search finds the target in O(log η) queries, where η is the prediction error. A sorted array is a path graph, so a natural generalization is searching a tree. Each query to a node returns the neighbor on the path toward the hidden target. Without a prediction, centroid search needs O(log n) queries. The paper asks whether a predicted node s can bring the cost down to something that depends on dist(s, t).
official.method:
The paper proves that O(log dist(s,t)) is impossible on general trees. It then gives 'k-spine search' for trees of pathwidth k. Using a recursive decomposition (Suderman's 'main path'), removing a spine path leaves subtrees of pathwidth at most k-1. The algorithm runs doubling binary search along the spine from the point nearest the prediction, finds which off-spine subtree holds the target, and recurses. This takes O(k log dist(s,t)) queries. In the implementation, the prediction is queried first, and the search then starts from the lowest decomposition component consistent with the direction the oracle returns (Appendix C).

Experiments: four graphs from the Network Repository (Luxembourg road network, sc-msdoor, soc-orkut-dir, soc-orkut) are each turned into a DFS spanning tree rooted at a low-degree peripheral vertex (for directed graphs, after taking the undirected largest connected component). The exact pathwidth is k = 5-6. For each prediction error d, ordered (prediction, target) pairs at tree distance d are sampled uniformly. All three algorithms run on the same pairs: centroid search (no prediction), k-spine search, and naive trace (walk from the prediction toward the target, which takes d+1 queries). The reported quantity is the average number of oracle queries at each d.
official.claim: On DFS trees of four real-world graphs (pathwidth 5-6, 115K-3.1M nodes), k-spine search uses fewer average oracle queries than both centroid search and naive trace over an intermediate range of prediction errors: d = 10-22 (Luxembourg), 10-43 (sc-msdoor), 10-53 (soc-orkut-dir) and 10-67 (soc-orkut). Inside that range it typically uses about 11-14 queries, against roughly 14-17 for centroid search.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Zoomed pre-crossing results. The shaded region marks distances where k-spine search uses fewer average oracle queries than both baselines.
official.metric: Average number of oracle queries at a fixed prediction-error distance d (lower is better). No error bars, seeds or per-d sample counts are reported.
official.comparison: k-spine search (Algorithm 1, prediction-based) vs. centroid search (no prediction) and naive trace (follow the oracle from the prediction), on identical sampled (prediction, target) pairs
official.falsification_criterion: With a reasonably large number of sampled pairs per d, k-spine search's average query count is not below both centroid search and naive trace over most of the stated d interval on some dataset, or the empirical crossing with centroid search falls far below the reported value (e.g., below d = 15 on sc-msdoor or the Orkut trees).

title: Semiparametrically Efficient Inference for Kernel Measures of Noise Heterogeneity
claim_source: Figure 3, page 10 (data-generating details in Appendix 12.4, page 48)

official.background: Many diagnostics fit a regression and then check whether the residuals are independent of the covariates. Examples are goodness-of-fit tests for additive noise models and additive-noise causal discovery. Kernel dependence measures such as HSIC can detect any such dependence, but here the residuals come from a fitted, often flexible regression, so first-stage estimation error can itself create apparent dependence between covariates and residuals. Naive plug-in residual methods then give miscalibrated tests and confidence intervals. Standard first-order semiparametric debiasing of scalar HSIC does not help, because its efficient influence function vanishes at independence.
official.method:
The target is the RKHS cross-covariance operator Psi_0 between covariates and residuals R = Y - E[Y | W]; its squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm is HSIC. The authors build a Hilbert-valued one-step estimator of Psi_0: a cross-fitted plug-in estimate plus its efficient-influence-function (EIF) correction. The nuisances (the regression m and a second nuisance v) are fitted with kernel ridge regression. When Psi_0 != 0, a delta-method confidence interval for ||Psi_0||^2 is ||Psi_hat_n||^2 +/- 2 z_{1-alpha/2} sqrt(2 sigma_hat_n^2 / n), which attains the semiparametric efficiency bound (the appendix suggests centering it on the U-statistic version). The plug-in baseline uses the same delta-method construction but omits the EIF correction term.

Figure 3 setting (Appendix 12.4): W = (X, T) with X ~ Bernoulli(1/2) a group indicator and T ~ Unif[-pi, pi]. Y = m(X, T) + sigma(X) eps with eps ~ N(0, 1) and m(x, t) = 1.5 (0.2x + sum_{k=1}^5 [0.30/k sin(kt) + 0.25/k cos(kt) + 0.22/k x sin(kt) + 0.18/k x cos(kt)]). Under the alternative, sigma(0) = 0.35 and sigma(1) = 0.55. Each dataset has n = 120. The kernel on X is the discrete kernel 1{x = x'}, so HSIC equals a scaled MMD between the residual laws of the two groups, and the residual kernel l is Gaussian. The experiment uses 4-fold cross-fitting with KRR nuisances; kernel bandwidths and ridge parameters are chosen by cross-validation within the training folds. Empirical coverage of the true ||Psi_0||^2 and mean CI width are measured at nominal levels 0.5 to 0.95.
official.claim: In the covariate-adjusted two-group residual model with n = 120, debiased delta-method CIs for ||Psi_0||^2 (HSIC; the figure caption says 'for Psi_0') have empirical coverage close to nominal (about 0.50, 0.59, 0.67, 0.81, 0.93, 0.96 at nominal 0.5-0.95). Their mean width is about 0.016-0.045, roughly 2.5-3x narrower than the plug-in (no-EIF-correction) CIs, whose width is about 0.048-0.117 and which over-cover (about 0.67 at nominal 0.5).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Delta-method CI calibration for Psi_0 when W = (X, T).
official.metric: Empirical coverage of the true ||Psi_0||^2 (closer to nominal is better) and mean CI width (lower is better), plotted against nominal coverage. Error bars are shown on the plot, but the paper does not say what they represent or how many repetitions were run; they look like Monte Carlo intervals over repetitions.
official.comparison: Debiased (EIF-corrected one-step) delta-method CI vs. plug-in delta-method CI with the EIF correction omitted, on identical data and nuisance fits
official.falsification_criterion: On replicated datasets from the Appendix 12.4 alternative (n = 120), the debiased CI's coverage departs from nominal by more than Monte Carlo error at several levels, or its mean width is not clearly smaller (e.g. less than 1.5x narrower) than the plug-in CI's width.

title: The Future of Facts: Tracing the Factual Generation-Verification Gap

official.background: Language models are often said to verify answers more reliably than they generate them (the generation-verification or GV-gap), and this asymmetry underlies self-improvement and best-of-N methods. For factual knowledge it is unclear how training creates, preserves or removes the gap, because real pretraining data makes it impossible to know how often a model has seen a given fact. This paper injects synthetic facts with invented entities into open models by fine-tuning, so data exposure is controlled, and tracks generation (recall) and verification (recognition) separately across acquisition, continual learning and updating.
official.method:
The authors generate 150 synthetic single-hop facts (25 per category: politics, medicine, religion, science, society, societal bias), each a triplet of invented entities such as (Hoibalbali, CureOfDisease, Blue Striped Axzazari), with 10 paraphrased training sentences per fact (1,500 sentences; made with Gemini 2.5 Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.5, released with the code). Instruction-tuned Gemma-3 4B/12B, Llama-3.2 3B/11B, Phi-4 Mini 3.8B/14B and Qwen-3 4B/14B are fully fine-tuned (AdamW, constant LR with warmup, per-model batch size and LR in Appendix Table 1, e.g. Qwen-3 4B BS 16 / LR 7e-6, Llama-3.2 3B BS 32 / LR 3e-6) on only the paraphrased sentences, each wrapped as a user message in the chat template, for up to 12 epochs.

After every epoch the model is evaluated, with a reason-then-answer prompt, on (i) a generative question per fact ('What is the cure for Blue Striped Axzazari disease?'), graded by whether the correct entity appears (programmatic grading; an LM judge gives similar results), and (ii) verification questions that ask whether a candidate answer is correct or incorrect (both phrasings, to counter sycophancy), including corrupted candidates. Verification is reported as balanced accuracy (alpha_u = 0.5, so chance = 0.5). Generation and verification curves are plotted per epoch, and the shaded GV-gap region spans the epochs where verification is above chance but generation lags behind.
official.claim: When synthetic facts are injected by full fine-tuning, verification (balanced accuracy) is above chance at epochs where generation is still near zero in all 8 models (for Gemma-3 4B/12B verification is already ~0.60 before any fine-tuning): e.g. after ~1-2 epochs Gemma-3 12B verifies at ~0.70 while generating at ~0.07, and Llama-3.2 3B at epoch 4 verifies at ~0.62 vs. ~0.18 generation; in Phi-4 Mini 3.8B the gap stays open through 12 epochs (~0.70 vs. ~0.32).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4.1: Verification develops before generation during knowledge acquisition. Fine-tuning loss (top) and generation/verification accuracy (bottom) for four open model families at two scales each. Verification capabilities consistently emerge before generation, opening a GV-gap (shaded region) that closes as both capabilities saturate. The location of the gap is not visible in the loss curve.
official.metric: Per-epoch generation accuracy (fraction of generative queries answered with the correct entity) and verification balanced accuracy (chance 0.5), averaged over 150 synthetic facts; higher is better. No error bars or seeds are reported; values below are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Verification accuracy vs. generation accuracy of the same fine-tuned model on the same facts at the same epoch, across 8 models (4 families x 2 scales).
official.falsification_criterion: In a reproduction on one or more of these models with the released data and hyperparameters, generation accuracy reaches its plateau at the same epoch as or before verification rises meaningfully above 0.5, or there is no epoch where verification is clearly above chance while generation is still near zero.

title: Learn from your own latents and not from tokens: A sample-complexity theory

official.background: Token-level self-supervised objectives (masked-language modeling, diffusion, next-token prediction) need enormous datasets, and methods such as data2vec and JEPA instead train networks to predict their own latent representations. How much this improves data efficiency is not understood theoretically. The paper studies this question on the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), a synthetic probabilistic context-free grammar with a fixed tree of depth L, v symbols per level, m production rules per symbol and s children per rule. Prior work shows that for RHM data, supervised learning needs about m^L samples and token-level SSL about v·m^(L+1) samples to recover the latent tree. Both grow exponentially in depth.
official.method:
Iterative Latent Clustering (ILC, Algorithm 1): starting from visible tokens, at each level ℓ the algorithm splits the current sequence into s-tuples, estimates for each observed tuple its empirical context vector (the empirical distribution of a symbol Z in a cousin tuple, i.e. one whose parent is a sibling of the tuple's parent), clusters these vectors with k-means (k = v), and relabels each tuple by its cluster index to obtain the level-(ℓ+1) sequence. This repeats up to level L−1. Theorem 1 proves that P ≳ v·m^3 samples (up to log factors, independent of L) suffice to recover all non-root latents, under balance/separation assumptions.

Numerical check (Figure 3 left): sample a fixed-tree RHM with L = 5, s = 3, v = 8 and varying m (6 to 32), run ILC on P samples, and measure clustering reconstruction accuracy of the latent hierarchy against the true latents. P* is the number of samples at which accuracy reaches 50%. The exponent alpha in P* ∝ m^alpha is fit by least squares in log-log space with Monte-Carlo resampling over the per-m mean and std of P* across simulations (Appendix F; reported uncertainty is 2σ).
official.claim: For the iterative latent-clustering algorithm on RHM data (L = 5, s = 3, v = 8, m from 6 to 32), the sample size P* at which hierarchy reconstruction accuracy reaches 50% scales as m^alpha with alpha = 3.1 ± 0.3, and accuracy curves for all m collapse when P is rescaled by v·m^3 (transition at P/vm^3 of order 1). This is far from the token-level SSL exponent L+1 = 6.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Recursive clustering recovers the RHM hierarchy at the predicted scale. Left: Clustering reconstruction accuracy of the iterative clustering algorithm using k-means (L = 5, s = 3, v = 8). Right: Class reconstruction accuracy of SLC architecture (L = 4, s = 3, v = 10) trained end-to-end, evaluated by linear probe on the highest level latents ĥ^(L−1). In each panel, the main plot is a scaling collapse, effected by rescaling number of samples by predicted sample complexity P ∼ vm^3. Insets show raw data (top left) and inferred sample complexity (bottom right) P* for which accuracy reaches 50%. Monte-Carlo fitting P* ∝ m^α (grey-dots) gives α = 3.1 ± 0.3 (ILC) and α = 2.9 +0.4/−0.3 (SLC), see Section F for details.
official.metric: Clustering reconstruction accuracy of the latent hierarchy (higher is better) vs. number of samples P; P* = P at 50% accuracy; alpha = fitted exponent of P* ∝ m^alpha, ± is the 2σ range from 300 Monte-Carlo refits (Appendix F)
official.comparison: Fitted ILC sample-complexity exponent (alpha ≈ 3, per Theorem 1) vs. the token-level SSL scaling P ∝ v·m^(L+1) = v·m^6 established in prior work (red dotted guide in the inset; Figure 12 shows the curves do not collapse under m^(L+1) rescaling)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running ILC with k-means on RHM data (L = 5, s = 3, v = 8, several m between 6 and 32), the fitted exponent of P*(m) falls outside roughly [2.8, 3.4] (e.g. is near 4 or above), or accuracy curves fail to collapse when P is rescaled by v·m^3 while they do collapse under a different power of m.

title: Is Backpropagation Optimal? When Synthetic Gradients Improve Sample Efficiency

official.background: Backpropagation is the default way to compute gradients in neural networks whenever the model is differentiable. The paper treats backprop as a Monte Carlo estimator of each node's gradient and synthetic gradients (each node predicts its incoming gradient from its local input, as in decoupled neural interfaces) as the bootstrapped, TD-like alternative. It argues that synthetic gradients can estimate the gradient with lower mean squared error than backprop when the gradient feedback is uncertain (noisy terminal feedback, stochastic computation, or sparse connectivity) and each node's local input is sufficient to predict the mean of its incoming gradient. In those conditions they could train faster per sample. Earlier work found synthetic gradients worse than backprop, but it tested them on deterministic, densely connected networks with clean data.
official.method:
The task is an MNIST contextual bandit trained with policy gradient (REINFORCE). The context is an MNIST image, the policy samples a digit label, and the reward is 1 for the correct label and 0 otherwise. During training the reward is flipped with probability p_flip = 0.4; evaluation uses the noiseless reward. The policy is a SparseNet: 5 sparse layers of width 200, neuron output dimension 10, 5 slots per neuron and 5 randomly chosen, fixed parents per neuron. Each neuron routes its local input over slots with softmax key matching and outputs a tanh mixture. Each neuron also has a synthetic-gradient predictor: a separate linear head per slot, mixed with the same routing weights, that predicts the gradient arriving at the neuron's output from its local input only. The predictors are trained alongside the policy, using the same batch as each policy update.

In synthetic gradient propagation (sgprop) the gradient passed to each neuron mixes the backpropagated gradient with the synthetic prediction, g = λ·(backprop) + (1−λ)·(synthetic), applied recursively through the network. In the Table 4 ablation λ is fixed at 0.5. Backprop and sgprop both train the same SparseNet for 1000 steps with learning rate 1e-3 (Adam) over 3 seeds. Evaluation reward is measured on clean rewards. Per-sample gradient-estimation MSE is measured on validation images, relative to the mean of the ground-truth backpropagated gradients.
official.claim: On the MNIST contextual bandit with noisy rewards, a SparseNet trained with synthetic gradient propagation (fixed λ = 0.5, same samples and learning rate as backprop) reaches a higher clean evaluation reward than the same SparseNet trained with backpropagation at every checkpoint: 0.474 ± 0.0065 vs. 0.363 ± 0.0091 at step 600 and 0.602 ± 0.027 vs. 0.521 ± 0.02 at step 1000. Its per-sample gradient-estimation MSE is about 18x lower at step 1000 (21.0 ± 0.73 vs. 380 ± 15, ×10^-3).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Evaluation reward and gradient estimation MSE at different training steps. All values in panel (b), including uncertainties, are multiplied by 10^-3. The evaluation-reward ranking of the four methods aligns with their gradient-estimation MSE: lower MSE corresponds to higher evaluation reward.
official.metric: Evaluation reward on clean labels (higher is better) and per-sample gradient-estimation MSE ×10^-3 (lower is better); ± is the standard error of the mean over 3 seeds
official.comparison: SparseNet sgprop (λ = 0.5, synthetic-gradient predictors trained on the same batch as the policy) vs. SparseNet backprop, same architecture, learning rate 1e-3, 1000 steps
official.falsification_criterion: When rerun under the same settings, sgprop's evaluation reward at steps 400-1000 is not higher than backprop's by more than the combined SEMs, or sgprop's gradient-estimation MSE is not clearly below backprop's.

title: PICID: A Modular Evaluation Infrastructure for Reproducible PHM Across Tasks and Domains

official.background: Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) uses machine learning to detect faults, classify them (diagnostics) and predict remaining useful life (prognostics) for engineered assets such as engines, batteries, bearings and hydraulic rigs. Reported results in PHM are hard to reproduce or compare, because protocol choices such as splits, preprocessing, label alignment, windowing and metrics are usually implicit and ad hoc; the authors' audit found public code for only 8 of 329 papers from 2022 to 2025. The paper proposes PICID, a library that fixes these protocol choices as executable, leakage-safe components, so that different model families can be compared on identical data contracts across tasks.
official.method:
PICID loads raw unit trajectories, applies split-safe preprocessing that is fitted on the training partition only, aligns targets to the transformed time grid, windows sequences into supervised samples, and evaluates every model through a shared wrapper and evaluator interface. The benchmark runs 13 models (Linear/Exp/MLP; LSTM, CNN-1D, TiDE; the transformers Timeseries Transformer (TST), Spacetimeformer (STF), Crossformer (CF) and PatchTST (PTST); XGBoost; TabPFN and TabDPT) on 6 prognostics and 6 diagnostics datasets, using the same family instantiated as a classifier or a regressor.

For diagnostics, the datasets are N-CMAPSS multi-source concept classification (NC-D), four HSF15 hydraulic component tasks (accumulator 4-way, cooler 3-way, pump 3-way, valve 4-way), and MZVAV building faults. HSF15 features are min-max scaled, summarized with time-domain and spectral statistics, concatenated and rescaled, and the label is the last label in each window. Gradient-trained models (including LSTM, CNN-1D and all transformers) search over sequence length {1, 10, 50} and learning rate {1e-3, 5e-4, 1e-4}, with batch size 512, up to 200 epochs and early stopping, and are selected on validation F1. Each configuration is run with 5 seeds, and the metric is test macro-F1 (x100).
official.claim: Under PICID's identical preprocessing, windowing and splits, all four transformer models (TST, STF, CF, PTST) score test F1 <= 65.94 on NC-D and on each of the four HSF15 hydraulic diagnostics tasks, while both LSTM and CNN-1D score >= 87.53 on every one of those five tasks (e.g. HSF15-A: LSTM 94.59 ± 0.97, CNN-1D 94.03 ± 1.98 vs. best transformer STF 40.01 ± 5.75).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Main evaluation results. Top block: prognostics, measured by MAE in the normalized target space (×100) (↓). Bottom block: diagnostics, measured by F1 score (×100) (↑). Models are grouped by family: simple baselines, deep sequence models, transformers, tabular models, and tabular foundation models. Bold/underline denote the best/second-best result.
official.metric: Macro-F1 x100 on the test split (higher is better); ± is the std over 5 seeds
official.comparison: Transformer family (TST, STF, CF, PTST) vs. deep sequence models LSTM and CNN-1D, same pipeline and the same hyperparameter search
official.falsification_criterion: Running PICID's released configurations with 5 seeds, any transformer reaches within a few F1 points of the weaker of LSTM/CNN-1D on NC-D or on any HSF15 task, or LSTM/CNN-1D fall below about 85 F1 on these tasks.

title: LEIA: Learned Environment for Interactive Architected Materials

official.background: Designing architected materials (lattices whose mechanical properties come from their geometry) needs many nonlinear finite-element (FEM) simulations, which are slow. Neural surrogates can speed this up, but engineers need accurate stress fields, not just displacements. For materials with history-dependent internal state (viscoelasticity), the current displacement alone does not determine stress, so a surrogate that predicts displacement, or even the internal variables, and then recovers stress through the constitutive law can still give poor stress.
official.method:
MicroPlate's viscoelastic regime is a homogeneous plate (363 nodes, 1,000 trajectories of 100 steps) under finite visco-hyperelasticity with inertia (Arruda-Boyce equilibrium plus 3 non-equilibrium branches, 18 internal-variable components). Each trajectory applies 50 random loading actions (stretch, twist, two shears, each in {-1, 0, +1} per step) and then the exact reverse 50 unloading steps. Data are split 80/10/10 with seed 42; the test set has 100 trajectories.

Four baselines (MeshGraphNets, UPT, PointNet, Transolver) are trained end-to-end on the same splits in two variants that differ only in the output layer. In the indirect variant (22 outputs: displacement, 18 internal-variable components, pressure), stress is recovered through the constitutive law. In the stress-head variant (9 outputs: displacement plus 6 Cauchy stress components, supervised with FEM stress), stress is predicted directly. Outputs are standardized per component. Metrics are the median per-frame displacement relative L2 error and the median per-frame Pearson correlation between predicted and FEM von Mises stress fields, under teacher forcing (one step ahead from the ground-truth state) and under 100-step autoregressive rollout. LEIA itself (Perceiver tokenizer with a stress head plus an action-conditioned latent transformer) is reported for reference.
official.claim: On the MicroPlate visco-hyperelastic plate under teacher forcing, replacing indirect stress recovery (via predicted internal variables) with a direct 6-component stress head raises median von Mises correlation from <=0.26 to >=0.94 for all four baselines (MGN -0.009->0.987, UPT 0.257->0.951, PointNet 0.091->0.943, Transolver 0.108->0.941).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Stress-prediction strategies on MicroPlate's load-reverse visco-hyperelastic plate. 3 visco-hyperelastic branches, 100-step load-then-reverse protocol. Both the teacher-forcing and AR (autoregressive) columns report without / with the stress head. Medians across 100 test trajectories. The Space column indicates whether the model operates directly on mesh nodes (phys.) or on a compressed latent representation (latent).
official.metric: Median (over 100 test trajectories) per-frame Pearson correlation between predicted and FEM von Mises stress (higher is better); displacement relative L2 error in % (lower is better). No ± reported; single training run per configuration.
official.comparison: Each of MGN, UPT, PointNet, Transolver without the stress head (stress via predicted 18 internal variables + pressure and the constitutive law) vs. the same architecture with the stress head (direct Cauchy stress output); LEIA shown for reference.
official.falsification_criterion: With matched training, at least one baseline without the stress head reaches teacher-forcing von Mises correlation above about 0.6, or at least one baseline with the stress head stays below about 0.8, so the gap of roughly 0.7 or more does not hold across architectures.

title: Conservative neural posterior estimation via distributionally robust training

official.background: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) trains a conditional density estimator, usually a normalising flow, on simulated (parameter, data) pairs to approximate the posterior of a simulator whose likelihood cannot be evaluated. When simulations are expensive and the training set is small, NPE overfits the empirical loss and produces overconfident posteriors: their credible regions contain the true parameter less often than the nominal level. In scientific uses such as cosmology this overstates how tightly parameters are constrained. Earlier conservative variants (balanced NPE, coverage-regularised NPE) add heuristic penalties.
official.method:
DRO-NPE replaces the empirical NPE loss with its worst case over a 2-Wasserstein ball of radius ε around the empirical distribution of simulated pairs z = (x, θ). In practice it minimises the tractable upper bound L_NPE(q_φ; P_n) + ε·Ω(φ; P_n), where Ω = ( (1/n) Σ_i ||∇_z log q_φ(θ_i | x_i)||² )^{1/2} is the root-mean-square gradient of the log-density with respect to both the data and the parameters at the training pairs (Proposition 4.2). ε is chosen by Bayesian optimisation (10 iterations) on a 10% validation split, minimising the estimated KL-based miscalibration kl^q_cal with summary S(θ; x) = q_φ(θ | x), and the model is then retrained.

All methods use the same BayesFlow coupling flow (six affine coupling layers, tanh MLP activations), AdamW with learning rate 5e-4, batch size 64, 1000 epochs, and no early stopping. Baselines are standard NPE, CR-NPE (Falkiewicz et al. 2023; λ = 5, M = 16; trained until loss becomes NaN or 1000 epochs) and Bal-NPE (Delaunoy et al. 2023; λ = 100). In the cosmology task the data are the standard d_x = 39 dimensional CAMELS power-spectrum summary of high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulations, and the parameters are θ = (Ω_m, σ_8). There are 1,000 simulations, of which 900 are used for training and 100 for testing on one fixed split, with five independent training runs per method. Expected coverage of the highest-posterior-density region is computed by SBC with S(θ, x) = log q_φ(θ | x).
official.claim: On CAMELS cosmology (900 training simulations, d_x = 39, θ = (Ω_m, σ_8)), DRO-NPE's expected coverage is at or above the nominal level for most of the range, about 0.62 at nominal 0.5 and 0.83 at nominal 0.9. Standard NPE (about 0.07 and 0.18), Bal-NPE (about 0.18 and 0.43) and CR-NPE (about 0.27 and 0.60) are all below the diagonal at every nominal level. DRO-NPE also has the lowest test NLPD (about -1 vs. about 38 for NPE).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Cosmology results: expected coverage, NLPD, and kl^q_cal for DRO-NPE (green), CR-NPE (magenta), Bal-NPE (yellow), and standard NPE (blue).
official.metric: Expected coverage of the HPDR vs. nominal coverage 1 − α (on or above the diagonal = calibrated or conservative; below = overconfident), plus test NLPD (lower is better) and kl^q_cal (lower is better). Lines/points are means over five training runs on the same train–test split, with shaded bands/error bars showing the standard deviation across those runs. All values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: DRO-NPE vs. standard NPE, CR-NPE and Bal-NPE, using the same flow architecture, training protocol and fixed 900/100 CAMELS split
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining on the CAMELS 39-dimensional summaries with the 900/100 split, DRO-NPE's expected-coverage curve falls clearly below the diagonal (e.g. coverage < 0.4 at nominal 0.5), or it is not clearly above CR-NPE's and standard NPE's curves at mid-range nominal levels.

title: A Matter of TASTE: Improving Coverage and Difficulty of Agent Benchmarks

official.background: Conversational tool-use benchmarks such as τ2-Bench score an agent by whether the final database state after a dialogue with a simulated user matches the state produced by a gold tool-call sequence. Writing such tasks by hand is slow and costly, frontier models are approaching the ceiling on existing task sets, and hand-written tasks tend to reuse a narrow set of tool combinations. An automatic way to generate valid, harder, and more structurally diverse tasks would let these benchmarks keep up with model progress.
official.method:
TASTE reverses task construction: it first samples tool sequences, then writes tasks around them. Stage 1 trains a trigram 'Adaptive Contrastive' model over tool names, with separate count tables for sequences an LLM judge (Gemini-3-Flash) marks plausible or implausible, sampling from the ratio of the two; it is trained online for 3,000 iterations starting from the τ-Bench Verified gold sequences. Stage 2 samples 2,000 unique sequences and picks K medoids (K = 50 Airline, 114 Retail, 114 Telecom, matching the original task counts) with K-medoids under a weighted Levenshtein distance. Stage 3 has Gemini-3-Flash instantiate each sequence into a user instruction plus database records, validates it with rule-based checks and a hint-assisted verifier agent, then has Gemini-3-Pro 'evolve' it (less cooperative or mistaken user, decoy database records) while keeping the gold tool-call sequence, and re-validates.

The resulting τc-Bench is evaluated with the standard τ2-Bench harness at default settings and final-state reward. Six agent LLMs are paired with two user simulators (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5.2), and pass^1 on τc-Bench is compared with pass^1 on the τ-Bench Verified tasks of the same domain for the same agent/user pair.
official.claim: With a Gemini-3-Flash agent and Gemini-3-Flash user simulator in the τ2-Bench harness, pass^1 falls from 0.88 on τ-Bench Verified Retail to 0.44 on τc-Bench Retail (114 tasks each), and from 0.90 to 0.55 on Telecom; across all 11 agent/user pairs and three domains, τc-Bench pass^1 is lower in 31 of 33 cells (one tie, one increase).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main Results: Performance of agents on τ-Bench Verified (τBV) and on our generated tasks (τc-Bench), across three domains and two user simulators. For the airline domain, we additionally report pass^3 alongside the standard pass^1 scores. ∆% denotes the relative change (Ours−τBV)/τBV × 100.
official.metric: pass^1 task success rate under final-state reward (higher is better); point estimates only, no ± reported (single run per task; with 114 tasks the binomial SE is about 0.03-0.05)
official.comparison: Same agent/user pair on τc-Bench (TASTE-generated tasks) vs. τ-Bench Verified, per domain (Airline 50, Retail 114, Telecom 114 tasks)
official.falsification_criterion: Running the released τc-Bench Retail tasks and the τ-Bench Verified Retail tasks with a Gemini-3-Flash agent and Gemini-3-Flash user gives a pass^1 gap much smaller than the reported 0.44 (e.g. under 0.15), or τc-Bench scores are not lower than τ-Bench Verified for most agent/user pairs.

title: VeriTrip: A Verifiable Benchmark for Travel Planning Agents over Unstructured Web Corpora

official.background: Travel-planning benchmarks for LLM agents (TravelPlanner, ChinaTravel, TripTailor) give the agent clean structured APIs for flights, hotels and attractions, so they test constraint satisfaction but not whether an agent can find the facts itself in noisy web content. Deep-research benchmarks test information seeking but usually grade free-form reports with an LLM judge, which misses fabricated details. VeriTrip combines the two: agents must search a frozen, noisy multimodal web snapshot to build an itinerary, and every factual cell of the output is checked automatically against a hidden, human-verified knowledge base.
official.method:
The Multimodal Retrieval Base (MRB) holds 8,210 documents and 4,146 images scraped from Ctrip/Trip.com, 12306 and RedNote for 15 cities in China and the US, with ads and PII removed but conflicting or outdated user content kept. Agents get docSearch (Qwen3-Embedding-8B dense retrieval, top-10 snippets), imgSearch (DINOv2 ViT-S/14), getDocument, and three structured restaurant tools. Each of the 228 queries (78 simple, 76 medium, 74 complex) has text constraints plus a heavily cropped photo of a target POI. Complex queries have more travel days, more travelers and more stated preferences (2-8 vs. 1-4). Models run in a ReAct loop and must output a fixed JSON itinerary schema.

Evaluation is programmatic: Delivery Rate (DR, valid JSON), Factual Reliability (FR, fraction of transport IDs, times, POI and hotel names that match the VKB, exact or fuzzy), Preference Fulfillment Rate (PFR, rule checks for the stated transport mode, room type, must-see attractions, meal preferences and inner-city transport), micro Pass Rate on commonsense constraints (PRmi), and Average Margin over a TSP-optimal route (AM). Eleven MLLMs are evaluated (8 without thinking, 3 with thinking).
official.claim: On VeriTrip, Preference Fulfillment Rate is lower on complex than on simple queries for all 11 evaluated MLLMs, by 9.7 to 30.0 points (e.g., Claude-4.5-Sonnet 64.10 -> 50.00, GPT-4o 45.20 -> 32.53, o3 55.38 -> 27.57, Qwen3-VL-235B 66.46 -> 36.49), while Factual Reliability is higher on complex queries for all 11 models (by 2.1 to 11.3 points).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Main results of different MLLMs on VeriTrip. AM is measured in units of 10 km. Tool Calls indicates the number of tool calls. The colored values indicate the performance delta (Complex score - Simple score) for each metric. Red denotes an improvement, while green denotes a degradation. All subsequent experiments followed this setting.
official.metric: PFR and FR in % (higher is better); single run per model and difficulty level, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Same model, same toolset and prompt, evaluated on the 78 simple vs. 74 complex VeriTrip queries
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the models on the VeriTrip simple and complex splits shows a PFR drop of less than about 5 points for several models, or a PFR increase for any model, or FR no longer higher on complex queries for most models.

title: Personal Visual Memory from Explicit and Implicit Evidence

official.background: Long-term memory systems for personalized AI assistants (Mem0, MemOS, LightMem, RAG variants) are built and evaluated almost entirely on text. When conversations include images, these systems usually turn each image into a generic caption and store it like any other text. Existing benchmarks rarely punish this, because the facts needed for later questions can usually be recovered from the text alone. Images, however, often carry personal information the text never states, such as a recurring pet, a family member, or a cat tree in the background that implies the user owns a cat. Whether caption-based memory loses this information is the question the paper tests.
official.method:
The authors build a synthetic benchmark: 10 PersonaHub-derived personas, each with a social graph, user-owned assets (objects, pets) and about 172 temporally ordered events (1,717 events, 1,718 images, roughly 131K text tokens per persona). An LLM writes multi-turn conversations of three kinds: explicit-entity (an image shows a recurring person or asset), implicit-fact (a latent user fact is visible only in the image, or needs image plus dialogue), and distractors (unrelated or hard-negative images, e.g. a friend's living room). Images are generated with Nano Banana Pro, conditioned on entity and location reference images, and then manually filtered. The benchmark has 696 multiple-choice questions in four categories: Target Person, Target Asset, Implicit Fact (Visual-Only), and Implicit Fact (Multimodal).

VisualMem keeps MemOS as the text-memory backend and adds a visual-memory module. Each image is interpreted together with its surrounding conversation session to resolve identity and ownership. Ambiguous images go into a pending state and are re-evaluated later against accumulated memory. Confirmed images are turned into structured records (relationships, face/object/pet/location references, durable user facts), and the facts are also forwarded to MemOS. At question time, entity-centric queries go to the visual store and other queries go to text memory or to both. For all methods on this benchmark, Gemini-Pro-3.1 is used for both memory construction and question answering.
official.claim: On the authors' visual memory benchmark (696 multiple-choice questions, Gemini-Pro-3.1 for all methods), VisualMem reaches 84.1% overall accuracy versus 56.0% for MemOS, the strongest memory baseline and VisualMem's own text backend, and beats it in every category (Target Person 95.0 vs 45.0, Target Asset 91.1 vs 59.9, Implicit Visual-Only 77.9 vs 52.1, Implicit Multimodal 83.4 vs 64.8).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Evaluation results on our visual memory benchmark. We report performance for four task categories: Target Person, Target Asset, Implicit Fact (Visual-Only), and Implicit Fact (Multimodal). Each category is evaluated under a multiple-choice setting, and we report accuracy. Tokens denotes the amount of memory content provided to the answering model at inference time.
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy (%), higher is better; single run, no standard deviations or confidence intervals reported. Tokens = memory content passed to the answering model.
official.comparison: VisualMem (MemOS + visual memory, 1980 tokens) vs. MemOS (1187 tokens), Mem0, LightMem, SimpleMem, Self-RAG and HippoRAG2, all with Gemini-Pro-3.1; Full Context (325K tokens) and Oracle are reference upper bounds, not competitors
official.falsification_criterion: With the same benchmark and answering model, VisualMem's overall accuracy is not clearly above MemOS's (e.g. a gap under about 10 points), or MemOS matches VisualMem on Target Person/Target Asset.

title: Political Neutrality as Balanced Approval: A Large-Scale Human Evaluation of AI Responses
claim_source: Figure 3 (a and b), page 7; numbers from Table 1, page 7

official.background: LLMs are now a common source of political information, and AI companies and the U.S. government want 'politically neutral' models, but there is no agreed, testable definition of neutrality. Existing evaluations mostly measure slant along a single liberal-conservative axis with proprietary methods or LLM judges. This paper defines a neutral response as one that gets maximal and equal approval from people on opposing sides of a specific issue, and measures this with a large human survey.
official.method:
The authors picked 20 contested U.S. policy issues, each with a canonical survey question that splits respondents into a 'for' and an 'against' side (mapped to liberal/conservative per issue in Table B.1). For each issue they took 10 Reddit-sourced user prompts (two in each of five valences from Strongly For to Strongly Against). Each prompt was answered by 8 model/stance combinations: the default response of GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3 Flash Preview, Grok 4.1 Non-reasoning and Llama Maverick, plus three GPT 5.4 responses written from the 'for' side, from the 'against' side, and 'balanced' (one short paragraph per side and a closing sentence acknowledging trade-offs), giving 1,600 responses.

7,434 U.S. Prolific participants each got 4 random issues; for each they answered the canonical question (which sets their side) and rated one random, unlabelled response on seven 5-point Likert statements. Ratings are mapped to 0-1 (0, 0.25, ..., 1). The main analysis uses 'I approve of this AI response': per model/stance it averages approval among participants on the conservative side (s_cons) and liberal side (s_lib) over all 20 issues (Figure 3a, with 95% CIs), and separately fits a linear regression on ratings pooled over all 20 issues and all seven Likert statements (not only 'I approve'), with fixed effects for each model x stance x participant-side cell plus prompt charge, issue, Likert statement and demographics, and SEs clustered at the question and participant level (Figure 3b; Appendix D.3). The empirical maximum-equal-approval (MEA) response per issue is the response on the Pareto frontier of (s_cons, s_lib) minimising |s_cons - s_lib|.
official.claim: Averaged over all 20 issues, GPT 5.4's balanced response gets nearly equal approval from conservative-side and liberal-side participants (about 0.68 vs 0.69; mean s_cons - s_lib = -0.01, with overlapping 95% CIs and nearly identical regression coefficients), whereas GPT 5.4's default response to the same prompts leans liberal (about 0.60 vs 0.72; s_cons - s_lib = -0.12, with non-overlapping 95% CIs); the balanced response is the empirical MEA response on 60% of issues versus at most 15% for any other model/stance.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Summary of our results over all 20 issues. (a) Approval scores per model and model stance, from participants on the more conservative (x-axis) and more liberal (y-axis) side of the issue, averaged across all issues. Shaded lines indicate 95% confidence intervals. The red/blue arrows indicate the loss of approval from one-sided to balanced responses for conservative/liberal participants. (b) Approval regression coefficients for model, model stance, and participant side interaction terms, with 95% confidence intervals. See full model specification in Appendix D.3.
official.metric: Mean approval score on 'I approve of this AI response' mapped to 0-1 (higher is better), split by participant side; error bars in Figure 3 are 95% confidence intervals (3a: of the mean; 3b: coefficients of a regression pooled over all seven Likert statements, SEs clustered at question and participant level). Table 1 values (including MEA rate) have no error bars.
official.comparison: GPT 5.4 balanced vs. GPT 5.4 default (and the other four model defaults) on the same 200 prompts and participant pool, comparing the gap between conservative-side and liberal-side approval
official.falsification_criterion: Recomputing from the released PARETO data (or a new survey with the released prompts and responses), either the GPT default's liberal-minus-conservative approval gap is not significantly positive (95% CIs overlap), or the GPT balanced response shows a gap of comparable size (e.g. |s_cons - s_lib| >= 0.05 with non-overlapping CIs), or the balanced response is not the most frequent empirical MEA response across the 20 issues.

title: SCDBench: A Benchmark for LLM-Based Smart Contract Decompilers
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (replicated on a second 600-contract sample in Table 23, page 22)

official.background: More than 99% of Ethereum smart contracts are deployed without verified source code, so auditors and users see only EVM bytecode. Traditional decompilers recover function selectors and low-level pseudocode but not compilable Solidity. LLMs can produce source-like Solidity that may compile, but there has been no shared benchmark for checking whether that output compiles, recovers the right interface, and behaves like the original. SCDBench provides 600 verified Ethereum contracts (200 each in easy, medium and hard complexity strata) with bytecode, ground-truth source and replayable semantic test cases, and it scores decompilers in four cumulative stages: format completeness, compilability, ABI recovery and semantic consistency.
official.method:
Each model gets the contract bytecode as EVM assembly text, plus non-unique function-selector and event-signature candidate mappings (from 4byte.sourcify.dev) when available. It must return three XML-style blocks: a compiler JSON (version and settings), self-contained Solidity with no imports, and a target contract name (exact prompts in Appendix E.1). An output passes compilability if it has the required format and compiles with solc, using its own stated compiler settings, into a valid artifact for the named contract. Scoring is cumulative over all 600 contracts, so format failures also count as compile failures.

Zero-shot compilation repair (marked †): if an output has the required format but fails to compile, the same model is called once with the generated output and the solc error message (prompt in Appendix E.2). The repaired output is used if one is available; otherwise the original is kept. Models, all via OpenRouter: Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.3-Codex with high reasoning effort, GLM-5 with high thinking, and GLM-5 (instruct) without thinking. Each setting is a single run.
official.claim: On the 600 SCDBench contracts, one same-model compilation-repair call raises the share of decompiled outputs that compile for every model: GPT-5.3-Codex from 421/600 (70.2%) to 542/600 (90.3%), Opus 4.7 from 56.8% to 69.2%, GLM-5 from 36.8% to 67.2%, and GLM-5 (instruct) from 24.0% to 64.3%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Compilation success by complexity. A contract passes if the recovered Solidity compiles to a valid target artifact. Each complexity stratum contains 200 contracts. Blue highlights the best unrepaired result, and green highlights the best result after zero-shot repair.
official.metric: Compilation success rate (higher is better): contracts whose output has the required format and compiles to a valid target artifact, over all 600 contracts (200 per stratum). Single run, no error bars; the binomial SE at n = 600 is about 2 percentage points.
official.comparison: For each model, the initial zero-shot decompilation vs. the same output after one same-model repair call given the solc error, on the same contracts
official.falsification_criterion: With the released prompts and data, one repair call raises a model's total compile rate by less than about 5 percentage points (e.g. GPT-5.3-Codex stays under 75%, or GLM-5 stays under 45%), or the gain disappears on the hard stratum.

title: The Best-Laid SCHEMEs: Coordinated Sabotage and Monitoring in Multi-Agent Systems

official.background: Agentic coding systems increasingly split work across several model instances editing a shared codebase. That opens a threat that single-agent sabotage evaluations miss: a team of agents whose individually harmless-looking edits add up to a hidden malicious outcome while the legitimate task still passes. Before investing in monitors for this threat, it matters whether frontier models can actually carry out such coordinated sabotage on real code, and how well a trusted monitor catches it.
official.method:
SCHEME has 17 task instances (11 main/side pairings across 7 settings, built on 8 open-source libraries such as fairlearn, skfolio, pycasbin, lightkurve, sympy). Each pairs a legitimate software-engineering main task (one analyst agent runs an evaluation script and writes a report; 1-3 developer agents reimplement removed functions or fix bugs) with a covert side task that changes the evaluation script's output. Side tasks are joint-only: knowledge is split across agents and each agent has disjoint file write permissions, so no proper subset can succeed. Agents communicate only via append-only channel files (BUS topology, one shared channel, in the main run). Agents are explicitly instructed to pursue the side task.

Each instance is run 5 times per model (N=85 trajectories per model) with GPT 5.1 Codex (medium reasoning) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (high thinking), temperature 1.0, 32k max output tokens per generation. Automated scorers check the main task (reimplemented functions correct, report produced) and the side task (evaluation script output meets sabotage criteria). Sabotage success is the per-trajectory rate at which both main and side task pass.
official.claim: On all 17 SCHEME instances under the BUS topology (5 runs each, N=85 per model), Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves 84% sabotage success (main and side task both pass) versus 46% for GPT 5.1 Codex, with non-overlapping Wilson 95% intervals; Codex is limited by the side task (47% vs. Gemini 94%) while main-task pass is similar (89% vs. 85%).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Per-trajectory main-task, side-task, and sabotage success rates by knowledge variant. Single groups the 5 pairings that exist only in a concentrated variant; Concentrated and Distributed are the matched halves of the 6 pairings that exist in both knowledge variants; All aggregates across the three groups. Codex (solid) vs. Gemini (hatched); error bars are Wilson 95% confidence intervals.
official.metric: Per-trajectory pass rate (%) for main task, side task, and joint sabotage success; higher sabotage success = more capable attacker. Error bars are Wilson 95% binomial confidence intervals.
official.comparison: Gemini 3.1 Pro vs. GPT 5.1 Codex on the same 17 instances, same harness and prompts, 5 epochs each
official.falsification_criterion: On a rerun of the benchmark, the gap in sabotage success between Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT 5.1 Codex shrinks so the Wilson 95% intervals overlap (e.g. Gemini below ~75% or Codex above ~57%), or the ordering reverses.

title: OpenClawBench: Benchmarking Process-side Anomalies in Real-world Agent Execution Trajectories

official.background: Agent benchmarks usually score whether a task was completed, but an agent can pass the task oracle while still behaving unreliably along the way, for example writing to external state before resolving ambiguity or ignoring tool errors. The paper calls this the Outcome-Process Gap and argues that detecting such process-side anomalies needs trajectory-level supervision that is separate from task success. It releases OpenClawBench, a dataset of real OpenClaw agent executions on BFCL tasks with anomaly labels, and uses it to train a small detector that flags anomalous trajectories.
official.method:
OpenClawBench collects 31,264 OpenClaw agent runs on BFCL tasks from 6 open-weight source models (DeepSeek-R1, GLM-4.5-Air, gpt-oss-20B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), normalizes each into ReAct-style steps (thinking, action, feedback), and labels each trajectory with the FullTax LLM-annotation protocol as normal or one of 5 anomaly subtypes. Final released labels come from a single-call relabel by DeepSeek-V4-Pro, keeping only high-confidence labels: 23,857 train and 2,646 test trajectories (test anomaly rate 14.8%). Silver labels agree with the human binary label on 280/300 Gold-300 trajectories.

The detector is Gemma 3 12B Instruct with rank-32 LoRA (alpha 64, dropout 0.05, all attention and MLP projections, AdamW, peak lr 1.5e-4, cosine with 3% warmup, global batch 32, max length 8192, bf16) trained to emit one token from a 6-symbol vocabulary (normal + 5 subtypes); binary anomaly = any non-normal output. Normals are downsampled once (seed 42) to about 1:2 anomaly:normal, giving about 9,809 training examples; training runs in two stages: an initial 3-epoch run to step 921, then a resume from that checkpoint under a 10-epoch (3,070-step) schedule that was stopped manually at step 1,520 (about 4.95 epochs; lowest dev loss). Baselines on the same test split and prompt template: base Gemma 3 12B (no fine-tuning, greedy) and GPT-5.4 zero-shot (reasoning_effort=medium, JSON output mapped to the same labels).
official.claim: On the OpenClawBench silver test split (n=2,646, 14.8% anomalous), the LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma 3 12B detector reaches binary anomaly F1 0.729 (precision 0.660, recall 0.813), versus 0.426 for zero-shot GPT-5.4 and 0.372 for the un-fine-tuned Gemma 3 12B, with the gain coming from precision (predicted-anomaly rate 18.2% vs. 41.6% for GPT-5.4).

title: Information-Directed Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Table 4 (Appendix D), page 18; eta = 0.5 subset shown in Table 1(b), page 8

official.background: In offline-to-online learning, a policy or reward model is warm-started from a fixed offline dataset and then refined with a limited number of online interactions. The offline data shrinks uncertainty but does not remove the need to explore: it changes which uncertainty remains. The paper argues that online exploration should target this residual uncertainty, measured by the mutual information between the unknown parameters and the online trajectories conditional on the offline data, and that information-directed sampling (IDS) does this better than probability matching (Thompson sampling, TS) when the warm-start posterior is informative but biased.
official.method:
IDS with regulariser eta picks the action minimising Delta(a)^2 / (g(a) + eta), where Delta(a) is the expected instantaneous regret under the posterior and g(a) is the information gain about the reward parameters. In the linear contextual bandit, rewards are r(s, a) = phi(s, a)^T w* + noise (sigma = 0.05), with phi a fixed nonlinear random-feature map (state and action concatenated with quadratic and interaction terms, random Gaussian projection, tanh, l2-normalised; state dim 16, action dim 4, feature dim d = 128). All methods share one Bayesian linear-regression posterior (prior precision 1) that is warm-started on N offline samples and updated online in closed form.

The offline data comes from a biased behaviour policy with parameter w_behav = w* + beta * delta, beta = 6, so the warm-start posterior is shifted. A candidate action set of size M = 256 is sampled once and held fixed. IDS estimates Delta by Monte Carlo over 64 posterior samples and computes g(a) = 0.5 log(1 + phi^T Lambda^-1 phi / sigma^2) in closed form. Baselines are greedy (posterior mean), UCB and TS on the same posterior. The metric is cumulative regret after T = 200 online steps, mean and std over 20 seeds, for N in {20, 50, 100}.
official.claim: In the biased-warm-start linear contextual bandit (T = 200, 20 seeds), every IDS variant (eta in {0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5}) has lower cumulative regret than Thompson sampling at N = 20 (3.57 ± 1.67 to 7.29 ± 1.79 vs. 10.64 ± 1.52) and at N = 50 (1.67 ± 1.89 to 2.51 ± 0.65 vs. 4.73 ± 0.76).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Full η sweep for the biased linear contextual bandit. Final cumulative regret over T = 200, mean over 20 seeds. Bold marks the best IDS variant per row.
official.metric: final cumulative regret over T = 200 online steps (lower is better), mean ± std over 20 seeds
official.comparison: IDS_eta (eta = 0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5) vs. Thompson sampling, plus greedy and UCB, all on the same warm-started Bayesian linear-regression posterior
official.falsification_criterion: With a biased behaviour policy (beta = 6) and N = 20 or 50 offline samples, vanilla IDS (eta = 0) or IDS_0.5 does not achieve lower mean cumulative regret than TS by more than about one seed std.

title: ElegantVLA: Learning When to Think for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models

official.background: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models control robots by running a vision encoder, a large language model and an iterative action head (diffusion or flow) at every control step, which limits control frequency. Existing acceleration methods (token pruning, token caching, layer skipping) usually speed up one component with a fixed rule. Consecutive control steps are often highly redundant during smooth motion but not during contact or grasping, so computation could be allocated adaptively per step without retraining the base policy.
official.method:
ElegantVLA wraps a frozen VLA policy with a small scheduler that, at every control step, picks a Vision-LLM compute level (5 levels: 0 = full vision encoder + LLM; 1 = recompute vision encoder and only the first and last LLM layers, reusing cached intermediate LLM states; 2/3/4 = skip vision encoder and LLM for 1/2/3 consecutive steps and reuse the cached visual-language representation) and an action-head level (3 levels over the M refinement/denoising steps: 0 = recompute all; 1 = reuse cached updates for middle steps 1..M-2; 2 = recompute only the first step and reuse cached updates for the rest). The scheduler observation is [first-LLM-layer CKA similarity to the last full-compute anchor, gripper speed, end-effector translation speed, end-effector rotation speed, episode progress t/T_max].

The scheduler is trained with Maskable PPO in two stages: stage 1 adds dense shaping rewards (success minus FLOPs cost, plus penalties for disagreeing with a rule-based teacher and for long reuse horizons); stage 2 drops the teacher terms and optimizes task success and efficiency. The base model is never modified. Evaluation is in SimplerEnv with GR00T on six Google Robot tasks (200 episodes per task); speedup is the FLOPs reduction relative to full-computation GR00T. Baselines FastV and VLA-Cache are applied to the same GR00T model.
official.claim: On GR00T in SimplerEnv Google Robot (6 tasks, 200 episodes each), ElegantVLA reaches 75.00% average success at 2.35x FLOPs speedup, versus 71.08% for full-computation GR00T, 71.00% for FastV (1.13x) and 68.67% for VLA-Cache (1.13x).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Simulation results on GR00T in SimplerEnv. Each cell reports success rate (%, ↑) / speedup (↑). ElegantVLA improves the overall success rate from 64.00% to 65.88%, with 2.35× and 2.55× average speedup on Google Robot and WidowX, respectively.
official.metric: Average task success rate (%, higher is better) and average FLOPs speedup over full GR00T (higher is better). No error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: ElegantVLA vs. full-computation GR00T, FastV and VLA-Cache on the same frozen GR00T policy, Google Robot suite
official.falsification_criterion: A trained ElegantVLA scheduler on GR00T Google Robot either does not reach roughly 2x or more average FLOPs speedup, or its average success falls clearly below full-computation GR00T (e.g. more than a few points below 71.08%) or below FastV/VLA-Cache.

title: Token Inflation: How Dishonest Providers Can Overcharge for Large Language Model Usage
claim_source: Figure 1, page 4 (per-block-count means in Figures 4 and 5, pages 15-16)

official.background: Commercial reasoning LLM APIs bill per token but hide the reasoning trace, so users cannot check the hidden token counts they pay for. Several auditing frameworks have been proposed to verify these counts without exposing the trace. One is CoIn, where the provider commits the hidden trace as fixed 256-token blocks in a Merkle tree and a third-party auditor samples blocks and checks them with learned semantic-similarity scorers (token-to-block and block-to-answer) followed by a rule-based and a learned (RNN) verifier. This paper argues that such audits only check evidence the provider itself supplies, so a dishonest provider can inflate counts while still passing.
official.method:
The authors run CoIn's official models and pipeline on Glaive reasoning-v1-20m, splitting each reasoning trace into 256-token blocks with CoIn's block-generation code and keeping samples with 2 to 7 original blocks (about 97% of samples). Verifier settings are a 0.75 probing ratio and a 0.5 threshold for both the rule-based and learned verifiers. Starting from the honest trace, the attacker appends adversarial blocks one at a time and re-runs both verifiers after each insertion. It stops when either verifier rejects the trace or after 1000 added blocks. Inflation per sample = 100 * (accepted added blocks) / (original blocks), which equals token-count inflation because all blocks are 256 tokens.

The simplest attack is random block reuse (RB): each added block is a copy of a block sampled uniformly from the honest trace. Other variants are duplicate-all (DA, repeatedly append the full trace), highest-scoring block (HSB, repeatedly append the block with the largest combined CoIn score), hash-unique versions of each (insert one random valid token before or after the copied block so the hashes differ), and fabricated blocks from a T5 or LoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-1.5B generator trained on GCG-optimized blocks. A trace counts as evading the audit only if both verifiers accept it.
official.claim: On Glaive reasoning-v1-20m traces with 2-7 original 256-token blocks, CoIn's official rule-based and learned verifiers both accept traces inflated by block reuse, with mean per-sample token-count inflation of 549.9% for random block reuse, 1,469.0% for duplicating the full trace, and 536.8% for random reuse with one inserted token per copy to make block hashes unique.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Mean per-sample inflation percentage across eight CoIn attack variants, grouped by number of original reasoning blocks. Diamonds indicate the mean inflation for each original block count.
official.metric: Mean per-sample inflation percentage of committed blocks (equivalently tokens) accepted by both CoIn verifiers, higher means a stronger attack; no ± reported, per-sample spread shown as scatter points
official.comparison: Honest trace (0% inflation, accepted) vs. reuse-inflated traces that are still accepted by both verifiers; across eight attack variants
official.falsification_criterion: Running CoIn's official verifiers (probing ratio 0.75, threshold 0.5) on Glaive traces, random-block-reuse traces are rejected after few added blocks, so mean accepted inflation is far below ~550% (e.g. under 100%), or duplicate-all inflation is far below ~1,469%.

title: Native Audio-Visual Alignment for Generation

official.background: Joint audio-video generation models synthesize a video and its soundtrack together so that speech matches lip motion and sounds line up with visual events. Open-source systems mostly use dual-tower designs (separate audio and video streams linked by late cross-modal attention, e.g. Ovi, LTX, MoVA) or a fully unified design that puts text, audio and video tokens into one attention space (daVinci-MagiHuman). The paper argues that the first weakens fine-grained audio-video co-evolution and the second entangles semantic conditioning with low-level synchronization.
official.method:
NAVA is a 6.3B-parameter MMDiT with 30 blocks initialised from Wan2.2-5B (Wan2.2-VAE for video latents, LTX2.3-VAE for audio latents). The first 10 blocks are Hierarchical Alignment Layers: modality-specific projections followed by joint self-attention over concatenated audio and video tokens (audio RoPE rescaled by the video/audio token-rate ratio), with text and optional reference-timbre tokens injected only through cross-attention. The remaining 20 blocks are Unified Fusion Layers with shared parameters for audio and video, again with context via cross-attention. In Timbre-in-Context Conditioning, a timbre encoder maps each reference utterance to a context token that is inserted into the prompt with its speech span as <S>, timbre token, span text, <E>, and read through the same cross-attention pathway.

Training is three-stage multi-task (T2AV, TI2AV, T2A, T2V, TIA2AV) on about 15M clips, with 20% random masking of the cross-modal (audio-video) entries of the joint attention, intra-modal attention kept intact, and 20% timbre-token dropout. At inference, condition-factorized CFG adds separate text, audio-video alignment (full prediction minus the prediction with audio-video interaction masked) and timbre guidance terms. Evaluation on Verse-Bench (speech, sound effects, instruments) uses SyncNet Sync-C/Sync-D, ImageBind score, a video quality score, WER, Audiobox-Aesthetics PQ and FD. All prompts are rewritten with Gemini-3-Flash for each model, and baselines are run in their base versions without super-resolution, distillation or post-processing.
official.claim: On Verse-Bench, NAVA (6.3B) gets the best lip-sync scores among open joint audio-video generators, Sync-C 7.791 and Sync-D 7.566, vs. Ovi 1.1 7.484/7.979, MoVA 7.289/7.808, daVinci-MagiHuman 7.149/7.816 and LTX 2.3 7.248/7.690, along with the best video quality (0.659 vs. at most 0.636).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: General capabilities on Verse-Bench. We compare representative audio-video generation models in terms of synchronization, video quality, and audio quality. NAVA achieves the strongest overall synchronization and video quality, with competitive audio quality and the fewest parameters.
official.metric: SyncNet Sync-C (higher is better) and Sync-D (lower is better); also video quality score (higher is better). Single numbers, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: NAVA vs. Ovi 1.1 (10B), MoVA (A18B/32B), daVinci-MagiHuman (15B), LTX 2.3 (19B), all run by the authors on Verse-Bench with Gemini-rewritten prompts and no post-processing
official.falsification_criterion: Running NAVA and the baselines on Verse-Bench under the paper's protocol, some baseline matches or exceeds NAVA's Sync-C or has lower Sync-D, or NAVA's Sync-C lead over the best baseline (Ovi 1.1) falls within the variation seen across sampling seeds.
