title: Near-Optimal Decentralized Stochastic Convex Optimization over Networks
claim_source: Table 3, page 43 (Appendix F.1); Table 2 on page 12 shows the same numbers without std

official.background: In decentralized stochastic optimization, M workers minimize an average of local convex objectives using local stochastic gradients and gossip averaging with neighbors over a fixed network. A key question is how many workers can be used under a total sample budget N while keeping the centralized O(1/sqrt(N)) statistical rate. The best prior method, DAT-SGD (Eisen et al.), keeps this rate for M up to about rho*sqrt(N), where rho is the network's spectral gap, while centralized accelerated minibatching reaches N^{3/4}. This paper proposes an accelerated decentralized method claimed to reach rho*N^{3/4}, with only logarithmic dependence on data heterogeneity, and backs it with a synthetic benchmark.
official.method:
DDA-SGD (Algorithm 1) runs in macro steps of B synchronous rounds. In each macro step every worker draws B stochastic gradients at a fixed one-step-delayed query point q_{t,i} and averages them, while in the same B rounds it runs B steps of Nesterov-accelerated gossip (V = Y^{(s-1)} + beta_g (Y^{(s-1)} - Y^{(s-2)}), Y^{(s)} = (1 - alpha_g) V + alpha_g V P) on the current primal copies X_t, giving mixed copies X~_t. The next query is Q_{t+1} = X~_t + m_t (1 + m_{t+1}) (X~_t - X~_{t-1}); then locally Z_{t+1} = Z_t - eta_t G_t and X_{t+1} = (1 - theta_t) X_t + theta_t Z_{t+1}. Each worker outputs its column of X~_T. Two schedules: the 'theorem' schedule (alpha_g = 1/2, beta_g = (1 - sqrt(rho/2))/(1 + sqrt(rho/2)), theta_t = 2/(t+2), m_t = (t-1)/(t+2), eta_t = eta (t+2)/2) and a 'constant momenta' variant (theta_t = 0.1, m_t = 0.9, eta_t = eta/0.1, alpha_g = 1/2, beta_g = 0.9).

Benchmark (following Eisen et al.): worker i has f_i(x) = 1/2 ||A_i x - b_i||^2 with A_i in R^{50x50} i.i.d. standard normal, b_i = A_i (x# - delta_i), x# ~ N(0, I/d), delta_i ~ N(0, zeta^2/d I); stochastic gradients add N(0, sigma^2/d I) noise; all workers start at a common x0 ~ N(0, I). Ring (weights 1/3) and 2D torus (weights 1/5) gossip matrices, M in {4, 9, 25, 49, 100}. Every method runs 10^5 communication rounds with one stochastic gradient per worker per round (N = 10^5 M). Baselines: D-SGD (last iterate) and DAT-SGD (averaged iterate, exchanges two vectors per round). Stepsize tuned per configuration over {1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3, 5e-3, 1e-2, 5e-2, 1e-1}; for DDA-SGD B is tuned jointly over 20 values from 1 to 5000. Metric is (1/M) sum_i ||x_i - x*||^2, mean and sample std over 3 seeds.
official.claim: On the synthetic least-squares benchmark with sigma^2 = zeta^2 = 1 and 10^5 rounds, DDA-SGD with constant momenta reaches lower final error than DAT-SGD on every ring and torus size M in {4, ..., 100}, e.g. 6.3e-10 vs 3.0e-5 (ring, M = 49) and 3.0e-10 vs 9.1e-7 (torus, M = 100); the smallest margin is about 7x (ring, M = 100: 9.2e-5 vs 6.7e-4).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Final error for sigma^2 = zeta^2 = 1, the top-left panel of Fig. 2. The parenthetical number on each error is the standard deviation across three seeds, in the same units. The integer after a DDA-SGD entry is the selected block length. The lowest error in each row is in bold.
official.metric: Final mean squared distance to the minimizer, (1/M) sum_i ||x_i - x*||^2, lower is better; value(std) is mean and sample standard deviation over 3 seeds
official.comparison: DDA-SGD (constant momenta and theorem schedule) vs. DAT-SGD and D-SGD under the same number of rounds and samples, each with its stepsize tuned on the same grid
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the benchmark (sigma^2 = zeta^2 = 1, 10^5 rounds, tuned stepsizes), DDA-SGD with constant momenta does not beat DAT-SGD by a clear factor (e.g. at least 3x, well outside seed std) on most of the 10 (graph, M) configurations, or loses to DAT-SGD in any configuration.

title: Learning What Not to Impute: An Uncertainty-Aware Diffusion Framework for Meaningful Missingness

official.background: Standard imputation methods assume every missing cell hides a regular value that should be filled in. In many tables, though, some cells are missing because the value genuinely does not exist (for example, employment income for an unemployed respondent, or battery life for a book), while others are missing only because of how the data was recorded. Both show up as the same 'na' token. Filling in the meaningfully missing cells distorts the data and removes information, so a method has to decide not only what value to impute but whether to impute at all, without labels saying which kind of missingness each cell is.
official.method:
Diff-Joint trains a diffusion model (EDM backbone) on a joint state (x, c), where x is the completed table and c is a binary mask marking meaningfully missing (MM) cells. It starts by randomly filling missing cells and setting c = 0, then alternates: (i) fit the diffusion model on the current joint state; (ii) draw K = 30 conditional samples per row given the observed cells, set each imputed value to the sample mean (continuous) or mode (discrete), and compute a per-cell uncertainty score (sample std or entropy). Within each MM candidate column, k-means with k = 2 splits missing cells into high- and low-uncertainty groups; a cell is marked MM if it falls in the high-uncertainty group OR the majority of sampled masks say MM. The final output keeps na where c = 1 and the imputed value elsewhere. Ten outer iterations are used on the synthetic data, and the MM candidate columns are assumed known.

The synthetic dataset is a 5-variable Bayesian network (C1, C2 continuous; D1, D2, D3 discrete; 14,000 train / 6,000 test rows, full generative spec in Appendix C.1) in which D2, D3 and C1 take a true 'na' state under specified conditions. Observation-induced missingness is then added under MCAR, MAR or MNAR at 10-40%. The metric ACC_out is token-level accuracy on test-set missing cells in the discrete MM candidate columns: a cell counts as correct only if the predicted state (a regular category or na) matches the ground truth. Baselines (Mean/Mode, missForest, CMAE i.e. CACTI without embeddings, DiffPuter) always impute a regular value.
official.claim: On the synthetic Bayesian-network data with 10% MCAR observation-induced missingness, Diff-Joint reaches 78.34% token-level accuracy on missing discrete cells versus 35.21% for the best baseline (CMAE), 31.74% for DiffPuter and 30.40% for missForest and Mean/Mode, and it stays ahead of every baseline at all ratios (10-40%) and mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Method comparison on Bayesian Network data under various missing mechanisms/ratios.
official.metric: ACC_out: test-set token-level accuracy on missing cells in discrete MM candidate columns (higher is better), counting na as a valid predicted state; mean over 5 seeds, no ± reported in this table. RMSE_out on continuous non-MM columns (lower is better) is also reported.
official.comparison: Diff-Joint vs. CMAE, DiffPuter, missForest and Mean/Mode under matched data, missingness mechanism and ratio
official.falsification_criterion: On regenerated Bayesian-network data at 10% MCAR, Diff-Joint's ACC_out is not clearly above the best baseline (e.g. the gap is under ~10 points instead of ~43), or Diff-Joint fails to beat the baselines at a majority of the 12 ratio/mechanism settings.

title: Generating Financial Time Series by Matching Random Convolutional Features

official.background: Financial applications such as risk estimation, hedging and portfolio optimisation need many plausible future price paths conditioned on recent history, but usually only one historical path of a few thousand daily observations is available. Adversarial training (GANs) tends to overfit or memorise in this regime, so recent work instead trains generators to match the mean of a fixed, untrained feature map (typically truncated or randomised path signatures) between real and generated paths. Signatures at tractable truncation depths can miss relevant properties such as long-range or oscillatory autocorrelation, while random convolutional feature maps (Rocket, Hydra) are known to be strong unsupervised features for time series classification but are not differentiable and so cannot supervise a generator.
official.method:
The paper introduces SOCK, a differentiable random convolutional feature map. Each input path is augmented (posneg(int(X)): the path, its cumulative sum, and positive/negative parts), normalised, and randomly projected to M = 256 channels; channels are split into groups of width 2 and convolved with K = 8 random zero-sum, l1-normalised kernels of length 9 at dilations 1, 2, 4, 8. At each time step a softmax at temperature tau = 0.1 over the K kernel responses gives 'win probabilities', and the feature for each kernel is the standard deviation of its win probability over time (soft-deviation pooling). Features are standardised per coordinate using the real training segments.

A conditional GRU generator (hidden size 128) maps a context of q = 5 past steps plus Gaussian noise to a T = 64-step future. It is trained for 100k AdamW steps to minimise the squared distance between the batch mean of SOCK features of real joined past+future segments and generated ones, with the random SOCK parameters resampled every R = 100 steps. Baselines use the same generator and protocol with truncated signature features (Sig, depth 3), randomised signatures (rSig, resampled every 100 steps), and the conditional Sig-Wasserstein GAN objective (cSig); Diffusion-TS (DTS) is run with the authors' code. On V10 (3-dimensional VAR with X_t = phi1 X_{t-5} + phi2 X_{t-10} + eps, r = omega = 0.8), each model is trained on a single path of length 2048 and evaluated on 2048 independent out-of-sample continuations of length 2048. The RNN metric trains a GRU classifier to tell real from generated joined segments on half the evaluation set and reports |accuracy - 0.5| on the other half (averaged over 10 classifier trainings).
official.claim: On the synthetic V10 dataset, the generator trained by SOCK feature matching reaches an RNN discriminative score of 0.12 ± 0.03, versus 0.24 ± 0.04 for the best baseline (truncated-signature matching, Sig), 0.29 for rSig, 0.37 for Diffusion-TS and 0.38 for cSig; it also has the lowest autocorrelation error (ACF 0.026 ± 0.002 vs. 0.055 ± 0.01 for the best baseline, DTS).
official.claim_caption: Figure 7: Detailed results on synthetic datasets. Each cell reports the mean metric value across 5 seeds (standard deviation in parentheses), where seeds vary both the data draw and training randomness. Cell color encodes the mean value (lighter is better). The color is based on the averaged metrics.
official.metric: RNN discriminative score |accuracy - 0.5| of a GRU real-vs-generated classifier (lower is better; 0 means indistinguishable); ACF = mean absolute difference of channel-wise autocorrelations up to lag floor(T/3) (lower is better). Values are mean (std) over 5 seeds, each seed resampling the training path, evaluation paths and training randomness.
official.comparison: SOCK feature matching vs. Sig, rSig, cSig (same GRU generator and training protocol) and Diffusion-TS, all trained on one length-2048 V10 path with q = 5 context and T = 64 horizon.
official.falsification_criterion: With the paper's protocol on V10, the SOCK-trained generator's mean RNN score over 5 seeds is not clearly below the best baseline's (e.g. the gap to Sig or rSig falls within one seed standard deviation), or SOCK's ACF error is not below all baselines.

title: HyFAD: Hybrid Time-Frequency Diffusion with Frequency-Aware Embedding for Time Series Imputation
claim_source: Table 9 (Appendix A.13.3), page 21; same means in Table 1, page 8

official.background: Multivariate time series from sensors and medical records often have missing entries, and imputation fills them in from the observed values. Diffusion models such as CSDI are strong imputers, but they add and remove isotropic Gaussian noise only in the time domain. Real series concentrate most of their energy at low frequencies, so weak mid- and high-frequency components get over-smoothed. This matters most when observations are sparse.
official.method:
HyFAD keeps CSDI's temporal/feature transformer backbone and conditioning, and adds a second, frequency-domain diffusion process that is coupled with the time-domain one. At every forward step, Gaussian noise is first injected into an orthonormal real DFT (rDFT) representation of the series and then into the time domain. A balancing coefficient lambda (0.75 on PhysioNet) sets the share of time-domain noise. In reverse (DDIM-style, deterministic, 50 steps), a cascaded two-branch network first predicts and removes the time-domain noise and then the frequency-domain noise. Training minimizes a time-noise loss, a frequency-noise loss and a consistency loss (weight omega = 0.4), restricted to the masked target positions.

The frequency branch replaces the standard sinusoidal step embedding with a 'frequency-aware' one, which modulates it per frequency band using a noise-aware gate, a low-to-high stage schedule and a missing-aware band reliability weight. On PhysioNet (4000 ICU records, 35 features, 48 hourly steps), 10/50/90% of the observed values are held out as imputation targets. MAE and RMSE are computed on those targets. Removing the frequency process from both diffusion stages reduces HyFAD to CSDI.
official.claim: On PhysioNet with 90% of observed values held out as targets, HyFAD reaches MAE 0.448 ± 0.003 and RMSE 0.782 ± 0.028 (5 runs). CSDI gets MAE 0.492 ± 0.0005 and RMSE 0.851, and LSCD gets MAE 0.492 and RMSE 0.845, so HyFAD's MAE is about 9% lower.
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Detailed comparison of HyFAD, LSCD and CSDI.
official.metric: MAE and RMSE on the held-out imputation targets (lower is better), mean (std) over 5 independent runs; 95% CI and Welch-style p-values are also reported
official.comparison: HyFAD vs. CSDI (its time-domain-only counterpart) and LSCD, with the same CSDI data preprocessing, train/val/test splits and evaluation
official.falsification_criterion: On PhysioNet at 90% missingness, over several seeds, HyFAD's mean MAE is not clearly below CSDI's, for example a gap under ~0.01 or within the run-to-run std.

title: NIV: Neural Axis Variations for Variable Font Generation

official.background: Variable fonts (OpenType) let one font file vary continuously along design axes such as weight (wght), width (wdth), slant (slnt) and optical size (opsz). The variation is stored in the gvar table as per-point displacement 'tuples' that are active over regions of the design space and combined with tent-function weights. Building these tables by hand takes expert designers a lot of work, so most fonts remain static. The paper asks whether a neural model trained on existing variable fonts can predict these per-point displacements for any static font, including multi-axis interactions, and so convert it into a working variable font automatically.
official.method:
NIV is a non-autoregressive transformer encoder (d=256, 6 blocks, 8 heads) over a glyph's ordered control points plus 4 phantom points. Each point carries normalized (x, y) coordinates (scaled by 2/UPM), an on/off-curve/phantom indicator, and contour-position features. Axis conditioning uses a 'Property Embedding': each of the A axes has a learned positive and a learned negative embedding (2A in total); the corresponding embedding for each active axis (selected by a binary mask) is weighted by the absolute axis value (the paper says 'the product of the absolute axis values'), all weighted embeddings are summed and the resulting vector is normalized, then used to produce the scale and shift of AdaLN in every block. A point-wise head regresses (dx, dy) per point, trained with MSE against the total ground-truth displacement at the tuple's peak axis coordinate (the sum of all tuples of that glyph weighted by their tent functions). Data come from the 733 variable Google Fonts (filtered to wght, wdth, opsz, slnt tuples; composite glyphs and glyphs with more than 500 points are excluded), using a font split with 15% of fonts held out for test. Training: AdamW, lr 2e-4, micro-batch 32, bf16, 80 epochs, about 4 days on one RTX 3090.

For Table 13, the same trained font-split model is evaluated two ways on the font-split test set. 'Joint axes' feeds the full multi-axis vector v at once (Eq. 7). 'Additive per-axis' runs the model once per active axis a in S, each time with only that axis unmasked, and sums the predicted deltas (Eq. 8). Test RMSE is the root of the mean squared Euclidean per-point displacement error, averaged over all points (including phantom points) and all test (glyph, tuple) examples.
official.claim: On the font-split test set, conditioning NIV jointly on all active axes gives test RMSE 0.05205 ± 0.00088, whereas summing separate single-axis predictions from the same model gives 0.05737, showing that the model relies on cross-axis interactions.
official.claim_caption: Table 13: RMSE for additive, per-axis decomposition versus a joint conditioning, on the font-split dataset. For the main method we report mean ± one standard deviation (1σ) over 3 runs to indicate statistical stability.

title: TS-ICL: A Flexible Time-Indexed Foundation Model for Time Series via In-Context Learning
claim_source: Table 13, page 35 (also Figure 3b, page 6, and Figure 4b, page 7)

official.background: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as Chronos-2 and TiRex give strong zero-shot forecasts, but they are built on regular, patch-based grids. They do not natively impute missing values, and most cannot use exogenous covariates. Tabular foundation models adapted to time series (TabPFNv2.5-TS, TabICLv2-TS) can impute and can use covariates, but they rely on handcrafted time features and are slow at inference. Real-world series, for example in energy, are often partially observed and come with informative covariates such as weather, so one zero-shot model that imputes with covariates is useful in practice.
official.method:
TS-ICL is a 27M-parameter probabilistic encoder-regressor Transformer that works on timestamp-value pairs rather than a fixed grid. A Perceiver-style encoder compresses each channel (target and each covariate, channel-independently) into M latent tokens. A channel mixer lets the target tokens cross-attend to the covariate tokens. A temporal query module embeds any timestamp with frequency features and cross-attends to the latent tokens, giving a representation H(t). An in-context regressor treats the observed (H(t), value, covariates) pairs as a training set and predicts dense quantiles at the target timestamps (smoothed pinball loss). Imputation uses a dedicated imputation checkpoint trained on real and synthetic series, with covariate-target structures generated from random DAGs whose non-root nodes apply structural causal mechanisms sampled from a registry (linear, MLP, convolutional, GRU-based RNN, polynomial, discretize, product).

Evaluation is zero-shot on the known-covariates part of fm-impute-bench: 6 energy datasets (PV-OCC, PV-PACA, Wind-HDF, Wind-GE with irradiance or wind-speed covariates; Load-France 21/22 with temperature), four-week windows, and four masking scenarios (50% or 70% pointwise missingness, two or four disjoint one-day gaps), giving 24 tasks and about 1K windows. Baselines are TabPFNv2.5-TS and TabICLv2-TS (with and without covariates, using the TabICLv2-TS feature pipeline), TS-ICL without covariates, and ridge regression on the covariates. Metrics are NMAE and CRPS (computed as a weighted quantile loss), averaged arithmetically across tasks, plus pairwise per-task win rates.
official.claim: On the 24 known-covariate imputation tasks of fm-impute-bench, TS-ICL with covariates reaches mean CRPS 0.074 (NMAE 0.077), against 0.115 (0.121) for TabPFNv2.5-TS and 0.134 (0.141) for TabICLv2-TS, both also given the covariates, and beats TabPFNv2.5-TS w/ covariates on 95.8% (23/24) of tasks by CRPS.
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Aggregated imputation performance metrics across the 24 tasks of the known covariates setting in fm-impute-bench (mean ± std). Best in bold.
official.metric: CRPS (weighted quantile loss) and NMAE, lower is better, arithmetic mean over 24 tasks; ± is the std across tasks (not across seeds; no seed variation is reported). Pairwise CRPS win rate per task from Figure 4b.
official.comparison: TS-ICL (w/ covar) vs. TabPFNv2.5-TS (w/ covar) and TabICLv2-TS (w/ covar) on the same windows and masks; also vs. TS-ICL w/o covar, TFMs w/o covar, and ridge on covariates

title: Where, What, Why, and Importance: Structured Defect Grounding for Text-to-Image Feedback

official.background: Text-to-image models still produce localized failures such as malformed hands, garbled text, or content that contradicts the prompt. Scalar preference scores cannot say where a defect is, what kind it is, why it is wrong, or how much it matters, and recent dense-feedback methods (RichHF, ImageDoctor) predict heatmaps that do not bind a reason or severity to each individual defect and are not a native output of autoregressive vision-language models. A detector that outputs an explicit set of defect instances would be useful both for evaluating generators and as a spatial reward for training them.
official.method:
The authors build SDG-30K: 30,096 images (1024x1024) generated from Pick-a-Pic prompts by FLUX.2-dev, Z-Image-Turbo, LongCat-Image and SANA-1.5 (about 7.5K each), with human-drawn bounding boxes labelled artifact or misalignment plus short descriptions; Gemini 3 Pro expands the descriptions, writes a three-step reasoning trace, and assigns a 1-100 importance score. The split is prompt-disjoint: 28,945 train and 1,151 test images. Each defect is a (box in [0,1000] coordinates, type, description, importance) tuple, and the model outputs a variable-length JSON list of them after a <think> trace.

The SDG detector is Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, first SFT-trained (vision encoder frozen, coordinate jitter of +/-10) on the reasoning trace plus defect set, then trained with GRPO (8 samples per prompt) on a format-gated reward of 0.6 localization (Hungarian matching with DIoU cost) + 0.25 description cosine similarity + 0.15 importance accuracy. Evaluation (SDG-Eval) matches predictions to ground truth of the same type by class-aware Hungarian matching on IoU and reports, per type, BoxF1 at IoU 0.1 and 0.5 on images that contain that defect type, plus image-level detection F1, clean-image accuracy, description cosine and importance accuracy. Baselines GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3 Pro are prompted zero-shot with the same structured output format.
official.claim: On the SDG-30K test set, the GRPO-trained 4B SDG detector reaches BoxF1@0.5 of 0.263 (artifact) and 0.387 (misalignment), above the best zero-shot proprietary VLM, Gemini 3 Pro, at 0.200 and 0.307 (GPT-5.4: 0.035 and 0.292).

official.metric: BoxF1@0.5 (higher is better): F1 of predicted vs. ground-truth boxes of the same defect type after Hungarian matching at IoU >= 0.5, computed on test images with at least one ground-truth defect of that type. Single run; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: SDG (SFT) and SDG (GRPO), Qwen3-VL-4B fine-tuned on SDG-30K, vs. zero-shot GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3 Pro given the same structured-output prompt; human re-annotation (16 independent annotators) as an upper bound.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-evaluating the released SDG GRPO checkpoint and zero-shot Gemini 3 Pro on the released SDG-30K test split with SDG-Eval gives SDG artifact or misalignment BoxF1@0.5 that is not higher than Gemini 3 Pro's, or SDG's artifact/misalignment BoxF1@0.5 falls clearly below the reported 0.263/0.387 (e.g. below 0.200/0.307).

title: Symb-xMIL: Symbolic Explanations for Multiple Instance Learning in Digital Pathology

official.background: Multiple instance learning (MIL) models in digital pathology classify a whole-slide image from a bag of patch embeddings, and are usually explained with heatmaps that give each patch a relevance score. Heatmaps are first-order: they do not say whether the model needs two tissue types together (AND), accepts either one (OR), or treats one as evidence against the prediction (NOT). Symbolic XAI (Schnake et al.) aligns a model with logical formulas over input features, but it uses Harsanyi-dividend relevances and was not designed for bags of instances. This paper adapts it to MIL so that a model's decision for a bag can be described by the best-matching logical rule over semantic patch groups.
official.method:
Each instance in a bag is mapped to a semantic group (here: digit 4, digit 7, or R = any other digit). For each subset S of the groups, the MIL model is run on the sub-bag containing only instances from those groups, giving f(X_S) (the empty bag gives output 0). A logical query q over the groups defines a binary indicator λ_q(S) (e.g. for 4 ∧ 7, λ = 1 iff both 4 and 7 are in S). The alignment score is the correlation across all 2^3 = 8 subsets between λ_q(S) and f(X_S); the best query is the one with the highest score. The query space has 39 non-redundant formulas over {4, 7, R} built with ∧, ∨, ¬ (Appendix A). The baseline (original Symbolic XAI, Appendix B) instead correlates λ_q(S) with the Harsanyi dividend μ(X_S) = Σ_{L⊆S} (-1)^{|S|-|L|} f(X_L).

Data: three synthetic MNIST-bag datasets whose bag label is 4 ∧ 7 (both digits present), 4 ∨ 7 (either present) or 4 → 7 (4 absent or 7 present); 2000 train, 500 validation and 200 test bags each, with bag size sampled from 1 to 30 during training so the model stays accurate on small sub-bags. Model: a two-layer CNN encoder trained end-to-end with TransMIL from scratch, early stopping (up to 200 epochs); test accuracy is reported as 99.99%. Alignment scores are averaged over the positive (y = 1) test bags.
official.claim: On all three synthetic MNIST-bag MIL datasets, Symb-xMIL's top-ranked query among 39 is the ground-truth rule, with mean alignment 0.951 (4 ∧ 7), 0.992 (4 ∨ 7) and 0.967 (4 → 7) versus 0.761, 0.675 and 0.779 for the runner-up query; the original Harsanyi-based Symbolic XAI, applied to the same models, ranks the true rule first only for 4 → 7 (0.666) and ranks 4 ∧ 7 sixth and 4 ∨ 7 fourth.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Results of simulated experiments. The top row shows the Top-3 symbolic queries aligned with the Transformer-based MIL model trained to learn the logic of each dataset. The bottom row shows the ground-truth queries corresponding to the other two synthetic datasets. The alignment score (see Eq. 1) is averaged over all test bags with a positive label (y = 1). Symb-xMIL identifies the ground-truth rules with the highest correlation in all cases.
official.metric: Mean alignment score (Pearson correlation over the 8 subsets between query indicator and model output, averaged over positive test bags), higher is better; rank of the ground-truth query among 39. No ± reported (single trained model per dataset, no seeds).
official.comparison: Ground-truth query vs. all other 38 queries under Symb-xMIL alignment; and Symb-xMIL (raw sub-bag predictions) vs. original Symbolic XAI (Harsanyi dividends) on the same trained TransMIL models.
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining the MIL models (several seeds), the ground-truth rule is not the top-ranked Symb-xMIL query on one of the three datasets, or its margin over the runner-up shrinks to near zero (e.g. under 0.05); or the Harsanyi-based Symbolic XAI also ranks the ground truth first on 4 ∧ 7 and 4 ∨ 7, removing the claimed advantage.

title: Lean4Agent: Formal Modeling and Verification for Agent Workflow and Trajectory
claim_source: Table 6 and Table 7, page 14 (same numbers as Table 1, page 7)

official.background: LLM agents are often run through explicit multi-step workflows (graphs of LLM steps that read and write variables), but there is no formal way to check whether a workflow's natural-language specification is self-consistent before running it, or to find which step caused a failure afterwards. Mathematics solved a similar ambiguity problem with dependent-type formal languages such as Lean. This paper asks whether Lean4 can model agent workflows and whether passing its formal check actually predicts better task performance.
official.method:
FormalAgentLib is a Lean4 library that models an AgentSPEX YAML workflow as a typed graph of nodes and edges (Layer 1, structural checks) and attaches Hoare-style pre- and postcondition predicates to every LLM step (Layer 2). The predicates, including graph-level ones about information flow and context visibility (e.g. evaluateChoicesIndependent), are annotated automatically by an LLM from the step instructions. Under the LLMExec assumption (an LLM step whose preconditions hold produces its postconditions), Layer 2 checks that every step's preconditions are entailed by the parameters and the postconditions of its predecessors; a workflow passes or fails this check.

Experiment: Claude-Opus-4.6 generates 40 candidate workflows per task; those failing the workflow-language linter are dropped, Layer-2 specs are generated and verified, and 3 verification-passing and 3 verification-failing workflows are picked at random. Each workflow is run with 5 models (GPT-5.2, GLM-5, Kimi-K2.5, Gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen-3.5-27B) via the AgentSPEX engine (temperature 1.0, context 163,840) on a random 50-problem hard subset of SWE-Bench-Verified and a random 100-question subset of ELAIP-Bench (multiple-choice AI-paper understanding). The metric is the mean task pass rate of the 3 passing workflows minus that of the 3 failing workflows.
official.claim: Workflows that pass FormalAgentLib Layer-2 verification outperform verification-failing workflows in task pass rate averaged over 5 models, by 14.80 points on a 50-problem hard SWE-Bench-Verified subset (58.27% vs 43.47%, 95% CI [10.00, 19.60]) and by 9.07 points on a 100-question ELAIP-Bench subset (36.60% vs 27.53%, 95% CI [5.66, 13.07]).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: SWE-Bench Jimenez et al. [2024] subset's results with 95% CI. Table 7: ELAIP-Bench-Verified Dai et al. [2025] subset's results with 95% CI.
official.metric: Task pass rate (%), higher is better, averaged over 3 workflows per group; Diff. = passed minus failed. Lower/Upper CI are 95% paired bootstrap CIs from 10,000 resamples (the paper does not say exactly what is resampled; most likely problems). No seed repeats are reported.
official.comparison: 3 randomly chosen verification-passing workflows vs. 3 randomly chosen verification-failing workflows (all generated by the same LLM for the same task), each run with the same 5 execution models on the same problems
official.falsification_criterion: With freshly generated workflows split by FormalAgentLib Layer-2 verification, the passing group's mean pass rate is not higher than the failing group's, or the average gap falls well below the reported CI (under 10.00 points on the SWE subset or under 5.66 points on the ELAIP subset), or the gap's CI includes zero.

title: STREAM: Stochastic Riemannian Flow Matching with Anisotropic Decoder for Digital Histopathology Image Generation
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (seed re-measurement in Table 24, page 33)

official.background: Synthetic histopathology images could ease patient-privacy limits on data sharing and supply training data for pathology foundation models. Current state-of-the-art histopathology generators (ZoomLDM, PixCell) run diffusion in a VAE latent space conditioned on a pathology vision foundation model (VFM) embedding, so most of their output diversity comes from the conditioning and they need a VFM at inference. Recent natural-image work (RAE, SVG) instead generates directly in frozen VFM feature space. Pathology VFM patch tokens are L2-normalized on the unit hypersphere, which suggests that flow matching should respect that geometry instead of treating the features as Euclidean.
official.method:
A frozen UNI encoder (ViT-L/16) maps each 256x256 patch at 20x to 256 L2-normalized tokens of dimension 1024 on the unit sphere. Stage 1 trains a LightningDiT-XL (about 676M parameters, 95k steps, batch 1024) with Riemannian flow matching on the product of spheres. The source is uniform on the sphere, the conditional path is the SLERP geodesic perturbed by tangent Gaussian noise with a Brownian-bridge schedule sigma(t) = sigma_max sin(pi t), and the network predicts the normalized data endpoint under a chord (ambient L2) loss. Sampling uses 25 Riemannian midpoint steps (NFE = 50).

Stage 2 trains a ViT-XL pixel decoder from scratch (90k steps, batch 512, L1 + LPIPS + cosine round-trip + adversarial loss with a Kaiko ViT-S/8 discriminator). Its training features are corrupted with anisotropic tangent noise: a small sigma_H = 0.002 along the top-k* left singular vectors of the trained DiT's velocity-field Jacobian at t = 0.99 (cached per k-means centroid and token, with k* set by a 0.90 energy threshold) and a large sigma_L = 0.02 along the complement. All baselines (ZoomLDM, PixCell, RAE, SVG, REPA-E) are retrained by the authors on the same data with the same UNI encoder and their published hyperparameters, with only the step count changed so that every method (STREAM included) trains for the ImageNet-equivalent of 80 epochs given its batch size, and all are evaluated with 50k generated samples against the same reference set.
official.claim: On TCGA-BRCA 20x patches with the same frozen UNI encoder, STREAM reaches generation FID 6.16, against 15.84 for the Euclidean VFM-latent baseline RAE and 17.37 for SVG at matched NFE = 50. It also beats the strongest overall baseline, ZoomLDM, at 7.43. A three-seed re-measurement gives 6.12 +/- 0.04 vs. 15.88 +/- 0.04 for RAE.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Generation results on BRCA and COADREAD 20x patches (256x256), with all six methods on the same UNI encoder. All metrics lower-is-better; best bold, second-best underlined within each block. LPIPS is reconstruction-only.
official.metric: gFID (FID of 50k generated images against real images, lower is better). Table 3 is a single run with no error bars. Table 24 gives mean +/- SD over 3 sampling seeds at 50k samples with trained weights fixed, so it does not include training-seed variance.
official.comparison: STREAM vs. RAE and SVG (diffusion in the same UNI latent space), plus ZoomLDM, PixCell and REPA-E (VAE-latent models using UNI for conditioning or alignment), all retrained on BRCA by the authors
official.falsification_criterion: A STREAM model retrained on BRCA UNI features with the paper's settings does not reach a clearly lower gFID than RAE trained on the same features at matched NFE, for example if the gap shrinks from about 9.7 to a few points or reverses. A secondary check is STREAM failing to beat ZoomLDM's 7.43.

title: Generative Molecular Morphing for Flexible-Size Design via Unbalanced Optimal Transport
claim_source: Table 8, page 19 (appendix B.4); the corresponding joint plots are Figure 4, page 8

official.background: Diffusion and flow-based generative models for 3D molecules fix the number of atoms before generation begins: the atom count is drawn from the training-set empirical distribution and then held constant along the trajectory. Because many molecular properties (lipophilicity, drug-likeness, molecular weight) are tightly coupled to molecular size, fixing the size first prevents the model from learning the joint distribution of size and property, and makes it impossible to target property values whose natural molecule sizes were never seen in training. It also blocks tasks where the starting structure is given, such as growing a molecule out of a fixed scaffold.
official.method:
Morph models molecule generation as a jump-flow process on geometric graphs: continuous 3D positions evolve under a flow-matching ODE while a continuous-time Markov chain performs discrete jumps that insert nodes, delete nodes, and substitute atom and bond types. The state space is the disjoint union over atom counts n up to n_max, quotiented by SE(3) x S_n, so the number of nodes can both grow and shrink during sampling. Training uses Conditional Generator Matching: a network regresses the conditional velocity and the conditional jump rates along paths between paired endpoints (g0, g1).

To define those paths when the prior graph and the data graph have different sizes, the authors align them with unbalanced optimal transport. Edge-edit costs are set to zero and the node matching is lifted to an (n0+n1)x(n0+n1) assignment problem with slack rows/columns priced by w_del and w_ins, solved exactly with the Hungarian algorithm and then rotationally aligned with Kabsch. The resulting assignment partitions nodes into matched (Gaussian interpolation of positions, scheduled type substitution), inserted (sampled insertion time, position drawn around the target with shrinking variance, new node and its edges sampled from a per-node Gaussian mixture model), and deleted (sampled deletion time, attributes frozen at the prior until removal). For the claim below, a size- and property-conditioned model is trained on QM9 with RDKit-computed logP as the conditioning value; the prior atom count n0 is drawn uniformly rather than from the data, so the sampler must itself move to the atom count appropriate for the requested logP.
official.claim: A logP-conditioned Morph trained on QM9 hits the requested logP with MAE at most 0.292 and validity at least 0.949 for targets in the well-supported range logP in {-1, 0, 1, 2, 3} (e.g. logP=0: MAE 0.257, validity 0.968), while degrading at the distribution edges: logP=-4 gives MAE 1.495 at validity 0.825 and logP=4 gives MAE 0.659 at validity 0.788.

title: UniSHARP: Universal Sharp Monocular View Synthesis

official.background: Feedforward monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting methods such as SHARP and Flash3D predict a renderable Gaussian scene from a single image in under a second, but they are trained on narrow-FoV perspective photos and assume a pinhole camera, so they cannot take wide-FoV, fisheye or 360-degree equirectangular panoramas directly. Workarounds such as splitting a panorama into cubemap faces produce seams. Many real capture devices (robots, AR/VR, 360 cameras) use these non-pinhole lenses, so a single model that does single-image novel view synthesis for any camera type would be useful.
official.method:
UniSHARP replaces SHARP's image-plane Gaussian parameterization with a ray-distance one inspired by UniK3D: every pixel has a predicted unit ray r_p and radial distance d_p, and Gaussians are placed at d_p r_p. A UniK3D ViT-L encoder (pretrained) predicts rays and two radial-distance layers; two layers of 'Geometry Anchored Gaussians' are initialized on the native-resolution ray grid (visible surface plus a second layer for disocclusions), and a Gaussian decoder fusing 2D semantic and 3D ray-based features predicts 14-channel residuals (offsets, inverse distance, scale, rotation, color, opacity). For panoramas, the second layer is randomly dropped during training with a latitude-dependent probability. Loss = L1 color + opacity BCE + perceptual loss + source/rendered-target inverse-depth L1 + TV, floater-suppression and multi-scale Sobel depth regularizers. One model is trained on a mixture of perspective (RealEstate10K, DL3DV, WildRGB-D), wide-FoV (OmniRooms-Wide), fisheye (ScanNet++) and panoramic (HM3D, OmniRooms) data, with UniK3D pseudo-depth where ground-truth depth is missing; Adam, 10^6 iterations, 8 H20 GPUs.

Evaluation uses a single-source, multi-target protocol: the first frame of each predefined evaluation group is the source and subsequent valid frames are targets, with pairs filtered to source-target overlap > 60%, camera distance < 0.5 m and index gap < 10. PSNR, SSIM (RGB, 11x11 Gaussian window) and LPIPS (AlexNet) are computed on valid pixels, averaged over targets then sequences. For panoramas (equirectangular), the baselines PanoDreamer (optimization-based single-image-to-360 with diffusion + 3DGS) and Matrix3D (diffusion-based) are run with official checkpoints and defaults on the same source-target pairs. Replica is out-of-domain (not in training); HM3D's evaluation split is held out from HM3D training data.
official.claim: On single-image panoramic novel view synthesis, UniSHARP beats the strongest baseline Matrix3D on HM3D (PSNR 29.244 vs 23.398, LPIPS 0.065 vs 0.114) and on the out-of-domain Replica dataset (PSNR 30.182 vs 25.379, LPIPS 0.038 vs 0.069), evaluated on the same source-target pairs.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Quantitative comparison on panoramic novel view synthesis. Results are reported on real and simulated ERP datasets using PSNR↑, SSIM↑, and LPIPS↓; best results are shown in red.
official.metric: PSNR (dB, higher is better), SSIM (higher is better), LPIPS-Alex (lower is better), averaged over target views then sequences; single numbers, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: UniSHARP vs. PanoDreamer and Matrix3D on HM3D, OmniRooms and Replica equirectangular panoramas
official.falsification_criterion: With the same evaluation protocol (overlap > 60%, distance < 0.5 m, index gap < 10, first frame as source), UniSHARP's PSNR advantage over Matrix3D on HM3D or Replica shrinks to below about 1 dB, or Matrix3D matches or beats UniSHARP on LPIPS.

title: Partially Performative Prediction
claim_source: Figure 1, page 11 (per-algorithm versions in Figures 2-3, page 38)

official.background: Performative prediction studies settings where deploying a predictive model changes the data distribution it will later be evaluated on, as when credit applicants change their features in response to a scoring rule. Classical treatments make this shift purely endogenous: the population depends only on the deployed model. Real distributions also drift for exogenous reasons the learner does not control. This paper models the data at round t as a mixture D_t(theta) = (1 - alpha_t) D(theta) + alpha_t P_t of a performative component and a time-varying exogenous component P_t. It asks how retraining algorithms behave when the target (the performatively stable point theta_t^PS) moves over time.
official.method:
The authors define performative stability regret, the sum over t of PR_t(theta_t) - PR_t(theta_t^PS), and bound it for repeated risk minimization (RRM), repeated gradient descent and greedy/lazy SGD. The bounds have the form O(1 + sum_t Delta_t^PS), where the path length Delta_t^PS is driven by alpha_t * W1(P_t, P_{t+1}). The prediction is that when P_t drifts randomly, faster-decaying alpha_t gives smaller regret. When P_t is fixed, the path length is zero, and a larger alpha_t only weakens performativity and so should give smaller regret.

Experiment (Section 6, Appendix G.1): credit default data (actionable-recourse version, 17 standardized features). The loss is regularized logistic loss with lambda = 1 over the unit l2 ball. Features follow a Gaussian N(m, Sigma) fitted to 1500 signed points, and strategic response gives D(theta) = N(A theta + m, Sigma) with A = 0.1 * diag(p_mod), where the last 11 coordinates are modifiable. The exogenous component is P_t = N(m_t, Sigma), with m_t either drawn i.i.d. from the unit ball each round ('random') or drawn once and held fixed ('stationary'). The schedules compared are alpha_t = 1 and alpha_t = t^-b for b in {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2}. T = 2000 for RRM and 1000 for lazy SGD (r = 1, averaged over 10 runs). theta_t^PS is computed by a bilevel fixed-point iteration (20 outer steps, 60 inner steps of size 0.2, 512 MC samples), and risks are evaluated with 16384 common random samples.
official.claim: In the credit-scoring simulation with a randomly drifting exogenous component, RRM's stability regret is ordered by how fast alpha_t decays. At T = 2000 (log T of about 7.6), log Reg_T^PS is roughly 5.7 for alpha_t = 1 (near-linear growth), 2.8 for t^-0.25, 0.7 for t^-0.5 and about -0.15 for t^-1 (flat). With a stationary exogenous component the order reverses: alpha_t = 1 gives the lowest regret (log Reg of about -0.58) and t^-2 the highest (about -0.475).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Performative stability regret of A_RRM (left) and A_SGD-lazy with r = 1 (right) in the credit scoring experiment, for varying alpha_t. We consider a randomly varying (top) and a stationary (bottom) exogenous component P_t.
official.metric: log of cumulative performative stability regret Reg_T^PS (lower is better), plotted against log T. No error bars are shown. RRM is deterministic given the sampled m_t, and the lazy SGD curves are means over 10 runs with no spread reported.
official.comparison: RRM (and lazy SGD) under the alpha_t schedules 1, t^-0.25, t^-0.5, t^-1 and t^-2, with random vs. stationary exogenous P_t
official.falsification_criterion: With random P_t, RRM regret is not monotonically smaller for faster-decaying alpha_t (e.g. alpha_t = t^-1 does not end well below t^-0.5, or alpha_t = 1 does not grow roughly linearly in T). Or, with stationary P_t, alpha_t = 1 does not give the lowest RRM regret.

title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Multi-Agent Coordination in Language Agents
claim_source: Figure 5(b), page 8 (baseline CI from Table 1, page 6)

official.background: LLM agents are increasingly expected to work alongside other agents over long horizons, but most agent benchmarks test single agents, short interactions, or rigidly structured multi-agent tasks. ALEM is a JAX benchmark built on Craftax-Coop dynamics (a procedurally generated survival/crafting world). Each episode it samples coordination tasks (synchronous joint actions, timed handovers), soft role specialisation and an explicit communication channel, and a single scalar alpha sets coordination difficulty. With the benchmark, the authors ask whether zero-shot LLM teams can coordinate and which harness components (communication, scratchpad memory, reasoning) make coordination possible.
official.method:
Homogeneous teams of LLM agents (the prompts describe 3-agent tasks) play ALEM on the Hard setting (alpha = 0.9) through a text interface. At every step, each agent gets the game rules, a text rendering of its local observation, the last eight observations and actions, teammate messages, its private scratchpad, the visible coordination constraints, and the legal actions. It must return a structured response with exactly one action, plus optional reasoning, a broadcast message and a scratchpad update. Rewards are normalised per category: Base% (ordinary achievements and health) and Coord.% (27 coordination achievements), each a percentage of the maximum achievable reward, averaged over agents.

In the ablation, the default harness (communication, scratchpad memory and reasoning all on) is compared with the same harness with the broadcast communication channel removed. Everything else stays the same: Gemma-4-31B-it served with vLLM, reasoning enabled, Hard difficulty, 20 seeds. Results are cross-seed means with 95% stratified bootstrap CIs (rliable). The same ablation was also run on Gemini-3.1-Pro-High (10 seeds, API).
official.claim: On ALEM Hard (alpha = 0.9), removing inter-agent communication from Gemma-4-31B-it teams cuts coordination reward from 8.8% (95% CI 6.9-10.9) to 3.8% (CI roughly 2.5-5.2) of the maximum, with non-overlapping CIs, while Base% does not fall (7.3% -> 8.3%).
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Harness and team-composition ablations on Hard. Left: we ablate communication, scratchpad memory, and reasoning for Gemini-3.1-Pro-High and Gemma-4-31B-it. Bars show Coord.% and Base%, each normalised by the maximum achievable reward in that category, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Right: we compare heterogeneous teams against their constituent homogeneous baselines. Bars show mean Total% with 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals; the dashed line marks the average homogeneous-team baseline, and the text annotation reports the difference relative to that baseline.
official.metric: Coord.%: coordination reward as a % of the maximum achievable (higher is better). Error bars are 95% stratified bootstrap CIs over 20 seeds. Base% is reported alongside.
official.comparison: Gemma-4-31B-it, default harness (communication + memory + reasoning) vs. the same harness without communication, both on Hard. Secondary: the same ablation on Gemini-3.1-Pro-High (17.5 -> 5.3 Coord.%).
official.falsification_criterion: Over 20 seeds on Hard with Gemma-4-31B-it, the no-communication Coord.% has a 95% CI that overlaps the full-harness CI, or the drop is much smaller than the reported ~5 points (e.g. under 2 points).

title: Querying Counterfactuals on Tissue Graphs with Supervised Disentanglement
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (extended in Table A6, page 35)

official.background: Single-cell perturbation models (scGen, CPA, optimal-transport and flow-matching methods) predict how cells respond to a stimulus that is applied uniformly and treat cells as independent. In tissue, a cell's expression also depends on its spatial neighbors, so a natural question is what a cell would express if its neighbors were different or changed their own expression. Spatial transcriptomics makes this measurable, and recent spatially-informed methods (MintFlow, Concert, SpatialProp) each address one specific kind of neighborhood intervention. This paper formalizes 'tissue graph counterfactuals' as edge perturbations (rewiring a cell's neighbors) and node perturbations (changing neighbors' expression) and proposes a model for both.
official.method:
Cellina is a VAE with a negative-binomial decoder p(x | z, s) over two latents: an intrinsic z from an MLP encoder on the cell's own counts, and a spatial s from an MLP encoder on the Gaussian-kernel-weighted, degree-normalized average of neighbors' log-normalized expression (no self term). Supervised disentanglement anchors z to cell type with a classifier loss and adversarially removes spatial-domain information from z with a discriminator trained in alternating steps. Cellina-GAT replaces the fixed neighbor aggregator with a multi-layer GATv2 over the cell's local subgraph (no self-loops) and adds a contrastive loss on s that uses spatial neighbors as positives and cells from other domains as negatives.

Perturb-FISH task (node perturbation): human melanoma xenograft from Binan et al. (2025) with in situ CRISPR knockouts of NF-kB-pathway genes in cancer cells; 154,111 cells, 154 genes kept, 9 knockouts with measurable effects. During training, T cells whose neighbors include perturbed cancer cells are held out. At inference, 6,000 control T cells are sampled, the expression of their neighbors is set to the per-gene mean of a given KO cancer population, and the predicted T-cell expression is compared with the held-out T cells that actually neighbor that KO. Because most of the response is a shared shift common to all KOs, the average perturbation shift is subtracted from both predicted and observed log fold-changes ('KO-specific' score). The main metric is Pearson r between predicted and observed KO-specific log fold-changes of the top DE genes, averaged over the 9 KOs, repeated over 5 seeds.
official.claim: On the in vivo Perturb-FISH melanoma xenograft, predicting how control T cells respond when their neighbors take on a knockout cancer profile, Cellina-GAT reaches a KO-specific Pearson r of 0.40 ± 0.07 and Cellina 0.33 ± 0.08, versus 0.16 ± 0.06 for SpatialProp and 0.06 ± 0.06 for a mean-shift baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Node perturbation performance for the Perturb-FISH in vivo CRISPR KO dataset. KO-specific effect; mean over 9 KOs, ± std over 5 seeds. A Cellina variant (gray) is best on Pearson, Signed Precision and RMSE_LFC. Spatial competitors in orange.
official.metric: Pearson r between predicted and observed KO-specific log fold-changes (average perturbation shift removed), higher is better; mean over 9 KOs, ± is std over 5 random seeds. Signed precision, E-distance and RMSE of logFC also reported.
official.comparison: Cellina and Cellina-GAT vs. SpatialProp (spatial GNN for neighbor perturbation) and a mean-shift baseline, all under the same node-perturbation protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Perturb-FISH node-perturbation evaluation over 5 seeds, Cellina-GAT's (or Cellina's) mean KO-specific Pearson is not clearly above SpatialProp's, e.g. the gap is below about 0.1 or within one seed std.

title: Ultra Flash: Scaling Real-Time Streaming Video Generation to High Resolutions

official.background: Autoregressive (causal, chunk-wise) video diffusion models such as Self Forcing and CausVid can stream text-to-video in real time on one GPU, but only at about 480P. Generating high-resolution video directly is too expensive. The usual fix is a cascade: generate at low resolution, then run a super-resolution (SR) model. When the low-resolution latents are upscaled by plain interpolation before the SR model, the result has aliasing and temporal incoherence, so the SR stage has to add a lot of noise to cover it up. That makes SR training and few-step distillation harder. This paper aims to make the cascade streamable at 1K and 2K resolution.
official.method:
Ultra Flash cascades a low-resolution streaming generator (Self Forcing, 480P latents), a causal streaming latent upsampler, a generative SR model and a high-resolution decoder. The SR model is Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with its input projection widened from c to 2c channels, and the new weights are zero-initialized. The upsampled LR latent is concatenated with the noise latent along the channel dimension. The model is trained with flow matching on LR-HR pairs made by an AIGC-oriented degradation pipeline, using condition noise injection and condition dropout. Inference uses multi-step ODE sampling with CFG.

The latent upsampler is a 'causal memory network': an input 3x3 conv followed by three stages. Each stage has N_b CausalMemBlocks (the current frame's features are concatenated with the previous frame's features, passed through three 3x3 convs with ReLU, plus a 1x1 skip), then PixelShuffle spatial upsampling and a channel-transition conv. For 1K output it upsamples 2x spatially in latent space. It is trained with MSE plus an optical-flow-warped temporal consistency loss (eWarp). Table 5 swaps this upsampler for bilinear or bicubic latent interpolation in front of the same multi-step SR model at 960x1664 and measures the quality of the SR output with CLIP-IQA+, MUSIQ and NIQE.
official.claim: At 960x1664 output, feeding the multi-step generative SR model latents from the 8-block causal memory upsampler instead of bicubic latent interpolation raises CLIP-IQA+ from 0.625 to 0.671 and MUSIQ from 69.1 to 72.4, and lowers NIQE from 4.65 to 4.18, while adding 8 ms of latency.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Ablation: upsampling strategy. Impact on downstream SR quality and latency overhead.
official.metric: CLIP-IQA+ (higher is better), MUSIQ (higher is better), NIQE (lower is better) on the SR output; no error bars, seeds or number of evaluation videos are reported
official.comparison: Causal memory upsampler (4 and 8 blocks) vs. bilinear and bicubic latent interpolation, with the same downstream multi-step SR model
official.falsification_criterion: With the same SR model and prompts, swapping bicubic latent interpolation for the trained causal memory upsampler gives no consistent improvement in CLIP-IQA+, MUSIQ and NIQE (e.g. a CLIP-IQA+ gain well under ~0.04 or a MUSIQ gain under ~3 points, or gains within the spread across prompts/seeds).

title: TRL-Bench: Standardizing Cross-Paradigm Representation-Level Evaluation of Tabular Encoders

official.background: Tabular encoders (generic text models run on serialized tables, table-pretrained transformers, column-centric models, self-supervised learners trained per table, and meta-pretrained priors such as TabPFN/TabICL) are usually evaluated inside their own end-to-end pipelines, with different predictors, fine-tuning budgets and task setups. That makes it unclear whether the representations themselves differ. TRL-Bench freezes each encoder, exports its row, column or table embeddings, and evaluates them with the same lightweight downstream heads, so models from different training paradigms can be compared directly.
official.method:
TRL-RBench (row level) has two task types. Row prediction: 50 OpenML tables (from TabArena, OpenML-CC18, OpenML-CTR23) with 123 hand-curated target columns (77 classification, 46 regression). Each encoder sees only the non-target columns and produces one row embedding, which is reused to predict every target. Record linkage: 16 entity-matching datasets rewritten as labelled row pairs: 8 clean DeepMatcher (DM-C), 4 dirty DeepMatcher (DM-D) and 4 WDC Products sizes. The two row embeddings are concatenated and fed to a probe, with the original pair-disjoint splits.

Every supervised probe is trained twice on the frozen embeddings, once as a linear head and once as a one-hidden-layer MLP (hidden 256) with Adam, and the canonical score is the average of the two. Metrics: AUROC and macro-F1 averaged over classification targets; SGM_0.01 of nRMSE over regression targets (lower is better); binary F1 of the match class averaged over linkage datasets. Results are 5-seed means. Models include BERT, GTE, TABBIE, TUTA (transfer-based), TabICL, TabPFN (prior-based) and eight target-table learners (VIME, SCARF, DAE, TabBinning, SAINT, SubTab, TabTransformer, TransTab).
official.claim: Under identical frozen-embedding probes, TabICL row embeddings give the best row prediction of all 14 encoders (AUROC 0.816 ± .001 vs. next best 0.794; regression SGM 0.505 ± .001 vs. next best 0.556 ± .003), yet on clean record linkage (DM-C) TabICL reaches only F1 0.316 ± .011 against BERT's 0.418 ± .004.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Row-level results across four evaluation categories. Row prediction averages over 77 classification and 46 regression targets (TabTransformer: 63 targets due to categorical-feature requirement). SGM is SGM_0.01(nRMSE). Linkage columns report binary F1 (match class) on DM-C, DM-D, and WDC. See Appendix H for the convention. Rank columns aggregate ranks over individual targets (classification, regression) or datasets (linkage). Formula of metrics in Appendix H.
official.metric: Row prediction: AUROC (higher better) averaged over 77 classification targets and SGM_0.01(nRMSE) (lower better) over 46 regression targets; clean linkage: binary match-class F1 (higher better) averaged over 8 DeepMatcher clean datasets. Each score is the average of a linear and an MLP probe; ± is the spread over 5 seeds (the paper does not say whether it is std or SE; probe-seed variation only, not variation across datasets).
official.comparison: TabICL vs. BERT (and the other 12 encoders: GTE, TABBIE, TUTA, TabPFN, VIME, SCARF, DAE, TabBinning, SAINT, SubTab, TabTransformer, TransTab) under the same probe protocol, on row prediction and on clean record linkage.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if, with the same protocol, TabICL's classification AUROC or regression SGM is not best among the encoders (e.g. BERT or VIME within seed spread of it), or if TabICL's DM-C linkage F1 matches or exceeds BERT's (gap of 0.10 F1 shrinking to within the seed spread).

title: SynIB: Informational Bottleneck for Maximizing Synergy in Multimodal Learning
claim_source: Figure 8, page 9 (also Figure 10 right, page 19, and Figure 9, page 14)

official.background: Multimodal models are meant to exploit synergy, meaning label information that is only available from the joint use of several modalities (for example an XOR of one bit from each modality). In practice, standard cross-entropy training of fusion models tends to rely on unimodal or redundant cues and does poorly on examples that need cross-modal reasoning. Existing fixes either change the architecture or rebalance how much each modality contributes. Neither targets synergy directly in the training objective.
official.method:
SynIB adds a confidence penalty to the usual cross-entropy loss of a fusion model: L = CE(q(y|x1,x2), y) + λ Σ_i KL(q(·|x̃_i, x_¬i) || r), where r is a uniform reference (Bernoulli(0.5) for binary tasks) and x̃_i is modality i with some coordinates replaced by noise via x̃ = (1−M)⊙x + M⊙ε. Only the fusion logit is regularized. The model is pushed to be uncertain whenever one modality is corrupted, so it cannot stay confident by using one modality alone. The mask M is either random (each coordinate corrupted independently with probability π=0.5 on PID-XOR), learned (an inner loop of 20 Adam steps finds the smallest mask that breaks a unimodal head, and SynIB corrupts its complement), or an oracle that corrupts exactly the synergistic blocks.

PID-Controlled XOR (App. F.2): two 32-d modalities, each split into unique (6), redundant (6), synergistic (6) and noise (14) blocks. Each sample's binary label is carried by a single source drawn from the mixture (pU1, pU2, pR, pS) = (0.45, 0, 0.45, 0.10). For synergistic samples, bits b1 = b and b2 = b⊕y are sign-encoded through random projections into each modality's synergy block, so neither modality alone predicts y. 1800 training samples, 200 validation, 4000 test. Encoders are 2-layer MLPs (32→1024→1024), with unimodal heads (weight λ_uni = 1.0) and an MLP fusion head (2048→128→128→1). Training runs for 30 epochs over 3 seeds. Vanilla fusion is the same network trained without the KL term; App. A.1 gives λ = 10 for the learned-mask run.
official.claim: On PID-Controlled XOR with mixture (pU1, pU2, pR, pS) = (0.45, 0, 0.45, 0.10), vanilla fusion reaches only 0.50 test accuracy on synergistic examples (chance), while SynIB with learned masking reaches 0.89 (random masking 0.87, oracle 0.91), with U1 and R accuracy unchanged at 0.99.

Per-source training (solid) and validation (dashed) accuracy across 30 epochs, mean ± standard error over three seeds. Sources are colored by type: unique-to-modality-1 (U1, blue), redundant (R, green), and synergistic (S, red). Final synergy test accuracies (annotated per panel): 0.50 vanilla, 0.91 oracle, 0.87 random, 0.89 learned. PID mixture (pU1, pU2, pR, pS) = (0.45, 0, 0.45, 0.10). Vanilla fusion (left) fits U1 and R on both splits, but synergy validation stalls at chance while training accuracy climbs, the signature of memorization on the scarce synergistic examples. The three SynIB variants (M*, MRandom, MLearned) close this gap, lifting synergy validation accuracy without degrading U1 or R.

title: Mult-DPO: Multinomial Direct Preference Optimization for Recommender Systems

official.background: LLM-based recommenders are often aligned to user preferences with DPO, which assumes one preferred and one dispreferred response per context. Recommendation feedback is set-wise instead: for a user context there are several positive items (liked, clicked) and many negative items (unobserved or rejected), and every positive should outrank every negative with no order within either set. Extending DPO to this setting through the Plackett-Luce model requires marginalizing over all orderings of the positives, which is exponential in the number of positives. Existing workarounds either use one positive per context (S-DPO, DMPO) or sum independent pairwise losses (LiPO-BT), which drops the joint set-wise structure.
official.method:
Mult-DPO replaces the marginalized Plackett-Luce likelihood with a multinomial surrogate: the probability that k independent draws from the categorical distribution over candidates (weights w(e|x) = exp(reward)) hit each positive exactly once and no negative. With the DPO reparameterization w(e|x) ∝ (πθ(e|x)/πref(e|x))^β, the loss is L = -β Σ_{e∈positives} log(πθ(e|x)/πref(e|x)) + k log Σ_{e∈all candidates} (πθ(e|x)/πref(e|x))^β, i.e. each positive is contrasted against the same total candidate weight. The authors prove it upper-bounds the exact marginalized PL-DPO loss, with a gap of at most (k-1) log(1 + A/B), where A and B are the total positive and negative weights.

Experiments fine-tune Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct from the same SFT initialization and reference policy on Goodreads, MovieLens-10M (rating-5 items as positives, randomly sampled unrated items as negatives) and Reddit-V2 conversational recommendation (recommendations from different Reddit users on the same conversation pooled as multiple positives). All methods use AdamW with learning rate 1e-6; β is chosen per method on a validation set with 200 sampled candidates (β=0.005 is reported as optimal for Goodreads). Test NDCG@5/15/20 is computed against the full item catalog. Baselines: BigRec and D3 (SFT), vanilla DPO, DMPO, S-DPO, LiPO (BT).
official.claim: On Goodreads with the Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone, Mult-DPO reaches full-catalog test NDCG@5/15/20 of 0.0947/0.1292/0.1406, above the strongest baseline LiPO (BT) at 0.0862/0.1198/0.1294 and above every SFT and DPO-style baseline (e.g. S-DPO 0.0762/0.1105/0.1192).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison between Mult-DPO and DPO-style baselines on the test sets of Goodreads, MovieLens-10M, and Reddit-V2. Evaluation is conducted with the entire catalog as the candidates. Most results are significant as standard error is between 0.0020-0.0035 for N@5, N@15 and N@20.

title: FOGO: Forgetting-aware Orthogonalization Optimizer

official.background: Neural networks trained by gradient descent tend to overwrite what they learned earlier when the data distribution shifts. This is catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, and the authors argue a milder version also happens inside ordinary training when dominant mini-batch gradients suppress rare directions. Most anti-forgetting methods work at the level of data (replay buffers) or loss (regularizers like EWC). This paper asks whether an optimizer can reduce forgetting by itself, building on orthogonalized-momentum optimizers like Muon.
official.method:
FOGO starts from Muon's Newton–Schulz orthogonalized momentum, keeping a slow and a fast momentum stream. Each row of the orthogonalized updates is projected to a low dimension d with a fixed Rademacher random matrix, and the two streams are fused there by SLERP. A spherical codebook of centroids (an online EMA of k-means-style statistics) stores recurring update directions. Each step, components of the projected update that conflict with centroids (cosine < -ϵ_st) are removed and over-aligned components are slightly deflated (short-term filtering). At task boundaries, important centroids are frozen, and later updates have their components along those frozen directions removed with importance weights (long-term protection). The corrected projected update is lifted back to parameter space by a closed-form proximal least-squares step, then rescaled and applied with weight decay.

For the claim: PACS Domain-IL, 7 classes, 4 domains (Photo, Art Painting, Cartoon, Sketch) presented sequentially, 80/20 train/test split, 224×224 images. The model is an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 with frozen BN statistics, trained 15 epochs per domain at lr 5e-5, batch 32, grad clip 1.0. It is combined with ER (buffer 100, replay batch 32, α=1.0), and only the optimizer is changed (Adam, Muon, CBP, FIRE, FOGO). FOGO hyperparameters are in Appendix D.2.1: codebook 64 / proj dim 128 for backbone stages, 32 / 64 for the head, up to 21 frozen centroids per stage, µs=0.95, µf=0.35, ξ=0.3, ϵ_st=0.15, ϵ_lt=0.10, γ_lt=0.6 (0.4 head), λ_prox=1.0, update scale 0.1. Metrics are averaged over 3 random domain orders × 2 seeds.
official.claim: On PACS domain-incremental learning with ER replay (ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18), replacing Muon with FOGO lowers Average Forgetting from 7.56 ± 0.90% to 4.21 ± 0.85% (Adam: 9.81 ± 1.62%) without lowering Average Performance (90.24 vs 89.20%).

official.metric: Average Forgetting AF (%), lower is better; ± is std over 6 runs (3 random domain orders × 2 seeds). AP (%) is also reported, higher is better.

title: Dirichlet-Guided Group Forecasting for Alleviating Over-smoothing in Time Series Forecasting

official.background: Multi-step time series forecasters often over-smooth: they follow the coarse trend of the future but lose peaks, oscillations and regime changes. The paper argues that this happens because the same history can lead to several qualitatively different futures (latent dynamical modes) while each training input comes with only one realized future, so squared-loss training averages incompatible modes into a flat trajectory, and naive multi-head models collapse every head onto the same target. A forecaster that keeps distinct mode-conditioned futures should produce sample sets that both cover the realized future and keep its shape.
official.method:
DGF is built on a pretrained Moirai backbone (small or base), which is fully fine-tuned. From the encoder representation h, K heads give mode-conditioned predictive distributions q_k(Y|X), and a separate head gives Dirichlet concentrations alpha_k = alpha_min + softplus(e_k). Sampling is hierarchical: for each of B mini-groups, draw pi_b ~ Dir(alpha), then for G samples in the group draw a mode z ~ Cat(pi_b) and a trajectory from q_z.

Training uses a GRPO-style objective. Each trajectory gets reward lambda1 * (-MSE to ground truth) + lambda2 * dynamics reward (L1 differences in first and second differences, normalized FFT amplitude spectrum, and a history-to-forecast transition penalty). Sample-level advantages are normalized within each mini-group and update log p(z|pi_b) + log q_z(Y); a Dirichlet-level advantage (mini-group mean reward normalized across groups) updates log p(pi_b|alpha); a capped pairwise distance between the K head means is added as a diversity regularizer. K, B, G, gamma, lambda2, lambda3 and the learning rate are selected on validation; up to 200 epochs with early stopping. Table 3 evaluates the generated sample set with the STRIPE protocol: MSE and DILATE of the mean over samples ('mean') and of the best sample ('best').
official.claim: On the STRIPE-protocol Traffic and Electricity benchmarks, DGF on Moirai-base lowers mean-sample MSE versus full fine-tuning of the same backbone from 0.407 to 0.295 (Traffic) and 0.171 to 0.128 (Electricity), each ±0.01 over 5 runs, and also lowers best-sample MSE and DILATE.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Forecasting results on the Traffic and Electricity datasets, averaged over 5 runs (mean ± std). Metrics are scaled for readability. Lower values are better.
official.metric: MSE and DILATE (lower is better) of generated forecast samples, 'mean' = average over samples, 'best' = best sample (oracle); mean ± std over 5 runs. Metrics are 'scaled for readability' with no scaling stated.
official.comparison: DGF (Moirai-base) vs. Moirai-base fully fine-tuned with the standard supervised objective vs. zero-shot Moirai-base. The STRIPE, DeepAR, N-BEATS etc. rows are on a different scale and appear to be copied from the STRIPE paper, so they are not part of the claim.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same backbone, data split and number of samples, DGF's mean-sample MSE on Traffic or Electricity is not lower than supervised full fine-tuning by more than the run-to-run std, or the gap is far smaller than the reported ~27% (Traffic) / ~25% (Electricity).

title: Attention-Discounted Adaptive Sampler for Masked Diffusion Language Models
claim_source: Table 19 (Appendix G), page 20; summarized in Figure 2 (third row, page 8) and Table 2 (page 8)

official.background: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) such as LLaDA and Dream generate text by iteratively unmasking positions, and can reduce the number of denoiser forward passes (NFE) by revealing several tokens per step. This parallelism is fragile: tokens that are each confident may be mutually inconsistent when committed together. Common training-free samplers (Top-k, Fast-dLLM, EB-Sampler) decide how many tokens to reveal but rank candidates by token-wise confidence, ignoring interactions among the positions selected in the same step. Accuracy therefore collapses at high parallelism (low NFE), which is the regime where diffusion decoding would be most useful.
official.method:
ADAS changes only the order in which candidates are added to the set S of positions to unmask in one step; the base sampler's stopping rule is unchanged. With confidence c_i = max_x p(x_i | revealed context) and A the final-layer self-attention averaged over heads (A_is = attention from masked position i to masked position s), ADAS greedily picks the remaining candidate maximizing u(i | S) = c_i − α Σ_{s∈S} A_is (1 − c_s), i.e. confidence discounted by attention to already-selected positions weighted by their uncertainty, and appends it while the sampler's admissibility rule holds. For Top-k the rule is |S| ≤ k, so the number of tokens per step and the NFE are the same as plain Top-k. α = 40 is used everywhere (chosen once on LLaDA HumanEval, Appendix D). Accessing the attention requires disabling FlashAttention in the last layer only.

Evaluation uses lm-eval-harness 0.4.8 (few-shot seed 1234): GSM8K 8-shot (generation length 256), MATH500 4-shot, MBPP 3-shot, HumanEval 0-shot (length 512), temperature 0, with LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base. Top-k decoding unmasks exactly k tokens per step, giving NFE = length / k; k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}.
official.claim: With LLaDA-8B-Base and fixed Top-k decoding at k = 8 (identical NFE: 32 for GSM8K, 64 for the others), Top-k+AD beats confidence Top-k on all four benchmarks: GSM8K 42.46 vs 22.67, HumanEval 20.12 vs 5.49, MATH500 19.20 vs 3.40, MBPP 25.20 vs 7.00.
official.claim_caption: Table 19: Results on LLaDA-8B-Base with Top-k stopping rule. Each cell reports score on the first line and average NFE over samples on the second line. For GSM8K and MATH500, score is accuracy; for HumanEval and MBPP, score is Pass@1.

title: Express Language Modeling

official.background: Exact causal attention costs time quadratic in sequence length and, during decoding, a KV cache that grows linearly with the number of generated tokens. This is a bottleneck for reasoning models, which generate thousands of tokens per question. KV cache compression methods (StreamingLLM, SnapKV, ExpectedAttention, KeyDiff, Knorm) keep only a subset of key-value pairs, but mostly lack guarantees on the attention output. Thinning-based approximations such as Thinformer have strong guarantees, but only for unmasked (non-causal) attention.
official.method:
Express is a meta-procedure that turns a halving algorithm (one that picks half of a set of points while preserving kernel averages) into a streaming, updatable weighted cache of bounded size (at most 6·n_out for target size n_out = 2^h). The first n_out key-value pairs are stored exactly; later tokens arrive in batches of 2^m·n_out that are uniformly subsampled and then thinned to n_out with COMPRESS2 (a generalization of the COMPRESS algorithm of Shetty et al. that applies the halving algorithm to small groups of geometrically increasing size); whenever the cache reaches 4·n_out it is halved twice. Thinformer Express uses kernel halving with the key-value attention kernel of Thinformer (Eq. 3) as the halving algorithm, and each new query attends over the new token plus the weighted cache (weights enter both numerator and denominator of softmax attention). Defaults are inflation factor m = 2⌊h/2⌋ and δ = 1/2, plus 32 exact sink tokens and a 32-token recent window.

For memory-constrained decoding, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B generates solutions to the 500 MATH-500 problems (temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, max_new_tokens 32768), graded with the PRM800K grader. Prompt keys and values are computed exactly; the approximation is applied only during decoding, in all 32 layers. Thinformer Express is swept over h ∈ {6, 7, 8, 10, 12}; baselines (from kvpress 0.3.0, with the batch-to-online conversion of Devoto et al. except for StreamingLLM) are swept over target cache sizes {250, 500, 1k, 1.5k, 2k, 3k, 4k}. Curves plot mean accuracy against realized mean cache size: for each threshold and problem, the configuration with the largest realized cache size below the threshold is used.
official.claim: On MATH-500 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, at a mean KV cache size of about 500 Thinformer Express reaches about 0.79 accuracy vs. about 0.70 for the best baseline (ExpectedAttention), 0.68 for SnapKV and 0.63 for KeyDiff; at about 750 it reaches about 0.85 vs. about 0.79; and it retains 99% of exact-attention accuracy (about 0.90) with 61% of the cache.

On competition-level MATH-500 problems that benefit from step-by-step reasoning, Thinformer Express improves both the cache size-accuracy trade-off (left) and time-accuracy trade-off (right) of long-form decoding. Error bands display ±1 standard error across all 500 benchmark questions.

title: AVIS: Adaptive Test-Time Scaling for Vision–Language Models

official.background: Vision-language models improve on reasoning benchmarks when they use chain-of-thought and test-time scaling such as self-consistency over several sampled rollouts, but this multiplies inference cost. Images and videos also produce long visual-token prefixes that dominate prefill cost. The paper treats inference compute as two coupled knobs: how many visual tokens go to the language model (Visual Context Scaling, VCS) and how many reasoning rollouts are sampled (Visual Reasoning Scaling, VRS). It asks whether choosing both per query can beat fixed settings at the same compute.
official.method:
AVIS runs on Qwen2.5-VL-7B in CoT mode (<think>/<answer> format). For VCS it uses adaptive Key Diversity Visual (KDV) pruning before LLM prefill. Each visual token gets a score r_i equal to minus the head-averaged cosine similarity between its normalized attention key and that head's mean normalized key. Tokens with r_i >= -cos(tau), tau = pi/4, are kept, which prunes about 75% of visual tokens on average with a per-sample ratio. For VRS it uses self-consistency with majority voting over K rollouts (greedy decoding for K=1; temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.9 for K>1). All rollouts share one prefill and KV cache.

K in {1,3,5,7} is chosen per query by a small difficulty predictor: 1D Conv–GroupNorm–SiLU layers over the visual token embeddings, then global average pooling and an MLP. It is trained to predict whether the base model is right on at least 50% of 10 rollouts, on a curated calibration set of 4,000 image and 1,000 video multiple-choice questions. A fixed non-monotonic binning maps the predicted solvability p̂ to K: 1, 5, 7, 5, 3, 1 across six bins. The bin edges are set once on the calibration set to meet the compute budget. FLOPs are reported relative to Vanilla (no pruning, K=1), and evaluation uses VLMEvalKit.
official.claim: At roughly matched compute (~0.42–0.46× Vanilla FLOPs), AVIS on Qwen2.5-VL-7B scores higher than both fixed configurations (ρ=0.6, K=1 and ρ=0.85, K=5) on all six benchmarks. Its margins over the better fixed configuration are MathVista 68.1 vs 66.6, MathVerse 58.9 vs 56.5, MME 2364 vs 2311, CVBench 73.1 vs 71.4, BLINK 56.7 vs 54.5 and TreeBench 37.5 vs 36.8.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Matched-FLOPs comparison. We compare AVIS against fixed configurations chosen to approximate its average compute budget (∼45% of Vanilla FLOPs).
