title: Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking in Masked Diffusion Language Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (absolute accuracies in Figure 1, page 5; binomial SE bands in Figure 8, page 15)

official.background: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) such as LLaDA and Dream generate text by progressively unmasking tokens, several per step, which promises faster inference than autoregressive decoding. Once a token is unmasked it cannot be revised, so early mistakes propagate. Training-free 'remasking' methods (WINO, Saber, COVER) revert low-confidence tokens back to the mask state and report accuracy and speed gains, but mostly against fixed-K high-confidence sampling, at single operating points, and at large block lengths where confidence-based unmasking is known to degrade. This paper asks whether remasking still helps when compared against a tuned confidence-threshold unmasker (Fast-dLLM) along the full accuracy-compute frontier.
official.method:
Generation is zero-shot with length 256 and greedy decoding (temperature 0), semi-autoregressive with block length BL in {32, 128}, on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, evaluated on GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval and MBPP. Fast-dLLM unmasks every masked position in the active block whose confidence exceeds a threshold lambda1 (plus the single most confident position as fallback). WINO uses the same unmasking rule but appends a block of 'shadow' mask tokens (one per active-block position, same positional embedding, blocked from attending to the original token) so the shadow output approximates a leave-one-out re-prediction; already-unmasked tokens whose shadow confidence for the current token falls below lambda2 = 0.8 are remasked, with a loop-guard that limits remasks to |U_{t+1}| - 1. Saber and COVER use their official implementations with default hyperparameters.

Pareto frontiers of accuracy vs. NFEs are traced by sweeping lambda1 in {0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} (Fast-dLLM, WINO, COVER) or Saber's remasking budget in {2, 4, 8}. Table 1 reports, for each method, its best accuracy along its frontier minus Fast-dLLM's best accuracy at the same block length.
official.claim: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct with greedy decoding, WINO's best accuracy differs from Fast-dLLM's best by at most 1.22 points on all four benchmarks at BL=32 (+0.60 GSM8K, -0.20 MATH-500, +1.22 HumanEval, +0.00 MBPP), but improves on GSM8K and MATH-500 by +3.64 and +3.20 at BL=128, where WINO still stays below Fast-dLLM at BL=32.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Difference in top accuracy, Δ (%), between each remasking method and Fast-dLLM, each evaluated at its optimal point along its Pareto frontier (setup of Figures 1 and 7).
official.metric: Difference in top accuracy (percentage points) along each method's Pareto frontier, remasking method minus Fast-dLLM; higher favors remasking. Greedy decoding, single run, no seed error bars; Figure 8 shows +/-1 binomial standard error of test-set accuracy.
official.comparison: WINO (and Saber, COVER) vs. Fast-dLLM unmasking alone, each at its best point over the same lambda1 sweep, at BL=32 and BL=128
official.falsification_criterion: At BL=32 on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, WINO's best accuracy beats Fast-dLLM's best by more than ~2 binomial SEs on one or more benchmarks (e.g. >2.3 points on GSM8K); or at BL=128 WINO's GSM8K/MATH-500 gain over Fast-dLLM disappears (<1 point); or WINO at BL=128 matches or exceeds Fast-dLLM at BL=32 in top accuracy.

title: Strategic Decision Support for AI Agents
claim_source: Figure 2, page 3 (full per-pair curves in Figure 4, page 10, and Figure 5, page 25)

official.background: LLM agents increasingly act on behalf of users and can draw on costly support: asking a human, gathering more evidence, calling a tool, or consulting a stronger model. Calling support every time is wasteful, but skipping it when it would have fixed a wrong answer can be consequential. Agents left to decide for themselves are poorly calibrated about when support will actually help. The paper frames this as minimizing how often support is used while bounding the 'missed-support error': the fraction of instances where support would have materially improved the output but the agent acted alone.
official.method:
Strategic Oversight for Support-seeking (SOS, Algorithm 1) runs online over a stream of inputs. For each input x_t the agent produces an unsupported answer y0, a score s_t in [0,1] is computed, and support is sought with probability 1 if s_t ≥ λ_t and with exploration probability µ otherwise. When support is sought, the supported answer y1 is produced and g_t = 1 if support was beneficial (on WikiSQL/DDXPlus/MATH: y0 wrong and y1 correct). The threshold is updated as λ_{t+1} = λ_t − η·[(g_t a_t / p_t)(1 − p_t)1{s_t < λ_t} − α] and, for parameterized scores, score parameters θ are updated by importance-weighted squared-loss SGD toward g_t ('calibration-on-the-fly'). Score families: Confidence (the black-box signal ĝ_LLM, thresholded as-is with only λ adapted; despite the name, it is elicited alongside y0 as the LLM's self-reported probability that support would lead it to a different, correct answer, so higher means more need for support), Representation (σ(θᵀφ(x)) on a frozen embedding of the prompt x: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, gemini-embedding-2, or, for white-box Qwen-2.5-7B only, the LLM's hidden state at the final input token), and Anchored (σ(logit(ĝ_LLM) + θᵀφ(x))).

The baseline, LLM-decides, lets the agent itself choose whether to seek support after producing y0. Its missed-support rate on each task-model pair is used as SOS's target α, so the comparison is support rate at matched missed-support error. Tasks: DDXPlus (support = follow-up findings and labs), WikiSQL (support = writing and executing SQL on the table), VirtualHome (support = scene-specific object locations), MATH levels 4-5 (support = targeted hints from DeepSeek). Agents: Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o-mini. Per-pair hyperparameters (η, γ, µ, λ0) are in Table 3 of the appendix.
official.claim: With Gemini-2.5-Flash as the agent, SOS with the best learned score reaches a cumulative support rate of 0.27 vs. 0.45 for LLM-decides on WikiSQL (missed-support error 0.41 vs. 0.44) and 0.27 vs. 0.49 on DDXPlus (missed-support error 0.53 vs. 0.52).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Our method invokes decision support substantially less often than an LLM-decides baseline, while matching its error rate. For each of four agentic applications: information gathering (DDXPlus), tool use (WikiSQL), human-in-the-loop planning (VirtualHome), and collaborative human–AI reasoning (MATH), all using Gemini-2.5-Flash, we report two pairs of bars. The left pair (solid) shows the cumulative support rate: the fraction of inputs on which the agent requests external support. The right pair (hatched) shows the cumulative missed support error rate: cases where support would have materially improved the output but was not requested. In each pair, the left bar is the LLM baseline (the agent deciding for itself when to ask for support) and the right bar is our best learned method.
official.metric: Cumulative support rate (fraction of inputs on which support is requested, lower is better) at the end of the stream, at matched cumulative missed-support error (fraction of g = 1 instances where support was not requested). Single run; no seeds, error bars or confidence intervals reported. Values are printed on the bars.
official.comparison: SOS (best score variant: Representation-Gemini on WikiSQL, Anchored-MiniLM on DDXPlus per Figure 4 labels) vs. LLM-decides (the agent choosing for itself whether to seek support), with SOS's target α set to LLM-decides' missed-support rate on that task-model pair.
official.falsification_criterion: Running SOS (Representation or Anchored score with calibration-on-the-fly) on WikiSQL or DDXPlus with Gemini-2.5-Flash at α equal to LLM-decides' missed-support rate gives a final support rate not clearly below LLM-decides (e.g. a gap under ~0.08 instead of ~0.18-0.22), or gives the reduction only with a missed-support error clearly above LLM-decides'.

title: M*: A Modular, Extensible, Serving System for Multimodal Models

official.background: Modern multimodal models (unified image models like BAGEL, omni models like Qwen3-Omni, speech LMs, VLAs, world models) are built from several heterogeneous components (encoders, transformer backbones, flow/diffusion heads, audio codecs) that different requests traverse along different paths, often with non-autoregressive loops, internal parallelism and streaming between components. LLM serving systems such as vLLM and SGLang assume a single autoregressive loop, and their multimodal extensions (vLLM-Omni, SGLang-Omni) model the network as a flat DAG of stages, which cannot express loops across stages or parallelism inside a stage and only allows placement per stage. This limits performance and requires per-model glue code.
official.method:
M* represents a model as a directed computation graph of components plus a finite set of named 'Walks' (subgraphs for phases such as prefill or decode), built from Sequential, Parallel, Loop and DynamicLoop primitives and streaming edges with chunk policies. A request is a series of Walks chosen by a per-model state machine. The runtime (HTTP server, a Conductor tracking per-request Walk state, one single-process Worker per GPU) executes nodes with a FlashInfer paged-attention KV-cache engine or a stateless engine, both supporting continuous batching, CUDA-graph replay and torch.compile; workers schedule batch N+1 asynchronously while batch N runs.

For Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct, the Thinker streams hidden states to the Talker (FixedChunkPolicy, K=1) and the Talker streams codec frames to Code2Wav (LeftContextChunkPolicy). The deployment is disaggregated over 2 H200 GPUs: Thinker on one rank, Talker+Code2Wav colocated on the other. The authors attribute the gain to running the whole Talker (including the multi-token code-predictor loop) as one CUDA graph (vLLM-Omni disables CUDA graphs for the code predictor) and to colocating Talker and Code2Wav in one process (both baselines use separate processes per stage). The benchmark is the Seed-TTS evaluation set, max_tokens=256, greedy decoding on all sub-models, system prompt matching vLLM-Omni's official example, batch sizes B in {1, 4, 8, 16, 32}, 3-5 warmup requests then 10-160 timed requests in offline waves of B.
official.claim: Serving Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B text-to-speech on Seed-TTS over 2 H200s at batch size 16, M* reaches about 88 audio-seconds per wall-clock second versus about 32 for vLLM-Omni and 22 for SGLang-Omni (2.7x and 4.0x), with p50 real-time factor 0.17 versus 0.46 and 0.74.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Qwen3-Omni Seed-TTS, 2-GPU. (a) RTF (lower is better). (b) Audio throughput (higher is better).
official.metric: Audio throughput (audio seconds generated per wall-clock second, higher is better) and per-request real-time factor (processing wall time / generated audio duration, p50 bars with p95 hatched, lower is better). Values are printed on the plot; no error bars, seeds or run-to-run variance are reported.
official.comparison: M* vs. vLLM-Omni (vllm v0.21.0) and SGLang-Omni (commit 4a3960) on the same model, benchmark, hardware (2x H200, Thinker / Talker+Code2Wav disaggregated) and batch sizes
official.falsification_criterion: With the same model, Seed-TTS inputs, greedy decoding and 2-GPU disaggregated placement, M*'s audio throughput at B=16 is less than about 2x vLLM-Omni's, or its p50 RTF is not clearly below vLLM-Omni's across batch sizes.

title: The Hidden Power of Scaling Factor in LoRA Optimization

official.background: LoRA fine-tunes a frozen weight matrix through a low-rank update ΔW = (α/r)·BA. In practice the scaling factor α is set by rank-tied heuristics (α = r or α = 2r) and is treated as interchangeable with the learning rate η, since both appear to scale the step size. Practitioners also report that LoRA needs learning rates about 10× larger than full fine-tuning (FFT). If α and η actually play different roles in optimization, the usual heuristics leave performance unused and add extra hyperparameter search.
official.method:
The authors do supervised fine-tuning of Llama 3-1B on a 100k-example subset of Tulu 3 (max length 1024 tokens) for one epoch with AdamW and batch size 32, using LoRA on the model. Fit quality is measured as the expected negative log-likelihood (eval loss) on 10k held-out Tulu 3 examples. Starting from a common baseline (η_FFT = 2×10⁻⁵, the best FFT learning rate, and α₀ = 16), they trace two scaling paths for each rank r ∈ {1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256}: η-scaling, L(r, m·η_FFT, α₀), and α-scaling, L(r, η_FFT, m·α₀), sweeping the multiplier m from 1 up to several hundred.

The claim compares the minimum eval loss along each path at a fixed rank. The paper's method, LoRA-α, follows from this result: it sets α = 256·√r (Variant I, for LLMs) or α = √r/σ_A (Variant II, analytic) and keeps the FFT learning rate.
official.claim: For LoRA fine-tuning of Llama 3-1B on Tulu 3 at rank 256, increasing α at the fixed FFT learning rate (2×10⁻⁵) reaches a minimum eval loss of about 0.74, while increasing the learning rate by the same multipliers at α=16 bottoms out at about 0.80; α-scaling reaches lower minimum loss than η-scaling at every rank shown.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Hyperparameter analysis of Llama 3-1B on the Tulu 3 dataset. (a) Evaluation loss as a function of the learning rate η across different ranks r and scaling factors α. Gray lines denote linear fits of the minimum loss for each (r, α). Increasing α lowers the optimal loss and shifts η* downward. (b) Scaling paths defined in Eq. (2) relative to the baseline (η_FFT = 2 × 10⁻⁵, α₀ = 16), where η_FFT denotes the optimal FFT learning rate. Varying α reaches lower-loss regimes that are inaccessible via η-tuning alone. (c) Optimal scaling factor α* as a function of rank r, evaluated at η_FFT. The observed sublinear trend and large magnitude of α challenge conventional scaling heuristics.
official.metric: Eval loss (per-token NLL on a 10k-example Tulu 3 proxy set), lower is better; minimum over the multiplier sweep. Single run per configuration; no error bars or seeds reported. Values read off the plot are approximate (±0.01).

title: Magnifying What Matters: Attention-Guided Adaptive Rendering for Visual Text Comprehension

official.background: Visual Text Comprehension (VTC), also called optical context compression, renders long text into images so that a vision-language model (VLM) reads it as visual tokens, giving roughly 3x or more token compression compared with feeding the raw text. Existing VTC pipelines render text with fixed, content-agnostic typography. The paper reports that VLMs often attend to the correct evidence region in their middle-to-late layers even when they answer wrongly, and that enlarging the ground-truth evidence on the page fixes many failures. This suggests that the model's own attention could be used to decide what to magnify.
official.method:
AGAR (Attention-Guided Adaptive Rendering) is a training-free wrapper with two forward passes. The context is rendered at a 9 px base font, together with a word-to-bounding-box map. One forward pass of the VLM on (page image, question) extracts the post-softmax attention from the last query token to every image patch. This attention is averaged over heads and over the upper half of decoder layers ([a, b] = [0.5, 1.0]), and the top-K patches are taken (K = 8 for single-page short-form QA). Every rendered word whose box overlaps a selected patch is marked, and the character spans of those words are merged.

The page is then re-rendered with only those spans at 1.5x font size, with all other layout unchanged, and the VLM answers from the new page. Its first-pass answer is discarded. Weights and prompt are unchanged. Baselines use the same backbone (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct): Plain VQA on the original page; Random, which magnifies K random patches; Uniform, which scales the whole page font to match AGAR's visual-token count; and VQA emphasis methods adapted to VTC (VEA-Br, VEA-Con, CGR, VAR, AGLA).
official.claim: On single-page HotpotQA (distractor mode, 7,404 validation samples) rendered as images for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, AGAR reaches 46.9 F1 / 34.3 EM vs. 39.7 / 29.2 for Plain VQA and 41.8 / 30.9 for the best baseline (Random F1, VEA-Con EM), a +5.1 F1 margin.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Short-form single-page QA on Qwen3-VL-8B. Each cell shows the metric followed by its relative change (%) vs. Plain VQA. Avg. text tokens ≈ 805 (∼3× compression).
official.metric: F1 and EM (higher is better) on the official validation split; single run, no error bars or seeds reported

title: Learning-Augmented Approximation for Unrelated-Machines Makespan Scheduling

official.background: Makespan minimization on unrelated machines (R||Cmax) assigns n jobs to m machines, where job j takes p_ij on machine i, so that the maximum machine load is as small as possible. It is NP-hard: the classical Lenstra-Shmoys-Tardos (LST) LP-rounding algorithm gives a 2-approximation, and going below 3/2 is NP-hard. (1+ε)-approximation schemes exist only for a fixed number of machines and are exponential in m. Learning-augmented algorithms use a (possibly wrong) prediction of part of an optimal solution to get near-optimal results when the prediction is good, while keeping a worst-case guarantee when it is bad.
official.method:
The algorithm receives a predicted assignment for the 'heavy' jobs (processing time > εT for a target makespan T); jobs may be left unpredicted. For each critical threshold T, the inner layer fixes the predicted heavy assignments, enumerates every augmentation adding at most K extra heavy assignments (search budget K), solves a residual LP for the remaining jobs over a range of edge thresholds τ, and rounds with Shmoys-Tardos. The outer layer runs this over all critical thresholds, adds the LST 2-approximation schedule as a candidate, and returns the best schedule found. False negatives (heavy jobs left unpredicted) can be recovered by the K-search; false positives (heavy jobs fixed to the wrong machine) cannot.

Experiments: m = 10 machines, n = 100 jobs, p_ij i.i.d. Uniform[1, 100]; OPT computed with OR-Tools CP-SAT; LPs solved with HiGHS via SciPy; ε = 0.01. Predictions are the heavy assignments of an optimal schedule with a fraction ρ− (swept over 0 to 1 in steps of 0.001) of them removed (false negatives); the x-axis is the resulting error measure R−_OPT/OPT. The metric is Cmax/OPT for K = 0, 1, 2 and for the LST 2-approximation, averaged over 30 seeds.
official.claim: On m = 10, n = 100 uniform instances with false-negative prediction errors, increasing the search budget K lowers the makespan: K = 2 stays exactly optimal (Cmax/OPT = 1.00) up to R−/OPT ≈ 0.14 and reaches only ≈ 1.04 at R−/OPT ≈ 0.37, while K = 0 rises to ≈ 1.15 and K = 1 to ≈ 1.06 (LST 2-approximation ≈ 1.26).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Numerical results. (a) and (b) show the change in makespan as the false-negative and false-positive rates are varied, respectively. title: From Uncertain Judgments to Calibrated Rankings: Conformal Elo Estimation for LLM Evaluation

official.background: LLM-as-a-judge leaderboards are a cheap substitute for human preference campaigns like Chatbot Arena, but judge verdicts are biased and noisy, and the Elo ratings they produce may not match the human Elo scale. Standard practice converts each judged battle into a hard win/tie/loss label before fitting a Bradley–Terry (BT) model, which throws away how strongly the judge preferred one answer. The paper asks whether keeping that strength-of-preference information makes judge-derived Elo ratings closer to human Elo ratings for models the calibration never saw, and then wraps the estimates in conformal intervals.
official.method:
On LMArena 100K (55 models), each of 8 open-weight judges scores ~25,000 battles: each completion is graded 1–10 on six criteria, the per-criterion differences are averaged, and the score difference s(x) is averaged over both presentation orders. Hard-Elo fits a regularised BT model (λ = 0.01) to labels y ∈ {0, 0.5, 1} given by the sign of s (a sign flip on swapping gives a tie). Soft-Elo uses the same BT fit but with the soft target σ(β s(x)), where β is fit by maximum likelihood to human non-tie labels on battles not involving the held-out model.

Evaluation is leave-one-model-out (Algorithm 1, Appendix A.8): for each held-out model m, fit anchor strengths on battles not involving m, then fit only θ_m on m's battles with anchors frozen; the human reference Elo for m is computed by the same two-step procedure with human labels. Metric is mean absolute error between judge-derived and human-derived Elo (Elo = 1500 + 400/ln10 · θ) over the 55 held-out models, per judge.
official.claim: On LMArena 100K with leave-one-model-out evaluation over 55 models, replacing hard win/tie/loss labels with calibrated soft targets σ(β*·s) lowers held-out Elo MAE against human Elo for all 8 judges, by 39–73% (mean 45.9 → 17.9 Elo; e.g. DeepSeek-V3.2 63.4 → 17.1, Qwen3-32B 27.5 → 16.7), while Spearman ρ changes by at most ±0.012.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Hard-Elo vs. Soft-Elo results for held-out Elo estimation across the eight judges, sorted by MAE reduction. β* is the cross-fold mean defined in Eq. 6. ∆ρ reports the change in Spearman rank correlation relative to Hard-Elo.
official.metric: Held-out Elo mean absolute error vs. human-derived Elo (lower is better), over 55 leave-one-model-out folds; no ± reported in Table 2 (single run, deterministic given cached annotations). Appendix D.3: over 200 bootstrap refits of the human reference, Soft-Elo has lower MAE in all 200 (mean reduction 27.25 Elo, 95% range [23.26, 30.83]).
official.comparison: Soft-Elo (BT on σ(β*s) targets) vs. Hard-Elo (BT on ternary labels), same judge annotations, same BT model and regularisation, same held-out protocol, for each of 8 judges.
official.falsification_criterion: Using the released judge scores and the LOO protocol, Soft-Elo fails to reduce held-out Elo MAE for most judges, or the mean MAE reduction is far below the reported 45.9 → 17.9 (e.g. Soft-Elo mean MAE above ~30 Elo), or Spearman ρ drops by more than ~0.02.

title: Towards more general control of diffusion models using Jeffrey Guidance
claim_source: Figure 2(b), page 7 (Jeffrey guidance); Figure 7, page 17 (standard-guidance baseline); numbers in Section 4.1.1 text

official.background: Guidance lets a pretrained diffusion model be steered at sampling time without retraining, but it usually targets a single condition (e.g. a class) rather than a whole target distribution over some feature. Jeffrey's rule of conditioning updates a joint distribution so that the marginal over a feature y matches a prescribed target p*(y), while keeping p(x | y) fixed and staying as close as possible (in KL) to the original model. This gives a principled way to steer a generator toward a distribution of features, for example making the generator's Inception-embedding distribution match the training data, which is exactly what FID measures.
official.method:
For a deterministic feature y = u(x), the Jeffrey-updated model is p*(x) = p(x) rho(u(x)) with density ratio rho(y) = q_data(y) / q_theta(y). Here u is the Inception network used by FID, and rho is estimated by probabilistic classification: a single fully connected (linear/logistic) layer is trained with cross-entropy for 15 epochs (lr 1e-3) to separate Inception embeddings of training images from those of the model's own generated samples, and rho = D/(1-D). The ratio estimator never sees the test set.

At sampling, the guided score is s_theta(x_t, t) + lambda * grad_{x_t} log rho(u(x0_hat(x_t, t))), where x0_hat is the Tweedie estimate of the clean image. Guidance is applied only for timesteps t <= delta (delta = 10 means only the last denoising steps). The CIFAR-10 model is the public DDIM checkpoint (ermongroup/ddim), sampled with DDIM, 100 steps, eta = 0.2. The baseline 'standard guidance' (Appendix D.2, Figure 7) uses ancestral sampling: draw a target embedding y from the training embeddings, then guide with grad log N(y; u(x0_hat), I), with lambda controlling the Gaussian variance. FID is computed on 10k samples against the CIFAR-10 test set, and on 50k samples against the training set.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with the public DDIM checkpoint, Jeffrey guidance on Inception embeddings (best setting around delta = 10, lambda = 5) lowers test-set FID (10k samples) from about 9.76 unguided to about 6.71, whereas the ancestral-sampling standard-guidance baseline reaches only about 8.7 at its best setting.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: FID as a function of the guidance scale lambda for different values of delta. On CIFAR-10, guidance improves over the unguided baseline (lambda = 0) on both train and test sets for appropriate choices of (lambda, delta). We observe that larger values of delta, corresponding to guidance applied earlier in the diffusion process through x0_hat, require smaller guidance scales to remain stable, whereas smaller delta allows for stronger guidance as it is applied closer to the end of the trajectory. Similar trends are observed on FFHQ, showing that the behavior extends to higher-resolution data.
official.metric: FID on CIFAR-10 test set (10k generated samples), lower is better. Single run per setting; no error bars on the test-set curves. Bootstrap 95% CIs (10 resamples of 49k) are shown only for the train-set FID in Figure 6 and are described as small.
official.comparison: Jeffrey guidance (best lambda, delta) vs. unguided sampling (lambda = 0) vs. the authors' standard-guidance baseline (best lambda, delta), all with the same CIFAR-10 DDIM checkpoint and sampler
official.falsification_criterion: With the same checkpoint, sampler and evaluation, no (lambda, delta) setting of Jeffrey guidance brings 10k-sample test FID below about 8 (i.e. it fails to beat the best standard-guidance FID of about 8.7 by a clear margin), or the gain over the unguided ~9.8 disappears.

title: Existence Precedes Value: Joint Modeling of Observational Existence and Evolving States in Time Series Forecasting
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (per-dataset results in Table 7, pages 18-22)

official.background: Real-world time series are often incomplete and irregular: sensors go dormant, transmissions are delayed, and sampling is event-driven. Impute-then-forecast pipelines treat missing values as defects, and continuous-time models (Neural ODEs, continuous-time graph networks) handle irregular history but assume that the timestamps of future valid observations are known at inference time. This paper argues that whether a future observation will exist at all is itself a forecasting target, and proposes predicting future observability jointly with future values.
official.method:
Timeflies takes the history X, a missing mask M (1 = observed) and a missing-interval sequence I = log(1 + distance to the last missing event) and predicts future values Y and observation probabilities p_obs over horizon H. A value stream and an observation stream are patch-embedded (non-overlapping patches, mask-aware normalization using only observed entries). A patch reliability score from the mean mask and mean interval gates how much observation information enters the value tokens; in the value-stream attention the map is Softmax(A_val) + A_rel * Softmax(A_obs), with A_rel = sqrt(rho rho^T). A dual head outputs observation logits from both streams and a value forecast Y = Z_val + p_obs * Z_obs. The loss is MSE on observed future positions plus eta (= 1.0) times focal BCE on the observation labels.

Evaluation is on the Shadow benchmark: 15 GIFT-Eval public datasets plus 16 proprietary hourly e-commerce datasets with natural missingness, split 80/10/10, with series grouped into No (0%), Low (0-10%], Medium (10-40%] and High (>40%) missingness regimes and short/medium/long horizons. Baselines (PatchTST, iTransformer, Crossformer, FEDformer, OLinear, WPMixer, TimeMixer, DLinear, FACT, MICN) receive zero-filled inputs plus observation masks. The joint metric OVJE = -(1/T) sum_t [o_t log(p_t q_t) + (1 - o_t) log(1 - p_t)], with q_t = exp(-sMAPE_t), i.e. Bernoulli NLL of the observation forecast plus the sMAPE on observed positions; lower is better. Scores are averaged over horizons within each dataset, then over datasets within each regime.
official.claim: On the Shadow benchmark, Timeflies gets the lowest OVJE in every missingness regime: 0.611 vs. 0.762 for the best baseline (OLinear) under High missingness, 0.914 vs. 1.176 (FACT) under Medium, 0.762 vs. 0.924 (PatchTST) under Low, and 0.477 vs. 0.639 (FACT) with no missingness; averaged equally over the four regimes it is about 22.5% below FACT.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Forecasting results on Shadow benchmark. For each missing-ratio regime, we first calculate the average of the test metrics across forecasting horizons for each dataset, and then report the arithmetic mean of these scores for all datasets within the same regime. See Tab. 7 for full results.
official.metric: Observation-Value Joint Entropy (OVJE), lower is better; two-stage arithmetic mean (over horizons within a dataset, then over datasets in a regime). Single runs; no error bars, seeds or variance are reported.
official.comparison: Timeflies vs. 10 baselines (FEDformer, PatchTST, Crossformer, iTransformer, DLinear, TimeMixer, OLinear, WPMixer, MICN, FACT) adapted to the missing-aware setting with zero-filled inputs and masks, on the same Shadow splits
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running on Shadow (or on its public GIFT-Eval part), some baseline matches or beats Timeflies' OVJE in a regime, or Timeflies' margin over the best baseline in the High and Medium regimes shrinks to a few percent or reverses across seeds.

title: Reward Modeling for Multi-Agent Orchestration

official.background: LLM multi-agent systems increasingly rely on a trained orchestrator: an LLM that writes a plan specifying the sub-agents, their roles and how they interact, which other LLM agents then execute. Training such orchestrators with RL (e.g. MAS-Orchestra, GRPO with a final-answer reward) is very expensive, because every reward requires executing the full multi-agent rollout. Test-time scaling via majority voting or trajectory-level judges also requires running every candidate to completion. A reward model that scores the orchestration plan alone, before any sub-agent runs, could make both selection and training far cheaper.
official.method:
Orch-RM is a Bradley-Terry reward model r(x, z) over (query, orchestration plan) pairs. It is initialized from Skywork-Reward-LLaMA-3.1-8B and trained per domain on self-supervised preference pairs built from the released MAS-Orchestra artifacts. Two kinds of pairs are used: 'specialized over base' (plans from the trained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct MAS-Orchestra orchestrator are preferred over plans from the untrained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 10 samples each per query) and 'correct over incorrect' (plans from MAS-Orchestra training logs whose execution gave a correct vs. an incorrect final answer). The two are mixed per query (12 SoB + 4 CoI pairs in the implementation section).

For test-time scaling, the MAS-Orchestra orchestrator samples N=8 plans per query. Each verifier scores the plans, and only the top-scoring plan is executed by GPT-OSS-120B sub-agents. Accuracy is that plan's final-answer accuracy. Baselines that also score plans only are LLM judges (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4-mini), log-probability, and four off-the-shelf Skywork reward models. The reference points are MAS-Orchestra without verification (= majority vote here) and a trajectory-level GPT-5-mini judge. Test sets: AIME 24&25 (60 problems) and BrowseComp+ (200 questions), plus HotpotQA (200) and GPQA (199, OOD).
official.claim: With best-of-8 selection over MAS-Orchestra orchestration plans, Orch-RM reaches 68.33% on AIME 24&25 and 14.00% on BrowseComp+. This beats MAS-Orchestra without verification (63.33% / 9.50%), its own untrained initialization Skywork-Reward-LLaMA-3.1-8B (61.67% / 11.50%), and every other orchestration-level verifier (best: 66.67% on AIME, GPT-5.4-mini judge; 12.00% on BrowseComp+, Skywork-V2-Llama-3.2-3B), at the same 2.38M / 8.26M verification tokens as the Skywork baselines.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance of Orchestration-Level Automatic Verification Methods for MAS Test-Time Scaling. We compare Orch-RM primarily against orchestration-level verification methods (bottom two blocks). Trajectory-level baselines are included for reference, including MAS-Orchestra without verification as a lower bound (LB), and an oracle reward model that always selects the best answer as an upper bound (UB). Acc.: Best-of-N accuracy (N=8 across all benchmarks), reported in percentages. #Tok (M): Total number of tokens (input + output) used for verification. Boldface and underline indicate the best and the second best results among orchestration-level methods.
official.metric: Best-of-N accuracy (%) with N=8, higher is better; single run, no error bars reported. #Tok (M) = total verification tokens.
official.comparison: Orch-RM vs. no verification (MAS-Orchestra / majority vote), the untrained Skywork-Reward-LLaMA-3.1-8B it is fine-tuned from, other Skywork reward models, log P, and LLM-as-a-judge on plans (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4-mini), all selecting among the same 8 sampled orchestrations.
official.falsification_criterion: On AIME 24&25 or BrowseComp+, Orch-RM's best-of-8 accuracy does not exceed both the unverified MAS-Orchestra baseline and the untrained Skywork-Reward-LLaMA-3.1-8B selector. Alternatively, averaged over several resamplings of the 8 candidate plans, the gap is within the run-to-run spread.

title: SpatialClaw: Rethinking Action Interface for Agentic Spatial Reasoning

official.background: Vision-language models still struggle with spatial reasoning: judging metric distances, camera and object motion, viewpoint changes and relative directions from images or video. A common fix is to give the VLM specialist perception tools (segmenters, depth and pose estimators). This paper argues that the action interface through which those tools are invoked matters as much as the tools themselves. Existing spatial agents either write one complete program and run it once (single-pass code), or call named tools one at a time with typed JSON arguments (structured tool-calls). The first cannot react to intermediate results, and the second cannot freely combine tool outputs with arbitrary numerical code.
official.method:
SpatialClaw is a training-free agent in which the VLM writes one Python cell per step, executed in a persistent IPython kernel pre-loaded with the input frames (at most 32, long edge 768 px), metadata, perception tools (tools.Reconstruct wrapping Depth Anything 3 DA3Nested-Giant-Large, which gives depth, intrinsics, extrinsics and point maps; tools.SAM3 for text/point/box-prompted masks), utility wrappers, numpy/scipy/matplotlib, a show() function that puts images into the next step's context, a vlm helper for grounding and side questions, and ReturnAnswer(). A separate planner call (no images) writes an analysis plan first. Each step's stdout, condensed tracebacks, new-variable summaries and shown images are fed back. The loop runs for up to N_max = 30 steps, and the same system prompt is used for every benchmark.

For the action-interface comparison (Table 2), all variants use Gemma4-31B, the same toolset and the same system prompt, and differ only in response format and the prompt section describing the interface. Single-Pass Code writes one complete program before seeing any execution feedback. Structured Tool-Call keeps the multi-step loop but allows exactly one JSON tool call per step, whose arguments must be literals or previously bound names (no arbitrary Python expressions); the call is translated to Python and run on the same kernel. No-tool is the backbone reasoning in thinking mode without tools. Evaluation covers 20 benchmarks, capped at 1,000 samples per benchmark (random subset with a fixed seed). Scoring is per-sample accuracy for categorical questions and mean relative accuracy (MRA) for numerical ones, averaged per benchmark.
official.claim: With a Gemma4-31B backbone and identical tools and system prompt, the multi-step persistent-kernel code interface (SpatialClaw) averages 59.9% over 20 spatial benchmarks vs. 56.7% for structured JSON tool-calls and 55.2% for single-pass code, with the largest gaps on multi-view tasks (MindCube 72.8 vs. 62.4 vs. 57.5; MMSI 51.3 vs. 43.0 vs. 42.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Action interface comparison. All variants use the same toolset. "Structured Tool-Call" exposes the tools through a JSON command interface (Chen et al., 2026). "Single-Pass Code" generates one complete program before execution. (Table 3, cropped alongside: Comparison with other spatial agents. All use the same Gemma4-31B backbone model. *: video or multi-image not supported.)
official.metric: Per-benchmark score (accuracy for categorical questions, MRA for numerical ones, unweighted mean over samples), higher is better; average is the unweighted mean over 20 benchmarks. Single run; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: SpatialClaw (multi-step code in a persistent kernel) vs. Structured Tool-Call (one JSON tool call per step) vs. Single-Pass Code vs. No-tool, all with Gemma4-31B and the same toolset
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the three interfaces with Gemma4-31B on the same benchmarks, SpatialClaw does not beat Structured Tool-Call on MindCube and MMSI by several points (e.g. the MindCube gap falls below ~5 points), or its 20-benchmark average is not above both baselines.

title: Learning the Context of Errors: Black-Box Online Adaptation of Time Series Foundation Models
claim_source: Figure 4, page 8 (ORCA per-cell values in Table 1, page 7; seed spread in Table 9, page 26)

official.background: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as Chronos-2, Moirai-2, TiRex, TimesFM-2.5 and Sundial forecast zero-shot, but streaming data drifts and there is a gap between pre-training data and any specific deployment, so online adaptation helps. Most existing online adaptation methods need white-box access (fine-tuning weights) or grey-box access (gradients through the frozen model). If TSFMs are served as closed APIs, only black-box methods that see inputs and outputs are possible, and the existing ones (ELF, a parallel lightweight forecaster ensemble; δ-Adapter's Ada-Y variant, which corrects outputs from the prediction alone) give small gains.
official.method:
ORCA treats the TSFM as a frozen black box (gradients are disabled; the open-source models simulate an API). A Linear Adapter takes the context C_t = [X_t, Y_t^base] (look-back window L = 520 concatenated with the base model's median forecast), applies moving-average decomposition (kernel 25 for H > 30, 7 otherwise), separate trend and seasonal linear layers, and linear channel mixing, and outputs a residual ΔŶ_t; Y_t^ada = Y_t^base + ΔŶ_t. A Boltzmann Router keeps EMAs (α = 0.2) of the absolute errors of the base and adapted forecasts per channel and mixes them with weight c_t = softmax(-ε/τ), τ = 0.1, giving Y_t^comb.

Training is online: once a horizon's ground truth is fully observed, the snapshot (X_t, Y_t^base, Y_t^GT) goes into a FIFO buffer (3000 snapshots). Every H steps the adapter does 10 AdamW steps (lr 1e-4, batch 256, sampling with exponential decay favouring recent snapshots) on a loss (1/(H·D))(||Y^GT − Y^ada||² + c̄_t ||Y^ada − Y^prior||²), where c̄_t is the channel-mean of the router confidence c_t and Y^prior = Y^base + output of a frozen (stop-gradient) copy of the adapter from the previous cycle; there is a 50-epoch warmup when the buffer first fills. Datasets are split 7:1:2 chronologically and MSE (normalized by a dataset-level scalar) is reported on the test portion for H ∈ {30, 96, 336}. Baselines ELF and δ-Adapter (Ada-Y) are run under the same protocol; the metric is the relative MSE drop versus the vanilla zero-shot TSFM, averaged over horizons, then over 8 datasets × 5 TSFMs.
official.claim: Across 8 datasets (ETTh1/h2/m1/m2, Exchange, Weather, Electricity, Traffic) and 5 frozen TSFMs, averaged over H ∈ {30, 96, 336}, ORCA reduces test MSE versus the zero-shot base model by 6.29% on average, while the black-box baselines ELF and δ-Adapter (Ada-Y) reduce it by only 0.47% and 0.79%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Heatmaps illustrating the relative MSE drop (%) achieved by various online adaptation methods compared to the vanilla zero-shot TSFMs across 8 datasets and 5 base models. Green cells indicate a reduction in MSE (improvement), while red cells indicate an increase in MSE (degradation).
official.metric: Relative MSE drop (%) versus the vanilla zero-shot TSFM (higher is better), averaged over 3 horizons and then over 40 dataset×model cells. Figure 4 reports a single run; Table 9 gives ORCA's spread over seeds 42/43/44 as an overall average of −6.34 ± 0.18 pp (SD across seeds). No seed spread is reported for the baselines.
official.comparison: ORCA vs. black-box online adapters ELF and δ-Adapter (Ada-Y), plus black-box adaptations of DSOF, TAFAS and SOLID, all wrapped around the same frozen TSFMs on the same streaming test split.

title: What Drives Test-Time Adaptation for CLIP? A Controlled Empirical Study from an Update Perspective
claim_source: Table 12 and Table 11 (Appendix F.4-F.5), page 23; summarized in Figure 4(b) and Figure 3(b) on pages 4-5

official.background: CLIP's zero-shot accuracy drops under distribution shift, and many test-time adaptation (TTA) methods for CLIP have been proposed that adapt on the unlabeled test stream. A common family, parameter-based TTA, is often credited to the gradient update itself: for each test image it builds augmented views, keeps the most confident ones, and takes a gradient step on an unsupervised entropy objective. The paper re-implements more than 20 methods in one codebase (TTABC) and asks which part of this pipeline actually produces the gain. Its answer is that the quantity and quality of test-time evidence (how many augmented views there are, and which of them are kept) matter more than how strongly or how long the model is optimized.
official.method:
Two representative parameter-based methods are used with CLIP ViT-B/16 on ImageNet-A (7,500 images, 200 classes): TPT, which tunes 4 learnable text-prompt tokens initialized as 'a photo of a', and TPS, which learns per-class shift vectors added to the text prototypes (prototypes built from templates plus GPT-4 descriptions). For each test image, AugMix produces 63 augmented views plus the original (N = 64). The views are ranked by prediction entropy, the top fraction p is kept, and one SGD step (lr 5e-3) minimizes the marginal entropy of the averaged prediction over the kept views. The parameters are reset after every sample (episodic), and the prediction is made on the original image after the update.

The evidence-quality ablation (Table 12) varies only the selection ratio p in {1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1}, with entropy or maximum-softmax-probability (MSP) as the ranking score. The optimization-depth ablation (Table 11) keeps p = 0.1 and varies only the number of gradient steps per sample from 1 to 20, recording wall-clock time.
official.claim: On ImageNet-A with CLIP ViT-B/16 (64 AugMix views, 1 step), keeping only the top 10% lowest-entropy views instead of all views raises accuracy from 50.75% to 58.47% for TPS (+7.7) and from 49.07% to 52.03% for TPT (+3.0). For TPS this exceeds the gain from going from 1 to 20 gradient steps (58.47% to 59.21%, +0.7).
official.claim_caption: Table 11: Scaling Adaptation Steps. Accuracy (%) and total inference time (seconds) on ImageNet-A as the number of per-sample gradient steps increases. Table 12: Impact of Confidence Filtering Strategies. Top-1 Accuracy (%) of TPT and TPS on ImageNet-A across different view selection ratios (p).
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%) on ImageNet-A, higher is better; single run with a fixed seed and no error bars (the binomial SE over 7,500 images is about 0.6 points)
official.comparison: Same method and backbone, with the view-selection ratio p = 1.0 (all 64 views) vs. p = 0.1 (top 10% by entropy), 1 step; secondarily, 1 vs. 20 adaptation steps at p = 0.1
official.falsification_criterion: With the same setup, entropy-based top-10% filtering improves TPS by less than about 3 points over using all views (or improves TPT by less than about 1.5 points), or going from 1 to 20 steps improves TPS by more than filtering does.

title: Free Heavy-Tailed Lunch for Muon: A Theoretical Justification of Empirical Success
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (full learning-rate grid in Figure 4, page 32)

official.background: Optimisers with matrix-valued updates such as Muon (normalised steepest descent in the spectral norm, with momentum) train Transformers well, but existing convergence theory does not show an advantage over Euclidean methods: the bounds pick up a dimension-dependent norm-equivalence factor and assume bounded-variance noise. Stochastic gradients in language modelling appear heavy-tailed (bounded p-th moments, p < 2). This paper analyses normalised steepest descent with momentum in general norms under heavy-tailed noise stated in the optimiser's own geometry. It shows that Muon reaches nuclear-norm stationarity with an optimal sample complexity whose dimension dependence is milder than that of Euclidean methods. The theory predicts that, among Schatten-r geometries, moving from r = 2 (Euclidean) to larger r should improve training.
official.method:
The algorithm is NSSD-M: momentum m_t = β m_{t-1} + (1-β) g_t, then x_{t+1} = x_t + η · argmin_{||d||≤1} <m_t, d>, with the norm taken as the Schatten-r norm on each weight matrix. r = 2 gives Euclidean normalised SGD with momentum, and r = ∞ gives the spectral geometry of Muon. Intermediate r values are computed with a full SVD. All 2-D parameters except the input and output embeddings are trained with the Schatten-r method; embeddings and all other parameters use AdamW.

The setup is the 70M-parameter Pythia architecture, pre-trained from scratch on FineWeb-Edu for 1.4B tokens (Chinchilla-optimal), with sequence length 2048, batch size 512, β = 0.95 and weight decay 0.1. The learning-rate schedule is WSD with 5% warmup and 20% cooldown. Learning rates are swept over {0.005, 0.0075, 0.01, 0.0125, 0.015, 0.03, 0.06} for each r in {1, 8/7, 4/3, 3/2, 2, 3, 4, 8, ∞}, with seeds 0, 1 and 2. The metric is final perplexity at the best learning rate for each geometry.
official.claim: Pre-training Pythia-70M on 1.4B FineWeb-Edu tokens, with the learning rate tuned for each geometry, the spectral geometry (Muon, r = ∞) reaches a final perplexity of 33.34 ± 0.02, against 40.18 ± 0.09 for Euclidean normalised SGD with momentum (r = 2); both are best at learning rate 0.015. Perplexity improves steeply from r = 1 (88.89) to r = 3 (34.51), then plateaus.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Final perplexity for Schatten-r geometries. Figure 4: Full result grid for the Schatten-r sweep. The value represents the mean final perplexity ± its standard deviation over the seeds 0, 1, 2. Optimal learning rates per geometry are marked with black borders, the overall best result with an orange border.
official.metric: Final perplexity (lower is better); ± is the std over seeds 0, 1 and 2
official.comparison: NSSD-M in Schatten-∞ (Muon) vs. Schatten-2 (Euclidean) geometry, and the trend across r ∈ {1, 8/7, 4/3, 3/2, 2, 3, 4, 8, ∞}. Model, data, token budget and learning-rate grid are the same for every geometry.
official.falsification_criterion: With the learning rate tuned over the same grid, r = ∞ does not beat r = 2 in final perplexity by a margin well above the seed std (for example, the gap is under about 2 perplexity points instead of about 7), or perplexity does not drop sharply from r = 2 to r ≥ 3.

title: RepFusion: Leveraging Multimodal Priors for Denoising in Representation Space
claim_source: Figure 1, page 2 (TextEmbed-RAE 0.57 also in Table 6, page 16)

official.background: Modern text-to-image diffusion systems often use a large language model only as a static text encoder, while a newly trained diffusion transformer (DiT) does all the denoising. Representation autoencoders (RAEs) move diffusion from compressed VAE latents into semantic feature spaces such as CLIP features. These are the same features that multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) already read through an MLP projector. This raises the question of whether a pretrained MLLM can also read noisy versions of those features and give a more useful conditioning signal to the denoiser than text embeddings alone.
official.method:
RepFusion uses a LLaVA-style MLLM (causal 7B LLM + CLIP-L/14 at 336 px, which gives N = 576 visual tokens). The MLLM's own MLP projector is reused to feed the noisy RAE latent z_t (plus a timestep embedding) into the frozen LLM after the caption tokens. The last N hidden states, one per visual token, condition a 1.3B DiT through token-wise AdaLN-Single modulation. Only the projector and the DiT are trained, with a flow-matching (v-prediction) loss in CLIP-feature space and timestep shift alpha = 12. By default the MLLM is rerun at every denoising step. Images are decoded with an RAE ViT-XL decoder.

The TextEmbed baseline uses the same frozen 7B LLM as a static text encoder (Sana-style: last-layer text-token embeddings followed by RMSNorm) to condition a newly initialized 1.3B DiT in the same latent space. All models are pretrained on BLIP-3o 31M for 10 epochs (160k steps, batch 2,048, lr 3e-4, AdamW, cosine schedule) and evaluated on GenEval without SFT. Figure 1 shows each conditioning strategy trained in both a VAE latent space (DC-AE f32) and the RAE (CLIP) space.
official.claim: With the same frozen 7B LLM and a 1.3B DiT trained on the same 31M pairs in RAE (CLIP-feature) space, conditioning the DiT on MLLM outputs computed from the noisy latents (RepFusion) reaches GenEval 0.70, compared with 0.57 for conditioning on static LLM text embeddings (TextEmbed-RAE), a gap of +0.13. In VAE space the gap shrinks to +0.07 (0.54 vs. 0.47).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: GenEval comparison when switching from VAEs to RAEs for three conditioning strategies: TextEmbed (conditioning a DiT with an LLM's last-layer text token embeddings following recent T2I practice), Transfusion, and RepFusion. All three variants in this comparison use a 7B LLM, TextEmbed and RepFusion also use a 1.3B DiT. RepFusion feeds noisy visual representations into a pretrained MLLM and uses the resulting outputs to condition a DiT. It benefits most significantly from the transition, achieving a 30% relative gain (+0.16 absolute improvement), compared to 21% (+0.10) for TextEmbed and 11% (+0.06) for Transfusion.
official.metric: GenEval overall score (higher is better). Single run per configuration; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: RepFusion-RAE vs. TextEmbed-RAE (same 7B LLM, same 1.3B DiT, same data and schedule); Transfusion-RAE (7B, fully trainable) shown as a second reference
official.falsification_criterion: In a matched retraining (same frozen MLLM, same DiT size, same data and steps, RAE space), RepFusion's GenEval is not clearly higher than TextEmbed's, e.g. the gap falls below ~0.05, which is roughly the spread one might expect from seed and sampling noise on GenEval's 553 prompts.

title: Forced Deferral: Manipulating Routing Decisions in Multimodal LLM Cascades
claim_source: Figure 9 (Appendix B), page 14; same pattern for the JS metric in Figure 2a (page 6) and Figure 10

official.background: Serving a large multimodal LLM (MLLM) for every image question is expensive, so providers use cascades: a cheap weak model answers first, and the query is deferred to an expensive strong model only when the weak model's confidence (answer-token probability, perplexity, or sample consistency) falls below a threshold calibrated on clean data. Because the weak model's confidence controls how compute is allocated, a user who wants strong-model answers has an incentive to lower that confidence on purpose. This paper asks whether an image perturbation can force such deferrals without knowing the cascade's confidence metric or threshold.
official.method:
The Forced Deferral Attack (FDA) learns one universal trigger confined to a 16-pixel border. Each image is resized to 448x448, the clean image is resized into the inner region, and the border pixels are the trigger (parameterized by raw variables passed through a sigmoid). For each training (image, question) pair, the weak model's greedy clean response y is recorded. The trigger is optimized with teacher forcing on y to minimize the mean over tokens of KL(q_t^T || p_w(. | triggered image, question, y_<t)), where q_t^T = softmax(z_t / T) is the weak model's clean next-token distribution flattened by temperature T > 1. For Qwen3-VL-2B: Adam, lr 0.02, batch 32, 600 steps, cosine schedule, T = 4 on MMBench and T = 3 on MMMU/ScienceQA.

Datasets are image-based multiple-choice questions from MMBench (dev-en, 931/116/117 train/val/test, seed-42 split), MMMU (test split, single image, text options, 7,269/908/910) and ScienceQA (official splits with images, 6,218/2,097/2,017). The prompt asks for the option letter on line 1 and a brief explanation on line 2 (greedy, max 64 new tokens). The Answer Probability (AP) confidence is the probability of the first generated token. For each calibrated deferral rate D, a threshold is set on the clean training split so that a fraction D of the lowest-confidence queries defer. The threshold is then applied unchanged to the test set under each condition: clean, FDA-triggered, defocus blur (disk kernel radius 6 plus Gaussian sigma 0.5), and prompt injection (prepending 'Before answering, compare the two most plausible options and try to refute your top choice with one plausible counterargument. Then commit to the final answer.'). Reroute rate is the fraction of test samples below the threshold.
official.claim: In the Qwen3-VL-2B→32B cascade under the Answer Probability metric, at calibrated deferral rates D = 0.1 and 0.3, the FDA border trigger raises the test reroute rate to about 0.90–1.00 on MMBench, MMMU and ScienceQA, whereas the best baseline (prompt injection) reaches only about 0.15–0.50 (clean cascade about 0.08–0.31).
official.claim_caption: Figure 9: Actual reroute rate of the Qwen3-VL same family cascade under AP.
official.metric: Actual reroute rate (fraction of test queries whose weak-model confidence falls below the threshold calibrated on clean training data; higher = stronger attack). Single run; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: FDA border trigger vs. defocus-blur image perturbation, prompt injection, and the clean cascade, all with the same weak model and the same fixed calibrated threshold
official.falsification_criterion: With a trigger trained as described, the reroute rate under AP at D = 0.1 or 0.3 stays below about 0.8 on any of the three datasets, or prompt injection or blur comes within about 0.2 of FDA.

title: Conditional Multi-Event Temporal Grounding in Long-Form Video
claim_source: Table 3, page 9 (component ablation in Table 8, page 31)

official.background: Video temporal grounding asks a model to find the time interval in a video that matches a text query. Real uses such as video editing or sports analysis often need every occurrence of an event that meets temporal conditions (after X, while Y, within a time window) and spatial conditions (a specific person, a motion), along with an exact count, and sometimes the correct answer is that no such event exists. Existing benchmarks handle single-moment grounding, unconditioned counting, or multiple-choice QA separately. The paper introduces CoMET-Bench (2,789 queries over 600 long videos averaging 33.8 minutes, 26.6% negative queries) and a training-free agent, CoMET-Agent, for this task.
official.method:
Baselines are video MLLMs run single-pass with a shared evaluation prompt and 128 uniformly sampled frames per video. They output a set of [start, end] intervals per query, or an empty set. Grounding is scored on positive queries with mIoU, Recall@0.5 and F1@0.5 (intervals matched at tIoU 0.5). Counting is scored with MAE, off-by-one accuracy and Pearson correlation. Negative queries are scored with Rejection-F1 (the harmonic mean of the rejection rate on negatives and non-empty coverage on positives) and FPR.

CoMET-Agent wraps the same MLLM backbone in four steps. (1) A Planner agent picks a hyperparameter profile and trims the video if the query names a time window. (2) The video is split into coarse event nodes by change-point detection on DINOv2 frame-similarity features. A Filter agent drops irrelevant nodes, and the remaining nodes are split into action nodes by change-point detection on RAFT optical-flow similarity. Edges between nodes are weighted with Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B. (3) A Verifier agent goes through the candidate action nodes, adds neighbours whose edge weight exceeds a threshold to give more context, checks the query conditions, and writes verified nodes to a Global Memory Bank (summary, timestamps, confidence) with deduplication. (4) An Aggregator agent turns the memory bank into the final intervals and count. Nothing is trained.
official.claim: On CoMET-Bench, CoMET-Agent with a Qwen3-VL-8B backbone raises grounding F1@0.5 from 3.4% (Qwen3-VL-8B single-pass) to 8.8% and Rejection-F1 from 52.1% to 57.4%. With a GPT-5 backbone it raises F1@0.5 from 10.1% to 16.2%.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Main results on CoMET-Bench across three evaluation aspects. Counting: MAE (↓, mean absolute error), OBO (↑, off-by-one accuracy), Pearson (↑, Pearson correlation). Grounding: mIoU (↑), R@0.5 (↑, Recall at tIoU 0.5), F1@0.5 (↑). Negative: Rej.-F1 (↑, harmonic mean of negative-rejection rate and positive-coverage rate), FPR (↓, fraction of negative queries with non-empty prediction). Bold marks the best score per metric; underline marks the second best.
official.metric: F1@0.5 on positive queries (tIoU threshold 0.5, higher is better), plus Rejection-F1 on negative/positive coverage (higher is better). Single run, no error bars. The authors say open-source inference uses deterministic greedy decoding.
official.comparison: CoMET-Agent vs. the same backbone used single-pass with 128 uniform frames (Qwen3-VL-8B; also GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Flash). The strongest non-ours baseline overall is Gemini 3 Flash single-pass (F1@0.5 14.6%), and the best other agent is VideoARM (13.0%).
official.falsification_criterion: A faithful reimplementation of CoMET-Agent on Qwen3-VL-8B, evaluated with the released CoMET-Bench toolkit, does not clearly beat single-pass Qwen3-VL-8B on F1@0.5 (for example, a gain under about 2 points, or below 6% absolute), or the GPT-5 version does not exceed GPT-5 single-pass F1@0.5 of 10.1%.

title: Probabilistic Signature Inversion: Learning Conditional Distributions from Truncated Signatures
claim_source: Table 7, page 19 (summary version in Table 1, page 8)

official.background: The signature of a path (its sequence of iterated integrals) determines the path uniquely, but in practice only a truncated signature can be computed, and the truncated map is many-to-one. Existing inversion methods (insertion, Fourier/Legendre basis recovery, optimization) return a single path and ignore this ambiguity. The paper treats inversion as learning the conditional distribution of paths given their truncated signature, and measures how much ambiguity remains with the Bayes reconstruction error: the expected integrated squared distance between a path and an independent draw from the conditional distribution given the statistic. For Gaussian process families this error has a computable value when the conditioning statistic is a set of linear statistics. That value is an upper bound on the error under truncated-signature conditioning, because the signature contains at least as much information.
official.method:
The linear statistic of depth r is L(r)(X) = (X_T, ∫ t X_t dt, ..., ∫ t^{r-1} X_t dt). For log-GBM (dX = ν dt + σ dB, X_0 = 0, T = 1) the Bayes error under L(r) has the closed form E(L(r)) = 2 a_r T^2 E[σ^2] with a_r = r / (2(2r-1)(2r+1)), averaged over the parameter prior µ, σ ~ U[1.5, 2.5]. Since the time-augmented (TA) truncated signature generates a finer σ-algebra than L(r), the TA Bayes error is at most the LS value, with equality for r ≤ 2.

The estimator is a signature-conditioned flow-matching model with a 1D DiT backbone (patch size 8, 128-dim tokens, 7 blocks, 8 heads; conditioning injected via AdaLN-Zero). It is trained on 100k simulated log-GBM paths of length 1001 (parameters sampled per path) for 100 epochs (AdamW, lr 2e-4, batch 64). The conditioning vector is either the LS coordinates (taken from the TA log-signature) or the full TA log-signature at depth r (computed with iisignature, then level-wise scaled by x ↦ sign(x) log(1 + k!|x|)). At test time, for each of 1000 held-out reference paths, the model draws 30 samples with 1000 Euler steps. The empirical Bayes error is the mean discrete path MSE between the reference and its samples.
official.claim: On log-GBM at truncation depth r = 4, the sampler conditioned on linear statistics reaches path MSE 0.261 ± 0.005, matching the closed-form Bayes oracle of 0.260. The same sampler conditioned on the time-augmented log-signature reaches 0.197 ± 0.006, about 24% below the oracle bound.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Bayes reconstruction error with confidence intervals and inter-sample spread ratio. LS Oracle is analytic for log-GBM; for log-fBM and OU, it reports the mean with 95% confidence intervals based on the t-distribution over 10 numerical seeds. LS, TA, and TLL report full-sample empirical path-MSE means with normal-approximation 95% bootstrap half-widths, computed as 1.96 times the bootstrap standard error.
official.metric: Empirical Bayes reconstruction error (mean discrete integrated squared path error between reference and sample, over 1000 references × 30 samples; lower is better). ± is a 95% bootstrap half-width (1.96 × bootstrap SE) over the evaluation set, not over training seeds. The log-GBM LS Oracle is analytic.
official.comparison: Flow-matching sampler with TA-signature conditioning vs. the same sampler with LS conditioning and vs. the analytic LS Bayes oracle, all at depth 4 on the same log-GBM evaluation set
official.falsification_criterion: The claim is refuted if a reproduced LS-conditioned sampler's error at r = 4 differs from 0.260 by more than its bootstrap uncertainty plus a few percent, or if the TA-conditioned sampler's error is not clearly below 0.260 (for example above about 0.24).

title: OmniTraffic: A Controllable Generation Pipeline and Benchmark for Spatio-Temporal Traffic Reasoning

official.background: Roadside traffic cameras record lane usage, queues, special vehicles, incidents and signal phases, and multimodal LLMs are increasingly proposed as a natural-language interface to such footage. Existing traffic VQA benchmarks mostly test passive recognition on single images or videos from real cameras, which offer no control over intersection layout, viewpoints or signal phases and are expensive to annotate with lane-level structure. As a result, it is unclear whether MLLMs can reason about intersection topology, align views with a bird's-eye-view (BEV) map, or track how traffic evolves over time.
official.method:
OmniTraffic rebuilds 12 real intersections as controllable 3D simulation scenes and renders synchronized multi-view, multi-timestep images together with structured metadata (lane topology, vehicle-to-lane assignment, signal phases, events). Rule-based templates turn the metadata into VQA pairs, which are then converted to four-option multiple-choice questions with distractors drawn from the same scene. Real surveillance footage from South Korea and Tianjin adds human-annotated questions for perception and temporal tasks. A 3,204-item human-verified test set covers 11 categories at three levels: L1 perception, L2 spatio-temporal reasoning (including View-BEV Mapping, which asks a model to match directional camera views to a BEV layout), and L3 signal-phase decision support.

Eleven MLLMs (e.g. Gemini-3-Pro-Thinking, GPT-5.2, Grok-4, Claude-Sonnet-4.5-Thinking, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking) are evaluated zero-shot. They use greedy decoding (temperature 0, at most 500 output tokens), the prompt template in Fig. 22, and a regex extraction of the A/B/C/D label, with up to three retries when no label can be parsed; responses that are still unparseable are scored as wrong. The metric is exact-match accuracy. Ten non-expert humans answer the same questions on a web platform without external aids.
official.claim: On the 3,204-item OmniTraffic test set, all 11 evaluated MLLMs score between 9.2% and 39.2% on View-BEV Mapping, against 100.0% for non-expert humans, and the best model overall (Gemini-3-Pro) reaches 72.4% average accuracy, against 92.9% for humans.

title: BALTO: Balanced Token-Level Policy Optimization for Hallucination Mitigation

official.background: In retrieval-grounded generation, LLMs often make faithfulness hallucinations: short unsupported spans (a wrong number, date or entity) inside answers that are otherwise correct. RL with a response-level faithfulness reward gives the same scalar advantage to every token, so one wrong number also penalises all the supported content. This can push the model toward short, conservative answers. The paper asks how to assign token-level credit so that RL removes hallucinated spans without making answers less informative.
official.method:
During GRPO-style training (verl, 8 rollouts per prompt, batch 256, lr 1e-6, asymmetric clipping 0.2/0.28), an LLM verifier (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) extracts checkable factual claims from each rollout, checks each claim against the reference documents, and for unsupported claims returns the minimal erroneous text span. These spans are aligned to rollout tokens. Tokens in the minimal erroneous spans are labelled hallucinated (H), tokens in supported claims are labelled faithful (F), and all other tokens (including the non-erroneous tokens inside a hallucinated claim) are neutral.

BALTO replaces the response-level group-relative advantage with a per-token advantage: -1 for hallucinated tokens, +N-/N+ for faithful tokens (so the advantages in each response sum to zero; if N+ = 0 only the -1 penalty is applied), and 0 for neutral tokens and for all tokens of responses with no hallucination. The clipped objective is normalised over |H|+|F| tokens only. Baselines are trained with the same verifier: GRPO_B (binary hallucination-free reward), GRPO_D (fraction of faithful claims as reward), and FSPO (GRPO_D reward and advantage, with the advantage sign inverted on faithful-claim tokens in negative-advantage responses and on hallucinated-claim tokens in positive-advantage responses). Evaluation uses the same verifier. Faith. is the percentage of test responses with no hallucinated claim.
official.claim: With Qwen3-8B trained and evaluated on RAGTruth, BALTO reaches 98.4% faithfulness (share of hallucination-free responses), vs. 92.0% for the strongest baseline GRPO_D, 89.8% for GRPO_B and 73.1% for FSPO, while also having the highest Q-Score (70.0 vs. 67.9 for GRPO_D).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results (%) on ConFiQA, RAGTruth, and FinLLM-Eval using Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B. Bold and underlined scores represent the best and second-best results. [ref.] denotes the reference method for relative metrics, with Info. computed against Base and WR computed against BALTO.
official.metric: Faithfulness (%) = fraction of test responses with no claim judged unsupported by the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B evaluator, higher is better; Q-Score = Faith. x Info. No error bars: the paper reports no seeds, number of runs, std or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: BALTO vs. the RL baselines GRPO_B, GRPO_D and FSPO (same Qwen3.5-35B-A3B verifier and verl RL hyperparameters), plus SFT/DPO on verifier-corrected data, all trained from Qwen3-8B on the RAGTruth training split and evaluated on its test set
official.falsification_criterion: In a matched re-run on RAGTruth with Qwen3-8B, BALTO's faithfulness is not clearly above GRPO_D's (for example, a gap well under the reported 6.4 points, or within the variation seen across seeds), or BALTO reaches its faithfulness only with a Q-Score below GRPO_D's.

title: Closing the Approximation Gap in Simulation-free Latent SDEs

official.background: Latent SDE models explain irregularly sampled, noisy time series as readouts of a latent stochastic process. They are fit by variational inference (VI), which needs a posterior over latent paths. Simulation-based VI integrates the posterior SDE at every gradient step, which is accurate but slow. Simulation-free VI methods such as SDE Matching and SVISE instead parameterize the posterior's Gaussian one-time marginals and derive a drift from them, so samples at any time can be drawn directly. However, the one-time marginals do not determine the path law: many drifts produce the same marginals. Each existing method fixes one drift, which restricts the posterior family. When posterior uncertainty is high, this can hurt both inference and the learned dynamics.
official.method:
By the Fokker–Planck equation, any two drifts with the same one-time marginals q(x,t) differ by a q-divergence-free vector field. Only the path KL term of the ELBO depends on that choice. It is minimized by adding to a reference drift f_q (the SDE Matching 'square root' drift, eq. 4) the q-divergence-free component h of the residual r = f_p − f_q, which comes from a q-weighted Helmholtz decomposition. Helmholtz-SDE approximates h by whitening x so that each marginal is standard Gaussian, expanding r in normalized Hermite polynomials up to degree ℓ (coefficients by Gauss–Hermite quadrature or Monte Carlo), and solving for the optimal divergence-free field in that subspace. Training is ordinary simulation-free stochastic VI: random observation index, random KL time, Gaussian samples, and a corrected drift f_q + ĥ in the path-KL estimate. All experiments use ℓ = 1.

Noisy Lorenz setup (Appendix D.1): 3-D stochastic Lorenz (10, 28, 8/3) with process noise σ = 5 on T = 5, observed every Δt = 0.25 through a standardizing linear map with noise η = 0.3; 1024 training and 2048 test trials. The model has a K = 4 latent SDE with a neural-network prior drift, fixed identity diffusion, a learned Gaussian initial state and a linear-Gaussian readout (C, d learned; observation noise variance fixed at η²), learned jointly with the posterior. The ℓ = 1 Helmholtz correction is estimated by Monte Carlo (Stein estimand, N_mc = 1). The posterior uses Gaussian marginals with dense covariance, amortized by a GRU encoder plus an MLP over time; the same amortization is used for SDE Matching. Baselines: simulation-free SDE Matching and SVISE/ARCTA, and simulation-based SING and Latent SDE, run from their authors' codebases.
official.claim: On the noisy Lorenz attractor, Helmholtz-SDE learns a prior with symmetric KL 0.06 ± 0.00 to the true prior's one-time marginals and autocorrelation error 0.024 ± 0.002, against 0.26 ± 0.01 / 0.057 ± 0.001 for SDE Matching and 0.35 ± 0.02 / 0.052 ± 0.002 for SVISE. Its test negative ELBO is about 48 nats, against about 69 (SDE Matching) and 65 (SVISE).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Helmholtz-SDE closes the gap between simulation-based and simulation-free VI algorithms on the noisy Lorenz attractor. nELBO and posterior predictive LL at unobserved times are averaged over trials; sym KL is averaged over one-time marginals. Autocorr error is the entrywise RMSE of the global 3×3 autocorrelation matrix, over lags τ ∈ [0, 2]. Errors are ±2SE over 10 replicates.
official.metric: Symmetric KL (nats) between learned and true prior one-time marginals, averaged over time (lower is better); autocorrelation error = entrywise RMSE of the global 3×3 autocorrelation matrix over lags τ ∈ [0, 2] (lower is better); negative ELBO per trial (lower is better, bar chart); posterior predictive LL at unobserved times (higher is better). ± is 2 standard errors over 10 replicates.
official.comparison: Helmholtz-SDE (ℓ = 1) vs. the simulation-free baselines SDE Matching and SVISE, with matched model, data and amortization. Simulation-based SING and Latent SDE are shown for reference.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same data-generation settings and 10 replicates, Helmholtz-SDE's symmetric KL to the true prior is not clearly below SDE Matching's (e.g. less than a 2× reduction, or overlapping ±2SE), or its autocorrelation error is not below both simulation-free baselines, or its negative ELBO is not lower than SDE Matching's by well over the error bars.

title: Structure-Semantic Co-optimized Latent Diffusion Model for Fast Visual Anagram Synthesis

official.background: Visual anagrams are images that show one concept (e.g. 'a girl') and a different concept (e.g. 'an elderly man') after a fixed transformation such as a flip or rotation. Zero-shot methods generate them with pretrained text-to-image diffusion models by denoising the image and its transformed view in parallel, each conditioned on its own prompt, and averaging the two noise predictions at every step. Existing methods mostly use slow pixel-space models at 256x256. Moving this to a fast few-step latent model (SDXL-Turbo) is attractive, but the paper argues that naive noise averaging then produces structural conflicts between views and diluted semantics.
official.method:
S2CO-Anagram runs multi-view parallel denoising with SDXL-Turbo (T=4 steps, CFG w=1.5, 512x512). At each step the latent z_t and its transformed view g(z_t) are passed through the UNet with prompts P1 and P2, and the two noise predictions are fused. Three components are added on top, with a K=5 inner optimization loop per denoising step: (1) Null-Text Structure Alignment (NTSA): the null-text CFG embedding is updated by gradient descent (lr 0.1) on a View-Cycle Low-Frequency Consistency loss, the squared difference between the low-frequency 1D-DCT components (lowest th=5 percent along h and along w) of the Tweedie-predicted clean latents of view 1 and of view 2 mapped back by g^-1; (2) Semantic Enhancement (SE): z_t is updated by gradient ascent (lr 0.5) on the sum of cross-attention activations for the key word of each prompt, restricted to locations above the 60th percentile; (3) Attention-guided noise fusion: the two noise predictions are combined with per-pixel weights proportional to each view's key-word attention map instead of a plain average. Final images average D(z0) with the inverse-transformed decode of g(z0).

Evaluation uses the CIFAR10 2-views prompt-pair set (from Anagram-MTL): for each prompt pair, 10 images with different seeds, metrics averaged. Metrics are A_min (worse of the two view-prompt CLIP similarities), concealment score C (softmax-based CLIP discrimination between views/prompts), A_avg (mean view-prompt CLIP similarity), and LAION Aesthetics Predictor V2 score (AS). The ablation in Table 2 switches each component on or off; the all-off row is plain SDXL-Turbo multi-view denoising with average noise fusion.
official.claim: On CIFAR10 2-views with SDXL-Turbo (T=4), adding NTSA, SE and attention-guided fusion to plain averaged multi-view denoising raises A_min from 0.2463 to 0.2726, C from 0.6672 to 0.6918, A_avg from 0.2658 to 0.2824 and aesthetic score from 4.64 to 6.14, with NTSA alone accounting for most of the gain (A_min 0.2703, AS 5.58).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Quantitative ablation study on the contributions of the key model components. (Image also shows Table 1, the cross-method comparison, and Table 3, the DCT threshold ablation.)
official.metric: A_min, C, A_avg (CLIP-based, higher is better) and LAION aesthetic score AS (higher is better); averaged over prompt pairs x 10 seeds; no error bars or std reported
official.comparison: Full S2CO-Anagram vs. the same SDXL-Turbo multi-view denoising with all three components disabled (average fusion), plus single- and double-component variants
official.falsification_criterion: With all settings matched, the full method fails to beat the all-off baseline on A_min by a margin larger than the seed-to-seed spread of the mean, or NTSA alone does not improve A_min and AS over the all-off baseline.

title: SDS-LoRA: Overcoming Anisotropic Gradient Scaling in Low-Rank Adaptation
claim_source: Table 11 (Appendix G), page 21; the ViT-Base rows also appear as Table 3, page 8

official.background: LoRA fine-tunes a large pretrained model by learning a low-rank weight update ΔW = sBA, but it still trails full fine-tuning. The paper argues that part of this gap comes from how gradients flow through the low-rank factors. The full gradient G is multiplied by the singular values of B (for A's gradient) and of A (for B's gradient). When those singular values are skewed, the gradient is pushed toward a few dominant directions ('anisotropic gradient scaling'). This lowers its effective rank and worsens how well the implied update approximates G.
official.method:
SDS-LoRA reparameterizes the update as ΔW = s(Q_B A + B Q_A^T). Q_A and Q_B are orthonormal bases of the row space of A and the column space of B, obtained by QR decomposition of A^T and B, and they are treated as constants (detached) in the backward pass. The gradients are then ∇A = s Q_B^T G and ∇B = s G Q_A, so the singular values of A and B never scale the gradient. The forward pass can still represent any rank-r update. Training starts with T = 10 warm-up iterations of standard LoRA. The warm-up ΔW is then converted via truncated SVD (A = Σ V^T / 2s, B = U Σ / 2s, Q_A = V, Q_B = U) and the optimizer state is reset. During main training, Q_A and Q_B are recomputed on a schedule with k = 5 phases, where the update interval in phase i is i steps.

For the vision experiments, ViT-Base (224px, patch 16) gets LoRA adapters on the 'query' and 'value' projections. It is trained with AdamW (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, no weight decay), a cosine schedule and batch size 64; for Cars, 5 epochs at learning rate 5e-3. The scale is s = α/√r with α = 4 (rsLoRA-style) for all methods except plain LoRA, which uses s = 2. The baselines are LoRA, rsLoRA, LoRA+ (learning-rate ratio 4), PiSSA and DoRA, all reproduced by the authors in the same setup. Results are mean ± std over 3 trials.
official.claim: On Stanford Cars with ViT-Base, SDS-LoRA reaches 80.41 ± 0.20% top-1 accuracy at rank 8, vs. 79.05 ± 0.25% for the best baseline (LoRA+). At rank 32 it reaches 82.95 ± 0.25%, vs. 81.48 ± 0.20% for the best baseline (plain LoRA).

official.metric: Top-1 test accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is std over 3 trials
official.comparison: SDS-LoRA vs. LoRA, rsLoRA, LoRA+, PiSSA and DoRA at the same rank (8 and 32), with the same backbone, epochs, learning rate and batch size; full fine-tuning (84.26 ± 0.19) shown as reference
official.falsification_criterion: With ViT-Base on Cars, at rank 8 or rank 32, some baseline's mean accuracy comes within about one seed std of SDS-LoRA's, or exceeds it.
