title: Geometry-Aware Post-Hoc Uncertainty Quantification in Operator Learning

official.background: Neural operators such as Transolver are fast surrogates for PDE solvers on irregular meshes and point clouds, but they produce deterministic point predictions with no uncertainty estimate. Deep ensembles are the standard way to add calibrated uncertainty but multiply training cost. Cheaper post-hoc methods (Laplace approximation, input perturbation) work in weight or input space and can be poorly calibrated, especially when the geometry varies across samples. A post-hoc method that gives ensemble-quality calibration from a single trained operator would make UQ practical for large geometry-varying PDE datasets.
official.method:
REEF-GP keeps a pretrained Transolver frozen and fits a Gaussian process to its pointwise residuals, v(x) − Gθ(u,a)(x). Each GP input is the query coordinate x, the input-function encoding u (if present), and hidden features h taken from three Transolver layers (first, one picked by CKA, last). The kernel is a product k_space(x,x') · k_fun(u,u') · k_base(ρ(h),ρ(h')), where ρ is a spectral-normalized MLP. Noise is heteroscedastic, with a variance σψ²(z̄) given by a spectral-normalized network, plus a global noise term σn². All hyperparameters are trained by minimizing the exact GP negative log marginal likelihood on random subsets of Ns = 5,000 points per step, with early stopping on validation loss.

For inference, K GP experts share the hyperparameters, each conditioned on a different random subset of Ns training points. Their predictions are combined with a uniformly weighted generalized product of experts, and the resulting mean and variance are added to the frozen Transolver prediction. Baselines use the same Transolver backbone and data split (ShapeNet Car: 500 train / 100 val / 250 test cars, 3,500 surface points each, predicting surface pressure). They are a deep ensemble of 5 independently trained Transolvers, MC Dropout (p = 0.1, 50 passes), PNO, input perturbation (Gaussian noise σ = 1e-2, 50 passes), last-layer Laplace (LUNO-LA), and DVE-spatial. Metrics are test-set NLL, CRPS, NIS and energy score.
official.claim: On ShapeNet Car (3D surface pressure, 500 training cars), REEF-GP fitted post hoc to a frozen Transolver reaches test NLL 2.84 ± 0.09. This is lower than the 5-member deep ensemble (4.16), PNO (4.98 ± 1.52), input perturbation (13.44 ± 1.14) and LUNO-LA Laplace (33.55 ± 23.43), while rL2 stays at the base model's level (8.52 vs 8.62%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Evaluation metrics on representative 2D (Airfoil) and 3D (ShapeNet Car) benchmarks. Lower is better (↓). Best in bold, second best underlined. Base is the deterministic Transolver without UQ; rankings exclude Base. REEF-GP is our approach. Metrics are defined in Appendix H.
official.metric: Gaussian negative log-likelihood of the test-set pointwise predictions (lower is better; definition in Appendix H). ± is the spread over the 5 random seeds {0,1,2,3,4} that the paper uses for all experiments; the tables do not say outright whether it is a standard deviation, though the paper's figures use ±1 std over the same seeds. The deep ensemble has a single value with no ±.
official.comparison: REEF-GP vs. Deep Ensemble (5 Transolvers), MC Dropout, PNO, Input Perturbation, LUNO-LA and DVE-spatial, all on the same Transolver backbone and the same ShapeNet Car split

title: Offline Preference-Based Trajectory Evaluation
claim_source: Table 8, page 19 (appendix); aggregate in Table 2d, page 8

official.background: Agent benchmarks usually score each trajectory by binary terminal success, and compare systems by success rate. This throws away partial progress and how quickly the agent got there, so many instance-level comparisons between two systems are ties. Ties shrink the effective sample size, make it harder to separate systems, and may contribute to apparent benchmark saturation. The paper proposes comparing pairs of trajectories directly through temporal preferences over their return-versus-time profiles. It also measures how much signal this recovers.
official.method:
A trajectory is a nondecreasing normalized return curve f(t) in [0, 1], and g(R) is the first step at which return R is reached (infinity if never). Metric baselines are success rate SR = 1[g(1) < inf], partial return PR = max_t f(t), and reference-free SPL = success / trajectory length. Each metric gives a pairwise preference Δ = μ(f) − μ(f′). The proposed preferences are computed directly on a pair of trajectories. Lexicographic Return (LR) is sgn[g′(R*) − g(R*)] at the highest return level R* where the two times-to-return differ. Return-Paired Preference (RPP) sums, over the segments of the sorted union of both trajectories' return levels (plus 0 and 1), the segment width times sgn[g′(R̂k) − g(R̂k)], with ∞ − ∞ = 0. Interval-Paired Preference (IPP) does the same with the time increments between consecutive levels.

Tie rate is the percentage of instance-level comparisons (pairs of systems on the same task instance) with Δ = 0. It is averaged over tasks within each benchmark and then over benchmarks. The benchmarks are AgentBoard (6 tasks, 12 models, with subgoal progress scores), OpenHands-Index (4 tasks, success and step count only), TheAgentCompany (partial terminal score and step count), TALES (Jericho and ScienceWorld, about 50 models), and a self-generated sub-goal RL set (Taxi, DoorKey, FourRooms). Tasks with fewer than 30 instances are removed.
official.claim: On AgentBoard trajectories (6 tasks, 12 models), the trajectory preferences LR, RPP and IPP tie on 33.3%, 34.9% and 36.1% of instance-level comparisons. Success rate ties on 78.9% and partial return, the strongest scalar baseline, on 43.5%. Averaged over all five benchmarks, ties fall from 74.9% (SR) and 49.7% (PR) to 33.9-35.1%.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Tie rate (% of instance comparisons with zero difference), averaged within benchmark.
official.metric: Tie rate: % of instance-level system-pair comparisons with zero preference, lower is better. Computed exactly with no error bars, averaged over tasks within a benchmark.
official.comparison: LR, RPP, IPP (trajectory preferences) vs. SR, PR, SPL (scalar metrics turned into preferences), on the same logged trajectories
official.falsification_criterion: Recomputing tie rates on the public AgentBoard logs, RPP (or LR) ties on about as many comparisons as PR (e.g. a gap under 5 percentage points), or SR's tie rate is far below about 79%.

title: Beyond Domains: Reusing Web Skills via Transferable Interaction Patterns

official.background: LLM web agents usually act by calling one low-level browser tool (click, fill, select) per LLM call, so long tasks need many sequential, costly LLM calls. Skill-library methods (ASI, SkillWeaver, PolySkill) compress repeated action sequences from past successful trajectories into callable skills, so that one skill call replaces several LLM-generated primitives. These libraries are retrieved mostly by instruction text or site metadata, so they are rarely reused on websites from new domains, where the wording differs even when the interaction (e.g. fill a form and press submit) is the same.
official.method:
SkillMigrator stores each induced skill as a 'transferable interaction pattern' (TIP): a one-sentence intent, an operation template (e.g. search, fill-and-submit, click-by-text) mined by clustering training trajectories on action shape, a slot schema in which each slot has a descriptor and a synonym set, and the cleaned accessibility-tree skeleton of the page where the skill was induced. At test time, for each planner subtask, skills from one global library are scored by α·cosine(embedding of subtask + page summary, embedding of skill descriptor) + (1−α)·(1 − normalized tree edit distance between the stored skeleton and the live page's tree), using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and APTED, with α = 0.6. If the top score is at least β = 0.20, slot values are matched from the subtask's instantiation dict (or extracted from the instruction) and slots are bound to live page controls via two Hungarian assignments over embedding similarities, and the template's deterministic plan emits the primitives with no LLM call. Otherwise the agent falls back to a ReAct step.

Baselines are ReAct (no skills), ASI and PolySkill, with skills induced from the same training trajectories using each method's own pipeline. title: HumanoidArena: Benchmarking Egocentric Hierarchical Whole-body Learning
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (in-GMT success rates with seed std in Table 1, page 8)

official.background: Humanoid robots doing whole-body interaction (kicking a ball, sitting on a sofa, stepping between desks) are often controlled hierarchically. A high-level visuomotor policy predicts an intermediate whole-body action, and a low-level general motion tracker (GMT), an RL-trained controller, turns it into stable joint targets. If the intermediate action is a shared interface, a policy trained with one tracker could in principle be deployed with another. Existing benchmarks do not test whether this works. HumanoidArena is a simulated benchmark of 7 leg-critical tasks built to measure that policy-tracker interface directly.
official.method:
In Isaac Lab, a Unitree G1 humanoid is teleoperated through VR, from an egocentric view, to collect 100 successful demonstrations per task per GMT backend (TWIST2 and SONIC). Both backends receive the same 40D canonical action: planar root motion, root height, root orientation, 29 joint targets and binary hand open/close. A GMT-specific adapter maps this action into each tracker's input format. High-level policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, Flow Matching, pi0.5; LeRobot implementations, 100k gradient steps each) take the egocentric RGB image, a 64D proprioceptive state and the task instruction, and predict the 40D action. A separate policy is trained per task and per GMT.

In-GMT evaluation deploys a policy with the tracker that produced its training data. Cross-GMT evaluation deploys the same trained policy with the other tracker. Every configuration is run with 3 seeds x 20 rollouts = 60 episodes on identical held-out initializations. The paper reports the absolute drop Delta_cross = SR_in - SR_cross and the retention Ret = SR_cross / SR_in.
official.claim: Diffusion Policy trained on TWIST2 demonstrations and deployed with the SONIC tracker loses most of its success rate on all 7 tasks: Football 46.7% -> ~21.7%, DoubleDesk 10.0% -> 0%, P&PBox 50.0% -> 0%, OpenDoor 68.3% -> 0%, SitSofa 73.3% -> 0%, Boxing 51.7% -> ~1.7%, VisNavi 30.0% -> ~16.7% (retention 0-56%). Across all 4 policies, 22 of the 28 TWIST2->SONIC entries reach 0% retention.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Cross-GMT evaluation. T->S denotes policies trained on TWIST2 demonstrations and deployed with the SONIC backend, while S->T denotes the reverse direction. Each policy entry reports absolute cross-GMT drop Delta_cross (lower is better) / relative transfer retention Ret (higher is better), computed with respect to the corresponding matched in-GMT performance. AFR (lower is better) denotes the task-level average fall rate under each cross-GMT deployment direction, measuring tracker-induced stability failures.
official.metric: Task success rate over 60 rollouts (3 seeds x 20), higher is better. The table reports absolute drop Delta_cross (points) and retention Ret = SR_cross/SR_in. In-GMT SRs come with mean +/- std over 3 seeds (Table 1). Cross-GMT entries have no error bars.
official.comparison: The same trained high-level policy deployed with its training GMT (in-GMT) vs. with the other GMT (cross-GMT). The headline case is DP trained on TWIST2 data and deployed with TWIST2 vs. with SONIC.
official.falsification_criterion: Using the released TWIST2 demonstrations and the paper's evaluation protocol, a Diffusion Policy deployed with SONIC keeps SR within about one in-GMT seed std (<=12 points) of its TWIST2 in-GMT SR on most of the 7 tasks. Equivalently, retention is above roughly 80% on most tasks rather than near 0%.

title: Learning from the Self-future: On-policy Self-distillation for dLLMs

official.background: Diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) such as LLaDA generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens in any order rather than left to right. Their reasoning can be improved by RL with verifiable rewards (e.g. diffu-GRPO), but that uses sparse outcome rewards and needs thousands of optimization steps. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD), where one model acts as both student and a teacher that sees privileged information, gives dense supervision and has worked for autoregressive LLMs. There, the privileged information (a reference solution) is appended to the prompt and the loss is a per-token KL, which assumes left-to-right generation and does not fit dLLMs.
official.method:
d-OPSD (on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LoRA r=128) has the student sample a full denoising trajectory for a prompt (resampling up to k=8 times until the final answer is correct). At each denoising step t, the student input is the current partially masked sequence; the teacher input is the same sequence with a random 25% (rho_teacher = 0.25) of the still-masked positions filled in with the student's own final answer tokens, i.e. the 'self-future' used as suffix conditioning. The teacher is frozen at the initial policy. The loss is the reverse KL between student and teacher token distributions, averaged over the top-k most confident masked positions that the teacher would unmask at that step (step-level supervision), with pointwise KL clipping at 0.05, averaged over steps.

The AR-style OPSD baseline (Table 4) follows Zhao et al. (2026): the teacher instead gets the dataset's reference reasoning solution appended to the prompt as a prefix, while the step-level divergence, model, and training setup are kept the same. Both are evaluated at generation length 256 (block diffusion, block length 32, 128 denoising steps) on GSM8K and MATH500 test sets, reporting the best accuracy over checkpoints evaluated every 25 steps up to step 500.
official.claim: With LLaDA-8B-Instruct at generation length 256, using the model's own sampled answer as suffix privileged information (d-OPSD) beats the AR-style OPSD teacher that prefixes the reference solution: GSM8K 81.0 vs. 78.4 and MATH500 37.2 vs. 33.4 (base model 76.0 / 31.8).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Reasoning performance Comparison between AR-style OPSD and our approach. Generation length is 256. Our teacher construction outperforms the AR-style baseline.
official.metric: Test accuracy (%) on GSM8K and MATH500, higher is better; single run, best checkpoint over evaluations every 25 steps; no error bars reported
official.comparison: d-OPSD (self-generated answer as suffix teacher context) vs. AR-style OPSD (reference solution as prefix teacher context) vs. untrained LLaDA-8B-Instruct, with the same step-level reverse-KL objective
official.falsification_criterion: Under matched training budget and checkpoint selection, AR-style OPSD reaches GSM8K accuracy within ~1 point of d-OPSD, or matches/exceeds it on MATH500 (gap < ~2 points), or the gap disappears across seeds.

title: CEO-Bench: Can Agents Play the Long Game?
claim_source: Table 3, page 9 (baseline details in Appendix B, Table 4, page 30)

official.background: Most agent benchmarks (SWE-bench, WebArena, tau-bench) test short episodes with a clear goal and quick feedback. Real-world work often needs long chains of decisions under uncertainty: reading noisy signals, coping with delayed consequences, adapting to a changing environment, and coordinating many interdependent actions. Earlier long-horizon simulations such as Vending-Bench involve a narrow set of decisions in a mostly stable world. CEO-Bench asks whether current LLM agents can run a simulated software startup for 500 days and grow its cash.
official.method:
The simulator models a subscription-software company that starts with $1M cash and zero customers; the score is cash on hand at day 500, and the run ends in bankruptcy if cash drops below zero. Agents act once per simulated week (unlimited turns) through a Python package (34 tools: pricing, ads, development/R&D, capacity, support, enterprise deals, market research, social media) and a 19-table SQL database. Customer preferences, channel effectiveness and competitor moves are hidden and stochastic. Each model is run 3 times with random seed 42 at maximum reasoning effort, using the authors' minimal terminal harness (bash, read-file, edit-file), which clears history each week and keeps only the system prompt and an agent-editable memory file. The best run is the bankruptcy-free run with the highest ending cash; if all runs went bankrupt, it is the run that lasted longest.

The rule-based baseline makes no LLM calls. It fixes a price book, model tiers and quotas; spends $200/day on global development plus fixed targeted development and (from day 20) targeted ads on the highest-yield channel for the chosen customer groups, while cash stays above a floor; sets ops spend to max(100, 0.05 x active subscribers); and adjusts capacity toward 80% utilization. A grid of 24 configurations (Table 4, Appendix B) was evaluated on seed 42. The best one (mid price book, target S1 only, heavy spend, $100K floor) ends with $15.76M.
official.claim: On the 500-day CEO-Bench simulation (seed 42), every evaluated LLM agent's best of 3 runs finishes below the rule-based baseline's $15,756,408: the best agent, Claude Fable 5, reaches $12,630,078 (and goes bankrupt in 1 of 3 runs), GPT-5.6 Sol $11,313,982, Claude Opus 4.8 $2,399,209, and all other models finish below the $1M starting cash.
official.claim_caption: Table 3. Benchmark results summary. Most models fail to avoid bankruptcy or finish below the initial $1,000,000 cash balance. Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 4.8 are the only evaluated models whose best runs finish above the starting balance, and all evaluated models remain below the rule-based baseline and the estimated upper bound of attainable final cash. CEO-Bench presents a challenging task for existing models.
official.metric: Final cash on hand at day 500 in USD (higher is better), best of 3 runs per model; no error bars on cash. Mean survival days ± std over the 3 runs is reported separately.
official.comparison: 16 LLM agents (same minimal harness) vs. the best grid-searched non-LLM rule-based policy, all on seed 42
official.falsification_criterion: The released rule-based configuration does not reach about $15.76M on seed 42, or a rerun of a top agent (e.g. Claude Fable 5 or GPT-5.6 Sol, same harness, max reasoning effort) finishes above the rule-based baseline's final cash.

title: Dual Dimensionality for Local and Global Attention
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (3-seed numbers in the text of Section 3.1, page 6)

official.background: In decoder-only Transformers every previous token contributes keys and values of the same dimensionality, however far it is from the token being predicted, and the KV cache that stores them dominates memory at long context. Methods such as Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) shrink the per-token representation, but uniformly across all positions. The authors hypothesize that nearby tokens need rich representations for next-token prediction, while distant tokens mainly act as long-range memory and can use far fewer dimensions. If true, KV dimensionality could be allocated by token distance instead of uniformly.
official.method:
Distance-Adaptive Representation (DAR): for each token j, hidden state h_j is also projected to a bottleneck h_j^D = h_j W_down (d_down < d) and back up, h'_j = h_j^D W_up. When a query at position i attends to token j, keys and values are computed from the full h_j if i - j < w (local window, default w = 128) and from h'_j otherwise, using the same W_K, W_V and RoPE in both paths. Training uses the plain next-token loss with no auxiliary losses; W_down and W_up are learned through the distant positions. The Uniform reduction baseline applies the same bottleneck d_down to all tokens regardless of distance (equivalent to w = 0); Vanilla is the standard full-dimensional model (d = 512).

All three are pretrained from scratch with the Pythia-70M architecture and Pythia recipe: 19,073 steps, batch size 256, sequence length 2,048, on the first 10B tokens of the deduplicated Pile. Evaluation is perplexity on subsets of FineWeb-Edu, C4 and WikiText-103 (rolling evaluation for documents longer than 2,048 tokens); Rel.(%) is the per-dataset perplexity ratio to Vanilla averaged over the three corpora.
official.claim: At the Pythia-70M scale with d_down = 128 and w = 128, DAR reaches relative perplexity 99.68 ± 0.57% of Vanilla over 3 seeds, while Uniform reduction to the same dimension reaches 103.82 ± 0.91% (single-seed Table 1: DAR 99.12% vs. Uniform 103.52%, with lower perplexity on all three corpora).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: DAR validation at the Pythia-70M scale. DAR is run with window size w = 128 across all bottleneck dimensions. Perplexity is reported on three evaluation corpora: a subset of FineWeb-Edu, C4 and WikiText-103. Rel. is the average per-dataset perplexity ratio relative to Vanilla, reported as a percentage (lower is better).
official.metric: Relative perplexity Rel.(%) = mean over FineWeb-Edu, C4 and WikiText-103 of perplexity / Vanilla perplexity (lower is better). The ± values are the paper's spread over 3 pretraining seeds (the paper does not say whether it is std or another statistic), computed relative to the mean Vanilla perplexity across seeds and given only for the d_down = 128 setting; the table itself is single-run with no error bars.
official.comparison: DAR (full-dimensional local window of 128 tokens, d_down-dimensional distant tokens) vs. Uniform reduction (d_down for all tokens) at matched d_down, with the full-dimensional Vanilla model as reference
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining DAR and Uniform reduction at d_down = 128 with the same recipe gives a Rel.(%) gap between them that is within about one seed std (roughly under 1.5 points), or DAR's relative perplexity is not lower than Uniform's on the three corpora.

title: EfficientRollout: System-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for RL Rollouts
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (repeated-seed numbers in Appendix F.2, page 27)

official.background: In on-policy RL post-training of LLMs (e.g. GRPO), generating rollouts dominates step time, because responses are long and decoded token by token, and a few long-tailed responses decide when the rollout finishes. Speculative decoding (SD) cuts latency without changing the output distribution, but it is hard to use in RL for two reasons. A fixed drafter falls out of step with the policy as training changes it. And early in a rollout the active batch is large and compute-bound, so parallel verification can make SD slower than plain autoregressive (AR) decoding.
official.method:
EfficientRollout is self-speculative decoding with a drafter derived from the target model. At the start of every training step, the current policy's FFN and QKVO projection weights are quantized to 4 bits with round-to-nearest (RTN), served with the Marlin W4 kernel in vLLM. The quantized copy drafts tokens and the full-precision policy verifies them with standard rejection sampling, so sampling stays lossless. A calibrated roofline model predicts the SD-over-AR speedup from the current batch size B, sequence length S, block efficiency tau and draft length gamma. SD is switched on, and stays on for the rest of the rollout, once the predicted speedup is at least 1.05. The draft length is picked adaptively from {5, 7, 9, 11} based on the block efficiency measured in previous steps, with a patience window.

Setup: GRPO in veRL with vLLM rollouts. Qwen2.5-7B trained on SimpleRL-8k-hard with train batch 128, group size 8, temperature 1.0, max response 8k, for 100 steps on one 8xA100-80GB node with data parallelism. Baselines in the same stack: veRL (AR) without SD, history-based drafting (Spec-RL, lossy lenience e^0.5), learned auxiliary drafting (EAGLE3, gamma=3), and always-on quantized self-SD with the best fixed gamma. Metrics are per-step averages of rollout-generation time and full training-step time.
official.claim: In GRPO training of Qwen2.5-7B on SimpleRL-8k-hard (8xA100, 100 steps), EfficientRollout cuts mean per-step rollout-generation time from 82.4 s (veRL AR) to 62.4 s (-24.2%) and step time from 132.6 s to 111.9 s (-15.6%). Final model quality is preserved; the learned-auxiliary EAGLE3 baseline reaches only 81.9 s.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: End-to-end training acceleration across models and rollout decoding methods. We report SD-specific preparation time, average block efficiency τ (γ̄ denotes the average draft length), per-token acceptance rate α, rollout-generation time, and training-step time. Signed percentages denote relative changes from the veRL (AR) baseline. In arrow-marked columns, bold and underlined entries indicate the best and second-best values within each model group.
official.metric: Per-step averaged rollout-generation time and training-step time in seconds (lower is better). Table 2 is a single run with no error bars. Appendix F.2 reports that over 3 paired data-order seeds the reductions are 22.2% ± 1.8 pp (rollout) and 14.0% ± 1.5 pp (step), mean ± SD.
official.comparison: EfficientRollout vs. veRL (AR), history-based drafting (Spec-RL), learned auxiliary drafting (EAGLE3) and always-on quantized self-SD, all run in the same veRL+vLLM stack on the same hardware
official.falsification_criterion: In the same setting, EfficientRollout's rollout-generation time reduction over veRL (AR) for Qwen2.5-7B comes out well below the ~20% band reported (e.g. under 15%, or several seed-SDs below 22.2%), or the training reward / validation accuracy curve departs noticeably from AR.

title: OrthoReg: Orthogonal Regularization for Hybrid Symbolic-Neural Dynamical Systems
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (repeated in Table 4 'Medium' block and Table 5 'Regular' block, pages 21-22)

official.background: Hybrid dynamical-system models write the vector field as a symbolic part (a sparse combination of library functions such as polynomials and sin/cos, as in SINDy) plus a neural residual that captures effects the library cannot express. To keep such a model interpretable, the neural part should not relearn terms the symbolic part could have represented. APHYNITY-style L2 regularization of the neural part guarantees this when the symbolic structure is fixed, because the problem reduces to a projection. When the symbolic support is instead discovered with an L1 sparsity penalty, coefficient shrinkage leaves in-library residual structure that the neural part can absorb. The result is redundant models and worse recovery of the true symbolic terms.
official.method:
The model is f̂(x) = Σ_j w_j φ_j(x) + f̂_aug(x; ϑ). The library is PolynomialLibrary(degree 2) ⊕ FourierLibrary(1 frequency) (M = 20 feature-component pairs for the 2-D pendulum), and f̂_aug is a 3-hidden-layer tanh MLP of width 128. Training uses vector-field regression on smoothed finite-difference derivative targets, with Adam (lr 0.0089, 2000 full-batch epochs, 1000 trajectories). OrthoReg minimizes L_fit + µ‖w‖₁ + λ Σ_j ⟨f̂_aug, φ_j⟩_D², where ⟨·,·⟩_D is the empirical inner product over training states (λ = 0.005, µ = 0.003). The Hybrid L2 baseline is identical except that the regularizer is λ₂‖f̂_aug‖_D² (λ₂ = 0.005, µ = 0.001). Both sets of hyperparameters were chosen by a validation sweep on held-out in-distribution prediction loss. Coefficients are thresholded at 1e-3 to count terms and compute F1 against the true support.

The data come from a modified damped pendulum θ̈ + 0.2 θ̇ + sin θ = 0.3 cos(3θ) + 0.25 e^{−θ} + 0.15 tanh(θ̇), simulated with odeint over T = 6 with 100 time points. The three forcing terms lie outside the library by construction ('medium' library mismatch). OOD-T3 uses trajectories generated with all system parameters scaled by 1.2 and evaluates derivative MSE, normalized by the squared norm of the target.
official.claim: On the modified damped pendulum with medium library mismatch, OrthoReg recovers the symbolic support better than the L2-regularized hybrid (F1 0.93 ± 0.15 vs. 0.61 ± 0.03; 3.6 ± 1.3 vs. 6.8 ± 0.4 active terms). Its OOD-T3 (parameters ×1.2) normalized derivative MSE is 0.02 ± 0.00 ×10² vs. 7.90 ± 4.02 ×10² for L2, but it has higher in-distribution error (derivative MSE 1.89 vs. 1.41 ×10⁻²).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Damped Pendulum results. Scale factors ek inside parentheses are powers of ten; x/ẋ are state/derivative spaces.
official.metric: F1 of recovered symbolic support vs. ground-truth terms (higher is better); number of active terms after thresholding at 1e-3 (lower is better); normalized derivative MSE on OOD-T3 trajectories (lower is better). ± is presumably std over the 5 seeds the paper mentions, but the table does not define it

title: Compute Efficiency and Serial Runtime Tradeoffs for Stochastic Momentum Methods
claim_source: Figure 1 (right panel; left panel for the a = 0.9 contrast), page 2

official.background: Momentum methods such as heavy ball (HB) speed up gradient descent on quadratics from O(κ) to O(√κ) iterations when gradients are exact, but this acceleration is known to vanish for SGD at small batch sizes. Practitioners care about two separate quantities: serial runtime (the number of steps to reach a target loss) and compute efficiency (the inverse of the total number of gradient queries, i.e. batch size × steps). Larger batches reduce serial runtime for free only while steps-to-target fall as 1/B. The paper asks how HB and accelerated SGD (ASGD, a two-term momentum family that includes Schedule-Free and AdEMAMix-like schemes) trade off these quantities as the batch size grows.
official.method:
The setting is online noiseless linear regression with Gaussian covariates x ~ N(0, H) and y = <w*, x>. H has a power-law spectrum λ_i ∝ i^(-a). ASGD updates μ_t = β μ_{t-1} + (1-β) g_t and w_{t+1} = w_t - η(μ_t + ζ g_t). HB is the special case ζ = 0, and SGD has no momentum. The theory predicts that for rapidly decaying spectra (a > 1), ASGD has better small-batch compute efficiency than HB/SGD and reaches the accelerated (saturated) step count at a smaller batch size (about d^(1/2) vs. d^(a/2) for HB). For slowly decaying spectra, ASGD and HB should roughly coincide.

Experiments (Section 5): dimension D = 50,000, up to N = 500,000 samples, batch sizes from 1 to 1024 (up to 4096 in the a = 0.9 panel), averaged over 50 seeds. Each method is tuned separately at each batch size over a grid: η ∈ {1e-5, 3e-5, 1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10}, β ∈ {0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99, 0.999, 0.9999}, ζ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99} (ζ = 0 for HB). Figure 1 plots the best-tuned number of steps needed to reach a fixed target loss (2.16 for a = 0.9; 0.0071 for a = 2) against batch size.
official.claim: In synthetic linear regression with power-law spectrum a = 2 (target loss 0.0071), tuned ASGD reaches the target in about 2,900 steps at batch size 1 versus about 12,000 for tuned HB and 13,000 for SGD (about 4x fewer). The gap shrinks as batch size grows, and ASGD and HB nearly coincide (about 180-210 steps) from B = 256 to 1024. With a = 0.9, ASGD and HB nearly overlap at all batch sizes.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Batch-size tradeoffs for stochastic momentum methods in synthetic linear regression with power-law spectra. Plots show the number of serial steps needed to reach a fixed target loss as the batch size varies, after tuning hyperparameters for each method. (Left) For slow decaying power law spectra, HB and ASGD do not yield better CE, but they decrease the serial runtime. (Right) For fast decaying spectra, ASGD has better CE than HB, but has a shorter linear scaling window before it begins trading off CE for serial runtime. Experimental details are provided in Section 5.
official.metric: Number of serial steps to reach a fixed target loss (lower is better), with hyperparameters tuned per method and batch size, averaged over 50 seeds. No error bars or seed spread are shown. Values are read off a log-scale plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Tuned ASGD vs. tuned heavy ball (ζ = 0) vs. tuned SGD at each batch size on the same synthetic problem
official.falsification_criterion: On the a = 2 problem with per-batch-size tuning over the stated grid, ASGD at B = 1 needs about as many steps as HB (e.g. less than a 2x reduction), or ASGD's advantage does not shrink toward HB's step count at large batch sizes (B ≥ 256).

title: Calibrating Generative Models to Feature Distributions with MMD Finetuning

official.background: Generative models of molecules trained on broad drug-like chemical space can produce individually plausible molecules whose distribution of chemical features differs substantially from a specialized target class, such as known antibiotics. Directly finetuning the pretrained model on the small target set can overfit and gives the user no control over which features are matched. The paper asks how to calibrate a pretrained generator so that the distribution of user-chosen, possibly non-differentiable features of its samples matches a target distribution given only feature-space samples.
official.method:
kCGM (kernel Calibrating Generative Models) finetunes a pretrained generative model p_theta to minimize an unbiased finite-sample estimator of the squared kernel maximum mean discrepancy between the feature distribution of generated samples and the empirical distribution of target features, plus lambda times the KL divergence to the pretrained model. Because gradients are score-function (REINFORCE) gradients over the sampling trajectory log-probability, the feature map h may be black-box and non-differentiable. Per-sample MMD coefficients are coupled across the minibatch, so the authors introduce an MMD-specific leave-one-out baseline (plus the standard leave-one-out baseline on the KL coefficients) as a control variate.

In the small-molecule experiment the pretrained model is G2PT-small (1M parameters, autoregressive graph transformer) trained on GuacaMol, and the target is a set of 174 antibiotics. Three feature spaces are used: 256-bit radius-2 Morgan fingerprints with the Tanimoto kernel, generic Murcko scaffolds embedded with ChemNet and reduced to 64 PCs with the energy-distance kernel, and 11 RDKit molecular descriptors with the energy-distance kernel; chemically invalid generations map to the zero vector. Baselines are CGM (Smith et al. 2026, CGM-relax; matches only the target feature mean) run on the same features with the same KL regularizer, and direct autoregressive-likelihood finetuning on the 174 antibiotics with the same KL regularizer. Each method sweeps five values of lambda; Table 1 linearly interpolates each method's curve to a common KL-to-pretrained of 25 so methods are compared at matched distance from the pretrained model. All methods train 500 epochs at batch size 192 and are evaluated with 9,600 samples, over 3 seeds.
official.claim: On the 174-antibiotic G2PT task at a matched KL-to-pretrained budget of 25, kCGM trained on Morgan fingerprints reaches Morgan MMD^2 = 0.005 (SEM 0.00017) versus 0.014 (0.00019) for CGM on the same features, while also keeping chemical validity at 95% (0.2%) versus 67% (0.093%) for direct finetuning, which reaches a comparable Morgan MMD^2 of 0.007 (7e-05).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Best metric values for runs with KL budget 25. Entries show linearly interpolated mean (SEM) at KL-to-pretrained equal to 25. SEMs are interpolated by treating the two neighboring estimates as independent and propagating variance under the linear interpolation weights. Bold indicates the best method for each metric; underline indicates the second-best method.
official.metric: Squared MMD between generated and target Morgan-fingerprint distributions under the Tanimoto kernel, computed only on chemically valid generations (lower is better), and fraction of chemically valid generations (higher is better); parentheses are the standard error of the mean over 3 seeds, linearly interpolated to KL-to-pretrained = 25 with variance propagated across the two neighboring lambda runs
official.comparison: kCGM Morgan vs. CGM Morgan vs. direct finetuning vs. the pretrained model, all finetuning the same pretrained G2PT-small on the same 174 antibiotics with the same KL regularizer, compared at KL-to-pretrained = 25
official.falsification_criterion: At KL-to-pretrained = 25, kCGM Morgan's Morgan MMD^2 is not clearly below CGM Morgan's (e.g. the 0.005 vs. 0.014 gap shrinks to within a few SEM, or CGM matches/beats kCGM), or direct finetuning does not lose a large amount of validity relative to kCGM (e.g. its validity is not far below 95%).

title: Learning When to Denoise: Optimizing Asynchronous Schedules for Latent Diffusion

official.background: Multi-representation latent diffusion models such as Semantic-First Diffusion (SFD) denoise two latent groups for each image: a texture latent from an image VAE, which is decoded to pixels, and a semantic latent compressed from DINOv2 features. The semantic group is denoised ahead of the texture group, asynchronously, so global structure forms before detail. In SFD the size of this lead is a fixed temporal offset found by a small grid search. Since sample quality depends strongly on this schedule, learning it from data could improve both convergence speed and final quality.
official.method:
Semantic local time is set to the global sampler time τ, and texture local time follows a learned schedule t_tex(τ; ρ). Its derivative is a normalized non-negative degree-4 polynomial (softplus coefficients), so the schedule is monotone and convex, with t_tex(0)=0, t_tex(1)=1 and t_tex(τ) ≤ τ, which means semantics always lead. The flow-matching loss is a weighted sum of texture and semantic component losses (group weights w_tex = 1, w_sem = 2).The texture term is reweighted by stop-gradient(t'_tex(τ)), so the marginal weighting over local noise levels does not change when the schedule changes. The schedule objective also adds a kinetic-energy regularizer λ·E[t'_tex² ||v_tex||² + ||v_sem||²], with λ = 4e-2.

Stage I is a 10K-step joint probe that trains a temporary denoiser (its architecture is not stated in the paper) together with ρ on the flow loss plus the kinetic regularizer (learning rate 1e-2 for ρ, 1e-4 for the denoiser). ρ is averaged over the last 5K steps and then frozen. Stage II trains a fresh LightningDiT-XL/1 (675M parameters) from scratch on the SFD-released ImageNet-256 latents with this fixed schedule and the unchanged SFD losses (including REPA), at batch size 256. Evaluation uses unguided sampling with dopri5 ODE integration (250 NFEs) and FID on 50K samples against the ADM reference statistics. Everything except the schedule and the corrected loss weighting is the same as SFD-XL.
official.claim: On class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 with a LightningDiT-XL/1 backbone and SFD latents, replacing SFD's hand-tuned semantic-first offset with the learned schedule lowers unguided FID-50K at 400K training iterations from 3.53 to 2.87. The learned schedule also gives lower FID at every other matched budget (e.g. 70K: 8.79 to 6.89; 1M: 2.82 to 2.37).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Unguided FID convergence. All entries use 675M-parameter XL backbones. Baseline numbers are from Pan et al. [18], Peebles and Xie [19], Yao et al. [26], Yu et al. [27].
official.metric: Unguided FID-50K vs. ADM reference statistics (lower is better); single run per setting, no error bars reported
official.comparison: Learned asynchronous schedule (Ours) vs. SFD's fixed semantic-leading offset at the same training-iteration budget, same backbone, latents, auxiliary losses and sampler
official.falsification_criterion: With the same SFD codebase and latents, a model trained for 400K iterations under the learned schedule does not reach FID clearly below a matched SFD fixed-offset model (e.g. gap well under the claimed 0.66), or the SFD baseline rerun gets much closer to 2.87 than the reported 3.53.

title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems
claim_source: Table 4, page 19 (Appendix C.1; same numbers without error bars in Table 1, page 9)

official.background: In image restoration there is a distortion-perception (DP) tradeoff: estimators that minimize MSE give blurry, over-smoothed images, while posterior samplers give sharp, realistic images that are less faithful to the ground truth. Which balance is best depends on the user, so it would be useful to have one model that can move along the DP frontier at inference time. Existing methods either fix one operating point, need paired supervised training or auxiliary models, or move along the frontier by retuning sampler hyperparameters.
official.method:
A flow map v_theta(x, s, t) is trained from scratch (Song UNet, about 128M parameters, Lagrangian self-distillation loss) on unconditional clean images. It predicts the average velocity of the flow-matching ODE over the interval [s, t]. The authors define an 'average denoiser' D_{s,t}(x) = x + (1 - s) v_theta(x, s, t). At t = s this is the ordinary MMSE (Tweedie) denoiser; at t = 1 it transports the noisy input to the end of the flow, so its outputs follow the data distribution. The lookahead t is therefore a knob between low distortion and high perceptual quality.

For inverse problems the denoiser is placed in a Plug-and-Play loop (Algorithm 1): a gradient step on 0.5||y - f(x)||^2, re-noising to level s_k = k/N, then x_{k+1} = D_{s_k, t_k}(z~_k) with t_k = min(s_k + Delta, 1). With Delta = 0 this is exactly PnP-Flow (Martin et al., 2025); 't = 1' means Delta = 1. Both rows use the same network and the same solver hyperparameters, tuned for PSNR (on AFHQ random inpainting, N = 300 iterations, learning-rate exponent alpha = 0.05). The task is random inpainting with 90% of pixels missing and Gaussian noise sigma = 0.01. Metrics are PSNR, LPIPS, DISTS and FID, computed over 100 test images.
official.claim: On AFHQ 256x256 random inpainting (90% missing, sigma = 0.01), with the same flow map and solver, switching PnP-Flow from t = s to t = 1 lowers LPIPS from 0.162 +/- 0.013 to 0.122 +/- 0.012, DISTS from 0.135 +/- 0.008 to 0.095 +/- 0.006 and FID from 13.49 to 9.11, while PSNR drops from 24.99 to 23.23 dB.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Quantitative results for random inpainting (90%) with sigma = 0.01 on CelebA and AFHQ. Best results are in bold.
official.metric: LPIPS and DISTS (lower is better), FID (lower is better), PSNR (higher is better). Metrics are averaged over 100 samples. The paper does not say what the +/- values are (Appendix C.1 only says 'corresponding error bars'); they appear to be per-sample spread from one run, since no seeds are reported. FID has no error bar.
official.comparison: PnP-Flow with lookahead t = 1 (the proposed flow-map average denoiser) vs. PnP-Flow with t = s (the standard instantaneous MMSE denoiser, i.e. the published PnP-Flow method), using the same trained flow map and solver settings

title: Pose6DAug: Physically Plausible Multi-View Object Swapping for Robot Data Augmentation

official.background: Vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies often fail on object instances whose appearance or geometry differs from their training data, and collecting new multi-view teleoperation demonstrations for each failure is expensive. Existing augmentation alternatives each have drawbacks: 2D video-editing models (e.g. VACE) edit each camera view independently and can produce multi-view-inconsistent or physically implausible objects, while simulation-based trajectory adaptation (e.g. MimicGen) needs simulator access and often fails to produce valid rollouts for hard object geometries.
official.method:
Pose6DAug takes a successful multi-view episode with a source object and replaces the object with a target object while keeping the robot's recorded action trajectory. The target mesh is reconstructed with SAM3D from a single rendered image of the target object (the simulator's ground-truth asset is not used directly), assumed to share the source mesh's canonical frame, and given the source object's per-timestep world-frame 6D pose (from simulator state in RoboCasa). The source object is masked out and the background filled with a video inpainting model (VOID); the target mesh is rendered into each calibrated camera view at the shared pose and composited back-to-front, with robot/gripper pixels restored on top. Random rotations/flips, translations along the gripper approach axis, and vertical rescaling (when the target is too short for the gripper) diversify the episodes.

Experiments use the RoboCasa365 Counter-to-Cabinet pick-and-place task and GR00T-1.5. Eight hard target meshes (base-policy success <= 30%) are paired with same-category source episodes from the training set; Pose6DAug and VACE (Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B, applied per view) each produce 176 augmented episodes with the same pairings, while MimicGen (32 attempts per pair, only successful rollouts kept) yields 33. For Table 1, GR00T-1.5 is fine-tuned for 30K steps on the original demonstrations plus each method's augmented episodes (AdamW, lr 1e-5, cosine decay), and evaluated on failure episodes, i.e. object instances on which the base policy never succeeded, split into ID and OOD object categories.
official.claim: On RoboCasa365 Counter-to-Cabinet failure episodes, GR00T-1.5 fine-tuned on original data plus Pose6DAug augmentations reaches 22.8% average success rate, versus 16.4% with the same number of VACE-edited episodes and 15.8% with MimicGen (base policy 0.0%); turnover ratio is 24.5% vs. 18.2% and 17.2%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Overall performance on failure episodes. Success rate (%) and turnover ratio (%) evaluated on failure episodes: instances where the base policy never succeeded in completing the task with the target object. Results are split into in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) object categories unseen during training, and averaged over 3 independent seeds. Higher is better for both metrics. Bold indicates the best result.
official.metric: Success rate (%) on failure episodes, higher is better; turnover ratio (%) = fraction of never-succeeding meshes that achieve at least one success. Reported as means over 3 seeds; no standard deviations or intervals given.
official.comparison: Pose6DAug vs. VACE (per-view 2D video editing, matched pairings and 176 episodes) vs. MimicGen (simulation-based, 33 valid episodes) vs. base GR00T-1.5 policy, all fine-tuned with the same recipe
official.falsification_criterion: With matched pairings and episode counts, the Pose6DAug-augmented policy's average success rate on failure episodes is not above the VACE-augmented policy's, or the gap is within seed-to-seed variation across 3 seeds.

title: ConnectomeBench2: A Unified Benchmark for Automated Connectomic Proofreading

official.background: Connectomics reconstructs neurons and their synapses from 3D electron-microscopy volumes. Automatic segmentation leaves two kinds of errors: split errors, where one neuron is broken into pieces, and merge errors, where several neurons are fused. Correcting them by hand ('proofreading') is the main bottleneck in building whole-brain wiring maps. Earlier automated proofreading systems were usually trained and evaluated on one species and one error type, and earlier benchmarks were too small to train on. This paper releases a large multi-species benchmark built from expert proofreading edits and trains a single vision model on it.
official.method:
The dataset takes non-reverted expert proofreading edits from four public connectomes (MICrONS mouse, FlyWire fly, H01 human, Fish1 zebrafish). Positives are real merge edits (fixing split errors) and real split edits (fixing merge errors). Negatives are synapse partners and spatially adjacent segments (for split-error correction) and skeleton junctions on proofread neurons (for merge-error identification). Each sample is rendered as 3 orthographic mesh-geometry views (7 channels: normals, depth, two segment masks, silhouette) and 4 EM slice views (3 channels: EM plus two segment masks). Train/val/test splits are assigned by (80 µm)^3 spatial cubes (75/12.5/12.5).

The model is one ImageNet-initialized ViT-B/16 (224x224) with two patch embeddings, a 7-channel one for geometry and a 3-channel one for EM, feeding a shared encoder. Classification heads on the CLS token cover split-error correction, merge-error identification and an auxiliary synapse task, and a CNN decoder predicts a 2-channel mask for merge-error correction. It is trained jointly across species, modalities and tasks with masked cross-entropy (label smoothing 0.1) plus a permutation-invariant CE+Dice mask loss, using AdamW with a cosine schedule for 20 epochs. At test time, view probabilities are averaged within each operation and thresholded at 0.5. Table 1 compares the full model with geometry-only and EM-only variants. The text says modalities and channels can be ablated independently at inference time, and channel dropout is used in training.
official.claim: On the held-out spatial test split, the jointly trained mesh+EM ViT-B reaches 93.0% [92.7, 93.2] per-operation balanced accuracy on merge-error identification, versus 90.6% [90.4, 90.9] for geometry-only and 91.1% [90.9, 91.4] for EM-only. On split-error correction it reaches 97.0% [96.9, 97.2] versus 96.2% and 94.2%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Peak performance and ablations on the held-out test set. Per-sample (one prediction per operation; views aggregated). bAcc is reported at threshold 0.5 alongside mIoU (mask GT is rendered on geometry views only, so the EM-only row's mIoU is '—'). Brackets are 95% cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals.
official.metric: Per-sample (per-operation, views averaged) balanced accuracy at threshold 0.5, higher is better; brackets are 95% cluster-bootstrap CIs over operations (one training run, no seed variance reported)
official.comparison: Full ViT-B (geometry + EM views) vs. the same ViT-B with only geometry views and with only EM views; human expert reference (93.0% split, 84.1% merge) is also reported
official.falsification_criterion: On the released test split, the full mesh+EM ViT-B's merge-error bAcc is not above both single-modality variants by more than their CIs (e.g. a gap under ~1 point), or its split-error bAcc does not exceed the geometry-only variant.

title: Reward-free Pretraining for Reinforcement Learning via Occupancy Coverage Maximization

official.background: In sparse-reward reinforcement learning the agent gets no useful signal until it reaches the goal, so the behavior it starts with matters a lot. Reward-free pretraining lets the agent interact with the environment before any reward is defined. Many intrinsic-reward methods (RND, SMM, APT, CIC) collect diverse data during pretraining, but their objectives change as the data changes, so the final policy may only visit a small region even though the replay buffer is diverse. When the downstream reward cannot be evaluated offline to relabel stored data, what transfers is the policy itself, so the final policy's coverage is what matters.
official.method:
ROVER pretrains a stationary policy to minimize the squared RKHS norm of the kernel mean embedding of its discounted state occupancy, J(pi) = ||mu_{d^pi}||^2, which with a Dirac kernel equals the sum of squared state-occupancy probabilities (equivalent to maximizing Rényi-2 entropy or matching the uniform distribution in MMD). Each round it collects transitions with the current policy, learns an L1-normalized state representation phi with an InfoNCE next-state prediction loss, fits a linear transition operator by kernel ridge regression from state-action features phi(x) ⊗ e_a to next-state features (with a Nyström approximation), and then runs closed-form policy mirror descent using the dual gradient of J through the resolvent (I - gamma T P_pi)^{-1}. The transition operator is augmented with a virtual absorbing 'sink' state with norm epsilon so that unsupported state-action pairs are routed to the sink instead of to zero.

Figure 3 evaluates coverage on two custom MiniGrid-style environments with 4 discrete actions: Maze (108 states) and Multiple Rooms (5 rooms in a corridor, 109 states, horizon 300), with either one-hot state observations or 84x84 RGB pixels. Baselines are CIC, SMM, ICM-APT and RND (following the URLB codebase). The bottom row ('Resampling') takes each method's final pretrained policy and plots the percentage of states visited as a function of the number of environment observations collected by rolling out that policy (up to 10 x 10^3). The top row ('Replay') plots coverage of the replay buffer during pretraining (up to 100 x 10^3).

title: CoDMD: Copula-aware Distribution Matching Distillation for Fast Video Generation

official.background: Video diffusion models such as Wan-2.1 need about 50 denoising steps with classifier-free guidance (100 network evaluations) per clip, which is slow to deploy. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student by pushing its output distribution toward the teacher's with a reverse-KL gradient built from the difference between a frozen teacher score and an online 'fake' score model. At 4 steps, DMD-distilled video models often show weak or collapsed motion, broken layouts and oversaturation. The authors argue this happens because DMD's gradient is coordinate-wise and does not constrain relations across samples or across frames.
official.method:
CoDMD adds a relational regularizer to standard DMD that reuses the teacher and fake-model predictions already computed in each DMD step. At batch level, each video is average-pooled over frames and space to a C-dim channel vector and a B_g x B_g cosine-similarity matrix is built (gathered across GPUs); at frame level, each frame is pooled over space and an F x F cosine-similarity matrix is built per video. This is done for the student output (S_stu), the teacher prediction (S_real) and the fake-model prediction (S_fake). The loss is KL(softmax((S_stu - (S_fake - S_real))/tau) || softmax(S_stu/tau)) with the target detached, tau = 0.1. The total generator loss is L_DMD + 0.1 * L_batch + 0.1 * L_frame.

The official 50-step Wan-2.1-T2V teachers (1.3B and 14B) are distilled into 4-step students at 832x480, 81 frames, CFG 3.5, using text prompts only (no real videos). The 1.3B setting uses batch size 128, student lr 2e-6, fake-score lr 4e-7 and 5 fake-score updates per student update. Models are scored with the VBench protocol (Quality, Semantic and Total scores). All baselines are re-evaluated in the authors' codebase; DMD is the primary baseline and is the same recipe with the relational weights set to 0.
official.claim: Distilling Wan-2.1-T2V-1.3B into a 4-step student, adding the copula-aware relational loss to DMD raises the VBench Total score from 83.38 to 84.46 (Quality 84.53 -> 85.50, Semantic 78.78 -> 80.27), with a similar gain at 14B (83.81 -> 84.87).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: VBench results for Wan-2.1-T2V on 480p resolution. A full per-attribute breakdown is provided in Appendix C, where CoDMD leads on the majority of individual VBench dimensions.
official.metric: VBench Total score (higher is better), plus Quality and Semantic sub-scores; single run, no ± reported
official.comparison: CoDMD (DMD + batch- and frame-level relational loss, lambda = 0.1) vs. plain DMD, both 4-step students of the same Wan-2.1-T2V teacher, evaluated in the same codebase; rCM, sCM, DCM, AVD and the 50-step teacher also listed
official.falsification_criterion: A 4-step DMD student and a CoDMD student trained under the same recipe on Wan-2.1-T2V-1.3B differ by less than about 0.5 VBench Total points, or the gap falls within the spread across training seeds.

title: On the Sparsity-Storage-Accuracy Tradeoff in Parsimoniously Activated Dictionary Learning
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (same numbers with more decimals in Table 10, page 23; the ablation in Table 4, page 8)

official.background: Dictionary learning represents each data vector as a sparse combination of learned atoms. Classical L1 sparse coding controls how many coefficients each sample uses, but not how many atoms the whole dataset uses, and that second number determines storage cost. A family of methods adds a row-wise L-infinity penalty that charges for each atom used by any sample, but their two regularization weights have to be tuned by grid search. This paper derives that objective as MAP estimation under a Beta coefficient prior plus a latent per-atom activation variable. From that derivation it gets closed-form estimates of lambda1, lambda2 and the activation threshold delta, so the method is claimed to need no hyperparameter search while reconstructing better with fewer active atoms.
official.method:
PADL minimizes ||X - DR||_F^2 + lambda1 ||R||_1 + lambda2 sum_k ||r_k||_inf over a dictionary D (unit-norm columns) and coefficients R projected to [0,1], using alternating projected gradient descent. After a warm-up phase of t_s iterations with (lambda1, lambda2, delta) = (0, 1, 0), it fits Beta(1, beta) to the empirical coefficients, sets lambda1 = beta - 1 and lambda2 = 1, solves Eq. 13 for the optimal activation threshold delta*, reinitializes, and trains. At test time D is fixed and only R is solved.

Data: CIFAR-100 and SVHN images converted to grayscale, cut into non-overlapping 8x8 patches (d = 64), with 20,000 random training patches and 2,000 test patches. The nominal dictionary has K = 128 atoms. The matched baseline 'L1-Regularized DL' is the same learner without the L-infinity term (also listed as 'w/o L-infinity' in the Table 4 ablation). The metrics are test-patch RMSE, PSNR and SSIM, given as mean +/- std over 10 repeated runs.
official.claim: On CIFAR-100 grayscale 8x8 patches with a 128-atom dictionary, PADL reaches test PSNR 20.56 +/- 0.55 dB versus 18.98 +/- 0.54 dB for the same dictionary learner with only L1 regularization (RMSE 0.099 +/- 0.009 vs 0.112 +/- 0.006), over 10 runs.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Reconstruction performance comparison on CIFAR-100 and SVHN. For recent baselines and PADL, results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over 10 repeated runs.
official.metric: Test-patch PSNR in dB (higher is better); RMSE and SSIM are also reported. +/- is the standard deviation over 10 repeated runs.
official.comparison: PADL (L1 + row-wise L-infinity, data-estimated lambda1, lambda2, delta*) vs. L1-Regularized DL (same pipeline without the L-infinity term), on CIFAR-100. Other baselines (KSVD, DDL, GDDL, BPFA, IBP, CRsAE, JumpReLU SAE) are listed for context.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same protocol and 10 runs, PADL's mean CIFAR-100 PSNR exceeds the L1-only baseline's by less than about 0.55 dB (one std), or not at all; or PADL does not reach that PSNR with fewer active atoms than the L1-only dictionary.

title: Robust Diffusion Models via Divergence-Induced Weighted Denoising

official.background: Diffusion models are trained with a weighted mean squared error on the denoising residual, so every training image counts equally however corrupted or atypical it is. When part of the training set is corrupted, those images pull the model toward generating artifacts. The paper asks whether swapping the quadratic loss for a bounded-influence transformation, derived from an f-divergence, makes diffusion training robust to such contamination, as redescending losses do in robust M-estimation.
official.method:
With the standard ε-parameterization, the per-step mismatch is m_t = w_t ||ε − ε_θ(x_t, t)||^2, with w_t = β_t^2 / (2 α_t (1 − ᾱ_t) σ_t^2). Standard DDPM (KL) minimizes m_t. The proposed objective minimizes h_G(m_t), so each sample's gradient is multiplied by the influence weight h'_G(m_t). For squared Hellinger (HD), h_HD(m) = 4(1 − e^{−m/4}) and the weight is e^{−m/4}. For the negative exponential divergence (NED), h_NED(m) = E[e^{1−U_m}] − 1 with log U_m ~ N(−m, 2m); it has no closed form, and the weight h'_NED(m_t) is approximated with 64-node Gauss–Legendre quadrature over U_m. The update is θ ← θ − η h'_G(m_t) w_t ∇_θ||ε − ε_θ(x_t, t)||^2; nothing else in DDPM training changes. Baselines: Huber loss (δ=1.0) and clipped MSE (threshold τ=10); the paper does not say whether these act on the raw residual or on m_t.

Setup: 35M-parameter DDPM U-Net (128 base channels, multipliers (1,2,2,2), attention at 16×16), linear β schedule from 1e-4 to 0.02, T=1000, Adam lr 2e-4, batch 128, bf16, gradient clipping 1.0, 100K steps, unconditional. Contamination: a fraction ε of CIFAR-10 training images is replaced by a uniform mixture of four corruptions (8×8 patch noise, Gaussian blur σ=1.5, salt-and-pepper p=0.05, contrast shift ±0.4). FID uses 5K samples from a 50-step DDIM sampler, computed against the clean test split.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with 30% of training images corrupted, training the DDPM with the HD or NED divergence-induced loss gives FID 56.2 and 55.1, versus 94.0 for Huber loss and 90.5 for clipped MSE (single seed, 100K steps).

official.metric: FID on 5K samples vs. the clean CIFAR-10 test split (lower is better). Table 3 is a single seed (42) with no error bars; Table 2 gives mean ± std over 3 seeds (42, 123, 456) for KL/HD/NED only.
official.comparison: HD and NED losses vs. Huber (δ=1.0) and clipped MSE (τ=10), with identical architecture, hyperparameters and budget, at ε = 0.30 (with ε = 0.10 and 0.20 as supporting rows)
official.falsification_criterion: At ε=0.30, averaged over several seeds, the better of Huber and clipped MSE reaches FID within the cross-seed std of HD/NED, or below them; or the HD/NED advantage at ε=0.30 shrinks to a few FID points.

title: MotionHalluc: Diagnosing Kinematic Hallucinations in Fine-Grained Motion Reasoning
claim_source: Table 9 (Appendix H.1), page 22; reconstructed-motion version in Table 3, page 7

official.background: Motion instruction generation asks a model to compare a query video of someone exercising with a reference video and produce corrective feedback (e.g. 'keep your torso more upright'). Large multimodal models often produce instructions that sound plausible but do not match the actual kinematic difference: they get the direction backwards, name the wrong joint, or compare mismatched phases of the movement. MotionHalluc is a benchmark of 1540 closed-form questions over 553 Fit3D video pairs (32 fitness actions) that tests these three failure modes, Directional (DH), Attributional (AH) and Temporal (TH) hallucination. The paper also asks whether giving the model explicit kinematic measurements reduces these errors.
official.method:
Benchmark tasks: DH is binary yes/no on whether a human-annotated instruction is accurate for (query, reference); half the items are 'Reversed', with the videos swapped so the correct answer is No. AH is a 2-way choice between a true instruction and a GPT-5-perturbed one (same joint or different joints). TH is a 3-way choice of which reference clip matches the query clip's action phase. Overall accuracy is the mean of DH, AH and TH accuracies. Videos are sampled at 4 FPS; open-source models use greedy decoding, and API models are averaged over 3 runs.

PPV (Perceive-Parse-Verify) is training-free. (1) Get 3D motion for both videos: 4D-Humans reconstruction plus DTW alignment, or, in the PPV-GT variant, Fit3D ground-truth motion capture (22-joint HumanML3D skeleton). (2) A text-only semantic parser (gemini-3-flash-preview) turns the action description and each candidate instruction into structured calls from a fixed library of 4 frame-localization functions (extremum of a joint angle, joint-axis offset, pelvis height, or bone-to-world-direction angle) and 4 measurement functions (three-joint angle, joint-axis offset, pelvis Y, bone-to-world angle). (3) These are executed on both motion sequences, and the resulting query vs. reference measurements are given as text to the evaluated model along with the original videos and question.
official.claim: Adding PPV kinematic measurements computed from ground-truth motion raises overall MotionHalluc accuracy for all five evaluated LMMs, with paired 95% bootstrap CIs on the gain excluding zero, e.g. LLaVA-OV-1.5-8B 48.37 -> 59.65 (+11.28 [9.07, 13.51]), InternVL3.5-8B +6.58 [4.16, 9.08], Qwen3-VL-8B +4.96 [2.60, 7.29], Gemini-3-Flash +18.03 [15.30, 20.62].
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Overall accuracy under Base and PPV-GT. Accuracy is reported in percent; gains (PPV-GT minus Base) are in percentage points. Brackets denote 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Gains use unrounded scores. The LOAO range gives the minimum and maximum gains across 32 action exclusions.
official.metric: Overall accuracy (%) = mean of DH, AH, TH accuracies, higher is better. Brackets are percentile 95% CIs from 10,000 action-stratified cluster bootstrap resamples (video pairs as clusters, same draws for Base and PPV-GT). The LOAO range is the min-max gain over 32 leave-one-action-out evaluations.

title: SteerVTE: Seamless Video Text Editing with Style and Glyph Control

official.background: Visual text editing means replacing the text in an image or video with new text while keeping the original font, color and effects and leaving everything else unchanged. Image text editors are strong, but applying them frame by frame causes flicker and style drift. Editing only the first frame and propagating it with image-to-video generation loses fidelity to the source video. General video editing models built on video foundation models (Wan, HunyuanVideo, LTX) have weak text-rendering priors and tend to produce garbled or unedited text. Video text editing therefore needs character-level accuracy, style fidelity and temporal coherence all at once.
official.method:
SteerVTE freezes the VACE 14B video diffusion transformer and adds a Text Context Adapter (LoRA rank 64 plus two linear connectors) that injects three signals. (1) Mask-guided positional conditioning: VAE latents of the masked foreground and background, the downsampled mask, and the VAE latent of a line-level glyph image of the target text rendered in a neutral font. (2) A style encoder: Qwen2.5-VL-3B reads the masked text crop from one source frame with a prompt about typography; its last two hidden states are projected and fed in by cross-attention. (3) A character-level glyph encoder: each target character is rendered separately and encoded with PP-OCRv3, then fed in by cross-attention. Training follows a three-stage curriculum: connectors only on 500k easy synthetic images; connectors plus LoRA on 300k real image edits derived from AnyWord-3M; then 200k hard synthetic 49-frame videos with flow matching plus the GLAS loss (a mask-weighted latent loss with gamma = 3.0, plus an OCR feature/CTC loss on decoded frames with lambda = 0.1, applied only for t < 0.3).

Evaluation uses VTE-Bench-Synth: 100 synthetic videos (50 easy, 50 hard) with ground-truth edited videos. Five frames are sampled per video and OCR'd with PP-OCRv4, which differs from the PP-OCRv3 used in training. The text metrics are precision, recall, F-score, NED (1 minus normalized Levenshtein distance) and sentence accuracy (exact string match). Baselines get the source video, mask (if supported), a line-level glyph image and the prompt 'Change the text from {source} to {target}, while keeping the text style consistent.' All open-source models use 20 sampling steps. Seedance 2.0 is called through its official 480p API.
official.claim: On VTE-Bench-Synth (100 synthetic videos), SteerVTE reaches sentence accuracy 0.61 and NED 0.962, compared with 0.33 and 0.863 for the strongest baseline, Seedance 2.0. Every open-source video editor, including its own backbone VACE given the same mask and glyph image, scores NED at or below 0.16, and the per-frame image editor FLUX-Text scores 0.28.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative comparison on VTE-Bench-Synth. SteerVTE consistently outperforms other approaches across all metrics, including OCR accuracy and style consistency. Bold is the best.
official.metric: Sentence accuracy (exact OCR match with PP-OCRv4, higher is better) and NED (higher is better), averaged over 5 sampled frames and 100 videos. Single run, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: SteerVTE vs. FLUX-Text (per-frame image editing), VACE, VideoPainter, VIVA, UniVideo, Kiwi-Edit and Seedance 2.0 on the same benchmark inputs (Table 1); Appendix Table 7 adds STRIVE*, TextCtrl, AnyText2 and FLUX2, all of which score below Seedance 2.0.

title: GeoFidelity-Bench: Evaluating Block-Conditioned Geographic Fidelity in Text-to-Image Street-View Generation
claim_source: Table 6, page 7 (per-model values from Table 5, page 6)

official.background: Text-to-image models can produce believable street scenes for a prompt like 'a street in New York City', but standard metrics (FID, CLIPScore, LPIPS) measure image quality or text alignment and cannot tell whether an image looks like the requested place or just a generic version of the city. GeoFidelity-Bench tests geographic fidelity at the level of named street blocks: each block (a named OpenStreetMap way, or a segment of one) has a panel of real Mapillary street-view images, so generated images can be compared with the real appearance of that street and with other streets in the same city.
official.method:
The benchmark has 112 named street blocks in 25 cities, each with a filtered panel of real Mapillary images (7,563 block-image assignments, at least 25 and on average 67.5 per block; four images per block are held out as real queries and the rest form the reference panel). Prompts come in three levels sharing a photorealistic, daytime, clear-weather suffix: L0 'taken in {city}, {country}'; L1 'taken on {street} in the {neighborhood} district of {city}, {country}'; L2 = L1 plus 'near GPS coordinates ({lat}, {lon})'. Six open-weight models (SDXL, SD 3.5 Large, FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.1-schnell, PixArt-Σ, HunyuanDiT) each generate four 1024×1024 images per block and prompt level, with fixed per-model settings (e.g. SDXL 30 steps, guidance 5.0, fp16) and a shared negative prompt (not used for FLUX). L0 images for a block are drawn from a pool of city-only generations for its city.

The main metric, CosSim, encodes every image with DINOv2 ViT-B/14, averages the embeddings within the four-image generated panel and within the block's reference panel, and takes the cosine similarity of the two means. The prompt ablation computes, for each (model, block) pair, CosSim(L1) − CosSim(L0), and reports the mean over the 672 pairs with a 95% interval from 5,000 bootstrap resamples of the matched pairs, plus a city-balanced estimate that averages within each city first.
official.claim: Adding the street and neighborhood names to a city-only prompt (L1 vs. L0) raises DINOv2 panel CosSim to the target block's real reference panel by +0.036 on average over 672 matched (model, block) pairs (bootstrap 95% CI [0.029, 0.042]; city-balanced +0.042 [0.025, 0.060], positive in 21 of 25 cities), and the gain is positive for all six models (e.g. SDXL 0.512 → 0.536, SD 3.5 Large 0.432 → 0.515).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Prompt-ablation uncertainty checks for CosSim. Matched units are (model, block) pairs; city-balanced units give each city equal weight.
official.metric: CosSim: cosine similarity between mean DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings of the four-image generated panel and the block's real reference panel, higher is better. Brackets are 95% bootstrap intervals; the paper states they use 5,000 resamples of the matched (model, block) pairs, and for the city-balanced column says only that estimates average within each city first and then weight cities equally (no separate resampling unit is specified). Table 5 per-model values have no error bars.

title: Learning to Trigger: Reinforcement Learning at the Large Hadron Collider

official.background: LHC experiments keep only a tiny fraction of collisions, using triggers that accept an event when a score (for example total jet transverse energy H_T, or an autoencoder anomaly score) exceeds a threshold. The background acceptance rate has to stay inside a fixed bandwidth (here 100 ± 10 kHz), but pileup and detector conditions drift during a run. Static, hand-tuned thresholds then fall out of the band, and simple feedback controllers such as PID react only to the scalar rate error. The paper casts online threshold tuning as reinforcement learning: keep the rate in the tolerance band while maximizing efficiency on rare signal processes.
official.method:
A single scalar threshold is controlled for each trigger (H_T, or the AD reconstruction-loss score from an autoencoder with latent dimension 2). At each micro-step (5,000 events; chunks of 50K events on MC and 20K on CMS) the policy sees a recurrent summary of the last K event scores plus pileup (N_pv), controller context (threshold, observed rate, last change) and near-threshold occupancy features. It picks a discrete threshold increment, clipped by a safety shield. The reward (Eq. 2) combines rate tracking around the target r_B* = 0.25% with tolerance τ = 0.025%, a mix of tt̄ and h→4b signal efficiencies (α = 0.7), and a move penalty (λ1 = 0.25, λ2 = 1.0). GRPO is adapted with γ = 0, sampling G candidate increments and normalizing rewards within the group. GFPO samples G = 64 candidates and keeps K = 16 before normalizing. GFPO-F keeps the 16 with the smallest window rate error. GFPO-FR keeps feasible (in-band) candidates first, ranked by signal efficiency, and pads with the closest-to-feasible candidates if needed. The update is skipped when no candidate is feasible.

Policies are trained on the first 80% of the Monte Carlo background stream, frozen, and deployed with argmax actions and no gradient updates on real CMS Open Data Run 283408 (1.99M background events; the AD autoencoder is trained on Run 283876). Baselines: constant threshold, PID, DSPOT, DQN, DQN-F, PPO, ADT, GRPO, Lagrangian GRPO (L-GRPO) and CPO (with group-relative advantages). InBand is the fraction of steps whose observed background rate lies within [0.225%, 0.275%] (90-110 kHz). The first 10 calibration chunks are excluded.
official.claim: With MC-trained policies frozen and deployed zero-shot on CMS Run 283408, GFPO-F keeps the AD-trigger background rate in the 90-110 kHz band on 0.689 ± 0.04 of steps, vs. at most 0.541 for every baseline (PPO, ADT, GRPO, L-GRPO, CPO; PID 0.405), and on the H_T trigger on 0.99 vs. at most 0.905 (CPO; PID 0.432).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Single-trigger control on CMS data (zero-shot transfer). MC-trained policies from Table 1 are frozen and deployed on real collision data without fine-tuning. GFPO-FR (ours) attains the highest signal efficiency on both triggers and the highest InBand on AD; GFPO-F (ours) attains the lowest MAE on both. See Appendix F.4 for results on online training for CMS data.
official.metric: InBand fraction (higher is better): fraction of control steps with background rate inside r_B* ± τ. Values in parentheses are std over 3 training seeds; many entries show (0) because the frozen argmax policy is deterministic or the method is non-learning. MAE, P95|e| and overall and in-band signal efficiencies are also reported.
official.comparison: GFPO-F and GFPO-FR vs. Constant, PID, DSPOT, DQN, DQN-F, PPO, ADT, GRPO, L-GRPO and CPO, all trained on the same 80% MC and deployed frozen on the same CMS run
official.falsification_criterion: On the AD trigger, frozen GFPO-F's InBand on CMS Run 283408 falls to within seed std of the best baseline (about 0.54), or a re-run baseline (e.g. GRPO or CPO) reaches about 0.69; or on H_T, GFPO-F does not exceed CPO's 0.905.

title: AsyncOPD: How Stale Can On-Policy Distillation Be?

official.background: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student LLM on its own sampled rollouts, using token-level feedback (a local KL loss) from a teacher. Like RL, it is bottlenecked by rollout generation: for long reasoning traces, a synchronous pipeline spends most of its time waiting for generation while the learner sits idle. Asynchronous pipelines overlap rollout, teacher scoring and learner updates, but then the learner trains on stale data produced by an older student, and because full-vocabulary teacher logits are too expensive to store, teacher scores are only available on a finite cache of actions. The paper studies which OPD estimators survive staleness and builds a fully asynchronous OPD system, AsyncOPD, from those choices.
official.method:
All schedulers use the same reverse-KL OPD estimator: at each visited prefix, the rollout worker caches m next-token samples from the rollout-time student (m = 64, 'MC64', or m = 1, 'MC1') with their log probabilities; the teacher (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507) scores those cached tokens; the learner recomputes the advantage A_theta = log q - log p_theta under the current student and applies the unclipped old-to-current importance-sampling surrogate -(1/m) sum_i rho_theta(a_i) sg(A_theta(a_i)). Students are Qwen3-{1.7B,4B,8B}-Base trained on DeepMath problems filtered to difficulty >= 6, with up to 16,384 response tokens, batch size 256.

Three schedulers are compared for 100 training iterations on one 8-GPU node with one GPU reserved for the teacher. Strict sync time-shares the other 7 GPUs between rollout and training. Two-step-off (VeRL-style) and AsyncOPD split them into 4 rollout GPUs and 3 FSDP trainer GPUs; two-step-off fixes a 2-update lag but waits for complete rollout batches, while AsyncOPD streams individual samples through FIFO queues (queue depth tau = 4), pauses rollout only for weight sync, and keeps in-flight prefixes. Training throughput is response tokens consumed by the learner per second of wall-clock time, excluding the first 5 updates; final AIME24 Avg@32 is also reported.
official.claim: With a Qwen3-1.7B-Base student and the MC64 estimator on one 8-GPU node, AsyncOPD trains at 23.4k tokens/s versus 14.2k for two-step-off and 8.7k for strict sync (2.70x sync), while its final AIME24 Avg@32 (9.38) is not lower than strict sync (8.85).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: AsyncOPD scheduler results for Qwen3-Base models. Train tok/s is training throughput; parentheses show speedup over the matched strict-sync baseline. Overlap is concurrent OPD-stage activity. Avg@32 is final AIME24. AsyncOPD achieves the highest throughput and overlap in all matched settings while maintaining comparable final accuracy.
official.metric: Training throughput in response tokens/s consumed by the learner (higher is better), excluding the first 5 warm-up updates; also final-checkpoint AIME24 Avg@32 (%). Single run per cell; no error bars reported.
official.comparison: AsyncOPD (streaming async scheduler) vs. two-step-off and strict synchronous schedulers, same student, teacher, data, estimator (MC64, A_theta, no clip, IS) and hardware.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the matched setup, AsyncOPD's throughput is not clearly higher than two-step-off (e.g. less than ~1.3x two-step-off, or below 2x strict sync), or its final AIME24 Avg@32 falls clearly below strict sync.
