title: FlowR2A: Learning Reward-to-Action Distribution for Multimodal Driving Planning

official.background: End-to-end driving planners increasingly output several candidate trajectories and pick one. Scoring-based planners (VADv2, Hydra-MDP) score a fixed vocabulary of 8192 trajectories using dense simulator-derived rewards, but cannot generate trajectories outside that vocabulary. Anchor-based planners (DiffusionDrive, iPad) generate proposals from anchors, but supervise only the proposal closest to the single human ground-truth trajectory, so many proposals get no training signal and can be poor. The paper argues that learning a reward-conditioned generative model of actions gets the dense supervision of the first family and the generation of the second, and that this shows up as a proposal set that is good on average, not just in its best member.
official.method:
For every NAVSIM navtrain scene, each of 8192 vocabulary trajectories is simulated to get reward labels: seven scalars (the PDM score and the NAVSIM v2 sub-scores NC, DDC, TLC, EP, LK, HC, with EP replaced by a safety-gated, per-scene-normalized variant) plus two per-timestep arrays (TTC-time, and ego area on-road/on-route) that replace the binary TTC and DAC labels. Continuous rewards (EP, PDM score) get Gaussian noise (σ = 0.05) during training. A reward encoder embeds each reward (randomly replaced by a per-reward null token, for classifier-free guidance) and an MLP fuses them. A 4-block transformer flow-matching decoder (x-prediction, AdaLN reward conditioning, cross-attention to Transfuser ResNet-34 scene features) is trained to generate trajectories conditioned on (scene, reward), sampling vocabulary pairs inversely to score density. A small transformer mode selector predicts NAVSIM sub-scores to rank proposals and is fine-tuned in a second stage on the decoder's own proposals.

At inference, each proposal is generated with 20 Euler steps, CFG scale 5 under a high-reward condition (NC, HC, per-timestep arrays at their maximum, target PDM score drawn from U[0.9, 1.0]), starting from the imitation-learning head's trajectory noised to t_init ~ U[0.5, 0.9]. For Table 3, 64 proposals are generated per scene to match iPad. Each proposal is scored by the NAVSIM simulator on navtest, and the table reports the score of the selected proposal when choosing among 1, 4 or all proposals, plus the mean ± std of scores across all proposals.
official.claim: On NAVSIM v1 navtest with 64 proposals per scene, the average PDMS over all of FlowR2A's proposals is 89.4 (±7.4 spread), vs. 77.9 (±22.4) for iPad and 60.3 (±33.1) for DiffusionDrive, and FlowR2A's best-of-4 PDMS (91.8) already exceeds iPad's PDMS with all proposals (91.5).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Quantitative comparison of proposal quality. We report PDMS, EP, and TTC on navtest when selecting among different numbers of proposal candidates. Mean and standard deviation of all proposals' scores are reported to reflect the average quality of proposals. Ours generates 64 proposals in total to match iPad [17].
official.metric: NAVSIM PDMS (higher is better), plus EP and TTC sub-scores. In the 'Mean over All Proposals' columns, ± is the standard deviation of scores across proposals (and scenes), not across seeds; no seed variation is reported. FlowR2A results in the main tables are described as averaged over three inferences.
official.comparison: FlowR2A (ResNet-34, 64 proposals) vs. anchor-based iPad (64 proposals) and DiffusionDrive (20 proposals), all evaluated by the authors on navtest proposal sets
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained FlowR2A's mean PDMS over all 64 proposals is not clearly above iPad's (e.g. the gap shrinks below ~5 PDMS from the reported 11.5), or its per-proposal score spread is not much tighter than iPad's.

title: HelpBench: Assessing the Ability of LLMs to Provide Privacy, Safety, and Security Advice
claim_source: Table 3, page 24 (summary in Table 1, page 6, and Section 5.1.3)

official.background: People increasingly ask LLMs for help with digital privacy, safety and security (PSS) problems such as recovering a locked account, judging whether a message is a scam, or dealing with harassment and stalking. Bad advice in this domain can cause account compromise, financial loss or physical risk, yet there was no help-seeking benchmark for consumer PSS advice comparable to HealthBench or LegalBench. HelpBench fills this gap with realistic, open-ended questions and expert-written per-question rubrics, so that model advice can be scored automatically and repeatedly.
official.method:
HelpBench has 450 questions, 50 for each of nine topics (accounts, moderation tools, security tools, privacy tools, compromise, platform actions, scams, harassment, data concerns), sampled from Reddit help-seeking posts (2021-2024), stratified by length, whether existing practices are mentioned, and need type, then rephrased with Gemini 2.5 Flash and manually checked. Each question has an expert rubric of positive and negative factual criteria worth 1, 2, 3 or 5 points, plus shared delivery criteria (tone, relevance, clarity). A response's score is (points for met positive criteria + points for avoided negative criteria) / maximum points.

An auto-rater (the prompt in Appendix E, run on Gemini 2.5 Pro at temperature 0) judges each criterion as met or unmet; its scores correlate with expert scores at Pearson r = 0.85 (0.96 factual, 0.78 delivery). 18 models from 7 families (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, GLM, Qwen) are queried 5 times per question with default parameters through their chat versions (40,500 responses). Scores are averaged over the 5 responses per question, then over the questions in each category.
official.claim: Averaged over 18 LLMs, HelpBench scores are highest on scam questions (88%) and lowest on moderation-tool questions (77%), and every one of the 18 models scores higher on scams than on moderation tools (gaps from 3 points for Gemini 3.1 Pro, 85% vs. 82%, to 16 points for Qwen 3, 78% vs. 62%).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: The average performance of each model, both overall and for questions within a given category. Performance is averaged first per question—where we scored five separate responses from the same model for the same question—and then per category. Each row below this average shows the average standard deviation across the five responses obtained per question.
official.metric: HelpBench rubric score in percent (higher is better), auto-rated by Gemini 2.5 Pro, averaged over 5 responses per question and then over the 50 questions per topic. The second line under each cell in Table 3 is the average standard deviation across the 5 responses to a question (spread across responses, not a standard error or CI). The paper reports a Kruskal-Wallis test showing topic differences are significant (p < 0.05) for 17 of 18 models.
official.comparison: Scores on the 50 scam questions vs. the 50 moderation-tool questions for the same model, same rubric scoring and same auto-rater
official.falsification_criterion: Generating 5 responses per question from one or more of the listed models on the scams and moderation-tools questions and scoring them with the released rubrics and auto-rater prompt (Gemini 2.5 Pro, temperature 0), the scam score is not clearly higher than the moderation-tool score (e.g. the gap is under ~3 points averaged over the models tested, or reverses for a model whose reported gap is 7+ points, such as GPT 5.0 at 93% vs. 81%).

title: Do Thinking Tokens Help with Safety?

official.background: Reasoning models generate a long thinking trace before answering, and it is widely assumed that this deliberation should help safety: the model can notice that a request is harmful and refuse, while still helping on benign requests that only look harmful. Safety is measured by two competing rates, attack success rate (ASR, compliance on harmful prompts) and over-refusal rate (ORR, refusal on benign prompts). Prior work found that safety alignment in instruction-tuned models is shallow and set by the first few output tokens. This paper asks whether reasoning models actually deliberate about safety in their thinking traces, or whether the refusal/compliance decision is already fixed before any visible thinking.
official.method:
Models (Qwen3-8B, Olmo-3-7B-Think, Phi-4-Reasoning, GPT-OSS-20B) generate one completion per prompt with vLLM in BF16 using each model's default sampling settings (Qwen3-8B: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20), with a 16,384-token thinking budget. Prompts are a harmful pool (WildJailbreak 2,000 adversarial-harmful test samples + FORTRESS 500) and an expanded benign pool of 6,750 (OR-Bench-Hard, FalseReject, CoCoNot contrast split, PHTest, ORFuzzSet). Only the final response (after the thinking block) is labelled: it is a refusal if at least 3 of 4 guardrail classifiers (WildGuard, Qwen3Guard, Granite Guardian 3.3-8B, GPT-OSS-Safeguard-20B) say refusal; 2-2 ties count as compliance.

The feature h0 is the final-layer hidden state of the first token of the thinking trace. An l2-regularized logistic regression is trained to predict the final refusal/compliance label: features are standardized and projected onto the top 100 principal components, both fit inside each training fold of 5-fold stratified cross-validation, giving one out-of-fold probability per example. AUROC is computed on these probabilities; balanced accuracy uses a Youden-J threshold chosen on the other four folds. The control ('Text') is the same probe on a TF-IDF representation of the first generated token's identity. Results are reported per pool (Harmful, Benign) and pooled.
official.claim: On Qwen3-8B, a linear probe on the first thinking token's final-layer hidden state predicts the final refusal/compliance outcome on harmful prompts with AUROC 0.948 ± 0.010 (balanced accuracy 0.878 ± 0.019), versus 0.492 ± 0.042 for a TF-IDF probe on the first token's identity; across all four models the within-pool representation AUROC is 0.840-0.948.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: First-token probe AUROC and balanced accuracy (BAcc) values decomposed by probe type. Rep. uses h0, and Text uses the first thinking-token TF-IDF feature. A linear probe on h0 predicts the final refusal/compliance outcome, while text-only controls have far less predictive power.
official.metric: AUROC and balanced accuracy of out-of-fold (5-fold CV) probe predictions, higher is better; ± is presumably the half-width of a 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples), per the paper's general footnote on uncertainty; Table 1 does not say explicitly
official.comparison: Logistic probe on the first thinking token's hidden state h0 ('Rep.') vs. logistic probe on the TF-IDF feature of the first generated token ('Text'), same labels and CV protocol, per model and per pool (Harmful, Benign, Pooled)
official.falsification_criterion: With the same models, prompt pools and labelling, the h0 probe's harmful-pool AUROC for Qwen3-8B falls well below ~0.93 (outside the reported CI), or within-pool AUROC across models drops toward the text-only control (e.g. below ~0.75), showing the outcome is not strongly decodable before visible thinking.

title: Neglected Free Lunch from Post-training: Progress Advantage for LLM Agents

official.background: Process reward models (PRMs) score individual steps of an LLM's output and help with best-of-N selection, monitoring and failure diagnosis. They are hard to build for LLM agents, because long-horizon, stateful, stochastic environments make step-level human annotation and Monte Carlo rollouts very expensive, and task-specific PRMs generalize poorly. Earlier 'implicit reward' work used the log-ratio between a fine-tuned policy and its reference as a reward, but that derivation assumes deterministic transitions, which agents interacting with tools and users do not have.
official.method:
The paper shows that under a KL-regularized RL objective in a stochastic MDP, β times the log-probability ratio log π*(a|s) − log π_ref(a|s) between the optimal policy and its reference exactly equals the optimal advantage function (Proposition 1); this is called progress advantage. It argues clipping-based objectives (DAPO, Dr. GRPO) impose an approximate, local KL constraint, so the same signal is used for them too (Proposition 2). It is computed from public checkpoint pairs with no extra training, e.g. Qwen3.5-9B vs. Qwen3.5-9B-Base and gemma-4-E4B-it vs. gemma-4-E4B. Per-token advantages are aggregated within each step (MEAN/MIN/MAX/...) and across steps (MEAN/MIN/MAX/LAST/...) into a trajectory score; the paper picks the best of 25 (token, step) combinations per setting.

Test-time scaling: for each task, 8 trajectories are sampled from the behavior policy (WebShop: first 100 tasks of items_shuffle_1000, 30-step limit, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, thinking disabled, vLLM). Each scoring method picks the highest-scoring trajectory, and the metric is the success rate of the selected trajectories. Baselines: Mean-of-N (average success of the 8), greedy decoding, trained reward models WildReward-8B and ThinkPRM-7B/14B, and training-free confidence scores Self-Certainty, DeepConf Tail and DeepConf Bottom-10%, all scoring the same 8 trajectories.
official.claim: On WebShop best-of-8 selection with Qwen3.5-9B as the agent, progress advantage (Qwen3.5-9B vs. Qwen3.5-9B-Base log-ratio) selects trajectories with a 42.0% success rate, versus 33.0% for the best baseline (ThinkPRM-14B), 30.0% for DeepConf B10 and 26.4% for Mean-of-N.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Test-time scaling through best-of-8 sampling. We compare reward scoring methods across four benchmarks and two LLM backbones, reporting the success rate (%) of the selected trajectory. Our progress advantages successfully boost the success rate, especially when the non-zero-temperature exploratory behavior is beneficial to the task, i.e., WebShop and τ²-Airline.
official.metric: Success rate (%) of the selected trajectory over 100 WebShop tasks, higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Progress advantage vs. WildReward-8B, ThinkPRM-7B, ThinkPRM-14B, Self-Certainty, DeepConf Tail, DeepConf B10 and Mean-of-N, all selecting from the same 8 sampled trajectories per task
official.falsification_criterion: With Qwen3.5-9B on the same WebShop split, progress advantage's best-of-8 success rate is not clearly above the best baseline scorer (e.g. less than ~5 points above ThinkPRM-14B or DeepConf), or is no better than Mean-of-N, ideally checked over several sampling seeds.

title: Soft Token Alignment for Cross-Lingual Reasoning

official.background: Multilingual LLMs often give different reasoning and answers to the same question asked in different languages. Earlier work suggests that middle layers hold fairly language-agnostic meaning, but the final layers become language-specific as the model commits to discrete tokens in one script. 'Soft tokens' (probability-weighted mixtures of vocabulary embeddings, as in inference-time Soft Thinking) are not tied to any one token or script. The paper asks whether aligning soft tokens across languages during supervised fine-tuning gives a better cross-lingual training signal than discrete tokens or hidden states.
official.method:
SOLAR adds an auxiliary loss to standard SFT on parallel multilingual reasoning traces (M-s1k: 1,000 s1k problems translated into 10 languages, 10,000 examples). In the same teacher-forced forward pass used for cross-entropy, each response position's next-token distribution is top-k filtered (k=30), renormalized at temperature tau=1.0, and used to weight the input embedding matrix, which gives a soft-token embedding. These are mean-pooled over all response positions (prompt positions are excluded) into one d-dimensional summary per example. For each non-English example, the loss is L_CE + lambda * (1 - cos(e_bar_en, e_bar_l)), with lambda=0.5. The English summary is held fixed (stop-grad), and English examples use only L_CE.

Qwen3-4B (non-thinking mode) gets full-parameter fine-tuning with LLaMA-Factory: 5 epochs, batch size 32, lr 1e-5 with cosine decay, max length 16,384, bf16. Baselines trained on the same data are plain SFT, MidAlign (middle-layer contrastive alignment), MAPO (DPO with NLLB translation-consistency preferences) and AlignX. Evaluation covers MGSM, AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and GPQA Diamond (the XReasoning multilingual versions) in 7 languages (En, Fr, Ja, Sw, Te, Th, Zh), decoding at temperature 0.6, top-k 30, top-p 0.95, max 32,768 tokens. Accuracy is averaged over 5 sampling runs (MGSM, GPQA) or 10 (AIME).

Its cross-lingual consistency is 41.51%, against 37.76% for SFT and 38.98% for MidAlign.

title: SpatialFlow-GRPO: Where Spatial Credit Drives Image Editing

official.background: Online RL post-training (Flow-GRPO, DanceGRPO) has improved instruction-based image editing, but these methods score each edited image with a single whole-image reward and apply the same advantage to every latent position. In edits that touch several regions, some regions may succeed while others fail or the background is damaged, and a single scalar cannot tell the policy which part of the image deserved the credit or blame. The paper asks whether assigning reward to semantic regions and keeping that spatial structure in the policy update improves editing models.
official.method:
A region-aware reward model, SFReward (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct fine-tuned with LoRA on the 14,276-sample SFReward-14K dataset), outputs bounding boxes, semantic labels and semantic-consistency scores for each edited region, a background-preservation score, and image-level perceptual-quality scores. Region rewards are sqrt(phi(IF_{i,r}) * AES_i)/C. Advantages are z-normalized within each (instruction, region label) group, mixed with the global sample-level advantage as (1-alpha)A_global + alpha*A_region with alpha warmed up from 0 to 0.5 over the first 500 steps on a cosine schedule, and painted onto the latent positions under each box (background elsewhere; fallback to the global advantage for sparse groups).

The policy objective uses one shared importance ratio per region (exp of the mean per-position log-ratio inside the region), a PPO-clipped loss averaged within each region, and power-weighted aggregation across regions with weights proportional to (|M_r| + tau)^beta, beta = 0.7. The Flow-GRPO baseline uses the same SFReward, but only its sample-level VIEScore-style score sqrt(min(o_i) * min(q_i))/C, with the same training data (EditScore-RL-Data 9-category subset), base model and sampling settings. Main setup: OmniGen2 with LoRA r=32, G=12 samples per instruction, 48 instructions per round, 20 inference steps, 2000 training steps, 512x512 cap. Evaluation: GEdit-Bench and ImgEdit-Bench overall scores, and the authors' MultiEditBench (500 prompts with 2-5 simultaneous edits, judged by GPT-4.1 with the VIEScore protocol).
official.claim: On OmniGen2, with the reward model, training data and sampling held fixed, SpatialFlow-GRPO beats Flow-GRPO on GEdit-Bench (7.29 vs. 6.99 overall; base 6.42), ImgEdit-Bench (3.74 vs. 3.66) and MultiEditBench (avg 8.11 vs. 7.52, ahead at every 2- to 5-edit level).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Standard benchmark results. Overall is the score after post-training, and ∆ is the gain over the corresponding base model without RL. Table 3: Full MultiEditBench results. MEB Score is reported by the number of simultaneous editing regions. Avg is the equal-weighted average over the four difficulty subsets. ∆ Avg denotes the improvement over the corresponding base model and is omitted for standalone reference editors.
official.metric: GEdit-Bench overall and ImgEdit-Bench overall (higher is better); MultiEditBench average of 2/3/4/5-edit subset scores from GPT-4.1 VIEScore judging (0-10, higher is better). Single numbers with no error bars, although Appendix says main RL comparisons were repeated with different seeds.
official.comparison: SpatialFlow-GRPO vs. Flow-GRPO (same SFReward reward model, using its sample-level score) vs. the base model without RL, on OmniGen2; the same comparison on FLUX.2-klein-4B is also reported.
official.falsification_criterion: A matched re-run on OmniGen2 where SpatialFlow-GRPO's GEdit-Bench overall does not exceed Flow-GRPO's, or where its MultiEditBench average is not clearly above Flow-GRPO's (e.g., the 0.59-point gap shrinks below seed-to-seed variation).

title: EO-WM: A Physically Informed World Model for Probabilistic Earth Observation Forecasting

official.background: Earth Observation (EO) forecasting predicts future multispectral satellite images (here, Sentinel-2 from EarthNet2021) from past observations and meteorological forcing. Observations are sparse and cloudy, and the same weather can lead to different land-surface outcomes, so probabilistic models are natural. Standard EarthNet2021 metrics only check agreement with a single realized future. They do not test whether a model's predictions respond in the right direction when the weather forcing changes, which is what a weather-driven 'world model' should do.
official.method:
EO-WM is a latent video diffusion model: an EO-VAE tokenizer fine-tuned on EarthNet2021 plus a 387M-parameter MMDiT backbone trained from scratch with flow matching (12 double-stream and 14 single-stream blocks, hidden size 768). It takes 10 context frames and predicts 20 future 4-band (B/G/R/NIR) frames at 128x128. Weather is split into a per-tile monthly climatological mean, added once at the input, and an anomaly (weather minus climatology) that enters a spatial condition. That spatial condition is reinjected into the video tokens every four double-stream blocks through zero-initialized gates. Cumulative heat, water-deficit and compound stress indices (running sums of ReLU-gated standardized temperature and precipitation anomalies) are also added to the spatial condition. For the main results, inference uses 5 samples averaged into an ensemble mean, with no classifier-free guidance.

The Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark has 422 pairs from 380 locations in the EarthNet2021 seasonal test set. Each pair is the same location and season in two different years, filtered for cloud quality and matched initial state. The Directional Hit Rate (DHR) is the fraction of target frames where the sign of the predicted NDVI difference between the two windows matches the sign of the ground-truth difference. Only frames with ground-truth |difference| > 0.02 count, and hits are pooled over pairs. 0.5 is chance. Baselines (SimVP, PhyDNet, PredRNN, PredRNN v2, TAU, Earthformer, Latte) are trained on the same split with the same weather variables. Wan2.1-Fun-V1.1-1.3B-InP is fine-tuned from its pretrained checkpoint in four stages. Generative models are evaluated with the mean of 5 samples.
official.claim: On the Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark (422 same-location cross-year pairs), EO-WM reaches a Directional Hit Rate of 0.6522, against 0.6050 for the best baseline (fine-tuned Wan2.1-Fun-InP, a 7.8% relative gain) and 0.5551 for the best deterministic model (Earthformer).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison of deterministic and generative models on the Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark. "*" indicates that the model is finetuned from its pretrained weight. DRRmean: mean value of DRR. PDCsp: Spearman paired divergence correlation.
official.metric: Directional Hit Rate (DHR, higher is better, 0.5 = chance), pooled over pairs on frames with ground-truth NDVI difference > 0.02. Single run; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: EO-WM (5-sample ensemble mean, no CFG) vs. SimVP, PhyDNet, PredRNN, PredRNN v2, TAU, Earthformer, Latte and fine-tuned Wan2.1-Fun-InP, all given the same 10 context frames and weather inputs
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained EO-WM does not beat a matched Wan2.1-Fun-InP or Earthformer baseline on DHR for the released benchmark pairs, or its margin over Wan2.1 (0.047) falls inside the variation seen across training seeds or sampling seeds.

title: RoPEMover: Depth-Aware Object Relocation via Positional Embeddings

official.background: Moving an object within a single photo means more than translating pixels: the object has to keep its identity, the region it leaves must be filled in plausibly, occlusion order with other objects must be right, and shadows and reflections must follow it. Two-stage pipelines (remove then insert, or copy-paste then harmonize) tend to leave shadows behind or produce a pasted look, while video-prior methods such as ObjectMover need large purpose-built training sets. Instruction-tuned diffusion transformers can edit images from text but give only coarse spatial control.
official.method:
RoPEMover fine-tunes Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 with rank-16 LoRA adapters (attention, MLP and modulation layers; text encoder and VAE frozen). Given an image, an object mask and a drag (dx, dy, s), the rotary positional embeddings of the image tokens inside the source mask are replaced with those of the translated and scaled position (Eq. 3) for the first 20 denoising steps. In addition, a MoGe-2 depth map normalized to [1, 2] is written into the first complex component of the otherwise unused temporal axis of Qwen-Image's 3D RoPE. At inference the target depth is synthesized from the source depth: Laplace inpainting of the object region, a per-pixel warp of the object depth plus a user depth offset, and z-buffer compositing.

Training has two stages: Stage 1 uses 5,000 paired CLEVR scenes rendered in Blender (one object moved, everything else fixed), 2 epochs of 5,000 steps; Stage 2 fine-tunes on ~165 captured real photo pairs (repeat factor 30, 2 epochs). Evaluation is on ObjMove-A (200 captured scenes with a ground-truth target image, from the ObjectMover paper) at 512x512, with CLIP, DINO and DreamSim computed on the target-object crop, the source-region crop and the background, plus full-image PSNR.
official.claim: On ObjMove-A, RoPEMover removes the object from its source location much more cleanly than every baseline: source-region DINO 87.37 vs. 78.49 for the best baseline (MagicFixup) and source-region DreamSim 0.1012 vs. 0.1853 (MagicFixup); it also gives the best target-object DreamSim (0.1180 vs. 0.1379 for Inpaint4Drag) and PSNR (24.97 vs. 24.06 dB for ObjectMover).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison on the ObjMove-A benchmark. For CLIP, DINO, and PSNR scores, higher-is-better; for DreamSim lower-is-better.
official.metric: DINO score on the source-region crop (higher better), DreamSim on source and target crops (lower better), full-image PSNR (higher better); single numbers with no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: RoPEMover (Stage 2, 5k CLEVR + real) vs. 11 baselines: ChronoEdit, 3DiT, DragAnything, DragDiffusion, Inpaint4Drag, MagicFixup, GeoDiffuser, Qwen-Image (base), Flux Kontext, FreeFine, ObjectMover
official.falsification_criterion: On ObjMove-A, a reproduced RoPEMover does not beat the strongest baseline on source-region DINO by a clear margin (e.g. reaches below ~80 vs. MagicFixup's ~78.5) or its source-region DreamSim is not clearly below ~0.185.

title: Flexformer: Flexible Linear Transformer with Learnable Attention Kernel
claim_source: Table 8 (Appendix C), page 16; means also in Table 1, page 7

official.background: Softmax attention costs O(N^2) time and memory in the sequence length N. Kernel-based linear attention replaces the softmax similarity with an inner product of feature maps phi(q)^T phi(k), which brings the cost down to linear in N. Fixed random-feature kernels such as Performer and RFA (unbiased estimates of the softmax kernel) often lose accuracy. Learnable feature maps such as Hedgehog and Polaformer do better, but how expressive their kernel family is has not been characterized. The question is whether a more expressive learnable kernel gives better accuracy on long-sequence tasks while keeping linear cost.
official.method:
Flexformer starts from the random-Fourier-feature decomposition of the softmax kernel: exp(x^T y / sqrt(d)) = exp(||x||^2 / 2sqrt(d)) * exp(-||x-y||^2 / 2sqrt(d)) * exp(||y||^2 / 2sqrt(d)). The middle Gaussian term is approximated with Fourier features [cos(w_i^T x), sin(w_i^T x)]. Instead of sampling the frequencies w_i from a fixed Gaussian, Flexformer treats them as trainable parameters (stationary variant, Flexformer_s). The nonstationary variant (Flexformer_n), based on Yaglom's theorem, learns frequency pairs (w_1i, w_2i) and uses features of the form cos(w'_1i^T x)cos(w'_2i^T x) and sin(w'_1i^T x)cos(w'_2i^T x). It also replaces the fixed 2sqrt(d) scale in the norm term with a learnable exp(tau). Parameters are independent per head. The resulting features are used in standard linear attention, sum_j phi(Q_i)^T phi(K_j) V_j / sum_j phi(Q_i)^T phi(K_j).

For LRA (ListOps, Text, Retrieval, Image, Pathfinder; lengths 1K-4K), the models are trained from scratch with the hyperparameters of the official LRA implementation. Each method only swaps the attention module. Results are test accuracy, given as mean ± std over 3 seeds.
official.claim: On the LRA byte-level document retrieval task (AAN, 4K bytes), Flexformer_n reaches 73.94 ± 0.66% test accuracy, against 68.67 ± 0.63% for Hedgehog and 68.05 ± 0.63% for Skyformer (the best baselines) and 64.49 ± 0.61% for the softmax Transformer. On LRA Image it reaches 45.42 ± 0.32% vs. 43.56 ± 0.30% (Cosformer, the best baseline), and its 5-task average is 59.99 ± 0.25 vs. 57.47 ± 0.23 (Hedgehog).
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Mean and standard deviation of performance metrics on the LRA benchmarks. All reported metrics represent test accuracy (%), where higher values indicate better performance. The best results for each benchmark are in bold, and the second best in underlined.
official.metric: test accuracy (%), higher is better, mean ± std over 3 random seeds
official.comparison: Flexformer_n (and Flexformer_s) vs. Transformer, Reformer, Longformer, Linear Transformer, BigBird, Performer, RFA, Skyformer, Cosformer, Hedgehog, Polaformer on LRA under the official LRA hyperparameters
official.falsification_criterion: With matched LRA training, Flexformer_n's Retrieval accuracy does not beat Hedgehog's (or the best linear-attention baseline's) by more than about 1 point (roughly 2 seed stds), or its Image accuracy does not beat Cosformer's by more than the seed std.

title: OperatorSHAP: Fast and Accurate Shapley Value Estimation for Neural Operators

official.background: Neural operators such as Fourier neural operators learn PDE solution maps and accept inputs on any grid, which matters for physical data that come on irregular or varying meshes. Shapley-value attributions are a standard way to explain predictions, but per-sample estimators like KernelSHAP or RegressionMSR need thousands of model evaluations per explanation, and amortized explainers like FastSHAP assume a fixed, homogeneous input vector, so they cannot handle inputs whose grid changes between samples. Gradient methods like Integrated Gradients are cheap but give zero attribution when the explained quantity is piecewise constant (for example a thresholded decision).
official.method:
OperatorSHAP treats each spatial point as a player in a non-atomic game and targets the Aumann–Shapley value. For an input u0, baseline ū (zero) and query point x*, the game v(S) is the change in the backbone output at x* when the input is switched from baseline to u0 on region S. The explainer is itself a neural operator (same family as the backbone, e.g. an FNO) that takes u0 plus a Gaussian bump (width 0.05) marking x* and outputs an attribution density field. During training, each sample is pinned to one grid size n in {8, 16, ..., 1024}; the density is integrated over the n grid cells to get a discrete attribution vector, which is fit with the FastSHAP weighted MSE (v(S) − φ̂ᵀ1_S)² on coalitions drawn from the Shapley kernel, with hard normalization for efficiency. One trained explainer per PDE and readout is then used at every resolution.

In the 'decision readout' game the coalition value v(S) is 1 if the backbone prediction at x* for the masked input u_S = ū + 1_S ⊙ (u0 − ū) is closer to the prediction for u0 than to the prediction for the baseline ū, and 0 otherwise (so v(∅) = 0 and v(Ω) = 1). Evaluation uses 30 test inputs × 3 query points (domain center, 1/4 and 3/4). Baselines are RegressionMSR and KernelSHAP (shapiq implementations) with 2n backbone evaluations per query point (minimum 1024) and Integrated Gradients with 50 steps. The reference attribution is RegressionMSR with 3·10⁵ backbone evaluations. Metrics are Pearson correlation and NRMSE against the reference, plus Shapley-kernel-weighted R² (faithfulness) over 10,000 random coalitions.
official.claim: On Burgers 1D with the thresholded decision readout at n = 256 players, OperatorSHAP's attributions reach median Pearson correlation 0.975 [IQR 0.964, 0.983] with the reference, versus 0.178 [0.083, 0.446] for RegressionMSR and 0.193 [0.093, 0.385] for KernelSHAP at a budget of 1024 backbone evaluations (median NRMSE 0.232 vs. 1.221 and 3.391).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Attribution quality across resolutions n for the point readout and the decision readout of App. D.6 on two PDEs and MGN Cylinder. Each (PDE, n, method) entry reports the median over 30 test inputs and three query points per input on the top line and the inter-quartile range in brackets below. Metrics are the Shapley-kernel weighted R² (faithfulness), and Pearson correlation and NRMSE against the reference attribution. RegressionMSR (RMSR) and KernelSHAP (KS) use a budget of 2n (minimum 1024) backbone evaluations per query point, IG uses a 50-step Riemann sum, and OperatorSHAP (OS) uses one query-conditioned model per PDE and readout at all resolutions. MGN Cylinder uses 10 test inputs. On the decision readout, the gradient of the game vanishes, so IG attributions are identically zero and their Pearson correlation is undefined (–). Bold marks the best median and every median within one standard error of it over the test inputs, compared at three decimals. All PDEs are in Tabs. 3, 4 and 8.
official.metric: Pearson correlation with the reference attribution (higher is better); also NRMSE (lower is better). Values are medians over 30 test inputs × 3 query points with inter-quartile range in brackets; no seeds or standard errors are reported in the table.
official.comparison: OperatorSHAP (one amortized explainer for all resolutions) vs. RegressionMSR and KernelSHAP at 2n = 1024 backbone evaluations per query point; Integrated Gradients gives identically zero attributions on this game.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same setup (Burgers 1D, decision readout, n = 256, reference RegressionMSR at 3·10⁵ evaluations), OperatorSHAP's median Pearson falls to within the IQR of RegressionMSR or KernelSHAP at 1024 evaluations, or the RegressionMSR/KernelSHAP median Pearson is above about 0.9.

title: Disentangling Continuous-Time Latent Dynamics: Identifiability of Latent SDEs via Diffusion Shifts

official.background: Causal representation learning tries to recover latent causal variables from nonlinear mixtures of them, which is impossible without extra structure such as multiple environments or temporal dependence. Existing identifiability results for time series are almost all discrete-time, while work on continuous-time stochastic differential equations (SDEs) usually assumes the state is observed directly. This paper asks when a latent SDE observed only through an unknown nonlinear invertible map can be recovered, and shows that two environments sharing the same drift but with different diagonal diffusion covariances suffice, provided the coordinate-wise variance ratios between the two environments are pairwise distinct. In that case the latent coordinates are identified up to permutation, scaling and a constant shift, with no sparsity assumption on the drift.
official.method:
Data: latent SDE dz = f(z) dt + Σ_e^{1/2} dW in d = 5 dimensions, simulated by Euler-Maruyama with Δt = 0.005, 20 stored points per trajectory (19 transitions), initial state N(0, 0.25 I), 10,000 trajectories per regime. Three drift families: dense linear OU (A = -(MMᵀ + 0.5 I), M Gaussian), sparse linear OU on a directed 5-cycle (diagonal -1, off-diagonal 1.5·Unif(0.8, 1.2)), and a nonlinear sparse drift f_i(z) = -z_i + 1.5 Σ c_ij tanh(z_j) on the same cycle. Observations x = g(z), where g is a 3-layer MLP with Haar-random orthogonal weights, Gaussian biases and leaky-tanh activation tanh(u) + 0.1u (final layer a pure rotation). Regime conditions: Σ_1 = diag(0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5) throughout; Distinct ratios uses Σ_2 = diag(2.0, 1.5, 0.8, 0.5, 0.4); One regime uses only Σ_1; Proportional diffusions uses Σ_2 = 2Σ_1 (all ratios equal 2).

Estimator, Stage 1: an encoder h_θ (MLP, 4 hidden layers of width 256, ELU), a shared drift model and per-regime diagonal log-variances are trained jointly (Adam, lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, 20,000 steps) to minimize the Euler-Maruyama Gaussian transition negative log-likelihood of encoded consecutive pairs, minus log|det Dh_θ(x_{t+Δt})| (computed by finite differences), averaged over regimes. Stage 2 (sparse families only) freezes the encoder and fits a sparse drift to finite-difference velocities with an L1 Jacobian penalty, then thresholds at τ = 0.05 to get a graph. The main metric is MCC: mean absolute Pearson correlation between true and learned latent coordinates after Hungarian matching. The monomial score (how close the mean |D(h∘g)| is to a permutation-scaling matrix) and graph match rate (GMR) are also reported.
official.claim: On d = 5 synthetic latent SDEs under leaky-tanh MLP mixing, the two-stage estimator recovers the latent coordinates with MCC 0.9976-0.9977 (± ≤ 0.0002) under Distinct ratios for all three drift families, versus at most 0.8087 ± 0.0428 under the One-regime and Proportional-diffusions controls (0.70-0.81 depending on family).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Synthetic d = 5 results under three-layer leaky-tanh MLP mixing. Entries are mean ± s.d. over five training seeds. Bold highlights the identifiable condition (Distinct ratios); the other two conditions are controls. GMR is omitted for the dense linear family because sparse graph recovery is not the target there.
official.metric: Mean correlation coefficient (MCC, higher is better) between true and learned latents after Hungarian matching; ± is standard deviation over 5 training seeds (data-generating drift and mixing fixed across seeds). Monomial score and graph match rate (GMR) also reported.
official.comparison: Same estimator, data generator and mixing under three diffusion-regime conditions: Distinct ratios (identifiable) vs. One regime and Proportional diffusions (controls that violate the separation assumption S4)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the d = 5 leaky-tanh setup, Distinct ratios fails to reach MCC near 0.99 for some drift family, or one of the controls reaches MCC within about 0.05 of Distinct ratios (e.g. above 0.95), so the gap predicted by the theory does not appear.

title: SEAD: Competence-Aware On-Policy Distillation via Entropy-Guided Supervision
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (also Table 2, page 7, the 2^3 ablation)

official.background: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a small student language model on its own sampled rollouts, using per-token corrections from a larger teacher (typically a reverse-KL loss on the teacher's logits). This avoids the exposure bias of training on fixed teacher traces and is used to transfer math reasoning from large to small models. Standard OPD applies the same divergence to every token, at every training step, for every prompt. The paper argues that teacher feedback is only useful when the student's rollouts are coherent, so supervision should depend on the student's current competence.
official.method:
SEAD changes the vanilla OPD loss in three ways. (1) Token zones: for each rollout token it computes the teacher and student entropies (teacher entropy approximated over the top-k vocabulary) and uses percentile thresholds (50/40/10) to sort tokens into three zones. Zone A (both entropies low) gets no gradient. Zone B (teacher entropy low, student entropy high) gets reverse KL. Zone C (teacher entropy high) gets forward KL weighted by λ. The loss is normalized by |B ∪ C|. (2) KL annealing: the forward-KL weight on Zone C is multiplied by α(t), which follows a cosine decay from 0.8 to 0 over training. (3) Curriculum: before training, each prompt's difficulty is set to 1 − (pass rate over 8 student rollouts). Prompts are then shown once, from easy to hard, with Gaussian noise (σ = 0.02) added to break ties.

Setup: student OLMo-3-7B-Instruct-SFT, teacher OLMo-3(.1)-32B-Instruct. Training is one epoch on a deduplicated DAPO-Math-17K in verl, with 96 prompts per step, one rollout per prompt at temperature 0.7, up to 16,384 tokens, one clipped update per batch (ε = 0.2), and peak LR 5e-9 with linear warmup and decay. Evaluation uses greedy Pass@1 on MATH-500, Minerva-Math and OlympiadBench, and Pass@32 (average pass rate over 32 samples) on AMC23, AIME24 and AIME25. The baseline is vanilla OPD with full-token reverse KL (k = 1), run under the same setup.
official.claim: On OLMo-3 (7B student, 32B teacher), full SEAD reaches a six-benchmark average accuracy of 64.0, compared with 59.2 for vanilla OPD with reverse KL (+4.8). The largest per-benchmark gains are AMC23 (89.8 vs. 80.9), AIME24 (53.9 vs. 47.9) and AIME25 (42.5 vs. 37.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results on OLMo model pair (OLMo-7B student, OLMo-32B teacher).
official.metric: Accuracy (%), higher is better. Pass@1 (greedy) on MATH-500, Minerva and OlympiadBench; Pass@32 average on AMC23, AIME24 and AIME25; Avg. is the unweighted mean of the six. Single runs, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: SEAD (token zones + KL annealing + curriculum) vs. vanilla OPD (full-token reverse KL), same student, teacher, data and training budget. GRPO (58.0) and OPSD (58.2) are also reported.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running vanilla OPD and SEAD with the stated setup, SEAD's six-benchmark average is not clearly above OPD's (e.g. the gap is under ~2 points, or within the spread across a few seeds).

title: Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop Instead of Act?

official.background: LLM agents that search, browse and run commands are usually evaluated on whether they complete tasks. Many real instructions are ambiguous, contradictory, or cannot be satisfied in the environment, and a reliable agent should stop and abstain instead of continuing to call tools. Unlike single-turn LLM abstention, the need to abstain may only become clear after the agent interacts with the environment, so it matters both whether the agent abstains and how soon. The paper builds a benchmark of more than 28,000 instructions across WebShop, Terminal-Bench 2.0 and AbstentionBench-derived QA, finds that most agents abstain late or not at all, and proposes CONVOLVE to improve timely abstention.
official.method:
The WebShop part of the benchmark has 500 abstention-warranted instructions: 249 request-based rewrites (Subjective Preference, Underspecified Intent, False Premise or Contradiction; made by an LLM and manually reviewed) and 251 Missing Target tasks, in which the original instruction is kept but the ground-truth products are removed from the catalog and the Lucene index is rebuilt. Agents get at most 10 turns. AbsRec@K is the fraction of abstain-warranted instances on which the agent correctly abstains by step K; abstaining before the warranted step counts as wrong. Timely recall is AbsRec@1 for request-based tasks and AbsRec@2 for Missing Target tasks. SPL rewards successful abstention and penalizes longer paths.

CONVOLVE (built on Agentic Context Engineering) runs an agent on training episodes. After each episode a reflection model analyses the trajectory for abstention-relevant signals, and a curator model distills these into short stopping rules added to a structured playbook. The playbook is appended to the unchanged WebShop system prompt at test time, and no model weights are updated. The 500 abstention-only WebShop tasks are split, stratified by scenario and grouped by original goal, into 20 training, 8 validation and 101 held-out evaluation tasks, with one offline epoch and at most two reflection/update rounds per example. The baseline is the same model on the same 101 tasks without the playbook (all other settings fixed). An in-context-learning variant is also reported. 'Llama-3.3-70B + 70B' means the 70B agent using a playbook learned from 70B trajectories.
official.claim: On the 101 held-out abstention-warranted WebShop tasks, adding a CONVOLVE playbook learned from 20 Llama-3.3-70B trajectories raises Llama-3.3-70B's timely abstention recall from 26.7% to 57.4%, AbsRec@10 from 83.2% to 100.0%, and SPL from 55.3 to 78.9, compared with the same model without the playbook.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: CONVOLVE improves abstention on WebShop. Trained variants use 20 trajectories.
official.metric: Timely recall (AbsRec@1 for request-based, AbsRec@2 for Missing Target), AbsRec@10 and SPL, all in %, higher is better; single run, no ± or seeds reported
official.comparison: Llama-3.3-70B + CONVOLVE (70B-learned playbook) vs. Llama-3.3-70B base (no playbook) under identical settings; in-context learning (55.4 / 97.0 / 77.2) also reported
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning Llama-3.3-70B on the held-out abstention tasks with and without a CONVOLVE playbook learned from 20 training trajectories gives a timely-recall gain well below ~30 points (e.g., under 10 points), or no gain at all.

title: Few-Step Boltzmann Generators via Scalable Likelihood Flow Maps

official.background: Boltzmann generators fit a generative model to (biased) molecular-dynamics samples and then reweight its samples with self-normalized importance sampling to recover the equilibrium Boltzmann distribution. This needs the model's exact likelihood for every sample. Expressive continuous flows only give likelihoods by integrating the velocity divergence over hundreds of steps. Few-step flow maps need costly Jacobian log-determinants (FALCON). F2D2, a 'likelihood flow map', distills sampling and log-density change into a few network evaluations, but it trains the log-density head with Hutchinson's trace estimator, which is noisy and needs a JVP.
official.method:
SCALLOP keeps the F2D2 likelihood-flow-map setup: a network with shared DiT blocks (6 shared, plus 3 for each readout head; 6.25M parameters) outputs a flow-map velocity u_theta(x_t,t,s) and a log-density-change head D_theta(x_t,t,s). It is trained with flow matching, Lagrangian self-distillation (LSD), and a divergence-matching term. The only change is that divergence matching swaps the Hutchinson target (eps^T grad v eps) for a Conditional Divergence Matching target (Eq. 17; vectorized as Eq. 20). Using the chain rule d_t log p_t = grad log p_t · v_t + ∂_t log p_t, it regresses D_theta onto the closed-form conditional space and time scores of p_t(x_t | x1) for the linear interpolant x_t = (1-t)x0 + t x1, combined with the teacher velocity v_t(x_t). This target has the same gradient as exact divergence matching, needs no Hutchinson estimator or JVP, and is vectorized so D_theta predicts the Jacobian diagonal, which is summed to give the divergence. Both SCALLOP and F2D2 use the vectorized objective and the same architecture. Training: AdamW lr 1e-4, batch 1000, 4M updates, EMA 0.999, random-rotation augmentation, mean-centering, t sampled in [0, 1-1e-5], (1-t) weight on the divergence loss.

Evaluation: draw 2e5 samples with their log-likelihoods using 4/8/8/16 Euler-like flow-map steps for ALA-2/3/4/6. Compute SNIS weights against the AMBER energy, clipping logits at 0.002. Report Kish ESS, the energy-histogram 2-Wasserstein distance (E-W2), and the torsion-angle 2-Wasserstein distance (T-W2) against reference MD data. Data and splits (1e5 train) come from the Sequential Boltzmann Generators release (Tan et al. 2026a).
official.claim: With the same DiT backbone and the same number of steps, SCALLOP gets a higher SNIS effective sample size than F2D2 on all four alanine systems (ALA-2 0.088 vs 0.066, ALA-3 0.088 vs 0.079, ALA-4 0.067 vs 0.053, ALA-6 0.042 vs 0.033, all ±0.001). It also gets a lower energy W2 on ALA-3/4/6 (1.596 vs 2.155, 1.545 vs 4.209, 5.845 vs 10.140).
official.claim_caption: Results on ALA-N systems, with N = 2, 3, 4, 6. Results are obtained from three random seeds with 2 × 10^5 samples, reported as mean ± std. The best results are in bold, and the second-best results are underlined. Values of SBG-IS, FALCON, and FALCON-A are from Rehman et al. (2026).
official.metric: Kish ESS of SNIS weights over 2e5 samples (higher is better) and energy-histogram 2-Wasserstein distance E-W2 (lower is better); mean ± std over 3 random seeds
official.comparison: SCALLOP (Conditional Divergence Matching, vectorized) vs. F2D2 (Hutchinson divergence matching, vectorized). Same architecture, training budget, data and NFE, all run by the authors
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained with matched settings, SCALLOP's ESS is not above F2D2's by more than the seed std on ALA-2 (or the other systems), or SCALLOP's E-W2 is not clearly below F2D2's on ALA-3/4/6.

title: On the Nonlinearity of Learning Rate Scaling for LLM Training

official.background: Tuning the learning rate directly at large scale is too expensive, so practitioners fit a scaling law on cheaper runs and extrapolate. The usual assumption is that the optimal learning rate is log-linear (a power law) in training tokens D and model size N. If that law bends at larger scales, extrapolated learning rates are wrong and the target run wastes compute. The paper tests this assumption on GPT-2-style models and asks which quantity (raw learning rate or effective learning rate) and which axis (D or N) extrapolate best under a fixed fitting budget.
official.method:
12-layer GPT-2-style models (nanoGPT; hidden size 256 to 2048, 22M to 707M parameters) are trained on FineWeb-100B with AdamW (weight decay 0.1, beta1 = beta2 = 0.95, batch 0.52M tokens; the embedding layer uses a separate AdamW with fixed learning rate 0.0036), a WSD schedule (1000-step warmup, steady phase, 5000-step decay from saved checkpoints) and a log2 learning-rate grid with unit steps, for data budgets from 5B to 100B tokens. The effective learning rate is eta_eff(t) = ||w_hat_{t+1} - w_hat_t||_2 with w_hat = w/||w||, averaged over all non-embedding weights and over training steps. For each (D, N), the optimum eta* (or eta_eff*) is the minimizer of a cubic polynomial fitted to validation loss vs. log eta (or log eta_eff).

Extrapolation is tested on the held-out 707M model. Under a compute budget beta times C = 6 N_test D_test, the D-axis strategy fits log eta* (or log eta_eff*) vs. log D using the 707M model at smaller data budgets (alpha_1 D_test = 5B, alpha_2 = beta - alpha_1); the N-axis strategy fits vs. log N using smaller models at D_test. The fitted law predicts the optimum at (D_test, N_test); for eta_eff the prediction is mapped back to a learning rate (the paper does not spell out how), and the resulting run's validation loss is compared to the true optimum. The extra compute ratio (ECR) is the extra tokens needed (via a power-law fit L0 + A D^-gamma to the predicted run's loss curve) to reach the optimal loss, as a fraction of 6 N_test D_test.
official.claim: At (D_test, N_test) = (100B, 707M) with a fitting budget of 20.64% of the target run's compute, extrapolating the optimal effective learning rate along the data axis costs 1.29% extra compute (log-LR error +0.1271), versus 2.21% for the effective learning rate along the model axis (the strongest alternative), 8.65% for the raw learning rate along the data axis and 7.87% for the raw learning rate along the model axis; at 13% budget (D-axis only) the gap is 1.21% vs. 16.96% for the raw learning rate.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Prediction error, validation loss gap, and extra compute ratio for each fitting setup across some budget ratios, tested on (D_test, N_test) = (100B, 707M). Bold indicates the lowest ECR within each beta block. For some small beta using D-dim fit, there is no N-dim correspondence. We always set alpha_1 D_test = 5B, alpha_2 = beta - alpha_1.
official.metric: Extra compute ratio ECR (%), lower is better; also log LR prediction error and validation loss gap (1e-4). Single test configuration; no seeds or error bars reported.
official.comparison: D-axis fit of eta_eff* vs. D-axis fit of eta* and N-axis fits of eta* and eta_eff*, all under the same fitting compute budget, evaluated at the held-out 707M / 100B-token configuration
official.falsification_criterion: Using the same sweep grid and fitting protocol, the D-axis eta_eff* fit at 13-21% budget does not give a clearly lower ECR (or smaller absolute log-LR error) than the D-axis eta* fit at (100B, 707M), e.g. the eta* fit's ECR is within ~2x of the eta_eff fit's; or, at 20.64% budget, the D-axis eta_eff* fit does not beat the N-axis eta_eff* fit.

title: GLACIER: Rethinking Mass Spectrum Prediction as an Object Detection Problem

official.background: Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) is used to identify unknown small molecules: one predicts the spectrum of each candidate structure and ranks the candidates by similarity to the measured spectrum. The best current spectrum predictors (ICEBERG, FraGNNet, MARASON) are two-stage: a fragmentation simulator first enumerates candidate fragment subgraphs and a second network then scores their intensities. This is slow (CPU-bound enumeration) and depends on heuristics. The paper treats the task as object detection on the molecular graph and proposes a single-stage, DETR-style model.
official.method:
GLACIER encodes the molecule (atom/bond features plus adduct and collision energy) with a Graphormer, producing atom embeddings and a graph token. A DETR-style transformer decoder with learnable queries cross-attends to these. Each query yields atom affinities, which LinSATNet projects into soft top-k' breakpoint masks for cardinalities 0 to 3, plus a softmax over cardinality. Fragments are the connected components left after removing the predicted breakpoint atoms. In training, queries are matched to MAGMa-derived breakpoint labels with the Hungarian algorithm. An intensity decoder pools each fragment's features from the shared atom embeddings (masked cross-attention, then a transformer encoder over fragments) and predicts 26 intensities per fragment (13 hydrogen shifts x charge retention/migration).

The loss combines the breakpoint set loss, a spectral cosine-distance loss on the predicted spectrum, and a teacher-forced auxiliary intensity loss that uses the MAGMa fragments. The weight of the auxiliary loss starts at 1 and decays exponentially after 2,500 steps. An optional contrastive finetuning (CF) step, taken from ICEBERG 2.0, follows. Retrieval ranks up to 256 candidates by the similarity between predicted and experimental binned spectra (0.01 Da bins on MassSpecGym); the main text does not name the exact ranking score.
official.claim: On the MassSpecGym mass-challenge retrieval task (up to 256 same-mass candidates, official MCES split), GLACIER without contrastive finetuning reaches Recall@1 of 69.69% (99.9% CI 68.16-71.21), against 63.95% (62.39-65.58) for ICEBERG 2.0 with contrastive finetuning, the strongest baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Retrieval accuracy (mean with 99.9% confidence intervals upon bootstrapping, 20,000 resamples) on the MassSpecGym dataset [3]. GLACIER surpasses all baselines in retrieval accuracy. Note that MolSpecFlow [32] does not have an open-source implementation and only reports on the mass challenge. It also uses a different bin width (0.1 Dalton) instead of the bin width adopted by MassSpecGym (0.01 Dalton); the comparison has to be made with extra care.
official.metric: Recall@1 retrieval accuracy (%), higher is better; parentheses are 99.9% bootstrap confidence intervals over test spectra (20,000 resamples), not over training seeds
official.comparison: GLACIER (w/o CF and w/ CF) vs. NEIMS (FFN/GNN), FraGNNet, MolSpecFlow and ICEBERG 2.0 on the same MassSpecGym split and candidate sets
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained GLACIER (w/o CF) on the official MassSpecGym split has a mass-challenge Recall@1 whose 99.9% bootstrap CI overlaps ICEBERG 2.0's (62.39-65.58), e.g. a mean below about 67%.

title: From Failure Taxonomy to Intervention: A Diagnostic Methodology for Industry-Scale AVLM in Video and Live-Streaming Platform Moderation

official.background: Video and live-streaming moderation systems usually feed a vision-language model with video frames plus an ASR transcript of the audio, which loses prosody, non-speech sounds and other acoustic context. The paper describes building an in-house Audio-Visual-Language Model (AVLM) for TikTok-scale moderation and organizes the lessons as a taxonomy of failure types, each mapped to an intervention. One failure type is 'proxy-sufficient representation collapse': pretraining the audio pathway on audio-to-text (ASR-style) supervision yields features good for transcription but poorly usable by the language decoder for audio question answering (AQA).
official.method:
The AVLM couples an in-house audio encoder to a pretrained vision-language backbone through a lightweight projector (the full AVLM is described as 2B-scale). Training has three stages: Stage I weakly supervised audio-text alignment (~1M hours of pseudo-labeled ASR data), Stage II supervised audio adaptation of encoder and projector (~200k hours of in-house audio covering ASR, AST, diarization, audio events, intent), and Stage III full-model multimodal instruction tuning.

Cross-modal continuation (CMC) is added to the audio-data mixture before Stage III: from timestamp-aligned audio-transcript pairs split at a valid word boundary, the model receives the audio prefix and is trained to generate the transcript suffix (continue the language from the audio context). Low-confidence alignments and too-short examples are removed, and CMC makes up 20% of the audio-data mixture. Table 3 compares the pre-instruction-tuning checkpoint trained without vs. with CMC on ASR (LibriSpeech-Other, FLEURS overall WER/CER) and AQA (MMAU, MMSU accuracy).
official.claim: Adding cross-modal continuation (20% of the audio-data mixture) before instruction tuning improves audio QA while also improving transcription: MMAU 34.2 -> 52.5 and MMSU 18.98 -> 40.98 accuracy, with LibriSpeech-Other WER 13.40 -> 10.41 and FLEURS overall WER/CER 29.26 -> 17.98.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Effect of cross-modal continuation (CMC) on transcription and AQA-style capability.
official.metric: WER/CER on LibriSpeech-Other and FLEURS (18 languages, overall), lower is better; accuracy on MMAU and MMSU, higher is better. Single runs, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Same AVLM pre-instruction-tuning checkpoint trained without vs. with CMC data in the audio mixture (the 'without CMC' row equals the Stage II baseline in Table 4)
official.falsification_criterion: In an audio-LLM trained with ASR-style audio-text alignment, adding audio-prefix-to-transcript-suffix continuation data (~20% of the mix) at matched budget does not raise MMAU/MMSU accuracy by a clear margin (e.g. under ~5 points), or it raises AQA only at the cost of worse WER on LibriSpeech-Other/FLEURS.

title: AETDICE: Unified Framework and Offline Optimization for Nonlinear Multi-Objective RL
claim_source: Table 1, page 9 (near-identical values in Appendix Table 4, page 24, which states 5 seeds)

official.background: Multi-objective RL turns a vector of returns into one scalar through a scalarization function. When that function is nonlinear, it matters whether it is applied to each trajectory's return (Expected Scalarized Return, ESR, which needs policies that depend on accumulated reward) or to the expected return (Scalarized Expected Return, SER, which needs optimization over the whole occupancy distribution rather than local Bellman updates). Offline methods exist for linear scalarization and for SER (FairDICE), but not for ESR or for objectives that put nonlinearity at both levels. That rules out preferences such as 'reward specializing within an episode but stay balanced across episodes'.
official.method:
The AET objective is J(pi) = G(E_tau[F(R(tau))]), where F is a trajectory-level transformation of the return vector and G is a concave aggregation over expected utilities. The state is augmented with the accumulated reward vector and the timestep, and a transformed per-step reward r~(s~_t, a_t) = F(R_acc_t + r_t) - F(R_acc_t) for t >= 1, with r~(s~_0, a_0) = F(r_0), telescopes to F(R(tau)). With linear G this reduces to single-objective offline RL in the augmented MDP (the paper's ESR-IQL baseline uses IQL here). With concave G, AETDICE solves a finite-horizon DICE problem over augmented-state visitation distributions with per-timestep Pearson chi^2 regularization to the data distribution (coefficient beta, swept log-scale), a slack variable k and its dual mu, and time-indexed dual nu_t. The policy is then extracted by weighted behavior cloning with the optimal ratios w*_t.

For the claim, on D4MORL MO-Ant-v2 (expert-uniform split, 50k transitions, H = 500, per-objective rewards min-max normalized), F(x) = exp(x/50) elementwise (convex, increasing marginal utility) and G(x) = sum_i log(x_i). Baselines, all offline on the same data: OptiDICE with linear scalarization at weights [1,0], [0.5,0.5], [0,1] (Lin-w); FairDICE (linear F, concave G); ESR-IQL (convex F, linear G); and AET-ESR (AETDICE run with the ESR objective, i.e. linear G). All are evaluated on the convex-F + concave-G utility.
official.claim: On D4MORL MO-Ant expert data with convex F(x)=exp(x/50) and concave G(x)=sum_i log x_i, AETDICE reaches an AET utility of 13.69 ± 0.05, above the best baselines Lin-[0.5,0.5] (13.04 ± 0.02), FairDICE (13.04 ± 0.07) and AET-ESR (13.04 ± 0.12), with ESR-IQL at 12.24 ± 0.01.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results on MO-Ant with convex trajectory-level utility F. Linear is abbreviated as Lin.
official.metric: AET utility G(E[F(R)]) evaluated on rollouts (higher is better), mean ± std over random seeds (5 seeds per Appendix Table 4; Table 1 does not state the count)
official.comparison: AETDICE (convex F + concave G) vs. OptiDICE linear scalarization at three weights, FairDICE, ESR-IQL and AET-ESR, all trained offline on the same MO-Ant expert dataset and evaluated on the same objective
official.falsification_criterion: On MO-Ant expert with this F and G, AETDICE's utility is not higher than the best baseline (FairDICE or Lin-[0.5,0.5]) by more than the seed std, e.g. the gap shrinks from about 0.65 to under about 0.1.

title: CoMet: Context and Multiplicity Decomposition for Multimodal Uncertainty Estimation
claim_source: Table E.1, page 24 (averages in Table 1, page 8)

official.background: Multimodal LLMs need a score that says how likely a given answer is to be wrong, for self-evaluation, abstention, or hallucination detection. In open-ended visual question answering there is no fixed answer set to compute an entropy over, so existing methods either ask the model about its own confidence (P(True), verbalized confidence), use the likelihood of the generated answer, or sample many answers and measure their consistency. Sampling-based methods are slow and sensitive to decoding settings, and self-reported confidence is often poorly calibrated.
official.method:
CoMet defines a binary 'match' variable m (is answer candidate y valid for image x and question t) and takes the Rényi-2 entropy of the match-conditioned posterior p(y | x, t, m=1). Under a uniform p(y | t) this splits into a context term u_t (how many answers the question allows) and a multiplicity term u_x|t = 2 log Z1 - log Z2, where Z1 and Z2 are the mean and mean-square of the match probability over candidates. Match probabilities come from the frozen MLLM used as a verifier (calibrated sigmoid of the log-odds of 'Yes' vs 'No'), and candidates for each question come from clustering questions in the Cambrian instruction-tuning data (200k image-question pairs, 32 candidates each). u_t is approximated with an LM's probabilities of the candidates, weighted by lambda (0.25 for Qwen3VL-2B).

A light Transformer head (about 50M parameters) on frozen MLLM features is trained to regress Z1, Z2 and u_t from (x, t) alone, then its attention-pooling and last linear layers are adapted on 900 MMMU-val plus 10k held-out VQA v2 samples. At test time it needs one pass with no generation. Uncertainty quality is measured as AUROC for separating correct from incorrect model answers (soft VQA score thresholded to binary), and compared against Consistency (entropy/max over 5 samples), NLL, Verbalized confidence, P(Correct), and VL-Uncertainty, all applied to the same frozen backbone.
official.claim: On a 10k random subset of VQA v2 with the frozen Qwen3VL-2B-Instruct backbone, CoMet's uncertainty score reaches AUROC 0.833 for detecting incorrect answers, versus 0.630 for the best baseline (VL-Uncertainty), 0.624 for Consistency (Ent), and 0.600 for P(Correct).
official.claim_caption: Table E.1: Open-ended VQA results. We report AUROC (AUC), AUPRC (AP), and FPR@95 of uncertainty estimation methods on open-ended VQA benchmarks. "GF" denotes generation-free.
official.metric: AUROC of uncertainty score for separating correct vs. incorrect answers (higher is better); AUPRC and FPR@95 also reported. No ± reported (single run).
official.comparison: CoMet (generation-free, trained head) vs. Consistency (Ent/Max), NLL, Verbalized Conf, P(Correct), VL-Uncertainty on the same frozen Qwen3VL-2B-Instruct and the same 10k VQA v2 samples
official.falsification_criterion: With the same backbone and VQA v2 subset, CoMet's AUROC is not clearly above the best baseline (e.g., margin below about 0.05), or any baseline reaches AUROC within 0.05 of CoMet.

title: Validating Causal Abstraction Metrics on Simulated Complex Systems
claim_source: Figure 3, page 8 (values in Figure 7, page 21; power curves in Figure 4, page 9)

official.background: Scientists and AI interpretability researchers propose high-level explanations of low-level systems (e.g. an ideal gas law for interacting particles, a symbolic program for a transformer), but there is no agreed metric for whether such an explanation is valid. Causal abstraction formalizes validity as consistency between interventions on the high-level model and the corresponding interventions on the low-level model under an abstraction map. Existing operationalizations mostly take the set of relevant low-level variables as given, and do not test whether the variables left out of the explanation are really causally inert, so they can accept explanations that silently ignore hidden causal pathways.
official.method:
The paper defines the Causal Abstraction Error (CAE): sample multi-node interventions (top-down CAE↓ samples macro-interventions and grounds them to compatible micro-interventions via the inverse value map; bottom-up CAE↑ samples micro-interventions and lifts them), run both the micro-model M and the macro-model E, map M's output to the macro level, and average a dissimilarity (e.g. MSE) between the two. The faithfulness test adds the dummy variable Φ (all unmapped micro-variables) to the intervention pool with some probability; when chosen, the unmapped micro-variables are overwritten with noise (Gaussian for continuous, uniform {-1,0,1} for integers, resampling for Booleans) while nothing changes on the macro side. CAE_NF variants exclude Φ.

Six controlled experiments (Appendix C) each pair a valid and an invalid (M, E, τ) that are observationally indistinguishable. Two isolate faithfulness: (1) Hidden confounder: a Lotka-Volterra macro-model where the micro-model has an unmapped resource variable r that scales final prey by (1+γr), with γ=0 in the valid case and γ>0 in the invalid case; (2) XOR backup path: E is X→M→Y with unmapped a, b; in the valid M, y=m=x, in the invalid M, y = m ∨ (a ⊕ b). Each metric is computed 100 times on the valid and on the invalid condition, and a Mann-Whitney U test decides whether they are separated.
official.claim: On the hidden-confounder and XOR-backup-path controlled experiments, both faithfulness-aware CAE variants (CAE↓, CAE↑) separate the invalid from the valid abstraction at p<0.001 (Mann-Whitney U over 100 runs; invalid scores ≈1.0 and ≈0.17 respectively), whereas both faithfulness-free variants (CAE↓_NF, CAE↑_NF) and IIA do not reach significance (invalid scores ≈0).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Controlled failure modes. Each cell reports whether a metric significantly separates the valid and invalid abstraction over 100 runs using a Mann–Whitney U test. CAE is the only family that detects all six targeted invalidities.
official.metric: Significance of a Mann-Whitney U test between 100 metric scores on the valid vs. 100 on the invalid abstraction (*** = p<0.001); cell color is Cohen's d. Metric scores are normalized errors (lower = more valid). No ± reported; the 100 runs are the spread.
official.comparison: CAE↓ and CAE↑ (with faithfulness test over unmapped variables) vs. CAE↓_NF and CAE↑_NF (same metric without it), plus IIA and ~30 observational/functional/information-theoretic baselines, on the same valid/invalid pairs.
official.falsification_criterion: On Experiments 1 or 2, a CAE_NF variant also separates valid from invalid at p<0.05, or a faithful CAE variant fails to reach p<0.001 over 100 runs (or gives clearly non-zero scores on the valid condition).

title: World from Motion: Generative Dynamic Gaussian Reconstruction from Monocular Video

official.background: Monocular 4D reconstruction recovers a dynamic scene's geometry, appearance and motion from one casual video so that it can be rendered from new viewpoints and times. Optimization-based dynamic 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) methods such as MoSca and WorldTree recover well-observed regions accurately but fail on unobserved regions and novel-view dynamics. Video generative models can fill these gaps but are not multiview-consistent enough for precise reconstruction. Hybrid methods such as CAT4D and ViDAR give blurry or inconsistent results.
official.method:
An initial dynamic 3DGS is built from the input video with an off-the-shelf method (WorldTree or MoSca). It is rendered along both the input and the target camera trajectories into per-frame 4D buffers: RGB, opacity, depth, normals and a rasterized 3D world-space scene flow (per-Gaussian displacement between consecutive frames). A Wan 2.1 14B video DiT with ReCamMaster-style input-video and camera conditioning receives these buffers through a VACE-style adapter and generates the target-trajectory video. Only the adapter blocks (initialized from Wan 2.1 VACE 14B), the camera encoder and the base DiT's self-attention layers are fine-tuned; all other weights stay frozen. It is trained with flow matching on MultiCamVideo pairs whose initial reconstructions come from Shape of Motion or WorldTree. At inference, a classifier-free-style guidance on the 4D-buffer tokens steers generation toward the reconstruction.

Distillation: J virtual cameras (J = 8 on DyCheck, per the supplement) are chosen by farthest-point sampling on the input trajectory and held fixed over time; test cameras are never used. A video is generated for each, and the dynamic 3DGS is re-initialized, with extra Gaussians backprojected from Depth Anything v3 depth of the generated views. It is then re-optimized (Gaussians and motion) with L1+SSIM+LPIPS losses on the input video and on the generated videos (down-weighted, λ_tgt = 0.5), plus depth, 3D track and ARAP terms. 'Ours (distill)' is this refined 3DGS rendered at held-out DyCheck test views under a static-camera protocol.
official.claim: On DyCheck under the static-camera protocol (covisible region), WorldTree + World from Motion (distill) reaches mPSNR 20.06 / mSSIM 0.721 / mLPIPS 0.187, versus the input WorldTree reconstruction at 19.28 / 0.714 / 0.246 and the strongest baseline ViDAR at 19.44 / 0.711 / 0.224.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative results on the DyCheck dataset. We evaluate under the static-camera protocol using three regions (Full, Valid, Covisible), and additionally report results with per-frame pose optimization for comparison with prior work. All metrics are computed over the corresponding evaluation masks, except for the full (unmasked) evaluation.
official.metric: Masked PSNR (higher better), masked SSIM (higher better), masked LPIPS (lower better) on held-out DyCheck test views over the covisible mask, averaged over the benchmark scenes; no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: WT + Ours (distill) vs. WorldTree (its own initialization), ViDAR (generative hybrid), MoSca and Shape-of-Motion, all re-evaluated with fixed test-camera poses
official.falsification_criterion: Running the WorldTree + WfM distillation on DyCheck does not beat both WorldTree and ViDAR on covisible mPSNR and mLPIPS. Concretely, mPSNR does not exceed 19.44 or mLPIPS is not below 0.224.

title: VLA-Corrector: Lightweight Detect-and-Correct Inference for Adaptive Action Horizon

official.background: Vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies such as π0.5 generate a chunk of future actions per forward pass and execute the first H of them open-loop, which cuts the number of expensive policy calls but leaves the robot blind to new observations for H steps. Small slips or collisions during that window can compound into task failure. Shorter horizons restore reactivity but multiply policy calls, so a fixed horizon trades robustness against compute. The paper asks whether the robot can keep long chunks by default and cut them short only when execution visibly drifts.
official.method:
VLA-Corrector leaves the VLA weights frozen. A ~40M-parameter residual MLP (the corrector) is trained on demonstration data to predict the change in the VLA's own visual-encoder latent k steps ahead, given the current latent and the executed action (loss: L2 plus a cosine term). At run time the Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) computes E_t = 1 - cos(predicted latent change, observed latent change) at every control step, keeps a 15-step window, and fires an interrupt when E_t exceeds median + 3·MAD for 5 consecutive steps (hysteresis off-threshold median + 2·MAD, 10-step cooldown). On interrupt, the remaining actions in the chunk are discarded and the policy is queried again.

That single recovery query uses Online Gradient Guidance (OGG): during flow-matching denoising, the first action of the current clean-chunk estimate is passed through the corrector, and the velocity field is nudged by η = 1 times the gradient of 1 - cos(predicted effect, ΔZ_exp - ΔZ_dev), where ΔZ_exp is the latent change expected at the last stable step and ΔZ_dev is the drift actually observed since then. Subsequent calls use ordinary inference. On RoboTwin v2.0, all 50 tasks are run in clean and randomized configurations with 50 paired-seed episodes each, comparing fixed-horizon H = 50, fixed H = 30 (chosen to match VLA-Corrector's per-step latency), and VLA-Corrector at H = 50.
official.claim: On RoboTwin v2.0 (all 50 tasks, clean + randomized, 5,000 episodes per method, same frozen π0.5), VLA-Corrector at H = 50 reaches 73.1% overall success [95% CI 71.9, 74.3], above the latency-matched fixed-horizon H = 30 baseline at 69.4% [68.1, 70.7] and the H = 50 baseline at 65.4% [64.1, 66.7], while using fewer policy calls per episode than H = 30 (6.88 vs. 9.41).
official.claim_caption: Table 2 RoboTwin v2.0 evaluation. Success rate (%, ↑), average policy calls per episode (↓), and per-step wall-clock latency (↓). The benchmark covers all 50 tasks in clean and randomized configurations, with 50 episodes per task/configuration (5,000 episodes per method); the same frozen π0.5 backbone is used throughout.
official.metric: Task success rate (%), higher is better, pooled over 50 tasks × 2 configurations × 50 episodes; brackets are 95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes (no seed std). Policy calls per episode and ms/step are also reported.
official.comparison: VLA-Corrector (LVM truncation + OGG, H = 50) vs. fixed-horizon π0.5 at H = 50 and at H = 30 (latency-matched), same frozen backbone and paired initial conditions/seeds
official.falsification_criterion: With the same backbone and protocol, VLA-Corrector's overall success is not above the latency-matched H = 30 baseline by more than the CI half-width (~1.3 points), or its gain requires more policy calls per episode than the H = 30 baseline.
