title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (unfiltered numbers: Table 22, Appendix U, page 31)

official.background: Many everyday programming tasks are 'fuzzy functions' that are easy to describe but hard to write as rules, such as triaging log lines, repairing malformed JSON or classifying intent. Developers increasingly call a remote LLM API on every input for these, which costs money, needs network access, and is not reproducible when providers update models. The paper asks whether a large model can instead be used once per function to compile a natural-language specification into a small artifact that a tiny local model executes offline.
official.method:
A PAW program has two parts. An off-the-shelf Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 'pseudo compiler' rewrites the user's specification into a clean restatement plus a few input-output examples (the pseudo-program). A second, trained Qwen3-4B 'LoRA compiler' reads the spec, the pseudo-program and 64 learned prefix tokens; its prefix hidden states are mean-pooled, passed through an MLP, and mapped to mixing coefficients over shared LoRA bases (rank 64, 64 bases per module type, all attention and MLP projections), giving about 38.5M LoRA parameters per function. The frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter runs with this LoRA attached and the pseudo-program prepended to the input.

Only the LoRA compiler and mapper are trained, by next-token likelihood of the target output through the frozen interpreter, for 3 epochs on FuzzyBench-10M: (spec, input, output) triples generated by gpt-5.2 across 800+ task categories, split 80/10/10 by specification. The evaluation set is the 'verified' test split, keeping examples where gpt-5.2 and gpt-5-mini agree on the output. Baselines are direct prompting of Qwen3 0.6B/4B/8B/14B/32B (spec plus input, single sample), scored by exact match.
official.claim: On held-out FuzzyBench test specifications (verified split), Qwen3-0.6B executing PAW-compiled programs reaches 73.78% exact match, higher than direct prompting of Qwen3-32B (68.70%), Qwen3-14B (63.96%) and the same Qwen3-0.6B base (9.84%); on the unfiltered test split the ordering also holds (PAW 57.20% vs. Qwen3-32B 53.20%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Main results. FuzzyBench reports verified-test EM; unfiltered results appear in Appendix U. Following the WRENCH benchmark setup of ALCHEmist [Huang et al., 2024b], SMS uses F1 and the rest use Acc. Contained indicates the program is self-contained and executable without internet access. PS is per-program shipping size; for prompting baselines this is the prompt/spec size, and for PAW it is the deployed PEFT adapter (Q4_0 quantized for Qwen3 0.6B and Qwen3.5 0.8B; fp32 for GPT-2). †: numbers taken from Huang et al. [2024b], which uses 10-sample majority voting; the reimplementation row uses single-sample for fairness. *: zero F1 due to zero recall.
official.metric: Exact-match accuracy on the FuzzyBench verified test split, higher is better; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: PAW (frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter + compiled LoRA + pseudo-program) vs. direct prompting of Qwen3-0.6B, 4B, 8B, 14B and 32B on the same test examples
official.falsification_criterion: Re-evaluating the released PAW compiler/interpreter and prompting Qwen3-32B on the same FuzzyBench verified test split gives PAW an exact match that is not higher than Qwen3-32B's (or the gap shrinks to around 1 point or less, which the authors themselves say they would not interpret).

title: K9-Bench: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs on Canine-Centric Videos

official.background: Video benchmarks for multimodal LLMs are almost entirely about humans, so it is unclear whether these models can follow animal behaviour, such as a dog's posture, ear and tail cues, and its interactions with people over long clips. This matters for pet-welfare monitoring and home robots. K9-Bench is a video question-answering benchmark built from 907 YouTube videos of domestic dogs, with 4,744 five-way multiple-choice questions in five categories (posture, action sequence, context, cause-effect, interaction), generated by Gemini-2.5-Flash from an expert-built canine behaviour ontology and filtered to remove questions that text-only LLMs can answer.
official.method:
Questions and correct answers are generated by Gemini-2.5-Flash from the video (and audio) plus a canine-behaviour knowledge base; four distractors are generated from a text narration of the video. A 'deaf-blind' filter removes any question that a majority of three text-only frontier LLMs answer correctly (removing 42.58% of 8,263 QAs), and GLM-4.5-Flash rewrites questions to strip speaker identities and audio references.

Open-source models (Qwen3-VL 4B/8B/32B Instruct and Thinking, InternVL-3.5 8B/14B) receive 32 uniformly sampled frames plus the question and are asked to give a free-form answer (Thinking variants get up to 2,048 response tokens). The answer is embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B and compared by cosine similarity to the five options; it counts as correct only if similarity to the ground-truth option exceeds 0.5 and no wrong option has a higher similarity. The metric is accuracy over all 4,744 questions (chance is 20%).
official.claim: On K9-Bench (4,744 five-way questions, 32 frames, embedding-matched free-form answers), Qwen3-VL Thinking variants score below their Instruct counterparts: 4B 22.4% vs. 27.6%, 8B 25.3% vs. 28.8%, 32B 30.7% vs. 31.4%, and no open-source model exceeds 33.0% (InternVL-3.5-14B).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: MCQ evaluation results on K9-Bench: Closed-source models lead overall, while open-source models show varied strengths, particularly in interaction and context reasoning. * indicates models evaluated with 32 frames. † indicates models evaluated using a 1 FPS setting.
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy (%) over all 4,744 questions, higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Qwen3-VL-{4B, 8B, 32B}-Thinking vs. Qwen3-VL-{4B, 8B, 32B}-Instruct under the same 32-frame input and the same embedding-based scorer; InternVL-3.5-8B/14B as the other open-source references
official.falsification_criterion: Re-evaluating with the released data and the paper's protocol, Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking matches or beats Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (or 4B-Thinking matches or beats 4B-Instruct), or Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct accuracy differs from 28.8% by more than a few points, or an open-source model of these sizes scores well above 33%.

title: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction
claim_source: Table 5, page 23 (Appendix D.2); greedy-decoding counterpart in Table 1, page 7

official.background: LLMs used in high-stakes settings should be able to abstain when they are likely to be wrong. Selective prediction (SP) does this by answering only when a confidence score is above a threshold, trading coverage (fraction answered) against selective risk (error rate on the answered fraction). It is usually summarized by the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC). Existing RL alignment either rewards only correctness (RLVR) or adds a calibration penalty (RLCR, a Brier score on verbalized confidence). Calibration does not guarantee that correct answers are ranked above wrong ones by confidence, and that ranking is what SP depends on.
official.method:
RLSR is GRPO with a reward derived from AURC. Using the weighted form AURC = (1/N) Σ α_i·1{wrong_i}, with α_i = H_N − H_{N−r_i} (r_i = rank of sample i in ascending order of verbalized confidence, H = harmonic numbers), the authors 'lift' it to two-sided rewards: each rollout gets reward +α_i if correct and −α_i if wrong. Ranks are computed over an effective batch that pools all B×G rollouts (B = 48 prompts × G = 32 rollouts = 1536), and GRPO advantages are then computed within each prompt group without std normalization. A binary format reward enforces <think>, <answer>, <analysis>, <confidence> tags.

Base model Qwen2.5-7B (no SFT), LoRA rank 1 (α = 32) on all linear layers, no KL term, BNPO loss, TRL + vLLM, lr 1e-5 constant schedule with 5% warmup, 1 epoch over 20,000 HotPotQA-Modified examples (from the RLCR paper), max completion 1536 tokens, rollout temperature 0.7. RLVR (binary correctness reward) and RLCR (correctness minus Brier score) use identical hyperparameters. In-domain evaluation is HotPotQA-Modified and HotPotQA-Vanilla. Out-of-domain evaluation is SimpleQA, TriviaQA, GPQA, Math500, GSM8K and CommonsenseQA, with correctness from exact match, math-verify or a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct judge. AURC is computed from the verbalized confidence.
official.claim: For Qwen2.5-7B trained on HotPotQA, RLSR reaches in-domain AURC 0.478 ± 0.006 versus 0.509 ± 0.012 for RLCR and 0.537 ± 0.008 for RLVR, and out-of-domain AURC 0.412 ± 0.009 versus 0.443 ± 0.009 (RLCR) and 0.453 ± 0.006 (RLVR) (5 seeds, temperature 0.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: The AURC (mean ± std) of Qwen2.5-7B trained on HotPotQA over 5 seeds at T = 0.3.
official.metric: AURC of verbalized confidence (lower is better), averaged over 2 in-domain or 6 out-of-domain datasets; mean ± std over 5 evaluation sampling seeds at T = 0.3 on a single trained checkpoint per method (training seeds not varied)
official.comparison: RLSR vs. RLCR and RLVR, all GRPO-trained from Qwen2.5-7B on HotPotQA-Modified with identical hyperparameters
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining all three methods with the stated recipe, RLSR's in-domain AURC is not lower than RLCR's by more than the seed std (e.g. the gap is under about 0.012), or RLSR's out-of-domain AURC is not lower than both baselines.

title: B-CALM: Bias-Limited Bayesian Borrowing for RCT-Anchored Treatment Effects under Covariate Mismatch
claim_source: Table 1, page 10 (per-cell results in Appendix C, Table 3, pages 26-27)

official.background: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) give unbiased treatment effects for the trial population, but they are usually too small to estimate how the effect varies across patients (the conditional average treatment effect, CATE). Observational studies (OS) such as EHR cohorts are much larger, but treatment is confounded and the two sources often measure only partly overlapping covariates. The question is how to let the OS reduce uncertainty about the trial CATE without the biased OS taking over the estimate and producing overconfident intervals.
official.method:
B-CALM models both sources on a shared latent state z, reached through source-specific encoders that are learned jointly in general. The RCT outcome surface is mu(z) + a*tau(z). The OS surface is mu(z) + a*tau(z) + b0(z) + a*b_delta(z), where b0 is a baseline bias and b_delta is a comparative (treatment-contrast) bias. Priors on b0 and b_delta control how much the OS can inform the trial CATE tau. A tight prior on b_delta (sigma_delta -> 0, prior mean 0) fully borrows the OS treatment contrast, while b0 still absorbs baseline bias. A diffuse prior (sigma_delta -> infinity) returns the contrast to RCT-only inference.

In the synthetic experiments the encoders are fixed identity maps, and mu, tau, b0 and b_delta are linear in a prespecified polynomial-trigonometric basis, so the Gaussian posterior and the 90% credible intervals are closed-form. sigma_delta is chosen per replicate by empirical-Bayes model averaging over {0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, inf} with fixed asymmetric prior weights (Algorithm 2, Appendix B.3). The data come from a 3-d latent state (shifted for OS units) that generates trial covariates (W, U) and OS covariates (W, V) through noisy linear maps. The grid crosses 3 covariate-overlap regimes, 3 OS-bias regimes (none, baseline-only, comparative) and a comparative-bias strength sweep {0, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0} on the balanced DGP, with n_r in {250, 500}, n_o = 5,000, confounded OS treatment assignment and 50 replicates per cell (24 cells). Each replicate is scored on 600 fresh draws from the trial covariate distribution. Baselines fitted under the same harness are RCT-only, OS-only, pooled (b0 = b_delta = 0), a causal forest on the pooled data, and R-OSCAR/MR-OSCAR/CALM, which coincide in this harness and are reported as one OSCAR/CALM row.
official.claim: Averaged over the 24-cell synthetic factorial grid (50 replicates per cell), B-CALM's pointwise 90% credible intervals cover at 0.939, and its CATE RMSE is 0.206 vs. 0.318 for RCT-only, with a negative-transfer rate of 0.023. Pooled borrowing and the causal forest under-cover (0.581 and 0.811 coverage; negative transfer 0.292 and 0.299), and OSCAR/CALM reaches 0.890 coverage with RMSE 0.228.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Synthetic factorial study: metric averages over the full condition grid (24 cells × 50 replicates; Appendix B.2). Cov. and Width refer to pointwise 90% credible intervals evaluated on trial-distribution covariates; NT is the negative-transfer rate relative to RCT-only. R-OSCAR, MR-OSCAR, and CALM coincide in this harness and are reported as one OSCAR/CALM row. Per-cell results: Appendix C, Table 3.
official.metric: CATE RMSE (lower is better); empirical coverage of pointwise 90% intervals (target 0.90); mean interval width; negative-transfer rate = fraction of replicates where the method's RMSE exceeds RCT-only's on the same replicate (lower is better). Baseline intervals come from each method's own procedure: Gaussian posterior for RCT-only, OS-only and pooled, asymptotic influence-function SEs for CF, and a 200-replicate trial bootstrap for OSCAR/CALM. Table 1 gives grid averages with no error bars; Table 3 gives per-cell RMSE as mean ± across-seed std.
official.comparison: B-CALM vs. RCT-only, OS-only, pooled RCT+OS, causal forest on the pooled data, and the OSCAR/CALM calibrated-borrowing family, all fitted on the same simulated datasets
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the factorial grid, B-CALM's average 90% coverage falls clearly below nominal (e.g. under 0.88), or its average RMSE is not clearly below RCT-only's (e.g. above 0.28), or pooled and causal-forest coverage under comparative bias does not fall well below B-CALM's (e.g. on the balanced DGP at bias strength 1.0, n_r = 500, the paper reports pooled 0.071 and CF 0.229 vs. B-CALM 0.897).

title: Decentralized Aggregation of LLM Predictions via Wagering Mechanisms

official.background: When several LLMs, each with different expertise or access to private context, answer the same question, their probabilistic predictions can be combined, but someone has to decide how much weight each model gets per question. Centralized methods (stacked generalization on hidden states, learned routers) need access to every model's internals or inputs. Decentralized methods either use fixed weights or self-reported confidence or perplexity, which break down when models are miscalibrated and can be gamed by a participant that wants more influence. This paper asks whether a wagering mechanism, where each model reports a prediction plus a wager used as its aggregation weight, can learn good per-question weights without central access.
official.method:
WALLA pays each agent i the net payout pi_i = w_i (s(p_i, y) - b_{-i} - c3 w_i), where s is the Brier score (c1 = 1, c2 = 1/2), c3 = 1/2, and b_{-i} is a leave-one-out baseline: the wager-weighted average of the other agents' scores (WALLA I) or the score of the wager-weighted pool of their predictions (WALLA II). The best-response wager is then (expected score advantage / 2 c3)^+, and the aggregate prediction is the wager-weighted linear pool. Each LLM keeps its frozen prediction (from output-token logits) and trains a separate 2-layer MLP wager head (hidden sizes 512, 256, sigmoid output, Adam, batch size 100) on its own last-layer hidden state, regressing with MSE onto the hindsight-optimal wager ((s_i - b_{-i})/2c3)^+, which it can compute from its own payout alone. All agents' wager heads train simultaneously.

Scenario I (Table 2): M in {4, 8, 12} copies of Llama3-Aloe-8B answer yes/no PubMedQA questions (dataset balanced between yes and no, maybe dropped, 8:1:1 split). For each question, one randomly chosen copy receives the relevant abstract and the rest receive none. Aloe alone gets AUC 82.39 with the abstract and 60.65 without. Baselines: UniformAvg, SelfCertainty (KL-from-uniform confidence weights), PackLLM (inverse input perplexity weights), which are all decentralized and learning-free; and the centralized RouterDC, NIRTRouter, RouteLLM, and StackedGen (an MLP on concatenated hidden states).
official.claim: On PubMedQA with 12 Aloe-8B copies, one of which receives the relevant abstract, WALLA I's wager-weighted aggregate reaches AUC 82.10 ± 0.35 and ACC 86.66 ± 0.32, versus 73.65/78.97 for the best decentralized baseline (PackLLM) and 63.10/66.17 for uniform averaging, roughly matching the centralized StackedGen (82.26 ± 0.32 AUC).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Homogeneous models (Aloe) on PubMedQA with private contexts. For each question, one of M ∈ {4, 8, 12} models is randomly selected to receive a relevant abstract; the rest receive none. (Footnote: Aloe achieves AUC=82.39, ACC=87.57, ECE=7.38 with abstract and AUC=60.65, ACC=63.10, ECE=7.83 without.)
official.metric: AUC and accuracy of the aggregated prediction on the test split, ×100, higher is better; ± is a 95% confidence interval over five independent runs (learning-free baselines are deterministic and have no interval)
official.comparison: WALLA I (decentralized learned wagers) vs. UniformAvg, SelfCertainty, PackLLM (decentralized, learning-free) at M = 12; secondary: vs. centralized StackedGen and RouteLLM w/ context
official.falsification_criterion: With M = 12, WALLA I's AUC falls within ~2 points of PackLLM's (i.e., at or below ~75.7), or its accuracy does not exceed PackLLM's 78.97 by more than the run-to-run CI; for the secondary parity claim, WALLA I's AUC falls more than ~2 points below StackedGen's.

title: RustMizan: A Compilable, Contamination-Aware Benchmarking Framework for Rust Vulnerabilities

official.background: LLM agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, but most vulnerability benchmarks use small non-compilable snippets taken from diffs, test only binary detection, and ignore that public datasets may already be in models' training data. RustMizan is a benchmark of 42 real Rust memory-safety CVEs from the RustSec advisory database, each packaged as standalone compilable programs at three levels of context (whole crate, single file plus dependencies, single function plus dependencies), with ground truth for detection, CWE class, and function- and line-level localization. Because the same vulnerability appears at each level, the multi-level design allows a controlled study of how much code context helps or hurts an agent.
official.method:
The dataset has 173 compilable variants (77 crate-level, 39 file-level, 57 function-level), built manually from both the vulnerable (pre-patch) and, where available, patched (post-patch) versions; patched variants are labelled non-vulnerable. Single-file crates have no crate-level variant, and the function-level variant is skipped when the file is essentially one function. Each variant is analyzed by an agent in a Docker sandbox (rust:1.84.1) built with Inspect-AI, using a ReAct scaffold with bash access (message limit 100, 3600 s wall clock). The agent can explore, build and run the code, and must write results.json with is_vulnerable, cwe_type, vulnerable_functions and vulnerable_lines. The same prompt (Appendix F) is used for Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT 5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Qwen 3.6 Plus.

Line localization is scored as micro-averaged F1: TP, FP and FN are computed by set intersection between the predicted and ground-truth (file, line) pairs and summed over all variants at a given context level. Figure 4 reports this Line F1 separately for the crate, file and function variants of the vanilla (unmutated) dataset.
official.claim: On the vanilla RustMizan dataset, all four agents localize vulnerable lines better with function-level context than with the whole crate: Line F1 rises from 17.9 to 39.4 (Claude Sonnet 4.6), 15.6 to 24.7 (GPT 5.4), 16.6 to 41.3 (Gemini 3.1 Pro), and 10.7 to 37.2 (Qwen 3.6 Plus).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Line localization F1 across context levels (crate, file, function). Function-level context consistently helps. The crate-to-file differences vary across the models.
official.metric: Line localization micro-F1 (%), higher is better; single run per model, no error bars or seeds reported; values are the bar labels printed in the figure
official.comparison: Function-level variants (57) vs. crate-level variants (77) (and file-level, 39) of the same CVEs, same agent scaffold, prompt and model
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the agent with the released harness on the vanilla crate- and function-level variants, function-level Line F1 is not clearly higher than crate-level Line F1 (e.g. within a few points, or within the run-to-run spread of repeated runs) for most of the models tested.

title: Beyond Modality Fusion: Deep Ensembles for Multimodal Classification

official.background: In multimodal classification, late-fusion networks concatenate features from modality-specific encoders and classify them jointly. When one modality is much more predictive than the other (modality imbalance), jointly trained late-fusion networks often underuse the stronger modality and can do worse than the best single-modality model. Many methods (OGM-GE, InfoReg, MMPareto, AUG, ReconBoost, LFM) modify gradients or losses to balance learning across modalities. This paper asks whether simply training unimodal networks independently and averaging their logits, with no explicit fusion, does better.
official.method:
A heterogeneous deep ensemble (HeDE) trains n1 classifiers on modality 1 and n2 on modality 2, each independently and from a different initialization, and classifies by averaging their output logits (not probabilities). A homogeneous ensemble (HoDE) uses only one modality. For a fair comparison, an ensemble of N unimodal networks is matched to a late-fusion network with the same modality-specific encoders, which differs only in its head: a single linear layer on the concatenated features. The imbalance-aware baselines change training but not parameter count.

On CREMA-D (audio-visual emotion recognition), the authors build a clean split in which actors are disjoint between train and test, because the commonly used split leaks actor identity. Audio (log-magnitude STFT spectrograms, nfft 512, hop 353, at 22,050 Hz; the MMPareto baseline instead uses 128-bin Kaldi mel-filterbank features) and video (a single frame, 224x224) are each encoded by a ResNet-18 trained from scratch. Audio unimodal models: SGD, lr 0.1 with cosine schedule, wd 1e-4, batch 32, 64 epochs. Video unimodal models: wd 1e-3, batch 64, 256 epochs. Late-fusion models: video hyperparameters, 64 epochs. Baselines were run from their official code with the modifications listed in Appendix C. The HeDE in Table 1 has size 2 (one audio + one video ResNet-18), matching the two-encoder late-fusion networks in parameter count.
official.claim: On the actor-disjoint CREMA-D split, a heterogeneous deep ensemble of one audio and one video ResNet-18 (logit averaging) reaches 71.1 ± 3.1% accuracy, beating every imbalance-aware late-fusion method with the same encoders; the best of these, AUG, reaches 65.0 ± 1.6% and vanilla late fusion 56.7 ± 1.6%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Mean accuracy and standard deviation across 5 runs on the clean CREMA-D split.
official.metric: Top-1 test accuracy (%) on the clean CREMA-D split, higher is better; ± is std across 5 runs
official.comparison: HeDE (size 2) vs. Vanilla late fusion, OGM-GE, LFM, AUG, InfoReg, MMPareto, ReconBoost (each a single two-encoder late-fusion network), plus audio-only and video-only HoDEs of size 2
official.falsification_criterion: With an actor-disjoint CREMA-D split, matched ResNet-18 encoders and 5 runs, the size-2 HeDE's mean accuracy fails to exceed the best imbalance-aware late-fusion baseline (AUG or LFM) by more than one std, or a baseline matches or beats it.

title: RABBiT: Rapidly adaptive BOLD foundation model via brain-tuning for accurate zero-shot and few-shot prediction of speech-elicited responses in the brain
claim_source: Table 3, page 23 (Appendix E.5); curves in Figure 4a, page 10

official.background: Encoding models that predict fMRI responses to natural speech usually fit a separate voxel-wise ridge regression for each participant. This needs a lot of fMRI data per person and hundreds of millions of readout parameters. Recent foundation-style brain encoders (e.g. TRIBEv2) predict group responses zero-shot, but they are large and not built for cheap adaptation to a new individual. A model that predicts the shared response across listeners and adapts to a new listener from a few minutes of data would make population-scale language neuroscience much cheaper.
official.method:
RABBiT is an audio-to-fMRI encoder (~12.9M trainable parameters) trained on the Friends subset of CourtoisNeuroMod (6 participants, ~565K TRs) and projected to 30 bilateral HCP-MMP1 ROIs on fsaverage6 (~41K vertices). Wav2Vec2.0-base is brain-tuned with rank-8 LoRA. A 2-layer Temporal Brain Transformer (8 heads, hidden 256) uses one learned query per ROI that cross-attends over the speech tokens and produces a per-ROI latent z_i. A Shared-Idiosyncratic Decomposition (SID) maps z_i to vertices as pi_i(z_i) Phi_i + rho_i(z_i) Delta_{i,s}, where Phi_i is a shared rank-100 basis and Delta_{i,s} is a per-subject rank-15 deviation basis (initialized from PCA/SVD of training responses). For an unseen subject, Delta is replaced by the average over the training subjects.

Few-shot adaptation: on the Narratives story 21styear (19 held-out participants after one exclusion), the last 400 TRs are a fixed test segment and a contiguous prefix of 200/400/800/1200/1600 TRs (~5-40 min) is the calibration data. RABBiT freezes everything except the per-ROI deviation coefficient maps rho_i (~115K parameters) and trains them with a correlation loss plus an anchor penalty (lambda=5e-5). Baselines fit on the same calibration window: (a) voxel-wise ridge (FIR delays, CV alpha, ~222M parameters) on pretrained Wav2Vec2.0 features, (b) the same ridge on multi-brain-tuned Wav2Vec2.0 features, and (c) No-SID RABBiT, where SID is replaced by a per-ROI linear readout (~10.6M parameters) that is fine-tuned the same way. The metric is per-subject vertex-mean Pearson r on the test segment over language ROIs, compared with paired two-sided t-tests across the 19 participants.
official.claim: On 21styear (n=19 unseen participants), with 10 minutes of calibration data RABBiT few-shot (updating ~115K parameters) beats the No-SID fine-tune by Δr=+0.021 (paired p<0.001), which in turn is a non-significant +0.005 over brain-tuned voxel-wise ridge (p=0.108); RABBiT few-shot vs. that ridge is p<0.001 (~+0.026 summing the two adjacent Δs). RABBiT few-shot significantly beats ridge at every calibration size from 5 to 40 minutes.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Pairwise paired two-sided t-tests on the language-aggregate saturation curve. n=19 participants on 21styear; ∆r between consecutive sorted conditions.
official.metric: Language-aggregate per-subject vertex-mean Pearson r on a fixed held-out 400-TR test segment (higher is better); Δr between conditions with paired two-sided t-tests across 19 participants. No seeds or CIs are given for the Δ values; Fig. 4a shows ±SE bands across participants.
official.comparison: RABBiT few-shot (SID deviation coefficients only) vs. No-SID direct fine-tune vs. brain-tuned-feature voxel-wise ridge (and pretrained-feature ridge in Fig. 4a), all trained on the same per-participant calibration window
official.falsification_criterion: At 10 minutes of calibration on 21styear, RABBiT few-shot's language-aggregate test r is not significantly higher (paired test across participants) than a properly tuned voxel-wise ridge on brain-tuned Wav2Vec2.0 features, or the gap falls well below about +0.02 r.

title: Graph Sparse Sampling: Breaking the Curse of the Horizon in Continuous MDP Planning
claim_source: Table 2, page 22 (Appendix B.4); plotted in Figure 2b, page 8

official.background: Online planning in continuous MDPs is usually done with tree search (MCTS with Double Progressive Widening, or Voronoi-based variants such as VPW). Because each state-action pair gets its own sampled successors, the tree branches, and in the worst case the sample budget needed for a given accuracy grows exponentially with the planning horizon (as for Kearns et al.'s Sparse Sampling). This paper proposes a planner that shares one sampled set of successor states across all candidate actions at each depth, which avoids branching, maps onto large fixed-shape GPU batches, and under overlap conditions gives error bounds polynomial in the horizon.
official.method:
Graph Sparse Sampling (GSS) builds a layered graph of depth T from the root state. Forward pass: at each depth t, every one of the C_t state nodes draws K_t candidate actions from an action proposal; a state proposal q_t^s is then fitted and a single shared next layer of C_{t+1} states is drawn from it. Leaves get a tail value from a single rollout of a rollout policy. Backward pass: every (node, action) pair gets a self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) backup over the whole next layer, Q = sum_j rho(j) [r + gamma V_{t+1}^j] / sum_j rho(j) with rho(j) = p(s^j_{t+1} | s, a) / q_t^s(s^j_{t+1}); node values are the max over sampled actions, and the root returns the argmax action. Because Lunar Lander's transition noise is 3D in a 6D state (singular density), the backup uses a smoothed transition density: a Gaussian kernel with bandwidth (0.02, 0.02, 0.005, 0.02, 0.02, 0.002) added to the linearized transition, giving a closed-form Gaussian density. Implemented in JAX.

Lunar Lander (Mern et al. 2021; Appendix B.4): state (x, z, theta, vx, vz, omega), action (Fx in [-5,5], T in [0,15], delta in [-1,1]), dt = 0.4, Gaussian noise on vx, vz (std 0.1) and omega (std 0.01), reward -1000 for crash/out-of-bounds, 100 - |x'| - vz'^2 on landing, -1 otherwise, gamma = 0.99. GSS uses planner horizon 12, rollout and closed-loop cap 24, a brake-near-ground guide/rollout policy, actions mixed from expert primitives, the rollout action, noisy rollout actions and uniform samples, and a next-state proposal that is a diagonal Gaussian fitted to the top-80% (by sample-plus-rollout score) sampled successors, inflated by 1.1. Five budgets range from 10 actions / 384 states (xs) to 50 / 2048 (xl). Baselines DPW and VPW (POMDPs.jl, Julia) use the same brake-near-ground guide and rollout policy, a 35-step closed-loop cap, and per-action wall-clock budgets 0.0001-1.0 s; (c_uct, k_a, alpha_a, k_s, alpha_s) = (60, 1.45, 0.6, 0.1, 0.3).
official.claim: On continuous Lunar Lander with 100 seeds, GSS at the 'large' budget (40 actions, 1536 states per layer, 0.053 s per decision) reaches discounted return 78.641 ± 0.108 (SE), above every DPW and VPW budget from 0.01 s to 1.0 s; the best tree result is VPW at 0.01 s with 74.402 ± 0.353 and the best DPW is 73.582 ± 0.208.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Lunar Lander planner performance from Figure 2b. Return entries are discounted mean episode return ± SE over 100 seeds.
official.metric: Mean discounted episode return over 100 seeds, higher is better; ± is standard error over seeds
official.comparison: GSS (budgets xs to xl) vs. DPW and VPW tree search at per-action budgets 0.01, 0.0316, 0.1, 0.316 and 1.0 s, all using the same brake-near-ground guide and rollout policy

title: MobileWan: Closing the Quality Gap for Mobile Video Diffusion
claim_source: Table 7, page 12 (the matched Wan2.2-5B comparison is also in Table 5, page 12)

official.background: Text-to-video diffusion transformers that give good quality have billions of parameters and need server GPUs. Earlier on-device video generators use much smaller backbones (0.4 to 1.8B parameters) so they fit the memory and latency limits of a phone, and their quality falls clearly short of server models. The paper asks whether a server-scale 5B video DiT (Wan2.2-5B) can instead be compressed and reformulated so that it runs on a phone NPU while keeping close to server-level quality.
official.method:
Starting from Wan2.2-5B fine-tuned to 81x480x832 at 16 FPS, the authors apply four steps in sequence. (1) Learned self-attention head pruning (about 23% of heads) uses per-head sigmoid gates, a sparsity penalty, temperature annealing and high-noise-biased timestep sampling, followed by fine-tuning. (2) Recurrence distillation turns all 30 blocks into a hybrid attention: softmax attention within a local temporal chunk (chunk size 4 latent frames, overlap 2) and causal linear attention with learnable polynomial feature maps for all earlier chunks. The feature maps are first pretrained block-wise with all other weights frozen, then the whole DiT is fine-tuned; at inference the DiT runs as an RNN with constant-size state. (3) Step distillation to 3 sampling steps; the variant carried into Table 5 and the final MobileWan VBench numbers is DMD2 (the DMD loss plus an adversarial loss from a lightweight convolutional discriminator on teacher-network features, which also needs real video data). It scores 84.03 VBench Total at 3 steps in Table 3, versus 83.20 for plain DMD and 82.44 for D-DMD at 3 steps. (4) An efficient VAE decoder (LightX2V with an extended causal look-back window) is fine-tuned.

Quality is measured with VBench (Total, Quality and Semantic scores) on the standard VBench prompt set at 81x480x832. The final 3-step system with the optimized decoder is reported as MobileWan, and the authors state that its DiT checkpoint and sampling code are released. Table 7 lists MobileWan next to server models and to earlier mobile models, including the authors' own Neodragon.
official.claim: MobileWan (DMD2 step-distilled to 3 sampling steps, optimized decoder, 81x480x832) reaches VBench Total 83.79 (Quality 85.16, Semantic 78.32). That is higher than the best previous mobile model from the same group, Neodragon (81.61), and higher than the full-step fine-tuned Wan2.2-5B model it was derived from (83.12).
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Comparisons with SOTA generic and on-device video diffusion models on VBench.
official.metric: VBench Total score (higher is better), plus Quality and Semantic sub-scores. Single runs; no error bars or seed variation are reported.
official.comparison: MobileWan vs. Neodragon (previous state-of-the-art mobile video DiT) and vs. the fine-tuned Wan2.2-5B starting model; the other mobile and server rows are numbers cited from other papers
official.falsification_criterion: Running the released MobileWan checkpoint and sampling code through the standard VBench protocol gives a Total score at or below Neodragon's 81.61, or clearly below the fine-tuned Wan2.2-5B's 83.12 (for example, by more than about 0.5 points).

title: Inertia-1: An Open Exploration of Wearable Motion Foundation Models
claim_source: Table 3, page 7 (full-finetuning numbers in Table 13, page 24)

official.background: Wearable accelerometers record large amounts of unlabeled motion data (e.g. NHANES, UK Biobank), while labeled datasets for human activity recognition (HAR), freezing-of-gait (FoG) detection and disease prediction are small and use different sensors, placements and sampling rates. Previous studies of motion foundation models each varied one design choice under its own setup, so it is unclear whether large-scale self-supervised pretraining reliably helps and which choices matter. Inertia-1 is a benchmark-style study that compares pretraining objectives and sensing configurations under one shared protocol.
official.method:
Ten (pre)training approaches are run with a shared configuration: 30 s windows of 20 Hz triaxial wrist accelerometer data, small encoders (~3-10M parameters), AdamW with lr 2e-4, batch 1024, and pretraining on NHANES 2011-2014 accelerometry (~14,000 participants). Self-supervised objectives include masked patch reconstruction (PatchTST: patch length 10, mask ratio 0.4, MSE on masked patches), autoregressive next-patch prediction (ART Transformer, ARG GRU), DINO, SimCLR, SSL-Wearables, RelCon and Self-PAB. The supervised baselines are a 1D ResNet-style CNN (5.0M) and a 1D ViT (5.4M) trained from scratch on each downstream task.

For the claim, each pretrained encoder is frozen and a linear classifier is trained on each of 10 HAR datasets (lr 1e-3, weight decay 0.01). The metric is AUROC on each dataset's test split. The supervised CNN/ViT are trained end-to-end on the same windows.
official.claim: With linear probing, a PatchTST encoder pretrained on NHANES outperforms both supervised-from-scratch baselines (CNN, ViT) in AUROC on OPPORTUNITY (89.8 vs. best supervised 72.9), MHEALTH (98.2 vs. 93.8) and HHAR (93.5 vs. 89.1).
official.claim_caption: Table 3 | Comparisons of SSL models and supervised baselines across all HAR datasets. We report the linear probing AUROC of each model. AUPRC and full finetuning results are in Table 10 & 13.
official.metric: Test AUROC (%) of a linear probe on frozen pretrained features, higher is better; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: NHANES-pretrained PatchTST (and other SSL encoders), linear probe, vs. supervised CNN and ViT trained from scratch on the same HAR dataset and input configuration (20 Hz, 30 s, triaxial accelerometer)
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction in which the NHANES-pretrained PatchTST linear probe does not beat the best supervised baseline by at least ~3 AUROC points on OPPORTUNITY, MHEALTH and HHAR, or in which the OPPORTUNITY gap shrinks well below the reported ~17 points.

title: Constrained Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Efficient Inference over Finite Automata

official.background: Structured outputs such as JSON function calls or SQL are usually enforced in autoregressive LLMs by masking out invalid next tokens left to right. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) such as Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B break this assumption: at each denoising step they sample many positions at once from a fully factorized (mean-field) distribution. Locally valid tokens can then combine into an invalid sequence, so the autoregressive masking trick does not carry over. Without a constraint mechanism, dLLMs often produce malformed structured output, especially under temperature sampling or with few denoising steps.
official.method:
The constraint is written as a finite automaton (a DFA for the function-calling tasks, built from the given function schema). The automaton is treated as a chain-structured graphical model (an HMM whose latent states are automaton edges) whose support is exactly the set of accepted length-L strings. At each denoising step, the dLLM's mean-field prediction p_theta(x0_i | x_t) reweights the emission factors of this chain. A sample x0 is then drawn exactly from the constrained posterior p_theta(x0 | x_t) * 1[x0 in C], using a backward pass and ancestral sampling. Greedy decoding takes the argmax under the same distribution. Every intermediate prediction is valid, so the final output satisfies the constraint by construction. Per-position marginals under the constrained distribution replace the model's usual confidence score when choosing which positions to unmask ('Mar' remasking). A log-depth tree version of the sampler (divide and conquer on midpoint states) cuts the sequential depth from O(L) to O(log L).

For BFCL, both Dream-v0-Instruct-7B (entropy remasking) and LLaDA-8B-Instruct (low-confidence remasking, block size 32) generate 256 tokens in 128 denoising steps. The metric is exact match against the ground-truth function call, at temperature 0 (greedy) and temperature 1 (sampling). The baseline is the same model with the same settings but no constraint.
official.claim: On BFCL-Live in JSON format with Dream-7B-Instruct, constrained decoding raises exact-match accuracy from 63.9% to 71.5% under greedy decoding and from 22.3% to 69.0% under temperature-1 sampling, compared with unconstrained decoding of the same model.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparing unconstrained (Base) and constrained (Ours) accuracy (%) under greedy decoding and stochastic sampling on Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B. CS is the baseline constraint satisfaction rate; our method guarantees 100% constraint satisfaction by construction. For function calling, we report both JSON and Python formats; for BFCL, L/NL denote Live and Non-Live settings.
official.metric: Exact-match accuracy (%) against the ground-truth function call, higher is better. No error bars or seed counts are reported for Table 1. CS is the unconstrained baseline's constraint-satisfaction rate.
official.comparison: Dream-7B-Instruct with the paper's automaton-constrained decoding (constrained-marginal remasking) vs. the same model decoded without constraints, same sequence length (256) and steps (128), at T=0 and T=1
official.falsification_criterion: With the same model, prompts, and decoding settings, either (a) under T=1 the constrained decoder's BFCL-Live (JSON) accuracy is not far above unconstrained sampling (e.g. the gain is under ~20 points instead of ~47), or (b) under greedy decoding it does not beat the unconstrained baseline by several points (the paper reports +7.6).

title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?

official.background: Automated failure attribution uses an LLM to read a failed agent trajectory and say which agent made the decisive error, at which step, and of what type. This feedback is useful for debugging and for self-improving agents, but the earlier Who&When benchmark has only 184 text-only traces. Who&When Pro builds 12,326 failed traces across text, image and video tasks (26 source benchmarks, 15 agent frameworks) and uses it to compare LLMs and attribution protocols.
official.method:
Traces are built by taking a successful agent trajectory, injecting one taxonomy-conditioned erroneous action at step t, replaying steps 1..t-1 exactly (warm start with cached tool outputs) and letting the agent continue; traces that end in task failure are kept, so step t (and its agent) is the decisive error by construction. Each trace has labels for agent, step and failure mode (perception, reasoning, planning, action, verification, coordination). Human review of 100 traces accepted 94% of step labels.

Three attribution protocols from Zhang et al. are compared. All-at-Once: the LLM gets the full trajectory in one prompt and predicts agent, step and failure mode together. Step-by-step: the LLM reads the trajectory step by step and stops once it believes the decisive error has occurred. Binary-search: the LLM recursively compares trajectory halves to localize the step. The task's ground-truth answer is not given. The comparison uses a stratified subset of 1,444 traces that keeps the modality and error-category distribution. Step is exact-match accuracy of the predicted decisive step; each cell is averaged over the three modalities (text-only models are evaluated on text only) and over three seeds.
official.claim: On the 1,444-trace ablation subset, All-at-Once attribution gives higher Step accuracy than Step-by-step for all 10 evaluated LLMs, by 7.6 percentage points on average (e.g., GPT-5.4 65.5 vs. 55.8, Qwen3.5-122B 63.5 vs. 56.1, Gemma 4 59.7 vs. 51.4).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Comparison of attribution method performance on the ablation set. Each cell reports the metric averaged over the three modalities. † Text-only models whose results are not directly comparable with the rest of multimodal models. Best per column in bold, second-best underlined.
official.metric: Step accuracy (%), exact match of predicted decisive step against the injected step, higher is better; averaged over three modalities and three seeds. No standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: All-at-Once vs. Step-by-step (and Binary-search) prompting protocols, same model and same trace subset, for each of 10 LLMs
official.falsification_criterion: Running both protocols with the same model on the released ablation subset (or a stratified sample of it) gives Step-by-step Step accuracy equal to or higher than All-at-Once, or an All-at-Once advantage much smaller than the reported ~7-10 pp for models such as GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemma 4, Llama-4 Maverick or Qwen3.5-122B.

title: Conditional Optimal Bridge for Riemannian Activation Steering

official.background: Activation steering changes an LLM's behavior at inference time by editing its residual-stream activations, using desired and undesired example activations, without any fine-tuning. Most methods add a fixed or activation-dependent direction. They lack a principled population-level objective, and they can hurt unrelated capabilities when applied to prompts the contrastive data do not cover. This paper casts steering as a Schrödinger Bridge between the undesired and desired activation distributions on the hypersphere. It derives from the bridge both a query-adaptive steering field and a support score for gating out-of-distribution prompts.
official.method:
At a fixed layer, last-token activations are normalized to the unit sphere. On the contrastive samples, a discrete static Schrödinger Bridge is fitted with Sinkhorn (5 sweeps): the reference weights are exp(-d_S(h-_j, h+_i)^2 / 2ε), where d_S is geodesic distance and ε is the squared median 5-NN geodesic distance. The fitted endpoint potentials weight two kernel sums over the desired and undesired samples. The steering field is the Riemannian gradient of their log-ratio, which amounts to attraction toward weighted desired samples and repulsion from weighted undesired ones. Each token's activation takes K = 10 geodesic Euler steps along the normalized field, with step Δ = (T/K)·s(x0)·g·θ0. Here s is a von Mises–Fisher alignment coefficient (κ = 20) based on the mean-difference axis μ, θ0 is the angle between x0 and μ, and g is the support gate. The original activation norm is restored after steering.

For the in-distribution results in Table 1, the gate is off (g = 1), and the horizon T is set per model (about 0.6 for LLaMA3.1-8B, Appendix G.3). On TruthfulQA, there are 5,918 question–answer pairs, used with two-fold cross-validation over the 817 questions: steering is fitted on one fold and evaluated on the other. Generation uses temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9 and repetition penalty 1.1. Truthfulness and informativeness come from the public AllenAI fine-tuned LLaMA2-7B truth and info judges. True×Info is the share of answers labelled both true and informative. The baselines (RepE, ITI, CAA, MiMiC, Linear-AcT, ODESteer, SphericalSteer) are implemented in the ODESteer codebase. Baselines with a comparable steering-strength parameter get the best result from a small sweep (T = 4-6 plus T = 1 for LLaMA3.1-8B); the others use the settings reported in their papers.
official.claim: On LLaMA3.1-8B (base), TruthfulQA True×Info is 68.1 ± 1.3% with ungated COBRAS steering, above every baseline steering method run under the same protocol. The best baseline is SphericalSteer at 63.5 ± 0.9%, followed by ODESteer at 62.5 ± 2.6% and CAA at 61.0 ± 2.0%. The unsteered model scores 43.0 ± 1.5%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance of steering methods on Helpfulness (UltraFeedback), Truthfulness (TruthfulQA), and Detoxification (RealToxicityPrompts) for four LLMs. Results are means ± standard deviations over three runs with different seeds. Primary metrics are highlighted in light purple.

official.comparison: COBRAS (ungated) vs. RepE, ITI, CAA, MiMiC, Linear-AcT, ODESteer and SphericalSteer on LLaMA3.1-8B, using the same two-fold TruthfulQA split, judges and generation settings
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same protocol, COBRAS's mean True×Info on LLaMA3.1-8B comes within about one seed std of the best baseline (e.g. SphericalSteer or ODESteer), or falls below it.

title: SLVMBench: Skill Learning from Video Memory

official.background: Video LLMs are increasingly used to power agents that must perceive a live video stream while drawing on things they saw much earlier. Existing benchmarks test these abilities separately: streaming benchmarks (StreamingBench, OVO-Bench) need only 10-20 minutes of memory, long-video benchmarks (VideoMME, LVBench) test passive comprehension without real-time questions, and skill-learning benchmarks (VideoMMMU, DemoICL) use a short tutorial shown immediately before the task. SLVMBench asks whether a model can learn a procedural skill from a tutorial video, keep it in memory through a long stream of unrelated video, and then apply it to answer a question about an ongoing target video paused at a decision point.
official.method:
Each item consists of a tutorial video, a sequence of unrelated distractor videos, a target video truncated at a manually calibrated cutoff t_c, and a five-option multiple-choice question (next-step prediction, step ordering, subgoal, parameter recall, tool configuration, safety check, mistake detection, conditional branching). Videos are YouTube how-to content published after January 2025; tutorial-target pairs are matched by hand, QA candidates are drafted by Gemini-2.5-Pro and then manually rewritten so they cannot be answered from common sense. There are 2,261 questions over 1,220 videos.

Three settings are evaluated with the same questions: (1) w/o Tutorial: only the target video up to t_c; (2) w/ Tutorial: the full tutorial immediately followed by the truncated target; (3) w/ Tutorial (Long): tutorial, then distractor videos, then the truncated target, with total length uniformly distributed from 10 minutes to 2 hours in 10-minute steps. Non-streaming open models (including Qwen3-VL-8B) receive 64 uniformly sampled frames from the whole concatenated stream, greedy decoding (temperature 0), a fixed zero-shot system prompt requiring a single-letter answer, and accuracy is computed by exact letter match.
official.claim: With 64 uniformly sampled frames, Qwen3-VL (8B) scores 33.44% without the tutorial and 49.21% with the tutorial placed immediately before the target (+15.77), but only 34.72% [95% Wilson CI 32.8, 36.7] when distractor videos are inserted between tutorial and target (+1.28 over baseline), i.e. the long gap removes almost all of the tutorial's benefit.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Main results on the SLVMBench reported in Accuracy (%). We compare model performance across three settings: (1) w/o Tutorial (baseline), (2) w/ Tutorial (immediate application), and (3) w/ Tutorial (Long) (episodic reasoning after a 2-hour distractor). ∆ and ∆L represent the performance gain attributed to tutorial knowledge over the baseline. Models are categorized into proprietary systems and open-source architectures, with the latter further divided into non-streaming and specialized streaming models. "Frames" denotes the total number of frames sampled per evaluation instance. Wilson 95% confidence intervals are provided for w/ tutorial (Long) results.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on 2,261 five-option multiple-choice questions (chance 20%), higher is better; greedy decoding, single deterministic run; 95% Wilson score intervals are reported only for the w/ Tutorial (Long) column, no error bars for the other two settings
official.comparison: Same model and same questions across three input conditions: w/o Tutorial vs. w/ Tutorial vs. w/ Tutorial (Long). The same pattern is reported for other models (e.g. GPT-5.2 42.68 / 57.94 / 44.89; VideoLLaMA3-7B 35.34 / 53.38 / 35.98; video-SALMONN 2+ 64 frames 37.64 / 63.64 / 47.24).
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Qwen3-VL-8B on SLVMBench with 64 frames, either the w/ Tutorial accuracy is not clearly above the w/o Tutorial accuracy (gain under ~5 points), or the w/ Tutorial (Long) accuracy retains most of the short-tutorial gain (e.g. more than ~8 points above the no-tutorial baseline, outside the reported CI).

title: Higher-Order Cell Tracking Transformer
claim_source: Table 5, page 8 (per-sequence curves in Figure 2, page 9, and Figure 3, page 18)

official.background: Cell tracking in live-imaging microscopy links segmented cells across frames into lineages, including through cell divisions. Recent learned trackers such as Trackastra embed each detection (node) with a Transformer and score links by node-embedding similarity. Tracking errors are costly to fix by hand, so it matters how quickly a tracker improves from a small amount of user feedback (human-in-the-loop correction). The paper argues that node-embedding models handle divisions poorly and that per-edge representations are both more accurate and easier to correct.
official.method:
HOCT is a two-stage Transformer. It runs 4 node self-attention layers with 3D RoPE over 19 hand-crafted per-cell features (position, size, intensity, inertia tensor, border distance). It then builds one token per candidate link (edge) and refines these tokens with 4 edge-attention layers, biased by the 3D distance between the line segments of each pair of edges. A per-edge logit goes through a parental softmax per target node and temporal gap, and an ILP solver turns the edge probabilities into lineages. The model is trained on 16 Cell Tracking Challenge (CTC) datasets.

Incremental correction: both HOCT and Trackastra + Attrackt start from CTC-pretrained weights that never saw bacteria data. They are corrected on the three bacteria validation sequences from the Trackastra benchmark for 20 rounds of 20 annotations each (400 total). HOCT labels 20 candidate edges per round, keeps its backbone frozen, and refits a logistic-regression head on the frozen edge embeddings (L-BFGS, class-balanced BCE, adaptive L2, and a consistency loss toward the current ILP solution). Edges are chosen by random, uncertainty (closest to 0.5), or solution-distance sampling. Trackastra labels 20 nodes per round, each giving 1-2 ground-truth parent links. Its variants are ILP pinning only (random, confidence), a learned linear map on the embeddings, LoRA fine-tuning (rank 32, 2000 steps per round), and LoRA with the Attrackt unsupervised loss. The metric is AOGM averaged over the three sequences, reported as the relative reduction from round 0.
official.claim: On the three bacteria validation sequences, after 20 rounds of 20 annotations (400 total), refitting a logistic head on frozen HOCT edge embeddings with uncertainty sampling reduces mean AOGM by 58.6% (1418 → 587). The best Trackastra + Attrackt strategy (LoRA + unsup) reduces it by only 6.75% (4951 → 4617). Every HOCT strategy, including random sampling (−43.8%), beats every Trackastra strategy.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Incremental correction on the bacteria validation sequences. Both systems annotate 20 elements per round for 20 rounds (400 total). AOGM is averaged over three sequences (lower is better). Δ denotes relative improvement from round 0. HOCT uses a frozen backbone with a refitted linear head; Trackastra strategies use LoRA fine-tuning, a learned linear map of the embeddings, and/or ILP constraint pinning. LoRA + unsup requires pretrained per-detection autoencoder embeddings and MLP_E/MLP_D weights (Appendix D); we pretrain both directly on the validation sequences before round 0.

title: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning
claim_source: Table 10, page 33 (values also in Figure 1b, page 2, and the CIFAR-10H row of Table 2, page 9)

official.background: Epistemic uncertainty (model ignorance, as opposed to irreducible label noise) is usually evaluated through surrogate tasks: out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, active learning and selective prediction. Many standard epistemic scores, such as mutual information or predictive variance, are in fact estimates of the regret, the excess loss of the model over the Bayes-optimal predictor at an input. The true regret cannot be computed on single-label datasets, so it is rarely evaluated directly. Datasets with many human labels per input, such as CIFAR-10H (about 50 labels per CIFAR-10 test image), give an empirical reference for the true label distribution and make the regret measurable. The paper asks whether the surrogate tasks and the regret task agree on which uncertainty method is best.
official.method:
Fourteen uncertainty quantification methods from the probly library (MC-Dropout p=0.1/0.5, DropConnect p=0.5, last-layer Laplace, SWAG, MFVI-BNN, Deep Ensemble with 5 members, BatchEnsemble, SubEnsemble, SNGP, DDU, Evidential, PostNet, NatPN) use ResNet-18 trained from scratch on 45,000 CIFAR-10 training images. The probly benchmark checkpoints are used for three seeds. Each method's epistemic estimate (log-loss decomposition, e.g. mutual information; K/alpha0 for Dirichlet methods) is used as the score for every task on the same network.

Regret task: for each CIFAR-10 test image, the true log-loss regret is the model's cross-entropy against the CIFAR-10H annotator distribution minus that distribution's entropy (the Bayes risk). Accepting the fraction kappa of inputs with the lowest score gives a regret-coverage curve. Its area is normalized to n-AuReC = (AuReC - oracle)/(random - oracle), lower is better. OOD detection: AUROC of the same score with CIFAR-10 test images as in-distribution data, CIFAR-100 as near-OOD and the OpenOOD v1.5 far-OOD sets as far-OOD. Methods are ranked by each metric (mean over seeds). Agreement is the Spearman correlation between two tasks' rankings over the 14 methods, and the stability reference is the Spearman correlation between rankings from two seeds of the same task.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10H with 14 probly methods on ResNet-18 (log loss), the method ranking by the regret task (n-AuReC) correlates with the ranking by OOD-detection AUROC at Spearman 0.18 (near-OOD, CIFAR-100) and 0.04 (far-OOD), while each task's ranking is stable across seeds (0.93 regret, 0.91 near-OOD, 0.91 far-OOD). The regret ranking agrees closely with selective prediction (0.96).
official.claim_caption: Table 10: Rank agreement between the tasks on CIFAR-10H. Spearman correlation between the method rankings of two tasks over the fourteen methods of Table 9 (+1: identical rankings); the values of Figure 1(b). Diagonal (italic): the agreement of two seeds of the same task, mean over the three pairs of seeds. Last two rows: the raw log-loss regret area and the test accuracy, as references. Tables 29 to 45 give the other datasets.
official.metric: Spearman rank correlation between method rankings over 14 methods (+1 identical, 0 unrelated). Rankings use means over 3 seeds; the diagonal is the mean over seed pairs of the two-seed ranking correlation. No error bars are reported on the correlations. Per-method seed std of the underlying metrics is in Table 18 (median at most 0.021).
official.comparison: Cross-task rank agreement (Regret,log vs. OOD near/far) vs. within-task seed-to-seed rank agreement (diagonal), on the same trained networks
official.falsification_criterion: Recomputing the 14-method rankings on CIFAR-10H gives a Regret(log)-vs-OOD Spearman correlation near the seed-to-seed agreement (e.g. above about 0.7 for near or far OOD), or the regret ranking itself is unstable across seeds (two-seed correlation well below 0.9).

title: MM-IssueLoc: A Controlled Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Evidence in Multimodal Repository-Level Issue Localization

official.background: Repository-level issue localization means finding which files and functions must be edited to fix a reported GitHub issue, and it comes before patch generation in automated software engineering. Real issues often attach screenshots, error dialogs, rendered UI or logs, yet localization benchmarks are mostly text-only, and the multimodal SWE-bench variant only scores end-to-end repair, so nobody can tell whether an image helped find the right code. MM-IssueLoc is a benchmark that isolates localization and treats the presence of images as a controlled variable.
official.method:
The benchmark has 652 real issue/PR instances from 608 GitHub repositories in 23 languages, with 1,050 issue images. The gold files are the files the merged fixing PR edited (function-level gold exists for 343 instances). The metric is strict Acc@K: an instance counts as solved only if every gold file appears in the system's top-K ranked list. Each instance can be run text-only (images removed) or with images, and nothing else changes.

MM-IssueLoc-VL-Embedding is a dense retriever initialized from Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B or 8B. The query is the issue text plus at most two images, and the candidates are file or function strings. It is fine-tuned with InfoNCE (tau = 0.05) and in-repository hard negatives on a separate training set (13,196 file-level and 13,769 function-level rows, disjoint from the benchmark by instance_id). Training is a file-level stage followed by a function-level stage, with the vision encoder frozen. For the ablation, the same trained (full two-stage) retriever ranks the repository's candidate files with and without the issue images in the query, and file Acc@5 is compared.
official.claim: On the 652 MM-IssueLoc instances, removing issue images from the query lowers file Acc@5 of the authors' trained multimodal retriever from 32.06 to 27.15 (2B) and from 32.82 to 28.38 (8B), while the strongest agent (OpenHands GPT-5.2) changes by only 0.31 points (38.96 vs 38.65).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: With-image versus no-image ablation on MM-IssueLoc. ∆ is no-image minus with-image file Acc@5. Negative values mean that removing images hurt the cell.
official.metric: Strict file-level Acc@5 in % (all gold files must be in the top 5; higher is better). Single run with no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Same model with issue images vs. text-only query: MM-IssueLoc-VL-Embedding-2B and -8B (retrievers), AgentLess GPT-5.2, OpenHands GPT-5.2, and OpenHands Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (agents)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the released MM-IssueLoc-VL-Embedding-8B (or 2B) on the 652 instances gives a with-image minus no-image File@5 gap that is clearly smaller than about 4 points (for example under 2 points) or has the opposite sign.

title: Audio-Visual Flamingo: Open Audio-Visual Intelligence for Long and Complex Videos
claim_source: Table 6, page 28 (same OmniVinci and AVF-Instruct numbers also appear in Table 1, page 9)

official.background: Most video LLMs process only visual frames and short clips, while real-world video such as movies, lectures and podcasts is long and carries much of its information in speech, sound and music. Open audio-visual (omni) LLMs exist, but they are mostly trained on separate unimodal audio and video corpora and on short clips. The strongest systems are closed or released as weights only, without their data or training recipes. This paper builds an open audio-visual LLM aimed at long, complex videos and releases its data and training recipe.
official.method:
AV-Flamingo (AVF) keeps the OmniVinci architecture: a SigLIP vision encoder with Dynamic S2 compression, the AF-Whisper audio encoder (30-second sliding windows), 2-layer MLP adaptors, time-interleaved audio and visual tokens with Constrained Rotary Time Embeddings, and a Qwen2.5-7B LLM. It is initialized from the OmniVinci checkpoint and fully fine-tuned. Pre-training (AVF-Stage1) uses unimodal audio/image/video data plus AV-Skills-Short (about 3.8M synthetically annotated captions and QA pairs on videos up to 60 s, max input 5 min, 16K context). Mid-training adds AV-Skills-Long (about 3.2M instances on 1 to 15 minute videos, max input 15 min, 32K context) together with downsampled AV-Skills-Short, audio, music and speech data and the authors' Audio-/Video-Think-Time data (Table 5), which produces AVF-Instruct. A later SFT+GRPO stage on timestamped chain-of-thought data (AV-Think) produces AVF-Think and is not part of this claim.

Table 6 evaluates OmniVinci, AVF-Stage1 and AVF-Instruct on DailyOmni and WorldSense (joint audio-visual QA) and Video-MME (video QA, without subtitles), all reported as accuracy.
official.claim: Fully fine-tuning OmniVinci on the AVF data mixtures (unimodal data plus AV-Skills-Short in short-context pre-training, then AV-Skills-Long plus replay in long-context mid-training) raises DailyOmni accuracy from 66.5 to 72.4 (+5.9 points). The same comparison gives WorldSense 48.2 to 50.3 and Video-MME 67.3 to 70.7.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Ablation study on the effect of AV-Skills-Short and AV-Skills-Long. AVF-Stage1 isolates the contribution of AV-Skills-Short during pre-training, while AVF-Instruct adds AV-Skills-Long during mid-training. Higher is better.
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy (%), higher is better; single numbers with no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: AVF-Instruct vs. OmniVinci (its initialization checkpoint, same architecture and size); AVF-Stage1 is an intermediate checkpoint
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating the released AVF-Instruct and OmniVinci checkpoints with the same protocol on DailyOmni gives a gap well under ~5.9 points (e.g. under 2 points), or OmniVinci scores higher.

title: OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models

official.background: Consumer wearables (iPhone, Apple Watch) record minute-level activity, heart rate, sleep and workout data, but the large datasets used to train wearable foundation models (Apple's WBM, Google's LSM-2) are private and the models are not open. This paper releases OpenMHC, data from 11,894 My Heart Counts study participants (67M wear-hours, 19 minute-level channels), with open reimplementations of WBM and LSM-2 and a benchmark with three tracks: health-outcome prediction, imputation and forecasting. Missing data is the norm in this setting (devices get taken off for charging, sleep or showering), so how well models fill gaps directly affects how useful the data is downstream.
official.method:
Single-day imputation task: each sample is one participant-day as a 19 x 1440 minute-level matrix. Six pre-defined masking approaches hide observed values: three structural ones (random 30-minute channel patches at ratio 0.5; 30-60 minute time blocks across all channels at ratio 0.25; whole channels or a whole device group) and three semantic ones (every channel except the two sleep indicators during detected sleep; heart rate and active energy during workouts; heart rate and active energy during runs of at least 5 minutes above 160 BPM). Test users are capped at 91 days. Error is MAE on masked positions for the 7 continuous channels and 1 - ROC AUC for the 12 binary channels.

Methods compared under the same participant-level split (60/10/30) and masks: statistical baselines (Mean, Mode, Linear interpolation, LOCF, temporal mean/mode), PyPOTS neural imputers (BRITS, DLinear, FEDformer, TimesNet) tuned by Bayesian optimization, and the authors' reimplementation of LSM-2, a ViT-style masked autoencoder on daily minute-level data trained with adaptive and inherited masking. The aggregate skill score is S = 1 - geometric mean of clipped error ratios against LOCF, aggregated with the four channel categories as equal-weight buckets; 95% CIs come from 1000 participant bootstrap resamples.
official.claim: On OpenMHC single-day minute-level imputation, the reimplemented LSM-2 reaches an aggregate skill score of +61.4% (95% CI +60.2 to +61.9) over LOCF, compared with +21.5% (+20.3 to +22.2) for linear interpolation, the best other single-day method, and +6.8% for BRITS, the best other neural imputer.
official.claim_caption: Table 3 | Imputation Results. We report Average Rank R, Aggregate Skill Score S (in %; 0 = LOCF reference), and Channel-Specific Skill Scores for the following channels: Activity, Physiology, Sleep, Workout. Finally, we also report performance on all Semantic masking approaches (see Appendix F). Single-day imputation method results are in the upper section of the table; long-context imputation method results (>= 7 x 1440 time steps) are below. Values are point estimates on the held-out test split; sub/superscripts give the 95% bootstrap percentile confidence interval (1000 resamples).
official.metric: Aggregate skill score S in % relative to the LOCF reference (higher is better; geometric-mean error reduction across masking approach x channel tasks, MAE for continuous and 1 - ROC AUC for binary channels). Sub/superscripts are 95% bootstrap percentile CIs over 1000 resamples on the held-out test split; single training run, no seed variance reported.
official.comparison: LSM-2 vs. Linear interpolation, LOCF, Mean, Mode, Temporal mean/mode, BRITS, DLinear, FEDformer, TimesNet, all on the same test users and pre-defined masks
official.falsification_criterion: With the same split and masks, LSM-2's aggregate skill score over LOCF falls within the CI of linear interpolation (around +21.5%), or a retrained LSM-2 lands far below +61.4% (e.g. below +40%) while the baselines reproduce.

title: Think, Plan, Paint: Layout-Aware Reasoning for Controllable Image Generation in Unified Models

official.background: Unified multimodal LLMs that both understand and generate images still struggle to follow prompts with complex spatial constraints (counts, relative positions, attribute binding). One fix is to have the model first emit a layout (bounding boxes) and then render the image conditioned on it, as PlanGen does, but existing unified models predict the layout directly from the prompt with no explicit reasoning step, which the authors argue produces incomplete or inconsistent layouts for complicated instructions.
official.method:
ATLAS fine-tunes a unified autoregressive/diffusion (Transfusion-style) model, BAGEL-7B (ATLAS-7B) or Hunyuan Image 3.0 (ATLAS-80B), to generate in three stages in one sequence: Think (a text chain of thought about objects, counts and spatial relations), Plan (a layout of label-box pairs, where each box is written with dedicated coordinate tokens <pos_x_k>/<pos_y_k>, k in 0..999), and Paint (diffusion of image latents conditioned on prompt, reasoning and layout). Training data are (prompt, reasoning, layout, image) quadruples: Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B annotates boxes for only the prompt-relevant objects and then writes a reasoning chain that leads to that layout, with an LLM filter rejecting inconsistent chains; these are mixed with layout-only, image-only, layout-aware understanding and editing data (5M samples total; 7B: batch 256, lr 2.5e-5). A Flow-GRPO stage then aligns the Paint stage with the layout; it does not affect the layout-planning claim.

Layout-planning evaluation (Table 2): given only the text prompt, the model generates a layout, which is scored without rendering an image, by Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B (spatial-relation score, following T2I-CompBench's spatial protocol) and by a rule-based clause checker (whether each object is present and each stated spatial relation holds). Prompts are the T2I-CompBench spatial subset and the authors' 500-prompt ATLAS-Reasoning benchmark. 'w/o Think' is ATLAS trained to generate the layout directly from the prompt without the reasoning chain.
official.claim: At 7B scale, adding the Think (layout-aware chain-of-thought) phase before layout planning raises layout quality on the T2I-CompBench spatial subset from 67.31 to 82.30 (Qwen3-VL judge) and from 54.63 to 72.96 (rule-based clause accuracy), and on ATLAS-Reasoning from 34.56 to 54.72 and 32.41 to 48.67; both variants far exceed PlanGen (37.31 / 29.84 on T2I-CompBench spatial).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Layout Planning Evaluation. Comparison of generated layout quality against baselines. We report both spatial relation scores judged by Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B and rule-based clause checking accuracy on T2I-CompBench (Spatial) and ATLAS-Reasoning benchmarks.
official.metric: Layout spatial-relation score judged by Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B and rule-based clause-checking accuracy, both higher is better; single numbers, no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals reported for this table
official.comparison: ATLAS-7B (Think + Plan) vs. ATLAS-7B w/o Think (layout predicted directly from prompt) vs. PlanGen; the same comparison at 80B is also reported
official.falsification_criterion: A BAGEL-7B model fine-tuned to emit reasoning before the layout does not beat an otherwise identically trained direct-layout model by a clear margin (e.g., under ~5 points rather than ~15-18) on T2I-CompBench spatial layout scores under either evaluator, or the gap vanishes across training seeds.

title: Adaptive Adversaries: A Multi-Turn, Multi-LLM Benchmark for LLM Agent Security
claim_source: Table 8, page 17 (summarised in Section 5.1 and Figure 3, page 5)

official.background: LLM agents read external content (documents, emails, tickets) that an attacker can control, so they are exposed to prompt injection and multi-turn manipulation. Static attack datasets measure robustness against a fixed set of inputs, but an adaptive attacker that learns from the defender's earlier replies may find failures that fixed pools miss. This paper builds Security Arena, a 21-scenario benchmark where an attacker LLM adapts across rounds against a defender LLM, with executable per-scenario success checks, and argues that aggregate attack success rates hide model-specific weaknesses that differ across scenarios.
official.method:
Each scenario defines a defender role and task, an attacker-controlled input surface, and an executable success check on the defender's structured output. In a battle the attacker LLM writes the attacker-controlled input, which is inserted into the scenario template; the defender answers in a fresh session each round (no prior-round history), while the attacker keeps all its prior inputs, the defender responses, and scorer feedback. A battle lasts up to 15 rounds and stops at the first scored success; ASR@15 is the fraction of battles with at least one success. In memleak the defender is a coding assistant whose supplied context contains a previous user's secret, and success is the session canary or the exact password appearing outside the refusal window. In paperaccept the defender is a meta-reviewer and the attacker controls an author rebuttal containing purported authority; success is SUBMISSION_ID_4991 receiving an acceptance verdict.

The July precision study fixes Claude Opus 4.6 as the attacker and runs 60 battles per defender (Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro) on memleak, paperaccept and meetingnotes, all under the same scaffold. Each cell combines 15 baseline-arm battles from the provenance study with 45 new battles. A separate three-attacker replication (20 battles per attacker-defender cell, Table 6) shows the same pattern.
official.claim: With a Claude Opus 4.6 attacker and 60 battles per defender, Opus 4.6 as defender leaks the memleak secret in 38/60 battles (63.3%, Wilson 50.7–74.4%) vs. 14/60 for GPT-5.4 and 12/60 for Gemini 2.5 Pro, while on paperaccept the ranking reverses: Gemini is compromised in 47/60 (78.3%, 66.4–86.9%) vs. 0/60 for Opus and 1/60 for GPT-5.4.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: July fixed-Opus-attacker precision study, including all nine cells.
official.metric: ASR@15: fraction of battles with at least one scored success within 15 rounds (higher = less secure defender). Intervals are Wilson 95% binomial intervals over battles; no seeds.
official.comparison: Defender models Claude Opus 4.6 vs. GPT-5.4 vs. Gemini 2.5 Pro on the memleak and paperaccept scenarios, same Opus 4.6 attacker, scaffold and 15-round cap
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the two scenarios with an Opus attacker and ~60 battles per defender, either Opus's memleak ASR is not clearly above both other defenders (e.g. its Wilson interval overlaps theirs), or Gemini's paperaccept ASR is not clearly above both Opus and GPT-5.4; i.e. the opposite-direction ranking across the two scenarios does not hold.

title: CryptanalysisBench: Can LLMs do cryptanalysis?

official.background: LLMs are starting to contribute to mathematics and software security, and cryptanalysis (finding practical attacks on cryptographic schemes) lies between the two. It is also unusually easy to grade: a practical attack either wins a formally specified security game (key recovery, IND-CPA/CCA, forgery, collision) or it does not. Earlier LLM evaluations used toy ciphers or CTF challenges with planted bugs. This paper asks whether LLM agents can break real primitives submitted to NIST standardization competitions, whose weaknesses were not deliberately inserted.
official.method:
CryptanalysisBench has 191 tasks, each a reference C implementation of one scheme (block ciphers, hash functions, AEADs, KEMs, PKEs, signatures) taken mostly from the AES, SHA-3, Lightweight Cryptography and PQC competitions. Tier 1 is 49 schemes with known practical breaks (FEAL-4, AIMer and 47 NIST candidates eliminated early, plus SIKE). Tier 2 is 142 schemes with no known practical break, run at full strength and as easy/medium/hard scaled-down variants. The agent runs in a Docker container (8 CPUs, 20 GB RAM, 10 GB storage) with the source code and a CLI client. A separate challenger container holds all secrets and answers only the oracle queries the chosen security game allows, over HTTP. The agent picks a game and must submit a self-contained /app/attack.sh. Verification re-runs it against fresh sessions; decision games (IND-CPA/CCA) need at least 17 wins out of 20.

Agents use the Harbor framework (v0.13.1) with the terminus-2 scaffold. The agent gets 2 hours of wall-clock time to explore and the attack script gets another 2 hours at verification. Internet access is allowed only for installing packages; searching for the target or its known attacks is forbidden, and logs are audited for this. Every task is run twice per model, and a task counts as broken if either run produces a winning attack. Five models are evaluated with this same setup: GLM-5.2 (open weights), Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.

official.claim_caption: Table 2: Success rates on CryptanalysisBench. Tier 1 reports the percentage of tasks broken on the original specification. Tier 2 reports per-variant success rates across the easy, medium, and hard scaled-down configurations. A task is counted as broken if the agent produces a working attack in at least one of two independent runs.
