title: IGGT4D: Streaming 4D Instance-Grounded Geometry Transformer

official.background: Feed-forward spatial foundation models such as VGGT and Depth Anything 3 (DA3) predict camera poses and 3D geometry directly from a set of images. However, they attend over the whole image set at once, so a growing video stream has to be reprocessed from scratch. Streaming variants (CUT3R, StreamVGGT, Stream3R, LingBot-Map) keep an online state instead. They are geometry-only and usually much less accurate than the offline models. Embodied agents need online geometry together with object identities that stay consistent over time.
official.method:
IGGT4D starts from the DA3-Giant geometry Transformer (40 blocks of interleaved intra-view and cross-view attention) and adds causal masks to the cross-view and camera attention, so each frame only attends to itself and earlier frames. At inference, camera and cross-view KV caches are reused frame by frame. A 'Tri-DPT' head decodes depth, a ray map, and an 8-dim instance feature map, with the instance branch attending to the depth and ray features. Training uses first-frame geometric normalization (poses expressed in the first camera's frame, scale taken from the first frame's point cloud), L1 depth/ray/point/camera losses, and a multi-view contrastive instance loss. The training data is InsScene4D-147K, a new dataset with pseudo-labelled geometry and instance masks. Training runs on 16 H20 GPUs: 6 epochs on geometry only, then 9 epochs joint. Ground-truth camera poses are injected with 20% probability during training.

For the claim, pose and reconstruction are evaluated with the DA3 benchmark protocol on HiRoom, ETH3D, 7Scenes and ScanNet++. Frames are reordered so that each frame overlaps an earlier one. Predicted poses are aligned to ground truth with RANSAC-based evo alignment, then depths are TSDF-fused and compared to ground-truth point clouds. Streaming baselines (CUT3R, StreamVGGT, Wint3R, Stream3R, LingBot-Map) run frame by frame, except Wint3R (sliding window 4, stride 2) and LingBot-Map (full attention over the first 8 frames, then streaming).
official.claim: Under DA3's benchmark protocol, averaged over HiRoom, ETH3D, 7Scenes and ScanNet++, streaming IGGT4D reaches pose AUC@3 0.4464 and reconstruction F1 (predicted poses) 0.6678. The best streaming baseline, LingBot-Map, reaches 0.3060 and 0.5228.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Geometry benchmark on HiRoom, ETH3D, 7Scenes, and ScanNet++. (a) Camera pose estimation (AUC@3, AUC@30). (b) 3D reconstruction (F1-score) without (w/o p.) and with (w/ p.) ground-truth camera poses. Methods are grouped into full-attention (offline) and streaming (online). Best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underline, respectively.
official.metric: Pose: AUC@3 / AUC@30 over min(RRA, RTA), higher is better. Reconstruction: F1-score of the TSDF-fused point cloud vs. ground truth, with predicted poses (w/o p.) and GT poses (w/ p.), higher is better. Single numbers with no error bars or seeds.
official.comparison: IGGT4D (streaming) vs. streaming baselines CUT3R, StreamVGGT, Wint3R, Stream3R, LingBot-Map on the same sequences; offline full-attention models (VGGT, MapAnything, Pi3X, DA3) shown for reference
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the DA3 benchmark with the released IGGT4D checkpoint and LingBot-Map gives an average AUC@3 gap below about 0.05, or an average F1 (w/o p.) gap below about 0.05. Either result would leave IGGT4D not clearly ahead of the best streaming baseline.

title: Masked Visual Actions for Unified World Modeling
claim_source: Table C1, page 17 (appendix; same means appear in Table 2, page 7, without error bars)

official.background: Pretrained video generation models encode strong priors about how objects move and respond to contact, so they are attractive as robot world models that predict what happens when a robot executes an action. The open question is how to feed actions to such a model. Low-dimensional joint or end-effector commands are embodiment-specific and not aligned with the pixel space the model was trained on; sparser visual signals such as a drawn end-effector pose or robot skeleton are more visual but still require the model to infer geometry and contact. If the action signal does not transfer across robots, the world model has to be retrained for every new embodiment.
official.method:
Masked Visual Actions express an action as a partially revealed video: the pixels occupied by the robot (or any chosen entity) over time are shown, the rest of the frame is set to uniform gray, and the model generates the full video from this masked video plus a reference first frame. Training masks come from SAM 3 segmentations of the robot in DROID videos (prompt 'A robotic arm') and from URDF renderings of the robot from its recorded joint states with refined camera calibration (DROID), plus robot-only renderings in RoboCasa simulation; rendered robots are translucent with the gripper fingers colored bright red. About 1,000 DROID demonstrations (two external cameras) and 4,000 RoboCasa examples are used; DROID scenes from the CLVR and RAD labs are held out for testing. The base model is Wan-Fun-Control 2.2 14B; the masked video is encoded with the model's own autoencoder and concatenated as conditioning, and the model is LoRA-finetuned (rank 256, batch size 4, ~10,000 steps).

For the conditioning ablation, the same base model is trained on the same DROID data but conditioned on (a) a visualization of the end-effector pose (IRASim-style) or (b) a rendered robot skeleton (VAP-style). All variants are evaluated by reconstruction of held-out ground-truth videos given the first frame and the action signal: on held-out DROID scenes (n=50), on real-world clips of a Franka with an unseen custom 3D-printed gripper (n=13), and on BEHAVIOR-1K clips of the bimanual R1-Pro robot, an embodiment unseen by all methods (n=50). For BEHAVIOR the baselines' visualizations are drawn for both arms.
official.claim: On 50 BEHAVIOR-1K clips of an unseen bimanual robot, the model conditioned on masked visual actions reconstructs the ground-truth video with PSNR 22.90 ± 0.52 vs. 19.58 ± 0.34 for the same model trained on the same data with skeleton conditioning (and 19.23 ± 0.34 with end-effector conditioning), and LPIPS 0.123 ± 0.007 vs. 0.162 ± 0.007.
official.claim_caption: Table C1: Reconstruction metrics across datasets (mean ± SEM; best per column in bold).
official.metric: PSNR (higher is better), SSIM (higher is better), LPIPS (lower is better) between generated and ground-truth video; ± is the standard error of the mean over clips (n=50 for BEHAVIOR-1K and DROID, n=13 for real world). Single training run per variant; no seed variation reported.
official.comparison: Masked visual actions vs. end-effector-pose visualization and robot-skeleton visualization, all with the same base model (Wan-Fun-Control 2.2 14B, LoRA) and the same DROID training data. Ctrl-World, Wan-Move and Wan2.2-I2V are also reported as external baselines.
official.falsification_criterion: On BEHAVIOR-1K, a skeleton- or end-effector-conditioned model trained on the same data and base model comes within about 1 dB PSNR of the masked-visual-action model (a gap comparable to the reported per-method SEMs of 0.34-0.52 dB), or matches/beats it on LPIPS.

title: ITPEval: Benchmarking Formal Translation Across Interactive Theorem Provers

official.background: Interactive theorem provers (Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle, HOL Light) each have their own logic, tactic language and library, so a theorem proved in one cannot be reused in another. Automatically translating formal statements and proofs between provers would let verified results move across ecosystems and would add training data for learning-based provers. Before this paper, the only benchmark for this task was Babel-formal, which covers 14 Lean-Rocq files. ITPEval builds a four-way aligned benchmark and asks which part of the problem is hard: differences in logical foundations, or differences in libraries and proof style.
official.method:
The benchmark has two tiers. Tier A (controlled) is Babel-formal extended to all four provers: 16 self-contained, axiomatized items (64 files, 660 lemmas) that define their own objects and assumptions and use no prover libraries. Tier B (ecosystem) has 58 of Wiedijk's 'Formalizing 100 Theorems' that are formalized in all four provers (232 files, 4,924 lemmas), taken from Mathlib, Rocq libraries, Isabelle/AFP and HOL Light core. These files use library lemmas, local helper lemmas and prover-specific automation. Tier B also includes 316 miniF2F statements, which are used for statement translation only. Every item exists in all four provers, so there are 12 directed source-target pairs per item: 16x12 = 192 Tier A instances and 58x12 = 696 Tier B instances for proof translation.

In proof translation, the model receives a complete proof file in the source prover and must output only raw code for a complete file in the target prover. An output counts as passing only if the target prover accepts the entire file with exit code 0, with no sorry or placeholders and every lemma proved. Checking runs through the authors' itpeval verifier, which uses state-isolated warm backends. Five models are evaluated zero-shot with greedy decoding (T=0), one sample per instance (pass@1): GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Qwen3-235B-A22B.
official.claim: On zero-shot proof translation (pass@1, verified by the target prover), GPT-5.5 translates 57/192 (29.7%) of the controlled Tier A (Babel-formal) directed pairs but only 36/696 (5.2%) of the ecosystem Tier B (Formalizing 100 Theorems) pairs. All five models score lower on Tier B (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro: 18.2% vs 1.4%).
official.claim_caption: Table 4. Proof translation pass@1 rates on 888 directed pairs. Tier A is consistently much easier than Tier B.
official.metric: Proof-translation pass@1 (%): the fraction of directed source-target file pairs whose single greedy output compiles in the target prover with no placeholders. Higher is better. Per-tier numbers have no error bars. Appendix Table 9 gives 95% Wilson CIs only for the overall rates (GPT-5.5 overall 10.5% [8.6, 12.7]).
official.comparison: The same model and protocol on Tier A (Babel-formal, 192 directed pairs) vs Tier B (Formalizing 100 Theorems, 696 directed pairs), for each of five LLMs.
official.falsification_criterion: Running GPT-5.5 (or the strongest available model) under the same protocol gives Tier A and Tier B proof pass@1 rates within a few percentage points of each other, or Tier B at or above Tier A. A Tier A rate far below 29.7% for GPT-5.5 would also cast doubt on the reported numbers.

title: Total Variation Distance Estimation in Autoregressive Models

official.background: Two engines serving the same LLM weights can produce different output distributions because of batching, kernels, quantization or bugs. Comparing them needs a distance between distributions over length-n sequences. KL divergence is the usual choice because it decomposes per token, but it becomes infinite when supports differ (e.g. under top-k truncation). Total variation (TV) distance is bounded and robust to this, but has no chain rule. The paper studies how many prefix queries are needed to estimate TV between two autoregressive models under sample access, exact logit access, and noisy logit access, where the returned probabilities are unbiased but noisy (relative variance σ²), as on real inference engines.
official.method:
Using the mixture representation TV(π, µ) = E_{X∼(π+µ)/2}[|π(X) − µ(X)| / (π(X) + µ(X))], the estimator draws a trajectory X from the mixture and estimates π(X) and µ(X) by multiplying per-token probabilities, each averaged over r repeated noisy oracle queries. The single-level estimator uses one fixed repetition count r, which has a bias floor set by r. Algorithm 3 is a multilevel Monte Carlo version: it writes the level-L estimator as a telescoping sum over levels with increasing repetition counts r_0 < r_1 < ... < r_L, estimates each coupled increment Z_ℓ(X) − Z_{ℓ−1}(X) on the same trajectory X, and uses more cheap low-r samples and fewer expensive high-r samples.

Synthetic test (Appendix B.1–B.2): the binary autoregressive hard instance from Section 3.2 with n = 128, block-index length 12, p_active = 0.4, α = 0.49, so TV(π, µ) = 0.388 by enumeration. The noisy oracle adds zero-mean Gaussian noise with std σ·sqrt(p̂(1 − p̂)) to each realized next-token probability (unclipped; the r-averaged probability is clipped to [1e-12, 1] before the log). The single-level estimator with r = 256 is compared with 2-, 3- and 4-level schedules sharing the top level r = 256 ((32,256), (8,32,256), (1,8,32,256)) at matched oracle-call budgets, for σ ∈ {0.04, 0.5, 0.8}. The metric is the mean absolute error against the true TV.
official.claim: On the synthetic instance (true TV = 0.388) at noise level σ = 0.04, the 4-level schedule (1, 8, 32, 256) has mean absolute error of about 0.02 at ~5×10^5 oracle calls versus about 0.10 for the single-level r = 256 estimator at the same budget, and stays below the single-level error at every budget up to ~10^7 (the paper says it matches the single-level accuracy with roughly 7× less budget).
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Mean absolute error against oracle-call budget for 1-, 2-, 3-, and 4-level instantiations of Algorithm 3 on the synthetic hard instance, at three noise levels σ ∈ {0.04, 0.5, 0.8}. Column titles report the variance ratio ρ_ℓ at each level of the deepest schedule.
official.metric: Mean absolute error of the TV estimate against the enumerated true TV 0.388 (lower is better), as a function of oracle-call budget; error bars are shown but what they represent and the number of repetitions per point are not stated for this figure (Figure 11, same instance, uses 64 repetitions per point). Values below are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Multilevel Algorithm 3 (2-, 3-, 4-level schedules with top level r = 256) vs. the single-level estimator with r = 256, at matched oracle-call budget on the same synthetic instance and noise oracle
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the synthetic experiment at σ = 0.04, the 4-level schedule's mean absolute error at budgets around 5×10^5 to 2×10^6 oracle calls is not clearly lower (e.g. less than 2× lower) than the single-level r = 256 estimator's at the same budget.

title: Optimal Recalibration of an Online Predictor

official.background: A classifier trained to minimize loss often outputs poorly calibrated probabilities, and in an online stream with distribution shift its miscalibration can grow. Recalibration post-processes a given 'hint' forecast sequence online so that the new predictions are calibrated while losing little under a proper loss such as the Brier score. Calibeating asks for more: beat the hint's loss down to its refinement score (the loss of the hindsight per-value label average). Prior online methods achieved good calibration and calibeating rates only separately or with a worse epsilon dependence.
official.method:
The recalibration algorithm treats calibration and loss preservation as two simultaneous Blackwell approachability objectives (an 'imbalanced' extension of prior work), achieving (epsilon, epsilon^2)-recalibration in T ~ epsilon^-3 rounds. For simultaneous calibration and calibeating, the calibeating algorithm of Foster and Hart (FH23) is run first and its output is fed as the hint to an independent instance of the recalibration algorithm (C+R).

Experiment (Section 9.1): a 40-layer DenseNet-BC with a single sigmoid output is trained on CIFAR-10 cats vs. dogs (10k train, 1k validation; 89.6% test accuracy). The 2,000 test images are reshuffled and replayed for 100 passes (T = 200,000). From step 100,000 onward each label is flipped independently with probability 0.2, while the network's per-image predictions stay fixed. Four online forecasters are compared on the same stream: Hint (raw sigmoid output), Calibeating (FH23), Recalibration (Theorem 5), and C+R. Metrics are cumulative over the full stream: Brier score, K1 (ECE-style l1 calibration error), K2^2, and 0-1 accuracy at threshold 0.5; 20 random seeds (label flips and data order).
official.claim: On the CIFAR cats-vs-dogs stream with label flips (p = 0.2) after step 100,000 (T = 200,000, 20 seeds), calibeating followed by recalibration (C+R) achieves both a lower Brier score than calibeating alone (0.13314 ± 4.5e-4 vs. 0.13865 ± 5.4e-4) and a much lower K1 calibration error (0.01319 ± 4.5e-4 vs. 0.05771 ± 5.1e-4), with K1 close to recalibration alone (0.01188) and accuracy unchanged (82.41% vs. 82.43%).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: CIFAR-2 cats vs. dogs classification with partial concept drift (flip probability β = 0.2 after step 100,000 with T = 200,000 for 20 random seeds). Cumulative metrics over the full stream. Note that “Hint” and “Calibeating” are deterministic, and the randomness comes from random flipping and data order.
official.metric: Cumulative Brier score (lower is better), K1 calibration error (lower is better), K2^2 (lower is better), accuracy (higher is better); mean ± spread over 20 random seeds (the paper does not say whether ± is std or standard error)
official.comparison: C+R vs. Calibeating (FH23) alone, plus Recalibration alone and the raw Hint, on the same stream
official.falsification_criterion: With the same stream setup, C+R's Brier score is not below Calibeating's, or C+R's K1 is not clearly below Calibeating's (e.g. not under about half of it), beyond the seed spread.

title: Importance-Aware OBS Pruning for Diffusion Models

official.background: Text-to-image diffusion models have billions of parameters and run many denoising steps, so they are expensive to deploy. OBS-Diff adapts Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) second-order pruning to diffusion models in a one-shot, training-free way. Its layer-wise reconstruction objective treats every spatial location of the image equally, so at high sparsity it can keep the background intact while damaging the prompt's main subject. This paper asks whether weighting the pruning objective toward perceptually important image regions preserves generation quality better at the same sparsity.
official.method:
The method keeps the OBS-Diff pipeline (layer-wise OBS with Cholesky-based inverse-Hessian updates, timestep weights α_t following OBS-Diff's logarithmically decreasing schedule) and changes only the Hessian. For each calibration sample and timestep, a spatial importance map is computed as the classifier-free-guidance delta |ε(x_t,t,c) − ε(x_t,t,∅)|, averaged over latent channels and min-max normalized per sample and timestep, then scaled by λ (A_t = λ M_t). Layer input activations are multiplied token-wise by A_t, and the Hessian H = 2 Σ_t α_t E[X'X'^T] is accumulated from these importance-filtered activations. Saliency is w_q^2 / (2 [H^{-1}]_qq) as in standard OBS. For structured pruning, the same aggregation strategy as OBS-Diff is used.

Setup: PixArt-Σ; calibration on 1,000 GCC3M (Conceptual Captions) samples, batch size 2, 10 inference steps, CFG scale 4.5 during pruning; λ = 1.0; evaluation images generated with 25 steps, CFG 7.0, from 1,000 MS-COCO 2017 val prompts. Metrics are CLIP Score, ImageReward and MUSIQ.
official.claim: For structured pruning of PixArt-Σ, importance-aware (CFG-mask) OBS beats OBS-Diff on ImageReward at every reported sparsity: 0.79 vs. 0.74 at 20%, 0.54 vs. 0.38 at 30%, and 0.30 vs. -0.04 at 40%. It also beats OBS-Diff on MUSIQ at every sparsity (68.64 vs. 65.17 at 40%).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Quantitative comparison between OBS-Diff and Ours (CFG) on PixArt-Σ using 1000 samples from GCC3M for structured pruning.

title: AgentKVShift: Efficient KV Cache Reuse for Agentic Memory Systems

official.background: Memory-augmented LLM agents store past interactions as structured memory units (notes with LLM-written summaries, keywords and tags, or graph nodes) and retrieve a few of them for each query. Every retrieved unit must be encoded into key-value (KV) states during prefill, and this dominates latency. Prefix caching does not help because the set and order of retrieved memories change per query. Selective-recompute methods built for RAG, such as CacheBlend and ProphetKV, reuse cached KV states for most tokens and recompute only a small fraction r. The authors argue that these methods lose much of their accuracy on metadata-rich agentic memories.
official.method:
Each memory chunk's KV states are cached once and reused under a new context. AgentKVShift computes, for each retrieved chunk, the per-token L2 divergence between fresh and reused K, and separately V, at the first layer (as in CacheBlend). It then selects separate top-b probe sets for K and V (b = ceil(r*n)), with per-token weights w_j = min(divergence_j, 1); probe sets and weights are fixed at layer 1 and reused at all layers. At every layer the union of the K and V probe tokens is recomputed fresh, and the chunk-level offset mu_hat is estimated as the mean of (fresh - reused) over the probes, separately for K and V. Every non-probe token is corrected as K_reuse + w_j * mu_hat (and the same for V), while probe tokens keep their fresh states. The method needs no training. The motivation is that an SVD of the reuse residual shows it is dominated by a shared per-chunk offset.

The claim is evaluated on LoCoMo (10 long multi-session conversations with QA). Memories are built with A-Mem (note-based) and LiCoMemory (graph-based) using each system's default ingestion and top-k=10 retrieval. The models are Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. All KV-reuse methods use check layer 1 and recompute ratio r=0.1. Answers are scored by token-level F1, ROUGE-1 and BLEU-1 against the gold answers. Full recompute (no KV reuse) is reported as the upper bound.
official.claim: On LoCoMo with A-Mem memories and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at recompute ratio r=0.1, AgentKVShift reaches 0.319 F1 (full recompute 0.339), versus 0.178 for CacheBlend and 0.125 for ProphetKV; AgentKVShift is best among KV-reuse methods in all 6 model x memory-system settings of Table 1.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: F1, ROUGE and BLEU-1 scores on LoCoMo using recompute ratio, r=0.1. Best KV-reuse result is bold,
official.metric: Token-level F1 against gold answers (higher is better); ROUGE-1 and BLEU-1 also reported. Single numbers with no seeds, std or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: AgentKVShift vs. CacheBlend and ProphetKV at the same recompute ratio r=0.1, same model, memory system and retrieval; full recompute as the reference upper bound
official.falsification_criterion: With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on LoCoMo/A-Mem at r=0.1, AgentKVShift's F1 is not clearly above CacheBlend's (e.g. the gap is under ~0.05 F1 instead of ~0.14), or AgentKVShift falls far below full recompute (e.g. a relative drop over 20% instead of ~6%).

title: HierFlow: Hierarchical Coupled Dual-Space Search for Automatic Agentic Workflow Generation
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (cost comparison with Flow on MATH in Table 6, page 23)

official.background: Agentic workflows organise how an LLM decomposes a problem, calls tools and checks intermediate results. Automatic workflow generation searches over such workflows, but existing methods either search offline for one workflow per dataset (ADAS, AFlow), train a workflow designer (MaAS, DyFlow), or refine at test time in a single representation such as a task graph (Flow). The paper asks whether a training-free, per-query search that couples a task-decomposition graph with executable code for each subtask produces better workflows than these approaches.
official.method:
For each query, an LLM initiator proposes K = 3 candidate task decompositions (DAGs of subtasks); the best by an LLM-plus-structural score is executed layer by layer. For each subtask, a small MCTS-style search over executable code sub-workflows (depth 3, branching 3, budget 5 expansions) starts from a direct input-output attempt; candidates must pass a sandboxed executability check with mock inputs and are scored by an LLM evaluator. If a subtask fails or its scores vary too much, the upper level revises the DAG (refinement budget 20) and resumes from the earliest unfinished subtask.

A gate decides whether to run the code search for a subtask: search is triggered when (log remaining search space) x (predictive entropy of the evaluator's rationale) exceeds tau = 4. All LLM calls use gpt-4o-mini; results average 3 independent runs. Benchmarks use a 1:4 train/test split (HotpotQA: 1,000 sampled examples, 800 test; MATH: 486 test; MBPP: 341 test; GSM8K: 1,055 test; HumanEval: 131 test), and training-free methods are evaluated on the test split only.
official.claim: With gpt-4o-mini as the only LLM, HierFlow outperforms Flow (the training-free, query-level baseline) by 4-6 points on three benchmarks: MATH accuracy 53.70 ± 0.91 vs. 48.15 ± 1.13, HotpotQA F1 71.75 ± 0.58 vs. 67.63 ± 0.73, and MBPP pass@1 82.40 ± 0.77 vs. 77.71 ± 0.89.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Overall performance of manual and automatic workflow generation methods across different scenarios. The lower-right subscript reports the standard deviation. The best results are highlighted in bold, and the runner-up results are underlined.
official.metric: MATH accuracy, HotpotQA F1, MBPP pass@1 (higher is better), mean ± std over 3 independent runs
official.comparison: HierFlow vs. Flow, both training-free and query-level with gpt-4o-mini; also vs. Vanilla, CoT, SC@5 and the offline/trained methods ADAS, AutoFlow, AFlow, MaAS, DyFlow
official.falsification_criterion: On the same test splits with gpt-4o-mini, HierFlow's mean over 3 runs is not above Flow's by more than the run-to-run std on MATH, HotpotQA or MBPP, or HierFlow does not beat self-consistency with five CoT paths (SC@5: 49.18 MATH, 68.50 HotpotQA, 73.61 MBPP) by a clear margin.

title: FrED: External Data Influence Estimation via Domain Knowledge Graph Grounding
claim_source: Table 7, page 22 (Appendix F); FrED's numbers also appear in Table 1, page 7

official.background: Training data attribution asks which training examples are responsible for a given model output, which matters for copyright and accountability in generative models. The strongest attribution methods (TRAK, D-TRAK, DAS) need gradients from the model, which is infeasible for closed or very large models. Black-box alternatives score training images by embedding similarity to the output (e.g. CLIP cosine), but these score poorly on the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), a counterfactual benchmark that checks whether summed attribution scores predict how the model's loss changes when it is retrained on random halves of the data.
official.method:
FrED scores each training image X_j for a target image C without touching the model. A latent score S_lat,j combines a likelihood term, the ViT-g-14 (OpenCLIP, LAION-2B) similarity p(c|x_j) raised to the 10th power, with a distinctiveness prior p(x_j) that down-weights training images in dense regions of the embedding space. A domain score comes from an art-history knowledge graph (painting and artist metadata from WikiArt, Wikipedia and DBpedia, embedded with Node2Vec); generated images, which have no metadata, are projected into the graph space by a CLIP-style contrastive alignment between ViT-g-14 image embeddings and Node2Vec embeddings. The final weight is alpha_j = S_lat,j x (1 + W / (k + R_dom,j)), where R_dom,j is the sample's integer rank under the domain score (an asymmetric, RRF-style boost).

Evaluation follows the D-TRAK ArtBench protocol: a 256x256 Stable Diffusion model fine-tuned with LoRA (r=128) on ArtBench-2 or ArtBench-5, the same 1,000 generated targets plus validation images, and LDS computed as the Spearman correlation between summed attribution scores and the actual diffusion loss across 64 random 50% training subsets (3 seeds each), averaged over targets. The authors reuse D-TRAK's pre-generated images and model weights. Table 7 ablates the formulation, starting from plain ViT-g-14 cosine similarity p(c|x_j).
official.claim: On ArtBench-2 validation images, FrED reaches LDS 29.10 ± 0.65% versus 12.30 ± 1.00% for plain ViT-g-14 similarity with the same encoder (ArtBench-5 validation: 28.90 ± 0.35% vs 9.30 ± 0.75%).
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Ablation study of our proposed attribution framework. LDS scores are reported. Our results show that raising the similarity score to a power (p5 and p10) significantly improves accuracy by rewarding the most relevant images and driving unimportant scores toward zero. Furthermore, our Asymmetric Rank Boost outperforms standard fusion by using the Domain's ranking to guide the visual comparison, ensuring the final attribution is both visually and semantically correct.
official.metric: Linear Datamodeling Score in % (Spearman correlation, higher is better). ± is described in Appendix D.4 as a 95% bootstrap confidence interval (64 resamples) over the evaluation set.
official.comparison: Full FrED (Asymmetric Rank Boost) vs. the un-sharpened visual baseline p(c|x_j) (ViT-g-14 cosine similarity), with sharpened, prior-weighted, domain-only and linear-hybrid variants as intermediate ablations; all on the same targets and LDS ground truth.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the D-TRAK ArtBench-2 LDS protocol, FrED's validation LDS is not clearly above ViT-g-14 cosine similarity (e.g. below ~20% against a ~12% baseline), or the gap shrinks to within the reported intervals.

title: CORVUS: Context Optimization and Reduction Via Underlying Synchronization for LLM Coding Agents

official.background: LLM coding agents keep an append-only trajectory of reasoning, tool calls and tool outputs. When an agent reads a file, the full contents are stored as a fixed snapshot in the history. Files then change because of the agent's own edits, so the history fills up with duplicate and outdated copies. Agents re-read files (26% of Claude Sonnet 4's file reads on SWE-PolyBench_Verified were re-reads) and sometimes edit against stale text, and both effects inflate token cost and the number of reasoning cycles. Existing context-management methods (sliding windows, summarization, observation masking) shrink the trajectory only after the redundant content has already been added.
official.method:
The baseline is a 'Minimum Viable Agent' built on the Strands Agents framework with the tools common to 14 production and research coding agents: read_file, fs_write (write/edit, e.g. str_replace), list_directory and execute_bash. CORVUS changes only file reading. It replaces read_file with sync_file(f), which returns just the marker 'sync: f' and adds f to a synced file set. Before every reasoning cycle, a context-sync step reads the current contents of every file in the set from the repository and appends them as a 'synced context' block at the end of the prompt (prompt = system message + tool schemas + message history + synced context). So at most one current copy of each synced file is ever in the prompt. All other tools, prompts and settings are identical between the two agents.

Both agents run on all 382 SWE-PolyBench_Verified instances (Python, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript) and on 191 sampled SWE-Bench Pro instances with above-average patch size, with Claude Sonnet 3.7, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5 and Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B via AWS Bedrock, all at temperature 0. The metrics are input and output tokens summed over all reasoning cycles of a task, averaged over instances, plus the resulting dollar cost. Pass@1 is reported as a guardrail.
official.claim: On SWE-PolyBench_Verified with Claude Sonnet 4.5, CORVUS reduces average accumulated input tokens per task from 1,673,332 (append-only baseline) to 829,579 (-50.4%) and cost from $5.27 to $2.62 per instance, with comparable pass@1 (Table 5 'overall pass rate', benchmark scope not stated: 28.10% baseline vs. 29.49% CORVUS).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Token cost comparison between Baseline and CORVUS on two benchmarks.
official.metric: Average total input tokens summed across all reasoning cycles per task (lower is better), averaged over the 382 instances; single run at temperature 0, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: CORVUS (sync_file + per-cycle context sync) vs. the identical Minimum Viable Agent baseline that embeds read_file outputs in the trajectory, same model, tools, prompts and instances
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both agents on SWE-PolyBench_Verified (or a random subset of it) with Claude Sonnet 4.5 at temperature 0, CORVUS's average input tokens per task are not substantially lower than the baseline's (e.g. a reduction under ~20%), or the reduction comes with a clear drop in pass@1 (more than a few points).

title: ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow

official.background: Latent world models predict the future in a compact representation space rather than in pixels, which makes them cheaper than video diffusion models and useful for robot planning. Existing latent world models, including JEPA-style models, work in discrete time steps and can suffer representation collapse, because the encoder and the latent predictor are trained jointly through an indirect consistency loss. The paper asks whether modelling the latent dynamics as a continuous-time ODE in physical time gives better long-horizon video prediction and planning representations.
official.method:
ODEWorld encodes 256x256 frames with a frozen DINOv2 encoder (16x16x768 features), with a separately trained RAE-style image decoder (L1 + LPIPS + GAN losses) mapping DINO features back to pixels. A cross-attention dynamics encoder f_dyn(s_t; s_0) maps the current DINO features, conditioned on the initial frame s_0, to a single 768-d latent token z_t; a cross-attention decoder g_dyn(z_t; s_0) reconstructs s_t. A 3-layer MLP velocity field v_theta(z_t, tau; z_0, c) takes the concatenation of z_t, z_0 and the goal condition c (goal image) as input, with the rescaled physical time tau injected via FiLM layers, and is trained so that it matches the target latent velocity obtained by a Jacobian-vector product of f_dyn with the feature-space velocity ds/dt (estimated by a 5-tap Savitzky-Golay filter, kernel [-2,-1,0,1,2]/10), under stop-gradient. The loss is reconstruction + velocity MSE with equal weights 1.

At inference, z_0 = f_dyn(s_0; s_0) is integrated forward with RK4, and each predicted z_tau is decoded via g_dyn and the DINO image decoder. Video prediction is evaluated on LIBERO (all 130 tasks, 6,500 demonstrations, re-rendered at 256x256) for 16-frame and 64-frame fragments with PSNR and LPIPS against ground truth. Baselines, trained by the authors on the same data: LDP (SD-VAE latent planner, open-loop autoregressive rollout, goal-image conditioning added) and V-JEPA 2 (ViT-L/16 checkpoint fine-tuned on LIBERO agentview video with CLIP language conditioning, plus a separately trained convolutional pixel decoder).
official.claim: On LIBERO video prediction, ODEWorld reaches PSNR 20.53 / LPIPS 0.109 on 16-frame fragments and 19.46 / 0.134 on 64-frame fragments, versus 17.60 / 0.157 and 16.47 / 0.166 for the strongest baseline, V-JEPA 2 (about +3 dB PSNR at both horizons).
official.claim_caption: Table 1 Comparison on video prediction quality and latency.
official.metric: PSNR (higher is better) and LPIPS (lower is better) of predicted frames vs. ground truth; latency in seconds on one A100 also reported. Single numbers, no error bars, no seeds or number of evaluation clips reported.
official.comparison: ODEWorld vs. V-JEPA 2 and LDP, all trained by the authors on LIBERO and evaluated on 16- and 64-frame fragments
official.falsification_criterion: A re-trained ODEWorld fails to beat a comparably trained V-JEPA 2 (or LDP) on PSNR and LPIPS at both 16 and 64 frames on LIBERO, or the PSNR gap over V-JEPA 2 shrinks to well under 1 dB.

title: CENDRe: Concept Extraction with Natural Domain Representations
claim_source: Table 6, page 21 (Appendix D.1.3); summarized in Figure 2, page 8; significance tests in Figure 9, page 23

official.background: Concept extraction (CE) explains a trained network globally by clustering its latent activations into recurring patterns ('concepts'), localizing each concept in the input, and scoring how much it matters for each class. For time-series CNNs, existing CE methods (ECLAD-ts, MultiVISION) work only in the time domain, need the number of concepts K to be fixed by hand, and localize concepts with heuristics (upsampled activation maps or full receptive-field patches) that may not match the regions the model uses. Faithful localization matters because the concept importance scores are computed from those masks.
official.method:
CENDRe builds per-timestep latent descriptors (LADs) by linearly upsampling activation maps of selected probe layers of a trained 1D CNN to a common length and concatenating them. It runs mini-batch k-means on all LADs to get J = 50 micro-centroids, then clusters the micro-centroids into K concepts, either by cosine-distance agglomerative clustering with K chosen to maximize the mean silhouette score (CENDRe_silhouette, default) or by HDBSCAN (CENDRe_HDBSCAN); CENDRe_kMeans instead runs k-means on LADs with a fixed K. Each concept is localized by the ReLU of the input gradient of a contrastive presence score (Eq. 3: inverse-distance similarity to the assigned micro-centroid minus mean similarity to micro-centroids of other concepts), averaged over the timesteps assigned to that concept (time mask = ReLU of the gradient of this sample-level presence w.r.t. the input); inserting an rFFT 'virtual inspection layer' (phi^-1 o phi, no learnable parameters) gives the frequency mask ReLU(Re(x_f ⊙ ∇_{x_f} presence)). A class-wise importance I_{c,k,ch} is the inner product of the concept mask with the noise-tunnel-smoothed gradient of the class logit, averaged over samples and normalized, then reduced to a class-agnostic I_{k,ch} (Eq. 5).

Evaluation: binary synthetic datasets (SyntheticLocal: shapes such as square, circle, triangle injected into a noisy sinusoid, 9 variants) with ground-truth primitive masks. InceptionTime10, ResNet1D-18 and DenseNet1D-121 are trained with AdamW (lr 1e-4, wd 1e-7, early stopping) over seeds 0-10. Each CE method runs on 256 samples. Alignment is the Relevance Mass Accuracy of the normalized concept mask inside the primitive mask. Soft Importance Correctness sIC = sum_{k,ch} max_p A_{p,k,ch} |I_{k,ch}| / sum_{k,ch} |I_{k,ch}| (Eq. 7). Fixed-K methods (ECLAD-ts, MultiVISION, CENDRe_kMeans) are swept over K in {2,4,6,8,10} and reported at the K with the best sRC; the automatic CENDRe variants run once.
official.claim: On the 9 SyntheticLocal datasets (33 runs each: 3 CNN architectures x 11 seeds), CENDRe's automatic variants achieve higher soft importance correctness than prior CE methods: family mean sIC 0.858 ± 0.107 (HDBSCAN) and 0.792 ± 0.110 (silhouette) vs. 0.722 ± 0.105 for MultiVISION and 0.556 ± 0.262 for ECLAD-ts, with CENDRe_HDBSCAN best on all 9 datasets.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Distributional summary (mean ± std, 95% CI) of sIC across CE methods and datasets.
official.metric: Soft Importance Correctness (sIC, in [0,1], higher is better). ± is std over the 33 runs per dataset (3 architectures x 11 seeds); the family Mean row pools all 9 datasets x 3 architectures x 11 seeds (297 runs per method). Brackets are the paper's 95% Student-t CI for the mean. The paper also reports paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected, per architecture over 99 matched pairs (9 datasets x 11 seeds).
official.comparison: CENDRe_HDBSCAN and CENDRe_silhouette (automatic K, J = 50 micro-clusters) vs. ECLAD-ts and MultiVISION (K swept over {2,4,6,8,10}, best-sRC K reported), on the same trained models and data. CENDRe_kMeans (0.658) is an internal variant.

title: TrajWiki: Source-Grounded Memory Trajectories for Long-Horizon Dialogue Agents

official.background: LLM dialogue agents that run over many sessions cannot keep the whole history in context, so they rely on external memory. Most memory systems (Mem0, A-MEM, LangMem) store flat records that are overwritten or retrieved independently. This makes it hard to answer multi-hop or update-sensitive questions that need evidence scattered across sessions, and hard to trace which source utterances support an answer.
official.method:
TrajWiki converts each dialogue exchange into an immutable episodic snapshot of extracted claims linked to the source messages. It appends each snapshot to the most compatible memory trajectory or starts a new one, recording claim-level ADD/REVISE/DEPRECATE edits. The trajectories are then compiled by an LLM into a persistent 'Memory Wiki' of index, entity, topic and inventory pages, each linking to trajectories. At query time the query is routed to the top t = 15 wiki pages, the union of their linked trajectories forms the candidate set, the top k = 15 trajectories are selected by relevance plus coverage minus redundancy, and these are expanded into source-linked snapshots for evidence-grounded answer synthesis. Embeddings use Qwen3-Embedding-8B; the backbone here is GPT-4o-mini.

In the Table 10 follow-up, the memory stores are frozen and answer generation is rerun on 200 LoCoMo multi-hop queries with GPT-4o-mini, identical answer instructions and a common 32K input-plus-output cap. 'No Wiki Routing' bypasses query-time wiki routing and ranks trajectories directly from the same frozen trajectory store. A method-blinded Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge labels each answer CORRECT, PARTIAL or wrong. JudgeScore = 100 (N_correct + 0.5 N_partial) / N. The 95% CIs on the differences come from 10,000 paired query-bootstrap draws.
official.claim: On 200 LoCoMo multi-hop queries with GPT-4o-mini and frozen memory stores, full TrajWiki scores 42.0 JudgeScore versus 31.3 when Memory Wiki routing is bypassed (difference -10.8, 95% paired-bootstrap CI [-16.0, -5.5]), while also using fewer generation input tokens (19.3K vs 30.9K).
official.claim_caption: Answer-level ablations on 200 LoCoMo multi-hop queries. The full and ablated settings use frozen memory stores and a common 32K input-plus-output cap. Score differences are relative to Full TrajWiki, with 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 paired query-bootstrap draws. Strict accuracy and gold-reference coverage are percentages; input tokens are mean generation inputs, not full-pipeline deployment costs. title: Group Perspective Matters: Regulating Debate Relationships Can Mitigate Blind Conformity in Multi-Agent Debate
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (GPT-4o-mini replication in Table 3, page 15)

official.background: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) has several LLMs answer a question, read each other's answers, and revise over several rounds. A known failure is blind conformity: a correct minority agent switches to the incorrect majority answer. Existing fixes filter which peer messages are passed on using self-reported confidence (CortexDebate) or perplexity (MAD-M2), but these signals are poorly correlated with correctness. The paper instead regulates who listens to whom, and how each agent samples, based on group-level agreement signals.
official.method:
Three copies of the same frozen LLM (Qwen3-8B), each with a distinct persona prompt, debate for 3 rounds. After each round, every pair of agents gets an evidence score: the mean of the cosine similarities (rescaled to [0,1]) between BGE-M3 embeddings of their summarized conclusions and of their reasoning. Subjective Logic turns each agent's row of evidence into belief masses toward each peer plus an uncertainty mass (base weight = number of agents).

A Selection RL-Agent maps the concatenated beliefs, uncertainties and one-hot IDs to independent Bernoulli probabilities, which decide whether agent i sees peer j's response in the next round. A Behavior RL-Agent takes each agent's evidence (fused with its selected peers' evidence via Dempster's combination rule) and outputs that agent's temperature and top-p in [0,1] for the next round. Both small policies are trained jointly with HAPPO using a shared terminal reward of +1 for a correct final answer. The LLM itself is not fine-tuned. For math, training uses the GSM8K training set; evaluation is on GSM8K (ID) and AIME24, GSM-Hard, MATH-500 (OOD), all baselines using the same personas.
official.claim: With Qwen3-8B (3 agents, 3 rounds) and policies trained only on GSM8K, DEAR reaches 73.5% accuracy on out-of-distribution GSM-Hard vs. 61.8% for the best multi-agent baseline (DMAD) and 60.3% for CoT-SC (16 samples), and 85.0% on MATH-500 vs. 78.8% for DMAD, while using fewer tokens per task (6.2K vs. 23.4K on GSM-Hard).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison on Qwen3-8B. We highlight the optimal and suboptimal results. Acc. (%) denotes accuracy, and T. (K) represents the average tokens per task.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on a 400-example random subset of each benchmark, higher is better; average tokens per task (K), lower is better. Single run; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: DEAR vs. CoT, CoT-SC, Majority Voting, MAD, DMAD, CortexDebate, MAD-M2(O), ECON, all with Qwen3-8B and identical personas
official.falsification_criterion: On the same 400-example GSM-Hard subset (or a comparable random subset), a re-trained DEAR does not exceed the best of DMAD/MAD/MAD-M2(O) with the same personas by more than ~5 accuracy points, or on MATH-500 does not exceed DMAD at all.

title: Information-Geometric Forward Policy Training in GFlowNets

official.background: GFlowNets learn a stochastic, step-by-step construction policy whose distribution over finished objects should be proportional to an unnormalised reward. They are trained with balance objectives such as trajectory balance (TB), and the forward policy is usually updated with plain (Euclidean) gradient steps on its parameters. Because the thing being optimised is really a probability distribution over trajectories, the paper argues the update should use the Fisher-Rao geometry of that trajectory distribution, i.e. a natural gradient. It derives the trajectory Fisher, shows that it splits into per-step terms (exactly block-diagonal and occupancy-weighted for tabular policies), and studies when exact, sampled or structure-based approximations of it are good enough.
official.method:
Target: a triangle-count exponential random graph model on n = 6 nodes, p_β(G) ∝ exp{β T(G)} with β = 0.2, where T(G) counts triangles. That gives 15 possible edges and 2^15 = 32,768 terminal graphs. The GFlowNet visits the 15 edges in a fixed order and decides include/exclude for each, so every graph has a unique length-15 trajectory. The forward policy is tabular (one softmax logit vector per state), trained with the squared TB loss (Eqs. 14-15) together with a learned log Z. Because every graph has a unique trajectory, the backward policy is trivial here (P_B = 1).

Natural variant: the forward-policy gradient h is preconditioned with the exact tabular trajectory Fisher from Corollary 1, F = ⊕_s d_θ(s) C(π_s), where C(π) = Diag(π) − ππᵀ and the state occupancies d_θ(s) are computed exactly by forward dynamic programming. The update is θ ← θ − η (F + λI)^{-1} h. Backward-policy and log Z parameters always get Euclidean updates. Euclidean variant: the same setup with θ ← θ − η h. Both are run for 15,000 steps over 5 seeds. TB loss and the exact KL(q_θ ‖ p_β) over all 32,768 graphs are tracked.
official.claim: On the triangle-count ERGM (n = 6, β = 0.2) with a tabular forward policy, exact natural-gradient TB training brings KL(q_θ‖p_β) to about 2×10⁻³ by about 4,000 steps, while Euclidean TB is still at about 2.4×10⁻² after 15,000 steps. The TB loss is about 5×10⁻⁸ vs. about 4×10⁻² at 15,000 steps.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: TB loss (left; geometric mean with ±1 std in log space) and KL(q_θ‖p_β) (right; mean ± std) on the triangle-count ERGM (n = 6, β = 0.2), over five seeds.
official.metric: Exact KL(q_θ ‖ p_β) over all terminal graphs (lower is better; mean ± std over 5 seeds) and TB loss (lower is better; geometric mean ± 1 std in log space over 5 seeds). Values below are read off the log-scale plot and are approximate; the bands are very narrow.
official.comparison: Natural-gradient forward-policy update with the exact occupancy-weighted tabular Fisher vs. Euclidean gradient update, same TB objective, environment and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both variants (n = 6, β = 0.2, 15,000 steps, 5 seeds), the Euclidean run reaches a final KL within a factor of ~2 of the natural-gradient run, or the natural-gradient run does not reach a lower KL by step 4,000 than the Euclidean run reaches by step 15,000. The same holds for Euclidean step sizes tuned over a reasonable grid.

title: Safe Evolution with Circuit Anchors
claim_source: Figure 5, page 9 (endpoint safety numbers for Standard from the text of Sec. 4.4, page 8)

official.background: Self-evolution algorithms let an LLM improve its reasoning by training on self-generated problems with RL, but they optimize only for task reward. Fine-tuning is known to erode safety alignment, so a model that self-evolves may become a stronger reasoner while losing its tendency to refuse harmful requests. The paper asks whether safety can be preserved during self-evolution without giving up the capability gains, and without the cost of running a separate safety reward model during training.
official.method:
Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE) first uses pre-trained per-layer transcoders and the circuit-tracer toolkit to find a 'safety circuit': transcoder features whose attribution to refusal on harmful prompts (1,429 prompts from Do-Not-Answer, DAN and Malicious Instruct, intersected across datasets) exceeds a threshold, about 1.2-1.8% of all transcoder features. During evolution, a KL penalty between the original model's and the current model's activations on these features (computed through the frozen transcoders on M = 64 reference samples per step) is subtracted from the evolution objective with weight lambda.

The comparison runs three instruction-tuned models (Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2B-IT, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) through 500 steps (batch 32) of EVOL-RL (GRPO on self-generated math problems) or Abs-ZERO (proposer-solver self-play), each under three conditions: Standard (unconstrained), +RM (Beaver-Cost safety reward model added to the reward), and +CAE. Safety score is the refusal rate on the held-out AdvBench set (520 prompts); capability score is average accuracy over the original algorithms' evaluation benchmarks.
official.claim: After 500 steps of EVOL-RL self-evolution, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct's AdvBench refusal rate falls from 96.22% to 72.13% without constraints, while with circuit anchoring it stays at about 96% and capability rises by a similar amount (about 22.5% -> 34.7% for CAE vs. about 34.5% unconstrained); the same pattern holds for Qwen3-4B (99.04% -> 69.85% unconstrained) and Gemma-2-2B (98.65% -> 75.38%).
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Safety-capability trajectories during evolution across three model families. Standard evolution improves capability but severely degrades safety. +RM partially preserves safety at the cost of reduced capability gains. +CAE maintains high safety while achieving comparable capability improvement to unconstrained evolution. The CAE trajectories cluster tightly in the upper-right region across both algorithms, demonstrating consistent safety preservation regardless of the underlying evolution method.
official.metric: Safety score = refusal rate (%) on AdvBench, higher is better; capability score = average benchmark accuracy (%), higher is better. No error bars, no seeds reported (single runs).
official.comparison: +CAE vs. Standard (unconstrained) vs. +RM (Beaver-Cost reward-model constraint), same model, algorithm, 500 steps
official.falsification_criterion: With CAE applied to Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct under EVOL-RL for 500 steps, the AdvBench refusal rate drops by more than ~5 pp below the initial model (i.e. below ~91%), or the capability gain is substantially smaller than unconstrained evolution's (e.g. less than half), or unconstrained evolution does not cause a large (>10 pp) refusal drop.

title: Ask-E: An Environment for Calibrated Question Generation

official.background: Models are improved and measured by training and testing them on problems at the edge of their ability, but writing such problems needs a writer who is more capable than the model, which gets harder as models improve. Ask-E turns this around and evaluates a model as the question writer: given a target difficulty range defined by two existing 'boundary' language models, the asker must write a math question that exactly one of the two can solve. The question writer is graded by the behaviour of the solvers rather than by a stronger supervisor.
official.method:
Each session picks a pair of boundary solvers from a set of 20 models (17 open-weight checkpoints from 1.5B to 27B, served with vLLM, plus 3 Gemini Flash API models), giving 190 unordered pairs. The asker gets 4 probing rounds: in each round it writes a question (in #Reasoning#/#Draft#/#Question# sections), both solvers answer it statelessly at temperature 0.7, and the asker sees each solver's boxed answer plus a short summary. In the 5th round it writes a final question, which it does not see answered. The prompts and token budgets are in Appendices B and F.

The final question is answered by both boundary solvers and three times by a cross-check solver (Gemini 3.1 Pro, thinking low). If the three cross-check answers disagree the session is 'bad cross-check'. Otherwise the session is 'calibrated' if exactly one boundary solver matches the cross-check answer (math-verify plus string fallbacks plus an LLM equivalence check), 'too easy' if both match, and 'too hard' if neither matches. Each asker runs every pair 10 times (1,900 sessions). The metric is the fraction of calibrated sessions.
official.claim: On the 190-pair Ask-E math benchmark, Gemini 3.1 Pro calibrates 44.9% of sessions, above every other tested asker (Qwen3.5-27B 37.4%, DeepSeek V4 Pro 37.2%), and Qwen3.5-27B (37.4%) beats Qwen3.5-4B (27.2%), with non-overlapping 95% CIs in both comparisons.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Benchmark performance of five models on Ask-E. (Left) Calibration rate across all sessions. Error bars correspond to 95% confidence intervals computed across 10 independent runs of all 190 boundary pairs. (Right) Breakdown of generated question outcomes into too easy, calibrated, too hard, no question (no parseable final question), and bad cross-check (the three cross-check answers disagree) categories.
official.metric: Calibration rate (% of 1,900 sessions where exactly one boundary solver matches the cross-check answer), higher is better; error bars are 95% confidence intervals across 10 independent runs of all 190 pairs
official.comparison: Asker models Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.5-4B and Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, each run on the same boundary set, dialogue protocol and grading
official.falsification_criterion: Under the paper's protocol, Gemini 3.1 Pro's calibration rate falls within the 95% CI of Qwen3.5-27B or DeepSeek V4 Pro, or Qwen3.5-27B's rate is not clearly above Qwen3.5-4B's (overlapping CIs or reversed order).

title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
claim_source: Table 1, page 10 (ablation in Table 2, page 11; relaxed |Δz| < 1 threshold in Table 5, page 23)

official.background: LLM coding agents are increasingly used to run statistical analyses end-to-end: inspect a dataset, write code, compute a p-value and draw a conclusion. Executing code correctly is not the same as choosing a valid test: agents often apply a method whose assumptions the data violate (outliers, heteroskedasticity, clustering, censoring), producing a precise but wrong p-value and a false discovery. Existing data-analysis benchmarks score executable workflows or factoid answers and rarely check whether the p-value matches a valid reference analysis. The paper builds P-Bench, 425 open-ended hypothesis-testing tasks on real economics, biology and medical data (Easy 203 / Hard 222), and trains an open-weight agent, Fisher-R1, for this task.
official.method:
Each P-Bench task gives the agent a research question, a data description and a CSV; the agent works in a multi-turn loop in an R sandbox (<think>/<code>/<observation>/<answer> tags) and must report a p-value and a reject/fail-to-reject decision at alpha = 0.05. The hidden answer key comes from a logged run of the canonical reference analysis (replication scripts, re-implemented methods sections, or course notes) and is expert-audited. Raw = decision matches the key; Strict = Raw and |z(p̂) − z(p*)| < 0.5 with z(p) = Φ⁻¹(1 − p/2). Each model gets 3 independent rollouts per task (inference temperature 0.3, top-p 0.9); pass@1 is the mean per-trial success (± std over the 3 runs), pass@3 is any-of-three.

Fisher-R1 starts from Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/14B. Training data are 8,642 synthetic tasks: an LLM writes simulation code and questions over a grid of method × scenario × sample size × effect size (null/borderline/medium) × prompt style (hint/non-hint) × seed, plus missing-value and outlier perturbations; the answer key is the canonical method run on the simulated data. SFT (LlamaFactory, 3 epochs, lr 1e-5) uses 3,851 Claude-Sonnet-4.6 trajectories filtered for correct decisions and p-values. RL (verl, DAPO, 1 epoch, lr 1e-6, G = 8, clip 0.2/0.28, max response 4,096 tokens) uses reward 0.9 · exp(−|min(z(p̂),5) − min(z(p*),5)|) + 0.1 · [decision correct], set to 0 for malformed trajectories.
official.claim: On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-7B (SFT + DAPO) raises Strict pass@1 over its untrained Qwen2.5-Coder-7B backbone from 36.3 ± 5.5 to 65.7 ± 1.2 on P-Easy and from 13.2 ± 0.5 to 30.6 ± 1.2 on P-Hard (Raw pass@1: 61.4 → 87.0 and 37.5 → 63.4); the 14B version likewise improves P-Hard Strict pass@1 from 23.7 ± 1.6 to 33.0 ± 1.7.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on P-Bench. Raw denotes correct conclusion direction, while Strict additionally requires |Δz| < 0.5, where z is the two-sided z-score derived from the reported p-value. pass@1 is reported as mean±stdev over three independent runs.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on P-Bench, higher is better. Strict = correct reject/fail-to-reject decision and |Δz| < 0.5 between reported and reference p-value; pass@1 is mean ± std over 3 independent runs (3 rollouts per task); pass@3 has no error bar.
official.comparison: Fisher-R1-7B vs. its backbone Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (and Fisher-R1-14B vs. Qwen2.5-Coder-14B), same agent loop, R sandbox, prompts and decoding settings
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating the released Fisher-R1-7B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on P-Bench with the same harness (3 runs), the Strict pass@1 gain is below ~15 points on P-Easy or below ~8 points on P-Hard, or a model retrained with the described SFT + DAPO recipe does not beat the backbone by more than a few std on Strict pass@1.

title: A Distribution Mapping Approach to Counterfactually Fair Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Figure 2a (and 2b), page 9; the N = 1000 CFSMDM value is from Table A4, page 39

official.background: Offline reinforcement learning policies used in settings such as digital health can treat people differently because of a sensitive attribute (sex, ethnicity, education), even when that attribute is left out of the state, because states and rewards carry information about it. Counterfactual fairness (CF) asks that a policy's action distribution for a person stay the same had their sensitive attribute been different, with all exogenous noise held fixed. An earlier preprocessing method (CFSDP, Wang et al. 2025) makes RL counterfactually fair by replacing states and rewards with estimated counterfactuals, but it assumes the noise is additive. This paper relaxes that assumption to noise that enters monotonically, which allows nonadditive transition and reward models.
official.method:
CFSMDM (counterfactually fair sequential marginal distribution mapping) preprocesses offline trajectories before policy learning. For each state component and the reward at each time step, it fits conditional quantile models given (Z, previous state, previous action) (or (Z, state, action) for the reward), finds the quantile level of the observed value under the observed Z, and reads off the value at the same quantile level under each alternative Z, propagating sequentially through the trajectory. The augmented state is the vector of counterfactual states under every value of Z, and the augmented reward is the P(Z)-weighted average of counterfactual rewards. A policy is then learned on the augmented data with fitted Q iteration (FQI, 200 iterations). In the simulation, quantiles are fitted with linear quantile regression (statsmodels QuantReg, polynomial and interaction terms, quantile levels 0.01-0.99).

Data come from CMDP 1 (Appendix O): binary sensitive attribute Z, bivariate state, binary action, cube-root (nonadditive) transitions and reward with Gaussian noise, and sensitive-attribute strength δ. Experiment 1 uses T = 20, δ = 2.0, a uniformly random behaviour policy, and N ∈ {100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000} training individuals. The baselines are Full (uses Z as a state), Unaware (drops Z), Random, FLAP_M and ECOCF_M (single-stage marginal distribution mapping adapted to RL) and CFSDP (additive-noise counterfactual preprocessing with a neural transition model). The CF metric is the maximum over pairs (z, z') of the fraction of (individual, time) pairs where the policy's action differs between the factual and counterfactual trajectories, computed on 10,000 simulated individuals over 20 steps using the true CMDP. Policy value is the discounted cumulative reward on 10,000 simulated individuals.
official.claim: On the nonadditive-noise simulation (CMDP 1, T = 20, δ = 2.0), CFSMDM's CF metric is about 0.04 for N ≥ 500 (0.038 ± 0.012 at N = 1000), while FLAP_M, ECOCF_M and CFSDP stay around 0.13-0.15 and Unaware around 0.33; CFSMDM's policy value (about -3.3) is somewhat lower than FLAP_M/ECOCF_M (about -3.05).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Experiment results under nonadditive noise (CMDP 1): (a) CF metric vs. Sample size (N); (b) Policy value vs. Sample size (N); (c) Policy value vs. CF metric; (d) CF metric vs. Size of effect of Z on St and Rt (δ). Results are aggregated over 50 replications with different random seeds. Point represents the empirical mean. Shaded area represents the band between 0.025 and 0.975 empirical quantiles.
official.metric: CF metric (fraction of individual-time steps where the factual and counterfactual actions differ, max over attribute pairs; lower is fairer) and discounted cumulative reward (higher is better). Points are means over 50 seeds; shaded bands are the 2.5%-97.5% empirical quantiles over seeds. Figure values below are read off the plot and are approximate; the ± for N = 1000 is the std over 50 seeds from Table A4.
official.comparison: CFSMDM vs. FLAP_M, ECOCF_M, CFSDP (fairness-aware preprocessing baselines), and Unaware/Full/Random, all with FQI policy learning on the same simulated data
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running CMDP 1 (T = 20, δ = 2.0, N = 1000, 50 seeds), CFSMDM's mean CF metric is not clearly below the best of FLAP_M, ECOCF_M and CFSDP (e.g. the gap is under ~0.05, or CFSMDM's 2.5-97.5% band overlaps the baseline's mean), or CFSMDM's CF metric does not fall as N grows.

title: When Latents Forget Pixels: Restoring Fidelity in Diffusion Transformer Super-Resolution
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (same numbers repeated in Table 6, page 18)

official.background: Generative super-resolution (SR) built on large latent diffusion or flow-matching models produces realistic textures but often hallucinates details that are not supported by the low-resolution (LR) input, such as wrong text characters. The authors argue that one cause is the VAE bottleneck: the LR image is only seen by the model after VAE compression, which discards fine spatial detail, and the frozen VAE decoder loses further detail when rendering the output. Fixing this matters for any application where SR output must stay faithful to the observed image.
official.method:
PGSR adapts a frozen FLUX.1-dev flow-matching transformer for x4 SR with a ControlNet branch (initialized from a FLUX SR ControlNet) and rank-16 LoRA adapters, conditioned on the VAE latent z_lr of the bicubic-upsampled LR image, with cached empty-text embeddings (the implementation also adds a few learnable leading text tokens with a small learning rate and L2 regularization, Appendix A). A small pixel encoder reads the upsampled LR image before VAE compression and produces a latent-resolution feature plus three multi-scale taps. Condition-side trajectory guidance adds the latent-resolution feature to z_lr through a gated residual (z_lr + lambda * sigmoid(g) * W_p(p_lr)) before the ControlNet. Decoder-side pixel grounding (DFM) adds zero-initialized projections of the multi-scale taps to the frozen VAE decoder's activations before each of three upsampling blocks. The VAE and FLUX backbone stay frozen.

Training uses flow-matching loss plus low-noise-gated LPIPS and L1 image losses (lambda_perc = 0.05, lambda_pg = 0.05). Stage 1 trains on DF2K with bicubic x4 pairs (512x512 HR crops, 60 epochs, effective batch 256); Stage 2 fine-tunes with Real-ESRGAN second-order degradation on DF2K+LSDIR+FFHQ+OST, with DFM and image losses enabled. Inference uses 20 sampling steps, denoising strength 1.0, and 512-pixel tiles with 64 overlap. The ablation in Table 2 removes the condition-side pathway, the decoder-side pathway, or both ('w/o Pixel-Grounded', the latent-only FLUX SR baseline), and evaluates PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on DIV2K-Val (bicubic x4) and RealSR.
official.claim: On DIV2K-Val x4 SR, adding both pixel-grounded pathways to the same FLUX.1-dev ControlNet SR model raises PSNR from 23.68 to 25.89 dB and lowers LPIPS from 0.2431 to 0.2104 versus the latent-only variant (and beats the strongest single-pathway variant, w/o Decoder-Side at 24.78 dB / 0.2188, by 1.11 dB); on RealSR PSNR rises from 22.15 to 24.75 dB and LPIPS falls from 0.2789 to 0.2596 (strongest single-pathway variant: 24.22 dB PSNR, 0.2626 LPIPS).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Architecture ablation of pixel-grounded pathways in PGSR. The left table reports quantitative results on DIV2K-Val and RealSR, while the right panel shows a representative visual ablation. Removing either the condition-side trajectory guidance or the decoder-side grounding degrades reconstruction and perceptual quality, and the full design gives the best results on both datasets.
official.metric: PSNR (dB, higher is better), SSIM (higher is better), LPIPS (lower is better) on DIV2K-Val and RealSR at x4. Single run (seed 42); no error bars or seed spread reported.
official.comparison: Full PGSR vs. the same FLUX.1-dev ControlNet+LoRA SR model without pixel grounding ('w/o Pixel-Grounded'), and vs. variants without only the condition-side or only the decoder-side pathway.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining the latent-only and full PGSR variants under the same recipe gives a DIV2K-Val PSNR gap well below ~2.2 dB (e.g. under 0.5 dB), or the full model does not beat the latent-only variant on both PSNR and LPIPS on DIV2K-Val and RealSR.

title: Parameter Exploration for RLVR via Variational Learning
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (multi-seed check for Olmo3 in Appendix G, page 21)

official.background: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), usually with GRPO, improves LLM reasoning but depends on the model's own rollouts. When all rollouts for a prompt get the same reward, the group-relative advantage is zero and the prompt gives no learning signal. Common fixes explore in the action space, for example by raising sampling temperature, adding entropy bonuses or penalizing high-covariance tokens. These change the variance of the token distribution but cannot reorder tokens, and they can produce degenerate outputs. The paper asks whether exploring in parameter space, by sampling perturbed policies from a learned posterior over weights, gives a better RLVR learning signal.
official.method:
Training uses the IVON variational optimizer instead of AdamW, so the model keeps a diagonal Gaussian posterior over weights with mean m and variance sigma = 1/sqrt(lambda (h + delta)), where h is a learned diagonal Hessian (initialized to a constant h0 at the start of RLVR) and lambda is the effective sample size (1e9 for Olmo3, 1e10 for Qwen2.5-Math). Rollouts are generated from perturbed weights m + sigma * z. In C3PO (chunked noising), each step draws N = 4 independent weight samples; each generates G/N = 4 rollouts per prompt, and the GRPO advantage is computed over the combined group of 16 rollouts. A fresh weight sample is used for the gradient update, with sequence-level importance-sampling masking (Seq-MIS, ratios outside [0.5, 2] masked), which the authors say is needed for training to converge.

Setup: Olmo-3-1025-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B are first warm-start SFT'd with IVON for 2 epochs on a ~2M-example subset of Llama-Nemotron Post-Training data (DeepSeek-R1 responses), then trained with token-level GRPO on DAPO-MATH-17k (32 prompts x 16 rollouts per step, binary reward, 559 steps, max 4096 tokens, temperature 1.0, no KL term). The baselines start from the same SFT checkpoint: GRPO with AdamW (lr 1e-6), GRPO+entropy regularization, GRPO+Polaris temperature switching (1.0 to 1.4), and GRPO+KL-Cov. Evaluation is unbiased pass@1 over 8 samples (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95) on AIME'24/'25/'26, MATH-500, AMC 2023 and Minerva, averaged over the six benchmarks.
official.claim: With Olmo-3-1025-7B on DAPO-MATH-17k at near-identical FLOPs per step, C3PO (N=4, lambda=1e9) reaches a six-benchmark average math pass@1 of 44.04 ± 0.46, above GRPO (42.99 ± 0.51) and every action-space exploration baseline (EntReg 42.44, KL-Cov 42.29, Polaris 41.47). The same ordering holds on Qwen2.5-Math-7B: C3PO 46.88 ± 0.38 vs. GRPO 45.37 ± 0.35 and Polaris 45.78 ± 0.32.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: A comparison of all methods across common mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Methods with multiple noise samples outperform GRPO on average. Both models benefit most from C3PO's increased group diversity. The largest gains are on the harder AIME problems. We report the unbiased Pass@1 across 8 samples, and its standard error.
official.metric: Unbiased pass@1 from K=8 samples per problem (higher is better), averaged over 6 math benchmarks; ± is the standard error over evaluation samples for a single training run, not over training seeds. Appendix G reports 3 training seeds for GRPO vs. C3PO on Olmo3 only: mean gain +0.89 points, positive on all 3 seeds, paired t-test p = 0.027.
official.comparison: C3PO vs. GRPO (AdamW) and GRPO + EntReg / Polaris / KL-Cov, all starting from the same SFT checkpoint with 16 rollouts per prompt and the same training steps
official.falsification_criterion: On Olmo3, C3PO's six-benchmark average pass@1 does not exceed GRPO's by more than the reported standard error (about 0.5 points), or the gain is not positive across 3 training seeds; or some action-space baseline matches or beats C3PO.

title: DegradeQuery: Counterfactual Tuple Pretraining for Context-Aware PROTAC Degradation Prediction
claim_source: Table 14, page 16 (Appendix A.4); same numbers summarized in Table 2, page 8 and Figure 2, page 7

official.background: PROTACs are bifunctional molecules that degrade a target protein by recruiting it to an E3 ubiquitin ligase, so whether degradation happens depends jointly on the degrader molecule, the target protein and the recruited E3 ligase. Public PROTAC databases record thousands of molecule-target-E3 entries, but measured degradation endpoints (DC50, Dmax, percent degradation) are expensive and exist for only a small fraction: in the PROTAC-8K benchmark only 1,502 of 8,636 records carry a binary active/inactive label. Standard supervised training discards the other 7,134 records, and the main prior approach to using them (DegradeMaster) assigns activity pseudo-labels. The question this paper addresses is whether the label-missing records can be used as a pretraining signal without inventing activity labels for them.
official.method:
DegradeQuery encodes the molecule with a three-layer residual message-passing network over 15-dimensional atom features summed with a 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprint (radius 2, both projected to 256 dims), and encodes the target protein and the E3 ligase with a shared 150-feature sequence encoder (amino-acid composition, length/unknown-residue features, 128 hashed di-/tri-peptide counts) into separate 256-dim embeddings. A fusion module concatenates the three embeddings, their three pairwise elementwise products and the absolute target-E3 difference; an optional cell-line assay descriptor is added only in the supervised stage.

In counterfactual tuple pretraining (CTP), each recorded train-side tuple (molecule, target, E3) is scored by a scoring head and contrasted, with an InfoNCE-style ranking loss (temperature 0.1, 3 counterfactual samples per tuple), against alternatives formed by replacing the target, the E3, or both, drawn from the empirical train-side marginals. An auxiliary SimCLR-style molecule-consistency loss over subgraph-masking / SMILES-enumeration views is added with weight 0.1. No degradation pseudo-labels, teacher models, distillation or ensembles are used, and test/query tuples are excluded from the pretraining tuple set. The pretrained encoder is then fine-tuned on the 1,202 labeled training rows with a class-weighted focal loss (gamma = 1.0) and evaluated on the 300-row official test split at a fixed threshold of 0.5. The baseline, DegradeQuery-Sup, is the identical architecture and fine-tuning recipe with random initialization instead of CTP.
official.claim: On the official PROTAC-8K split, initializing from counterfactual tuple pretraining raises test AUROC from 0.8777 +/- 0.0031 (DegradeQuery-Sup) to 0.8996 +/- 0.0039 (Full CTP) and accuracy from 0.7840 +/- 0.0072 to 0.8233 +/- 0.0058 over five paired seeds, a mean paired AUROC gain of +0.0219 with 95% CI [0.0136, 0.0303]; pretraining on only the 7,134 label-missing records recovers the same gain (0.9007 +/- 0.0032, +0.0230 over Sup with CI [0.0173, 0.0287]).
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Official-split results over five paired seeds. Values are mean +/- standard deviation. Confidence intervals are for paired differences. Lower is better for Brier score and expected calibration error (ECE); higher is better otherwise.
official.metric: AUROC and accuracy on the 300-row official PROTAC-8K test split, higher is better; +/- is the standard deviation over 5 paired seeds (seeds 1-5), and bracketed intervals are paired 95% confidence intervals over the same seeds
official.comparison: DegradeQuery-CTP (full and unlabeled-only pretraining) vs. DegradeQuery-Sup, identical architecture, protein/molecule features, supervised loss, labeled training split, model-selection rule and 0.5 decision threshold; the only difference is whether the encoder is initialized from counterfactual tuple pretraining
official.falsification_criterion: Under the matched protocol with 5 seeds, CTP's mean test AUROC fails to exceed Sup's by more than one seed standard deviation (i.e. a gain below roughly 0.004), or the paired 95% CI for the CTP - Sup AUROC difference includes zero. Equivalently, if unlabeled-only CTP (pretraining on the 7,134 label-missing records alone) does not improve over Sup.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Probabilistic Constrained Clustering from Entangled Pairwise Supervision

official.background: Pairwise constrained clustering uses weak supervision of the form 'these two items are / are not in the same cluster'. Existing deep constrained clustering methods assume hard must-link/cannot-link labels. In practice, pairwise labels are often real-valued and mix three things: genuine ambiguity between the items, systematic bias of the specific annotator (e.g. blind spots for unfamiliar classes), and random recording errors. The paper calls this setting uncertainty-aware probabilistic constrained clustering (UPCC) and asks whether a learner can recover a clustering that reflects the underlying relation rather than annotator bias and noise.
official.method:
ProbPair trains an autoencoder (500-500-2000 encoder, 10-d embedding, SDAE-pretrained) so that sigmoid((cos(z_a, z_b) - m)/T), with learnable m and T, fits each soft pairwise label y in [0,1] under binary cross-entropy, plus a reconstruction loss from normalized embeddings (lambda_rec = 0.02). Weighted ProbPair additionally weights each constraint by an information-based decisiveness score kappa_i (Eq. 9). Final clusters come from K-means on the normalized embeddings.

ECI-PP wraps Weighted ProbPair in an Estimator-Corrector-Integrator loop: K=5 cross-fitted Estimators give out-of-fold beliefs for each constraint; a small expert-specific Corrector MLP (64-16) predicts the discrepancy between belief and label from [belief; pair descriptor] and corrects the label; the remaining gap gives a reliability weight w_i = (1 - gap_i)^10; the Integrator is trained with the ProbPair objective on the fused target y_BC = (y + n_i y_cor)/(1 + n_i) with n_i = 10 w_i, with w_i also multiplying each per-constraint loss term. Estimators are warm-started from (y, kappa) and in later rounds retrained on the Integrator's relations and weights (y_int, w); the outer loop runs a fixed 500-epoch budget, and K-means on the normalized Integrator embeddings gives the clusters. Constraints in the multi3 setting are made by three MLP 'expert' classifiers, each trained with 10% of labels on familiar classes and 0.01% on its unfamiliar classes; a pair's label is the inner product of the two predicted class distributions, then replaced by Uniform(0,1) with probability 0.3. 9k constraints in total (3k per expert).
official.claim: On Reuters under the multi3 multi-expert setting (corruption probability 0.3, 9k constraints, pretrained backbone), full ECI-PP reaches test NMI 69.7 ± 2.3 versus 59.2 ± 3.8 for Weighted ProbPair (the same model without the ECI pipeline), and ARI 76.5 ± 2.5 versus 65.0 ± 5.7.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Ablation under the pretrained multi3 setting (p_corr = 0.3, 9k constraints). Results are mean±std over five runs; best and second-best results are bold and underlined, respectively.
official.metric: Test-set clustering NMI (also ACC, ARI), in %, higher is better; mean ± std over five runs
official.comparison: ECI-PP (Full) vs. Weighted ProbPair, plus ablations w/o cross-fitting, w/o Corrector, w/o screening, 1-pass ECI, all under identical constraints and pretrained initialization
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same Reuters multi3 setting, ECI-PP's mean test NMI over five runs is not clearly above Weighted ProbPair's (e.g. the gap shrinks below about 4 NMI points, within one baseline std), or Weighted ProbPair matches or exceeds ECI-PP.
