title: HandEdit: A Unified Benchmark for Egocentric Human-to-Robot Dexterous Hand Image Editing
claim_source: Table 4, page 10 (Hand-only); the same pattern appears in Table 6, page 11 (Hand-Arm: Interaction 0.595 vs. 0.421, VLM 0.786 vs. 0.856)

official.background: Egocentric videos of human hands manipulating objects are abundant, but robot policies with dexterous hands cannot use them directly because human and robot hands look and move differently. One way to bridge this gap is to edit human-hand frames into images of a specific robot hand or hand-arm, defined by its URDF, while keeping the scene, the object state and the hand-object contact. No dataset or benchmark existed for this URDF-conditioned editing task. Generic editing metrics (PSNR, LPIPS, VLM judges) also may not show whether the correct robot was produced or whether the interaction was preserved.
official.method:
HandEdit builds pseudo-GT targets from five egocentric hand-object datasets. The pipeline segments the human hand or arm (SAM3), inpaints the background (ProPainter), retargets the MANO/3D hand pose to a target robot URDF (with IK and a virtual base for hand-arm robots), renders the robot, composites it into the scene, and harmonizes the result. The test set has two tracks, Hand-only and Hand-Arm, each with 1K images and 13 target embodiments. Eleven commercial and open-source editors receive the source image, a render of the target URDF, and a fixed text template (Table S17). Each editor runs with its default inference settings.

Outputs are scored with embodiment-aware metrics and a GPT-4o judge. Interaction = 1 - LPIPS between the source and the edited image on a dilated object-contact mask M_O (Eq. 8). Structural fidelity = (1 + cos) / 2 between DINOv2 features of the edited ROI and the pseudo-GT ROI (Eq. 4). The VLM score is sqrt(SC * PQ), where Semantic Consistency and Perceptual Quality are GPT-4o rubric scores normalized to [0, 1] (Eq. 2; each is the minimum over its sub-criteria, Fig. 4). The paper's argument for its metric suite is that the VLM judge and the embodiment-aware metrics rank editors differently.
official.claim: On the HandEdit Hand-only test track, GPT-Image-2 has a much higher Interaction score than GPT-Image-1.5 (0.703 vs. 0.435) and also scores higher on structural fidelity (0.780 vs. 0.730). Its GPT-4o VLM score is lower (0.663 vs. 0.765). So the VLM judge ranks the two editors in the opposite order from the interaction-preservation metric.
official.claim_caption: Table 4. Hand-only Embodiment-Aware Metrics and VLM Judgment. Best and second-best model scores are bolded and underlined, respectively.
official.metric: Interaction = 1 - LPIPS on the object-contact region; Struct Fidelity = DINOv2 cosine similarity to the pseudo-GT ROI; VLM = sqrt(SC*PQ) from a GPT-4o judge. All higher-is-better and averaged over the test images. No error bars, seeds or CIs are reported (single run per editor).
official.comparison: GPT-Image-2 vs. GPT-Image-1.5, both evaluated with the same URDF-reference-conditioned prompt template, the same test images and the default API settings
official.falsification_criterion: On the Hand-only test set (or a sizeable random subset of it), GPT-Image-2's Interaction score does not clearly exceed GPT-Image-1.5's (a gap well below ~0.27), or GPT-Image-1.5's VLM score is not higher than GPT-Image-2's. Either result means the reported rank reversal does not hold.

title: Doomed to Re-Annotate, Forever: The ImageNet Story

official.background: Top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet-1k validation set is still the most widely reported number in visual recognition, yet its original 2012 labels are single-label, often wrong, and miss other objects in the image. Earlier relabeling efforts (ReaL, multilabel annotations, ImageNetMultiLabel) kept the original problematic class taxonomy. This paper re-annotates all 50,000 validation images from scratch as multilabel, localized annotations with revised class definitions (ReImageNet / ReGT), and asks how model accuracy and model rankings change when evaluated on corrected labels.
official.method:
Seven trained in-house annotators labeled every ImageNet-1k object that is noticeable at first viewing, with bounding boxes and attributes, assisted by OWLv2 proposals and OpenCLIP top-20 predictions, followed by a verification pass using MLLM predictions localized by SAM3. They report that 3.8% of images contain no ImageNet-1k class (set N, excluded from evaluation), 33.3% are multilabel, and about 12% of the original labels are incorrect.

Evaluation uses top-1 ReaL-style accuracy (Eq. 1): a model's single prediction counts as correct if it lies in the image's ReGT label set extended with equivalent class pairs (e.g. laptop = notebook computer). The same models are scored on the same 48,114 images (A\N) against the original labels (ImGT) and against ReGT. Models: MLLMs (GPT-5.4, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-it, Gemma-4-31B-it) prompted open-world with free-text answers mapped to classes via a text encoder (Qwen3-Embedding-8B / SigLIP 2 text encoder), zero-shot VLMs (SigLIP so400M/14-384, SigLIP 2 so400M/16-384, SigLIP 2 ViT-g-opt-384), DINOv3 ViT-7B with k-NN (k=11), and supervised ImageNet classifiers (EfficientNetV2-XL, EfficientNet-L2, EVA-02 ViT-L-14-448 from timm).
official.claim: On the 48,114 ImageNet-1k validation images with at least one valid class, switching from the original labels to ReGT raises top-1 accuracy much more for language-supervised models (Gemma 4: 69.48 -> 74.87, +5.39; Qwen3-VL +6.09; SigLIP2 +2.61) than for supervised ImageNet classifiers (EffNet-L2 +0.70; EVA-02: 91.33 -> 91.38, +0.05).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Recognition accuracy Acc on image categories defined in Fig. 4 for MLLMs (top), VLMs (middle) and supervised models (bottom). Subscripts denote the number of images in a category. Images in N contain no valid ImageNet-1k class and are excluded from evaluation. Increase in accuracy on ReGT with respect to ImGT is shown for A\N48114.
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%) on A\N (48,114 images), higher is better; correct if the prediction is in the label set (ReGT labels plus equivalent classes, or the original label for ImGT). Single run, no error bars or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: Same model, same images: accuracy against ImGT vs. against ReGT; compared across model families (MLLMs and VLMs vs. supervised ImageNet models).
official.falsification_criterion: Using the released ReGT labels, the ImGT->ReGT gain for an open MLLM (Gemma 4 or Qwen3-VL) or zero-shot SigLIP 2 is not clearly larger than for EVA-02 / EfficientNet-L2 (e.g. the language-supervised gain falls below ~1.5 points, or the supervised models gain comparably).

title: InstructVVT: Instruction-Driven Video Virtual Try-On without Auxiliary Spatial Priors

official.background: Video virtual try-on replaces the clothing of a person in a video with a reference garment, and must keep identity, body shape, motion, camera, background and temporal coherence intact. Existing video try-on systems get their editing control from auxiliary spatial priors such as human or garment masks, parsing maps, DensePose, skeletons or garment lines. These come from external estimators or manual annotation, which can fail on in-the-wild videos with occlusion, large camera motion or several people. General instruction-guided video editors avoid these priors, but they tend to drift from the reference garment and change regions that should stay the same.
official.method:
InstructVVT is a latent video Diffusion Transformer (Wan2.1-style backbone) whose only inputs at inference are the source video, a reference garment image and a natural-language instruction. It uses three conditioning pathways. (1) The source-video VAE latent is concatenated channel-wise with the noisy latent before a widened patch embedding; the new channels are zero-initialized. (2) A Qwen3-VL-8B MLLM with LoRA and learnable query tokens reads four sampled source frames, the garment and the instruction. An MLP connector projects the query-token hidden states into 'edit tokens', which replace the T5 text embeddings in DiT cross-attention. (3) The VAE-encoded garment passes through a separate garment patch embedding, and the resulting tokens are concatenated with the video tokens in DiT self-attention, then discarded before decoding.

Training runs three supervised flow-matching stages on TripVVT-10K, 10K synthesized ViViD video triplets and about 100K synthesized image triplets (8 H100s, 60K steps in total, batch 1). DiffusionNFT post-training follows (180 steps, batch 30, 40 H100s). Its reward is the expected 0-5 score computed from the first-token logits of the score tokens of a frozen Qwen3-VL-32B prompted with a try-on rubric, normalized to [0, 1]. Evaluation on TripVVT-Bench uses 100 in-the-wild videos (49 frames, 832x480) with MLLM-generated instructions. title: Harness the Memory: A Holistic Evaluation of Memory Substrates in Memory Agents
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (M5 confirmed as best fixed substrate in Table 12, page 37)

official.background: Long-horizon LLM agents need persistent memory, and many memory designs exist: vector indices, gist records, note graphs, knowledge graphs, hierarchical trees, distilled strategies, LoRA adapters and KV-cache or full-context buffers. Published systems are usually evaluated on one or two dialogue benchmarks, with different backbones and pipelines. That makes it hard to tell which storage medium (the 'substrate') should be used in which regime. This paper holds the harness, backbone, prompts, auxiliary LLM and judge fixed and varies only the memory substrate, across user-centric QA (LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, MemoryAgentBench) and agent-centric tasks (ALFWorld, BigCodeBench-Hard).
official.method:
The paper implements 11 memory methods (M1-M11) in one harness. Every substrate that embeds text uses text-embedding-3-small, and GPT-4o-mini is the auxiliary LLM for memory writing and management. M1 is dense-vector top-k over utterances and M2 is BM25 top-k (both k=10 on LoCoMo). M3 is a ReadAgent-style gist index: an LLM picks which pages to expand. M4 is A-Mem evolving notes. M5 is a LightRAG dual-level graph: at write time GPT-4o-mini extracts entities and relations into a KG next to a chunk vector index, and at read time 'mix' mode fuses KG traversal with dense chunk search by reciprocal rank fusion. M6 is a RAPTOR collapsed tree and M8 is MemSkill-style skill bundles read by a zero-shot LLM. M9 is a LoRA adapter (r=8) trained on auxiliary QA pairs, M10 is the full context truncated at the window, and M11 is an EpiCache-style episode re-prefill.

For the claim, each substrate ingests the 10 LoCoMo dialogues and answers all 1,986 questions with the Qwen3-8B backbone (vLLM, temperature 0). The metric P4 is the fraction of answers that GPT-4o-mini, as a judge with fixed templates, labels correct. Each substrate keeps the hyperparameters of its reference implementation, so retrieved-token budgets differ across substrates.
official.claim: On LoCoMo (1,986 questions) with Qwen3-8B, the LightRAG-style dual-level graph substrate M5 reaches LLM-judge accuracy P4 = 0.648. That is above all 9 other substrates; the next best are full context M10 at 0.589, gist index M3 at 0.562 and dense vector M1 at 0.561.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Memory substrates on LoCoMo, LME-S, and MAB (LRU, TTL, CR). P4 ↑: LLM-judge score; E15 ↓: per-query latency (s). Within each model band, green and red mark the per-column best and worst; bold marks the per-model P4 winner on each benchmark.
official.metric: P4: GPT-4o-mini LLM-judge accuracy (higher is better), single greedy run. No CI for this cell. Appendix E.1 states that rerun variation is at most 0.02 on the [0,1] scale (M2 and M10 reproduce bit for bit).
official.comparison: M5 (dual-level KG + vector graph) vs. M1 dense vector, M2 BM25, M3 gist index, M4 evolving notes, M6 hierarchical tree, M8 skill bundles, M9 LoRA adapter, M10 full context, M11 episode re-prefill. Same backbone, auxiliary LLM, encoder, prompts and judge.
official.falsification_criterion: On LoCoMo with Qwen3-8B, M5's P4 is not higher than every other substrate's P4, or its lead over the best other substrate (the paper reports M10 at 0.589) is 0.02 or less, i.e., inside the reported rerun variation.

title: ChainSpace: A Chained-Reasoning Paradigm for Spatial Intelligence

official.background: Spatial-intelligence benchmarks and training sets for multimodal LLMs usually pose independent question-answer pairs about a video, which lets models answer from local cues or priors without keeping a coherent picture of the scene. The paper argues that spatial reasoning should instead be posed as chains of dependent questions over a shared spatial state, so that later answers must stay consistent with constraints established earlier, and that such chained supervision is a more data-efficient training signal.
official.method:
ChainSpace-Pipeline generates training data in simulation: ProcTHOR houses, AI2-THOR exploration trajectories, and for each trajectory four 3-round question chains (object count, appearance order, relative direction, route plan) whose later rounds depend on earlier answers. About 50K chained samples are used to fully fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (ViT frozen, 1 epoch, lr 1e-7, DFT loss, 8x H20).

Evaluation uses ChainSpace-Bench (326 real RoomTour3D videos, 1,304 three-round chains, human-annotated) scored by per-question accuracy and a weighted Chain-Aware Score that rewards pairwise and full-chain correctness. The key control (Table 5) is an Independent-QA model trained on the same videos, questions and answers with the previous ground-truth answer pasted into each later question, so only the cross-round dependency structure differs.
official.claim: Holding backbone, videos, questions, answers and training configuration fixed, chained supervision improves Qwen3-VL-8B on ChainSpace-Bench (avg. question accuracy 0.3344 -> 0.3510, Chain-Aware Score 0.1522 -> 0.1687) whereas the de-chained Independent-QA control does not (0.3236, 0.1482), and the chained model also beats the control on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and MindCube.
official.claim_caption: Controlled comparison of different training paradigms on ChainSpace-Bench and external spatial reasoning benchmarks. All settings use the same backbone. Independent-QA uses the same videos, questions, answers, supervision content, and training configuration as ChainSpace-Pipeline, while removing cross-round dependencies.
official.metric: ChainSpace-Bench avg. question accuracy and Chain-Aware Score; VSI-Bench (MRA/Acc), MMSI-Bench (Acc), MindCube (Acc)
official.comparison: ChainSpace-Pipeline-8B vs. Independent-QA Control (8B) vs. untuned Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
official.falsification_criterion: Chained-trained model does not exceed the Independent-QA control on ChainSpace-Bench Chain-Aware Score, or the difference is within run-to-run variance across seeds.

title: Conditional Evaluation of Language Models with Cheap Auxiliary Signals
claim_source: Table 2, page 10 (per-cell results in Tables 3-26, Appendix G, pages 21-28)

official.background: Aggregate benchmark accuracy hides where an LLM succeeds or fails, so evaluators increasingly want conditional performance profiles: accuracy as a function of a metadata axis such as difficulty level, grade or question length. Estimating such a profile from gold labels alone is noisy when only a few items can be graded. Cheap signals such as LLM-judge scores, pairwise comparisons against anchor models, self-reported confidence and judge disagreement can be collected for every item, but they are often biased or miscalibrated, so using them as substitute labels changes what is being estimated. The paper asks how to use such signals to reduce variance without introducing bias into the conditional profile.
official.method:
For candidate model m, item i has a profiling covariate Z_i (e.g. MATH-500 difficulty), gold correctness Y_im (observed only on a uniformly random labeled subset L of size n out of a pool T of M = 500 items) and a K = 6 cheap-signal vector S_im observed for all items: mean of 3 pointwise judge scores, variance of those scores, three pairwise win/tie scores vs. anchors (Ministral 3B, Claude Haiku 3, Claude Opus 4.6; both orderings averaged), and self-reported confidence. The judge is Claude Opus 4.6. Each signal is standardized within each benchmark/model pair. LACE estimates the profile at z as theta_hat(z) = Ybar_L(z) - beta_hat(z)^T {Sbar_L(z) - Sbar_T(z)}, where the bars are Gaussian-kernel-weighted local means over L or T, and beta_hat(z) = {Sigma_SS(z) + lambda I}^{-1} Sigma_SY(z) is a local ridge coefficient (Sigma_SS computed on the full pool T, Sigma_SY on L). Fixed hyperparameters: lambda = 0.3, bandwidth h = b = 1.5 x 1.06 sd(Z) M^{-1/5}, no per-cell tuning. All eight benchmarks use Gaussian smoothing: the ordered discrete axes (MATH-500 level, ScienceQA grade, GSM8K solution steps) are first jittered to Z_i = g_i + U_i with U_i ~ Uniform(-0.4, 0.4); the other five use token length directly (Appendix H).

Evaluation: 8 benchmarks (MATH-500, ScienceQA, MMLU, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, ARC; 500 items each, profiling axes in Table 1) x 3 candidates (Claude Haiku 3, Ministral 3B, Qwen3 32B) = 24 cells. For each cell, B = 100 random permutations give nested labeled sets of n in {50, 100, 200}, shared by all methods. The target is the full-pool gold kernel profile on a grid of 20 points spanning the 5th-95th percentiles of Z. RE = mean naive MSE / mean method MSE over splits (naive = kernel mean of gold labels in L). Baselines include logistic plug-in estimators (judge-only and multi-signal with Z), augmented plug-in, global CV, per-signal CV, scalar prediction CV (PPI++-style), Local PPI, PPCI and StratPPI, all fit with logistic C = 1.
official.claim: Across 24 benchmark-model cells and label budgets n in {50, 100, 200} (pool M = 500), LACE achieves an overall geometric-mean relative efficiency over the gold-label-only kernel estimator of 5.528 [5.181, 5.898], versus 2.647 [2.277, 3.078] for the strongest baseline (multi-signal logistic plug-in), and is best in all 72 cells.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Overall results. Entries are geometric-mean RE [95% MC CI] across the 24 benchmark-model cells at each label budget; Overall aggregates all 72 cells. Each cell is a ratio of mean MSEs over the same B = 100 label splits. Intervals apply the paired delta method within each cell; budget columns combine cellwise log-RE variances across independent cells, and the Overall column treats the three nested budgets within each cell jointly, using the label-split permutation as the joint resampling unit, so its variance includes the cross-budget covariances induced by the nested prefixes. Target: realized full-pool gold kernel profile; randomness: matched L-draws conditional on T.
official.metric: Relative efficiency (ratio of mean profile MSE of the naive estimator to that of the method over the same 100 label splits; higher is better), aggregated as a geometric mean over cells; brackets are 95% Monte Carlo confidence intervals from a paired delta method over label splits, conditional on the fixed item pool.
official.comparison: LACE (feasible) vs. Plug-in (judge), Plug-in (multi), Aug. plug-in, Global CV, Per-signal CV, Residual-only, Scalar prediction CV, Local PPI, PPCI, StratPPI, all on identical labeled subsets and signals.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same signals, label budgets and fixed hyperparameters, LACE's overall geometric-mean RE is not clearly above the multi-signal plug-in's (e.g. the 95% intervals overlap), or the plug-in or another baseline beats LACE in a substantial number of the 72 cells.

title: Beyond Suspicious Steps: Ontological Trust in Long-Horizon Agents
claim_source: Figure 5, page 9 (cross-model means in Table 39, page 44)

official.background: LLM agents running long multi-step tasks can drift away from what the user authorized without any single step looking wrong: each tool call is legitimate, but the trajectory gradually takes on a broader role, pursues an adjacent goal, or relies on evidence the user never gave. Existing monitors check rule compliance per step (AgentSpec), judge safety from a step or short window (R-Judge), give a verdict on the full record (AgentAuditor), or run a structured multi-agent defense (MAS-Shield). None of them directly estimates whether the current trajectory prefix still corresponds to the delegated task, which is what this paper calls ontological trust.
official.method:
RGE is an online monitor. A one-time setup pass (two LLM calls before the trajectory starts) turns the task into a set of completion gaps (core/support, each with closure evidence) and a compact task-domain profile for the parser. At each step, one LLM call parses the current action-observation pair (conditioned on the task, prior prefix and a task memory) into typed fields; everything after that is deterministic. The fields are combined with fixed weights into Role, Goal and Evidence consistency scores, whose complements form a deviation vector z_t = (r_t, g_t, e_t). An instantaneous score u_t = α_r r_t + α_g g_t + α_e e_t + λφ_t (φ_t a geometric-mean coupling term active only when all three axes exceed 0.40; λ = 0.25) is accumulated as s_t = γ s_{t-1} + u_t plus a short-horizon EMA. A trajectory is flagged if u_t or s_t crosses its threshold or a step is labeled reanchor/contain, with all thresholds set by one sensitivity κ = 0.5, fixed across domains and models.

The evaluation corpus has 248 trajectories built from 80 source tasks in OSWorld, FinanceBench and EICU-AC, all generated by Claude Opus 4.6 as the actor: 80 benign reference executions, 81 prefix-paired drift variants (role-drift, role-expansion, goal-rewrite, latent hijacking, evidence fracture; benign prefix then divergence at an annotated onset step) and 87 pseudo-consistency variants. Each monitor replays trajectories step by step and a trajectory is positive if any step raises an alarm. Baselines (AgentSpec, R-Judge with k=1 and k=3 steps of context, AgentAuditor on the full record, MAS-Shield) run under their default decision rules with the same estimator LLM (GPT-4o, Qwen3.5-9B or Gemma-4-E4B-it). Metrics: Drift F1 on drift trajectories, Pseudo F1 on pseudo-consistency trajectories, and Benign Coverage = 1 - FPR on benign trajectories, each averaged over the three benchmarks.
official.claim: With Qwen3.5-9B as the estimator and averaged over OSWorld, FinanceBench and EICU-AC, RGE reaches 96.70% Drift F1 at 97.33% Benign Coverage, while the best baseline that keeps benign coverage above 95% (AgentAuditor) reaches 35.60% Drift F1, and MAS-Shield reaches 65.20% Drift F1 only at 4.93% Benign Coverage; the same pattern holds with GPT-4o (97.93% vs. at most 45.37%).
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Benchmark-averaged baseline comparison under default protocols. Cells report Drift F1, Pseudo F1, and Benign Coverage by monitor and estimator setting (Appendix E.9).
official.metric: Drift F1 (%) on prefix-paired drift trajectories and Benign Coverage (%) = 1 - false-positive rate on benign trajectories, both higher is better, averaged over three benchmarks; single run, no error bars or seeds reported for this comparison
official.comparison: RGE vs. AgentSpec, R-Judge (k=1), R-Judge (k=3), AgentAuditor and MAS-Shield, each using the same estimator LLM on the same 248 trajectories under its default decision rule
official.falsification_criterion: On a rebuilt corpus of prefix-paired drift and benign trajectories with Qwen3.5-9B (or GPT-4o) as the estimator, RGE's Drift F1 is not at least ~30 points above the best baseline whose Benign Coverage is ≥ 95%, or RGE's Benign Coverage falls well below 95%.

title: EditBridge: Towards Faithful and Efficient Ultra-High-Resolution Image Editing

official.background: Diffusion-based instruction image editors such as Qwen-Image-Edit and FLUX Kontext run at about 1K resolution or below, because attention cost grows quadratically with token count. The usual way to get 2K or 4K edits is to edit at low resolution and then apply a separate super-resolution model. That model never sees the original high-resolution source, so it invents textures that contradict the source in unedited regions and produces over-smoothed or over-sharpened artifacts. The paper asks whether the HR source can be used during upscaling, faithfully and cheaply.
official.method:
EditBridge is a two-stage pipeline built on Qwen-Image-Edit. Stage 1 edits the downsampled source at low resolution with the pretrained model. Stage 2 is a diffusion (Brownian) bridge whose start point is the upsampled LR edit and whose end point is the HR edited image. A DiT, fine-tuned with LoRA (r = 128, all linear layers, Prodigy optimizer), predicts the bridge velocity while the HR source latent is concatenated along the sequence dimension as a condition. Default inference uses one bridge step.

To keep the HR conditioning affordable, Prior-Guided Block-wise Sparse Attention (PG-BSA) takes the argmax target-to-source attention correspondence from the LR editing stage, upsamples it by 2x with nearest-neighbour expansion, and limits each target token's cross-attention to a k x k window of source tokens around its matched anchor. Text, target and source tokens otherwise attend only within their own segment (implemented with VMoBA and FlashAttention). Training data: 5,000 1K/2K pairs and 1,500 4K pairs, with HR sources from Aesthetic-4K/Aesthetic-Train-V2, instructions from Gemini 3 and targets from Nano Banana Pro. Evaluation follows ScaleEdit: HaarPSI against the source over the whole image, masked PSNR/SSIM/MSE on unedited regions, and masked LPIPS on edited regions.
official.claim: At 2K resolution, EditBridge preserves unedited regions better than every SR and HR-editing baseline (mPSNR 18.64 vs. best baseline 17.24 for DiT-SR; mSSIM 0.871 vs. 0.827; mLPIPS 0.390 vs. 0.470 for PiSA-SR) while taking 4.08 s per image vs. 14.82 s for the fastest baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative comparison results. ↑/↓ indicate whether higher/lower values are better. Bold numbers represent the best results.
official.metric: Haar(PSI) up, masked PSNR/SSIM up and MSE down on unedited regions, masked LPIPS down on edited regions, wall-clock time per image (s) down; single numbers, no error bars, seeds or evaluation-set size reported
official.comparison: EditBridge (LR edit + bridge refinement with PG-BSA) vs. LR edit followed by DiT4SR, DiT-SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR; HiFlow; ScaleEdit; and direct HR inference with the base model, at 2K
official.falsification_criterion: On a 2K editing benchmark scored with the ScaleEdit protocol, EditBridge does not beat the best SR baseline (e.g. DiT-SR) on mPSNR by a clear margin (the paper reports +1.4 dB) or is not faster than DiT-SR's LR-edit + SR pipeline.

title: Monroe: A Molecular Foundation Model for In-context Probabilistic Inference
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (adaptation-strategy selection that defines MiniMolPFN is Table 2, page 8)

official.background: Bioassay activity prediction for small molecules is data-limited: wet-lab measurements are expensive, so downstream datasets often have only hundreds of labelled compounds. Molecular foundation models (MFMs) try to solve this by pretraining a general-purpose molecular encoder and adapting it to each small downstream task, conventionally by training a task-specific MLP head on the embeddings or by fine-tuning the encoder. Both adaptation routes fit free parameters on very little data and need per-task hyperparameter choices, which is exactly the regime where overfitting bites. The paper asks whether a prior-data-fitted tabular model (TabPFN), which performs amortized in-context prediction in a single forward pass with no gradient updates, is a better downstream adapter — and whether that holds for existing MFMs, not just for the authors' own model.
official.method:
The paper introduces Monroe, a sparse GRIT graph transformer (the paper gives no parameter count) pretrained on 81M PM6 molecules plus 1.56M PCBA bioassay molecules over 1152 tasks, with uncertainty-weighted multi-task loss balancing, a conformer-denoising objective, embedding decorrelation, and stereochemistry-aware graph rewiring. For downstream use the encoder is frozen: embeddings z = f(G) of the labelled support molecules, together with their labels, are passed to TabPFN as an in-context training set, and TabPFN returns a posterior-predictive distribution for each test molecule in one forward pass.

The claim selected here concerns the downstream-adaptation half of that pipeline applied to an existing model. The authors take MiniMol, a published MFM, and compare three adaptation strategies on the same 28 Polaris tasks (Table 2): its Native adaptation (the adaptation originally proposed for that model; for MiniMol, Table 10 states this is frozen features plus a trained residual-MLP head, selected on best validation loss, up to 50 epochs with patience 5), frozen pretrained embeddings fed to TabPFN (PT_PFN), and embeddings from an encoder fine-tuned on the downstream task fed to TabPFN (FT_PFN). For MiniMol specifically, Native and PT_PFN therefore consume the same frozen encoder embeddings and differ only in the predictor placed on top. PT_PFN wins within-model (92.9% vs 57.1% for Native), so MiniMol PT_PFN is carried forward as a new method named MiniMolPFN and evaluated against all other methods on Polaris (28 tasks) and MoleculeACE (30 activity-cliff regression tasks) in Table 1. All methods are run by the authors on identical splits and seeds, and winners per task are decided by Tukey HSD plus Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control at alpha = 0.05.
official.claim: On the 30 MoleculeACE activity-cliff tasks, swapping MiniMol's native adaptation for TabPFN in-context prediction over the same frozen MiniMol embeddings (MiniMolPFN) lowers overall RMSE from 0.703 ± 0.018 to 0.642 ± 0.004 and raises the win rate from 10.0% to 70.0%; on the 28 Polaris tasks it raises the win rate from 42.9% to 75.0% and improves mean leaderboard rank from 11.39 to 5.82.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Model performance on Polaris and MoleculeACE. Error bars report the mean standard deviation across seeds.
official.metric: MoleculeACE overall RMSE (lower is better), averaged over the 30 tasks; ± is the paper's 'mean standard deviation across seeds', defined in Appendix D as the per-task standard deviation across seeds averaged over tasks (deliberately not a standard error of the mean), so it measures typical per-task run-to-run spread rather than uncertainty on the 30-task average. The seed variance has different sources per arm: for native MiniMol it is 5 fine-tuning/head-training seeds with an 80/20 train-val split, for MiniMolPFN it is TabPFN's internal random state; Win % is the fraction of tasks on which a method is best or statistically indistinguishable from the best under Tukey HSD + Benjamini-Hochberg FDR at alpha = 0.05 across all seven compared methods; Polaris Rank is mean rank on the consolidated leaderboard (Table 8), reported without error bars

title: Manifold Drift in Flow Preference Optimization: A Root Cause of Reward Hacking

official.background: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has been adapted to flow-matching image generators (FlowDPO) by replacing log-likelihoods with flow-matching regression errors on winner and loser samples. Reported side effects include degraded image quality and reward hacking. The paper argues that the cause is 'manifold drift': the preference update changes the transport trajectories, so generated samples can leave the support of the pretrained model (e.g. raising an OCR reward while visual quality collapses). It asks whether a preference objective can shift mass toward preferred regions while keeping samples on the pretrained data manifold.
official.method:
THERMODPO-weighted (Eq. 11) adds a winner-side anchor to FlowDPO. With per-sample flow-matching errors l = ||v(x_t,t) - (x_1 - x_0)||^2 and Delta = l_theta - l_ref for the winner (w) and loser (l), the loss is E[ tau(t) * log(1 + exp((Delta_w - Delta_l)/tau(t)) + exp((1-t)^2 * l_theta^w / tau(t))) ], with temperature schedule tau(t) = t/beta. The first two terms are a temperature-scaled FlowDPO loss; the third is a reconstruction anchor on the preferred sample that is strongest near the data endpoint (t = 0). Time convention: t = 0 is data, t = 1 is noise.

Toy benchmark (Sec. 5.1, App. E.1): data lie on the surface z = f(x,y) = [1.2 exp(-(x-3)^2) + 1.2 exp(-(x+3)^2) - 0.9 exp(-x^2)] * (1 - 0.15 y^2), x in [-5,5], y in [-1,1]. Points with |x +/- 3| < 1 are preferred, |x| < 1 dispreferred. A reference flow-matching model (3-layer MLP, hidden 128, SiLU) is pretrained for 10K steps (batch 512, Adam, lr 1e-3). Each method is then fine-tuned from this reference on the same winner/loser pairs for 10K steps (batch 512, Adam, lr 1e-4, grad clip 1.0) and evaluated on 10,000 samples. title: Grounded-Exo2Ego: Structured Semantic Grounding for Robust Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (std in Table 4, Appendix B.1, page 17)

official.background: Exo-to-ego video generation takes one third-person (exocentric) video plus a target first-person camera trajectory and generates the corresponding egocentric video. It is useful for AR/VR and for turning third-person footage into first-person training data for robots. It is much harder than ordinary novel-view synthesis: the usual conditioning signal, a rendering of a monocular 3D reconstruction from the target camera, is full of holes and distortions at the ego viewpoint, and ground-truth ego cameras calibrated to the real world are misaligned with the monocular reconstruction. The prior method in this exact setting, EgoX, relies mainly on that geometric rendering.
official.method:
The model is LTX-2.3 fine-tuned with rank-256 LoRA on self- and cross-attention. Geometric anchoring: exo depth from MoGe-2 is lifted to a mesh and rasterized at the ego camera; the rendering and exo video are VAE-encoded and appended as extra tokens along the sequence dimension (IC-LoRA style; render tokens share the noisy latent's (f, x, y) RoPE coordinates per Sec. 3.4, though Appendix D.1 says they are x-shifted by the ego width, near-blank tokens are masked out). Ego cameras are re-localized into the MoGe-2 reconstruction via a non-rigid alignment to a Depth-Anything-3 multi-view reconstruction (only camera depth changes). Output is 33 frames at 448x448.

Semantic grounding (the contribution tested here): a VLM (CapRL-Qwen3VL-4B) captions the first frame of each clip (Appendix D.2: captioning covers all ego and exo cameras, and ego phrases are prioritized when the noun phrases are unioned); Gemma-3-12B deduplicates and ranks the object phrases by relevance to the camera wearer, and the top K=10 are kept; each phrase is encoded by Gemma-3, padded to L=10 tokens with shared learned registers, and projected into the DiT cross-attention space. SAM3 segments each phrase in the first exo frame and the masks are reprojected into the ego view. In cross-attention, a video token may attend to object k's token packet only if it lies inside object k's mask (ego tokens use the reprojected ego mask, exo tokens the exo mask); all tokens still attend to the full scene caption. During training the reprojected masks are replaced by ground-truth ego masks with probability 0.5. Table 2 compares 'Ours (no obj tok, mask, synth)' (geometry-only, same data, re-localization and sequence concat) against 'Ours (no synth)' (adds object tokens and mask gating), both trained on real EgoExo4D data only and evaluated on EgoX's New Action and Unseen splits.
official.claim: With backbone, real training data, camera re-localization and sequence-concat conditioning held fixed, adding mask-gated object tokens raises object IoU from 0.374 ± 0.007 to 0.418 ± 0.004 on EgoExo4D Unseen and from 0.501 ± 0.005 to 0.569 ± 0.005 on New Action, and raises PSNR from 15.67 to 16.00 dB (Unseen) and 17.69 to 18.39 dB (New Action).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Ablation studies on EgoExo4D. TOP: the components each variant uses. BOTTOM: results, averaged over five independent generations (standard deviations in Appendix B.1). Loc Err and Contour are normalized by the image side length. Bracketed EgoX values are the two metrics its paper does not report, which we measured ourselves. Rows marked * are our own re-implementations of EgoX, ported to the LTX-2.3 backbone so that the comparison isolates one component at a time; EgoX's released code targets a different backbone, so these were rebuilt to the best of our ability from the paper and the reference implementation, and they may understate what the original authors would achieve. The unmarked EgoX row carries the numbers reported in their paper.
official.metric: Object IoU (higher is better, SAM2-Large masks matched by DINOv3 + Hungarian, EgoX protocol); also Loc Err, Contour Chamfer (lower is better), PSNR (higher). Mean over 5 independent generations of one trained model; ± is std across those generations (not across training seeds).
official.comparison: Ours (no synth) [object tokens + object mask gating] vs. Ours (no obj tok, mask, synth) [geometry-only], same LTX-2.3 backbone, data, re-localization and conditioning. Also reported: Ours (no obj mask, synth) with ungated object tokens, and the full model with synthetic data.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both variants under matched settings, the grounded model's object IoU on Unseen and New Action is not higher than the geometry-only model's by more than the run-to-run spread (or the gap is much smaller than ~0.04-0.07 IoU), or PSNR does not improve.

title: Evaluating Multimodal Narrative Understanding of Popular Hollywood Films
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (discussed in Section 5.2, 'Vision is not sufficient for film narrative understanding')

official.background: Multimodal language models are starting to be used for computational analysis of film, but benchmarks built on Hollywood films are unstable because of copyright: clips get taken down and YouTube links rot. The authors build a collection of 61 popular (top-100 by Variety box office for their year) sound films from 1929-1963 that are likely in the US public domain, verified against copyright registration and renewal records, and write a 4-way multiple-choice benchmark about long-form narrative (temporality, plot, character, setting, perspective, representation, symbolism, object identification). The question is how well current video, vision-language and audio-visual models understand whole films.
official.method:
Co-authors watched each film and wrote 779 four-option MCQs, referring to scenes by plain-language description rather than timestamps. To remove questions answerable from memory, all questions were posed to Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT 5.5 with only the film title and year; questions were added in ascending order of how many of the three models answered them correctly until the average closed-book accuracy reached about 25%, leaving the benchmark B of 628 questions. Human experts reach 82.0% on a 133-question sample.

Several paradigms are compared on B. End-to-end: vision-language models get 256 uniformly sampled frames (no audio); the audio-visual setting gives Gemini 3 Flash the full video including the audio track. Socratic (two-stage): Gemini 3 Flash is the captioner and produces either frame captions (from a 0.5-fps frame strip, no audio) or clip captions (from shot-boundary-respecting ~60-second video chunks that include audio, shots detected with TransNetV2); the timestamped captions are concatenated into a chronological history and given, with the question, to a QA backbone (Qwen3-VL-8B, GPT-5-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5 or Gemini 3 Flash). The metric is accuracy, with the widest 95% Wald CI reported as ±3.9 pp.
official.claim: Holding the QA backbone fixed in the Socratic pipeline, replacing Gemini 3 Flash frame captions (no audio) with clip captions (with audio) raises accuracy on the 628-question benchmark from 36.8% to 48.1% for GPT-5-mini, 35.0% to 45.9% for Claude Haiku 4.5, and 46.0% to 58.9% for Gemini 3 Flash; end-to-end, Gemini 3 Flash on the full video with audio scores 61.1% vs. 39.3% with 256 frames.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Accuracy on B. The largest 95% Wald confidence interval is ±3.9%. Bold indicates best overall; underline marks the within-subgroup leader significantly better than the runner-up (whose 95% CIs do not overlap).
official.metric: 4-way MCQ accuracy (%) on B (628 questions, chance 25%), higher is better; single run per configuration, no seeds; the paper reports only that the widest 95% Wald (binomial) confidence interval is ±3.9 pp
official.comparison: Socratic frame-based captions vs. clip-based captions with the same QA backbone (GPT-5-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash); and Gemini 3 Flash end-to-end with 256 frames vs. full video with audio
official.falsification_criterion: For any of GPT-5-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5 or Gemini 3 Flash, Socratic clip-caption accuracy does not exceed frame-caption accuracy by more than ~8 pp (i.e., the 95% CIs overlap), or Gemini 3 Flash full-video accuracy is within the CI of its 256-frame accuracy.

title: Guidance For Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation
claim_source: Table 2 (Appendix H), page 20; summarized in Figure 2, page 8

official.background: Amortized simulation-based inference (SBI) trains a neural posterior estimator on simulations drawn from a fixed training prior p(θ). When scientists change the prior to q(θ), the trained model's posterior is wrong, and re-simulating and retraining is expensive. PriorGuide adapts a diffusion-based SBI model at test time by adding a guidance term to its score, but it approximates the prior ratio with a Gaussian mixture and the reverse transition kernel with a Gaussian, which biases the result, especially when q has little overlap with p.
official.method:
The base model is a Simformer (score-based diffusion, VP-SDE) trained on 50,000 simulations from p(θ). The guided score is s_ϕ(θ_t, x, t) + ∇_θt log q(θ_t, x)/p(θ_t, x). The joint log ratio over diffused states is learned by a small network a_ψ(θ_t, x, t) (4-layer MLP, width 256, SiLU, Fourier time embedding) with a density-ratio-estimation loss (NRE: logistic classification, or KLIEP). Samples from q(θ_t, x) are never drawn; instead the q-side expectation is replaced by an importance-weighted expectation over p-samples with weight r(θ_0) = q(θ_0)/p(θ_0) (Proposition 1), so no new simulator calls are needed. Training data: the 50,000 original pairs plus 420,000 base-model posterior samples (1,000 for each of 420 observations), AdamW, batch 4,096, lr 3e-4, 10,000 iterations. At sampling time the gradient ∇_θt a_ψ is added at each of 25 reverse-SDE steps, with no Langevin correction.

Baselines under the same setting (frozen base model, no new simulations, prior change seen only through q/p): PriorGuide (50-component diagonal GMM fit to the log prior ratio, 4 Langevin corrections per step) and WSM (same MLP and data, learns an additive score correction by prior-ratio-weighted denoising score matching). Gaussian Linear 6D: x | θ ~ N(θ, 0.1 I_6). OOD regime: training prior p = N(0, -0.1·1 1ᵀ + 1.1 I_6), target prior q = N(1.1·1, 0.2·1 1ᵀ + 0.8 I_6); the ground-truth posterior is closed form. Evaluation: 10 observations drawn from the target marginal, 5,000 posterior samples per method per run, 3 runs per observation, C2ST against 5,000 ground-truth samples.
official.claim: On Gaussian Linear 6D with an out-of-distribution prior shift, DRE-based guidance (NRE) reaches C2ST 0.58 ± 0.05 against the analytic target posterior, vs. 0.69 ± 0.08 for PriorGuide and 0.67 ± 0.06 for WSM (unguided Simformer 0.70 ± 0.06); MMD is 0.02 vs. 0.06 for both baselines.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Posterior inference performance (θ) under prior shift. Mean (standard dev.) over 10 simulated observations, where each observation's value is averaged over 3 independent runs. Bold indicates the best result or one not significantly worse than the best (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired by observation, p > 0.05). Gray rows are shown for reference only and are excluded from the comparison. All evaluation metrics are computed using 5,000 posterior samples per method run: C2ST, MMD, and W2 are calculated between these 5,000 generated samples and 5,000 reference (ground-truth) posterior samples, while RMSE is computed between the 5,000 generated samples and the true parameters θ*.
official.metric: C2ST accuracy (lower is better, 0.5 = indistinguishable from the true posterior); mean (std) over 10 observations, each averaged over 3 runs. The std is the spread across observations, not seeds. Bold = best or not significantly worse by a one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p > 0.05).
official.comparison: Ours (NRE) and Ours (KLIEP) vs. PriorGuide and WSM, all with the same frozen Simformer, same data and same sampler; Simformer without adaptation as a reference
official.falsification_criterion: With the stated priors, NRE-guided C2ST on Gaussian Linear 6D OOD is not lower than both PriorGuide's and WSM's by more than about 0.05 (one across-observation std), or a paired test across observations finds no significant difference from the better baseline.

title: AutoSaddler: Automatic Harness Optimization with Durable Updates from Agent Execution Traces

official.background: LLM agents often fail on long-horizon tasks because small local errors compound over many steps. The external 'harness' around the model (system prompts, tool definitions and implementations, and runtime control logic such as hooks and the agent loop) can strongly affect reliability, but designing it by hand is slow and has to be redone for each new model or domain. Prior automatic methods either optimize only the prompt (GEPA) or let a coding agent edit the whole harness freely (Meta-Harness). This paper asks whether an offline, mini-batch optimization loop driven by diagnosis of failed execution traces can produce harness changes that generalize to unseen task groups.
official.method:
AutoSaddler treats the harness as code with three parameter groups (prompt, tool, middleware). Each iteration runs the current harness on a small mini-batch of training tasks (the paper reports six training-scenario executions per iteration, and an epoch over the 75 train tasks spans 25 iterations). A Claude Agent SDK 'Diagnosis-Patch' agent then reads the mini-batch execution traces (failed and successful) and the harness source, and writes a structured patch drawn from a fixed taxonomy (prompt-rule, new-tool, tool-argument, implementation, tool-description, PreToolUse hook, infrastructure and agent-loop changes). The schedule is phased: one epoch of 'capability' (code) patches, then 'steering' (text) patches. The patch is kept as a candidate only if it improves the same mini-batch, and only then is it evaluated on the dev set. A Reflection agent records fixed/regressed/still-failing/still-passing lessons in a DAG of past harnesses (EvoDAG), and an Evolution agent proposes the next harness by selecting from or merging earlier candidates. After the budget runs out (2 epochs on GAIA2), the candidate with the best dev score is evaluated once on the test set.

On GAIA2 the base harness is the default ReAct agent in Meta's ARE environment, and Claude Opus 4.6 serves as both task agent and optimizer. The splits are by persona Universe: train is Universe 29 (75 tasks), dev is Universe 30 (65), and test is Universes 21/22/27 (107/112/81). Success is judged by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, following the GAIA2 protocol. GEPA (system-prompt evolution) and Meta-Harness (an unconstrained coding agent over the repository, trained on train ∪ dev with at least as many task executions) are adapted to GAIA2 by the authors. Each method runs one optimization, and the selected harness is executed three times on the test set.
official.claim: On held-out GAIA2 Universes 21, 22 and 27 (300 tasks) with Claude Opus 4.6 as the agent, the AutoSaddler-optimized harness reaches 62.0 ± 1.2 average Pass@1, versus 54.6 ± 2.5 for GEPA, 53.2 ± 2.2 for Meta-Harness and 53.0 ± 1.5 for the default agent.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Test-set Pass@1 results on GAIA2, reported as mean ± standard deviation over three runs. Values in parentheses indicate the number of tasks; boldface denotes the best result.
official.metric: Pass@1 success rate (%) on the test universes, higher is better; ± is std over three repeated test executions of the single harness each method selected (it does not cover optimization-run variance)
official.comparison: AutoSaddler-optimized harness vs. GEPA-optimized and Meta-Harness-optimized harnesses and the unmodified default ReAct agent, all with the same Opus 4.6 task agent and splits
official.falsification_criterion: A re-run AutoSaddler optimization on Universe 29/30, evaluated on Universes 21/22/27, fails to beat the best of the default agent and GEPA by more than their combined test-run spread (e.g. its average Pass@1 is below about 58%), or the default agent re-run on the test universes scores within a few points of the AutoSaddler harness.

title: DPIAgent: Divide, Protocol, Isolate for Agentic Reproduction Test Generation

official.background: Reproduction test generation means writing, from a bug report, a test that fails on the buggy code and passes once the fix is applied. Such tests rarely exist when an issue is first filed, and they are needed to validate automated or human fixes. Current LLM agents (SWE-Agent, OpenHands, TraeAgent and others) handle this in a single loop that mixes exploring the code with writing the test. The authors argue that this mixed objective leads to goal drift: the agent starts editing tests before it understands the root cause.
official.method:
DPIAgent is built on SWE-Agent and splits each run into two phases within one agent context. In Phase 1 (defect exploration), the agent has only file-viewing, bash and graph-based code-search tools over a pre-built repository graph (RPG). It must call ready_to_write_test with a six-field structured summary: bug location, root cause, expected vs. actual behavior, reproduction strategy, reference tests and test plan (Protocol). In Phase 2 (test generation), the full trajectory stays in context, the exploration tools are removed and replaced by edit and bash, and the system prompt is switched (Isolate). The claim below uses no test selection, i.e., a single run per instance with the original issue text.

Evaluation uses SWT-Bench Verified (433 Python instances from SWE-bench) with the official Docker harness. Success rate S is the fraction of instances where the generated tests include at least one fail-to-pass test and no test goes from passing to failing after the golden patch. Change coverage, coverage and TDD coverage are also reported. Every method is run with the same backbone LLM, and each result is averaged over 3 runs. The SWE-Agent baseline uses the SWT-Bench test-generation prompt.
official.claim: On SWT-Bench Verified with GPT-5-Mini as the backbone, adding DPI to SWE-Agent raises the reproduction success rate from 60.12% to 74.28% (+14.16 points) and TDD coverage from 54.29 to 62.22, without test selection.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance results on SWT-Bench Verified. Ours applies DPI on top of SWE-Agent, without test selection. † Results reported from the public leaderboard.
official.metric: Success rate S (% of 433 instances with a valid fail-to-pass test suite, higher is better), averaged over 3 runs. Table 1 gives no error bars. Table 2 (page 7) gives Total F2P counts with ± std over the 3 runs: SWE-Agent 273.7±1.5, DPI 331.0±2.0.
official.comparison: DPIAgent (SWE-Agent + DPI, no test selection) vs. plain SWE-Agent, both with GPT-5-Mini on SWT-Bench Verified. The other baselines in the table (TraeAgent, Mini-SWE-Agent, OpenHands, Claude Code, Aider, Terminus-2) are also given for context.
official.falsification_criterion: With GPT-5-Mini on SWT-Bench Verified, averaged over 3 runs, SWE-Agent + DPI improves success rate over plain SWE-Agent by less than about 5 points, or not at all.

title: DDMS: Discriminative Distillation of Multi-view Foundational Features into Single-view Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (protocol in Appendix D.1, page 23)

official.background: Self-supervised 2D foundation features such as DINOv2 are widely used as dense descriptors, but they are learned from single images. They are not trained to be consistent across viewpoints, and similar-looking but geometrically different regions can end up close in feature space. Earlier 3D-aware fine-tuning methods have two problems. Methods that render features through 3D Gaussians (Fit3D, SnD) smooth features across views and lose local discriminability. A descriptor-style method (MEF) improves matching but weakens semantic transfer. The paper asks whether the internal features of a multi-view geometry model can be distilled into a single-image encoder so that its features become more consistent across views and more distinctive, while staying close to the original DINOv2 feature space.
official.method:
Teacher: DINOv2 features of each view are concatenated with block-19 features of a frozen Depth-Anything-3 Giant model run jointly on N = 4 posed views. A 1x1 conv and a 3x3 conv predict a residual added to the DINOv2 feature. The fusion module and LoRA adapters on DINOv2 are trained (DA3 stays frozen) for 20k steps on ScanNet++ training scenes (AdamW, lr 1e-4) with two losses. The first is a differentiable average-precision ranking loss (Smooth-AP style, temperature 0.01), computed on M = 2 of the 4 views: for each query pixel, candidates in the other view whose 3D point lies within 0.05 m are positives and candidates beyond 0.15 m are negatives, with 1,024 candidates per query filtered for reprojection and visibility validity. The second is a hinge anchor on cosine distance to the frozen DINOv2 feature (delta = 0.2, lambda_anchor = 0.2).

Student: a single-view DINOv2 with rank-32 LoRA and a 3x3 conv head is trained for 20k steps (AdamW, lr 1e-4, cosine schedule). It uses an L1 loss between L2-normalized student and frozen-teacher features on M = 3 views, plus the same ranking loss on the student features, applied to pairs of a reference view and each other view (lambda_disc = 0.2, thresholds 0.05/0.10 m, temperature 0.02, 15-px negative exclusion radius). At test time only the student runs, on one image. Evaluation on ScanNet SuperGlue test pairs (1,500 pairs): dense features are sampled on a 324x242 grid, every grid point with valid depth in view 1 is matched to its nearest neighbor in view 2 (no ratio test), and PCK@10px/20px is computed against ground-truth correspondences from depth and poses.
official.claim: With a DINOv2 ViT-B backbone, the DDMS student reaches PCK@10px of 66.01 and PCK@20px of 78.48 on ScanNet nearest-neighbor geometric correspondence. The strongest 3D-aware baseline built on the same backbone, MEF, reaches 39.17 / 55.06, and frozen DINOv2 reaches 21.72 / 36.11. With ViT-S the numbers are 61.35 / 74.24 for DDMS vs. 38.54 / 54.30 for MEF.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Direct feature evaluation compared with recent 3D-aware feature finetuning methods [69, 68, 50]. Benchmarks cover ScanNet [10] feature separation and geometric correspondence, Navi-Wild [24] object correspondence, SPair-71k [37] semantic keypoint matching, and DAVIS [42] mask propagation. Best and second-best results are highlighted within each backbone group. Our method achieves the best separation, outperforms existing methods by a large margin on ScanNet, and performs strongly in all cases.
official.metric: PCK@10px and PCK@20px (%) of dense nearest-neighbor matches on a 324x242 grid over the ScanNet SuperGlue test pairs; higher is better; no error bars or seeds reported (single run)
official.comparison: DDMS student vs. frozen DINOv2, Fit3D, MEF, SnD and SnD (+blending), all from the same DINOv2 ViT-B (or ViT-S) initialization using released checkpoints, evaluated with the same protocol and input resolution
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained DDMS ViT-B student, evaluated with the same ScanNet protocol, scores below about 50 PCK@10px, or fails to beat the MEF checkpoint by at least 10 points when both are run through the same evaluation code.

title: Joint Optimization of Tool Creation and Use for Large Language Model Agents

official.background: Tool-augmented LLMs are limited to the APIs that humans have written. Tool-creation methods such as LATM, CRAFT, TroVE and KTCE prompt a frozen LLM to write reusable Python tools at inference time. The model that writes the tool is never trained, and nothing pushes it to write schemas that it, or another model, can actually call. The paper asks whether training one model with reinforcement learning to both write and use tools gives tools that generalize better than prompting or distillation.
official.method:
SMITH fine-tunes Qwen3-4B-Instruct (LoRA r=64, alpha=128) with DAPO for 60 gradient steps on 13 Reasoning-Gym task families. Each batch is split evenly between build tasks and use tasks. In a build task the policy sees N=4 easy question-answer pairs and writes a Python function plus an OpenAI-compatible JSON schema. In a use task the policy sees only tool schemas from a tool pool (1 correct tool and 2 distractors) and must call the right tool to answer a question within T=5 turns. Build rewards come in two separate axes: (i) a format reward (0.5 if code and schema are consistent) plus an evaluation reward, which is the fraction of K=16 hard held-out questions answered correctly through the tool by an evaluator model that is periodically synced from the policy; (ii) an LLM-judge quality score (a Qwen3-30B-A3B judge), with -0.5 for a syntax error and the score halved when schema and code disagree. The use reward is final-answer correctness, scaled down as more turns are used. Tool induction uses easy curriculum bands and tool evaluation uses the hardest band.

Evaluation is single-shot build-then-use: one tool is built from easy examples and applied unchanged to hard test questions. A question counts as correct only if the tool is invoked and the answer matches. RG (Unseen) is the macro-average accuracy over 10 Reasoning-Gym tasks never used in RL training. All baselines use Qwen3-4B-Instruct. LATM* is the same build-then-use scaffold with the untrained model and a rewritten prompt. CRAFT, TroVE and KTCE are inference-time scaffolds. ReTool is a 4B model distilled from Qwen-32B code-execution traces. LATM (distill GPT-4.1) is the 4B model fine-tuned on GPT-4.1 tool-writing trajectories by rejection sampling.
official.claim: On the 10 held-out Reasoning-Gym tasks (RG Unseen), SMITH-trained Qwen3-4B-Instruct reaches 79.9 ± 2.2 macro accuracy, versus 58.3 for the same LATM build-then-use scaffold on the untrained 4B model, 65.8 ± 4.1 for the 4B model distilled from GPT-4.1, 63.2 ± 0.4 for ReTool (4B distilled from Qwen-32B) and 74.1 for LATM with Qwen3-30B-A3B.
official.claim_caption: Table 1 | Reasoning-Gym results (Qwen3-4B-Instruct); CRAFT, TroVE, KTCE, ReTool, LATM-distill, and SMITH report mean±std over seeded re-evaluations. SMITH leads held-out generalization (RG Unseen 79.9) over distilled models (ReTool 63.2, LATM-distill 65.8) and every scaffolding baseline, using 32× fewer output tokens than standard CoT. Fixing baseline grading bugs raises TroVE's RG (Unseen) from 40.6 to 55.9 and KTCE's from 48.7 to 65.1. RG (Seen/Unseen): macro-average over training/held-out tasks. *LATM prompt rewritten for schema clarity. I/O: input / output tokens.
official.metric: RG (Unseen) macro-average accuracy (%) over 10 held-out tasks, higher is better; ± is std over seeded re-evaluations of one trained model (not over training runs); LATM* rows have no std
official.comparison: SMITH (RL-trained 4B) vs. same-backbone LATM* (untrained 4B, same scaffold), LATM distilled from GPT-4.1 (4B), ReTool distilled from Qwen-32B (4B), and LATM* with Qwen3-30B-A3B; CRAFT/TroVE/KTCE also in the table

title: StreamPI: Streaming Multimodal Temporal Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Models

official.background: Strong vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies such as π0.5 predict each action chunk from a single observation, with no access to earlier frames. This rules out tasks that need memory (e.g., tracking which cup hides an object) and gives up the depth and motion cues that come from seeing several frames. Earlier multi-frame VLAs feed a window of frames at every step, which raises latency, or add a video encoder whose new parameters can disturb the pretrained representations.
official.method:
StreamPI fine-tunes π0.5 without adding any parameters. Each time step's multi-view images and the language instruction form one 'atomic temporal unit' (the instruction is repeated for every frame). Inside a unit, attention is bidirectional. Across units, a block-wise causal mask applies, and position embeddings are extended to cover the longer sequence. At inference, earlier units are kept in a KV cache, so only the new frame has to be encoded. T streaming frames are used (T = 3 or 5). In training, the interval between frames is drawn uniformly from [3, 7] (random-interval training), and temporal masking hides the earliest k frames, with k random.

The π0.5 recipe (optimizer, learning-rate schedule) is unchanged and all weights are fully fine-tuned. Simulation evaluation uses a fixed interval δ = 5. On CALVIN, the authors compare StreamPI (T = 5) with a single-frame π0.5 baseline and with MemoryVLA, using the standard 5-task chained evaluation. The metrics are the success rate at each chain position and the average number of tasks completed in a row (avg. sequence length, 0-5).
official.claim: On the CALVIN long-horizon benchmark, StreamPI (π0.5 with 5 streaming frames) reaches an average sequence length of 4.547, compared with 4.313 for single-frame π0.5. The gap grows along the chain: success on the 5th consecutive task is 85.0% vs. 79.5%, while on the 1st task it is 96.9% vs. 94.2%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance comparison on CALVIN [29]. Success rates (%) at each sequence position and average sequence length are reported.
official.metric: Average completed sequence length out of 5 chained tasks (higher is better) and success rate (%) at each chain position. No error bars, seeds or number of evaluation chains are reported.
official.comparison: StreamPI (T = 5) vs. single-frame π0.5 (and MemoryVLA) on CALVIN; the paper does not state which CALVIN split was used
official.falsification_criterion: Fine-tuning π0.5 with StreamPI's block-causal multi-frame mask (T = 5, random interval in [3, 7]) and fine-tuning a single-frame π0.5 baseline under the same recipe gives an average sequence length gap that is well below about 0.23 (e.g., under 0.1), or that is within seed-to-seed variation.

title: TreeGraft: Adaptive Multi-Drafter Grafting for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (full per-benchmark values in Table 11, page 29; repeat-run stability in Table 10, page 28)

official.background: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference: a cheap drafter proposes tokens and the target model verifies them in parallel. Tree-based variants such as EAGLE-2 propose a tree of candidate continuations, so more tokens are accepted per verification. Existing tree methods use one drafter for every drafting step, which forces a trade-off. A tiny drafter is fast but builds poor trees, and a larger drafter builds better trees but adds latency at every step. The paper asks whether two drafters of different cost can share a single draft tree, with the expensive drafter used only at steps where it pays off.
official.method:
TreeGraft builds one shared draft tree over D=5 drafting steps (frontier width W=10, m=10 children per node, verification budget 63 nodes, temperature 0). Each step is handled either by a training-free n-gram 'small' drafter or by a pretrained 'middle' LLM from the target's family. At small-drafter steps, the standard EAGLE-2 rule applies: only the nodes generated at the previous step are scored and expanded. At middle-drafter steps, the candidate pool is every tree node the middle drafter has not yet visited, so it can rescore earlier nodes and reopen under-ranked paths. New children are attached without overwriting existing branches (non-destructive grafting). The final tree is pruned by cumulative path score to the budget and verified by the target with the usual lossless rule.

A lightweight learned scheduler decides at each step whether to call the middle drafter. It is an MLP distilled from an offline value system fitted on call/skip trajectories from 6 target-middle pairs and 5 benchmarks. Baselines are All Small (n-gram drafter at every step) and All Mid (middle drafter at every step), with identical tree budget and verification. The metric is wall-clock speedup over plain autoregressive decoding with the target, measured on 2x A100 at batch size 1 with 80 sampled examples per benchmark and max_new_tokens=256.
official.claim: With target Qwen3-32B and middle drafter Qwen3-0.6B, TreeGraft averages a 1.47x speedup over autoregressive decoding across 6 benchmarks (Alpaca, GSM8K, HumanEval, NQ, CNN/DM, MT-Bench). The All Small baseline averages 1.21x and All Mid 1.19x, and TreeGraft beats the better of the two on every one of the 6 benchmarks.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Online evaluation results. Values are speedups over autoregressive target decoding. TG denotes TreeGraft; S and M denote All Small and All Mid. The five-task average is the arithmetic mean over Alpaca, GSM8K, HumanEval, NQ, and CNN/DM; the overall average includes MT-Bench. Blue rows denote held-out target–middle pairs, green columns denote the held-out MT-Bench task, and orange cells denote their intersection. For LLaMA pairs, 70B, 8B, 3B, and 1B refer to LLaMA 3.3-70B, LLaMA 3.1-8B, LLaMA 3.2-3B, and LLaMA 3.2-1B, respectively. The full speedups are in Table 11.
official.metric: wall-clock speedup over target-only autoregressive decoding (higher is better); single timing run, no ±; a repeat run of this pair gave 1.473x vs. 1.470x (Table 10)
official.comparison: TreeGraft (learned scheduler, n-gram small + Qwen3-0.6B middle) vs. All Small (n-gram only) and All Mid (Qwen3-0.6B only) dynamic-tree speculative decoding, same tree budget, decoding parameters, hardware and evaluation samples

title: VIPER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Vision-Language Models in Veterinary Pathology
claim_source: Appendix Table 11, page 25 (overall drop and P-value in Section 5.2, page 8)

official.background: Pathology vision-language models (VLMs) are evaluated almost entirely on human, mostly oncology, data, often from educational or web-derived question sets that models may answer from text cues alone. Toxicologic pathology, where pathologists examine rat tissue in preclinical drug-safety studies, has no vision-language benchmark. VIPER is a benchmark of 1,251 questions on 419 H&E rat histology ROIs from seven organ systems, authored and validated by board-certified veterinary pathologists, and built so that questions should not be answerable without looking at the image.
official.method:
Each question is tied to one 1,024×1,024 ROI cropped from TG-GATEs or MMO whole-slide images. A veterinary pathologist wrote one seed question per ROI; GPT-5.2 turned it into an MCQ (5 options), a KPrim item (4 true/false statements) and a free-text question. MCQ and KPrim candidates were adversarially filtered: GPT-5.2 answered them without the image (temperature 0, 3 trials, shuffled options), and any MCQ answered correctly in any trial or KPrim scoring ≥3/4 in the worst trial was regenerated or dropped. Final set: 419 MCQ, 414 KPrim, 418 free-text.

Scoring: MCQ by exact match, averaged over 5 cyclic-shift orderings of the options (chance 20%); KPrim by the ETH half-point rule (4/4 → 1, 3/4 → 0.5, else 0; chance 18.75%); free text by a GPT-5.4 judge using 0.7·diagnostic accuracy + 0.3·completeness with a per-question rubric. All models are run once at temperature 0, with no tools or retrieval. For the image ablation (Appendix Table 11), each lead model (ToxScribe-Qwen, PathChat+, GPT-5.4) is re-run on the same questions with the correct image ('Normal'), a solid black image, a random other benchmark image (MCQ only), or no image.
official.claim: On VIPER, GPT-5.4 scores 58.5 on MCQ and 54.3 on KPrim with the correct image, but only 30.5 and 25.1 when the image is removed (drops of 27.9 and 29.2 points; free text 55.1 → 25.6), and 34.2/31.0 with a black image; the overall no-image drop is 29.0 points (P < 0.001, paired bootstrap).
official.claim_caption: Appendix Table 11: Image ablation across lead models on VIPER. “Normal” is the question’s correct image; “Black” a solid black image; “Random” a randomly-chosen other benchmark image; “No image” drops the image entirely. Right-most column is the Normal − No-image gap. The Random condition is reported on MCQ only; the KPrim and free-text random-image conditions used an earlier protocol and are omitted for comparability.
official.metric: Per-format score in % (MCQ accuracy averaged over 5 option rotations; KPrim ETH half-point score; free text LLM-judge score), higher is better. Table 11 has no error bars; the text reports P < 0.001 (paired item-level bootstrap) for the overall no-image drop. Table 1 gives 95% bootstrap CIs of about ±4 points per format for the image condition.
official.comparison: Same model (GPT-5.4), same questions, with the correct image vs. no image (and vs. a black image / random other image).
official.falsification_criterion: Running GPT-5.4 (or the same model snapshot) on the released VIPER MCQ and KPrim questions, the no-image score is within about 10 points of the with-image score on either format, or the no-image MCQ score is well above chance (e.g. >45%) while with-image stays near 58%.

title: Sparse Koopman Autoencoders Identify Local Dynamical Regimes in Multibasin Systems
claim_source: Table 6, page 19 (Appendix D.2); headline version in Table 1, page 7

official.background: Koopman autoencoders (KAEs) learn an encoder into a latent space where one linear matrix K advances the dynamics, plus a decoder back to the state. Systems with several basins of attraction generally cannot be linearized by a single continuous finite-dimensional global embedding, so a plain KAE has to compromise between incompatible local linearizations. This paper proposes that a sparse latent code, in which the set of active coordinates (the support) selects which columns of K and the decoder are used, lets one model represent several local linear regimes without basin labels.
official.method:
Each model has an encoder, a linear decoder with unit-norm columns, and a dense latent transition K, trained jointly on windows of L = 8 steps with prediction, reconstruction and latent-linearity losses (plus an l1 penalty λsp = 3e-3 on the code for sparse models). Sparse encoders are LISTA (MLP pre-code followed by Q = 2 learned shrinkage steps, 256 sign-split coordinates) or a Sparse MLP (ReLU hidden layers and ReLU on the output code, with l1). The matched dense control in Table 6 is an MLP with ReLU hidden layers and a linear (dense) output code and no l1. Dense MLP and the two intermediate MLP encoders share initial weights, training windows and validation/test starts. Training uses AdamW for 200,000 steps, 2,048 fixed windows per system and seed, with 15 seeds (0-14) per system.

Forecasts use periodic re-encoding: roll K forward m steps, decode, re-encode the predicted state, and repeat, with m chosen per trained model from {10, 25, 50, 100} by validation MSE at H = 500. The benchmark has 15 procedurally generated 2D multibasin systems (potential wells around known attractors plus transition dynamics). Test MSE is measured on 100 uniform initial conditions per system and seed at horizons H = 100, 500, 1000. The score is the interquartile mean over seeds within each system, then the arithmetic mean over systems.
official.claim: On the 15-system 2D multibasin benchmark at horizon H = 1000, sparse-code KAEs have mean forecast MSE 0.106 (LISTA) and 0.0897 (Sparse MLP) versus 0.229 for a matched dense-code KAE with ReLU hidden layers, with significantly lower MSE in 13 and 14 of 15 systems respectively and significantly higher in none.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Sparsity mechanisms of the encoder on the multibasin benchmark (15 systems, 15 paired seeds; tests of Appendix C). MSE: means over systems of per-system seed IQMs; **: significantly lower than Dense MLP in all 15 systems; §[1/15]: significantly lower than Sparse MLP with λsp = 0 in 1 system at every horizon. Sparsity rows, as means over systems on 64 held-out trajectories per run: exactly zero encoded coordinates; coordinates with |zi| ≤ 10^-3 in the direct K^h rollout over 8 steps; and exactly zero activations in each hidden layer of the encoder MLP (for LISTA, its pre-code MLP).
official.metric: Re-encoded forecast MSE on held-out starts, lower is better; mean over systems of per-system interquartile means over 15 seeds. No ± in the table; significance from one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction per system. The text gives a paired seed-bootstrap 95% CI for the l1-free Sparse MLP vs ReLU-hidden Dense MLP ratio at H = 1000 of 1.97 [1.36, 2.85].
official.comparison: LISTA and Sparse MLP (sparse codes) vs. Dense MLP with ReLU hidden layers (dense code, same hidden-layer sparsity), all with dense K and the same training setup; also the l1-free Sparse MLP (ReLU on the code only) as the one-component step
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining on the multibasin systems with 15 seeds, the ReLU-hidden dense-code KAE reaches H = 1000 MSE within about 1.3x of LISTA/Sparse MLP, or the sparse models are not significantly better in a majority of the 15 systems.

title: AdapToPASS: Ambiguity-aware Adaptive Spherical Transformer for Panoramic Semantic Segmentation

official.background: Panoramic (360°) semantic segmentation is used for robot navigation and VR. Recent spherical Transformers (HEAL-SWIN, SphereUFormer, SO3UFormer) work directly on the sphere and avoid equirectangular distortion, but they are trained and evaluated on panoramas with a canonical upright orientation and fixed viewpoint. Handheld or robot-mounted 360° cameras rotate, zoom and move, and segmentation accuracy drops when test panoramas are transformed in ways not seen in training. The paper asks whether an architecture that adapts its attention range to local ambiguity is more robust to such unseen spherical transformations.
official.method:
AdapToPASS is a U-shaped icosphere Transformer built on SphereUFormer. Each Adaptive Spherical Attention (AdaSpA) block does local self-attention over icosphere neighbourhoods with a learned geodesic-distance bias; a small MLP predicts a per-token ambiguity score c_i in [0,1] that rescales the geodesic distance (scale between 0.8 and 1.6), so ambiguous tokens aggregate wider context. A 'Bifocal' design adds a full-resolution Acuity Stream (rank-7 icosphere, one AdaSpA block) whose features are gated into a Lateral U-Net stream on the rank-6 icosphere, and the two streams' predictions are fused. Training uses class-balanced cross-entropy + Lovász loss plus a truncated per-class signed-distance-field (SDF) boundary regression loss (weight 0.5), an SDF/softmax sign-alignment loss (0.1) and an ambiguity regulariser. Model size is 14.78M params, ERP input 512×256, AdamW lr 1e-4, 300 epochs per Appendix B.4 (Appendix A.2 says 400), batch 4/GPU, no data augmentation.

Robustness protocol: all models are trained only on the original, untransformed Stanford2D3D training set (80:10:10 split, all classes). Test panoramas are transformed with five families (Rotation in yaw/pitch/roll; Scale via spherical Möbius zoom; Translation via depth-based camera shift; Orientation Shift = rotation + zoom; Viewpoint Shift = rotation + translation) at three severities (mild, robust, stress; parameter grids in Appendix Table 4), with identity transforms excluded. Baselines (SFSS, SGAT4PASS, Elite360D, HEAL-SWIN, SphereUFormer, SO3UFormer) are retrained from scratch with RGB only at comparable size, and all predictions are evaluated on a common uniformly sampled sphere.
official.claim: On Stanford2D3D test panoramas under robust-level unseen spherical transformations, AdapToPASS obtains higher mIoU than the best of six retrained baselines in every family: Rotation 51.52 vs. 46.88, Orientation shift 46.61 vs. 41.95, Translation 62.90 vs. 57.21, Viewpoint shift 45.20 vs. 36.64, and Scale 62.23 vs. 60.13.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: mIoU comparison under unseen spherical transformations on the Stanford2D3D benchmark. Results are reported across mild, robust, and stress settings, including rotation (Rot.), Scale, Orientation Shifts (Ori.), Translation (Trans.), and Viewpoint Shifts (View.). Higher is better.
official.metric: mIoU (%) on the transformed Stanford2D3D test set, higher is better; single run, no ± or seeds reported
official.comparison: AdapToPASS vs. SFSS, SGAT4PASS, Elite360D, HEAL-SWIN, SphereUFormer and SO3UFormer, all trained by the authors from scratch on untransformed training data and evaluated on the same transformed test sets
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining AdapToPASS and the strongest baselines (SO3UFormer, SphereUFormer) on untransformed Stanford2D3D, AdapToPASS's robust-level mIoU does not exceed the best baseline by a margin larger than seed-to-seed variation on Rotation, Orientation shift, Translation and Viewpoint shift (e.g. the Rotation gap of ~4.6 mIoU vanishes).
