title: GenScale: A Benchmark for Relative Object Scale in Image Generation and Editing

official.background: Text-to-image models now produce photorealistic, prompt-aligned images, but they often draw familiar objects at implausible sizes relative to each other, for example a banana as large as a bicycle. Existing benchmarks fold this into broader compositional, spatial, or physical-commonsense checks. GenScale makes real-world relative object scale its own evaluation target. Its unit is an anchor-target object pair grounded in physical-size metadata, and pairs are scored by a judge calibrated against human raters. The authors report a recurring failure they call mean regression: small objects are rendered too large and large objects too small.
official.method:
Task 1 is text-only generation from prompts naming 2-4 non-human objects drawn from a pool of 97 COCO/LVIS categories with stable physical size. Object sets are kept only if the largest-to-smallest characteristic-length ratio lies in [4, 20]. There are two scenarios with 200 prompts each. S1 (Natural Depth, 570 pairs) allows realistic perspective and depth ordering. S2 (Same Plane, 573 pairs) asks for the objects to sit on roughly the same depth plane, so image-space proportions should directly reflect real-world ratios. Every anchor-target pair in each generated image is scored on a five-point ordinal scale: 1/2 = target severely/slightly too small, 3 = plausible (within about ±20%), 4/5 = slightly/severely too large.

The judge is Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. It sees the image, the object names, their physical reference lengths, the expected ratio, and the rubric. It is queried 5 times per pair and the scores are aggregated by majority vote, with the median used when there is no unique mode. Pairs with missing, merged, or unidentifiable objects are excluded. Against the consensus of nine human raters on 527 pairs, the judge reaches Pearson r = 0.832 and QWK = 0.820. Reported metrics are scale error = mean |s − 3|, Plausible = % of pairs with s = 3, and MR (mean regression) = % of pairs where a physically smaller target is judged too large or a physically larger target is judged too small. The 95% CIs come from 2,000 image-level bootstrap resamples. Seven generators are evaluated: Nano Banana 2, GPT-Image-2, Z-Image-Turbo, Grok Imagine, Qwen-Image 2512, FLUX.2, and SD3.5-Large.
official.claim: On GenScale Task 1, all seven generators show more mean-regression error under same-plane prompts (S2) than natural-depth prompts (S1). For open-weight Qwen-Image 2512, S2 has scale error 1.105 [1.036, 1.179] vs. S1 0.703 [0.623, 0.786], plausible rate 27.0% vs. 53.1%, and MR 67.6% vs. 37.5%.
official.claim_caption: Table 30: Task 1 full results. Results are split by S1, S2, and all Task 1 entries. Error is mean |s − 3| with 95% CI in brackets. Plausible denotes score 3; Too small denotes scores 1–2; Too large denotes scores 4–5; Severe denotes scores 1 or 5. MR denotes mean-regression error.
official.metric: Scale error = mean |s − 3| over valid anchor-target pairs (lower is better), with brackets giving a 95% CI from 2,000 image-level bootstrap resamples; Plausible % (score 3, higher is better); MR % (mean-regression error, lower is better). No seed variation is reported; each prompt is generated once.
official.comparison: The same generator on S2 (Same Plane) vs. S1 (Natural Depth) prompts, scored by the same calibrated Gemini judge.

title: When Metropolis and Hastings Meet Bradley and Terry: Exact MCMC From Preference Voting
claim_source: Figure 2, page 10 (setup in Appendix C.1, pages 26-28)

official.background: Metropolis-Hastings (MH) samples from a target distribution if it can evaluate ratios of the target density. When the target is 'outputs of a generative model that a judge considers to have property M', that density is not available. What is available is pairwise preference votes from a human or LLM judge. Under a Bradley-Terry (BT) preference model, the MH density ratio equals the judge's win-rate odds, but the sampler only sees a finite number of binary votes, not the odds. The paper proves that no fixed-budget procedure can reproduce the oracle BT-MH acceptance probability exactly (Theorem 1). It then proposes an acceptance rule that still yields a chain whose stationary distribution is exactly the target (Theorem 2).
official.method:
Pref-MH: from current state x, propose x' ~ q(.|x), query the judge N times on (x, x'), let K be the number of votes preferring x', and accept with probability min{1, r0(x,x') * K / (N - K + 1)}, where r0 = p0(x')q(x|x') / (p0(x)q(x'|x)). The invalid plug-in baseline uses the same N votes but accepts with min{1, r0 * K/(N - K)}, with acceptance set to 0 when K = 0 and 1 when K = N. Oracle MH uses the true latent score s.

Synthetic setup (Appx. C.1): state space k in {0,...,240}; base p0(k) proportional to exp(-((k-68)/56)^2 / 2); latent score s(k) = 5k/240 + 0.9 g(60,13) + 0.7 g(130,21) + 1.0 g(200,13), where g(a,tau)(k) = exp(-((k-a)/tau)^2 / 2); target pi(k) proportional to p0(k) exp(s(k)). Votes come from K ~ Binomial(N, sigma(s(k') - s(k))). The proposal is symmetric: with probability 0.88 a uniform draw over {0,...,240}, otherwise a lazy nearest-neighbour move (stay 1/2, step +-1 with 1/4 each, mass that would leave the space stays at the boundary). All chains start at k = 0 and run 150,000 steps without burn-in removal. Every 500 steps the TV distance between the cumulative empirical distribution of visited states and pi is computed, for N in {1, 2, 4}.
official.claim: On the 241-state synthetic target, Pref-MH's cumulative empirical TV distance to the true target keeps falling to about 0.04 after 150,000 steps for N = 1, 2 and 4, close to Oracle MH (about 0.02). The plug-in MH sampler, using the same votes and proposal, plateaus at about 0.52 (N = 1), 0.38 (N = 2) and 0.22 (N = 4).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Synthetic validation of MH methods. Cumulative empirical total variation distance (TV) between the sampled chain and the true target. The distribution is visualized in Fig. 5 in the Appx.
official.metric: Total variation distance between the cumulative empirical state distribution of the chain and the exact target (lower is better). No error bars; apparently a single chain per method. Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Pref-MH (N-vote rule) vs. plug-in MH (empirical win-rate odds) at matched N in {1, 2, 4}, same proposal kernel and initialization; Oracle MH as reference
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the setup, the plug-in sampler's TV at 150k steps for some N in {1, 2, 4} is not clearly above Pref-MH's (e.g. within about 0.05), or Pref-MH's TV stops decreasing at a level well above Oracle MH (e.g. above 0.1 after 150k steps).

title: What Is Worth Representing? Representational Empowerment for Continual Model Construction

official.background: An agent that builds models of the world under limited resources has to decide what to represent, not only how to fit parameters or causal structure inside a fixed vocabulary. The paper calls this continual model construction: the agent builds a task-specific model for each environment and keeps a library of reusable elements across environments. It proposes representational empowerment (RepEmp), a version of empowerment defined over edits to the agent's own representation instead of over external states, as the criterion for which elements to build and keep. It compares RepEmp with environmental empowerment (EnvEmp) and information gain (InfoGain).
official.method:
Exp. 2 is an agent-based simulation of a causal-discovery task. For each of 30 seeds, a linear SEM over 10 variables is sampled (edge probability .25; values x in {1..16}; child = e + w*parent + Gaussian noise). Each seed has a curriculum of 5 training and 5 held-out tasks, and each task exposes an overlapping window of 4-7 variables. At every step the agent makes two choices: an observation granularity (coarse: 2 bins, medium: 4 bins via ceil(x/4), fine: 8 bins via ceil(x/2)) and an intervention on a variable-property pair. Each task allows 1,000 interventions (10 episodes x 100 steps). The agent keeps a Bayesian belief graph across task boundaries, and an edge counts as learned when its posterior exceeds .5. In the default 'R-medium' regime the observation noise is (sigma_coarse, sigma_medium, sigma_fine) = (2.0, 0.5, 3.0), so medium is the most reliable granularity.

Each condition pairs a granularity rule with an intervention rule, each drawn from RepEmp, EnvEmp, InfoGain, or uniform random. For granularity, RepEmp is the mutual information between candidate interventions and goal-achievement outcomes on a fixed probe-goal set under the current belief model (I(U; Gamma_G(l) | M_t)). EnvEmp counts distinguishable commandable states (log2 of B(l)^|reach|). InfoGain scores the probability of detecting unresolved structure times its remaining posterior entropy. 'Factored' uses RepEmp for granularity and EnvEmp for interventions. Performance is the F1 of the learned graph against the ground-truth graph, projected through the chosen discretization, over 150 seed-task instances per split. Table 2 swaps one rule at a time starting from the Factored condition.
official.claim: In the R-medium noise regime, with EnvEmp interventions held fixed, choosing observation granularity by RepEmp gives held-out graph-recovery F1 of .703 (SEM .021), compared with .425 (.014) when granularity is chosen by InfoGain and .376 (.015) when it is chosen at random.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Exp. 2: Graph recovery when medium is optimal. Absolute F1 (mean, SEM; 150 seed-task instances per split). Table 2: Exp. 2: One-factor-at-a-time ablations. Held-out F1 (mean, SEM) when one decision is replaced and the other is held at the specified criterion.
official.metric: Held-out edge F1 of the belief graph vs. ground truth (higher is better), mean with SEM in parentheses over 150 seed-task instances (30 seeds x 5 held-out tasks)
official.comparison: RepEmp vs. InfoGain vs. random granularity selection, all with EnvEmp intervention selection, using the same graphs, curricula and task order
official.falsification_criterion: In a faithful reimplementation of the R-medium regime, RepEmp granularity selection does not beat InfoGain granularity selection on held-out F1 by clearly more than the combined SEM (e.g., a gap well below the reported .278), or RepEmp does not mostly choose medium granularity (the paper reports 63% medium).

title: Detect Anything in Graphic Design: Element-Level Rewards for Autoregressive Detection

official.background: Graphic designs (posters, ads, infographics) are built from layered elements that occlude each other, but they are usually shared as flat raster images. Recovering the elements, their full (amodal) extent and their stacking order is the first step toward re-editing such images. Existing detectors treat objects as an unordered set and predict only visible regions. VLM-based autoregressive detectors can emit elements in sequence, and they are commonly post-trained with GRPO using a sequence-level detection reward, which gives every element the same advantage regardless of whether it was a good or bad prediction.
official.method:
DAD is Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA (rank 32) that outputs a sequence of elements in compositional (bottom-to-top layer) order, each as an amodal bounding box (coordinates in [0, 1000]) plus a text/visual label. It is first supervised fine-tuned (DAD-SFT, 650k steps) on DAD-10M excluding the RL and test splits, then trained with RL for 5,000 steps on 19,195 filtered designs with 16 rollouts per image, lr 5e-7, KL beta 0.04. The reward is IoU-weighted F1, computed separately for text and visual elements and averaged.

EleRPO replaces GRPO's uniform sequence-level advantage with an element-level one. For rollout i and element k, the reward is the change in F1 from adding element k, ΔF1(k), minus the mean ΔF1(k) over rollouts in the same cluster; clusters come from k-means (number chosen by silhouette score) on the prefix score F1(k-1). Rewards are divided by the per-position RMS over rollouts that have at least k elements, and the final token advantage is the average of this element-level advantage and the standard GRPO sequence-level advantage, used in the usual clipped PPO/GRPO objective. No extra reward model or re-rollouts are needed.
official.claim: Starting from the same DAD-SFT checkpoint and RL configuration, EleRPO reaches 79.7 IoU-weighted F1 on the DAD-10M test set (5,000 designs), versus 74.2 for GRPO and at most 74.1 for the other fine-grained RL methods (GRPO-λ 73.0, GTPO 74.1, PRIME 73.3, VinePPO 58.0, SPO 57.9).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison of EleRPO with existing RL methods on DAD-10M.
official.metric: IoU-weighted F1 (x100, higher is better) on the DAD-10M test set; single number per method, no error bars or seed count reported
official.comparison: EleRPO vs. GRPO, GRPO-λ, GTPO, PRIME, VinePPO and SPO, all applied to DAD-SFT with the same RL configuration (5,000 steps, 16 rollouts per image)
official.falsification_criterion: Under matched RL training from the same SFT checkpoint, EleRPO's test IoU-weighted F1 does not exceed GRPO's by a clear margin (e.g. the gain is below ~2 points or within the run-to-run spread across seeds).

title: HyCO: A Hybrid Neural Solver for Combinatorial Optimization
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (repeated in Table 6, Appendix B.1, page 19)

official.background: Neural solvers for combinatorial optimization such as the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) fall into two families. RL solvers like POMO build a tour one node at a time: they are fast, but errors compound over long horizons, so they degrade badly on large instances. Diffusion-model solvers like DIFUSCO generate the whole tour at once: they avoid horizon compounding, but generating a large solution from scratch is hard. The paper asks whether combining them (RL for the start of the tour, diffusion for the rest) beats either one alone.
official.method:
HyCO runs a pretrained RL policy greedily to build a tour prefix. At each step it checks two signals: the entropy of the RL policy, and the KL divergence between the RL policy's top-M actions and a prior from a single denoising probe of a prefix-conditioned diffusion model (Prefix_Difusco, a DIFUSCO GNN trained with a masked loss on random prefixes of optimal tours). The first time either signal exceeds its threshold, HyCO hands over once (no further triggers).

At the handover it runs two tracks. (i) Hybrid path: replace the RL action with the diffusion model's best next action and let RL finish the tour. (ii) DM proposals: for each top RL candidate action (up to 0.8 cumulative probability), run conditional diffusion completion (50 DDIM steps for TSP-500/1000) and greedily decode a tour. It returns the shortest tour among all candidates. Optimality gap is measured against Concorde.
official.claim: On TSP-500 and TSP-1000 with greedy decoding, HyCO (POMO + Prefix_Difusco) reaches optimality gaps of 3.56% and 4.58%, vs. 15.62% and 15.38% for standalone POMO and 8.23% and 9.91% for standalone Prefix_Difusco, and also beats Prefix_Difusco with 16 samples (4.58% and 6.07%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Results on large-scale TSP problems. RL, SL, G, and S denote Reinforcement Learning, Supervised Learning, Greedy decoding, and Sample decoding, respectively. * indicates the baseline for computing the performance gap. The TIME reports the average inference time per instance.
official.metric: Optimality gap (%) of average tour length relative to Concorde, lower is better; no error bars (single deterministic greedy run)
official.comparison: HyCO(POMO+Prefix_Difusco) vs. its RL backbone POMO (greedy), its DM backbone Prefix_Difusco (greedy), and Prefix_Difusco with 16 parallel samples, on the same TSP-500/TSP-1000 test sets
official.falsification_criterion: With the same backbones, HyCO's gap on TSP-500 (or TSP-1000) is not clearly below both standalone POMO and standalone Prefix_Difusco, e.g. HyCO comes within about 1 percentage point of Prefix_Difusco's greedy gap, or does not beat Prefix_Difusco(16 samples).

title: Inference Time Nash Alignment

official.background: Aligning an LLM with human preferences usually means fine-tuning (RLHF, DPO), which needs large preference datasets, substantial compute and access to model weights. Inference-time alignment, such as Best-of-N sampling with a reward model, avoids training but usually assumes a scalar Bradley-Terry reward, which cannot represent preferences that are intransitive or otherwise not reducible to a single score. The paper studies inference-time alignment with a general pairwise preference model, framed as finding the Nash equilibrium of a two-player zero-sum game between policies.
official.method:
For each prompt, N = 64 responses are sampled from a base SFT model (LLaMA3-SFT 8B). A pairwise preference model (LLaMA3-PM 8B) scores every ordered pair to build an empirical N x N preference matrix. Best-of-Nash (BoN) solves the zero-sum matrix game by linear programming and outputs the equilibrium mixed strategy over the 64 responses. Nash Mirror Descent (NMD) approximates the same equilibrium with closed-form optimistic mirror-descent updates (beta = 1) and returns the averaged iterate.

Evaluation uses 100 sampled prompts from each of TLDR, HelpSteer2 and UltraFeedback. Each output is compared with the dataset's reference answer by an LLM judge (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, temperature 0, prompt in Appendix E.1), queried twice with the response order swapped; a win or loss counts only if both orders agree, otherwise it is a draw. The metric is expected win rate EWR = win + draw/2. The base SFT row is the base policy's own sample without any selection.
official.claim: With LLaMA3-SFT as the base policy, LLaMA3-PM as the preference oracle and N = 64 samples, Best-of-Nash raises expected win rate against the reference answers from 44.1% to 68.8% on HelpSteer2 and from 23.9% to 48.8% on UltraFeedback (NMD: 67.8% and 46.7%), and from 62.9% to 73.5% on TLDR.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of expected win-rate (EWR) across three datasets. BoN and NMD sample N = 64 responses from LLaMA3-SFT and we use LLaMA3-PM as preference model; beta = 1 for NMD.
official.metric: expected win rate EWR = win + draw/2 vs. the dataset reference response, judged by DeepSeek-V4-Flash with order swapping; higher is better; 100 prompts per dataset, no seeds or intervals reported
official.comparison: Best-of-Nash and NMD (N = 64, LLaMA3-PM oracle) vs. the base LLaMA3-SFT policy without selection
official.falsification_criterion: On 100 HelpSteer2 or UltraFeedback prompts, Best-of-Nash (or NMD) with N = 64 does not improve EWR over the base SFT policy by more than about 10 points (roughly two binomial standard errors), or the improvement disappears under a different judge.

title: Length Generalization for Transformers via Compression
claim_source: Figures 1-3 (Appendix C), page 16; exact values stated in the Appendix C text

official.background: The C-RASP hypothesis says a transformer length-generalizes on a task (trained on short strings, correct on longer ones) if and only if the task can be expressed in the C-RASP language. A known puzzle is bounded parity, PARITY_k (even number of a's, at most 2k a's): it is C-RASP-definable for every k, yet transformers fail to length-generalize on it even for moderate k. The paper proves that tasks definable in the fragments C-RASP+ / C-RASP_1 need a training sample at most exponential in the size of the smallest formula. COUNT_k and MAJ_k have formulas of size O(log k), while PARITY_k needs size Omega(k). The theory therefore predicts that the first two length-generalize easily and PARITY_k gets harder as k grows.
official.method:
Using the codebase and training setup of Huang, Yang et al. (2025) (github.com/lacoco-lab/length_generalization), the authors train one identical 4-layer, 2-head, 256-dim transformer per task and per k in {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}. The model is a binary recognizer over the alphabet {a, b}: the input is <BOS> w <SEP> y <EOS> and the loss is taken only at the answer position. The predicates are COUNT_k: |w|_a > k; MAJ_k: |w|_a > k and |w|_a > |w|_b; PARITY_k: |w|_a even and |w|_a <= 2k. Training uses Adam with lr 1e-3 and batch size 64, and stops after 100% in-distribution accuracy on three consecutive evaluations or at 60K steps.

Training lengths are [0, M] with M = 50 (M = 256 for k = 64). The three test sets are t0 = [0, M] (in-distribution), t1 = [M+1, 2M] and t2 = [2M+1, 3M]. Sampling is label-balanced: draw a length L, draw a label y ~ Bernoulli(1/2), draw |w|_a uniformly among the counts consistent with y, then randomly permute. PARITY_k negatives are split evenly between 'odd count' and 'even but > 2k'.
official.claim: With the same 4-layer transformer and training recipe, COUNT_k and MAJ_k length-generalize nearly perfectly for every k in {2,...,64} (t2 accuracy >= 93.8% and >= 96.8%), whereas PARITY_k degrades with k: t2 accuracy is 84.2% at k=8, 82.5% at k=16, 85.6% at k=32 and 74.2% at k=64, against 98.4% (COUNT_64) and 99.8% (MAJ_64).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Length generalization accuracy of T on COUNT_k tasks. Figure 2: Length generalization accuracy of T on MAJ_k tasks. Figure 3: Length generalization accuracy of T on PARITY_k tasks.
official.metric: Classification accuracy (%) on t2 = lengths [2M+1, 3M] (higher is better); single run per configuration, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: PARITY_k vs. COUNT_k and MAJ_k at matched k, same architecture, optimizer and training-length range
official.falsification_criterion: For k >= 8, PARITY_k t2 accuracy is comparable to COUNT_k/MAJ_k (e.g. within a few points, above ~93%), or across several seeds the PARITY_k vs. COUNT_k/MAJ_k gap at k = 64 is not consistently present.

title: Training-Free Task Vectors for LLM Behavioral Control
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (standard deviations in Table 8, page 20)

official.background: Task vectors (fine-tuned minus pretrained weights) let practitioners add, remove, or combine behaviors by weight arithmetic, but each one needs a fine-tuning run that already shows the behavior. Activation steering vectors find behavioral directions without training, but they only act at inference time through a forward-pass hook. A way to turn steering directions into persistent, composable weight edits without training would make post-training behavioral control (e.g. amplifying or suppressing evil, hallucination, or sycophancy) much cheaper.
official.method:
Steering vectors are built following the Persona Vectors protocol: for each trait, 20 questions are paired with 5 trait-inducing and 5 trait-suppressing system prompts, with 10 completions sampled per prompt. Completions are filtered by a GPT-4.1-mini judge (coherence >= 50, trait score >= 50 for positive and < 50 for negative). The steering vector s_l is the difference between the mean completion-token activations of the positive and negative sets at module l, and mu_l is the module's mean input, estimated from the same data.

TFTV turns s_l into a rank-one update of each attention output projection W_l = sum_i sigma_i u_i v_i^T: TFTV = s_bar_l (sum_i sign(mu_l^T v_i) sigma_i v_i)^T, where s_bar_l = s_l/||s_l||. Each W_l in a selected layer range is updated as W_l <- W_l + alpha * TFTV (Llama: layers [14,20) for evil and sycophancy, [13,30) for hallucination; alpha swept over {0.01..0.05}). The baseline is Persona-Vector inference steering at layer 16, with its coefficient swept over {0.4..1.2}. For each method, the configuration with the highest trait score subject to mean coherence >= 70 is reported. Trait expression is scored 0-100 by GPT-4.1-mini on 200 generations (20 questions x 10 samples, temperature 1, no system prompt), and utility is zero-shot MMLU (lm-eval-harness) and GSM8K.
official.claim: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, TFTV addition edits reach trait scores of 63.26 (evil), 98.55 (hallucinating) and 94.64 (sycophantic), versus 14.06, 61.51 and 63.86 for Persona-Vector inference steering. TFTV's MMLU stays within 0.15 points of the base model's 68.26, while steering's MMLU is 67.29-67.41.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: TFTV increases trait manifestation without damaging utility. We report trait scores, MMLU scores, and GSM8K scores. Higher values are better. Base model scores are provided for reference. Best results among training-free editing methods are in bold. The last two columns refer to methods that require fine-tuning.
official.metric: GPT-4.1-mini trait-manifestation score, 0-100, higher means stronger trait, mean over 200 generations; ± in Table 8 is the std across the 20 prompt-level means (not seeds). Zero-shot MMLU accuracy (%), higher is better.

title: Why Learning Rediscovers the Closed-Form Diagonal Regularizer
claim_source: Tables 2 and 3, page 8 (per-window values in Table 11, page 24)

official.background: Recovering the modal amplitudes of a field (e.g. a room's acoustic eigenmodes) from a few sensors is an ill-posed inverse problem, so a Tikhonov penalty is needed. Besides its strength, the penalty has a per-mode shape that decides how strongly each mode is shrunk, and the best shape depends on the truncation noise that discarded higher modes add to every measurement. Whether that shape must be tuned or learned per room, or can be fixed in closed form from the excitation statistics alone, decides whether learned regularizers are worth building for such problems.
official.method:
Each room is a random convex 2D polygon; Laplacian eigenpairs are computed by FEM and pressure fields by an FDTD solver excited with a broadband click. The estimator keeps K = 50 modes and observes through M = 8 microphones placed uniformly at random; the remaining modes act as truncation noise. Stacking T snapshots gives a linear model y = Φ̃ a0 + η, solved by Tikhonov regression â = (Φ̃ᵀΦ̃ + αΓ)⁻¹Φ̃ᵀy with diagonal Γ. Quality is the normalized modal MSE P = Σ_k E[(â_k − a0_k)²] / Σ_k Var(a0_k) (0 = perfect, 1 = guessing zero).

The closed form uses Γ_k = λ_k^|s|, where |s| = 1.13 is a single population exponent fitted by OLS in log space to the modal variances (σ²_k ∝ λ_k^−|s|). The per-room power-law oracle sweeps Γ_k = λ_k^p over a 61-point grid on p ∈ [0, 6], grid-searching α at each p, and keeps the best (p, α) for that room; the closed form also has α grid-searched. The relative cost δ(T) = (P(|s|, T) − P(p*, T)) / P(p*, T) is computed per room and summarized by its median over the 187 in-scope rooms (K_total > K) of a 197-room validation set, at T ∈ {1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2100}. As a secondary check, M3 (a 4,930-parameter CondNet that maps per-mode features to a per-room diagonal Γ, with the strength α learned jointly as a single scalar, trained end to end through a differentiable closed-form Tikhonov solve on 800 rooms, 5 seeds) is compared to the closed form.
official.claim: On the 187 in-scope simulated rooms (K = 50, M = 8), the fixed closed-form penalty Γ_k = λ_k^1.13 has a median relative cost versus per-room power-law oracle tuning of at most 0.61% for T ≤ 50, 1.46% for T ≤ 100, and 5.83% over all windows (max at T = 1000), and the learned per-room diagonal model M3 does not improve on it (P = 0.7245 ± 0.0021 vs. 0.7264 at T = 1; 0.6051 ± 0.0027 vs. 0.6035 at T = 100; 0.1339 ± 0.0003 vs. 0.1308 at T = 1000).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Replacing per-room power-law oracle tuning with the closed form costs little at the population median, and most at long observation windows. The relative cost δ is the extra modal error of the closed form as a fraction of the oracle error, reported as the largest median over the in-scope rooms within each regime. Table 3: M3 matches the error of the closed form at every tested window and recovers little of the gap to the oracle, although its seeds learn different spectra. P is the normalized modal error, lower is better, and M3 entries are mean and standard deviation over seeds. The gap is the closed form's error minus the oracle's.
official.metric: Normalized modal MSE P (lower is better) and relative cost δ = (P_closed − P_oracle)/P_oracle, median over rooms. Table 2 reports medians over the 187 in-scope rooms with no error bars (Table 11 gives per-window medians with IQR and 95th percentile across rooms, but over in-scope and boundary rooms together, so its T = 1000 median reads 5.6% rather than 5.83%); ± in Table 3 is std over 5 training seeds of M3.
official.comparison: Closed-form Γ_k = λ_k^|s| (one exponent for all rooms) vs. per-room power-law oracle (best p and α per room); secondary: closed form vs. learned per-room diagonal regularizer M3
official.falsification_criterion: In a faithful re-simulation, the median relative cost of the closed form exceeds the oracle by substantially more than the reported values (e.g. > 2% for T ≤ 50 or > ~10% at any T), or a learned per-room diagonal regularizer (M3-style) reduces median P below the closed form by clearly more than its seed std at T = 100 or T = 1000.

title: MoME: Mixture-of-Memory Embeddings for Context-Aware Sparse Lookup
claim_source: Table 17, page 22 (Appendix A.9.1); same data plotted in Figure 2, page 8

official.background: Conditional-memory methods add large token-indexed embedding tables to a transformer. Each token looks up a few rows, so capacity grows with little extra compute. Examples are Value Embedding (a per-token table added to the attention value stream), STEM, Per-Layer Embedding, and Engram/Bigram (n-gram hashed tables). In all of these the row that gets read is a fixed function of the token (or n-gram) identity. The same surface token (e.g. 'bank' or 'python') therefore always retrieves the same memory, whatever its meaning in context. The paper asks whether making the lookup context-dependent gives better language modelling for the same memory budget and FLOPs.
official.method:
MoME replaces each token-indexed row of a value-embedding style table with M memory slots, E_mem in R^{N x M x d_value}. In a memory-augmented block, the row is chosen by the token (f(x_t) = token id by default, so N = V). A per-head linear router on the hidden state h_t entering the block produces M slot logits. The router takes the top-K slots (K = 2), weights them with a sigmoid normalised over the selected slots, and sums them into one memory vector per value head. That vector is added to the attention value v_{t,i} through a per-head gate 2*sigmoid(W_gamma h_t + b_gamma). All heads in a layer share one table but route independently. Memory blocks sit on alternating layers.

In the scaling sweep, the backbone is nanochat d12 (12 layers, d_model 768, 6 heads of dim 128, 32k BPE vocabulary). Every run is trained on FineWeb-Edu to a target of 3e18 training FLOPs (about 3.3B tokens), with 524,288-token batches, 2048-token context, and Muon plus AdamW (memory table AdamW lr 0.2, wd 0.001). The memory budget is swept over 3 to 24 'blocks' of about 25.2M parameters each (75.5M to 604M). Bigram (modded-nanogpt style: a hash of the previous and current token indexes a shared d_model table added to the residual stream through hidden-state-conditioned gates) gets the same parameter count at each budget. MoME scales the slot count M at each budget. Validation bits-per-byte is measured on 20,971,520 held-out FineWeb-Edu tokens, averaged over seeds 42, 43 and 44.
official.claim: On the nanochat d12 backbone at 3e18 training FLOPs, MoME reaches lower validation bpb than an equal-memory Bigram table at every budget, and the gap grows with memory. At 302M memory parameters it scores 0.8569 ± 0.0002 vs. 0.8606 ± 0.0012, and at 604M it scores 0.8533 ± 0.0003 vs. 0.8571 ± 0.0010 (the no-memory base is 0.8785).
official.claim_caption: Table 17: Memory-size scaling sweep on the 12-layer nanochat backbone trained at 3e18 FLOPs (~3.3B tokens), with block counts {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24}. Blocks is the memory expansion factor; each block adds ≈ 25.2M parameters to the memory table. Values are 3-seed means ± std. The Base-model row is the no-memory baseline imported from Table 2. Bigram and MoME share the same memory budget at each block count, so the rows are directly comparable. Figure 2 plots the val bpb column vs. memory.
official.metric: Validation bits-per-byte on FineWeb-Edu (lower is better); mean ± std over 3 seeds (42, 43, 44). Train bpb and CORE are also reported, but CORE differences are mostly within std.
official.comparison: MoME (K=2, slot count M scaled with budget) vs. Bigram (hash table size scaled with budget), with matched memory parameters at each of 8 budgets, the same backbone, data and training FLOPs
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining nanochat d12 at 3e18 FLOPs with 302M (or 604M) memory parameters, MoME's mean validation bpb is not lower than Bigram's by more than the seed std (e.g. the gap is under about 0.0015 bpb), or Bigram matches or beats MoME.

title: VisInteract: Towards Dynamic Interactive Text-to-Visualization under Imperfect Queries

official.background: Text-to-Visualization systems turn a natural-language request and a database into a chart. Real requests are often ambiguous, incomplete or factually wrong (for example, a year missing from the database, or a chart type that does not fit the data), but existing benchmarks and methods assume a well-specified query and produce one chart in a single pass. Recovering what the user actually wants requires asking clarifying questions and reacting to feedback on draft charts, and existing benchmarks do not measure this ability.
official.method:
VisInteract-Bench has 1,098 samples built from the 11 BIRD Mini-Dev databases. Each sample pairs an imperfect query (1-3 of 14 injected ambiguity, incompleteness or factual-error templates) with a hidden set of natural-language key features and a validated ground-truth Altair chart. A simulated User Agent answers ask_user_text questions (it sees only the key-feature types the question touches) and, through ask_user_vis, compares a rendered chart with the ground-truth chart and returns a 1-10 satisfaction score plus a critique. A Code Judge and a Chart Judge (Qwen3.5-plus) decide for each key feature whether the submission satisfies it. Merge Task Score is the fraction of samples in which every key feature passes both judges.

Vis-MCTS runs MCTS over tool calls (execute_sql, execute_altair, ask_user_text, finish). It has 10 rollouts, depth up to 20, progressive widening (C_pw=2, alpha=0.5, child cap K_max), UCT with c=2 and temperature 0.8. Clarification answers and visual critiques are shared across rollouts. The terminal ask_user_vis score is split by an LLM into data, design and intent scores (weights 0.4/0.4/0.2) and backpropagated only to SQL, Altair and question nodes respectively. The method returns the terminal chart with the highest user score. The main baseline, Best-of-N (ReAct), runs 10 independent ReAct chains with the same tools, successor constraints, depth cap, temperature 0.8 and User Agent, and returns the chain whose terminal chart gets the highest ask_user_vis score.
official.claim: On VisInteract-Bench (1,098 samples) with Qwen3.5-flash as the backbone, Vis-MCTS reaches a Merge Task Score of 51.46% vs. 38.06% for Best-of-N (ReAct) under the same 10-rollout budget (+13.40). With Gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview the scores are 57.19% vs. 40.92% (+16.27).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Main results on VisInteract-Bench. † Non-interactive methods. ‡ Interactive methods. Within each backbone, the best result is highlighted in blue and the second-best in light blue.
official.metric: Merge Task Score (%), higher is better: the share of samples where all key features pass both the Code Judge and the Chart Judge (Qwen3.5-plus). Each number is the mean of three independent evaluation runs. The table has no per-cell error bars; the text says only that the mean std is about 0.86.
official.comparison: Vis-MCTS vs. Best-of-N (ReAct) with N=10 (strongest baseline), plus ReAct, MultiVis-Agent, Self-Correction LLM and nvAgent, all on the same backbone and the same simulated User Agent
official.falsification_criterion: On the full benchmark with Qwen3.5-flash, Vis-MCTS's Merge Task Score is not clearly higher than Best-of-N (ReAct) with N=10: for example, the gap is under about 3 points (a few times the reported std of about 0.86), or Best-of-N matches or beats Vis-MCTS.

title: Learning Options for Compositional Motor Control with Adapter Banks

official.background: Skilled motor control seems to rely on a finite set of reusable primitives that can be recombined into new movements. Neuroscience theory (Logiaco et al. 2021) proposes that such primitives could be low-rank perturbations of a shared cortical recurrent network, selected through thalamocortical loops. That theory does not say how such a system would be learned. The paper asks whether a recurrent controller with a bank of selectable adapters can be learned end-to-end from demonstrations of closed-loop arm control. It also asks whether the learned primitives can be resequenced into movements the network never saw, better than a standard multitask RNN that is conditioned on a rule input.
official.method:
The setting is closed-loop control of a two-link, six-muscle arm (motornet RigidTendonArm26 with Hill muscles), following Lazzari and Saxena (2025). The teacher is a multitask RNN that receives a one-hot rule input over 10 tasks (5 half and 5 compound movements: reach, clockwise and counter-clockwise circles, figure-8, inverted figure-8), together with go cue, speed, target and proprioceptive feedback. The student (CABRA) has a shared LSTM core (H=256) and a bank of K=10 full-rank residual adapters, Delta_k(h) = W_out tanh(W_in h). Codes 0-4 are reserved for extension and codes 5-9 for retraction. A CompILE-style encoder reads the teacher's demonstrations, segments each one into 2 parts and picks one code per segment with Gumbel-softmax. The decoder rolls out the arm in closed loop, with the selected adapter perturbing the hidden state. The student is trained only on the 5 compound trajectories and never sees the rule input. Training uses hand-trajectory L1 to the teacher, KL terms, and auxiliary DIAYN and muscle-excitation losses, with Adam at lr 1e-4 for 30k iterations.

Transfer test: both trained networks are frozen. For each one, only a T x 10 matrix of logits is optimized. A temperature-0.5 softmax turns it into per-timestep weights over the 10 rule inputs (teacher) or the 10 adapter codes (student). The optimizer is Adam at lr 0.1 for 350 steps, minimizing hand L1 to a synthetic 'two-petal' target: reach extension, then circle retraction, then circle extension, then reach retraction. These pairings did not appear in either network's training data. Optimizer, initialization, target and evaluation are identical for the two networks.
official.claim: When a soft 10-way policy over the task interface of a frozen network is optimized for 350 steps to produce the novel two-petal trajectory, the adapter-bank student reaches a final hand L1 of about 0.005, while the rule-input-conditioned teacher plateaus at about 0.04 (roughly 8x worse).
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Out-of-distribution compositional transfer. (A) The two-petal target trajectory, composed of four movement segments stitched together in a novel combination. (B) Hand L1 during transfer optimization, in which both networks are frozen and a 10-dimensional soft policy over the network's task interface is optimized for 350 steps via gradient descent. Final teacher L1 ≈ 0.04; final student L1 ≈ 0.005. (C) Final teacher (top) and student (bottom) hand trajectories under the optimized policies. Open circle marks the home position; star marks the reach target. (D) Final policies. Top: teacher rule-input weights over time. Bottom: student adapter-code weights.
official.metric: Hand-trajectory L1 error to the target (m, lower is better) at the end of transfer optimization. Single run, no error bars.
official.comparison: Frozen CABRA student with an optimized soft policy over adapter codes vs. frozen multitask teacher RNN with an optimized soft policy over rule inputs. Optimizer, target, initialization and step budget are identical.
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining both networks as described, the student's final transfer L1 on the two-petal target is not clearly lower than the teacher's (for example, less than 2x lower), or the gap disappears across independent training seeds.

title: Large Language Models Develop Belief State Geometry In-Context
claim_source: Figure 5 (bottom row), page 9; all parametrizations and LLMs in Appendix L

official.background: LLMs can predict sequences from processes they never saw in training (in-context learning), but it is unclear what internal representation supports this. Computational mechanics predicts that an optimal predictor of data from a hidden Markov model (HMM) must track the belief state, the posterior over the HMM's hidden states given the token history, and toy transformers trained on HMM data are known to encode this belief state linearly. The paper asks whether off-the-shelf LLMs, prompted only with HMM-generated tokens, form the same representation. A key alternative is that the model represents only the next-token distribution (NTP), which for many HMMs carries strictly less information than the belief state.
official.method:
Token sequences of length 20,000 are sampled from 3-state, 2-symbol HMMs (e.g. Wing(α=0.98, x=0.4), Strata(α=0.97, t0=0.38, t1=0.54); transition matrices in Appendix C.1, Eqs. 9–10, stationary initial distribution). The two symbols are written as the letters F and Q separated by spaces ("F Q F ...") so that each HMM symbol is one LLM token. Qwen3.5-9B is run on each sequence, and residual-stream activations after each layer's MLP (before the next LayerNorm) are recorded. The ground-truth belief state η at each position is computed by Bayesian filtering (Eq. 3) and the ground-truth NTP by ηM (Eq. 5).

Probes use positions t ≥ 15,000 (the last 5,000 tokens, after in-context prediction has converged). For each sequence and layer, an ordinary-least-squares linear regression from activations to belief states is fit on a random 20% of positions (1,000) and scored by R² on the held-out 80% (4,000), then averaged over 10 sequences. The comparison baseline is a linear regression from the ground-truth NTP (or log-NTP) vector to the belief state on the same sequence and split. This baseline needs no LLM, and it bounds how much belief information a pure NTP representation could linearly carry. Activations exceeding it means they hold belief information beyond the NTP.
official.claim: For Qwen3.5-9B prompted with Wing(α=0.98, x=0.4) data, held-out R² of linearly decoding the belief state from residual activations is ≈0.99 at layers ≳6, versus ≈0.88 from ground-truth NTP or log-NTP. For Strata(α=0.97, t0=0.38, t1=0.54) it is ≈0.96–0.97 at layers ≳2, versus ≈0.89 (log-NTP) and ≈0.80 (NTP).
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Activations capture more than only short-suffix beliefs and next-token (log) probabilities (NTP/log-NTP). Top: We decode the full HMM's belief from only the last k tokens, using activations from true-HMM, 1-HMM, and 0-HMM sequences. Bottom: Activations decode belief states better than the ground-truth NTP or log-NTP can. Mess3 is omitted, since its emission matrix is invertible. Error bands are 95% confidence intervals across 10 sequences.
official.metric: Held-out R² of a linear regression onto the 3-dim belief state (higher is better), averaged over 10 sequences. Error bands are 95% CIs across the 10 sequences and are visually negligible.
official.comparison: Activations → beliefs probe R² (per layer) vs. ground-truth NTP → beliefs and log-NTP → beliefs regression R² on the same sequences and train/test split
official.falsification_criterion: For Wing or Strata with these parameters, activations → beliefs R² does not exceed max(NTP → beliefs, log-NTP → beliefs) R² by more than the across-sequence 95% CI at any middle or late layer of Qwen3.5-9B, or the margin is far below the ~0.08–0.10 R² read off the figure.

title: Learning Fractional-Order Dynamics from a Single Trajectory
claim_source: Figure 2 (middle column, 'noise scale' panels), page 9; setup in Appendix A.1, page 14

official.background: Many signals (EEG, heart rate, network traffic, finance) show long-range dependence: correlations decay as a power law instead of exponentially, so Markovian state-space models fit them poorly. Discrete-time fractional-order linear time-invariant (FOLTI) systems model this with the Grünwald–Letnikov difference operator, which weights the whole past trajectory with power-law coefficients set by an unknown fractional order α. Identifying α and the system matrix A jointly from a single trajectory is a nonlinear problem with strongly dependent data, and existing methods either estimate α with a separate proxy (wavelets) or truncate the memory to an augmented Markov state.
official.method:
The model is Δ^α x_{s+1} = A x_s + η_s with η_s ~ N(0, σ² I), where (Δ^α x)_s = Σ_{j=0}^{s} Ψ(α, j) x_{s−j} and Ψ(α, j) = diag(ψ(α_i, j)), ψ(α_i, j) = Γ(j − α_i)/(Γ(−α_i)Γ(j+1)); each coordinate i has its own order α_i ∈ (0, 1). FO-GS (Algorithm 1) works row by row: for each coordinate i and each candidate α on a uniform grid over a search interval, it computes the fractional-difference row Δ^{α} X_t^{(i)} over the full history, fits the i-th row of A by ordinary least squares on X_t = [x_0, ..., x_{t−1}] (eq. 7), and evaluates the profiled squared-residual loss (eq. 8). It keeps the α with the smallest loss and the corresponding OLS row.

Synthetic setup (Appendix A.1): 2-dimensional systems, α_i,⋆ ~ U[0.1, 0.5] independently, A⋆ with eigenvalues ~ U[−0.5, 0.5], initial state ~ N(0, 4.0²). FO-GS searches [0.05, 0.55] with 20 grid points per coordinate and ridge 1e−6. Baselines: FO-BS (Chatterjee & Pequito 2022: binary search on α with tolerance 1e−2 over [0.05, 0.55], then OLS on a truncated lifted state with memory p = 40, ridge 1e−6) and FO-WT (Flandrin: Haar-wavelet estimate of α, min level 2, linear detrending, then OLS with ridge 1e−6). MSE of α and of A is averaged over 5 random systems × 20 Monte Carlo rollouts. In the noise sweep, t = 200 and σ ∈ {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40}.
official.claim: On synthetic 2-D FOLTI systems with a single trajectory of length t = 200, FO-GS has roughly half the MSE of the better baseline (FO-BS or FO-WT) for both α and A at every noise level σ from 0.05 to 0.4, with non-overlapping 95% CIs: e.g. at σ = 0.1, α-MSE ≈ 0.015 vs. ≈ 0.033 (FO-BS) and A-MSE ≈ 0.010 vs. ≈ 0.021 (FO-WT); at σ = 0.4, α-MSE ≈ 0.025 vs. ≈ 0.050 and A-MSE ≈ 0.017 vs. ≈ 0.027.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Comparison of the MSE on synthetic FOLTI system identification. Shaded regions indicate 95% confidence intervals (CI). Columns: varying trajectory horizon t (σ = 0.1), varying noise scale σ (t = 200), varying number of grid points M (σ = 0.01, t = 100); top row MSE of α, bottom row MSE of A.
official.metric: Mean squared error of the estimated fractional order α and of the estimated system matrix A (lower is better), averaged over 5 random systems × 20 rollouts; shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals. Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: FO-GS vs. FO-BS (binary search + truncated lifted-state OLS) and FO-WT (wavelet α estimate + OLS) on the same synthetic systems and trajectories
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the Appendix A.1 noise sweep (t = 200), FO-GS's mean MSE for α or for A is not clearly below the better of FO-BS and FO-WT (e.g. less than ~1.5× lower, or overlapping 95% CIs) at σ ≥ 0.05.

title: Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training

official.background: RL post-training with verifiable rewards is now a standard way to improve LLM reasoning. One tempting data-design choice is to train on small, individual skills, because rewards and verifiers are easy to write for them, and hope the model learns to compose those skills at test time. The paper asks whether that works. It models a reasoning task as a dependency graph of skill invocations and defines three levels of compositionality: single-skill chains (one skill repeated), multi-skill chains (different skills interleaved), and branch-merge graphs (non-linear dependencies). It then tests transfer in both directions on data-structure tasks from DSR-Bench, which have exact, programmatically checkable answers.
official.method:
Tasks come from five data-structure domains (array, BST, counting Bloom filter, hashmap, min-heap) plus segment-tree construction. An atomic task is one skill invocation on a given state (e.g. one insert into a given array). A compound task is a chain of invocations whose final state must be returned: Level I stacks inserts only; Level II interleaves inserts (p = 0.7) and deletes (p = 0.3); Level III is segment-tree construction (SplitInterval, MakeLeaf, MergeSummaries, AssembleNode) with a pre-order output. Problem length is the initial structure size and, for compound tasks, also the number of operations. All data is generated synthetically, with values either integers in 0-100 or English-alphabet strings depending on the domain, and deterministic tie-breaking so each prompt has one correct answer.

Starting from Qwen3-4B-Instruct, RL-Atomic is trained with GRPO only on atomic tasks and RL-Compound only on compound tasks, both at problem lengths 5-10, with a binary reward (the extracted \boxed{} answer matches ground truth after normalization). Training uses verl + vLLM, 30 steps, batch 128 prompts, 5 rollouts per prompt, lr 5e-6, KL coef 0.001, entropy coef 0.001, max response 4096 tokens (8192 / 16384 for lengths 11-20 / 21-30). Both models and the untrained Base are evaluated on held-out atomic and compound tasks at lengths 5-30 (accuracy = exact match of the final state), averaged over 3 runs.
official.claim: With Qwen3-4B-Instruct trained at lengths 5-10, RL-Compound beats RL-Atomic on compound tasks at test length 10 at every level (Level I ~0.41 vs ~0.22, Level II ~0.44 vs ~0.25, Level III ~0.53 vs ~0.00), while on atomic tasks the two stay within ~0.03 of each other at length 10 for Levels I and II and both stay at 0.95 or higher for Level III.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Evaluation on three compositionality types with Qwen3-4B-Instruct, averaged across three runs with the standard deviation shown as a shaded region. Rows evaluate atomic (decomposed skill) and compound (composed task) tasks. RL-Atomic trains on atomic tasks, while RL-Compound trains on compound tasks. Models are trained on small problem lengths (5-10) and evaluated on larger ones (up to 30). Results show a consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry.
official.metric: Exact-match accuracy of the final data-structure state, higher is better; mean over 3 runs with std shown as a shaded band. Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: RL-Compound (GRPO on compound tasks) vs. RL-Atomic (GRPO on atomic tasks), same base model and same number of training steps, with the untrained Base model as reference; evaluated on both atomic and compound tasks.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running GRPO on Qwen3-4B-Instruct with matched settings, RL-Atomic's compound-task accuracy at length 10 comes within about one std of RL-Compound's (e.g. a gap under ~0.08 on Level I or II), or RL-Compound's atomic-task accuracy falls clearly below RL-Atomic's (by more than ~0.05 at lengths 10-15).

title: Geometric Gain Graph: Zero-Token Graph Construction for Multi-Hop RAG
claim_source: Table 6 (Appendix C.1), page 16; same F1 values in Table 1, page 7

official.background: Multi-hop question answering needs a retriever to find several documents that are each relevant to the question but carry different information. Dense retrievers tend to return near-duplicates of the query (a 'similarity trap'), while graph-based RAG systems such as LightRAG and HippoRAG2 build entity graphs with many LLM calls during indexing (millions of tokens) and either drift off-topic or remain bound to surface similarity. The paper asks whether a graph built only from document embeddings, with no LLM tokens spent on indexing, can retrieve better multi-hop evidence.
official.method:
G3RAG builds a document-only graph from passage embeddings (NV-Embed-v2 or Qwen3-8B-embed). For two passages with cosine similarity x, the edge weight is g_ij = x * sqrt(1 - x^2) (cos θ · sin θ), kept only for x in [0.1, 0.7]. A hub penalty multiplies each edge into node j by exp(-β ρ_j), where ρ_j is j's mean cosine similarity to all nodes (β = 0.7 on MuSiQue, 0.1 elsewhere). Rows are normalized into a transition matrix T.

At query time, dense retrieval returns k = 10 candidates; an LLM filter (Llama-3.3-70B) keeps s = 2 seed passages. A uniform vector over the seeds is multiplied once by T (one diffusion step, no PageRank iterations), and the seeds plus top diffused nodes form n = 5 passages given to Llama-3.3-70B with HippoRAG2's QA prompt. HippoRAG2 uses the same embedder, generator, prompts, k = 10, n = 5 and its own s = 5. Evaluation uses 1,000 sampled questions per dataset from HippoRAG's curated MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA with HippoRAG2's passage corpora.
official.claim: On MuSiQue (1,000 questions, NV-Embed-v2 embeddings, Llama-3.3-70B reader, 5 retrieved passages), G3RAG reaches answer F1 52.28 vs. 47.60 for HippoRAG2, a +4.68 point gain with paired-bootstrap 95% CI [2.35, 7.02] (p = 0.00018).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Statistical significance of F1 differences using Nv-embed-v2. ∆ denotes G3RAG minus HippoRAG2 in F1 points. Confidence intervals are for ∆, and significance is assessed at p < 0.05.
official.metric: QA token-level F1 (higher is better) on 1,000 questions; single run. The CI is a paired bootstrap over questions, not over seeds; no seed variance is reported
official.comparison: G3RAG vs. HippoRAG2 (strongest graph baseline) with identical embedder, generator, prompts and final 5-document budget
official.falsification_criterion: With the same setup on MuSiQue, G3RAG's F1 does not exceed HippoRAG2's, or the paired-bootstrap 95% CI of the difference includes 0.

title: FlashBoB: I/O-Efficient Exact Backward-over-Backward for Softmax Attention
claim_source: Table 1 (left panel), page 8; extended sweep to N = 262,144 in Table 10 (Appendix K), page 31

official.background: Some training methods differentiate through a gradient computation: Hessian-vector products for second-order optimizers such as Sophia-H, test-time training, gradient-written memory and meta-learning. When the model contains softmax attention, this requires the derivative of the attention backward pass itself (backward-over-backward, BoB). FlashAttention makes the forward and first backward passes I/O-efficient, but has no double backward, so exact attention BoB falls back to PyTorch autograd, which materializes N x N tensors and runs out of memory at modest sequence lengths. Hand-written HVP kernels (from GradMem) and FlashBack reduce but do not remove this cost.
official.method:
Given upstream matrices U_Q, U_K, U_V for the first-backward outputs (dQ, dK, dV), BoB computes the gradients of Phi = <dQ,U_Q> + <dK,U_K> + <dV,U_V> with respect to Q, K, V and dO. FlashBoB shows that the softmax double backward introduces only two row-wise scalars (alpha, E) that enter all outputs affinely, so the row-side outputs can be accumulated without knowing the scalars first and corrected at the end of each row block.

This gives an exact two-pass Triton kernel in the FlashAttention execution model: Pass 1 holds a query-row block in SRAM, streams key/value blocks, recomputes probability tiles from the saved log-normalizer L, and writes (alpha, E) plus the row-owned outputs d~(Q) and d~(dO); Pass 2 holds a key/value block, streams row blocks, reads (alpha, E) and writes d~(K), d~(V) once per block. No N x N tensor is written to HBM and no global atomic adds are used. In the benchmark, PyTorch SDPA computes the forward and first backward and only the attention double backward is replaced.
official.claim: On an isolated causal attention layer (batch 4, 12 heads, d = 64, BF16 inputs with FP32 reductions, one A100 80GB), FlashBoB computes exact attention BoB faster than PyTorch autograd (MATH, which fits only up to N = 4,096) and the GradMem HVP-M / HVP-S kernels at every N from 256 to 8,192 (e.g. 25.80 ms vs. 89.14 ms for HVP-S at N = 4,096; 95.11 ms vs. 356.84 ms at N = 8,192, 3.75x), with far lower peak memory (1,702 vs. 55,971 MiB at N = 8,192), and keeps running at N >= 16,384 where all three baselines run out of memory.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Isolated attention-layer BoB scaling at d = 64 (NVIDIA A100 80GB) and d = 128 (NVIDIA B300), with batch 4, 12 heads, causal mask, and BF16 inputs with FP32 reductions. Peak memory reports the lowest-memory baseline that fits (HVP-M) versus FlashBoB; full four-method memory tables through N=262,144 are in Appendix K. OOM denotes out of memory; best values are bold.
official.metric: wall-clock time per BoB call in ms (lower is better; median of 100 CUDA-synchronized timed iterations after 25 warmup iterations) and peak memory via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated in MiB (lower is better). No ± reported; single-run medians.
official.comparison: FlashBoB vs. MATH (PyTorch autograd double backward), HVP-M and HVP-S (GradMem-derived hand-written HVP kernels), same shapes and hardware
official.falsification_criterion: At d = 64 on an A100 80GB, FlashBoB is not at least ~2x faster than the faster of HVP-M/HVP-S at N = 4,096 or 8,192, or its outputs disagree with the autograd reference beyond BF16/FP32 reduction-order error, or FlashBoB also runs out of memory at N = 16,384 while a baseline does not.

title: Displacement Geometry Captures Platonic Shared Reality Across Models and Modalities
claim_source: Table 6 (Appendix C), page 17; paired tests in Table 5 (Appendix B), page 17; summarized in Figure 2a (page 5) and Section 4.3 (page 6)

official.background: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) says independently trained models converge on a shared statistical model of reality. Both the supporting evidence (mutual-kNN overlap) and the counter-evidence (alignment degrading at scale) define 'shared reality' through sample proximities. This paper asks a different question: after aligning two models' representation spaces, does the vector from sample i to sample j point in the same direction in both? If it does, models could share relational geometry even when the aligned positions of individual samples differ.
official.method:
For each model, take hidden states after a transformer block (mean-pooled over tokens for LLMs, CLS or global average pooling for ViTs), reduce them to a common dimension with PCA (500 by default; 20 and 100 also reported) and whiten them (covariance^-1/2). For each model pair, fit a single orthogonal Procrustes rotation (rotation/reflection only, no scaling) on 10,000 matched Flickr30k image-caption items, then evaluate on 10,000 disjoint held-out items. PCA, whitening and the rotation are fit only on the alignment split. After alignment, each model's mean (passed through its own PCA and whitening) is added back.

Two cosine metrics are computed on the held-out items: Pointwise = cos(a_i, b_i), averaged over individual items, and Cross-Model = cos(a_i - a_j, b_i - b_j), averaged over 10,000 random unordered pairs. The mean shift cancels in Cross-Model but not in Pointwise. The model set has 44 encoders: 25 ViTs (supervised, CLIP, DINO, MAE, SigLIP, I-JEPA; base/large/huge) and 19 LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Mistral, OLMo, Bloomz). Results are grouped into vision-vision (V-V), language-language (L-L) and vision-language (V-L) pairs. Randomly initialized models serve as a null and give Cross-Model near zero.
official.claim: At the sample level (Flickr30k, PCA-500, rigid Procrustes alignment), Cross-Model displacement similarity exceeds Pointwise similarity in all three modality groups: V-V 0.45 ± 0.07 vs. 0.31 ± 0.13, L-L 0.73 ± 0.07 vs. 0.36 ± 0.08, V-L 0.31 ± 0.02 vs. 0.19 ± 0.04. The paired median differences are 0.231 ± 0.008 (V-V), 0.387 ± 0.007 (L-L) and 0.146 ± 0.002 (V-L), all with p < 0.0001.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Comparison: Pointwise vs. Cross-Model similarity across different PCA dimensions.
official.metric: Mean cosine similarity on held-out items or pairs, higher means more agreement. In Table 6, the paper does not define ± (caption and text are silent); it may be a spread over model pairs, but the paper does not say so. In Table 5, ± is the bootstrap SE of the median paired difference (Cross-Model - Pointwise) across model pairs, with Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted).
official.comparison: Cross-Model (displacement direction) similarity vs. Pointwise (aligned position) similarity, computed with the same Procrustes rotation on the same model pairs and held-out data; randomly initialized networks as a null for Cross-Model
official.falsification_criterion: With the paper's protocol on Flickr30k (PCA-500, whitening, orthogonal Procrustes fit on 10k items and evaluated on 10k disjoint items), the paired Cross-Model - Pointwise difference is not clearly positive (e.g. median D < 0.1 for L-L or ≤ 0 for V-L) over a representative set of model pairs. A weaker refutation: Cross-Model for trained pairs is not clearly above the random-init null.

title: From Experts to Sub-experts: Fine-grained Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for MoE LLMs

official.background: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs usually works either on fixed weight matrices (LoRA) or on whole experts: Expert-Specialized Fine-Tuning (ESFT) updates only the experts the router uses most on the target data. The paper argues that whole experts are still too coarse, because inside an activated expert only a small fraction of the intermediate (FFN) channels respond strongly to a given task. Updating whole experts therefore spends trainable parameters on channels that do little for the task.
official.method:
NSFT (Neural Sub-expert Fine-Tuning) splits each GLU expert along its intermediate dimension into groups of G consecutive channels (sub-experts; default G = 16 on OLMoE). On the target training data it accumulates each channel's SiLU gate activation over the tokens routed to that expert, normalizes these values within the expert, and multiplies by the expert's routing frequency in that layer. Channel scores are summed per group, groups in a layer are ranked, and the smallest set whose cumulative score reaches τ = 0.2 is made trainable (the same threshold ESFT uses to select whole experts). All other parameters stay frozen.

Because only part of each expert is updated, NSFT multiplies the learning rate per expert by min(d_expert / K, 5), where K is the number of selected channels. It also multiplies gradients per group by a clipped, entropy-tempered ratio of the group's activation energy to the mean energy of the selected groups, and refreshes these coefficients online every 5 steps with EMA 0.9 (dynamic gradient scaling). Training recipe for all methods: 2 epochs, global batch 8, AdamW (β2 = 0.95), peak LR 3e-5 with linear decay to 3e-6, packed sequences of length 8192, bf16, seed 1234. ESFT and LoRA use weight decay 0.1, NSFT uses 0. LoRA is rank 32 or 64 (α = 64 for r32) on the MLP projections.
official.claim: On OLMoE fine-tuned separately on each domain at τ = 0.2, NSFT beats expert-level ESFT while training fewer parameters: SciRiFF 44.38 / 42.05 vs. 40.15 / 38.08 (4k / 8k), RAG-Instruct 70.36 vs. 64.47, TableQA 24.13 vs. 19.47. The in-domain average across six domains is 46.62 vs. 43.42 for ESFT and 43.38 for LoRA-r64, and the general-benchmark average is about the same as ESFT's (45.96 vs. 46.24).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: In-domain fine-tuning results on OLMoE under threshold τ = 0.2. Each domain column reports the result after fine-tuning on the corresponding domain dataset, while Train. denotes the percentage of trainable parameters. Avg. and General Avg. denote the average in-domain performance and the average general-benchmark performance, respectively.
official.metric: In-domain score on each domain's evaluation set after fine-tuning on that domain (higher is better), plus the mean of GPQA, MMLU-Redux, C-Eval and IFEval ('General Avg.'). Single run with seed 1234; no error bars or seed variance reported.
official.comparison: NSFT-OLMoE (τ = 0.2, G = 16, learning-rate scaling + dynamic gradient scaling) vs. ESFT-OLMoE (τ = 0.2) and LoRA-r32/r64. All use the same data, epochs, batch size and learning-rate schedule. Base model and Full FT are shown for reference.

title: GeoPair: Geometry-Preserving Cross-Layer Factorization for Training-Free Transformer Compression

official.background: Post-training compression of large language models by matrix factorization replaces each weight matrix with a cheaper structured approximation, using a small calibration set so that the approximation preserves layer outputs rather than raw weights. Most methods factorize each layer on its own. Sharing one dictionary (basis) across several layers could save more parameters, but each layer has its own activation statistics and hence its own whitening transform, which makes direct sharing awkward. The prior cross-layer method, Basis Sharing, averages the covariances of adjacent layers into one global whitening and only pairs neighbouring layers, which the authors argue distorts each layer's geometry.
official.method:
GeoPair pairs weight matrices that share an input dimension (across layers and projection types) and approximates each pair as W1 ≈ D C1, W2 ≈ D C2 with a shared dictionary D. It minimizes the sum of each layer's calibration-whitened error, ||L_i W_i − L_i D C_i||_F^2, where L_i is the Cholesky factor of that layer's own regularized Gram matrix X_i^T X_i + ηI. Optimization alternates between a coefficient update and a closed-form dictionary update obtained by solving a two-term generalized Sylvester equation via simultaneous diagonalization; D is initialized from the SVD of [W1 W2]. Coefficients are made column-sparse with Hard Thresholding Pursuit (2 HTP iterations, 10 conjugate-gradient iterations, KS ratio 2.5). Pairs are chosen by maximum-weight matching (Edmonds' Blossom) on a whitened, shift-minimized normalized Frobenius distance between weight matrices.

Calibration uses 256 FineWeb samples, with no fine-tuning after compression. Models are evaluated zero-shot on PIQA, HellaSwag, LAMBADA (OpenAI), ARC-e, ARC-c, SciQ, RACE and MMLU (average accuracy) and on WikiText and LAMBADA perplexity. In Table 6, Llama2 7B is compressed at compression ratios 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 and compared with Basis Sharing, CoSpaDi (grouped) and a dense GeoPair variant (GeoPair*, no sparsification, Basis-Sharing grouping).
official.claim: On Llama2 7B at compression ratio 0.4 with no fine-tuning, full GeoPair reaches 55.8% average zero-shot accuracy over 8 benchmarks and WikiText perplexity 15.64, versus 47.8% and 25 for CoSpaDi (grouped) and 42.9% and 39.6 for Basis Sharing.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Performance comparison of different compression methods. We denote GeoPair* as our method with dense factorization (no sparsification) using basis-sharing grouping, and GeoPair as our full pipeline with both sparsification and optimal grouping.
official.metric: Average zero-shot accuracy over PIQA, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, ARC-e, ARC-c, SciQ, RACE, MMLU (higher is better), plus WikiText and LAMBADA perplexity (lower is better). title: M-plicits: Neural Implicit Surfaces via Nested Multiscale Residuals
claim_source: Table 3, page 9 (per-mesh comparisons in Figures S22-S25, pages 18-20)

official.background: Surfaces can be reconstructed from oriented point clouds as the zero-level set of a neural signed distance function (SDF). Single large sinusoidal MLPs (SIREN) are slow to query, which hurts sphere tracing and marching cubes. Grid-based encodings such as Instant-NGP are fast but tend to fit measurement noise into the surface, and earlier multiscale methods (BACON, IDF) can produce artifacts or off-surface blobs. The paper asks whether a coarse-to-fine residual SDF can be fast to render and also robust to noisy input points.
official.method:
M-plicits represents the SDF as a sum of three SIRENs: f1 (coarse, (128,2), omega0 = 30) trained over the whole domain, then residuals r1 ((256,2), omega0 = 45) and r2 ((400,2), omega0 = 100) with f2 = f1 + r1 and f3 = f2 + r2. Each residual is trained only inside a narrow band {|f_i| < delta_i} around the previous level's zero set, where delta_i = (1 + eps) * max_j |f_i(x_j)| over the input points. Each level uses a data loss (f(x_j) = 0 and gradient aligned with the input normal N_j) plus an Eikonal loss over its band. Eikonal samples come from dithering around the input points with rejection outside the band, and extra data samples are taken along the normals (f(x_j + t N_j) = t). The coarse SIREN acts as a low-pass prior, so noise is not fitted.

For the noise test, the vertices of Stanford and Thingi32 meshes are displaced along the ground-truth normal by up to 1% of the bounding box. Each method fits the noisy oriented point cloud. The zero-level set is extracted with marching cubes at 512^3, 500K points are sampled on the mesh, and L2 Chamfer distance and IoU are computed with PyTorch3D; the evaluation protocol says this is done "against the input point cloud" (Sec. 4), without saying whether the clean or the noisy cloud is used for Table 3. Baselines are iNGP (coarse and fine), IDF and BACON (8th-layer output).
official.claim: On Stanford + Thingi32 with 1% vertex noise along the normals, M-plicits (fine) reaches mean Chamfer distance 3.36e-5 vs. 2.80e-4 for iNGP fine (about 8x lower) and 1.68e-3 for BACON, and mean IoU 0.582 vs. 0.322 for IDF (the best baseline on IoU) and 0.309 for iNGP fine.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Quantitative robustness to noise. CD (↓) and IoU (↑) for Stanford and Thingi32 under vertex noise. Bold, italic, underlined = best, second, third.
official.metric: L2 Chamfer distance (lower is better) and IoU (higher is better), mean and median over the dataset's meshes. Single run, no seeds or error bars reported.
official.comparison: M-plicits coarse/medium/fine vs. iNGP coarse, iNGP fine, IDF, BACON, all fit to the same noisy point clouds
official.falsification_criterion: On the 1%-noise Stanford + Thingi32 set, iNGP fine's mean Chamfer distance comes within a factor of ~2 of M-plicits fine, or iNGP fine matches or beats M-plicits fine on a majority of meshes, or M-plicits fine's mean IoU is not clearly above that of iNGP fine and IDF.

title: The Shape of Events: Edge-Based Inductive Biases via Cross-Domain Distillation
claim_source: Table 13 (Appendix A.10), page 24; cue-conflict values also in Appendix C.1 / Figure 11a (page 29) and Figure 2b (page 5)

official.background: ImageNet-trained CNNs are known to prefer local high-frequency texture over global object shape, and this texture bias is linked to fragility under color shifts, noise and other distribution shifts. Event cameras record only per-pixel brightness changes, so event data mostly carries edges and contours, but the event domain lacks diagnostic benchmarks for measuring what inductive bias such data gives a model. The paper distills an event-trained classifier into an RGB ImageNet classifier so that the standard RGB diagnostics (cue-conflict shape bias, hue rotation, ImageNet-C, band-limited noise, linear-probe transfer) can be used to characterize that bias.
official.method:
The teacher is the public DiST ResNet-34 trained on N-ImageNet (ImageNet re-recorded with an event camera from a monitor; 48.43% top-1), kept frozen. The student is an RGB ResNet-34 trained from scratch on ImageNet-1k with standard logit distillation: L = (1 - alpha) CE(y, p_s(x_strong)) + alpha T^2 KL(p_t(x_event) || p_s(x_weak)), where x_event is the instance-paired N-ImageNet sample, x_strong is the RGB image under a strong pipeline (RandomResizedCrop, flip, RandAugment, RandomErasing) and x_weak is a Resize/CenterCrop view. ED_Student uses alpha = 0.2 and T = 3.0. The baseline is the same ResNet-34 trained with alpha = 0 (cross-entropy only).

Both models use AdamW, lr 2e-3, weight decay 0.05, batch 512, 120 epochs with 5-epoch warmup then cosine, seed 1, and DDP on 8x A100. Shape bias is measured with the bethgelab/model-vs-human cue-conflict benchmark (Geirhos et al.) under the 16-class restricted-argmax protocol: the fraction of shape decisions among trials where the model picks either the shape or the texture class.
official.claim: On ImageNet-1k with a ResNet-34 trained under an identical recipe, adding event-teacher distillation (ED_Student, alpha = 0.2) raises cue-conflict shape bias from 0.212 (baseline) to 0.375, also well above the matched non-event distillation control Canny_Distilled (0.270; same α = 0.2, T = 3.0 recipe with an RGB Canny-edge teacher), while clean top-1 drops from 73.9% to 69.7%; ED_Student also scores higher than the baseline on ImageNet-Sketch (28.1 vs. 23.7, but Canny_Distilled reaches 27.9) and under band-limited noise at 0.95π (57.5 vs. 44.3; Canny_Distilled 35.6).

title: StarWM: Self-Supervised Trained Attention Routing for Robust World Models
claim_source: Table 6 (Appendix D.2.1), page 25; summarized in Figure 5 and Figure 1 (right) in the main text

official.background: Reconstruction-based world models such as DreamerV3 learn latent dynamics by reconstructing every pixel, so their representation capacity is spent in proportion to pixel area rather than relevance; with distracting video backgrounds the latent fills up with background content and policies degrade. Reconstruction-free alternatives avoid this bias but lose pixel-level grounding. The paper targets visual control from images when the background is a distracting video.
official.method:
StarWM modifies only the encoder and decoder of DreamerV3. A cross-attention module with N learnable queries attends over the encoder's spatial feature map (keys = features + 2D sinusoidal positions; values = features + normalized coordinates). The attended tokens become the RSSM input (the 'dynamics stream'). The attention parameters are trained only by self-supervised dynamics objectives, namely inverse dynamics (predict the action from consecutive attention-pooled features) and temporal contrastive learning, while stop-gradients prevent reconstruction and RSSM losses from moving the attention.

A dual-stream decoder paints the dynamics-stream features back onto the attended locations (spatial broadcast) and fills the rest from a residual stream: a Gaussian-bottlenecked VAE path over the full encoder output that absorbs background for the reconstruction loss but is never fed to the RSSM and is dropped during imagination. Policy learning is DreamerV3's actor-critic in imagination, unchanged.
official.claim: On DeepMind Control with random-frame video backgrounds (VHR, 1M env steps), default reward-free StarWM obtains a higher final return than all four baselines (DreamerV3, DenoisedMDP, Iso-Dream++, R2-Dreamer) by margins far beyond seed std on 4 tasks: Walker Walk 851 ± 51 vs. best baseline 517 ± 68, Walker Run 435 ± 73 vs. 191 ± 3, Cheetah Run 469 ± 44 vs. 213 ± 45, Cartpole 563 ± 50 vs. 144 ± 3.

title: Learning Provable Neural Network Observer for Uncertain Dynamical Systems
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (trajectories in Figure 3, page 9; observer-level RMSE in Table 6, Appendix F.1, page 20)

official.background: Controllers for uncertain dynamical systems, such as drones near the ground or underwater vehicles in turbulent flow, often depend on an observer that estimates the state and the unknown disturbance online. Neural network observers can capture nonlinear disturbances better than classical ones such as extended state observers (ESO). Prior work (Chen et al. 2023) certified their Lyapunov stability with a Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) on the network weights. Enforcing that LMI throughout training produces large semidefinite programs that are slow or intractable for wide or deep networks.
official.method:
The observer augments a known linear model (A, B, C, B_omega) with a neural network pi_theta (tanh residual network) driven by the scaled output error. It produces a state estimate x_hat1 and a lumped-disturbance estimate x_hat2 (Eq. 2). Training has two stages. Stage I (point-guided Lyapunov pre-training) samples error states eta_i from a truncated normal on a compact domain and minimizes the mean of ReLU(F_V(eta_i, theta) + xi) + gamma||theta||^2. F_V is the quadratic-Lyapunov decrease bound of Eq. 6 with V = eta^T P eta, decay rate rho and disturbance-derivative bound M_w. Stage II starts from the Stage I weights and minimizes phi(lambda_max(H(theta))) + beta||theta||^2 until the LMI H(theta) < 0 of Lemma 2 holds, which gives a global stability certificate. Both stages use Adam.

For the Quad-UAV experiment, a 12-state quadrotor with a ground-effect force f_G = g2 R(z) / (h + g1)^2 * T_cmd (g1 = 0.1 +/- 0.01, g2 = 1.0 +/- 0.25 perturbed) is controlled by a fixed PID controller. The observer's disturbance estimate f_a_hat is subtracted from the thrust command (T'_cmd = T_cmd - f_a_hat). Hyperparameters are pre-training 100k epochs at lr 0.01, fine-tuning 15k epochs at lr 0.01, epsilon = 0.01, P = diag(1,1,1,0.1 x9, 1,1,1,0.1 x9), rho = 0.1, M_w = 0.5, xi = 10, beta = 0.01 and phi(lambda) = 1e5 * lambda for lambda > 0. The baseline Neural Lander learns a feedforward ground-effect compensator from 40,000 collected data points, using the hyperparameters of Shi et al. 2019. The metric is vertical trajectory tracking error in landing and take-off.
official.claim: On the simulated Quad-UAV with ground effect, PID + the LMI-certified neural network observer has a vertical tracking error of 0.1471 ± 0.0602 m in landing and 0.0002 ± 0.0000 m in take-off. PID + Neural Lander has 0.5732 ± 0.1188 m and 0.2444 ± 0.0297 m, and plain PID has 2.2006 ± 0.1456 m and 0.1255 ± 0.0266 m.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparative analysis of tracking errors and data requirements for Quad-UAV control. Here, "per task" means that once the environment or disturbance changes, new data must be collected and the model must be retrained. The label "once" means that the same trained parameters can be reused across changes in the environment as long as the underlying system is unchanged.
