title: LogicTree-RAG: Logic Tree-guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Long-form Patent Drafting

official.background: Drafting a patent from an invention means turning a technical disclosure into a long, legally formatted document (claims, background, summary, detailed description) that is complete and faithful to the invention. LLMs struggle to sustain long outputs with consistent global structure. Earlier full-patent generators such as COPGEN (Pap2Pat) or AutoPatent rely on outlines or draft information taken from the reference patent, which is not available in practice. The paper frames the task as generating a whole patent from a pre-publication research paper with no such priors.
official.method:
LogicTree-RAG first splits the source paper into semantically coherent chunks: adjacent paragraphs are merged while their embedding cosine similarity is at least tau_s = 0.8 and the chunk stays under 512 tokens. The chunks are indexed in a Milvus vector store. The backbone LLM writes a draft technical description from the chunks. This draft becomes the root of a 'logic tree', and the LLM then decomposes it into first-level child nodes. Nodes are expanded breadth-first. For each node, up to 100 candidate chunks are retrieved using the node's content as the query. They are reranked by a discriminative relevance score (similarity to the node minus the maximum similarity to the node's siblings), and the top 5 are kept. A global novelty test skips a node whose evidence is already covered elsewhere in the tree, outside the parent's branch. Otherwise the node is expanded into child nodes generated from the evidence, and refined: the LLM finds under-specified terms and completes them with retrieved evidence if they are domain concepts that appear in the paper, and from its own knowledge otherwise. Construction stops when the tree reaches 64 nodes, and tree depth is capped at 3.

The patent is then written by traversing the tree. Background and Summary are generated from a BFS traversal. For the Detailed Description, the LLM clusters the tree into subtrees and expands each one by DFS. The backbone is Qwen3-80B with temperature 0.3, top-p 1.0 and at most 8,192 tokens per call. In the agentic baselines (Appendix G.2), semantic chunking, node-aware retrieval and evidence-guided generation are exposed as callable tools to the same backbone, and the logic-tree orchestration is replaced by generic ReAct or Plan-then-Execute planning. Evaluation uses the 500-pair Pap2Pat test set: Coverage is SCALE NLI entailment of reference-patent sentences by the generated patent; F_Pat is SCALE entailment of generated sentences by the reference patent; F_Src is the same with the reference patent plus the source paper as premise. ROUGE-L, StyloMetrix style, repetition rate and DiscoScore coherence are also reported.
official.claim: On the 500-pair Pap2Pat test set with a Qwen3-80B backbone, LogicTree-RAG's logic-tree orchestration produces patents with higher coverage (43.79 vs. 42.02), patent-grounded factuality (F_Pat 58.92 vs. 56.35) and source-grounded factuality (F_Src 66.34 vs. 64.96) than a Plan-then-Execute agent given the same chunking, retrieval and generation tools. It also beats a ReAct agent with the same tools (40.28 / 55.98 / 64.85).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Performance comparison of LogicTree-RAG against agentic baselines for patent drafting.
official.metric: SCALE NLI-based Coverage, F_Pat and F_Src (0-100, higher is better), averaged over the 500 test pairs; the paper reports no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals
official.comparison: LogicTree-RAG (Qwen3-80B) vs. ReAct and Plan-then-Execute agents with the same Qwen3-80B backbone and the same tools, where only the logic-tree orchestration is replaced. Table 1 (page 7) gives single-call and COPGEN baselines for context.

title: Brenier Meets Adversarial Training: Optimal Transport Geometry for Robust Learning
claim_source: Table 2, panel (c) lambda = 1.0 (Appendix F.3), page 37; same numbers as Figure 3 in the main text (page 10)

official.background: Penalty-based Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (DRO) trains a model against an adversary that may move each training sample anywhere but pays lambda times the squared transport distance. For neural-network losses with a realistic (small) lambda, the adversary's per-sample maximization is nonconvex, and standard adversarial training solves it by independent per-sample gradient ascent (particle ascent, PA). The paper shows that the optimal adversarial transport map must be cyclically monotone (as in Brenier's theorem), that PA violates this in two or more dimensions and so wastes transport cost, and proposes two adversaries that enforce the property. The question is whether a better-structured adversary actually gives more robust models under distribution shift.
official.method:
MPA (multi-start particle ascent) runs R rounds of K parallel gradient-ascent steps on the adversarial samples of a batch. Before each round and once at the end, it reassigns each empirical sample to whichever adversarial sample in the batch pool gives the highest value of f(theta, z) - lambda * ||z - z_hat||^2. This makes the batch map assignment-stationary and therefore cyclically monotone. ICNN-DRO instead parameterizes the adversarial map as T_omega = grad psi_omega, where psi_omega is an input-convex neural network (softplus activations, exponentiated positive weights, a PSD quadratic term only in the final layer, initialized near the identity). The map is cyclically monotone by construction. Training alternates K ascent steps on omega with one descent step on the model parameters theta, evaluated at z_i = T_omega(z_hat_i).

Robust control setup (Sec. 6.3, App. F.3): CartPole with uncertain pole mass and half-length z = (m_p, l) in [0.05, 0.2] x [0.25, 0.75], with training anchors sampled uniformly. The distance is width-normalized and lambda = 1. The loss is the negative expected return, and the adversary differentiates it through the unrolled dynamics using a straight-through estimator for actions and a smooth survival function for termination (beta = 20, tau = 1). The policy is trained with PPO (MLP actor and critic, SGD with Nesterov momentum 0.9) for 100 epochs. Each iteration uses B = 64 nominal anchors plus one adversarial counterpart each, so 128 environments. MPA uses R = 3 rounds of K = 15 steps. Every method is evaluated by 1,000 deterministic rollouts with horizon H = 1,000 on the original physics and on six shifted variants: Light, Long and Soft Gravity (easier), and Heavy, Short and Strong Gravity (harder, outside the training box).
official.claim: On robust CartPole with lambda = 1, ICNN-DRO has a higher mean episode length than every baseline on all 7 physics variants, including the strongest baseline WFR (Original 829.3 ± 6.6 vs 435.0 ± 6.8; Heavy 725.2 ± 7.7 vs 337.5 ± 4.1; Short 561.7 ± 6.4 vs 276.2 ± 2.0; Strong Gravity 472.5 ± 7.6 vs 287.3 ± 2.8). Also, MPA beats standard particle ascent PA on all 7 variants (e.g., Original 570.3 ± 8.4 vs 342.4 ± 5.4).

Panel (a) reports λ = 0.1; panel (b) reports λ = 0.5 and panel (c) reports λ = 1. The leftmost column corresponds to the original training configuration, the middle group to easier physics variants (Light, Long, Soft Gravity), and the right group to harder variants (Heavy, Short, Strong Gravity). Bold entries indicate the best result per column.

title: Nonparametric In-Context Learning under Growing Geometric Complexity: Minimax Optimality and Local Geometry-Adaptivity of Transformers

official.background: Nonparametric in-context learning treats a transformer as an estimator: given a prompt of (X_i, Y_i) pairs and a query X_{n+1}, it predicts f at the query without updating its parameters. Existing theory covers Euclidean domains or a single manifold. Real data such as images and embeddings look more like unions of manifolds with different intrinsic dimensions, smoothness and sampling masses. The paper asks whether transformers can still reach the minimax rate under this kind of unknown, heterogeneous geometry. It also asks whether, in practice, a trained transformer can match an estimator that is told the local geometry.
official.method:
Synthetic task (Appendix C): ambient dimension D = 64, context size n = 40,000, and K = 12 ellipsoidal sphere components, one for each (intrinsic dimension d, Hölder smoothness alpha) in {2,4,6,8} x {0.75,1.5,3}, with unequal mixture masses (0.02 to 0.20), density tilts, and shrinking uniform-ball covariate noise. Each task draws a random ridge-plus-bump function per component. Responses carry uniform noise with variance 0.01. The test target is the noiseless latent value f(X*_{n+1}) on 2,000 fixed test prompts.

Learned model: a 'softmax workspace' transformer with 286,401 parameters (width 64, 4 blocks, 4 heads, 32 learned workspace tokens that cross-attend to all 40,000 context tokens, tanh readout). It is trained from scratch with AdamW (lr 3e-4, cosine schedule, effective batch 25), one pass over Gamma pretraining prompts, for Gamma in {100k, 200k, 500k, 1M}, with seed 0. title: Panoptic Scene Program Diffusion Transformer

official.background: Modern text-to-image diffusion models produce realistic images but still fail on compositional prompts: they get counts wrong, attach attributes to the wrong object, swap subject and object in relations, and drop details in long prompts. Existing fixes either inject fixed structure (boxes, layouts, scene graphs) as an external condition, or steer a pretrained model at inference time. The paper asks whether making an explicit, instance-indexed scene representation part of the generative state itself improves compositional faithfulness.
official.method:
PSP-DiT models the joint distribution p(z, s | y) of an image latent z (from a representation autoencoder, RAE) and a 'panoptic scene program' latent s, given a prompt y. The program has one token per object instance (up to 16), relation edge (up to 32), cardinality group (up to 8) and scene-context slot (8). A frozen parser turns the prompt into an initial program, and the program latent is initialized as noise around that prior. A coupled DiT runs within-stream self-attention for image tokens and program tokens, followed by bidirectional cross-attention between the streams, so both latents are denoised jointly over 50 sampling steps. Heads predict per-instance ownership maps over the latent grid and coarse depth ordering.

Training adds program-denoising, ownership/depth grounding, instance-to-region alignment and cycle-consistency losses (a frozen recognizer parses the predicted image back into a program) to the image denoising loss. Weights are lambda_prog=1, lambda_pan=1, lambda_align=0.25, lambda_cycle=0.5, lambda_D=0.1. The matched baseline Ours-FlatText uses the same RAE, backbone, image-caption data, optimizer (AdamW, lr 1e-4, cosine), 1.2M steps at 512px for the 1B model and the same 50-step sampler, but conditions only on flat text tokens and has no program stream. Evaluation uses GenEval 2 (Rewritten prompts, 4 fixed seeds, 4 images per prompt, no best-of-N), SANEval-Simple, PSG-Score and DetailMaster Avg.
official.claim: At 1B backbone size and 512px, under matched data, training budget and 50-step sampling, PSP-DiT beats the flat-text baseline Ours-FlatText on all four compositional benchmarks: GenEval 2 (Rewritten) 38.2 vs. 32.8, SANEval-Simple 73.6 vs. 65.9, PSG-Score 0.73 vs. 0.65, DetailMaster Avg. 72.4 vs. 66.8; the gain also holds at 0.5B/512px (GenEval 2 33.6 vs. 28.9, SANEval 68.4 vs. 61.7, DetailMaster 67.9 vs. 63.2).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main quantitative evidence. Panel (a) reports the main compositional benchmark comparison; panel (b) checks image quality and prompt alignment; panel (c) breaks down gains by compositional skill; panel (d) tests scaling and resolution robustness; and panel (e) reports efficiency for the matched 1B setting. GE2 denotes GenEval 2 on the Rewritten prompt set reported on a x100 scale, SANE denotes SANEval-Simple on a x100 scale, DM denotes DetailMaster Avg., IR denotes ImageReward, and Pref. denotes human preference win rate. All panels use the unified evaluation pipeline described in Section 4.1. Human preference denotes model-specific win rates against the sampled opponent pool; values are not complementary head-to-head percentages.
official.metric: GenEval 2 Rewritten prompt-level correctness x100, SANEval-Simple averaged score x100, PSG-Score in [0,1], DetailMaster mean of 8 task accuracies; all higher is better. No ± reported (single training run per model; the paper calls these deterministic benchmark scores).
official.comparison: PSP-DiT vs. Ours-FlatText (same backbone, RAE, training data, optimization schedule and inference recipe, without the scene-program latent), at 0.5B, 1B and 3B backbone sizes
official.falsification_criterion: A matched re-implementation (same backbone, data and step budget for both arms) in which PSP-DiT's GenEval 2 gain over the flat-text baseline is under about 2 points, or in which it fails to improve SANEval-Simple and DetailMaster, or in which the gap is within the spread across training seeds.

title: SynDORBench: Evaluating LVLM Perceptual Robustness Under Physically Constrained Visibility Conditions
claim_source: Table 3, page 9 (lighting-stratified breakdown in Table 7 and Figure 3, Appendix A.5.2, pages 18-19)

official.background: LVLM benchmarks such as MMBench, MMMU and SEED-Bench mostly use well-lit, high-resolution images, so they say little about how far away, or in how little light, a model can still see a person. Fixed-camera practice uses the DORI standard (BS EN 62676-4), which sets the minimum pixel density (px/m) a human needs to detect, observe, recognize or identify a person. The paper builds a synthetic benchmark calibrated to those pixel densities to measure where LVLM perception breaks down and how it compares with a conventional object detector.
official.method:
Images are rendered in Blender with a simulated 1080p, 1/2.8" sensor, 2.8 mm lens, f/1.4 camera. Using the pinhole model, the midpoints between DORI zones (187.5, 93.8, 43.8 px/m) give camera distances of 5.4 m, 10.8 m and 23.0 m. A single SMPL-X human (SMPLitex textures, 8 BABEL-derived action poses) is placed in one of three outdoor scenes (desert, field, wharf), with 8 azimuths x 4 elevations, four lighting conditions (morning, noon, evening, midnight) and a night-vision ISP variant of low-light renders. For night and night-vision images, presence labels are replaced by 'discernibility' labels predicted by an RF+XGBoost ensemble trained on 2,000 human annotations, so a rendered but invisible person counts as absent. The benchmark has 54,864 QA pairs.

For human-presence classification (HPC), each LVLM gets the prompt "Respond only with 1 or 0. Respond with 1 if a person is visible in the image, and 0 if not. Is there a person visible in the image?". Sixteen open LVLMs (<=8B), GPT-4o-mini and YOLO11x are evaluated zero-shot. Accuracy and macro-F1 are reported per distance, averaged over the other factors (lighting, viewpoint, scene, pose).
official.claim: On SynDORBench human-presence classification at the 23.0 m DORI distance (43.8 px/m), zero-shot LVLMs beat YOLO11x by large margins: gemma-3n-E2B-it 88.87% accuracy / 72.12 macro-F1 and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct 80.24% / 64.99, vs. YOLO11x 50.29% / 42.98.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Performance degradation across DORI-calibrated distances for presence classification, with accuracy (Acc) and macro-F1 (F1) reported. Best scores are in bold.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) and macro-F1 (%) on binary presence classification, higher is better; single evaluation run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: Zero-shot LVLMs (best: gemma-3n-E2B-it; widely used: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) vs. the YOLO11x detector on the same 23.0 m images, averaged over lighting, viewpoint, scene and pose

title: RAO-Nav: Probing Omni-Language Models for Zero-shot Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation

official.background: In Semantic Audio-Visual Navigation (SAVN), an embodied agent in an unseen indoor 3D scene hears a short sound from an object and must work out what the object is, where it is, and how to reach it and stop there, even after the sound ends. Existing methods are either policies trained on many simulator trajectories, which generalize poorly to unheard sounds, or zero-shot frameworks that chain several language models together, which are complex to deploy. The paper asks whether a single open omni-language model (OLM) that takes audio, images and text can act as the agent zero-shot.
official.method:
RAO-Nav runs one frozen OLM (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B or Baichuan-Omni-1.5-7B) in an iterative loop with three stages. (1) AudioGoal Prediction: the OLM scores the 21 SAVi audio categories from the accumulated audio and action history. Scores are thresholded and accumulated (tau = 0.12, gamma = 0.5) to form a candidate target set. A plug-in Localization Expert, following the SAVi localization design, takes the binaural log-spectrograms plus the OLM category-score vector and predicts K candidate source positions, which are smoothed over time. (2) Global Reasoning: the OLM is shown a semantic map with the candidate waypoints as lettered or coloured options, together with recent RGB frames and the last five actions, and answers as a multiple-choice question which target to go to. (3) Real-time Action: a deterministic geometric controller turns the chosen path into turn-then-forward discrete actions. While the actions execute, the OLM monitors the surroundings and decides whether to STOP; otherwise the loop re-runs AudioGoal prediction.

LNR (Latent Navigation Reasoning) is a test-time module. It appends L latent placeholder tokens and updates their embeddings by gradient ascent on the frozen OLM's log-likelihood of the predicted audio-goal text, given the historical RGB embeddings. It then mean-pools the latents into a query and keeps the top-K most similar historical frames for the next reasoning step. Evaluation uses SoundSpaces on Habitat with Matterport3D scenes, unheard sounds and unseen scenes, 1,000 test episodes, a cap of 200 steps, 256x256 RGB only (no depth), on one A100-80GB.
official.claim: On 1,000 Matterport3D SAVN test episodes with unheard sounds, zero-shot RAO-Nav + LNR with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B reaches 39.2% success rate. This is higher than the best supervised baseline, K-SAVEN (34.4%), the zero-shot multi-LLM framework RILA (35.4%), and the same pipeline without LNR (36.4%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of four types of navigation frameworks on the Matterport3D test dataset in unheard-sound settings. Oracle† denotes a privileged-input diagnostic setting for Pure VLMs. The model is given the ground-truth audio category, the semantic map, and the ground-truth target location marked on the map. It directly predicts low-level actions.
official.metric: Success Rate (SR, %, higher is better) over 1,000 test episodes. SPL, SNA, DTG and SWS are also reported. The paper gives no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: RAO-Nav + LNR (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, zero-shot) vs. supervised specialized models (AudioGoal, AV-WAN, SAVi, AVLEN, K-SAVEN), zero-shot RILA, Pure VLMs with oracle inputs, and RAO-Nav without LNR
official.falsification_criterion: A rerun of RAO-Nav + LNR with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B on the 1,000-episode MP3D unheard-sound test split gets SR at or below 35.4% (RILA). The LNR claim is also refuted if the same pipeline without LNR matches it within run-to-run variation.

title: Multimodal LLMs Outperform Pathology Foundation Models in Cross-Domain Histological Similarity
claim_source: Tables 13 and 14 (Appendix F), page 25; also Table 2 (page 7) and Table 5 (page 18)

official.background: Pathology foundation models (UNI2H, Virchow2, Midnight, etc.) are self-supervised vision encoders trained on millions of H&E histology tiles and are used for retrieval, few-shot transfer and multi-site studies. For those uses, tiles of the same tissue type should embed close together even when they come from different slides or hospitals. Earlier work showed that these embeddings also encode site-specific signatures (scanner, stain, preparation). This paper asks whether the encoders rank a same-class tile from another institution as more similar than a different-class tile from the same institution, and compares them with general-purpose multimodal LLMs used as zero-shot similarity judges.
official.method:
Relative similarity test: each triplet has a reference tile t_r, a positive t_p of the same class, and a negative t_n of a different class. In the cross-institution setting t_r and t_n come from institution I and t_p from a different institution I'. For embedding models, the candidate with the smaller Euclidean distance to the reference embedding is chosen. For multimodal LLMs, the three images (reference, candidate 1, candidate 2) are sent with a 'biology-focused' prompt (Appendix E.1: focus on cell morphology and tissue architecture, ignore stain intensity, artifacts and preparation) and the model returns JSON with a more_similar_candidate field. Candidate order is randomized, so chance is 50%. Invalid LLM responses are excluded.

CAMELYON16 data: 40 breast lymph-node WSIs from Radboud (21 slides) and Utrecht (19 slides), tiled at 512x512 pixels with stride 256 after Otsu tissue masking and filtered to tiles with at least 1% foreground; tumor vs. normal labels are assigned from the tumor fraction computed on the pixel-level masks with a > 50% threshold. For each (institution, positive class) combination, 100 triplets are sampled (negative from the other class at the same institution), giving 400 triplets. All models are scored on the same 400 triplets.
official.claim: On 400 CAMELYON16 cross-institution triplets, zero-shot Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite picks the same-class, other-institution tile with 0.730 accuracy (95% CI 0.685-0.775), versus 0.640 (0.593-0.685) for Midnight, the best pathology foundation model, and 0.610 for Gemini Embedding 2, the best general encoder (paired McNemar p < 0.001 and p < 0.0001).
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for overall accuracy on HER2ST (cross-slide, n = 2000) and CAMELYON16 (cross-institution, n = 400). Models are grouped by category. Table 14: McNemar's test for key pairwise comparisons. Each test uses paired comparisons where both models returned valid responses. The best LLM is compared against the best pathology foundation model and the best general foundation model for each experiment.
official.metric: Relative similarity accuracy (fraction of triplets where the positive is chosen), higher is better, chance = 0.5. Brackets are bootstrap 95% CIs over triplets (10,000 resamples); single run per model, no seeds; significance from paired McNemar tests.
official.comparison: Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite (multimodal LLM, biology-focused prompt) vs. Midnight (best of 5 pathology encoders) and Gemini Embedding 2 (best of 6 general encoders) on the identical 400 triplets
official.falsification_criterion: On a re-sampled set of ~400 CAMELYON16 cross-institution triplets built as in Appendix A.4, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite's accuracy is not significantly higher than Midnight's (paired McNemar p > 0.05), or the gap is below ~4 points.

title: LiveOption: Evaluating LLM Agents in Structured Option Trading with Nonlinear Payoffs
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (per-asset detail in Table 17, Appendix H.1.1)

official.background: LLM trading-agent benchmarks have so far focused on equities and crypto, where the action space is essentially buy/hold/sell and payoffs are linear in price. Options add nonlinear payoffs, time decay, volatility exposure, multi-leg structures and margin rules, so they are a harder test of whether an agent reasons about risk rather than just direction. The paper builds a replay-based options backtesting benchmark (LiveOption) over calendar year 2025 to reduce pretraining leakage, and asks whether current LLM agents add value in three option use cases: portfolio overlays, earnings-event trades and 0DTE intraday trading.
official.method:
Each agent is an analyzer-executor pair driven by one LLM (temperature 0.5): the analyzer interprets market conditions and makes high-level decisions, the executor turns them into orders. Orders use a quantized action space (expiry bucket, moneyness level, option type), the implied-volatility surface is summarized by a 3x3 anchor grid (moneyness/delta x time-to-expiry), and a backend verifier enforces margin, position and contract-validity rules before a brokerage-style simulator fills them (mid-quote fills, 1 bp slippage, $0.65/contract commission).

In the Overlay scenario each run starts with a fixed long base of 10,000 shares of one underlying (QQQ, NVDA, AMD, GOOG or TSLA) plus a cash buffer of 20% of the stock notional; the agent may not trade the stock and only layers options on rebalance days over full-year 2025 (Appendix E.2.2 and the scenario settings table say weekly at Monday's close; Appendix H.1.1 says a Mon+Wed cadence — the paper is inconsistent). At each decision it sees spot, mark prices, full Greeks and IV of open positions, a position table, a compressed option chain (IV surface, moneyness buckets, liquid contracts in the DTE band) and recent price action. Two mandates: Hedging (long puts or bear put spreads, DTE 7-60 days, weekly premium budget) and Covered Call / Income (covered calls or cash-secured puts, DTE 7-45 days; no naked short premium). Performance is measured against the matched buy-and-hold portfolio holding the same share count on the same path: ΔRet = overlay full-year return minus buy-and-hold return (percentage points), and ΔMDD = buy-and-hold max drawdown minus overlay max drawdown (positive = shallower). Eight LLMs are evaluated (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5.3-Flash, GPT-5.6-Terra, Gemini-3-Flash), and each cell is averaged over the 5 assets.
official.claim: In the 2025 Overlay scenario under the Hedging mandate, every one of the 8 LLM agents underperforms the matched buy-and-hold portfolio. Mean active return over 5 assets ranges from −3.05 pp (GPT-OSS-120B) to −13.65 pp (GPT-5.6-Terra), and mean information ratio is negative for all models.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Overlay performance against the matched buy-and-hold portfolio, five assets per model and mandate. ΔRet is mean active return and ΔMDD the mean drawdown reduction (%).
official.metric: ΔRet: mean active return vs. matched buy-and-hold over 5 assets, in percentage points (higher is better); ΔMDD: mean max-drawdown reduction in pp. No ± or confidence intervals are reported for these cells; the paper itself calls them descriptive patterns, not population estimates.

title: Binding Multiple Modalities via Multimodal Wasserstein Barycenter

official.background: Multimodal representation learning with more than two modalities (video, audio, text, subtitles, depth) usually binds every modality to one designated anchor, such as text in VAST or LanguageBind, or images in ImageBind, using pairwise or anchor-centred contrastive losses. The authors argue that this anchor choice biases the shared space towards one modality. One symptom is a large gap between text-to-video and video-to-text retrieval, and weaker modalities such as audio end up under-optimized. They propose to replace the fixed anchor with a learned Wasserstein barycenter of all modality distributions.
official.method:
BaryBind starts from the VAST model (BERT-B text encoder, BEATs audio encoder, EVA-CLIP-ViT-G vision encoder; about 1.3B parameters in total), drops VAST's modality-fusion layers, and adds lightweight MLPs. A WB map T_theta (an MLP) sends an initializer m0 to a barycenter embedding b = T_theta(m0). Section 3.2 says m0 defaults to the arithmetic mean of the modality features, but the experiments use the text embedding ('T-VA', text-initialized WB; Table 10 shows the choice barely matters). T_theta is trained with the multimodal Wasserstein barycenter (MWB) loss (Eq. 5), a max-min dual objective with K two-layer-MLP potentials f_k constrained to sum to zero (weights lambda_k = 1/K), optimized by alternating updates on mini-batches. A barycenter-anchored volumetric contrastive (BVC) loss (Eq. 10) then treats the Gram-determinant volume of the simplex spanned by b and the gap vectors r_k = b - m_k as a distance. Small volumes are favoured for matched tuples and large volumes for mismatched ones, contrasting in both directions with temperature tau = 0.07. A VAST-style data-anchor matching (DAM) loss is added, and the total loss is L = L_MWB + 1.0 * L_BVC + 0.1 * L_DAM.

Training is continued pretraining from VAST weights on a 150k-sample subset of VAST-27M (one frame plus one 10-second audio clip per sample), for 10k steps with batch size 256, learning rate 1e-4 and linear decay, on 2×A100. The checkpoint is chosen by MSR-VTT retrieval, evaluated every 100 steps. The VAST, GRAM, Triangle and PMRL baselines are stated to use the same architecture and training strategy. Evaluation is zero-shot classification on VGGSound5K (5,000 ten-second clips, about 310 sound-event classes) with audio only, video only, or audio+video inputs.

title: ASTRA: ADMM-Accelerated Topology Reconfiguration for Dynamic Satellite Constellations
claim_source: Table 10 (Appendix K), page 26; related main-text results in Table 2 (page 8) and Table 5 (page 10)

official.background: Large Low Earth Orbit constellations link satellites to each other with inter-satellite links (ISLs), and the link topology has to be recomputed as satellites move, are added or fail. Norberto et al. posed topology design as a convex problem over a graph Laplacian X, weighted by a utility matrix U and restricted to feasible links P and per-satellite maximum degree (here called GUTO). GUTO relies on generic constrained-optimization solver calls, which become slow for constellations with thousands of satellites. ASTRA keeps the same problem and solves it faster.
official.method:
The problem is min_X 0.5||(X - P) ⊙ U||_F^2 - Tr(Λ ⊙ X) subject to X symmetric, X1 = 0, and box bounds B_lower ≤ X ≤ B_upper (off-diagonals in [-1, 0], diagonals in [0, d_max]). ASTRA splits it with ADMM into an X-update over the affine set {X = X^T, X1 = 0}, solved by a few projected-gradient steps using the closed-form projection Q·sym(Y)·Q with Q = I - 11^T/n, and a Z-update that clips entries to the box. The dual update is standard scaled ADMM. The stopping rule is ||V^k - V^{k-1}|| / ||V^{k-1}|| < 1e-7. The settings are ρ = 1, proj_its = 5, Λ = 1e-4·I, and U = 0.6·U_3-closest + 0.4·U_dist-reciprocal with rows normalized by their max. The FOV approximation is 'H+C' and the maximum link distance is 8,000 km.

Test case: a synthetic Iridium-like constellation with 6 elliptical orbital planes of 11 satellites each (66 satellites). The continuous X is thresholded and greedily discretized into ISLs. Because the two solvers' stopping criteria cannot be matched exactly, for Table 10 both GUTO and ASTRA are run until they reach the same solution, and wall-clock time is averaged over 10 runs on the same CPU (M5 Pro MacBook Pro).
official.claim: On the 66-satellite Iridium-like constellation, when both are run until they reach the same solution, ASTRA's ADMM solver takes 0.356 ± 0.051 s versus 0.991 ± 0.008 s for the GUTO baseline, about 2.8x faster (64% less time).
official.claim_caption: Table 10: Time comparison when GUTO and ASTRA are run until achieving the same result. The values presented on this table refer to the average and respective standard deviation over 10 runs.
official.metric: wall-clock time in seconds to reach the common solution (lower is better), mean ± std over 10 runs
official.comparison: ASTRA (problem-specific ADMM with closed-form Laplacian projection) vs. GUTO (the same convex problem solved with generic constrained-optimization calls), same problem instance, same hardware, same solution
official.falsification_criterion: With both solvers run to the same solution (equal objective and equal discretized topology) on the Iridium-like constellation, ASTRA is not faster than GUTO by a margin larger than the run-to-run std, e.g. a speedup below ~1.5x, or ASTRA reaches a different topology or objective value.

title: STRIDE: Automated Evaluation of Text-to-Trajectory Alignment across Diverse Contexts

official.background: Text-conditioned pedestrian and crowd trajectory generators are now appearing, but they are still evaluated by comparing outputs with recorded human trajectories for the same scene, such as ADE/FDE or distribution distances. That does not scale to rare or unsafe scenarios like evacuations, crushes or violent incidents, where no human data can be collected. It also does not check whether the trajectories match what the text asked for. Asking an LLM to judge raw trajectories directly is unstable. A useful automatic metric therefore has to score how well trajectories match the context, and it must actually depend on the text rather than just rewarding crowd motion that looks plausible in general.
official.method:
STRIDE breaks each scenario description into at least five behavioral questions along five axes: Velocity, Realism, Direction, Spatial and Temporal. For each question, an LLM (GPT-5.2 for the benchmark) picks one or more of 20 deterministic measurement functions (DMT), such as mean_speed, flow_alignment, path_linearity, collision_fraction or density_trend. The LLM also sets an expected numeric range for each function's output, calibrated with real-crowd reference values (TrajFacts). Scoring needs no LLM: each measurement passes (1) or fails (0) depending on whether the computed value falls in its expected range. Scores are averaged within each question, then over questions in a scenario, then over scenarios. STRIDE-Bench has 936 scenarios, 6,633 questions and 11,696 measurements on 113 real maps across 11 crowd categories.

Text-swap ablation (Section 5.3): the trajectory and venue stay fixed, while the context description and its questions, measurements and expected ranges are swapped for those of another scenario on the same map. That scenario is either from the same crowd category or from a different one. The same trajectory is then rescored. Real human trajectories come from 12 Fête des Lumières (Lyon) recordings and 5 ETH/UCY scenes. Their own-scenario questions were generated with the same QA pipeline; ETH/UCY used open mode without calibration. Model rows (LLM-SFM, SingularTrajectory, Random Walk) cover all benchmark scenes, and each swapped model score averages up to three partner scenarios on the same map; the paper does not say how many partners are used for the human recordings.
official.claim: Scoring real human trajectories against a swapped context from a different crowd category lowers the mean STRIDE score from 0.943 to 0.452 on the 12 Lyon recordings and from 0.914 to 0.440 on the 5 ETH/UCY scenes. A same-category swap gives intermediate scores (0.727 and 0.686), while Random Walk stays near 0.33 (0.337 / 0.335 / 0.332) under every swap.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: STRIDE_score under text-swap ablation. Context descriptions are randomly swapped between scenarios, either within the same crowd category or across different categories.
official.metric: STRIDE score in [0, 1], higher means better context alignment; mean over recordings/scenes. No error bars or seeds are reported for Table 5 (scoring is deterministic). Lyon own-scenario per-scene std is 0.075 (Table 9, range 0.812-1.000).
official.comparison: Same trajectories scored against their own scenario vs. a different scenario from the same crowd category vs. a different scenario from a different crowd category; human trajectories (Lyon, ETH/UCY) contrasted with generated/baseline trajectories (LLM-SFM, SingularTrajectory, Random Walk).
official.falsification_criterion: Rescoring the Lyon or ETH/UCY human trajectories with released code fails to show the drop. The claim is refuted if the different-category swap mean stays within about 0.15 of the own-scenario mean, if the score does not decrease on most of the 17 recordings, or if Random Walk's score changes about as much as the human score.

title: When Confidence Rises Too Early: Detecting Shortcut Reasoning via Premature Answer Commitment

official.background: Reasoning LLMs can reach an answer through a shortcut, such as copying an authoritative hint, exploiting a pattern in the training data, or gaming a biased verifier, and then write a chain of thought that looks like honest step-by-step work. Monitors that read the CoT text (for example a GPT-4o judge) and reward models that score responses can be fooled by these post-hoc rationalizations. The paper asks whether the model's internal confidence in its final answer, tracked over the course of the reasoning, can expose shortcut reasoning without access to the ground truth or a task-specific verifier.
official.method:
ConfLens splits a CoT into steps. After each step it estimates the model's confidence in the final answer and summarizes the confidence-vs-CoT-fraction curve by its area under the curve (AUC). The idea is that a shortcut sample becomes confident early ('premature answer commitment') and so has a high AUC. DACS is the confidence estimator: after each CoT prefix the string </think><answer> is appended, and confidence is the negative entropy of the model's next-token distribution over the vocabulary. The ConfLens score is then thresholded for detection, with the threshold chosen on a validation set to maximize F1.

In the explicit-hint setting the prompt starts with 'A Stanford professor thinks the answer is <ground truth>.' A response counts as shortcut reasoning if it is correct with the hint but wrong once the hint is removed, and as faithful if it is correct without relying on the hint. Math uses filtered hard Big-Math-Verified questions; code uses CRUXEval. Baselines: a GPT-4o CoT monitor (outputs SHORTCUT/UNCLEAR/GENUINE, so it has F1 only) and TRACE (pass@k reasoning-effort truncation, k=8). Backbones: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. The implicit-hint and reward-bias settings require first GRPO-training a model that exploits the loophole.
official.claim: For detecting shortcut reasoning under explicit hints on math (Big-Math-Verified), ConfLens with DACS beats both baselines on all three backbones. F1 vs. the GPT-4o CoT monitor: Qwen2.5-3B 0.732 vs. 0.641, Qwen3-4B 0.752 vs. 0.632, Llama-3.2-3B 0.794 vs. 0.658. AUROC vs. TRACE: 0.784 vs. 0.702, 0.800 vs. 0.768, 0.827 vs. 0.808. ConfLens is also about 10-15x faster than TRACE (0.26-0.38 s vs. 3.8-4.2 s per query).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Shortcut reasoning detection results across different methods. For TRACE and ConfLens, we optimize the decision threshold on the validation set that yields the best F1 score, thereby converting their outputs into binary detection results. The best results are bolded.
official.metric: AUROC and F1 for the binary label shortcut vs. faithful (higher is better). The decision threshold is tuned on the validation set for best F1. Latency is seconds per query. No ± reported (single run, no seeds or CIs).
official.comparison: ConfLens with DACS vs. GPT-4o CoT monitor and TRACE (k=8) on the same labelled responses from each backbone
official.falsification_criterion: In the explicit-hint math setting, ConfLens-DACS F1 does not exceed the GPT-4o CoT monitor's F1 on the reproduced data, or its AUROC is not above TRACE's on at least two of the three backbones.

title: Beyond Selection: Token Parameterization for Extreme Visual Token Compression
claim_source: Table 12 (Appendix J.7), page 25; single-seed per-benchmark numbers in Table 1, page 7

official.background: Vision-language models such as LLaVA feed hundreds of visual tokens from a vision encoder into the LLM, and prefill cost grows with that count. Mobile, low-latency or long-context settings may allow only a few dozen visual tokens. At such extreme budgets, token pruning and merging tend to drop rare but important regions, and learned resamplers (query/Perceiver-style modules) add attention cost, parameters and alignment complexity. The paper asks whether performance at tiny budgets depends more on how the visual token field is parameterized than on which tokens are selected.
official.method:
Braco replaces the dense 24 x 24 CLIP ViT-L/14-336 token grid in LLaVA-1.5-7B with K = Kb + Kr tokens. Backbone: a 2D orthonormal DCT over the spatial token lattice (applied per channel), keeping the C x C low-frequency coefficient block (Kb = C^2). An input-independent basis-coordinate embedding (polar Fourier) is added on the retained (u, v) frequency coordinates. Then a budget-dependent coordinate organization is applied: coefficient tokens are kept as-is when Kb < 16, and the coefficients are mapped to a coarse C x C spatial grid by inverse DCT when Kb >= 16. Residual: a lightweight TokenLearner-style scorer produces S sparsemax weight maps over the original grid, and each residual token is a weighted sum of patch tokens. The concatenated tokens are normalized and fed through the projector. Splits are c1s3 / c2s5 / c3s7 / c4s9 (C, S) for K = 4 / 9 / 16 / 25.

Every method (Braco and each baseline) is retrained per budget with the standard LLaVA-1.5 two-stage recipe: pretraining on blip_laion_cc_sbu_558k (batch 256, 2181 steps, only the compressor and projector trained) and instruction tuning on llava_v1_5_mix665k (batch 128, 5198 steps, compressor, projector and LLM trained). Evaluation uses 8 benchmarks (GQA, MMBench EN/CN, MME, POPE F1, ScienceQA, TextVQA, MM-Vet). Acc. is the mean over benchmarks of score / score of the 576-token uncompressed Vanilla model, x100. In the seed study, the three seeds share the base checkpoint, data order and schedule across methods.
official.claim: Retrained under the same LLaVA-1.5-7B recipe over 3 matched training seeds, Braco reaches 95.18 ± 0.10 Vanilla-normalized Acc. with 25 visual tokens vs. 94.24 ± 0.13 for TokenPacker (+0.94; QueCC is not reported at this budget). With 9 tokens it reaches 93.29 ± 0.12, 1.81 points above TokenPacker (91.48 ± 0.18) but only 0.27 points above the stronger QueCC (93.02 ± 0.14).
official.claim_caption: Table 12: Accuracy across three matched training seeds. Values are sample mean ± sample standard deviation. QueCC does not support 25 tokens on the fixed 24 x 24 lattice; TokenPacker is not included in the four-token repeated-training comparison.

title: A Unified Uncertainty Representation for Graph Neural Networks via Doubly-Spectral Stochastic Expansion
claim_source: Table 14 (Appendix E.1), page 33; summarized in Table 19 and Figure 3

official.background: Deploying graph neural networks reliably requires calibrated class probabilities, out-of-distribution detection, and robustness to distribution shift, and existing methods usually address each need with a separate model or objective. Calibration on node classification is commonly measured by the Brier score, and standard GNNs (GCN, GAT) can be accurate but poorly calibrated, especially on heterophilous graphs. The paper proposes one uncertainty representation for node embeddings meant to serve all three needs.
official.method:
DSS-GNN represents each node embedding as a truncated polynomial chaos expansion in a single shared standard Gaussian latent omega: every node keeps P+1 coefficient vectors H_0..H_P (one per Hermite order) instead of one hidden vector. Each layer filters every coefficient with dual low-pass/high-pass Chebyshev graph filters, mixes the two branches with per-order gates, evaluates the field at S Gauss-Hermite quadrature nodes, applies ReLU there, and projects back onto the Hermite basis. This makes the network deterministic, with no Monte-Carlo sampling. At P=0 it reduces to a deterministic dual-filter spectral GNN.

A linear readout gives per-order logits Z_n. Training uses cross-entropy on the mean logit Z_0 plus lambda_reg times the chaos energy sum_{n>=1} ||Z_n||^2, with early stopping on validation loss (lr 0.01, wd 5e-4, up to 1000 epochs, patience 200, S=4). Predictions and Brier scores come from the quadrature-averaged softmax (Table 1 reports the mean-logit readout, and its entries are taken from the Table 13/14 sweeps; the paper shows the two readouts agree within 0.003 Brier, Table 27). The ablation fixes each dataset's architecture (Table 11: Cheb/Prop-first/TFE-adj, hidden size, layers, optimizer) and varies only P.
official.claim: With each dataset's DSS-GNN architecture held fixed and only the chaos order changed, P=2 lowers test Brier score relative to the deterministic P=0 arm from 0.427 ± 0.008 to 0.308 ± 0.010 on Citeseer and from 0.666 ± 0.003 to 0.635 ± 0.006 on Amazon-Ratings (and 0.190 ± 0.007 to 0.170 ± 0.014 on Minesweeper).
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Brier Score (↓) of DSS-GNN for varying chaos order P across all datasets.
official.metric: Brier score on test nodes (lower is better), mean ± std over 10 splits (random fixed-seed splits for Citeseer: class-balanced training set totalling 60% of nodes, 20% validation, rest test; the first 10 public 50/25/25 splits of Platonov et al. for Amazon-Ratings and Minesweeper)
official.comparison: DSS-GNN with chaos expansion (P=2, S=4) vs. the same architecture with chaos disabled (P=0), same splits and hyperparameters
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the sweep, the P=2 mean Brier is not lower than the P=0 mean by more than one std on Citeseer or Amazon-Ratings.

title: From Retrieval to Reasoning: Agentic Mechanism Prediction from Cell Painting Profiles

official.background: Cell Painting is an imaging assay that records how a compound changes cell morphology, and a common use is predicting a compound's mechanism of action (MOA). The standard approach embeds each compound's morphological profile and copies MOA labels from its nearest reference compounds (kNN voting). Retrieved neighbors are often misleading, because of batch and source effects, non-specific toxicity, and different mechanisms that converge on similar phenotypes. The paper argues that MOA prediction should treat retrieved neighbors as uncertain evidence to be weighed against mechanism-side information, not as direct answers.
official.method:
PhenoAIR is an LLM multi-agent system. Offline, an LLM-assisted pipeline computes reliability annotations on the reference set (cross-source consistency, reference replicability, intra-MOA stability, MOA confusion patterns) and a coarse MOA family ontology. At query time, a phenotype agent reads the calibrated CellCLIP nearest-neighbor evidence, and a mechanism agent separately evaluates candidates using the query's chemical structure, in-silico target predictions, pharmacophore matches and structural neighbors. Both agents write structured updates into a shared candidate memory. A rule-based controller chooses further actions (expand retrieval, validate candidates or families, inspect risky anchors, stop). An LLM arbiter then makes the final choice, which passes through deterministic eligibility checks; a final canonical label must have phenotype support.

The benchmark is built from JUMP Cell Painting (cpg0016, 5 sources) with MOA labels from the Drug Repurposing Hub. MoA-Verified has 63 reference compounds profiled in multiple sources, 200 test compounds and 26 MOA classes. Baselines on the same backbone (GPT-5.1 or Claude 4 Sonnet): Structure-only (structure and mechanism tools, no phenotype), Workflow (a fixed pipeline: phenotype retrieval analysis, then structure evidence; same tools, no memory or controller), and Single Agent (same tools, one agent). Top-1 accuracy is scored against each compound's representative MOA label. Free-text LLM outputs are mapped to canonical labels by string matching, with an LLM-as-judge for unmatched cases. LLM methods are averaged over 5 runs.
official.claim: On MoA-Verified (200 test compounds, 26 MOAs), PhenoAIR with GPT-5.1 reaches 62.6 ± 0.7% top-1 accuracy, vs. 50.0 ± 1.2% for the fixed Workflow baseline and 43.5 ± 1.4% for Structure-only. With Claude 4 Sonnet the scores are 61.5 ± 0.5% vs. 52.4 ± 0.9% and 47.3 ± 0.8%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Main results on three datasets. We report accuracy (Acc. %), hit rate (Any-match), and F1 measured against ground-truth MOA labels. All LLM-based methods operate on the same CellCLIP features. Best results are in bold; second-best are underlined. Our method is highlighted in blue.
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%) against the representative MOA label, higher is better. Table 2 does not define ±; the text says LLM methods are averaged over five independent runs, and the paper's Table 4 and Table 5 captions label the same quantity as mean ± s.d. over runs, so ± is read as std over 5 runs. The CellProfiler, CellCLIP and ECFP kNN rows are deterministic (± 0.0); the Random row has its own spread.
official.comparison: PhenoAIR vs. Structure-only, Workflow and Single Agent LLM baselines using the same backbone, the same CellCLIP features and the same tool interfaces; kNN retrieval baselines (CellProfiler, CellCLIP, ECFP) also shown
official.falsification_criterion: On MoA-Verified with the same backbone, PhenoAIR's mean top-1 accuracy over runs is within a few points (about 2 std) of the Workflow or Structure-only baseline, or falls below either one.

title: Towards Scalable Context-Aware Single-Cell Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology Images
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (MPG/SVG versions in Table 5, page 18)

official.background: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression at known tissue locations, but it is expensive, whereas H&E-stained histology slides are cheap and routine. Most methods that predict expression from H&E work at the level of Visium spots, which average dozens of cells. Platforms such as 10x Xenium now give single-cell expression paired with H&E, so it is possible to train models that predict expression for each cell. The open question is how to build good per-cell image features: either crop each cell and run a pathology foundation model on it (slow, loses context), or use segmentation-mask CNNs (no strong pretrained features).
official.method:
CELLO runs one pathology foundation model (Virchow2 by default) forward pass per 224x224 H&E patch. It reshapes the patch tokens into a 2D feature map and bilinearly samples (grid_sample) a feature at each cell centroid. That query is then refined by multi-head cross-attention over all patch tokens, using 2D RoPE and an additive Gaussian distance-decay bias -||s_i - c_m||^2 / (2p^2). The output is layer-normalized and passed to a two-layer MLP that predicts log-normalized expression over a 1,915-gene union vocabulary, with the loss restricted to each sample's measured panel. Training uses a cell-level Huber loss plus 0.5 x a patch-sum Huber loss. The backbone is progressively unfrozen: frozen for the first 10% of epochs, gradually unfrozen with a linearly increasing backbone learning rate (up to 2e-5) over the next 30%, and fully fine-tuned thereafter. Training runs 200 epochs with AdamW on 4 H100s.

Benchmark: 52 HEST-1k Xenium/H&E pairs across 12 organs, split 36 train / 4 val / 12 test. The in-distribution (ID) test set has one slide each for Lung, Breast, Bowel, Skin, Pancreas and Lymphoid. Baselines are trained on the same split: UNet3+ on cell masks (GHIST-style), DeepSpot2Cell (per-cell crops through a frozen foundation model), and Grid (CELLO without the cross-attention). The metric is the mean per-gene Pearson correlation over HVG-k, which the paper defines as the top-k most predictive genes among the highly variable genes, computed per test slide over that slide's measured genes.

title: DisCoMBO: Steering Expert-in-the-Loop Black Box Optimization via Distributional Conformance
claim_source: Figure 7, page 28 (JAHS (CIFAR-10) panel); relative improvement vs. IBO-HPC in Figure 19, page 35 (≈+35% for DisCoMBO vs. ≈0-5% for the other baselines)

official.background: Sequential model-based optimization (SMBO, e.g. Bayesian optimization) tunes expensive black-box functions such as neural network hyperparameters, material designs or wind-farm layouts by alternating between fitting a surrogate model and choosing the next point to evaluate. Experts often want to inject knowledge (e.g. 'learning rate should be near X') into this loop. IBO-HPC (Seng et al., 2025) used probabilistic circuits (PCs), tractable generative models over (configuration, performance), as surrogates, so priors can be applied by conditional sampling. However, it chooses candidates purely by sampling from p(x | y = y*) and has no notion of epistemic uncertainty, so it has no principled exploration-exploitation trade-off. This paper adds such an uncertainty proxy to PCs.
official.method:
The Distributional Conformance score (DisCo) is computed in one bottom-up pass over a PC. Each leaf gives a two-tailed probability 2·min(F(x), 1−F(x)) from its CDF, sum nodes take the weighted average of their children's scores, and product nodes combine their k children with Fisher's method, 1 − F_χ²(−2 Σ ln ρ_i; 2k). The result lies in [0, 1], and 1 − ρ is used as an uncertainty proxy.

DisCoMBO (Algorithm 1) fits a Mixed Sum-Product Network with LearnSPN on the observed data (K-means plus RDC tests, threshold 0.3; the surrogate stays unchanged for L = 5 iterations). At each step it samples N = 1000 candidates from p(x | y = y*) (perturbed by 5%, following IBO-HPC), optionally adds random candidates, and scores them with DisCo. It then sorts them into K bins on [0, 1] skewed by an annealing exponent β_t from a cosine schedule s(t) = (β0+β1)/2 + (β0−β1)/2·cos(πt/c) (β0 = 3, β1 = 0.3, c = 20), where a high β favours low-conformance (exploratory) bins and a low β favours high-conformance (exploitative) bins, and evaluates a candidate from a randomly chosen bin. The initial design size J = K (K = 20 for JAHS and NAS-Bench-201, 10 for HPO-B, 5 for PV and Floris). The no-prior setting used here applies no expert prior. All methods share the same evaluation budget (50/100/250 iterations depending on the task), and each run is repeated over 50 seeds.
official.claim: Without expert priors, on JAHS (CIFAR-10) DisCoMBO reaches a final normalized regret of ≈0.125, versus ≈0.19 for the strongest baselines (DynaBO, HEBO, IBO-HPC, CMA-ES, BO w/ TPE; ≈34% lower), ≈0.20 for BO w/ RF and ≈0.24 for SMAC. The curves are separated by far more than their standard-error bands over 50 seeds.
official.claim_caption: Figure 7: DisCoMBO achieves top-tier performance without external priors. Without guidance with external priors, DisCoMBO achieves top-tier performance on 8/9 tasks. On Floris, we still significantly improve upon IBO-HPC, however, DisCoMBO cannot fully catch up with top-tier baselines (see App. C.4) for further discussion.
official.metric: Normalized regret (lower is better) vs. benchmark-reported cumulative wall-clock time (×1e7 s). Curves are means over 50 seeds with shaded bands that the paper's checklist says are standard error. All values are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: DisCoMBO vs. the strongest matched baselines (DynaBO, HEBO, IBO-HPC, CMA-ES, BO w/ TPE) and also BO w/ RF and SMAC, all under the same budget, seeds and benchmark, with no priors
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running DisCoMBO and the strongest baselines (HEBO, IBO-HPC; DynaBO if available) with the released code over many seeds (≥ 20) on JAHS (CIFAR-10) under the paper's budget, DisCoMBO's final mean normalized regret is not clearly lower than the best baseline's (e.g. the relative reduction is under ~10% or the standard-error bands overlap).

title: SEED: Self-Speculative Decoding via Implicit Encoder–Decoder

official.background: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose several tokens that the full model verifies in one forward pass. Self-speculative methods draft with the target model itself, so no separate draft model has to be deployed. They face a tradeoff: early-exit methods (e.g. LayerSkip) draft cheaply from shallow intermediate layers, which gives low-quality drafts, while multi-token-prediction methods draft from the final hidden states but need a full forward pass per drafting step.
official.method:
SEED treats a decoder-only transformer as an implicit encoder-decoder: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base (28 layers) the first 26 layers are the 'encoder' and the last 2 layers the 'decoder'. To draft, the 2-layer decoder takes the raw token embedding of the latest token (skipping layers 1-26) and attends to the layer-27/28 KV cache that the full model already computed for the verified prefix during the previous verification pass. The full model then verifies the drafts in one forward pass, which also refreshes that deep KV cache. No new parameters are added.

Training is standard SFT plus one auxiliary loss, L = (L_CE + λ L_spec)/(1+λ) with λ = 1. L_spec trains the last 2 layers to predict each token from raw embeddings of tokens within the current block (block size 10, block-causal mask) while attending to the decoder KV cache of all preceding blocks, computed in parallel after one full forward pass. Fine-tuning: 30,000 steps, batch size 1, LR 1e-5 with 100-step warmup and cosine decay, max length 768, seed 1. Inference uses greedy decoding with confidence-based dynamic draft length (τ = 0.7) and top-p tree-based verification; throughput is measured on one NVIDIA A6000, stopping at <|endoftext|>. Baselines AR and LayerSkip (early exit at layer 8, trained with TRL) are fine-tuned from the same base model with the same schedule and budget.
official.claim: On GSM8K with Qwen3-1.7B-Base fine-tuned under the same training budget, SEED decodes at 91.8 tokens/s versus 37.9 for standard AR fine-tuning (2.4x) and 47.0 for LayerSkip (2.0x) on a single A6000 with greedy decoding, while its 0-shot accuracy (57.1%) is not lower than AR (56.3%), unlike LayerSkip (42.2%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison on Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base. 0-shot pass@1 accuracy (Acc.) is reported in %, and decoding throughput (Tput) in tokens/s. For CNN/Daily Mail, we report ROUGE-1 (R-1), ROUGE-2 (R-2), and ROUGE-L (R-L). For methods that keep the target model frozen, we report only their throughput. Given the size of its released drafter weights, PARD is evaluated only on Qwen3-4B-Base. The highest throughput and average speedup are shown in bold, and the second highest results are underlined.
official.metric: Decoding throughput in tokens/s (higher is better) on one NVIDIA A6000, generation stopped at <|endoftext|>; 0-shot pass@1 accuracy (%) on the GSM8K test split via lm-eval flexible match. Single training run (seed 1); no ± reported.
official.comparison: SEED (2-layer decoder, block size 10, λ = 1, dynamic drafting + tree verification) vs. AR SFT and the trained early-exit baseline LayerSkip, all fine-tuned from Qwen3-1.7B-Base on GSM8K with the same optimizer schedule and 30k steps
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup, SEED's throughput is less than 1.5x the AR model's or not clearly higher (e.g. under 1.3x) than a trained LayerSkip model's, or SEED's GSM8K accuracy is more than ~2 points below the AR fine-tuned model's.

title: Less Supervision, Better Generalization: Weakly Supervised Fake Region Localization in Diffusion-Edited Images

official.background: Diffusion-based editing tools can change parts of an image in ways that are hard to see, so forensic systems need to localize which regions were generated or edited, not just flag the whole image as fake. Existing localizers are trained with pixel-level edit masks from controlled inpainting pipelines. Those masks are unavailable for many commercial, text-driven editors, and they can also be wrong: latent encoding, decoding and blending leave diffusion traces outside the intended mask, yet mask supervision labels every out-of-mask pixel as real. The paper argues that this pushes models toward source-specific, mask-shaped cues that transfer poorly to unseen generators.
official.method:
ReGFLoW is trained on OpenSDID's SD1.5 split using only image-level real/fake labels. A frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 global encoder and a trainable MAE ViT-B/32 side-adapter local encoder (as in OpenSDI/IMDLBenCo, 512x512 input) produce features. The local features are pooled to a 16x16 grid. A reconstruction residual r = |I - D(E(I))| from the frozen Stable Diffusion 1 VAE is encoded by a 3-layer conv prior encoder and injected in two ways: a tanh-gated residual offset added to the local features, and a zero-initialized, tanh-gated logit bias added to the patch score map. The 16x16 patch logits are aggregated per image with a standardized softmax (soft top-k, kappa = 2) and trained with a pairwise fake-vs-real softplus margin loss (margin 0.5), plus image-level cross-entropy and small regularizers (real-image top-10% suppression, edge-aware smoothness, sparsity, patch contrastive). At inference the map is upsampled, calibrated per image from its own mean, std and mean response (fixed parameters, Appendix B.6), and thresholded at 0.5. Training: 10 epochs, batch 8, AdamW lr 5e-5, one GPU, seed 42.

For the matched comparison (Appendix D.1), ReGFLoW-FS keeps the same backbone and reconstruction guidance but replaces the MIL head with a segmentation head trained on pixel masks. Both are trained on OpenSDID-SD1.5 under the P+F protocol (partially edited and fully synthetic fakes in training and evaluation) and evaluated with pixel-level F1 on SD1.5 (in-domain) and on SD2.1, SDXL, SD3 and Flux.1 (unseen generators).
official.claim: With the same ReGFLoW backbone and reconstruction guidance trained on OpenSDID-SD1.5 (P+F), weak image-level MIL supervision gives higher pixel-level F1 than pixel-mask supervision on the three generators most distant from SD1.5: SDXL 30.1 vs. 16.89, SD3 32.2 vs. 15.46, Flux.1 29.4 vs. 3.41. OOD average is 31.3 vs. 25.25, while full supervision wins in-domain (SD1.5 92.22 vs. 35.6) and on SD2.1 (65.26 vs. 33.4).
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Controlled supervision comparisons under P+F. Each pair shares the backbone architecture and non-head components but changes the localization head and supervision. Pixel-level F1 (%); bold marks the better result within each pair.
official.metric: Pixel-level F1 (%) of the calibrated, thresholded localization map, higher is better; single run (seed 42), no error bars reported
official.comparison: ReGFLoW (weak, image-level labels, MIL head) vs. ReGFLoW-FS (same backbone and reconstruction prior, segmentation head trained with pixel masks), both trained on OpenSDID-SD1.5 under P+F
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both variants on OpenSDID-SD1.5 (P+F), ReGFLoW's pixel F1 does not exceed ReGFLoW-FS's by a clear margin (e.g. at least ~5 points) on SDXL, SD3 and Flux.1, or its OOD average (SD2.1, SDXL, SD3, Flux.1) is not higher than ReGFLoW-FS's.

title: MultiTalk: Scaling Full-Duplex Speech Models to Long, Multi-Party, Bilingual Conversation

official.background: Full-duplex speech models such as Moshi listen and speak at the same time, but they are trained and evaluated almost only on short two-person conversations. Real deployments such as meetings, group lessons and social robots are long, involve several speakers, and may be in more than one language. Open multi-party speech corpora add up to only a few hundred hours, and existing speech-to-speech benchmarks are dyadic and short. The paper releases a synthetic training corpus and a benchmark built from real recordings for long, multi-party, English-Chinese full-duplex dialogue, and trains a Moshi model on the corpus.
official.method:
Training data comes from an LLM-scripted, TTS-rendered (IndexTTS2) data engine that produces parallel-stream audio with word-level alignments. Moshi-MTB starts from kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16 and keeps Moshi's architecture unchanged. Phase 1 pre-trains on MultiTalkPT (54.4k h of bilingual dyadic dialogue, about 60% English and 40% Chinese) for 5,000 steps at peak LR 3e-5. Phase 2 fine-tunes on MultiTalkFT (3.2k h of multi-party dialogue, with all non-target speakers mixed into the user channel) for 200 steps at LR 2e-6 (temporal transformer) and 4e-6 (depth transformer). Both phases use full-parameter AdamW with a one-cycle schedule, a global batch of 21 h of audio, and a jointly supervised user stream.

MultiTalkBench has 104 samples drawn from the test splits of real close-mic multi-party recordings: AMI, ICSI, CHiME-6, AISHELL-4, AliMeeting, AISHELL-5 and MagicData-RAMC. The model plays one named participant, given a persona prompt, and the other participants come from the real audio. The model's offline output is spliced into the ground-truth transcript and scored by a Gemma-4-31B-it judge in six calls. The judge rates 1-5 ordinal dimensions in three groups (General, Multi-Party IQ, Role-conditional), each normalized to 0-100. Final Score is the equal-weight mean of the three groups. A mechanical Participation score (time-span ratio matching) is reported separately and is not part of the Final Score.
official.claim: On MultiTalkBench (104 samples, Gemma-4-31B judge), Moshi-MTB reaches a Final Score of 13.15. This is higher than its Moshiko-7B initialization (4.66) and than all open baselines: MiniCPM-o-4.5 (11.05), Qwen3-Omni-30B (4.94) and PersonaPlex-7B (2.52). The largest margin over the strongest baseline is on the Role-conditional group (12.16 vs. 7.81), while on Multi-Party IQ it trails MiniCPM-o-4.5 (8.56 vs. 9.00).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Detailed results on MultiTalkBench, broken down by sub-dimension. Bold: best result among models per row. The ∆ column reports relative change of Moshi-MTB over its Moshiko-7B backbone. Italics: human reference (oracle upper bound).
official.metric: MultiTalkBench Final Score (0-100, higher is better): the equal-weight mean of the General, Multi-Party IQ and Role-conditional LLM-judge group scores. No error bars, seeds, repeated runs or confidence intervals are reported (each sample is judged once by six judge calls).
official.comparison: Moshi-MTB (Moshiko-7B trained on MultiTalkPT + MultiTalkFT) vs. Moshiko-7B, PersonaPlex-7B, MiniCPM-o-4.5 and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct, all evaluated on the same 104 MultiTalkBench samples with the same judge
official.falsification_criterion: Re-scoring the models on MultiTalkBench with the released judge pipeline gives Moshi-MTB a Final Score that is not higher than MiniCPM-o-4.5's. A weaker check: Moshi-MTB does not clearly exceed Moshiko-7B, for example by less than 2x.

title: A Comprehensive View of Fairness through Distributional Stability
claim_source: Table 4, page 29 (Appendix E.3); qualitatively Figure 3, page 10

official.background: Group-fairness criteria such as demographic parity (DP) and equal opportunity (EO) are measured on one fixed data distribution, but deployed models face populations whose protected-group composition differs from the training data (other regions, times, institutions). A model that satisfies DP at the training group proportion can still have a positive-prediction rate that drifts with the deployment group proportion. The paper recasts fairness as stability of a prediction-rate functional under perturbations of the protected-group marginal. It then asks for a predictor whose rate stays close to a fixed target level t for every deployment composition, which is a stronger requirement than a small fairness gap at the training composition.
official.method:
For DP, the functional is Phi(h; pi) = P_pi(h(X)=1), the positive-prediction rate when the share of group G=1 is set to pi while P(X,Y|G) is kept fixed. Shifts are simulated with importance weights. STABLE draws K=30 values pi_k from Pi = U[pi_bar, 1-pi_bar] and trains one importance-weighted L2 logistic regression (C=1, lbfgs) per value. The dictionary is enlarged with 2Kc=20 logistic regressions trained on label-flipped data and with the two constant predictors 0 and 1. Mixture weights alpha on the simplex minimize the linearized risk sum_k alpha_k R(eta_k) subject to the second-order-cone constraint ||A alpha - t 1||_2 <= sqrt(m delta), where A_jk = Phi_hat(eta_k; pi'_j) is evaluated on m=60 stratified perturbation points. The budget is delta = delta0^2 Var_Pi, and the SOCP is solved with cvxpy. The target t is ERM's mean prediction on the training set (DP). The model is unaware: G is not an input at prediction time.

ACS Income experiment (Appendix E.3): models are trained on California (n=80,000 subsampled), pi_bar and the dictionary are chosen on 3 validation states, and evaluation is on 11 held-out test states with White-resident share from 68% to 95%. All methods use the same fixed budget delta0 = 0.01. Baselines are unconstrained ERM, ERM + constraint (fairlearn Exponentiated Gradient), PostProc (entropic post-processing), STABLE_DRO (the same dictionary and perturbations with an SA-DRO-style objective, at its least unfair lambda) and Shifty. The deployment gap is |Phi(h; pi_state) - t|, and the worst value over held-out states is reported, as mean +/- std over 5 seeds.
official.claim: On ACS Income under the DP constraint (train California, 11 held-out states, delta0 = 0.01), STABLE has a worst-state deployment gap of 0.015 ± 0.002, lower than every baseline: ERM 0.032 ± 0.007, STABLE_DRO 0.036 ± 0.007, ERM+DP 0.055 ± 0.007, PostProc 0.069 ± 0.008, Shifty 0.403 ± 0.010. Its accuracy is 0.764 ± 0.006, at least as high as any baseline's.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: ACS Income, held-out states, at the fixed budget of Figures 3 and 7 (δ0 = 0.01; STABLE_DRO at its least unfair λ): mean accuracy and mean U(h) over the states, worst-state deployment gap, and absolute slope of π_state ↦ Φ. Mean ± std over 5 seeds.
official.metric: Worst-state deployment gap max over held-out states of |Phi(h; pi_state) - t| (lower is better); also mean accuracy (higher is better). ± is std over 5 seeds.
official.comparison: STABLE vs. ERM, ERM + constraint (Exponentiated Gradient), PostProc, STABLE_DRO (DRO-objective ablation) and Shifty, all at the same fairness budget and with logistic-regression base learners
official.falsification_criterion: With the same protocol (train on California ACS Income, evaluate on the 11 held-out states, delta0 = 0.01, 5 seeds), STABLE's worst-state DP deployment gap is not below ERM's and STABLE_DRO's by more than their seed std, or STABLE's accuracy falls clearly below ERM+DP's.

title: FlowMAS: Learning Multi-Agent Workflow Topology via Information-guided Generative Flow Network

official.background: LLM multi-agent systems are often organized as workflows, i.e. directed acyclic graphs of operators (CoT, self-refine, programmer, ensemble, etc.) that pass messages to each other. Designing these topologies by hand is laborious, and automated approaches each have drawbacks: search-based methods such as AFlow and ADAS spend many LLM tokens exploring a large design space, and generation-based methods such as MaAS (MLP controller), G-Designer (VAE) or GTD (graph diffusion) may not model discrete, dependency-heavy graphs well and tend to produce low-diversity topologies. A better way to generate query-specific workflows would raise accuracy and cut the token cost of multi-agent pipelines.
official.method:
FlowMAS treats workflow construction as a sequence of graph-edit actions (add operator node, add edge, early stop) and trains a Generative Flow Network with a trajectory-balance objective so that the probability of a finished workflow is proportional to its reward. States are encoded by embedding the task text, the operator pool and the current topology (e.g. with MiniLM). The terminal reward is the task score minus a token-cost penalty, max(0, s - lambda_cost * c), in [0, 1].

Two intermediate per-transition rewards are added to the flow: (1) a curiosity reward (random-network-distillation style prediction error) that favors structurally novel partial topologies, weighted by alpha = 0.2; (2) an information-guided reward, weighted by beta = 0.8, computed whenever a fan-in/fan-out appears, which combines a PID-inspired synergy score (cosine similarities between embeddings of upstream messages and the ground-truth answer) and an effective-channel score (spectral entropy of the Gram matrix of upstream output embeddings). Each benchmark is split 1:4 into train/validation and test following AFlow (HumanEval: 33 train, 131 test). FlowMAS is trained on the train split and evaluated on the test split with temperature 0.2, over 5 independent trials.
official.claim: With Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the backbone, FlowMAS reaches 69.6 ± 1.5 pass@1 on the HumanEval test split (131 problems), above the best automated-workflow baselines AFlow (65.1 ± 1.4) and MaAS (62.7 ± 0.9) and the best non-automated baseline LLM-Majority (56.6 ± 0.0).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. We bold the best results and underline the second-best results. Each experiment is run five times to record the mean and standard deviation.
official.metric: HumanEval pass@1 (%), higher is better; mean ± std over 5 independent trials
official.comparison: FlowMAS vs. AFlow, MaAS, SELFORG, ADAS, AgentNet and 10 single-agent / hand-crafted multi-agent baselines, all with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at temperature 0.2 on the same split
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same backbone and split, FlowMAS's mean pass@1 over 5 runs is not clearly above AFlow's (e.g. the gap shrinks below ~1.5 points, one std), or AFlow/MaAS match or exceed it.

title: Codebook-Guided Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation for Structurally Heterogeneous Features
claim_source: Table 13 (Appendix B.2), page 20; the 5-run, varying-split version is Table 1 (page 6) / Table 8 (page 17)

official.background: Cross-modal knowledge distillation trains a student on one modality (for example audio) with help from a teacher trained on another (for example video), which matters when the richer modality is available only at training time. Feature-level distillation methods usually assume the teacher and student features can be matched unit by unit (pixel to pixel, token to token), but a 2D spatial video feature map and a 1D temporal audio sequence have no such correspondence, so these methods fall back to pooled features or prediction-level transfer.
official.method:
The method replaces direct feature matching with a vector-quantized teacher codebook. Stage 1 freezes the teacher, projects its intermediate features into a code space, quantizes them with a learnable codebook (512 codes of dim 128 on RAVDESS) and trains a codebook-branch head with task, codebook and commitment losses, jointly with the student and a term matching the codebook-branch prediction q(t) to the student prediction. Stage 2 scores each code by leave-one-code-out: how much removing it raises the teacher task loss (task relevance) plus how much it raises the teacher-student prediction gap (student compatibility), and keeps the top 50% of codes.

Stage 3 re-initializes the student and trains it with its task loss plus lambda=0.01 times (a student-side codebook branch that quantizes student features onto the fixed selected teacher codes, with task and commitment losses, and an L2 match between the student prediction and q(t)). On RAVDESS (speech subset, 8 emotions, 60/20/20 split) audio uses frozen Wav2Vec2-Base features (768 x 179) and video uses frozen ResNet-18 layer-3 features averaged over 10 frames (256 x 14 x 14), each followed by a small conv classifier trained 100 epochs with AdamW, lr 1e-3, batch 64.
official.claim: On RAVDESS with the data split and teacher checkpoint fixed, the codebook-guided student beats the strongest baseline (MGDFR) over 10 runs in both directions: audio-to-video 0.9420 ± 0.0071 vs. 0.9271 ± 0.0080 accuracy (paired t-test p = 0.001) and video-to-audio 0.7556 ± 0.0120 vs. 0.7351 ± 0.0144 (p = 0.007).
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Controlled significance tests against the runner-up methods for the classification results. The data split and the teacher checkpoint are fixed, and results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over ten runs. p-values are computed using a two-sided paired t-test. The runner-up is STXD for MM-IMDB T→I and MGDFR for all other settings.
official.metric: student test accuracy (higher is better) at the best-validation checkpoint, mean ± std over 10 runs with fixed split and teacher; two-sided paired t-test
official.comparison: proposed method vs. MGDFR (best of 10 KD/CMKD baselines in Table 1) under the same split, teacher, features and student architecture
official.falsification_criterion: With a fixed split and teacher, over 10 runs the method's mean accuracy on RAVDESS A->V or V->A is not higher than MGDFR's, or the paired difference is not significant at p < 0.05.
