title: Why Cross-Skeleton Retargeting Is Non-Identifiable: Structural Limits of Generative Motion Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 10 (extended with length-controlled SIF in Table 27, page 30; six-robot replication in Tables 28, 29 and 32, pages 32-33)

official.background: Cross-skeleton retargeting asks a model to take a motion clip on one body (a human, a coyote) and produce a motion on a different body that keeps both the action and the particular way the source clip performs it. Progress is usually measured by an action-level retrieval AUC: is the generated motion recognizable as the requested action on the target body? That test cannot tell a model that transfers the source clip apart from one that ignores the source and outputs a typical motion for the action. The paper argues that in sparse multi-body motion libraries the source-conditioned map is non-identifiable under standard objectives. Matching each body's latent marginals leaves a free relative 'gauge' between bodies (Theorem 1). Squared-error regression onto random same-action targets converges to the cell mean (Proposition 1.1). The paper proposes Source-Instance Fidelity (SIF) to detect this.
official.method:
SIF is computed per (source skeleton, target skeleton, action) group with at least three source clips. For every pair of source clips i, j and their outputs, both sides are cropped to their common duration and Procrustes-aligned (removing translation, rotation and isotropic scale), and per-frame discrepancies d_src(i,j) and d_out(i,j) are computed. SIF is the Pearson correlation between {d_src} and {d_out} within a group, macro-averaged over groups. A model that ignores the source scores near 0, and a correct map scores near 1. The paper also reports output variation (median ratio of output spread to source spread), action AUC, and a realism score (share of outputs whose nearest real G1 pose is within the 95th percentile of held-out real motion).

In the human-to-G1 study, BONES-SEED provides human motion-capture clips with retargeted counterparts on the Unitree G1 humanoid. The authors select 90 action groups with 3-4 clips each (355 clips). One small transformer (4 layers, width 256) is trained three ways with the same data, number of steps and optimizer. (1) The unpaired objective is two VAEs, one per body, coupled through a shared Gaussian latent and each trained only on its own motions (Theorem 1 class). (2) The averaging objective regresses each human clip with squared error onto a robot clip from the same group, drawn at random at every step (Proposition 1.1 class). (3) The true-pair model is the same regressor trained on the true counterparts. Two reference rows need no training: the true counterpart itself and a random same-action G1 clip.
official.claim: On human-to-G1 retargeting (BONES-SEED, 90 action groups, 355 clips, identical test items), the same transformer trained on true pairs reaches SIF +0.900 with output variation 0.52, while the unpaired shared-latent objective reaches only +0.203 / 0.001 and the random same-action squared-error objective +0.379 / 0.05. Both degraded objectives collapse output variation to at most a tenth of the true-pair model's.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Human-to-G1 evaluation on identical test items (90 action groups, 355 clips). SIF uses raw scoring; variation is the median ratio of output spread to source spread; realistic is the share of outputs whose nearest real G1 pose lies within the 95th percentile of held-out real motion.
official.metric: SIF (Pearson correlation of source-pair vs. output-pair distances, raw scoring, higher is better) and output variation (median ratio of output spread to source spread; collapse = near 0). No error bars or seed counts are reported for Table 2.
official.comparison: Same 4-layer transformer, same data, steps and optimizer: trained on true human-G1 pairs vs. the unpaired VAE objective (Theorem 1 class) vs. random same-action pairing with squared error (Proposition 1.1 class). Reference rows: the true counterpart (+0.960) and a random same-action clip (-0.008).
official.falsification_criterion: Under matched training, the random-pairing squared-error model or the unpaired shared-latent model reaches SIF within about 0.2 of the true-pair model, or keeps output variation above about half of the true-pair model's, or the true-pair model fails to reach SIF of about 0.6 or more.

title: OFBD: Object-Focused Background Debiasing for Long-Tailed Learning

official.background: Real-world image datasets are long-tailed: a few head classes have many examples and most tail classes have very few, so classifiers trained on them do poorly on tail classes. Existing fixes re-balance sampling or losses, change the architecture, or add augmentation, which mostly make up for the small number of samples. This paper argues that tail classes also suffer from background bias: with few, low-diversity images, tail-class backgrounds are correlated with the label, so the network learns background shortcuts instead of object features.
official.method:
OFBD is a plug-in added on top of an existing long-tailed method. FG-CutMix is a CutMix variant that keeps a selected 'foreground' region of the image and pastes in background from another image. N random region proposals are generated. A small RL region selector, operating on the encoder feature map, samples K=6 of them without replacement. It is trained with a GRPO-style clipped objective (advantages normalized within the K-candidate pool), a KL penalty (beta=0.02) to a frozen previous-epoch reference selector, and an auxiliary CE term (alpha=1.0) aligning selector confidence with the reward. The reward is 1 if the classifier gives the mixed image a higher probability for the foreground-source class than for the background-source class, and 0 otherwise. Mixed labels are corrected as in CutMix, and FG-CutMix is applied with probability 0.5. The K mixed samples are aggregated into a single feature f^a with mixed label y~.

BFR (Background-guided Feature Rectification) is parameter-free and is applied to the final conv feature map of the original sample. It first computes SimAM-style neuron scores S_du = sigmoid((F_du - mu_d)^2 / (4(sigma_d^2+eps))), with mu_d and sigma_d^2 taken over spatial locations. Effective channels at location u are those with S_du >= S̄_u, the mean score over channels at u (Eq. 6). The mean of S_du over these channels gives a foreground contribution T_u. The background score is B_u = sigmoid((mean T - T_u)/(std T + eps)). The pooled feature becomes f' = (1/HW) sum_u (1 - lambda B_u) F_u with lambda=0.5, and f' is fed to the classifier and, when present, the projection head. The loss is L = 0.5[l_LT(h(f^a), y~) + l_LT(h(f'), y)] + 0.8 x L_RL, where l_LT is the base method's long-tailed loss. For CIFAR the setup is ResNet-32, 200 epochs, batch 256, SGD (momentum 0.9, wd 5e-4), LR warmed up to 0.15 over 20 epochs and decayed 0.1x at epochs 160 and 180. Contrastive baselines keep their original contrastive objectives unchanged.
official.claim: On CIFAR-100-LT with imbalance ratio 100 (ResNet-32), adding OFBD to the strongest baseline, MKP, raises overall Top-1 accuracy from 53.21% to 54.42% (+1.21) and Few-class accuracy from 34.91% to 37.29% (+2.38), with Many-class accuracy 67.28% vs 67.57%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparisons on CIFAR-LT [4] datasets with varying imbalance ratios (r). Results are reported across all classes as well as different groups based on training sample sizes ("Many", "Med", and "Few"). For each method, the first row reports the original baseline accuracy, and the second row shows the performance after applying OFBD.
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%) on the balanced test set, higher is better. Table 1 reports single numbers with no error bars, and baselines are single reproduced runs with fixed seeds. The only spread in the paper is Appendix Table 17, where the K=6 OFBD entry is 53.96 ± 0.19. The paper does not say what ± denotes or which base method and setting it uses (likely BCL+OFBD on CIFAR-100-LT r=100). No spread is reported for MKP or MKP+OFBD.
official.comparison: MKP (CVPR'26) vs. MKP + OFBD (FG-CutMix + BFR), with the same ResNet-32 backbone, schedule and data. The authors reproduced the baselines with official code and fixed seeds. For reference, OFBD on BCL: 51.84 -> 54.19 (+2.35); on GBG: 51.92 -> 54.23 (+2.31).
official.falsification_criterion: Over several seeds, MKP+OFBD's mean overall accuracy on CIFAR-100-LT (r=100) beats MKP's by less than ~0.5 points, or by less than the seed std of either run.

title: Social Choice Foundations for Simulation-Augmented Generation

official.background: Simulation-augmented generation (SAGE) answers contentious user queries by consulting LLM simulations of individuals from a target population and synthesizing their views. Querying every simulation at inference time is too slow and costly, so a router must pick a small set of k simulations to query. The open question is how to pick them so that their responses still proportionally represent the whole population of simulations, in the sense that any large enough group with cohesive views gets a fair share of the k slots.
official.method:
Representation is measured with metric proportional justified representation plus (mPJR+): a slate X of k points satisfies it if, for every l in [k], every unselected candidate c and every group S of at least l*n/k voters, at least l slate members are within distance max_{i in S} d(v_i, c) of some member of S. The proposed router, Predictive Route-then-Simulate, runs the Spatial Expanding Approval Rule (SEAR: grow balls around all candidates at a common rate; when the voters inside a candidate's ball have total remaining budget >= n/k, select it and deduct n/k from those voters' budgets) on predicted viewpoint embeddings theta_i(p), which serve as both voters and candidates. It then queries only the k selected simulations.

In the experiments, psi is the preference embedding model embeddings-for-preferences-st5-xl (Blair et al. 2026). The proxy theta is a LoRA fine-tune (r=8, alpha=16, q/v modules, lr 1e-5, 1 epoch, loss = MSE + 1 - Pearson over pairwise distances) of a copy of psi that maps 'User: {user context}\nQuestion: {prompt}' to the embedding of that user's simulated response. Ground truth for evaluation is c_i(p) = psi(A_i(p)), the embeddings of all n simulated responses, used as both voters and candidates when checking mPJR+ (He et al. 2026 FPT verifier). On Remesh, the simulators are Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct role-play prompts for n = 310 participants (demographics, past answers and agree/disagree votes as context), and the evaluation uses 1,000 Claude-generated prompts on 10 related topics. Baselines: k-means on the same theta embeddings (taking the simulation nearest each center) and uniform random selection. The oracle (SEAR on the true c_i) satisfies mPJR+ by construction.
official.claim: On Remesh (n = 310 simulated participants), routing with SEAR on predicted viewpoint embeddings satisfies mPJR+ on a larger share of test prompts than both k-means on the same embeddings and random selection at every k from 3 to 10. For k = 6-10 it leads the best baseline (random) by about 16-22 points: roughly 65 vs. 47% at k = 6, 58 vs. 36% at k = 8 and 47 vs. 28% at k = 10. k-means reaches only 11-25% at these k.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: mPJR+ Satisfaction Rate by Simulation Selection Method. Left: Remesh; right: Reddit AITA. Solid: Route-then-Simulate with SEAR (ours), k-means, random; dashed: Simulate-then-Route SEAR (oracle).
official.metric: Percentage of test prompts whose k selected simulations satisfy mPJR+ with respect to the true response embeddings of all n simulations (higher is better). The figure has error bars of about ±4 points, but the paper does not say what they are. There is one proxy-training seed (seed 42).
official.comparison: Predictive Route-then-Simulate with SEAR (ours) vs. the same pipeline with k-means in place of SEAR vs. random selection of k simulations. All routed methods use the same proxy embeddings. The oracle Simulate-then-Route SEAR (100% by construction) serves as an upper bound.
official.falsification_criterion: On Remesh test prompts with a re-trained proxy, SEAR's mPJR+ satisfaction rate is not higher than both random and k-means by more than about 5 points at each k in 6-10. Alternatively, random or k-means matches or beats SEAR at any k in 3-10.

title: TrackFish3D: Self-Supervised 3D Tracking of Schooling Fish from Multi-view Videos
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (per-scene breakdown in Table 12, page 23)

official.background: Studying collective fish behaviour needs dense, identity-consistent 3D trajectories for every fish in a school. Multi-camera 3D tracking has to solve two coupled problems: matching 2D detections of the same fish across synchronized cameras (spatial association) and linking the resulting 3D points over time (temporal association). Schooling fish look almost identical and occlude each other often, so appearance-based re-identification works poorly, and identity labels, temporal annotations and 3D ground truth are rarely available for training.
official.method:
TrackFish3D takes per-camera, per-frame 2D detections (from SAM 3 or YOLO26+SAM2) plus calibrated cameras. Each detection is turned into a 9-D geometry-only feature (normalised centroid, box size, camera index, detector score, back-projected world-ray direction), encoded by a small MLP, and processed jointly with all other detections in the frame by a 4-layer transformer with 2D RoPE. A pairwise head predicts whether two detections from different cameras are the same fish. Training labels come from geometry alone: a cross-camera pair is a pseudo-positive if its triangulated point reprojects inside both bounding boxes, weighted by reprojection error (confidence-weighted BCE). After a 100-epoch warm-up on this loss, an InfoNCE contrastive loss (same multi-view group = positive) and a temporal loss (an MLP predictor maps a group embedding at frame t to its matched group at t+1, weighted MSE) are added; training runs 400 epochs total, about 655K parameters, no identity labels or 3D ground truth.

At inference, cross-view pairs are scored by A = 0.6*P + 0.4*(cos(h_i, h_j)+1)/2 (cosine of transformer embeddings rescaled to [0,1]), matched with Hungarian per camera pair, merged, triangulated by DLT and validated by reprojection; groups are linked over time with a cost combining 3D distance and embedding similarity, with predictor-based embedding roll-forward for gaps and post-hoc fragment merging. All 13 baselines, including SAM3 + Hungarian + 3D constant-velocity Kalman linking (3D-SORT), use the same detections, calibration and post-processing (gap interpolation, ghost-track removal), and learned baselines are fine-tuned on the same training split. SynFish is an Unreal Engine 5 synthetic dataset with 3 cameras; training uses 8 scenes and testing 6 held-out scenes (4, 5, 8, 16, 16, 16 fish; one test rig unseen in training).
official.claim: On the 6 held-out SynFish test scenes, TrackFish3D with SAM 3 detections reaches 95.8% 3D MOTA (IDSw 0.0, MT 95.8%), versus 87.7% (IDSw 4.0, MT 77.1%) for the strongest baseline, SAM3 + Hungarian + 3D-SORT Kalman linking, using the same detections and post-processing.
official.claim_caption: Tab. 2: 3D tracking results on the SynFish test set, averaged over 6 held-out scenes (4–16 fish). Best result in each column among methods with MOTA>0 is bolded; per-scene breakdown is in Appendix Table 12.
official.metric: 3D MOTA (higher is better), averaged over 6 test scenes, with predictions matched to ground truth under a fixed 3D distance threshold per frame. Single run; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: TrackFish3D (SAM3) vs. SAM3 + 3D-SORT (strongest baseline), SAM3 + Hungarian/Greedy, MCTR, ReST, ASNet, Self-MVA, SambaMOTR, MOTIP; all on identical SAM 3 detections and calibration
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining TrackFish3D on the 8 SynFish training scenes (or several seeds of it) and evaluating on the 6 test scenes gives average MOTA within about 2 points of the 3D-SORT baseline (87.7%), or below it; or the 16-fish scenes (test4-test6) no longer show a clear advantage over 3D-SORT.

title: AdaM-Rec: Adaptive Modality Routing for Multimodal Recommendation
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (the static grid it compares against is Figure 3, page 9)

official.background: Multimodal recommenders usually fuse text and image signals in a fixed way, assuming the relative value of each modality is the same for every request. In practice it varies: an appearance-driven query ('sneakers with a thick wavy sole') benefits from visual evidence, while a specification-driven one ('70W MacBook USB-C charger') can be hurt by visually similar but functionally wrong items. The paper studies query-based personalized recommendation, where a user issues a natural-language query and the system must recall and rank items from the full catalogue using both the query and the user's history.
official.method:
Offline, an MLLM (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) turns every item into a structured text profile, while the item's raw text description is embedded with a text encoder (Qwen3-Emb.-0.6B) and its main image plus raw text with a multimodal encoder (Qwen3-VL-Emb.-2B). For each user, the profiles of the items in their history are summarized by the LLM policy (Qwen3-8B) into a preference profile. At query time, recall takes the top α·K items by text-embedding similarity and the top β·K items by multimodal-embedding similarity (α + β = 1, K ≤ 1000), adds positive items of the 5 most preference-similar users, and ranks candidates by the LLM's expected 1–5 relevance score given query, user preferences and item profile.

The routing parameters (α, β, K) are chosen per user and query: the LLM initializes them from similar users' routing parameters, rewrites the actual query into pseudo-queries of the same granularity that point to the user's own relevant positively interacted items, runs both recall branches on each pseudo-query, observes the rank of the known target in each branch, and iteratively updates (α, β, K) with a memory of past steps. The ablation 'w/o Adaptive Modality Routing' replaces this with the best static setting found by grid search in Figure 3 (α = β = 0.5, K = 800) while keeping the rest of the pipeline.
official.claim: On TAIRA's Amazon Beauty query-based recommendation set (374 user-query pairs, full-corpus ranking), the full AdaM-Rec with adaptive modality routing reaches candidate Recall 0.4278 and HR@40 0.2193 / NDCG@40 0.1077, versus 0.3743 and 0.1898 / 0.0866 when routing is replaced by the best static split (α = β = 0.5, K = 800).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Ablation studies on agent policy and core components. The metric "Recall" denotes the HR of candidates recalled with routed parameters. "@K" denotes the HR and NDCG scores computed over top-K ranked items. Bold highlights the default config and the strongest policy variant.

title: Unveiling the Value of Motion for Cinematic Camera Trajectories
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (supported by Tables 13, 16, 17, 18 in Appendix H, pages 21-22)

official.background: Text-conditioned camera trajectory generators (CCD, E.T., GenDoP) and their evaluators (CLaTr) represent a camera path as a sequence of absolute per-frame poses. Human descriptions of camera motion ('dolly in, then pan right') describe how the camera moves rather than where it is, so the paper argues that pose-centric inputs make text-trajectory alignment harder than necessary, and that this matters both for retrieval-style evaluation and for generation.
official.method:
POSE9D represents each frame as the 6D continuous rotation of R_t concatenated with translation t_t (9 dims). DIRSPEED computes frame-to-frame velocities, Δt_t = t_t − t_{t−1} and ω_t = log_SO(3)(R_{t−1}^T R_t) (zero at t=1), and splits each into a unit direction and a log-speed: d = v/(||v||+ε), s = log(||v||+ε), giving an 8D per-frame vector [d_tr, d_rot, s_tr, s_rot].

Alignment is measured with a purely contrastive evaluator: a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder (pooled EOS, trainable linear 768→256 head) and a 4-layer Transformer trajectory encoder (d_model 256, CLS pooling, ~3.6M params), trained only with symmetric InfoNCE (τ = 0.1, false-negative masking of captions with text-text cosine > 0.99), AdamW lr 2e-4 cosine, batch 64, up to 150 epochs with early stopping. Training pairs are CineScript trajectories (extracted with VIPE from ~28K movie clips) and motion captions generated with the E.T. motion-tagging + Mistral-7B pipeline. Retrieval is trajectory-to-text on the validation set (2,578 clips per Table 12). The same evaluator is trained once with DIRSPEED inputs and once with POSE9D inputs.
official.claim: With an identical purely contrastive text–trajectory evaluator (3.6M params) trained on CineScript motion captions, DirSpeed inputs give higher trajectory-to-text retrieval than Pose9D inputs: R@1 25.2 vs. 17.8, R@10 49.0 vs. 31.4, MedR 11 vs. 51, AlignScore 66.3 vs. 46.6; the gap also holds inside the CLaTr evaluator (R@1 19.7 vs. 6.9).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Alignment evaluator validation on motion captions. We compare CLaTr and our purely contrastive protocol under both trajectory representations.
official.metric: Trajectory-to-text retrieval on the CineScript validation set: R@1/5/10 (higher better), median rank (lower better), AlignScore = 100 × mean clipped cosine of matched pairs (higher better). Single runs; no seeds, std or confidence intervals reported.

title: AdaOcc: Adaptive 3D Occupancy Prediction for Embodied Tasks

official.background: 3D semantic occupancy prediction labels every voxel in a local 3D volume around an agent as empty or as one of several semantic classes, giving robots a dense map for navigation and manipulation. Most existing methods use dense voxels or Gaussian primitives, assume a fixed sensor setup, and run with a fixed compute budget. The indoor benchmark Occ-ScanNet (built from ScanNet RGB-D scans) asks a model to predict a 60x60x36 grid at 0.08 m voxels from RGB images. The recent Gaussian-based method SplatSSC is the strongest prior method that uses the same depth prior from RGB (Depth Anything v2).
official.method:
AdaOcc is a point-based occupancy predictor. A dual-branch encoder extracts multi-scale image features (default C-RADIOv3-B; the AdaOcc† variant uses SplatSSC's EfficientNet encoder) and geometric features: depth maps estimated from the RGB input by Depth Anything v2 are lifted to a 3D point cloud, voxelized, encoded with a sparse 3D CNN and compressed into three orthogonal feature planes (xy, xz, yz). Query points are initialized by sampling locations from this point cloud. A 6-layer decoder, following OPUS, refines each query by sampling image and plane features around its reference point and predicts a growing number of semantic points per query (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 across layers). The predicted points are voxelized for evaluation.

Training uses focal loss on semantic logits, density-aware Chamfer distance to ground-truth occupied voxel centers, and a new containment loss (C.P.O.) that penalizes predicted points that land in supervised empty space by their Smooth-L1 distance (plus a margin m = 0.04) to the nearest occupied voxel box. Progressive query learning raises the active query count by 100 every 40 epochs up to 500, over 200 epochs. For Table 4, AdaOcc† (EfficientNet encoder) is evaluated at 500 queries and SplatSSC is trained with 1131 anchors, both on Occ-ScanNet-mini, with latency and memory measured on one NVIDIA H20 GPU.
official.claim: On Occ-ScanNet-mini with the same EfficientNet image encoder, AdaOcc† with 500 queries reaches 57.97 mIoU and 65.16 IoU at 64.4 ms per sample, versus 48.46 mIoU and 60.86 IoU at 85.1 ms for the best SplatSSC setting (1131 anchors).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Efficiency and adaptability analysis on the Occ-ScanNet-mini dataset using a single NVIDIA H20 GPU. All results use the same EfficientNet image encoder as SplatSSC for a controlled comparison. (a) Query-number ablation for AdaOcc†. (b) Anchor-number ablation for SplatSSC. (c) Decoder-layer output ablation for AdaOcc†. Within each panel only the listed factor is varied while all other settings are fixed.
official.metric: mIoU over 11 occupied semantic classes and occupied (binary) IoU, higher is better; latency (ms) and memory (MiB) on one H20 GPU, lower is better. Table 4 has no error bars. Table 13 (p. 22) gives 5-seed std for the default RADIO-encoder AdaOcc on the same split: 0.20 mIoU, 0.10 IoU (mean 58.46 / 65.41). No seed spread is reported for AdaOcc† or SplatSSC.
official.comparison: AdaOcc† (EfficientNet encoder, 500 queries) vs. SplatSSC (EfficientNet encoder, 1131 anchors, the best of 600/1131/1911/2596 anchors), same dataset split and same GPU
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained under matched conditions, AdaOcc† at 500 queries does not exceed SplatSSC's best anchor setting by at least ~5 mIoU on Occ-ScanNet-mini, or it does not beat SplatSSC on IoU, or it is not faster per sample on the same GPU.

title: CellMSA: Context Modeling for Single-Cell Representation Learning

official.background: Single-cell RNA-seq profiles are high-dimensional, sparse and affected by batch effects, which makes learning good cell representations hard. Most single-cell foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer, etc.) encode each cell on its own, and the few that use multi-cell context (CellPLM, STATE, Stack) compress each cell and use only cells from the same batch. The paper asks whether giving the model a richer context of related cells, analogous to the multiple sequence alignment used in protein structure models, gives better cell embeddings for downstream tasks such as cell type and disease-state classification.
official.method:
For each target cell, CellMSA builds an MSA-like context of 40 retrieved cells: 16 of the same type and batch, 16 of the same type from other batches, and 8 from biologically similar cell types (from a hierarchical clustering of cell-type mean profiles). Each cell is a scGPT-style sequence of gene tokens with binned expression values; context rows get a relation-type embedding. A low-dimensional CellMSA-Module (AlphaFold-style outer-product mean and pair-weighted averaging) summarizes the context into a gene-pair representation, which a GenePairformer injects as an attention bias while encoding the target cell; the <cls> output is the cell embedding. The model is pretrained for one epoch on ~109M CELLxGENE human cell observations with masked gene expression modeling (the same gene positions are masked in the target and context rows), expression-profile reconstruction from the cell embedding, and a cell-level InfoNCE contrastive loss (positive from the same cell type, negatives from the same batch).

For classification, cell embeddings are extracted from the pretrained model and a three-layer MLP head is trained on top (the paper describes no CellMSA fine-tuning; all foundation-model baselines are explicitly run zero-shot with official checkpoints and default settings). Ground-truth labels of validation and test cells are not used to build their context: HVGs + PCA + KNN in PCA space determine the cell type used to select their context cells. Data are split by donor 7:1:2 and the experiment is repeated five times. Tasks: cell type annotation on Tabula Sapiens-Blood (cell types with at least 1% of cells) and 3-way proximal tubule state classification (aPT, dPT, dPT/DTL) on the Kidney Atlas (healthy, AKI and CKD donors).
official.claim: With frozen embeddings and the same MLP head over 5 donor-split runs, CellMSA reaches higher accuracy than the strongest baseline on Tabula Sapiens-Blood cell type annotation (0.962 ± 0.002 vs. CellPLM 0.931 ± 0.003) and on Kidney Atlas PT cell state classification (0.958 ± 0.004 vs. Stack 0.936 ± 0.008; macro-F1 0.931 ± 0.006 vs. best 0.912 ± 0.009).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Results of cell type and cell state classification. Entries with ± report mean and standard deviation over five runs.
official.metric: Classification accuracy (and macro-F1) on the held-out donor test split, higher is better; ± is std over five random donor splits/runs
official.comparison: CellMSA embeddings vs. scVI, scGPT, Geneformer, STATE-SE, Stack and CellPLM embeddings, each with the same three-layer MLP head and splits
official.falsification_criterion: CellMSA's mean accuracy does not exceed the best baseline by more than the run-to-run std on either task (e.g. Blood accuracy at or below ~0.935, or PT accuracy at or below ~0.944 when CellPLM/Stack are rerun under the same protocol).

title: Beyond Spatial-Domain Supervision: A Relation Constrained Space for Multi-Modal Image Fusion
claim_source: Table 3 (row (a)(4) 'w/o RCS' vs. 'Full Model (Transformer)'), page 9; same rows repeated in Table 7, page 23

official.background: Multi-modal image fusion (MMIF) merges two registered images of the same scene, such as infrared + visible or MRI + PET, into a single image. No ground-truth fused image exists, so nearly all learned fusion networks are trained with losses that pull the output toward the source images themselves (intensity and gradient L1 to the max of the two sources, SSIM, etc.). The paper argues that treating both sources as simultaneous targets forces a pixel-level compromise or a bias toward one modality. It proposes supervising fusion in a learned feature space built from frozen pretrained models instead.
official.method:
A learnable feature adapter (LFA) takes frozen DINO (layers 4 and 8) and CLIP (layer 6) features of each source image, projects them to a 16x16 token grid with 256 channels, and aligns them with an MLP. A pair encoder then produces pair-conditioned representations z_A and z_B plus three per-token relation parameters: sharedness m, dominance d and coordination radius r. The fused image is encoded with the same adapter as the self-pair (F, F) to give z_F. A frozen token-wise MLP G_shr, pretrained CDDFuse-style, splits each representation into a shared part c and an offset u = z - c. The relation-constrained supervision (RCS) is L_rel = L_shr + L_cmp + L_crd. L_shr is the cosine distance of c_F to c_A and to c_B. L_cmp = (1-m)·cosdist(u_F, d·u_A + (1-d)·u_B). L_crd is a hinge max(0, ||u_F|| - r).

Training: the fusion network (two-branch encoder-decoder; CNN, Mamba or Transformer blocks) is warmed up for 20 epochs with the conventional loss ||F - max(A,B)||_1 + 2·||∇F - max(∇A,∇B)||_1. The adapter is pretrained for 50 epochs with a self-supervised margin ranking loss (matched source pairs and matched source-fused triples must score higher than pairs with one source swapped for an unpaired image). Training then alternates for 5 rounds: 30 adapter epochs with the fusion net frozen, then 20 fusion epochs with the adapter frozen, using only L_rel. Settings are AdamW, lr 3e-4 halved every 10 epochs, batch 4. IVF trains on 1,000 MSRS pairs and tests on 50 RoadScene pairs. MIF uses 200 Harvard Medical pairs. The 'w/o RCS' ablation replaces RCS with conventional source-preservation supervision on the same backbone.
official.claim: With the same Transformer fusion backbone, replacing conventional source-preservation supervision with relation-constrained supervision improves all 7 fusion metrics on both RoadScene IVF and MRI-PET MIF, e.g. RoadScene MI 2.803 -> 3.179, Q_AB/F 0.497 -> 0.564, Q_M 0.581 -> 0.643; MRI-PET AG 8.604 -> 9.690, Q_AB/F 0.541 -> 0.627, Q_P 0.405 -> 0.481.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Ablation study of the proposed method on the IVF RoadScene and MIF MRI-PET datasets. The best results are highlighted in bold. More ablation variants are provided in the appendix.
official.metric: No-reference fusion metrics AG, EN, SD, MI, Q_AB/F, Q_M, Q_P (all higher is better), averaged over test pairs; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: Full model (Transformer backbone, relation-constrained supervision) vs. the same backbone with RCS replaced by conventional source-preservation supervision ('w/o RCS')
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining the Transformer backbone with conventional source-preservation loss and with RCS under the same schedule gives RCS no improvement in MI and Q_AB/F on RoadScene or MRI-PET, or an improvement smaller than the run-to-run spread across seeds.

title: Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via False Discovery Controlled Visual Data Splitting

official.background: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate objects: they say an object is in an image when it is not, usually because the language prior wins over weak visual evidence. Training-free decoding methods such as VCD, MARINE and AGLA reduce this by contrasting logits from original and altered visual inputs. However, they judge each object query on its own and give no explicit control over how many hallucinated objects are kept per image. This paper treats the problem as multiple hypothesis testing and aims to control the false discovery rate (FDR) of hallucinated objects within each image while keeping power, the fraction of truly present objects that are retained.
official.method:
CORAL is training-free. For each image, the patch-level visual embeddings v from the vision encoder are perturbed with a single shared Gaussian noise draw Z with opposite signs: v+ = v + τZ and v- = v - τZ, where τ is calibrated once per backbone by a coarse sweep (τ ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 1.00}) on a small subset disjoint from the evaluation images at q = 0.1 and then kept fixed; the paper does not report the selected τ values (Appendix C.2, Figs. 10-11). For each generated token, the model computes logit differences Δ+ = logit(y|v) - logit(y|v+) and Δ- = logit(y|v) - logit(y|v-) under the same prompt and decoding history. It then forms the Gaussian-mirror statistic Δ = |Δ+ + Δ-| - |Δ+ - Δ-|. For an object that spans several tokens, the object-level statistic is the minimum Δ over its tokens.

FDR at threshold s is estimated as #{Δ ≤ -s} / max(#{Δ ≥ s}, 1). The threshold T_q is the smallest s whose estimated FDR is at most q = 0.1. Objects with Δ ≥ T_q are kept and the rest are suppressed. On POPE (MSCOCO, 500 images, 6 yes/no questions per image, random/popular/adversarial negative sampling), the paper reports per-image FDR and power, averaged over images. The comparison covers Regular decoding, VCD, MARINE and AGLA, with each baseline run at its published default hyperparameters, on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B.
official.claim: On POPE-MSCOCO adversarial at target q = 0.1, CORAL achieves higher overall power than the strongest baseline (AGLA) on all three backbones: LLaVA-OneVision-7B 88.33 ± 1.45 vs. 75.77 ± 1.28, Qwen2.5-VL-7B 83.63 ± 1.55 vs. 73.99 ± 1.11, InternVL3-8B 87.59 ± 1.33 vs. 81.36 ± 1.78, with comparable or lower FDR (0.069-0.084 vs. 0.078-0.090).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Evaluation of overall FDR control and overall power across multiple LVLM architectures on MSCOCO (3000 runs). Overall FDR and power denote averages of per-image FDR and power. Bold indicates the best result and underline indicates the second-best result.
official.metric: Overall power (%), the mean over images of per-image power (higher is better), with overall FDR as a secondary check (lower is better). ± is the std over 3000 evaluation resamplings in which model outputs are held fixed (Appendix B.7), not over independent seeds or runs.
official.comparison: CORAL vs. Regular decoding, VCD, MARINE and AGLA (baselines run at their papers' default hyperparameters) on three LVLMs, POPE-MSCOCO adversarial split
official.falsification_criterion: On POPE-MSCOCO adversarial, CORAL's overall power does not exceed AGLA's by more than a few points (for example, less than about 3 points, roughly two reported std) on at least two of the three backbones, or CORAL's overall FDR is clearly higher than AGLA's.

title: Beyond Prediction: Steering VLM Agents with Retrospective World Modeling

official.background: VLM agents trained with RL for multi-turn tasks (grid puzzles, embodied navigation, manipulation) increasingly reason with an internal 'world model': they describe the current state and predict the next state before acting (e.g., VAGEN). This prediction is open-loop: nothing checks whether the executed action actually explains the observed state change, and the agent still learns only from sparse end-of-episode rewards. The paper asks whether adding a backward check, inferring which action caused an observed transition, gives a useful dense training signal.
official.method:
Retrospective World Modeling (RWM) extends VAGEN's reasoning trace (<Obs> state, <Rea> candidate action, <Pred> predicted next state, <Ans> action) with a <Retro> step. After a transition (s_t, s_{t+1}) is observed, the same policy VLM, given a history-agnostic prompt containing only the two textual belief states and the candidate action set, scores every action from the logits of the action tokens. The Self-Consistency Reward is the normalized margin between the executed action's score and the best other action's score, r^i_t = (v^{a_t} - max_{a != a_t} v^a) / (S_max - S_min). It is assigned back to turn t and added to the extrinsic reward with weight alpha (r_t = r^e_t + alpha * r^i_t).

The policy (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) is trained with PPO and a value head. In the 'Base' configuration both VAGEN-Base and RWM-Base use standard token-level GAE with sparse task and format rewards; RWM-Base additionally receives the self-consistency reward. ('Full' adds Bi-Level GAE and a GPT-4.1-nano LLM-as-judge reward to both.) Training: batch 128, actor lr 1e-6, critic lr 1e-5, max 4 turns per episode. Evaluation: success rate at temperature 1.0, averaged over 3 evaluation runs on 128 generated test cases per environment. FrozenLake is 4x4 and non-slippery; Sokoban Standard is 6x6.
official.claim: With a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone and identical sparse-reward PPO (token-level GAE), adding the retrospective self-consistency reward (RWM-Base) raises test success rate over the prospective-only VAGEN-Base from 0.43 to 0.75 on FrozenLake (4x4) and from 0.41 to 0.58 on Sokoban (6x6 standard).

We adopt Qwen2.5-VL-3B as the backbone for the trained models. The best and second-best performance among open-source models/methods are highlighted in bold and underline, respectively.

title: PatchKV: Weight Space Compensation of KV Cache
claim_source: Figure 2(a), SQuAD panel, page 6 (the 73% figure is stated in Sec. 3.2, page 7)

official.background: In long-context LLM serving where one context is read once and queried many times, the KV cache grows linearly with context length and dominates memory and bandwidth per query. Token-eviction (e.g. KVzip) and cache-approximation (e.g. Attention Matching) methods shrink the cache, but accuracy degrades sharply at aggressive budgets (the paper studies cache ratios of at most 20%), because facts needed by later queries are dropped. The paper asks whether a context-specific weight update can carry part of the information lost by compression, so that the cache can be smaller without changing per-query cost.
official.method:
PatchKV takes an off-the-shelf compressed cache (here KVzip, which evicts KV pairs that get low attention during a teacher-forced 'repeat the context' pass) and computes a patch ΔW to the MLP down-projection of every transformer block. Reference sequences derived only from the context (repeat-context: the context re-fed after a 'Repeat the previous context' prompt; self-study: the full-cache model's own answers to fixed generic instructions such as 'Aggregate all key facts'; joint: both) are teacher-forced through the model twice: once attending to the full cache (teacher) and once to the compressed cache (student). For each reference token, the target is t_i = W(h_i − h'_i) + (z_i − z'_i), where h is the MLP intermediate activation and z the attention output, and ΔW solves the ridge regression ΔW = T^T H' (H'^T H' + λI)^{-1} with λ = λ0·||H'^T H'||_F^2 / tr(H'^T H'). Blocks are patched sequentially (later blocks see student activations from already-patched earlier blocks), and the sufficient statistics are accumulated in 5K-token chunks.

The patch is merged into the weights and the model then answers downstream questions using only the compressed cache. The evaluation varies the KV cache ratio b/n ∈ {0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and compares PatchKV (three reference-query variants) against the same compressed cache without a patch ('Cache-only') and the full KV cache.
official.claim: On SQuAD with Qwen2.5-7B-1M and KVzip compression, adding the PatchKV weight patch (joint reference queries) raises exact-match accuracy from about 12% to about 68–75% at KV cache ratios 0–0.02 and from about 17% to about 81% at ratio 0.05 (full KV ≈ 93%). With no cache at all, PatchKV recovers up to 73% of full-KV accuracy (as stated in Sec. 3.2).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Benchmark results using Qwen2.5-7B-1M with PatchKV applied on top of (a) an eviction based method (KVzip) and (b) an approximation based method (Attention Matching). In (b), † marks shortened (tiny) task variants for SCBench retrieval tasks.
official.metric: SQuAD exact-match accuracy (%), higher is better; single runs, no error bars or seeds reported; values read off the plot (approximate)

title: On the Complexity of Preference-Based Bandits
claim_source: Figure 1(a), page 9 (repeated with d = 15 and d = 20 in Figure 2, page 26)

official.background: In preference-based (dueling) bandits a learner picks a pair of arms each round and sees only which arm won, drawn from a Bradley-Terry model P(x beats x') = sigmoid(f*(x) - f*(x')), while it is scored on the reward of the arms it plays. This setting models recommendation, ranking and RLHF-style feedback. Because the sigmoid link is non-linear, existing algorithms and their regret bounds pay a problem-dependent constant kappa = sup 1/sigmoid'(f*(x) - f*(x')), which grows like exp(2S) with the reward range S. The paper argues that preference feedback need not cost this factor in the leading regret term.
official.method:
GINOP (Generic INformative OPtimism) computes at each round the maximum-likelihood reward estimate f_hat_t under the Bradley-Terry log-loss and a log-loss confidence set F_t. It then plays the pair (x, x') that jointly maximises f_hat_t(x) + f_hat_t(x') + omega_t(x, x'), where omega_t is the largest disagreement over F_t on the reward gap f(x) - f(x'). Both arms are chosen in a single optimisation step, and the bonus is zero for identical arms.

In the linear case (f*(x) = <theta*, x>), omega_t(x, x')^2 is proportional to beta_t ||x - x'||^2 in the norm induced by H_t^{-1}, where H_t = sum_s sigmoid'((x_s - x'_s)^T theta_hat_t)(x_s - x'_s)(x_s - x'_s)^T. This curvature-weighted design matrix replaces the unweighted V_t used by the baselines (Appendix E.1). In the experiment: d = 10, S = 2, theta* in the radius-S ball, 30 arms drawn uniformly from {-1/sqrt(d), 1/sqrt(d)}^d, horizon T = 2000, 20 independent trials, and cumulative regret is reported. Baselines are MaxInP (no tuning); CoLSTIM with c = C_thresh = eta = sqrt(d log T), tau = t0 = d|X|, p_t = min(1, sqrt(d/(t - tau)) log(dT)); and FGTS.CDB with eta = 0.25, mu = 1/(10 e^S sqrt(T)).
official.claim: In the linear Bradley-Terry dueling bandit (d = 10, S = 2, 30 arms, T = 2000, 20 trials), GINOP reaches cumulative regret of about 400 at T = 2000, versus about 1,330 for FGTS.CDB, 2,150 for CoLSTIM and 2,400 for MaxInP. Its regret curve flattens while the baselines' curves grow nearly linearly.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: We benchmark GINOP against several baselines across different settings, reporting in each case the cumulative regret over a horizon of T = 2000 rounds, averaged over 20 independent trials and considering an action set of 30 arms. (a) In the linear setting, we take d = 10 and benchmark against MaxInP (Saha, 2021), CoLSTIM (Bengs et al., 2022), and FGTS.CDB (Li et al., 2024). (b) In the kernelized setting, we adopt the Ackley function as the reward and employ the Matérn kernel with smoothness parameter ν = 2.5; we benchmark against POP-BO (Xu et al., 2024), MaxMinLCB (Pásztor et al., 2024), and MR-LPF (Kayal et al., 2025). (c) In the neural setting, we consider a cosine reward function and benchmark against the neural-network-based approaches NDB-UCB and NDB-TS (Verma et al., 2025).
official.metric: cumulative regret at round T = 2000 (lower is better), mean over 20 independent trials. Shaded bands are shown but the paper does not say what they represent (std or CI). Values are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: GINOP vs. MaxInP, CoLSTIM and FGTS.CDB on the same synthetic linear instances and horizon
official.falsification_criterion: With the stated setup, GINOP's mean cumulative regret at T = 2000 is not clearly below FGTS.CDB's, the strongest baseline (for example, less than about a 2x gap, or overlapping across-trial standard deviations), or it is not below MaxInP and CoLSTIM.

title: I Have a Stream: Making Self-Supervised Learning Work on Continuous Video
claim_source: Table 13 (Appendix A.2), page 15; single-seed versions of the same comparison in Table 4 (page 9) and, for ViT-S, Table 3 (page 8)

official.background: Self-supervised image encoders such as MAE, DINO and MoCo v3 are trained on shuffled, multi-epoch image collections in which each batch holds diverse, unrelated images. A camera, robot or embodied agent instead sees a temporally ordered video stream in which consecutive frames are near-duplicates. The paper asks whether SSL can learn good image representations from scratch when frames are consumed in temporal order through sliding-window batches, with no global shuffling, no multi-epoch replay and no long-term replay buffer. It reports that contrastive and distillation methods degrade badly in this setting and that MAE degrades less but still trails i.i.d. MAE trained on the same frames. It attributes the gap to high intra-batch similarity (near-duplicate frames within a batch), not to the overlap between consecutive batches.
official.method:
Streaming protocol: a walking-tour video (WT++12h = one 12-hour London walking tour, 60 FPS subsampled by k = 16 to 3.75 FPS, 1280×720) is consumed in temporal order. Each step takes a sliding window of B = 2048 consecutive frames with stride s = 1. DataDrop keeps a random 25% of the window, giving an effective batch of 512; dropped frames are not forwarded. Training is from random init with a ViT encoder, AdamW (betas 0.9, 0.95), base lr 4e-5 for ViT-B scaled by Beff/256, and a constant lr after linear warm-up. The streaming MAE baseline is standard MAE (mask ratio 0.75, normalized-pixel loss, decoder dim 512, depth 8, a single 224×224 random-resized crop with horizontal flip, no color jitter) trained under the same protocol, also with DataDrop.

StreamMAE keeps the MAE objective and changes only the input pipeline and regularization: color jitter (MoCo v3 settings, p = 0.5), a linear drop-path schedule reaching 0.25 in the last block, and two-stage cropping with motion-biased crop selection. A fixed-size first-stage crop is chosen and the standard MAE random-resized crop is then applied inside it. With probability 0.5, the first-stage crop is the one of K = 4 random candidates with the highest mean patch-level L1 frame difference from the previous frame; otherwise standard random resized cropping is used. Evaluation is end-to-end fine-tuning: a linear per-patch head on ADE20K (40k steps, 512 crops) and Cityscapes (20k steps, 1024 crops), following Kerssies et al., and the MAE fine-tuning protocol on ImageNet-1K.
official.claim: With ViT-B/16 pretrained from scratch on the WT++12h stream, StreamMAE beats streaming MAE after end-to-end fine-tuning: Cityscapes 69.5 ± 0.4 vs. 58.9 ± 0.5 mIoU and ADE20K 32.9 ± 0.6 vs. 26.6 ± 0.2 mIoU. This matches or exceeds i.i.d. MAE trained on the same frames (68.1 ± 0.4 and 32.8 ± 0.1).
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Results across repeated downstream fine-tuning runs for fixed ViT-S/16 and ViT-B/16 checkpoints pretrained on WT++12h. We report mean and standard deviation over two seeds for ImageNet-1K and three seeds for ADE20K and Cityscapes.
official.metric: Validation mIoU after full fine-tuning, higher is better; ± is std over 3 fine-tuning seeds of one fixed pretrained checkpoint (2 seeds for ImageNet-1K top-1). Pretraining variance is not reported.
official.comparison: StreamMAE vs. streaming MAE (with DataDrop, the stronger baseline config) on the same WT++12h chronological stream, same backbone, iterations and effective batch size; i.i.d. MAE on the same frames as a reference
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running ViT-B/16 pretraining on WT++12h with both methods, StreamMAE's Cityscapes mIoU exceeds streaming MAE's by less than ~3 mIoU, or its ADE20K mIoU by less than ~2 mIoU. That is roughly a third of the reported gaps, which are already well beyond the fine-tuning std.

title: A Matched-Budget Audit Framework for Recaptioned Image-Text Supervision Distributions
claim_source: Table 5, page 7 (bootstrap SDs in Appendix Table 19, page 22)

official.background: Text-to-image models are now usually trained on recaptioned corpora, where a vision-language model (VLM) replaces web alt-text with dense descriptions. Public recaption releases are mostly compared by mean caption length or by downstream text-to-image benchmark scores, which mix the caption corpus with the training recipe. This paper treats a recaptioned corpus as a supervision distribution set by a captioning policy, a captioner and a source corpus, and audits it directly at the caption level before any generator is trained. It also releases its own recaption corpus (about 490M images), written with a policy that phrases captions like user prompts.
official.method:
The released captions ('Ours') are produced by Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8 under a prompt-ordered policy (dominant subject first, then scene structure, then camera framing). For each of four source corpora (DataComp, LAION-pop, PD12M, Danbooru), Ours is paired with a public reference recaption of the same source rows (Recap-DataComp, LAION-pop-Llama, PD12M released, Danbooru-Florence). Each caption is cut to its first B = 64 whitespace-delimited words.

A claim extractor (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8) reads each 64-word window caption-only and returns 'controllable basic units' (CBUs): claims of eight types (object, attribute, relation, count, style, camera, lighting, text-rendering). Each CBU is then re-asked against the paired image by two judges, the Qwen3.5-397B model and Gemma-4-31B-IT, with deterministic schema-constrained answers (supported / unsupported / uncertain). Supported CBU per caption is the mean number of claims a judge labels supported; Risk is unsupported CBUs divided by all claimed CBUs. About 5,000 paired captions per surface are judged.
official.claim: At a 64-word budget, on all four cross-corpus pairs and under both judges, the released captions yield more image-supported claims per caption (Gemma judge: DataComp 8.00 -> 12.94, LAION-pop 10.22 -> 13.61, PD12M 8.23 -> 13.53, Danbooru 6.15 -> 11.85) and lower unsupported-claim risk (e.g. Gemma 0.219 -> 0.081 on DataComp) than the reference recaptions of the same images; the gain holds on the length-matched LAION-pop pair (180.3 vs 182.9 lexical units).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Cross-corpus results at B = 64. Cells a -> b report Ref->Ours (bold = Ours). Pool-wins counts the seven prompt pools where Ours raises prompt-mass support; Qwen and Gemma Judges re-ask the same CBUs on approximately 5,000 paired captions per surface; Risk is unsupported / claimed CBU. Per-pool deltas in Appendix Figure 3, full descriptors in Appendix Tables 14, 16.
official.metric: Supported CBU per caption (higher is better) and Risk = unsupported / claimed CBU (lower is better), at B = 64 on about 5,000 paired captions per surface. Table 5 shows no error bars; Appendix Table 19 gives caption-level bootstrap SDs (2,000 resamples) of about 0.04-0.06 for supported CBU/cap and 0.001-0.003 for risk.
official.comparison: Released prompt-ordered captions (Ours) vs. the public reference recaption of the same source rows, per source corpus, under the same extractor, budget and two judges.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same 64-word truncation, extractor and judge setup on a random sample of paired captions, the reference surface reaches supported CBU per caption within about 1 of Ours or lower risk than Ours on any pair (in particular the length-matched LAION-pop pair), or the ordering flips under the independent Gemma judge.

title: RelationVGGT : Visual Geometry Transformers for 3D Spatial Relation Segmentation

official.background: Open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding methods (LangSplat, OpenGaussian, feed-forward models built on DUSt3R/VGGT-style geometry backbones) segment objects named by a text query. They do not handle spatial relations between objects, such as 'the desk the monitor is resting on'. The closest prior method, RelationField, learns relation features inside a per-scene radiance field. It needs calibrated camera poses and hours of optimization per scene, and finding a target means searching the whole 3D volume. The paper defines a feed-forward, pose-free task: given unposed multi-view images, a mask of a subject object in one reference view, and a relation phrase, segment the target object in every other view without being told its category.
official.method:
RelationVGGT extracts frozen DINOv2 features and Pi3 geometry-encoder tokens for every view and fuses them per patch with an input mixer (a linear projection plus a few RoPE transformer blocks). The reference-view tokens are multiplied by the downsampled subject mask, which keeps only subject patches. The tokens of all target views are concatenated into one sequence and passed through a ViT-S-sized relation transformer that alternates cross-attention to the masked subject tokens with global self-attention across all target views. A DPT head upsamples the result to per-pixel relation features at 512×388. The relation phrase is embedded with Jina Embeddings v3. The mask is sigmoid(feature · text embedding) thresholded at τ = 0.3, with no negative prompts and no post-processing. Training uses a multi-query sigmoid focal loss (several compatible phrasings of the same relation each supervise the same target mask) plus a Dice loss.

Training data comes from 900 ScanNet++ scenes labelled automatically: Set-of-Mark prompting of Qwen3-VL-8B on posed frames, keeping relations proposed in at least 3 frames, geometric filtering with 3D boxes and centroids, and GPT-5.2 rephrasing of predicates. Training runs 200 epochs on 4 H200 GPUs (AdamW, lr 1e-4, cosine decay). Evaluation uses a hand-annotated benchmark of 119 queries: 40 on ScanNet++ (26 from RelationField plus 14 new), 31 on LERF (3 scenes) and 48 on Replica (8 scenes). Baselines are optimized per scene from posed images. RelationField receives the target category name for object retrieval; RelationField† uses only its relation embedding.
official.claim: On the hand-annotated 3D spatial-relation benchmark, feed-forward RelationVGGT (unposed images, no target category given) reaches mIoU 0.445 on ScanNet++ (40 queries) vs. 0.307 for per-scene-optimized RelationField, and 0.446 vs. 0.349 (best baseline, OpenGaussian) on Replica (48 queries). Its 3-split macro average is 0.382 mIoU / 0.549 mAcc vs. RelationField's 0.303 / 0.480.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative comparison on the Replica, LERF, and ScanNet++ benchmarks. RelationField† denotes the relation-only variant without target-object retrieval; Avg. is the macro average across the three benchmarks.
official.metric: mIoU of the predicted target masks across target views (higher is better), plus mAcc = fraction of queries with IoU > 0.25. Single run, no error bars or seed variation reported.
official.comparison: RelationVGGT vs. LangSplat, OpenGaussian, RelationField (given the target category for object retrieval) and RelationField† (relation embedding only), all evaluated on the same benchmark queries
official.falsification_criterion: With RelationVGGT retrained on the auto-annotated ScanNet++ data and evaluated on the same benchmark, its ScanNet++ mIoU does not clearly exceed RelationField's (e.g. a gap well under the reported 0.138), or its Replica mIoU does not exceed the best baseline's.

title: Mixture-Trained Merging for Unified Multi-Objective Models

official.background: Post-training one language model to be good at several things at once (math, code, instruction following, think/no-think modes) is usually done on a single training trajectory, which makes the result sensitive to data ratios, ordering and stopping. Weight-space merging of separately trained experts is a modular alternative, but merging experts that were each fine-tuned on a single objective often degrades one domain or collapses behavioral modes. The paper argues that whether branches can be merged depends on how they were trained, and that branches trained on objective-biased data mixtures stay compatible in weight space.
official.method:
Starting from Qwen3-4B-Base, the paper fine-tunes two branches with full SFT on 10K examples each, using prompts from Dolci-Instruct-SFT (math and code categories) with responses generated by Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 in no-think mode (AdamW, LR 2e-5 constant with 3% warmup, effective batch 128, max length 10,000, loss on assistant tokens only, plateau-based early stopping on validation token accuracy). Hard branches are trained on a single domain (math only, code only). Soft branches are trained on complementary mixtures: the math-leaning branch on 70% math / 30% code and the code-leaning branch on 30% math / 70% code, with the same total size of 10K examples.

Each pair of branches is linearly merged as θ_base + (1−a)(θ_math − θ_base) + a(θ_code − θ_base), sweeping the code-expert ratio a from 0.1 to 0.9 in steps of 0.1. Each merged model is evaluated on MATH-500 and MBPP+ with NeMo-Skills (average of one greedy and three sampled generations at T = 0.7, top-p = 0.95). The full MTM method (iterative rounds, MOBO over the merge simplex, mixture propagation) is not needed for this claim.
official.claim: On Qwen3-4B-Base, linearly merging hard (single-domain) math and code experts drops MATH-500 accuracy from about 85-86 at code-expert ratios 0.1-0.3 to about 66 at 0.5 and about 47-52 at 0.7-0.8, whereas merging soft branches trained on (0.7, 0.3) math/code mixtures keeps MATH-500 at about 82-85 across ratios 0.1-0.8, with MBPP+ staying at about 66-69 for both.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Domain-expert merging on Qwen3-4B-Base. Following Section 5, Hard branches are trained on single domains, whereas Soft branches use complementary Math/Code mixtures with a (0.7, 0.3) split.
official.metric: MATH-500 and MBPP+ accuracy (pass@1 averaged over 4 generations per prompt), higher is better; single training run per branch (seed 42), no error bars; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Linear merges of hard single-domain branches vs. linear merges of soft mixture-trained branches, same base model, data sources, training size and merge-ratio sweep
official.falsification_criterion: With hard and soft branches trained as described, the soft merge's MATH-500 accuracy at code-expert ratios 0.5-0.8 is not at least ~15 points higher than the hard merge's, or the hard merge does not lose more than ~15 MATH-500 points between ratio 0.3 and ratio 0.7.

title: ATI-VLA: Action-Centric Predictive Vision–Language–Action Models via Actionable Alignment Then Adaptive Injection

official.background: Vision–language–action (VLA) models map camera images and a language instruction to robot actions. 'Predictive' VLAs also forecast future observations or world states, hoping this look-ahead improves action generation. The authors find that predictive VLAs often do no better than direct action models such as OpenVLA-OFT. They give two reasons: the predicted-observation representations are poorly aligned with the action space, and adding a prediction loss to the action loss creates conflicting gradients that slow and destabilise training.
official.method:
ATI-VLA uses the OpenVLA-OFT framework with an OpenVLA-7B backbone (LoRA rank 32, alpha 64) and trains in two stages. Stage 1 (alignment): the current observation and action are encoded by modality-specific encoders and vector-quantized into one shared codebook. A unified self-attention/cross-attention decoder then predicts the future observation and the future action (n steps ahead) from these discrete latents, trained with a weighted sum of observation and action prediction losses. The module is then frozen.

Stage 2 (injection): the frozen Stage-1 module maps the current observation to a quantized predictive latent. At every s-th LLM layer (s = 8 for the 32-layer LLaMA-2-7B), a lightweight side path refines this latent with a residual FFN. The action-query tokens cross-attend to it, and the result is added back scaled by a learnable scalar beta_l. Stage 2 is trained with the action loss only. On RoboTwin 2.0 the action chunk size is 25 and the batch size is 32. The comparison baseline is OpenVLA-OFT, reproduced by the authors (marked †).
official.claim: On four RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual tasks (100 trials each), ATI-VLA reaches a 72.3% average success rate vs. 58.8% for the authors' reproduction of its base model OpenVLA-OFT. It wins on every task: Click Bell 91 vs. 78, Open Laptop 87 vs. 66, Place Container Plate 90 vs. 82, Place Bread Skillet 21 vs. 9.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Simulation Results on RoboTwin 2.0 Benchmark. Comparison of task success rates. "†" indicates our reproduced results.
official.metric: task success rate (%), higher is better, over 100 evaluation trials per task; no seeds or error bars reported for RoboTwin
official.comparison: ATI-VLA vs. OpenVLA-OFT† (same OpenVLA-7B backbone and framework, reproduced by the authors). RDT, ACT, DP and π0 numbers are also listed but were not re-run under matched conditions.
official.falsification_criterion: Training OpenVLA-OFT and ATI-VLA under the same RoboTwin 2.0 data and budget gives an average success-rate gap well below 13.5 points (e.g. under ~5 points), or ATI-VLA fails to beat OpenVLA-OFT on most of the four tasks.

title: World Motion Models: Flexible Sequence Modeling of SE(3) Trajectories

official.background: Agents that act in the physical world need a generative prior over how things move in 3D: how a scene will evolve, how a body or robot should move to reach a goal, and how one embodiment's motion maps to another's. Existing motion models are usually tied to one morphology (SMPL humans, MANO hands, a specific robot) or operate in dense observation spaces such as pixels, point tracks or 3D flow, so a separate model and interface is needed for each task. The paper proposes one representation and one model for many of these tasks.
official.method:
A dynamic scene is represented as a set of rigid SE(3) trajectories, one per entity (a body joint, robot link, object, or tracked scene point). Each pose at each time step is one token, a 9-vector made of the position x and two points x + δr1 and x + δr2 built from the first two rotation-matrix columns (δ = 0.2). Each entity also carries a time-constant feature: for TraceGen this is the DINO feature at the query pixel. A transformer with per-token AdaLN conditioning, learnable registers and factored attention (time-axis, entity-axis, register-only and full) is trained with flow matching in which every token gets its own independently sampled noise level. At inference, observed tokens are set to noise level 0 and unknown tokens to 1, so the same network can do future prediction, infilling, policy or retargeting.

For the TraceGen benchmark, the model receives a single RGB-D start frame and a language instruction and predicts the 3D motion of 400 keypoints over 32 steps. Each keypoint is an entity with a 3D position plus an orientation from local Procrustes on the tracks, starting at t=0. Separate checkpoints are trained per dataset (Droid, EpicKitchen) and jointly on both, at training windows of P=128 randomly sampled trajectories or all P=400. Even when trained with P=128, the model infers all 400 trajectories at test time. Metrics are MSE, MAE and endpoint MSE of the 3D trajectories (each ×100), following the TraceGen protocol.

title: From Isolated feature to Orbits: Discovering Music Concepts via Multi-SAE Alignment

official.background: Music foundation models such as MuQ and MusicFM learn frame-level audio representations that work well on downstream tasks, but it is unclear how musical concepts are organized inside them. Probing tests whether predefined labels are linearly recoverable, and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) find individual features that are labelled after the fact. Many music concepts are relational instead of isolated: the 12 major chords form a cycle under pitch transposition, so finding the whole ordered set ('orbit') at once would let a few labelled anchors name all of its members.
official.method:
Each 30-second training segment is pitch-shifted to five views at -2 to +2 semitones (torchaudio phase vocoder, resampled to keep frames aligned), and S = 3 consecutive views are sampled at random for each training example; frame-level representations are extracted from a frozen foundation model (MuQ layer 2 or MusicFM layer 4, d = 1024, 25 fps). One Top-K SAE (K = 48) is trained per view on 326 Slakh2100 songs, with a shared pre-encoder bias and a shared Top-K support mask: the K indices are chosen jointly from the RMS-normalized activations, taking the max over views, so the same feature index is pushed to encode adjacent transpositions of one concept. After training, a successor map inside the middle SAE is built from decoder cosine similarities (reference is the middle SAE, s = 1: the destination j of feature i maximizes the mean of cos(w_i in SAE-2, w_j in SAE-1) and cos(w_i in SAE-1, w_j in SAE-0); the transition is accepted if the larger of these two cosines is at least tau, and when several features map to the same destination only the most confident transition is kept). Iterating this map gives rings (cycles), fixed points and open chains.

For chord recognition, the recovered 12-feature major-chord and minor-chord rings are labelled with a few anchor examples (a batched script for the tables). Activations are smoothed with a 9-frame moving average and averaged within each chord segment, and the argmax over the 24 (root, quality) features is taken; no-chord segments come from the reference no-chord labels under Oracle Bd and from discovered silence features under Est. Bd. No classifier is trained on the ring activations. Segments come from reference chord boundaries (Oracle Bd) or from peaks of a discovered chord-boundary feature (Est. Bd). Baselines: a supervised 25-class linear probe on the same frozen layer, decoded with the same oracle-boundary procedure (Probe); a standard single SAE whose features are picked by cosine similarity to the probe weights (s-SAE); and the released LVCR chord-transcription checkpoint. The metric is mir_eval weighted chord recall on POP909, RWC and Slakh2100.
official.claim: Using MuQ layer-2 representations and oracle chord boundaries, the unsupervised orbit-recovered major/minor chord rings (o-SAE) reach Root WCR of 85.29 / 86.21 / 84.67 on POP909 / RWC / Slakh2100, within 1.4 points of (and on POP909 and RWC above) a supervised 25-class linear probe on the same layer (84.17 / 86.01 / 86.05).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Weighted Chord Recall (WCR) across Different Models.
official.metric: Root weighted chord recall (%, mir_eval Root vocabulary, higher is better); MajMin WCR also reported. Single numbers with no error bars; seed variation is shown only qualitatively in a radar plot (Appendix I.2, Figure 18).
official.comparison: o-SAE chord rings (MuQ layer 2, Oracle Bd) vs. the supervised linear probe on the same layer and decoding; also vs. s-SAE (probe-matched standard SAE features), LVCR, and the same pipeline on MusicFM layer 4
official.falsification_criterion: With MuQ layer 2, K = 48 and oracle boundaries, the recovered chord rings score more than about 3 Root WCR points below the matched linear probe on any of the three datasets, or 12-member major and minor chord rings are not recovered from the multi-SAE alignment at all.

title: Controllable Multi-label Video Safety Detection via Adaptive Tversky Policy Optimization
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (Qwen3-VL-8B replication in Table 6, Appendix F, page 20)

official.background: Automated moderation of video content usually treats harmful-video detection as binary (safe vs. unsafe), although unsafe videos often belong to several harm categories at once (e.g. violence and abuse), and moderation pipelines need different precision-recall operating points for different audiences and categories. Vision-language models (VLMs) can classify videos zero-shot but do poorly on the multi-label version of the task. The paper fine-tunes VLMs with reinforcement learning (GRPO) for multi-label video safety detection and asks how the set-level reward should be designed.
official.method:
The model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, videos sampled at 1 FPS) receives the video plus category definitions and outputs reasoning and a predicted set of unsafe categories P, compared with the ground-truth set G via TP = |P ∩ G|, FP = |P \ G|, FN = |G \ P|. Training is a 1-epoch LoRA SFT warmup (rank 64, lr 1e-5) on 11,036 SafeWatch-Bench training videos under two minutes, then 3 epochs of GRPO (group size 8, temperature 1.0, KL coefficient 0.01) from that same SFT-1ep checkpoint. Baselines are GRPO with an Exact Match reward and GRPO with the Static Tversky Reward (STR) TP / (TP + α FP + β FN) with fixed α, β (α = β = 1 gives the Jaccard reward).

ATPO-G (Global Adaptive Tversky Reward) keeps the Tversky form but adapts α, β during training with a feedback controller: batch-level FP and FN counts from the rollouts are smoothed by an EMA (λ = 0.95), the observed ratio r_t = (FN_ema + ε)/(FP_ema + ε) is compared with a target r*, a logit is updated u_{t+1} = u_t + η (log r_t − log r*) with η = 0.01, and α = 2(1 − σ(u)), β = 2σ(u) (so α + β = 2). ATPO-C does the same per category with micro-aggregated rewards. Evaluation is on the SafeWatch-Bench-Real (820 videos) and SafeWatch-Bench-GenAI test subsets with the example-based Jaccard index, micro/macro F1 and binary F1.
official.claim: Starting from the same SFT-1ep Qwen2.5-VL-7B checkpoint, GRPO with the adaptive G-ATR reward (ATPO-G) reaches a Jaccard index of 75.44 on SafeWatch-Bench-Real and 74.29 on SafeWatch-Bench-GenAI, versus 70.09 and 69.12 for GRPO with the static Tversky reward (STR) and 63.36 and 62.23 for GRPO with Exact Match; ATPO-G also beats STR on macro F1 (76.10 vs. 63.88 Real, 74.46 vs. 64.38 GenAI).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Training comparison on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. GRPO uses static rewards (Exact Match and STR), whereas ATPO-G and ATPO-C use adaptive rewards G-ATR and C-ATR, respectively. All RL methods start from the SFT-1ep checkpoint. Micro, Macro, and Binary denote F1 scores. Bold and underlining indicate the best and second-best results per column.
official.metric: Jaccard index (example-based intersection over union of predicted and true label sets, %, higher is better); also micro, macro and binary F1. Single training run per method; no error bars or seeds reported (checklist answers [No] for statistical significance).
official.comparison: GRPO with adaptive Tversky reward (ATPO-G / ATPO-C) vs. GRPO with static Tversky reward (STR) and Exact Match reward, all from the same SFT-1ep checkpoint, same training data and same GRPO configuration
official.falsification_criterion: Re-training from a matched SFT-1ep checkpoint, ATPO-G's Jaccard on SafeWatch-Bench-Real is not more than ~2 points above GRPO with STR (α = β = 1), or the gap falls within the run-to-run spread observed over several seeds of each method.

title: KaliBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tool Use on Kali Linux with Runtime-Free Verifiable Rewards

official.background: LLMs are increasingly asked to turn an analyst's request into a concrete command for a security tool, but command-line interfaces are unforgiving: a wrong flag, alias or argument order makes the command fail. Existing cybersecurity benchmarks test knowledge (multiple choice) or end-to-end agent behaviour (CTFs), and function-calling benchmarks assume tools are described by JSON schemas in the prompt. KaliBench measures schema-free natural-language-to-CLI translation for Kali Linux tools, scoring tool choice and each argument separately so that failures can be attributed to tool selection or to argument construction.
official.method:
The dataset has 8,504 query-command pairs over 1,642 Kali tools, generated by Qwen3-Max from official tool documentation and filtered by LLM verification, sandboxed execution in a kali-linux-everything Docker image, and human review. It is split into a 5,000-example test set (all 1,642 tools) and a 3,504-example training set. Each example stores the tool name, alias-aware optional flag-value pairs, and ordered positional arguments. Model outputs are parsed with Python's shlex and scored deterministically: Tool Accuracy, Optional-Argument F1 (alias-aware), Positional-Argument F1 (multiset), Total Score (mean of tool and argument scores), and Exact Correct (tool and all arguments match).

Each model is evaluated in three prompt modes: Unrestricted (query only), Restricted (query plus a random list of 20 candidate tool names including the correct one), and Hinted (Restricted plus the official documentation of the candidate tools, truncated to an 8,192-token input budget). Models under 72B (including Qwen3-8B) run locally with vLLM in BF16, and models of 72B or more run through the OpenRouter API; all use temperature 0.2 with 8,192 input and 8,192 output tokens, and documentation is truncated only when the prompt exceeds the input budget. Table 1 reports all metrics for 24 open-weight configurations, including Qwen3-8B with thinking disabled.
official.claim: For Qwen3-8B (non-thinking) on the 5,000-query KaliBench test set, adding 20 candidate tool names (Restricted) raises Tool Accuracy from 68.9% to 95.6% but Exact Correct only from 18.3% to 24.1%, while also adding tool documentation (Hinted) raises Exact Correct to 73.1% (Optional-Argument F1 43.4% -> 88.2%); the same pattern holds on the 24-model average (Tool Acc. 72.0 -> 95.2, Exact Correct 22.3 -> 28.3 -> 73.1).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Open-weight model query-to-command performance across three modes. Columns report Unrestricted (U), Restricted (R), and Hinted (H). † indicates thinking-enabled models, and ⋆ denotes cybersecurity-tuned models. Bold/underline mark the best and second-best within each size group. Models are sorted by Averaged Total Score. MoE parameters use Total/Active (e.g., 685/37B).
official.metric: Exact Correct, Tool Accuracy, Optional-Argument F1 (%), higher is better. The paper reports one number per model and mode (temperature 0.2), with no standard deviations, repeated seeds or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: Same model (Qwen3-8B, thinking off) under Unrestricted vs. Restricted vs. Hinted prompts; secondarily the average over all 24 open-weight configurations.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if, for Qwen3-8B, the Restricted-minus-Unrestricted gain in Exact Correct is comparable to the gain in Tool Accuracy (e.g. Exact Correct rises by more than ~15 points), or if Hinted mode does not raise Exact Correct by at least ~30 points over Restricted.

title: Choosing Before Acting: Comparative Value Estimation for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agents
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (95% CIs for CITA from Table 8, Appendix J, page 26)

official.background: LLM agents that solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls are hard to train with reinforcement learning, because a final success/failure reward says little about which intermediate tool choice caused the outcome. Step-level rewards help, but getting them usually needs human labels, unstable LLM judgments, or costly extra rollouts in a stateful environment. Logged trajectories also only show the tool that was actually called, never the value of alternatives at the same decision point. The paper asks whether an agent can learn to estimate, before acting, how likely each candidate next tool call is to lead to final task success, and use that estimate to pick tools and to shape RL rewards.
official.method:
CITA trains a Comparative Inference Model (CIM) that takes a tool-use context s (query, previous calls and outputs) and a candidate next call a, and outputs a value V(s,a) in [0,1] (estimated probability of final success) and a confidence c(s,a). It uses the LLM backbone as a text encoder, followed by an 8-layer transformer head (hidden 768). It is trained on pairs (s, a_f, a_c, v_f, v_c) from three sources: (1) logged trajectories, where two different next tools observed under the same context get their empirical downstream success rates as labels; (2) a Bayesian simulator over the tool-transition graph, with Beta-sampled node success and edge reliability probabilities, where two continuation paths from a fork are scored by the product of these probabilities; and (3) an LLM that imagines continuations for a factual and an alternative tool and judges success, repeated M times. The loss is BCE on each value, a squared-error loss on the value gap, a consistency term and a confidence-calibration term, trained progressively and with a phase-aware source mixture.

The policy (Qwen2.5-7B or Llama3.1-8B, first SFT'd with LoRA on successful episodes) is then trained with GRPO (group size 6, LoRA rank 64). At each step the policy samples K = 3 candidate tool calls and the frozen CIM executes the one with the highest V*c. The reward is 0.4 x a task-level matching reward + 0.6 x the confidence-weighted mean of CIM values over the executed steps. The same CIM-guided selection is used at inference. Tool F1 compares the generated tool set with the reference trajectory; Task Success Rate (TSR) is judged by GPT-4o from the full trajectory with a fixed prompt.
official.claim: On TOUCAN with a Qwen2.5-7B backbone, CITA reaches 54.23 ± 2.22 TSR and 59.67 ± 1.88 Tool F1, versus 32.68 TSR and 42.74 Tool F1 for the strongest of 11 baselines (ReAct), a gap of about 21.5 TSR and 17 Tool F1 points; CITA is also best on all six benchmark-backbone settings (e.g. Toolathlon/Qwen TSR 47.82 vs. 32.74 for WebDreamer).
