title: Drive vs. Decay: On the Training Dynamics of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
claim_source: Table 4 (image columns), page 9; per-seed values in Tables 19 and 20 (Appendix I.4), pages 46-47

official.background: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) such as I-JEPA learn representations by predicting the embedding of a masked target view from a context view. Because the all-constant solution also minimises the prediction loss, JEPAs can collapse to low-rank embeddings, and the usual safeguards (asymmetric predictor, stop-gradient, EMA teacher) are mostly heuristic. The paper linearises the JEPA gradient flow around the collapsed fixed point and finds that each mode escapes collapse when a ratio µ = γ/σ of a 'drive' term (view alignment) to a 'decay' term (predictor-induced contraction) exceeds 1. A large or poorly initialised predictor increases decay, so the theory suggests starting the predictor near the identity.
official.method:
ResidualPred replaces the standard I-JEPA transformer predictor with an identity-biased version: each predictor attention block adds a fixed diagonal logit bias β_init · I (β_init = 10, unchanged across all experiments) before the softmax, Attention(Q,K,V) = Softmax(QK^T/√d + β_init · I) V, so that at initialisation every token attends almost only to itself and the predictor acts close to the identity in token space. Nothing else changes: same loss, optimiser, EMA teacher, masking and encoder; there is no added loss term or per-step cost, and the predictor is trained jointly as usual.

Image protocol (Appendix I.4): I-JEPA with a ViT-Small/4 encoder on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (64 tokens) and ViT-Small/8 on STL-10 (144 tokens), context retention p_m1 = 0.85, AdamW, 100-epoch cosine schedule, otherwise following the I-JEPA training recipe of Assran et al. (2023). Representations are evaluated with a linear probe on the frozen encoder; seeds: 3 on CIFAR-10 and STL-10, 5 on CIFAR-100.
official.claim: In I-JEPA pretraining for 100 epochs, replacing the standard predictor with ResidualPred raises linear-probe accuracy from 64.55 ± 1.71 to 68.61 ± 0.59 on CIFAR-10 (ViT-S/4, 3 seeds), from 36.83 ± 1.49 to 40.85 ± 0.66 on CIFAR-100 (ViT-S/4, 5 seeds), and from 71.25 ± 1.14 to 75.31 ± 0.78 on STL-10 (ViT-S/8, 3 seeds).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: ResidualPred across tabular and image datasets. Linear-probe accuracy (%). More ImageNet results: Appendix I.5, Figure 6c.
official.metric: Linear-probe top-1 test accuracy (%) at epoch 100, higher is better; ± is the standard deviation over seeds (3 seeds for CIFAR-10 and STL-10, 5 for CIFAR-100)
official.comparison: I-JEPA with ResidualPred predictor vs. I-JEPA with the standard transformer predictor, same encoder, data, masking, optimiser, schedule and seeds (matched initial µ and effective rank at epoch 0)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running I-JEPA with ViT-S/4 on CIFAR-100 (or CIFAR-10) for 100 epochs with ≥3 seeds per arm, ResidualPred's mean linear-probe accuracy is not higher than the standard predictor's by more than the larger of the two seed stds (e.g. a gain under ~1.5 points on CIFAR-100), or the per-seed ranges overlap substantially.

title: Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow

official.background: Offline multi-agent RL learns coordinated policies for several agents from a fixed dataset, without collecting new data. Expressive generative policies (diffusion or flow matching) can represent the many coordination modes in such data, but they do not know which modes have high value. Policies trained to maximize a learned Q-function, held back by a fixed regularization coefficient, tend to collapse onto a single mode. When several agents drift at once, this can produce joint actions that never appear in the data and break coordination. The paper asks whether value maximization can be moved from training time to test time, so that the behavioral prior keeps all its modes and samples are only pushed toward high value at deployment.
official.method:
SCOUT trains two separate components on the offline data. The first is a per-agent flow-matching behavioral prior (velocity field v_{w_i}(t, o_i, x_t), sampled with 10 Euler steps). The second is a decomposed critic {Q_i(o_i, a_i)}, trained by TD learning on the additive (VDN) target Q_tot = sum_i Q_i, where the next-state actions are produced by the same refinement procedure with L_train steps (particles aggregated by mean for the target, Table 4). No actor is trained to maximize Q.

At test time, each agent independently draws P = 10 action particles from its flow prior. It refines them for L_test steps of a Stein-variational-gradient update: a kernel-smoothed gradient of Q_i plus an RBF repulsion term (adaptive median bandwidth), with step size ε = 0.02, clipping, and temperature α = 1.0. It then executes the particle with the highest Q_i. Setting L_test = 0 reduces to best-of-P sampling from the prior. L_train and L_test are chosen per dataset from a small grid on a held-out split of the offline data (Table 5: Hopper-Medium uses L_train = 2, L_test = 3; Hopper-Medium-Replay uses L_train = 3, L_test = 0). Main baseline: MAC-Flow, which uses the same flow-matching backbone but distills a joint flow into one-step per-agent policies with training-time Q-maximization.

title: Efficient Memory Crystallization for Graph Learning under Non-Stationary Distribution Shifts

official.background: GNNs deployed in practice see test graphs whose distribution drifts continually (new regions of a social network, new time steps of a citation or transaction graph). Continual test-time adaptation updates a pre-trained GNN on each unlabeled target graph in turn without source data, and has to avoid forgetting earlier domains. The most recent graph-specific method, GCAL, replays memory graphs produced by a separately trained generative model (a VGAE), which is costly in time and GPU memory and scales poorly as domains accumulate.
official.method:
EMC replaces the generator with a training-free, closed-form memory. For each incoming target graph, node features are propagated K hops (H = Â^K X); nodes are grouped by predicted class into sub-classes, and confidence-weighted aggregation gives compact memory embeddings H' (memory size set to 1% of the graph's nodes). The memory graph structure A' is built by cosine-similarity thresholding of H', and memory features are solved in closed form as X' = (QᵀQ + αL')⁻¹QᵀH' with Q = Â'^K (Dirichlet-energy-regularized reconstruction).

Memory representations evolve across domains by a fixed convex combination with the previous step's memory. The GNN is updated on each target graph by minimizing entropy on the current graph plus β times the KL divergence between current and stored predictions on all past memories. Evaluation follows the GCAL benchmark: pre-train on source domains, adapt sequentially over the remaining domains (Twitch-Explicit, Facebook-100, Elliptic, OGB-Arxiv), and report Average Performance (AP over all domains after the last step), forgetting, wall-clock runtime and peak GPU memory, all on one Tesla V100 32GB.
official.claim: With a GCN backbone, EMC completes continual test-time adaptation far faster and with far less GPU memory than GCAL on all four benchmarks (runtime 74.6 vs. 217.5 s on Twitch, 18.8 vs. 1675.2 s on Facebook, 22.8 vs. 707.2 s on Elliptic, 25.0 vs. 1362.8 s on Arxiv; GPU 855 vs. 11160, 3006 vs. 17108, 189 vs. 5534, 299 vs. 22342 MiB) while matching or exceeding GCAL's AP (55.95 vs. 55.65, 53.10 vs. 52.72, 56.76 vs. 56.57, 19.32 vs. 14.15).

title: LUMOS: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs
claim_source: Table 3, page 7 (CoT version in Table 9, Appendix D.2, page 21)

official.background: Studies of what an LLM 'knows' usually look only at outputs or internal states and do not check what the model actually saw during training. So they cannot tell memorization from generalization, or missing knowledge from failed retrieval. OLMo 2 publishes its full pretraining corpus, so for each fact you can count how often the model was exposed to it and then relate that count to accuracy, consistency, self-verification and internal probing signals.
official.method:
For the factual domain, the authors sample chunks of DCLM, the Wikipedia part of Dolma 1.7, and peS2o. They extract entities (DBpedia for web, OpenAlex Concepts for academic) and count exact-string occurrences across the entire OLMo 2 pretraining mix with an Aho–Corasick automaton. Head entities are the high-frequency entities that account for the top third of the frequency mass. Tail entities are sampled from entities that occur exactly once in the corpus, matched in number to the head group. For each selected chunk, Qwen 2.5 32B generates an entity-grounded 4-option MCQ (CRAFT framework), and a cross-encoder filters the chunks for factual density.

OLMo 2-Instruct 7B, 13B and 32B answer each MCQ with a fixed prompt that asks for a single letter (zero-shot or with 5 fixed examples). Each question gets K = 11 generations: 1 greedy and 10 at temperature 1.0. Accuracy is the mean fraction of the 11 answers that are correct, averaged over questions. Decisional Consistency (DC) is the mean fraction of answers that agree with the most common answer.
official.claim: Under zero-shot MCQ prompting, OLMo 2-Instruct is much more accurate on questions about head (high-frequency) entities than on questions about tail entities that appear exactly once in pretraining: 86.54% vs. 53.64% at 7B, 87.73% vs. 60.92% at 13B, and 92.20% vs. 68.23% at 32B. The gap remains 21–26 points with 5-shot prompting. Tail accuracy still stays well above the 25% chance level.

title: Cephalonauts One: A deep fMRI dataset for decoding naturalistic speech in the human brain
claim_source: Figure 3, page 8 (numeric ranges from Section 4.2 text, page 8)

official.background: Decoding perceived speech from non-invasive fMRI benefits from subject-specific decoders, and earlier work suggests that decoding accuracy grows mainly with the amount of data recorded per subject. Existing speech fMRI datasets are broad but shallow: Narratives and Le Petit Prince offer about 2 hours per subject, and LeBel et al. offer up to 16 hours for 3 subjects. Cephalonauts One records 30 hours of whole-brain 3T fMRI (TR 520 ms) for each of 3 French-speaking subjects listening to the podcast Les Pieds sur Terre. It is released with aligned text and audio embeddings and a held-out-session retrieval benchmark, and the paper uses it to test whether decoding keeps improving up to 30 hours per subject.
official.method:
Each subject has 24 sessions of five 15-minute runs. fMRI is preprocessed with DeepPrep and projected onto fsaverage5 (20,484 vertices); each vertex time series is detrended, z-scored and smoothed with a 4-TR moving average. Stimulus events are placed every 4 TRs (2.08 s). Each event's target is the concatenation of a Qwen3-Embedding-8B embedding of the preceding 20 transcript words (4096-d) and an LCO-Embedding-Omni-7B embedding of the preceding 10 s of audio (3584-d). Each event is paired with the fMRI frame recorded 2.5 s later.

The decoder is a one-hidden-layer MLP (hidden 4096, GELU, dropout 0.5) trained with a CLIP contrastive loss (temperature 0.02) using AdamW (lr 3e-4, wd 3e-4, batch 2048, up to 100 epochs). It uses early stopping on validation Median Relative Rank with patience 5. There are 5 folds: sessions 19-23 each serve as the test session once, the next session in that set is used for validation, and training draws from the remaining 22 sessions. Training size is varied from about 1 h to about 27 h. At test time the predicted embedding must retrieve the true segment among the ~2,000 segments of the held-out session by cosine similarity. The paper reports Median Relative Rank (MRR, chance 0.5), Top-10@2000 (chance ~0.5%) and mean cosine similarity.
official.claim: For each of the 3 subjects, increasing within-subject training data from ~1 h to ~27 h improves held-out-session retrieval: Top-10@2000 rises from about 3.8-6.4% to 22.3-27.3%, Median Relative Rank falls from about 0.11-0.19 to 0.022-0.034, and cosine similarity rises from about 0.075-0.090 to 0.144-0.155. The curves are roughly linear on log-log axes with no clear saturation.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Speech decoding performance versus training-set size. Test performance is shown versus training hours for each subject, using Median Relative Rank, Top-10@2000, and Cosine Similarity. Lower is better for Median Relative Rank; higher is better for the other metrics. Error bars show one empirical standard deviation across five folds with distinct held-out test sessions. Performance improves with additional subject-specific data, with no clear saturation. Chance level is 0.5 for Median Relative Rank and ~0.5% for Top-10@2000.
official.metric: Median Relative Rank (lower is better), Top-10@2000 retrieval accuracy in % (higher is better) and mean cosine similarity between predicted and true embeddings (higher is better); error bands are one empirical standard deviation across 5 folds with different held-out test sessions

title: Less Decoder is More Encoder: Geometric Representation Learning from Novel View Synthesis
claim_source: Table 8, page 19 (appendix D.2); same SNAP/DINOv3 numbers in Table 4, page 17

official.background: Feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) models learn to render unseen views of a scene from a few posed images, which in principle requires 3D reasoning and needs only posed images rather than dense 3D labels. In practice their internal representations transfer poorly to geometric tasks such as correspondence or pose estimation. The authors argue this happens because expressive decoders absorb the spatial reasoning and pixel-space targets push the encoder toward low-level image statistics. If NVS pretraining can be fixed, it would give a self-supervised route to geometric features that today come mostly from 3D-supervised models such as VGGT.
official.method:
SNAP takes N reference images (256x256; up to N = 6 during training), turns each into patch features with a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B (layer 11), projects them and processes them jointly with a 16-layer multi-view transformer using full cross-view self-attention and 2D RoPE, with no camera poses given. The output scene tokens Z are the representation. During pretraining, a pose-conditioned decoder (8 blocks alternating PRoPE cross-attention to Z with self-attention among target queries restricted by a BlockNN mask, set to RF = 1, i.e. a per-patch residual MLP) predicts the frozen DINOv3 feature map of a target view from its camera. The loss is L1 on l2-normalised features plus an L1 penalty on spatial finite differences. Training uses RealEstate10K, DL3DV and Co3Dv2 (~117k sequences), 40k steps, batch 256, AdamW, EMA weights for evaluation.

For the claim, features are evaluated without any trained head: each source keypoint's feature is compared with the full target-view feature map and the predicted match is the soft-argmax of the similarity map (temperature 0.02). PCK is reported at thresholds 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 (normalized image distance), aggregated over multiple random seeds (~2 million pairs in total). Baselines are the frozen DINOv3 ViT-B teacher features and V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L features under the same protocol. Hypersim is not in SNAP's pretraining data.
official.claim: With training-free soft-argmax matching on frozen features, SNAP reaches PCK@0.1 of 55.35 ± 0.98 on held-out Hypersim, vs. 29.29 ± 0.73 for its frozen DINOv3 ViT-B teacher and 21.45 ± 0.52 for V-JEPA 2.1-L (RealEstate10K: 78.21 vs. 45.83 and 35.85; DL3DV: 58.74 vs. 28.00 and 24.55).

PCK (%) at thresholds 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 for DINOv3 [15] (ViT-B), SNAP (ViT-B), and V-JEPA 2.1-L [58], using global soft-argmax matching (τ = 0.02). Values are mean ± CI. Hypersim is held out from SNAP's training. Best results are highlighted in bold.

title: StepCAD: Mesh-to-CAD Code Generation via LLM Policy and Geometry-Guided Search

official.background: Mesh-to-CAD reconstruction tries to recover an executable, editable parametric CAD program (here CadQuery Python code) that reproduces a given 3D mesh. This matters for reverse engineering scanned parts, topology-optimized designs and AI-generated meshes. Recent learning-based methods (CAD-Recode, Cadrille, CADEvolve) predict the whole program in one autoregressive pass from a point cloud. Errors in the program structure or in continuous parameters such as extrusion depths and radii are then never corrected, and accuracy drops sharply on complex shapes.
official.method:
StepCAD has two stages: a state-conditioned LLM policy (Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B with Point-MAE geometry tokens, trained on the authors' ARCADE-1.5M dataset) proposes a seed CadQuery program, and a geometry-aware beam search then refines it. The search is training-free and uses only the target mesh and an executable seed program. It visits operations in execution order (beam width K = 2). At each operation it applies four local edits, executes every candidate in CadQuery and keeps the top-K by volumetric IoU against the target mesh. The edits are: (1) continuous refinement, i.e. Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (6 random initial samples, then 10 iterations of 4 candidates each) of the operation's scalar parameters within +/- min(max(0.2|v|, 0.005), 0.3); (2) sketch modification, which slices the target mesh with the operation's workplane (trimesh.section), simplifies the largest closed loop with Ramer-Douglas-Peucker and refits circles or line/arc sketches; (3) complement cut, which computes the overshoot S(p) minus the mesh with manifold3d, clusters its planar faces and appends the best cut-extrude found by grid search over depths, for up to two rounds; (4) operation skipping, which deletes the operation if that raises IoU. Refinement takes about 66 s per sample.

For the chosen claim, the authors run the search on top of programs produced by the public CAD-Recode checkpoint, without any retraining, on a 1,200-sample subset of CADBench. CADBench pools DeepCAD, Fusion 360, ABC Easy/Medium/Hard, MCB (Mechanical) and Objaverse (Organic). They compare IoU before and after search.
official.claim: Applying StepCAD's training-free, IoU-guided program search to CAD-Recode's output programs on the same 1,200 CADBench samples raises mean IoU from 0.597 to 0.745 (+0.148). The share of samples with IoU >= 0.90 rises from 29.2% to 45.8%.
official.claim_caption: Table 10: Search applied to CAD-Recode programs on the same 1,200-sample CADBench subset, without retraining.
official.metric: Mean volumetric IoU between the executed CAD program and the target mesh (higher is better), plus the percentage of samples above IoU thresholds 0.80/0.90/0.95. Single run; no standard deviations, confidence intervals or seeds are reported.
official.comparison: CAD-Recode public checkpoint output (seed programs) vs. the same programs after StepCAD geometry-aware beam search, on the same 1,200-sample CADBench subset

title: TreeWalker: Partial Evaluation for Grouped Tree-Ensemble Inference
claim_source: Table 10 (Appendix F), page 23; G=128 rows also in Table 3, page 9

official.background: Many applications score a gradient-boosted tree ensemble on groups of rows that share most feature values: discrete-time survival models expand each patient into G time steps, ranking models score every item in a search session, and what-if (scenario) analyses perturb a few inputs of one row. Standard tree inference walks every tree once per row, so the identical constant-feature prefix of each walk is repeated G times. Fast-inference systems such as compiled trees (lleaves, tl2cgen) or QuickScorer cut per-node or per-walk cost but do not exploit this shared structure across the rows of a group.
official.method:
TreeWalker applies partial evaluation to grouped inference: features constant across the group are static and the varying features are dynamic. For each tree it walks once per group with a row bitmask. At constant splits it advances in O(1) for all rows. At varying splits it partitions the bitmask into left/right masks, skips empty sides (unsplit shortcut) and recurses. At leaves it adds the leaf value to every active row. The default evaluator precomputes all varying-feature predicate masks once per group (sort plus sweep against deduplicated thresholds); the 'trace' evaluator instead evaluates each varying predicate per active row. It reads standard LightGBM/XGBoost models and leaves training unchanged. The baseline is 'TreeWalker (full walk)': the same 16-byte-node data layout and binary, but each row walks every tree independently, which isolates the algorithmic effect from data-layout effects.

Scenario-analysis benchmark (Appendix F): UCI Default of Credit Card Clients (30,000 rows, 23 numeric features). One LightGBM model (T=500 trees, max depth L=8, num_leaves=255, binary objective, seed 42) is trained, and 2,000 test rows are drawn as base rows. Each base row expands into G variants (variant 0 unperturbed) that multiply k selected features (from credit limit, bill amounts, payment amounts, ordered by gain importance) by log-uniform factors in [0.5, 2] while all other features stay bit-identical. The sweep is k in {1,2,4,8} and G in {4,16,64,128}. Latency is single-threaded, pinned to one core, as the median of per-block medians in a blocked paired protocol. Speedup = full-walk latency / TreeWalker latency. The table also reports the trace-evaluator work ratio W/(G*T*L) and its Corollary 1 prediction (dv+1)/L.
official.claim: On the credit-card scenario-analysis benchmark (LightGBM, T=500, L=8), TreeWalker is faster than the same-layout row-independent full walk in all 16 (k, G) cells on both Intel and Arm. At G=128 the speedup is 15.15x/12.82x/10.32x/8.12x on Intel (9.21x/8.38x/7.37x/6.22x on Arm) for k=1/2/4/8, and speedup rises monotonically with G for every k.
official.claim_caption: Table 10: Full scenario-analysis sweep. Speedup is algorithmic speedup over the same-layout full walk. Work ratios are W/(G·T·L) under the trace and default (precompute) evaluators; the trace prediction under this baseline is (dv + 1)/L with L = 8.
official.metric: Algorithmic speedup = full-walk latency / TreeWalker latency (higher is better), latency = median of per-block medians in us per scenario set. The table shows no ± values. The paper reports paired-bootstrap 95% intervals with a median half-width of 0.87% (Intel) / 0.98% (Arm) and about 2% at the 95th percentile across the grid. The trace work ratio W/(G*T*L) is a deterministic counter (identical across machines).
official.comparison: TreeWalker (default precompute evaluator) vs. TreeWalker (full walk), the same data layout and binary evaluating rows independently, on the same model, groups, and core
official.falsification_criterion: With the same model and scenario generation, TreeWalker's speedup over a row-independent walk of the same layout is below about 2x at G=128 for any k, fails to rise with G, or TreeWalker is slower than the full walk at G>=16. title: Mitigating Over-squashing without Rewiring: A Sheaf Effective Resistance Perspective

official.background: Message-passing graph neural networks compress information from exponentially many nodes into fixed-size vectors (over-squashing), which hurts tasks with long-range dependencies. Over-squashing is usually treated as a property of the graph topology: effective resistance between two nodes bounds how sensitive one node's output is to the other's input, and rewiring methods add or remove edges to reduce it. This paper argues that the bottleneck can instead be reduced by changing the cellular sheaf (learned restriction maps) attached to a fixed graph. It defines a sheaf effective resistance and proves that it bounds the Jacobian sensitivity for flat vector bundles.
official.method:
FlatNSD is Neural Sheaf Diffusion restricted to flat vector bundles, written as a message-passing network: each node v gets one learned orthogonal d×d restriction map F_v (built from Householder reflections), and a layer computes h_v^(t+1) = φ_t(h_v^(t), Σ_{u∈N_v} Â_uv ψ_t(h_u^(t))), with ψ_t(h_u) = −F_u h_u up to weight matrices, Â the normalized adjacency, and F_v^T applied in the update. The restriction maps are produced by a small GNN (GCN, GIN or SAGE, giving FlatNSD_GCN / _GIN / _SAGE) on the original graph. The graph is never rewired.

For graph classification on the TUDatasets Enzymes, IMDB, Mutag and Proteins, the authors follow the protocol of Nguyen et al. [2023] and Liang et al. [2025]: GNN-specific hyperparameters are frozen, and only rewiring-related hyperparameters (for the baselines) or sheaf-related hyperparameters (for FlatNSD: stalk dimension d ∈ {2,...,5}, restriction-map GNN type, 1-5 GNN layers) are tuned by grid search. Graph-classification settings (Table 4): 4 layers, 64 hidden channels, dropout 0, learning rate 0.001. Baselines are GCN, GIN and SAGE without rewiring and with SDRF, FOSR, BORF, DR, GTR, LASER and GOKU. The metric is test accuracy.

title: Rethinking Long-Video Efficiency: A Joint Allocation Perspective on Frames, Pixels, and Front-End Latency

official.background: Long-video question answering with vision-language models (VLMs) is limited by a visual-token budget. The usual efficiency methods keep frames at native resolution and decide which frames (keyframe selection) or which tokens (token pruning) to keep. The paper argues that two other levers are neglected: per-frame resolution can be lowered to afford many more frames, and the cost of decoding video frames before the model runs (front-end latency) grows with the number of candidate frames decoded, which keyframe-selection methods inflate by decoding densely.
official.method:
LoHi feeds the VLM two streams in a single forward pass, with no training. A low-resolution video stream (Lo-V) of N=128 uniformly sampled frames resized to scale r=0.25 goes through the model's native video pathway (3D mRoPE), and K=8 of those same 128 frames are also given at native resolution (r=1.0) as separate images through the image pathway (Hi-I). A text cue between them says the video is low-resolution temporal context and the following K images are high-resolution key frames. Only 128 frames are decoded per video, and the total visual-token budget (~5,760) matches the default 16 frames at native resolution.

LoHi-SemDiv picks the K Hi-I frames from the 128 Lo-V frames by greedy maximization of log det(L_S + I), where L = diag(q) E E^T diag(q), E are L2-normalized CLIP image embeddings of the frames, and q_j is the min-max normalized CLIP query-frame cosine similarity raised to the power alpha=5. The main comparison baseline, Low-Res-Base, is a single video stream of 256 uniformly sampled frames at r=0.25 with the same token budget. Prior baselines (CLIP-TopK, AKS, BOLT keyframe selection; VisionZip, FlashVid token pruning) decode 256 native-resolution frames and select 16 frames or prune 93.75% of tokens. Evaluation uses lmms-eval with greedy decoding, no subtitles, on Qwen3-VL-4B.
official.claim: On Qwen3-VL-4B at a matched ~5,760 visual-token budget, LoHi-SemDiv (128 frames at r=0.25 + 8 native-resolution frames) beats the dense Low-Res-Base (256 frames at r=0.25) on all three benchmarks: VideoMME 66.81 vs 64.44, MLVU 74.38 vs 69.36, LVBench 45.90 vs 43.71 (average 62.36 vs 59.17), and also exceeds the best prior keyframe-selection/token-pruning baseline average (BOLT, 57.13).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Performance Comparison on Qwen3-VL-4B. Avg. is the mean over three benchmarks.
official.metric: multiple-choice accuracy (%), higher is better; single greedy-decoding run, no ± reported. Appendix C.11 (Table 28) gives a McNemar p=0.011 for LoHi-SemDiv vs Low-Res-Base (+2.15) on the 2,232 subtitle-available VideoMME questions evaluated without subtitles.
official.comparison: LoHi-SemDiv vs Low-Res-Base (256F@0.25), the strongest matched baseline, and vs CLIP-TopK, AKS, BOLT, VisionZip, FlashVid, all at ~5,760 visual tokens and at most 256 decoded frames, same backbone and evaluation protocol
official.falsification_criterion: With Qwen3-VL-4B, greedy decoding and the same budgets, LoHi-SemDiv does not beat Low-Res-Base on the three-benchmark average, or its margin on MLVU falls below ~2 points, or it is not above Low-Res-Base on VideoMME.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Best Arm Identification with Fixed-Budget under Differential Privacy

official.background: In fixed-budget best-arm identification (BAI), a learner pulls arms of a multi-armed bandit for a fixed number of rounds T and then recommends the arm with the highest mean; performance is the probability of recommending a wrong arm, which decays exponentially in T. When rewards are sensitive (clinical trials, online experiments), the whole adaptive transcript (which arms were pulled and the final recommendation) must be differentially private, because the sampling sequence itself leaks information about rewards. This paper characterises the best achievable error exponent under pure ε-DP for Bernoulli arms and proposes an algorithm that attains it asymptotically.
official.method:
AO-Pri-BAI keeps, for each arm, a Laplace tree (continual-release mechanism) over its rewards, so the private running mean m_{a,t} is a sum of O(log T) noisy node values; all decisions use only these private means (initialised to 1/2). Each round, a min-learner samples an alternative instance θ from a Gibbs distribution restricted to instances where the current private leader is not best, with density ∝ exp(-β_t Σ_a λ_{t,a} d_ε^Ber(θ_a, m_{a,t-1})) (implemented by rejection sampling), where d_ε^Ber(p, q) = inf_u [ε·|p - u| + KL(Ber(u)||Ber(q))] is a privacy-aware divergence. A max-learner (AdaHedge) updates the sampling design λ_t with loss ℓ_{t,a} = 1 - d_ε^Ber(μ'_a, m_{a,t-1})/ε. The played distribution mixes in uniform exploration: (1 - γ_t)λ_t + γ_t·uniform with γ_t = t^{-α}. After T rounds, a final θ is sampled from a Gibbs distribution ∝ exp(-Σ_a N_{a,T} d_ε^Ber(θ_a, m_{a,T})) and its argmax arm is recommended.

Baselines: UNIFORM is AO-Pri-BAI with AdaHedge removed (always samples arms uniformly, same private Laplace trees and final rule). DP-TT-FB is the fixed-confidence DP Top-Two algorithm of Jourdan and Azize (2025) made to stop after T pulls and recommend the latest private empirical best arm; it uses the Geometric Private Estimator (GPE). Setting: ε = 0.1, α = 1/4, β_t = 2√(t+1); a 50-arm Bernoulli instance with one arm at 0.95, 4 arms at 0.925 and 45 arms at 0.50; 500 independent trials per algorithm and budget; metric is the fraction of trials recommending the best arm.
official.claim: On the 50-arm Bernoulli instance (best 0.95, four at 0.925, 45 at 0.50) with ε = 0.1, AO-Pri-BAI reaches accuracy about 0.95 at T = 2M and about 0.99 at T = 5M, while DP-TT-FB plateaus around 0.84-0.86 and UNIFORM reaches about 0.51 (2M) and 0.89 (5M); DP-TT-FB is better only at small budgets (below about 700k).
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Comparison of AO-Pri-BAI to Uniform and DP-TT-FB on the 50-arm instance.
official.metric: Empirical accuracy (probability of recommending the best arm, higher is better) over 500 independent trials; shaded bands are ±1 standard error; values below are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: AO-Pri-BAI vs. DP-TT-FB (fixed-budget adaptation of DP Top-Two) and UNIFORM (AO-Pri-BAI without the AdaHedge design learner), all ε-DP, on the same instance and budgets
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the 50-arm instance at ε = 0.1 with T = 2M (and/or 5M) and several hundred trials, AO-Pri-BAI's accuracy is not clearly above DP-TT-FB's (e.g. the gap is under ~0.05 or within ~2 SE), or AO-Pri-BAI does not exceed ~0.9 accuracy at T = 2M.

title: When Debate Helps: Proposal Supply and Verification-Aware Readout in Multi-Agent Reasoning
claim_source: Table 3, page 10 (CIs for T - F in Table 9, page 18; free-generation accuracies in Table 10, page 18)

official.background: Multi-agent debate, where several LLM agents propose answers, read each other's responses and revise, often fails to beat simple majority voting. Prior theory shows that symmetric, truth-agnostic interaction is a martingale: mixing proposals creates no expected drift toward the correct answer. This paper argues that debate can beat voting only if (1) the agents surface a correct answer that the majority misses, and (2) the readout uses answer-specific evidence to pick that correct minority answer. The second requirement is an empirical question: does a model's answer actually move toward the truth because a peer's reasoning is correct, rather than just because an answer is repeated?
official.method:
The authors model the readout as Latent Verification Debate (LVD): a Dirichlet posterior over candidate answers in which each answer gets its proposal count plus a non-negative verification pseudo-count; correct minorities are recovered only when correct answers receive more verification mass. To test this without changing the candidate set, they take saved four-agent debate traces on GPQA and MMLU-Redux (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, verification debate prompt) and, per backbone-dataset pair, uniformly sample 50 traces whose initial proposals contain at least one correct and one incorrect answer. The question, target agent, its initial response, prompt and candidate set are fixed; only the peer evidence shown to the target agent varies.

Three probes are run. (i) Trace effect: the margin m = log p(gold) - log p(designated wrong answer) is computed under a neutral peer context N and under the original context T containing a correct peer response from the trace; Delta m_trace = m(T) - m(N), averaged over recovery cases (target initially wrong, correct peer available), with a 95% CI. (ii) Answer-stripped rationales: matched correct and wrong peer rationales are stripped of all stated answers/option references and length-matched; T - F is the difference in gold-vs-all-wrong log margin after the correct vs. wrong rationale. (iii) Free generation: fresh answers are generated after d = 3 peer messages under correct support and controls (neutral, answer withheld, shuffled rationale from another question); Delta Acc is correct-support minus neutral accuracy.
official.claim: With the candidate set held fixed, an original correct peer response raises the gold-vs-wrong log-probability margin over a neutral context in all four backbone-dataset cells (Qwen3-4B GPQA 8.15 [4.96, 11.41], MMLU-Redux 11.40 [9.02, 13.97]; OLMo3-7B GPQA 4.57 [3.65, 5.50], MMLU-Redux 5.47 [4.52, 6.43]), and answer-stripped, length-matched correct rationales beat wrong rationales by T - F = 2.01 to 5.50 (all 95% CIs exclude zero).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Controlled fixed-proposal evidence for verification-aware readout. Trace effect is the answer-margin shift from an original correct peer response relative to neutral context; W-hat is its median equivalent controlled support over recovery cases. T - F is the gold-margin difference between answer-stripped correct and wrong rationales. Delta Acc is correct-support accuracy minus neutral accuracy at d = 3. All entries use the main readout configuration; secondary configuration controls are reported in the appendix.
official.metric: Log-probability answer margin shift (nats; higher = more favorable to gold). Delta m_trace is a mean over recovery cases with a 95% CI; T - F is a mean margin difference with 95% CI (Table 9). Delta Acc is free-generation accuracy difference on 50 questions, no error bar.
official.comparison: Same target agent, question, initial response and candidate set under: original correct peer response vs. neutral peer context; answer-stripped correct rationale vs. length-matched answer-stripped wrong rationale; correct support (d = 3 messages) vs. neutral, answer-withheld, and shuffled-rationale controls.
official.falsification_criterion: On a fresh sample of 50 mixed-proposal traces per cell, the 95% CI of Delta m_trace includes or falls below zero for any backbone-dataset cell, or the answer-stripped T - F gap is not positive with a CI excluding zero (which would mean the shift comes from answer repetition, not the content of correct reasoning).

title: DICE: Decoupling Capability from Intervention Necessity in LLM Tutoring

official.background: LLM tutors are usually trained to produce the next teacher utterance at every student turn, so they assume an intervention is always needed. In practice this leads to two failure modes: over-intervention, where the tutor keeps questioning a student who has already answered correctly, and false acceptance, where the tutor approves a wrong answer. The authors argue that this happens because training labels come from annotators who see the gold solution, and that a tutor should decide explicitly whether to intervene before deciding what to say.
official.method:
DICE splits tutoring into an explicit action-selection step and a generation step. A policy (Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct with a LoRA adapter) picks one of six pedagogical actions per turn: a0 accept-and-advance (non-intervention), arithmetic repair, conceptual hint, handle question, ask for justification, or refocus subgoal. It is trained on about 20k GPT-5-annotated decision states from DICE-Bench, which is built from SocraTeach (GSM8K/MAWPS) problems with generated easy (q-) and hard (q+) skill-preserving variants. Training weights each intervention label by its Intervention Value (IV): the simulated student's judged progress after that action minus its progress after a0, estimated with rollouts. A KL term keeps the policy close to the SFT policy. At inference, DICE-Cost intervenes only if the best active action beats a0 by a log-probability margin λ = 0.25. When a0 is chosen, an acceptance verifier and a final-answer guard (exact match against the reference answer) can block the accept.

In the session-level evaluation, a tutor guides a simulated student (Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, temperature 0.6) through a triplet q- → q → q+ under a shared 20-turn budget. The data is 750 problems, i.e. 250 triplets. All tutors use Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct as the teacher. The baselines are StratL-style steering, a MathDial fine-tuned tutor, Socratic prompting and SocraticLM. Metrics: All-3 success (all three variants solved), average variants solved, average turns used, over-intervention (the tutor intervenes when the student's latest response is already correct), and unsafe final-answer acceptance.
official.claim: In session-level tutoring on DICE-Bench (250 triplets, 20-turn budget, Qwen-2.5-1.5B student), DICE-Cost has an over-intervention rate of 0.028 vs. 0.420 for SocraticLM (0.768 for StratL). It also reaches All-3 success 0.564 vs. 0.440 for the best baseline (StratL) and uses 11.94 vs. 14.88 average turns (SocraticLM).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Session-level tutoring results on DICE-Bench. Each session contains the triplet (q−, q, q+) under a shared 20-turn budget. All-3 reports full triplet success, Vars. is the average number of variants solved, and UnsafeAcc. is unsafe final-answer acceptance. Higher is better for success metrics and Vars.; lower is better for Turns, OverInt., and UnsafeAcc. Best values are bolded and second-best values are underlined.
official.metric: Over-intervention rate (lower is better), All-3 success rate (higher is better), average turns per session (lower is better); single run, no ± reported (n = 250 sessions; binomial SE for All-3 is about 0.03)
official.comparison: DICE (MAP, Cost λ=0.25, Threshold τ=0.8) vs. StratL, fine-tuned MathDial, Socratic prompting and SocraticLM, all with the same Qwen-2.5-7B teacher, Qwen-2.5-1.5B student and 20-turn budget

title: LogSig-SSM: Time-Series Modelling with Multi-Scale Log-Signature Compression for State-Space Models
claim_source: Table 7 (Appendix C), page 18; summarized in Table 4 (page 10) and Table 1 (page 8)

official.background: Long, high-frequency and irregularly sampled multivariate time series are hard to model. Neural CDEs and rough differential equations (NCDE, NRDE, Log-NCDE) handle irregular sampling but are slow on long sequences. Selective state-space models such as Mamba scale linearly with length, but they degrade on very long inputs. A single Mamba block also uses a diagonal state transition, so it cannot represent cross-channel path features such as Lévy areas. The paper asks whether compressing the series into windowed log-signature tokens before a Mamba backbone fixes both problems.
official.method:
LogSig-SSM tokenises a series x ∈ R^{dx×T} offline. At strided anchors (stride s) and for each of K window scales (length L_k, truncation depth m_k), it computes the truncated log-signature of the piecewise-linearly interpolated window with iisignature (Lie-basis coordinates). The per-scale vectors are concatenated into one token U_τ ∈ R^{D_tot} per anchor, which gives a token sequence of length T' ≈ T/s. A learned linear embedding W_in maps each token to the scan width d, and the token sequence is then processed by a stack of standard Mamba blocks followed by a classifier head. On UEA every window uses depth m_k = 2. The selected configs are in Table 11; for example, EthanolConcentration uses windows [18, 132], depths [2, 2], stride 66, 6 blocks, d = 16 and N = 256.

Tuning protocol (Appendix F): two-stage Optuna with 100 trials per stage. Stage 1 searches the tokeniser (stride, number of scales, window lengths, optional global branch) with a small reference Mamba. Stage 2 searches the Mamba backbone (lr, d, blocks, state size, conv width, expansion, normalisation) together with a local neighbourhood of the tokeniser. The ablation variants in Table 7 use the same protocol and budget: other window descriptors (depthwise conv, standard conv, Catch24 statistics, wavelet scattering) feed the same Mamba backbone, and the log-signature tokens also feed S5 and Transformer backbones. Evaluation follows the Log-NCDE protocol on six long UEA datasets: 70:15:15 split and test accuracy averaged over five random splits.
official.claim: On UEA EthanolConcentration (4 classes, T = 1,751, 3 channels), LogSig-SSM reaches 51.4 ± 6.9% test accuracy versus 27.9 ± 4.5% for Mamba on raw input. It also beats the same Mamba backbone with standard-convolution tokens (33.6 ± 5.6%) and the same log-signature tokens with a Transformer (36.0 ± 3.4%) or S5 (25.6 ± 2.7%) backbone. It does not beat the strongest matched tokeniser, wavelet-scattering tokens + Mamba (53.5 ± 4.0%). Averaged over six long UEA datasets it scores 71.7% versus 58.6% for raw Mamba.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: UEA ablations (% accuracy ↑, mean ± std over five splits). Top: tokeniser variants with the Mamba backbone fixed. Bottom: backbone variants with the log-signature tokeniser fixed. All variants share the same window positions, token dimensions where applicable, and Optuna budget (Appendix F). Bold = best per column.
official.metric: Test classification accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is std over five random 70:15:15 splits
official.comparison: LogSig-SSM (log-signature tokens + Mamba) vs. raw-input Mamba, the same Mamba with other window tokenisers (depthwise conv, standard conv, Catch24, wavelet scattering), and log-signature tokens with S5 or Transformer backbones, all tuned with the same 200-trial Optuna budget
official.falsification_criterion: Under the Log-NCDE UEA protocol with five splits, LogSig-SSM's mean accuracy on EthanolConcentration is not above both raw-input Mamba and ConvMixing-Mamba by more than about one std (e.g. below ~40%), or its six-dataset average does not exceed raw Mamba's by several points.

title: METRO: Metric-Enhanced Token Routing Operator
claim_source: Table 12 (Appendix G.4), page 29; Transolver value from Table 5, page 15; matched Transolver vs. M-Transolver sweep over slice counts in Table 10, page 27

official.background: Slice-and-process neural operators such as Transolver handle PDEs on irregular meshes by softly assigning the N mesh points to a small number G of latent tokens (slices), mixing the tokens with attention, and broadcasting back. In Transolver the assignment score is a dot product between a point's feature and a learned per-slice prototype. The paper argues that this score yields either unbounded linear decision regions or, under feature normalization, isotropic Euclidean clustering, so slices cannot form local, direction-dependent receptive fields that match thin, elongated flow features such as boundary layers and wakes.
official.method:
METRO replaces the dot-product slice score with a log-Gaussian score: for slice g with learnable center mu_g and diagonal positive precision P_g = diag(softplus(p_hat_g) + eps), the logit is S_{n,g} = -1/2 (x_n - mu_g)^T P_g (x_n - mu_g) + 1/2 log det P_g, where x_n is a linear projection of the point's features. Softmax over g gives routing weights A_{n,g}; slice tokens are the column-normalized weighted averages of value projections, processed by the usual Transformer block (M-Transolver) or Mamba block (M-LaMO), and broadcast back with A. Everything else (layers, heads, channels, losses, optimizer, schedule) follows Transolver.

For Elasticity (972 points per sample, point-cloud input of 2D coordinates, target von Mises stress; 1000 train / 200 test) the configuration is 8 layers, 8 heads, D = 128 channels, G = 64 slices, relative-L2 loss, AdamW, lr 1e-3, batch size 1, cosine annealing, 500 epochs (Table 7).
official.claim: On the Elasticity benchmark, replacing Transolver's dot-product slice routing with Mahalanobis routing (M-Transolver, G = 64) gives relative L2 error 0.44 ± 0.015 (x10^-2, 4 runs), vs. 0.64 for Transolver and 0.50 ± 0.021 for the best baseline (LaMO).

title: Order Matters: Competition-Guided Query Ordering for RNN-Based Object Detection
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (seed repeats in Table 18, page 22)

official.background: DETR-style object detectors predict a set of boxes from a fixed set of object queries and use one-to-one Hungarian matching during training, so they need no non-maximum suppression (NMS). In practice several queries still converge on the same object with similar scores. These duplicates make the matched query switch between training steps, which slows convergence. Decoder self-attention is thought to suppress duplicates implicitly, but it processes queries in parallel and has no notion of which query should win. Classical NMS resolves duplicates by sorting candidates by score and handling close overlaps in that order. This paper asks whether giving the decoder that kind of explicit order helps.
official.method:
DETRNN replaces the self-attention sub-layer in selected decoder layers with a bidirectional RNN (a Mamba block in the main experiments) and leaves cross-attention and the FFN unchanged. Before each such layer, Competition-Guided Query Ordering (CGQO) sorts the queries using the previous predictions. Queries are ranked by confidence, and the top one becomes a pivot. Every remaining query whose similarity to the pivot, (1−α)·IoU(boxes) + α·cos(class-score vectors), is at least a pivot-specific density-adaptive threshold T_i (Eq. 3) is grouped right after the pivot. The group is then removed and the process repeats until all queries are ordered. No queries are discarded, and gradients do not flow through the ordering indices. The Bi-RNN processes the queries in this order and in reverse. For Def-DETR++ the module is inserted in the last two decoder stages, and CGQO is recomputed before each stage. The full model also uses IOF-PE (Appendix C): for adjacent boxes in the CGQO order, the Intersection-over-Foreground area(b_i ∩ b_{i+1})/area(b_{i+1}) (arguments swapped for the reverse pass, 0 at boundaries) gets a sine-cosine embedding that replaces the query as the input to Mamba's Δ (discretization-step) branch, while B and C are still generated from the query.

Setting for the claim: COCO train2017 → val2017, ResNet-50 backbone, 900 queries, 1× schedule (12 epochs), Def-DETR++ training recipe (total batch size 16, learning rate 2e-4 for the encoder-decoder and 2e-5 for the backbone, weight decay 2e-5), run on 8 RTX 4090/3090 GPUs. The baseline is the same Def-DETR++ with standard decoder self-attention. CGQO hyperparameters (α, τ_min, τ_max) are fixed and listed in Appendix B.
official.claim: On COCO val2017 with a ResNet-50 backbone, 900 queries and a 12-epoch schedule, adding DETRNN to Def-DETR++ raises AP from 47.6 to 48.7 (+1.1). Over three seeds DETRNN gives 48.73 ± 0.15 AP, and FLOPs barely change (300G vs. 301G).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results on COCO val2017 with ResNet-50 and 900 queries. Under unified 1× / 2× schedules, DETRNN consistently improves AP across baselines with comparable FLOPs / FPS.
official.metric: COCO box AP on val2017, higher is better. Table 1 reports single numbers with no error bars. Table 18 reports mean and std over 3 seeds for the DETRNN variants only (Def-DETRNN++: 48.7, 48.9, 48.6; std 0.15). The baseline is a single run.
official.comparison: Def-DETR++ (self-attention decoder) vs. Def-DETRNN++ (CGQO + Bi-RNN in the last two decoder stages), with the same backbone, query count, schedule and training recipe
official.falsification_criterion: With matched 12-epoch R50 training of both models, Def-DETRNN++ does not exceed the Def-DETR++ baseline by clearly more than seed noise (e.g. a gain under about 0.5 AP), or the baseline itself reaches about 48.5 AP or more.

title: ColdDDI: Evaluating Knowledge Utilization in Cold-Start Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction
claim_source: Table 4, page 7 (confidence intervals in Table 33, Appendix C.6, page 44)

official.background: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) predictors are most needed for new drugs that have no recorded interactions yet. Drug-wise splits capture this: S0 (both drugs seen in training), S1 (one unseen), S2 (both unseen). Existing benchmarks report one aggregate score per split, so they cannot tell whether a model succeeds because it uses pharmacological evidence (for example, a shared metabolizing enzyme) or for other reasons. ColdDDI is a DrugBank-derived benchmark that stratifies each interaction by mechanism and by whether the knowledge graph contains a mediator linking the two drugs, so that this question can be studied.
official.method:
ColdDDI is built from DrugBank 5.1.13 with a seven-step filter: 1,900 approved small-molecule drugs and 565,731 positive pairs. The task is binary DDI detection, with unrecorded pairs sampled 1:1 as negatives (fixed for val/test, resampled each training epoch). Drugs are split into seen (G1) and unseen (G2) sets, and all methods train on pairs within G1. Each positive pair is labeled PK or PD by keyword matching on its DrugBank interaction-type description. It is labeled Type A if the DrugBank KG contains a shared mediator with a compatible action-role combination: for PK pairs, a shared enzyme or transporter (e.g., substrate-inhibitor, substrate-inducer); for PD pairs, a shared target (e.g., agonist-agonist, antagonist-antagonist). Otherwise it is Type B. This gives four subtypes: PK-A, PK-B, PD-A, PD-B.

Eight conventional DDI models (including the KG-based EmerGNN and TIGER) and a LoRA-fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B prompted with one-hop KG facts written as sentences (P4, 'LLM-FT') are trained and evaluated on S2 of a stratified 800-drug subset over 3 seeds. Per-subtype Recall is computed on positives of that subtype. Per-subtype AUC-ROC compares that subtype's positives against the full S2 negative pool. The A-B gap is 0.5*(M_PK-A + M_PD-A) - 0.5*(M_PK-B + M_PD-B).
official.claim: On the fully inductive S2 split (800-drug subset), EmerGNN's Recall is 0.777 ± 0.037 on PK-A and 0.743 ± 0.086 on PD-A pairs but only 0.308 ± 0.039 on PK-B and 0.436 ± 0.109 on PD-B, an A-B Recall gap of +0.388 ± 0.078 (95% CI [+0.194, +0.582]) and an AUC-ROC gap of +0.227 ± 0.031. The fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B shows the same pattern (Recall gap +0.398 ± 0.105, AUC gap +0.229 ± 0.051), while TIGER, which has the same KG access, shows only +0.071 ± 0.052.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: S2 Recall and AUC-ROC by mechanism subtype on the 800-drug subset (3-seed mean±std). Best in bold. † MKG-FENN's uniformly high Recall and near-zero Recall gap are saturation artifacts (see Table 3). On the 800-drug subset, it predicts 98.29% of S2 pairs as positive, with precision 0.503. These Recall entries are excluded from bolding.
official.metric: Per-subtype S2 Recall and AUC-ROC (higher is better) and the A-B gap; mean ± std over 3 seeds (42, 43, 44). Table 33 gives pointwise 95% Student-t intervals over the 3 per-seed gaps.
official.comparison: Within each method: Type A (shared KG mediator) vs. Type B (no mediator) S2 positives, for EmerGNN and LLM-FT; across methods: their A-B gap vs. that of TIGER, which uses the same KG.
official.falsification_criterion: On a reconstructed ColdDDI S2 split, EmerGNN's A-B Recall gap falls within about one seed std of zero (e.g., below +0.1), or its Type A AUC-ROC is not clearly above its Type B AUC-ROC (gap below about +0.1).

title: Spectral Geometry of Attention: From Information Routing to Uncertainty
claim_source: Table 8, page 22 (with Table 1, page 9 and Table 5, page 21)

official.background: Uncertainty estimators for LLMs that use output probabilities (perplexity, token entropy, sequence likelihood) can fail when task-relevant distinctions are compressed before they reach the logits, especially in long-context tasks. Single-pass attention-based estimators such as RAUQ instead read signals from attention heads during generation. This paper treats each attention map as a linear operator between weighted function spaces on the token sequence. It argues that the standard Euclidean spectrum of attention is biased by attention sinks, and that an 'intrinsic' probability geometry gives a cleaner measure of how much token-dependent information a head routes. It then uses this measure as the attention signal in an uncertainty estimator.
official.method:
For an attention map A (n x n, row-stochastic, causal), the Token Difference Operator is D = Omega_mu^{-1} A^T Omega_pi A, with output measure pi = (1/n) 1 and input measure mu = A^T pi (the average attention row). The signal is its normalized participation ratio PR(D) = (1/n) tr(S)^2 / tr(S^2), computed from the similar symmetric matrix S = Omega_mu^{-1/2} A^T Omega_pi A Omega_mu^{-1/2}, so no eigendecomposition is needed.

SAUQ copies RAUQ's recurrence unchanged and swaps in this signal. In each middle-third layer (layers 10-22 of LLaMA-3.1-8B), one head is selected per layer as the argmax over heads of PR(B B^T), where B is the generated-token block of the attention map at the final step. At each decoding step t, s_t = PR(D) is computed for that head over the full prefix. The confidence recurrence is c_1 = p_1, c_t = 0.2 p_t + 0.8 s_t c_{t-1}, where p_t is the probability of the generated token. The per-layer uncertainty is 1 - mean_t log c_t, and the sequence score is its maximum over the middle layers. RAUQ uses the same recurrence, alpha, layer range and max aggregation, but with its own head choice and its previous-token attention score as s_t. The paper notes that SAUQ changes the estimator in two places, head selection and signal (Appendix B.6). Evaluation uses LM-Polygraph with greedy decoding and the Normalized Prediction Rejection Ratio (PRR) metric, following the RAUQ setup.
official.claim: On XSum summarization with LLaMA-3.1-8B, SAUQ's PRR exceeds RAUQ's by +0.121 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [+0.037, +0.212]; 0.42 ± 0.07 vs. 0.30 ± 0.08 SE), and the gain remains +0.060 after controlling for input and output length.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: Difference in PRR between SAUQ and RAUQ on LLaMA-3.1-8B, pooled and after stratifying by output length and by input × output length.
official.metric: Normalized Prediction Rejection Ratio (PRR, higher is better). The difference Delta = PRR_SAUQ - PRR_RAUQ, with a 95% CI from a stratified paired bootstrap over evaluation instances (5000 resamples). The ± values in Table 5 are bootstrap standard errors. Decoding is greedy, so there are no seeds.
official.comparison: SAUQ (intrinsic TDO participation-ratio signal) vs. RAUQ (previous-token attention signal and RAUQ's own head choice), with the same recurrence, alpha = 0.2, layer range and protocol, on LLaMA-3.1-8B
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same LM-Polygraph XSum protocol on LLaMA-3.1-8B, a paired bootstrap 95% CI for PRR(SAUQ) - PRR(RAUQ) that includes zero or lies below it, or a pooled difference well below +0.037.

title: RoSA: Rotational Sparse Adaptation for Memory-Efficient Fine-Tuning

official.background: Full fine-tuning of a 7B LLM with AdamW needs far more GPU memory than inference, mostly for optimizer states, gradients and activations, so it does not fit on commodity 40 GB GPUs. PEFT methods such as LoRA cut memory by restricting what can be trained. Layer-wise methods such as LISA and BAdam instead train only some layers at a time. RoSA asks whether a structured layer schedule (freeze an input-side prefix, rotate a trainable block over the later layers) can keep near-full-fine-tuning accuracy within a 40 GB budget, and whether that structure beats random layer sampling at the same memory.
official.method:
On Llama-2-7B, RoSA permanently freezes the input embeddings and Transformer Layers 0–7. It keeps the final Transformer layer and the output head always trainable (the 'anchor') and splits Layers 8–30 into consecutive groups of b layers (default b = 8). Each epoch exactly one group plus the anchor is trainable. When a group becomes active, its optimizer states are created fresh, and they are deleted when it leaves (cold start). Inside the active layers, the optimizer is NanoAdam: optimizer states and adaptive updates cover only a subset of parameters chosen by bottom-ρ weight magnitude (ρ = 0.2), and the mask is refreshed every 600 steps (lr 1e-4, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95). Backpropagation stops at the frozen prefix. The forward pass still runs through all layers, and no activation checkpointing is used.

Training is on the commonsense reasoning fine-tuning setup, and evaluation is average accuracy over 8 tasks (BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-E, ARC-C, OBQA). Settings: cutoff length 256, global batch 128, micro-batch 1, 4×A100 40GB. A 1-cycle run takes 3 epochs (each group visited once) and the default 2-cycle run takes 6. The LISA baseline uses 8 active layers, 3 epochs, the same batch settings, and the best of a five-point learning-rate sweep (1e-4). Peak VRAM is the per-GPU system peak.
official.claim: On Llama-2-7B commonsense reasoning (8-task average), RoSA with one rotation cycle (3 epochs, group size 8) reaches 79.10% at 34.9 GiB peak VRAM, compared with 70.05% for LISA (8 active layers, best of 5 learning rates, 3 epochs) at 30.71 GiB. At matched memory, RoSA with group size 6 reaches 78.50% at 30.93 GiB, 8.45 points above LISA.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Layer-wise and memory-efficient baselines on Llama-2-7B commonsense reasoning. † Does not fit into 40 GB GPUs at cutoff length 256; run on 80 GB GPUs.
official.metric: Average accuracy (%) over 8 commonsense reasoning tasks (higher is better), plus peak VRAM in GiB (lower is better). Single runs with no error bars. Appendix E reports one extra RoSA seed (2-cycle config) at 79.49% vs. 79.61%.
official.comparison: RoSA (group size 6 and group size 8, 1 cycle) vs. LISA (8 active layers), all run by the authors with the same cutoff length, batch size and epoch budget. Full fine-tuning (AdamW, 78.5 GiB, 79.99%) is the reference upper bound.
official.falsification_criterion: With a matched learning-rate sweep for both methods, LISA comes within about 2 points of RoSA's average accuracy at similar peak VRAM (≈31 GiB), or RoSA group size 6 falls well below 78.5% / RoSA 1-cycle well below 79.1%.

title: An Information-Theoretic Evaluation Framework for Benchmark and Model Diagnosis in Knowledge Tracing
claim_source: Table 8 (Appendix E.3), page 20; supported by Table 9 (page 20) and Table 2 (page 6)

official.background: Knowledge tracing (KT) models predict whether a student will answer the next item correctly from their past item-response history, and they are ranked almost entirely by global AUC and accuracy. Such aggregate scores cannot show whether a model's improvement comes from already-easy predictions, from hard but structured cases, or from near-random cases, nor whether a benchmark is close to saturation. The paper proposes reading model performance along a shared, causally computed uncertainty coordinate to locate where remaining headroom lies.
official.method:
For each held-out prediction point, a Context Tree Weighting (CTW) model (maximum depth D = 6) is run causally over a token stream of past item-response tokens 'I:item|R:resp' plus a query token 'Q:item' for the current item, giving an anchor probability p_ctw and an uncertainty coordinate H(p_ctw) in bits. Points are split into five fixed-width entropy bands [0,0.2), ..., [0.8,1.0] (and, as a robustness check, into equal-frequency quintiles). CTW and the bucketing are computed out-of-fold under five-fold cross-validation, with all compared predictors joined on the same held-out rows.

The probe CTW+NN-SKT adds a learned SimpleKT residual to the CTW logit, p = sigmoid(logit(p_ctw) + f_phi(history, current item)), trained with validation-NLL model selection (<= 50 epochs, patience 4). The paper reports, within each band, probe minus CTW in accuracy, Brier score and log-loss (nats). The datasets are NIPS 2020 Education Challenge Task 3/4 and KDD Cup Algebra 2005 at question level.
official.claim: In the highest CTW-entropy band [0.8, 1.0], the CTW+NN-SKT probe improves accuracy over the CTW anchor by +0.0905 [0.0898, 0.0913] on NIPS Task 3/4 and +0.0285 [0.0252, 0.0317] on Algebra 2005 (Brier -0.0388 and -0.0685), and this gain is much larger than in low-entropy regions (NIPS quintile Q1 +0.0094 vs. Q5 +0.1570; Algebra Q1 -0.0001 vs. Q4 +0.0433); the paper's paired high- vs. low-band tests give p = 1.16e-8 (NIPS) and 1.71e-5 (Algebra).
official.claim_caption: Table 8: CTW+NN-SKT gains in the highest-entropy band, [0.8, 1.0], on each reference's own coordinate. Entries are five-fold means [95% t intervals]; log-loss is in nats.
official.metric: Probe minus CTW anchor on matched held-out predictions: accuracy (higher better), Brier and log-loss in nats (lower better). Table 8 gives five-fold means with 95% t intervals over folds (folds share training data); Table 9 quintile values have no error bars.
official.comparison: CTW+NN-SKT (CTW logit plus SimpleKT residual) vs. the CTW anchor alone, in the highest CTW-entropy band compared with the lowest band/quintile
official.falsification_criterion: With a depth-6 item-token CTW anchor and a SimpleKT residual probe on the same five-fold splits, the probe's accuracy gain over CTW in the [0.8, 1.0] band is not clearly larger than in the lowest-entropy band/quintile (e.g. NIPS high-band gain not several times the Q1 gain), or the high-band gain falls outside roughly +0.06 to +0.12 on NIPS or is not positive on Algebra.

title: CausalBind: Causal Modeling and Learning for Protein-Molecule Virtual Screening

official.background: Virtual screening ranks millions of candidate molecules against a protein target before any wet-lab work. The strongest scalable methods are retrieval-based: they embed molecules and protein pockets into a shared space and screen by similarity. These models align whole-molecule against whole-pocket embeddings, but real binding is driven by a small contact interface and a few local interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, salt bridges). The authors argue that dense holistic alignment therefore mixes binding determinants with nuisance global correlations, which hurts transfer to unseen targets and scaffolds, and is especially visible on LIT-PCBA, a benchmark built to suppress property-based shortcuts.
official.method:
CausalBind keeps the retrieval/contrastive training setup of HypSeek but replaces dense alignment with a structurally constrained cross-modal interaction. Three encoders are used: Uni-Mol for molecule and pocket 3D structure and ESM2 for protein sequence. A Perceiver-style cross-attention block with K learnable concept queries decomposes each modality into K concept tokens of dimension d_c. For each branch (mol, poc) and (mol, seq), a K x K learnable parameter matrix is passed through Gamma(M) = tanh(M) + 1 and a straight-through threshold at tau = 0.5 to give an effective mask; the mask gates the matrix of concept-pair inner products, and the retained entries are averaged into a scalar pair score. These scores feed an InfoNCE contrastive loss over the minibatch, plus an L1 sparsity penalty on the continuous masks and the geometric regularizers inherited from HypSeek.

Three variants differ only in how the interaction is constrained: CausalBind_SP uses the learnable sparse concept-pair mask (K=128, d_c=1024, lambda_spa=1e-4, L=4 Perceiver layers); CausalBind_LR factorizes the raw mask as U V^T with rank r=1; CausalBind_EMB applies the mask after pooling into embedding space. Training uses the same curated ChEMBL/BindingDB/PDBBind assay pool as LigUnity and HypSeek, with every assay whose target UniProt ID appears in DUD-E, LIT-PCBA or DEKOIS 2.0 removed, so evaluation is cross-dataset generalization rather than a random split. All models in Table 2 are trained for 50 epochs on four A100s under the same pipeline and evaluated at the last checkpoint.
official.claim: Retrained under the authors' own matched pipeline, CausalBind_SP beats the stronger reproduced retrieval baseline HypSeek on LIT-PCBA (AUROC 0.635 ± 0.006 vs 0.603 ± 0.009; BEDROC80.5 0.088 ± 0.007 vs 0.067 ± 0.007; EF@1% 7.55 ± 0.73 vs 5.62 ± 0.71) and on DUD-E AUROC (0.939 ± 0.004 vs 0.914 ± 0.013), over five runs.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Ablation and diagnostic study on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA. CausalBind_SP is the sparse mask, CausalBind_LR is the low-rank mask, and CausalBind_EMB is the pooled embedding-space mask. -L_spa removes the sparsity penalty from CausalBind_SP, while +L_spa tests an optional sparsity penalty on CausalBind_LR without changing its rank-one parameterization. M_emb^{r=1} replaces the pooled embedding mask with a rank-one mask. Rows report mean ± std over five runs.
official.metric: AUROC, BEDROC80.5 and EF@1% (all higher is better), averaged over the 102 DUD-E and 15 LIT-PCBA targets; ± is std over five training runs
official.comparison: CausalBind_SP vs LigUnity and HypSeek, all retrained by the authors for 50 epochs on the same training pool, same four-A100 pipeline, last checkpoint
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same training pool and schedule, CausalBind_SP's LIT-PCBA AUROC and EF@1% fail to exceed a retrained HypSeek by more than one std over runs, or the ordering reverses on either benchmark.

title: Rationale-Guided Policy Optimization: Learning to Reason with Adaptive Rationale Scaffolding
claim_source: Table 5 (Appendix D.1), page 34; summarized in Figure 2 and Section 5.1 on page 7

official.background: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR, e.g. GRPO) improves LLM reasoning only when the policy sometimes samples a correct answer. On problems that are too hard for the current model, every rollout in a group fails, the group-normalised advantage is zero, and training gets no signal. Datasets often contain reference solutions, but supervised imitation of them can push the model toward off-policy text, copy errors in the references, or teach it to rely on a hint that is absent at test time. The paper asks how to use reference rationales to get past this reward sparsity without these failure modes.
official.method:
RGPO keeps the ordinary unguided GRPO update and adds a second, guided pass. Each training problem has a hint level g that starts at 0; after each epoch g goes up by one if none of the problem's unguided rollouts was correct and down by one otherwise (clipped to [0, N]). For problems with g > 0, the model samples extra responses from a prompt that includes the first g/N of the reference rationale. A guided response is accepted only if its verifier reward is strictly higher than the best unguided rollout (reward gate, δ = 0). Accepted responses are trained with an SFT loss conditioned on the original prompt without the hint, added to the RL loss with weight λ.

The claim comes from the controlled simulation (Section 5.1, Appendix C.4, Table 4). There are 40 decision types (32 easy, 8 hard) with 16 actions each. Easy decisions start with valid-action probability of about 0.78-0.89; hard decisions have one valid action and a uniform initial policy. Easy problems have 2-5 easy decisions; hard problems have 5-7 decisions, 4 of them hard. The policy can either reason (reward 1 only if every decision is valid) or answer directly among 100 answers (initial probability 0.2). Each problem has a reference rationale that is systematically wrong for 3 of the 8 hard types; hint levels are g ∈ {0, 1, 2} (none, first half, full trajectory plus answer), and the policy follows a revealed step with probability 0.7. There are 512 train and 256 test problems per seed, 25% hard. Training uses K = 4 unguided and K' = 4 guided rollouts, batch 32, 3 epochs (16 updates per epoch), plain gradient ascent with learning rate 64, no KL, and λ = 1. Accuracy is the exact no-hint success probability p_θ(x) averaged over a split, so evaluation has no sampling noise.
official.claim: In the controlled simulation, after 3 epochs RGPO reaches 99.5 ± 0.2% no-hint accuracy on held-out hard problems, versus 0.0 ± 0.0% for GRPO and 12.8 ± 5.6% for the best baseline (RL + SFT on the reference, and also RGPO without the reward gate), while keeping easy-problem test accuracy at 99.3 ± 0.1%.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Final no-hint accuracy (%) in the controlled simulation after three training epochs. Values are mean ± standard deviation over five seeds. The hard test split is the primary diagnostic: it contains problems for which successful unguided reasoning trajectories are initially extremely unlikely.

title: Learnable Spectral Activations
claim_source: Figure 4, page 7 (numbers in Section 4.2 text, page 8; Table 8, page 30; convergence in Appendix B.2, Figure 10)

official.background: Implicit neural representations (INRs) fit a signal such as an image or audio clip with a small MLP that maps coordinates to values. How well they fit depends heavily on the activation function: SIREN uses sin(ω0 u) and FINER uses a variable-periodic sin((|u|+1)u), and both control which frequencies the network can express. The paper argues that the bottleneck is also how each neuron combines several harmonics, and that making the activation's harmonic profile learnable improves fitting of signals with localized structure such as image edges.
official.method:
Learnable spectral activations (LSA) replace the fixed nonlinearity in each hidden layer with a residual truncated Fourier series φ(u) = u + Σ_{k=1..K} a_k sin(2πku), applied elementwise. The K coefficients a_k are shared across all neurons of a layer, initialized from N(0, 1e-3²) so the network starts near identity, and trained jointly with the weights (coefficient learning rate 2× the weight learning rate).

Kodak image fitting (Section 4.2, Appendix A.2/C.1): each of the 24 768×512 RGB images is fitted separately by a coordinate MLP with raw coordinates in [-1,1]² (no Fourier features), width 256, four nonlinear layers and a linear RGB output. LSA uses K = 32 (199,043 parameters). SIREN uses ω0 = 30; FINER uses ω0 = 30 and first-layer bias scale √2/2. All methods: Adam, 5,000 updates, minibatches of 65,536 pixels, learning rate 5e-4 decayed exponentially to 0.1×, seed 0. The reported PSNR is the best full-grid PSNR among evaluations every 100 steps (in-sample fitting). LSA's learning rate was picked from 3 candidates on six calibration images (kodim02, 05, 07, 10, 13, 23) and then frozen.
official.claim: When fitting each of the 24 Kodak images with a matched 4-layer, width-256 coordinate MLP for 5,000 Adam updates, LSA (K = 32) reaches a mean PSNR of 38.11 dB vs. 37.32 dB for FINER and 34.99 dB for SIREN, with higher PSNR than FINER on 21/24 images and than SIREN on 24/24 images.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Per-image Kodak fitting comparison under fixed configurations. Per-image PSNR is shown for LSA, FINER, SIREN, and STAF under 5,000-update fits.
official.metric: Best full-grid RGB PSNR (dB) per image after 5,000 updates, higher is better; the means in the legend are across the 24 images and the legend std is the spread across images, not over seeds (one seed per image). The per-bar error bars are not defined in the paper.
official.comparison: LSA vs. FINER and SIREN with the same MLP backbone, optimizer, batch size, schedule and step budget; only the activation (and LSA's coefficient learning rate) differs. STAF (35.37 dB) is also shown, with a separately tuned configuration.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the 24 fits for each method under the stated protocol, LSA's mean PSNR does not exceed FINER's, or LSA beats FINER on fewer than about 16 of 24 images (no consistent paired advantage), or LSA does not beat SIREN on nearly all images.

title: ElasticFit: Fit-Aware 3D Object Insertion via VLM Reasoning and Generative Adaptation

official.background: Inserting a new object into an existing 3D scene from a language instruction (for AR/VR, interior design or embodied AI) requires choosing a location that matches the instruction and also making the object physically fit there: resting on the intended surface, not intersecting nearby geometry, and sometimes changing shape to fill a gap. LLM/VLM-based layout methods such as LayoutGPT, Holodeck and LayoutVLM reason over object poses and bounding boxes. This coarse representation can leave inserted objects floating, penetrating geometry or unsupported in cluttered, irregular scenes.
official.method:
ElasticFit renders the scene from the user's viewpoint and builds an XYZ buffer and a semantic instance-ID buffer. It then queries a VLM (Gemini-3.1 Pro Preview) with the rendered view, a Set-of-Mark image of visible object IDs, and the instruction. The VLM returns structured JSON: anchor object, target pixel and support object, optional orientation cues (look_at_uv, top_uv), snapping behavior, and, when adaptive generation is enabled, object-generation fields and canonical object scale. The target pixel is checked against the ID buffer, snapped to the predicted support object if needed, and lifted to a 3D support point. A 'ghost box' (maximum fitting volume) and a yaw/pitch orientation are built from it. Stage 3 fits the object with a collision- and support-aware pose search over mesh geometry, then runs a short PyBullet rigid-body settling simulation plus a conservative grounding correction. The full method also generates the object (SDXL-style image, then TRELLIS 3D lifting) and adapts it rigidly, uniformly or elastically.

For the baseline comparison (Table 2), ElasticFit runs in a placement-only setting: object generation and deformation are disabled, and all methods insert the same fixed target asset into the same Replica scene for the same prompt. The task set is the Common Placement Set: 60 tasks (S001-S060), 12 each for distance, directional, facing, alignment and against-wall relations. The baselines are the authors' single-object adaptations of LayoutGPT (direct CSS-style pose prediction, no refinement), Holodeck (LLM relation constraints plus AABB-based candidate search) and LayoutVLM (VLM program plus bounding-box differentiable optimization). All use the same LLM/VLM backbone. Support Success Rate (SupR) counts a task as supported if |z_bottom - z_sup| <= 0.02 m and footprint coverage >= 0.08, where z_sup is the 95th-percentile height of support-object points under the object footprint.
official.claim: On the 60-task Common Placement Set in Replica scenes with fixed target assets, placement-only ElasticFit reaches a Support Success Rate of 91.7%, versus 48.3% for the best adapted baseline (LayoutGPT), 43.9% for LayoutVLM and 41.7% for Holodeck. It also reaches a Spatial Relation Success Rate of 69.7% versus 50.8% for the best baseline.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Baseline comparison on the Common Placement Set. Note. SRS = Spatial Relation Success Rate, CFR = Collision-Free Rate, SupR = Support Success Rate, and CPS = Contextual Plausibility Score. Higher is better for all metrics. Scores are reported in percent except CPS.
official.metric: Support Success Rate (SupR, % of 60 tasks, higher is better); secondary: Spatial Relation Success Rate (SRS). Single run, no error bars or repeated-run variability reported (the paper says explicitly that it does not quantify repeated-run variability).
official.comparison: ElasticFit (placement-only: VLM grounding + geometry/physics-aware refinement) vs. adapted LayoutGPT, Holodeck and LayoutVLM, all with the same scenes, prompts, fixed assets and Gemini-3.1 Pro Preview backbone
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the comparison on the same kind of task set gives an ElasticFit SupR that is not clearly above the best baseline (e.g., a gap under ~15 percentage points, roughly 9 of 60 tasks), or some baseline reaches SupR comparable to ElasticFit's.
