title: WASD: Wasserstein-based Knowledge Distillation for Large Language Models

official.background: Knowledge distillation for LLMs trains a small student to match a large teacher's next-token distribution at every position, and the choice of divergence (forward KL, reverse KL, total variation, generalized JS, skew KL, α-β, and so on) is the main design choice. All of these compare probabilities index by index over the vocabulary, so moving probability from 'sofa' to 'couch' costs as much as moving it to 'apple'. This paper asks whether a divergence that knows which tokens are semantically close, via optimal transport over the teacher's token-embedding space, gives a better distillation signal.
official.method:
WASD replaces the per-token divergence with a debiased Sinkhorn divergence between teacher and student next-token distributions, with transport cost C given by cosine distances between the teacher's token embeddings (computed once, kept fixed). The cost is sparsified to each token's k = 8 nearest non-self neighbors (symmetrized, plus zero-cost self-loops). Instead of backpropagating through the solver, the loss is sum_i sg(phi_i^(p,q) - phi_i^(q,q)) q_theta(i), where phi^(p,q) is the student-side dual potential from 10 Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations between teacher p and student q, and phi^(q,q) comes from 10 fixed-point iterations of the student self-transport problem; its gradient equals the Sinkhorn divergence gradient (Theorem 3). Entropy regularization ε = 0.001; student temperature scaling of 2 during training.

Table 2 setup: teacher GPT-2 XL (1.5B), student GPT-2 Base (0.1B), distillation data databricks-dolly-15k, no OpenWebText pretraining loss, no SFT initialization of the student, no on-policy generation, AMiD/DistiLLM codebase defaults (lr 1e-4, 20 epochs, best checkpoint by validation ROUGE-L). Each divergence (KL, RKL, Sym-KL, Jeffrey, TV, GJS, SKL, SRKL, α-β, CSD, WASD) is swapped into the same pipeline. Evaluation: ROUGE-L on Dolly Eval, Self-Instruct, Vicuna, Super-NaturalInstructions and Unnatural Instructions, with 5 sampling seeds (10, 20, 30, 40, 50).
official.claim: Distilling GPT-2 XL (1.5B) into GPT-2 Base (0.1B) on Dolly with the divergence as the only change, WASD reaches an average ROUGE-L of 22.47 over five instruction-following benchmarks, versus 21.46 for the best baseline (CSD), 20.53 for TV and 17.17 for forward KL, with the largest per-benchmark gain on Super-NI (28.63 ± 0.17 vs. 25.86 ± 0.31 for CSD).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: ROUGE-L scores on five general instruction-following benchmarks for GPT-2 XL (1.5B) → GPT-2 Base (0.1B), varying divergences. All results are obtained using our implementation, where all methods share identical teacher and student initialization. Performance is averaged over five evaluation seeds. Bold and underline indicate the best and second-best performance, respectively.
official.metric: ROUGE-L (higher is better) per benchmark and the unweighted average over 5 benchmarks; ± is std over 5 evaluation (sampling) seeds of a single trained model, not over training seeds
official.comparison: WASD (Sinkhorn divergence) vs. KL, RKL, Sym-KL, Jeffrey, TV, GJS, SKL, SRKL, α-β and CSD, all with identical teacher, student initialization, data and training pipeline
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the divergence-only GPT-2 XL → GPT-2 Base distillation, WASD's average ROUGE-L is not higher than CSD's by more than the training-seed spread (e.g. gap < 0.3 points), or is not clearly above forward KL (gap < 2 points).

title: The Labeling Problem in Hallucination Detection Benchmarks: An Empirical Evaluation
claim_source: Table 6, page 20 (same p1/p2 κ values in Table 1, page 7)

official.background: Hallucination detectors for LLMs are usually benchmarked on open-domain QA datasets (TriviaQA, HotpotQA, TruthfulQA). An LLM answers each question, and an automated rule (a ROUGE-L or BERTScore threshold, NLI entailment, or an LLM judge) compares the answer with short reference answers and labels it hallucinated or not. Those labels then serve as ground truth for scoring detectors. The paper argues that these labelers often apply reference faithfulness (anything not supported by the reference counts as a hallucination) when the intended target is factual correctness (only contradictions or false specific claims count). The two criteria disagree whenever a correct answer adds true detail that is missing from the short reference, so faithfulness-style labelers over-label hallucinations.
official.method:
The authors sample 300 validation questions (TriviaQA 100, HotpotQA 101, TruthfulQA 99) and generate one answer per question from each of Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (T = 0.7, top-p = 0.95, max 128 new tokens, seed 42), giving 900 question–answer pairs. A primary annotator labels all 900 under a factual-correctness protocol: an answer is a hallucination if it contradicts the reference or contains a specific verifiable claim that is false, and external sources may be consulted when the reference is insufficient. A second annotator labels 300 of them (κ = 0.808).

The LLM judge GPT-5-mini labels every pair with each of three prompts (Appendix B), returning strict JSON {label, confidence}. p1 is a terse faithfulness prompt: 'A hallucination is any claim that is not supported by, or contradicted by, the reference answer … Do not use external knowledge.' p2 is a factual-correctness decision-tree prompt stating that 'absent from reference' is not 'contradicted by reference' and that only explicit contradictions or false specific details count. p3 extends p2 with edge-case handling. Agreement with the primary human labels is measured with Cohen's κ separately for each generator's 300 answers. Paired p1 vs. p2 differences are tested with a 2,000-resample item-level bootstrap CI for Δκ and McNemar's exact test on item-level correctness.
official.claim: With GPT-5-mini as the hallucination judge, replacing the faithfulness prompt p1 with the factual-correctness prompt p2 raises Cohen's κ against human factual-correctness labels from 0.530 to 0.756 (Llama-3-8B answers, Δκ +0.226 [+0.127, +0.328]), from 0.498 to 0.770 (Gemma-2-9B, +0.272 [+0.179, +0.360]) and from 0.194 to 0.626 (Mistral-7B, +0.432 [+0.332, +0.533]), with McNemar p < 0.0001 in each case.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Paired prompt comparisons for GPT-5-mini against the primary human labels. In each contrast, prompt a is the prompt before the arrow and prompt b is the prompt after the arrow. κa and κb denote the Cohen's κ agreements of prompt a and prompt b with the human labels, respectively; ∆κ = κb − κa. Brackets give 95% nonparametric bootstrap intervals for ∆κ with 2,000 item-level resamples. McNemar's p is the exact two-sided paired test over item-level correctness disagreements between the two prompt variants. L=Llama-3-8B, G=Gemma-2-9B, M=Mistral-7B.
official.metric: Cohen's κ between judge labels and primary human labels (higher is better), computed per generator on 300 answers; brackets are 95% nonparametric bootstrap CIs for Δκ (2,000 item-level resamples); McNemar exact two-sided p on paired item-level correctness. Single judge run per prompt, no seed variation reported.
official.comparison: GPT-5-mini with prompt p2 (factual correctness) vs. the same judge with prompt p1 (reference faithfulness), on identical question–answer pairs and human labels
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running GPT-5-mini with the published p1 and p2 prompts on the released 900 labeled pairs gives a p1→p2 κ gain whose bootstrap 95% CI includes zero for any generator, or a gain far below the reported range (e.g. under +0.10 on Llama-3-8B or Gemma-2-9B answers).

title: MedZERO: Self-Evolving Agents for Open-Ended Medical Reasoning Through Controlled Knowledge Accumulation

official.background: Self-evolving LLM frameworks, where a model generates its own training tasks and learns from solving them, have mostly worked in domains with exact verifiers such as math and code. Medical reasoning is open-ended and only partly verifiable, and progress often depends on bringing in external knowledge, so self-consistency rewards and naive reuse of self-generated facts can reinforce errors. The paper asks whether a self-evolving loop built for partial verifiability and controlled knowledge reuse can improve medical QA without any human-labelled training data.
official.method:
MedZERO alternates two GRPO-trained agents initialised from the same base model (Qwen3-4B-Base or Qwen3-8B-Base). An Examiner generates a medical question, a local option set (M options) and candidate knowledge triplets. It is rewarded for option-level frontier difficulty: the frozen Reasoner gives K free-form answers without seeing the options, a mapper model maps each to an option, and the reward is -|agreement - gamma|. It also gets a diversity reward and an evidence-grounding reward (weight 0.05). After Examiner training, regenerated questions whose agreement score falls in [0.3, 0.8] (K_cur = 9 samples) become the Reasoner curriculum, and their triplets are deduplicated and added to a persistent KG on top of PrimeKG. Triplets produced during Examiner optimisation are kept only in a temporary buffer and then discarded.

The Reasoner answers curriculum questions with multi-turn tool use (retrieval over PrimeKG plus the persistent KG, optional web search via Tavily) and is trained with GRPO (4 rollouts) on a majority-consistency reward over mapped options plus a grounding reward. Evaluation is open-ended: the Reasoner sees only the question stem, writes a free-form answer, and a Qwen3-4B-Base mapper maps it to the benchmark option. Accuracy is reported on MedBullets op4/op5 (308 each), MedBrowseComp (50, rule-based matching), MedXpertQA text (2,450), MMLU-Pro health (818) and PubMedQA labelled (1,000), with the average taken over the six scores.
official.claim: With Qwen3-4B-Base, MedZERO reaches a six-score average accuracy of 35.6% under open-ended evaluation, versus 21.2% for the strongest self-evolving baseline (Absolute Zero), and beats it on every benchmark; excluding MedBrowseComp (42.0% vs. 0.0%), the five-score mean is still 34.3% vs. 25.5%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on Qwen3-4B-scale backbones under open-ended evaluation.
official.metric: Accuracy (pass@1, higher is better) after open-ended generation and LLM-based answer mapping; the average is unweighted over six scores. Single numbers with no error bars. The only variance estimate in the paper is a separate fixed-curriculum experiment (Table 3a) where three Reasoner-training seeds give a four-score mean of 36.84 ± 0.34 (sample std).
official.comparison: MedZERO vs. Absolute Zero, SPIRAL, Agent0 and the untrained base, all on Qwen3-4B-Base
official.falsification_criterion: A rerun of MedZERO and Absolute Zero from Qwen3-4B-Base with the same open-ended evaluation protocol where MedZERO's five-score mean (excluding MedBrowseComp) does not beat Absolute Zero by clearly more than run-to-run variance (e.g. a gap under about 3 points), or where the gap disappears once Absolute Zero gets the same retrieval and web tools at evaluation time.

title: Decision-Focused Learning in MDPs: An Occupancy Measure Approach

official.background: Decision-focused learning (DFL) trains a predictor of optimization-problem parameters end to end on the quality of the decisions it induces, instead of on prediction error. When the downstream problem is a Markov decision process (MDP) whose rewards and transitions are predicted from features, existing DFL methods differentiate through the KKT conditions of the Bellman optimality equations (in practice a QP relaxation solved with qpth). This requires solving a |S||A| x |S||A| linear system per gradient step, which becomes prohibitive as the state or action space grows.
official.method:
The MDP is written as the occupancy-measure linear program max r_theta^T y s.t. H_theta y = gamma, y >= 0, where the predicted transitions enter the flow-constraint matrix H_theta. With a strictly positive initial distribution the optimal basis is non-degenerate, and the Jacobian of the solution is obtained in closed form by inverting only the |S| x |S| basis matrix (Eq. 3-4). Training uses an augmented Lagrangian loss: minus the true reward of the predicted occupancy, plus a dual term with the true LP's optimal dual and a quadratic penalty rho * ||H_true y - gamma||^2 (Eq. 5). DFL-Sketch additionally averages solutions over K = 8 Gaussian row sketches of the constraints during training.

DFL-SA is DFL-Sketch combined with a learnable soft state-aggregation layer (Algorithm 1: aggregate, sketch-and-solve the aggregated LP, average, lift, apply the augmented Lagrangian loss):a softmax membership matrix W (|S| x M) builds an aggregated MDP (Eq. 8) with M << |S| states, the aggregated LP is solved and differentiated (an M x M basis solve), and the aggregate occupancy is lifted back via W. In the scaling experiment (Appendix B.4) the task is an inventory MDP with Poisson demand whose rate lambda is predicted by an MLP (32, 32) from features; |S| = 101 net-inventory states, |A| = 31 order quantities, discount beta = 0.95 (gamma in the LP is the initial-state distribution); Table 2 lists 10 training and 50 test samples for the |S| = 36 inventory, and B.4 does not restate them for |S| = 101. Baselines run under the same setup: Two-stage (MSE on the MDP parameters, then solve), DFL-QP (KKT/QP-based DFL of Wang et al. with qpth), DFL-LP, DFL-Feas (feasibility-penalty constrained DFL of Mandi et al.), and DFL-Sketch.
official.claim: On the larger inventory MDP (|S| x |A| = 101 x 31), DFL-SA (M = 30) trains in 862.8 +/- 12.2 s versus 34791.0 +/- 756.4 s for KKT-based DFL-QP (about 40x faster) while reaching test regret no worse than DFL-QP (39.187 +/- 5.198 vs. 44.545 +/- 5.823).
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Larger inventory MDP, |S| x |A| = 101 x 31 = 3131 (mean ± standard error over 10 seeds).
official.metric: Total wall-clock training time in seconds (lower is better) and test regret (lower is better); +/- is the standard error of the mean over 10 seeds.
official.comparison: DFL-SA (M = 30) vs. DFL-QP (KKT-based DFL), with Two-stage, DFL-LP, DFL-Feas, DFL-Sketch and DFL-SA (M = 10, 20) as additional rows, all on the same inventory MDP and seeds.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if, run on the same hardware with comparable solver settings, DFL-SA (M = 30) is not at least roughly an order of magnitude faster to train than DFL-QP, or if its mean test regret is worse than DFL-QP's by more than the combined standard errors.

title: Trajectory Planning without Trajectory Data: A Manifold-Guided Approach

official.background: Generative trajectory planners such as Diffuser learn a distribution over whole expert trajectories and plan by conditional sampling. They need costly trajectory supervision, and they generalize poorly to start-goal pairs whose connecting trajectories were missing from training, even when every intermediate state was observed. The paper asks whether a planner can be built from state-only data: learn the distribution of feasible states, then build paths that stay on that learned state manifold.
official.method:
Ariadne trains a generative model (a flow-matching MLP for Maze2D: 4 hidden layers, width 128, lr 5e-4 for large and 1e-4 for medium, batch 64) on individual maze states only, with no trajectories or transitions. At inference it estimates the local normal space at the current state by eigendecomposing the Hessian of log-density. For flow matching this Hessian is approximated by (J+J^T)/2 of the model output at time 0.98. Eigen-directions with eigenvalue below a threshold (-0.0001 for Maze2D) count as normals.

A path from start x0 to goal x1 is built by integrating a 'Correction-Projection ODE' with explicit Euler and operator splitting. Each step moves along the straight-line direction x1 - x0, adds a correction term (2-4t)·phi that restores progress toward the endpoint, and then projects out the normal components (projection scale 1.0). Arc-length step size is 0.02. The resulting state sequence is executed in the D4RL Maze2D environment and scored with the standard D4RL normalized score.
official.claim: On D4RL Maze2D, Ariadne trained only on state observations scores 55.69 (Medium) and 50.63 (Large). This beats the state-only geometric planner Follow-the-Energy (16.29 / 16.41) and Diffuser* (52.70 / 41.98), a Diffuser trained with trajectories reaching the evaluation targets withheld.

title: CANDO: Cooperative Agentic Network for Layout Design Optimization
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (paired tests in Table 17, page 28)

official.background: Layout generation benchmarks (PubLayNet, RICO, posters) mostly place axis-aligned boxes on rectangular canvases and score results with distributional metrics such as FID and mIoU, which reward matching the dataset prior. Real facility layouts (fuel/service sites) need irregular site boundaries, element orientations, access-point-aware placement and vehicle-routing feasibility. The paper introduces ALPS-Bench (1,000 professionally annotated real facility layouts with a design manual of hard and soft constraints; 900 dev / 100 held-out test) and asks whether a training-free cooperative multi-agent LLM system can satisfy these constraints better than single-model and single-agent approaches.
official.method:
Each instance gives a polygonal premise, access points, a fixed set of elements (class and shape), and a design manual. Hard constraints are containment, non-overlap and routing feasibility (checked with Voronoi-based motion planning for predefined vehicle scenarios); soft constraints are proximity, compositionality and orientation. HCM = 0.2*HC_geometric + 0.8*HC_flow; SCM = 0.6*PR + 0.3*CO + 0.1*OR. The constraint-satisfaction score is CS = SCM if HCM = 1, else 0.5*HCM*SCM. RE compares path length, turns and clearance against the withheld ground truth, and AGG = (CS + RE)/2. CS needs no ground-truth layout.

CANDO: an ICL Initializer retrieves similar dev-set layouts with weighted kNN over hand-crafted features, generates K_init candidates and keeps the one with the best overlap/containment proxy. Then a loop of Historian (sliding window of feedback changes, W=6), Planner (supervisor plus per-category workers, using coordinates and a rendered image), Generator (K=6 candidates across 8 repair strategies) and a deterministic tool-based Verifier runs as CoDe block-wise best-of-N: N=4 parallel branches, block size B=10, T=20 refinement steps. The Single-Agent baseline uses the same GPT-5.2 backbone and has the same evaluation scores and toolset, but it is one agent refining sequentially for up to T=200 steps.
official.claim: On the ALPS-Bench held-out test set (100 layouts), CANDO (CoDe, GPT-5.2) reaches constraint-satisfaction score CS 0.78 ± 0.35 and AGG 0.60 ± 0.25, vs. 0.47 ± 0.37 and 0.40 ± 0.27 for a tool-equipped Single-Agent on the same GPT-5.2 backbone. The paired CS difference is +0.318 (95% bootstrap CI [0.246, 0.392], Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.001), and CANDO uses T=20 refinement steps against the baseline's 200.

Symbols indicate the generation paradigm: ♦ diffusion-based, ▲ single-LLM/MLLM, and • agentic.

title: SLDR: Defending Against Malicious Fine-tuning via Selective Layers Recovery and Dynamic Routing

official.background: Fine-tuning-as-a-service lets users adapt an aligned LLM with their own data, but an attacker can mix a small fraction of harmful instruction-response pairs into otherwise benign task data, so that the fine-tuned model still does the task but stops refusing harmful requests. The service provider then wants to restore refusal behavior without losing the task accuracy gained from fine-tuning. Existing defenses either constrain fine-tuning (and often cost downstream accuracy) or repair the whole model afterwards (pruning, perturbation, one-shot re-alignment), which entangles safety repair with task behavior.
official.method:
Before any fine-tuning, SLDR probes the aligned model layer by layer: it scales all attention and MLP weights of one layer by (1 + α) and by (1 − α), α ∈ {0.1, 0.2}, counts keyword-detected refusals on an over-refusal prompt set, and assigns each layer a signed score κ_l = max_α (c⁺ − c⁻)/α. Only the two endpoint layers, l_max = argmax κ_l and l_min = argmin κ_l, are kept. After the user's (possibly poisoned) LoRA fine-tuning (Stage 1: 1000 samples, poison ratio ρ = 0.1, 20 epochs, lr 1e-5), Stage 2 trains a LoRA recovery adapter (q/k/v, rank 32) only on l_min and l_max with 100 harmful-prompt/safe-response pairs (lr 5e-4, 20 epochs), with all other parameters frozen.

At inference, a router takes the ℓ2-normalized last-token hidden state at layer l_max of the recovered model, computes the mean cosine-similarity gap between harmful and benign reference prompts, and applies the recovery adapter only if this score exceeds τ = 0; otherwise the attacked task model answers unchanged. Harmful Score (HS) is the percentage of BeaverTails test responses that Llama-Guard-3-8B labels unsafe; Finetune Accuracy (FA) is SST2 test accuracy (872 samples).
official.claim: On Llama3.1-8B-Instruct fine-tuned on SST2 with 10% harmful data (|D_train| = 1000), SLDR achieves Harmful Score 0.08 ± 0.10 versus 1.88 ± 0.36 for BDS (the strongest baseline) and 4.18 ± 0.32 for One-shot FT over 4 seeds, while keeping SST2 accuracy at 92.92 ± 0.33 (BDS 91.37 ± 0.50).
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Multi-seed stability analysis on Llama3.1 with the SST2 dataset.
official.metric: Harmful Score (% of BeaverTails outputs judged unsafe by Llama-Guard-3-8B, lower is better) and Finetune Accuracy (% SST2 test accuracy, higher is better); mean ± std over 4 seeds {0, 1, 2, 42}
official.comparison: SLDR vs. BDS and One-shot FT under the same attacked fine-tuning setup (Llama3.1, SST2, ρ = 0.1, |D_train| = 1000)
official.falsification_criterion: Over several seeds, SLDR's mean Harmful Score is not clearly below BDS's (e.g. the gap is within one std of either method), or SLDR's SST2 accuracy falls clearly below BDS's.

title: Explicit Geometric Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language-Action in Autonomous Driving
claim_source: Table 5, page 8 (same numbers for baseline and GeoCoTDrive in Table 2, page 7)

official.background: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for end-to-end autonomous driving predict future ego trajectories from camera images and text, using a pretrained vision-language model. Their intermediate reasoning happens in a 2D semantic token space, while driving actions depend on precise 3D geometry. Prior work adds geometry either through 3D perception supervision (agent and map tokens) or by injecting global features from a geometric foundation model such as VGGT or Depth Anything into the VLM. This paper asks whether geometry helps more when it is retrieved only from the image regions that matter for the current planning decision.
official.method:
GeoCoTDrive takes a front-view image, driving command and ego status, and first autoregressively generates a few 2D bounding boxes of planning-relevant regions (critical objects, road boundaries, conflict areas, occluded areas, dense object areas), followed by a <GEO_COT> token. A frozen geometric foundation model (Depth Anything V3 METRIC-LARGE by default, last backbone layer) encodes the same image; a regular K-point grid (grid size ablated in Table 11, 1x1 to 5x5; 4x4 = 16 tokens per box ties for best there, and the paper does not name a default) is bilinearly sampled from its feature map inside each predicted box, projected by an MLP aligner into the LLM embedding space, and inserted into the context at <GEO_COT>. The model then continues decoding the trajectory as text tokens. Training uses ground-truth boxes for sampling; inference uses the predicted boxes.

Grounding supervision comes from PlanningGrounding, 146K box annotations produced by Gemini-3.1 and human-checked (102K from NAVSIM). Training has two stages, each 3 epochs with cosine LR: Stage I fine-tunes vision encoder + LLM on driving QA (NAVSIM-Traj + PlanningGrounding), Stage II freezes the vision encoder and trains LLM + geometric aligner on grounding-then-trajectory sequences. On NAVSIM the base VLM is Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The ablation compares (i) Baseline: the same VLA without geometry tokens (its numbers are identical to the Stage-I-only row of Table 12, so it appears not to receive Stage II training), (ii) Global: global geometry tokens from the same foundation model interleaved into the context, (iii) GeoCoT: region-sampled geometry tokens.
official.claim: On NAVSIM navtest (NAVSIMv1, non-reactive), with a Qwen2.5-VL-3B VLA, interleaving geometry tokens sampled from predicted planning-relevant regions raises PDMS to 87.6, versus 85.9 for the same model without geometry and 85.8 with global geometry tokens, with DAC 95.6 vs. 94.0/94.1 and TTC 95.0 vs. 94.4/94.2.

title: MESSENGER: Memory-Enhanced Sequential Scene Flow Estimation via Autoregressive Next-Frame Forecasting

official.background: Scene flow is the per-point 3D displacement field between consecutive LiDAR (or RGB-D) frames, used in motion segmentation, dynamic reconstruction and SLAM. Most learned estimators work on frame pairs and ignore longer temporal context. Multi-frame methods (Flow4D, MambaFlow) stack frames, so their cost grows with sequence length, and they only estimate flows between observed frames. GenFlow3D, a diffusion-based estimator with a GRU state, can also predict future flows, but its errors grow quickly as it extrapolates further into the future.
official.method:
MESSENGER processes a LiDAR sequence one frame at a time. At the coarsest level of a hierarchical point encoder, it keeps a FIFO memory buffer of the last M = 6 frames' coarse flows, GRU hidden states and per-point uncertainties. For each new frame, a cross-attention read-out (query from the latest hidden state, keys and values from stored states and flows) followed by an MLP forecasts the current coarse flow from history alone. This forecast is refined with the current frame's geometry and cost-volume features, and multi-scale diffusion decoders (as in GenFlow3D/DifFlow3D, 4 stages, 1-step DDIM at inference) upsample it. A per-point uncertainty, the clamped normalized norm of (forecast flow − refined flow), down-weights unreliable stored flows when memory is read. For future frames no new point cloud is available, so the model rolls out autoregressively from memory.

Evaluation follows GenFlow3D: nuScenes (650 training / 200 test sequences per the paper's split) and Argoverse 2 (700 training / 150 evaluation scenes), 8192 sampled points per frame, ground and points beyond 35 m removed, ground truth from odometry and tracking. For prediction, H = 6 frames are observed and flows for the next K = 4 frames are predicted. Metrics are EPE3D (mean end-point error in m, lower is better) and Acc3DS (fraction of points with small error, higher is better).
official.claim: For future scene flow prediction with H = 6 observed frames, MESSENGER's EPE3D at the 4th predicted frame (SF_{H+4}) is 0.025 on nuScenes and 0.062 on Argoverse 2, vs. 0.088 and 0.192 for GenFlow3D (71.6% and 67.7% lower), and it has lower EPE3D than GenFlow3D at every horizon k = 1 to 4 on both datasets.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison of scene flow prediction results on nuScenes [59] and Argoverse 2 [60]. We set the observed frames as H = 6 and predict future frames with the intervals of k = 1, 2, 3, 4.
official.metric: EPE3D (m, lower is better) and Acc3DS (higher is better) on predicted future flows; single numbers, no ± or seed count reported
official.comparison: MESSENGER vs. GenFlow3D (ICCV'25) under the same prediction protocol (H = 6 observed frames, K = 4 future frames) on nuScenes and Argoverse 2
official.falsification_criterion: With both models trained and evaluated under the same protocol, MESSENGER's SF_{H+4} EPE3D is not clearly lower than GenFlow3D's (e.g. less than ~30% lower, versus the claimed ~70%), or GenFlow3D matches or beats it at any horizon k = 1 to 4.

title: SteerCast: Retrieval-Based Latent Steering for Decoder-Only Time Series Forecasting
claim_source: Table 2, page 6 (per-horizon numbers in Table 30, Appendix D, page 28)

official.background: Decoder-only time-series foundation models such as Time-MoE, Timer-XL and TimesFM are fine-tuned per dataset and forecast autoregressively, but they still make systematic errors on atypical patterns and their errors build up over long horizons. Improving them usually means more training, ensembling or scaling. Retrieval-augmented forecasting (RAF, RAFT) instead feeds similar historical windows to the model, but prepending retrieved sequences uses up the model's fixed context window and adds attention cost. This paper asks whether retrieved training examples can instead correct an already fine-tuned forecaster at inference time by editing its hidden states, with no parameter updates and no extra input tokens.
official.method:
SteerCast builds a key-value memory from the training split only. For each univariate training window x with true continuation y, the fine-tuned forecaster F produces its own prediction y_pred. The key is the mean over time of F's final-layer hidden states on x. The value is a steering vector Δ = h([x; y]) − h([x; y_pred]), where h concatenates the last-token residual-stream state at every block's output. At test time, the query's key retrieves the top-k nearest entries by Euclidean distance, and their Δ are averaged.

During autoregressive generation, each layer's hidden state at every forecast step is updated as h + λ·α·Δ^(l)/||Δ^(l)||. Here α = b + ReLU(−cos(h, Δ^(l)) + m)^p is a cosine gate with (b, m, p) = (0.1, 0.1, 1.25), and λ = 0.01. k is chosen per dataset on the validation split (Table 17; for Time-MoE, k = 1 on ETTh1 and ETTh2). In the fixed look-back setting (Table 2), the input length is 512 for all horizons {96, 192, 336, 720}, and one database built at 512→96 is reused for every horizon. Baselines: FT (the fine-tuned backbone alone), RAF (training-free; retrieved history/future pairs prepended as in-context examples) and RAFT (retrieved future segments used alongside the input in a trained pipeline). The metric is MSE averaged over the four horizons, computed on all channels, with the last 20% of each series as the test split.
official.claim: With Time-MoE in the fixed look-back setting (input 512, one 512→96 database reused for horizons 96-720), SteerCast lowers horizon-averaged test MSE relative to the same fine-tuned model from 0.407 to 0.394 on ETTh1 and from 0.537 to 0.488 on ETTh2, and also beats RAFT (0.402 and 0.518).

official.metric: MSE on the standardized test split, averaged over horizons {96, 192, 336, 720} (lower is better). Point estimates only; no ± or seed variation is reported.
official.comparison: SteerCast applied to fine-tuned Time-MoE vs. fine-tuned Time-MoE alone (FT), RAF and RAFT, under the same 512-step look-back and data splits.

title: Rethinking Contrastive Loss in CLIP Post-training: A Complementary Framework with Frozen Text Encoder

official.background: CLIP is the standard vision encoder inside VLMs such as LLaVA. Post-training, meaning a short refinement of a pretrained CLIP on a small image-text corpus, is a cheap way to improve it without retraining from scratch or breaking compatibility with downstream systems. Earlier post-training methods (CLIP-Refine, KUEA) avoid the standard contrastive loss, because prior work reported that it causes catastrophic forgetting at the small batch sizes affordable in post-training. This paper argues the forgetting comes mostly from using the pretraining temperature (τ ≈ 0.07) rather than from too few negatives, and proposes a recipe that keeps the contrastive loss with a much smaller τ.
official.method:
ComCLIP freezes CLIP's text encoder and post-trains only the vision encoder for 1 epoch, using the sum (all weights 1.0) of three losses on the l2-normalized post-projection image embedding u: (i) symmetric InfoNCE between u and the frozen text embeddings with a fixed temperature τ = 0.01; (ii) an MSE anchoring loss ||u(x) − u0(x)||² to a frozen copy of the original CLIP vision encoder; (iii) a relational distillation loss: row-wise KL(P_dino || P_clip) between softmax(T = 0.1) distributions over the batch cosine-similarity matrices of u and of frozen DINOv2 ViT-L/14 (with registers) features. Training uses AdamW, learning rate 1e-6, weight decay 0.1, 410-step linear warm-up, global batch 1,024 on 8 A800 GPUs, standard per-sample CLIP augmentation, and is built on the KUEA codebase.

The baseline is CLIP-Refine (self-distillation with image-text soft labels), reproduced from its official code with its original hyperparameters for 1 epoch. For the Table 2 claim, both start from OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/16. ComCLIP is trained on CC3M and CLIP-Refine on COCO Caption, each method's best setting. Linear probing is the average over 5 datasets: ImageNet-1K, SVHN, GTSRB, CLEVR Distance, CLEVR Counts.
official.claim: On OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/16, ComCLIP post-trained 1 epoch on CC3M reaches a 5-dataset average linear-probe accuracy of 48.99 ± 0.35, versus 42.28 ± 0.62 for CLIP-Refine (COCO Caption), over 3 seeds (Welch p = 4e-4), while 12-dataset zero-shot accuracy is at parity (63.00 ± 0.13 vs. 62.87 ± 0.11).

title: VINCIE-NExT: Unlocking Video Editing from Images via In-Context Modeling
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (Seed1.6-VL re-judging in Table 4, Appendix D.1, page 25)

official.background: Instruction-guided video editing needs (source video, instruction, edited video) triplets, which are expensive to annotate and hard to synthesize at scale, while image editing already has millions of such pairs. Applying image editors frame by frame causes flicker, and pipelines that build video editing pairs from flow, depth or segmentation tools accumulate errors. The paper asks whether editing ability can be transferred from images to videos so that a video editor needs much less paired video editing data.
official.method:
VINCIE-NExT factorizes video editing as Video → Image → Image → Video: pick a keyframe I_s from the source video V_s, edit it into I_t, then generate the edited video V_t conditioned on V_s, I_s and I_t. All segments are flattened into one interleaved text/visual token sequence and modeled by a single 3B MM-DiT (initialized from the VINCIE text-to-video backbone, SD3-inflated video VAE and Flan-T5 frozen) trained with a flow-matching loss on any contiguous sub-chain. A position encoding (TDF3D-RoPE) adds an inter-shot offset component to an intra-shot component so that the same spatial location in different shots has zero relative spatial offset; training images get a random temporal index (TPR). Training data: 1.20M OmniEdit image editing pairs, 2.45M OpenVE video editing pairs reformatted into sub-chains, and 1.63M (video, frame, edited frame) triplets built with GPT-4o instructions and Seedream 4.5 edits. Training is 32 H100s for about 150 h (256×256 then 640×480).

Inference uses Chain-of-Editing: stage 1 generates the edited keyframe (V→I→I) by the model itself, using the temporal mid-frame as I_s; stage 2 generates the video (V→I→I→V) with the edited latent inserted without VAE decoding; up to 65 frames at 12 FPS, 32 sampling steps, CFG 2.5. Evaluation is on OpenVE-Bench (431 clips, 8 categories), where Gemini 2.5 Pro scores each output 1–5 on instruction compliance, consistency/detail fidelity and visual quality/stability, averaged into a category score and an overall score.

title: OmniCapBench: A Deep-Structured Evaluation Framework for Fine-Grained Audio-Visual Captioning

official.background: Omnimodal LLMs are increasingly asked to describe long audio-visual videos, and audio-visual captioning is a natural diagnostic task for them. Existing caption benchmarks either score the whole free-form caption with one global LLM judge, which gives coverage but no error localization, or ask sparse QA/cloze probes, which localize errors but cover little of the video. In both cases an LLM must reason over long, unstructured generated text, so scores can depend heavily on which LLM is used as the judge.
official.method:
OmniCapBench (786 videos, 12.8 hours) asks the evaluated model to output a structured JSON of atomic units in three tracks: References (persistent people, objects, scenes with IDs), Events (timestamped audio events and dialogue) and Shots/Subshots (timed visual segments that cross-link to reference and event IDs). Scoring is two-stage. Deterministic rules first drop structurally invalid units (undefined IDs, reversed time spans, impossible event-shot links) and match shots and events to the ground truth by temporal IoU; references and subshots are matched by a bounded LLM matcher that only compares local candidate pairs. An LLM judge then scores semantic equivalence only on the matched unit pairs, bidirectionally (recall: ground truth to prediction; precision: prediction to ground truth).

For the judge-sensitivity test (Section 4.3, Table 5), the same model predictions are scored with three judges, weak (Qwen3.6-27B), mid (GPT-4o) and strong (Gemini-2.5-Pro), under three protocols: holistic whole-caption judging in the style of UGC-VideoCap, QA-probe judging in the style of Omni-Cloze, and OmniCapBench's bounded local judging. The claim is that the OmniCapBench score barely moves across judges while the baseline protocols move a lot.
official.claim: Scoring identical model predictions with weak (Qwen3.6-27B), mid (GPT-4o) and strong (Gemini-2.5-Pro) judges, holistic UGC-VideoCap-style scores range from 71.24 to 93.92 (22.7 points) and Omni-Cloze-style QA scores from 53.49 to 61.17 (7.7 points), whereas OmniCapBench scores stay within 56.82-58.24 (1.4 points).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Judge sensitivity. Stability across judges.
official.metric: Aggregate caption score (0-100) under each protocol; stability is the spread across the three judges (smaller is better). Single values, no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: Spread across judges of OmniCapBench's bounded local LLM scoring vs. holistic whole-caption LLM judging (UGC-VideoCap style) and QA-probe judging (Omni-Cloze style), on the same predictions
official.falsification_criterion: Re-scoring the same predictions with the three judges gives an OmniCapBench spread comparable to or larger than the QA-protocol spread (about 7.7 points), or the holistic-protocol spread is not several times larger than OmniCapBench's.

title: MindVLM: Neural-Grounded Visual Captioning via Subject-Aware Semantic Evidence Selection

official.background: Brain captioning tries to generate a text description of what a person saw from their fMRI response. Most work on the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) trains fMRI-to-text models on MS-COCO captions, but NSD subjects viewed square crops of the COCO images, so about 18% of images lose objects that the captions still mention. The paper argues that this mismatch makes COCO captions a poor training target and proposes using fMRI to select which parts of the (known) stimulus image the brain response supports, then letting a frozen vision-language model (VLM) describe only those parts.
official.method:
For each subject, a 4-layer, 4-head ViT encoder maps nsdgeneral voxels to neural tokens. Neural tokens and the frozen VLM's visual tokens (CLIP ViT-L/14-336 for LLaVA-v1.5-7B) are mean-pooled, linearly projected to a shared space, and trained with a symmetric CLIP-style contrastive loss on image-fMRI pairs (150 epochs, batch 1000, AdamW, lr 7.5e-3 cosine; no text and no LLM in training; about 45 min per subject).

At inference, the projected local tokens give a neural-by-visual similarity matrix A; the top q% of entries are kept and any visual token with a kept entry is selected. The full image is encoded unchanged, and an attention mask restricts LLaVA to the selected visual tokens; it is prompted with 'Please describe the image as simply as possible.' (max 32 new tokens). For Table 2, each MindVLM-LLaVA caption and each MS-COCO reference caption is scored against the NSD stimulus crop with CLIPScore and with SigLIP; MindVLM's score per image is averaged over subj01, 02, 05 and 07, and a paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples) over the 1,000 shared test images gives the CI.
official.claim: On the 1,000 shared NSD test images, MindVLM-LLaVA captions (averaged over 4 subjects) align with the cropped stimulus better than the MS-COCO reference captions under two independent reference-free scorers: CLIPScore 66.85 vs. 65.26 (Δ +1.59, 95% CI [1.23, 1.95]) and SigLIP 29.61 vs. 28.83 (Δ +0.78, 95% CI [0.44, 1.13]).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Reference-free Validation.
official.metric: Reference-free image-text alignment between caption and the NSD stimulus (CLIPScore and SigLIP score), higher is better; Δ is the mean paired difference with a 95% CI from a paired bootstrap over test images (10,000 resamples); single training seed (2025)
official.comparison: MindVLM-LLaVA captions (fMRI-selected visual tokens) vs. human MS-COCO captions, both scored against the same NSD stimulus crops
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining the per-subject encoders and regenerating captions, the paired CLIPScore or SigLIP difference (MindVLM minus COCO) has a 95% bootstrap CI that includes 0 or is negative.

title: CompactSplat: Spatially Adaptive Gaussian Distribution for Feedforward Scene Reconstruction

official.background: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting models (pixelSplat, MVSplat, DepthSplat, SurfSplat, ...) predict a 3D scene from two posed input images in a single forward pass, with no per-scene optimization. Almost all of them predict one or more Gaussians for every input pixel, which wastes primitives on flat, textureless regions and gives large, redundant representations. The question is whether allocating Gaussians according to image content can cut the primitive count substantially without losing novel-view rendering quality.
official.method:
CompactSplat reuses the DepthSplat/SurfSplat encoder: a multi-view Swin transformer with plane-sweep cost volumes, a Depth Anything V2 monocular branch (ViT-S/B/L for Ours-S/B/L), a 2D U-Net, cascade depth refinement, and a DPT head that predicts a full-resolution Gaussian attribute map A_base. SurfSplat's surface continuity prior and forced alpha blending are also kept. A Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) splits each input image into a quadtree, starting from 16×16 blocks: a block is split into four while its maximum per-channel intensity range exceeds a threshold τ, stopping at 1×1. A Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) builds an average-pooled pyramid of A_base and, for each quadtree leaf, grid-samples attributes from the pyramid level that matches the leaf's depth. The decoded scale multiplier is multiplied by the block size (s_k = Δs_k ⊙ b_k), so one Gaussian covers each leaf.

Training uses MSE + 0.05·LPIPS on rendered target views. Stage 1 fixes τ = 0 (dense, one Gaussian per pixel); stage 2 samples τ ~ U(0, 0.02) at each iteration, so a single checkpoint works at any τ. Ours-S trains for 300K iterations at batch size 16, Ours-B/L for 600K iterations at batch size 8, on A100s. Evaluation follows the standard two-view RE10K protocol at 256×256 (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), plus the HRRC protocol (rendering at 2× and 4× resolution, i.e. 512 and 1024) from SurfSplat. Compactness is reported as Gaussians per pixel (GPP) and total Gaussian count.
official.claim: On RealEstate10K (two 256×256 input views), CompactSplat-L uses 72.6k Gaussians (0.554 per pixel) versus 131.1k (1.0 per pixel) for SurfSplat and still matches it at standard resolution (PSNR 27.567 vs. 27.537, SSIM 0.892 vs. 0.892, LPIPS 0.117 vs. 0.112) while beating it under 4× high-resolution rendering (1024×1024 PSNR 25.252 vs. 24.897, LPIPS 0.276 vs. 0.320).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Novel view synthesis performance on the RealEstate10k dataset. *Note: Due to architectural constraints, YonoSplat is evaluated at 224 × 224 resolution, which may yield marginally inflated metrics compared to the standard 256 × 256 resolution used by other baselines.
official.metric: PSNR (higher is better), SSIM (higher is better), LPIPS (lower is better) on RE10K test novel views at 256×256 and HRRC at 512×512 and 1024×1024; Gaussians per pixel (GPP) and total Gaussian count (lower is better). Single numbers, no error bars or seed counts reported.
official.comparison: CompactSplat-S/B/L (same checkpoint family, inference threshold giving 0.554 GPP) vs. one-Gaussian-per-pixel baselines MVSplat, TranSplat, DepthSplat, SurfSplat, YonoSplat and multi-Gaussian-per-pixel pixelSplat (3 GPP) and HiSplat (1.75 GPP), all listed in the same table on the RE10K test set (the paper does not say whether baseline numbers were re-run or taken from prior work).
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained CompactSplat at about 0.55 GPP on RE10K comes in clearly below SurfSplat at 256×256 (e.g. PSNR more than ~0.3 dB lower), or does not beat SurfSplat's 1024×1024 HRRC PSNR; or the reported GPP turns out to need far more Gaussians to reach the stated quality.

title: Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck

official.background: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) mixes conditional and unconditional predictions of a diffusion model to strengthen conditioning, but applying it at every denoising step hurts sample diversity and FID. Interval Guidance (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024) showed that turning CFG on only during part of the trajectory helps, but the interval is set by hand. This paper casts the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and argues that conditional information only becomes useful after a Fisher-information balance point, which suggests a data-driven rule for when to switch CFG on.
official.method:
At each reverse step the model is run on a mini-batch with conditional and null labels. A batch-wise guidance-gain statistic is computed: ΔĴ(t) = mean over the batch of ||s_θ(x_t, t, c)||² − ||s_θ(x_t, t, ∅)||², where s_θ is the score obtained from the predicted velocity (for SiT). Scanning from t = T toward 0, CFG is off (plain conditional prediction, scale 1) until ΔĴ(t) first crosses a threshold n/(m(t)β*). From then on, standard CFG with scale ω is applied for all remaining steps. In the released Appendix D code for SiT, the rule is implemented as log(max(E_cond − E_uncond, 0) + 1e-12) > −log β*, with mean-squared (per-pixel) score norms, and CFG is also forced on once t ≤ guidance_high. The activation time is shared by the whole batch, and it is training-free.

For the chosen claim: SiT-XL/2 (REPA) on class-conditional ImageNet 256×256, SDE (Euler–Maruyama) sampler, 50 steps, 10k samples, batch size B = 32. Interval Guidance baseline: ω = 1.8, t_l = 0, t_h = 0.7. Ours: ω = 1.9, log β* = 5.9. Each is run with three random seeds, and FID and IS are reported.
official.claim: On ImageNet 256×256 with SiT-XL/2 (REPA), SDE sampler, 50 steps, 10k samples and B = 32, adaptive CFG activation (ω = 1.9, log β* = 5.9) gives FID 4.98 ± 0.06 and IS 298.1 ± 2.6 over 3 seeds, vs. FID 5.18 ± 0.08 and IS 284.1 ± 3.3 for Interval Guidance (ω = 1.8, t_h = 0.7). It has lower FID and higher IS on every seed.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Multi-seed stability. FID and IS over three seeds on SiT-XL/2.
official.metric: FID (lower is better) and IS (higher is better) on 10k samples; ± is std over 3 random seeds (0, 1, 2)
official.comparison: Information-bottleneck adaptive CFG activation vs. Interval Guidance (fixed interval t ∈ [0, 0.7]), same model, sampler, step count, sample count and batch size; guidance scales differ (1.9 vs. 1.8)
official.falsification_criterion: Over 3+ seeds in this setting, the adaptive method's mean FID is not lower than Interval Guidance's by more than about one seed std (i.e. gap under ~0.08), or its IS gain disappears. Another refutation: the gain vanishes when Interval Guidance is run at the same ω = 1.9.

title: SeoulMMOD: A Large-Scale Multimodal Origin-Destination Flow Benchmark

official.background: Origin-destination (OD) flow forecasting predicts how many trips will go from each zone to each other zone in the next hours, which feeds timetable planning, bus control and shared-fleet rebalancing. Public OD benchmarks usually cover one transport mode, or at most two, and span weeks to months, so it is hard to tell whether a demand change is a shift between modes or a change in total travel, or whether models generalize across years. SeoulMMOD releases three years (2023-2025) of hourly OD flows for six intra-urban modes (metro bus, local bus, subway, walk, car, other) across Seoul's 25 districts (625 OD pairs) and 426 sub-districts (181,476 OD pairs), estimated from KT mobile-network signalling data published by the Seoul Metropolitan Government, plus travel time/distance, calendar, rainfall and POI signals.
official.method:
Task: given the past T hours of OD flow for all P = Z² OD pairs and M = 6 modes, predict the next H hours (T = H; H ∈ {6, 12, 24}). The main split is chronological 70/10/20 train/val/test within calendar year 2024. All learned baselines run through BasicTS-compatible configs with Adam, up to 100 epochs, early stopping (patience 10 where enabled), masked-MAE loss, and checkpoint selection on validation MAE; metrics are MAE, RMSE and wMAPE in trip-count units after inverse scaling.

For the joint-vs-separate comparison (Section 4.4), four spatio-temporal models (STID, AGCRN, STAEformer, MTGNN) are trained at the district level, 24h→24h horizon, in two ways: 'Joint' uses the six modes as input and output channels of one model (output dimension 6, no explicit cross-mode mechanism); 'Sep' trains one model per mode. Per-mode and average test MAE are compared.
official.claim: At the district level (625 OD pairs, 24h→24h, 2024 test split), training one STID model per mode lowers average MAE from 24.63 (joint six-mode model) to 20.34 (−17.4%), with Sep better on all six modes; the average-MAE advantage also holds for AGCRN (30.37 → 26.13, Sep better on all six modes) and MTGNN (27.40 → 23.91, though Sep is worse on 'other').
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Joint training vs one model per mode for four spatio-temporal models at the district 24h horizon. Bold marks the lower MAE per (model, mode). ∆ is (Sep − Joint)/Joint.
official.metric: Test MAE in estimated trips per OD pair per hour, lower is better; single run per setting, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: One model per mode (Sep) vs. one joint six-output model (Joint), same architecture, split, horizon and training protocol; STID is the primary (cheapest) case, AGCRN, STAEformer and MTGNN are the other three
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running STID on the district 24h→24h task (ideally over several seeds), the per-mode models' average MAE is not clearly below the joint model's (e.g. the relative reduction is under ~5% or within seed-to-seed spread), or Sep loses on several modes.

title: Where to Look Matters: Rethinking Sub-Volume Sampling in 3D Medical Self-supervised Learning
claim_source: Table 9, page 20 (Appendix C.1; same means as Table 1, page 6)

official.background: Self-supervised pretraining for 3D medical images (CT/MRI) typically trains on fixed-size sub-volumes drawn by random cropping from each scan. Even after foreground cropping, random crops often land on body boundaries, homogeneous tissue or regions already seen, so much of the fixed crop budget goes to low-information views. The paper asks whether choosing where to crop, rather than cropping uniformly at random, improves the representations learned by existing 3D medical SSL methods without changing their objectives or architectures.
official.method:
VolumeProbe-Lite builds, offline and without training, a per-volume bank of K = 40 crop centers in normalized coordinates. Each volume is divided into a coarse 4x4x2 grid of bins; bins are scored by A(v) + alpha*I(v), where the anatomy term A is a location prior (1 minus a z-down-weighted distance to the volume center) plus a margin from the volume boundary, and the informativeness term I is the normalized mean gradient magnitude plus normalized intensity entropy. The top M = 24 bins are refined into the bin center plus up to six axis-offset neighbors, rescored on a crop-sized local patch, and K centers are picked greedily by maximizing A + alpha*I - beta*D, where D is an axis-wise product redundancy penalty against centers already in the bank (alpha = beta = 1, eta = 0.35).

During pretraining, 70% of crop centers are drawn from the cached bank (each center jittered per axis by a uniform integer offset within +/-round(0.05 x the crop size on that axis), then clipped to the image) and 30% by standard random cropping; everything else follows the official VoCo / S2DC / MedGMAE recipes (VoCo-10k corpus of ~9.9k CT volumes, 100k steps; VoCo uses one 64^3 crop, S2DC one 96^3 crop). The pretrained encoders are fine-tuned as Swin-UNETR (VoCo, S2DC) for segmentation on BTCV, AMOS, WORD and Atlas-MRI with 1%, 10% and 100% of labels (1000 epochs for 100%), reporting Dice. The baseline is the same SSL method with random cropping.
official.claim: Replacing random cropping with VolumeProbe-Lite during VoCo pretraining raises AMOS 100%-label segmentation Dice from 84.44 ± 0.1 to 87.52 ± 0.1 (WORD 100%: 84.06 ± 0.2 to 85.56 ± 0.2), and for S2DC raises AMOS 100% Dice from 84.68 ± 0.2 to 87.17 ± 0.1; for VoCo on AMOS 100% it also beats the strongest matched non-random sampler, Uniform-Grid bank sampling (85.79; Table 4, page 7, single run without std).
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Multi-run robustness on segmentation tasks. Dice Score (%) is reported as mean±std over three independent runs.
official.metric: Dice score (%) on the official test split, higher is better; ± is std over three downstream fine-tuning runs (different optimization seeds for 100% labels), not over pretraining runs
official.comparison: VoCo + VolumeProbe-Lite vs. VoCo with random cropping; S2DC + VolumeProbe-Lite vs. S2DC with random cropping; same data, steps, crop size and downstream protocol. Secondary: VoCo + VolumeProbe-Lite vs. VoCo with matched Uniform-Grid / Center-Biased bank sampling (same 70/30 bank/random mix, Table 4)
official.falsification_criterion: With matched pretraining (same corpus, steps and settings) and the same fine-tuning protocol, VoCo + VolumeProbe-Lite does not exceed random-crop VoCo on AMOS 100%-label Dice by clearly more than run-to-run std (e.g. gain under ~1 Dice point), or the gain disappears when pretraining is repeated with a different seed.

title: MvFFN: Multi-view Floor-Plan Feed-Forward Network for Unposed Wide-Baseline Panorama Layout Reconstruction

official.background: Reconstructing a multi-room floor plan and the camera poses from a few unposed, wide-baseline 360° indoor panoramas is useful for real-estate tours, AR and digital twins, but existing systems assume known poses, small baselines or human-in-the-loop correction. Modular pipelines that first estimate poses, then per-view geometry, then vectorize a top-down layout tend to produce duplicate or missing walls and wrong junctions when poses and fused geometry are noisy. The paper asks whether predicting local cross-view wall instances and within-room wall connectivity directly from the images gives more accurate structured floor plans.
official.method:
MvFFN is a feed-forward multi-view transformer over panorama column tokens (EfficientNet-v2 + height compression, 256 column patches per view). Stage 1 trains a 12-layer VGGT-style alternating-attention geometry branch to predict 3-DoF camera poses, floor boundaries, floor point maps and wall-line parameters. It is conditioned on camera rotations from 2-view CovisPose + spanning tree, and its early global attention is masked using CovisPose correspondences. Stage 2 freezes this branch and trains a semantic branch fused with the frozen geometry tokens, plus a 4-layer query decoder. For every anchor column it predicts the Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) field: which columns in all views belong to the anchor's wall and to its next K-1 = 2 clockwise adjacent walls in the same room.

A deterministic Layout Chaining step clusters these dense predictions into global wall instances and directed within-room adjacency, takes longest paths as room wall sequences, fits wall lines from predicted point maps, and intersects consecutive walls to obtain corners. Baselines are modular pipelines: CovisPose+greedy spanning tree poses, LGT-Net per-panorama boundaries (pretrained ZInD checkpoint), and either LGT heuristic post-processing (LGT-PP) or RoomFormer/PolyRoom fine-tuned on ZInD-XV top-down density maps. A GT-pose LGT-PP variant is included as a control. Evaluation uses instance-matched wall and junction precision/recall/F1 and matched-wall distance on 5-view and 8-view test tuples of ZInD-XV.
official.claim: On ZInD-XV, MvFFN + Layout Chaining reaches 5-view wall F1 88.1 and junction F1 73.3 (8-view: 88.4 / 75.0), versus 73.4 / 57.3 (8-view: 74.5 / 59.1) for the strongest modular baseline CovisPose + LGT-Net + LGT-PP, and it also beats that baseline given ground-truth poses (74.4 / 58.1; 8-view 75.3 / 59.9).

title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (CBraMod rows); parameter-matched adapter control in Table 15, page 27

official.background: EEG foundation models (EFMs) such as CBraMod, LaBraM, CodeBrain and CSBrain are pretrained on large multi-subject EEG corpora and then fine-tuned with a classification head for downstream tasks. The paper argues that pretrained EFM tokens make subject identity easy to read out, so in cross-subject (subject-disjoint) evaluation the downstream head has to discount subject-specific structure while also learning the task. It proposes splitting the pretrained tokens into a task 'content' branch and a subject 'style' branch before classification.
official.method:
DEFT is a post-backbone adapter (about 2.07M parameters). The backbone token grid Z (M channel groups x W windows x D) is averaged over channel groups to a window sequence. A Recursive Gaussian Disentangler runs four alternating precision-weighted Gaussian (Kalman-style) updates: a style branch with identity transition and a content branch with a gated mixture of 16 learnable transition matrices, where each branch update first subtracts a learnably gated copy of the other branch's current estimate. The window-level content and style are put back into the token grid with a residual (z_mw - mean_w + c_w), and only the content tokens go to the classification head.

Training loss = cross-entropy on the content branch + λ_ord·max(0, m + Var(S) − Var(C)) + λ_sty·Var(S) (temporal variance across windows) + λ_con·supervised contrastive loss on trial-pooled style vectors with same-subject positives (subject-balanced sampler; subject IDs used only in training) + λ_rec·reconstruction of the mixed window features from content via FiLM parameters predicted from pooled style. The backbone, adapter and head are all fine-tuned (AdamW, lr 1e-4, batch 64, 20 epochs; CBraMod weights λ_ord 0.1, λ_sty 0.01-0.02, λ_con 0.2, λ_rec 0.02). The vanilla baseline fine-tunes the same backbone and head without the adapter. Checkpoints are selected on a subject-disjoint validation split.
official.claim: With the CBraMod backbone under subject-disjoint evaluation, DEFT reaches balanced accuracy 0.7292 ± 0.0059 on MentalArith. (binary workload) and 0.5579 ± 0.0310 on BCIC-IV-2a (4-class motor imagery), beating a parameter-matched Generic Adapter (0.6597 ± 0.0371 and 0.4806 ± 0.0403; +0.070 and +0.077) and vanilla fine-tuning (0.6316 ± 0.0148 and 0.4630 ± 0.0327; +0.098 and +0.095).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on six representative downstream datasets. All metrics report multi-seed mean±std over available seeds. Bold marks the best value in each metric column, and Delta is the absolute improvement of DEFT over vanilla fine-tuning. Chance B-ACC is 0.250, 0.111, 0.200, 0.500, 0.333, and 0.500 for BCIC-IV-2a, FACED, ISRUC-S1, MentalArith., BCIC-Speech, and Mumtaz2016, respectively.
official.metric: Test balanced accuracy (B-ACC), higher is better; mean ± std over seeds 0-2
official.comparison: DEFT adapter + fine-tuning vs. (a) a parameter-matched Generic Adapter (MLP between backbone and classifier, task loss only, same subject-balanced sampler) and (b) vanilla fine-tuning (backbone + head), all from the same public CBraMod checkpoint, same split, same backbone update policy
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running CBraMod Generic Adapter vs. DEFT (and vanilla vs. DEFT) for 3 seeds on the paper's subject-disjoint splits, the mean B-ACC gain of DEFT over the Generic Adapter on MentalArith. or on BCIC-IV-2a is below ~0.03 or not larger than the seed std of either arm.

title: VC-OPD: Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning

official.background: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has improved reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs), but its sequence-level reward gives little credit assignment to individual tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) fixes this by letting a larger teacher score every token of student-generated responses, giving a dense per-token signal. Standard OPD, however, weights all teacher-preferred tokens equally, even though many tokens in a VLM's reasoning are generic templates or language-prior continuations that do not depend on the image. The paper asks whether focusing distillation on image-dependent tokens improves multimodal reasoning.
official.method:
VC-OPD has two stages. Stage I warm-starts the student with supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated responses whose boxed final answer is correct. Stage II is on-policy distillation: the student samples a response under the real image; the teacher scores the same response twice, once with the original image and once with a counterfactual image (default: 60% patch dropout). The per-token direction term is log p_teacher(original) - log p_student (the standard reverse-KL OPD signal, normalized). The visual-dependence score is log p_teacher(original) - log p_teacher(counterfactual); it is turned into a soft weight sigmoid((delta - tau)/T), tuned so roughly 10% of tokens are emphasized, and then mass-normalized so the weights in each response sum to the number of response tokens. The token advantage is weight x direction, used in a policy-gradient loss.

Main setting: student Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, teacher Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, training on ViRL39K (~39K verifiable visual reasoning examples) for 200 optimization steps with the verl framework (lr 5e-6, max response length 8192). Baselines from the same student checkpoint: GRPO, PAPO, and RKL (vanilla reverse-KL on-policy distillation). Evaluation is exact-match accuracy at the '@8' setting with temperature 1.0 on seven benchmarks (Geometry3K, MathVerse, MathVista, We-Math, MMMU-Pro, LogicVista, Super-CLEVR Counting), with the unweighted mean reported.
official.claim: With a Qwen2.5-VL-7B teacher and Qwen2.5-VL-3B student trained on ViRL39K, VC-OPD reaches 48.87 average exact-match accuracy over seven multimodal reasoning benchmarks, vs. 46.64 for reverse-KL on-policy distillation (RKL) and 44.47 for GRPO, and beats RKL on all seven benchmarks.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on multimodal reasoning benchmarks. We report exact-match accuracy under the @8 setting with inference temperature 1.0. Avg. denotes the unweighted average over all listed benchmarks.
official.metric: Exact-match accuracy (%) after answer extraction, @8 setting at temperature 1.0, unweighted mean over 7 benchmarks; higher is better. No ± reported (single run, no seeds or confidence intervals).
official.comparison: VC-OPD vs. RKL (vanilla on-policy distillation), GRPO and PAPO, all from the same Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct checkpoint and 7B teacher, same data and training budget
official.falsification_criterion: Under the 7B-teacher / 3B-student setting, VC-OPD's 7-benchmark average is not clearly above RKL's (e.g. gain under ~1 point, or within the run-to-run spread across a few seeds), or VC-OPD fails to beat RKL on most of the seven benchmarks.

title: What DNA Foundation Models Learn Beyond Sequence Composition

official.background: DNA foundation models (FMs) are often evaluated on genomic classification tasks such as promoters, enhancers, splice sites and transcription-factor binding. Many of these tasks can be partly solved from short-motif frequencies and nucleotide content alone, yet FM evaluations rarely include a simple compositional control such as normalized k-mer counts. The paper asks whether frozen FM embeddings carry predictive information beyond global k-mer composition, and which models actually add value when combined with it.
official.method:
The authors use 57 classification datasets from the DNA Foundation Models Benchmark (Feng et al., 2025), with the train/test splits that the benchmark provides. For each sequence they compute L1-normalized global 6-mer frequencies (4096 dimensions, K6) and frozen, mean-pooled final-layer embeddings X from five FMs: NTv3-650M, Caduceus-Ph, HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2 and Evo2-1B. No features are scaled.

In the T6 incremental-utility protocol, a Random Forest is trained on K6 alone and on the concatenation [K6; X] (fixed order: 6-mer then FM). Model selection happens within the training split by stratified 4-fold CV (shuffle, seed 42) over 200 or 500 trees, with max depth 20, sqrt feature subsampling and min split size 2. Tuning uses AUROC for binary tasks and accuracy for multiclass tasks. The selected model is refit and evaluated on the held-out test split. The reported quantity is ΔMCC = MCC([K6; X]) − MCC(K6) per dataset, summarized as mean, median and the count of datasets that improve.
official.claim: Under a matched Random Forest protocol on 57 genomic classification datasets, concatenating frozen mean-pooled NTv3-650M embeddings with 6-mer frequencies improves test MCC over 6-mer features alone on 46/57 datasets (mean ΔMCC +0.072, median +0.055), whereas HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2 and Evo2-1B lower mean MCC (−0.016, −0.034, −0.075).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Incremental utility in the T6 protocol, using exact 6-mer frequencies and frozen, mean-pooled FM embeddings. Differences are test MCC of [6-mer; FM] minus test MCC of 6-mer alone. Positive/negative/tie counts are based on unrounded dataset-level differences.
official.metric: Test MCC difference (higher = FM adds value), [6-mer; FM] minus 6-mer alone, per dataset; mean, median and count of improved datasets over 57. Single run per dataset; no error bars, seeds or significance test reported for this comparison.
official.comparison: Random Forest on [6-mer; FM embedding] vs. the same Random Forest protocol on 6-mer frequencies alone, for each of five FMs
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the matched protocol (with the 6-mer baseline refit under the same CV) gives NTv3 a mean ΔMCC near zero or negative, or improves clearly fewer than half of the 57 datasets; or HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2 and Evo2 show gains comparable to NTv3.

title: Variance-Optimal State Resampling for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (VSR repeat runs: Table 7, page 26)

official.background: In GRPO-style RL with verifiable rewards, a rollout group where every sample fails (or every sample succeeds) has zero group-relative advantage and gives no gradient. On hard tasks most groups launched from the initial prompt fail, so much of the rollout budget is wasted. Intermediate states partway along a trajectory often give mixed outcomes, which carry learning signal, but on-policy rollouts from the prompt rarely reach them. The paper asks which state distribution minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator under a fixed rollout budget. Under homogeneity assumptions it derives a Neyman allocation µ(s) ∝ d^π(s) σ^π(s), where σ^π(s) is the standard deviation of the reward from state s.
official.method:
VSR (Variance-driven State Resampling) is a plug-in to GRPO/GiGPO. It keeps a recency-windowed replay buffer of prefix states taken from recent successful trajectories, which stands in for d^π. A replay ratio ρ of each batch is launched from buffered prefixes instead of fresh prompts. Prefixes are sampled in proportion to a zero-cost score σ̂ = sqrt(p̂(1−p̂)) with p̂ = (1−α)·p0(x) + α·R(τ), where α is the prefix's normalized position in the trajectory and p0(x) is the success rate of the prompt's fresh rollout group. Prefix tokens are masked out of the loss, and the usual group-relative loss is applied to the newly generated continuations. No density-ratio correction is applied.

In the agentic setting, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct are trained with GiGPO as the base algorithm on Sokoban and three BabyAI levels (SynthLoc, OneRoom, MiniBoss). The buffer is filled only from the model's own trajectories, with no expert cold start. Hyperparameters (Table 5): replay ratio 0.3, recency window 5 steps, group size 8, batch size 32, learning rate 1e-6, no KL penalty, max response length 256, 150 updates for 1.5B, on one H200. GiGPO and VSR+GiGPO use matched model, environment, reward and training settings. Success rate is averaged over 128 fixed map seeds per environment.
official.claim: On BabyAI with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, adding VSR to GiGPO raises average success over SynthLoc/OneRoom/MiniBoss from 30.4% to 47.6% (SynthLoc 32.3→51.2, OneRoom 27.9→54.6, MiniBoss 30.9→36.9). Three independent VSR runs average 48.2 ± 2.4 SD.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Agentic-task success rates (%) on Sokoban and BabyAI. Best result is in bold.
official.metric: Task success rate (%) over 128 fixed map seeds per level, higher is better. The Table 2 entries are single training runs with no error bars. The only reported run-to-run spread is for VSR on Qwen2.5-1.5B BabyAI (runs 47.6/50.8/46.1, mean 48.2 ± 2.4 SD).
official.comparison: VSR+GiGPO vs. GiGPO under matched model, environment, reward and training settings (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, BabyAI average)
official.falsification_criterion: A matched reproduction gives a BabyAI average for VSR+GiGPO that is not clearly above GiGPO. For example, the gap is under about 5 points, or it falls within the run-to-run spread of the two methods when each is trained with several seeds.

title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks

official.background: Neural networks can memorize their training data, including random inputs and wrong labels, yet still learn features that generalize. Recent work on language models (Merullo et al., 2025) argued that the top of the Fisher information (loss-curvature) eigenspectrum holds generalizing structure while low-curvature directions hold memorized samples, so projecting weights onto top Fisher directions can remove memorized content. The intuition is that the Fisher is an average of per-sample Fishers: directions shared across many samples add up, while sample-specific directions are diluted by a factor of about 1/|D|. This paper tests that picture in controlled settings where the memorized content is known: CIFAR-10 image classifiers with injected noise, a small transformer doing in-context regression, and a solvable linear model.
official.method:
Input-noise setting: the CIFAR-10 training set is augmented with 500 synthetic images (1% of the training set). Each is sampled from a Gaussian whose mean and variance match a randomly chosen CIFAR-10 class, and it is given the label of an independently chosen random class, so it can only be fit by memorization. A ResNet-20 is trained to 100% training accuracy (200 epochs, SGD, lr 0.1 decayed 10x at epochs 100 and 150, batch size 128, weight decay 1e-4, momentum 0.9).

For one layer at a time, the exact per-layer Fisher F = (1/N) Σ_i Σ_c p(c|x_i) s_ic s_ic^T, with s_ic the gradient of log p(c|x_i) with respect to that layer's weights, is computed over the full training set (CIFAR-10 plus Gaussian images) and diagonalized (no K-FAC approximation). The layer's weights are then projected onto the span of the top-k eigenvectors, all other layers are left unchanged, BatchNorm statistics are re-estimated, and accuracy is measured on CIFAR-10 train, CIFAR-10 test and the Gaussian set (under their assigned labels) as a function of k.
official.claim: Projecting the first conv layer of a ResNet-20 (trained on CIFAR-10 plus 500 memorized Gaussian images) onto its top k ≈ 45 Fisher eigenvectors keeps CIFAR-10 train/test accuracy at about 94%/78% (vs. 100%/83% unprojected) while accuracy on the memorized Gaussian images is only about 23%; the same projection on the last layer gives no such separation.
official.claim_caption: Figure 1: Layer-dependent decoupling of memorization and generalization via Fisher projection: memorized Gaussian images. Classification accuracy as a function of the number of retained top Fisher eigenvectors k, computed over the full training set (CIFAR-10 and Gaussian images) for a single layer of a ResNet-20. Green: CIFAR-10 test; blue: CIFAR-10 train; red: memorized Gaussian samples. A) In the first layer, CIFAR-10 train and test accuracy rise in tandem and reach a maximum at k ≈ 45, while accuracy on memorized Gaussian samples remains at ≈ 30%, demonstrating selective de-memorization at negligible cost to generalization. B) In the last layer, all three curves rise sharply even for very small k, with no separation between them at any point, indicating that memorized and structured representations have merged and can no longer be separated.
official.metric: Classification accuracy (higher is better) on CIFAR-10 train, CIFAR-10 test, and the 500 Gaussian images under their assigned labels, as a function of the number k of retained top Fisher eigenvectors. Shaded bands are shown but not defined in the caption (Appendix Fig. 7 reports per-layer curves averaged over n = 4 models). Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Accuracy on clean CIFAR-10 (train and test) vs. accuracy on memorized Gaussian images after the same first-layer Fisher projection, across k; also first layer vs. last layer.
official.falsification_criterion: After retraining the setup and projecting the first conv layer onto its top-k Fisher eigenvectors (Fisher computed on the full training set), there is no k at which CIFAR-10 test accuracy is within ~5 points of the unprojected model while Gaussian-set accuracy is below ~40%, i.e. the clean and memorized curves rise together as they do for the last layer.

title: DIGS: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation

official.background: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) asks which Gaussians belong to the object named by a free-form text query. Most methods give each Gaussian a single semantic feature (a CLIP embedding or an instance ID), usually learned by 1-4 hours of per-scene gradient training. Recent closed-form approaches such as Splat Feature Solver remove that training. Either way, a Gaussian that sits on the boundary between two objects must commit to one feature, which blurs or aliases rendered mask edges and hurts retrieval accuracy.
official.method:
DIGS starts from a fixed, pre-reconstructed Mip-Splatting scene (30k iterations) and runs two training-free stages. Stage 1 (class-agnostic mapping) streams the training frames. For each frame it computes SAM ViT-H automatic masks (after mask NMS), Hungarian-matches them on IoU to a label map rendered from the current state, and back-projects the matched labels onto each pixel's top-K contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian keeps an evidence accumulator, updated by a tempered Dirichlet rule H_ij += eta_i W_ij with eta_i = tau / (S_i + W_i + tau), and sparsified to its top-M labels. A visibility-aware decay is applied first, and per-instance match/miss counters filter out unstable instances. Label maps are rendered by 'late argmax', which takes the argmax over labels of the alpha-weighted sum of each contributing Gaussian's top-M distribution, instead of giving each Gaussian a hard label before rendering. Hyperparameters: tau=5, M=3, gamma=0.95, theta_iou=0.4, lambda=0.7.

Stage 2 renders each stable instance in isolation from its top-B training views and averages Open CLIP ViT-B/16 image embeddings of the crops. In the LLM+CLIP variant, GPT-4.1 receives paired context and isolated view crops of the instance and writes a one-line attribute description. That description's CLIP-text embedding is fused as lambda*visual + (1-lambda)*text with lambda=0.7. A query is CLIP-text-encoded and matched by cosine similarity to pick one instance. The deployed numbers also apply retrieval thresholds: a top-1/top-2 cosine-margin filter Delta_min=0.12 and an absolute fused-cosine floor sigma_abs=0.25 (Appendix D.1). The paper does not say what is output when a query is rejected. For an accepted query, the predicted mask is the late-argmax label map at the test view restricted to that instance. Evaluation follows the OpenGaussian 3D-native protocol on LERF-OVS (4 scenes) with mIoU and mAcc@0.25.
official.claim: On LERF-OVS under the OpenGaussian 3D-native protocol, DIGS (LLM+CLIP) reaches 71.95 mean mIoU versus 62.16 for the authors' reproduction of the training-free Splat Feature Solver and 60.55 for their reproduction of LaGa, and DIGS has the higher mIoU on every one of the four scenes.

official.metric: mIoU (%) per scene and mean over the 4 LERF-OVS scenes, higher is better; mAcc@0.25 also reported. Single run, no error bars or seeds reported (the paper's checklist answers [No] on statistical significance).
official.comparison: DIGS (LLM+CLIP) and DIGS (CLIP only) vs. Splat Feature Solver† and LaGa† (both re-run by the authors under the same protocol); other rows are copied from papers or re-evaluated by OpenGaussian.
