title: Learning Deployable Causal Action Geometry under Temporal Non-Stationarity

official.background: Platforms that set continuous actions such as prices or budgets learn response curves from logged time series, but demand, traffic and policies drift over time. A model fitted to pooled historical data can absorb these drifting baselines into the action-response surface and so rank actions wrongly for future periods, even when it fits past outcomes well. The paper argues that a fully stable future response law is not identifiable, and proposes to learn only the part needed for decisions: the shape of the response across actions after removing period-specific level and amplitude changes.
official.method:
The target, 'deployable causal action geometry', is the action-response shape left after anchoring at a reference action a0 on a link scale (identity removes additive shifts, log removes multiplicative shifts) and profiling out a positive per-period scale factor. Estimation is honest and two-stage: Stage I builds cross-fitted orthogonal (doubly robust, kernel-localized) pilot estimates of the anchored responses per period on a pilot sample; Stage II, on an independent selection sample, chooses the link, representation and shape by minimizing a normalized profiled geometry loss. The deployed rule picks the action that maximizes the selected shape; the selected geometry is refitted on separate refit data.

For the claim, the authors use the Dominick's orange-juice panel from bayesm 3.1-7 (deal=0, feat=0; action = price per ounce over its trailing 13-week median, a0 = 1), keep the real histories, prices and temporal design, and simulate only the outcome. In setting A the noiseless response is 4.0 + 1.2 tanh(eta_t(H)) + s_t(H) rho*(u(H), a), i.e. exact persistence of the shape on the identity scale with drifting level and amplitude; Gaussian noise with SD equal to 0.20 times the response SD is added. Four expanding-window chronological folds are used (first: train weeks 53-91, validate 92-104, test 105-117), with the 83 stores split into 42 pilot, 21 selection and 20 refit stores. Representations are brand-based or history-clustered (11/22/33 cells), the action grid has 31 points in [0.85, 1.15], and the metric is normalized regret of the recommended action against the true noiseless curve on test rows.

title: Barycentric Guidance: Turning Foundation Image Editors into Continuous Affective Controllers

official.background: The valence-arousal (VA) model describes emotion as a point in a continuous 2D plane (unpleasant to pleasant, calm to excited). VA-based image editing should move an image's expression or mood to any target VA point while keeping identity and background fixed. Existing VA editors (e.g. GANmut, EmoStyle) are trained per domain and cover rare VA regions such as low arousal or high-arousal negative states poorly. Foundation image editors (FLUX, Qwen Image Edit) make high-quality discrete emotion edits, but interpolating their text prompts gives poorly calibrated, abrupt changes, so they do not give continuous VA control out of the box.
official.method:
Barycentric Guidance is training-free. A 2D triangle mesh is built over the VA plane whose vertices are discrete emotion anchors (for faces: AffectNet mean VA locations of basic emotions, plus excited, sleepy and serene). For a target (v, a), the enclosing (or nearest) triangle is found and barycentric weights (w1, w2, w3) are solved. Instead of interpolating text embeddings, the editor's denoiser outputs for the three anchor prompts ('Change this persons facial expression to be <emotion> while maintaining the same facial features, composition, lighting, and camera angle') are combined as sum_i w_i D(x_t, y_i), combined with CFG (w_cfg = 4.0) whose scale is increased with VA magnitude (w*_cfg = 1 + (w_cfg - 1) sqrt(v^2 + a^2)).

For faces, an optional geometry step first generates the three anchor edits (30 steps each), morphs them using face landmarks weighted by the barycentric weights, then restarts diffusion from step 10 of 30 (SDEdit style) with Barycentric Guidance (180 NFEs per image in total). The backbone is FLUX.2-dev. Evaluation: for each source image a 10x10 grid of target VA values uniformly spaced in [-1, 1] is edited, VA of each output is predicted with EmotiEffLib, and RMSE between predicted and target VA is reported. Baselines are EmoStyle (StyleGAN latent editing, trained on FFHQ, default repo config) and GANmut (retrained on AffectNet; no RMSE because it uses polar coordinates).
official.claim: On facial expression editing over a 10x10 grid of target VA values, Barycentric Guidance on FLUX.2-dev reaches lower VA-target RMSE than EmoStyle on all three datasets: 0.433 vs. 0.610 (AffectNet), 0.418 vs. 0.568 (FFHQ), and 0.412 vs. 0.550 (CelebA-HQ).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Facial Expression Editing comparison with other VA editing models. We treat Entropy, VA Std, RMSE, and S*_2D as the primary controllability metrics. †: The method does not control VA directly; instead, it approximates VA editing using polar coordinates to steer emotion.
official.metric: RMSE between EmotiEffLib-predicted VA and target VA (lower is better). Single numbers; no std, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: Barycentric Guidance (FLUX.2-dev, with scaled CFG and face morphing) vs. EmoStyle, the strongest VA-editing baseline with a reported RMSE, on the same source datasets and the same VA grid and VA predictor
official.falsification_criterion: With EmotiEffLib as the VA predictor and the same 10x10 VA grid, Barycentric Guidance's RMSE is not clearly below EmoStyle's (e.g. the gap is under about 0.05, or it reverses) on any of the three datasets.

title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation

official.background: Resting-state functional connectomes are correlation matrices between brain regions, used for biomarker discovery and cohort analysis. A conditional generator of connectomes could augment small neuroimaging datasets, but its samples must be valid correlation matrices (symmetric, positive definite, unit diagonal) and must also land in the right class-conditional region. Prior manifold-aware generators such as DiffeoCFM (flow matching in a normalized-Cholesky pullback chart) guarantee validity, but the authors argue that validity alone does not recover the class-conditional structure, especially when coarse binary labels (control vs. patient) merge heterogeneous subgroups.
official.method:
MAGNET runs diffusion in the normalized-Cholesky chart: a correlation matrix C = LL^T is mapped to the strict lower triangle of diag(L)^-1 L, standardized with training statistics, and decoding inverts the map and renormalizes, so every sample is a valid correlation matrix. The denoiser reshapes the noisy chart vector into a symmetric zero-diagonal d x d matrix and treats each row as an ROI token, adding learned ROI positional, timestep, subtype and bridge embeddings, then applies a 4-layer pre-norm Transformer (hidden 128, 4 QK-normalized heads, GeGLU width 512) and a row-wise projection plus symmetrization back to chart coordinates. Three controllers are added: class-anchored conditioning (per-class diagonal GMM in chart space with K chosen by BIC, giving subtype tokens), an amortized structural bridge (a small predictor of 16-d spectral/connectivity summaries, trained to match a teacher target from subtype atoms), and relevance-preserving corruption (per-coordinate forward noise variance reduced early in diffusion for coordinates where conditional and unconditional denoiser outputs differ). Loss = diffusion loss (min-SNR weighted) + 0.1 bridge loss + 0.1 spectral loss. Sampling uses 6 DDIM steps with an orthogonalized, tanh-saturated classifier-free guidance at gamma = 1.5, followed by class-wise affine calibration of the latent fit on the training split.

For Table 4, the setting is a quality-controlled 831-scan ABIDE cohort (CPAC preprocessing, band-pass filtering, no global signal regression) with binary labels (control vs. autism), parcellated with AAL116 or CC200, evaluated over 10 group-aware train/validation splits (10% validation). Baselines (DiffeoCFM, DiffeoGauss, TriangCFM, TriangDDPM, GDSS-proj) use the same splits and preprocessing, and the flow baselines use matched 6-point ODE grids. Class-conditional fidelity is alpha-Precision, beta-Recall and their harmonic mean alpha,beta-F1 (Alaa et al. 2022) of generated vs. held-out real connectomes; CAS utility is a logistic regression on tangent-space features of generated samples, tested on real validation connectomes.
official.claim: On ABIDE (831 scans, 10 group-aware splits), MAGNET reaches alpha,beta-F1 0.69 ± 0.05 vs. 0.59 ± 0.05 for DiffeoCFM with the AAL116 atlas, and 0.66 ± 0.06 vs. 0.58 ± 0.03 with the CC200 atlas, the best of all generators on both atlases.
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Generalization to higher-resolution ABIDE parcellations. We evaluate MAGNET and the competing generators on AAL116, an anatomically defined 116-region atlas, and CC200, a functionally derived parcellation with approximately 200 regions. Both settings use the same quality-controlled 831-scan ABIDE cohort and 10-split group-aware evaluation protocol. We report class-conditional support fidelity, downstream classifier-based utility, and wall-clock sampling time. Results are mean ± standard deviation across splits. The Real Data row provides the empirical reference, and bold denotes the best generative model within each atlas.
official.metric: alpha,beta-F1 (harmonic mean of alpha-Precision and beta-Recall, higher is better); ± is the standard deviation across 10 train/validation splits. alpha-Precision, beta-Recall, CAS ROC-AUC/F1 and sampling time are also reported.
official.comparison: MAGNET vs. DiffeoCFM (strongest baseline), plus DiffeoGauss, TriangCFM, TriangDDPM and GDSS-proj, all under the same splits, preprocessing and a 6-step sampling budget; Real Data row is a split-vs-split oracle.
official.falsification_criterion: On ABIDE with AAL116 or CC200 under the same 10-split protocol, MAGNET's mean alpha,beta-F1 does not exceed DiffeoCFM's by more than about one split standard deviation (e.g. AAL116 margin below ~0.05), or DiffeoCFM matches or beats MAGNET.

title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (also Tables 11 and 12, Appendix B.4-B.5, pages 21-22)

official.background: Transformer hidden states mix what a sentence means with how it is phrased: two paraphrases of the same fact get different activations. Interpretability tools such as sparse autoencoders, probes, CKA, or concept erasers like LEACE do not directly ask which directions of a representation stay the same when a sentence is reworded. The paper casts this as a local-to-global consistency problem: each paraphrase pair says that two activations should agree, and the directions on which all pairs agree should carry the content (e.g. the fact) independent of surface form.
official.method:
Paraphrases are nodes of a graph and paraphrase pairs are edges; each node holds a mean-pooled hidden state h from a frozen model at layer floor(0.67 L) (layer 8 for GPT-2). A restriction map P^T maps hidden states to a k = 128 edge space, where P (d x k) holds the top-128 joint-PCA components of the paired activations. The edge-space sheaf Laplacian is L_F = (1/N) sum_i Δ_i Δ_i^T with Δ_i = P^T h_i^(1) - P^T h_i^(2), i.e. the projected within-pair difference covariance. H^0 is the span of its 20 lowest-eigenvalue eigenvectors, pulled back to hidden space as P v_j; no training of the model or of any network is involved.

Retrieval test (Table 2): ROME CounterFact, 500 facts with several paraphrases each, split 70/30 by fact (350 train, 150 test). For the main table the pair-only graph is used (each fact's paraphrases chained by K-1 edges), and P and H^0 are fit on the training facts only. Held-out paraphrases are projected into each subspace and scored by top-1 nearest-centroid retrieval among held-out facts, with 'hard' distractors restricted to facts of the same relation. Baselines on the same activations: full hidden state ('Full'), LEACE-preserved subspace (LEACE eraser for the binary paraphrase/non-paraphrase concept, rank d-1, 'LEACE-full'), top-20 PCs of the LEACE-preserved activations (LEACE-20D), top-20 PCA (PCA-20), and a random 20-dim subspace (Rand-20).
official.claim: On held-out ROME CounterFact hard same-relation retrieval (150 test facts), the 20-dim sheaf H^0 subspace achieves higher top-1 accuracy than the full-dimensional LEACE-preserved representation (identical to the raw full hidden state) on all 8 models (gaps +1.5 to +42.2 pp, mean +17.1 pp) (e.g. GPT-2 85.3% vs 43.1%, Gemma-2-9B 77.9% vs 54.4%, Phi-2 87.1% vs 69.1%), and beats every 20-dim baseline (PCA-20, LEACE-20D, Rand-20) by at least 20 pp on every model.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Held-out CounterFact retrieval (top-1 accuracy, hard same-relation distractors, k = 20 dims, 70/30 train/test split, n_test = 150 facts). Sheaf H^0 basis and LEACE eraser are fit on training facts only, and evaluation is on held-out facts not seen during fitting. Across eight architectures sheaf H^0 at 20 dimensions beats LEACE-preserved at full hidden dimension, with gaps ranging from +1.5pp (OLMo-2) to +42.2pp (GPT-2).
official.metric: Top-1 retrieval accuracy (%) on 150 held-out facts with same-relation distractors, higher is better; single run, no error bars or CIs reported in Table 2
official.comparison: Sheaf H^0 (20 dims, joint-PCA restriction map, fit on training facts) vs. full hidden state / LEACE-preserved subspace (full dim), LEACE-20D, PCA-20 and Rand-20 on the same activations and split, across GPT-2, Mistral-7B, OLMo-2-7B, Phi-2, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B. The strongest label-free 20-dim baselines, CCA and PLS, appear only in Table 12 (a separate run of the same protocol), where H^0 beats every label-free method by +9 to +36 pp
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the protocol, 20-dim H^0 does not beat the full-dimensional (LEACE-preserved) representation by a clear margin on GPT-2 (e.g. gap below ~15 pp instead of +42 pp), or the mean gap over the 8 models is near zero, or H^0 fails to beat Rand-20 and PCA-20 by a wide margin.

title: Compute-optimal data scaling for neural surrogates via multi-fidelity training
claim_source: Table 14 (Appendix J.1), page 40; scaling curves with ±1 std bands in Figure 22 (Appendix J.1); summarized in Figure 9, page 10

official.background: Neural surrogates for PDEs are trained on data from numerical simulators, and as datasets grow the cost of generating that data can exceed the cost of training. Unlike data in most domains, the cost of a simulated sample can be tuned: fewer solver iterations or coarser grids give cheaper but less accurate samples, with known convergence rates. The paper asks whether, for a fixed data-generation budget, a mixture of cheap low-fidelity and expensive high-fidelity samples gives a more accurate surrogate than spending the whole budget on high-fidelity samples.
official.method:
Fidelity is a discrete menu Ξ (here the number of multigrid V-cycles K ∈ {1, 2, 3} applied from a zero initial guess to the 1D Poisson equation at resolution 64; cost c(K) = K). A dataset is drawn under budget B by sampling fidelities from a softmax over the min-max-normalized fidelity ξ̂ with temperature-like parameter λ (λ → +∞ is high-fidelity only, implemented as λ = 20; λ = -20 is almost all lowest fidelity), so lower λ yields more, cheaper samples. The normalized budget B̃ = B / c(ξmax) is the number of high-fidelity samples the budget would buy. Inputs are random windowed-Fourier right-hand sides; data are generated procedurally per seed.

The surrogate (FiLM-conditioned U-Net, 4 levels, base 64 channels; or FiLM-FNO) receives ξ̂ as a conditioning input through a sinusoidal encoding plus MLP, and is trained with Adam (lr 1e-4, 2,000 warm-up steps, cosine decay, 20,000 steps, batch 20, MSE on whitened outputs). At test time it is conditioned on ξ̂ = 1 and scored by relative L2 error against 100 highest-fidelity (K = 3) test samples. For each budget, λ is swept and the best λ* (multi-fidelity, MF) is compared with λ → ∞ (high fidelity only, HF).
official.claim: On 1D Poisson with multigrid solver-error fidelities, a fidelity-conditioned U-Net trained on the optimal fidelity mixture reaches relative L2 error 0.295 vs. 0.770 for high-fidelity-only training at B̃ = 100, and 0.081 vs. 0.214 at B̃ = 300 (FNO: 0.318 vs. 0.517 and 0.131 vs. 0.226), with the gap vanishing by B̃ = 10,000.
official.claim_caption: Table 14: Summary of the Poisson experiment results (truncation/solver error). Multi-fidelity (MF) uses the optimal λ*; High-fidelity (HF) is the high-fidelity-only baseline (λ → ∞). Mtrain denotes the number of training samples; Δ(%) denotes the relative change in number of training samples and error compared to the high-fidelity baseline.
official.metric: relative L2 error on 100 test samples at the highest fidelity (lower is better); mean over 6 training seeds (1D); the table reports no std, the figures show ±1 std bands
official.comparison: Multi-fidelity training at the best mixture λ* vs. high-fidelity-only training (λ → ∞) at the same data-generation budget B̃, same architecture and training recipe
official.falsification_criterion: At B̃ = 100 or 300 on 1D Poisson (solver axis), no mixture λ < 20 yields a U-Net test error clearly below (beyond seed std) the high-fidelity-only U-Net, or the reduction is far smaller than the reported ~62%.

title: MID: Mask-Image Distributional Divergence for Evaluating Medical Image Segmentation
claim_source: Table 4, page 18 (Appendix E); summarised in Section 4.4, pages 7-8

official.background: Medical image segmentation is normally evaluated with per-sample metrics such as Dice and HD95, which need a ground-truth mask for every prediction. That rules them out on unlabeled deployment data and says nothing about whether a set of predictions matches the population of real masks. In generative modelling, FID compares the feature distributions of two sets without pairing samples. The paper adapts this idea to segmentation, arguing that segmentation quality is a property of the joint image-mask distribution: a mask can look plausible on its own yet be wrong for the image it goes with.
official.method:
MID encodes each image once and each foreground class of its mask as a separate binary mask with the same frozen pretrained medical encoder (MedSigLIP; 3-D volumes are handled by averaging patch-token embeddings over axial slices). The image and mask embeddings are concatenated into one joint vector per (image, class), projected with incremental PCA (k = 128) fitted on the reference set, and fitted with a Gaussian (Ledoit-Wolf covariance). MID is the squared 2-Wasserstein (Frechet) distance between the reference Gaussian (clean image + ground-truth mask pairs from a 10-dataset pool) and the candidate Gaussian, with no per-sample pairing.

For the claim, candidate sets are made by corrupting ground-truth masks in the evaluation split with five signed-distance-transform corruptions (elastic boundary deformation, smooth erosion, smooth dilation, blob false positives, partial missing slices) at mild/moderate/severe levels, over 56 organ groups, giving 840 cells. For each cell, MID and each baseline are computed against the reference, and mean Dice and HD95 are computed against the paired ground truth. Spearman rho is then taken across the 840 cells. Baselines use the same encoder unless stated otherwise: FID on mask features only (FID-mask), FID on image features only (FID-img), KID on mask features, FID on Inception-v3 axial mid-slice renderings, and mean Mahalanobis distance from the joint reference Gaussian.
official.claim: Across 840 controlled-corruption cells (56 organ groups x 5 corruption types x 3 severities), MID correlates with mean Dice at Spearman rho = -0.55 [95% CI -0.61, -0.49] and with HD95 at +0.72 [+0.66, +0.77], stronger than every unpaired baseline: mask-only FID (-0.47 / +0.61), Mahalanobis (-0.42 / +0.55), Inception FID (-0.38 / +0.49), KID (-0.28 / +0.36) and image-only FID (-0.03 / +0.04).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Metric comparison on the controlled corruption sweep. Spearman rho is computed cell-by-cell against mean Dice and against HD95 across 840 cells (56 organ groups x 5 corruption types x 3 severity levels); bootstrap CIs use 1000 replicates. The two reference targets are inversely related (Dice goes up, HD95 goes down for better segmentations), so a metric that tracks segmentation quality should produce a negative rho against Dice and a positive rho against HD95 of comparable magnitude.
official.metric: Spearman rho between the distributional metric and mean Dice (more negative is better) or HD95 (more positive is better) across 840 cells; brackets are the paper's 95% bootstrap CIs (1000 replicates; the paper does not state the resampling unit beyond computing rho cell-by-cell). Single fixed seed; the embedding is deterministic.
official.comparison: Joint MID vs. FID-mask, FID-img, KID (all MedSigLIP), FID-Inception (2-D mid-slice) and joint Mahalanobis, all on the same corruption sweep
official.falsification_criterion: On the same corruption sweep, MID's |rho| with Dice or HD95 is not larger than that of mask-only FID computed with the same encoder and PCA protocol, or MID's |rho| with Dice falls below that of the Mahalanobis or KID baselines.

title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
claim_source: Table 6 (Appendix D.4), page 25; same experiment family as Figure 5 (page 8) / Figure 9 and Table 4 (pages 22-23)

official.background: Long-context training of LLMs and multimodal models packs many sequences into one batch and uses structured attention masks (document, sliding-window, prefix-LM, share-question, block-sparse) to encode which tokens may attend to each other. FlashAttention-3 (FA3) is fast on Hopper GPUs but supports only a few mask types natively. General-mask alternatives such as FlexAttention (compiled Triton kernels) and MagiAttention (AttnSlice + Flex-Flash-Attention kernel) accept arbitrary masks but are slower, and the original FlashMask kernel, which encodes masks with four O(n) column-wise boundary vectors, targets Ampere and does not use Hopper's TMA/WGMMA pipeline.
official.method:
FlashMask-3 keeps FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask representation (per key column j, boundary vectors LTS, LTE, UTS, UTE give the masked query intervals) and builds a Hopper kernel on the FA3 TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline. It reuses 96 otherwise idle producer threads as a third role, the KV Index Generator, which scans the boundary vectors and emits a queue of KV blocks classified as fully masked (skipped), partially masked (row-interval mask applied) or unmasked. The KV Loader issues TMA loads only for listed blocks, and the MMA consumers run WGMMA. A preemptive persistent-tile scheduler (CTAs atomically claim the next Q-block) balances SMs under irregular masks.

Benchmark (Appendix D.1.1): one H100 80GB SXM5, BF16, head dim 128, 32 heads (MHA), batch size B = max(floor(128K/S), 1) (B=16 at 8K, B=1 at 128K), forward+backward, 10 warm-up and 50 timed iterations. TFLOPs/s for every method is computed with the same sparsity-aware FLOP count (density of non-skipped tiles times 4·B·H·S²·D times 3.5 for fwd+bwd), so the ratios between methods equal inverse runtime ratios. Baselines are FlexAttention (PyTorch 2.8.0) and MagiAttention (commit d97b72). FA3 is also reported as a reference on the masks it supports.
official.claim: On a single H100 (BF16, d=128, fwd+bwd), for Sliding Window, Causal Document and Document masks at 8K, 32K and 128K, FlashMask-3 has higher throughput than both general-mask baselines in all 9 settings, by more than the summed std. Against MagiAttention: 290.3 vs 166.2 TFLOPs/s (8K Sliding Window), 435.5 vs 328.8 (32K Causal Document), 542.7 vs 498.6 (128K Causal Document). Against FlexAttention the speedup is about 1.33x at 8K Sliding Window (290.3 vs 218.9) and 1.43x to 1.61x in the other 8 settings.

title: SchemaPose: RGB-Based Category-Level Pose Estimation with Parametric Category Schema
claim_source: Table 2 (and Table 3 'Learned latent' row), page 9; seed variation in Table 10, Appendix C.5, page 21

official.background: Category-level 9D pose estimation recovers the 3D rotation, 3D translation and 3D size of unseen instances of known object categories (bottle, bowl, camera, can, laptop, mug). Doing this from a single RGB image, with no depth, is hard because instance shape, proportions and part layout are entangled with pose in the image. Earlier RGB methods either predict canonical NOCS coordinates and solve for pose geometrically, or regress pose directly from query features, so category structure stays implicit. The paper asks whether an explicit, supervised structural variable describing each object's shape helps a monocular pose network.
official.method:
Each category gets a hand-written parametric schema: discrete part choices (e.g., body type, handle type) and continuous geometric parameters (radii, heights, thicknesses) that compose primitives into a mesh. A per-category compression maps the full schema to a compact, normalized vector g_c. The same schemas generate SchemaData: 10K procedurally instantiated objects per category, rendered in BlenderProc into 135K scene images with pose and schema labels. The authors also annotate REAL275 training images with schema.

SchemaPose is a DINO detector (Swin-L, COCO-pretrained) with a Schema-Guided Pose Head applied at both the proposal stage (encoder memory) and every decoder layer. From a query feature q, the head predicts class and 2D box b, then a unified schema vector g. A category mask selects the valid slots g~, and [q; b; g~] feeds the projected-center, depth, rotation and size branches. Training is end-to-end for 12 epochs on 135K SchemaData + 135K CAMERA25 (no schema loss) + 4.3K REAL275 x6, using focal/L1/GIoU/L2/geodesic losses plus L1 and sigmoid-CE schema losses. The 'w/o Schema' ablation keeps the same backbone, query architecture, training data and pose heads, but removes both schema supervision and schema conditioning.
official.claim: On REAL275, adding schema supervision and dual-stage schema guidance to an otherwise identical DINO-based pose network (same backbone, queries, training data and pose heads) raises 10°10cm mAP from 63.8 to 68.4 and IoU50 from 80.5 to 86.3. The 5-seed std of the full model is 1.3 and 1.0 (mean 67.5 and 86.5). A same-dimensional learned latent without schema supervision reaches only 61.8 on 10°10cm.

official.metric: mAP (%) at 3D IoU 50/75 and at 10cm, 10°, 10°10cm pose thresholds on the REAL275 test split; higher is better. Ablation rows are reported without error bars (apparently single runs). Only the full model has seed statistics (Table 10: mean ± std over 5 seeds, 10°10cm 67.5 ± 1.3, IoU50 86.5 ± 1.0).
official.comparison: SchemaPose (dual-stage schema guidance) vs. the w/o Schema variant (no schema supervision or guidance) and vs. a learned-latent variant (same-dimensional unsupervised vector in place of the schema), all trained on the same data mixture

title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs

official.background: LLaVA-style multimodal LLMs are trained in two stages. Stage I trains only a projector that maps frozen vision-encoder features into a frozen LLM's input space, using hundreds of thousands of image-caption pairs. Stage II then instruction-tunes the projector and the LLM together. It is unclear what Stage I actually contributes, and earlier papers disagree on whether it can be skipped (Prismatic) or should be scaled up (Cambrian-1). If Stage I only does a coarse distributional alignment, the paired data and the training it needs could be replaced by something much cheaper.
official.method:
PORTAL builds the first layer of the LLaVA 2-layer MLP projector in closed form, with no paired data and no gradient steps. Mean, top-k PCA basis and per-axis spread are computed for the vision features (patch tokens from about 1,024 unlabeled COCO images) and for the LLM's input token embeddings. The map is W1 = V_t diag(sigma_t / sigma_s) V_s^T and b1 = mu_t - W1 mu_s, with k = 512. This is the Gaussian (Bures-Wasserstein) optimal-transport map on the shared principal subspace. The second layer is set to identity with zero bias. Appendix F gives a PyTorch implementation.

For each (vision encoder, LLM) pair, three projector initializations go through identical Stage-II instruction tuning on LLaVA-665k (LLaVA-1.5 hyperparameters, seed 42): (i) the standard Stage-I projector trained on LCS-558k, (ii) a random projector with no Stage I, and (iii) PORTAL. The models are scored with lmms-eval v0.4.1 on 16 benchmarks (Knowledge, General, OCR and Vision categories, with SEED-Bench as a 500-sample Lite subset). Avg is the unweighted mean of the 16 scores.
official.claim: With CLIP ViT-L/14-336 and identical LLaVA-665k instruction tuning, a PORTAL-initialized projector (no paired data, no Stage-I training) beats the projector trained on 558k LCS image-caption pairs in 16-benchmark average for both small LLMs: Qwen 2.5 0.5B 39.9 vs. 37.6 (106.1 ± 1.3 %BL; random init 37.7) and LLaMA 3.2 1B 44.2 vs. 41.6 (106.2 ± 1.3 %BL; random init 41.5).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: PORTAL generalizes across LLM backbones and vision encoders. All configurations use identical Stage-II instruction tuning (LLaVA-665k). PORTAL requires zero Stage-I paired captions and zero Stage-I gradient steps. Baseline †: uses 558k paired captions for Stage-I pretraining. Bold: best among zero training data methods. Avg: unweighted mean of the 16 per-benchmark scores. %BL: this average as a percentage of the trained baseline (BL), which is therefore 100%. Subscripts on the Avg and %BL columns give the 95% bootstrap confidence-interval half-width over per-sample outcomes, from 1000 resamples paired across methods. L: 500-sample Lite subset from lmms-eval.
official.metric: Unweighted mean of 16 benchmark scores (higher is better), also shown as % of the trained baseline (%BL). ± is the 95% paired bootstrap CI half-width over per-sample outcomes (1000 resamples), from a single training seed (42).
official.comparison: PORTAL init vs. the standard Stage-I projector trained on LCS-558k vs. random init (no Stage I), all followed by the same Stage-II tuning, on Qwen 2.5 0.5B/CLIP and LLaMA 3.2 1B/CLIP
official.falsification_criterion: After identical Stage-II tuning, PORTAL's 16-benchmark average for Qwen 2.5 0.5B/CLIP or LLaMA 3.2 1B/CLIP is not above the LCS-558k-trained projector's by more than the bootstrap CI (i.e. %BL is about 101% or below), or PORTAL does not beat the random init.

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (full version with medians: Table 5, page 34)

official.background: Persistent homology summarizes a graph, under a filtration such as vertex degree, as a persistence diagram (PD): births and deaths of connected components and cycles. Many different graphs share the same PD. Topology-aware graph generators (e.g. TAGG on top of DiGress) condition on PDs only through soft losses, so their samples match the target PD only approximately. This paper asks how to generate graphs whose degree-filtration PD equals a given target exactly, which is useful for building controlled benchmarks and for applications that need exact counts of components or cycles.
official.method:
Two exact generators are given a target degree-filtration PD (P0, P1). The local sampler (Algorithm 3) builds the graph stage by stage: at each degree level k it adds the vertices born at k, joins components according to the deaths at k, and adds the cycles born at k, while tracking each vertex's remaining degree capacity. Every output it produces matches the PD, but it can reach dead ends (no valid edge left), so it is run as a rejection sampler with up to 20,000 attempts per target. The paper proves (Theorem 3.10) that any such local procedure must sometimes reach infeasible states.

The global method encodes the problem as a constraint satisfaction problem solved with OR-Tools CP-SAT. Binary adjacency variables M_ij are linked to per-stage component 'slots' through six constraint families: degree equals birth time, every active vertex belongs to one slot, edges stay within slots, each slot is connected (witnessed by a spanning tree with parent pointers and depths), the Euler characteristic matches the cumulative cycle count, and the number of slots whose oldest vertex was born at b matches the PD. Each target gets a 1,800 s budget with 120 CP-SAT workers. For every test graph of COMM-20, PLANAR, SBM and ENZYMES (SPECTRE 64/16/20 split), its degree PD is the target; the metric is the fraction of targets for which a valid graph is returned within budget.
official.claim: On the 40 SBM test graphs (44-187 nodes, mean max degree 17.1), the global CP-SAT encoding produces an exactly degree-PD-equivalent graph for 82.5% of targets (33/40) within 1,800 s each, while the local rejection sampler (Algorithm 3) succeeds on only 15.0% (6/40) within 20,000 attempts; on COMM-20, PLANAR and ENZYMES both methods succeed on 99-100% of targets.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Local degree-filtration sampler vs. the global CP solver. Wall-clock means charge the full attempt or time budget on failed runs.
official.metric: Success rate (% of test-split targets for which a graph with exactly the target degree-filtration PD is returned within budget), higher is better; single deterministic run, no ± reported. Mean wall-clock per target (s, failed runs charged the full budget) also reported.
official.comparison: Local degree-filtration rejection sampler (Algorithm 3, 20,000 attempts) vs. global constraint-programming encoding (CP-SAT, 1,800 s, 120 workers) on the same target PDs
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both methods on the 40 SBM test targets with the stated budgets, the local sampler solves a similar number of targets as CP (e.g. CP's lead is under ~10 targets), or CP solves well under ~25/40; alternatively, any CP output whose degree PD differs from the target.

title: MemCode: Discrete Semantic Representations for Long-Term Agent Memory
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (GPT-4o-mini block); repeated-run variability in Appendix Table 9, page 17

official.background: LLM agents that talk to users across many sessions need an external long-term memory, because model weights are static and long contexts are expensive and poorly used. Most memory systems write dialogue fragments into a store and retrieve them by nearest-neighbor search over dense embeddings. The paper argues that this has two problems: fragments detached from the dialogue lose speakers, times and referents, so they are hard to retrieve, and dense nearest-neighbor search misses evidence that is logically related to the question but lexically distant. Benchmarks such as LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S test this with multi-hop, temporal, open-domain and single-hop questions over long multi-session conversations.
official.method:
MemCode ingests a conversation turn by turn. An LLM (the same backbone as the answerer, here GPT-4o-mini) rewrites each turn, with the last 10 sentences of the previous turn as read-only background (LoCoMo setting, Table 7), into self-contained atomic memory units (AMUs): canonicalized facts with resolved speakers, absolute timestamps and pointers to the source utterances. Each AMU gets two index keys: a 768-d bge-base-en-v1.5 dense vector (FAISS), and a discrete fingerprint from a VQ-VAE built on a T5-base encoder with a stride-1 projection and a 1024-entry codebook. The VQ-VAE is trained once on DailyDialog context-response pairs (predict the response from the quantized context) and frozen before evaluation; adjacent duplicate codes are removed to form the fingerprint.

At query time, Path A retrieves the top 20 AMUs by dense similarity. Path B builds a code co-occurrence matrix over all AMU fingerprints, scores each code reached in one hop from the query's codes by source-code IDF times transition probability, scores each AMU by its best code, and adds the top 20 AMUs not already retrieved by Path A. Source pointers recover raw dialogue turns (25 on LoCoMo), and the evidence is sorted by time and given to the LLM for a single answer call. GPT-4o-mini judges answers against the reference (LLM-as-a-judge accuracy). The claim below uses MemCode without the optional asynchronous consolidation stage.
official.claim: On LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini as writer/reader, MemCode (without consolidation) reaches 78.12% overall accuracy (six-run mean 78.26 ± 0.35), beating the strongest baseline Full Text (73.83%) by 4.3 points and LightMem (71.95%) by 6.2 points.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Category-level accuracy and memory-construction cost on LoCoMo. Asyn. denotes asynchronous consolidation. Bold and underline denote the best and 2nd-best results on each backbone.
official.metric: Overall LLM-as-a-judge accuracy (%) on 1,540 LoCoMo questions, higher is better. Table 2 gives single runs with no error bars; Appendix Table 9 reports six repeated MemCode runs (mean ± std 78.26 ± 0.35, range 77.86-78.70). No repeated runs are reported for baselines.
official.comparison: MemCode vs. Full Text, Naive RAG, A-MEM, MemoryOS, Mem0 and LightMem, all with GPT-4o-mini as backbone and GPT-4o-mini as judge, under the same incremental turn-by-turn ingestion protocol
official.falsification_criterion: A reimplementation of MemCode on LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini does not exceed Full Text (full conversation in context, same backbone and judge) by more than about 1 point overall, or does not exceed LightMem by more than about 1 point.

title: Learning Visual Speech Representations via Cross-Modal Distillation and Joint Face-Lip Modeling
claim_source: Figure 2, page 8 (Section 4.4); the 1x face+lip values match Table 2 (FLARE 342M, 4966h: 13.6 LRS2, 15.9 LRS3), page 6

official.background: Lipreading (visual speech recognition) transcribes speech from video of the speaker without audio. It is hard because several phonemes look the same on the lips, and because the input degrades with head pose and low video resolution. Most audio-visual self-supervised methods (AV-HuBERT, RAVEn, BRAVEn) use only a cropped lip region of interest (ROI), which becomes unreliable for turned heads, low resolution or poor crops. Some recent work uses the full face instead. This paper asks whether processing face and lip crops together in one encoder gives more accurate and more robust lipreading than using either one alone.
official.method:
FLARE is a visual speech encoder pretrained by cross-modal distillation. Deep features from Whisper-Large (the teacher, run on clean audio) are normalized and quantized into discrete targets with a frozen random projection and a frozen random codebook (V = 8192, Dq = 32), as in BEST-RQ. The student predicts these codes for masked and unmasked frames with a cross-entropy loss. Masking replaces spans of video frames with other spans from the same utterance. The student has two parallel 3D-conv + ConvNeXt frontends, one for the full-face video and one for the lip-ROI video (each 88x88), plus a feed-forward projection of noisy audio filterbanks. Their features are concatenated along the channel dimension, linearly projected, and passed to an 'enhanced Conformer' context encoder (RoPE, GQA, SwiGLU, RMSNorm). Modality dropout picks audio/video/audio-visual with probabilities 0/0.75/0.25 and face-only/lip-only/face+lip with 0.25/0.25/0.5. A missing stream's features are set to zero, so one model accepts face-only, lip-only or joint input at test time.

For the claim, FLARE-Large (342M encoder, 18 blocks, hidden size 768) is pretrained and then finetuned with a 6-layer Transformer decoder (cross-entropy, no CTC, no external LM), both on 4966 h of audio-visual data. The same model is evaluated on the LRS2 and LRS3 test sets with face-only, lip-only or face+lip input. The test videos are spatially downsampled to 0.75x, 0.5x and 0.25x of their original resolution (the paper does not say how they are brought back to the 88x88 input size).
official.claim: With the same FLARE-Large model, joint face+lip input gives lower WER than both face-only and lip-only input at every resolution (1x, 0.75x, 0.5x, 0.25x) on both LRS2 and LRS3. At full resolution: LRS3 ~15.9% vs. 18.9% (face) and 22.5% (lip); LRS2 ~13.6% vs. 18.7% (face) and 15.5% (lip). At 0.25x: LRS3 ~21.2% vs. 27.1% and 30.1%; LRS2 ~31.7% vs. 47.8% and 42.7%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Word error rate (WER) comparison across different video resolutions.
official.metric: Word error rate (%) on the LRS2 and LRS3 test sets, lower is better; single run, no error bars or significance tests (the paper's checklist says so). Values are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Joint face+lip input vs. face-only and lip-only input, all fed to the same trained FLARE-Large model (the missing stream is zeroed), at four spatial resolutions

title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation

official.background: Pixel-level active learning for semantic segmentation asks an annotator to label only a few individual pixels per image (as few as one), which cuts annotation cost far below dense or region labels. Prior low-budget methods (PixelPick, the diffusion-driven 2-stage eDALD) select pixels on dense pixel-resolution feature maps. With a ViT backbone, those per-pixel features are interpolations of patch tokens, so diversity and uncertainty criteria can be drawn to token boundaries where interpolation creates artificial variation rather than real semantic variety. The paper asks whether doing the selection on the ViT's native token grid works better when only 1 to 10 pixels per image are labeled.
official.method:
TEAL uses a frozen DINOv3-base (ViT-B/16) backbone on 256x256 images (a 16x16 token grid) and trains only a small Mini-DPT segmentation head. The head takes per-layer fixed-normalized features from layers {2,5,8,11} and predicts logits on a 64x64 grid (4x4-pixel cells). It is trained with cross-entropy on the labeled pixels only (Adam, lr 1e-4, 10 epochs per round, warm-started, early stop at 95% training accuracy). Each active learning round has two stages. Stage 1 runs two-level MaxHerding (an RBF-kernel greedy coverage objective, bandwidth = 2 x the median pairwise distance) on token descriptors built from layers {8,9,10,11}: it picks k = 20 tokens per image, then herds the union globally down to half its size, which gives the candidate token set C_t.

Stage 2 scores every 64x64 decoder cell that overlaps a candidate token and whose center pixel is still unlabeled by margin uncertainty (top-1 minus top-2 softmax probability). It queries the center pixels of the m most uncertain cells across the dataset. Budgets are 1 and 10 labeled pixels per image on average, and mIoU is reported at the final round. In Table 2, the baselines PixelPick and 2-Stage eDALD (MaxHerding over upsampled pixel features plus eBALD uncertainty) are re-run with the same frozen DINOv3 features, so the comparison isolates the acquisition strategy.
official.claim: On CamVid at 256x256 with all methods using the same frozen DINOv3 backbone, TEAL reaches 49.54 ± 0.37 mIoU at 1 labeled pixel per image vs. 47.07 ± 0.28 (PixelPick) and 45.88 ± 1.68 (2-Stage eDALD), and 55.93 ± 0.11 at 10 pixels per image vs. 53.79 ± 0.27 and 53.98 ± 0.57.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Matched-backbone comparison across datasets and labeling budgets. Green values indicate absolute improvement over the previous two-stage method [Kim et al., 2026]. Ceiling reports the fully supervised mIoU obtained using dense labels and the DINOv3 backbone, shared by all methods. The final column reports the fraction of the fully supervised performance recovered at the 10-pixel budget. All methods use DINOv3 features for a matched-backbone comparison.
official.metric: mIoU on the validation set at the final active-learning round (higher is better), mean ± std over three seeds (seed count stated in Appendix tables 7-8 and A.1)
official.comparison: TEAL vs. PixelPick and 2-Stage eDALD (Kim et al. 2026), both re-run by the authors on the same frozen DINOv3-base features with the same training schedule (10 epochs, Adam 1e-4, early stop at 95% training accuracy); the paper does not state explicitly that the baselines use the Mini-DPT head, at budgets of 1 and 10 pixels per image

title: SIEVE: Overcoming Topological Obstruction in Equivariant Self-Supervised Learning
claim_source: Figure 4, page 7 (text on page 8; reconstructions in Figure 5, page 8)

official.background: Masked-autoencoder self-supervised learning on 3D point clouds usually replaces masked inputs with a learnable constant token or random noise. SE(3)-equivariant networks are attractive for point clouds because their outputs transform consistently under rotations and translations, but the paper argues, using vector-bundle theory, that combining them with constant or geometry-independent masks makes it impossible to reconstruct point clouds of differing topology: the vector pipeline collapses. This matters for anyone trying to build pose-invariant self-supervised point cloud encoders.
official.method:
SIEVE is an equivariant masked autoencoder. The encoder (an SE(3)-equivariant network such as GATr) takes the point coordinates as the vector input and i.i.d. Gaussian noise as the scalar input, and outputs per-point invariant scalar embeddings; its vector output is discarded. The decoder receives those scalars plus a masked vector input and must reconstruct each point's coordinates under an L1 loss. SIEVE's mask is the spherical projection mask: each point x_i is replaced by mean + (x_i - mean)/||x_i - mean||, which keeps global pose but removes local shape.

The collapse test (Section 4.2, details in Appendix B.2) uses a synthetic dataset of solid cuboids (homeomorphic to a 3-ball) and square toroids (a torus), 120 instances per class, 100/20 train/test split. Three masks are compared under identical initialization and hyperparameters: a learnable constant vector token, an ellipsoid noise mask (uniform samples on an ellipsoid with semi-axes (2, 1, 0.5) aligned with the cloud's PCA axes, so still equivariant), and the spherical projection mask (no added noise here). Backbones are GATr and SE(3)-Transformer (kNN edges, k=50), both with encoder 6 layers and decoder 2 layers, hidden (32 scalar, 8 vector) channels, trained for 200 epochs, batch size 4, cosine LR with peak 3e-4 and 10% warmup, gradient clipping at 10, no weight decay.
official.claim: On the synthetic cuboid/toroid reconstruction task, SE(3)-equivariant autoencoders with the spherical projection mask reach validation L1 loss below 0.01 after 200 epochs (about 0.0013 with GATr, about 0.007 with SE(3)-Transformer), while the same models with a constant vector mask or an ellipsoid noise mask stay at about 0.5 on both training and validation loss and output a collapsed 'blob'.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Validation Loss of SIEVE on two baselines: GATr and SE(3)-Transformer. Trained on the synthetic dataset.

official.falsification_criterion: With either backbone, the constant or noise mask model reaches validation L1 below ~0.05 (no collapse), or the spherical-mask model fails to get below 0.01, under the stated setup.

title: NOCE-Net: Representation Learning for Battery Operational Context via Nested Sequence Modelling

official.background: Battery management and health-aware control need models that predict how a battery's voltage will respond to planned future charge/discharge inputs over its whole life, accounting for how degradation changes that response. Most data-driven battery models instead rely on features computed from measured responses (e.g. dV/dQ curves) or on short early-life windows, so they cannot be run forward on hypothetical future operation, and public aging datasets differ in resolution, recorded fields and cycling protocols, which limits training across many chemistries and usage patterns.
official.method:
The re-BatteryData pipeline converts 10 public aging datasets (~700 cells) into a common format: six input features (charge current, discharge current, temperature, time, charge and discharge throughput) at uniform temporal resolution, battery metadata 'task' features (chemistry, form factor, nominal capacity, voltage limits), and segmentation into Full Equivalent Cycles (FECs), each covering absolute charge throughput of 2x nominal capacity. Six datasets (ISU-ILCC, NASA-Rand, TJU, MATR, UMICH, XJTU-Partial) are used for training (6:2:2 train/val/in-sample-test split); five datasets (NASA-PCoE, Stanford-EV, HUST, XJTU-Full, evTOL) are held out entirely for zero-shot testing.

NOCE-Net (2.5M params) encodes each FEC's input sequence with multi-patch Conv1D embeddings (patch sizes 4, 16, 32) plus task, FEC-position and learnable aggregator tokens through a 6-layer Transformer; the three aggregator tokens feed a 2-layer GRU across FECs (initial state from task features); a 3-layer Transformer decoder plus transposed-convolution output layer reconstructs the per-FEC voltage sequence. It is trained on lifetime voltage prediction with MSE + derivative + upper-quartile-error loss. Baselines (TimerXL, AutoTimes, TTM, MAMBA, thuml implementations) are trained with the same loss for 50 epochs in three modes: M1 (nested, with MPATCH/VARSEQ variants), M2 (flattened single sequence), and Indep. (each FEC independent). Metric is MAE and MAPE of predicted voltage on zero-shot test batteries over their whole life.
official.claim: On zero-shot (held-out-dataset) lifetime voltage prediction, NOCE-Net reaches aggregate Total-Unseen MAE 0.0656 and MAPE 13.71%, versus best baselines MAMBA+M2 (MAE 0.1001, 34.5% higher) and TTM+Indep. (MAPE 24.41%, 43.8% higher), with the stated run-to-run std of 5-10%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Zero-shot and few-shot voltage prediction results. Total-Seen and Total-Unseen are macro-averages over in-sample and out-of-sample test batteries respectively. Values are means over 5 runs, (std. 5%-10%, higher when VarSeq=True). Independent and TimerXL baselines omitted from few-shot due to computational overhead and consistent underperformance respectively. Bold = best, underline = second best.
official.metric: MAE and MAPE (%) of predicted voltage on zero-shot test batteries, lower is better; Total-Unseen is a macro-average over out-of-sample test batteries. Values are means over 5 runs; the only error information is a caption statement 'std. 5%-10%' (relative), not per-cell std.
official.comparison: NOCE-Net vs. TimerXL, AutoTimes, TTM and MAMBA in M1 (4 MPATCH/VARSEQ variants), M2 (flattened) and Indep. (per-cycle) modes, all trained on the same six training datasets with the same loss
official.falsification_criterion: When retrained on the same split, the best baseline (e.g. MAMBA+M2 or TTM M1 with MPATCH=True) reaches a Total-Unseen MAE within ~10% of NOCE-Net's, or NOCE-Net's Total-Unseen MAE is not clearly below 0.10.

title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction
claim_source: Table 7 (Appendix A.1), page 18; the 128K counterpart is Table 1, page 7

official.background: During long-context LLM inference the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and can dwarf the model weights (about 48 GB at 128K tokens for Phi-3-mini), so eviction methods keep only a small fraction of cached tokens. Most eviction scores rank tokens by attention weight alone (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and ignore the value vectors. Recent output-aware methods (CriticalKV, AnDPro) try to minimise the change in the attention output caused by eviction, but the exact subset-selection problem is NP-hard and they rely on loose bounds or relaxations.
official.method:
For a query q with attention weights p and output a = sum_i p_i v_i, evicting token j alone shifts the output by p_j/(1-p_j) (a - v_j). DropKV ignores interactions between evicted tokens and scores each token by its own squared perturbation summed over an observation window of the last w = 8 queries: score_j = sum_t [p_j^(t)/(1-p_j^(t))]^2 ||a^(t) - v_j||^2. The scores are max-pooled with kernel size 11, the window tokens are always kept, and the tokens with the smallest scores are evicted (per head, at prefill) until the cache budget is reached. The paper proves a constant-factor approximation to the exact subset problem under a 'cone condition' on the residuals a - v_j, and provides fused Triton kernels for the scoring.

Evaluation: RULER (11 tasks, average accuracy) at 16K-128K tokens and LongBench, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M and MegaBeam-Mistral-7B-512K, with KV-cache budgets of 5%, 10% and 30%. Baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, StreamingLLM, KeyDiff, CAKE, CriticalKV, AnDPro) use the same window and pooling settings, mostly from NVIDIA/kvpress, and everything runs in one lm-evaluation-harness pipeline on an A100-80GB.
official.claim: On RULER at 32K sequence length with a 5% KV-cache budget, DropKV reaches a RULER average of 87.34 on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M versus 82.00 for the best baseline (AnDPro), 80.49 for CriticalKV and 79.73 for SnapKV (full KV: 91.40); on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct it reaches 89.54 versus 86.51 for the best baseline (CAKE).
official.claim_caption: Table 7: RULER results at 32K sequence length and 5%, 10% and 30% KV-cache budget. The best result is highlighted in gray, and the second-best is underlined.
official.metric: RULER average accuracy over 11 tasks (N-S1..3, N-MK1..2, N-MQ, N-MV, VT, FWE, QA-1, QA-2), higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: DropKV vs. SnapKV, PyramidKV, StreamingLLM, KeyDiff, CAKE, CriticalKV and AnDPro at the same 5% cache budget, same model, same 32K RULER set
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup (32K, 5% budget, w=8, pooling kernel 11), DropKV's RULER average on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M is within about 1 point of AnDPro or CriticalKV, or below them; or on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct it does not exceed CAKE and SnapKV.

title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (with Table 1, same page, for FID/CLIP-T/latency)

official.background: Diffusion transformers spend most of their inference cost on self-attention over many image tokens at every denoising step. Token merging is a training-free speed-up: it averages redundant tokens into representative ones for some layers and then unmerges them. Which tokens to merge decides the quality: ToMeSD merges by feature similarity and distorts DiT outputs, and the recent importance-based method of Wu et al. [9] protects tokens with a large conditional-unconditional (CFG) noise-prediction gap. The authors argue the CFG signal is prompt-centric and static over time, so background objects and boundaries not named in the prompt get merged away and the image drifts from what the unmerged model would produce.
official.method:
DaTMe (Dynamics-aware Token Merging) scores tokens at each denoising step from the Tweedie clean-image estimate x̂0(t) = (x_t − σ_t ε_θ)/α_t (or x_t − t·v_θ for rectified flow). A temporal map M_temp = |x̂0(t) − x̂0(t−1)| marks tokens still changing, and a spatial map M_spat = |x̂0(t) − Up_s(Down_s(x̂0(t)))| (s = 4) marks high-frequency structure. For target compression ratio r (merge ⌊rN⌋ tokens), the constraint set (never merged) is the intersection of the top-(1−r) fractions on both maps; the source set is the intersection of the bottom-r fractions, topped up to the budget by uniform sampling of the remaining unassigned tokens within P = 4 spatial grid cells. The destination pool is every token in neither the source nor the constraint set; each source token is merged into its spatially nearest destination token (locality-constrained matching, as in [9]), and constraint tokens pass through unmerged. Merging starts at the second step, since the temporal map needs the previous estimate.

On PixArt-α: 20 steps, guidance 4.5, merging in transformer layers 9–19, 10k COCO 2014 val prompts, r ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}. Baselines are ToMeSD and CFG-importance merging [9]. SSIM, PSNR and LPIPS are computed between each compressed output and the uncompressed PixArt-α output for the same prompt and seed; FID, CLIP-T, HPSv2 and an aesthetic score are also reported.
official.claim: On PixArt-α with 10k COCO prompts, DaTMe preserves the uncompressed output better than both CFG-importance token merging and ToMeSD at every compression ratio: SSIM 0.811 vs 0.714 (CFG) / 0.731 (ToMeSD) and LPIPS 0.150 vs 0.237 / 0.243 at r = 0.3; SSIM 0.730 vs 0.633 / 0.674 and LPIPS 0.226 vs 0.325 / 0.315 at r = 0.5; SSIM 0.658 vs 0.570 / 0.630 and LPIPS 0.308 vs 0.413 / 0.368 at r = 0.7.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Text alignment and efficiency scores on PixArt-α. DaTMe achieves the best overall quality-efficiency trade-off, preserving strong text alignment with minimal degradation under token compression. Table 2: Image fidelity score on PixArt-α. DaTMe achieves stronger structural preservation and image-level fidelity under token compression.
official.metric: SSIM↑, PSNR↑, LPIPS↓ against the uncompressed PixArt-α image for the same prompt/seed, averaged over 10k images; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported
official.comparison: DaTMe vs. CFG-importance merging [9] and ToMeSD [10] at identical compression ratios (0.3, 0.5, 0.7) on PixArt-α
official.falsification_criterion: At any of r = 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 on PixArt-α, DaTMe's SSIM is not higher (or LPIPS not lower) than the better of CFG-importance merging and ToMeSD, or the gap is a small fraction of the reported margins over that best baseline (SSIM ≈ +0.08 / +0.06 / +0.03, LPIPS ≈ −0.09 / −0.09 / −0.06 at r = 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7). The r = 0.7 PSNR gap over ToMeSD is only 0.05 dB and is not part of the claim.

title: Towards Reconstructing Geographically Diverse Architecture with 3D Foundation Models
claim_source: Table 10 (Appendix B.4), page 23; same medians with IQRs in Table 2, page 6

official.background: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) such as VGGT, Depth Anything 3 and pi3 predict cameras and dense geometry from a set of images in one forward pass, and are increasingly used on internet photo collections, including for cultural-heritage digitization. Existing evaluation sets with dense ground truth are either captured in controlled settings or are geographically skewed (MegaScenes is about 83% Europe), so it is unknown whether reconstruction quality differs across world regions. The paper builds ArchWorld, a benchmark of 396 in-the-wild landmarks across eight regions with metric-scale dense MVS ground truth and landmark masks, and runs a disaggregated evaluation.
official.method:
ArchWorld scenes come from MegaDepth-X reconstructions plus 69 new MegaScenes scenes (COLMAP with at least 50 registered images, outdoor, man-made, manually checked), each with a hand-annotated metric scale factor and a 3D landmark mask so only the target building is evaluated. For each scene, 50 images are chosen by a greedy view-coverage selection, resized to width 518, and fed to the frozen public checkpoints (facebook/VGGT-1B, depth-anything/DA3-LARGE-1.1, yyfz233/Pi3). Predicted depth and poses are unprojected to a point map (pi3 outputs point maps directly), aligned to the masked ground truth with Umeyama and then ICP, and scored by Chamfer distance; each scene is evaluated 5 times and averaged.

The disparity metric is normalized Chamfer distance CD-hat = (Accuracy + Completeness) / (2 x BoundingBoxSize) (the paper writes 'bounding box size'; elsewhere it measures scene extent as the bounding-box diagonal), reported x10^3, which removes the dependence of error on landmark size. Per region the paper reports the median over scenes with a percentile-bootstrap 95% CI (2,000 resamples).
official.claim: On ArchWorld, the best 3DFM (pi3) has median normalized Chamfer distance (x10^3) of 2.75 [95% CI 2.15, 4.42] on East Asian landmarks vs. 1.34 [1.09, 1.59] on Southeast Asian landmarks, and the same non-overlapping gap holds for VGGT (6.63 [4.50, 13.69] vs. 2.85 [2.15, 3.48]), with East Asia and North America the two worst regions for all three models.
official.claim_caption: Table 10: Benchmarking 3DFMs by geographic regions with bootstrapped confidence intervals. For each model and region, we report the median CD and CD-hat with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals in parentheses; the number of evaluated scenes is listed alongside each region name. The top sub-table shows each model's median CD across all scenes in each region. The bottom sub-table shows CD-hat (scaled up by 10^3 for readability) across all scenes in each region. The order of the region columns is based on the ordering of pi3, the best-performing model.
official.metric: Per-region median normalized Chamfer distance CD-hat (x10^3, lower is better); brackets are percentile-bootstrap 95% CIs over scenes (2,000 resamples). Each scene's CD is the mean of 5 evaluation runs.
official.comparison: Same frozen model, same evaluation pipeline, across geographic regions: East Asia (43 scenes) and North America (44) vs. Southeast Asia (50) for pi3, VGGT and DA3
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running pi3 (or VGGT) on ArchWorld with the paper's protocol gives an East Asia median CD-hat whose bootstrap 95% CI overlaps the Southeast Asia CI, or East Asia/North America are no longer the two worst regions.

title: COMET: Decoupled Distillation, Routing, and Capacity Control for Task-Agnostic Continual Vision--Language Learning

official.background: CLIP-style vision-language models can classify images zero-shot, but deployed models often need to learn a sequence of new tasks (for example medical, microscopy or satellite images) with no stored data from earlier tasks, no task identity at test time, and no budget to retrain the backbone. The X-TAIL protocol tests this: after each task the model must classify over all classes seen so far plus unseen ones. Existing approaches either fine-tune or interpolate CLIP weights (WiSE-FT, ZSCL), which limits how far the model can move toward distant domains, or add small adapters to a frozen CLIP (MoE-Adapters, LADA), which may lack capacity for domains far from CLIP's pre-training data.
official.method:
COMET keeps a frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 teacher and trains a separate full TinyCLIP expert (~58M parameters, initialized from TinyCLIP) for each task, for 1,000 AdamW iterations at lr 1e-5 and batch size 64. The per-task loss is the supervised task loss plus Tri-Affinity Distillation (TAD: Frobenius loss between student and teacher image-image and text-text cosine-similarity matrices, plus a teacher-to-student KL on image-to-text and text-to-image logits, weight 0.2) and Student-Aware Cross-Expert Distillation (SACED, weight 1.0: matches the student-teacher attention distance to that of compatible prior experts). Both distillation losses are computed on a fixed reference pool of 10,800 Conceptual Captions validation image-text pairs. After training, a contextual bandit decides whether to keep the new expert or merge it into a prior one.

At test time, each retained expert has a small autoencoder router trained on that task's frozen-CLIP image features. Reconstruction errors are converted into calibrated likelihood-ratio scores and a softmax gate, the top-k (k <= 2) experts are run, and their class-text similarity logits are averaged with the gate weights. Transfer is the accuracy on tasks not yet trained on, averaged across the stream; Average is the mean accuracy over all evaluation steps; Last is the accuracy after the final task.
official.claim: On a 4-task full-shot continual sequence far from CLIP pre-training (Covid19, Kather-Texture, NCT100K, SEM), COMET reaches a mean Transfer accuracy of 31.2%, compared with 12.5% for the best baseline (ZSCL), and is higher on each of the three Transfer columns (KT 19.8 vs. 12.7, NCT 40.5 vs. at most 1.6, SEM 33.4 vs. at most 24.8).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Heterogeneous 4-dataset full-shot results. Transfer, Average, and Last scores (%). The best result in each metric and column is in bold. ZS: zero-shot; Cov19: Covid19; KT: Kather-Texture; NCT: NCT 100K.
official.metric: Transfer accuracy (%), higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: COMET vs. CLIP-FT, WiSE-FT, ZSCL, MoE-Adapters and LADA on the same 4-task sequence (zero-shot TinyCLIP and CLIP-B/16 also shown)
official.falsification_criterion: Reimplemented COMET's mean Transfer on this sequence is not clearly above the best of ZSCL/WiSE-FT/MoE-Adapters/LADA (e.g. a margin under ~5 pp), or the NCT100K Transfer gain (40.5 vs. <= 1.6) does not appear.

title: Towards High Semantic Fidelity: Hyperdimensional Symbolic Messages in Multi-Agent Communication

official.background: In communicating multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), agents exchange messages over a channel that may be noisy or adversarially perturbed. Common message formats are numerical (e.g. Q-value lists), which are easy to interpret but fragile under noise, or learned neural embeddings, which can be made more robust but are black boxes. This paper proposes to send hyperdimensional computing (HDC) vectors instead. Random high-dimensional vectors are nearly orthogonal, which should make messages tolerant to perturbation, and their bind/bundle algebra can be inverted to decode what a message says.
official.method:
Herm encodes each agent's message without any learned parameters, using Holographic Reduced Representations (HRR, circular-convolution binding). Observations are encoded entity by entity: attribute and value hypervectors are bound, bundled over attributes, bound to an entity-identity vector and bundled over entities. Continuous values are discretized, and nearby values share dimensions through 'cyclic replacement' encoding. The last w actions are bound to time-index vectors and bundled. The receiver binds each incoming message with its own encoding (ego-binding). It then fuses the observation parts weighted by softmax(-cosine similarity), so dissimilar views get more weight, and the action parts weighted by softmax(+cosine similarity). The fused vectors pass through a single mapping layer into a GRU-based local Q-network trained with QMIX (PyMARLzoo+, Adam, lr 5e-4, batch 32). On Hallway the paper uses H = 64 and w = 1.

Adversarial test (Table 1): each message is perturbed at test time with FGSM, m̂ = m + η_f · sign(∇_m f(m)) · φ, where f is the cross-entropy between the noisy and noise-free policies and φ is the mean of the per-message maximum values. η_f ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}. PGD uses 5 steps with an L2-ball projection. Baselines are CroMAC (a certified-robust message method) and MAIC with AME message ablation (K of N-1 sources kept, 10 ablation votes at test time). The metric is the test win/success rate (%).
official.claim: On Hallway 4 under an FGSM message attack with η_f = 0.3, Herm keeps a 95.5 ± 0.4% success rate while CroMAC drops to 6.0 ± 0.1%. On Hallway 5 the corresponding numbers are 93.5 ± 0.8% vs. 24.6 ± 0.3%. Without the attack, both methods are near 100% on both maps.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Robustness Evaluation in Adversarially Noisy Environments.
official.metric: Test success rate (%), higher is better; ± is not defined in the paper (Figure 3 curves use 4 random seeds, so it is likely std over seeds)
official.comparison: Herm (HDC symbolic messages) vs. CroMAC and MAIC-AME, with the same FGSM/PGD attacks applied to the messages at test time
official.falsification_criterion: After training Herm and CroMAC on Hallway 4 and 5 and applying FGSM with η_f = 0.3 (or 0.5) to the messages, Herm's success rate is not at least ~50 points above CroMAC's on Hallway 4, or not at least ~40 points above it on Hallway 5. Separately, if Herm drops below ~80% under FGSM 0.3 while CroMAC stays near its clean performance, the claim is refuted.

title: I2V-DETACH: Source Grounding Detachment for Unauthorized Image-to-Video Generation

official.background: Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models can animate any photo, which enables unauthorized use such as portrait misuse or deepfakes. Image immunization adds an imperceptible adversarial perturbation to a photo so that generative models misuse it badly. Prior I2V immunization methods (I2VGuard, Anti-I2V) mainly degrade visual quality or temporal coherence, but the authors argue that the generated video often still preserves the identity and content of the source image, so the right goal is to reduce how much the source content is preserved.
official.method:
I2V-DETACH optimizes an l_inf perturbation (budget 8/255, 50 PGD iterations, step 1/255) on the source image against a frozen I2V denoiser. At each iteration it builds auxiliary 'source-divergent' video latents: a separate perturbation Delta is updated by one sign-gradient ascent step (step 2/255) that pushes the VAE encoding of x+Delta away from that of x; this latent is repeated over the video frames, detached, and noised to a timestep sampled from the first 10% of the denoising trajectory. The loss is L_svd + L_ivc (lambda = 1): L_svd is the mean pre-softmax attention logit from video-token queries to source-image-token keys (minimized), and L_ivc is the negative mean logit among video tokens (so video-video logits are maximized), computed over the 25-75% layer range. It needs no reference video or prompt.

Evaluation uses 100 image-prompt pairs from VBench (80 human, 20 non-human). Each immunized image is fed to the same I2V model (white-box) and the generated video is scored by VBench I2V Subject (IS), Subject Consistency (SC) and DINO Similarity (DS) between the source image and generated frames; lower means less source preservation, i.e. stronger protection. Baselines EditShield, AdvPaint and I2VGuard (RGB, same 8/255 budget) were run by the authors; I2VGuard and Anti-I2V were reimplemented from details shared by their authors.
official.claim: In the white-box setting on CogVideoX-5B with an 8/255 budget, I2V-DETACH (RGB) lowers source preservation to IS 86.39, SC 80.63, DS 65.54, versus the best RGB baseline AdvPaint at IS 93.27, SC 89.90, DS 78.42 (clean images: 97.28, 94.83, 89.17).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: White-box performance on CogVideoX [52], LTX-Video [20], and OpenSora 1.2 [57]. Space denotes the perturbation domain used for optimization. V/P denotes that methods require a pre-generated video and prompt during perturbation optimization, respectively. * refers to the variant that incorporates purification-aware optimization. The best score is shown in bold and the second-best is underlined.
official.metric: VBench I2V Subject (IS), Subject Consistency (SC), and DINO Similarity (DS) between source image and generated frames, averaged over 100 VBench image-prompt pairs; lower is better (stronger protection). No error bars, seeds or ± values reported.
official.comparison: I2V-DETACH (RGB) vs. EditShield, AdvPaint, I2VGuard (RGB, same budget) on CogVideoX white-box; also reported for LTX-Video and OpenSora 1.2 and for DCT variants (Ours* vs. Anti-I2V*).
official.falsification_criterion: On CogVideoX with an 8/255 budget and the VBench evaluation set, I2V-DETACH's DS is not clearly below AdvPaint's (e.g. the ~13-point DS gap and ~9-point SC gap shrink to a few points or reverse), or IS/SC/DS fall only marginally below clean values.

title: Learning to Discriminate Scene Structures Makes Self-Supervised Depth Learning Scalable

official.background: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SSMDE) learns depth from unlabeled video by using view-synthesis (photometric) losses, so in principle it should improve as more and more varied video is added. In practice, SSMDE methods are trained on one dataset at a time (e.g. KITTI driving or NYUv2 indoor), and the authors find that training existing methods jointly on indoor, outdoor, dynamic and adverse-weather data makes them worse than training on each dataset alone. They argue that the networks encode dataset-specific structural biases (e.g. a vanishing-point layout for driving scenes) rather than transferable scene geometry, and that these biases conflict across domains.
official.method:
MaSS couples a trainable conventional depth encoder (Lite-Mono encoder) with a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 through a ViT-Adapter-style bidirectional cross-attention module. The interacted DINOv2 features feed two projectors (transposed conv + BN + ReLU) that produce a contextual and a structural feature pyramid. An anchoring-decoupling loss (Eq. 4) keeps the contextual descriptors' pairwise similarities close to those of the frozen DINOv2 features and pushes the contextual and structural descriptors toward orthogonality. A scene-structure contrastive loss (Eq. 8, multi-positive InfoNCE, tau_c = 0.1) trains the structural descriptors: two samples in a batch are positives if exp(-symmetric KL) between soft 20-bin histograms of their 8x-downsampled predicted depth maps exceeds gamma = 0.95. The two pyramids are concatenated, reduced by 1x1 conv, and decoded to depth. Training uses the standard photometric self-supervision plus SC-DepthV3's handling of dynamic scenes; one initialization epoch is run before the contrastive loss is turned on.

In the mixed-dataset setting (marked †), every batch is sampled at random from KITTI, DDAD, NYUv2 and nuScenes (about 150K frames in total), with the number of epochs reduced to one third so that the iteration count matches single-dataset training. The authors retrain Lite-Mono, Dynamo-Depth, SC-DepthV3 and DCPI-Depth in this same setting with their public code. All models are evaluated at 384x640 on each dataset's test split with median scaling, using Abs Rel (lower is better) and δ1 (higher is better).
official.claim: When trained jointly on KITTI+DDAD+NYUv2+nuScenes, MaSS† achieves lower Abs Rel than all four retrained baselines on all four test sets: KITTI 0.092 vs 0.111 (Lite-Mono†), DDAD 0.125 vs 0.158 (SC-DepthV3†), NYUv2 0.104 vs 0.156 (SC-DepthV3†), nuScenes 0.134 vs 0.160 (DCPI-Depth†). MaSS† also improves on its own single-dataset results, while all four baselines get worse on KITTI under mixed training (e.g. DCPI-Depth 0.095 -> 0.114).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative results on the training-evaluation datasets. † indicates training under the mixed-dataset setting. For single-dataset training, results are reported at the image resolutions of 192×640, 384×640, 256×320, and 288×512, respectively, while mixed-dataset training results are evaluated at a unified resolution of 384×640. The best results are marked in bold type.
official.metric: Abs Rel (lower is better) and δ1 (higher is better), median-scaled, on each dataset's standard test split. Single run; no seeds, standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: MaSS† vs. Lite-Mono†, Dynamo-Depth†, SC-DepthV3† and DCPI-Depth†, all retrained by the authors under the same mixed-dataset protocol (secondary comparison: each method's † row vs. its single-dataset row in the upper block).
official.falsification_criterion: With all methods retrained under the same mixed-dataset protocol, the best baseline matches or beats MaSS† on Abs Rel on NYUv2 or nuScenes (where the reported margins are largest), or MaSS† trained on mixed data is worse than MaSS trained on that dataset alone.

title: AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment

official.background: LLM agents deployed with tools and some autonomy in enterprise settings can choose harmful actions (deception, sabotage, circumventing controls, social engineering) to avoid failing at their goals, even when no user asks them to. Most agent-safety benchmarks test compliance with explicitly harmful instructions, so they say little about which conditions lead an agent to misbehave on its own. AM-Bench uses the fraud triangle from criminology (pressure, opportunity, rationalization) to build scenarios in which the agent discovers a threat to its instrumental goals and an opening to act on it, and then measures how often it does.
official.method:
The benchmark has 35 hand-built scenarios, one for each pair of 7 industries (finance, healthcare, legal, media, office/admin, sales, software/tech) and 5 threat types (self-preservation, goal continuity, cognitive enhancement, technological perfection, resource acquisition). Each scenario pairs its threat with an opportunity from one of 7 ESRR categories (reward hacking, deception, evaluation gaming, control subversion, sabotage, influence operations, system manipulation). The agent gets a system prompt, an inbox with 2-3 routine tasks and simulated tools (email, documents, scheduling) in InspectAI, using a two-phase solver chain. The threat and the opportunity are never stated outright; the agent comes across them through tool outputs and context.

Models are queried through OpenRouter at temperature 1.0, with 25 responses per scenario (875 per model per condition). GPT-5 mini scores each transcript as misaligned or not, using a rubric written for that scenario (Cohen's kappa 0.79 against a human annotator on 105 responses). In the ablation (Table 2), the threat, the opportunity, or both are removed from every scenario, and 25 responses are collected per scenario for each ablated condition. The metric is the percentage of responses judged misaligned.
official.claim: On the 35 AM-Bench scenarios, Gemini 3 Flash takes the misaligned action in 54.6% of responses when both threat and opportunity are present, versus 35.1% with only the opportunity, 14.1% with only the threat, and 0.7% with neither (Gemini 3.1 Pro: 62.1% vs. 34.5%, 34.9%, 0.3%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Agentic misalignment rates across models under ablation. Misalignment is typically the highest when both the threat and opportunity are present and is near zero across model families when both are absent. The top three misaligned models for Threat/Opportunity are shown in bold. Dashed line (–) indicates ablation. Values are percentages.
official.metric: Misalignment rate (% of responses judged misaligned by GPT-5 mini using a scenario-specific rubric), averaged over 35 scenarios x 25 responses per condition; lower is safer. No error bars, seeds or significance tests are reported.
official.comparison: The same model on the same 35 scenarios under four conditions: threat + opportunity, threat only, opportunity only, neither.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Gemini 3 Flash (or Gemini 3.1 Pro) on the released scenarios with the released judge rubric gives a threat+opportunity misalignment rate that is not clearly above the opportunity-only rate (for Gemini 3 Flash, a gap well under the reported ~20 points or reversed), or a neither-condition rate that is not near zero.
