title: CME–SpectrumBench: Can LLMs Analyze Condensed Matter Spectral Data?
claim_source: Figure 2 (a, b), page 3; numbers for Gemini 3.1 Pro also stated in the text on page 3

official.background: Scientific LLM benchmarks mostly test symbolic or theoretical reasoning, not the extraction of quantitative information from noisy experimental data. In condensed matter physics, ARPES and RIXS spectroscopies produce 2D intensity maps over energy and momentum, and analysis is an inverse problem: recovering dispersions, line widths, phonon energies or doping from a spectrum blurred by noise and instrumental resolution. Because the needed information is spread over the whole array (~10^5 tokens as text), this is also a test of dense long-context reasoning, and of whether LLMs could act as data-analysis assistants.
official.method:
A purpose-built simulator generates ARPES and RIXS spectra for 38 question categories, each at 5 noise (ARPES) or convolution (RIXS) levels, for 190 questions. Questions are almost all three-shot: the prompt gives three example spectra with their answers, then a test spectrum, and asks for a number or an array of numbers. Spectra are given as text tables (100x100 = 10^4 pixels at standard resolution, intensities normalized to a max of 1000 and rounded). Each answer is scored with a Lorentzian, Score = γ²/((x − x0)² + γ²), with γ = 0.005/Å in momentum, 0.003 eV in energy, 0.01 in doping; array answers are scored element-wise and averaged. A model's score is averaged over repeated responses per question, then over all 190 questions ("all"); "min."/"max." are averages over the lowest/highest noise-or-convolution level only.

Direct prompting puts the data in the prompt and scores the printed answer. Advanced prompting ("Code") gives the same questions with the datasets as .csv files and a Python interpreter; the code's numerical output is scored. "ReAct" additionally prompts the model to run its code on the example datasets and compare with the example answers to debug. A handwritten analysis script by a graduate student is the reference (where several fitting options existed, all were run and the best score per question kept).
official.claim: On the 190-question CME–SpectrumBench at standard resolution, Gemini 3.1 Pro scores 0.34 under direct prompting but about 0.46 with a Python interpreter and ReAct prompting (all spectra), and 0.48 vs. about 0.68 on minimum-noise/convolution spectra; Claude Opus 4.5 goes from about 0.05 (direct) to about 0.28 (ReAct), all spectra.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: (a) More recently released, closed–weight (proprietary) models generally perform better. Models with asterisks (*) are open–weight. Note expanded axes scaling, which top out at 1. Min./max. refer to spectra with minimum and maximum noise or convolution. (b) Advanced prompting improved scores, particularly for questions with minimal noise and convolution (min.), but gains were marginal when experimental complications were severe (max.). A solid black line denotes identical scores under direct query and advanced prompting. The legend applies to both subfigures.
official.metric: Mean Lorentzian score in [0, 1] (higher is better; 0.5 means an error of about one experimental standard deviation), averaged over repeated responses per question and then over questions. No error bars are reported for the leaderboard. Values other than those stated in the text are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Same model on the same questions under direct prompting vs. code-interpreter (Code) and code-interpreter + ReAct prompting; handwritten code (0.45 all, 0.61 min.) as reference.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Gemini 3.1 Pro (or Claude Opus 4.5) on the released questions, the ReAct/Code score averaged over all 190 questions is not clearly above the direct-prompting score (e.g. a gain under ~0.05 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, or under ~0.1 for Opus 4.5), or the gain on minimum-noise spectra disappears.

title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference

official.background: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) builds expressive variational distributions by mixing an explicit conditional q(z|ε) over an implicit mixing variable ε. Sampling is easy, but the exact ELBO gradient needs the marginal score ∇z log q(z), which is intractable because it integrates over ε. UIVI estimates this score by running MCMC on the reverse conditional q(ε|z), and AISIVI uses importance sampling with a conditional normalizing flow as proposal; both add an inner approximation that is costly and can be unstable.
official.method:
DIVI trains a separate score network sψ(z) (an MLP) to approximate the marginal score by denoising score matching: it regresses sψ(z) onto the tractable conditional score ∇z log qφ(z|ε) on samples (ε, z) drawn from the semi-implicit hierarchy, whose minimizer is the marginal score. Training alternates a ψ-step (several score-matching updates on fresh samples) with a φ-step that applies the pathwise ELBO gradient (∇z log p(D,z) − sψ(z)) ∇φ hφ(u,ε), using the learned score as a plug-in in place of the intractable marginal score. No reverse-conditional sampling is needed.

Conditioned diffusion benchmark: a 100-dimensional Euler-Maruyama discretisation (Δt = 0.01) of the double-well SDE dx = 10x(1−x²)dt + dw, x0 = 0, observed every 5 steps with Gaussian noise σ = 0.1. The variational family is Gaussian conditional with ε ~ U[0,1]^100, a two-hidden-layer ReLU MLP (width 128) for the mean and a learned global diagonal variance; all methods share this family. SIVI, UIVI, AISIVI and DIVI train for 10,000 iterations (lr 1e-3, batch 128, step decay 0.7 every 1,000, 5,000-step linear annealing); KSIVI for 100,000. DIVI's score MLP has 3 hidden layers of width 128, is warm-started for 2,000 epochs, then gets 5 updates per VI step on 2,048 samples. The metric is the expected log marginal likelihood (ELM): the sum over coordinates of the log of a 1-D Gaussian KDE fitted to 100,000 model samples, averaged over 1,000 SGLD reference posterior samples (SGLD: 1,000 particles, 100,000 iterations, step size 1e-4).
official.claim: On the 100-dimensional conditioned diffusion posterior, DIVI reaches an expected log marginal likelihood of 75.162 ± 0.02, higher than AISIVI (74.687 ± 0.03), KSIVI (74.808 ± 0.04, with 10x the iterations), SIVI (58.309) and UIVI (21.866), and closest to the SGLD reference (75.316), while using the least wall-clock time (335 s vs. 736 s for AISIVI and 756 s for UIVI).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Conditioned diffusion results for expected log marginal likelihood and wall-clock time.
official.metric: Expected log marginal likelihood (ELM) of SGLD reference samples under coordinate-wise KDE of model samples, higher is better; ± is standard error over 10 independent runs. Wall-clock time is end-to-end training time including warmup, reported without error bars.
official.comparison: DIVI vs. AISIVI, UIVI, SIVI (same variational family and 10K iterations) and KSIVI (100K iterations) on the same conditioned diffusion target
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the benchmark with 10 seeds, DIVI's mean ELM is not higher than both AISIVI's and KSIVI's by more than a few standard errors (e.g. the gap to the best baseline falls below ~0.1), or DIVI's training wall-clock time is not clearly below AISIVI's and UIVI's under the same hardware.

title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (FLOPs/latency in Table 1, page 7; average budget 44.64% in Table 4, page 9)

official.background: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving combine perception, language reasoning and trajectory prediction in a single LLM-based model, but running a dense LLM backbone on every frame costs onboard compute, latency and energy. Existing efficiency work for driving VLAs shortens the token sequence (fewer vision tokens, shorter chain-of-thought). This paper instead skips LLM layers, choosing per frame how many to skip and which ones, on the premise that routine scenes need less capacity than complex ones.
official.method:
The base model is SimLingo (InternVL2-1B: InternViT-300M plus the Qwen2-0.5B LLM with 24 layers). The LLM is split into Lpre = 4 prefix layers that always run and Lsub = 20 routable layers. Five extra tokens are appended to the input. Three are scene-aware tokens: a scene-deviation token from cross-attention between an EMA history of pooled visual features and the current visual tokens, plus path and speed decision-deviation tokens computed from the ego-motion-aligned difference between the waypoints predicted at t-1 and t-2. The other two are a budget query and a layer-routing query. A budget MLP reads the budget-query hidden state after prefix layer 2 and picks one of K = 10 discrete budgets b (floor bmin = 0.2). The chosen budget is sinusoidally embedded by a budget encoder, and at the end of the prefix a routing MLP reads the routing query concatenated with this budget embedding and selects k = floor(24·b) - 4 of the 20 routable layers via Gumbel-Softmax top-k. Skipped layers are bypassed through the residual connection.

Training has two stages on SimLingo's dataset, using 2× RTX 4090. Stage 1 is SFT for one epoch (~90k steps) with a uniformly random budget b ~ U[bmin, 1] and the budget scheduler frozen, trained with SimLingo's waypoint and language losses plus diversity and balance regularisers; the prefix layers are tuned with LoRA. Stage 2 is GRPO for ~40k steps (group size 4). It unfreezes the budget scheduler, the budget query, the scene-aware encoders and the LoRA of the first half of the prefix layers, with an L2 anchor loss to their Stage 1 values. The routing scheduler, budget encoder, routing query and later prefix layers stay frozen. It uses a reward that trades off waypoint loss against the full-budget loss and penalises the budget. Evaluation is closed-loop Bench2Drive in CARLA (220 routes), reporting Driving Score (DS) and Success Rate (SR). Compute is LLM-only FLOPs ≈ 2·P_active·(N_in + N_out). 'SimLingo+SA@b' is the same trained model run with its budget fixed at b.
official.claim: On Bench2Drive closed-loop evaluation, SimLingo+SA with its learned adaptive budget cuts LLM compute from 0.59 to 0.27 TFLOPs per decision (-53.5%; ~45% average active budget) while keeping Driving Score at 84.87 vs. 85.07 for dense SimLingo. The same model forced to a fixed 40% budget (0.24 TFLOPs) drops to DS 78.20 and SR 59.09%, vs. 65.45% for adaptive.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison with SOTA driving methods on the closed-loop benchmark.
official.metric: Driving Score (0-100, higher is better), Success Rate (%), and LLM TFLOPs per decision (lower is better). Bench2Drive values are means over 3 random seeds with no std or other error bars reported.
official.comparison: SimLingo+SA (adaptive budget) vs. dense SimLingo (non-inferiority on DS at much lower compute) and vs. SimLingo+SA@40% (fixed budget at similar compute)
official.falsification_criterion: The claim is refuted if a reproduced SimLingo+SA averages at least ~1.5 DS points below dense SimLingo under the same evaluation, or uses more than ~0.35 TFLOPs (more than ~60% of SimLingo's), or if a fixed 40% budget model matches adaptive SA's DS/SR within a few points.

title: ControlJEPA: Principled Trajectory Regularization via Lyapunov Tube Loss

official.background: Fine-tuning language models with next-token prediction (NTP) puts no constraint on the shape of the hidden-state trajectory across token positions. Recent JEPA-style regularizers (LLM-JEPA, Semantic Tube Prediction / STP) add auxiliary losses that push these trajectories to be straight, which was reported to improve accuracy and data efficiency in fine-tuning. STP penalizes only the angle between displacement vectors, not how far the hidden state drifts from a reference path. This paper replaces the angle penalty with a Lyapunov-style contraction condition on the size of the deviation from a reference line, and claims better downstream accuracy than both standard fine-tuning and STP.
official.method:
For each semantic segment (dataset-provided, following STP), take the final-layer hidden states at two anchor positions t_start and t_end, form the reference secant v_geo = h_tend - h_tstart, and for each intermediate position compute the transversal error e_t = (I - v̂v̂ᵀ)(h_t - h_tstart). The Lyapunov candidate is V_t = ||e_t||² / ||v_geo||². The Lyapunov Tube Loss is the mean over valid transitions in the segment of σ(V_{t+1} - γV_t - τ), with σ = softplus or ReLU, and the training objective is L_NTP + λ·L_Lyap. No architecture change.

The setup follows STP: same codebase, splits, decoding and validation for all methods, 5 seeds (82, 23, 37, 84, 4). Baselines are plain NTP fine-tuning, NTP + LLM-JEPA loss, and NTP + STP loss, using their published dataset-tuned epochs and learning rates; ControlJEPA keeps those and tunes only λ, γ, τ (the ablations use λ = 0.05, γ = 0.95, and accuracy is reported flat for λ in [0.01, 0.08]). The metric is task accuracy on GSM8K (and five other benchmarks) after fine-tuning.
official.claim: Fine-tuning on GSM8K (Figure 3a setting, apparently Llama-3.2-1B) with the Lyapunov Tube Loss gives about 42% accuracy, versus about 36.5% for NTP + STP, about 36.5% for NTP + LLM-JEPA and about 32.5% for plain NTP fine-tuning, with error bars of about ±1 point or less.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Accuracy and generalization performance of L_NTP, LLM-JEPA, STP, and ControlJEPA across (a) Datasets, (b) Model families, and (c) Model sizes.
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on the GSM8K test set, higher is better; bars are means over 5 seeds (82, 23, 37, 84, 4) with error bars that the paper's checklist describes only as 'variability across experimental runs' (std vs. SE not stated); values are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: ControlJEPA (NTP + λ·Lyapunov Tube Loss) vs. NTP + STP, NTP + LLM-JEPA and plain NTP fine-tuning, same model, codebase, splits and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: With the same base model, GSM8K data and baseline hyperparameters, ControlJEPA's mean accuracy over seeds is not at least ~3 points above NTP + STP (the paper reports ~5-6 points), or the difference is within the seed spread.

title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
claim_source: Table 9, page 26 (Appendix E); same means in Table 2, page 7

official.background: Reinforcement learning improves the clinical reasoning of LLMs, but medical RL pipelines usually depend on expert-labelled questions or costly synthetic data. The medical literature contains many unlabelled clinical case reports that trace a patient from presentation to treatment. Document-grounded self-play (a proposer writes questions from documents and a reasoner learns to answer them) could turn such reports into RL training signal without labels. The authors argue that existing self-play methods (e.g. SPICE) do poorly here because the proposer keeps asking about the same salient clue in each report, and because rewarding only intermediate difficulty lets through badly formed or shallow questions.
official.method:
CasePlay alternates GRPO updates of a proposer and a reasoner, each warm-started separately from Qwen3-8B-Base by SFT on the same small warm-start dataset (5 epochs, lr 1e-5), over 4,281 PubMed Central case reports (2020-2025). Before training, the proposer extracts up to M = 4 knowledge points per report; each of the Np = 4 proposer rollouts for a report is conditioned on one knowledge point chosen round-robin, plus the full report, and outputs a multiple-choice question, a reasoning chain and a target answer. The frozen reasoner answers each question 4 times without the report, giving a learnability reward 1 - 2|acc - 0.5|, and also scores the question (with target answer and reasoning chain) on three rubric dimensions: clue integration, reasoning depth and option quality. Each reward component is normalised within the group and combined as learnability + 0.2 x (sum of rubric components).

Valid questions go into a buffer; the reasoner is then trained with GRPO on them (8 samples per question, binary correctness reward, no access to the report). Training runs 15 iterations of 10 proposer steps + 10 reasoner steps, batch 128, lr 1e-6, max output 8,192 tokens. Baselines R-Zero, SPICE and DARC use the same warm-start data. Evaluation is average accuracy over 8 samples (temperature 0.6) on seven benchmarks; the headline clinical benchmark is LiveClin (1,450 text-only questions). Table 9 reports mean ± std over three training seeds and 95% bootstrap CIs over runs and questions.
official.claim: With Qwen3-8B-Base and the same SFT warm-start, CasePlay reaches 72.3 ± 0.8 accuracy on LiveClin (text-only), above DARC (70.5 ± 0.7), SPICE (67.1 ± 1.2) and R-Zero (66.0 ± 1.5), and 66.2 average across seven benchmarks versus 65.0 for DARC.
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Full results for the main self-play comparisons.
official.metric: Avg@8 accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is std over three training seeds; 95% CIs by percentile bootstrap over training runs and evaluation questions. No std is given for the seven-benchmark average.
official.comparison: CasePlay vs. self-play baselines R-Zero, SPICE and DARC, all trained from the same SFT warm-start on the same case-report corpus
official.falsification_criterion: Over three seeds, CasePlay's mean LiveClin accuracy is not above DARC's by more than the seed std (about 0.8 points), or it fails to exceed SPICE's LiveClin accuracy by a margin outside the bootstrap CIs.

title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (CXR-CounterFact-Single columns); paired differences from Table 14, Appendix I, page 19

official.background: Medical vision-language models (Med-VLMs) can score well on benchmarks while relying on textual priors and disease co-occurrence patterns instead of the image. They then fail on subtle findings and on overlapping conditions. The paper argues that fine-tuning data dominated by templated text makes the language signal drown out the visual one. It proposes data selection as the fix: choose the training samples whose learning signal actually depends on the image, rather than scoring each image-text pair as a whole.
official.method:
For each training sample, ViCoR computes two gradients of a final-answer-token loss over the parameters that will later be fine-tuned (the LoRA parameters): one with the real image (joint) and one with the image replaced by a dataset-level per-channel mean image (shortcut). The residual g_delta = g_joint - g_short is the image-dependent update. The visual-necessity score is S_vis = 1[E_delta >= tau_E] * E_delta * w_s * w_d. Here E_delta = ||g_delta||, w_s = log(1 + clip(||g_short|| / ||g_delta||, 0.05, 20)) measures how strongly the shortcut dominates, and w_d = 1 - [cos(g_delta, g_short)]_+ rewards residuals that point away from the shortcut gradient. S_vis is multiplied by a calibration factor B_i, which rewards answers that map to a fixed clinical vocabulary and concise answers, and softly penalizes answers with more than 2 labels. The resulting score defines a 3K candidate pool. The final K = 20% subset is then picked greedily, MMR-style (lambda = 0.85), using cosine similarity over a lightweight descriptor (length features, a 32-bucket MD5 answer hash, residual statistics). All hyperparameters are listed in Appendix C.

The selected subset is used to fine-tune Qwen3-VL-4B or InternVL3.5-4B with LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, all attention and MLP projections, lr 1e-4, cosine schedule, 3 epochs, effective batch 16, bf16). Baselines get the identical recipe: Full (100% of the pool), Random 20%, GraNd, LESS, Self-Filter and Adapt-infinity at 20%. Models are evaluated zero-shot on four external benchmarks (OmniMedVQA, GMAI-MMBench, MedBLINK, DrVD-Bench), and the Avg. column is the unweighted mean of the four. The CXR-CounterFact-Single pool has 40,000 examples: single-disease CXR-CounterFact items plus sampled normal cases, after Qwen3-4B-based denoising, task classification and removal of fill-in-the-blank items.
official.claim: When selecting 20% of the 40K CXR-CounterFact-Single pool, ViCoR gives the highest four-benchmark average on both backbones. title: When Empathy Misses the Goal: A Benchmark for Goal Displacement in LLM Advice
claim_source: Table 34, page 62 (Appendix L); also Figure 3a, page 9

official.background: LLM assistants giving advice can respond warmly while failing to move the user toward their stated goal, for example reassuring someone in distress without naming the binding deadline or eligibility rule that decides their situation. Existing benchmarks measure instruction compliance, sycophancy, or safety, not whether actionable content survives once the supportive text is set aside. The paper calls this failure 'goal displacement', builds a 230-scenario benchmark (GDB) to measure it, and asks which post-training stage suppresses it.
official.method:
GDB scenarios are single-turn user prompts in a 2 × 2 grid of hard constraint × emotional distress: F1 (constraint only, 65), F2 (constraint plus distress, 65), F0 (distress only, 35; failure is unsolicited problem-solving) and F3 (neither, 65). Each response gets a Displacement Severity (DS) score from 0 to 3 via a 'deletion test': remove the purely supportive sentences and judge whether a complete, goal-advancing reply remains (DS ≥ 2 if the remainder is noticeably thin or nearly empty). A response counts as displaced when the mean DS of the two raters is ≥ 2; the displacement rate (DR) is the share of displaced scenarios in a family.

For the post-training probe (Appendix L), allenai/OLMo-2-1124-7B (Base), -SFT and -DPO each generate one response to all 230 scenarios (temperature 0.7, single turn, no system prompt, max tokens 4096). Each response is scored by two LLM judges, GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2, with the released rubric; their DS scores are averaged and thresholded at ≥ 2. Stage transitions are compared per family with McNemar tests on the paired scenario outcomes. The same procedure is applied to Qwen2.5-7B Base→Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.2→v0.3.
official.claim: On the 65 F2 (constraint + distress) GDB scenarios, OLMo-2 7B's displacement rate is 52.3% for both Base and SFT checkpoints and falls to 13.8% for the DPO checkpoint (−38.5 pp, McNemar p < 0.001), so the reduction happens at preference optimization, not at SFT.
official.claim_caption: Table 34: Per-family pairwise displacement comparison. n = scenario count per family (same 230 scenarios for all comparisons). DR values are averaged-judge displacement rates (%). ∆DR in percentage points. p = McNemar test (exact or asymptotic with continuity correction as indicated).
official.metric: Displacement rate on F2 = % of scenarios whose judge-averaged DS (GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2) is ≥ 2; lower is better. One sample per scenario per checkpoint, no seeds or error bars; significance is a paired McNemar test over scenarios.
official.comparison: OLMo-2-1124-7B-SFT vs. OLMo-2-1124-7B-DPO (and Base vs. SFT) on the same 65 F2 scenarios, same generation settings and judges
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning the three OLMo-2 checkpoints on the F2 scenarios with the released judge pipeline, the SFT→DPO drop in F2 displacement is small (e.g. under ~15 pp or not significant by McNemar), or Base→SFT also shows a comparably large drop, so that the reduction is not concentrated at the DPO stage.

title: ProtGlycanDock: Towards Accurate Protein-Glycan Docking with Tailored Dataset, Benchmark and Model

official.background: Glycans are flexible, branched sugar polymers that bind proteins noncovalently and govern processes such as metabolism, immune response and pathogen recognition, but their complexes are hard to solve experimentally. Computational docking would fill the gap, except that existing docking programs and structure prediction models were built for small molecules and proteins, and the few protein-glycan complex benchmarks that exist contain fewer than 100 samples and cannot be used for training. The authors curate ProtGlycanDock, 1,781 repaired noncovalent protein-glycan complexes from the PDB split into 1,374 training, 125 validation, 134 glycan-holdout test and 148 protein-holdout test samples, and run ten existing methods on it under a blind docking setting.
official.method:
All ten baselines are evaluated blind: no ground-truth receptor structure and no binding-site information are given. The two physics-based methods (AutoDock Vina, Vina-Carb) and the two machine-learning docking models (DiffDock, SurfDock) are run on AlphaFold 3-predicted receptor structures with RDKit-generated glycan conformers, with DeepPocket-predicted pockets defining the search box for the Vina methods and SurfDock's own surface preprocessing and SurfScore ranking used for its pose selection. The six molecular structure prediction models (RoseTTAFold All-Atom, Chai-1, Boltz-2, AlphaFold 3, Protenix v0.5.0, Protenix-constraint v0.5.3) take a protein sequence plus a glycan specification (CCD codes with covalent bonds for AlphaFold 3, Boltz-2 and the Protenix models, a SMILES string for Chai-1, an sdf conformer for RoseTTAFold All-Atom); for AlphaFold 3, Chai-1, Boltz-2 and the Protenix models the output sample with the highest ranking score is taken as the prediction, and Protenix-constraint additionally receives the DeepPocket-predicted pocket as a constraint.

A prediction counts as geometrically correct when Ligand RMSD (glycan RMSD after superposing predicted onto ground-truth protein) is below 2 Angstrom, and as both geometrically correct and physically plausible when it additionally passes every PoseBusters test. Each model is run with inference seeds 42-46, and the table reports mean and standard deviation over those five seeds. The paper's own contribution, finetuning Protenix and Protenix-constraint with glycan topology embeddings and a Carbohydrate Intrinsic (CHI) energy loss, is reported in the same table but is not part of the claim below.
official.claim: Under blind docking on ProtGlycanDock, Protenix-constraint produces roughly twice as many geometrically correct and PoseBusters-valid predictions as SurfDock, the best docking model: 22.2 (0.7) vs 10.6 (0.8) of 148 protein-holdout samples, and 20.6 (0.5) vs 9.4 (0.5) of 134 glycan-holdout samples.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Benchmark results on ProtGlycanDock. Mean (standard deviation) of each metric is given. The best, second-best, and third-best results are denoted by bold, underline, and italic, respectively. Abbr., PB-valid: passing all PoseBusters tests, FT.: Finetuned; Topo.: Topology; Emb.: Embedding.
official.metric: Number of predictions with Ligand RMSD < 2 Angstrom that also pass all PoseBusters tests (higher is better); value in parentheses is the standard deviation over inference seeds 42, 43, 44, 45, 46
official.comparison: Protenix-constraint v0.5.3 (molecular structure prediction with DeepPocket pocket constraints) vs SurfDock (best of the four docking methods: AutoDock Vina, Vina-Carb, DiffDock, SurfDock), both run blind by the authors on the same test sets with the same five seeds
official.falsification_criterion: SurfDock, or any other docking baseline, reaches within one seed standard deviation of Protenix-constraint on the count of Ligand RMSD < 2 Angstrom and PoseBusters-valid predictions on either test set, or Protenix-constraint's count falls to SurfDock's level.

title: Rethinking LLM Fine-Tuning via Weight Space Reparameterization: Preserving Safety during Downstream Adaptation
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (attack-wise breakdown in Table 18, page 24)

official.background: Fine-tuning a safety-aligned LLM on a benign downstream task, such as math word problems, often erodes its refusal behavior, so jailbreak attacks succeed more often afterwards. Existing defenses mix in safety data, filter training data, constrain updates, or patch the weights after fine-tuning. Many of them protect specific neurons or parameters in the model's original coordinates. The paper argues that safety information is spread across many coordinates there, so freezing a subset of raw weights protects safety only partially.
official.method:
WSR-Tune builds a safety-conditioned basis for each target linear layer W_l (attention q, k, v and MLP up, down in every layer). It collects the layer's input activations on safety examples (Circuit Breakers harmful prompts with refusals), eigendecomposes H_l H_l^T = U_l Σ_l U_l^T and reparameterizes the weight as W~_l = W_l U_l (output basis V_l = I). It scores each coefficient of W~_l by the magnitude of the safety-loss gradient summed over the safety corpus, freezes the top ρ = 10% within each layer with a stop-gradient mask, and fine-tunes the remaining coefficients on the downstream task.

All methods fine-tune the full model for 3 epochs (effective batch 16, max length 1024, bf16, AdamW, cosine schedule, seed 42) on GSM8K for the Llama-2 Chat models, with method-specific learning rates (full-parameter FT uses 5e-5). Safety is the attack success rate (ASR) on AdvBench harmful prompts, averaged over Direct prompting and three HarmBench-generated jailbreaks (AutoDAN, PAIR, PAP). An attack counts as a success if the response does not start with a HarmBench refusal keyword. Downstream performance is 5-shot GSM8K accuracy.
official.claim: On Llama-2-7B-Chat fine-tuned on GSM8K, WSR-Tune (10% of reparameterized coefficients frozen) reaches 6.90% average jailbreak ASR at 38.99% GSM8K accuracy. Full-parameter FT gives 20.78% / 41.17%. The baselines with comparable accuracy all have higher ASR: SafeInstr 13.55% / 38.44%, SEAL 12.75% / 38.89%, Resta 10.56% / 36.92%. The only baselines with lower ASR (AsFT 5.27%, SafeDelta 5.57%) fall below 20% accuracy.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison across various chat and instruction-tuned models. Safety is measured by Jailbreak (JB) AVG (averaged over Direct, AutoDAN, PAIR, and PAP; lower is better), and downstream performance is measured by task accuracy (higher is better). Specifically, we use GSM8K for the Llama-2 Chat models and MATH for the Llama-3 Instruct models. We also report changes relative to Full Params FT: ∆S (safety, lower is better) and ∆D (downstream, higher is better). We further define ∆Overall = −∆S + ∆D to summarize the safety–utility trade-off.
official.metric: Average attack success rate over Direct/AutoDAN/PAIR/PAP on AdvBench (keyword-based refusal check; lower is better) and 5-shot GSM8K accuracy (higher is better). Single run (seed 42); no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: WSR-Tune vs. Full Params FT, SafeInstr, Resta, SEAL, AsFT, Lisa, SafeDelta, SN-Tune, RSN-Tune under the same downstream fine-tuning pipeline on Llama-2-7B-Chat / GSM8K
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup, WSR-Tune's average ASR is not clearly below that of SafeInstr, SEAL and Resta (e.g. above about 10%) at GSM8K accuracy within about 1 point of theirs, or its GSM8K accuracy falls well below 38%. Either result would refute the claim; so would re-running with other seeds and finding the gaps within run-to-run variance.

title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation

official.background: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) trains an amortized conditional density estimator q(z | x) on simulated (x, z) pairs by maximizing log-likelihood. With flexible families such as Gaussian encoders or normalizing flows this objective is unbounded: the model can shrink its predicted variance around each training point. Early stopping is then what sets the posterior scale, but along the training trajectory the mean and variance are fitted to the same pairs. As the mean overfits, the in-sample residuals shrink and the variance becomes overconfident, so early stopping has to trade an underfit mean against an overconfident variance. This matters most when simulations are expensive and the training set is reused for many epochs.
official.method:
Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE) splits the N training pairs into K = 10 folds. Stage 1 trains, for each fold k, a mean regressor mu_{-k}(x) with MSE loss on the other K-1 folds; with M > 1, mu_{-k} is the average of M networks trained on the same data from different initializations. Each training pair then gets an out-of-fold residual r_i = z_i - mu_{-k(i)}(x_i). Stage 2 fits a conditional density q_psi(r | x, mu) to these residuals by maximum likelihood; for the Gaussian family this is a mean-zero diagonal Gaussian. At test time the posterior is q_psi(z - mu_{-1}(x) | x, mu_{-1}(x)), using the fold-1 mean regressor.

On the Gaussian–Gaussian problem, z ~ N(0, I_200) and x | z ~ N(z, 0.25 I_200), so the exact posterior is N(0.8x, 0.2 I_200). Each seed uses N = 10,000 training pairs and 1,000 test pairs, with the same simulations shared across methods, over 10 seeds. Baselines are standard NPE (Std-NPE) with a diagonal Gaussian encoder and Std-NPE-mixture, a uniform mixture of K' independently initialized Std-NPE fits (deep ensembles), with K' chosen to roughly match CF-NPE's compute. Every network's depth, width, learning rate, weight decay, dropout and batch size are tuned with Optuna (100 trials each); mixtures inherit the base method's hyperparameters.
official.claim: On the Gaussian–Gaussian problem (d = 200, N = 10,000) with a diagonal Gaussian posterior family, CF-NPE with M = 3 reaches held-out log-likelihood -128.42 ± 0.10 nats, versus -141.30 ± 0.11 for standard NPE and -133.28 ± 0.11 for the roughly compute-matched 30-member standard NPE mixture (analytic posterior: -122.84).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Gaussian–Gaussian problem (d = 200). Held-out log-likelihood (nats, mean ± standard error over 10 seeds), χ²_d (target 1), and posterior-mean MSE under each approximating family. MSE standard errors are at most 0.001, except 0.003 for Std-NPE (standard NPE) with the NSF approximation. Bold marks entries within one standard error of the best within an approximating family. The reference rows are analytic.
official.metric: Held-out test log-likelihood in nats (higher is better), mean ± standard error over 10 seeds. Reduced chi-square χ²_d (target 1) and posterior-mean MSE are secondary.
official.comparison: CF-NPE (M = 1, 3, 10; K = 10 folds) vs. Std-NPE and Std-NPE-mixture (K' = 10, 30), all with a diagonal Gaussian approximating family, on identical simulations per seed
official.falsification_criterion: With tuned networks, CF-NPE (M = 3) does not beat Std-NPE-mixture K' = 30 in test log-likelihood by clearly more than the reported seed standard errors (paper: -128.42 ± 0.10 vs. -133.28 ± 0.11, a gap of about 4.9 nats), or CF-NPE (M = 1) does not beat single Std-NPE (paper: -133.92 vs. -141.30).

title: Robustness of Internal Signals for Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models

official.background: Vision-language models often mention objects in captions that are not in the image. A popular family of detectors scores each generated token using only signals from the captioning model's own forward pass: output logits ('black box', e.g. NLL, entropy) or hidden states and attention ('white box', e.g. IC, CL, GLSim, SVAR, PAS). White box methods usually score higher on benchmarks, but it is unclear whether they actually check the image or exploit shortcuts such as the fact that hallucinated objects tend to appear late in a caption. The paper tests this with several interventions and argues that some white box detectors rely on token position rather than visual evidence.
official.method:
LLaVA-1.5-13B (llava-hf) captions 5,000 randomly chosen MSCOCO 2014 val images (seed 0) with the prompt 'Describe this image in detail', greedy decoding, max_new_tokens=512. CHAIR string matching against COCO annotations labels each mentioned object as hallucinated or not (first occurrence of each object, first token of multi-token words; systematic false matches like 'orange' are filtered). The hallucination rate is 22.8%. Seven detectors give a per-object score: black box NLL and Entropy; white box Internal Confidence (logit-lens on image patches), Contextual Lens (image-patch vs. text-token cosine similarity), GLSim (global/local similarity), SVAR (attention from the token to image patches) and PAS (attention from the token to earlier caption tokens). The token-position heuristic (index of the object's first token in the caption) is a reference.

Blank-image test: keeping the original caption and its original CHAIR labels fixed, the authors recompute every detector's scores with the image replaced by a blank gray image (teacher-forcing the caption) and compare AUPRC with the original-image scores. A visually grounded detector should fall to roughly the hallucination rate (random AUPRC); a detector that ignores the image should keep its performance.
official.claim: On LLaVA-1.5-13B captions of 5,000 COCO val images, replacing the image with a blank gray image barely changes AUPRC for attention-based PAS (0.514 -> 0.509) and SVAR (0.493 -> 0.445), whereas NLL (0.447 -> 0.181), Entropy (0.451 -> 0.217) and IC (0.504 -> 0.236) drop to about the random baseline of 0.228.
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Detection methods that depend on token position (i.e., SVAR, PAS for LLaVA-1.5-13B) exhibit less visual grounding than other detection methods. We compare detection method performance in AUPRC when using the original image (solid) compared to replacing the image with a blank gray image but retaining the original caption (hatched). A greater drop suggests greater grounding in visual signals, while negligible drops indicate little to no grounding in the image.
official.metric: Object-level AUPRC for detecting CHAIR-labelled hallucinated objects (higher is better; random = hallucination rate 0.228). No error bars in Figure 4 (single greedy run).
official.comparison: Each detector's AUPRC with the original image vs. with a blank gray image (same captions and labels); position-dependent attention methods (SVAR, PAS) vs. black box methods and IC
official.falsification_criterion: With a blank image, PAS or SVAR AUPRC falls by a similar amount to NLL/Entropy/IC (e.g. to within ~0.1 of the 0.228 random baseline), or NLL/Entropy/IC keep most of their original AUPRC.

title: Real In, Real Out: What If We Only Use Real Data for Scene Text Editing?

official.background: Scene text editing (STE) replaces the text in a cropped scene-text image with a new string while keeping its style (font, color, texture, lighting, perspective). Training normally needs paired images with the same style but different text, which almost never exist in real photos, so prior methods train mostly on rendered synthetic pairs and then suffer from a synthetic-to-real gap: leftover source strokes, misspellings, or a visibly synthetic look. The paper asks whether an STE model can be trained on real labeled text images only, by turning each image into its own training pair.
official.method:
Self-paired data (Alg. 1): for a real image I_tgt with label T_tgt of length L, the image is split along its long axis into L equal segments (Alg. 1; the appendix implementation splits the width into n_split in [2, L] equal columns, which may cut through characters); with probability p_shuffle = 0.7 the segments are randomly permuted (Shuffle), and then a consecutive subset of N <= L segments is kept and concatenated (Crop). The result is the pseudo-source I_src, whose reading order is destroyed but whose local style survives. The model is trained to reconstruct I_tgt from (I_src, T_tgt). Training data is U14M-Filter (3.22M real labeled text instances from Union14M); no synthetic data is used.

TextRIRO is a conditional latent diffusion model: SD 2.1 VAE (frozen), SD 1.5 U-Net (trained), a ViT style encoder (as in TextCtrl) whose multi-scale features are added into the U-Net ControlNet-style (trained), and a character-level text encoder pre-trained with an autoregressive STR objective (MAERec) on real text (frozen). Inputs are 64x256; inference uses 20 sampling steps and CFG 2.2. For RIROCommon, every image of six standard STR test sets (IIIT5K, SVT, IC13, IC15, SVTP, CUTE80) is given one equal-length and one variable-length target string; each STE model edits the image, and the output is read by an independent recognizer (SVTRv2). title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning

official.background: In online continual learning (OCL) a model sees a non-stationary stream of class-incremental tasks once (single pass, small batches), usually with a small replay buffer, and suffers catastrophic forgetting. Most OCL methods change the data, loss or gradient (replay, distillation, gradient projection) but feed the resulting gradient to a generic optimizer such as SGD or AdamW. This paper argues that the optimizer itself should be designed for OCL and proposes a drop-in replacement that can be put under any existing OCL method.
official.method:
SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation) keeps two copies of the weights: a fast 'plasticity' sequence φ and a slow 'stability' sequence θ. At each step the gradient (whatever the upstream OCL method produces, e.g. ER loss on stream + replay batch) is evaluated at the interpolated point x_t = (1 − β)φ_t + βθ_t; φ is updated by a base optimizer with that gradient, φ_{t+1} = Opt(φ_t, ∇L(x_t), γ) (SGD or AdamW, giving SPIN-SGD / SPIN-AdamW); then θ_{t+1} = θ_t + α(φ_{t+1} − θ_t). The final model is θ (Algorithm 1). All main results use α = β = 0.05.

Setup: randomly initialized ResNet-18, stream batch size 10, replay batch 64 from a reservoir-sampled buffer, CCL-DC experimental configuration (MOSE and SCR use the MOSE setup with an NCM classifier). Split CIFAR-100 is 10 tasks with buffer M = 2000. For each OCL method, SPIN-X uses the same learning rate and weight decay as X (Table 11; e.g. ER: SGD lr 0.01, AdamW lr 0.0005). Metrics: final Average Accuracy (Acc, mean accuracy over all tasks after the last task) and Averaged Anytime Accuracy (AAA, mean over tasks of the average accuracy on seen tasks after each task). Results are averaged over 5 runs.
official.claim: On Split CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, M = 2k, ResNet-18), replacing AdamW with SPIN-AdamW at the same learning rate raises the 11-method average final accuracy from 36.23% to 38.49% and AAA from 45.10% to 49.75%, and improves every one of the 11 OCL methods; for ER specifically Acc goes 33.07 → 35.92 and AAA 41.50 → 48.08 (SGD → SPIN-SGD: 27.94 → 33.31 Acc, 36.86 → 46.18 AAA).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Comparison of final Average Accuracy (Acc. %) using different optimizers on Split CIFAR-100 (M=2k) and Split Tiny-ImageNet (M=5k). Our SPIN is benchmarked against 4 standard optimizers across 11 SOTA OCL methods. Table 3: same for Averaged Anytime Accuracy (AAA %).
official.metric: Final Average Accuracy and Averaged Anytime Accuracy (%), higher is better; mean over 5 runs, no std or confidence interval reported
official.comparison: Each OCL method trained with SPIN-AdamW vs. AdamW (and SPIN-SGD vs. SGD) with identical learning rate, weight decay and all other settings; RMSprop and Adam are additional baselines
official.falsification_criterion: Rerunning ER on Split CIFAR-100 (M = 2k) over 5 seeds, SPIN-AdamW's mean Acc is not higher than AdamW's by more than the seed std (paper gap: 2.85 points Acc, 6.58 points AAA), or SPIN-AdamW does not beat AdamW on the majority of a few re-run methods (e.g. ER, DER++, ER-ACE).

title: When Copying Is Hard: Copy-Constrained Decoding for Exact Span Reproduction
claim_source: Table 15 (Appendix H.1), page 21; averaged over backbones in Table 2 (page 7) and frozen-model rows of Table 1 (page 7)

official.background: LLMs are often asked to reproduce a span from their context verbatim: a contract clause, a quoted methods sentence from a paper, a code snippet, or an API key or credential string. Even when the target is in the prompt, models drift mid-span (substituting a plausible but wrong token) or overrun or stop short of the span boundary, and a single wrong character makes the output unusable. Existing copy-aware decoding methods (LLMA, CopySpec) mainly speed up generation and keep the base model's output unchanged, and rule-based copy constraints do not know where a requested span begins and ends.
official.method:
CopyGen is a plugin of small MLP heads on top of a frozen LLM's final hidden state. At each step it computes the grounding length m_t (longest suffix of the output so far that occurs contiguously in the source). If m_t is at least τ = 5, a trigger head fed LN([h_t; log(1+m_t)]) decides between COPY and ordinary generation. In COPY mode a length head on the same input predicts a tentative copy length in log space, and the candidate source continuations are replayed token by token through the frozen model. For each replayed token the raw source margin Δ (logit of the source token minus the best other logit) is shifted by a bounded learned bias b = 8·tanh(f_bias(LN([h̄; Δ]))), where h̄ is the frozen model's replay hidden state at that proposal position. The decoder emits the longest prefix whose adjusted margin is above γ = 0, and falls back to one-step source-aware generation otherwise.

The heads are trained for one epoch (AdamW, lr 1e-4, grad accumulation 16) with trigger, log-length and a hardness-weighted hinge loss on adjusted margins (in-span tokens vs. boundary-crossing tokens), using the benchmark train splits. Decoding is greedy (temperature 0). The benchmark has four tasks: Contract (JSON-formatted clause extraction from SEC EDGAR contracts, 141 test items), Literature (verbatim evidence spans from PubMed Central articles, 145 test), Code (explain and then reproduce a snippet from FastAPI/SQLModel/Starlette, 229 test), and Random Sequence (copy a synthetic OpenSSH-style private key, 250 test). The metric is exact match after stripping leading and trailing whitespace and empty lines.
official.claim: With a frozen Qwen3-8B and greedy decoding, CopyGen raises exact match over the best of the base model and five source-aware decoding baselines (LLMA, CopySpec, PICARD-style, Longest-Copy, CopySpan) on Contract (34.75 vs. 16.31), Literature (86.21 vs. 77.93) and Random Sequence (90.40 vs. 69.20), while decoding at about 15x the base model's throughput on average (842 vs. 55 tokens/s).
official.claim_caption: Table 15: Full comparison with source-reuse and constrained-decoding baselines. Baselines are grouped into lossless source-reuse acceleration (Lossless), rule-based source constraints (Rule-based), and learned copy mechanisms (Learned); CopyGen is listed separately. Each cell reports EM and tokens/s. Throughput of Longest-Copy is omitted (–) as it is not meaningful without model verification. Best results within each backbone are highlighted in bold.
official.metric: Exact match (%) on each task's test set, higher is better; single deterministic (greedy) run, no error bars; the paper marks bold results as significant with a two-tailed paired t-test at p < 0.05 (Tables 1 and 2). Throughput in tokens/s on one RTX PRO 6000.
official.comparison: Qwen3-8B frozen + CopyGen vs. the same frozen Qwen3-8B with standard greedy decoding, LLMA, CopySpec, PICARD-style source-constrained decoding, a Longest-Copy rule, and CopySpan (span pointer-generator trained on the frozen LM), all on the same test sets
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Qwen3-8B (frozen) with CopyGen trained on the released train splits, EM on Contract, Literature or Random Sequence is not clearly above the base model and the best baseline (e.g. the gain on Random Sequence is under ~10 points, or the gain on Literature disappears).

title: HorizonComposer: Spatiotemporally Consistent Driving Video Editing with Enriched Traffic Semantics
claim_source: Table 5 (Appendix D), page 15; relative version in Table 1, page 8

official.background: Instruction-guided video generators can turn one recorded driving log into many variants (other weather, season or time of day), which is useful for stress-testing autonomous-driving perception. General-purpose video editors often corrupt traffic semantics while doing this: lane markings vanish, vehicles change colour or appear and disappear, and an imperfect reference frame causes flicker at the start of the clip ('temporal shock'). The paper aims to make global appearance edits on driving video while keeping road markings, vehicles and scene layout intact.
official.method:
HorizonComposer fine-tunes Cosmos-Transfer2.5 (a ControlNet-style diffusion transformer) with a frozen depth control branch (Depth Anything V2) and a fine-tuned visual branch that takes the source clip. It is also conditioned on an edited first frame (Qwen Image Edit during training; Nano Banana Pro at test time). Training data is a hybrid of real pose-aligned Boreas traversal pairs under different conditions and 28,348 synthetic pairs from Boreas, nuScenes and Waymo, made by editing the first frame with Qwen and propagating it with Cosmos-Transfer2.5 (depth weight 0.9, visual weight 0.1). This synthetic pipeline is the 'SyntheticPip' baseline.

Each training pair gets a dense per-pixel reward map built from SAM-based scene-change detection, SAM3 masks of lane lines, crosswalks and vehicles, an InternVL check on vehicle colour, FF-α/FF-β optical-flow consistency, and CLIP instruction success. The map is thresholded into a binary pixel mask I that is fed as an extra control input. Training follows CFGRL-style advantage conditioning with flow-matching loss and drops I with probability 0.3; at inference I = 1 everywhere, with reward guidance scale 2.0. At inference, N = 2 'thinking frames' with temporally reflected controls are prepended and later cropped. Training takes 28k steps at 480p on 2 H100s (48 GPU-hours). Lane = spatial IoU of SAM3 road-line masks between source and edited video; Car = fraction of IoU-matched SAM3 vehicle instances that InternVL judges to keep the same body paint.
official.claim: On global weather/season/time-of-day edits, HorizonComposer preserves road lines and vehicle appearance better than its own synthetic-pipeline baseline (SyntheticPip): Lane IoU 0.4848 ± 0.0030 vs. 0.4035 ± 0.0020 and Car 0.8358 ± 0.0037 vs. 0.7778 ± 0.0070 in-domain (150 Boreas/nuScenes/Waymo clips), and Lane 0.6220 ± 0.0062 vs. 0.5790 ± 0.0023 and Car 0.8578 ± 0.0019 vs. 0.7922 ± 0.0060 out-of-distribution (150 nuPlan clips).
official.claim_caption: Table 5: Quantitative Comparison on Driving Scene Editing. We evaluate models across temporal stability, instruction alignment, ODD preservation, and overall video quality. Values indicate means with standard deviations below. We report best and runner-up mean performances on In-Domain (ID) and Out-of-Distribution (OOD) scenarios.
official.metric: Lane↑ (SAM3 road-line mask IoU, source vs. edited) and Car↑ (fraction of matched vehicles whose paint colour InternVL judges unchanged); higher is better. ± is described only as 'standard deviations'; the paper does not say over what (seeds, runs or samples).
official.comparison: HorizonComposer vs. SyntheticPip (Qwen/Nano Banana first-frame edit + Cosmos-Transfer2.5 propagation, same backbone and same reference image), also vs. CCEdit and UniVideo, on the same ID and OOD test clips

title: Velocity Ambiguity Profiles: Time-Resolved Bayes-Risk Diagnostics for Flow Matching
claim_source: Section 5.4 and Appendix D.7 (velocity loss, page 48; Figure 4, page 9); Table 2, page 10 (FD and other deployment metrics; full version Table 15, page 48)

official.background: Flow matching trains a network to regress a velocity target at every interpolation time t, but the loss is normally reported as a single average over t. Part of that loss is an irreducible Bayes-risk floor (several data points remain plausible given the same noisy interpolant) and part is reducible estimation error that more data or a better estimator could remove. The paper defines the Velocity Ambiguity Profile A_v(t), the time-local Bayes-risk floor, so that the time-resolved loss splits as L_N(t) = A_v(t) + R(t; N), and asks whether the reducible part R(t) can be used to decide where along t training effort should go.
official.method:
Since A_v(t) is not observable on real data, the reducible error is estimated by a reference-relative proxy R̂(t) = L_N(t) − L_ref(t), where L_ref is the time-resolved validation loss of large-budget reference models (here five models trained on all 50,000 CIFAR-100 training rows). The proxy is frozen and used to define a training-time sampler q_4(t) ∝ R̂(t)^4 over 64 categorical time bins, with the standard MSE loss and no importance correction. The baseline samples t uniformly from the prescribed interval.

Data: CIFAR-100 images are passed through frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14; the 384-dim final-LayerNorm CLS feature is centered and globally RMS-scaled using the 50,000 training rows (no PCA or projection). Each target seed trains on 25 examples per fine class (2,500 total). The flow model is a fine-label-conditioned MLP (432 → 512 → 512 → 512 → 512 → 384), Adam, lr 3e-4, batch 512, linear path x_t = (1−t)a + tε with target ε − a. Both arms are compared on five paired training seeds; velocity loss is evaluated on a uniformly weighted 25-point time grid at the common step 11,500. For deployment, each arm's checkpoint (step 8,500 uniform, 10,500 guided) is integrated with 100-step Heun from paired noise to generate 6,000 features (60 per class), compared with a disjoint 6,000-feature test reference via global Gaussian Fréchet distance and other feature metrics.
official.claim: In CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature-space flow matching with 2,500 training examples, VAP-guided time sampling (q(t) ∝ R̂(t)^4) lowers uniformly evaluated velocity loss at step 11,500 by 6.78% versus uniform time sampling (paired 95% interval [−7.11%, −6.44%], 5/5 seeds), and its generated features have lower global feature FD (25.48 vs. 33.33, −23.6%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature-flow summary. Values are aggregate deployment metrics over five paired training seeds. Arrows indicate the preferred direction.
official.metric: Velocity MSE averaged over a uniform 25-point t grid (lower is better), relative change guided vs. uniform with paired 95% interval over 5 training seeds; global Fréchet distance between generated and held-out DINOv2 features (lower is better), mean over 5 paired seeds, no error bars reported
official.comparison: VAP-guided time sampler q_4(t) ∝ R̂(t)^4 vs. uniform time sampling, same architecture, data subset, optimizer and paired seeds
official.falsification_criterion: Over at least 5 paired seeds, the guided arm's uniform-grid velocity loss at a common training step is not lower than the uniform arm's by clearly more than seed variation (e.g. reduction under ~3% or not consistent in sign across seeds); secondarily, global feature FD of the guided arm is not lower than the uniform arm's.

title: FiLM-CAM: Keyed Feature Modulation for Conditional-Access Watermarking

official.background: Invisible image watermarks are used to flag AI-generated content and to trace provenance, but organisations often want to control who can embed, read, or remove their watermark. Today that is done by training a separate private encoder–decoder model for each organisation, which is costly to deploy and maintain. A single shared watermarking model whose behaviour depends on a secret key would let many private 'domains' share one backbone, provided that decoding with the wrong key really fails while image quality stays on par with the best open watermarking models.
official.method:
FiLM-CAM adds a Conditional Access Module to a watermark embedder–extractor pair. A 100-bit binary key is mapped by a three-layer MLP to a 64-dimensional embedding (shared by both networks), and linear layers turn it into FiLM scale/shift parameters (gamma, beta). In the embedder (a U-Net, 13.3M parameters, 256x256 input; the 100-bit message is projected to an image and concatenated with the cover) FiLM modulates the 256-channel bottleneck. In the extractor (ConvNeXt-Base, 224x224 input, globally pooled, BatchNorm) FiLM modulates the 1024-d pooled feature just before the 100-bit linear head. The residual is composed with the cover in an atanh/tanh 'logit' space with an image-dependent gain (kappa = 0.95, alpha = 100, eps = 1e-3).

Stage 1 training on 100K MIRFlickr images uses a correct-key loss (YUV + LPIPS + focal-frequency image loss, BCE message loss, GAN loss) followed, for the same sample, by a wrong-key step in which the extractor is trained to output the all-zero message for an independently sampled wrong key. Keys are sampled fresh at every iteration, so test keys are unseen. After 120 epochs, Stage 1 alternates with a Stage 2 removal-training stage in 5-epoch cycles (removal is not part of this claim). Evaluation: 5K COCO, 100 DIV2K and 5K SA-1B images, each with a random message and key; bit accuracy (BA) is measured with the correct key and with a wrong key.
official.claim: The clean FiLM-CAM model decodes its 100-bit payload with bit accuracy 0.99 under the correct key but only 0.53 / 0.54 / 0.53 (near the 0.5 chance level) under a wrong key on COCO / DIV2K / SA-1B, while keeping watermarked-image PSNR at 48.2 / 46.7 / 46.6 dB, comparable to or above the best baseline on each dataset (InvisMark 48.0 dB on COCO and 46.5 dB on DIV2K; PixelSeal 46.5 dB on SA-1B).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison with SOTA neural watermarking on COCO, DIV2K and SA-1B. † FiLM-CAM embeds a 100-bit watermark payload plus a separate 100-bit secret key (200 bits of information in total); only the 100-bit payload is recovered at decoding, and the key is not counted in capacity. bpp: bits per pixel
official.metric: Bit accuracy of the recovered 100-bit message (higher is better with the correct key; ~0.5 is the desired value with a wrong key); PSNR_W of the watermarked image vs. the cover (higher is better). Single numbers; no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: FiLM-CAM decoded with the correct key vs. the same model decoded with a random wrong key; image quality compared against TrustMark-Q, InvisMark, PixelSeal, RoSteALS, SSL, MBRS and Key-based FNNS.
official.falsification_criterion: A re-trained FiLM-CAM (same architecture and wrong-key training) gives wrong-key bit accuracy clearly above chance (e.g. >= 0.65) while correct-key bit accuracy stays ~0.99, or reaching ~0.99 correct-key and ~0.5 wrong-key bit accuracy is only possible at PSNR_W well below ~46 dB on DIV2K/COCO.

title: Primal-Dual Representation Learning for Low-Rank Constrained MDPs

official.background: Constrained MDPs (CMDPs) formalize safe reinforcement learning: maximize reward while keeping a cumulative utility or cost within a budget. Provable CMDP algorithms exist for tabular problems and for linear CMDPs with known features, but they do not cover continuous-state problems whose transition features are unknown. In unconstrained low-rank MDPs, representation learning (fitting transition features from data) has made exploration efficient. The paper extends this approach to low-rank CMDPs. This is harder because representation error affects both reward optimization and constraint satisfaction.
official.method:
The theoretical algorithm REP-PD-TEG collects data with a decaying epsilon-greedy mixture policy, fits low-rank transition features by MLE, builds covariance-based uncertainty bonuses, and plans with an optimistic Lagrangian (primal-dual) objective. For the tested claim, the authors' practical neural variant REP-PD-NN (Algorithm 3, Appendix H.2) replaces the full-batch MLE step with a mini-batch SPEDER-style representation objective. Reward and cost critics take the learned state-action representation phi(s,a) as input. The actor is trained with a SAC-style Lagrangian objective, and the multiplier lambda gets a dual update toward the cost budget after each episode.

The baseline uses the same Lagrangian SAC skeleton without the representation network: the critics and actor see raw (s, a). Any difference is therefore attributed to the learned representation. Both methods train for 1M environment steps on Safety Gym PointGoal1, PointPush1 and PointPush2 with 3 seeds and are evaluated at the final deterministic checkpoint.
official.claim: On Safety Gym PointGoal1, PointPush1 and PointPush2 after 1M steps, adding the learned representation (REP-PD-NN) to the same Lagrangian SAC backbone raises final evaluation return from about -1.4 (raw state: -1.38 ± 0.58, -1.40 ± 0.60, -1.40 ± 0.71) to near zero (-0.14 ± 0.03, -0.17 ± 0.12, -0.03 ± 0.01), with no increase in evaluation cost.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Safety Gym results for the practical neural implementation REP-PD-NN. Metrics are the mean and standard deviation over 3 seeds at the final deterministic evaluation checkpoint after 1M environment steps.
official.metric: final deterministic evaluation return (higher is better) and evaluation cost (lower is better), mean +/- std over 3 seeds at 1M environment steps
official.comparison: REP-PD-NN (Lagrangian SAC on learned SPEDER-style representation) vs. raw-state Lagrangian SAC with an identical training skeleton
official.falsification_criterion: On any of the three tasks, REP-PD-NN's mean final evaluation return does not exceed the raw-state baseline by more than the baseline's seed std, or REP-PD-NN's mean evaluation cost is clearly higher than the raw baseline's.

title: F2G-Pose: Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting for Direct RGB-D Category-Level Object Pose Estimation

official.background: Category-level RGB-D object pose estimation recovers an object's 3D rotation, translation and metric size for unseen instances of known categories, without a CAD model or reference views. It is hard because of intra-class shape variation, symmetries and partial, noisy depth. Deterministic methods rely on intermediate structures (canonical coordinates, correspondences, shape priors) that can compound errors, while diffusion-based methods such as GenPose++ sample many pose hypotheses and then score, filter and cluster them, which is slow (about 4 FPS) and makes the final accuracy depend on candidate extraction. The Omni6DPose benchmark (SOPE synthetic, ROPE real scanned objects, 149 categories) is the standard large-scale testbed.
official.method:
F2G-Pose takes an RGB crop and a segmented partial point cloud. A frozen RADIOv2.5 backbone produces dense image features (layers 8, 16, 23 fused with 1x1 convs and learned softmax weights, refined to 1024 channels); each 3D point gets the feature of the patch it projects to. The concatenated point-plus-feature set is tokenized by a DGCNN encoder into 128 tokens of dimension 512, which pass through Transformer blocks whose FFNs are Mixture-of-Experts layers (8 experts, top-2 routing, soft load-balancing loss with weight 0.01), and are pooled into a global object vector.

Two heads read the global vector in one feed-forward pass: a pose-size head that regresses a 6D continuous rotation, translation and metric size (Smooth L1 losses; rotation loss is the minimum over symmetry-equivalent ground-truth rotations), and a camera-frame shape-completion head (coarse 512 points, confidence-based fusion with observed points, upsampled to 2048 points, Chamfer-L1 supervision). The network is trained only on the SOPE training split (100 epochs, batch 512, AdamW, lr 1e-4) and evaluated on SOPE and ROPE with the Omni6DPose metrics: AUC of 3D-box IoU at 25/50/75%, VUS at joint rotation-translation thresholds, and mean rotation/translation error.

title: Rethinking Structured Generation: Can Graph-Based Reasoning Resolve Ambiguity?
claim_source: Table 13 (Appendix C.2.1), page 20; same means as Table 2, page 7

official.background: Structured generation maps natural language to formal outputs such as SQL queries or visualization specifications. It is usually trained and evaluated as a one-to-one mapping against a single reference, even though many inputs are underspecified and admit several structurally different but valid outputs (for example, different aggregations or execution-equivalent SQL). The paper argues that single-reference training suppresses valid alternatives and that selecting among sampled candidates by token likelihood or LLM judgment ignores relational structure.
official.method:
LLaMA-2-13B samples k = 5 candidate outputs per input (temperature 0.7, top-k filtering); the same pool is generated offline and shared by all candidate-based methods. Each candidate is deterministically converted into a typed graph: for nvBench, nodes are attributes, chart types, encoding channels, aggregation functions, filters, grouping fields and values, with edges such as attribute-to-encoding, aggregation-to-attribute and grouping dependencies; for Spider, nodes are tables, columns, operators, conditions, values and aggregation functions, with edges for table-to-column, joins, condition dependencies, operator-argument and condition-to-value links. Node features come from LLM contextual token embeddings. A 2-layer edge-aware GNN with mean pooling gives a graph embedding h_s, and three learned scoring heads over h_s, the input encoding h_x and their interaction (semantic, structural, relational) are summed linearly into Score(s, x). The highest-scoring candidate is the output.

The GNN and scorer are trained jointly, separately for each benchmark, with a multi-valid softmax loss (Eq. 6) that maximizes the total probability of all valid candidates in the pool, where validity means execution equivalence for Spider and comparable visual encodings for nvBench. Adam, lr 1e-4, batch 32, up to 10 epochs with early stopping, 3 seeds. The strongest baseline, Candidate + LLM Rerank, reranks the same candidate pool with an extra LLM pass that scores semantic plausibility.
official.claim: Selecting from the same 5 LLaMA-2-13B candidates, the graph-based multi-valid scorer reaches 58.9 ± 0.3 exact match on nvBench and 70.3 ± 0.4 on Spider, against 54.7 ± 0.4 and 66.8 ± 0.5 for LLM reranking, gains of 4.2 and 3.5 EM points.
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Performance stability across runs (mean ± std).
official.metric: Exact Match (%) against the reference structure, higher is better; mean ± std over 3 seeds (different initialization and decoding randomness)
official.comparison: Ours (graph scorer, multi-valid loss) vs. Candidate + LLM Rerank, Candidate + Likelihood and Deterministic LLM, all on the same LLaMA-2-13B outputs and prompts
official.falsification_criterion: With the same LLaMA-2-13B k=5 candidate pools, the graph scorer's EM is not above LLM reranking by more than about 1 point (a few seed std) on nvBench or on Spider.

title: Correct but Unselectable: The Hidden Interface Tax in Multi-Candidate Reasoning
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (counts in Appendix Table 5, page 16)

official.background: Small language models are often used with multi-candidate generate-then-rerank: sample several answers, then let a fixed verifier pick one. More samples do not always raise accuracy. A correct answer can be in the pool and still be lost because it is cut off, cannot be parsed, or uses the wrong answer format (for example a number where a choice letter is expected). The paper calls this loss the 'hidden interface tax'. It splits final accuracy into oracle coverage (some candidate is correct) times conversion (the verifier picks a correct one, given one is present).
official.method:
Qwen3-1.7B samples a raw pool of 16 candidates, each at most 128 new tokens. A fixed verifier-reranker scores candidates with two yes/no continuation scores and picks one. The verifier is Qwen3-1.7B fine-tuned on GSM8K training-split candidate pairs with a binary yes/no objective (checkpoint qwen3_17b_gsm8k512_verifier_yesno_v1). At most K = 8 candidates are kept. The answer is scored by numeric exact match on the final (boxed) span. Base sends the raw pool to the selector.

CACC (Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction) is a rule-based layer between the generator and the selector. It does not train or change either one. It has three parts. CCR (completion-centric replacement) repairs fragments and candidates with no final answer: it runs one extra batch of 4 completions of at most 160 new tokens per example and uses them to replace fragments. AMC (answer-mode compatibility) normalizes the final numeric span and protects boxed answers. SCH (selector-compatible hygiene) removes scaffold residue and near-duplicates. The rules come from a rulebook frozen offline from audited traces, and online routing uses no gold labels. After these steps the pool is merged, deduplicated, parse-checked and cut to K = 8, then passed to the same verifier.
official.claim: With the same Qwen3-1.7B generator, retained cap of 8, parser and fixed verifier, CACC raises final accuracy on GSM8K test (N = 1319) from 0.2873 to 0.3632 (379 to 479 correct, +7.59 pp). On competition_math numeric (N = 3199) it rises from 0.1519 to 0.2579 (486 to 825 correct, +10.60 pp). Oracle coverage rises from 0.4882 to 0.6391 and from 0.3210 to 0.4436.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Candidate-interface results. ∆Final and Ratio are computed against the Base row within the same dataset. † uses a Qwen3-8B proposer (different compute regime from the Qwen3-1.7B generator). Paired tests for CACC vs Base are in Appendix Table 10.
official.metric: Final accuracy (fraction of questions where the verifier-selected candidate parses to the gold numeric answer), higher is better. Oracle = some retained candidate is correct; V|O = Final / Oracle. Single run; the paper reports no error bars, seeds or paired test for these rows.
official.comparison: CACC vs. Base: the raw Qwen3-1.7B generate-then-rerank pool, with the same generator, retained cap, parser and verifier. The SP and CACC+SP rows use a Qwen3-8B proposer and are a different compute regime.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Base and CACC with Qwen3-1.7B (16 samples × 128 tokens, K = 8, same yes/no verifier, numeric exact match), CACC's final accuracy on GSM8K test exceeds Base by clearly less than ~7.6 pp (e.g. under 3 pp), or by less than ~10.6 pp on competition_math numeric (e.g. under 4 pp).

title: TENET: Time-point Encoding Network for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
claim_source: Table 1, page 6 (seed std in Table S3, page 23)

official.background: Unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) trains only on normal operation and must flag abnormal time points in sensor or server-metric streams. Most methods score anomalies by reconstruction or forecasting error, but normal data often contain fluctuations that are hard to reconstruct, so large errors do not always mean abnormal behavior. Latent one-class methods (Deep SVDD, THOC, DAGMM) score a learned representation instead. This paper argues that the bottleneck is how the scored representation is built, and that it should represent the current time point rather than summarize the whole window.
official.method:
TENET takes a window of length L = 20 ending at the current point. A temporal layer with separate parameters for each variable embeds the univariate window (value embedding concatenated with a lag embedding that is 0 at the current point). It starts an anchor state from the last time step's embedding and runs M = 2 blocks of anchored cross-attention: the query comes from the anchor and the keys and values from the whole window. A sigmoid gate mixes the query and the retrieved context, followed by an FFN. This gives one token per variable (d = 256). A 2-block Transformer then applies self-attention across the variable tokens, and the tokens are summed after a 2-layer GELU MLP and passed through a linear+GELU layer, giving the current-point system state c in R^256.

Training and scoring use the same fixed standard-normal NLL, A(X) = 0.5 ||c||^2 + const, minimized on normal training windows only (AdamW, batch 1024, 10 epochs, lr 1e-6 for PSM/SWaT/SWAN and 5e-5 for SMD). The anomaly score of time t is A(X_t). Baselines are rerun in a shared TAB-based pipeline (same loading, train-fitted StandardScaler, point-wise scoring, metric code) with their own recommended hyperparameters, over seeds {10, 23, 30, 31, 37}. Metrics are AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, VUS-ROC and VUS-PR (VUS tolerance range 0 to 10), with no score post-processing.
official.claim: On PSM, TENET reaches A-ROC 86.14 ± 0.69 and V-PR 74.21 ± 1.70, above every one of 19 baselines rerun in the same pipeline; the best baselines are CAROTS on A-ROC (75.48 ± 1.21) and GPT4TS on V-PR (56.14 ± 0.55).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Multivariate time series anomaly detection performance on real-world datasets. All metrics are reported in percent and averaged over five random seeds. Bold indicates the best score.
official.metric: AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, VUS-ROC, VUS-PR in percent (higher is better), mean over 5 seeds; ± is the std over 5 seeds from Appendix Table S3 (unavailable for IF, PCA, OCSVM, Chronos)
official.comparison: TENET vs. 19 baselines (classical: IF, PCA, OCSVM; latent one-class: DAGMM, THOC; reconstruction, forecasting and representation methods such as OmniAnomaly, CAROTS, SARAD, CrossAD, ModernTCN; foundation models TTM, Timer, Chronos, GPT4TS) on PSM
official.falsification_criterion: A faithful reimplementation of TENET trained on PSM as described (L=20, 10 epochs, lr 1e-6, fixed standard-normal NLL) gets A-ROC below about 76 or V-PR below about 57 averaged over 5 seeds, i.e. no longer clearly above CAROTS / GPT4TS under the same evaluation code; or a rerun of the best baseline closes the gap to within seed std.

title: MDMR-Bench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Multi-Reference Image Generation

official.background: Recent image generators (Qwen-Image-Edit, FLUX.2, GPT-Image, Nano Banana, Seedream) accept several reference images plus a text instruction, for example 'put the hat from Image 2 on the person in Image 1'. Existing benchmarks for this multi-reference setting are small, cover a narrow set of tasks, and mostly use a VLM that assigns a single holistic score per aspect, which is unstable across judges. Without a reliable benchmark it is hard to tell how far open-source models are behind proprietary systems and which multi-reference capabilities are still weak.
official.method:
MDMR-Bench has 2,390 cases with 2 to 4 reference images (from LAION and synthetic images) across five task families: Entity Fusion (936), Attribute Transfer (982), Multi-Element Extraction (101), Infographic Manipulation (278) and Visual Reasoning. For each case, Gemini-3-Pro generates a checklist of yes/no questions at the global and atomic level for five dimensions: Following, Consistency, Composition, Minimality and Quality. Each model generates one output per case at the closest supported resolution. Gemini-3-Pro (the default judge) then answers every checklist item for that output.

Each dimension is scored as its yes-rate. Overall is a weighted sum with weights 0.20/0.25/0.25/0.20/0.10 for Following/Consistency/Composition/Minimality/Quality. Scores are first averaged within each subtask, then across subtasks, then equally across the five task families. Six proprietary models (GPT-Image-2, Nano Banana Pro, Nano Banana 2, Seedream 5.0 Lite, Seedream 4.0, GPT-Image-1.5) and five open-source models (FLUX.2, Qwen-Image-Edit, BAGEL, DreamOmni2, OmniGen2) are evaluated on the same cases with the same checklists and judge.
official.claim: On MDMR-Bench under the Gemini-3-Pro checklist judge, every proprietary model scores higher Overall (77.5-88.8) than every open-source model (28.6-51.3); e.g. Nano Banana Pro scores 85.1 vs. FLUX.2 51.3 and Qwen-Image-Edit 49.9.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Primary leaderboard under the default Gemini-3-Pro judge, in percent. GPT-5.4 results are reported separately in Appendix A.2.
official.metric: Checklist Overall score in percent (weighted yes-rate, hierarchically averaged over task families), higher is better. No ± in Table 2; Appendix A.6 reports std over 3 independent generation+judge runs on the Multi-Element Extraction subset of 0.05-1.51 points for four proprietary models.
official.comparison: Proprietary models (GPT-Image-2, Nano Banana Pro, Nano Banana 2, Seedream 5.0, Seedream 4.0, GPT-Image-1.5) vs. open-source models (FLUX.2, Qwen-Image-Edit, BAGEL, DreamOmni2, OmniGen2), all evaluated on the same 2,390 cases with the same Gemini-generated checklists and Gemini-3-Pro judge.
official.falsification_criterion: With the released benchmark, checklists and evaluation code, FLUX.2 or Qwen-Image-Edit reaches an Overall score within about 10 points of Nano Banana Pro, or above the weakest proprietary model (GPT-Image-1.5, 77.5).
