title: PCFBench: How Far Can Large Vision-Language Models Go in Physics-aware Photonic Inverse Design?

official.background: Designing photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) is a manual inverse-design loop: an engineer inspects a cross-section image and the simulated mode field, works out why loss is high, and proposes a geometry change, which is then checked by slow FDTD simulation. Vision-language models (VLMs) could automate parts of this loop, but it is unclear whether they reason about waveguide physics or only recognise visual patterns. PCFBench is a benchmark of 26 tasks built from about 220K Meep FDTD samples across 18 fiber families, and its main finding is a 'perception-design gap': models that identify fiber geometry better do not make better physics-aware design decisions.
official.method:
Each benchmark sample pairs a 336x336 structure image (refractive-index map) with FDTD mode-field images at 1310 and 1550 nm, geometric parameters, and expert annotations. Family Classification gives the model the structure image and asks for one of 18 family labels (accuracy). Closed-Loop Improvement gives the structure image plus the 1550 nm mode field and asks for a new pitch value (numeric, 128-token budget); success is scored against family-specific expert physics rules (Appendix D.5). All queries use temperature 0.1, the system prompt "You are an expert in photonic crystal fibers.", fixed prompt templates with rule-based answer extraction, and a stratified 200-sample evaluation subset per task drawn with a fixed seed.

To ask whether the gap is visual or physical, the authors add k in {0, 2, 4, 8} in-context exemplars (labelled support examples) to the prompt for both tasks and report the mean over five random support-set draws, for Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-VL-72B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B.
official.claim: Adding in-context exemplars improves perception but not design: going from k=0 to k=8 exemplars raises family-classification accuracy for all five models (e.g. Qwen2.5-VL-7B .096 -> .172, GPT-4o-mini .130 -> .291, Gemini-3-Flash .668 -> .763), while closed-loop design success changes by at most .009 for any model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B .638 -> .641).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Family accuracy and closed-loop success with k in-context exemplars (mean over five support-set draws).
official.metric: Family classification accuracy and closed-loop improvement success rate (both higher is better) on the 200-sample subset, mean over five support-set draws; no std or CI is reported for Table 4. For scale, Table 22 gives paraphrase-sensitivity std at k=0 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B of .011 (family acc) and .021 (CL success).
official.comparison: Same model and test samples with k=0 vs. k=2, 4, 8 in-context exemplars, on a perception task (Family Acc) vs. a design task (CL Succ.)
official.falsification_criterion: For a model such as Qwen2.5-VL-7B, k=8 exemplars do not raise family accuracy by clearly more than the run-to-run spread (about .01-.02), or they raise closed-loop success by a similar or larger margin than family accuracy (e.g. CL success moves by more than about .03).

title: DRIVE: Fine-tuning via Data Contribution- and Diversity-aware Weighting with Prior Regularization

official.background: Fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a new task often causes catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities, and in practice the pre-training data is usually not available to replay. Per-sample loss weighting is a cheap lever that needs no extra data: some methods upweight hard samples to speed up adaptation, while FLOW upweights samples that the pre-trained model already fits well (easy samples) to limit forgetting. Each favours either retention or adaptation, and none has a single objective that also accounts for how diverse the weighted set is.
official.method:
DRIVE computes per-sample weights w (on the simplex) at every training step by maximizing J(w) = sum_i w_i c_i + eta log|Sigma_w| - tau KL(w || p). The contribution score is c_i = lambda a_i + (1 - lambda) t_i, with a_i = -loss of sample i under the frozen pre-trained model (for vision: the frozen ImageNet backbone with a task-specific linear-probe head trained on the downstream training set) (anti-forgetting, FLOW-like) and t_i = loss under the current model (task adaptation, hard-sample-like); lambda decays linearly from 1 to 0 over fine-tuning. Sigma_w = sum_i w_i x_i x_i^T is the weighted covariance of centered penultimate-layer features of the current model, projected to k = 128 dimensions with a fixed Gaussian random matrix, and its log-determinant rewards diversity. p is a uniform prior. The maximizer is found by the fixed-point iteration w_i proportional to p_i exp((c_i + eta x_i^T Sigma_w^{-1} x_i)/tau), at most 10 iterations, ridge 1e-5, over the current mini-batch plus a FIFO buffer of the 128 most recent samples; weights are then restricted and renormalized to the batch and used in a weighted cross-entropy loss. Defaults: eta = 1, tau = 10th percentile of pre-training loss.

Vision setup: ImageNet-1K-pretrained ResNet-50 is fully fine-tuned on CIFAR-10 (20 epochs, lr 5e-4), CIFAR-100 (25 epochs, lr 1e-3) or Flowers102 (25 epochs, lr 1e-2), SGD momentum 0.9, weight decay 5e-4, cosine schedule, batch size 128. Retention is measured as ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy after restoring the original ImageNet classification head; 'Avg Acc.' is the mean of ImageNet-1K accuracy and target test accuracy. Baselines (same training configuration; the paper reports a learning-rate search over {5e-2, 1e-2, 5e-3, 1e-3, 5e-4, 1e-4} on a held-out validation split for Standard FT, Linear Probe and DRIVE): Standard FT, Linear Probe, WiSE-FT, l2-regularization towards the pre-trained weights, DEFT-UCS, FLOW.
official.claim: With ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, DRIVE reaches the highest average of ImageNet-1K and target accuracy on all three datasets, beating the strongest baseline by 2.00 points on CIFAR-10 (84.17 ± 0.03 vs. FLOW 82.17 ± 0.02; Linear Probe 81.28), 1.54 on CIFAR-100 (72.34 ± 0.02 vs. FLOW 70.80 ± 0.03) and 0.88 on Flowers102 (83.85 ± 0.01 vs. Linear Probe 82.97 ± 0.02; FLOW 80.69).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Performance comparison of models fine-tuned on vision benchmarks (Accuracy in %). Best in bold, second in underlined.
official.metric: Avg Acc. = mean of ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy (original head restored) and target test accuracy, in %, higher is better; ± is reported but the paper does not say how many seeds the vision runs use (LLM results are mean ± std over 5 runs)

title: Inverse Modeling for Laser Pulse Shape Design in Inertial Confinement Fusion

official.background: In inertial confinement fusion (ICF), the laser pulse shape (the 3 ns temporal power profile driving the fuel pellet implosion) largely determines implosion performance, and small changes in timing or amplitude have nonlinear effects. Pulse design today relies on sweeps of expensive radiation-hydrodynamics simulations (LILAC) and expert iteration. An inverse model that maps desired implosion outcomes and pellet parameters directly to candidate pulses would make design exploration much cheaper.
official.method:
The authors generate 1 million LILAC simulations (pulse l as a length-256 sequence, pellet parameters p of size 5, implosion outcomes m of size 12) and train a surrogate S_phi(l, p) -> m (about 1.4% average error), which is then frozen. Inverse models G_theta(m, p) -> l are trained: a conditional DDIM diffusion model, deterministic LSTM and Transformer autoregressive predictors (MSE loss), and generative LSTM variants (Gaussian, mixture-of-Gaussians, categorical output).

The full objective is lambda_L L + lambda_S S + lambda_P P, where L is the reconstruction loss (diffusion noise MSE or autoregressive MSE/NLL), S is the MSE between target outcomes m and the frozen surrogate's prediction S_phi(G_theta(m, p), p) (added after a reconstruction-only warmup; for diffusion the clean pulse is estimated with the DDIM x0 formula), and P is a hinge penalty on total pulse energy exceeding that of the reference pulse. The ablation retrains each model without S. The 'm error' metric is the MAPE between the target outcomes and the surrogate's prediction on the generated pulse, on a held-out test set, over 5 training runs x 10 seeds.
official.claim: Training through the frozen surrogate (the S term) more than halves implosion-outcome error on the simulation test set: m error is 1.93 ± 0.046% vs. 4.50 ± 0.014% without S for the diffusion model, 1.65 ± 0.09% vs. 3.90 ± 0.011% for the LSTM, and 1.94 ± 0.11% vs. 4.40 ± 0.016% for the Transformer.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: ICF model performance. ± denotes standard deviation over seeds and training runs. For the predictive autoregressive models (LPDS_LSTM and LPDS_Transformer), diversity is not defined because they are deterministic. The LILAC-error column reports true simulator validation rather than surrogate evaluation and is available only for the strongest models because simulator access is limited. The ablation experiments for the loss terms were performed for a subset of the models due to computational constraints.
official.metric: m error: mean absolute percentage error (%) between target implosion outcomes and surrogate-predicted outcomes of the generated pulse (lower is better); ± is std over 5 training runs x 10 seeds
official.comparison: Full LPDS objective (L + S + P) vs. the same model trained without the surrogate loss S (L + P), for Diff, LSTM and Transformer
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining a model (e.g. the LSTM) with and without S under matched settings gives m errors whose gap is within a few std, or the model trained without S matches the full model's m error; also refuted if the gap vanishes when outcomes are evaluated with an independently trained surrogate or the true simulator.

title: Speeding up Log-Sum-Exp: Kernel Fusion at the Memory Wall, Integer Arithmetic at the Compute Wall
claim_source: Table 6 (Appendix A.2), page 15; summarized in Section 4.2, page 7

official.background: Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) is the numerically stable way to sum probabilities in log space, and ML code calls it constantly: per-token log-probabilities over the vocabulary in RLHF, sum nodes in probabilistic circuits, and weight normalization in particle filters. On GPU, torch.logsumexp runs as a chain of nine CUDA sub-kernels (max, subtract, exp, sum, log, ...) that send the input through HBM about 6 times per call, so it is about 6x slower than a plain torch.sum over the same tensor. Compilers such as torch.compile and XLA fuse the chain but keep a two-pass max-then-sum structure.
official.method:
FuseLSE is a single-pass CUDA kernel built on the pair-wise identity LSE(x, y) = max(x, y) + log(1 + exp(-|x - y|)), which folds each element into a running accumulator without a separate pass for the global max. For a float32 (B, N) input it launches one 256-thread block per row. Each thread reads its share of the row with float4 loads and folds the elements into a register accumulator using the SFU intrinsics __expf/__logf. The partial results are reduced with warp-shuffle butterflies and a small shared-memory buffer. Each input element is read from HBM once (about 1x input traffic), at the cost of N-1 log calls per row instead of one.

The claim comes from the appendix benchmark at (B, N) = (512, 128,256): per-call latency of eager torch.logsumexp, torch.compile(torch.logsumexp) (PyTorch 2.8), jax.nn.logsumexp under XLA (JAX 0.7.1), and FuseLSE on V100, H100, H200 and B300, excluding compilation time. The related benchmarks draw inputs from U(-100, 0). The paper's second kernel, IntLSE, replaces exp/log with integer arithmetic and matters only on CPU; it is not part of this claim.
official.claim: At (B, N) = (512, 128,256) float32, the single-pass FuseLSE kernel is 1.8-2.1x faster per call than both compiler-fused baselines (compile time excluded) on V100, H100 and H200: 0.310 vs. 0.605 (torch.compile) / 0.651 ms (XLA) on V100, 0.0894 vs. 0.163 / 0.184 ms on H100, and 0.0674 vs. 0.120 / 0.134 ms on H200. It is also 6.3-6.9x faster than eager torch.logsumexp on all four GPUs.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: LSE latency (ms) at (B, N) = (512, 128,256), excluding compilation; FuseLSE speedup in parentheses. –: toolchain does not support B300.
official.metric: Per-call LSE latency in ms (lower is better) and FuseLSE speedup; single reported values with no error bars or seed spread
official.comparison: FuseLSE vs. torch.compile(torch.logsumexp), JAX/XLA jax.nn.logsumexp, and eager torch.logsumexp, at the same shape on the same GPU, compile time excluded
official.falsification_criterion: On any of V100, H100 or H200 at (512, 128,256) float32, FuseLSE is less than ~1.5x faster than torch.compile or JAX/XLA (compile time excluded), or less than ~4x faster than eager torch.logsumexp.

title: Self-Evolution Reasoner: Continuous Optimization via Policy-Intrinsic Exploration and Exploitation

official.background: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR, e.g. GRPO) and on-policy context distillation (OPCD) let an LLM improve its reasoning from its own sampled solutions. Both need the policy to sample at least one correct solution per problem before they get any learning signal. On hard tasks where the model almost never solves a problem, training stalls. Adding expert solutions from a stronger model gets around this, but those solutions are off-policy, and the student cannot fully absorb reasoning from a distribution that differs from its own.
official.method:
SEPO (Self-Evolution Policy Optimization) uses the ground-truth label as a hint so that the model produces its own correct reasoning. For each problem, the student samples G = 8 unhinted rollouts. An EMA copy of the student (the teacher, EMA rate 0.05) is given the problem plus 'Correct answer: y*; reason as you naturally would without this hint' and samples H = 4 candidate reasoning traces. Only traces whose final answer passes the verifier are kept. The teacher, conditioned on a retained trace as a 'reference solution', then scores each student rollout token by token. The student minimizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence to this teacher over the student's top-100 tokens plus one tail bucket, with importance-ratio clipping at 2.0. Problems with no retained trace give no loss.

Baselines share the global batch (32 prompts), G = 8 and the EMA teacher. They are an enhanced off-policy GRPO (asymmetric clipping, off-policy correction), OPCD (Self) whose teacher context is one of the student's own correct rollouts, OPCD (Expert) whose context is a DeepSeek-V3.2 solution, and OPCD (Label) whose teacher sees only the label with no guided-deduction prompt. All methods train Qwen3-8B (non-thinking mode) with verl and FSDP2 on 8 H20 GPUs at lr 1e-5. The metric is test avg@16 (accuracy averaged over 16 samples), averaged over 3 seeds. Arrow Maze is a SynLogic task on which Qwen3-8B's initial pass@16 is exactly zero.
official.claim: On SynLogic Arrow Maze with Qwen3-8B (initial pass@16 = 0), SEPO raises test avg@16 to about 12.5 after 16 hours of training. Under matched conditions, GRPO and OPCD (Self) stay at about 0, OPCD (Label) at about 1 and OPCD (Expert) at about 4.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Training process on (a) Chemistry and (b) Arrow Maze tasks using Qwen3-8B. Shaded regions show the standard deviation across 3 runs. SEPO consistently maintains top performance throughout training, achieving effective improvements even on Arrow Maze where baselines fail.
official.metric: Test accuracy avg@16 (%, higher is better) vs. training wall-clock time. Curves are the mean over 3 runs; shaded regions are std across the 3 runs (no numeric std given for this figure).
official.comparison: SEPO vs. GRPO (off-policy), OPCD (Self), OPCD (Expert, DeepSeek-V3.2 contexts) and OPCD (Label), all trained on Qwen3-8B for 16 h with the same batch size, rollouts per prompt and EMA teacher.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same budget, SEPO fails to get clearly above 0 on Arrow Maze (e.g. it stays below ~5 avg@16 after 16 h). Or a baseline (in particular OPCD (Expert) or OPCD (Label)) reaches a final accuracy within the run-to-run spread of SEPO's.

title: End-to-End Neural Modeling of EM Response and Design Performance for Free-Form RFIC Passives

official.background: Passive matching networks in RF integrated-circuit power amplifiers are designed by repeatedly running finite-difference electromagnetic (EM) simulation, which can take up to 20 minutes per layout over the full frequency band. Neural surrogates exist, but most handle only templated layouts and predict only the EM response (S-parameters). The downstream design performance (input impedance, passive efficiency, max gain) is then computed by a circuit solver that is very sensitive to small EM-response errors. The paper targets free-form pixelated layouts and predicts both the EM response and the design performance under varying frequency and circuit context.
official.method:
Each layout is a binary 2x18x18 mask (two metal layers). A frequency-conditioned neural simulator (conv stem, layer norm, four residual blocks, with per-channel and per-position FiLM-style scale/shift predicted from a Fourier encoding of frequency) maps (mask, f) to a feature u. Two linear heads produce the explicit EM response S_hat (20 complex S-parameter entries, 40 reals) and a complementary response Z_comp. A circuit-conditioned neural solver (an MLP) takes (S_hat, Z_comp) plus Fourier-encoded capacitor values C1 and C2 and predicts design performance (complex Z_in, passive efficiency, max gain). Everything is trained end-to-end with normalized MSE on both the EM targets and the design targets (L_pred = L_EM + L_design), over 501 frequencies (10-60 GHz) and 200 sampled circuit contexts per layout. The paper also proposes an optional dependence regularizer lambda_corr * L_corr that penalizes the covariance between S_hat and Z_comp (stop-gradient on W_S and Cov(u), so it only affects Z_comp).

The ablation in Figure 9 trains the 21M-parameter input-matching model with and without Z_comp, so in the ablated model the solver sees only S_hat. The with-Z_comp model is the unregularized one (lambda_corr = 0): its per-target averages are identical to the lambda_corr = 0 run in Figure 18 (App. B.4), and it is trained and tested on the full (mixed) distribution. Data: 61,515 layouts (contour-seeded and random-path-seeded), split 7:1:2. Training uses AdamW (lr 1e-4, wd 1e-2, cosine to 1e-6) for 500 epochs, and the reported checkpoint has the best validation loss. The metric is test R^2 per target, averaged over output dimensions and frequency.
official.claim: For the 21M input-matching model on the full test distribution, adding the complementary response Z_comp raises frequency-averaged R^2 on every target, most clearly on |S| (0.9976 vs. 0.9884, with the ablated model dropping to about 0.95 near 60 GHz), and also on max gain (0.8971 vs. 0.8887) and |Z_in| (0.9878 vs. 0.9846).
official.claim_caption: Figure 9: Effect of the complementary response for the 21M input matching model.
official.metric: test R^2 per target (higher is better), averaged over output dimensions and the 501 frequencies; single training run per model, no error bars
official.comparison: 21M model with Z_comp vs. the same model and training setup without Z_comp (solver sees only the explicit EM response)
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained model without Z_comp reaches an average |S| R^2 within about 0.002 of the model with Z_comp (no high-frequency collapse), or the gap disappears across seeds.

title: Transporting Quantiles to Codebook: Scalable Vector Quantization without Codebook Collapse

official.background: VQ-VAE tokenizers map continuous encoder outputs to the nearest vector in a learned codebook so that autoregressive or masked generative models can work on discrete tokens. A well-known failure is codebook collapse: as the codebook grows, only a small fraction of codes is ever selected, so a larger vocabulary adds little capacity. Existing fixes either add auxiliary entropy losses, replace learned codebooks with fixed grids (lookup-free quantization, LFQ), or use optimal-transport assignment (OptVQ), each with trade-offs between utilization and quantization accuracy.
official.method:
FlowVQ defines a fixed prior codebook C0 in a Gaussian source space by mapping K Sobol points in [0,1]^d through the inverse Gaussian CDF, so each code covers roughly equal probability mass. A small flow-matching velocity field (4-layer MLP, hidden size 256, ~0.2M parameters) is trained jointly with the autoencoder to transport N(0, I) to the current encoder latent distribution. Every 1000 steps the codebook C1 used for nearest-neighbour quantization is recomputed as the ODE pushforward of C0 through the flow, so codes follow the latent density. The explicit codebook loss is dropped; the encoder still gets the commitment loss and the straight-through estimator.

Self-correction pushes N·K (N = 50) dense Sobol prior samples through the flow, assigns them to the nearest transported code, and moves each code toward its cluster centroid for a few k-means-style iterations. An optional online correction re-adds the standard codebook loss on real latents. On CIFAR-10 (32x32, downsampling f = 4 to an 8x8 token grid) all methods share the same VQ-GAN-style encoder/decoder (hidden 128, multipliers [1,2,4], perceptual + discriminator losses), batch size 128, AdamW at lr 1e-4, and 325K steps for |C| = 16384; the baselines use an auxiliary entropy loss by default, while FlowVQ does not.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 with identical encoder/decoder and training, FlowVQ uses 100% of the codebook at |C| = 10240 and 16384 (entropy 13.28 and 13.97 bits), while VQ-GAN collapses to 2.7% and 2.8% utilization (entropy 8.07 and 8.57). At |C| = 16384, d = 14, FlowVQ also reaches a lower rFID than every baseline: 1.40 vs. 1.65 for VQ-GAN, 1.72 for OptVQ and 2.03 for LFQ.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Evaluation of image quality and codebook utilization on CIFAR-10. By default, all baselines optimize the auxiliary entropy loss while FlowVQ does not if not specified. As the entropy maximization is tightly coupled in the OptVQ optimization process, we did not explore removing it.
official.metric: Codebook utilization (% of codes used on the evaluation set, higher is better) and code-usage entropy in bits (max log2|C|); reconstruction FID on CIFAR-10 (rFID, lower is better). Single runs, no ± reported.
official.comparison: FlowVQ (no entropy loss) vs. VQ-GAN, LFQ and OptVQ (each with auxiliary entropy loss) under the same architecture, latent dimension and codebook size

title: CoDeRNet: Selective Cross-Task Routing under Heterogeneous Supervision for Change Detection and Captioning

official.background: Change Detection & Captioning (CDC) takes a pair of remote-sensing images of the same place at two times and asks one model both to segment the changed pixels and to write a sentence describing the change. Detection gets dense pixel-level supervision while captioning gets only sentence-level supervision, so the two branches learn representations of different reliability. Earlier unified CDC models (MCINet, CTMTNet) share features or train the two heads jointly. This paper argues that information should instead be passed between the two branches selectively, only where the receiving branch needs help and the sending branch is reliable.
official.method:
CoDeRNet uses a weight-shared ImageNet-1K ConvNeXt-Base encoder on both images. At each scale it builds a change feature by a 1x1 convolution over [F_t0, F_t1, |F_t1 - F_t0|, F_t1 - F_t0], then projects it into separate detection and captioning branch features. The detection head is an FPN decoder trained with cross-entropy + Dice loss. The captioning head is a Transformer decoder over global, region-pooled (pool size 2) and local tokens, trained with token cross-entropy. The two losses are each divided by their own detached magnitude and summed.

Confidence-Decomposed Routing (CoDeR) moves features between branches. For target feature F_t and source feature F_s at the same scale, C_t = sigmoid(conv1x1(F_t)), C_s = sigmoid(conv1x1(F_s)), M = (1 - C_t) * C_s, and F_t' = F_t + M * g(F_s), where g is a light adapter. It is applied in both directions with separate parameters: caption to detection at 1/8 scale, detection to caption at 1/16 scale. The key ablation (Table 3(a)) compares this full model with the same jointly trained model with CoDeR removed, and with single-task models. Training: Adam with lr 1e-4 halved every 50 epochs, effective batch 64, 100 epochs on LEVIR-MCI, flips and 90-degree rotations with direction words in captions remapped, greedy decoding with max caption length 41. A run takes about 12 hours on one RTX 4090.
official.claim: On the LEVIR-MCI test set, adding bidirectional CoDeR routing to the otherwise identical jointly trained detection+captioning model raises captioning CIDEr-D from 136.18 to 141.79 and BLEU-4 from 64.41 to 66.27, while change-detection mIoU stays essentially unchanged (87.67 to 87.79); the CoDeR model also beats the strongest no-routing captioning baseline in the table, the captioning-only model (CIDEr-D 137.41, BLEU-4 63.18).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Ablation studies on LEVIR-MCI [25]. (a) Effect of joint training and explicit interaction, comparing single-task training, joint training without CoDeR, and joint training with CoDeR. (b) Effect of CoDeR directionality, comparing two single-direction settings with the bidirectional design. Bold indicates the best result in each column.
official.metric: CIDEr-D and BLEU-4 (higher is better) for captioning, plus METEOR and ROUGE-L; mIoU (higher is better) over building/road/no-change for detection. Single run per setting; no standard deviations or seeds are reported.
official.comparison: Joint Seg+Cap training with CoDeR vs. the same joint training without CoDeR (and single-task Seg-only / Cap-only models), all with the same ConvNeXt-B backbone, branch interfaces, decoders and training recipe. Note that for captioning the Cap-only model (CIDEr-D 137.41) is a stronger no-routing baseline than joint training without CoDeR (136.18), so the margin over the best no-routing baseline is about 4.4 CIDEr-D, not 5.6.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both variants (ideally over several seeds) gives a CIDEr-D gain from CoDeR that is near zero or within the seed-to-seed spread of either variant, or the with-CoDeR model does not exceed the without-CoDeR model on BLEU-4 and CIDEr-D.

title: Active Learning of Conditional Generative Models via the Transport Neural Tangent Kernel

official.background: In many scientific experiments the measured output for one input (a drug, a cell type, a weather station) is a whole distribution of samples, not a single number, and new measurements are expensive. Pool-based active learning picks which inputs to measure next, but existing methods for regression assume scalar or vector outputs and in effect only target the conditional mean. The paper shows that the 2-Wasserstein test risk of a conditional generative model splits into a mean term and a shape term, so mean-based acquisition ignores errors in the shape of the predicted distribution.
official.method:
The transport Neural Tangent Kernel (tNTK) is k(x, x') = ∫ Tr[D_θ T_θ(x)(y)ᵀ D_θ T_θ(x')(y)] dν(y): the inner product of parameter Jacobians of the transport map T_θ(x), which pushes a base measure ν onto the predicted conditional distribution, integrated over ν. In 1D with a monotone map this becomes k(x, x') = ∫₀¹ ∇_θ F_θ⁻¹(x; τ)ᵀ ∇_θ F_θ⁻¹(x'; τ) dτ, computed over the predicted quantile function. The tNTK is used as a GP covariance, and inputs are chosen greedily to minimize the average GP posterior variance (λ-regularized) over the pool plus the training set (Algorithm 1, the BAIT-style rule of Holzmüller et al.). As elsewhere in the experiments, the kernel uses last-layer parameters.

For conditional quantile prediction (Section 5.2, Appendix D.4), an MLP takes station (longitude, latitude, elevation) and outputs 32 non-crossing quantiles at τ_k = (2k-1)/64 (a base quantile plus softplus increments). It is trained with the squared W2 loss with early stopping, and the hyperparameters are chosen by CV and listed in Table S1. Dew Point uses 1000 randomly selected NOAA GSOD stations (2023-2025) with at least 512 daily measurements. Baselines use the same acquisition rule with the last-layer NTK of a network of the same size trained to predict the mean (NTK), the mean and variance (NTK mean-var), or the quartiles (NTK quartile). BALSA-EMD and random sampling are also compared. The metric is the change in test W2² risk from iteration 0, averaged over T = 5 AL rounds and K = 5 folds per seed.
official.claim: On the NOAA Dew Point conditional quantile task with B0 = 10 initial stations and B = 1 added per round, tNTK acquisition reduces Wasserstein test risk by −212.74 ± 11.73 (×10⁻³), compared with −159.24 ± 10.32 for the best NTK baseline (mean-var) and −76.55 ± 10.15 for random. With B0 + B = 5 + 5, tNTK reaches −442.25 ± 22.34, compared with −375.47 ± 22.57 for the best baseline (NTK quartile).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Change in Wasserstein test risk from iteration 0 (lower is better). For each seed, we average over T = 5 iterations and K = 5 folds; we then report mean ± standard error across N = 10 seeds, in units of 10⁻³. Column headers indicate B0 + B, the initial training set size and the number of conditions added per AL round. Best mean per column shown in bold.
official.metric: Change in Wasserstein (W2²) test risk from iteration 0, in units of 10⁻³ (lower/more negative is better). For each seed it is averaged over T = 5 AL iterations and K = 5 folds; ± is the standard error across N = 10 seeds.
official.comparison: tNTK vs. NTK (mean), NTK (mean-var), NTK (quartile), BALSA-EMD and Random, all using the same quantile network and the same greedy total-posterior-variance acquisition rule (except Random and BALSA-EMD)
official.falsification_criterion: On Dew Point at 10+1 (or 5+5), the best NTK-variant baseline comes within about one standard error of tNTK's mean risk reduction, or beats it.

title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution

official.background: In multi-objective RL an agent receives a vector of rewards (e.g. speed vs. energy, helpfulness vs. safety) and should perform well for any preference weighting of them. The optimal policy can change sharply with the weighting, so learning a single preference-conditioned policy, or sharing all trajectories across preferences, can cause negative transfer when objectives conflict. Approximating the Pareto front with few policies and little data is the core difficulty, and standard benchmarks measure it with the hypervolume (HV) and the number of distinct Pareto points found (cardinality).
official.method:
Routed ensemble policy learning (Algorithm 1) keeps N basis policies (N = 3 for MO-Gymnasium, Table 7). In each iteration a preference w is sampled and B trajectories are collected, each from a uniformly chosen basis policy. Each basis policy j is scored on each trajectory by its estimated scalarized return <w, sum_h sum_a r(s_h, a) pi_j(s_h, a)>, each trajectory is routed to the highest-scoring policy, and each basis policy is then updated only on its routed trajectories with the base learner F. Routing is a drop-in module on top of a published base learner, which for discrete MO-Gymnasium tasks is Pareto Q-Learning (PQL).

Baselines are PQL, MPMOQL and Envelope Q-learning with hyperparameters from their official implementations, plus a 'uniform assignment' ablation that assigns trajectories to the N basis policies at random instead of by score. All methods are trained for 10^4 time steps on the discrete benchmarks (Deep-Sea-Treasure, Fruit-Tree) and evaluated by hypervolume (HV) and cardinality of the resulting front.
official.claim: On discrete MO-Gymnasium tasks with a 10^4-step budget, routed ensembles on top of PQL (Algorithm 1, N = 3) reach a higher hypervolume than every baseline: Deep-Sea-Treasure HV 1.10 ± 0.00 (×10^3) vs. Envelope 0.79 ± 0.00, PQL 0.76 ± 0.30 and uniform assignment 0.62 ± 0.20; Fruit-Tree HV 9.30 ± 0.00 (×10^3) vs. uniform assignment 8.29 ± 0.38 and PQL 6.69 ± 0.95, with all 10 Deep-Sea-Treasure Pareto points recovered (cardinality 10 vs. at most 8.3).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of our approach with several baseline methods. We report the average success rate on Meta-World, HV and UT on MuJoCo, as well as HV and Cardinality on Grid-World.
official.metric: Hypervolume (×10^3, higher is better) and cardinality (×10, higher is better) of the learned Pareto front; ± is reported but not defined (seed count not stated)
official.comparison: Algorithm 1 (routed ensemble over PQL) vs. PQL, MPMOQL, Envelope, and uniform (random) assignment of trajectories to the same number of basis policies, under the same 10^4-step budget
official.falsification_criterion: With matched budgets over several seeds, Algorithm 1's HV is not above the best baseline (Envelope/PQL on Deep-Sea-Treasure, uniform assignment on Fruit-Tree) by more than the seed std, or uniform assignment matches routing on Fruit-Tree.

title: MedVTok: A General-Purpose Medical Visual Tokenizer

official.background: Multimodal medical AI systems need a visual front end that turns images into tokens a downstream model can consume. Existing medical visual tokenizers are usually tied to one modality or one dimensionality (2D images vs. 3D CT/MRI volumes), so multimodal systems end up with fragmented representations. A tokenizer that maps many modalities and both 2D and 3D inputs into one token space, while keeping both pixel-level fidelity and clinical semantics, would serve as a reusable interface across tasks.
official.method:
MedVTok is a transformer autoencoder (27-block encoder and decoder, d = 1152, encoder initialized from SigLIP2) with dimension-agnostic 4x16x16 patchification and RoPE over patch coordinates, trained with reconstruction (pixel, LPIPS, adversarial), KL, a slice differential regularization on 3D volumes, and Multi-Expert Representation Alignment (MERA). In MERA, a mean-pooled global representation of the tokens is contrastively aligned to features from a panel of frozen modality-specific expert encoders (projected into a shared space), and also back-projected into each expert's own space with a cosine loss. Training uses 28.8M 2D images and 70K volumes over 9 modalities in two 100K-step stages.

For the claim, every tokenizer is frozen. A global feature is taken from the CLS token (or equivalent global representation; tokenizers without one have all features concatenated), L2-normalized, and used for k-NN classification with cosine similarity and softmax-weighted voting (temperature 0.07). k is swept over {10, 20, 100, 200} on the validation set and the best accuracy is reported. Images are at 256x256 where possible. There are 9 benchmarks, one per modality: JSIEC (CFP), ChestCTScan (CT), HAM10K (dermoscopy), PolypDiag (endoscopy), BRISC (MRI), OCTDL (OCT), LungHist700 (pathology), BUSBRA (ultrasound), Kermany (X-ray). Retrieval Recall@1 uses the same features, with the train split as the gallery.
official.claim: With frozen features and k-NN classification averaged over 9 single-modality medical benchmarks, MedVTok reaches 80.23% accuracy, above the best semantic encoder MedImageInsight (76.21%) and the prior unified medical tokenizer MedITok (73.55%), with the largest gains on CFP/JSIEC (90.25 vs. 81.07 best other) and OCT/OCTDL (94.00 vs. 90.79).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Image classification and retrieval evaluation [Accuracy (%)↑, Recall@1 (%)↑]. *: semantic encoder.
official.metric: k-NN top-1 accuracy (%), higher is better, best over k in {10, 20, 100, 200} chosen on validation; Recall@1 (%) also reported. No error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: MedVTok vs. general tokenizers (SDVAE, TokenFlow, MingTok, UniTok, AToken), medical semantic encoders (BiomedCLIP, MedSigLIP, MedImageInsight) and medical tokenizers (PUMIT, MedVAE, MedITok), all frozen under the same k-NN protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same frozen-feature k-NN protocol, MedVTok's 9-benchmark average accuracy is not above MedImageInsight's (76.21%) and MedSigLIP's (74.12%), or its lead on JSIEC and OCTDL disappears.

title: From Structural Feedback to Prompt Policies: Learning Faithful Text-to-Image Prompt Editors
claim_source: Table 23, page 34 (Appendix G.7); Table 1 (page 7) reports slightly different single-run StruPO Lexica numbers (RR 69.64, SGR 80.74)

official.background: Automatic prompt optimizers for text-to-image models rewrite a user's prompt to get nicer images, but stylistic rewriting can silently drop objects, change attributes or break relations ('a tiger with a gold crown') while global text–image similarity such as CLIP score stays high. Prior structure-aware methods (OPT2I, VisualPrompter) diagnose missing scene-graph elements at test time and ask an LLM to revise the prompt iteratively. This paper asks whether that structural feedback can instead train a reusable editing policy that preserves the requested objects and relations in a single pass.
official.method:
StruPO parses the input prompt into a scene graph (object phrases with attributes, plus relation triplets) and calibrates it with one rendered image: GLIP-T grounding and BLIP-base relation verification filter ambiguous auxiliary elements (style/camera phrases), while core elements are always kept. A frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder plus a two-layer GCN (hidden 768) encode prompt tokens and graph elements; a BART-base editor outputs deletion, reordering and insertion actions applied to the input tokens. The editor is first supervised-fine-tuned on 144K Lexica-derived input/target pairs (56K updates), then trained with GRPO on 24K prompts (6K updates, N=4 rollouts, M=3 SD v1.5 images per rollout averaged before group normalization). The reward is 0.6 x the mean over constraints of clipped-log-transformed GLIP object and BLIP relation confidences + 1 x LAION improved-aesthetic score + 5 x CLIP similarity; only the GCN and editor are trained.

Evaluation uses Stable Diffusion v1.5 on a disjoint 2K-prompt Lexica test set, three images per prompt with matched seeds. Object recall (OR) and relation recall (RR) use thresholded GLIP/BLIP grounding on held-out images; SGR = (OR+RR)/2. The GPT-4o-SG-Iter baseline renders an image, gets a structural critique (missing objects, wrong attributes, broken relations), and has GPT-4o rewrite the prompt, for three rounds. The whole generation/evaluation pipeline is repeated with three independent seed lists.
official.claim: On the 2K-prompt Lexica test set with Stable Diffusion v1.5, StruPO reaches relation recall 69.51 ± 0.29 vs. 66.55 ± 0.32 for the three-round GPT-4o structural-feedback loop (GPT-4o-SG-Iter) and 61.20 ± 0.25 for Promptist, with SGR 80.67 ± 0.19 vs. 78.82 ± 0.20, while matching its aesthetic gain (AES∆ 0.63 vs. 0.61).
official.claim_caption: Table 23: Full 2K-prompt Lexica comparison over three independent matched seed lists (mean ± standard deviation).
official.metric: Relation recall RR (%, higher is better) from thresholded BLIP relation verification on generated images; also OR, SGR, AES∆ and Gemini-VQA. ± is std over three independent matched seed lists for image generation/evaluation (not over training runs). Table 21 separately reports StruPO RR 69.64 ± 0.31 over three training seeds.
official.comparison: StruPO (single-pass learned editor) vs. GPT-4o-SG-Iter (3 rounds of render, structural critique, GPT-4o rewrite), Promptist, VisualPrompter and a style-template baseline, all with matched prompts, sampler, seeds and three-image averaging.
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained StruPO editor evaluated under the same protocol fails to beat GPT-4o-SG-Iter on Lexica RR by more than about 1 point (the combined seed spread), or its RR falls to the level of Promptist (~61%).

title: Intrinsic Information Theoretic Analysis of ReLU Nets
claim_source: Figure 2, page 7; per-dataset-group correlations in Table 6 (Appendix G.4), page 30

official.background: Information-bottleneck style analyses of neural networks need estimates of the mutual information I(Y; T) between labels and hidden representations, but in high dimensions the usual estimators (binning, kernel density, k-nearest neighbours, variational bounds) depend on hyperparameters whose bias often dominates the signal. ReLU networks partition the input space into convex linear regions, each identified by a binary activation pattern, so every input carries a discrete region label. The paper asks whether this built-in discretisation can give an information estimate without any external bin width, bandwidth or cluster count.
official.method:
The paper decomposes I(Y; T) = I(Y; Pi) + I(Y; T | Pi) - I(Y; Pi | T), where Pi is the activation-pattern (region) label of a layer. The routing information I(Y; Pi) is estimated by a plug-in estimator: pass each held-out sample through the trained network, take the concatenated binary activation pattern of layers 1..l as its region id, build the count table of (label, region) pairs over data-supported regions, and compute the empirical discrete MI in bits (Eq. 4). Occupancy rho = |regions| / N is reported to flag saturation (rho near 1 means nearly every sample has its own region and the estimate approaches H(Y)).

Calibration (Study 1): fully-connected ReLU MLPs trained 150 epochs with SGD (lr 1e-3, momentum 0.9, batch 32, cross-entropy, He init, no regularisation), 5 seeds each, on Composite (synthetic 7-class 2D mixture, 2,000 held-out points), WBC (UCI breast cancer, 114 held-out points; depths 3/5, widths 5/9/25) and MNIST FC (PCA-10 rescaled to [-1,1], 10,000 test images; [3,3,3], [5,5,5], [7,7,7]); 75 networks in total. At the last hidden layer and last epoch, the routing estimate is compared with three baselines on the same held-out representations: uniform binning (K = 8 bins per unit on [-c, c], Miller-Madow corrected), k-means with K = |Y| clusters (Miller-Madow corrected), and the mixed continuous-discrete KSG estimator (k = 3, clipped at 0).
official.claim: Across 75 trained ReLU MLPs (Composite, WBC, MNIST PCA-10; last hidden layer, held-out data), the hyperparameter-free routing estimate I^(Y; Omega_D) correlates with Miller-Madow binning (K = 8) at Pearson r = 0.911 and with k-means (K = |Y|) at r = 0.922 (KSG k = 3: r = 0.892), and never exceeds H(Y).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Pointwise calibration of I^(Y; Omega_D) against three MI baselines: binning and k-means with the Miller-Madow correction, and the k-nearest-neighbour estimator KSG (last epoch, last hidden layer, held-out points). There is one marker per network (architecture and seed) on Composite (blue), WBC (orange), and MNIST FC (green). Pearson r pooled across all three datasets: r = 0.911 (binning, K = 8), r = 0.922 (k-means, K = |Y|), r = 0.892 (KSG, k = 3). WBC networks with KSG near zero: App. G.5.
official.metric: Pearson r between the routing estimate and each baseline estimate, one point per network (higher = better agreement); no error bars or confidence intervals on r are reported
official.comparison: Plug-in routing estimator vs. binning (K = 8, Miller-Madow), k-means (K = |Y|, Miller-Madow) and KSG (k = 3), all applied to the same networks and held-out points
official.falsification_criterion: On retrained networks under the same protocol, the pooled Pearson r between the routing estimate and binning (K = 8, MM) or k-means (K = |Y|, MM) falls clearly below ~0.9 (e.g. below 0.8), or the routing estimate exceeds H(Y) for some network.

title: Beyond Low-Pass Dynamics: Frequency-Selective Spiking Reservoirs with Resonant Neurons

official.background: Liquid state machines (spiking reservoir computers) pair a fixed, randomly connected spiking recurrent network with a trained linear readout, which avoids backpropagation through time and allows event-driven, low-energy inference. Almost all of them use leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons, which act as low-pass filters: they encode how much input arrives but not at which temporal frequencies. Harmonic resonate-and-fire (HRF) neurons follow damped-oscillator dynamics and respond preferentially to inputs near their resonance frequency. The paper asks whether a reservoir made of HRF neurons with heterogeneous resonance frequencies produces better representations and higher classification accuracy than an otherwise identical LIF reservoir.
official.method:
HRF-Res has two populations of N neurons, simulated with Euler steps of size Δt: a LIF encoder that receives the input through a fixed matrix U (plus bias b) and HRF feedback through W (rescaled to spectral radius ρ), and an HRF reservoir driven by LIF spikes through V. Each HRF neuron has a velocity x and position y with x_{t+1} = x_t + Δt(V s^LIF_t − γ⊙y_t − ε⊙x_t), y_{t+1} = y_t + Δt x_t, and spikes when y exceeds a refractory threshold (y is not reset). Per-neuron stiffness γ_i and damping ε_i are drawn uniformly around searched centres, giving heterogeneous resonance frequencies √γ_i. All weights are fixed; only a scikit-learn logistic-regression readout (L-BFGS, ℓ2 strength C) on the final HRF position state y_T is trained.

The baseline LIF-Res is identical except that the HRF population is replaced by LIF neurons with soft reset and per-neuron membrane time constants and thresholds drawn from log-uniform distributions. Each model gets its own random hyperparameter search under the same protocol (one seed per configuration, stratified 10% validation split of the training set; LIF-Res uses 100 trials, 80 for SHD, and the paper does not state the HRF-Res trial count), and the best configuration is re-run on the standard train/test split with 5 seeds that set all fixed weights (the same seeds for both models). On sMNIST (pixel-by-pixel, T = 784) both use N = 800; selected configurations are listed in Appendix Tables 5 and 6.
official.claim: With matched architecture, reservoir size (N = 800) and final-state logistic-regression readout, an HRF reservoir reaches 93.64 ± 0.25% test accuracy on sequential MNIST versus 67.00 ± 1.04% for an independently tuned LIF reservoir; on SHD (N = 3,000) the gap is 83.48 ± 0.44% vs. 72.95 ± 0.53%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: HRF-Res vs. LIF-Res. Both architectures are otherwise identical; hyperparameters for LIF-Res are independently re-tuned per dataset. Results are mean ± std over 5 seeds with final reservoir state readout. HRF-Res outperforms or matches LIF-Res on all four datasets, with accuracy gains up to +26.6% and lower energy consumption on most datasets. See Appendix A.5 for LIF-Res architecture details and Appendix A.4 for the evaluation protocol.
official.metric: Test classification accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is std over 5 seeds controlling the fixed reservoir weights (readout refitted per seed). Energy (J, model-based SOP estimate) is also reported.
official.comparison: HRF-Res vs. LIF-Res (HRF reservoir neurons replaced by heterogeneous LIF neurons, all else identical, hyperparameters re-tuned per dataset with the same search protocol)
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running sMNIST with N = 800 and the final-state readout, an independently and comparably tuned LIF-Res comes within a few points of HRF-Res (e.g. a gap under 10 points), or HRF-Res fails to reach about 90% accuracy with the reported configuration.

title: SAG-Sep: Sparse Augmented Graphs and Onion-Guided Search for Rounded Capacity Cut Separation
claim_source: Table 19, page 36 (paired statistics, Appendix D.6); mean gaps and runtimes from Table 3, page 11

official.background: Exact solvers for the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) tighten the LP relaxation with rounded capacity cuts (RCCs), but finding a violated RCC is NP-hard, and exact separation is far too slow on large instances. Solvers rely on the CVRPSEP heuristic, which works well on small instances but adds few useful cuts on large ones. NeuralSEP-style neural separators predict cut-defining customer subsets from the fractional LP solution, but rely on slow recursive graph coarsening. This paper proposes a single-pass neural separator and a training-free decoder that turns its node scores into many violated cuts.
official.method:
SAG-Sep encodes the current fractional LP solution as a sparse augmented graph: the LP-support graph (edges with x̄_ij ≥ τ1) plus synthetic edges to all 2-hop neighbours, each edge carrying (bottleneck flow along the widest shortest path, hop distance). The graph is replicated M = ⌈d(V+)/C⌉ times, replica m conditioned on m/max(M-1,1), and a six-layer transformer with edge-biased masked attention outputs, in one forward pass, a probability p_i^(j) that customer i belongs to an RCC-defining subset for vehicle-count level j. The threshold readout takes S^(j) = {i : p_i^(j) ≥ τ} (τ = 0.5) per replica.

Onion-Sweep (OS) reuses the same probabilities with no extra forward pass and no retraining: per replica it sorts customers by score, computes the RCC violation 2⌈d(P_r)/C⌉ − x̄(δ(P_r)) of every prefix incrementally, and emits the most violated prefix; across replicas it sorts by the mean score and emits each prefix at which ⌈d(P_k)/C⌉ reaches a new level. Violated, non-duplicate cuts are added and the LP is re-solved until no violated cut is found or a 3600 s root time limit is hit. The metric is the root optimality gap 100(U − L)/U against the best known solution, on the 10 NeuralSEP benchmark test instances per size, with one CPU thread for the LP and one NVIDIA L4 GPU.
official.claim: On the NeuralSEP CVRP benchmark at N = 50, 75, 100 and 200 customers, decoding the same SAG-Sep checkpoint with Onion-Sweep instead of the threshold readout lowers the root gap on all 40 instances, by a mean of 1.77 ± 0.29, 2.11 ± 0.51, 1.68 ± 0.28 and 1.49 ± 0.15 pp (mean gaps 2.60/3.80/5.43/7.62% vs. 4.37/5.91/7.11/9.10%), at equal or lower root runtime.
official.claim_caption: Table 19: Paired per-instance comparison of SAG-Sep+OS on the ten benchmark instances per size. W/L/T counts instances on which OS attains a better/worse/equal root bound; Δ is the opponent's gap minus the OS gap in percentage points (positive favors OS), reported as mean ± standard error and as the worst case over the ten instances.
official.metric: Root optimality gap (%) to the best known solution, lower is better; Δ = threshold gap minus OS gap per instance, reported as mean ± standard error over the 10 instances per size, with win/loss/tie counts and the worst-case Δ. One run per instance; no seeds.
official.comparison: SAG-Sep+OS vs. SAG-Sep with threshold readout (same trained encoder, same LP loop and time limit), paired on the same instances
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both decoders with the released checkpoint on the 10 benchmark instances at N = 50-200, OS fails to beat the threshold readout on most instances at some size, or the mean paired improvement falls below about 0.5 pp (or within two SE of zero) at any of these sizes.

title: Variational Consequence-Driven Offline Reinforcement Learning

official.background: Offline RL learns a policy from a fixed dataset, and the main failure mode is distribution shift: the learned policy picks actions the data does not cover and the value function overestimates them. The dominant fix is behavior regularization, which keeps the policy's action distribution close to the behavior policy's (MSE in TD3+BC, VAE density in SPOT, flow matching in FQL). The authors argue this ignores dynamics: in dynamics-sensitive states a small action deviation can lead to very different next states that are outside the data, so the constraint should be on the induced next-state (consequence) distribution instead. That distribution is intractable without a dynamics model, which motivates a cheap latent surrogate.
official.method:
StBR (Structural Behavior Regularization) trains, alongside a TD3-style actor-critic, a variational-information-bottleneck model (State Belief Gaussian Fitting): a Gaussian encoder p_theta(z|s,a), a decoder q_psi(s'|z) that reconstructs the next state, and a Gaussian state-belief encoder p_phi(z|s). The loss (Eq. 8) is next-state reconstruction + beta * KL(p_theta(z|s,a) || p_phi(z|s)) + KL(p_phi(z|s) || N(0,I)), so p_phi is fit to the aggregate latent of dataset actions. The policy loss (Eq. 12) is -Q(s,a)/alpha + lambda * KL(p_theta(z|s,a) || p_phi(z|s)) for a ~ pi(s), using the closed-form Gaussian KL, with alpha the minibatch mean |Q|. The policy is deterministic; 2 critics plus 2 target critics (Table 2 lists '4, including 2 target networks'), batch 256, 1M gradient steps, encoders 750-750 MLPs with latent dim 1.2 x state dim. For hopper-medium, lambda = 0.03, beta = 0.001 (beta = 0.003 for subsets below 10%).

For the dataset-size ablation, trajectory subsets of 1% to 100% of hopper-medium-v2 are sampled at random and both StBR and SPOT (a TD3-based method that regularizes the policy with a VAE estimate of the behavior action density) are trained on the same subsets. Scores are D4RL normalized returns, mean and std over 5 seeds.
official.claim: On D4RL hopper-medium-v2 trained on random trajectory subsets, StBR beats the VAE-based action-regularization baseline SPOT at 25% data (99.5 ± 1.5 vs. 83.6 ± 6.2) and at 10% data (97.2 ± 4.1 vs. 72.9 ± 4.5), and at every other size from 100% to 1%.

title: MEV: A Multi-Event Video Dataset for Long-Take Generation
claim_source: Table 2, page 8 (human-judged check on one fixed 128-prompt subset in Table 24, page 35)

official.background: Text-to-video datasets mostly contain short clips that show a single event, or long clips with one coarse caption. Models trained on them have little supervision for long, single-shot ('long-take') videos in which a subject performs several events in sequence, and they often drift, skip events or order them wrongly. MEV is a dataset of about 8k long-take videos (720p-4K) split into 25k events, each with human-verified start/end timestamps and event captions, plus global structured captions, camera-motion labels, semantic attributes and VBench quality scores. The paper argues that this event-grounded supervision improves multi-event video generation.
official.method:
MEV-Wan fine-tunes Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with a MinT-style multi-event adaptation: each DiT block keeps the global text cross-attention (fed the video-level middle caption) and adds a temporal cross-attention branch fed the ordered event captions, merged through a tanh gate initialised near zero, with ReRoPE (rescale length 8) binding event tokens to their frame ranges. Training samples are contiguous groups of 2-5 events from a video, with the 81 frames (480x832) allocated to events in proportion to annotated durations. LoRA rank 32 on q,k,v,o,ffn.0,ffn.2, AdamW, lr 1e-5, effective batch 128, 8 epochs, on the MEV train split (6,413 videos; 80/20 split at the original-video level).

Ultra-Wan is the matched baseline: the same backbone and MinT-style adaptation, fine-tuned on an UltraVideo-Long subset with the same number of videos. Its events come from temporal connectives ('then', 'after', 'before') in the summarized captions, with uniform temporal boundaries. Wan2.1-1.3B and the official LongLive checkpoint are evaluated without fine-tuning. Evaluation draws 128 prompts from the MEV test split five times and averages the results. MEV-Eval uses Gemini 2.5 Pro as a blinded judge, given the generated video, the global prompt, the ordered event captions and the normalised durations. It scores Event Execution Accuracy (EEA, fraction of events executed), Event Order Accuracy (EOA, pairwise order correctness), Temporal Grounding Accuracy (TGA, fraction of duration regions that mainly show their assigned event) and Boundary Transition Coherence (BTC, 1-5 rating per adjacent boundary, normalised to [0,1]).
official.claim: On the MEV test split (128 prompts x 5 random draws), Wan2.1-1.3B with MinT-style adaptation fine-tuned on MEV (MEV-Wan) scores EEA 0.61, EOA 0.45, TGA 0.60, BTC 0.64 under the Gemini 2.5 Pro MEV-Eval judge, versus 0.46, 0.33, 0.42, 0.50 for the identical adaptation fine-tuned on an equal-size UltraVideo-Long subset (Ultra-Wan), and above the strongest other baseline LongLive (0.47, 0.39, 0.46, 0.58).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: MEV-Eval event-centric generation results. Metrics are averaged over the same five random 128-prompt draws as Table 3.
official.metric: EEA, EOA, TGA, BTC in [0,1], higher is better, judged by Gemini 2.5 Pro; mean over five random 128-prompt draws from the MEV test split. No standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: MEV-Wan vs. Ultra-Wan (same backbone, adaptation and number of training videos, different training data/annotations); also vs. Wan2.1-1.3B and LongLive checkpoints without further fine-tuning
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both models under the matched recipe and judging with MEV-Eval, MEV-Wan's advantage over Ultra-Wan shrinks to within draw-to-draw variation on EEA and TGA (e.g. a gap under about 0.05), or Ultra-Wan or LongLive matches or beats MEV-Wan on most of the four metrics.

title: BudSplat: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting under a Rendering Budget
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (20/24/48-view results in Table 3, page 16)

official.background: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts Gaussian primitives directly from images in one network pass instead of optimizing each scene. As the number of input views grows (tens of views), pipelines such as AnySplat and WorldMirror produce millions of Gaussians, because repeatedly observed smooth regions generate many redundant primitives, and rendering cost scales with the number of visible Gaussians. Simple pruning by opacity or confidence tends to keep large, stable, smooth regions and drop thin structures and boundaries that matter for perceived quality. The question is whether a feed-forward model can keep only a small fixed fraction of Gaussians without losing rendering quality.
official.method:
BudSplat builds on an AnySplat-style pipeline: a pretrained VGGT backbone predicts dense points, confidences and image-aligned features from unposed views, and candidates are merged by spatial voxelization into Gaussians. Three additions are made. (1) A detail score per patch: tokens from VGGT layers {4, 11, 17, 23} pass through a rank-64 down-up projection, and the residual (token minus reconstruction) feeds a linear head; the score is trained with BCE against a target built from source-view rendering residuals and RGB/depth/normal gradients. (2) Importance-preserving voxel fusion: contributors in a voxel are weighted by softmax(1.0*confidence + 1.5*detail + 0.5*support prior). (3) Quality-aware pruning: each fused Gaussian is ranked by r = log(opacity + eps) + 1.0*D - 0.15*log(1 + voxel support), and the budget K = ceil(rho*M) is distributed over VGGT patch bins (base quota proportional to candidate count, rest by detail strength) and then filled by r within each bin. A soft gate with a straight-through hard mask makes this trainable.

Training: from VGGT weights, on a 0.7/0.3 mix of RealEstate10K and DL3DV, 8K steps, batch 1 per GPU on 8 H100s, 4-24 context views, 448x224 resolution, keep ratios sampled from {0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40}. Evaluation uses a low-overlap stress test derived from the NoPoSplat protocol (endpoint view overlap < 30%, intermediate target views), with all methods on the same context/target views and rendered at 448x224. Baselines (GGN, AnySplat, WorldMirror, and posed VolSplat) use official implementations. #GS is the number of Gaussians used for rendering.
official.claim: On RE10K under the low-overlap protocol, BudSplat keeping 5% of fused Gaussians matches or beats AnySplat in PSNR and SSIM with 14-20x fewer Gaussians: 22.48 vs 21.72 PSNR (65K vs 1298K Gaussians) at 16 views, 23.08 vs 22.69 (97K vs 1363K) at 32 views, and 23.52 vs 23.48 (173K vs 3461K) at 72 views; LPIPS is slightly worse at 32 and 72 views.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main quantitative comparison under increasing input views. We report PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and the number of rendered Gaussians (#GS). For our method, Oursρ denotes retaining a ρ-fraction of fused Gaussians after pruning. Pink and orange cells indicate the best and second-best results under each dataset and view setting, following the metric direction indicated by the arrows. OOM denotes out-of-memory during inference.
official.metric: PSNR (higher better), SSIM (higher better), LPIPS (lower better) on target views, plus #GS (number of rendered Gaussians, lower better). Single numbers, no error bars, seeds or confidence intervals reported.
official.comparison: BudSplat at keep ratio 5% (and 40%) vs AnySplat, WorldMirror, GGN (unposed) and VolSplat (posed reference) on identical context/target views
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running on the RE10K low-overlap split at 16/32/72 views, BudSplat at rho = 5% has clearly lower PSNR than AnySplat (e.g. more than 0.3 dB below) at any view count, or its #GS is not at least ~10x smaller than AnySplat's.

title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention
claim_source: Table 9 (Appendix C.2), page 20; summarized in the abstract and contribution 4

official.background: Transformers on 3D volumes (e.g. live-cell microscopy) patchify the volume and flatten it into a token sequence, which can be stored in raster, Morton (Z-order), block-contiguous or any other memory order for systems efficiency. If the positional mechanism is indexed by sequence position (learned absolute embeddings or 1D RoPE on the packed index), the model may learn the memory layout rather than the 3D geometry, so it breaks when the packing changes. The paper argues that for packed 3D fields, attention should be indexed by physical token-grid coordinates instead of memory order, and that this matters in particular for local-global attention that compresses distant context into block summaries.
official.method:
PACK3D is a local-global attention operator: exact attention over a coordinate-defined local neighborhood, plus attention from every token to one summary per contiguous 3D block, with a learned tokenwise gate mixing the two branches. Its only positional mechanism is axial RoPE: queries and keys (not values) are rotated by R(c_i), where c_i = (z, y, x) is the token's 3D grid coordinate and the head dimension is split across the three axes. Keys are rotated before being averaged into block summaries, so query-to-summary logits remain a weighted sum of query-relative 3D displacements.

For the claim used here (Appendix C.2), the authors build a controlled synthetic 3D labeling task with a fixed geometric rule. Each positional mechanism (none, learned PE, packed-sequence RoPE indexed by sequence position, axial grid-coordinate RoPE) is trained on raster-packed tokens and then evaluated on the same physical task after changing only the memory order of the tokens (Morton, block-contiguous, random). Coordinates and labels are held fixed; only the packing changes. The metric is Dice of the predicted labels.
official.claim: On a synthetic 3D labeling task trained on raster packing, learned PE and packed-sequence RoPE both reach 1.000 Dice on the training layout but drop to 0.449 (Morton), 0.418 (block-contiguous) and 0.378 (random) under test-time repacking, below the 0.554 no-position baseline, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE keeps 1.000 Dice under every repacking.
official.claim_caption: Task-level synthetic repacking benchmark. Each model is trained on raster-packed tokens and evaluated on the same physical 3D labeling rule after changing only the token memory order. Sequence-indexed mechanisms solve the training layout and collapse under repacking — below the position-blind baseline — while axial grid-coordinate RoPE is invariant.
official.metric: Dice of predicted labels on the synthetic task (higher is better); single values, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: Axial grid-coordinate RoPE vs. learned positional embeddings, packed-sequence (1D index) RoPE and no positional encoding, all trained on raster packing and tested on raster, Morton, block-contiguous and random packings of the same tokens
official.falsification_criterion: Under an equivalent synthetic setup, either (a) axial grid-coordinate RoPE loses noticeable Dice under Morton, block-contiguous or random repacking, or (b) learned PE / packed-sequence RoPE, after fitting the raster layout, do not fall clearly below their raster-layout Dice (e.g. stay above the no-position baseline) under repacking.

title: FairSplit: Decomposing the Embedding Space for Fair Classification

official.background: In-processing fair classification methods add a fairness objective during training so that a classifier's predictions depend less on a sensitive attribute such as gender or race, while keeping accuracy high. Most existing methods regularize the predictions directly and are designed only for binary targets with binary sensitive attributes. Real deployments often involve multiclass targets or sensitive attributes with more than two groups, such as intersectional groups like gender × age, and existing methods mostly cannot handle these settings.
official.method:
FairSplit trains an encoder f(x) = z together with a binary mask b that splits the embedding into a Fair Space z_f = b ⊙ z and a Sensitive Space z_s = (1 − b) ⊙ z. Only z_f is fed to a linear classification head. The loss is cross-entropy + structural compression (λ_f times the within-class variance in z_f, plus λ_s times the within-sensitive-group variance in z_s) + ρ_f·HSIC(Z_f, S) − ρ_s·HSIC(Z_s, S), with a Gaussian-kernel HSIC. Training alternates two steps. First, Adam updates the network with the mask fixed. Second, the mask is updated in closed form: b_j = V_j^(s) / (V_j^(y) + V_j^(s)), where V^(y) and V^(s) are the per-dimension within-class and within-group variances. The mask is then smoothed with an EMA (α = 0.99) and binarized at 0.5, so the size of the Fair Space is learned rather than fixed.

For the COMPAS experiment, the data uses ProPublica preprocessing restricted to African-American and Caucasian defendants. The target is binary two-year recidivism, and the sensitive attribute is gender × age (≤25 vs. >25), which gives 4 groups with p_min = 0.05. The encoder is an MLP with hidden layers [512, 256, 64]. Training uses Adam with lr 1e-3, StepLR (step 50, γ = 0.1), 150 steps in total, batch size 1024, and a 50-step classification-only warm-up for every fairness method. All methods share the FFB protocol. Each method's hyperparameters are grid-searched, and the configuration with the lowest mean validation ΔDP among those reaching ≥95% of ERM's validation AP is selected. For FairSplit on COMPAS, that is λ_f = 0.01, λ_s = 0.2, ρ_f = 0.3, ρ_s = 0.005, σ = 2. For HSIC(Y, S), it is λ = 200, σ = 1. ABCC is the area between the per-group CDFs of predicted probabilities, maximized over pairs of groups.
official.claim: On COMPAS with a 4-group intersectional (gender × age) sensitive attribute, FairSplit attains ABCC 1.2 ± 0.4. This is below HSIC(Y, S) at 6.7 ± 0.7, AdvDebias at 13.9 ± 3.1 and ERM at 17.9 ± 1.8, while all methods keep ≥95% of ERM's validation AP (FairSplit test AP 66.8 vs. 67.9 for HSIC(Y, S)).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Performance on multiclass and intersectional settings. UTKFace-AR has a 3-class age target and 3 racial groups, with F1 as utility. COMPAS has a binary target and an intersectional gender × age attribute, with AP as utility. Methods restricted to binary targets or sensitive attributes are omitted (Table 1). As in Table 2, all configurations achieve at least 95% of ERM's validation utility, and bold and underline mark the best and second-best results. Results are averaged over 5 seeds. With more than two groups, ∆π is the largest base-rate gap over pairs of groups and classes.
official.metric: ABCC (area between group-wise CDF curves of predicted probabilities, max over group pairs, in percent; lower is better), mean ± std over 5 seeds; test AP is reported as the utility check
official.comparison: FairSplit vs. HSIC(Y, S), AdvDebias and ERM, all with the same MLP encoder, training schedule and hyperparameter-selection rule (the other baselines are binary-only and cannot be run)
official.falsification_criterion: With the same protocol (≥95% of ERM's validation AP, lowest validation ΔDP selected), FairSplit's mean ABCC over 5 seeds is not clearly below HSIC(Y, S)'s, for example the gap is under about 2 points or within one seed std, or FairSplit only reaches low ABCC by falling below the 95%-of-ERM AP threshold.

title: CLaW: Codec-Guided Adaptive Latent Watermarking for Traceable Diffusion Image Generation

official.background: Text-to-image diffusion services increasingly need to trace a generated image back to the user who produced it, even after the image has been compressed, cropped, blurred or otherwise edited during redistribution. Existing watermarks either require retraining or fine-tuning the diffusion model, need slow diffusion inversion at detection time, perturb the initial noise so strongly that image fidelity drops, or (for post-hoc image watermarks such as RivaGAN) are fragile under image transformations. The paper targets multi-bit, user-specific watermarks that survive common transformations while keeping the image close to the unwatermarked generation.
official.method:
CLaW first pretrains a watermark codec in the latent space of a frozen VAE, following AquaLoRA: a secret encoder Es maps a 48-bit payload b to an additive latent residual δs = Es(b), the watermarked image is Dvae(Evae(x0) + δs), and a secret decoder Ds recovers the bits after an augmentation layer (identity, JPEG simulation, crop-and-resize, Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, color jitter). Loss: bitwise cross-entropy plus LPIPS (weight 5.0) and PRVL (weight 1.5) between VAE reconstruction and watermarked image. Trained on MS-COCO train at 512x512, AdamW lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 5, 40 epochs, StepLR (step 2, factor 0.8), warm-up with bit loss only. Es and Ds are then frozen.

At generation time the diffusion backbone (SD3.5-medium or FLUX.1-dev, 512x512, 50 FlowMatch-Euler steps, CFG 7.5, fp16) is untouched. The residual, scaled by the VAE scaling factor, is added to the noisy latent before each sampler update in the last 10% of steps (ρs, ρe = 0.9, 1.0) with a linear normalized schedule and α = 1.0. At each step in the window the current latent is VAE-decoded and passed through Ds; if the mean target-bit probability is below τ = 0.98 the gain is raised to clip(1 + 2.0·(τ − Pm), 0.75, 1.5). A terminal anchor 0.1·δ̄s is added to the final latent. Detection is one forward pass of Ds on the image; the decoded 48 bits are matched to the registry by maximum bit agreement, accepted only above a binomial false-positive threshold. Trace Acc. (Adv.) is trace accuracy after the post-generation attack suite (JPEG q=50, crop 0.8 + resize, blur r=3, Gaussian noise σ=25, brightness 1.5, 8 masks of ratio 0.18, 16 overlay strokes, adaptive noise 0.9).
official.claim: On SD3.5-medium, matching decoded 48-bit payloads against a registry of 10^6 users after common image attacks, CLaW reaches attacked trace accuracy 0.9649 vs. 0.8570 for RivaGAN and 0.4464 for DWT-DCT-SVD (0.9786 vs. 0.9001 at 10^5 users, 0.9861 vs. 0.9231 at 10^4), while clean trace accuracy is about 0.99-1.00 for all three.
official.claim_caption: Table 5: User-level traceability with increasing registry sizes. Trace accuracy is computed by matching each decoded 48-bit payload to a registry of candidate users. Higher is better.
official.metric: Trace accuracy (fraction of watermarked images attributed to the correct registered user under the binomial threshold), higher is better; '(Adv.)' is under the post-generation image-attack suite. Single run, no error bars reported.
official.comparison: CLaW vs. RivaGAN and DWT-DCT-SVD (the evaluated methods that decode explicit bit strings), same generated images/backbone, same 48-bit payloads and registries of 10^4, 10^5, 10^6 users
official.falsification_criterion: On SD3.5-medium with ~1,000 watermarked images and a 10^6-user registry, CLaW's attacked trace accuracy is not at least ~0.05 above RivaGAN's (e.g. CLaW below ~0.91 or RivaGAN above ~0.91), or CLaW's PSNR vs. the clean generation falls far below the reported ~41 dB at the stated settings.

title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models

official.background: Standard autoregressive (AR) image generators such as LlamaGen and RAR predict VQ image tokens in a fixed raster-scan order, so they cannot condition on non-contiguous context and cannot natively inpaint, outpaint or edit. Existing any-order generators (RandAR, MAR, discrete diffusion such as MaskGIT) are trained from scratch at roughly 3x the compute of raster-scan training, and discrete diffusion also gives up KV caching and AR serving stacks like vLLM. The paper asks whether an already-pretrained raster-scan AR model can instead be cheaply adapted into an any-order generator.
official.method:
Starting from a released raster-scan checkpoint (LlamaGen-L/XL or RAR-L/XL), the authors continue training on ImageNet-1k with the any-order objective: each training example gets a token permutation sigma, tokens are reordered by sigma, and the positional encoding (RoPE for LlamaGen, learned absolute table for RAR) is indexed by the spatial position sigma(t) rather than the sequence step. Two additions are made. (1) Future-aware positional embeddings: a learned table E (zero-initialized for LlamaGen, loaded from the checkpoint for RAR, trained at 10x the base LR) whose row for the next target position sigma(t+1) is added to the input at step t, with a learned null embedding at the final step; this tells the causal model which position it is predicting. (2) An ordering curriculum: sigma is raster scan with probability 1-alpha and uniformly random with probability alpha, with alpha ramped linearly from 0 to 1 over the first S_ramp epochs (e.g. LlamaGen-L: 100 adaptation epochs, S_ramp = 25; LlamaGen-XL: 25 epochs, S_ramp = 10). Other hyperparameters match pretraining (AdamW, cosine decay, bf16).

For inpainting and outpainting, the observed tokens are placed first in the generation order and the remaining tokens are sampled sequentially with the same causal model and KV cache, with no task-specific training. Inpainting uses center masks; outpainting extends a centered 128x128 crop to 256x256. Baselines are released ImageNet checkpoints of MaskGIT (original cosine schedule and Halton schedule) and MAR-L, evaluated with the same masks and protocol. FID, IS, Precision and Recall are computed over the full image on 50,000 validation samples with TF-Inception.
official.claim: On ImageNet 256x256 with identical masks, the adapted AR model reaches inpainting FID 6.21 and outpainting FID 5.84, lower than MaskGIT with the Halton schedule (7.82 / 7.91), MaskGIT cosine (10.44 / 12.17) and MAR-L (6.63 / 6.86), without any inpainting or outpainting training.

title: ACD-GS: Asymmetric Curvature-aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
claim_source: Table A6 (Appendix B), page 21; summarized in Table 3, page 8

official.background: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as millions of anisotropic Gaussians optimized for novel view synthesis. During training, Gaussians are cloned or split whenever their accumulated screen-space positional gradient exceeds a fixed threshold. This first-order signal does not tell real geometric edges apart from texture or noisy residuals, so the method creates many redundant primitives, which increases storage, memory and training time. Earlier density-control variants (AbsGS, Pixel-GS, GDAGS) change the gradient statistic but still rely on single-view first-order signals.
official.method:
ACD-GS replaces the densification step of 3DGS. From the rendered depth map it computes the absolute discrete Laplacian, clips it at mean + 3 std, normalizes it, and soft-thresholds it (tau = 0.15) into an edge-confidence map E. Each Gaussian samples E at its projected center (e_i), and its gradient is modulated asymmetrically: g_clone = g(1 - 0.8 e_i) and g_split = g(1 + 1.5 e_i), so cloning is suppressed and splitting promoted near depth discontinuities.

Before each densification step, K = 8 training views are rendered and their mean absolute RGB residuals are binarized. A Gaussian becomes a densification candidate only if the fraction of valid views in which its projected center lands on a high-residual pixel is at least tau_mv. The densification threshold is adaptive: it caps the number of densified Gaussians at 0.8% of the current count (top-10% fallback, lower-bounded by 0.8 x the base threshold). The opacity-pruning threshold is annealed linearly from alpha_min to alpha_max over training. Density control runs every 100 iterations from iteration 600 to the end of 30K iterations on one RTX 5090.
official.claim: On Tanks & Temples (Train, Truck; 30K iterations), ACD-GS ends with a mean of 0.64M Gaussians and 150.4 MB, against 1.35M / 319.5 MB for GDAGS (the most compact baseline) and 1.58M / 373.1 MB for vanilla 3DGS (a reduction of 53-60%), while its mean PSNR (23.37 dB) is within 0.4 dB of both (GDAGS 23.51, 3DGS 23.76).
official.claim_caption: Table A6: Per-scene quality and efficiency on Tanks & Temples.
official.metric: Final Gaussian count (M) and storage (MB), lower is better; test-view PSNR (dB), higher is better. Single runs, no error bars (the paper's checklist states that it reports no error bars or significance tests).
official.comparison: ACD-GS vs. GDAGS, AbsGS, 3DGS, Mip-Splatting, Pixel-GS and Mini-Splatting, all trained 30K iterations on the same scenes and GPU; GDAGS (smallest baseline) and vanilla 3DGS are the key comparisons
official.falsification_criterion: Re-training on Train and Truck, ACD-GS does not use at least ~40% fewer Gaussians (or less storage) than GDAGS/3DGS trained under the same setup, or its mean PSNR falls more than ~0.5 dB below 3DGS.
