title: Verifiable LLM-Guided Focal SMT Solving for Quantified Arrays

official.background: SMT solvers are central to software verification, but formulas that combine arrays with quantifiers are undecidable in general and often defeat standard quantifier-instantiation heuristics (E-matching, MBQI). This happens when the ground term needed to instantiate a quantifier, or the case split that makes the problem easy, is hidden behind auxiliary variables, guards and nested store/select terms. LLMs can often spot such semantic structure, but their outputs cannot be trusted as proofs, so the question is whether an LLM can guide a solver through an interface where the solver still certifies every answer.
official.method:
LinguaArray preprocesses a formula F into negation normal form with shortened identifiers (F'), then runs up to R = 10 rounds, each with two branches. UNSAT branch: the LLM proposes an Instantiation Focus Set (ground witness terms for universally quantified variables); positive universals in F' are replaced by the finite conjunction of their instances, and if the backend solver says this over-approximation is unsat, F is unsat. SAT branch: the LLM proposes a Constraint Focus Set (ground constraints such as i != j or array-cell assignments) that is conjoined to F'; if the solver finds this under-approximation sat, F is sat (an unsat result is accepted only after checking F' => c for every added constraint). Proposals that use unknown symbols or fail sort checking are discarded; failed proposals are fed back to the LLM in later rounds. When the rounds are exhausted, the backend solver runs on the original F for the remaining time. Every run has a 1200 s end-to-end timeout that includes LLM latency.

Benchmark: 1015 quantified-array instances from SMT-COMP 2025 / SMT-LIB (ABV 400 and ALIA 400 sampled uniformly with seed 42; all of ABVFP 60, ABVFPLRA 77, ANIA 78). Backends: Z3 4.15.0 (default) and CVC5 1.3.2 (tuned flags). LLM: DeepSeek-V3.2-chat at temperature 0. Controls run through the same harness with the same budget: Harness-only (empty focus sets) and Randomized (IFS witnesses sampled uniformly from well-typed ground subterms of F' by sort; CFS built from random well-typed atomic equalities, disequalities and order relations, resampled each round).
official.claim: On 1015 SMT-LIB quantified-array instances with a 1200 s end-to-end timeout, LinguaArray with Z3 and DeepSeek-V3.2 solves 701 instances (69.06%), versus 436 (42.96%) for the same harness with a randomized proposer, 143 for the harness with empty focus sets, and 141 for plain Z3.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results on five logics with a 1200s timeout (including LLM latency). LinguaArray uses DeepSeek-V3.2-chat. For each logic, we report #SAT / #UNSAT and success rate (SR).
official.metric: Number of instances solved (sat or unsat, solver-certified) within 1200 s, higher is better. Single run per configuration; no error bars in Table 1. Appendix D.1 reports 3 runs with the successor model DeepSeek-V4-Flash + Z3: 689.7 +/- 4.0 solved (sample std).
official.comparison: LinguaArray (Z3) vs. Randomized (Z3), Harness-only (Z3) and plain Z3; the same comparison with CVC5 as backend (659 vs. 445 vs. 322 vs. 321).
official.falsification_criterion: With the released code, Z3 4.15.0, a DeepSeek chat model at temperature 0 and the same 1015 instances and 1200 s budget, LinguaArray (Z3) solves no more than about 100 instances more than the randomized-proposer control (e.g. under ~540 vs. ~436), or the randomized control alone already reaches LinguaArray's count.

title: Escaping Path Mirages in Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

official.background: Offline goal-conditioned RL learns a policy that reaches any user-given goal state from a fixed dataset of trajectories, without further interaction. In long-horizon mazes with stochastic dynamics, value estimates compound errors, and rare lucky trajectories (for example, a random teleport that happens to land near the goal) make some routes look reliable when they mostly fail. The authors call this failure mode 'path mirage' and argue that methods which treat all dataset connectivity as equally trustworthy, such as HIQL or graph-based subgoal methods, keep routing through these risky branch points.
official.method:
Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP) is built on top of HIQL. A small decoder-only Transformer with Gaussian outputs is trained to autoregressively predict (action, next state) pairs. Each dataset state is scored by the discounted sum of predictive entropies over n = 5 steps. The top-α percentile of high-uncertainty states are clustered with K-means++ in a representation space (PCA for state observations) into N clusters. Every state is then assigned to its nearest center, and the dataset state closest to each center becomes a landmark. A pre-graph over landmarks uses edge weights -V(v, w) from the learned HIQL value. The distance d(s, g) is the shortest-path sum on this pre-graph, which avoids relying on one long-horizon value estimate.

For a given goal g, the planning edge cost is e_g(v_i, v_j) = E[d(s_k, g) - d(s_i, g)] with s_i drawn from cluster i and s_k drawn from every cluster reachable downstream of v_j. The cost becomes infinite if any downstream branch cannot reach g. Dijkstra on this goal-conditioned graph yields waypoints, which the HIQL policy follows in sequence. The value function and policy are trained with 'segmented learning': goals and transitions are sampled only within windows of M = 3 consecutive cluster segments of a trajectory. Training runs for 1M steps on state-based tasks, and results are averaged over 5 seeds. For pointmaze-teleport the hyperparameters are α = 1 and N = 100.
official.claim: On OGBench pointmaze-teleport-navigate, BGP reaches a 99 ± 2% success rate, compared with 45 ± 3% for the best baseline (CRL) and 18 ± 4% for its own backbone HIQL. On pointmaze-teleport-stitch it reaches 98 ± 2%, compared with 44 ± 2% (CRL) and 34 ± 4% (HIQL).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison on OGBench. We report the average success rate (%) with standard deviation (±) over 5 seeds. The best results in each row are highlighted in bold.
official.metric: Goal-reaching success rate (%) under OGBench's evaluation protocol (the paper gives no further detail on evaluation goals), higher is better; ± is standard deviation over 5 seeds
official.comparison: BGP (HIQL backbone + branch-aware graph planning + segmented learning) vs. HIQL, GCIQL, QRL, CRL, TMD, CGCIVL and GAS on the same OGBench datasets
official.falsification_criterion: A rerun of BGP on pointmaze-teleport-navigate or -stitch (5 seeds, 1M steps, α = 1, N = 100, M = 3) gives a mean success rate below about 60%, or a HIQL/CRL rerun with OGBench's official code comes within a few seed standard deviations of BGP.

title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science

official.background: Experimental design and protocol reproduction in AI-for-science need a retriever that finds method paragraphs satisfying several interdependent experimental conditions at once (e.g. a given cell line, cultured at 37 °C, not in DMEM). A paragraph often describes several experimental configurations, so a paragraph can mention every requested value and still not contain a single configuration that satisfies all of them. Existing scientific retrieval benchmarks test topical relevance, QA or claim verification, not this joint multi-constraint binding over unstructured methods text.
official.method:
ProSearch has 1,515 natural-language queries over six domains (Cell Culture, Immunotechnology, Electrochemistry, Organic Synthesis, Inorganic Materials, Polymer Materials), each with 3-5 explicit constraints (field, operator, value), including numeric and negation constraints. Each domain has its own corpus of method-section paragraphs (30k-93k paragraphs per domain) from 2020-2025 open-access papers. Queries were generated from GPT-5.2-extracted protocol records using expert-defined field templates. Relevance labels come from GPT-5.4 judging candidate paragraphs (exact-support and near-miss candidates mined from the records): a paragraph is relevant only if one experimental configuration in it satisfies all constraints. Expert audits agree with these labels 89.1% of the time.

For the reranking experiment, Qwen3-Embedding-8B (with the instruction 'Given a question, retrieve paragraphs that answer the question') retrieves the top-100 paragraphs per query. Six rerankers then reorder the same 100 candidates: BGE-Reranker-v2-m3 (0.6B, pointwise), Rank-R1-7B (setwise), Rank1-7B (pointwise reasoning), DIVER-GroupRank-7B (groupwise), ReasonRank-8B (listwise reasoning) and Qwen3-Reranker-8B (pointwise). The metric is nDCG@10 per domain, averaged over the six domains.
official.claim: Reranking the top-100 Qwen3-Embedding-8B candidates with Qwen3-Reranker-8B raises average nDCG@10 on ProSearch from 0.290 to 0.474, and every one of six rerankers improves on the first stage (the weakest, BGE-Reranker-v2-m3, reaches 0.396), with gains in all six domains.
official.claim_caption: Table 8: The performance of reranking models on ProSearch. We report nDCG@10 after reranking the top-100 candidate lists retrieved by Qwen3-Embedding-8B. Avg. denotes the average score across the six domains. The best score on each dataset is shown in bold and the second best is underlined.
official.metric: nDCG@10 (higher is better), per domain and averaged across the six domains; single deterministic run, no error bars or significance tests reported

title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
claim_source: Table 16 (Appendix H.1), page 24; means also in Table 3, page 8

official.background: LLM provers for Lean 4 work better when they are given the right premises (lemmas, definitions, instances) from libraries such as Mathlib4, which has hundreds of thousands of declarations. Existing neural premise selectors rank candidates by text similarity to the goal. The paper argues that this favours popular foundational lemmas, ranks each premise in isolation, and degrades when queries come from a different distribution (competition problems, informal statements), and that a declaration's position in the dependency graph is the missing signal.
official.method:
The authors extract a typed dependency graph from mathlib-4.22.0 (275k declaration and file nodes, 6.5M typed edges such as USES_CLASS, USES_INSTANCE, DEPENDS_ON). A query's positive premises are the declarations its verified proof depends on. DAPS embeds the query and each candidate and ranks by cosine similarity. A candidate's embedding is built from a frozen, contrastively warmed-up MGTE text encoder applied to the candidate and to up to n neighbours sampled from its 2-hop dependency subgraph (sample m neighbours, score them with a learnable FFN, keep the top n). The text encoder reads only the statement for queries, and name, category, signature, docstring, statement and proof for premises. For the candidate and each neighbour, a two-layer MLP fuses the frozen text feature with a type embedding, a hop-distance embedding (0/1/2) and a positional encoding over the sampled subgraph. An in-/out-degree embedding and a residual one-hot type embedding of the candidate are then added outside the MLP.

Training uses a group-level contrastive loss: for each query, every gold premise in a positive set gets its own log-term, all sharing one softmax denominator with the other positives and with negatives drawn from temporally preceding declarations, uniformly from the graph, and from other queries in the batch. Mathlib4-Heldout holds out whole source files from training (1,000 queries). ReProver, LeanHammer and Qwen3-Embedding-8B are retrained on the same Mathlib dependency data with their published recipes; MePo is used as released. Retrieval is scored by Recall@16 = |top-16 ∩ gold| / |gold| per query, averaged over queries.
official.claim: On Mathlib4-Heldout (1,000 queries from held-out Mathlib files), DAPS reaches Recall@16 of 78.74 ± 0.19, versus 67.33 ± 0.00 for LeanHammer retrained on the same dependency data, the strongest baseline (+11.41 points); at K=32 it is 89.25 ± 0.17 vs. 77.84.

title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication

official.background: Small language models (SLMs) deployed on-device often cannot fit a full vision-language model (VLM), so one modular option is to pair a small VLM with a text-only SLM. Such multi-agent systems usually pass information between the models as text: the VLM writes an answer or description and the SLM reads it. Text is a lossy channel for spatial layout, counts and fine-grained attributes, and an SLM has little capacity to recover what the text dropped. The paper asks whether a frozen VLM can instead pass its hidden states directly to a separately pretrained, frozen text-only SLM through a small learned codec.
official.method:
The frozen VLM (SmolVLM-256M, 30 layers, 576-dim) processes the image and question. Its 30 layers are split into B = 3 equal bands (L0-9, L10-19, L20-29), and each band is summarised as the mean over its layers of the last-token hidden state. A shared 2-layer MLP (576 -> 896, GELU, 896 -> 896; ~1.3M params) projects the three band vectors into the embedding space of the frozen SLM (Qwen2.5-0.5B, 896-dim). The three vectors are prepended as soft prefix tokens to the SLM's text embeddings (attended to, but excluded from the loss), and rank-4 LoRA on the q and v projections of all 24 SLM attention layers (~0.3M params) teaches the SLM to use them. The MLP and the LoRA are trained jointly with next-token cross-entropy (AdamW, lr 2e-4, cosine schedule, weight decay 1e-4, grad clip 1.0, effective batch 16, 5 epochs).

The matched text baseline ('Text communication + LoRA') has the VLM generate a short answer to the question ('Answer with a single word or short phrase'), inserts that text into the SLM prompt ('A vision model looked at the image and responded: ...'), and trains the same rank-4 q/v LoRA on the SLM. CLEVR uses 5,000 examples from MMInstruction/Clevr_CoGenT_ValA with a 4,000/1,000 train/test split. Free-form answers are scored by normalised matching: lowercase, strip articles and punctuation, map number words to digits, and accept an exact match or a match where every word of the shorter answer appears in the longer one.
official.claim: With frozen SmolVLM-256M and Qwen2.5-0.5B, Latent-Lens (1.6M trained params) reaches 81.0 ± 7.9% free-form accuracy on CLEVR versus 58.3 ± 5.7% for text communication with the same rank-4 LoRA, a 22.7pp gain.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on CLEVR, GQA (accuracy) and Flickr8k (BLEU-4). Source column lists the paper introducing each baseline. Trained conditions report mean ± sample standard deviation over three runs; frozen conditions are deterministic point estimates.
official.metric: Free-form VQA accuracy (%) on a 1,000-example CLEVR test split, normalised string match, higher is better; ± is the sample std over three training runs

title: Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics
claim_source: Table 1, page 8 (CEM-budget and wall-clock-matched SL-WM in Table 8, page 21)

official.background: Planning with a learned world model lets an agent reach goals it never saw in training without learning a policy, but search cost grows with the planning horizon and prediction errors pile up over long rollouts. So flat world-model planners such as DINO-WM work for goals tens of steps away but fail on tasks that need hundreds of steps. Earlier hierarchical world models add task-specific value functions, rewards, pre-trained skills or macro-actions to keep the high-level planner from exploiting model errors. The paper asks whether a hierarchy can be built from reward-free offline data alone and still plan long-horizon tasks to arbitrary goals.
official.method:
ID-WM has two learned models trained on reward-free offline trajectories. The high-level model is a conditional DDPM that, given the current latent state s_t, generates a state reachable within Delta steps (Delta = 5, i.e. 25 environment steps with frameskip). At inference, DDIM sampling makes the generated subgoal a deterministic function of the initial noise vector z, so z is treated as an implicit high-level action. The low-level model is a deterministic transformer world model following DINO-WM that predicts the next state from a history of states and actions.

Planning is MPC with CEM at both levels. The high-level CEM optimizes H_hi = 5 noise vectors to minimize the distance of the last generated subgoal to the goal, plus a hinge penalty on |z| above tau = 2 to keep z within the Gaussian support. For each subgoal, the low-level CEM searches an action sequence (horizon 5) whose predicted end state is closest to the subgoal; the actions are executed and the planner replans (up to 15 replans, 2000-step limit). The single-level baseline (SL-WM) runs CEM directly on the low-level world model with horizon 25 and the same samples (300), elites (30) and replans (15).
official.claim: On state-based PushT with random initial and goal states (no data augmentation, 50 start-goal pairs), ID-WM reaches success rate 0.77 ± 0.01, against 0.21 ± 0.04 for the single-level world model planner (SL-WM) with the same CEM budget and 0.21 ± 0.01 for the best other baseline (GCBC); final T-block coverage is 0.58 ± 0.01 vs. at most 0.31 ± 0.01.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison across environments. We report success rate (SR) and, for PushT, final coverage (Cov), as mean ± std over three seeds. PushT is evaluated with a fixed goal (Fix) and random goals (Rand.). Best results per row are in bold.
official.metric: success rate (agent and T-block both reach the goal; higher is better) and final T-block coverage of the goal (higher is better), each over 50 sampled start-goal pairs; ± is std over three seeds
official.comparison: ID-WM vs. HIQL, GCBC, Diffuser, Hierarchical Diffuser and single-level world-model MPC (SL-WM), all trained on the same offline PushT dataset; SL-WM uses the same CEM samples/elites/replans with flat horizon 25 versus ID-WM's 5 per level
official.falsification_criterion: On PushT (Random Goal), ID-WM's success rate is not clearly above SL-WM's and GCBC's (e.g. the gap shrinks to within a few seed stds, or ID-WM falls below about 0.4 while the baselines stay near 0.2).

title: From Clips to Streams: A Unified Framework for Streaming Sign Language Translation

official.background: Sign language translation (SLT) systems are almost always trained and evaluated on pre-segmented clips where each sentence's start and end are given. Real use involves continuous, untrimmed video in which the system must find where each sentence begins and ends (including rejecting non-signing intervals and handling co-articulated transitions) and translate it. The obvious approach is a cascade: segment first, then translate each segment with a separately trained translator. This paper defines a 'Streaming SLT' task that requires both outputs and argues that training segmentation and translation jointly works better than such a cascade.
official.method:
StreamSLST takes 15-second windows of 2D pose (77 COCO-WholeBody keypoints in five groups, normalized as in CoSign) and encodes them with group-wise ST-GCNs, then a 1D Deformable Transformer encoder-decoder with N = 30 learnable sentence queries. Each refined query feeds a segmentation head (center/width plus a foreground logit), a global sentence-count head, and a translation head: the query is concatenated with encoder features gathered at the query's predicted center (averaged over pyramid levels), linearly fused, and used to condition a 3-layer decoder initialized from (vocabulary-trimmed) mBART-large-cc25. Training uses Hungarian matching and loss weights (cls, giou, count, trans) = (2, 4, 2, 2), after a Stage-1 tri-modal contrastive pretraining (two masked pose views + window text) of the ST-GCN for 64 epochs. Training windows are sampled randomly so each contains at least one complete 1-20 s sentence; evaluation uses fixed-stride windows (stride 0.9W).

The cascaded baseline (Multi-Stage) uses the same intervals predicted by StreamSLST's segmentation head, but translates each interval with a separately trained GFSLT-VLP model whose RGB encoder is replaced by the same pose backbone; it is trained on fixed-length windows with the concatenated window subtitles as targets, and each localized segment is padded to window length by repeating the last frame. Because both systems share the intervals, F1 is identical and translation is scored on identical prediction-reference pairs (all pairs at tIoU >= 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, pooled per stream, averaged over streams and thresholds). Streaming-Phoenix-2014T is built by concatenating 2-K same-signer Phoenix-2014T clips (resampled to 12.5 fps, rest frames trimmed) with cubic-Hermite pose bridges whose lengths follow BOBSL inter-subtitle gaps.
official.claim: On Streaming-Phoenix-2014T, with identical predicted intervals (avg. F1 55.95), the jointly trained StreamSLST reaches threshold-averaged BLEU-4 8.16, BLEURT 31.87, CIDEr 7.89 and METEOR 17.30, versus 5.86, 17.46, 2.79 and 15.05 for the matched localize-then-translate cascade.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Localization and Translation performance on the synthetic test set of Streaming-Phoenix-2014T (left) and Streaming-CSL-Daily (right). Gray rows follow Table 1 and list published systems on the original Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily.
official.metric: Translation metrics on matched prediction-reference pairs, averaged over tIoU thresholds {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9}; higher is better. No ± reported: single run, no seeds or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: StreamSLST [mBART] (joint segmentation+translation) vs. Multi-Stage (Cascaded): same StreamSLST segment predictions, translated by a separately trained pose-input GFSLT-VLP trained on windowed targets
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both systems on Streaming-Phoenix-2014T (ideally over several seeds) and evaluating on the same intervals, StreamSLST's threshold-averaged BLEU-4 and BLEURT are not clearly above the cascade's (e.g. BLEU-4 gap under ~1 point or BLEURT gap under ~5 points, or the gaps fall within seed variation).

title: Dataset Mismatch Matters in Group Relative Policy Optimization for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards

official.background: GRPO-style reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards wastes many rollouts on prompts whose sampled responses are all correct or all wrong, giving zero group-normalized advantage. Selective-rollout methods (DAPO dynamic sampling, GRESO, AR3PO) cut this cost using only training-set statistics. But the training prompt pool usually differs from the benchmarks the model is evaluated on, so source-side rollout decisions may not help target performance. The paper asks whether a small amount of target-side feedback (gradients computed by the target owner on a held-out split, without sharing target prompts) can steer which source prompts get rolled out, improving both target accuracy and rollout efficiency.
official.method:
L2RR (learning-to-reweight rollout) keeps a sampling distribution q over the source prompts, initialised uniform. Each step it samples a batch from q, does a standard token-level GRPO update (no KL, group size up to G=8), then updates q with an exponentiated-gradient step. The gradient for each sampled prompt combines (a) a target term: minus the learning rate times the inner product between the target-validation gradient at the look-ahead parameters and the prompt's GRPO gradient minus the batch-mean gradient, and (b) a rollout-waste term lambda*(1 - p_e^z), where z counts the prompt's recent consecutive zero-advantage rollouts (lambda=0.25, p_e=0.5). Per-prompt group sizes are also reallocated (between G_min=4 and G=8) under a budget that shrinks for persistently degenerate prompts.

Main experiment: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B trained for 1000 steps (verl + vLLM, batch 256 prompts, lr 1e-6) on DAPO+MATH (DM) or a 30k OpenR1-Math subset (OR1). Targets are six math benchmarks (Math500, AIME24, AMC, Gaokao, Minerva, OlympiadBench), each split into fixed 10% validation / 90% test. L2RR uses the validation split for sampler feedback; all methods (DAPO, GRESO, AR3PO, L2RR) use it for checkpoint selection (every 50 steps, best macro-average validation accuracy). Test accuracy is avg@4 at temperature 1.0, top-p 0.7, mean +/- std over five training seeds.
official.claim: Training Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on DAPO+MATH, L2RR reaches 50.3 +/- 1.3% average test accuracy over six math benchmarks with 3.0M rollouts, versus 48.9 +/- 1.5% for AR3PO (2.5M rollouts), 47.8 +/- 1.6% for GRESO (3.3M) and 47.7 +/- 1.5% for DAPO (7.6M).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance (%) comparison across six math reasoning benchmarks. We train three models on source datasets DAPO+MATH (DM) and the Open R1 subset (OR1) and test on six benchmarks. # Rollout denotes cumulative source responses, in millions. RO ratio is the DAPO count divided by the method count. Accuracies are mean ± standard deviation over five training seeds.
official.metric: Average accuracy (%) over the 90% test splits of six math benchmarks (higher is better), avg@4; +/- is std over five training seeds. Cumulative source rollouts (millions) also reported.
official.comparison: L2RR vs. DAPO (dynamic sampling), GRESO and AR3PO, same shared GRPO settings and same validation-based checkpoint selection; the claim focuses on the Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B / DM row, with the other five model-source rows as secondary checks.
official.falsification_criterion: Over five seeds, L2RR's six-benchmark average is not higher than AR3PO's (or GRESO's) by more than the seed std, or L2RR needs substantially more rollouts than DAPO's 7.6M to reach its accuracy.

title: STEER: Route-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
claim_source: Table 12, page 20 (Appendix G.1); same runs as Table 4 IDs 1 and 4, page 9

official.background: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for end-to-end driving can emit a chain-of-thought before predicting a trajectory, but reasoning on every scene adds latency and can even lower planning quality ('overthinking'). Adaptive-reasoning methods choose per scene between a reasoning route and a direct answer; the prior explicit-routing approach (AdaThinkDrive) supervises this choice with scene-difficulty labels, which are costly and subjective. STEER asks whether the route choice can be learned from simulator rewards alone, without any difficulty labels.
official.method:
STEER fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL-8B (front camera image plus ego history in, 8 text waypoints out). The first generated token chooses the route: '<think> ... </think><answer>trajectory</answer>' (reasoning) or '<answer>trajectory</answer>' (direct). After driving-centric pretraining, a route-balanced SFT stage trains on both route targets for every prompt, with per-route length normalization and a term pushing the first-token route distribution toward uniform, so both routes stay available (about 49/51 reason/direct probability).

RL then uses GRPO with 16 rollouts per prompt and a PDMS-based reward on NAVSIM navtrain, plus two changes. (i) Routing uncertainty-aware rollout: from the binary entropy H of the first-token route probabilities, prompts with H > 0.5 get 8 forced-reasoning + 8 forced-direct rollouts, prompts with 0.25 <= H <= 0.5 get 4 + 4 + 8 on-policy, otherwise all 16 are on-policy (forced modes also need minority-route probability >= 0.05). (ii) Cross-route advantage: at the routing token only, a reasoning rollout gets advantage r_i minus the mean reward of the direct rollouts for that prompt (and vice versa), added with weight 0.05 on top of the usual GRPO content advantage applied to all tokens. The baseline 'vanilla GRPO' (Table 4 ID 1) uses the same backbone, initialization (route-balanced SFT), data, reward, split, 16-rollout budget and optimization settings, without (i) and (ii). Routing metrics are computed against the oracle route, i.e. whichever of the two routes gets the higher PDMS for that prompt.
official.claim: On NAVSIM v1 navtest, STEER's route-aware RL reaches 91.18 ± 0.25 PDMS and 81.09 ± 0.34% oracle-route accuracy, versus 89.45 ± 0.31 PDMS and 69.33 ± 0.68% for vanilla GRPO run from the same SFT checkpoint with the same data, reward and 16-rollout budget, while using fewer response tokens (315 vs. 363).
official.claim_caption: Table 12: Matched comparison with vanilla GRPO. Mean ± standard deviation over three evaluation seeds for IDs 1 and 4 of Table 4.
official.metric: PDMS (NAVSIM v1 closed-loop Predictive Driver Model Score, higher is better) and RouteAcc (% of prompts where the chosen route matches the oracle route, higher is better); also AUC, AvgRegret, average response tokens. ± is std over three evaluation seeds of one fixed trained checkpoint; training-seed variance is not reported.
official.comparison: STEER (uncertainty-aware rollout + cross-route advantage) vs. vanilla GRPO, both starting from the same route-balanced SFT model with identical RL data, reward, rollout budget and hyperparameters
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both arms under matched conditions gives a STEER PDMS gain over vanilla GRPO that is within the reported evaluation stds (0.31 and 0.25 PDMS) or reversed, or STEER's RouteAcc is not clearly above vanilla GRPO's (gap well below the reported ~12 points).

title: ShiftRAG: Bypassing the Textual Bottleneck via Decoupled Learning and Continuous Soft Tokens
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (full baseline list in Table 10, page 20; loss ablation in Table 3, page 8)

official.background: Retrieval-augmented generation for multi-hop question answering needs a retriever that separates the few supporting passages from many similar distractors. Decoder-only LLMs turned into text encoders (LLM2Vec, NV-Embed) are strong retrievers, but deep-layer token representations of decoder-only models tend to collapse into a low-dimensional subspace ('rank collapse'), which the authors argue blurs the fine distinctions needed to tell evidence from distractors. The paper proposes a single-backbone RAG system whose retrieval mode is trained with objectives meant to counter this.
official.method:
ShiftRAG uses one LLM (Gemma2-9B by default) with two separately trained LoRA adapters. The encoder-mode adapter (r = 16) uses bidirectional attention and mean-pooled embeddings, trained on the E5 retrieval data following LLM2Vec: 1,000 steps of masked next-token prediction warm-up, then 2,000 steps of contrastive training (3,000 total; global batch 16). The contrastive score is a layer-wise gap: for question q and document d, s(q,d) = max over 5 sampled lower layers l of [cos(e_q^L, e_d^L) - cos(e_q^L, e_d^l)], used in an InfoNCE loss with temperature 0.05 over positives and hard negatives (LGC loss). A soft-orthogonality loss (weight 1e-3) penalizes the squared Frobenius distance between the token-level cosine Gram matrix and the identity in the last 4 layers. At inference the final-layer cosine similarity is used for retrieval.

Retrieval is evaluated on the RaLa test configuration: 1,000 questions each for HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue with document pools of 6-12K passages, scored by Recall@K (K = 2, 5, 10). The decoder mode (soft knowledge tokens and generator LoRA) is not needed for this claim.
official.claim: With Gemma2-9B as backbone, ShiftRAG's encoder mode retrieves better than an LLM2Vec encoder fine-tuned on the same backbone on all three multi-hop benchmarks, e.g. HotpotQA R@2 0.6598 vs. 0.6130, 2WikiMultihopQA R@5 0.7109 vs. 0.6451 and MuSiQue R@2 0.4186 vs. 0.3598, and also beats NV-Embed-v2 (0.6318, 0.6632, 0.3781).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Retrieval performance. The best and second-best performances are presented in bold and underlined, respectively. LLM2Vec, OneGen, and ShiftRAG use Gemma2-9B as the backbone.
official.metric: Recall@K (higher is better) on 1,000 test questions per dataset; mean of 5 seeds, with only a 'maximum standard deviation ±0.05' stated for the whole table

title: AgentCBO: Causal Belief Routing for Bayesian Optimization under Unknown Graphs

official.background: Causal Bayesian optimization (CBO) chooses which variables to intervene on, and at what values, to minimize a target. It uses a causal graph to restrict the exploration sets (subsets of manipulable variables) and to build do-calculus priors for per-set Gaussian-process surrogates. In practice the graph is rarely known. Existing unknown-graph methods (CEO, GACBO, CBO-U) spend sample budget learning structure that may not matter to the optimizer, and hidden confounders make observational structure learning unreliable.
official.method:
AgentCBO keeps a single committed graph that routes a standard CBO loop (CEI acquisition, cost = |S|, epsilon-greedy observe/intervene schedule). Every 5 outer-loop steps a graph-update stack is re-run on the current observational data. A Language-Prior agent (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B served with vLLM, temperature 0.5) elicits pairwise causal beliefs and combines them with the PC algorithm to give a point DAG, a frozen backbone and a set of uncertain residual edge pairs. In the Calib variant, a Calibration agent may edit only residual pairs, and an edit is accepted only if it lowers a statistical structure score (holdout SEM NLL + CI-consistency penalty + sparsity). The Full variant adds a bounded Residual Repair agent (at most 5 edits). A deterministic commit gate (confidence threshold, the target must keep a manipulable ancestor, nSHD on the ancestor subgraph) decides whether the candidate replaces the current graph. On a commit, exploration sets and do-priors are rebuilt and archived interventional data are re-injected.

CompleteGraph (Appendix B.1) is a 7-variable SEM {F, A, B, C, D, E, Y} with two latent confounders U1, U2, manipulable variables {B, D, E}, and target Y to be minimized. Each run starts from 100 observational samples and has a budget of 50 outer-loop steps. The metric is the best Y reached, over 20 seeds.
official.claim: On the CompleteGraph hidden-confounder benchmark (n_obs = 100, T = 50, 20 seeds), AgentCBO-Calib reaches a best objective of -3.57 ± 0.07, versus -1.43 ± 0.55 for CEO, -1.23 ± 0.12 for GACBO, -0.57 ± 0.16 for CBO-U, -2.50 ± 1.21 for AgentCBO-Prior, and -2.48 ± 1.14 for known-graph CBO.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Main result matrix. Mean ± standard deviation of best objective Y* reached within 50 outer-loop steps, aggregated across 20 seeds per benchmark–algorithm pair. All benchmarks are minimization tasks. Bold marks the best displayed mean among methods other than the known-graph CBO reference baseline; ties at the displayed precision are bolded together.
official.metric: Best objective Y* reached within 50 outer-loop steps (minimization; lower is better), mean ± std over 20 seeds
official.comparison: AgentCBO-Calib (and Full, which gives the same number) vs. unknown-graph CBO baselines (CEO, GACBO, CBO-U), proposal-only AgentCBO-Prior, and the known-graph CBO reference, all on CompleteGraph with the same budget
official.falsification_criterion: Over 20 seeds on CompleteGraph, AgentCBO-Calib's mean best Y* is not clearly below CEO's and GACBO's (for example, it is above -2.5 or within one seed std of the best unknown-graph baseline), or it fails to beat AgentCBO-Prior's mean.

title: InformedXRD: Reproducible Benchmarks and Physics-Informed Evaluation for Powder Diffraction Symmetry Classification
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (Top-1 and hierarchy columns); Top-5 values and p-values in §6.1 text, page 8

official.background: Machine-learning models that classify crystal symmetry from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns are trained mostly on simulated data and tested on experimental patterns from the RRUFF archive. Each study uses its own hand-filtered RRUFF subset, its own label space (usually 230 space groups, even though powder diffraction cannot distinguish space groups within an extinction group) and flat Top-k accuracy, and few studies release checkpoints. As a result, published accuracies cannot be compared. The paper proposes a common evaluation standard and argues that evaluation choices change which conclusions are justified.
official.method:
Labels are the 99 extinction groups (EGs), the equivalence classes of space groups with identical systematic absences, from a released 230→99 mapping table. RRUFF-325 is a frozen, algorithmically curated set of 325 experimental Cu-Kα RRUFF scans, resampled to an 8501-point 2θ grid (5–90°, 0.01° step) and limited to the 'usable-or-better' and 'recoverable' Rietveld-fit strata (Rwp ≤ 0.22). The models are publicly released ViT checkpoints from Baggett et al. (2026). Two of them are compared here: the 'preferred-orientation-only' checkpoint and the 'final mixed-data calibrated' checkpoint, both scored with 99-way EG outputs on the same 325 patterns.

Top-1 and Top-5 EG accuracy are compared on the same cases with exact McNemar tests. The paper also reports hierarchy-aware error summaries over wrong Top-1 predictions: hop distance on the condensed translationengleiche subgroup DAG, the fraction of errors within 2 hops, and the branch-jump fraction. These summaries are compared with paired permutation tests.
official.claim: On RRUFF-325, the preferred-orientation-only ViT checkpoint beats the final mixed-data calibrated checkpoint at Top-1 (13.54% vs. 10.46%, exact McNemar p = 0.002), while the calibrated checkpoint beats it at Top-5 (43.69% vs. 40.92%, p = 0.012); hierarchy-aware summaries do not separate the pair (paired permutation p = 0.58).

title: Phase-wise MLLM Tuning for Multi-framework WebUI Code Generation
claim_source: Table 2, page 7 (also Table 4, page 8; seed std for the full method in Table 8, page 18)

official.background: Multimodal LLMs can turn a WebUI screenshot into HTML/CSS fairly well, but real projects often target React, Vue or Angular. When one model is fine-tuned on several front-end frameworks at once, the frameworks' different syntax and constraints can interfere through the shared parameters (negative transfer). The generated code then mixes syntax across frameworks (e.g. HTML class= in JSX, or Angular components without @Component) and fails to compile. The question is whether a training schedule that accounts for how similar and how gradient-compatible the frameworks are can reduce this interference.
official.method:
The backbone Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct is frozen. One shared adapter (r=16, alpha=32, layers 16-27) and four framework-specific adapters (r=8, alpha=16, layers 20-27; Vanilla, React, Vue, Angular) are trained on about 10.9k screenshot-code pairs built from DesignBench and WebCode2M. Before training, two pairwise signals are computed offline: heterogeneity, the normalized Jensen-Shannon divergence between distributions of normalized code (with variable names and literals suppressed), and compatibility, (1 + cos)/2 between per-framework loss gradients with respect to a zero-initialized shared adapter at layer 15, averaged over 100 batches. A partition objective (low within-phase heterogeneity, high within-phase compatibility) selects Phase 1 = {React, Vue} and Phase 2 = {Vanilla, Angular}.

Training runs phase by phase, 3 epochs per phase (batch size 32, lr 2e-4, cosine warmup). Each framework also has a fixed scalar gate on shared-adapter updates, set from its mean compatibility and heterogeneity (min-max normalized and averaged): React 0.96, Vue 0.95, Vanilla 0.49, Angular 0.00. The specific adapters update normally. The matched baseline 'Shared+Specific (no gate)' uses the same adapters trained jointly on all frameworks in a single phase with no gating. Evaluation is on the DesignBench Generation test split (about 290 samples per framework). CSR is the fraction of all test samples whose code compiles. CLIP similarity between the rendered output and the target screenshot is averaged over compiled samples only.
official.claim: On DesignBench Generation with a frozen Qwen2.5-VL-7B, phase-wise gated adapter tuning reaches average compilation success rate 0.9007 (CLIP 0.7950) vs. 0.8479 (CLIP 0.7468) for the same shared+specific adapters trained jointly without phases or gating; on Angular, CSR goes from 0.7389 to 0.8135.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Results on DesignBench Generation task. Best results are bold; second best are underlined.
official.metric: CSR (compilation success rate over all test samples, higher is better) and CLIP similarity (over compiled samples only, higher is better), macro-averaged over 4 frameworks. Table 2 reports means over 3 seeds with no error bars. Appendix Table 8 gives std over 3 seeds for the full method only: CLIP 0.7950 ± 0.0027, CSR 0.9007 ± 0.0024. No std is given for the baseline.
official.comparison: Ours (two-phase schedule + offline-derived gates) vs. Shared+Specific (no gate, no phase), the same adapter architecture trained jointly. Also vs. Specific Adapter only (0.8359 CSR) and the ScreenCoder / EfficientUICoder systems.
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both variants under the matched setup (same backbone, adapters, data, epochs), the phase-wise gated method's average CSR is not clearly above the joint Shared+Specific baseline's (a gap well below the reported 0.053, e.g. under about 0.01, or within seed spread), or its Angular CSR advantage disappears.

title: Z-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Transformers via Self-Reflection

official.background: Feature caching speeds up diffusion transformers without training by computing the full network only at some denoising steps and reusing or extrapolating the cached hidden features at the steps in between. With long cache intervals the predicted features drift from the true ones, and the error builds up within each cache window, which degrades image quality and prompt fidelity. The authors observe that this error drops sharply every time a full computation is performed, which suggests using the next full-computation step to go back and correct the steps that were cached.
official.method:
Z-Cache is a training-free wrapper around an existing cache predictor (TaylorSeer, SpeCa, MagCache, TeaCache). For a cache window between full-computation anchors a and b, the base predictor first forecasts the intermediate hidden features from the past anchors and the sampler runs provisional denoising steps up to b. The scheduled full computation at b is run on the provisional latent to obtain the future anchor H_b; then the same predictor is rerun with b added to the anchor set to produce a future-anchor prediction for each intermediate step. The two predictions are blended linearly, H_i = (1 - w_i) H_i^past + w_i H_i^future with w_i = (i - a)/(b - a). The provisional latents are discarded, the window is re-sampled from x_a using the blended features, and denoising continues from the reflected endpoint. No extra full-network evaluations are added; the FLOPs overhead is under 0.2% for TaylorSeer.

Evaluation (Appendix A.2.2): FLUX.1-dev, 200 DrawBench prompts at 1024x1024 with the default 50-step sampling. PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS are computed against the full 50-step FLUX.1-dev outputs for the same prompts and seeds; ImageReward is computed on image-prompt pairs. Each Base/+Z-Cache pair shares prompts, seeds and the base full-computation schedule; cache intervals are N = 6, 7, 8.
official.claim: On FLUX.1-dev with 200 DrawBench prompts at cache interval N = 6 (about 4.98x FLOPs speedup), adding Z-Cache to TaylorSeer lowers LPIPS against the full 50-step outputs from 0.4359 to 0.3914 and raises SSIM from 0.6302 to 0.6539 and PSNR from 28.84 to 29.22, at essentially the same FLOPs (745.54T vs. 746.47T); across all 12 Base/+Z-Cache pairs in Table 2, LPIPS, SSIM and PSNR improve every time.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Full paired results for cache predictors on FLUX.1-dev with DrawBench. Rows are grouped by the equivalent cache interval N. Bold quality metrics indicate the better value within each Base/+Z-Cache pair; gray rows identify +Z-Cache. Parameters are abbreviated in parentheses: TeaCache uses (L), where L = rel_l1_thresh; SpeCa uses (B, D, m, M) = (base, decay, min, max); MagCache uses (T, K, R) = (th, K, retention).
official.metric: LPIPS (lower is better), SSIM and PSNR (higher is better) against the full 50-step FLUX.1-dev output with the same prompt and seed; ImageReward (higher is better). Means over 200 DrawBench images; no standard deviations, confidence intervals or multiple seeds reported.
official.comparison: TaylorSeer vs. TaylorSeer + Z-Cache at matched cache schedule (N = 6, 7, 8); the same pairing for TeaCache, SpeCa and MagCache.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same TaylorSeer N = 6 schedule on FLUX.1-dev / DrawBench, TaylorSeer + Z-Cache does not lower LPIPS against full 50-step outputs (e.g. the gap is under ~0.01 or reversed), or the gain disappears at N = 8, or the gain requires noticeably more FLOPs than the base schedule.

title: MIRA: Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (SDs for MIRA_TENT in Table 12, page 17)

official.background: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed classifier on unlabeled target data under distribution shift, usually by minimizing the entropy of its own predictions (TENT and successors). Entropy minimization treats confidence as reliability, so under severe shift it can reinforce confident errors and leave the model miscalibrated. Uncertainty-aware TTA methods exist but usually need ensembles, repeated full-network stochastic passes, or posterior fitting on source data, which conflicts with cheap, source-free online deployment.
official.method:
MIRA keeps the backbone forward pass deterministic and perturbs only the last-layer classifier: for each target batch it caches features h_i, then samples K = 300 perturbed classifiers W + σ A_B ⊙ ε_W, b + σ a_B ⊙ ε_b with ε ~ N(0, I), where A_B and a_B are a fixed He-style scale sqrt(2/D) times a feature-wise factor from the batch's mean absolute feature (clipped to [0.25, 4]). For each candidate σ in a fixed 16-point grid (1e-5 to 5), using the same noise across σ, it computes batch-mean mutual information M(σ) = H(mean p) − mean H(p) and top-1 agreement A(σ); it selects the smallest σ with M(σ) ≥ min M + α(max M − min M) and A(σ) ≥ ρ (α = 0.03, ρ = 0.90; fall back to the MI condition alone, with log-linear interpolation between grid points).

With fresh samples at σ*, each sample gets a stop-gradient weight w_i = Norm(w_i^MI · w_i^conf), where w_i^MI is a softmax over −(MI_i − mean MI)/τ (τ = 0.25) scaled to unit batch mean and w_i^conf is the max mean-predicted probability normalized to unit mean. The loss is mean_i w_i (HE_i + γ EH_i) with γ = 1, applied to the parameters TENT adapts (normalization affine parameters); predictions are the Monte Carlo mean. For the claimed comparison, both TENT and MIRA_TENT use the AugMix ResNeXt on CIFAR-100-C, 15 corruptions at severity 5, 10,000 shuffled images per corruption, batch size 64, SGD lr 1e-3 with momentum 0.9, model reset between corruptions, identical ordered streams, seeds 1, 2, 3; metrics are macro-averaged over corruptions (ECE with 10 equal-width bins).
official.claim: On CIFAR-100-C (15 corruptions, severity 5) with the AugMix ResNeXt, attaching MIRA to TENT raises accuracy from 67.84 ± 0.05% to 68.69 ± 0.15% and lowers ECE from 0.0693 to 0.0452 and NLL from 1.2547 to 1.1940; on ImageNet-C with ResNet-50 the same pairing raises accuracy from 36.62 ± 0.12% to 39.45 ± 0.14% and lowers ECE from 0.0478 to 0.0361.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Plug-and-play evaluation: three-run means with accuracy ± SD. SDs for all metrics of MIRA_TENT are reported in Table 12. Bold: best accuracy, ECE, and NLL per dataset. Protocols: Appendix D.1–D.2.
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%, higher is better), ECE and NLL (lower is better), macro-averaged over 15 corruptions; ± is the sample SD over 3 seeds, reported for accuracy only in Table 2 (MIRA_TENT ECE SD is 0.0007 on CIFAR-100-C and 0.0022 on ImageNet-C per Table 12; no ECE/NLL SDs for TENT)
official.comparison: TENT vs. TENT + MIRA (MIRA_TENT) with matched model, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, streams and seeds
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both methods on CIFAR-100-C / ResNeXt with the stated protocol and 3 seeds, MIRA_TENT's mean accuracy is not higher than TENT's by more than ~0.3 points (about 2 SDs), or its mean ECE is not clearly below TENT's (e.g. less than 0.01 lower).

title: Reduced Cost Influence Functions for Predict-then-Optimize under Noisy Data

official.background: In predict-then-optimize pipelines, a regression model predicts the cost vector of a downstream linear program, and the quality that matters is the regret of the resulting decision rather than the prediction error. When part of the training labels is corrupted, ordinary least-squares fitting can push predictions across optimality-cone boundaries and flip decisions. The paper assumes a large noisy training set plus a small clean validation set, and asks how to reweight the training data so that downstream decisions become more robust, without changing the predictor or the LP solver.
official.method:
A reduced cost influence function (RCIF) is the first-order change in the reduced cost s_k(ĉ_v, B_v) = δ(B_v,k)ᵀ f_θ(z_v) at a validation point when a training point is upweighted: RCIF = δ(B_v,k)ᵀ ∇_θ f(z_v) I_θ(w_j), where I_θ is the standard influence function −H⁻¹∇ℓ. For each validation point, B_v is the optimal basis under the predicted cost. The point is 'correct' (σ_v = +1) if its true cost lies in the same optimality cone and 'incorrect' (σ_v = −1) otherwise. In the directed score Ψ^D_j = (1/m) Σ_v σ_v RCIF_{k*_v}, k*_v is the nonbasic direction with the smallest normalized reduced cost; for incorrect points the choice is restricted to directions where the true cost violates optimality (s_k(c_v,B_v) < 0).

Iterative Exp. Directed converts the accumulated scores into weights p_j ∝ exp(λ Σ_t Ψ_j^(t)) with λ = 0.05, refits a weighted least-squares linear predictor, and repeats for τ = 5 rounds. The clean validation set is folded into the final fit for all training-data methods. In the shortest-path experiment, PyEPO generates a 4×4 grid shortest-path problem (northwest to southeast corner) with feature dimension 30, polynomial degree 1, 400 train, 100 validation and 200 test points. A fraction β = 0.2 of the training labels gets added isotropic Gaussian noise (covariance 4I), and test regret is measured on clean test data.
official.claim: On PyEPO 4×4-grid shortest path with a linear least-squares predictor and 20% Gaussian-corrupted training labels, Iterative Exp. Directed RCIF reweighting reaches mean test regret 0.9437 ± 0.0172 over 100 seeds. This is lower than unweighted ERM (1.0029 ± 0.0169), validation-only ERM (0.9989 ± 0.0181), SPO+ Finetune (1.0042 ± 0.0176) and SPO Influence Weight (0.9560 ± 0.0158), with paired p < 0.048 against every method.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Mean test regret over 100 seeds under random LP setting, shortest path setting with a linear upstream, and shortest path setting with a neural-network upstream. Best per column in bold.
official.metric: Mean normalized test regret over 100 seeds (lower is better). The paper does not define ±; with 100 seeds it is most likely the standard error of the mean. Significance is from two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over seeds.
official.comparison: Iterative Exp. Directed (RCIF) vs. Unweighted ERM, RC Weight, Validation Only, SPO Influence Weight (influence-based reweighting with the SPO+ subgradient instead of reduced-cost directions), SPO+ Val Only and SPO+ Finetune, all on the same data, seeds and folded-in validation set
official.falsification_criterion: Over 100 seeds in the same shortest-path setting, Iterative Exp. Directed's mean regret is not lower than unweighted ERM's by clearly more than the ± (e.g. the gap is under ~0.03, versus the reported 0.059), or the paired test against SPO Influence Weight is not significant, or SPO Influence Weight has lower mean regret.

title: Beyond Unit-Circle Eigenvalues: Invariant Bases for Stable State Space Dynamics
claim_source: Table 20, page 30 (per-seed values in Table 23, page 31)

official.background: Diagonal state space models advance a latent state by applying the same diagonal transition at every step, so over a long autoregressive rollout any quantity the transition does not preserve drifts. Existing stabilisation methods (LRU-style or unitary recurrences) put every eigenvalue on the unit circle. That keeps the latent norm fixed, but it does not keep summed quantities such as total mass or linear momentum fixed, because whether a sum is preserved depends on the eigenvectors (the modal basis), not only the eigenvalues. For learned physics simulators this means a model can be numerically stable while still violating a basic conservation law.
official.method:
The Kronecker-Cayley transition (KC) splits the latent z into N object subspaces of width m. At each step a small MLP maps (||z_i - z_j||^2, action) to one symmetric scalar coupling w_ij per object pair. The couplings are placed in a graph Laplacian L (L_ij = -w_ij, L_ii = sum_k w_ik), so L has zero row sums. The generator is H = L ⊗ I_m and the step is the Cayley transform z_{t+1} = (Cay(L) ⊗ I_m) z_t, with Cay(L) = (I + iL/2)^{-1}(I - iL/2). It is computed through an N x N eigendecomposition and is diagonal in the eigenbasis of L. Zero row sums put the uniform vector in the eigenvalue-1 mode, so the sum over subspaces (1^T ⊗ I_m) z is preserved exactly at every parameter value. A tied linear read-out maps the physical linear momentum onto this zero mode.

For the N-body test, the charged (N = 5, 3D), gravitational (N = 10, 3D) and spring (N = 5, 2D) systems of the EGNN benchmark (3000/2000/2000 split) are encoded by a per-particle MLP encoder into subspaces of width m = 8, and decoded by a tied per-particle linear decoder. Training uses Adam at 1e-3, batch 32 and 200 epochs. Every transition shares this encoder and decoder. Baselines: level B (diagonal with unit-modulus eigenvalues), level C (B plus one mode per object fixed at 1 in the coordinate basis), a free diagonal, an LRU-style recurrence, and KC with an unconstrained decoder (KC-fd). Models are rolled out for T = 1000 steps in float32, and drift is |Q(T) - Q(1)| measured from the first decoded frame.
official.claim: On the EGNN charged, gravity and spring N-body systems at T = 1000 rollout steps, KC's linear-momentum drift is 2.2e-6, 3.6e-6 and 1.6e-6 (absolute units). Every diagonal baseline sharing the same encoder and tied decoder, and KC with an unconstrained decoder, drifts by 1.25 to 1.9e4; the best of them is level C at 2.66 (charged) and 3.92 (gravity) and level B at 1.25 (spring).
official.claim_caption: Table 20: N-body conservation at T = 1000, seeds 42 to 44. Drift in absolute units, geometric mean over the seeds that stayed finite. An asterisk marks a row where the free diagonal left the axis on one seed.
official.metric: Absolute drift of total linear momentum between the first decoded frame and step 1000, lower is better; geometric mean over seeds 42, 43, 44 (over the finite seeds for the free diagonal). No ± is reported; per-seed values are in Table 23.
official.comparison: KC vs. level B (unit-modulus diagonal), level C, free diagonal (level A), LRU-style recurrence (all with KC's per-particle encoder and tied decoder) and KC with an unconstrained decoder
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained on the EGNN N-body systems, KC's linear-momentum drift at T = 1000 is not several orders of magnitude below that of the level B / level C / LRU baselines (e.g. KC drifts above ~1e-3 on any system, or a unit-modulus diagonal baseline with the same tied decoder also stays near 1e-5).

title: A Scientific Claim Stability Framework for Evaluating MRI Morphometry Pipelines
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (per-pair values in Tables F6, F8, F9, pages 39-41)

official.background: Structural MRI morphometry pipelines (FreeSurfer, FastSurfer, SPM/CAT12) turn brain scans into region-of-interest (ROI) measurements that are used to support scientific statements such as 'Alzheimer's disease is associated with lower temporal cortical volume'. Pipelines are usually compared on measurement agreement, segmentation accuracy or downstream prediction. Two pipelines can agree closely on those measures yet point to different brain regions as the evidence for a conclusion. The paper proposes evaluating pipelines at the level of the scientific claims they support.
official.method:
For each analysis setting (dataset, pipeline, feature family, atlas, target, covariates), the framework fits ROI-wise OLS models x_ij = a_j + b_j*y_i + z_i'g_j + e_ij, where x_ij is the morphometric value of region j for scan i, y is the target (CN vs. AD, CN vs. MCI, MMSE or age) and z the primary covariates (age, sex, education, intracranial volume, as applicable). The signed coefficient for each region gives an evidence vector e. The support set S_k is a hybrid of BH-FDR-significant regions and a top-k (k = 20) fallback by |e|.

Experiment E4 compares FreeSurfer 8 and FastSurfer cortical (68 matched ROIs) and subcortical (64 matched ROIs) volumes on identical ADNI baseline scans (798 scans in the FastSurfer view) for 4 targets, giving 8 pairs. For each pair it computes evidence concordance (EC: Spearman correlation of the two evidence vectors over matched ROIs), support overlap (SO: Jaccard of the two support sets) and direction retention (DR: fraction of source-support regions whose sign is preserved). Table 2 reports medians over the 8 pairs under the primary specification and under cumulative extra covariates on an acquisition-complete subset.
official.claim: On ADNI baseline scans with primary covariates, FreeSurfer 8 and FastSurfer volume features give highly concordant ROI evidence (median Spearman EC 0.903 over 8 target/feature pairs) but nearly disjoint top-20 support regions (median Jaccard SO 0.098, direction retention 0.546).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: E4 sensitivity to sample selection and covariate adjustment (medians across eight FreeSurfer 8–FastSurfer claim-family comparisons). EC: evidence concordance (Spearman); SO: support overlap (Jaccard); DR: direction retention over source-support regions.
official.metric: Median across 8 comparisons of evidence concordance (Spearman, higher = more agreement), support overlap (Jaccard, higher = more agreement) and direction retention. No error bars in Table 2; Table F9 gives per-pair paired-bootstrap 95% percentile intervals (300 resamples), with EC lower limits 0.760-0.912 for 7 pairs and SO intervals as wide as [0.000, 0.667].
official.comparison: FreeSurfer 8 vs. FastSurfer cortical and subcortical volumes, same scans, targets (CN-AD, CN-MCI, MMSE, age) and design matrix; EC vs. SO within the same comparison.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running E4 with the stated specification gives median support Jaccard comparable to the evidence concordance (e.g. SO above about 0.5), or median EC well below 0.85, so that the 'high concordance but low support overlap' gap disappears.

title: Susceptibilities for Neural Networks Learning from Physical Data

official.background: When a neural network is trained on data from a physical system, the data distribution often depends on a physical parameter, such as the site-occupation probability in percolation. Susceptibilities come from singular learning theory and were proposed by Baker et al. (2025). They measure how a network's posterior-averaged loss responds to a perturbation of such a parameter of the data distribution. The paper asks whether susceptibilities can tell a practitioner which parts of the data are most useful for learning a given capability. If they can, they would be a tool for choosing training data.
official.method:
The data are percolating configurations on a 16x16 lattice. Each site is occupied independently with probability h, and a sample is kept only if an occupied cluster connects the bottom row to the top row (rejection sampling). The model is a 15M-parameter causal transformer (8 layers, width 256, 4 heads, 2D RoPE) whose inputs per site are the site coordinates, the occupation status and h. It is trained autoregressively with binary cross-entropy on a mixture of h values in [0.35, 0.6] (AdamW, batch 64, 262,144 steps of fresh data, peak learning rate 5e-4 with cosine decay). Using SGLD-style sampling around training checkpoints, the authors estimate a masked susceptibility chi_crit(h). It is restricted to the loss at critical sites, which are sites that must be occupied for the state to percolate. chi_crit(h) is positive and decreases with h throughout training (Figure 2). The authors read this as a prediction that small-h data makes percolation easier to learn.

To test this prediction, they retrain the same model with the mixing density u(h) proportional to exp(alpha*h) on [0.35, 0.6], with alpha from -16 (biased toward small h) to +16 (biased toward large h). Percolation ability is measured at each checkpoint on 16,384 samples from the uniform mixture. The model is given the bottom 8 rows of each sample as a prompt and generates the top 8 rows, and the score is the mean height of the tallest occupied cluster. A score of 16 means the model always generates percolating states; filling in the top rows with iid Bernoulli draws scores about 11.75.
official.claim: Models trained on data biased toward small h (alpha = -16, -8) learn to generate percolating states earlier: their mean generated max-cluster height jumps from about 12.5 to about 14 at roughly 3-5k training steps. Models biased toward large h (alpha = +8, +16) make the same jump only at about 8-15k steps.
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Biasing the training data towards smaller values of h makes learning percolation easier. We retrain the model with different training datasets parametrised by α and track the mean maximum cluster height generated by the model as a downstream measure of to what degree the model has learned percolation. When the dataset is biased toward small h (α < 0) the model learns percolation faster than when the dataset is biased towards large h (α > 0). For reference, we show the mean maximum cluster height when the model is replaced with a random Bernoulli model (baseline) and the optimal value for a model which always generates percolating configurations (optimal).
official.metric: Mean maximum cluster height (rows spanned by the tallest occupied cluster) in the generated top half, over 16,384 prompts from the uniform h-mixture. Higher is better; the maximum is 16. Plotted against training step on a log scale. No seeds, error bars or confidence intervals are reported. The values below are read off the plot and are approximate.

title: Visual-to-Executable Procedural Reconstruction of Buildings.

official.background: Procedural (shape-grammar) models of buildings, such as CGA programs, are compact, editable and reusable, but writing them by hand needs expert effort. Recovering such a program from a single in-the-wild photograph is hard: valid programs are non-unique, must obey strict grammar rules to execute, and photos have perspective distortion and occlusion. Asking a general LLM/VLM to write the low-level program directly is the obvious shortcut, but the generated code often fails to execute.
official.method:
The framework splits reconstruction into two levels. A fine-tuned Qwen-VL-7B predicts a Global Structure Layout Tree (a YAML split-and-repeat hierarchy of floors and tiles) from the facade crop and a SAM3 mask, and revises it for up to 2 rounds by rendering the tree into a schematic and comparing it with the image (visual-symbolic reflection). For each representative tile (window-like or entrance-like), a component predictor with CLIP + DINOv3 visual streams and a language decoder generates a YAML 'component parameterization' (arch presence/style, sill, grid rows/columns, frame, stairs, door hardware, etc.). A custom deterministic compiler turns the layout tree and the component YAML into executable CGA rules.

Table 3 compares three tile-level strategies on the same tile crops: (1) Direct Code, where Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview is prompted to write low-level CGA component code from the tile image; (2) Direct Middle Code, where Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview is prompted to output the structured component-parameterization YAML, which is then compiled by the same deterministic compiler; (3) Ours, the fine-tuned CLIP+DINOv3 predictor producing the same YAML. Execution success is the fraction of outputs that compile and run; attribute accuracy is exact match against annotated preset labels and is only defined for the two YAML-producing methods.
official.claim: For tile-level procedural component generation, producing a structured component-parameterization YAML that is deterministically compiled gives execution success of 0.95 (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, prompted) and 0.98 (fine-tuned predictor), versus 0.68 when Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview writes low-level CGA code directly.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Comparison of tile-level procedural generation strategies. Attribute accuracy is reported only for methods that explicitly predict tile-level structured attributes.
official.metric: Execution success rate (fraction of generated tile programs that execute; higher is better). Attribute exact-match accuracy is also reported. Single numbers, no error bars, seeds, or test-set size reported for this table.
official.comparison: Direct low-level CGA code generation by Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview vs. structured middle-code (YAML) generation by the same model and by the authors' fine-tuned CLIP+DINOv3 predictor, all followed by execution
official.falsification_criterion: With a comparable component schema and compiler, prompting the same frontier VLM to emit structured attributes does not raise execution success by a large margin (e.g., by less than ~0.15 absolute) over prompting it to emit raw CGA component code on the same tile crops; or direct CGA code generation already executes on ~0.9 or more of tiles.

title: Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models

official.background: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as Chronos, Moirai, TimesFM and Sundial are used zero-shot for probabilistic forecasting, and their quantiles or prediction intervals are only useful if they are calibrated: a predicted 10% quantile should be exceeded 90% of the time. Prior calibration evaluations of TSFMs pool all forecast steps and instances into one coverage score, which can hide errors that differ across horizons or across the model's own predicted values. Post-hoc recalibration (relabeling quantile levels with a monotone map fitted on held-out data) is a cheap fix, but it is unclear which kinds of miscalibration it actually removes.
official.method:
The authors define a hierarchy of calibration errors on the quantile grid {0.1, ..., 0.9}: PCE_pool (coverage error after pooling all horizons and instances), PCE_avg (coverage error computed per horizon step, then averaged), and QCE_avg (quantile-conditioned error per horizon, estimated by isotonic regression of the coverage indicator on the predicted quantile value, then averaged). They prove PCE_pool <= PCE_avg <= QCE_avg and show that a single global relabeling map can drive PCE_pool to zero but cannot push PCE_avg below half the horizon gap. 14 TSFMs are run zero-shot on the short-term task of GIFT-Eval; sampling models use 100 sample paths.

For recalibration, each of 42 GIFT-Eval configurations with at least 50 forecast windows is split chronologically: the earliest 20% of windows of every series are used to fit one non-decreasing level map (isotonic recalibration IR, KDE, or Platt scaling PS), pooled over horizons, and all metrics are computed on the remaining later 80% of windows before and after recalibration (series with a single window instead use a random 20% of series). Table 3 reports, per model, the relative change of the mean error over the 42 configurations.
official.claim: With isotonic recalibration fitted on the earliest 20% of forecast windows, Chronos-T5-Small's mean calibration error on the later windows of 42 GIFT-Eval configurations drops by 60.4% for PCE_pool but only 38.5% for PCE_avg and 31.1% for QCE_avg; the same ordering holds for Chronos-Bolt-Small (-24.5%, -8.9%, -6.8%), and for all 14 models the IR reduction in PCE_pool exceeds that in PCE_avg.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Relative change of the calibration errors after post-hoc recalibration under the chronological split, i.e., the change of each model's mean error over the 42 dataset configurations. Negative values are improvements, and bold numbers mark the best recalibration method for each model and metric. With a single exception, all errors decrease, but the gains are largest for PCE_pool and decrease for PCE_avg and QCE_avg, highlighting again that recalibration via CDF relabeling mainly targets probabilistic miscalibration.
official.metric: Relative change of each model's mean calibration error (PCE_pool, PCE_avg, QCE_avg) over 42 dataset configurations, after vs. before recalibration on the same test windows; negative is improvement. No ± reported (Table 8 gives standard errors across datasets for the raw, un-recalibrated errors only, e.g. Chronos-T5-Small PCE_pool 0.1035 ± 0.0112).
official.comparison: Each model's calibration errors on the chronological test windows before vs. after post-hoc relabeling (IR, KDE, PS); and the size of the reduction across the three metrics of the hierarchy
official.falsification_criterion: For Chronos-T5-Small with IR, the relative reduction of PCE_pool is not clearly larger than that of PCE_avg and QCE_avg (e.g. PCE_avg falls by about as much as PCE_pool), or the reduction in PCE_pool is far from ~60% (e.g. below 40%).

title: Beyond Token Representations: Explicit Visual Object Grounding for Video Reasoning Segmentation

official.background: Video reasoning segmentation (VRS) asks a model to segment, across all frames of a video, the object that an implicit query refers to (e.g. 'the tool used to cut the tomato'), so the model has to reason about which object is meant before it localizes it. Most current methods, starting with VISA, have a multimodal LLM emit one or a few special <SEG> tokens whose embeddings prompt a mask decoder such as SAM/SAM2, and then propagate keyframe masks with a tracker. The authors argue that these tokens carry little semantic or spatial information, so the decoder is poorly guided. Referring video object segmentation (RVOS) benchmarks such as MeViS are used as the same task with explicit queries.
official.method:
Spatial-aware prompt generation and refinement (SPGR): Qwen2.5-VL (3B or 7B, LoRA rank 16) is prompted with the video and query to output, for each frame, a bounding box and K=7 points with confidence scores in a fixed text format. The point set is then refined over several dialogue turns, where the MLLM is given its previous points and asked to keep the reliable ones and replace the rest (R=4 refinement steps during training, 2 at inference). Training losses are a point calibration loss (confidence vs. whether the point falls inside the GT mask), a box loss, BCE+Dice mask loss, and a cross-query consistency loss (weight 0.2) between predictions for the original query and an MLLM-generated auxiliary query (box IoU plus symmetric KL between Gaussians fitted to the two point sets; training only). The box and points prompt a frozen SAM2 on N=3 keyframes, chosen by the average of a SAM2 target-confidence score and the fraction of points inside the box, and frozen Cutie propagates the masks to the remaining frames.

The ablation 'Ours w/o SPGR' removes explicit box/point prompts and instead, following VISA, has the MLLM produce token-level target representations that prompt the mask decoder. Everything else is unchanged. Ablations follow UniPixel's protocol on MeViS and report region similarity J, contour accuracy F, and their mean J&F. Training samples T=4 frames per video at a 10-frame interval and uses AdamW at lr 1e-4 on 4 NVIDIA A40 GPUs.
official.claim: On MeViS with the Qwen2.5-VL-7B + SAM2 pipeline, replacing token-level target representations with the explicit box-and-point prompts of SPGR raises J&F from 45.5 to 60.1 (+14.6), and dropping only the point set lowers J&F to 49.5.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Ablation study on the SPGR module.
official.metric: J&F (mean of region similarity J and contour accuracy F, %), higher is better; single run, no error bars reported
official.comparison: Full model (explicit box + refined points) vs. 'Ours w/o SPGR' (VISA-style segmentation tokens) in the same pipeline; also vs. box-only ('SPGR w/o point') and points-only ('SPGR w/o box') variants
official.falsification_criterion: With a matched training setup on MeViS, the explicit-prompt model beats the token-based variant by less than about 5 J&F, or the token-based variant reaches J&F at or above 55.

title: Bridging CLIP with DINO: Cross-Modal Information Maximization for Online Test-Time Adaptation

official.background: Online test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a pretrained model on a stream of unlabeled, distribution-shifted test batches. Recent work uses CLIP as the backbone because it gives a zero-shot classifier for any class list, but under image corruptions CLIP's accuracy drops sharply and it makes confident errors. Entropy-minimization adapters such as TENT then reinforce those errors, and the predicted labels collapse onto a few classes. Methods such as BATCLIP, Mint and SubTTA adapt CLIP with multimodal alignment objectives, but all rely on CLIP's own text-aligned features.
official.method:
CDIM adds a frozen DINO v2-base (ViT-B/14, no ImageNet fine-tuning) next to CLIP ViT-B/16. For each batch, CLIP text prototypes T are projected into DINO space through the batch cross-covariance of the l2-normalized image features, M = (1/B) C^T D, T_D = colnorm(M^T T^T); DINO logits are 20 * D T_D, CLIP logits are 100 * C T^T, and the two are averaged. Only the affine parameters of the normalization layers in CLIP's image and text encoders are trained, with one gradient step per batch on GT-IM: the mean entropy over the samples kept by a gate (drop the ceil(0.05 B) samples with the highest negative log-sum-exp of the ensembled logits) minus the entropy of the full-batch mean prediction. T_D gets no gradient and DINO is never updated.

At prediction time, online logit adjustment subtracts log of an EMA (alpha = 0.9, initialized uniform) of the batch-mean softmax predictions from the ensembled logits. Evaluation is the standard online protocol: top-1 accuracy at severity 5, averaged over the 15 corruptions, with the model reset before each corruption. CIFAR100-C uses Adam, lr 5e-4, batch size 200 (BATCLIP's settings). The control in Table 9 adds the same DINO v2 logit ensemble (Eq. 3) to TENT and to BATCLIP.
official.claim: On CIFAR100-C (severity 5, online TTA, CLIP ViT-B/16 + DINO v2-base, batch size 200), CDIM reaches 48.2% mean accuracy, versus 44.6% for BATCLIP with the same DINO v2 logit ensemble and 40.0% for TENT with it.
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Accuracy (%) of TENT and BATCLIP with and without the DINO v2 logit ensemble (default setting: CLIP ViT-B/16 and DINO v2-base).
official.metric: Top-1 accuracy (%) averaged over 15 corruptions, higher is better. Table 9 has no error bars (single fixed seed). Table 7 gives CDIM 48.2 (std 0.1) over five seeds at B=200 on CIFAR100-C; no seed variation is reported for the baselines.
official.comparison: CDIM vs. BATCLIP + DINO v2 ensemble (strongest matched baseline) and TENT + DINO v2 ensemble, all with CLIP ViT-B/16 and DINO v2-base
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running both on CIFAR100-C under the stated protocol, CDIM's mean accuracy exceeds BATCLIP + DINO v2 ensemble by less than about 1 point, or CDIM falls well below 48.2% (e.g. under 47%).
