title: SEEK-VAU: Towards Evidence-Faithful Video Anomaly Understanding via Agentic Search
claim_source: Table 4, page 9; bootstrap CIs in Appendix F, page 19

official.background: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) asks a model to say whether a video contains an anomaly, what kind, when it happens, and why, with visual evidence. Most current systems, including multimodal LLMs and reasoning-tuned VAU methods, reason over a fixed bundle of frames chosen before inference (e.g. uniform sampling). If that bundle misses the precursor, trigger or aftermath of the event, the model cannot go back and look for it. The paper asks whether letting the model search the video itself, and check whether its evidence is sufficient before answering, recovers more of the anomaly event chain under the same frame budget.
official.method:
SEEK-VAU is a tool-using Qwen3-VL-8B policy with four actions: scan (6 uniform frames over the whole video, kept as a protected global map), seek (the policy picks a time interval, a text query and an event-chain role, and the tool deterministically returns 4 uniform frames from that interval, committed as an evidence window), verify (the policy labels its committed evidence sufficient/insufficient/redundant, gives an anomaly confidence and lists missing stages; only 'sufficient' allows finalization) and finalize (emits a structured case: existence, category, anomaly interval, evidence windows, explanation). An episode has at most 8 turns and 3 seeks, so at most 18 acquired frames, with at most 16 visible at once. Training is SFT on protocol traces built from SEEK-Bench train episodes, then trajectory-level GRPO (G=4, KL 0.1, lr 4e-7) with an answer reward (category, temporal IoU, QA judged by a fixed GPT-5.4 judge) and, in the full model, the EFCV counterfactual evidence reward.

The claim uses the matched acquisition-mode ladder (Table 4). All rows share the backbone, SEEK-Bench training episodes and targets, update count, answer reward, 18-frame cap, decoding, parser and evaluator. 'Two-stage matched' sees the 6-frame overview, then commits up to three windows at once before seeing any returned frame, gets 4 frames per window, and answers with no verify, replanning or EFCV. 'Closed-loop w/o verify' can choose later windows based on returned frames but has no verify gate. 'SEEK-VAU w/o EFCV' adds the verify gate, trained with the answer reward only. Evaluation is on the 576-episode, video-disjoint SEEK-Bench val split (from MSAD and ECVA videos): Temporal mIoU of the anomaly interval and Evidence F1 (one-to-one window matching at tIoU >= 0.3), both averaged over anomalous episodes, and QA accuracy judged for semantic equivalence.
official.claim: On the SEEK-Bench val split (576 episodes) with a matched Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, training and 18-frame cap, closed-loop search with a verify gate (SEEK-VAU w/o EFCV) beats one-shot two-stage retrieval by +6.2 Temporal mIoU (54.4 vs. 48.2), +11.6 QA accuracy (42.7 vs. 31.1) and +9.3 Evidence F1 (41.6 vs. 32.3), with paired-bootstrap 95% CIs of [+3.0, +9.2], [+7.0, +16.0] and [+5.0, +13.5].
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Matched acquisition-mode ablation.
official.metric: Temporal mIoU, QA accuracy and Evidence F1 (%, higher is better) on SEEK-Bench val. Single training run; no seed std. The only uncertainty reported is the paired validation-episode bootstrap 95% CI for this one contrast.
official.comparison: SEEK-VAU w/o EFCV (closed-loop seek with verify gate) vs. Two-stage matched (one-shot adaptive retrieval, no verify) under matched backbone, data, update count, answer reward and frame cap; the full SEEK-VAU with EFCV and Closed-loop w/o verify are additional rows.

title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations

official.background: Implicit neural representations (INRs) fit a small network that maps coordinates (time, pixel position) to signal values, and their quality depends mostly on how they represent high frequencies. Quantum INRs (QINRs) such as QIREN use data-reuploading quantum circuits, which compute finite Fourier series in the input, as feature extractors decoded by a classical layer. In existing multiband QINRs each quantum block works independently and their outputs meet only in the classical decoder. This paper asks whether letting quantum blocks share a coherent quantum memory register improves compact (few-hundred-parameter) signal fitting.
official.method:
SQMM maps a coordinate x through a fixed positional encoding (for 1D: the raw coordinate plus 16 dyadic sinusoidal frequencies) and per-band affine maps into rotation angles. It has 5 sequential quantum bands, each with 2 data qubits and [2, 3, 4, 4, 5] RY reuploads with local entangling layers, plus a shared 2-qubit memory register that is initialized from the encoding by RY/RX uploads. Each band reads the memory through controlled-RY couplings before its first upload and writes back through XY couplings (bands 1-4); the band's data qubits are then traced out and the memory state is passed to the next band. Every band emits Pauli Z and ZZ expectations, which are concatenated and decoded by an MLP with one hidden layer of width 5 and GELU. Total: 642 parameters in 1D. Simulation is exact (mixed-state, PennyLane + PyTorch) unless shots are specified.

Training: full-batch Adam, lr 0.03, MSE loss, bands added one at a time (one band per 25 updates for 300-epoch runs, 5-update fade-in), plus a spectral memory alignment loss (λ_align = 3) that matches the normalized Pauli-probed Fourier power spectrum of the memory after band i to the stop-gradient FFT power spectrum of the features of bands 1..i; this loss is switched off after four growth intervals. The Cello benchmark follows QIREN: the Bach cello excerpt sampled at 1000 points with stride 5, amplitude normalized, timestamps in [-1, 1], 300 epochs. Baselines (QIREN, IGA, FINER, SIREN, MSA-INR, CAFE (enc.)) are configured at a similar parameter budget (649-703), learning rate selected from [3e-2, 1e-3], trained for the same epochs and evaluated at their best-epoch weights.
official.claim: On the Cello audio reconstruction benchmark (1000 samples, 300 epochs, ~650 parameters), SQMM with exact expectations reaches MSE 0.48 ± 0.08 ×10^-3, versus 3.60 ± 0.60 for the best baseline CAFE (enc.), 3.73 ± 0.44 for FINER and 6.79 ± 0.35 for the quantum baseline QIREN; even with 2048-shot estimates SQMM reaches 0.76 ± 0.06.

official.metric: MSE ×10^-3 between reconstruction and normalized target signal, lower is better; mean ± SD over 5 runs (SQMM; Table 15 confirms 5 runs); baselines evaluated at best-epoch weights
official.comparison: SQMM (642 params) vs. QIREN (649), IGA (673), FINER (691), SIREN (673), MSA-INR (673), CAFE (enc.) (703), all fitted to the same Cello signal

title: Koopman Generative Operators for Efficient Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
claim_source: Table 5, page 21 (horizon averages in Table 1, page 7)

official.background: Probabilistic time-series forecasting asks a model for a full predictive distribution over future values, not just a point forecast, so that uncertainty can inform decisions in areas such as energy and finance. Diffusion and flow-matching forecasters can represent flexible distributions, but they need many iterative sampling steps at inference. Latent-dynamics models such as K2VAE are cheaper, but they tie uncertainty to a sampled initial latent state. The ProbTS benchmark compares these model families on standard datasets using CRPS (probabilistic accuracy) and NMAE (point accuracy).
official.method:
KGO normalizes the input with RevIN, splits it into non-overlapping patches and encodes them with an sLSTM. Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) then rolls the last latent state forward with powers of a learned linear operator K (spectrally normalized so ||K||_2 <= 1), which gives one latent per future patch. These latents feed two decoders. A residual-MLP decoder produces a deterministic forecast. Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM) lifts a noise/data interpolant conditioned on the KoPE latent, transports it with a closed-form affine map e^{(1-tau)A} z + (1-tau) b, and decodes the result. At inference tau = 0, so sampling takes a single step. An Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG) mixes the two forecasts with per-variate, per-horizon weights g in [0,1]. The model is trained end-to-end with an energy-score (sample CRPS) loss plus a quantile pinball loss.

Evaluation follows the ProbTS long-term protocol: context length 96, horizons {96, 192, 336, 720}, CRPS estimated from 100 samples, mean and std over 5 independent retraining runs. Baselines are TSDiff, CSDI, TimeGrad, GRU MAF, Trans MAF, GRU NVP and K2VAE.
official.claim: On ETTh2 long-term forecasting (context 96), KGO has lower CRPS than K2VAE, the strongest baseline, at every horizon: 0.134±0.001 vs 0.162±0.009 (H=96), 0.155±0.002 vs 0.186±0.018 (192), 0.173±0.002 vs 0.257±0.023 (336), 0.177±0.002 vs 0.280±0.014 (720). Averaged over horizons this is 0.160 vs 0.221, about 27% lower.

Each cell reports the mean ± standard deviation of the CRPS across 5 independent runs of retraining and evaluation. Red bold: best; blue underline: second best. Due to the excessive time and memory consumption, some results are unavailable and denoted as "–".

title: Heads That Write, Not Just Point: Image Retrieval Heads in Vision-Language Models
claim_source: Table 14 (Appendix J.2), page 25; same pattern for the four main models in Figure 3 (page 8) and Figure 7 (page 24)

official.background: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can take many interleaved images and text in one prompt, but to answer a question about one image they must first find that image in context ('in-context image retrieval'). Accuracy on multi-image benchmarks falls as the number of images grows, yet it is unclear which internal components perform this selection. Prior head-level analyses identify specialized heads by where they attend; this paper asks whether attention alone identifies the heads that the model actually relies on, or whether what a head writes into the residual stream also matters.
official.method:
Heads are scored on ICIR-MCQ, a probe built from MS-COCO images interleaved with MM-NIAH text passages: the model must pick which of four captions describes the one image that contains a queried category (5 or 6 candidate images, 6,000 samples). At the last token of the final category mention (the 'cattok'), the pointer criterion ranks each head by whether its attention mass over each image's visual-token span puts the target image first (R@1). The writer criterion trains, per head, a tiny dual-encoder probe (one linear layer on the head's value-weighted output and one on the mean-pooled LVLM image embedding, 256-d, InfoNCE) and ranks heads by R@1 of retrieving the target from a held-out pool of 1,200 images.

The union of the pointer top-100 and writer top-100 is split into three disjoint sets: overlap (in both), pointer-only, and writer-only. On Visual Haystacks (Yes/No questions such as 'In the image that contains a sofa, is there a bottle?', 1,000 samples per haystack size N), the top-K heads of each set (ordered by pointer rank, or by writer rank for writer-only) are zero-ablated before o_proj from the anchor-object token to the last prefill token, for K in {5,...,30}. Each arm is compared with ablating K uniformly random heads (mean of 3 seeds). Decoding is greedy, so runs are deterministic apart from the random-head draw.

title: Cool Graphs: Active Property Search Towards Quantum Nano-Refrigerators
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (per-topology breakdown in Table 7, Appendix J, page 19)

official.background: Nanoscale electronic junctions can, in some configurations, absorb energy from their bosonic (e.g. phonon) environment under a voltage bias, a necessary condition for a quantum nano-refrigerator. Checking a single configuration requires solving a many-body master equation whose size grows as 2^N in the number of orbitals, and under uniform random sampling of the physical parameters only about 1.2-9.2% of configurations show positive bosonic energy flux. Finding such configurations is therefore a rare-event search problem in which each oracle call is expensive, and the paper asks whether a learned surrogate with active learning can find them far more efficiently than random or standard Bayesian-optimization search.
official.method:
Each candidate is a rectangular grid of n sites (8 training topologies from 1x2 to 3x3) with parameters sampled from the ranges in Table 1 (site energies, inter-site coupling, decay constants, electrode and bath couplings, temperature). An oracle builds Born-Markov/secular rate matrices in the 2^N Fock space, solves for the steady state, and computes the bosonic energy flux F_E; the label is positive if F_E > 10^5 eV/s. The system is encoded as a graph (site nodes with features [alpha_i, T, eta_(i,L), eta_(i,R)], bath nodes with only T non-zero; site-site edges weighted by h_sys couplings and site-bath edges by W; features signed-log1p transformed and z-scored) and a GVAE (multi-head GAT encoder, auxiliary node/edge reconstruction decoders, attention pooling, MLP classification head; latent dim 32, hidden 128) is trained with reconstruction + KL + classification losses, in two stages.

Active learning starts from a 28,000-graph labelled pool. In each of 32 cycles, 10,000 candidates are freshly sampled, 20 MC-dropout forward passes estimate the predictive variance, the 500 most uncertain candidates are simulated with the oracle, and the GVAE is retrained on the enlarged pool (16,000 oracle calls per trajectory). Baselines at the same 16,000-call acquisition budget: random acquisition (same starting pool), and Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (one GP per topology, Matern-5/2 + white noise, EI or UCB on signed-log F_E, 2,000 calls per topology, 1,200 candidates scored per step, started cold from 12 random points). A five-member deep ensemble variant of the uncertainty acquisition is also reported.
official.claim: At a matched budget of 16,000 oracle calls, MC-dropout uncertainty-driven acquisition with the GVAE finds 4477 ± 105 positive-flux configurations, versus 670 ± 14 for random acquisition (6.68x enrichment, 3.58 vs. 23.88 oracle calls per positive) and 3073 ± 580 / 2923 ± 1076 for GP Bayesian optimization with UCB / EI.
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Search results at a matched budget of 16,000 oracle calls, three independent trajectories per strategy. The held-out rows are obtained by retraining a GVAE from scratch on the shared 28,000-graph initial pool plus that strategy's 16,000 acquisitions, giving a 44,000-graph pool in every case, so they isolate which points were acquired rather than how many; the rows above them concern the search itself, which for GP-BO uses no initial pool. Enrichment is the ratio of positives found to the random strategy at the same budget. The two GP-BO columns are the same Gaussian-process surrogate under different acquisition functions; it divides its budget evenly across the eight topologies, because a Gaussian process requires a fixed-dimensional input space, whereas the active-learning loop reallocates (Appendix J).
official.metric: Number of positive-flux configurations (F_E > 10^5 eV/s) among the 16,000 acquired points, higher is better; ± is the sample standard deviation over three independent search trajectories (different random seeds)
official.comparison: MC-dropout active learning (GVAE surrogate) vs. random acquisition from the same sampler and starting pool, and vs. per-topology GP-BO (EI and UCB), all with 16,000 oracle calls over the 8 training topologies
official.falsification_criterion: With the authors' sampler, oracle and protocol, MC-dropout acquisition finds fewer than ~3x the positives of random acquisition at 16,000 calls, or its mean positive count does not exceed the GP-BO (UCB) mean by more than the GP-BO trajectory spread (i.e. below ~3650).

title: LLMs as MDP Designers: A Dependency-Aware Agentic Framework for Automated Robot Policy Generation
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (Wilson CIs in Table 13, Appendix F.3, page 26)

official.background: Training a robot with reinforcement learning (RL) requires someone to formulate the problem as a Markov decision process (MDP): choose observations, actions, reward terms and termination conditions, and then implement them in a simulator. This is done by hand by experts and is easy to get wrong; a formulation can produce code that runs but a policy that never learns the task. The paper asks whether LLMs can do this design work automatically from a natural-language task description, so that the output is a standalone trained RL policy, and argues that general-purpose coding agents tend to produce executable environments with misaligned MDPs.
official.method:
ARPG is a multi-agent pipeline in which all agents use GPT-5.2. In the modeling phase, a parameter agent reads the task description and a robotics agent summarizes the robot's Isaac Lab Python/USD spec; then a fixed sequence of agents produces the objective, decision/state variables, constraints, a mathematical formulation (LaTeX) and finally a state-action-reward (SAR) MDP specification. Each agent outputs a self-assessed confidence score; below a threshold, an error-correction agent checks the artifact against an agent-specific checklist and the same agent is re-invoked with the diagnosis while upstream artifacts stay fixed. In the implementation phase, configuration agents generate Isaac Lab manager-based modules in three stages (scene/policy; action/observation/event/termination; reward), a coding agent assembles them, and runtime errors are routed back to the responsible module agent, with at most five revision rounds.

Baselines receive the same task description, robot/USD information and per-configuration Isaac Lab documentation: one-shot GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3, iterative GPT-5.2 (revises code from execution error logs, up to five rounds), and the off-the-shelf agents Codex (GPT-5.2) and Claude Code (Claude Sonnet 4.6). Tasks are CartPole, Ant, Humanoid, Franka Reach and Franka Lift in Isaac Lab 2.1.0 / Isaac Sim 4.5.0. Each method-task pair is run in 10 independent generation-and-training trials. PGSR (policy generation success rate) counts a trial as successful if the trained policy passes at least 16 of 20 fixed-seed evaluation episodes under automatic task criteria (e.g. Ant: survive 16 s, base height >= 0.31 m, mean forward velocity >= 0.5 m/s, up-projection > 0.93 and heading projection > 0.80 from 1 s to 16 s; Reach: end-effector error <= 0.10 m over the final 1-s hold for each of three 4-s targets). Trials that fail earlier count as failures.
official.claim: With 10 trials per cell, ARPG's policy generation success rate is 0.9 on Ant and 0.9 on Reach, versus at most 0.4 (Ant, Codex) and 0.3 (Reach, Claude Code) for every baseline, and ARPG has the highest PGSR on all five Isaac Lab tasks (summed over tasks, 36/50 successful trials vs. 13/50 for Codex and for Claude Code and 11/50 for iterative GPT-5.2).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Success rates across benchmark tasks. All results are reported as triplets in the order of MSR, EISR, and PGSR. Bold indicates the best value for each metric within a task. Corresponding 95% Wilson confidence intervals are provided in Appendix F.3.
official.metric: PGSR: fraction of 10 independent generation-and-training trials whose trained policy passes >= 16/20 fixed-seed evaluation episodes under task-specific criteria; higher is better. No ± in the table; the paper gives 95% Wilson intervals by success count (e.g. 9/10: [0.60, 0.98]; 4/10: [0.17, 0.69]; 3/10: [0.11, 0.60]). Table entries are MSR / EISR / PGSR triplets; the 50-trial totals in the statement are sums of the table's counts, not a statistic reported by the paper.
official.comparison: ARPG (GPT-5.2) vs. iterative GPT-5.2, Codex (GPT-5.2) and Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6), all given the same inputs and up to five execution-feedback revision rounds; one-shot GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3 are also reported but score 0 PGSR everywhere.
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running 10 trials per method on Ant and Reach, ARPG's PGSR is not clearly higher than the best of Codex and Claude Code (e.g. ARPG <= 0.6 or a baseline >= 0.7 on either task), or summed over the five tasks ARPG's successful trials are not well above the best baseline's.

title: Positional Encoding Is All You Need For Scalable Equivariance Constraint Relaxation

official.background: Equivariant networks build known symmetries (rotations, translations, permutations) into their layers, which often improves sample efficiency, but the constrained parameterization can make optimization harder, and the data may only approximately satisfy the symmetry. Recent work relaxes the constraint during training by adding non-equivariant dense branches in parallel to each equivariant layer and annealing them to zero, so the final model is strictly equivariant again. These dense branches greatly increase parameter count and training time. This paper proposes a cheaper relaxation: add a symmetry-breaking positional encoding (PE) to the input during training and anneal it away.
official.method:
The relaxed model is h_λ(x) = f_θ(x, λγp), where f_θ is the unchanged equivariant network, p is a positional encoding fixed in the canonical frame (not rotated with the input), γ is a learnable scalar initialized to 1, and λ(t) is a schedule that reaches 0 by the end of training, so the evaluated model is the original strictly equivariant architecture. For VN-PointNet (Vector Neurons, Sn × SO(3) equivariant), the best additive variant uses a sinusoidal per-point-index encoding p ∈ R^{N×3} (Eq. 4, Vaswani-style with 3 coordinates), added to the input points x' = x + λγp, with a linear decay λ(t) = 1 − t/T. The loss is L_task + β‖λ(t)γp‖² with β = 0.001 (concat variant: x' = [x, λγp] ∈ R^{N×6}, β = 0.005).

Setup: ModelNet40 classification, 300 points per cloud, SO(3)/SO(3) protocol (random rotations during both training and evaluation), training hyperparameters from Pertigkiozoglou et al. (2024): batch 32, Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, StepLR. The baseline CR method (Pertigkiozoglou et al.) adds a dense linear layer over flattened vector channels in parallel to every VN layer, annealed to zero; its schedule and β were tuned over the same search space (best: triangular schedule, β = 0.01). Validation is done with PE removed. Accuracy is the best validation instance accuracy over training, averaged over 5 seeds.
official.claim: On ModelNet40 under the SO(3)/SO(3) protocol (300 points), VN-PointNet trained with additive sinusoidal PE relaxation (PE removed at evaluation) reaches 79.6 ± 0.4% instance accuracy, above dense-layer constraint relaxation (74.0 ± 1.9%) and the strict VN-PointNet baseline (67.5 ± 0.5%), with essentially unchanged parameters (1.97M vs. 8.98M for CR) and time per epoch (27.9 s vs. 97.6 s for CR).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: ModelNet40 classification accuracy and training cost. Results for VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN under strict equivariance, dense-layer constraint relaxation (CR), and our positional-encoding relaxation (PE; additive and concatenative variants). Accuracy is the average best validation accuracy over training (mean ± std over 5 random seeds). All models are trained and evaluated on randomly rotated point clouds (SO(3)/SO(3)). "Parameters" counts trainable parameters in the trained architecture, and "Time per epoch" is computed by dividing total wall-clock training time on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 with batch-size 32 by the number of epochs.
official.metric: Instance accuracy on the ModelNet40 validation set (higher is better), taken as the best validation accuracy during training; mean ± std over 5 random seeds. Parameters and time per epoch on one RTX A6000 also reported.
official.comparison: VN-PointNet + PE (additive and concat) vs. VN-PointNet + dense-layer CR [Pertigkiozoglou et al.] vs. strict VN-PointNet, same training hyperparameters and same relaxation-hyperparameter search for PE and CR
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running VN-PointNet on ModelNet40 (SO(3)/SO(3), 300 points, 5 seeds) with additive sinusoidal PE annealed to zero gives a mean accuracy within about 2 points of a tuned CR run, or no more than a few points above the strict baseline (the paper reports +5.6 over CR and +12.1 over the baseline).

title: VIGOR: Visual Gain Ordering for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Language Models

official.background: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (e.g. LLaDA-V, Lumina-DiMOO) generate an answer by starting from a fully masked sequence and repeatedly unmasking ('committing') the masked positions they are most confident about, in blocks. Like autoregressive vision-language models, they hallucinate content that is plausible under language priors but not present in the image. The authors argue that in diffusion decoding part of the problem is the order of commitment: positions whose high confidence comes from language priors get committed early and then bias the remaining positions through bidirectional attention. Existing hallucination fixes (contrastive decoding, activation steering) were designed for left-to-right decoding and only change which token is chosen, not when a position is committed.
official.method:
VIGOR keeps the base model, block schedule, generation length and per-step unmask budget unchanged, and changes only the score used to pick which masked positions to commit at each denoising step. At every step it runs the usual image-conditioned forward pass and a second 'visual-ablation' pass in which the image input is replaced by [MASK] (projected image embeddings replaced by the [MASK] embedding for LLaDA-V; VQ image tokens replaced by [MASK] tokens for Lumina-DiMOO), with the text and current mask pattern unchanged. For each masked position the candidate token is the argmax of the image-conditioned distribution; its confidence under the two passes, c_img and c_noimg, gives the score s = (c_img - c_noimg) + log((c_img + 1e-8)/(c_noimg + 1e-8)). The top-k positions by s in the current block are committed to their image-conditioned argmax tokens. Decoding is greedy (temperature 0), so runs are deterministic; cost is about 2x the baseline decoding time.

Baselines on POPE are vanilla confidence-ordered decoding, VCD (logit contrast against a Gaussian-noised image, applied at every denoising step, with commit decisions driven by the clean branch) and ICT (head-level activation shifts from probes trained on clean/blurred image pairs, applied over the whole generation span). POPE asks balanced yes/no questions about whether an object is in an image (random, popular and adversarial negative sampling) over MSCOCO, A-OKVQA and GQA images; accuracy and F1 are reported for each of the nine subsets.
official.claim: On POPE-COCO with Lumina-DiMOO, VIGOR raises F1 to 79.3 / 79.3 / 74.8 on the random / popular / adversarial splits, versus 70.1 / 68.1 / 66.2 for the best adapted baseline (ICT) and 67.7 / 66.8 / 65.1 for vanilla decoding, a margin of at least 8.6 F1 points over every baseline on every split.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on POPE. We compare VIGOR against the vanilla Baseline, VCD and ICT. The values highlighted in green indicate the best metric under each setting. Arrows next to each value report the change vs. Baseline (↑/↓ = improvement on higher-/lower-is-better metrics).
official.metric: POPE F1 (higher is better; accuracy also reported). Single deterministic run with greedy decoding; no error bars or seeds reported.
official.comparison: VIGOR ordering vs. vanilla confidence ordering, VCD and ICT on the same Lumina-DiMOO checkpoint, same block schedule and generation settings
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Lumina-DiMOO on POPE-COCO (random, popular, adversarial), VIGOR's F1 is not at least ~5 points above both vanilla decoding and the best of VCD/ICT on each split, or VIGOR's gain over vanilla falls below ~5 F1 points on any of the three splits.

title: Manifold Embedding of Deep Image Features for Image Matching via Neural Adjoint Maps

official.background: Semantic correspondence means finding matching points between images of different object instances from the same category (for example two different cars). Features from foundation models such as DINOv2 and Stable Diffusion are strong descriptors, and zero-shot methods usually match them by nearest-neighbour (NN) search. NN matching has no notion of global structure, so dense matches are noisy and not smooth. Functional maps, which regularise matching through a low-dimensional spectral basis of the Laplace-Beltrami operator (LBO), work well for 3D shapes, but a flat image grid has no informative geometry from which to build such an operator.
official.method:
Each image's deep feature map is treated as a 2D surface embedded in feature space: every feature-map pixel is a vertex of a quad mesh whose d-dimensional position is its feature vector. A discrete LBO L = M^-1 K is derived with Galerkin's method using bilinear hat functions, the metric tensor g_ij = <d_i E, d_j E> of the embedding, four-point quadrature and a lumped mass matrix, so no kernel scale has to be chosen (unlike the graph Laplacian of Cheng et al. [16]). The first k = 50 eigenfunctions are computed with Lanczos. Stable Diffusion (v1.5) features are used to build the LBO.

For each image pair, a Neural Adjoint Map (NAM) h_theta (a bias-free linear layer plus a residual 2-hidden-layer MLP of width 128, LeakyReLU, output scaled by 0.01) is optimised from scratch with Adam (lr 1e-2, 200 iterations) to minimise ||Phi_s - Pi_ts h_theta(Phi_t)||_F^2, where Pi_ts is the NN correspondence between DINOv2-ViT-B/14 features of the two images. The final dense map is NN search between Phi_s and h_theta(Phi_t). Neural ZoomOut refinement is not used for the reported numbers. The evaluation is PCK@0.05 (threshold relative to image size) on the TSS dataset (400 pairs from FG3DCar, JODS, PASCAL).
official.claim: On TSS dense correspondence, the method (SD-v1.5 LBO + DINOv2-ViT-B/14 NAM, k = 50) reaches PCK@0.05 of 86.7 weighted average (84.3 unweighted), versus 78.7 (75.4) for nearest-neighbour matching on concatenated SD + DINOv2 features (FUSE) and 78.9 (75.6) for the spectral baseline of Cheng et al., and also above the best zero-shot NN baseline, CleanDIFT, at 85.5 (83.1).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative results (PCK@0.05↑) on the TSS dataset [85]. Methods are grouped into supervised, unsupervised and zero-shot. Our approach substantially outperforms all zero-shot baselines (bold face) and is on par with unsupervised task-specific methods. NN stands for nearest-neighbour matching. We report both the unweighted (Avg.) and weighted (Wtd. Avg.) averages over the three data subsets following [8] and [16], respectively. *: backbone fine-tuned on TSS.
official.metric: PCK@0.05 on TSS (higher is better), threshold 0.05 x image size; per-subset values plus unweighted (Avg.) and pair-count-weighted (Wtd. Avg.) averages. No error bars in Table 1; Table A9 reports 86.7 +/- 0.034 (std over 10 NAM initialisation seeds; the value matches the weighted average) for Ours; no variance is reported for any baseline.
official.comparison: Ours vs. zero-shot NN matching on DINOv1, DINOv2, DINOv3, Stable Diffusion, CleanDIFT, FUSE (SD + DINOv2) and Fuse2Match features, and vs. the functional-map method of Cheng et al. [16]

title: C-GRPO: Conformal Group Relative Policy Optimization

official.background: GRPO trains reasoning LLMs with RL by sampling a fixed group of G completions per prompt and using within-group reward differences as the advantage. A fixed G wastes compute on easy prompts, where all completions are correct and the advantage is zero, and under-explores hard prompts, where no completion succeeds. Adaptive-budget methods exist but use heuristic stopping rules. This paper uses split-conformal calibration to decide, per prompt, when enough rollouts have been drawn, aiming to cut training compute without hurting accuracy.
official.method:
C-GRPO samples rollouts on a budget grid K = {2, 4, 8, 16, 32}. For math, each prompt's extracted answers define an APS (adaptive prediction set) nonconformity score; on a held-out calibration set of 200 prompts, the current policy's scores give a conformal threshold q̂_k for each budget k. During training a prompt first gets k=2 samples; if the APS prediction set at threshold q̂_k is a singleton, sampling stops, otherwise the prompt is expanded to the next grid point, up to 32. The miscoverage level δ is set automatically from the policy's solve rate at k=32 (δ = clip(1 − solve rate + 0.05, 0.05, 0.95)), and thresholds and δ are re-calibrated every 50 steps with the current policy. Zero-variance groups are dropped and advantages are normalised over the whole batch.

Setup for the claim: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA (r=16, α=32, dropout 0.05), AdamW lr 2e-6, batch 4, 300 steps, 2,000 GSM8K training samples, KL β=0.05, binary verifier reward. Static GRPO baselines use the identical pipeline with fixed G ∈ {2, 4, 8, 10, 16, 32, 64, 128}. Metrics: k̄_train = mean rollouts per prompt at step 300; pass@1 = Ave@32 single-sample accuracy at temperature 1 on a held-out GSM8K test split of 200–400 problems.
official.claim: On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (LoRA, 300 steps), C-GRPO uses 10.4 training rollouts per prompt versus 32 for static GRPO (G=32), a 68% reduction, while reaching pass@1 57.2% versus 54.8%, i.e. not lower than G=32 (or any static G up to 128, best 55.3%).

official.metric: Mean training rollouts per prompt k̄_train at step 300 (lower is better) and pass@1 (%) on the held-out GSM8K test split (higher is better). Single run per method, no ±; the authors give a binomial standard error of 2.5–3.5 pp for accuracies near 57%.
official.comparison: C-GRPO (adaptive budget) vs. static GRPO trained at fixed G = 2, 4, 8, 10, 16, 32, 64, 128 under the same pipeline
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup, C-GRPO's mean training rollouts per prompt at step 300 are not well below 32 (e.g. above 16, i.e. under 50% savings), or its pass@1 is more than about 3 pp (one binomial SE) below static GRPO with G=32.

title: Learning Hierarchical Patch Splitting Policies for Faster Vision Transformers

official.background: Vision Transformers split every image into a uniform grid of patches, so sequence length, and the quadratic attention cost, depend only on resolution and not on content. Adaptive patchification methods such as APT give larger patches to visually simple regions to shorten the sequence before the transformer runs, but they decide where to split using pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy. Those heuristics can waste fine tokens on busy but task-irrelevant textures and under-resolve smooth but important regions, which limits how far the token count can be cut without losing accuracy.
official.method:
SPLIT keeps APT's multi-scale patch embedding but replaces the entropy rule with a learned decision network. For each coarse parent patch, a small cross-attention module uses the parent embedding as query and its four child-patch embeddings as keys/values; the pooled summary is concatenated with the parent embedding and passed to a two-layer MLP plus sigmoid to give a split probability. At inference a patch is split if p > 0.5. Classification uses a single splitting stage.

Training starts from an ImageNet-fine-tuned timm ViT checkpoint. A one-epoch warm-start trains the decision network with binary cross-entropy on pseudo-labels (split if any child's cosine dissimilarity to the parent exceeds a threshold tuned by dual ascent to hit the token budget) and also fine-tunes the backbone on these layouts. Then, with the backbone frozen, one epoch of PPO trains the policy: several masks are sampled per image, the cost is (task error + lambda * token fraction)/(1 + lambda), advantages are leave-one-out within the image, and lambda is updated by dual ascent toward the target token fraction rho. For Figure 5a, SPLIT and APT are compared on ViT-L at 336x336 with patch size 14 across several token budgets, reporting ImageNet-1K validation accuracy against the realized % of tokens.
official.claim: On ImageNet-1K with ViT-L at 336x336 (patch 14), SPLIT achieves higher validation accuracy than APT at every token budget tested, and the gap widens as the budget tightens: at about 55% of tokens SPLIT reaches ~87.6% vs. APT ~87.1% (about +0.5 pp), and around 68-70% tokens it is ~88.0% vs. ~87.6%.
official.claim_caption: Figure 5: Comparison of our method against APT. (a) Accuracy vs. % tokens for ViT-L 336/14. (b) Sequence length distribution at same mean % tokens.
official.metric: ImageNet-1K top-1 validation accuracy (%) vs. realized % tokens relative to the dense 577-token sequence; higher accuracy at equal tokens is better. No error bars or seeds reported; values are approximate readings from the plot.
official.comparison: SPLIT (learned cross-attention splitting policy, warm-start + PPO) vs. APT (entropy-based patch splitting) using the same multi-scale patch embedding and ViT-L 336/14 backbone, swept over token budgets.
official.falsification_criterion: At a matched token fraction of about 55-65%, SPLIT's ImageNet validation accuracy is not higher than APT's, or the gap is under roughly 0.2 pp (comparable to run-to-run noise), or the gap does not grow as the token budget shrinks from ~85% to ~55%.

title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction
claim_source: Table 15, page 31 (Appendix F.1); summarised in Section 4.3, page 8

official.background: Models that predict how cells respond to a genetic perturbation (for example a CRISPRi knockdown) are meant to help biologists choose which experiments to run. They are usually judged by aggregate accuracy over held-out perturbations, and simple linear baselines often match them on those benchmarks. To act on a single prediction, a user needs to know whether that particular prediction is reliable before running the experiment. The paper studies STATE-style predictors, where a frozen single-cell foundation-model encoder embeds control cells and a trained state-transition (ST) transformer decoder predicts post-perturbation expression. It proposes a per-prediction confidence score that can be computed without measuring the perturbation.
official.method:
Three frozen encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, Tahoe-x1) are each paired with an ST decoder with the same architecture and training recipe. The decoders are trained under the STATE few-shot protocol on the Replogle–Nadig CRISPRi panel. For each target cell line (HepG2, Jurkat, RPE1, K562), the decoder trains on all perturbations of the other three lines plus the training perturbations of the target line, and it is tested on the remaining 945–1,084 perturbations of the target line. That gives 12 encoder–cell configurations. SE+ST uses the published few-shot checkpoints of Adduri et al.; scGPT+ST and Tahoe+ST were trained by the authors with the same configuration. Each prediction averages 64 predicted cells into a pseudobulk over 2,000 HVGs. Accuracy is the per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC): the Pearson correlation across genes between the predicted change (ŷ_p − predicted control) and the observed change (y_p − observed control mean).

Predicted-NN-distance is min over training perturbations q of cosine_distance(Δ_pred_p, Δ_train_q), where Δ_pred_p = ŷ_p − predicted control and Δ_train_q = y_q − observed control mean, both over the 2,000 HVGs. It is compared with four other scores computed from the prediction and the training responses: (b) the norm of the predicted response, (c) the mean cosine distance to the ten nearest training responses, (d) the Euclidean distance to the nearest training response, and (e) the alignment of the predicted response with the leading axis of the training responses. Each score is evaluated by its Spearman |ρ| with per-perturbation PDC over the held-out perturbations of each configuration. The oracle distance, computed from the observed response instead of the prediction, reaches mean |ρ| 0.88 and serves as a reference.
official.claim: Across the 12 encoder–cell-line configurations, predicted-NN-distance has mean Spearman |ρ| 0.806 with per-perturbation PDC. That is higher than the ten-nearest-neighbour mean distance (0.784), alignment with the leading training axis (0.664) and Euclidean nearest distance (0.555), with paired Wilcoxon p < 0.01 for each. Predicted-NN-distance beats (c) and (e) in all 12 configurations and beats (d) in 11 of 12.
official.claim_caption: Table 15: Spearman |ρ| between each score and PDC on the held-out perturbations. (a) predicted-NN-distance (cosine, nearest training response); (b) norm of the predicted response; (c) mean cosine distance to the ten nearest training responses; (d) Euclidean distance to the nearest training response; (e) alignment of the predicted response with the leading axis of the training responses.
official.metric: Spearman |ρ| between the score and per-perturbation PDC on held-out perturbations (higher is better; the sign of ρ for the distances is negative). Point estimates only, with no error bars per configuration. Significance comes from a paired Wilcoxon test over the 12 configurations.
official.comparison: Predicted-NN-distance (a) vs. the predicted-response norm (b), the mean cosine distance to the 10 nearest training responses (c), the Euclidean nearest-training distance (d) and alignment with the leading training axis (e). All scores are computed from the same predictions and the same training responses.
official.falsification_criterion: With the same models and splits, predicted-NN-distance's mean |ρ| across configurations is not above that of score (c), (d) or (e), or it falls well below about 0.8 (e.g. below 0.7). For a reduced check on the 4 SE+ST configurations, it fails to beat (c), (d) and (e) in each cell line.

title: Practical Estimation of the Bayes Optimal Fairness-Accuracy Tradeoff with Soft Labels

official.background: The Bayes error is the lowest error any classifier can reach on a distribution. For binary classification it can be estimated without features or training, directly from soft labels c = P(Y=1|x) as the mean of min(c, 1-c), and this is used to benchmark models and detect overfitting. When a classifier must also satisfy a group-fairness constraint (demographic parity or equal opportunity), the best achievable error rises, giving a fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier. This paper asks whether that optimal frontier can also be estimated from soft labels and group membership alone, so that fair-classification algorithms can be compared against the theoretical limit.
official.method:
The Bayes-optimal lambda-fair classifier is a group-dependent threshold on the soft label: for DP, predict 1 iff c >= 1/2 + (2a-1)lambda/(2 pi_a); for EOP, iff c >= 1/(2 - (2a-1)lambda/pi_1a). The soft-label dataset {(c_i, a_i)} is split into D_alpha, used to estimate the priors pi_a, pi_1a and hence the thresholds, and D_beta, used to estimate the error R = mean((1-2c_i) I(c_i >= alpha_hat_{a_i})) + pi_hat and the unfairness (difference in estimated positive rates for DP, or soft-label-weighted TPRs for EOP between groups). Algorithm 1 runs a bisection search over lambda in [0, lambda_max] if the unconstrained (lambda = 0) unfairness is positive, or [lambda_min, 0] if it is negative (lambda_max = 1/inf|w|, which the paper states as max_a pi_a for DP and max_a pi_1a for EOP), recording (error, unfairness) points until the target unfairness is reached; lambda = 0 gives the unconstrained Bayes error. No features and no model training are needed.

CIFAR-10H: soft labels are averages of about 50 human annotations per CIFAR-10 test image (setup and code from Ishida et al.); the 10 classes are grouped into two binary partitions, one used as the label and the other as the sensitive attribute. Baselines trained or post-processed on the same data: Fairlearn Exponentiated Gradient (Exp-Grad), FairRet, OxonFair, and (DP only) MIFPO, which is fed the same soft scores. Results are averaged over 5 runs.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10H, the soft-label estimate of the optimal fairness-error tradeoff lies well to the left of every trained fair classifier: at near-zero unfairness the estimated error is about 0.08 (DP) and about 0.035 (EOP), versus about 0.10-0.12 for Exp-Grad and OxonFair under DP and about 0.13-0.17 for FairRet, Exp-Grad and OxonFair under EOP.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Unfairness-error tradeoffs on Cifar-10H and the Adult Dataset, for Demographic Parity (DP) and Equal Opportunity (EOP) constraints. The proposed estimate (green) establishes a lower bound against competing algorithms, except MIFPO (red), which computes a high-variance data-dependent lower bound different from the Bayes optimal. Dotted lines denote the unconstrained Bayes Optimal classifier at λ = 0.
official.metric: Test error rate (x-axis) vs. signed unfairness (DP or EOP difference, y-axis); a lower error at the same unfairness is better and the Bayes-optimal frontier should lower-bound all classifiers. Points are averaged over 5 runs; the main text does not define the error bars, and the paper's checklist says only that 'the experiments are performed with bootstrapping' (it does not say whether the bars are std, SE or a CI). Values below are read off the plot and are approximate.
official.comparison: Soft-label estimated Bayes-optimal tradeoff (Algorithm 1) vs. Fairlearn Exp-Grad, FairRet, OxonFair (and MIFPO for DP) on the same CIFAR-10H binary task
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the estimator and baselines on CIFAR-10H, some trained fair classifier reaches a test error at or below the estimated frontier at matched unfairness (e.g. EOP |unfairness| <= 0.02 with error <= ~0.04), or the estimated error at near-zero unfairness is not clearly below the best baseline (gap under ~0.02 for DP or ~0.05 for EOP).

title: Understanding the Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs

official.background: Chain-of-thought (CoT) training and prompting improve LLM reasoning, but it is not well understood why a model trained on short or partial reasoning traces can solve longer, unseen compositions of steps. The paper frames CoT as compositional out-of-distribution generalization: the model only sees in-distribution single-step transitions (state -> next update) and must chain them at test time. It proves that the target-task risk is bounded by the sum of per-step risks with a depth-independent O(k) factor, and an estimation term growing like sqrt(T/n) in the number of steps T. The experiments test the qualitative prediction that a shared step predictor trained with explicit intermediate states generalizes from short to long chains, while direct input-to-answer training does not.
official.method:
Atom-Task: sequences over a six-symbol alphabet are transformed by chains of five atomic operations (Reverse, Substitute symbol pairs, Duplicate each symbol, Deduplicate consecutive repeats, Rotate first element to the end). In the CoT format each step writes the remaining task chain, the current input, the output and the updated chain (explicit state tracking); the No-CoT format trains the model to emit only the final output. Training sets are matched to about 5,000 atomic transitions: Single-Step (5k one-step samples), Three-Step (1.66k three-step samples), Mixed 3+5 (833 three-step plus 500 five-step chains using at most 2 distinct operations).

Qwen3-4B is fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, all attention and MLP linear layers) for 3 epochs at lr 5e-5 on one RTX 4090, separately in CoT and No-CoT formats, and evaluated by exact-match accuracy on held-out 3-, 5-, 7- and 9-step test sets of 500 samples each (max_new_tokens 2048). Each configuration is run with seeds 42, 2026 and 12345.
official.claim: With Qwen3-4B LoRA-fine-tuned on Atom-Task chains of only 3 steps, CoT-format training reaches 95.73 ± 0.68 / 88.87 ± 1.54 / 79.27 ± 3.03 % exact-match accuracy on unseen 5-, 7- and 9-step chains, whereas No-CoT training on the same chains reaches only 30.20 ± 0.65 / 11.00 ± 0.85 / 5.13 ± 0.09 %; with single-step training only, CoT still gets 91.80 % on 3-step chains vs. 10.93 % for No-CoT.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Accuracy (%) by training data and test steps. All entries are means over 3 seeds (42, 2026, 12345); standard deviations are shown as subscripts.
official.metric: exact-match accuracy (%) on 500 held-out test chains per length, higher is better; mean ± std over 3 seeds (42, 2026, 12345)
official.comparison: CoT-format vs. No-CoT-format fine-tuning of Qwen3-4B on the same training chains (Single-Step, Three-Step, Mixed 3+5), evaluated on longer test chains
official.falsification_criterion: With 3-step training, CoT accuracy on 7- or 9-step test chains is not far above No-CoT accuracy (e.g. the gap is under ~20 points), or CoT accuracy collapses at 9 steps to the No-CoT level.

title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
claim_source: Table 7, page 23 (appendix); also Figure 4b, page 9, and Table 8, page 24

official.background: In stream classification the data distribution can change over time (concept drift). As a result, old training examples can conflict with the current concept and hurt a deployed model. The usual approach pairs incremental trees such as Hoeffding Trees with drift detectors that reset the model. Drift detectors only say when drift happened, not where in feature space, and the reset throws away information that might become relevant again. Recent work suggests that when instances can be stored, simply retraining batch learners on recent data beats incremental stream learners. This raises the question of whether a batch tree can learn which stored instances to keep.
official.method:
A Time Neutralising Tree (TNT) is a batch information-gain decision tree that also receives each instance's arrival index t during training. At each node it compares the best split on time with the best feature split. If BestTimeSplit > BestFeatureSplit + λ (λ = 0.2), it builds a subtree that splits only on time until purity, N_min = 20 or an information-gain floor τ = 0.05 is reached. It then runs a Mann-Whitney U test (α = 0.05) comparing each older time leaf's label distribution with the most recent leaf's. Leaves that do not differ significantly are kept, the rest are discarded ("neutralised"), and the feature split is recomputed on the kept instances. Time is not used at inference. Impure leaves use a logistic-regression model, and 15 split thresholds are considered per feature. Hyperparameters were tuned only on 5 synthetic streams.

Evaluation is test-then-train on 24 real and semi-real USP DS streams, with numeric features standardised. Batch models are retrained from scratch every 50 instances. DT_n is a scikit-learn decision tree (min_samples_leaf = 10) trained on the last n instances. TNT500 uses the same protocol on the last 500 instances, and TNT/DT∞ train on all past instances. The metric is Cohen's kappa over each block of 50 instances (the first 50 are a warm start), averaged over the stream and over 10 seeded replicates. Methods are ranked per stream with a Mann-Whitney U test (Holm-Bonferroni) and summarised as a mean rank and a critical-difference diagram.
official.claim: With the same 500-instance sliding window and the same retraining every 50 instances, TNT500 gets a higher mean prequential Cohen's kappa than a plain decision tree (DT500) on 17 of 24 USP DS streams and a better mean rank (4.79 vs. 5.21). The largest gains are on Yoga (0.55 vs. 0.47), Rialto (0.65 vs. 0.57) and Keystroke (0.88 vs. 0.83), with Insects-Reoccurring (0.60 vs. 0.56) among several streams gaining 0.04.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Cohen's Kappa for each method (column) and data stream (row). Bolded values indicate the statistically best performing method. Underlined values are used to indicate top performing methods when no single method is best. Mean rank per method is reported with a bold value indicating lowest (best) rank. * Dataset not large enough to statistically distinguish performance over entire stream.
official.metric: Cohen's kappa over consecutive 50-instance blocks, averaged over the stream and 10 replicates (higher is better). Table 7 reports no ± values. Significance is given only as per-stream Mann-Whitney U tests (bold/underline, Table 8 ranks) and a CD diagram (Fig. 3).
official.comparison: TNT500 vs. DT500, with the same window, retraining cadence and data. Secondary: TNT (all data) vs. DT∞, with mean ranks 5.21 vs. 7.02. Incremental trees and drift-detector-reset Hoeffding Trees are also listed.
official.falsification_criterion: Using the authors' protocol, TNT500's mean kappa is not higher than DT500's on most streams, or the specific gains on Yoga, Rialto, Insects-Reoccurring and Keystroke disappear (e.g. TNT500 − DT500 ≤ 0.01 on those streams over 10 replicates).

title: Should We Pay This Much for Robustness? Efficient Proxy Certificates with Marginal Guarantees

official.background: Randomized smoothing (RS) gives model-agnostic robustness certificates for any black-box classifier, but each certified input costs thousands of noisy forward passes (e.g. 2000), which is too expensive for large models or high-throughput deployment. Deterministic verifiers are cheap at test time but need white-box access and do not scale to large architectures. This paper asks whether one can drop pointwise soundness and instead guarantee only that, over future inputs (clean or adversarially perturbed), at most a fraction α are approved while their prediction is actually flipped, in exchange for certifying with one forward pass.
official.method:
ProxC replaces the expensive certificate with a thresholded proxy ĥ(z, λ) = I[f(z)_y > λ] evaluated on a single Gaussian-noised copy of the input (σ = 0.5). The threshold λ is calibrated on an unlabeled holdout set D_n with conformal risk control: the backbone RS certificate (2000 MC samples, 50 for the majority-vote label and 1950 for the certificate) is run once on each calibration point; points it certifies contribute zero risk, and λ* is the smallest value for which the one-point-corrected empirical rate of proxy approvals (on one noise draw per point) among non-certified points is ≤ α_r = c↓(α, B⁻¹), the Gaussian-smoothing lower bound of α at radius r (Eq. 6, Prop. 2). Smoothing bounds then transfer the marginal guarantee to all ℓ2 perturbations within radius r.

For Table 13 the backbone is the Cohen et al. (2019) ResNet-110 trained with σ = 0.5 noise on CIFAR-10. The RS certificate is computed once on all 10,000 test images; for each calibration size n, 500 random calibration sets are drawn and the remaining images serve as test points. Reported are the proxy's empirical false-approval risk (approved and not certified by the backbone) and certified ratio (CR, fraction approved), with α = 5%, at r ∈ {0, 0.12, 0.25, 0.5}.
official.claim: On CIFAR-10 (ResNet-110, σ = 0.5, α = 5%) with n = 500 unlabeled calibration points, the single-forward ProxC proxy at r = 0.12 has false-approval risk 2.80 ± 0.76% (target α_r = 2.97%) and certifies 47.0 ± 3.9% of test images, versus 71.1% for 2000-sample randomized smoothing; at r = 0 it gives risk 5.00 ± 0.93% (α_r = 5.00%) and CR 69.4 ± 3.4% vs. 81.3%.
official.claim_caption: Table 13: Effect of the calibration-set size n = |D_n| on CIFAR-10 (ResNet-110, σ = 0.5, α = 5%). Proxy risk and certified ratio (CR) in %, mean ± std over 500 random calibration splits; the test set is all images not used for calibration. Infeasible: 1/(n + 1) > α_r, so the proxy approves nothing.
official.metric: False-approval risk (%, should be ≤ α_r on average) and certified ratio (%, higher is better); ± is std over 500 random calibration splits
official.comparison: ProxC proxy certificate (1 forward per test point for the certification decision) vs. its randomized-smoothing backbone certificate (1950 forwards) on the same test images, across calibration-set sizes n from 25 to 5000
official.falsification_criterion: With n = 500 calibration points, the mean false-approval risk over many calibration splits clearly exceeds α_r (e.g. > 3.3% at r = 0.12 or > 5.5% at r = 0), or the proxy's mean certified ratio at r = 0.12 falls well below the reported range (e.g. < 39%, about two std below 47.0%).

title: FreeOcc: Decoupling Ego-Motion for Efficient 4D Occupancy Forecasting via Continuous Flow Matching

official.background: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts a sequence of future 3D voxel occupancy grids from recent LiDAR sweeps, which gives a motion planner the scene's future geometry without explicit detection or tracking. Recent world models (OccWorld, ViDAR, Copilot4D) learn to separate the ego vehicle's own motion from the motion of other agents using cross-attention or deep recurrence, which costs parameters and latency. FreeOcc's premise is that the ego vehicle's future trajectory is already known from the planner. An explicit SE(2) warp can therefore remove ego-motion, so the learned model only has to handle residual scene dynamics.
official.method:
Each of K = 4 past LiDAR sweeps is encoded into a BEV feature map by a PointPillars encoder with a sinusoidal range encoding and a ResNet-FPN. The sweeps are fused by a two-layer ConvGRU with timestamp embeddings and a delay-aware gate, giving a present-state map H_t. For each of N = 6 future steps (0.5 s apart), H_t is warped into the future ego frame with a bilinear SE(2) affine warp built from the known future ego pose (odometry in training, planner at deployment). A ConvGRU then adds a residual on top of the warped map, giving the BEV prior C_tau.

Each prior C_tau is decoded two ways. A discriminative 3D decoder predicts occupancy logits and a per-voxel log-variance. A 3D U-Net velocity field is trained with conditional flow matching on the binary occupancy grid, with loss weights that up-weight occupied voxels and voxels where the decoder is uncertain. At inference the flow model is integrated with a 10-step midpoint ODE. FreeOcc-E blends the two outputs per voxel with weight sigmoid(-log-variance) on the decoder. Training uses a composite loss (focal BCE, Lovasz, Dice, sparsity, temporal consistency, ray-traced free-space, mass conservation, velocity TV smoothness, range weighting, heteroscedastic uncertainty) on nuScenes with a 200x200x16 grid at 0.4 m over [-40, 40] m. The metric is class-agnostic voxel IoU against future LiDAR-derived occupancy, averaged over the 6 horizons.
official.claim: On nuScenes 4D occupancy forecasting (200x200x16 grid, 0.4 m, 6 horizons over 3 s), FreeOcc-E reaches 32.1% average class-agnostic mIoU against 28.9% for OccWorld retrained from scratch under the same protocol. FreeOcc-E is higher at every horizon (43.6 vs 39.7 at tau=1, 24.9 vs 21.6 at tau=6) and also higher on F1 (49.6 vs 44.8).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: 4D Occupancy Forecasting on nuScenes. Evaluated via Class-Agnostic 3D Voxel mIoU (%) ↑. * Indicates the models whose output point clouds we voxelize for evaluation.
official.metric: Class-agnostic 3D voxel IoU (%) per horizon and averaged, plus precision, recall and F1; higher is better. Single run; the paper reports no standard deviations, seeds or confidence intervals.
official.comparison: FreeOcc-E (uncertainty-blended decoder + flow-matching ODE) vs. OccWorld trained from scratch with its released code on the same data and metric; also vs. FreeOcc-D (decoder only, 28.4) and FreeOcc-G (ODE only, 30.3). 4D-Occ and ViDAR are evaluated by voxelizing their point-cloud outputs.
official.falsification_criterion: A faithful reimplementation of FreeOcc-E, trained and evaluated on nuScenes under this protocol, does not beat a retrained OccWorld on average mIoU by a clear margin (e.g. the gap is under about 1.5 points or reverses), or the gap disappears across a few seeds.

title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs

official.background: Multimodal LLMs are expensive to run on edge devices, and quantizing both weights and activations to low bit-widths (W4A8, W4A4) cuts memory and compute. Post-training quantization works at W8A8 but loses a lot of accuracy at 4-bit, especially for the small 2B-4B models suited to edge deployment. Quantization-aware training (QAT) can recover accuracy, but MLLMs face two extra problems: open multimodal fine-tuning data does not match the model's own output distribution, and quantization damages multimodal understanding and language modeling at the same time.
official.method:
ProQuant is a weight-activation QAT recipe for MLLMs (vision encoder frozen; LLM backbone weights and quantization scales trained with STE). Self-relabeling (SRL): the prompts of LLaVA-680K are kept but the responses are regenerated by the full-precision target model itself (vLLM sampling, top_p 0.8, top_k 20, temperature 0.7, max 512 tokens). Progressive block activation (PBA): for each decoder layer a vision-sensitivity factor tau (mean output-gradient magnitude on vision tokens divided by that over all tokens) is computed; quantization is first enabled for the 50% of layers with the highest tau, then 75%, 88% and 100% at 30%, 40% and 50% of training (logarithmic schedule), with the other layers running in full precision until activated.

The loss is alpha * forward KL + (1 - alpha) * reverse KL to the BF16 teacher plus beta * cross-entropy on the SRL labels. Training is 5 epochs on one 8xH200 node (per-device batch 32, grad accumulation 2, AdamW, constant LR). The LLM-QAT baseline is adapted to multimodal inputs and trained with the same data, budget and optimization settings. Evaluation uses LMMs-Eval on AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, MMMU, ScienceQA, SeedBench and TextVQA (Avg. is the mean of these seven) plus MME.
official.claim: On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct at W4A8, ProQuant reaches a 7-benchmark average accuracy of 72.54 (BF16: 73.63), vs. 65.94 for LLM-QAT trained with the same data, budget and optimizer, a gain of 6.6 points.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Weight-activation quantization results for Qwen VL series. The headers represent model architectures, bitwidth, quantization methods, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, MMMU, ScienceQA, SeedBench, TextVQA, average accuracy, and MME scores, respectively. The superscript † indicates down_proj activations are quantized to 8-bit under W4A4 settings.
official.metric: Average accuracy (%) over AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, MMMU, ScienceQA, SeedBench, TextVQA (higher is better); single run, no seeds or error bars reported
official.comparison: ProQuant vs. LLM-QAT (matched data, budget, optimization) and PTQ baselines SmoothQuant and MBQ, all at W4A8 on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct; BF16 as the reference
official.falsification_criterion: A matched re-run in which ProQuant's W4A8 average on Qwen3-VL-2B is not clearly above LLM-QAT's (gap well under the reported 6.6 points), or in which ProQuant falls more than about 1 point short of BF16 (73.63) where the paper reports a 1.09-point drop.

title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline For Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Table 4(a), page 8; full τ sweep for Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-8B in Tables 9 and 10 (Appendix F.6.2), pages 31–32

official.background: In RL post-training of LLMs (e.g. GRPO), rollout generation is often the bottleneck. Asynchronous pipelines let several generation instances produce samples that a separate trainer consumes through a queue. Within each decoding minibatch, prompts whose responses differ in length leave slots idle (padding and long-tail 'skewness' bubbles). Sorting prompts by predicted output length reduces this waste, but then short minibatches are dispatched first and long ones last. Samples reach the trainer fast at first and slowly later, so the queue fills and then drains ('sorting bubbles'). The paper proposes an offline scheduler meant to keep the local gain from sorting while keeping the dispatched load steady over time.
official.method:
ASP is a one-time offline pass over the prompt set. (1) A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-1.5B predicts each prompt's output length, and prompts are sorted by the prediction. (2) Dynamic programming splits the sorted list into minibatches of size b to b+κ (b = 32, κ = 2), maximizing the sum of per-minibatch utilization R_i = sum(predicted lengths) / (size × max predicted length). (3) Simulated annealing permutes the minibatches so that consecutive batch groups of k = 6 minibatches have nearly equal total predicted load (minimizing the variance of group loads; random pair swaps, temperature C/log(n+2), C = 1, 2×10^6 iterations).

For the ablation, the authors take 39,000 measured Qwen3-32B responses on DeepScaleR (8192-token cap) and keep the true lengths fixed. They build noisy predictions as l_i·exp(ν·ε_i) with ν calibrated so that Kendall τ = 0.64, then compare five schedules: C0 fixed-size minibatches of 32 in original order; C1 sorted by prediction, fixed size 32; C2 sorted plus DP boundaries (32–34); C3 the C2 minibatches randomly shuffled; C4 the C2 minibatches reordered by simulated annealing. All metrics are computed on true lengths: mean within-minibatch length std, mean padding rate (1 − mean/max length), and the coefficient of variation and max/min ratio of total response tokens per consecutive batch group.
official.claim: On 39,000 measured Qwen3-32B response lengths with predictions at Kendall τ = 0.64, ASP's balanced ordering (C4) reduces batch-group load CV to 0.070, from 0.401 for length-sorted DP minibatches (C2) and 0.162 for randomly shuffled minibatches (C3), and below the unsorted baseline (0.103), while keeping C2's mean padding rate of 0.224 (vs. 0.322 unsorted).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Ablation of scheduling steps. Panel (a) measures schedule properties using fixed response lengths; panel (b) executes real generation with simulated training-step durations and weight-refresh delays. Trend is the Spearman correlation between iteration index and iteration time; values near zero indicate little monotonic drift.
official.metric: Batch-group load CV (std/mean of total true response tokens per group of k = 6 consecutive minibatches), lower is better; mean padding rate, lower is better. Values are means over three seeds of the prediction noise; no std or error bars are reported.
official.comparison: C4 (DP minibatches + simulated-annealing balanced ordering) vs. C2 (same minibatches in sorted order), C3 (same minibatches randomly shuffled) and C0 (fixed-size minibatches in original order), on the same lengths and prediction vectors
official.falsification_criterion: With measured response lengths from a reasoning model on DeepScaleR and predictions at τ ≈ 0.64, C4's batch-group load CV is not clearly below both C3's and C0's (e.g. C4 ≥ 0.8 × C3), or C4's padding rate is not close to C2's and well below C0's.

title: SIMBAD: Spatio-Temporal Traffic Forecasting Robust to Aperiodicity
claim_source: Table 7 (Appendix D), page 20; same means as Table 2, page 7

official.background: Traffic flow forecasting on road-sensor graphs is usually handled with spatio-temporal graph neural networks. Many of these models also feed in periodic history (the same time slot one day or one week earlier) to exploit weekly and daily regularity. When traffic deviates from its usual pattern, for example because of an accident or an event, that history becomes misleading and periodicity-aware models degrade. This paper asks whether a cheap similarity signal, the L1 distance between the current window and its past-period counterparts, can be used to decide how much each sensor should trust its periodic history and its neighbours.
official.method:
SIMBAD takes a recent input (the last 12 five-minute steps) and periodic inputs (the 12-step windows 2 weeks, 1 week and 1 day before the target). For each sensor and period it computes the L1 distance between the recent window and the matching past window, passes it through a small predictor with an aleatoric-uncertainty head (trained with a Kendall-and-Gal-style loss against the actual L1 distance between target and past window), and turns the uncertainty-scaled distances into softmax weights (temperature 0.2) for aggregating the periodic inputs. A mask with a learnable threshold, sigmoid(λ − d) times confidence, zeros out periodic input for sensors whose history looks dissimilar; those sensors get extra weight on their recent input. Spatially, a self-adaptive adjacency matrix is built from node embeddings initialised from the similarity and uncertainty values, and the predefined road adjacency is reweighted by sigmoid(λ − L1 distance between neighbours' recent windows). The backbone stacks temporal self-attention, gated temporal convolution, spatial self-attention and K-hop graph convolution: 2 layers on the masked historical input using the self-adaptive adjacency, then 2 on the recent input using the reweighted road adjacency. Hidden size is 64, with 4 attention heads.

Training uses Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 64, L1 loss plus 0.1 times the uncertainty loss, up to 100 epochs with early stopping (patience 30), and a 6:2:2 chronological train/val/test split. The task predicts the next 12 steps, and the metric is MAE averaged over all 12 horizons on the test set. Baselines (GWNet, DCRNN, AGCRN, STSGCN, STAEformer, DSTAGNN, STWave, STIDGCN, DTRformer, LHMformer, ASTGCN, plus NLinear/DLinear in the appendix) were run by the authors with default or tuned hyperparameters. Appendix C says the conventional baselines take only the recent 12-step input; ASTGCN is the exception, since by design it also uses weekly and daily segments.
official.claim: On PEMS08 (12-step-ahead traffic flow, 6:2:2 split), SIMBAD reaches test MAE 12.58 ± 0.02, below every baseline the authors ran; the best is DTRformer at 13.50 ± 0.04, followed by LHMformer at 13.66 ± 0.07 and STIDGCN at 13.71 ± 0.10. On PEMS07, SIMBAD reaches 17.86 ± 0.02 vs. 19.20 ± 0.06 for STIDGCN.
official.claim_caption: Table 7: Standard deviation results on PEMS datasets.
official.metric: MAE averaged over the 12 prediction horizons on the test set, lower is better; ± is the standard deviation over repeated runs (the paper does not say how many runs or what varies between them)
official.comparison: SIMBAD vs. 13 baselines run by the authors (GWNet, DCRNN, AGCRN, STSGCN, STAEformer, DSTAGNN, STWave, STIDGCN, DTRformer, LHMformer, ASTGCN, NLinear, DLinear) on the same PEMS08 and PEMS07 splits
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining SIMBAD and the strongest baselines (DTRformer, LHMformer, STIDGCN) on PEMS08 with the stated setup over several seeds, SIMBAD's mean test MAE is not lower than the best baseline's by more than about 0.3 (a third of the reported 0.92 gap), or some baseline matches or beats it.

title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
claim_source: Table 9 (Appendix C), page 18; the uniform-sampling comparison also appears in Table 2, page 7

official.background: Multimodal LLMs answering questions about long (up to hour-scale) videos can only take a limited number of visual tokens, so they must trade temporal coverage (many low-resolution frames across the whole video) against spatial detail (few high-resolution frames). Uniform frame sampling keeps coverage but can miss or blur the decisive moment, while retrieval-based frame selection concentrates on a few clips but can lose context and fails when retrieval is noisy. The paper frames long-video QA as deciding how to split a fixed visual-token budget between global coverage and local high-resolution evidence, and where to spend the local share.
official.method:
AdaAlloc is training-free and uses Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct for every MLLM call. (1) Planning: from a sparse low-resolution overview of the video plus the question and options, the MLLM picks one of five global/local budget splits (global-only 1.0/0.0, global-heavy 0.7/0.3, balanced 0.5/0.5, local-heavy 0.3/0.7, local-only 0.0/1.0), writes evidence-seeking grounding queries, and proposes temporal seeds (explicit timestamps or windows). (2) Memory refinement: each query (plus the original question) is run through the UniversalVTG temporal grounding model (~60M params, top-5 proposals per query); its candidates plus the seeds form a temporal memory, which the MLLM edits by keeping, discarding, adjusting and merging intervals. (3) Answering: the final input concatenates sparse low-resolution frames over the whole video (global share of budget B) with denser, higher-resolution frames from the refined intervals (local share); frame resolution is set so the total stays within B. Videos where uniform sampling is already dense enough under B bypass planning and are answered from uniform frames.

The claim uses the 16K visual-token budget (equivalent to 64 uniform frames). Uniform sampling samples at 1 FPS then subsamples uniformly to the frame limit. Retrieval-only grounds the original question with UniversalVTG and answers only from frames sampled from the retrieved segments, with no planning or refinement. All methods use the same answerer, the same final-answer budget, and greedy decoding; evaluation is multiple-choice accuracy without subtitles.
official.claim: On LVBench (1,549 questions, avg. 67-minute videos) with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at a matched 16K visual-token budget, AdaAlloc reaches 51.7% accuracy vs. 42.7% for uniform sampling (+9.0) and 46.5% for retrieval-only (+5.2).
official.claim_caption: Table 9: Component ablation under the 16K visual-token budget. All variants use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with the same final-answering visual-token budget and answerer. Planning & refinement denotes overview-conditioned planning with temporal-memory refinement; variants that use it share the same overview planner, grounding model, and refinement procedure.
official.metric: Multiple-choice accuracy (%), higher is better; single run with greedy decoding, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: AdaAlloc vs. uniform sampling and vs. retrieval-only (UniversalVTG on the original question), same backbone, answerer and 16K final-answering token budget
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same backbone and 16K budget on LVBench, AdaAlloc's accuracy is less than ~3 points above retrieval-only, or less than ~5 points above uniform sampling.

title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing

official.background: Activation checkpointing (AC) saves training memory by discarding intermediate activations in the forward pass and recomputing them during backpropagation, at the cost of up to a third more compute. Because recomputing Transformer linear layers is expensive, practitioners usually use selective AC, which keeps linear-layer outputs in memory and so gives up much of the memory saving. This paper asks whether the recomputation itself can be approximated cheaply without letting errors build up through the backward pass.
official.method:
KEAP writes an FFN layer as a sum over its n hidden units (and attention as a sum over heads) and, during the AC recomputation, recomputes only k of the n components. Checkpoints are stored exactly from the full first forward pass, so approximation errors are reset at each checkpoint. Component importance is the l2 norm of each component's output, recorded during the exact forward pass. Three selection rules are compared: Rand-k/n (uniform random k components, rescaled by n/k, unbiased), Opt-k/n (independent Bernoulli sampling with probabilities proportional to the component norms, clipped below at eps = 0.06, rescaled, unbiased), and Top-k/n (deterministically keep the k largest-norm components, no rescaling, biased).

The main experiment trains a Llama-3-style 488M model (hidden 1280, 20 layers, 20 heads, Llama-2 32k tokenizer) from scratch on FineWeb for 9307 steps of 1M tokens (9.76B tokens, Chinchilla-optimal) with Muon, a cosine schedule, and the dense baseline's tuned learning rate. KEAP is applied to FFN layers, attention layers, or both, with selection either per token (token-level) or one mask per batch (batch-level), for k/n in {2/3, 1/3}. The metric is perplexity on a disjoint 25M-token FineWeb held-out set. Baselines are the exact-gradient model (Llama-488M with standard AC) and a smaller FLOP-matched model.
official.claim: With token-level KEAP applied to the FFN layers of a Llama-488M model at k/n = 1/3, Top-k selection reaches held-out perplexity 12.46, compared with 13.66 for Opt-k (norm-proportional sampling) and 14.70 for Rand-k, against 12.03 for exact-gradient training (+3.6% vs. +13.6% and +22.2%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: KEAP performance. We report the perplexity of a Llama-488M model under different AC strategies, using per-token (a) and per-batch (b) granularity during re-computation as described in Sec. 3.3. Δ PPL is the relative perplexity degradation compared to the vanilla baseline. AC-FLOPs denotes the analytic FLOP cost of the targeted FFN and attention-projection computations relative to standard backpropagation for the same modules. (details can be found in App. B).
official.metric: Perplexity on a 25M-token held-out FineWeb set (lower is better); ΔPPL is relative to the exact-gradient Llama-488M. Single training run per cell, so no ± is reported.
official.comparison: KEAP Top-1/3 vs. Opt-1/3 vs. Rand-1/3 (token-level, FFN layers), with the same model, data, token budget and learning rate; exact-gradient Llama-488M as reference.
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same setup (or the same comparison at the 134M ablation scale), Top-1/3 does not give clearly lower perplexity than both Opt-1/3 and Rand-1/3 (e.g. its perplexity is within about 1% of Opt-1/3 or higher), or Top-1/3 degrades perplexity by more than about 7% relative to exact training.
