title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
claim_source: Figure 2, page 8 (outcome distributions in Figure 7, page 50; reach rate in Figure 6, page 50)

official.background: In cooperative fleet problems (delivery vehicles, warehouse robots, drones), many identical agents with independent noisy dynamics must jointly cover a set of targets, so the operator has to decide both which agent goes to which target and how each agent gets there. Classical pipelines assign agents using nominal shortest-path costs, which ignore stochastic delays, while standard multi-agent RL (MAPPO, QMIX, etc.) learns over the joint state-action space, which grows exponentially with the number of agents and does not transfer to other fleet sizes. The paper asks whether the problem can be split into a learned single-agent routing problem plus an assignment step without losing much optimality.
official.method:
The paper writes the cooperative problem over probability measures with a terminal optimal-transport cost between the final agent distribution and the target distribution, and proves that the population cost-to-go is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transport cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go j_t(s, z) (exact when dynamics are deterministic). SALT turns this into an algorithm: a single shared target-conditioned policy π(a | s, z) and cost-to-go estimate ĵ(s, z) are learned with any single-agent RL algorithm (Q-learning, DDQN, PPO, A2C), pooling all agents' trajectories. During training, agents are assigned to targets at t = 0 by solving a Hungarian assignment with cost ĵ_0 (or randomly with probability α_k, decayed 0.5 → 0.05), and the assignment is kept fixed for the episode. At evaluation, the assignment is recomputed by the Hungarian algorithm at every time step.

Grid-world setup (Section 5.1, Appendix F.1): N = 7 agents, 11 × 30 grid, horizon T = 100, actions {up, down, left, right, stay}; agents start uniformly in the first column and targets are sampled uniformly from the last ten columns. With probability p ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.25} the chosen action is replaced uniformly by one of the other four, with noise drawn independently per agent (individual), shared per state-action pair (local), or shared by all agents (global). Stage cost 1 per step while active; an agent becomes inactive once it reaches its assigned target (SALT) or any unoccupied target (MARL baselines). All methods train for 320,000 episodes (2.24 × 10^8 interactions); all neural methods use two-hidden-layer 64-unit tanh MLPs (SALT-Q has no network; Table 3 lists no hidden size and a 0.25 → 0.02 learning rate), with 5 training seeds, and are evaluated on the same 50 evaluation instances per seed. Baselines are MAPPO, IPPO, HAPPO, QMIX, VDN and mean-field Q-learning (MFQ), which observe relative offsets to all targets and target-availability flags.
official.claim: In the 7-agent stochastic grid world, all four SALT variants have lower average travel time than every MARL baseline in all 9 noise settings; e.g. with individual noise at p = 0.1, SALT-PPO averages 30.2 steps vs. 47.8 for the best baseline (IPPO), and at p = 0.25, 38.3 vs. 55.8 (IPPO).
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Average travel time to targets as a function of noise probability p under individual, local, and global noise. Cells show the pooled arithmetic mean over 50 evaluation rollouts from each of 5 independently trained policies. Figure 7 shows the corresponding distributions. Brighter cells indicate worse relative performance. SALT variants consistently outperform standard MARL baselines.
official.metric: Average travel time to targets in environment steps, lower is better; each cell is the arithmetic mean of 250 outcomes (50 evaluation rollouts × 5 training seeds). No ± is reported for travel time; Figure 7 shows boxplots (IQR, min-max) of the pooled outcomes.
official.comparison: SALT-Q / SALT-DDQN / SALT-PPO / SALT-A2C vs. MAPPO, IPPO, HAPPO, QMIX, VDN, MFQ, same environment, episode budget, training seeds and evaluation instances
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the grid world (N = 7, 11 × 30, T = 100, 320k episodes, 5 seeds), the best SALT variant's mean travel time is not clearly below the best MARL baseline's (e.g. gap under ~5 steps, or overlapping IQRs) at p = 0.1 or p = 0.25 under individual noise.

title: Decoupled Mode Connectivity for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Vision-Language Models
claim_source: Table 4, page 16 (Appendix A); the same seed means are in Table 1, page 8

official.background: Prompt learning adapts CLIP to a downstream task by learning a few context vectors on few-shot data from 'base' classes. Training on base classes tends to weaken CLIP's zero-shot ability on unseen 'novel' classes. Methods therefore add regularizers to a single prompt, such as a cosine pull toward CLIP's hand-crafted text features or MergeTune's linear-mode-connectivity path. The paper argues that putting both the cross-entropy and the regularizer on one prompt forces a compromise. It claims the base-to-novel harmonic mean (HM) improves when each objective gets its own prompt.
official.method:
Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC) replaces MergeTune's continued-training stage. It starts from a CoOp (or KgCoOp/MMA) prompt fine-tuned on 16-shot base-class data and trains two prompts, both initialized from that checkpoint. The specialization prompt gets cross-entropy plus a 'Visual Anchor' KL term, which matches CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution for each image (temperature 2). The generalization prompt gets only the cosine regularizer toward CLIP's zero-shot text features. A corridor loss applies cross-entropy to a re-normalized interpolation of the two prompts' text features, with alpha sampled from U[0,1] at each step. Loss weights are lambda_gen = 8, lambda_VA = 0.5 and beta = 4. Learning rate and epochs follow MergeTune's defaults, and the main table uses batch size 32.

At test time, the two text-feature matrices are merged once with alpha = 0.20, which was selected on Flowers102 and Caltech101. Evaluation follows the standard CLIP ViT-B/16 base-to-novel protocol: classes are split in half, there are 16 shots per base class, and the metric is the HM of base and novel test accuracy. MergeTune is run from the same checkpoint and evaluated at its final prompt, while DMC is evaluated at its best base-validation checkpoint. Both use 3 seeds.
official.claim: On StanfordCars base-to-novel generalization with a CoOp-initialized CLIP ViT-B/16, DMC reaches HM 75.21 ± 0.10 versus 73.38 ± 0.37 for MergeTune from the same checkpoint (+1.83 HM, 3 seeds).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Seed variability for every row we trained ourselves: HM mean ± sample standard deviation over 3 seeds (DMC at α = 0.20; MERGETUNE at its final prompt). Per-cell companion to Table 1, which reports the same runs as means. Cells with σHM > 1 are bold and flagged as seed-fragile.
official.metric: Harmonic mean of base and novel top-1 accuracy (%), higher is better; ± is sample standard deviation over 3 seeds
official.comparison: CoOp + DMC (alpha = 0.20) vs. CoOp + MergeTune, both continued from the same fine-tuned CoOp checkpoint

title: Intent-Aware Caching for Efficient LLM Serving
claim_source: Figure 6a (ShareChat panel), page 8; numbers stated in Section 5.1

official.background: LLM serving systems use prefix caching: they keep the key-value (KV) states of previous conversation prefixes in GPU memory and reuse them when a later request starts with the same tokens, which skips redundant prefill and lowers time-to-first-token. In multi-turn chat, a cached prefix is only useful if the user sends another turn, and the delay before that turn varies widely, so the eviction policy decides how much reuse is actually achieved under limited GPU memory. Standard policies (LRU, LFU, GDSF) use only recency, frequency and size, and the learned policy LPC predicts only whether a conversation will continue; both leave a large gap to offline oracle policies that know future arrivals.
official.method:
IAC assigns each request a workload state (i, t): an intent i from 30 categories, predicted by a 3-layer MLP head on frozen multilingual-e5-large-instruct embeddings of the last up-to-four user queries, and the turn index t. From a log of recent conversations (in the main evaluation, the 40K conversations preceding the test trace) it estimates for each state the continuation probability P(t+1 | i, t) = C(i, t+1)/C(i, t) and a log-normal fit to the inter-turn delay, whose median M_{i,t} = exp(mu_{i,t}) is used as the reuse window. Unseen states get P = 0.5 and M = 150 s.

Eviction mimics the size-aware oracle TB+S. Each RadixTree leaf v in SGLang gets the priority tuple (1[age_v < M_{i_v,t_v}], P(t_v+1 | i_v, t_v), size_v), compared lexicographically, and the lowest-priority leaf is evicted. Baselines LRU, LFU, GDSF and LPC (trained on the same 40K-conversation split) and the TB+S oracle are run on the same replay of the next 10K ShareChat conversations, with original intra-conversation inter-turn delays, Poisson arrivals of new conversations, and a fixed KV-cache capacity in tokens. Cache hit rate is the number of input tokens served from cache divided by all input tokens.
official.claim: On the ShareChat replay trace at a 140K-token cache capacity, IAC achieves a 34.6% cache hit rate vs. 18.8% for LPC and 12.2% for LRU, and IAC is above every online baseline at all four capacities (80K-170K tokens).
official.claim_caption: Figure 6: Cache hit rate of IAC vs. the baselines. (a) On WildChat and ShareChat, two real workloads with original timestamps, IAC achieves the highest cache hit rate among online policies at every cache capacity. (b) On ShareGPT with synthetic Poisson arrival rates λ (new conversations per sec.), IAC consistently outperforms the online baselines even as higher λ increases cache contention.
official.metric: Token-weighted cache hit rate (cached input tokens / total input tokens), higher is better; single replay per setting, no error bars or seeds reported. Values other than 140K are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: IAC vs. LRU, LFU, GDSF and LPC (strongest online baseline) on the same ShareChat replay trace and cache capacity; TB+S oracle as upper bound
official.falsification_criterion: Replaying the ShareChat test trace (conversations 40K-50K by timestamp) at 140K-token capacity, IAC's hit rate is not clearly above LPC's (e.g. the gap shrinks below ~5 percentage points), or IAC falls below LPC at any of the 80K-170K capacities.

title: FlowMoP: Stochastic Multi-Person Motion Prediction

official.background: Multi-person 3D motion prediction forecasts the future body poses and global positions of several interacting people from a short observed history. Human motion is multi-modal (a person can turn, stop or keep walking), but most multi-person predictors are deterministic and output a fixed set of candidates per person. Benchmarks such as CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW score methods by the best of 6 predictions per agent, so a generative model that samples a full predictive distribution can be compared directly against these deterministic predictors.
official.method:
FlowMoP is a conditional flow-matching model for each focal agent. It splits motion into a global hip trajectory and root-relative joint offsets, in an agent-centric frame translated (not rotated) to the last observed hip position. The future is represented by clamped cubic B-spline control points (Ct = 8 for trajectory, Cp = 24 for pose on CMU-Mocap, for a 50-frame horizon); noise is sampled in control-point space, and a linear interpolant is trained to predict the velocity. A dual-stream transformer (L = 8 blocks, D = 256, adaLN timestep conditioning) runs self-attention over the fixed past tokens, while future tokens attend to the concatenation of past and future tokens. The loss is a frame-space velocity MSE (control-point velocities projected through the spline basis B, with exponentially increasing weights on later frames) for trajectory and pose, plus a final-frame joint-position loss on the one-step clean estimate, with weights 1, 5 and 0.5. Training uses AdamW at lr 1e-4 with a cosine schedule, logit-normal t sampling, context drop and data augmentation.

At inference, K = 100 noise draws are each integrated with 10 Euler steps, and the proposals are reduced to K' = 6 with weighted k-means on last-frame joint positions (cluster medoids are returned). Evaluation follows the T2P protocol: CMU-Mocap (UMPM) uses 3 agents, 15 joints, 1.0s observed and 2.0s predicted. Metrics are best-of-6 JPE (absolute joint error), APE (root-relative pose error) and FDE (final root error), all in mm.
official.claim: On CMU-Mocap (UMPM) at the 2.0s horizon, FlowMoP's best-of-6 errors are lower than those of EMPMP (re-run by the authors under the same protocol): JPE 237.4 vs 250.4 mm, APE 128.6 vs 146.5 mm, and FDE 159.3 vs 171.6 mm.
official.claim_caption: Comparison of best-of-6 JPE, APE, and FDE metrics (in mm) at different time horizons on CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW datasets. Lower values are better (↓), with the best results shown in bold. An asterisk (∗) denotes models we recomputed for this setup.
official.metric: Best-of-6 JPE, APE and FDE in mm at 1.0s and 2.0s (lower is better). Single numbers; no seeds, std or confidence intervals are reported.
official.comparison: FlowMoP (K = 100 proposals reduced to 6) vs. EMPMP* (recomputed by the authors) and DuMMF* (recomputed stochastic baseline); T2P, MRT, TBIFormer and JRT are also listed
official.falsification_criterion: A retrained FlowMoP does not beat a retrained EMPMP on CMU-Mocap 2.0s JPE and APE under the best-of-6 protocol, or the gap shrinks to within the run-to-run spread across several training seeds.

title: MAGE: Towards Generalizable Multi-timescale EEG Representations

official.background: EEG foundation models (LaBraM, BIOT, EEGPT, CBraMod, CSBrain) are pretrained self-supervised on large unlabeled EEG corpora and then adapted to tasks such as motor imagery, emotion recognition, sleep staging and abnormality detection. Nearly all of them cut the signal into fixed-length patches. A short patch resolves fast transients but not slow oscillations, and a long patch does the reverse, while different tasks depend on different frequency bands (mu/beta rhythms for motor imagery, delta waves for sleep). The paper asks whether a foundation model that tokenizes at several timescales and learns how to weight them per input generalizes better across tasks.
official.method:
MAGE tokenizes each EEG sample (19 channels, 200 Hz) into non-overlapping patches of 50, 100 and 200 samples (250 ms, 500 ms, 1 s); each patch is embedded with a temporal 1D-conv branch plus an FFT-magnitude linear branch. A 6-layer encoder (hidden dim 64, 4 heads, ~0.6M parameters) applies, at each timescale, temporal attention within each channel (with RoPE) followed by spatial attention across channels and an FFN. A small Aggregator (1D-conv temporal branch plus FFT magnitude/phase conv branches, then an MLP and softmax) outputs one weight per timescale; Gaussian noise (std 0.3) is added to its logits during training to avoid collapse onto one scale. Pretraining follows EEGPT: a student-teacher (EMA) alignment loss on 70%-masked tokens plus a reconstruction loss whose output is the aggregator-weighted sum of per-scale linear decoders (lambda_rec = 5, lambda_align = 1), on a 500-hour subset of TUEG (TUAB excluded), 50 epochs, AdamW lr 1e-4, batch 64, about 8 hours on one A100 40GB.

Downstream, the pretrained encoder is frozen; a conv layer maps the dataset's channels to 19, and the tokenization module, aggregator and one classification head per timescale are trained, with the prediction being the aggregator-weighted sum of per-scale heads (noise off at test time). Baselines use their published pretrained checkpoints with frozen encoders, training patch embedding (and channel conv where needed) plus a classifier head; Medformer is a supervised multi-scale model. For PhysioNet-MI (109 subjects, 4-class motor imagery, 64 channels, 4 s trials, high-pass 0.3 Hz, resampled to 200 Hz, per-channel z-score), the official evaluation set is the test set and the train set is split into 5 folds with a different validation set each time; results are mean ± std over the 5 runs.
official.claim: On PhysioNet-MI 4-class motor imagery with frozen pretrained encoders (Medformer, the supervised baseline, excepted), MAGE (0.6M parameters) reaches 62.31 ± 0.63 balanced accuracy and 49.78 ± 0.83 Cohen's kappa, versus 59.96 ± 0.86 and 46.66 ± 1.16 for the best baseline CSBrain (8.9M) and at most 57.64 for all other models.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of MAGE with existing foundation models across various downstream tasks, metrics, and test subjects. Numbers under model names indicate parameter sizes in millions (M). MAGE achieves a highest average ranking among all models. Bold indicates the best result, and underlined indicates the second best. The average rank is calculated across all metrics.
official.metric: Balanced accuracy and Cohen's kappa in % (higher is better); weighted F1 also reported. ± is std over 5 runs with different train/validation partitions of the PhysioNet-MI training subjects (fixed test set), not over pretraining seeds.
official.comparison: MAGE vs. Medformer, LaBraM, BIOT, EEGPT, CBraMod and CSBrain, all re-run by the authors under the same frozen-encoder protocol and subject splits
official.falsification_criterion: Pretraining MAGE as described and running the PhysioNet-MI 5-fold protocol, MAGE's balanced accuracy does not exceed CSBrain's (run with its published checkpoint under the same protocol) by more than about one fold std (~1 point), or MAGE falls below ~60% balanced accuracy.

title: Preconditioned Implicit Midpoint Langevin Sampling for Non-Smooth Bayesian Imaging
claim_source: Table 4, page 10 (geometric-phantom details in Table 3, page 9)

official.background: Bayesian imaging problems such as deblurring have posteriors exp(-f(x) - g(x)) with a badly conditioned smooth data term f (condition numbers around 1e5 or more at 256x256) and a non-smooth prior g such as total variation. Unadjusted Langevin samplers mix in a number of steps that grows with the condition number. Preconditioning with M close to the Hessian of f should fix this, but the explicit Euler discretisation used by preconditioned ULA/MYULA inflates the stationary variance of a mode by 1/(1 - delta*l/2) exactly at the large preconditioned steps that make it fast. The paper proposes an implicit-midpoint discretisation, which is exact on Gaussians at any step size, combined with preconditioning and an M-norm Moreau envelope for the non-smooth prior.
official.method:
P-IMLA_lambda updates X_{n+1} = -X_n + 2 prox^M_{(delta/2) U_lambda}(X_n + sqrt(2 delta)/2 M^{-1/2} xi_n), where U_lambda = f + g^{lambda,M} uses the Moreau envelope of g taken in the M-norm. For deconvolution with a Gaussian blur and periodic boundaries, f and M = H are Fourier-diagonal. The proximal step is solved by Picard iteration (K_P = 30), with the inner M-norm TV proximal computed by 2-block ADMM (K_in = 50, rho_a = 200). A cheaper variant, JP-IMLA, replaces the nested solve with one ADMM on the joint proximal; it gives SSE within 0.7% at ~60x lower per-iteration cost.

Setup: 256x256 phantom, Gaussian blur sigma_blur = 2.0, noise sigma = 0.05 (kappa_f = 4e5), anisotropic TV with rho_TV = 0.3, Moreau lambda = 5e-3 (kappa_eff^lambda = 201), M = H. P-IMLA_lambda runs N = 2,000 iterations with delta = 0.141. The comparator SP-MYULA runs X_{n+1} = X_n - delta M^{-1} grad U_lambda(X_n) + sqrt(2 delta) M^{-1/2} xi_n on the same smoothed target for N = 2e5 iterations at its largest stable step (delta = 9.45e-3); MYULA and SK-ROCK are also run. All chains start at X0 = 0 with no burn-in, and the posterior mean is averaged over the whole run. The metric is SSE = ||x_bar_c - x*||^2 of each chain's posterior mean against the ground-truth image, averaged over chains (± SE).
official.claim: On 256x256 TV-regularised Gaussian deconvolution, P-IMLA_lambda with 2,000 iterations gives a posterior-mean SSE 3.5-4.0x lower than preconditioned explicit-Euler SP-MYULA with 200,000 iterations on the same Moreau-smoothed target: geometric phantom 855.22 ± 0.66 vs. 3,432.0 ± 1.0, Shepp-Logan 1,013.99 ± 0.81 vs. 3,525.6 ± 1.0, cameraman 890.24 ± 1.19 vs. 3,460.4 ± 2.0. Unpreconditioned MYULA does not mix (SSE ~1e9).
official.claim_caption: Table 4: Cross-phantom matched-budget SSE (geometric: 8 chains; Shepp-Logan, cameraman: 4 chains; ± SE; ours N = 2,000, baselines N = 2×10^5). MYULA SSE ~10^9 on all three.
official.metric: per-chain posterior-mean SSE ||x_bar - x*||^2 against ground truth (lower is better), averaged over chains, ± standard error across chains (8 chains geometric, 4 chains Shepp-Logan and cameraman); includes the cold-start transient
official.comparison: P-IMLA_lambda (implicit midpoint, preconditioned, N = 2,000) vs. SP-MYULA (explicit Euler, same preconditioner and smoothed target, N = 2e5); MYULA and SK-ROCK as unpreconditioned references
official.falsification_criterion: With the stated settings, SP-MYULA at its largest stable step and 2e5 iterations reaches a posterior-mean SSE within ~20% of P-IMLA_lambda's on any of the three phantoms, or P-IMLA_lambda's SSE is not clearly below SP-MYULA's.

title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks

official.background: Classical and modern Hopfield networks retrieve a memory by converging to a stored pattern and then stopping, so retrieving a sequence of memories needs repeated reinitialization or delayed asymmetric couplings that are hard to analyze. This paper adds a slow feedback variable to the input-driven plasticity (IDP) Hopfield model so that the network moves on its own from one stored memory to the next along a prescribed transition graph. It derives closed-form conditions (escape times, a critical gain, fixed points of a saliency map) for when such sequential retrieval keeps going and when it collapses to the inactive state.
official.method:
The model is τx ẋ = −x + M diag(Φ(z)) Mᵀ Ψ(x), τz ż = −z + (κ/√N) A Mᵀ Ψ(x), where M = [ξ1..ξP]/√N holds mutually orthogonal ±1 patterns, A is the adjacency matrix of a deterministic transition graph (here a directed cycle of length L = 5 among P = 15 memories), κ is the gain, and τx/τz = 0.01. The fast state x relaxes to the memory with the largest saliency φ(zν); z decays for the current memory and grows for its successor, until the current memory loses stability and x jumps to the next one.

In the limit τx/τz → 0 the transition reduces to a scalar map Z ↦ Z⁺ on the successor's saliency at escape. With ψ(x) = x/(1+|x|) ('SmoothF') and φ(z) = |z| the map is explicit: Z⁺ = Z²/X², where X = e^{T_esc} is the smallest root in [1, Z) of 1/κ = −X(X−1)(X+1−2Z)/(2Z³). Fixed points exist only for κ ≥ κcrit = 1/G(X̄², X̄) ≈ 12.74 with X̄ = (5+√105)/8; above it there is an unstable fixed point Z̄1 and a stable one Z̄2 (≈ 6.78 at κ = 15), and the asymptotic escape time is ½ log Z̄2. The authors check this by simulating the full model (explicit Euler, N = 256, fast noise σ = 1e-6) from Z0 = 8.
official.claim: In full-model simulations with SmoothF activation, orthogonal memories, N = 256, P = 15 and a 5-cycle, retrieval collapses to the origin at subcritical gain κ = 9 but is self-sustained at κ = 15, with the saliency peaks converging to about 6.95, close to the predicted stable fixed point Z̄2 ≈ 6.78 of the reduced map (κcrit ≈ 12.74).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: (A) Fixed points of the discrete map Z+ = h(Z/X) with κ = 15 for the SmoothF activation, with predicted Z̄2 ≃ 6.78 (see Fig. 9 in Appendix E for ψ = tanh). Real solutions Z̄1, Z̄2 > 1 emerge only for κ ≥ κcrit ≃ 12.74; self-sustained transitions require Z0 > Z̄1. (B) SmoothF (blue) and Tanh (green) activation functions. (C, D) Orthogonal memories with SmoothF activation. (C) Subcritical gain (κ = 9): oscillations decay and retrieval collapses to the origin. (D) Supercritical gain (κ = 15): persistent oscillations converge to the stable fixed point Z̄2 ≃ 6.95, close to theoretical prediction, enabling reliable sequential retrieval. (E, F) Random memories with SmoothF activation. (E) Subcritical gain: cross-talk noise sustains small-amplitude transitions. (F) Supercritical gain: transitions persist but exhibit amplitude fluctuations without entrainment to Z̄2. (G,H) Random memories with Tanh activation. (G) Subcritical gain (κ = 3) leads to collapse, with slower decay due to cross-talk. (H) Supercritical gain (κ = 5) yields self-sustained transitions. title: NINJA: A Navigator–Inspector Joint Architecture for Context-Efficient Issue Localization

official.background: Issue localization means finding the files and functions that must be edited to fix a GitHub issue, given only the issue text and the repository. It is the first step of automated issue resolution, and better localization raises downstream fix rates. Most LLM-agent localizers run a single ReAct agent whose context keeps growing as it reads files and search results, so later decisions are made over a long, cluttered history, and the same agent has to trade off searching broadly across files against reading deeply inside a few.
official.method:
NINJA splits localization between a navigator and inspectors that run in separate contexts. The navigator sees the issue and the repository structure, keeps a global state (suspicious functions, explored files, a queue of pending files), searches for files by name or content, and calls a dispatch tool to send entry files to inspectors. Each inspector starts fresh with only the issue and its entry file. It uses function-level tools (list functions/classes, read a function or method, get callers/callees) to explore around that file, possibly crossing into other files, and returns suspicious functions with explanations and the files it visited. Dispatched files are processed in mini-batches of at most P = 2 parallel inspectors. After each batch the navigator updates its state and skips already-visited files, and it can run several dispatch rounds before outputting a ranked list of (file, function) locations.

For the chosen claim no fine-tuning is used: NINJA and all baselines run Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct with temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95 and a 32,768-token context budget per context. The baselines are the authors' own runs of the released implementations of SWERank+, LocAgent, CoSIL, OrcaLoca and RepoSearcher (toolset only, not retrained). Ground truth is the set of functions edited by the resolving patch. Function-level Acc@5 counts an instance as correct only if all ground-truth functions appear in the top 5 predictions. Each setting is evaluated three times.
official.claim: On SWE-Bench-Lite with off-the-shelf Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct (no fine-tuning), NINJA reaches function-level Acc@5 of 71.1 ± 0.4, versus 54.0 ± 0.2 for the strongest baseline (CodeRankEmbed embedding retrieval), 39.0 ± 0.7 for the best agent baseline run with the same model (OrcaLoca), 25.4 ± 3.0 for LocAgent, 24.6 ± 0.4 for CoSIL and 19.9 ± 1.5 for RepoSearcher.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Results on SWE-Bench-Lite. Best and second-best localization results are in bold and underlined, respectively. CodeRank, Haiku-4.5, and Qwen3-30B denote CodeRankEmbed, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct. NINJA-14B and NINJA-30B are obtained by applying agentic fine-tuning (SFT+PPO) to Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-30B, respectively.

title: Projected Neural Additive Models as Universal Approximators

official.background: Neural additive models (NAMs) predict with a sum of one-dimensional MLPs, one per input feature, which makes them interpretable but unable to represent interactions between inputs (their cross-derivatives are zero, so they cannot even represent x1*x2). MLPs capture interactions but are black boxes. Projected NAMs (PNAMs) insert a learnable linear map T before the additive model, so each 1D MLP acts on a learned linear combination of the inputs. The paper proves PNAMs are universal approximators with rate O(M^{-s/(N-1)}) in the number of projections M, and asks whether the learned projection gives a practical accuracy gain over NAMs while keeping the additive structure.
official.method:
A PNAM computes y_hat_i = sum_j zeta_ij * MLP_ij(z_j) + eps_i with z = T x, where T is an M x N learnable matrix and each basis is a 1D MLP (hidden layers 64 and 32, SiLU). Training minimizes cross-entropy plus regularizers with weights w1..w5 = 0.01 for classification: unsquared L2 on MLP weights, a norm penalty on basis outputs, an SVD-based penalty pushing T toward a rectangular diagonal (NAM-like) matrix, and L1 penalties on T and zeta. A NAM is the special case T = identity (M = N = 17).

The task is the DeepMind knot dataset (243,746 knots, 17 invariants standardized to zero mean and unit variance), predicting the signature as a 14-way classification. Split is 80/20 train/test with the training part further split 80/20 into train/validation. All models are trained for 50 epochs with no early stopping, Adam (lr 0.001, decayed by 0.995 per epoch) and batch size 256. Test accuracy is reported as mean ± std over 10 runs for the authors' MLP [17,64,32,14], the NAM (17 bases), and PNAMs with M = 8, 17, 64.
official.claim: On 14-class knot-signature classification, a PNAM with M = 17 projections (17 basis MLPs [1,64,32,14], ~2.1e5 parameters) reaches 95.0 ± 0.2% test accuracy versus 92.4 ± 0.2% for a NAM with the same 17 bases and parameter count, and PNAM accuracy rises monotonically with M (93.6% at M = 8, 95.9% at M = 64, matching the MLP's 95.8%).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Performance comparison of different neural network architectures for the multi-class classification problem of predicting the signature of mathematical knots. The first two rows are reproduced from Table 3 of Liu et al. [14]; see [14] for definitions of G and k. For the remaining rows, the mean and standard deviation of the test accuracy are computed over 10 runs. The last row incorporates the Fourier feature mapping described in Eq. (4).
official.metric: Test accuracy (higher is better), mean ± std over 10 runs
official.comparison: PNAM (learned, regularized T, M = 17) vs. NAM (T = identity, 17 bases of identical architecture) under the same training protocol; also PNAM M = 8/17/64 vs. the authors' MLP
official.falsification_criterion: Under the stated protocol, the M = 17 PNAM's mean test accuracy is within about 0.4 points (two std) of the NAM's, or falls below it; or PNAM accuracy does not increase from M = 8 to M = 17 to M = 64.

title: RAD-TFM: Robust and Domain-Adapted Tabular Foundation Models
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (raw-AUC view: Table 5, page 10 and Table 18, page 29; per-dataset AUCs: Tables 9-10, pages 24-25)

official.background: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) such as TabPFN V2 and TabICL are transformers pretrained only on synthetic datasets sampled from structural causal models (SCMs), then used for in-context classification on real tables with no gradient updates. The prior over SCM hyperparameters is fixed, so some regions of dataset space (feature counts, categorical ratios, nonlinearities, noise levels) are under-represented, and TFMs still lose to boosted trees on some benchmarks. Because the data generator is parameterized, it can be steered during continued training toward datasets the model handles badly, as long as those datasets stay realistic for a target domain.
official.method:
RAD-TFM continues training a pretrained TFM (TabPFN V2 open weights) on synthetic data from a distribution-shifting adversary. Domain adaptation: each real training dataset in a benchmark is encoded as a vector of meta-features (schema, geometry, learnability). Bayesian optimization finds SCM-prior parameterizations θ whose synthetic datasets cover parts of the real embeddings, and a mixture P over these θ is fitted by minimizing an entropy-regularized Wasserstein distance (Sinkhorn) to the real-embedding distribution. P is the reference distribution.

Robust training alternates two stages. In the max stage, with the TFM frozen, a black-box optimizer (Optuna/TPE) proposes 100 θ. For each θ, 20 datasets are sampled and the optimality gap is estimated as the TFM's cross-entropy minus the best cross-entropy among e = 7 baseline estimators fit to each dataset (the paper names XGBoost, CatBoost and Random Forest as examples but does not list all seven; after a fixed number of iterations the TFM with its original weights is added as a further baseline). In the min stage, θ is sampled from Q with q_i ∝ p_i exp(η·gap_i), where η is set by a KL budget ρ = 0.1·ρ_max to P, and the TFM is trained on the generated datasets (lr 1e-5, batch 64, 1k-3k datasets per epoch, 30 epochs for TabPertNet, at most 90k datasets in total). Evaluation uses no ensembling, ROC-AUC (one-vs-one for multiclass) normalized per dataset to [0,1] across the 8 compared models. The FT baseline fine-tunes TabPFN V2 on each evaluation dataset's training split for 10 epochs.
official.claim: On the TabPertNet benchmark (70 classification datasets, at most 10k rows and 500 features), TabPFN V2 after RAD-TFM continued training reaches mean normalized AUC 0.8486, vs. 0.7306 for frozen TabPFN V2, 0.7299 for per-dataset fine-tuned TabPFN V2 and 0.7404 for CatBoost, with 13 rank-1 wins vs. 9 and 2, and pairwise Wilcoxon p < 0.05 against every model.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Experiment results across three tabular dataset benchmarks. For consistency, we report normalized AUC, with values scaled to [0,1] for each dataset [25, 23]. For rank-1 wins, we do not count ties, only outright wins.
official.metric: Mean normalized ROC-AUC over 70 datasets (higher is better; per dataset, the worst of the 8 models = 0 and the best = 1), plus mean rank and outright rank-1 wins. No ± reported: single run, no seeds or error bars. Significance comes from a Friedman test and pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over datasets.
official.comparison: TabPFN V2 + RAD-TFM vs. frozen TabPFN V2, TabPFN V2 fine-tuned per dataset (FT), CatBoost, XGBoost, RF, LR and MLP (default settings), all on the same TabPertNet train/test splits, with no TFM ensembling
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction of RAD-TFM on TabPertNet does not beat both frozen and fine-tuned TabPFN V2 in mean normalized AUC with Wilcoxon p < 0.05, or the mean raw-AUC gain over frozen TabPFN V2 (paper: 0.8019 to 0.8185, +0.0166) is not clearly positive.

title: SituRecBench: Evaluating Frontier Models as Situated Recommendation Assistants in 3D Environments

official.background: Conversational recommender systems are moving from ranking items in a static catalog to acting as interactive assistants, for example a shopping assistant on smart glasses that sees what the user sees. Such an assistant has to find out what the user wants through dialogue, ground its suggestions in the products actually visible in the store, and guide the user physically to them. Existing benchmarks test either dialogue-based preference elicitation without spatial grounding, or embodied navigation driven by explicit instructions rather than latent preferences, so no benchmark evaluates these abilities together in a closed loop.
official.method:
SituRecBench builds two Unreal Engine 5 retail scenes, a Supermarket (233 products, 1,324 instances) and a Home Furnishings Store (222 products), with annotated product names, attributes, prices and locations. A VLM-driven simulated user (GPT-5.6 Sol in the main experiments) gets a private profile, shopping goal and budget, speaks, and takes one physical action per turn (move, turn, move_to_fixture/store, pick_up/check item, add_to_cart, ...), executed in UE5 via UnrealCV. The assistant VLM shares the user's egocentric RGB view with Set-of-Mark labels and also receives the store layout map with the user's pose, the full product catalog and a product-location index; each turn it outputs one dialogue action, an expected user action and a top-10 recommendation ranking. Episodes end on cart addition, 20 turns, 3 unsuccessful recommendations, moderator termination, or 3 consecutive motion stalls.

Seven assistants (Gemma 4 E4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, GPT-4o, Qwen3.6-Plus, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro) each run the same 100 tasks per environment (50 profiles x 4 tasks over the two scenes, 1,400 trajectories in total). Success Rate (SR) is the percentage of episodes ending with a non-empty cart. Each environment's 100 tasks are split (seed 42) into four disjoint subsets of 25, each covering all 25 profiles; tables report the mean of the four subset means and the sample SD across them.
official.claim: With GPT-5.6 Sol as the simulated user, Gemini 3.1 Pro as the assistant reaches a higher success rate than GPT-4o in both environments: 80.0 ± 5.7% vs 45.0 ± 6.8% in Supermarket and 66.0 ± 7.7% vs 35.0 ± 10.0% in Home Furnishings Store (100 tasks each).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Evaluation results of different VLM models as situated recommendation assistants, with GPT-5.6 Sol acting as the simulated user. Bold marks the best performance per environment.
official.metric: Success Rate (%) = share of episodes ending with an item in the cart, higher is better; ± is the sample SD of the means over four disjoint 25-task subsets (not seeds)
official.comparison: Gemini 3.1 Pro vs GPT-4o as assistant on the same 100 tasks per environment, same user simulator (GPT-5.6 Sol), prompts and termination rules; other assistants in Table 3 as context
official.falsification_criterion: On the same 100 tasks with the GPT-5.6 Sol user, Gemini 3.1 Pro's SR exceeds GPT-4o's by less than about 15 points in either environment, or is not higher at all.

title: Bias, Measurement Error, and Double-Dipping: When Can GNN Convolutions Help Brain Connectome Prediction?

official.background: GNNs are widely used to predict diagnoses or traits from fMRI functional connectomes. In these pipelines the noisy empirical connectivity matrix serves both as node features and, after thresholding, as the graph. Several benchmarks found that such GNNs do no better than graph-agnostic baselines. This paper treats the problem as errors-in-variables regression: the true connectome is latent, and the observed covariance from T time points is a noisy estimate. It splits the effect of a graph convolution into three parts: smoothing bias vs. variance reduction (an oracle graph), graph-estimation error (an independently estimated graph), and double dipping (the graph built from the same noisy sample as the features).
official.method:
Synthetic connectomes follow a latent community model with p = 20 ROIs in K = 5 balanced communities. Each subject has Σ(i) = F(i)F(i)ᵀ + ψ²I, where row j of F(i) is the fixed orthogonal centroid of ROI j's community plus N(0, σ²I_d) noise; σ ∈ {0.5, 1.0} sets how blurred the communities are. For each subject, T i.i.d. samples Z_t ~ N(0, Σ(i)) give the sample covariance Σ̂(i). The target is linear, y = ⟨B*, Σ⟩ + ε. The paper uses two coefficient patterns: 'single-community-aligned' (support on one full community block, so it is community-smooth) and 'within-community contrast' (B* = ½{(e_a − e_b)vᵀ + v(e_a − e_b)ᵀ} with v = 1_{C(a)}: the difference between two same-community ROIs' connectivity to their community, per Appendix A.4.3; the figure captions describe its overlay as a single in-community edge), whose predictive difference smoothing averages away.

Five feature maps are each fit by OLS with an intercept on standardized, vectorized features (n = 25,000 subjects, 80/20 train/test split): raw Σ̂ (no convolution), and one linear SageMean convolution R(A)Σ̂ with R(A) = D̃⁻¹(A + I). A is built by thresholding at δ (≈9.10 for σ = 0.5, ≈10.20 for σ = 1.0) one of the following: the true Σ (oracle), an independent second sample Σ̂⊥ of the same subject (A⊥), the same Σ̂ (Â, the standard pipeline), or the population mean Σ₀ (A_pop). The metric is held-out MSE normalized by an oracle reference ('ValMSE / Oracle'), plotted against T for 5 seeds.
official.claim: In the latent-community simulation (p = 20, K = 5, n = 25,000), with σ = 0.5 and the single-community-aligned target, smoothing over the oracle graph lowers normalized test MSE vs. raw Σ̂ at every T (≈1.63 vs ≈1.96 at T = 5; ≈1.31 vs ≈1.48 at T = 100). The independent graph recovers only part of this gain (≈1.41 at T = 100). The same-sample and population graphs do no better than raw. For the within-community-contrast target at σ = 1.0, the oracle helps only at small T (≈1.63 vs ≈1.74 at T = 5), and raw is better from T ≈ 30 on (≈1.09 vs ≈1.17 at T = 100).
official.claim_caption: Figure 3: Decoupling the effects for different values of β and latent structures. Center: true covariance Σ for two graph regimes (σ); overlays mark the support of two coefficient patterns (β). Left/right: normalized ValMSE vs. T for SageMean(A, Σ̂) and a no-conv baseline. Mean ± 1 SD over 5 seeds. p = 20, K = 5, n = 25,000; thresholds δ_{σ=0.5} ≈ 9.10, δ_{σ=1.0} ≈ 10.20.
official.metric: Validation MSE normalized by an oracle reference ('ValMSE / Oracle'), lower is better; error bars are ±1 SD over 5 seeds; values are read off the plot and approximate
official.comparison: Linear SageMean convolution of Σ̂ over the oracle, independent, same-sample and population graphs vs. raw Σ̂ (no convolution), all fit by OLS on the same simulated data
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the simulation with the stated settings, either (a) for σ = 0.5 and the single-community-aligned target, R(A_oracle)Σ̂ is not clearly below raw Σ̂ (gap within a few seed SDs) at small and large T, or A⊥ is not between the oracle and raw, or the same-sample graph clearly beats raw; or (b) for σ = 1.0 and the within-community contrast, the oracle still beats raw at T = 100 (no crossover).

title: A Topological Encoder Decoder Framework for Temporal Graph Learning
claim_source: Table 3, page 8 (per-baseline CollegeMsg detail in Table 11, page 29)

official.background: Most temporal graph learning methods treat future prediction as scoring candidate edges or node labels over a mostly fixed set of nodes. Many real temporal graphs (messaging, forums, blockchain token transfers) have heavy node churn: nodes appear, disappear and reappear, and new nodes form edges. In that setting the useful prediction target is the whole next graph snapshot, including which nodes are active, which is something standard discriminative temporal GNNs do not produce directly.
official.method:
TopoGED encodes each discrete-time snapshot with a degree-sublevel filtration descriptor: for n=10 degree thresholds it records the node count and induced-edge count at each level, so the last entries equal |V| and |E|. A V-EWMA forecaster predicts the next descriptor (and so the node and edge budgets) and the fraction of new nodes from the last k=5 snapshots. A memory module scores nodes seen in the last k snapshots by P(v,t) = exp(-(t - l_v)/lambda) * (deg_v/deg_max)^alpha * f_v^beta (recency, normalized degree, frequency) and samples the predicted number of reappearing old nodes without replacement. The predicted number of new nodes is then added as fresh IDs.

Edges are generated in four phases (old-old previously seen, old-old unseen, old-new, new-new), each with a per-type budget from forecast edge-type proportions. In each phase a one-layer GCN trunk with type-specific heads, trained with BCE and negative sampling, picks the top-scored candidates. Baselines (ROLAND, EvolveGCN, VGRNN, GC-LSTM, TGCN, HTGN) are trained for link prediction with grid search and used to build full predicted snapshots. Node F1 compares the predicted active node set with the true one by node ID, averaged over test snapshots, with a 70/15/15 temporal split and 3 runs.
official.claim: On CollegeMsg next-snapshot forecasting, TopoGED reaches node-set F1 0.44 ± 0.10 versus 0.04 ± 0.02 for the best temporal-GNN baseline (EvolveGCN). Across 14 datasets the macro-average node F1 is 0.49 ± 0.07 for TopoGED versus 0.05 ± 0.09 for the best baseline (GC-LSTM).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Forecast results. For each dataset and metric group, we report TopoGED and the strongest baseline. Structure metric wins is the number of times each model was closest to 0 percent error across assortativity coefficient, clustering coefficient, average degree, density, triangle count, extra edges, extra nodes, missing edges, and missing nodes. Node metrics display the F1 of all nodes. Edge metrics are the F1 scores across all edge types. Detailed results can be seen in Appendix F and E.2.
official.metric: F1 of the predicted active node set against the true node set (higher is better), averaged over test snapshots. The paper does not say whether ± is the std over the 3 runs or over test snapshots.
official.comparison: TopoGED vs. the strongest of ROLAND, EvolveGCN, VGRNN, GC-LSTM, TGCN and HTGN on each dataset, all run by the authors on the same splits
official.falsification_criterion: Retrained TopoGED on CollegeMsg gives node F1 within about one std of the best baseline (e.g. below about 0.15), or a properly built baseline snapshot (for example from the same temporal GNNs with a node budget, or a copy-last-snapshot heuristic) matches TopoGED's node F1.

title: Disentangling Channel Semantics in Vision Transformers via Token Decorrelation and Composition-Aware Modulation

official.background: Microscopy and remote-sensing images have many channels (fluorescence stains, brightfield, SAR and multispectral bands) that share one spatial layout but carry different information, and the set of available channels often varies between samples. Channel-adaptive Vision Transformers handle this by patchifying each channel separately, adding a learned channel embedding, and summarizing with a [CLS] token plus extra memory tokens (as in ChA-MAEViT). The authors argue that these context tokens collapse onto a few dominant channels when channels are highly redundant, so the global summary is biased and channel-specific information is lost. That hurts accuracy, especially when only some channels are available at test time.
official.method:
MuCa-ViT is built on top of ChA-MAEViT (ViT-Small, joint MAE reconstruction plus classification, trained 100 epochs) and adds two parts. Factorial Token Learning (FTL) computes a per-sample Gram matrix G = (1/D) CST CST^T over the [CLS] token and K memory tokens at the final encoder output (batch-normalized first). It adds the loss L_FTL = mean_b ||W ⊙ (G_b − I)||_F^2 to the task loss with weight λ_FTL = 0.1e-5. W puts weight 1 on all [CLS] entries and on the diagonal, and α = 0.1 on off-diagonal memory-memory entries. Memory tokens are initialized orthogonally, and 3 are used on JUMP-CP versus 4 for the baseline.

Channel Composition-Aware Modulation (CAM) passes the [CLS] token at block k through a two-layer MLP with SiLU to produce (γ, β). It then applies Z_patch ← (1+γ) ⊙ Z_patch + β to all patch tokens. On JUMP-CP, CAM is applied in the last two blocks (10–11). The baseline ChA-MAEViT* is the authors' rerun of the official code under the same training configuration (Appendix Table 4). The test set is JUMP-CP (8 channels: 5 fluorescence and 3 brightfield, 161 perturbation classes), evaluated on top-1 accuracy with all channels (Full) and with a subset of channels (Partial).
official.claim: On JUMP-CP with a ViT-Small backbone, MuCa-ViT (ChA-MAEViT + FTL + CAM) reaches 95.14 ± 0.32% top-1 accuracy with all 8 channels versus 90.52 ± 0.40% for the reproduced ChA-MAEViT. With partial channels it reaches 72.04 ± 0.14% versus 67.40 ± 0.65%.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Comparison of test accuracy (%) of channel-adaptive models. Full denotes inference using all channels, while Partial evaluates on a subset of channels. All results are reported as the mean ± standard deviation of three independent runs (n = 3). Values marked with * were reproduced using the official implementation.
official.metric: Top-1 test accuracy (%) on JUMP-CP, higher is better; ± is std over three independent runs (n = 3)
official.comparison: MuCa-ViT vs. the authors' reproduction of ChA-MAEViT (ChA-MAEViT*), both trained under the same 100-epoch protocol; the published ChA-MAEViT numbers (90.73 / 68.05) are also listed
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both models under the same protocol gives a full-channel gain on JUMP-CP that is not clearly larger than the run-to-run std (for example under about 1 pp), or MuCa-ViT does not beat ChA-MAEViT's 90.73% full / 68.05% partial.

title: Learning a Unified Cross-Model Semantic Dictionary via Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
claim_source: Figure 4, page 9 (seed standard deviations in Table 4, page 13)

official.background: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) break a model's activations into sparse, often human-interpretable concepts, but each SAE is specific to one model. Recent cross-model methods (USAE, SPARC) train one encoder/decoder pair per model and only align the latent indices, so a concept still lives in each model's own representation space and cannot be reused across models. This paper asks whether a single dictionary of concepts can be learned that is shared by several vision foundation models, with the model-specific parts split off into separate private dictionaries.
official.method:
GB-SAE takes final-layer token features from frozen ViT, SigLIP and DINOv2 on ImageNet-1K (Configuration I), maps each to d' = 768 with a frozen random orthogonal linear projector, and encodes all of them with one shared TopK-ReLU encoder (h = 6144 latents, K = 32). A global learnable sigmoid gate g splits each code z into a shared part z ⊙ g and a private part z ⊙ (1 − g). One shared decoder D^sh and one private decoder per model reconstruct the projected features. The loss is total reconstruction + 0.5 × shared-only reconstruction + 1.3 × cross-model alignment (a continuous Jaccard overlap of normalized shared codes between model pairs, plus a 0.2-weighted overlap-weighted magnitude term) + 0.2 × gate binarization penalty Σ g(1−g)/h. Training uses AdamW, lr 3e-4, batch 32, 30 epochs on precomputed features of the train set plus two augmented views per image.

Zero-shot cross-model retrieval: for each ImageNet validation image (50,000) and backbone i, the features are projected, encoded with the frozen GB-SAE, reconstructed with the shared branch only (z_i^sh D^sh), and mean-pooled over tokens. Queries from one backbone retrieve among features from a different backbone j ≠ i by cosine similarity. Instance Recall@k counts a hit if the same image is retrieved; Category Recall@k counts a hit if an image of the same class is retrieved. Baselines use the same pipeline with the private reconstruction z_i^pr D_i^pr, or the projected features a'_i directly, plus the analytic random-retrieval rate. No retrieval training is involved.
official.claim: On ImageNet-1K validation (50,000 images) with GB-SAE trained on ViT, SigLIP and DINOv2, zero-shot cross-model retrieval using shared-dictionary reconstructions reaches Category Recall@10 of 0.244 and Instance Recall@50 of 0.148, while private-branch reconstructions and projected raw features stay near random (Category R@10 about 0.01 or less, Instance R@50 about 0.003 or less).
official.claim_caption: Figure 4: Zero-shot cross-model feature retrieval using z_i^sh D^sh ("shared"; light and dark blue bars). We report Recall@k at instance and category levels. Multiples in parentheses denote improvements over random retrieval.
official.metric: Recall@k (k = 1, 5, 10, 50) at instance and category level, higher is better; values are means over 3 seeds; Table 4 gives the std over seeds (shared: 0.010-0.029 instance, 0.023-0.040 category; projected and private: ≤ 0.002 except private Category R@50 std 0.008). Values for the PROJ and PRIVATE bars are read off the plot and approximate.
official.comparison: Shared reconstruction z^sh D^sh vs. private reconstruction z^pr D^pr vs. projected features a' (all from the same frozen GB-SAE and projectors) vs. random retrieval
official.falsification_criterion: After training GB-SAE as described, shared-branch Category Recall@10 for cross-model retrieval is not clearly above the projected-feature and private-branch baselines (e.g. below 0.10, or within a few seed std of them), or Instance Recall@50 is near the random rate of 0.001.

title: Dual-Granularity Learning for Regression with Continuous Noisy Labels

official.background: Most work on learning with noisy labels targets classification. In regression the labels are continuous, so noise varies in size from sample to sample: small deviations still carry useful information about the true value, while large ones (outliers, badly corrupted annotations) make the exact label value unreliable. Existing robust-regression methods (robust losses, reweighting, mixup, sample selection) treat all corruption the same way. This paper argues that the two regimes need different mechanisms and proposes one framework that handles both.
official.method:
GRAIN puts three heads on a shared ResNet-50 feature extractor. (1) Fine-grained: a regression head is trained with a piecewise robust loss (quadratic within ±τ, sub-quadratic beyond it). Through its infimal-convolution form, the loss introduces per-sample residuals ξ_i = τ·tanh(h_res(z_i)), which a residual head learns against the target Ỹ_i − Y*_i. The threshold τ is re-set every epoch to a scaled (1.345×) median absolute deviation of the residuals Ỹ_i − Y*_i. (2) Coarse-grained: the label range is split into K equal-width bins (the width is set adaptively as a 10% quantile interval around the peak of a KDE of the noisy labels, which fixes K), a histogram head is trained with cross-entropy over bins, and a cross-bin contrastive loss pulls together the feature distributions of nearby bins and pushes apart distant ones, using unbalanced optimal transport under a Gaussian approximation. (3) Bridge: robust pseudo labels Y*_i are EMA-smoothed (α = 0.9) probability-weighted averages of bin representative values (an endpoint or midpoint of each bin) from the histogram head, keeping the smallest set of top bins that covers 68% of the probability mass. After a warm-up these pseudo labels drive bin assignment and give the residual targets. The total loss is λ_reg R_reg + λ_ce R_ce + λ_pos R_pos + λ_neg R_neg, with λ_ce = 1, λ_neg/λ_pos = 0.5, λ_reg ∈ {0.2, 0.5} (ramped up over 20 epochs) and λ_pos ∈ {0.01, 0.05}.

Noise on UTKFace (age, about 20k images): for each sample an integer variance σ² is drawn uniformly from [std_max], an offset is sampled from N(0, σ²) on a grid of M = 4000 sub-intervals of [y_min, y_max], and the noisy label is drawn uniformly from the clean labels in that sub-interval. std_max ∈ {30, 60, 90} gives an average noisy-label MAE of 7.04, 10.52 and 11.44. Data are split 4:1 into train/validation, model selection uses validation MAE, and test MAE is measured against clean labels. All methods use ResNet-50, the same basic augmentation (crop, flip, rotation) and 5 seeds; each baseline is run both plain and with the same histogram head and binning as GRAIN ('BIN').
official.claim: On UTKFace with simulated heteroscedastic label noise at std_max = 60, GRAIN (basic augmentation) reaches test MAE 7.54 ± 0.14, below the best of 22 baselines, SuperLoss (BIN) at 7.90 ± 0.19; GRAIN also has the lowest MAE at std_max = 30 (7.01 ± 0.10 vs. C-Mixup (BIN) 7.44 ± 0.25) and std_max = 90 (7.65 ± 0.12 vs. SuperLoss (BIN) 7.95 ± 0.19).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Mean ± standard deviation on UTKFace under simulated Gaussian label noise with corruption levels controlled by std_max, and on Bone-Age. The best baseline for each metric is highlighted in blue, and results from GRAIN and GRAIN-AUG are presented in boldface.
official.metric: Test MAE in years against clean labels (lower is better), mean ± std over 5 seeds (1-5); RMSE and R² also reported
official.comparison: GRAIN (no extra augmentation) vs. Vanilla, SuperLoss, RDI, AUX, C-Mixup, CDR, Selfie, CoTeaching, CNLCU-S, CNLCU-H and CoSelfie, each with and without a histogram head (BIN), all trained under the same backbone, augmentation and protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running UTKFace at std_max = 60 (5 seeds), GRAIN's mean test MAE is not lower than SuperLoss (BIN)'s by more than about one seed std (gap under ~0.15 years), or some other baseline matches it.

title: Efficient LLM Adaptation with Forward-Only Passes

official.background: LASER (Sharma et al., 2024) showed that replacing one feed-forward weight matrix of an LLM with a low-rank SVD approximation (keeping only the top singular components) can raise downstream accuracy on some tasks with no training. Finding which matrix and which rank to reduce takes an exhaustive sweep over every layer, both feed-forward matrices and 9 rank fractions, each evaluated on a validation set. LASER-Grad (Sreeram et al., 2025) narrows the search with singular-value gradients but needs backward passes and about twice the memory. This paper proposes ranking matrices using only forward-pass statistics, so the adaptation could run inside an inference server.
official.method:
For each feed-forward weight W (W_in and W_out in each of GPT-J's 28 layers), write W = Σ σ_i u_i v_iᵀ so the layer output Y is the sum of rank-1 activations Y^(i) = σ_i (X v_i) ⊗ u_iᵀ. Angle concentration AC(·) is the mean pairwise cosine similarity between the token rows of a matrix (Eq. 2). For the last m SVD components (smallest singular values; m = 50 for GPT-J, m = 20 for Bios Gender and Bios Profession), compute Δ_i = AC(Y^(i)) − AC(Y), and score W by its dispersion −Σ min(Δ_i, 0), averaged over D_subset (100 validation samples). Matrices are ranked by this score and the top j = 10 are kept.

Ours (hierarchical): each of the top-10 matrices is evaluated with 9 retained-rank fractions k ∈ {0.5, 1, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 90}% on D_subset, the top-10 (matrix, k) pairs are re-evaluated on D_std (20% of the dataset), and the best one is the final candidate. Accuracy is reported on the remaining 80% of the data. LASER (std) instead evaluates all 28 × 2 × 9 candidates on D_std. 'Speedup' is the ratio of counted forward-pass evaluations in the search (Eq. 7 vs. LASER's L × 2 × 9 × D_std), excluding the test stage, and Mem is an analytic peak-memory estimate (Table 1, Appendix E).
official.claim: On GPT-J-6B, the forward-only search (ours, hierarchical) finds single-matrix rank reductions with accuracy competitive with LASER's exhaustive search and the gradient-based LASER-Grad: average gain over direct inference across 8 datasets of +11.3 points vs. +8.24 for LASER (std) and +10.1 for LASER-Grad (std) (e.g. Bios Gender 70.9 → 97.5 for both ours and LASER, FEVER 50.2 → 58.4 vs. 56.2; but lower than LASER on Bios Profession, 79.1 vs. 82.1), while needing about 36.7× fewer counted search evaluations than LASER (std).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: GPT-J evaluation with reported accuracy (Acc, %), Speedup, and peak memory (Mem) in Gigabyte (GB). Our approach achieves the best average improvement in Acc and the best average Speedup. Moreover, our approach shows comparable Mem to Baseline and LASER [Sharma et al., 2024], and 1.9× lower Mem to LASER-Grad [Sreeram et al., 2025] due to our forward-only passes.
official.metric: Classification/QA accuracy (%) on the 80% test split, higher is better; single deterministic run, no error bars. Speedup is an analytic ratio of search evaluations relative to LASER (std); Mem is an analytic peak-memory estimate.
official.comparison: Ours (hierarchical) vs. LASER (std) exhaustive search and LASER-Grad (std), and the unmodified GPT-J baseline, on CounterFact, HotPotQA, FEVER, Bios Gender, Bios Profession, TruthfulQA, BigBench Epistemic Reasoning and BigBench WikidataQA
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the angle-concentration ranking on GPT-J, the top-10 matrices do not contain a candidate that gets close to LASER's exhaustive best (e.g. on Bios Gender the selected rank reduction stays well below 97.5%, or on FEVER below ~56%), or the average accuracy gain of the forward-only result falls clearly below LASER (std)'s +8.24 points.

title: EndoSCOP-V: A Multi-Turn Video Understanding Evaluation Framework for Multimodal Models in Endoscopy Reporting and Clinical Reasoning

official.background: Gastrointestinal endoscopy reports are built from a chain of dependent judgments made over video: whether a disease is present, where it is, what it looks like, how severe it is, and what intervention it needs. Existing multimodal endoscopy benchmarks are mostly single images, single turns and single pathologies, so they do not measure whether large multimodal models (LMMs) can do this multi-step structured reporting on real procedure video. EndoSCOP-V provides 1,307 real EGD and colonoscopy clips (mean ~174 s, mostly 1080p) from one hospital, with multi-turn questions derived deterministically from clinician-filled structured EHR reports covering 54 WEO MST 3.0 diseases.
official.method:
Each case becomes a multi-turn dialogue of multiple-choice, binary or multi-select questions (20,274 in total; 9 tasks, 30 sub-tasks) instantiated from 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates and the clinician-filled EHR report. Evaluation uses 'oracle forcing' with Markovian context pruning: each turn is posed with the gold answer to its parent question (or the disease name) given as a prefix, so every turn is graded independently of the model's own earlier errors. Phase 1 (disease identification) has no prefixes; later phases reveal the disease.

All models get a fixed system prompt ('an expert gastroenterologist and endoscopist reviewing a {procedure_type} video'), uniformly sampled frames with frame numbers overlaid (100 frames for Qwen and MedGemma models, 16 for Hulu-Med and ColonR1), and never the clinician keyframe; they must answer in a JSON schema with a regex fallback, and unparseable answers score 0. The primary metric is strict exact-match accuracy; 'NDR' excludes the 3,213 format-trivial Disease-Rejection (DI-R) yes/no items.
official.claim: On the full 20,274-question EndoSCOP-V benchmark, the generalist Qwen3.6-27B reaches 59.8% strict overall / 53.4% strict NDR accuracy, above the strongest medical-tuned models Hulu-Med-32B (55.0% / 46.9%) and MedGemma-27B (51.6% / 43.0%), with the paper's stated 95% CIs under ±1 pp on Set-A overall accuracy; all remain far below the 77.9% clinician panel (measured on a different question subset, Set B).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Accuracy (%). Best per column in bold. † ColonR1 is scored on its eligibility-filtered subset (9,897 questions across 668 cases from the 28 disease classes it was trained for). 95% CIs are under ±1 pp on Set-A overall accuracy, ±2.1 pp on Set B and ±∼10 pp on Set-C cells.
official.metric: Strict exact-match accuracy (%) on all questions (Strict Overall) and excluding the 3,213 DI-R items (Strict NDR), higher is better. Table cells carry no ±; the caption states 95% CIs are under ±1 pp on Set-A overall accuracy (±2.1 pp Set B, ±~10 pp Set C) without saying how they are computed, and gives no separate CI for NDR. No seeds or repeated runs are reported.
official.comparison: Qwen3.6-27B (generalist, 100 frames) vs. Hulu-Med-32B (medical-tuned, 16 frames) and MedGemma-27B (medical-tuned, 100 frames) on the same questions and protocol
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the released evaluation pipeline on the full benchmark, Qwen3.6-27B's strict overall accuracy is not more than ~2 pp above Hulu-Med-32B's and MedGemma-27B's (or its strict NDR not more than ~2 pp above theirs), or Qwen3.6-27B's score differs from 59.8% by more than ~2 pp.

title: MMGraph-Agent: Agentic Multimodal RAG via Cache-Inspired Multimodal Knowledge HyperGraphs

official.background: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers questions by retrieving evidence from documents that mix text, images, tables and charts, or from the web. Graph-based organizers such as GraphRAG or RAG-Anything use paid LLM calls to extract entities and relations, which is expensive. Agentic RL retrievers such as Search-R1 and MMSearch-R1 run several retrieval rounds, and the growing context can overflow the model's window. Offline private corpora and the live web are usually handled by separate systems. The paper asks whether a cheap hypergraph index plus a bounded-context RL agent can beat these baselines on multimodal QA.
official.method: MMGraph-Agent builds a multimodal knowledge hypergraph with no LLM calls. A rule-based parser splits documents into spaCy sentences and image units. spaCy NER extracts entities from each sentence, and all entities in one sentence form an n-ary hyperedge that carries the sentence as its payload. Entities, hyperedges and images are embedded with a frozen CLIP-ViT-L/14 encoder (D=768) into flat FAISS inner-product indices. At query time a two-tier cache is used: L2 holds the full hypergraph, and a per-trajectory L1 cache accumulates retrieved evidence and serves the Top-C (C=5) items. Each evidence block is truncated to 1,200 words and condensed into a digest of about 300 words, and the prompt is capped at 5,000 tokens. The policy is Qwen2.5-VL-3B. It emits , (Google Lens) or actions and is trained with GRPO (G=8, eps=0.2, KL 1e-3, lr 2e-6, 75 steps) on 600 in-domain examples with web search disabled. The reward is token-level F1 times a concave call-count bonus, minus a format penalty. Baselines (Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone, labelled Qwen2.5-3B in the table, or GPT-4.1-mini): NaiveGen (no retrieval), StdMMRAG (flat CLIP top-5 retrieval over 300-token chunks and images of the same corpus), SFT and GRPO on the same 600 examples (no retrieval), RAG-Anything (GPT-4o-built graph over the corpus, GPT-4.1-mini answerer) and MMSearch-R1 (GRPO web-search agent; in Knowledge-Only it answers via web search because it has no offline hypergraph). Retrieval-based methods share the CLIP embedder and rollout prompt. The metric is token-level F1 on a 640-item evaluation pool (16-32 items per dataset), averaged over three sampled runs at temperature 1.0.
official.claim: In the Knowledge-Only regime, MMGraph-Agent-3B beats the best of 8 matched baselines on DocBench (33.05 ± 4.4 vs. 22.39 ± 1.4 F1, MMSearch-R1), MMLongBench-Doc (20.64 ± 2.3 vs. 11.08 ± 1.1, MMSearch-R1) and NQ (24.42 ± 2.9 vs. 10.99 ± 1.1, RAG-Anything with GPT-4.1-mini).
official.claim_caption: Table 3: Main results on 23 multimodal QA datasets in Knowledge-Only, WebSearch-Only, and Knowledge+WebSearch. Token-level F1 (%) with std. over three runs; bold marks the best per row, † flags out-of-distribution (OOD) rows, and green is the gain over the second-best baseline.
official.metric: Token-level F1 (%) against the gold answer, higher is better; ± is the std over three sampled evaluation runs (temperature 1.0) on the same fixed 16-32 items per dataset, not over training seeds
official.comparison: MMGraph-Agent-3B (Qwen2.5-VL-3B, GRPO-trained, retrieving from the per-dataset hypergraph) vs. NaiveGen, StdMMRAG, SFT, GRPO, RAG-Anything and MMSearch-R1 on the same evaluation items; StdMMRAG and RAG-Anything index the same corpus, MMSearch-R1 answers Knowledge-Only questions via web search, and NaiveGen/SFT/GRPO retrieve nothing
official.falsification_criterion: On DocBench, MMLongBench-Doc or NQ, the reproduced MMGraph-Agent-3B F1 is within the run-to-run std of the strongest baseline (MMSearch-R1 or RAG-Anything), or below it.

title: TransMem: Transition-Aware Retrieval for Evolving Personal Memory

official.background: Personal assistants that remember users over long periods must handle preferences that change: a user who once liked quick solo workouts may later prefer group hikes. Retrieval-augmented and structured-memory systems (RAG, Zep, A-Mem, Mem0, LightMem) can surface relevant facts, but they return isolated snippets. Stale and current preferences can then appear side by side, and the model has to infer which one superseded the other. The question is whether storing the preference update itself as a retrievable unit improves question answering over long, topic-interleaved user histories.
official.method:
Construction (offline, per user): each message is routed by embedding similarity to a topic summary (macro gate, tau_macro = 0.65) and by entity overlap with that topic (micro gate, tau_micro = 0.25). Messages that are topically similar but have low entity overlap ('EVOLVE') go into a buffer. Once the buffer holds kappa = 5 messages, an LLM shift detector compares it with the top-10 retrieved historical facts and outputs shift events (old state, new state, type, rationale, valid time). Each event's old and new states are grounded to existing entity nodes (cosine >= 0.5 with BGE-M3 embeddings) and stored as a directed intra- or inter-topic transition edge carrying the record text. All messages are also ingested as normal facts in a Graphiti-based graph.

Retrieval (online): take the top-k normal facts by query similarity as factual anchors (k = 110 for Qwen3.5-27B at 128k). Then run a beam search (B = 3, at most 6 hops) over transition edges adjacent to the anchors' endpoints. Each candidate is scored by cosine against a trajectory state that starts at the query embedding and is updated as C <- gamma*C + (1-gamma)*E(edge), with gamma = 0.6 for 27B. A candidate is accepted if its score is >= 0.40 and has dropped by no more than 0.10 from the previous hop. The context is the factual anchors plus the accepted transition records, and the same backbone (Qwen3.5-27B) does both construction and answering. Baselines (NaiveRAG, RF-Mem, Zep, A-Mem, Mem0 graph variant, LightMem) are reproduced from open-source releases with the same backbone.
official.claim: On PersonaMem in the 128k-token regime (55 user cases, 2,161 quality-filtered four-option questions) with Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, TransMem reaches 64.69% overall accuracy, ahead of every reproduced memory baseline. The best baseline, A-Mem, scores 61.64% (+3.05 pp), followed by Mem0 at 60.85% and Zep at 60.30%.
official.claim_caption: Table 2: PersonaMem results in the 128k context regime. Best results in bold; second-best underlined.
official.metric: Overall multiple-choice accuracy (%), question-weighted across 7 categories, higher is better; single run, no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: TransMem vs. ZeroMem, NaiveRAG, RF-Mem, Zep, A-Mem, Mem0, LightMem, all with Qwen3.5-27B for memory construction and answering, on the same filtered PersonaMem-128k evaluation set
official.falsification_criterion: A reproduction on PersonaMem-128k with Qwen3.5-27B in which TransMem's overall accuracy does not exceed A-Mem's (or that of another reproduced baseline), or exceeds it by well under the reported 3 pp, would count against the claim.

title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
claim_source: Table 6, page 9 (per-model A/Bp/Bf/C in Table 3, page 7; per-model corruption results in Table S9, page 27)

official.background: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief (Sally-Anne style) probes at near-human levels but lose 20 or more percentage points when the same story is shown as images. The usual reading is that VLMs lack belief-reasoning machinery. This paper argues the gap is mainly perceptual: models fail to extract structured scene state (who is where, who was present when an object moved) from pixels, and given that state as text alongside the image, their reasoning is largely intact.
official.method:
Abstract 2D stimuli are multi-panel images (200x200 px per panel, 4-6 panels, no embedded text) of geometric 'characters' and objects, generated with PIL from 10 false-belief templates (Sally-Anne search/belief, reality-belief, knowledge access, unexpected contents, two rooms, perspective divergence, second-order belief) with 50 seeded variants each, 500 probes. Each probe is asked under several conditions with the question held fixed: A = image only; Bp = image plus a programmatically generated panel-by-panel narration of entities, positions and observable cross-frame events that never states that an agent did not observe something; Bf = Bp plus explicit visibility/absence statements (for the second-order template it also states the resulting first-order belief); C = text narration only. Controls on Bp: B_identity (per-panel entity lists only), B_static (+ per-panel positions, no events), and length-matched corruptions D_mismatch (another variant's Bp scaffold), D_noise (30% of names replaced), D_shuffled (panel sentences reordered).

Seven VLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Llama 4 Maverick, GPT-4.1-mini, Ministral-8B) are queried via OpenRouter with temperature 0, max 200 output tokens, single turn. Answers are graded deterministically (lowercase, prefix/alias match, no partial credit). Accuracy is reported as the 7-model mean over 500 probes; condition comparisons use McNemar's test on the 3,500 matched (model, probe) pairs with Bonferroni correction.
official.claim: On the 500 abstract-panel false-belief probes, adding the correct perceptual-grade scaffold Bp raises 7-model mean accuracy from 73.9% (image only) to 88.8% (+14.9 pp), whereas a length-matched scaffold taken from another probe variant (D_mismatch) gives only 74.7% (+0.8 pp, not significant) and noise/shuffle corruptions give at most 80.6%.
official.claim_caption: Table 6: Scaffold-content ladder and corruption controls on Stage 3 (7 models × 500 probes). No rung below Bf states a belief. † Six models; ∆ vs. their A (77.2).
official.metric: Accuracy (%) on 500 Stage 3 probes, averaged over 7 models, higher is better; no ± reported in the table; significance by McNemar on 3,500 paired (model, probe) observations (Bp vs A p ≈ 4e-63; D_mismatch vs A p = .38; D_noise and D_shuffled p < 1e-8)
official.comparison: Image + perceptual-grade scaffold (Bp) vs. image only (A) vs. image + length-matched corrupted scaffolds (D_mismatch, D_noise, D_shuffled), same models and probes
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running Stage 3 with the released generator, the Bp gain over A is small (e.g. under ~7 pp in the 7-model mean, or absent for most models), or a length-matched corrupted scaffold (especially D_mismatch) recovers a similar share of the gain as the correct Bp scaffold.

title: Locating and Repairing Domain Shift in VLM Trajectory Planning

official.background: Vision-language models (VLMs) fine-tuned as end-to-end driving planners get much worse when deployed in a city they were not trained on: a planner trained in Boston and run in Singapore has a much larger trajectory error. Standard unsupervised domain adaptation applies one objective uniformly across all layers (feature alignment such as MMD or DANN, or LoRA everywhere). Locate-then-edit methods such as ROME change a single site. The paper argues that cross-city shift is instead structured by modality (image vs. text tokens) and by layer, and that adaptation should be applied only where the shift is causally located.
official.method:
Each VLM (LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B, PaliGemma2-3B) is first LoRA fine-tuned on the source city (nuScenes Boston-Seaport) to predict 6 future waypoints (3 s at 2 Hz) from three consecutive front-camera frames, with the numerical ego-state text removed so the model actually uses the images. The Causal Importance Score (CIS) is computed by activation patching on N=100 scene-matched source/target pairs (matched on ego speed, following distance and lead velocity). For each layer l and modality m, the target's modality-m hidden-state rows at layer l are overwritten with the source's, and CIS is the mean per-waypoint L2 displacement of the predicted trajectory. Thresholding the image and text CIS curves at their elbows splits the layers into an align zone (high image CIS), a tune zone (high text CIS) and a freeze zone. On nuScenes these are {0,1}/{2-9}/{10-15} for LFM2-VL, {0-3}/{4-10}/{11-27} for Qwen2-VL and {0-24}/none/{25} for PaliGemma2.

CIS-Guided Selective Repair (CISR) then trains for 1 epoch with loss L_task + 0.5 * L_MMD. Layers in the align zone get attention-only rank-16 LoRA driven by a multi-scale RBF MMD between source and unlabelled-target mean-pooled image-token features. Layers in the tune zone get rank-16 LoRA on all projections, driven by the source trajectory loss. Layers in the freeze zone get no adapter. The ablation 'DPA-partition' keeps the same CISR operators but derives the zones from domain-probing accuracy (a per-layer domain-classification probe) instead of CIS; 'w/o CIS' uses a random partition. The metric is the cross-domain gap Delta_ADE = ADE(target Singapore) - ADE(source Boston).
official.claim: On nuScenes Boston-Seaport to Singapore, CISR with the CIS-derived layer partition gets a cross-city gap Delta_ADE of 2.3687 / 2.6287 / 2.4521 m on LFM2-VL / Qwen2-VL / PaliGemma2. With the same operators on a DPA-probing partition the gap is 2.6742 / 2.8643 / 2.7234 m (0.24-0.31 m worse), and with a random partition it is 2.7259 / 2.9851 / 2.8523 m.
