title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 6 (GradCAM and LogitLens comparisons: Tables 10 and 11, page 31)

official.background: Multimodal LLMs are usually scored on whether their answers are correct, not on whether the image evidence they used supports what they say. A model can mention 'traffic lights' correctly while its internal attention sits on the wrong region. Existing grounding datasets mostly cover objects, parts and referring expressions, so they cannot score lower-level concepts (colors, edges, textures, shapes) or higher-level ones (actions, spatial relations). VIGOR provides pixel-level evidence masks for concepts at four levels (primitive, intermediate, object, scene) so that a model's internal visual rationale for each concept it processes can be scored against ground truth.
official.method:
VIGOR has 1,000 images (drawn from COCO / LVIS / PACO / Visual Genome-type sources), 3,011 concepts and 31,433 masks. 18,038 masks are reused from source annotations and 13,395 are generated by proposal tools (SAM3, Grounded-SAM, CLIPSeg, CLIP-CAM, attention ensembles), then kept only when at least 2 of 3 MLLM verifiers select them. To avoid confounds from what each model chooses to mention, every image gets one fixed caption, written by gpt-5.4 to contain all annotated concepts, and all models are run on the same image-caption pair.

For each concept, the rationale map is the attention from the concept's caption tokens to the image tokens, averaged over matched tokens, all layers and all heads. It is reshaped to the visual-token grid, upsampled to image resolution and normalized to [0, 1]. Pixel-level AP ranks GT-mask pixels against background. Pointing Accuracy checks whether the argmax pixel falls inside the mask. Both are averaged over all (image, concept) pairs. The random baseline draws maps uniformly from [0, 1]. Appendix C.4 repeats the evaluation with GradCAM and LogitLens rationale maps in place of attention.
official.claim: On VIGOR with the fixed-caption protocol, concept-token attention rationales from InternVL3.5-8B reach an overall AP of 30.6 and Pointing Accuracy of 38.2. This is far above a uniform-random map (5.8 / 5.7) but far from full alignment, and no evaluated model (1B-38B, 4 families) exceeds 31.2 AP or 38.7 Pointing. For the same model, attention clearly beats GradCAM (16.3 / 19.6) and LogitLens (13.9 / 16.5).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: Main results on VIGOR benchmark. We report AP and Pointing Accuracy for overall grounding and for primitive, intermediate, object, and scene-level concepts. The best performing model in each column is bolded and the second best in underlined.
official.metric: Pixel-level Average Precision and Pointing Accuracy (%) between rationale map and GT rationale mask, higher is better, averaged over all image-concept pairs; no ± reported (single deterministic evaluation)
official.comparison: Attention-based rationale of InternVL3.5-8B (and the other 25 models) vs. a random rationale map; secondarily, attention vs. GradCAM vs. LogitLens rationale extraction on the same model
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running the released evaluation for InternVL3.5-8B gives an overall AP outside about 26-35 or a Pointing Accuracy outside about 34-43. Also refuted if GradCAM or LogitLens on the same model matches or beats attention AP, or if a re-run model in Table 2 reaches above ~40 AP.

title: Robust Flow Matching under Target Corruption and Label Noise

official.background: Flow Matching (FM) trains a generative model by regressing a neural vector field onto velocity targets along paths from noise to data, with a squared loss. Like any least-squares regression, it is sensitive to outliers: if a fraction of the training targets are corrupted (for example off-manifold samples or noisy images), the learned model reproduces them. Generic robust-regression fixes (L1/Huber losses, mixture-model reweighting such as DeepGUM) do not use the time structure of FM, where a corrupted endpoint displaces the interpolation state by t times the corruption, so corruption should be most visible at late FM times.
official.method:
FM-TRS (Temporal Residual Score) keeps one score per training sample: an exponential moving average (decay 0.99 in 2D) of that sample's squared FM residual ||v_theta(x_t, t) - (x1 - x0)||^2, computed at FM times drawn from the late-biased density pi(t) = 2t (t = sqrt(U(0,1))). The same sampled time and residual are used for the training loss. After a warmup of 25% of training (weights = 1), each sample's loss is multiplied by w_i = sigmoid(-(S_i - q)/tau), where q is the 70th percentile of the current score buffer and tau in {0.001, 0.01}.

2D setup: a spirals dataset plus extra corrupted samples equal to 20% of the clean set, drawn from a Gaussian blob N(mu, 0.3^2 I) placed at distance 4.0 from the clean centroid. Model: 4-layer MLP, width 256, SiLU, 64-dim sinusoidal time embedding; Adam, lr 1e-3, batch 4096; Euler sampling with 20 steps. Evaluation: W2, MMD and Coverage between 50,000 generated samples and the clean spirals distribution. Baselines share the backbone and only change the robustness mechanism: OT-FM, OT-FM with L1 or Huber (delta=1) loss, FM-DeepGUM (Gaussian-uniform mixture weights on EMA residual scores), and TRS with uniform instead of late-biased time sampling.
official.claim: On 2D spirals with 20% off-manifold Gaussian-blob target corruption, FM-TRS (tau=0.01) reaches W2 0.434 ± 0.011 and MMD 0.048 ± 0.007, versus 0.727 ± 0.018 / 0.129 ± 0.007 for FM-DeepGUM and 1.199 ± 0.097 / 0.279 ± 0.033 for standard OT-FM.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: 2D target corruption results for spirals. FM-TRS improves over robust-regression baselines under off-manifold target corruption. "Uniform" denotes TRS scoring with uniform rather than late-biased time sampling, and bold numbers indicate the best performance in each column.
official.metric: Wasserstein-2 distance and MMD to the clean distribution (lower is better), Coverage (higher is better); mean ± std over 3 seeds
official.comparison: FM-TRS (late-biased time sampling, tau 0.001/0.01) vs. OT-FM, OT-FM (L1), OT-FM (Huber), FM-DeepGUM, and FM-TRS with uniform time sampling, same MLP and training budget
official.falsification_criterion: Under the same corruption setup, FM-TRS's W2 is not clearly below FM-DeepGUM's (e.g. within one seed std, or not at least ~25% lower), or not substantially below OT-FM's.

title: SLIC: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning Small LMs for Multi-Turn Analog Circuit Optimization

official.background: Analog integrated-circuit sizing is a manual, iterative process: a designer adjusts transistor sizes, runs a SPICE simulation, and repeats until gain, power, bandwidth and phase margin all meet target. LLM agents could automate this loop, but foundry process design kits are proprietary, so sending them to hosted LLM APIs is usually not allowed. The paper asks whether a small (4B) model that can run locally can be trained with reinforcement learning from simulator feedback to do closed-loop, multi-turn circuit optimization.
official.method:
Qwen3.5-4B is first fine-tuned (SFT) on filtered multi-turn trajectories from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, relabelled in hindsight with their best-observed performance as the goal. It is then trained with multi-turn GRPO in an ngspice environment using the open 65 nm PTM CMOS models. The prompt contains an XML circuit description, target specifications, simulator feedback (performance and per-transistor operating region) and a list of admissible parameters. The policy outputs reasoning plus discretized relative updates (increase or decrease a parameter by a percentage). Rewards are domain-gated, so non-positive gain or more than 6 dB of peaking suppresses other credit. Successful designs score in [1, 1.5] with a bonus for specification slack, and validity and performance advantages are normalized separately.

Reward-Guided Rollout Steering (RGRS): at each turn G candidate responses are sampled from the same history and simulated. All of them contribute to a group-relative (per-turn) update, and one valid candidate is chosen to continue the trajectory (SLIC-Random picks it uniformly among eligible candidates). Training uses an 8-turn horizon. The baseline Tree MT-GRPO is the branching multi-turn GRPO of MT-GRPO with SLIC's reward and slack bonus: 4-turn horizon, branching factor 3, 3+9+27+27 = 66 candidate actions per task, compared with 64 for a SLIC-Random rollout, and the same tasks per step and other settings. Evaluation is 4-spec Pass@1 (all four specifications met within 5% tolerance under the validity gates) within 8 interaction turns on 840 in-distribution tasks from 35 amplifier topologies.
official.claim: On 840 in-distribution analog amplifier tasks (PTM 65 nm, ngspice), the 4B SLIC-Random policy reaches 87.1 ± 0.7% four-specification Pass@1 within 8 turns. Tree MT-GRPO, trained with the same reward and an approximately matched simulation budget, reaches 81.2 ± 1.3%, and the gap is largest on complex topologies (82.5 ± 1.0 vs. 68.4 ± 1.4).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: In-distribution evaluation at the PTM 65 nm technology node over 840 tasks with breakdowns by topology complexity. GPT-6-Astra is evaluated once on the full evaluation set. Bayesian Optimization uses 96 and 192 simulator calls per topology to match SLIC's total simulation budget. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best mean results in each column respectively.
official.metric: Cumulative 4-spec Pass@1 (%) within 8 turns, higher is better; ± is std over three evaluation runs of a single trained checkpoint (no training-seed variance reported).
official.comparison: SLIC-Random (multi-turn GRPO with RGRS, Qwen3.5-4B) vs. Tree MT-GRPO (same backbone, SFT init, reward and slack bonus, ~matched candidate-evaluation budget); also vs. single-turn GRPO, Bayesian optimization (TuRBO), SFT, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash THINK.
official.falsification_criterion: With matched SFT initialization, reward and simulation budget, retrained SLIC-Random does not exceed Tree MT-GRPO on in-distribution Turn-8 total Pass@1 by more than the run-to-run spread, or the complex-topology gap (about 14 points) largely disappears.

title: Curriculum proof repair with learned counterexamples
claim_source: Table 1, page 7 (per-suite); micro/macro averages in Table 4, Appendix C.1, page 18

official.background: LMs are increasingly used to write proof annotations (loop invariants, assertions) for program verifiers such as Verus, a verifier for Rust. The usual loop is propose, verify and revise, but Verus error messages only name the failed obligation (e.g. 'invariant not satisfied before loop'), not the program state that breaks it. This makes LM repair a matter of trial and error. Concrete counterexamples are more informative, but prior LM methods produce them through costly iterative refinement and validation.
official.method:
TopoVerus fine-tunes QwQ-32B so that, given a failed Verus proof and the verifier error, it emits in one response a structured counterexample ([State], [Execution Trace], [Violation]), a repair rationale and the full repaired program. SFT uses 461 repair trajectories from 249 programs, with reasoning written by a teacher model (Sonnet 4.6) that sees the reference proof (CTX-Init). Then comes GRPO on the same 249 programs, which do not overlap with the test set. The reward is gated by a Lynette safety check (only ghost/proof code may change) and a format gate. CTX-Binary uses only the binary Verus pass reward.

CTX-Dep (the full TopoVerus) adds a Topological Graph Reward. Offline, the canonical invariants of each training program's reference proof are tested for inductiveness over subsets to build a dependency graph, which is condensed into a DAG of SCCs. The reward is coverage (fraction of canonical invariants matched by substring or token-Jaccard >= 0.6) times edge satisfaction (fraction of inter-SCC dependency edges whose prerequisite invariant appears earlier in the output). At evaluation, models run 3 independent repair chains of up to 10 verifier-feedback iterations. Safe-Pass@k counts a problem as solved if a Lynette-safe, Verus-accepted proof is found in k chains.
official.claim: Over the 471 Verus problems in seven benchmarks, TopoVerus (CTX-Dep, QwQ-32B) reaches 61.6% / 72.2% micro-averaged Safe-Pass@1 / @3, vs. 55.9% / 65.9% for Sonnet-4.5 and 53.7% / 67.9% for the binary-reward RL ablation (CTX-Binary). The largest suite gain is on ObfsBench (266 problems): 69.9% Safe-Pass@1 vs. 62.0% (Sonnet-4.5) and 58.6% (CTX-Binary).
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Overall verification repair safe pass rates. Each cell reports Safe-Pass@k (%) across seven benchmarks. Cloud LLMs use iterative repair with verifier feedback; our models use 3 chains x 10 iterations. A solution is safe if Lynette confirms only ghost (proof) code changed.
official.metric: Safe-Pass@1 and Safe-Pass@3 (%), higher is better: a Verus-verified repair where Lynette confirms that only proof code changed, within 3 chains x up to 10 repair iterations. No error bars, and a single training run per variant.
official.comparison: CTX-Dep (GRPO with the Topological Graph Reward) vs. CTX-Binary (same SFT init and GRPO, binary verifier reward only) and vs. the strongest prompted cloud baseline Sonnet-4.5 with iterative verifier-feedback repair
official.falsification_criterion: Evaluating the released TopoVerus-32B under the paper's protocol does not beat Sonnet-4.5 on micro-averaged Safe-Pass@1 over the 471 problems, or the advantage on ObfsBench Safe-Pass@1 shrinks to within a few points. title: CP-MLPs: A Tensor-Rank Theory of Tied and Untied MLP Blocks
claim_source: Figure 2, page 8 (setup in Section 5.1 and Appendix D.2-D.5, Table 2 on page 21)

official.background: Transformer feed-forward blocks differ in their gate (ReLU, SiLU, identity) and in whether the same projection is used both to detect a feature and to carry its value. Tied blocks such as ReLU^2 and tied SwiGLU share one direction for both roles; untied blocks such as bilinear, ReGLU and SwiGLU use two separate projections. It is unclear how much of the reported benefit of GLU-style blocks comes from untying these roles rather than from the gate itself. This paper asks when untying reduces the number of hidden channels (width) needed to represent a given polynomial interaction.
official.method:
Each channel computes c_a * g(u_a^T x) * (v_a^T x). At degree two with an identity gate, a tied channel (v = u) contributes a signed square c(u^T x)^2, and an untied channel contributes c(u^T x)(v^T x), which is a difference of two squares. Theorem 4.6 proves that the minimum width to represent the quadratic form x^T M x is n+(M) + n-(M) for tied channels and max{n+(M), n-(M)} for untied channels, where n+ and n- count positive and negative eigenvalues. Untying therefore saves min{n+, n-} channels on indefinite targets and nothing on definite ones.

Experiment (Section 5.1, Appendix D): target y(x) = x^T Q x with Q = diag(1^{n+}, -1^{n-}, 0), d = 8, inputs x ~ N(0, I_8), N = 256 samples, six signatures (n+, n-) in {(1,0), (3,0), (1,1), (2,2), (3,1), (3,3)}. Models are scalar-output tied polynomial atoms sum_a c_a (u_a^T x)^2 and untied atoms sum_a c_a (u_a^T x)(v_a^T x), with no bias. The loss is MSE minimised with scipy L-BFGS-B (3000 iterations, ftol 1e-22, gtol 1e-15), 8 restarts with theta0 ~ N(0, 0.25), 3 seeds, best-of-restarts per seed and median across seeds. A configuration 'fits' if MSE < 1e-8 and 'fails' if MSE > 1e-1. Each model is evaluated at the predicted width m* and at m* - 1.
official.claim: On quadratic targets x^T Q x (d = 8) with signature (n+, n-), the smallest width reaching MSE < 1e-8 is exactly n+ + n- for tied atoms and max{n+, n-} for untied atoms across all six tested signatures. Examples are (3,3): tied 6 vs. untied 3; (2,2): 4 vs. 2; (1,1): 2 vs. 1. At m* - 1 the median MSE stays near 1 (the target-variance scale), and at m* it falls to about 1e-15 to 1e-9.
official.claim_caption: Figure 2: Quadratic targets with (n+, n-) positive and negative directions. Left: required widths match the predictions n+ + n- (tied) and max{n+, n-} (untied). Right: loss stays near the target variance below the predicted width and reaches machine precision at the predicted width.
official.metric: Minimum width reaching median MSE < 1e-8 (lower is better), and median best-of-8-restart MSE over 3 seeds at widths m* - 1 and m*. The figure shows no error bars; the threshold separation spans about 9 or more orders of magnitude.
official.comparison: Tied bilinear (squared) atoms vs. untied bilinear detector-value atoms, under the same data, optimizer and restarts, swept over target signature and width.
official.falsification_criterion: Refuted if, for some indefinite signature, untied atoms cannot reach MSE < 1e-8 at width max{n+, n-} despite reasonable restarts, or if tied atoms reach MSE < 1e-8 at a width below n+ + n-. The second outcome would contradict the theorem and would suggest a leak or bug.

title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation

official.background: Retrieval-augmented generation feeds retrieved document text into an LLM's context, which costs many tokens on long documents. Textual compressors (prompt pruning, extractive summarization) lose detail at aggressive ratios. Single-embedding injection methods such as xRAG compress a document into one vector and lose fine-grained content. Optical compression encoders such as DeepSeek-OCR show that a rendered page of text can be encoded into about 100 visual tokens with little loss. This suggests document context could be passed to an LLM in pixel space at a far smaller token budget.
official.method:
OpticalRAG splits each long document into 24,000-character chunks and renders them as 640x640 page images (DejaVu Sans Mono, 15 px font). Each page goes through the frozen DeepSeek-OCR DeepEncoder (SAM-ViT-B + CLIP-L), giving 100 visual tokens of dimension 1024 per page, and every token is stored in a per-document FAISS inner-product index. The multiple-choice prompt is run through frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Its last-layer hidden states are projected by a learned W_q (3584->1024) and max-pooled, and the result retrieves the top-256 visual tokens.

A query-conditioned cross-attention compressor reduces the 256 retrieved tokens to M=16 prefix tokens: depthwise-conv downsampling to 64 tokens, 2 cross-attention layers with 16 learned queries biased by the query vector, and a 2-layer MLP bridge into the LLM's embedding space. Only the compressor and bridge (about 30.7M parameters) are trained, first on text reconstruction (3,800 Wikipedia/C4 passages) and then on reading comprehension (11,400 SQuAD v2/DROP/CoQA examples). At test time, the 16-token prefix is prepended to the prompt and the answer is the argmax next-token logit over A/B/C/D. All baselines use the same Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone. The closed-book baseline sees only the question and options. Standard RAG feeds the top-5 BM25-ranked 1,200-character chunks as text.
official.claim: On LongBench-v2 (all 503 four-way multiple-choice questions) with frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, OpticalRAG with 16 injected tokens reaches an Overall score of 35.79. This beats the closed-book backbone (30.62, +5.17) and every text-compression baseline run by the authors: Selective Context 32.40 (about 5,512 context tokens), RECOMP 32.01 (about 6,954), Standard RAG 31.41 (about 1,623), LLMLingua-2 28.23 and xRAG 26.24.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Main results on LongBench-v2, Bamboo, and LooGLE-v2.
official.metric: LongBench-v2 official Overall accuracy (%; higher is better). Len is the average number of context tokens given to the LLM (excluding question and options). CAP is an author-defined score multiplied by ((12001)/(Len+1))^0.05 when the score is at least the closed-book score. No error bars: single training run and deterministic evaluation.
official.comparison: OpticalRAG (16 visual-prefix tokens) vs. closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Standard RAG (BM25 top-5 chunks), Selective Context, LLMLingua-2, xRAG and RECOMP, all with the same backbone and multiple-choice prompt
official.falsification_criterion: With the released checkpoint (or a retrained compressor), OpticalRAG's LongBench-v2 Overall score does not exceed the closed-book backbone by a statistically meaningful margin (e.g., a paired McNemar or bootstrap test over the 503 items is not significant), or it fails to beat the best text baseline (Selective Context, about 32.4). A retrain with a different seed that lands near 31-32 would also refute the claim.

title: Plug-and-Play ADMM for Inverse Problems with Flow Matching Denoiser

official.background: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods solve linear inverse problems such as inpainting, deblurring and super-resolution by alternating a data-consistency step with a pretrained denoiser that acts as an implicit prior. Recent work (PnP-Flow, Martin et al. 2025) uses a flow matching model as the denoiser inside forward-backward splitting (PnP-FBS). It re-projects each iterate onto the flow's interpolation path with fresh Gaussian noise at every step, and it depends on a hand-tuned time-dependent step size. The authors argue that this repeated noise injection over-smooths reconstructions and that the lack of explicit consensus between the data term and the prior makes the method fragile.
official.method:
PnP-ADMM replaces FBS with ADMM: an x-update solves the quadratic data-consistency problem argmin_x (1/2σ²)||Ax − y||² + (ρ/2)||x − (z − u)||² with conjugate gradient (max 10 iterations, tol 1e-5); the consensus input ẑ = x + u is projected onto the flow path, z̃ = (1 − t_k)ε_k + t_k ẑ; the denoiser is a one-step Euler flow map z = z̃ + (1 − t_k) v_θ(z̃, t_k); and the scaled dual u is updated by u ← u + x − z. The penalty ρ is fixed (500 for AFHQ-Cat, 1000 for CelebA) across all tasks, with t_k = k/N. Initialization: x_0 ~ N(0, I), z_0 = x_0, u_0 = 0, ε_0 = x_0; the method returns the final z.

Trajectory correction: ε_k is not a fresh Gaussian sample but a normalized time-weighted mix ε_{k+1} = (t_k ε_P + (1 − t_k) ε_R) / sqrt(t_k² + (1 − t_k)²), where ε_R ~ N(0, I) and ε_P = (z̃ − t_k z)/(1 − t_k) is the latent implied by the current denoiser output. All methods use the pretrained flow matching models of Martin et al. (2025) on CelebA 128×128 and AFHQ-Cat 256×256, evaluated on 100 random test images each. Random inpainting masks 70% of pixels uniformly at random, with measurement noise σ = 0.01. Each baseline uses its default hyperparameters, kept fixed across tasks.
official.claim: On random inpainting (70% of pixels missing, σ = 0.01), PnP-ADMM reaches PSNR 31.06 dB / SSIM 0.86 / LPIPS 0.04 on AFHQ-Cat and 30.80 dB / 0.89 / 0.03 on CelebA, and it is best on all six metrics among the five methods; the strongest baselines reach 29.53 dB / 0.83 / 0.10 on AFHQ-Cat (Flow Priors) and 29.99 dB / 0.86 / 0.05 on CelebA (D-Flow), while PnP-FBS with the same pretrained flow models reaches 25.23 / 0.69 / 0.37 and 23.57 / 0.72 / 0.19.
official.claim_caption: Table 1: Quantitative results on AFHQ-Cat and CelebA across various inverse tasks, averaged over 100 randomly selected test images per dataset. Best results are bold, second-best are shown in blue.
official.metric: PSNR (dB, higher better), SSIM (higher better), LPIPS (lower better), averaged over 100 randomly selected test images per dataset; no error bars or seeds reported
official.comparison: PnP-ADMM (ours) vs. PnP-FBS (Martin et al. 2025), OT-ODE, D-Flow and Flow Priors, all with the same pretrained flow matching models
official.falsification_criterion: Re-running random inpainting on 100 test images with the released pretrained models, PnP-ADMM fails to beat the strongest baseline (Flow Priors on AFHQ-Cat, D-Flow on CelebA) on PSNR, or a baseline matches or beats it on SSIM/LPIPS; a PSNR advantage over PnP-FBS below about 2 dB on either dataset would also refute the predecessor comparison.

title: Causal Concept Explanations for Deep Neural Models
claim_source: Table 2, page 9 (overall values in Sec. 5.5.2, page 8-9)

official.background: Concept-based explanations route a model's decision through human-interpretable concepts (e.g. 'left turn', 'has yellow belly'), but a concept can be predicted accurately while having little causal influence on the output, so the explanation looks right but misleads. This matters for troubleshooting and certifying learned policies in safety-relevant settings. The paper proposes to train concept models so that the output is causally driven by the concepts that are actually present, and to measure this with interventional mediation analysis.
official.method:
CCW-Net wraps a frozen backbone f: a concept encoder (MLP) maps the backbone latent Z to J concept vectors M_j, each passed through a squash nonlinearity so its length encodes presence (trained by a concept classification loss on the length), and a bias-free attention head maps M to the output, so a zero concept vector contributes nothing. Training uses task MSE + concept loss, plus (after a warmup) four causal alignment losses (necessity, sufficiency, independence, presence) whose counterfactual concept vectors come from a per-concept conditional normalizing flow. On CarRacing the concept dimension in Table 2 is D = 1, J = 3 mutually exclusive concepts (Straight, Left, Right), 15,102 recorded samples (latents, actions, labels) from the CW-Net release; training is 10 warmup + 40 alignment epochs, batch size 32, Adam lr 1e-3, all alignment weights 0.1, beta = 1. The baseline CW-Net (Kenny et al., 2026) uses the authors' architecture with scalar concepts and no alignment.

Evaluation (Sec. 5.4, App. F) does not use the flow or any training loss: for pairs of test sets A and B whose labels differ by swapping the active concept for a mutually exclusive one, each test input is matched to inputs in A and B by Gaussian-kernel matching on z-scored features (tau = 0.25, radius 1.5, 96 matches), hybrid concept vectors are built by taking each concept group from the A or B match, and each group's effect is its Shapley-averaged change in head output. rho_j is concept j's share of the summed effect norms; 'All Active' (rho_active) is the share carried by concepts labelled present, averaged over label combinations weighted by test counts. A faithful model has rho_active near 100%; spreading effect uniformly over 3 concepts gives about 33%.
official.claim: On CarRacing-v1 (released CW-Net latents, J = 3 concepts), CCW-Net routes 89.8 ± 2.5% of the output effect through the active concept, versus 33.1 ± 1.6% for CW-Net, at comparable concept accuracy (92.6 ± 0.4% vs. 90.0 ± 1.3%).
official.claim_caption: Table 2: CarRacing: fraction of the effect each concept carries (Eq. 7), per concept label combination, estimated as in Sec. 5.4. Active concepts are in bold. All Active and All Inactive are rho_active and rho_inactive. Each block's header gives the model's test action MSE (tMSE), concept accuracy on the Straight/Left/Right concept set (%), and DCI disentanglement / completeness / informativeness. Means over ten seeds with two-sided 95% Student-t intervals. CCW-Net shows superior causal effect routing through active concepts compared to prior art.
official.metric: rho_active, fraction (%) of the interventional indirect effect carried by concepts labelled active (higher is better); mean over ten seeds with two-sided 95% Student-t intervals
official.comparison: CCW-Net (D = 1, with causal alignment losses) vs. CW-Net (Kenny et al., 2026) on the same recorded latents and labels; CCW-Net without alignment losses is also reported
official.falsification_criterion: Retraining both models on the released CarRacing latents and applying the paper's matching estimator, CCW-Net's overall rho_active is not clearly above CW-Net's (e.g. the gap is under ~20 points or the 95% intervals over seeds overlap), or CW-Net's rho_active is well above the ~33% uniform level.
